_childDocuments_.review: ** note: my rating is neutral but since the average rating is "very positive" I felt a negative rating would be best **I love 90's FPS games. They're all about action, speed, accuracy, creative weaponry, diverse enemies, huge open maps, secrets to find, keys to collect, etc. etc. etc.WRATH clearly wanted to follow this model since it feels like a mix of Blood & Hexen, combining a hub based system of maps with Blood's type of enemies and weapons. On paper, this is a really great idea since both games are classics. In practice, somehow they managed to inherit the weakest elements of these games.The game gives you a wide arsenal of weapons which mostly feel solid. The sounds aren't as chunky as I'd have liked making the weapons sometimes feel weaker than they are and I do feel they lack some of the depth of modern "90s" style shooters like Ion Fury (which had the best combination of weaponry in decades) but for this style of game they're fine. 6/10The enemies are predictable - slow moving melee enemies, enemies that shoot, enemies that fly & shoot, enemies that throw stuff at you, etc. Their designs are quite good but the AI is very basic. I don't mind this however - intelligent AI is not something that would "work" in a game of this type. Part of the fun in these old games was knowing how to defeat the AI of the enemies after all. 5/10Map design is ... well ... I'm conflicted. If you've ever played Hexen, you'll know that by far the biggest flaw of the game was the maze-like maps where pushing a lever changed or opened something in a different area of the map or even in a different map altogether and you'd end up trying to figure out where to go next.Wrath falls into a similar trap. Trying to avoid linear maps, they give these massive mostly-open maps which are connected by a hub. The problem is that these maps often don't have clear identifiable elements to orientate yourself to and very often, I was unsure what I was supposed to do. There's no "goal", no mission, no explanation, nothing. The sad thing is, that the maps  are beautiful and fun to traverse as long as you don't get stuck. It's clear they had a good level designer but someone who doesn't understand the skill of "guiding" players towards a certain path. Unlike Hexen, the game doesn't even have a map to consult which is a massive mistake which is by far the biggest flaw of the game. 3/10The atmosphere is quite good and comparable to Quake but there were better examples of similar games with better atmosphere: Doom, Heretic, Hexen, etc. The "music" could have made a huge difference here but it's just ambient sound instead of actual music. The ambient sound is good but still.  7/10Graphics. There's a reason this is far down the list since you don't expect the best graphics for a game that tries to be over 25 years old. To be honest, the graphics mostly work great. If a screenshot of this game appeared in a 1996 games magazine you'd have thought it looked great. The textures feel properly retro and not faux-retro (you know, making it extra ugly just for the sake of being "retro"). 8/10I've seen a lot of people complain about the way you save the game and I have to agree with them. If you play on Easy or Normal, it's not too bad - you get enough "save points" but the more you increase difficulty, the less save points you get yet the more you'll need them. This is plain bad game design. The main problem is that the game has uneven difficulty spikes. You can easily get killed even on normal if you're not careful. This is often the problem with indie games because the old FPS games back in the day got beta-tested to death by a team of testers to iron out these difficulty spikes, something indie games don't have the budget to do. In most games this wouldn't be a problem since saving is painless but with a limited amount of save points, this is another major negative. 2/10While I do enjoy playing this game, the confusing map design, lack of a map to consult and limited save points means the game is a 5/10-6/10 in the end. You'll easily have fun for a few hours but after that, frustration may start to set in which is a darn shame.

_childDocuments_.review: Visually, this game is impressive. There's a lot of thought and expression behind the work done here that it definitely is memorable.... But the core gameplay, while not terrible, still feels like it's unpolished. It's easy to run out of ammo just playing the game normally, something I really only had to experience in other games like Quake when I was genuinely playing horribly. There are power ups that are interesting, but the inventory system makes it easy to overlook them unless you make a conscious effort to make use of them, which also kinda ruins the glee that used to come from coming across something like a quad damage power up and know there was about to be a frenzy of violence in the near future. Worse still is the save system, while I understand they are trying to make you be sparing by tying saves to Soul Tethers, I find myself collecting enough that I never have the tension that's normally associated with limited saves.Don't get me wrong, there IS promise behind this game, but it just feels like they needed to put it through a few more passes of Playtesting to just refine things just somewhat and this would have been an excellent game. As it stands, it's still worth a play, but I honestly feel like it's a remake of Arcane Dimensions.

_childDocuments_.review: Wrath's first episode is a masterclass in virtuoso Trenchbroom level design with clear lineage from Arcane Dimensions, and aside from some dodgy encounter design is an absolutely standout Quake / Hexen II / Unreal throwback with an identity all its own. It's moody, dense in atmosphere and nails its theme hard. Not a single dud level.Wrath's second episode is a real mixed bag, with the advantage of a really unique middle-eastern fantasy visual style that sells it. Some levels are mind-bendingly complex and beautiful to behold (Crystal Dunes and The Watchtowers are particular highlights), a couple that are just okay if visually sumptuous, and another that is little more than an ugly, featureless gauntlet of cheap ambushes and traps.Wrath's third episode is where the quality just takes an absolute nosedive into generic heavy-metal boomshoot cliché land. It's a fleshy hell dimension with an exceptionally drab colour palette and the occasional bit of mild body horror. Level design takes a huge backward leap into featureless box-rooms that amp the cheap ambushes up to 11, with the only challenge deriving from the measly scarps of health and armour doled out. The final boss is an absolute groaner that's simultaneously the worst and most obvious ending to the game possible.It's sorely disappointing that the back 3rd of the game was so clearly rushed after spinning its wheels in early access for nearly five years. We are all poorer for 3D Realms / Slipgate's continual unforced blunders and boneheaded management decisions. I hope that whatever KillPixel and co move onto next isn't allowed to be sullied in the same way.

_childDocuments_.review: I would honestly wait for this game to come out of early access before getting it. The core gunplay and mechanics are good, my biggest issue with this game is that once you've done one level, you've basically done them all. Once you run through a level you've encountered all the enemies in the game, and have all the guns in the game, and from then on you keep your guns, so whenever you start a new level from the hub, you'll start with all the guns and face the exact same enemies you've fought in the other levels. The levels themselves while pretty, all feel very samey, so it feels like you're just repeating the same thing over and over again.
_childDocuments_.name: WRATH: Aeon of Ruin

_childDocuments_.review: Out of all the 'boomer shooter' types, this one is perhaps the most faithful game of the era rather. The trailer on Steam doesn't really do the game justice either. It shows off a fast paced action game with loud guitar riff music, WRATH couldn't be further from that. While it IS a fast paced action game, the overall ambient of the game has this serene, ethereal and otherworldly feel to it. Even during boss fights which you'd think would be tense just has a soft and moody ambient playing in the background. The level design is quite stunning with some great vistas and atmospheric skyboxes.When it comes to gameplay the game has pretty good movement. You feel nice and fluid. Weapons are aesthetically fantastic, have good sound design and feel powerful. The game doesn't shower you with bullets however, so resource management is an important part of the gameplay. Instead of using your favorite weapon all the time the game forces you into situations where using the right weapon for the right situation will leave you less drained of your precious resources.The two cons I have for the game is the over abuse of monster spawning and how quick the AI reacts to you and how far they shoot you from. The monster spawning is an unfortunate necessary due to how the level design works, but I think it weakens the feel of the setting. Enemies don't feel like they are monsters that simply exist somewhere as most of them appear out of nowhere after you've triggered some event, which hurts the immersion. The designers also love abusing their Vortigaunt-inspired enemy who will start shooting at you the nanosecond you enter their FOV and shoot in constant bursts which can lead to a lot of peak-a-boo shootouts that honestly after a while get kind of worn out.This isn't my favorite boomer shooter, although it's very good. But in terms of aesthetic, atmosphere, ambiance and setting it is probably going to be one of the long lasting memories for me.
_childDocuments_.name: WRATH: Aeon of Ruin

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely one of the better throwback/"boomer" shooters to come out!The combat has a good rhythm to it and once you settle into the groove it feels great. Enemies pop and blow apart when you kill them which is really satisfying. The weapon lineup features usual suspects like a pistol, shotgun, automatic weapon, and some heavy hitting launchers, but they all look and feel good.The level design, in terms of architecture and spectacle, is a treat. However, some levels feel a bit too long for their own good. Each level on average took me around 40 minutes to complete. The quickest I completed a level was around 20 minutes, and the longest about an hour. That isn't necessarily a bad thing, but I felt that sometimes the levels didn't vary themselves up enough to feel like the length was justified. That said, I never felt navigation was too much of an issue. The levels can feel a bit overwhelming and sprawling, but I found that generally they guided me through without me getting lost or not knowing where to go. The one exception was a level very late into the game where I was locked into a small loop and I didn't know how to get a key to unlock a door, but I think it was a bug where I should have unlocked access to the key with a lever, but it failed to trigger, so I had to use noclip to access the cage with the key in it.Encounter design can feel a little uninspired too, with enemies just waiting in rooms or around corners to ambush you or having a mob spawn in when you pick up an item. It's fine and serviceable, but there's a lack of surprise and no fights that really use enemies in interesting or novel ways to make you think about your approach or require you to tackle them differently. But that said, I still found the combat remained enjoyable throughout the game thanks to the aforementioned rhythm and game feel.If you enjoy the dark fantasy aesthetic and combat loop and rhythm of Quake, then you'll probably find enjoyment in WRATH: Aeon of Ruin too. I certainly did.
_childDocuments_.name: WRATH: Aeon of Ruin

_childDocuments_.review: WRATH's ambiance, music, gameplay and level design are all in a league of its own. This game shouldn't be slept on for anyone who enjoys FPS, particularly the likes of Dusk and Doom (2016/Eternal). It's admittedly a bit steep at $25 for the three levels in the game, but I'm happy to pay it. If the developers meet half of their roadmap goals I think it'll be more than worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: Eh... The "difficulty" of the game comprises of ye olde spawn enemies behind you, or static spawn enemies in "ambush" spots  at awkward angles in the level, or just spawn a bunch of ♥♥♥♥ in at once in a very tight location and it all just opens fire on you at once. The first two don't really make the game harder, just more tedious to play. The third involves some skill to prioritize and kill high threat enemies quickly, but it begins to feel a little tired pretty quickly. I think it wants to be inspired by Doom's arena style game play, but doesn't quite understand what made that so much fun. What ends up happening is a cycle of progression through a level based on just learning what spawns where so you don't take damage from the static and spawned enemies. That's about it. The game didn't feel difficult in so much as it was hard for me to progress and kill things, it felt cheap in how it attempted to be difficult through the use of its enemy placement and spawn mechanics. You don't really have to learn mechanics, or weapon balance, or some kind of rock paper scissors, you just have to learn where enemies spawn. I feel like you can also tell which weapon the developer thought you should be using in each area based on the fact that an overwhelming majority of a single ammo type will spawn or drop for you. So there's less interplay of using specific weapons to kill specific mobs, and more of just use whatever gun mobs are actually giving you ammo for in a particular area.The art style is pretty cool. The movement is pretty decent. The gameplay loop, eh, it's just not there for me. Other reviewers have spoken about the game length as well. I don't know if I'll play it long enough to have an opinion about it.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game, I bought it after watching a couple of reviews and figured it was right up my street, ten minutes into the game I knew I'd spend a good amount of time on it.I like to think of this game as slightly more of a soulslike kinda thing, I always used to savescum a bit more than I should have so factoring in the limited saves, it was a bit of a difficulty spike for me, launching in on the outlander difficulty.However I think this is how the game should be played, making sure to check every corner indoors, ducking for cover against overwhelming numbers of difficult enemies, and then these tense, fast-paced outdoor battles, using your artefacts to try even the odds against those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ heretics, my god I hate those things.speaking of the enemies, they are all incredibly designed, providing a unique threat to each encounter, with different combinations and or numbers of these things, a couple gripes I do have though, include: the shotgun enemies are able to stay trained on you even behind cover, meaning that when you appear they pop ya instantly, not much but its a bit of a low blow gotta say, and then sometimes, ya throw a few too many heretics at the player, I love them, they hurt me in all the right ways but my got, when you have 5 high pressure flying enemies that are faster than you, and can kill you in no time at all, not to mention how spongy they are for the amount that are thrown at you, it gets a little repetitive.Speaking of repetitive, that has to be one of the only real issues I have with the game, I get that the whole thing has a bit of a quake-esk real gloomy vibe to it, but man each level looks damn similar to the last, I realise this is probably gonna change with each hub world introduced, but I do think each level needs a tiny bit more individuality, even if it just is changing some brick textures or lots of small things, especially for how long you are spent with them. I do love when the Priory's underbelly reveals itself to be a massive cavern filled with lava, and a dimly-lit red glow, we need more moments like these.I also think that the slag cannon and the wretcher serve much the same purpose, being big AOE weapons used to take down heavy enemies or larde groups of smaller ones, I only really used them both because i ran out of the other one's ammo pool, but I do think that only a little bit of tweaking is needed to give each of them more character, maybe making the wretcher's alt fire it's main one, and then changing the alt fire to something akin to like the BFG of the group, if nothing else is planned for that.But my god, the weapons in this game would give women hard-ons, they feel so damn good to use, some of the best I think, that shotgun is perfection and the Fang-spitter's alt fire sounds like a freight train, however I reckon it might need a little buff, gotta feel like a freight train too, also find I constantly have far too much ammo for it, maybe have the heretics be the only enemy to drop ammo for it. The coach gun has got to be my favourite pistol in a game, it does need a buff though, I really don't want to disregard it when the shotgun comes along, it's way too cool man.Perhaps to balance these changes, make enemies stronger, or throw more at us, just not those damn heretics.The soul tethers are phenomenal, they make the game so much more tense than any other shooter I've played, but I have noticed that there are vastly different amounts of tethers per level. For instance I started out with the priory, I was new to the game, I knew the difficulty would kick my ass, I wanted it to, barely scraping by with the barren amount of tethers given, comparing this to the undercrofts, I had 9 tethers leaving the level, I do think that these numbers should be evened out a bit, more bringing down the number of tethers in places where there are plenty, really robbing you of your sanity like that, perfect, also shrines are useless, either get rid of them or turn them into fast travel points if they aren't already, because unless they will serve a proper purpose in the full release, they're just useless compared to soul tethers.I think the movement is spot on, using your blade to work your way around the surprisingly brilliantly designed maps, is great fun, and I would say the combat of the game feels like a bit of a mix between Prodeus, with the indoor cover-ish but damn fast bludgeoning, and then Dusk when it comes to fighting in big open arenas with every projectile you can think of, a pinhead from killing the player, however there is a lot to get wedged or stuck on in these arenas, I also do think it is a bit of a disappointment that each enemy shows up in every level, I was looking forwards to fighting something new in each map, to find simply new environments, Like when the Oppressors are introduced underneath the Priory, that was real fresh.Overall I think this game is really bringing something special to the modern throwback FPS genre, and if this game is done well, it will stand out as one of the best, this is simply my findings while playing the game, and if I made and mistakes or points for criticism, please let me know. You're doing a damn good job, keep up the work and make the best game ya can.

_childDocuments_.review: If there was a neutral option, I'd probably give that to Wrath, but there's not, so it's gotta get a negative rating from me. I've tried really hard to enjoy this, but good lord I just can't. This game has some good things going for it, but mostly bad.The Good:Art direction - The one thing this game absolutely excels in is the art direction. Many of the areas throughout are simply beautiful, with a lot of thought going into particularly environmental design. It all looks really good, and unlike many other retro shooters, the locations look like tangible places rather than a hallway with fancy textures.Weapon design - All of the weapons have really interesting designs, I particularly like the look of the fang spitter. Not much to say on them, I just think they look cool.Music - This seems to be hit or miss with people, I think it's fine, it's all ambient background tracks, so it's never in your face.The Bad:Enemies - Literally every enemy in this game is awful in some way. I don't care much for their designs, they're all just "evil thing that wants to kill you", with one even just being a knock-off of the cacodemon from Doom 64. I do mean literally every enemy has something that makes them annoying, let's run through some.Shotgunners - Way too accurate, often hitting you with at least one pellet even if you're strafingMouth-cannon goobers - If they see you, they don't stop shooting. This is not hyperbole, they literally do not stop shooting until you break their line of sight, and to top it off when they die they explode. This is entirely unnecessary, because two other enemies leave an area of damage when they die, why do you need three of them doing that? Cacodemon - flying enemies are always a nuisance in pretty much any game, but these ones are atrocious. Their projectile is negligible, but if they're close enough they'll charge and try to bite you, which does a whole lotta damage and is very difficult to stop unless you use the fang spitter on them as they charge.There are other examples, but for brevity, I'll stop at those three.Levels - The levels are way, way too long. The average amount of time you'll be in any given level is around 20 to 50 minutes, varying along the way. I know there's only 15 normal levels (18 including the bosses), but this is just too much. Because the levels are so long, you just forget things that happen in them, leaving most set pieces forgettable and/or insignificant. This also ties into the save system problem.The save system - It's a novel idea, having limited saves and only getting them from items, but it quickly becomes an issue. Imagine a scenario where you have one save item (soul tethers, for future reference), and you use it. Then you make some progress, and you get ambushed by an executioner (since the game loves doing that) and because the level is so long, you just lost 10 minutes of progress, and have to do all of it again. Not fun in the slightest, this is actually one of the most rage-inducing aspects of the game, and the more I think about it the more my blood pressure skyrockets.Enemy ambushing - I didn't think much about this at first, but I read some other negative reviews of the game and starting noticing it more and more. There will be times where you see a couple enemies and start fighting them, only for a wall behind you to burst open and an enemy (usually the executioners or widows) will rush out and blindside you. There's no indicator that this will happen, nor anything leading you to believe the wall is suspicious (this could've been fine if the walls were cracked, leading the player to break it open and getting the drop on the enemy instead), and that wall will not burst open until you start fighting the other enemies. They purposefully make it so you cannot react to it unless you have played the level before and have prior knowledge. Absolutely awful.The mace - I was holding out hope that the super weapon would make the slog worthwhile, but it didn't. The silly goober mace (I can't remember the actual name and I don't care) does similar damage to a point-blank SSG blast, and collects a soul from each enemy killed, going up to 10. You can then right-click (or whatever your alt-fire bind is) and shoot some piddly energy balls. Keep in mind this is supposed to be this games equivalent to the BFG.Bosses - There are three bosses in the game, and I fought two of them, neither of which were good. The first boss is absolutely terrible, she floats in the middle of the arena, and after you damage her enough, she'll float up to the next floor of the arena, and you have to walk through the silly levitation gate so you can also float up there. The second boss is just a gimmick, you do stupid easy platforming to flip a switch to hurt him, three switches later and there's a second phase where you just shoot him until he dies. Lame. I didn't get to the final boss, but I watched a video of it and it looks similarly goofy and annoying.Conclusion:Do not buy this game ever, it's not worth the boredom and tedium. My personal breaking point was at the end of the level "The Blood Pits" (one of the levels in episode 3). I could see the exit portal and had placed my last soul tether, and then some enemies spawned, so I kill them, exit the level, and go to the next. I get 10 minutes in, and not a single soul tether to be found, nor a shrine (one-use saves found within the levels). I get killed by one of the mouth-cannon goobers death explosion, and my only reload option was the soul tether in the previous level. No shrine, no autosave, nothing. So I quit. I will be uninstalling and I never plan to go back and replay this, because there are much better options. If you want a throwback retro shooter, play Turbo Overkill, Dusk, Amid Evil, Cultic, whatever, just not this.

_childDocuments_.review: Another retro style shooter from 3D realms that gets the aesthetics of a 90's shooter so right but fundamentally misses the mark on gameplay. In this case, the game tries to be Quake but fails to understand (or capture) what made the game great. The enemies and weapons look fantastic but are utterly boring in practice. All weapons are direct fire and there are no interesting or dynamic enemy behaviours. Walk into a room and unload on enemies that essentially stand or float, rinse and repeat. The levels lack any interesting design or flair and enemy placement is careless and unimaginative. After finishing one level I couldn't remember a single interesting encounter and the entire experience felt like a repetitive slog. The hub is admittedly a cool idea, but a beautiful hub that leads to nothing of substance makes for a poor game. I know it's early access, but typically at this stage you need a compelling gameplay loop or some strong fundamental mechanics to build on. Wrath lacks any semblance of this and therefore has a tough uphill journey if it wants to become a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: In a recent flurry of retro FPS, Wrath is one of the good ones. That said, it's not without its flaws, and I'm gonna talk about them a bit here.Graphics and overall design direction are really good - chunky pixels, sombre mood and subdued colours coupled with eerie monsters and weird weapons set a very nice atmosphere. Environments maintain reasonable balance between recycling assets and creating unique locations, featuring both large open areas and tight interiors.Playing Wrath, however, left me with somewhat a weird feeling - like it either tries too hard not to be Quake... but at the same time perhaps too little in order to be its own thing. Movement, physics and core gameplay are pretty much perfectly familiar, but certain design choices throw you off that well known path, and not necessarily in a good way.Weapons are a prime example of this - they feel like being somewhat different to classic Quake arsenal was their main design goal, with usability left a bit somewhere behind - and yet they still fall into familiar archetypes, just introducing some awkwardness in usage.Enemies are quite different - they are far more numerous, but very delicate. Even the biggest types go down very quickly, you no longer have the feeling of "working" to kill any of them, but they almost all have very well aimed ranged attacks and pack a punch. Also, if you want to trigger enemy infighting, you gotta use special powerup for that.Remember how in Quake, you seen monsters patrolling their turfs and made a battle plan ahead before surprising that ogre with a double barrel? Here it's you that is getting surprised. All the time. To the point of it becoming boring and not surprising in the slightest. In Wrath, 95% of enemies do not exist in the game world - they are just spawned when you walk over a trigger. See that armour item laying in exposed place? You can bet your a** picking it up will trigger spawns all around that will cost you more armour, health and ammo to deal with than the pickup was worth in the first place."Arcane Dimensions" gets thrown a lot in the marketing materials - and level design certainly smells like it at times, but sadly is not in the same league, neither in visuals nor playability. Don't get me wrong, maps are well made and visually pleasing, but they lack the thick mood and intricacy of AD maps. They are absolutely huge and sometimes a bit confusing about where you're supposed to go. The vast open spaces don't work very well, though - they are populated with triggers spawning flyers that are usually hard to dodge given rough terrain geometry, which very often blocks your movement. There's also some limited platforming with the use of your starting weapon, but it's mostly annoying.Perhaps all those things mentioned above, along with dash functionality and no falling damage were supposed to make the game feel more like "modern" arena shooters, but they don't exactly work great on somewhat clunky Quake engine, while enemies are attacking you from very, very long distances.Devs decided to introduce limited save system - there are checkpoints, but in order to quicksave you need to use an collectable in-game item. I get the idea of wanting to rid of save scumming, but it never works well in practice. One of the great things about playing Quake was quicksaving ahead of an area filled with dangerous monsters and then running right into the hectic fray trying daring and stupid things, dying and trying over and over again until you finally learned how play like a god. Limited saves force you to play boringly and cautiously and repeat large chunks of linear gameplay if you die and it's mostly detrimental to the game's dynamic. Luckily, there are some ways around it you can find by googling a bit.Then there's the issue of the cursed development cycle. Wrath is over 3 years in early access now, which is really testing the patience of people who bought it. Supposedly the full release is somewhere near and lately devs posts regular blog updates about their progress. Right now there are 5 huge maps available, which each one should be taking about an hour to complete. All in all, it's a game worth recommendation, but you might want to search around for a good deal or wait for the full release.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: while the start of the game was strong, with effectively no updates in 2 years, I can't recommend this at all.An absolutely impeccable first person shooter. _childDocuments_.review: Late to the party from its entry into early access back during the boomer shooter revival, Wrath was well worth the wait in spite of a few setbacks.The GreatWrath's sheer atmosphere and sense of scale is unparalleled for a game in its genre. Levels are huge, often broken up into several distinct segments, and the sheer artistry at play with its designs and architecture are something to behold. The game's low-poly 3D style and colorful textures paint a vivid masterpiece every ten minutes that you can't help but stop to admire. The game has three hub worlds, each with entirely distinct themes that give the player the feeling of traveling to ethereal, ancient worlds. Movement is ace in this game as well, thanks to a great sense of momentum.The GoodWhile the game is built on a modified version of the original Quake engine, the game's combat pace has its own, unique flow. You will be bobbing and weaving between showers of projectiles just as often as you're backing away from hyper-aggressive melee attackers and walking around mines. Your weapons are fairly lethal, though larger enemies require you to mix and match your arsenal to take down quickly. Most fights can kill you in seconds if you aren’t crafty. Added into the mix are a set of inventory items, similar to the trappings available in Heretic. These artifacts are far more limited in availability, but can make an otherwise hopeless situation trivial with strategic use. The selection wheel slows down time while active, which makes them easy and convenient to use. Each episode also contains special powerup gates, which grant the player a unique ability to help traverse the map for a limited time. The game has a unique saving system as well, with a limited save item used in combination with checkpoint altars that keeps the action engaging as you progress through a map. Progression is souls-like in the best way. The saving system can be disabled in favor of traditional quicksaves, if preferred.The BadAs beautiful as Wrath’s sprawling environments may be, the game heavily suffers from the lack of any kind of automap system. Certain levels, especially those taking place in catacombs and tombs, can be outright hellish to navigate without any way to track your progress. As dense as these levels are, I found myself taking breaks periodically throughout single levels, only to have to re-learn the map’s layout by the time I came back to it. Every now and then, especially in the third episode, there might be one specific path in a room of four that I’d overlook and end up circling around the map over and over until I noticed it. Either an automap or a guidance system like in Elden Ring or Quake 2’s remaster would alleviate this frustration. The soundtrack (or lack thereof) is another mildly low point for me. A lot of it is haunting ambience - which sets the mood well for when you’re exploring, but in the thick of combat with enemies surrounding you some of the thrill is lost without any sort of music to accompany the combat. Finally, I found the journal to be rather underwhelming. The Bestiary and Weapons pages only offer artwork, without any sort of notes or descriptions. The UglyThe controller support in this game feels very primitive by today’s standards. There’s no ability to remap your buttons, with only a few presets on offer instead. More damning is the lack of a weapon wheel - which has proven to be an absolute necessity for games like this with large arsenals and frantic combat. Something to be aware of if you plan on playing on Steam Deck, or just using a controller in general.In ConclusionWrath is an incredible tribute to the art of level design, made up of a unique blend of gameplay elements that kept me coming back time after time until the end. It feels like a modern spiritual successor to the original Quake, and that alone should tell you everything you need to know. Easy recommendation, even if it can feel a little rough around the edges.

_childDocuments_.review: Love it so far, Exactly what you're looking in a Quake-like.Of particular note: the melee weapon is one of the best in an old school shooter. Most importantly its secondary attack  address the inherent issue of melee being awkward in FPV really well. On top of that it adds a good amount of depth to movement and strafe jumping; not only allowing you to make agile changes in direction but also turn slopes in the environment (like rocks) into ramps for elevation.On the critical side: it's a bit too easy. For context, my first playthrough was on hard, I never used the healing or invincibility rune, and I was making plenty of mistakes. I died once and that was when I wasn't paying attention. Health and ammo is everywhere so punishment is pretty tame.The time between firing the shotgun and being able to switch away from it is a tad slower than you might expect. It feels a little clunky and by the time you can switch you are usually better off just shooting it again; discouraging you from combo-ing your weapons effectively.Inside areas are a little homogeneous. I play a lot of games with maze-like level design but there were still a few times I found myself getting turned around and confused as to where I was.

_childDocuments_.review: WRATH: Aeon of Ruin has become a dirty enjoyable evocation of the past, which quite cleverly fills the void created by the long-awaited and perhaps never-made Quake sequel. It's beautiful, fast-paced, blood-and-guts-pumping entertainment, which may seem daunting at first due to its intensity, but believe me, if you give it a chance, you won't regret it. After that, there's no question, it's a must-buy for lovers of the genre, and highly recommended for everyone else, but I can tell you in advance that after the moments spent with the game, nothing will be as enjoyable and exciting as it was before.

_childDocuments_.review: A promising shooter for fans of Quake. Nice graphical style, nice art and sound direction. The lighting in the maps is good. Of course, this is early access so there is still a long way to go,  The weapons and the alt-fire modes are all fun and useful, but perhaps there could do with being a little more ammo for the pistol - the default starting firearm is something you should be able to use without worrying about ammo.The enemy designs are cool but there is balancing work to be done. Some enemies spawn behind you or break through walls and attack with no warning and no chance to respond until you've taken damage. At times it feels more like a health tax that you must pay to progress rather than a gameplay element you can use skill to overcome. If you die and respawn, you know where the ambushes come from and can pre-empt them. It feels a little cheesy. Also the giant acid-spitting enemies should probably not be used in indoor areas so much as they are prone to jamming on the scenery or getting stuck in choke points.Of course, I expect the above ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to be ironed out for full release, which is likely quite a long way off just now. I will be buying the full game on release and I expect any fans of 90s gothic horror shooters would enjoy this.

_childDocuments_.review: After reading a few of the reviews, I became morbidly curious (let's just say) and went ahead with blowing some of my money on this game to see if it really was as bad as people were saying.Now I realize... maybe I should've just taken their word for it.I will say, the general atmosphere and some of the weapon and monster designs are pretty cool, if fairly standard, and the movement is at least somewhat smooth.The positives end there, however, as there are myriad design choices that really make the game feel like it was specifically engineered to tick off the player. For one, the save system. Someone on this team must've thought that Daikatana's save gem system was such a wondrous idea, so they made these Soul Tethers (your save items in this case) so excruciatingly rare that you'll constantly be caught between wasting a Tether in a spot where you end up not having needed it or saving a Tether for when you do actually need it and then getting wrecked by the artificial difficulty before you even get there, which usually means that Tether will have been a waste anyway!And yes, the game does have a problem with artificial difficulty, too. The whole "dynamic difficulty that scales to how much you've gotten done and how full your arsenal is" sounds good on paper... until about your second level, where monsters spawn in such dense numbers that it'll never really be your fault if you die, like trying to mix the gameplay of much older shooters with the more chaotic (that the right word?) design of, say, Doom Eternal. Now, I would talk about how (I feel) levels drag on for way longer than they really should for this style of FPS, but it's a much smaller complaint that I won't really say much on.All in all, this just seems to be one of those games that was *designed* for gatekeepers who probably just want to get a quick high from bullying people who can barely last a minute in a game that tries way too hard to be hardcore to begin with. Maybe if there was just a normal difficulty select, free quick-saves on all but the very hardest difficulty (maybe reserve the Soul Tether system to this specific difficulty), etc. so that people would be able to play the game like they play any other retro (or at least retro-styled) FPS, I might be able to recommend this to people who genuinely do want to get into the genre. As it stands, though, this will continue to be one of my "guilty pleasures", if you will.By the way, I hear the original developers abandoned this project quite some time ago. I could be wrong about that (or anything else I've said in this review), though, so feel free to correct me wherever it's needed.

_childDocuments_.review: SOON™: Aeon of DelayReleased into Early Access: November 2019First delay: January 2021 -> Summer 2021Second delay: Summer 2021 -> Unspecified date in 2022Third delay: 2022 -> Spring 2023Fourth delay: Spring 2023 -> February 2024After five years, we were left with a game that is by no means terrible, but definitely not great either. The biggest issue lies within its small enemy roster that failed to keep me interested throughout the whole, 15 hour long experience. Not only that, but they do not thematically fit into the later levels. The levels, for the most part, don't offer anything unique, always baiting you on some central level theme, such as dunes, in the crystal dunes level, or flesh, in the last level of act 3, but these themes only appear in the fraction of the level, before you are immediately thrown into bland boring catacombs or caverns. So while their level layout is mostly good, given the bland environments, they quickly become forgettable. Not to mention the criminal underusage of the sigils.Lastly, there are some questionable design choices, or rather, things that weren't completely thought through. The first one being, the overabundance of long range combat. This mostly concerns the first act and some of the levels in the second. There's simply not enough weapons with super long range to justify this many long range encounters, where you enter vast open rooms and there's enemies shooting at you from every side and you have to back off and carefully pick them one by one with your unreliable ranged weapons. Luckily, later down the game, not only will you get more tools to handle enemies from long distances, but the levels also become more enclosed, as they should have been from the start, because close to mid range combat is where the gunplay shines the most.The second afterthought is the overabundance of the instakill pits. That, in and of itself, wouldn't be much of an issue, if it weren't for two things: extremely slippery movement, where even the smallest stair makes you fly a distance and limited save system. I'm not complaining about the number of saves or the fact that this the way you have to play the game, I know there's the option to turn the unlimited saves on. I was carrying over 20 saves by the time I finished the game. But when you KNOW your saves are limited, you don't save EVERY TIME and you only save occasionally, that's why falling into the pit that instantly ends your life often leads to losing minutes of your progress, which is a punishment that vastly exceeds the weight of the mistake, especially since most of the times, the slipperry movement is at fault. Solution? Make the lava pits have some kind of an exit and make the spike traps take away some amount of your HP and teleport you outside of them.These complaints aside, I was having fun at least 50% of the time that I spent with the game and while it is far away from being the best retro FPS shooter that I've played, I think it deserves at least a solid 6/10, which could have easily been 8/10, if there was more variety in the environments and ESPECIALLY in the enemy roster. I'll keep the review negative, though, because the process that lead to the release of this game should by no means be forgiven and forgotten and should be kept as an example of how not to produce a game in the early access.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't like having to choose between a Yes/No recommendation, as there is a lot of nuance that is lost in a binary choice. I'm also aware that this is an early access project that has been a labour of love made over many years. I'm a fan of the recent 3D Realms output and I'm confident that some of these issues will be worked on. If the below points end up being addressed by the time this is fully released, I would be happy to change my review to be more positive.-There is a consistent visual theme, with dark, moody art direction that is, on paper, everything I am looking for. However, there is a distinct lack of atmosphere. None of the spaces feel lived in, or foreboding. In fact, very few of the spaces have made me feel anything.-The movement is very quick but slightly inaccurate and janky, for lack of a better word. I feel like this could be easily remedied in the ongoing early access process.-The weapons have a gnarly chunky design, but feel very slightly underwhelming, especially in the sound department. Exploding cysts and jagged fang projectiles should feel a lot beefier and more visceral than they currently do.-Similarly to the weapons, the enemies have a very cool body horror aesthetic. However, their movement patterns and animations make them seem goofy instead of threatening. Some of the attack patterns seem more annoying and frustrating than they are threatening and engaging.-So far, there seems to be a lack of story, setting or worldbuilding. I don't think it's necessary to have a direct story, but there is no underlying drive or motivation other than to just complete levels for completions sake.During the middle of a combat encounter in The Hollow, I came to realise something: I don't care if I win or lose, outside of the fact that I arbitrarily prefer to win. I didn't feel any motivation to push through and continue, and my deaths didn't make me want to jump back in, try again and succeed. This is an extremely damning feeling. I have played though flawed games before, because they have a core element that keeps me coming back despite any issues. However, nothing presented in Wrath so far made me feel pumped or engaged, which is the main thing I want from an FPS

_childDocuments_.review: INCOMING LONGASS REVIEWI have a lot to say about Wrath, but I'll try to keep it coherent. I wanted to give a review to defend this game in light of all the negative reviews that it's been getting recently, because it is genuinely a very good game, and it doesn't really deserve the treatment it's been getting. Also, I'll try to avoid spoilers. INTROI bought this way back in 2018, when there were only 3 or 4 levels that were available, and after only a few minutes of playing it quickly became one of my favorite single player shooters, I still come back to it all these years later. What originally grabbed me about this game was that the developers decided to use the DarkPlaces engine, the same engine that Quake 1 used, and that's where a lot of Wrath's charm comes from. It's also the reason this game runs so well, I barely seen it hitch or stutter in my 52 hours of playing. But don't let that fool you into thinking this is just a thirty dollar Quake mod, the devs built this from the ground up, adding smooth animations, projectile bullets, destructible enemies and environments, an alt fire for every weapon, power-ups which can be stored and used at any point, and lots more mechanics that make this game so good.WORLD/ENVIRONMENTOne thing that Wrath understands very well is how important the world around the player is in terms of gameplay. It's the first thing that the player sees, it sets the story, dictates a lot of how the game is played, and keeps the player wondering what's next, encouraging them to play more. Wrath does all of this very well, with all of the stages flowing naturally while still staying true to Quake's level design, with winding corridors, surprise arena segments, elevator sequences and so on, but now with more open areas, props, environmental storytelling and detail that wouldn't be feasible back in 1996. Now, it's still pretty linear, like most games from the boomer shooter genre, but all the levels are very open, with most areas having at least a couple different ways to come at a fight, and it rewards exploration and experimentation, which brings me to how the Ruination Blade, your melee weapon, plays into the movement of the game. WEAPONS/ITEMS:I'll try not to spoil any of the other weapons, but The Ruination Blade is the very first thing the game gives you when you start the game, it's a big sword attached to your arm which you can use to plunge straight through weaker enemies, get to otherwise out of reach areas, quickly get out of precarious situations, or just make level exploration much faster. Blasting around with the speed boost from this thing is fun in and of itself, and unlike the melee weapon from Quake, which is painfully useless, I've always found myself using it from start to finish. It's a great way to introduce the combat of this game to the player. The rest of the weapons are very similar to Quake's weapons. You have a regular 'shotgun' type, a 'super shotgun', a fully automatic 'nailgun' type, and a 'grenade' launcher. All of which you'll find that you need to make use of from their respective strengths. They also all have an alt fire, so they don't really get boring to use, and it makes them even more unique from the Quake weapons. The items are great too, very useful for players who are new to the genre. While not necessary to the overall game design, they add a lot more options for combat without making the player overpowered. ENEMIES:One of the features of this game that I remember being advertised was destructible enemies, which is impressive to implement in the Quake engine. It's gross, and it clearly shows the player how close a particular enemy is to biting the dust, without being too distracting. Not all of the enemies are destructible, but the fact that we have as many as we do at the moment is more than enough for me. The enemies have improved a lot since 2018, their pathfinding used to be pretty rough, and a lot of the bigger enemies ate way too much ammo, in the same way some Quake enemies became a chore to fight, but all of these issues have since been ironed out a bit. A few of Wrath's enemies are very very similar to Quake's, but most of them are unique, and it does a good job of not showing almost all of the enemy roster in the first couple levels of the game, which is something I think Quake suffered from. VERDICT;A fantastic retro shooter that suffered from the effects of Covid, slowed down development time by a lot. It’s a shame because this game had a lot of momentum before the pandemic hit, but it didn’t stop it from ultimately being finished, which is pretty cool. Great game, worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: Entire playtime was played in Hard difficulty.This one pains me. I got this game back in 2021, beat the early access which only had the first act, and followed its development ever since it went into dev hell and back again. I carefully watched every single biweekly update, excited for what they were showing us. And now we're here. I played through the first act again which was just as good as I remembered it. And then I got into Act 2.Good lord, what a mess. The first thing you'll notice is the sheer size of the levels. In Act 1, yeah they were big, but still manageable and fun to explore. These levels, however, are MASSIVE. Like, some of these levels could be entire ACTS by themselves. And there are FIVE of them. And they're all filled with the Exact. Same. Enemies. Over and over again. The enemy pool is not the largest, and trying to fill a 15-20+ hour campaign with only like, what, 10-12 enemies? That gets boring REAL quick. And let me tell you about the absolute worst of them: the Executioner, a big hooded burly guy with 2 bladed arms. I do not mean it lightly when I say this, this is probably one of the most anti-fun enemies ever designed in boomer shooters. Even more than the chaingunner. Even more than the spike mines in scourge of armagon. What do they do? They charge at you. Which might have you thinking "bruh why are you complaining about that literally every game has charging enemies just avoid them when you see them coming lmao skill issue" which, normally I'd agree with you. Except... you never see them coming. They are placed almost *exclusively* in ambush spots right next to you around corners/behind you or are spawned right in your face. At this point you're probably thinking "well, surely you can just get out of the way before they hit you right?" No. You can't. When they see you, they charge *instantly*. Yeah, I mean that. *INSTANTLY*. You have NO time to react, and they can turn on a dime. And when they hit you, you just die. Straight up. Their charge deals an OBSCENE amount of damage. 50+. And that's with armor. If you're out of armor, it's an instant death 90% of the time. "There's no way an enemy like that lives long, though. It's probably pretty squishy to make up for the fact that it can one shot you." It's one of the tankiest enemies in the game <3. So, you have a tank that is extremely mobile, near instant reaction time upon seeing you, and has the ability to kill you just as fast. And they decided this would be a good enemy to ambush you with all the time? Like, I pushed through this game's shortcomings as long as I could, but I'm going to be honest, this enemy is singlehandedly making me consider just not finishing this game. Which is genuinely such a sad thing for me to say, because this game has a lot of things going for it. The movement is clean (blade dashing is probably my favorite method of movement in any shooter, up there with rocket jumping, which this game also has), the shooting is great, the weapons are impactful which each of them having an alternate fire, the overall art design is breathtaking to look at, especially for a game made on the Quake 1 engine. It's just... a few VERY large flaws that bring this game down and make it not as great as it should be. If you're one of those people that can push through it, I recommend this game on a sale. Otherwise, there are better options to spend your money on.

_childDocuments_.review: While I enjoyed playing an unfinished chunk of Wrath a couple of years back, the developer and publisher's communication strategy warrants criticism as the lack of transparency has soured the experience for me. The Steam FAQ, which is still pinned to the discussion board, states the game was supposed to fully release in "early 2020." Back in 2019 this suggested there would be a relatively short turnaround time from early access to launch that encouraged me to purchase the game. Obviously they didn't fulfil that schedule, which happens but it's now been over 18 months since the last content update in Jan 2021 and there's been no meaningful official updates on any of their social channels addressing why the game wildly missed its original release window let alone addressing its future. The only info being consistently released are context-free, bi-weekly bullet points paired with the odd featureless screenshot which offer no insight into the game's overall development status. Even if a release date was announced tomorrow, Wrath would stand as a cautionary tale of how to go about early access: a once promising title that squandered its momentum due to mismanagement.

_childDocuments_.review: A true Quake successor, or at least, what a spin-off SHOULD feel like. There are times where you might be guessing where to go, but if you put on your time traveling cap and set the year to the late 90's, you'll find every cliche is present in Wrath, whether it's old fashioned key searching or destroying spawned hordes of enemies from picking up an item of importance. Overall, you'll find a very familiar feeling that will traverse you back to the fundamentals of early 3D FPS games, and do so in a very refined and wrathful way. I've seen this game come a long, long, way, so I imagine the finished product will be all the more satisfying.

_childDocuments_.review: They have made a patch that has made some slight changes to the game. After giving it a try, I can say it's a bit better, but it still bothers me. I have made some edits to my review.________________I was really looking forward to this game, I really am! A retro FPS built on the Quake Engine? What's not to love!Well so far the graphics and atmosphere are freakin amazing. This is like if you took Blood and Quake and mashed them together. However I have been suffering from some slight frame rate issues and stutters here and there, even after lowering the graphics. Keep in mind I have a 4 year old budget PC, but it can play more graphical demanding games better. Maybe it's just some minor optimization needed, so I would expect this to be fixed with patches. It will be interesting to see how the rest of the maps will be.  Currently though the maps are HUGE, which is a good thing and a bad thing. The 2 maps we get are very nicely built with lots of detail, but like the cemetery map, everything just feels the same. Most of the map contains the same looking rooms and textures, so it all starts to blend into the same, and then you can easily get lost or forget where you have been. ________________Weapons look amazing and are fun to use, and I might say, this double barrel shotgun might be the best one made yet. The satisfaction of gibbing just about everything from it is just such a great feeling... though I feel it might start getting old the longer the game goes on, but that's hard to say when it's just 2 levels. They all have an alt-fire, but at the moment some do feel way to weak, or are too slow so you won't use them. There is also way too much ammo. I ran around with max ammo just about the entire play time. They made slight edits to the weapons to make them better for most enemies and more fair. Now some weapons feel like they can deal damage. I still say that the weapon count feels really low (they are only adding 1 more weapon in the game according to their roadmap,) and the fact you can pick up all the weapons in the first maps is kind of weird and kills the enjoyment of the drip of weapons as you progress in the game.________________And that f*cking godlike Andrew Hulshult soundtrack. So far the soundtrack only consists of ambient drones, which do sound really good. I do hope the soundtrack will be more than this, and have some great epics later in the game, or tracks with build ups. I've also have a complaint with the music. There seems to be no "Epic" music, like when you enter a big area and a ton of monsters spawn in. You would expect that the music would start pumpin getting you in the zone for this big fight you are in, but there is nothing! It's a huge let down.________________But there is some glaring problems that make this unplayable for me.The movement is just, bad. Unlike Quake where there is a build up for your speed, and then use strafing or jumping to build even more speed, here it's just a simple tap and you move full blast! I hate that I am struggling to have more precise movement, and ended up throwing myself off ledges, sliding down slopes with no possible way to stop, and getting stuck on parts of levels because I sent myself flying. With this huge movement speed, even letting go and waiting for your character to stop moving takes a moment to slowdown. Plus there is no mid air control. When this was literally the very first thing I noticed the moment I started playing, you know it's bad... now they don't have to replicate the Quake movement exactly, I just used it as an example. The movement speed is still 0-100 with no build up, so I was still having the same issues as stated before with the precise movement. They added in air-control, but it is so barely noticeable. At least now you can walk down slopes a bit easier and not fly over them.________________Enemies are very cool looking, but are dumb as bricks, and get stuck on stuff too easily. Some of the bigger monsters also seem to have lots of health and can take tons of ammo on you. So if you only had a pistol left, you probably won't be able to kill any of those monsters.  They did some changes to the monsters, now some don't feel as bullet spongy as before, but they are still dumb and still get stuck on walls and parts of the levels.________________The movement alone is why I can not recommend this. It really pains me to do that, but it's just bad, plain and simple. Once they fix that... IF, they fix that, then I would easily recommend checking it out, but right now I say wait on buying it. _childDocuments_.review: I completed this game as Outlander for the very first run, and I find the game way too easy. For the elevator level I used Blood Siphon (the health leech thing) and Cysts on the Heretics and no problemo. No need to use Aegis. I didn't need any other artifacts in any other part of the game.Basically you just need to use a bit of skill, aim, and casual zig-zagging in the elevator. No need to sweat, no tears. I found that Doom 2016 / Eternal had much harder encounters. The game is good, but it's way too easy for an experienced FPS-player:There's way too much ammo, there's way too much health, and generally *way* too much space to kite the hordes, way too few projectiles to dodge. Considering that I played it on the hardest possible option for the first run, I found the game easy. For the guns, I liked them with few notes: The Pistol is absolutely useless, unless using the 2nd fire mode with instantly changing to shotgun for a proper shot. Never change back. The Shotgun is your main pick for *every single situation*. The 2nd fire more seems to be too strong as it solves most of your problems close and far. It's like Cillit Bang - and the dirt goes boom. Machine-gun is a machine-gun, low damage high rate of fire. It's okay.Cyst-launcher is a cool weapon.I really liked / hated the fast running screaming little demons. They gave me the chills and few "oh ♥♥♥♥!"-moments. The rest of the enemies were mostly just.. fodder. I'll hope Wrath: Aeon of Ruin retail version has way more content than this. :)

_childDocuments_.review: This one had to grow on me a bit before I enjoyed it. I think part of that is the ammo scarcity combined with the fact that I did not realize how powerful the blade was at first. The secondary attack shreds enemies and is essential to enjoying the game.I really love Quake. I love the simplicity of it. Wrath really scratched the itch for more OG Quake, albeit with some differences. For one thing, Wrath's levels are massive. It's not uncommon to spend more than an hour in a level. There are tons more enemies because it's 2024 and our hardware can handle that in the Quake engine (DarkPlaces). Coupled with the high health of enemies, this game can be a slog, and you definitely shouldn't play it all in one sitting. The combat is slower and more methodical than a lot of other games in the genre.This game manages to be sort of like a combat puzzle in that certain weapons are needed for certain encounters. Coupled with ammo management, you are pretty much always thinking about what you're doing. It's not quite as simple as mindlessly shooting things, but it's far from as complicated as something like Doom Eternal. The game gets better in episode 2, when you get access to more weapons.There were a few times I got lost and couldn't figure out how to progress. Once or twice, I had missed a switch or something. Once, I didn't realize the floor under a health pickup was an elevator, having not stepped on it since I had full health, leading to 15 minutes of wondering around looking for the way forward. Other than those few times, the levels generally give good indication of where to go. Enemies act as signposting and keep you on the right track, despite the enormous maps. The levels are great. The three distinct episodes give you a variety of maps. Some of it was a bit bland at first, but I really enjoyed episodes 2 and 3. There are some cool environments in those two, and parts of episode 3 felt a lot like the original Quake.Enemy variety is a bit lacking, given how long the game is. Another five or so enemy variants would have gone a long way. As it is, you will find you are fighting a ton of the same enemies, some more annoying than others. Almost every weapon feels weak at first, but I think a lot of that is the sound and visual design of them. Once you figure out how to use them, they really do (mostly) pack a punch. A couple of them are unique designs and do fun things. You can even do some animation canceling with the lance and shotgun, a lot like Doom 2016 / Eternal.The items you pick up are a good addition. I found I held on to them more than I could have, but they ended up being really helpful in episode 3 and with the final boss. I liked most of them. The cruel aegis was useless 99% of the time, but everything else was cool. The item wheel makes them easier to use than items in other games, like Hedon and other Doom-like games with an inventory.There is a bit of story and lore in this game, but it is almost entirely forgettable. If you're looking for those things, this isn't the game for you.Overall, I very much enjoyed my time with this one.
_childDocuments_.name: WRATH: Aeon of Ruin

_childDocuments_.review: WRATH, AEON OF RUIN.That sounds like something you'd see on the cover of a heavy metal album, right?Instead what you get is Quake on Valium. This game features everything I don't like about Quake, and then adds in a few other things I don't like just to top it off. But let's start off with the good things, to not be a complete negative nancy. You know what's good about Wrath: Aeon of Ruin? It actually looks pretty nice. Now, time for everything bad about it. You move at the usual Boomer Shooter Protagonist Pace(tm), which is great, but unfortunately no one figured out that the reason this sort of pace is fun, is because it was usually used in games where you had relatively open and uncluttered environments to use your speed and mobility to do fun things. Wrath, meanwhile, somehow manages to make even those outdoor areas I was in feel like they were cramped, with constant waist-high fences and environmental clutter that John Wrath could not move around or over very well. John Wrath also jumps like a pensioner, which is fine, except that the game still wants you to do jumping stuff, aided by your melee weapon that has a charged lunge attack which can be used for extra jump distance. Developers, please, stop this. I do not want your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gimmick mobility options. There are three good mobility options I want in an FPS: Double Jump, Grappling Hook and Air Dash bound to its own damn key and without a charge-up. This wouldn't be so egregrious, mind you, if the lunge-dash wasn't oddly unreliable, anemic and failing it would usually condemn you to a tiresome walk back. It definitely made me feel some Wrath.Now, the main Quakeism(tm) that I feel infests Wrath, at least until I got really bored with it, is the level design. The levels are... labyrinthine in the worst of ways. I arrive, I have no idea why I'm there and I have no idea where I'm going. I know that keys need collecting, so collected they get, but I have no idea for what end goal. Am I delivering a package? A telegram? Am I going to hug the level boss? IS there a level boss? Who knows. It makes it hard to have any sort of internal compass for the level and just makes the whole thing feel kind of purposeless.It doesn't help that the soundtrack seems to consist purely of the ambient music that plays in a game like CULTIC between major engagements. Even if fifty zombies or meat mans or poison meat mans are chasing me around a graveyard, the soundtrack is encouraging me to take a nap instead of getting hype(which I would take in absence of anything to actually be hype about.).There's sometimes also some weird input lag on weapon switches and other little oddities.As for the weapons, I guess they're okay? You have stabby backup weapon, pistol, shotgun and machinegun as far as I got to see, so I don't really expect any kind of interesting arsenal. The weapons are... functional? But none of them ever really feel punchy. Even when the shotgun gibs someone, I just sort of accept it with an "eh" instead of getting excited about it. It lacks a... viscerality. It lacks some bass thumping.The enemies are... once again, really generic. There are guys that shoot at you, flying guys that shoot at you, guys that shoot at you and explode if killed, and big guys that charge at you and take a lot of hits to kill.Wrath really feels like a boomer shooter designed by committee, like... I never get a feeling of soul from it. Like the developer cared about or strongly felt about anything. It's like it was boiled and leeched of all colour and flavour. It's like something I would serve at a British dinner table. No matter what colour the environments might sometimes have, this is the beige hospital food of FPS games. Technically nourishment but mostly a reminder that there are better and more fun things out there you could be spending your time on instead.So yeah, no, deeply disappointing.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a soft recommendation. There are parts of this game that are really good. There are a lot of cool levels, fun weapons and cool looking enemies that are satisfying to gib. I think Wrath's main problems are related to pacing and level design. A lot of really good shooters will have breaks in the action where you can explore and take in the atmosphere. Or maybe solve a puzzle, or have a tense horror section in the dark. Anything to slow the game down and give the player a chance to catch their breath.Wrath is not like that. Every level is at 100% intensity all the time. Something is always charging at you, or teleporting behind you, or ambushing you from a cliff. This intensity is stretched out over it's enormous hour long levels, and it just gets exhausting after a while. This game has 19 credited level designers, long time quake modders and veterans of Arcane Dimensions. All skilled and experienced designers in their own right, but the end product is unfortunately less than the sum of it's parts. It's a real shame. This game clearly had a troubled development cycle, and my heart goes out to everyone who worked on it. I have other gripes. There is a real lack of enemy variety. The bosses have long invincibility phases. The music by Hulshult is mostly droning ambiance and not as memorable as his other work. But what really hurts Wrath is there are so many games out now that are just better. The retro FPS market is rapidly approaching total saturation, and there isn't much room for games that are just okay.

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty good, but very flawed.Pros:Half of the levels in the game are good/memorableVaried arsenal of useful and interesting weapons (all with their own secondary fire modes). including one of the best starting melee weapons in any shooter.Decent enemy variety.Consumable items are also varied and useful (and you get plenty of them)Mixed:Save system is interesting? It really just felt like checkpoints you could hold onto, but I imagine it could make the game much worse for those who aren't great at the platforming later on.Boss fights are very easy.Really not important, but I saw some "Get 100% of all secrets" type achievements, and those aren't fun to do in games like this. Many of them are VERY well hidden, but they often don't give much worth looking for (most often just some ammo/general consumable, much less the dark armor), so it would be a chore to seek them all. You can return to levels you've been to in order to find extra items/secrets/collectables, but only if you haven't left the hub for that area. After that they are just gone (for some reason).Cons:Weapon/enemy/item variety is not well spread out much of the game. You get most of them introduced in the first act of the game (first third). The worst is enemies, with the second act only introducing 1 enemy that only appears in act 2 — with act 3 thankfully having a few more — but it unfortunately means much of the game enemy variety is enemy limited. Level design is inconsistent; many of the levels are good, but many are just too many generic maze-like corridors later on. The last act only has one good level, one decent level, and 3 mediocre ones. Levels are also extremely long feeling (perhaps 2-3 times as long as they should be). Feels like they should be much smaller, but with more levels. Often a bit too easy to get lost in some samey looking areas where it shouldn't be possible to get stuck on where to go. Coffer keys also give a good reason why massive levels (where you can find the last key, but need it for the first chest you missed) in this setup feel awkward. At least the coffers don't give anything great, so you can just skip them. I suspect because the game has 15 levels and 3 boss levels with 18 level designers that each level was only worked on by one designer. No proof of this, but it would explain the massive variance in quality.Music mostly doesn't exist sadly.Overall? It's alright, but more of a $10-15 shooter and not a $25 one. Note that many of my hours were pointless backtracking for achievement secrets early on (which I regret because I eventually realized it isn't worth it/fun to do that in this game) and leaving it up time to time; I'd expect 10-15 hours out of it if you don't look around excessively, and 20-25 if you do.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:-The shooting mechanics are fun. The double-barrel shottie in particular is a joy to use.-The presentation is top notch. Dense gothic atmosphere like Quake 1, Blood 1, Heretic and Hexen. -Andrew Hulshult's score fits the game's setting like a glove. A foreboding, subtle score suitable for the gothic setting.Cons: The map design is where it falls over, it's too old school for its own good. Massive, labyrinth-like levels where you're obtusely hunting for keys, switches and doors were a plague upon FPSes of this era. Wrath sadly continues this tradition which should've been left in the '90s IMO. This is the reason I absolutely loathed Hexen. If I'm blindly searching around cleared environments for 15+ minutes looking for where to go next, that's a huge problem. I'll be refunding the game for now because of the antiquated, poor map design. I may revisit it when they launch in 2021, more likely when it's being sold at a discount.

It's smaller brother Coach Gun already shreds most enemies, but when you bring out the big boomstick — all bets are off. The chaingun analogue is also way more useful than I expected — and that's coming from someone who mostly ignores Nailgun in Q1.I have yet to hit a lot of the issues people complained about in other reviews — and if I do, I will update mine. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR; WRATH is a remarkable accomplishment, and a must for fans of the genre, as well as those looking for something different. Recommended.-As the somewhat murky pool of Retro-Shooters expands in every direction, here is an obsessively well-polished offering to the shrine of QUAKE. However, there is a lot more depth and challenge here than in many of the 'old gods'. I have always thought it a little reductive to call works such as this as solely homages. This is a wonderful, macabre and thorough game within and of itself. Sure, it's housed within an old engine, but the level design and attention to so many different details are not the work of mimicry, but of creation.As well as pulling off the basics flawlessly, WRATH takes some very bold design decisions and does an admirable job of mostly landing them correctly. The save system is odd, and can be incredibly punishing. However, it forces the player to cling to their life and monitor their resources at all times, especially on the Hard difficulty (which is properly hard) The bestiary is also low on direct information, but is, by it's mere existence, much more than many other games. The lore is also nebulous, and leaves a lot of room for interpretation, which is no bad thing, either. There are many risks, which is admirable by itself.The levels are long and labyrinthine in some places, and short and stacked in others. All are profoundly beautiful and merit many replays, to both root out all those sneaky secrets and to simply gawk at some of the marvellous architecture. The arsenal is varied, thoughtful and deep. Ammo management and use of the Relics are challenges, and there is much room open to experimentation. The enemy roster that you'll be fragging is a little narrow, but this is no bad thing. Study of your foes' strengths and weaknesses is key, especially on higher difficulty.The right-honourable Mr. Hulshult's soundtrack is more like the Nine Inch Nails' QUAKE soundtrack than  Mick Gordon's DOOM ETERNAL work, and in my opinion is all the more fantastic for it. It's beautifully ambient and opressive at times, and ethereal at others. The man can do absolutely nothing wrong.Indeed, this game was in the oven for a while, but it has crisped up nicely. There's plenty here for you to dig in to, explore and get massacred by. Let there be WRATH!

_childDocuments_.review: Even in early access I have to say: This game is SUPERB.This is everything I wanted and expected Quake 2 to be and more. It reminds me a bit  of the first time I played Future vs. Fantasy for Quake 1. Fresh, clever, and fun.The old strafe jumping has been replaced with a new mobility mechanic that is, in my opinion, quite innovative and fun. Weapons are unique and fun.  The graphics are a lovely callback to 90's fps gaming and then some.  The music is a droning ambient score that's extremely immersive.The only thing I might suggest to the developers is a minor sound redesign for some slightly punchier auditory queues while firing certain weapons, taking damage, or activating/using something of significance.Bottom line: This is a love letter to those who wanted a true sequel to the first Quake.
