_childDocuments_.review: WRATH: Aeon of Ruin is an old school, Doom-like, fast paced FPS. Oh I love the low-poly but high-detailed FPS.Player is in a peaceful place at first, walking around freely and choosing which map to enter through a portal. There are 6 maps in total, each has unique elements like churches, iceland, lava and giant trees, the map feels big since some contain several layers. I am familiar with all the monsters (no horror), weapons, color keys thing, This game runs smoothly, what I like the most is that the maps are rich and big. Unlike Doom make 1-1, 1-2 levels, WRATH puts things with the same theme into one big level, making no pause in the middle for a full experience, with lots indoor/outdoor places to visit, secrets, monsters, switches to explore. It took me around 25-40 mins to finish a level with a 50%-80% completion rate.   Player can do dash jumps for further places, and crouch jumps to reach secret spots. I enjoy the FPS+Action part, not only is it a good scheme for attack and defense, the secret hunting is fun, too.The downside is it is hard and I struggle not to die. Due to limited saving where the player can only save once at a specific place (white temple), death can mean losing lots of progress. Another thing is no map is supported, occasionally I am stuck at locked doors.It's so retro and fun. Great work!

_childDocuments_.review: What I love about this game is that there is no huge overarching story and no fluffed up crap. You literally just turn your brain off, enter a level, and start killing things. I found the gunplay to be very satisfying, as well as the movement, although at times it felt very slippery.I was lucky enough to get this game right after The Priory level was added, and the level design overall and overall visuals have been awesome, 10/10!One issue I do have is that I feel like Heretics are way overused to inflate the game's difficulty. I was already getting fed up with the game constantly throwing these giant floating bullet sponges at me throughout my playthrough, especially after The Priory, but then it all came full circle at the end of The Gardens level, which was the fourth level I played. When I got on the tiny elevator at the end, I was predictably spammed with about a dozen Heretics. With how often they pop up, I can't help but think they feel cheap, a little lazy, and a little boring to just pump bullet after bullet into.Overall though, this game was definitely worth my money and I can't wait to play future levels!

_childDocuments_.review: Straight up, this is the Quake II you've always wanted. ----GAME FEEL----- super responsive/tight control- incredibly satisfying weapon feedback- tricksy movement options via bunny hops and a dash from melee weapon's alt fire----LEVEL DESIGN----- overwhelmingly sprawling maps- full of secrets- clever interwoven paths - levels that feel more like entire regions open for you to explore- moody atmosphere, gothic architecture, swampy vegetation, etc- Hub world with region/map portals, but the hub world is actually interesting----GAMEPLAY----- tense, stressful, but super satisfying- "save scumming" delegated to a consumable/finite item, making for more strategic use of quicksaves- the save systems adds unbelievable tension and suspense to each of the numerous combat encounters- enemies are easily "readable" even from great distances- "solutions" to enemy combinations are fun to experiment with, and easy to start pinning down- sometimes a little heavy on their implementation of the "Heretic" enemy (Caco Demon - like), though this is less of an issue as your arsenal expands. -----------------------This game would have been an unquestioned all-time classic if it dropped during the "golden years" of the genre. Even in early access, there's a wwhhoollee lotta game here, and it's VERY much worth your time and money.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic. If you are a fan of 90s shooters, especially Quake, this game is for you. The level design is very well done and the hub reminds me a lot of the Arcane Dimensions mod/level pack for Quake. The guns feel and sound fantastic, has that nice "oomf" too them. Even the sound fx when selecting options in the menu has that nice "oomf". I was adjusting some settings and the sound fx for clicking on options was getting me all pumped up. The guns have alternate fire modes which all of them so far are really fun to use, especially the shotgun alt-fire (Shotgun is a blast to use). The Artifacts are consumable power-ups but it is a lot like Heretic where you collect the power-up and can use it whenever you want instead of it being activated on pickup. Difficulty seems good with the hardest one Nightmare being challenging but fair. I really enjoy the save system as it kind of tries to prevent save scumming. There are a few shrines in each map where you get to save once when you walk in them so like a regular checkpoint but you can still quick save as well with an item. The item is a consumable so you have to think about when to use it. You do get quite a bit per level so you can still save quite often but not all the time. Even though full release is not until next year I still recommend it in its current state. Looking forward to the full release.

_childDocuments_.review: This was very much an impulse buy for me. I never heard of this up until I just randomly came across it while browsing the internet. The premise sold me almost immediately. A classic-styled FPS run on Quake 1's Tech? Sign me right up. Immediately not even 5 minutes into this I had the absolutely biggest smile on my face. This game is nothing short of amazing.One of my favorite concepts this game runs with are the Soul Tethers, there's no regular save button in this game. You can't hit up your menu and save. Instead, the game offers these Soul Tethers as ways to save your game, but you have a limited amount. I dig the hell out of that, my only complaint is that by the time I was finished with the first area, I had so many Tethers just sitting in my inventory. I don't know if there will be less on the Hard Difficulty (I played on Normal). However, speaking of Artifacts, I found myself having almost no need of the other artifacts I picked up. The Life Siphon Artifact I didn't need because there are an absolutely insane amount of health drops. Small vials giving you 10 Health and Large vials giving you 30, and the 5 per kill from the Artifact felt like it was not a good trade off, I was better off backtracking for health I left behind. As for the Cruel Aegis, I simply just never found a reason to use it.These small gripes aside, I had an absolute blast playing this, the gameplay was fast paced and I felt a real rush when I found myself constantly swarmed by dudes, especially the Executioners who just hit like trucks, or the giant Stricken who at first seem simple to dodge, but as they get closer to death they fire multiple bombs in different patters every time, making dodging a sort of sweet science. I found use out of every weapon, even if the Blade was mostly just for jumping across ledges and platforms. The Shotgun was the star of the show, an absolutely powerful weapon, The Pistol had perfect range for sniping weaker enemies and I found a lot of use out of the Triple Barrel secondary fire. The Fang Spitter was absolutely necessary in dealing with tougher enemies especially from a range. And the Retcher was great in dealing with Executioners.For two levels, the price may look like a bit much. But these levels are so massive and filled to the brim with enemies they feel like one giant Doom or Quake episode mashed into one level. I absolutely do not regret buying this, and I cannot wait for the next level to be released.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish Steam let you rate games as "maybe." So this is a Quake-style game made by some prolific Quake modders. Sounds good, right? It's got sharp art direction, moves well, animates well, and sounds good. Seems like a sure-fire bet. But if you've ever dabbled enough in the Quake or Doom modding scene, you may know that modders can be a little... high on their own supply, let's say. By that I mean they make these games primarily for themselves and their friends. They build content for the unspoken language of their community, which may not include people outside of their immediate clique. They're insular, in other words. Which, when we're talking about a mod that only a couple hundred people at most might play, is fine! There's nothing wrong with making things for yourself. But when we're talking about a retail product, standards change. To some degree you have to think about mass market consumption, and people outside of your immediate circle. After just 45 minutes with Wrath: Aeon of Ruin, that insular modder vibe is all over this game. I want to love it, I really do. It's pushing a lot of the good buttons in my brain. But I feel like it's throwing me in to Episode 4 Map 6 with nothing but the starter pistol and leaving me to figure out the rest on my own. I'm sure that appeals to some of you out there, but I very quickly grew tired of getting lost only to be ambushed and instantly killed the moment I figured out where to go.This is a game that cracks the whip on you a lot harder than the material its paying tribute to. On Normal difficulty, you'll almost immediately start fighting multiple different enemy types that explode on death, leaving you to contend with their splash damage. Health is surprisingly scarce, too. And the save system is a consumable item you pick up in levels themselves, meaning you have to choose carefully when and how often you save, because you CAN run out of save items. Maps seem way too big and intricate for their own good. You had Doom, then Duke 3D had even bigger levels, but Wrath is on the next level. The first level is a snowy graveyard with underground catacombs, and it's nothing but a maze of identical side halls that all twist around, looping back into and forking off from each other everywhere. It is extremely easy to get turned around and not realize which direction is forward, and there's no map or anything to help you orient yourself. When you DO figure out where to go next, it's right back to the grind of monsters that feel a little too fast, a little too powerful, and a little too plentiful. There were times where I went from full health to dead within seconds and I didn't even know where I was being shot from. This is not a game for those expecting sympathy or a power fantasy. This is a game for people who want authentic boomer shooters that bite back, and bite hard. I don't know if that's who I am.Like, this game gives me more trouble on Normal difficulty than Doom 1 did on Ultraviolence. Maps shift too much from being completely wide open or labyrinthine; enemies are always coming from all directions and you're never given a chance to slow down and line up shots or even take cover. It's constantly whipping back and forth between pedal-to-the-metal hyper-aggression and spending what feels like ages trying to figure out which of these 17 identical hallways is the one leading to progression.The hub does offer other maps besides the snowy graveyard to explore, but they all ultimately devolve in to the same beats with the same six enemies.And that's not even talking about the guns. The guns look and feel great, but just like everything else, feel like they're tuned for people who are already experts at this game. The Shotgun has a wonderful alt-fire that sprays shrapnel around, but you REALLY have to commit to understanding timing its charge up sequence. Wrath's version of the chaingun is great, but it has a low ammo cap and refills can get pretty scarce, so I'm too afraid to use it a lot of the time. You're given an acid launching gun just in time for them to introduce enemies that sprint up in your face, meaning you're more likely to cause splash damage to yourself when you use it.Swallowing one's pride and playing on Easy mode mitigates some of this, but only some. It's still a deeply unforgiving game and you're still going to get very, very lost. You have to be really dedicated to wanting this kind of game, because it's an extremely hardcore one of those.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: this is an early access review, and reflects the game as I actually played it. First, I am a die-hard Linux user, and wishlisted this game not just because it looked amazing, but because native Linux was promised. Early Access does _not_ have a Linux build, but it will run very well in Proton. Wrath wears its Quake heritage on its sleeve, but it's fundamentally a different game. If you expect a highly polished, hard as nails gameplay loop exactly like Arcane Dimensions you may be a little disappointed. AD took years of work from a much larger community group than Kill Pixel, but that does not mean Wrath is bad. Wrath is different, and different is good.The art style and audio are both absolutely some of the most polished I've seen in 2019, with exceptional attention to visual detail, and subtle but brilliant audio and music touches. The game retains the dark, oppressive and moody atmosphere of Quake 1, but the gameplay is decidedly different from Quake. Romero-esque monster closets are not the norm here, nor will you find elaborate traps of spikes, pits, or crushing walls. (though I do secretly hope some will be added in future.) The movement of Outlander is still fast and feels at home in the faux-90s theme, but Quake veterans will notice an initially disorienting lack of air-control, at least until you realize you can spam the blade lunge to almost fly.Every weapon has a distinct use and their own strengths and weaknesses, and each has a unique and (at least situationally) useful alt-fie. Arsenal redundancy is nowhere to be seen, with no weapon upgrades that render old ones more or less useless, eg, the shotgun to super shotgun relationship in Quake 1. The guns have some obvious homages to Quake 1 too, especially the Fang Spitter, one of the most satisfying recreations of the original Nailgun, and the single best reason to mash the number 4 on your keyboard that has ever existed. The game also appears to have a difficulty ramp that increases with each level you play, so in the final game you can pick any level from the hub world first and use it as the intro level, with successive levels getting harder no matter what order you pick them in. This is very hard to notice with only 2 levels unless you're playing those two levels over and over, but community consensus is that it's definitely there. However, this has led to the criticism that the game is too easy, I think in part because the game is currently too short to really showcase just how hard it's going to get by the time you're fighting your way through the final stages of the finished product. I believe that this natural difficulty ramp and the ability to blade lunge (or as I like to call it, blade running) will result in a game that provides some genuinely tantalizing speedrunning and routing possibilities. Finally, this game represents the continuation of the Darkplaces project, which started as a source port/extension for Quake 1, continued to be developed as the engine for Xonotic, and is now once again being extended for Wrath. Veteran modders and mappers are already beginning to sink their teeth into the game as evidenced by the 3d Realms Discord, and the gift of new code development being released to the community after the game is released will be a boon to fans of Quake modding, open source software, and the FPS genre as a whole. If given the choice, I would definitely choose support this game again. Flawless 5/7, A++, no regerts, would buy again, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good FPS in the line of Quake 1! Blast through a beautiful pixel hell!  When I learned that WRATH is a game from the original developers of many classic FPSs, I was immediately intrigued! Quake 1 has very atmospheric memories with me. A feeling of pure hellish dungeons! I have never returned to that game. Partly because nostalgia is a ♥♥♥♥♥, and the memories tend to be better than the experience itself. The main reason is that I'm physically unable to play an FPS due to a handicap. So once in a while I let a friend play such a game to be able to experience it still, but also to educate millenials about classic games! WRATH faithfully met my expectations of a Quake 1 game, and that by itself is a success on its own! The game is brutal, spawns enemies behind you through opening secret rooms. The weapons are awesome! They have a very hellish theme, and every weapon has a burst fire that deals more damage, at cost of a disadvantage (accuracy, ammo consumption, reload time). The UI is very minimalistic, only ammo and health is shown. The game uses a tether-point system for saving. You get to pick up very limited amount of these points, and you can create a saving point with them whenever you please. In other words: limited amount of saving spots, but you choose where. You will probably die a lot, and this gives players control of the saves. The parts I've seen are good! I'm waiting for the final version, hoping for achievements and maybe a story? 85/100

_childDocuments_.review: Being a huge fan of quake 1 through qc, heretic, hexen and hexen II, etc i am very impressed with this and it's been exactly what i have been wanting. the dark arcane gothiness with the graves, statues, and architecture is resemblent of arcane dimensions and other good single player quake maps and is just so satisfying to the soul. the anglo-saxon early dark ages theme with the runes and such is on point. it feels the part, and i get sucked into it.it's been a while since a game has made me want to turn off the lights and play in the dark. i love the use of sprites, especially the soul tether. wrath uses the darkplaces engine, so it's basically all cpu and stays within 450-501fps on my 5.2 i5-9600kf/sapphire rx590 stock. thge game loads right away and runs buttery smooth.my fov is 100 and the strafe jumping and movement is right on point. you can really get some speed up with the blade jump.the presence of alternate fire is great. i love the blade jump. the weapons all feel good. the blade feels a little light and the guns could kick a bit more but overall the feel is good. the pickups could be a little louder. the weapon switching time is excellent. the shotgun reload time is great. the fang spitter is like having a more accurate but slower nailgun, and i absolutely love using it. of course, all the targets have been for the most part stationary. the retcher is basically a nade launcher, allowing you to get all those sweet angle shots.the textures come just right out of the box but you can enable linear filters if you want that late 90s early 2000s blurry look. personally this is probably the best work i've seen so far in the recent race to create old school mid to late 90s magic/rpg fps based shooters. but this is definitely more quake like and more my style. $25 well spent.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic boomer shooter that feels like a hodge-podge of mid to late 90's id Software games and I say that as an absolute compliment. This game is clearly inspired by Quake 1, going so far as to using the ACTUAL Q1 engine via the Darkplaces source-port, you can't get more authentic than that aside from actually running the game in Windows 98 with a Voodoo 3DFX card* on a CRT monitor.*Please don't try it at home, your precious 3DFX would probably blow up lmao.While yes, the foundations are Q1 inspired, it also feels like it has a ton of inspiration from Doom and Quake 2 by adding bio-mechanic monstrosities aside from the regular Lovecraftian eldritch abominations and Hexen's hub world for good measure. For being such an ancient engine and despite the graphics looking appropriately chunky and low-poly, it looks AMAZING due to a strong sense of grimdark aesthetics that wouldn't be out of place if it was indeed released in the late 90's.Also it runs above 144 FPS, so you can probably run this game at 4K on your favorite potato.As weapons go, they're your typical id Software-esque roster of weapons with even pressing the appropriate key to select them, like the initial blade that can lunge to your enemies and gib them in a single hit, your pistol, double barreled shotgun, machinegun that uses "fangs" as ammo (nice nod to the "nails" of Q1) and also a mine launcher similar to the one from Unreal Tournament, with green glowing blobs and everything.The saving system is pretty interesting IMO, you can save in three different ways, by regular autosaves that happen when you enter a new level, by using "shrines" that disappear after a single use and limited quick saves in the form of actual pickups called "Soul Tethers", so *Unless you're hoarding those precious tethers, I dunno.I haven't gotten too far yet, I've only finished the first level which is surprisingly huge, it took me about an entire hour to finish and I still got 14 more to go lol. As far as first impressions go, I definitely really like what I'm seeing right now and I'll probably update this review if anything major comes up.So yeah, I really like it! Give it a shot if you're craving for more of that Quake 1 goodness!

_childDocuments_.review: I have to commend the developers of this game. Not only have they taken the legendary Quake engine and bought it into 2019, but they've made a damned good game using it too! The game handles well and the the atmosphere, music and sound design all really come together to make a game that pulls you in. The weapons are mostly well thought out and are certainly interesting takes on the classic weapon loadouts of old. Andrew Hulshult once again works his magic and comes out with an incredibly atmospheric and moody soundtrack which fits the feel of the game perfectly.Unfortunately not every game is perfect, but with this being early access I can only hope that the developers take on board feed back from us. While I love this game, there are some annoyances which stop it from being incredible. Here are the things that I feel could do with looking at:Audio and Visual Feedback: One thing that really got to me was that I could never tell if I had actually picked up an item or not. Sure, you get the text and icon in the top left of the screen, but that's it. In Quake you got a sufficient sound and a brief flash on the screen to indicate that you've picked something up. In Wrath you might hear the pickup sound but 99% of the time you don't. It's not just items that suffer from this. When in combat you get no feedback as to whether you've hit an enemy or not. There's no sound and no effect, you just kind of keep shooting and hope that the enemy is getting hit. This is especially bad when fighting enemies at close range and long range. At close range you know you've hit the enemy but it's like you've just shot it with air and at range you can't tell if you're actually hitting the enemy or not.The Crosshair: Wait, I'm complaining about a crosshair? I must be nitpicking here! I don't have a problem with the crosshair itself, but not having an option to adjust it is a PITA. You'll lose it easily in the snow in the Undercrofts when fighting. Also, it's too damn small! I'm running at 1440p so I don't know whether the crosshair scales at all, but at this resolution you can barely see the crosshair at all! We just need some options to adjust it so that we can see it better.Weapon damage: This is a weird one to describe but with some of the tankier enemy types I find myself either chewing through ammo to take them down, or sometimes they will happily accept death and let me keep my ammo. I think this may possibly be something to do with the lack of feedback as described above, but it feels somewhat off. I find this mainly with the Fang Spitter. The secondary fire seems almost obsolete apart from using it against one enemy type to stunlock it. It uses twice the ammo, fires slower but overall seems like it has zero benefit over the primary fire mode.I must stress that the gripes above don't stop it from being a good game, they are just annoyances and I'm sure things like this will be looked at in the future.Overall I'm massively looking forward to when this gets a full release!

_childDocuments_.review: "Beauty is only skin deep"I would like to preface this review with stating that I have played games of this ilk for a great amount of time, and generally, may have a different perspective than a casual user due to my experience. The game was played to completion on the hardest difficulty.With that out of the way, lets start with the good. Wrath looks great! Very nice attention to detail in the texture work with only a scant few alignment issues, lightmap leaks, etc. This is to be expected of the people working on this, as they represent some of the most talented individuals in the quake community and otherwise. It is clear that a lot of work went into building a cohesive design language for the environments and weapons (not so much enemies). Now with the art covered, lets get down to it. Why is this review negative?Frankly, this game really fails to capitalize on any of what makes retrofps fun to begin with. And past that, its just further death by a thousand cuts. Starting simple, the movement. While this game rides on the coattails of Quake as hard as it possibly can, it managed to throw away the finely tuned physics of Quake very quickly. While there is some level of speed, and control, it falls flat as soon as you step on a slope. You lose control, you slide around and get stuck. It is admittedly hard to convey a feeling like this through text, but youll have to trust me on this, after playing quake, this games movement feels like an interpretation you explained to someone who doesnt speak the same language. Add on top of this really poorly interpolated strafe tilting and its a recipe for poor feeling at best, and motion sickness at worst. Moving on from movement, lets go to combat. The bread and butter of a FPS.Whoever designed the combat the combat in this game lacks a fundamental understanding of the core gameplay behind a proper fps. Enemies are placed haphazardly with little to no thought. So much so it feels randomized but clearly wasnt. There is no buildup. There is no Payoff. The combat is incredibly monotone, there is no kill or threat priority to speak of. The weapons dont really serve distinct roles beyond bad, and good (we'll cover the weapons later). There are very very limited setpieces that feel like a designed encounter meant to push the player, or cause them to behave in a certain way. To take cover, or make a cerebral play. This is just kind of a crying shame. The game goes as far as to warp enemies in, sometimes right on top of you, in an attempt to be a pseudo serious sam??? But what the combat designer here didnt understand is that every enemy in a serious sam game has a distinct purpose, and a heavy effect on the gameplay. The designers of serious sam understand this core principle incredibly well, and finely tune every encounter to push the player to his limit, but never past it. There is no such escalation in this game. Anyways, it is hard to talk about the combat without talking about the weapons, so, moving on. The weapons in this game are a mixed bag thus far. The wristblade is cool, and fun to move around with. The pistol sucks. The shotgun is good, but definitely too slow to cycle. You can see even they knew that in their EA trailer, where they sliced out frames of the video to make it look like it shoots faster. The bonergun has a very satisfying sound, but MAN is the damage weak, and the alt fire weaker. The biorifle is good, it one-shots most enemies. Not much to say about it. Ultimately across all of these, its clear the game designer felt alt fires were necessary, and being blunt, all of them are pretty much useless. Yes you COULD kill a few enemies at a time with the shotguns alt, but its so clunky and unfun to use that it just isnt worth it. Speaking of killing enemies, lets talk about them for a moment. The AI in this game is bad. Your enemies will get caught on corners, run into walls, teleport around, and generally be kind of laughable. It is clear this was a difficult task as the level designers used a lot of complex and organic shapes which the enemies have difficulty finding their way past. Most of the time you encounter a larger more difficult enemy, they will get stuck on a small corner and allow you to shoot them with absolutely no sense of urgency or danger. Often times they will also just flatout not be able to fit in passageways and doors. I touched on this briefly earlier, but theres not really any sense of cohesion, or design in the enemies. Theyre fairly generic monsters, whos themes dont match eachother, or the levels they are in, which is mostly fine, but they serve to alter combat very little, and thats kind of a disappointment after looking at quake where there isnt really a single enemy out of place. Im out of segues at this point, so lets do a miscellaneous section. The save system is silly. Theres no other way to say it. Its a cute thought by an overly proud game designer who came up with the idea, and wanted it in the game at all costs. At best, its meaningless because theres very little pickup balance in this game, you have max ammo, powerups, armor, everything, at all times. At worst, its frustrating and cataclysmically bad. Potentially losing you upwards of 30 minutes of progress because you forgot to save or didnt find a shrine. This is bad. There is no reality in which the decision to include this mechanic pays off. The player doesnt feel a sense of accomplishment for spending one of their 9 saves. Theres no strategy to it. Its just a guessing game with no reward. As a side note about the pickups, the designers decided to make their collision unfortunately small, so youll waste a lot of time missing pickups and having to walk back to pick them up. Ill also fit the music in here, because while the ambience is good, thats ALL there is. There is no peak, no triumph, just a slow drone, and its just sort of an ethereal bit that doesnt QUITE fit the gameplay. Just further minor disappointment really. -This review is continued in the comments because Steam will not allow me to post it at this length.

_childDocuments_.review: (I have mixed feelings about the game)6,25/10 OVERALL – I appreciate the remarkable throwback and love letter to games like Heretic, Quake and Hexen. The designers put significant effort into captivating the player with a graphical crisp game, intricate level design and artistic enemies—which are undeniably captivating adding a chef's kiss to the impressive weapons. However, the convoluted, lengthy and meandering level designs drain the exhilarating gameplay like a rock!—but does Wrath lie aeons deep in ruins—let’s dive into it, shall we?5/10 Fast-paced?The gameplay aims for relentless fast combat. But the sprawling level design disrupts the game flow and drains energy from exhilarating gunfights. Add secrets, chest-hunting and parkouring and you have a serious, unnecessary time sink that destroys the fast-paced action. A great fight returns this energy—but is often short-lived. (In stage 3 gameplay pick-up is way better)6/10 Sprawling levels designRich graphical and artistic artwork, styled in fire, ice, sand, snow and bloody swamps—evocatively portrays the setting and feels well. But the sprawl and size cause time sinks repeating the same section—don't forget about the secrets, chest-hunting and parkouring! Level design may feel monotonous and lack variation at times.The Sigils of Displacement adds a great and refreshing puzzle perspective. In ACT 3, the level design feels tighter, more focussed, and better paced—but may drain with sprawling level sizes.-	Suggestion - Cut levels in half and shorten the level time, giving the feeling of progression.8/10 Great weapon rosterAll weapons have unique primary and secondary fire modes well suited for defeating enemies. Some of the weapons require planning, thought or strategic effort. Most of all, they have a well-polished graphical design:-	RUINATION BLADE – Has a LOVELY charge-jump mechanic.-	SHOTGUN – Secondary fire feels ineffective. (I would suggest a slug shot like the pistol)-	CRYSTALLIZER – A unique secondary requires planning and accuracy for massive damage.-	DEVASTATION MACE – Like Hexen’s Blood Scourge! (So cool)6/10 Fine Artefact RosterThe standard artefacts like Healing, underwater breathing and secret finding are fin. Where artefacts like the void grenade and Vicious Animus work well. Other artefacts lack utility or don’t seem as effective to me.-	MARK OF REVELATION – Could be a one-per-level Sigil and frees up a slot for something else.-	VICIOUS ANIMUS / VOID GRENADE – A nod to the Morph Ovum and porkalator.-	FLASH OF RAGE - I would love it if it altered weapon fire, like a Tome of Power in Hexen.-	SHOCKWAVE – Why does this artefact already have a void grenade?-	CONFOUNDING ATTAR – often works quite iffy and enemies still attack you when charmed.-	RING OF DEFLECTION – Please allow free movement during use—instead of standing around.-	CRUEL AEGIS – The worst artefact. It combines well with the MACE OF DEVASTATION and when repeatedly used—RIP AND TEAR! But, when drained to 1 Hp, a torch can kill you.6.5/10 Mediocre EnemiesWell-rounded and captivating graphically styled enemies with a mix between mythical and horror. Mainly enemy spawn-in feels lazy and starts becoming annoyed and expected. (but I think this was because of time constraints) Many enemies feel like bullet sponges and show little impact when hit. Some enemies don’t fit a scenario entirely (like Cyst-enemies in Act 3—keep them in the swamp).-	FALLEN – Relevant when owning the MACE OF DEVASTATION.-	HERETIC – An awesome three-fanged flying head—Often gets stuck flying into level design.-	EXECUTIONER – Nice horror creature—outmatched by ledges, like claptrap and stairs!-	WRAITH / LURKERS / WIDOWS – I would love if Wraiths flutter out like a balloon when killed. LURKERS are boring and easy. And widows, I expect them—thus easily killed. (The gib makes me laugh though when they meet the business end of my shotgun when I jump the corner)6/10 – BOSSESWeird designs are an interesting addition. But boss fights feel simple overall, and vary their attacks but little. Sometimes the first and second bosses feel like gargantuan versions of standard enemies. Of course, not every boss must be the next souls-boss, but these fights leave something to be desired.)-	LORD OF ETHERION – Shows what to do in the beginning. After that, hit three switches and learn the bosses’ telegraph attack—this part is utterly annoying and lengthy. Use the centre stage as cover against his attacks and you’ll be fine (Why he destroys the sigil and pillars is beyond me)The overall rating is rather low and I wish was higher. I put every hour into the game to finish it as I long for these kinds of games. Thank you so very much for Wrath the Aeons of Ruin—I hope you have more in store for us in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR : Lazy Early Access Review, looks very promising but combat is currently a bit dull and far to easyPROS-Great visuals and presentation, it looks seriously good -Weapons firing fangs and cysts is metal as ♥♥♥♥-The shotgun and nail gun in particular both look and sound fantastic-Shotgun exploding enemies is spot on-Blade dash mechanic is a cool addition-Interesting powerup/save system-Sound in general is very strong CONS-Very very easy even on hard (which should be the new medium...)-Most enemies are pretty boring currrently and just repeatedly spam low damage projectile attacks (there is nothing like shambler or vore from quake 1 with high damage charging/homing attacks)-Combat in general feels spammy as you will only take damage due to there being so many enemies constantly shooting all over the place-Current arsenal has no high damage med/long range weapons (rocket launcher etc) making killing larger enemies at range a boring slog -Enemy types either all feel "one shotable" or very bullet spongy, there is no in betweenThe charging and ranged zombies "widow" and "wrath" have far to little health (and annoying flying enemies have too much...)-The large charging melee enemy type "executioner" is far to hard to dodge due to its broken hit box -The secondary fire on the shotgun looks great but pretty much completely useless in its current bouncing projectile form-The 3 shot burst secondary fire on the retcher/bio gun might as well be the primary fire, the secondary could then be something more interesting (timed grenade?)-having to switch to the arm blade to use the dash is a massive pain, making it an off hand weapon that just recharges would let you more easily use it during combatThere might seem to be many CONS here but I still really enjoyed what I played and think it looks very promisingHowever I would not make it through a whole game with the current difficulty/enemies

_childDocuments_.review: As a boomer shooter lover, I tried really hard to like this game, I even played it for 7 hours, but unfortunately it is so freaking unbalanced to the point where it's unplayable.When I first started it, I was thrilled by how well crafted the game was, sound design, aesthetics, and the first enemies (the zombies) had good dismemberment animations, after that, everything went downhill. The maps started to get very similar to each other, they stopped having soul, with each map the enemy pool was getting bigger and bigger to the point where you had to kill 400 of them in a single map, and the weapons started to get stale because you had the same weapons you had picked from the first two maps.However, the biggest problem of this game is the enemy design, I have played a huge amount of video games in my life, this one has arguably one of the worst, if not the worst, enemy design, and no I am not talking aestheticaly wise but mechanic wise. Aesthetics meh, could've been better could've been worse, but mechanics?! Every single enemy except from zombies spams projectiles as soon as they make eye contact with you, and they won't stop until they are dead. "Git gud" right? Yea, now imagine that 20 of these spamming proctile enemies are spawning every 5 seconds in close quarter rooms and can eat your healthbar like it's nothing even on medium difficulty. Wait what's that? You don't have armor? Well now you die in 3 hits from most enemies.I could see past all that, but man the game doesn't give you any meaningful gun to deal with all this BS, the spike thrower (i do not even know its name because i do not even care) which is your "rifle/smg" will run out of bullets in mere seconds so you'll barely be able to use it, and the shotgun cannot deal with anything if it's 10 meters away from you.So the game's logic is you have to keep your distance and play "sMaRt" and avoid projectiles but at the same time the only useful weapon you hold can only deal damage in close quarters. I know later on the game you get more guns but you have to finish the whole first world with these abominations, so the experience is already ruined for me. I won't play a game that may become good after 15 hours.I also forgot to mention that most enemies are bulletproof, that really helps to capture the feeling of horrendous balance, devs did a great job there not gonna lie.All in all, Wrath was a product that was worked on the first 2-3 levels, and then they handed it to AI. It's a boomer shooter that has horribly long maps, filled with hundreds of projectile spamming enemies that need 10 shots to die and soulless world. It's a shame because I was waiting for the finished product to finally play it but I was dissapointed. With all that being said, I may keep playing just for the sake of finishing another game.PS: Funniest part is they add like 20-30 secrets for every map, yea I will definitely explore the maps after having the most frustrating time of my life fighting 1.500 enemies and their 10.000 projectiles. It seems like devs took the "the more the better" a bit too literally. 3/10

_childDocuments_.review: As one of the most visually captivating and action packed FPS games I've seen in recent years, WRATH: Aeon of Ruin is a fantastic title that will keep you on your toes for hours of intense and devastating fun. The game brings a combination of FPS and action-packed levels that transport you back to the classic era of DOOM and Quake. You play as the Outlander and battle your way through hordes of old-school enemies delivering devastation with an arsenal of classic weaponry and abilities.The game's visuals are stunning and its soundtrack is a modern take on classic legends like Mick Gordon, Quake's own composer. WRATH's enemies are varied and abundant with some exceptional boss fights to boot. The hard-hitting, combat-heavy guns are also quite satisfying, giving you freedom to unleash carnage with your skills and weapons. The movement within the game is smooth and responsive, and its levels require strategy and sustained endurance.WRATH: Aeon of Ruin is a really great FPS game with stunning graphics and intuitive combat mechanics. The level of depth that you can explore in this game is remarkable and the added tactical elements let you customize weapons, armor, and abilities to suit your play style. If you're looking for an immersive and action-packed shooter, then WRATH: Aeon of Ruin is definitely worth a try.

_childDocuments_.review: Generic: Aeon of Boomeshooter!Before I say anything, I want to be perfectly clear: the game is ''good''. Actually, if someone asked me what game represent the most basic feature of the genre the most, I'd point them to this game.And... that's it: no further embellishments, no deep story (there's little, and it's all blatantly ''generic''), no mouth-watering designs. Just a few kinds of enemies (most of them copied, or at least their concept, from others more acclaimed games of the genre), a reasonable amount of guns and only a few maps that are worthy of even being mentioned.Basically, all the stuff that the other boomershooters, (and Quake, more prominently) have done, W:AoR does it too and does it decently. Not bad, but certainly not astonishingly.Speaking of which, I've read other reviews mentioning how this game was supposed to be released way early, and if so, they believed could have ''consecrated'' into the Olympus of the genre (since it was one of the first games to announced the return of the boomershooter ''wave'')... but I strongly disagree: even if the game had come out before, it'd not have helped, since all of its problems are structural (beside the lack of creativity).Even the save system, which is the only thing truly ''unique'', it is definitely not enough to be a true redeeming feature.And yet again, the game is ''good'', and a fairly good time-killer, which does it pretty well, since it does have only 5 (+1 boss fight, but it hardly counts) maps per hub (3) but their are all MASSIVE... and by the end of it, even with my love for secret hunting, I decided to skip them, just to finish it in ''Hard'' mode (which is not).So, to conclude, worth buying? overall, yes. Not a ''historical'' game, but a good game nonetheless.

_childDocuments_.review: Wrath is a very simple game on the paper. You go in a level (accessible from the hub world) kill bunch of a creepy monsters and complete the level by obtaining its relic, it's up to you if you want to find the secrets. Meanwhile it's a very basic concept it almost never fails to entertain when it's done right it is also somewhat old fashioned. And time to time you see there would be certain popular genres (and revival of the boomer shooter lasts back to a past few years, one of the most recent and iconic example is Iron Maiden which is also developed under 3D Realms) Luckily, WRATH is mostly done right. It tries to grab the best of parts of beloved franchises like Quake, Duke Nukem and Doom. 3D Realms indeed did a good job contacting KillPixel and supplying him with proper talents. The game has a great atmosphere and even greater monster designs accompained by a creepy and mystic selection of ingame tracks. To an extent, I agree to the critisms that levels feels and seem identical (also applies to the variety of creatures) however, given it's still in early access I am willing to give the benefit of doubt without a hesitation. Last two level updates clearly shows how complex could be the maps with open areas and how could they feel different to the rest (to name, the levels are The Priory and The Hollow). Gunplay and save system does not disappoint. The game could be indeed challenging if you prefer to play it on hard however, on normal it is pretty a casual boomer shooter. There are enough ammo and things that makes you able to create a checkpoint so you rarely stress out. That doesn't mean you should utilize your relics/ammo or checkpoints right but I can't quite say the game tries to be hard at the first place which is more than fair for the newcomers. Platforming with your blade (jumping after charging your blade) is an interesting take and it creates opportunities for a unique traversal. Hard to understand why would anyone hate on an uncompleted game. So far, devs did a good job delivering the promised updates. The rest of the levels, a mod support and multiplayer is still yet to come. Hopefully, this year the game will be finished and I'll update my review then. I have a strong belief that rest of the levels will surprise us even if not with this fast-paced and swift movement system and gunplay, I believe the multiplayer could be actually dope.

_childDocuments_.review: WRATH is a solid classic Quake style shooter. With suitably monstrous enemies that can die in a variety of ways, very satisfying feeling weapons and interesting, if sometimes confusing to navigate, levels (so far what is in the game anyway) that allow you to freely traverse and explore secrets in them with no major points of no-return, there's not much about this game that doesn't appeal to my appetite for 90s style shooters.Slight sources of annoyance can be the enemies' uncanny ability to shoot at you very accurately from extreme distances, though you can return fire with some weapons, and the occasional unfair feeling ambush that may result in a rapid death. Combined with the limited saves the game has, allowing you to save anywhere but requiring you to spend a "soul tether", an item you can find both in the open and hidden in secret areas, these can sometimes lead to a misplaced save requiring you to redo a part of the game several times. However, so far these situations have been fairly few and far between (NOTE: these experiences are from hard mode and do not necessarily apply to lower difficulties).If you've enjoyed other such shooters like DUSK or Amid Evil, I can heartily recommend this game for you. People who want more modern style shooter may not enjoy this as much however.

I'd enjoy an "ultra-violence" equivalent with less save items or something, but the game's hard mode feels like a perfect difficulty otherwise.I had a mouse skipping issue at first, but it was easily fixable, just do some digging in the discussion forums.

_childDocuments_.review: Jesus Christ, 3D Realms. This was fine for what it was. A nice good looking modernized play on Quake. I liked the aesthetics, I  mostly liked the gameplay, I liked the weapons. It had some problems but you could easily overlook them because it was early access. It'll work out (it wouldn't).That was in 2019 I think. because I can't look it up quickly anymore. The original date has been switched out everywhere with 2024. And for good reason. It was a meme of how embarrassing an early access game could be handled. Pople were mad af and for good reason. Endless empty promises for years and nothing ever came of it. So nice retconning there, 3D Realms.Then again the game itself is mostly okay despite some gripes I have with it. It would have been okay if they just gave us some new levels and worked out the kinks but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, they actually made some of the things worse AND didn't bother with some of the most egregious problems. But more on that later.The worst offender is this: You did pay full price for this and played all the way through? Multiple times even because there was nothing else to play since 2019? Congratulations. Guess what. Your entire progress is now inaccesible. You now have to replay all the ♥♥♥♥ you repleayed over the last 4 years because there wasn't any new levels. So if you just came back to play something new you first have to replay all the tired old early access content, too. Again. Why? _childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game, but unfortunately I cannot even fathom finishing the full 15h campaign. It looks great and is dripping with atmosphere, weapons are satisfying to use, there's a ton of secrets that are actually FUN to find (something which is very rarely done right)... So why the negative review?EVERY. ♥♥♥♥♥♥. ENCOUNTER. IS. EXACTLY. THE. SAME.I've spent 4h playing this game and I feel like I've already seen everything it has to offer.Every fight is just copy-pasted over and over and over and over again ad nauseam, you're just repeating the same exact process of fighting the exact same enemies in the exact same order in almost the exact same environment. Have no one playtested this ♥♥♥♥? Did no one mention how excruciatingly boring this game becomes after like 3h? I've watched a few minutes of a gameplay video from the final level of the game AND IT WAS EXACTLY THE SAME AS THE FIRST ONE. It's unbelievable.Enemies. Oh god, could they be any less interesting to fight? They're the most basic, braindead, default Quake archetypes that felt dated in the early 2000s. _childDocuments_.review: I have so many good things to say about this game. The level design is stellar, with each mission having tons of enemies to slaughter. The weapons are standard old-school FPS fare, but the addition of alt-fire modes make them all feel fresh and stand out in a sea of double-barrels, rocket launchers and nailguns.Even though there are only 5 levels (at the time of this review) they have a ton of replayability. Starting levels in a different order from the central "hub" world changes the enemy composition and weapon pickups in each level, creating a different experience for subsequent playthroughs.The movement in this game is a speedrunner's dream! If you like Quake 1/Source style air control and bunnyhopping, Wrath is the game for you. The arm blade weapon's alt-fire is a dash, and these can be chained with bunnyhops and slopejumps to gain insane speed and height. Levels that might take 30-40 minutes when focusing on combat can be completed in 2-3 minutes if you focus on speeding past everything.A large portion of my playtime has been spent doing individual level and whole game speedruns, blazing through as fast as I possibly can by dashing, bhopping, and boosting up level geometry. I've spent thousands of hours in Quake Champions, modern DOOM, TF2 and other movement focused arena/old-school shooters, and Wrath has some of the most satisfying high-skill movement I've ever experienced in any game.Whether you choose to fight and kill every enemy or zip past them all to get straight to the end-level objective, this game is amazing. It's taking longer than expected to release the finished product, but I assure you, the content that's here already is more than worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey there Jimmy! Do you want a new boomershooter?“Yes sir! I love them! I love Turbo Overkill, Ultrakill and Deadlink!”Well Jimmy, here is Wrath: a true to the bone Boomshoot with only some minor modernisations!“Ewww! This is so basic! There is no upgrades, no super-meta techniques, no unlocks! How can you like this?”Jimmy, I said it was a boomershooter. What did you expect?“I wanted, ya know, for it to have updated like so many games have in the past couple of years. We can’t keep doing this really old feeling stuff!”Jimmy, I think the genre name is now bunk.Wrath: Aeon of Ruin is another one of the modern boomershooter games that have been part of a relentless deluge since 2019. While it may seem like just another title in the pile, it started development long, long before the current wave and set itself up to be one of the core 4 titles from 3D Realms and New Blood. Development hell has held that back and now we have the final product: a lean, mean, FPS machine that absolutely reeks of quality and effort, but also one that shows its Quake heritage roots so clearly in its simplicity and quirkiness that it may not be advisable to the more fair-weather fan.One thing must be established before we go further: Wrath is based on Quake’s Darkplaces engine. This means that rather than being a modern engine like Unity having its art and environments simplified to make it look old, Wrath takes ancient tech and pushes it so damn hard it is surprising it does not come apart at the seams. Look at any screenshot of the game and consider: this is a minorly upgraded version of something that drove a 1996 title. It is both a technical and aesthetic success in almost every way and you have to respect the effort the developers had to put into this to make it work. And work the game does, for my word, it plays so very, very nicely.Like a lot of GZDoom based titles, Wrath takes the already fantastic basis of Quake and runs with it well. If you are familiar with any of the Quake source ports you will know how this will work. Shooting is great, the level design is classic and the movement is… generally fantastic (though we will get to that). Not only does running around the world feel smooth and responsive, the guns feel suitabily boomy and enemies have a habit of exploding in a very satisfying manner. It tickles the brain in ways only the most simple shooters can do so: you run, shoot and then explore on more or less autopilot, letting your instincts guide you. Pure, simple, cathartic fun. This is the strength of Wrath, and for all criticisms I may level at it, this factor alone makes up for every issue.There are issues however, and many of them are part and parcel of the Quake double edge sword: For all its strengths, there are weaknesses.As many who have played Quake can attest to, the air control when bumping against walls and scooting off ledges is somewhat… odd. While Wrath nicely adds more air control to the core, when a character hits a wall or slight ledge they can end up bouncing wildly and all the air control suddenly vanishes. In a lot of cases this is not noticeable, but on the more geometrically complex levels this can cause issues, especially with platforming. Levels like The Great Hollow are a platforming nightmare due to the fact you can easily bounce off a wall or an enemy, throwing you down to the bottom leading you to have one hell of a trek back. If the levels were small and easy to navigate, this would not be an issue, but they are not.The level design, while absolutely impeccable by Quake standards, is something that may put off the less experienced player. There is a very Quake mod mapper feel to it (and if you played Arcane Dimensions, you know that is not an insult) and that type of design can lead to insular thinking. For FPS vertens, this is fantastic. For someone who wants to complete a level in 10 minutes it is abhorrent. Typically the levels last for 45 minutes and tend to have over 10 secrets at minimum. This is, for the general player, too much to take in and as such I can imagine navigation will be a pain. For the player who loves big maps, this is one of the best titles I’ve seen for that, and maps like The Priory and The Crucible of Souls are incredible. For everyone else, it may be a bit much.Similarly there is the Quake / Doom modding mentality. For these games players can make do with the same enemies and weapons over and over. Wrath has that style of design where after completing one of the maps in a chapter, you have effectively seen the whole chapter, both weapon wise and enemy roster. While it makes up for this shortcoming in fantastic pacing and placements, for the fan of novelty it will get very old very fast.In a way this is Wrath’s key point: It is a “True boomershooter” through and through. It is very simple in its content and its character. Whole chapters feel the same, the story is irrelevant, and the same enemies appear through the whole title. It is the boomershooter fan’s boomershooter and absolutely nothing else. It is not the title to win over new fans or give those who are tiring of the genre something fresh.It is simple.It knows it.It doesn’t care.So Wrath: A hardcore boomershooter fan’s wet dream and a nightmare for everyone else. For those who are fed up with the genre, this will not win you over. For the dedicated, you will find very few titles that scratch the itch like this!

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly thought it was pretty goodThere was a lot more to the levels than I expected, and I really like the design approach they took to it: The levels are surprisingly long and they often do loop back around to areas where you've already been. However, often enough in these revisited areas (if not all of them) enemies will reappear (Not to be taken as "They Respawn". These are new enemies, like that of reinforcements). I never once got lost or thought "Where do I go now?" Wrath often follows the concept of "If you find enemies, you're going down the right path" which is great for an old school shooter like this.I only had a couple of complaints overall, but these are not deal breakers in the slightest. If you like DUSK, you'll like this.-Jumping just feels very... Meh. I get that you're probably not supposed to rely on it in combat, but it makes what little platforming in the game feel like a chore. Especially when you're searching for secrets and needing to climb on objects to get to them. Just... Oi. Getting a higher jump could save people a headache.-The first pistol I feel needs more of an identity/reason to exist. Once I got the shotgun, every time I attempted to use the pistol it just felt bad compared to every other weapon, giving it's usefulness lifespan equal to that of literal minutes. Which is a shame because I like the design of it. But it doesn't fire fast, isn't strong enough to be worth your time, and its alternate  felt really weak. If it had unlimited ammo I could understand this, but where it is now... I don't even think dual wielding them would even be enough to save it.-The enemy design I thought was pretty good. Rather unique looking as well, but my complaint here is about the large green "Cyst" guys (as in, the really big ones). Specifically, their final death explosion, I feel like every sphere does a little too much damage. Almost killing you outright if even one of them touches you. This rarely happens if you can keep your distance, but occasionally I found myself in the worst possible position when they go down, and in my attempts to escape, what feels like a pixel of green touches you and deals 90% of your health and armor in damage. If you are point blank and it does that much? Sure. That's on me/the player. But wowzers... They hurt more than a direct projectile attack.That's about it, and it's a very short list of complaints. I'll no doubt recommend this one if you like the more retro style shooters. Wrath doesn't do too much new, but sometimes that's exactly what you're looking for. Keep up the great work KillPixel <3

Full transparency: I got a key from a friend who has a humble choice subscription in exchange for a dollar.The game looks good, my favourite level by far when it comes to the presentation is the winter level (dont remember the name of it idc). The movement feels smooth allowing me to combine dashing with the blade and my quake strafe jumping skills, but thats about where the positives end.You can approach the levels in any order you want which is both cool and bad, this means that all levels have to be more or less the same difficulty wise. The encounters all feel designed like in a normal fps where you can quicksave, but here you have a limited amount of saves that you can increase by picking up a special item. The game doesnt feel designed around this and it seems like they just threw this in because they could and not because it makes the game better. I could go on and on (and I probably will when I get to making a video on it) but even if I will I dont think anyone will listen, especially the dev team.This is basically abandonware, as far as I know there isnt a single dev working on this full time. I want to see the rest of this game through because its gunplay is incredibly fun.I cannot recommend WRATH to the general gaming populace quite yet, since I was able to complete what is available so far in under 2 hours. But if QUAKE-type games are something you enjoy, or if you are willing to buy this game as an investment, by all means, go for it.Oh, I'm not surprised in the slightest. I frequent Early Access games a lot. For example, my most played game is DayZ. I would think it's a rather good deal if the price were reduced to $10 or $15, and increased as more content was added. Like I said, what is here is fairly good. Combine a heap of small annoying issues and an extremely short time to "beat" what's currently available, and I can't recommend this game to the "average" gamer. When I first glossed over the roadmap, I was under the assumption that 2 "levels" would be more than just a half hour to 45 minute zone. I thought something more along the lines of Ion Fury's levels, where there are multiple stages to each level. Anyways, if you enjoy QUAKE-like games and are willing to invest for a better experience down the line, it's more than likely worth the price for you, but I'm not going to tailor my review to a select group of people.

_childDocuments_.review: Wrath: Aeon of Run is like an amalgamation of Quake, Turok: Dinosaur Hunter, Daikatana, Arx Fatalis, Doom, Unreal, Chasm: The Rift, Heretic, Hexen and Powerslave (Exhumed).  Five years later and then this game is finally out of early access.  I have waited for this game out to come out in early access since 2019. The game starts off with a lone combatant named Outlander made his way to a derelict land being infested with corrupt deities and their bloodthirsty minions.  The Outlander must travel into five different levels on each hub in order to get the runes and defeat the boss at the end.   The weapons are unique with a primary fire and an alt fire, the enemies resemble something you see in cosmic horror or body horror movies, the music composed by Andrew Hulshult fits the atmosphere of the game, the levels are lengthy but interesting and the power-ups are useful items that can be used in time of need.   This game really has come a long way into something better than it is before.Overall rating: 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: WRATH: Aeon of Ruin plunges players into a retro-inspired world filled with frenetic combat and atmospheric environments. While the game excels in certain aspects, such as its arsenal of weapons, varied enemies, and rewarding pickups, it struggles with providing clear navigation, hampered by the absence of a compass directing players towards objectives.Let's delve into the positive side first. WRATH offers an array of satisfying weaponry that packs a punch, from classic firearms to arcane artifacts, each contributing to diverse combat encounters. The enemies you face are equally diverse, challenging you to adapt your strategies and keep the adrenaline pumping. Additionally, the pickups scattered throughout the game world provide essential resources and power-ups, incentivizing exploration and adding depth to gameplay.However, where WRATH falters is in its lack of guidance. The absence of a compass or clear directional indicators makes it frustratingly difficult to discern where to go next to progress the story or complete objectives. I often find myself wandering aimlessly through labyrinthine levels, leading to moments of confusion and tedium that detract from the overall experience.In conclusion, WRATH: Aeon of Ruin offers a mixed bag of thrills and frustrations. While its arsenal of weapons, diverse enemies, and rewarding pickups contribute to an enjoyable gameplay experience, the absence of navigational aids undermines the immersion and can lead to moments of frustration. With some improvements in guiding myself through its world, WRATH has the potential to truly shine as a modern homage to classic first-person shooters.

_childDocuments_.review: Miracle this game got off the ground. It's a technical and artistic achievement. But also flawed. When everything is full tilt in a fight, this game is insanely fun with a nice weapon roster, with some incredibly realised environments with incredible artwork. I love that we get to play a game that imagines a world where Quake stuck with its dark fantasy theme for a sequel. But it is also its own thing. It's also a challenging game, and if you choose to stick with the limited save system, you will find that they're pretty generous as long as you think about placing your saves. Also, make use of the artifacts, as they do a lot to level the playing field when you're low on ammo and health which will happen.There were some things that had me raging. The movement system isn't great when trying to navigate narrow pathways above lakes of lava. There's one level in particular in the final chapter that had me wanting to slam my keyboard through the window as your character feels like he bounces or slides a bit too much off the narrow surfaces. It's a movement system that otherwise works amazingly in insanely fast combat arenas, but less so for the sections that demand finesse. I also found chapter one to lean too much on certain monsters, and this game got better for me progressing past this chapter where the levels felt better balanced and paced with greater monster variety. Also the levels are quite big, and have a propensity for overstaying at times, but you can never say the devs didn't provide on content. Still, overall the levels are great especially past chapter 1 (in my opinion).Not my personal favourite of the new age 'boomer shooters', but absolutely worth a play and congrats to the devs for getting this over the line despite all the challenges it faced.
_childDocuments_.name: WRATH: Aeon of Ruin

_childDocuments_.review: If you're hurting for a singleplayer FPS to play, you could do worse than WRATH. There's a lot to like about this game. The aesthetic is great and the weapons and enemies have a very solid, classic boomer shooter design. And when the game is taking place in small or medium sized areas where you can use your whole arsenal, it scratches the boomer shooter itch perfectly.But the bulk of the game takes place in huge outdoor areas with extremely long lines of sight, and there's one weapon, the Fang Spitter (a reskin of the nailgun from Quake), that isn't totally useless at that range. And I'm not having fun constantly running out of Fang Spitter ammo while the game keeps spawning more and more enemies football fields away from me as I search around the massive map wondering where the ♥♥♥♥ I'm supposed to go.The potential for a great shooter is here, but the game tends to feel like a slog and and I wouldn't actually recommend it to anyone I know.

_childDocuments_.review: WRATH, a game being developed on the DarkPlaces engine. When people see this, they immediately jump to Quake, which is understandable, but the only thing they really have in common is the engine and some of the aesthetic.Firstly, WRATH doesn't use strafe jump movement, it uses a different mechanic which a lot of Quake die hards are not happy about. But people need to realise, it shares the same engine, it was never meant to be a spiritual successor and the movement mechanics are bloody fun! Jumping around and dashing with the blade is a really unique approach to movement.So far the full arsenal hasn't been released and a lot of tweaks are being made, but what we have is solid.The levels are actually quite large, ranging from 45 minutes to an hour in length approximately, and with 15 levels in total it's going to be a decent sized campaign. So far the first hub world and it's levels are very reminiscent of Soul Reaver, an aesthetic that was common during the late '90s and early '00s, and it's nice to see it being used again here.They've gone with an atmospheric soundtrack for WRATH and it's composed by... Andrew Hulshult! That's right, the one and only. He's quickly making a name for himself among these boomer shooters, and for a good reason.So if you're a fan of the first Quake, and strafe jumping never phased you or you just love boomer shooters, this is definitely one you should jump on!

_childDocuments_.review: I heard a lot of good things about this so I picked it up while it was on sale. Weapons, levels and enemies are all great, really shaping up to be a great shooter. However the movement really broke this game for me. You've got 'always sprint' on by default and it feels really disorienting to fight when you're moving so quickly. So i turn it off to have better control in combat but it also shows why its on by default. It breaks the when moving normally as every jump has no horizontal momentum and every time you go down stairs you stop dead with every step. I can see it being great now I've had more control over moving in combat, but these problems with the movement are a real problem for people who don't want to have sprint always on. If these issues are fixed in a future patch or by final release then I'd recommend this game highly. Until then I'd only recommend it if you play games with really quick movement.

_childDocuments_.review: The trailer is misleading - this game plays very slow. The main problem is the enemies suck. One of the enemies randomly shoots balls of energy in all directions when it dies sometimes, so I hope you didn't kill it up close with a shotgun. Anything that shoots a cyst is obnoxious because they will bounce off the walls in random directions and whether you get hit or not is mostly up to chance, and the slope of the wall and floor behind you. I've had a cyst follow me all the way down a spiral staircase, then explode, then deny the floor where it exploded for 5 seconds because the acid will continue to hurt you. The fat cyst throwers throw far too many cysts. They also explode on death because they weren't already annoying enough. Even if you dodge the three cysts that shoot out from its corpse, there's still an explosion that will cause you to take damage if you're too close. Some enemies spawn in the stratosphere for some reason. Some of the open areas of levels will have enemies attacking from all angles. The projectiles move too fast and have no sound effect at that distance, so you're just trying to dodge enemies you have no reason of knowing even exist yet (like the ones in the stratosphere). The dude that charges you that blocks bullets that you can't dodge is a fun one. Many enemies also have a tendency to fire at you without line of sight, so you'll often find yourself peeking around a corner into a hail of projectiles.Game is beautiful though. The two linear levels are okay. Abbey and Cemetary are obnoxious labyrinths with lots of backtracking. Enemies spawn far too many times in the same areas and it gets incredibly tedious.Weapons are a mixed bag. They feel okay individually, but don't feel like they have much of a purpose. The fang launcher does not have enough ammo capacity. The fang ammo is literally everywhere but you can only carry 100, so I hope you enjoy micro-managing your inventory. The cyst launcher is essentially the rocket launcher for this game, but the range is trash and the splash radius is too small.The movement is terrible. You change directions too quickly and you bounce off of everything when platforming. I tried to play the game without auto-run because I felt like I couldn't control where I was going, but you can't jump while walking, so you have to use auto-run. If you jump while walking, you lose all momentum. I don't know how the game has gotten to this point but still doesn't support basic movement.Basically, the game looks nice, but the creators forgot to design compelling encounters, weapons, and enemies. The environments would work better for some kind of RPG rather than what this is. I had 2-3 moments that put me on the edge of my seat where I thought "Oh, that was a nice bit of gameplay," but everything else was an absolute bore. Spare yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: I've just finished the Early Access version of this and I am delighted. Can't wait to see what the full version will bring!Sound & MusicThese are quite good, give a good atmosphere.GraphicsI don't know which Quake flavour they are using, but it works well - I especially loved the ability to disable texture filtering right from the settings panel. There are also several anti-aliasing options.I own a i7-6700K + GTX 1070 + 165hz QWHD gaming monitor and I have enabled DSR to push it to 4K and get even less jagged lines. So with everything set to the max, it was going at 165fps, so I set the GPU to use ULMB instead of G-Sync, Low Latency Mode to Ultra, and Vsync to Fast.I haven't tried on my laptop which only has a 630 UHD GPU but I think it should be all right.Level DesignHaving played all the Quake in the series and also having played Arcane Dimensions, the levels here feel really mysterious, and there are lots of open areas - probably something ID could not afford at the time because of technological constraints of the era. This game, similarly to the Arcane Dimensions mod, pushes this engine to the limits.GameplayThough it has many things in common with the original Quake, there are several variants that make this game different enough not to be considered simply another mod. The weapons feel great to use and are very effective. The enemies AI was ok-ish, sometimes I've seen them unable to get around a corner to get me, and there was another time when they could not get down a step.However, throughout the whole session the game managed to make me feel challenged but never frustrated.ControlsControls were great, though I've enabled an option to disable the bobbing when strafing, but I'm not sure it changed much, maybe it has reduced it.I have also noticed that the invert mouse axis option gets reset when you move in between areas, something the devs should look into fixing.Another thing I've noticed is that this game has inherited some of Quake own bugs - some background app forced me out of the game and when I came back I was strafing all the way to the right, just like a button was stuck - this is something I've experienced in the past with Quake games, I think the solution is to disable switching to windows unless CTRL+TAB / CTRL+ALT+Canc is pressed.An additional note about the UIWhen you begin, you create a profile, but there is no option to delete or rename a profile. I'm not sure how much I'd like to use profiles, I guess it's to play with different difficulties.Another note is the saving system - because it's so special you only have three restore options:Autosave; Shrine; Soul Tether;Unfortunately, they are always listed in a fixed order so you will never know which one was the last unless you remember where you were. Devs could look into this and put a timestamp.Again, can't wait to play the full version soon!
