_childDocuments_.review: Well, after 3+ years of missed release windows Wrath has crawled its way out of development hell. Was it worth the wait?No. I was hoping I would get to change this review to a positive one once the game released despite my issues with its dev cycle but unfortunately what's present is just not good. For the sake of brevity (and being able to keep my original review up), I'll bullet point the few things I did like and all the stuff I didn't:-Movement is tight. It's fluid and responsive and besides some jank on slopes, it was very smooth. The movement tech with the melee weapon's alt fire, which will launch you forward in midair, is very fun.-Weapons for the most part are a very traditional roster, but they have some unique designs and each has an altfire, though some of those altfires are much less useful than others. Ammo distribution for each weapon feels all over the place, however. Sometimes you have more than you know what to do with and sometimes you're squeezing through an arena with nothing but shotgun shells.-Levels are geometrically complex for the Quake engine and impressive in that regard, however...-While they are complex, they're visually uninteresting. Most levels are plagued by bland color palettes and setpieces, which is further exacerbated by the fact that each level in an episode looks almost identical to the other in design. This issue is only remedied in the final levels of the game.-Not only are levels uninteresting, they are way too long. Each level will take anywhere from 25 minutes to nearly an hour to complete. Enemy counts sometimes rival Serious Sam, averaging 3-400 per level. Every level in the game just drags on when you put these problems together.-Enemy variety is too lacking for how large each level is. Most enemies are introduced in the very first level you enter in the game (and weapons), with only a handful more being introduced after. Enemy encounters quickly become repetitive and forgettable, especially in levels that contain central hub areas, as more enemies will typically spawn any time level progression returns you to it.-While enemies are visually distinct and easy to recognize at a distance, most fulfill the same exact purpose. Most enemy behavior consists of stopping to shoot some form of projectile while you're within a certain distance of them or in their line of sight. There's very little to keep you on your toes and promote more creative movement other than strafing to the side. This is compounded by borderline nonsensical enemy placements that don't seem to have any real rhyme or reason as to why they're there.-All three bosses in the game are some of the worst ones I've ever seen in an FPS.-The music is largely forgettable due to being generic ambience, not even being close to what Doom 64 had. This is unfortunate, as it was composed by Andrew Hulshult, the de facto boomer shooter OST guy. I'm not sure if this is just a miss on his part or poor direction.Even trying to ignore all the flaws, Wrath is simply too generic of a retro FPS released way too many years too late. Nothing it does tries to push the genre forward, and what is there is so badly done it doesn't even work well as a Quake clone. Save your cash and throw it towards one of the many other retro shooters on the market right now, because Wrath misses the mark in almost everything it does.---------------------------------I don't typically put out reviews on a product that aren't explicitly about the product itself, but after being punked out of a release for at least the  I feel this is necessary to stand as a warning before purchasing this game.Wrath currently has the first episode available in early access: 5 levels and a hub world. With its original launch window, this was perfectly acceptable; a shareware-like build with the full release coming relatively soon. The original release window was set for early 2021 (early access began in late 2019). This was delayed during the 2020 holiday season to Summer 2021. Okay, fair enough, a few months' delay for polish and finish.Oh, how wrong we all were.August 2021 we get a blog post stating that it has been officially delayed into "sometime in 2022". They tell us that they're now going to give us bi-weekly update posts so we know what's going on with the state of the game. Okay, kinda sucks but hey, we get to see them finish the game up now, right?Pffffff.The first bi-weekly updates they release showed that the game was barely developed past what is in the early access build. The boss and its respective level for the first episode are not even blocked out yet. Enemies and weapons are still being developed and tested. Levels for episodes 2 and 3 are either still in the texturing/detail phase or not even blockmapped yet. This was supposed to release in early 2021? So we get these pitiful bi-weekly updates for about a year (seriously, just go to news history for the game and take a peek). September 2022 arrives, and at Realms Deep they announce their brand new release window of... Spring 2023? Wait, new window? Didn't they say the game was going to release in 2022? I mean, based on the posts we were seeing, the game didn't have a chance of hitting that release window, but seriously?And so here we are. I waited to see the clock tick over Summer and laughed as the  release window was missed, over two years since the initial one. The update we apparently got from the devs in a Discord channel over the following days? A delay to sometime next year and something they probably should have just said in the first place: "When it's done." Fantastic.So, surely they would update the currently available build with some of their new levels to hold us over while we wait, right? Nah, the developers have made their stance clear saying something along the lines of "We finished the early access roadmap, that's why we aren't going to update the public build until full release." The problem with that is that roadmap was based around a game that was supposed to come out over two  ago. If it had been the original yearish development time from early access release to full release the 5 level roadmap would have been perfectly acceptable. Ion Fury did a similar thing with its preview campaign and there was enough there to get an idea of how the game works, despite being short. Ion Fury, however, released in a timely manner after their preview campaign was dropped. Wrath has not. This game has sat as a digital paperweight since the last content update in January 2021, again, with the developers citing their "content complete" early access roadmap.I would not be as irritated as I am now if it wasn't for how much the userbase has been led on by multiple release windows and promises. If after the first delay the developers had been transparent instead of severely overestimating their ability to finish this game I would be significantly less mad. "Hey, we screwed up, gonna be a while, we're offering refunds if you want one or don't have faith in our game." Could have been as simple as that instead of constantly raising hopes only to consistently throw it all down the tube. There are people out there who preordered $120 limited box editions of this game who may not ever see those arrive.If this game ever does actually release I'm sure it'll be a pretty good boomer shooter strengthened by the engine it's running on. Until that happens though, . You're paying for nothing more than a shareware demo who's full version seems to be nowhere in sight. There are fully released, quality games that your $25 can be spent on over this.I dislike dragging developers through the mud like this because I'm sure they're working hard on finishing the game, but this has become a gross mismanagement of a product and expectations that should not be considered acceptable.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: Like that of what it inspires from Wrath, takes on a dark gothic horror aesthetic that is combined with adrenaline-filled action, combining the two in perfect harmony where it feels like 1996 all over again. Despite its very dedicated resemblance to Quake, Wrath adds a few modern twists of its own not only giving everything that was loved about Quake but brings it a new level.A full detailed video preview can be viewed here:Gameplay:The gameplay to Wrath is excellent. It is everything you could have ever hoped for from a game that not only takes most of its inspiration from the original Quake but is being developed on the very technology that Quake was initially built on. The pacing is extremely fast and the combat action-packed and adrenaline filled. It is an old-school FPS that has more depth to its gameplay than that of any other, all the while making secrets actually worthwhile seeking out. Wrath isn’t just attempting to be the next Quake; it is attempting to give everything that was loved about the game while bringing it to a whole new level. And so far, Killpixel is doing exactly that.Level Design:It is classic level design, but it is a classic design done extremely well. It is clear KillPixel have a complex and deep understanding of the level design from the game that Wrath’s inspiration clearly comes from and it really shows. Between the unique environments and atmosphere of each of the levels and the excellent design of their layout, they are nothing short of an absolute joy to play. If there is one gripe I would have with the levels it would be that there are only 2 available right now. I think it should have the first full episode available to play from the launch of Early Access. 2 levels and under 2 hours of gameplay for €21 doesn’t feel like much to play around with for the cost. Regardless of that one issue, however, of what is so far presented, gives a fantastic first impression that leaves you salivating for more. And I certainly can’t wait to see what new levels the developer has in store.Atmosphere:Much like Quake back in 1996, Wrath takes quite a different approach to its atmosphere compared to others in the genre. Unlike DUSK or Amid Evil which both take a much more action-orientated approach with their atmosphere, Wrath goes full-on with the horror theme.There is always a sense of darkness, death, decay and destruction about the atmosphere of each of the levels and that horror lays around each dark corner. To intensify this sense of horror, a fitting soundtrack accompanies it, acting more like a dark ambience as opposed to a music track. The tracks do have the odd action note to them to compliment the combat and fast pacing of the game, but the horror is definitely dominant over anything else. It is exactly the approach Id Software took, and it is working for Wrath like it worked for Quake. It is that horror theme that will separate Wrath from the others, giving it a special place in the modern old-school inspired FPS sense, just as it did for Quake back in 1996.Conclusion:Wrath: Aeon of Ruin is an absolute marvel of a game and the team of KillPixel truly are the necromancers of the Quake engine. Not only are they creating a modern game on a game engine that is over 23 years old, but they are pushing it to its absolute limits.Despite the age of the engine, Wrath is visually stunning and the sheer amount of enemies and the size of the maps are absolutely awe-inspiring. It truly is the Id Tech 2 engine on steroids. Technological astonishment aside, as a game Wrath is showing nothing but promise. It currently doesn’t present enough that I could call it outstanding, but never the less it shows a very bright future. From the combat to the level design to the atmosphere, Wrath is absolute bliss and is everything that fans of Quake could ever have hoped for.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fast pace FPS where you fight your way through a horde of enemies, throught different levels accessible through a HUB levels. It largely evokes the gameplay style of Duke Nukem 3D with a goth, kind of quake-like, aesthetic.Beware, it is still a work in progress, however the game that's already there has been a great deal of fun for me. If you are a fan of the genre, I definitely recommend it, if not now in its current state then further in the future when more content has been added.At first I noticed that there were only 5 weapons in total, which seemed likec a small amount to me, but then I realized that each weapon has an alternate mode (Right-click by default) which, when paired with several available consumables that give you momentary boosts, provide you with a diverse set of options to tackle the levels.The boosts are called artifacts and they vary in effects. (Vampirism, invincibility but your HP goes to 10 as a drawback, enemies fight eachother,etc..)I liked the enemy designs and variety. A thing that I believe was a great choice by the developer was the fact there are almost no hitscan enemies, meaning that you are more free to run around and rip and tear your foes. I won't spoil too much of the monsters because discovering them and adapting your weapon choice to better deal with them is a big part of the problem solving aspect of the game and, as such, a substantial part of the fun. I will say this, though. At least two or more of the projectile throwing mobs fire fast missiles, which require a good bit of focus dodge.A couple negatives I found on the enemies were that the pathing on  was a bit weird at times, I even had one run opposite from me in a straight line instead of charging me. Another bug that popped up was when I shot one of the big floating enemies as it spawns, it would stop floating and plummet to the ground. I also believe that the level design is good. It is linear enough that you rarely get lost trying to find a door you now have the key too open but the levels also branch out enough to give you a feeling of exploration and motivate you to inspect your environment with attention. The secrets are a fun and, if you are familiar with this game genre, expected part of the game. There are different levels of difficulty to secret hunting but, in general, they are hard enough to feel satisfying but not so hard that you feel you're wasting too much time trying to find them.As a final note, I will say that the developer definitely spent some time focusing on game balance. From how much damage you take and receive, to ammo management, to enemy numbers and to how fast you go and jump. I am very excited for how far the developer will be able to push this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Praise• Movement is very fun. There's a lot of airstrafing and somewhat a capacity for bunnyhopping, paired with a massively useful alt-fire on your knife that propels you forward. If you're used to Quake 1, or any Source Engine game with surf physics, this will feel like second nature to you, and you'll probably have more fun with the game than the general populous.• The general philosopy of combat seems to sit right in the middle of Quake and Serious Sam. The player has a high degree of movement relative to enemies like in Quake, and the enemies are plentiful and relatively low health like in Serious Sam. This may seem like a strange anthithetical mix, however, it never feels tedious to mow down hundreds of units, nor does it feel too forgiving with how it lets you disengage from encounters. In fact, a lot of fights seem built around this rapid disengagement on blind runs, since sticking around to see how things work may get you killed. Stuff deals a respectable amount of damage to you on Outlander, and map design usually ensures enemies are placed in a way that will catch you off guard, rather than bunching them up in a way that's easy to predict or disperse.• Enemies are highly aggressive. They react at a decent rate and pour out tons of attacks, yet don't just stand still like turrets when you play Quake on Nightmare. Every one of them has a quirk that makes them more than just target practice, like exploding on death, or charging toward you if you get too close, or altering their firing pattern. They are both predictable and unpredictable in a way that's highly satisfying, and they generally do a lot of damage, punishing you for poor play, yet never feeling too much like bull**** with how much agency the game gives you in terms of movement and legroom.• The weapons, in general, all serve a role, even the Pistol, and ESPECIALLY the Knife. It's actually commendable how nuanced the between-guns balance is, with one exception.• TL;DR, combat is REALLLY bouncy and frenetic and fun and sometimes tricky yet fair if you put forth any amount of effort to learn its rhythms. You can move fast, but can't move carelessly, and every enemy/arrangement thereof will have you dancing a different way. In this respect, it is almost perfect.Mixed Feelings• Artifacts can make the game too easy if you use them abundantly, to the point where it's simply intuitive not to. However, trying to beat certain segments without them at all is a very demanding task. It's like the game's telling me on a moment-to-moment basis "yeah don't use these unless you suck", and also, "you have to use these here to progress unless you played everything up until now pixel-perfect". At times it's hard to tell if the devs want me to replay sections to save up more supplies, or to just power through roadblocks effortlessly at the press of a button. I'd like to think I approach the vast majority of fights cautiously while minimizing damage taken, so it may very well be the latter, which isn't all that satisfying.For example, The Garden's final section locks you in a tiny elevator with several Cacodemon-type enemies, who are both tanky and highly aggressive, after you've expended all you ammo in the preceding parts of the map, which absolutely do not require Artifact usage, as The Garden is one of the easier maps in Act 1. If there is a way to do this section without using an invincibility powerup on Outlander, I haven't found it. Act 2 seems to ramp up the difficulty a bit as a standard, mostly in terms of Shrines and Armor being harder to come by, so you may find yourself utilizing Artifacts more as a legitimate part of the game rather than a free win button. However, even when integrating them in this matter, you still have way more of them than you'll ever need if you play to the game's rhythms properly, and so they /still/ feel cheap.TL;DR Artifacts present an enigma I don't know how to feel about. Sometimes I think I'd feel better accomplished if they weren't there, and instead Quake-1 esque timed powerups were meticulously placed in the parts of the map they're needed in.Criticism• Outlander difficulty needs to be unlocked now. If you don't want to play a massive campaign twice to get the good difficulty you're used to from EA, you have to type skill 3 in console and restart the maps.• Hitscan weapon shots can clip on edges and seem like they're making contact with the enemy when they aren't. Exacerbated by the lack of readable enemy blood effects. Highly unsatisfying.• The Shotgun's alt-fire may shoot off a wildly inaccurate shot. Why? Isn't this firing mode for precision? I'd rather it have a consistent spread pattern, even if that spread pattern means one of the pellets missing at super long ranges.• The Retcher has been heavily nerfed from its EA version, and needlessly so. It barely has any AoE damage, can't kill Widows in one hit, and can't kill a Cacodemon-equivalent enemy with 2 barrages (6 grenades), and that's IF they play nice and don't bounce around to throw off your aim. It feels pointless to use unless I wanna conserve ammo for other stuff or wanna meme on an Executioner running toward me with mines. Doesn't help that it's an arced weapon with poor collision detection upon touching an enemy's head (tends to phase through them). Most other weapons have a nice time-to-kill vs. ease of use ratio, and this one simply doesn't anymore. • The Priory is very hard to navigate. There's a hint in the form of a note that tells you "to open this gate, find the watchtower and climb the spiral staircase". GREAT! That'd probably help if I've seen a single spiral staircase or anything remotely resembling a watchtower up to that point. Then, when I figure it out, turns out I need a key too. Kinda just noclipped for a moment at that point to figure out the pathing since I couldn't be bothered to spend another hour looking. Frankly, an abomination of map design.• Acid throwing enemies have been heavily nerfed from EA. Honestly, they should've been, but not to this degree. The toad-like enemy's issue wasn't his direct damage output, but how his death projectiles bounced wildly and instantly killed you, unfairly punishing you for shooting him. He's kinda pathetic now, and so are his green zombie babies who deal chip damage upon being shot to death, when they used to make you explode when you were close to them. I want these enemies to be a real threat (which they presently aren't) without being nonsense (like before).• Act 2's new enemies suck. The invisible spiders deal teeny tiny chip damage even on the highest difficulty, and the floating yellow shield guys slow the game to a crawl since even if you're within their bubble and shoot them instead of it, you die from the ricochet.Quality of Life Suggestions• Make Outlander available from the start. No reason not to.• Make the Shotgun's Alt-Fire feel better, make the Retcher's damage output respectable, and improve grenade/hitscan hit detection.• Make weapon switching cache your inputs better. A lot of times I'll press 1 and then Mouse 2 to dash with the knife, but end up switching to another weapon and using its Alt-Fire, wasting ammo, because the game didn't cache my inputs properly.• Make Artifact activation more responsive. I've died a few times just because the game didn't recognize I used a lifesteal powerup.• There are severe performance issues on one Act 2 map (Watchtowers) and basically every Act 3 map (to varying degrees). 120 fps is basically essential for this game. Please optimize whichever troublesome textures/particles/lighting is causing this on these maps. A hunch tells me it's all the red stuff.• Up the contrast on The Red Throne on an internal level. This map is needlessly dark compared to every other.Do I recommend this? Hell yes. All in all a really great game that needs a few finishing touches I really hope it gets because there isn't much out there nearing this quality.

_childDocuments_.review: I completed WRATH: Aeon of Ruin on its medium difficulty in 23 hours. Each level took me, on average, 70 minutes to complete, which was unusually long for this kind of game. For comparison, each mission in the original Quake took me 10-15 minutes to complete, and each level in Amid Evil took 15-20. The first thing that stuck out to me about Wrath was its enormous levels. Not only are they wide-open and really good looking, the levels also complicate the usual Quake design in which central areas branch off into two or three paths. In Wrath, central areas often branch off into as many as five, six, or even seven paths, and each path then splits up further into two or three additional subpaths. Mentally mapping out where I had been and where I wanted to go next, on top of keeping track of item pickups and staying vigilant about ambushes, was surprisingly taxing.Wrath also had a tight resource economy. While I never completely ran out of ammo, I was never fully topped off. This meant that I had to make every shot count and deliberately manage my available resources. From conserving ammo by fighting with melee to memorizing ammo pickup locations to using consumable “artifact” abilities, managing Wrath’s limited resources made the game surprisingly difficult in a way that most shooters aren’t.The rest of Wrath looks, sounds, and plays great without straying too far from the Quake formula, much like 2018’s Amid Evil. The overall package is kind of like a more polished and cohesive take on 2015’s Arcane Dimensions, and since I think very highly of that mod, I would also highly recommend Wrath.

_childDocuments_.review: (Note, the displayed gametime is actually way longer than what the game took to beat. Don't leave your computer with the game on running kids)The game is good. Mostly.The core gameplay is very good. It's just Quake, but enemies don't take 5 SSG shots to kill, the guns have amazing feedback, well thought out secondary modes, the gore is satisfying, the movement control you get with your base melee is phenomenal, it feels good to move around in general and the environments are gourgeous.So why the negative review? Because of everything else. The enemies deal ridiculous damage on hard, especially the 2 endgame ones can oneshot you from pretty much any health. Everything explodes so you're very often punished by simple fodder just because you didn't have enough space or forgot they explode. I assume this is a deliberate mechanic to nerf the final weapon, but it doesn't help make gameplay fun. Quite the opposite. Even if you remember, you still often have to wait for the explosion to progress and over the course of the game (which is still very long), it adds up.Each weapon is good in a vacuum, but together they feel like something is missing. Your final nuke stores ammo only for one use, the crystal lazer is very gimmicky, the slag cannon is your best all rounder, but is incredibly ammo hungry and forces you to choose between 2 modes, meaning you often lack the ammo if the situation changes to call for the other mode. The amount of shotgun ammo incentivizes you to use the shotgun and only the shotgun, maybee switching to another weapon for long range encounters if you can kill the enemy faster than the secondary takes to charge up. The cyst launcher ends up as a generic dps weapon you only switch to because you have no ammo for others or you're full with cysts (heh).The artifacts ended up just how they end up feeling in every boomer shooter. Forgotten. They all have decently thought out functions and have their use in combat, but sorry, I'm not remembering to use, what, 9 weapons with alternate modes and 10 artifacts in a fast paced combat game. I'm not an MMO player.The enemy design is, while often annoying, pretty good. It is not good however for a game that takes double digit hours to finish. You will get tired of seeing the same faces over and over again.The levels are HUGE for a boomer shooter (Arcane dimensions scale, probably even bigger). It wouldn't be a problem, but the lack of gameplay variety makes them just a tedious slog, even if they look good.BUTI played to the end with the save tether system and my biggest advice is DO NOT DO THAT. You end up with the good 'ol hoarding mentality and it severely drags the game down. This is probably the biggest reason for me being tired with the game by the end of it.I have no comment on the bosses, they are fine. The final plot twist was something I was thinking about since the very start of Act II.

_childDocuments_.review: There have been a lot of throwback shooters lately aping the likes of Doom and Duke 3D. There is even Dusk, which takes on the task of tackling Quake. This is the realm that Wrath lives in, but with graphics out of Quake III. The game looks great and all the gore and particle effects are excellent. I haven't seen anything too crazy with the environments yet, but they're serviceable gothic levels in the vein of the original Quake. Gameplay wise I really am loving Wrath. The shooting feels great and punchy. Enemies explode appropriately in a way that feels good every single time. They ambush, they projectile spam, they're just nasty little ♥♥♥♥♥. So you have to get used to that Quake style of gameplay where you are moving a shooting a lot. Wrath is great at capturing that feeling. For negatives I guess I have to point out that it's not finished yet, but it's in early access so that's to be expected. One other negative, which could be rectified in time, is that I'm leaning on the shotgun like it's the only leg I've got. The acid launcher ammo is a little to rare to rely on, the nailgun is okay but lacks the fun factor of the shotgun, and the coach gun can go right in the trash like every other pistol in this kind of game. The blade arm is fun but a little too dangerous, this leaves the shotgun and nailgun as the only viable weapons in most instances. I hope they add some more crazy and fun weapons as the game continues. That's the one thing Wrath needs at this point. Overall, I'm usually wary of Early Access, but I'm glad I decided to support Wrath. Killpixel is doing a great job and I can't wait to see what the final game looks like.

_childDocuments_.review: I can completely understand some of the criticisms I've seen of Wrath already. I don't disagree with them. However, it's testament to it that, for me, it still rose above them and was mostly a blast to play through.Yes, the enemy variety is a little lacking. That said, the majority of the ones that are there are a joy to fight. I never stopped chuckling to myself when a Widow would screech at me and I'd greet it with a blast of the double barrel shotgun.The majority of the maps were a joy to explore, with some really neat features to each that made them distinct. There were only two I didn't enjoy, one because I got lost for a bit, and the other, because it felt like a trap fest and I just wanted out quick as possible.My two biggest criticisms of Wrath, and they're ultimately minor points, is that the 'bonus' items you pick up never really felt necessary, and that the save system is a bit obtuse. Now, the first might be mitigated on higher difficulties where they become more vital. The second, just seemed to be the result of a dumb lack of defaulting to your most recent save. So, tip to anyone reading this that hasn't played yet, when you load a game from the main menu, hover over each of the three options to see which states the most recent time/date. I assumed the most recent was at the top, used that one for half the game and it resulted in me thinking that your mid-level saves only stayed active for that session and disappeared when you closed the game. Note, that is why my play time is so high - I ended up leaving my system on overnight once to avoid losing progress.Ultimately, was the time and money I spent on Wrath worth it? Absolutely!

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't actually finished this game but i'll explain why later.One negative is that there's too many enemy types. Episode 2 felt like it should've been the cutoff for new foes. I specifically have issues with The Symbol, contextually it makes sense but there was already too many flying enemies.Another is the levels dragged on for far too long. My first run of the Crypt/Graveyard i stopped halfway through purely because I didn't think the level would take more than 10 minutes tops. In fact most levels range from 20-40~ mins depending on your skill level which can cause the game to become a slog to play through.Finally music. If you had pulled me aside and asked me if Wrath had a good ost i'd outright say "what music?" as you really needed to pay attention to it in order to know it existed in the first place. Ambient tracks can be done well if they're properly integrated into the levels. In Wrath you'd have a hard time noticing them. So much so that I wound up playing other music instead.Whoever was behind the art direction or the aesthetics of the game should be patting themselves on the bat because everything is pleasant to look at even with how hellish it can get.The guns are great. I love the pistol specifically as it was always a solid fallback weapon or something that i could comfortably shoot at range with. The alt fires/gimmicks add a lot to the weapon too, the lance being both a railgun and a shield you can use to close the distance with made it very versatile.Episode 2 is by far my favourite part of the game. The world actually feels like you've stumbled upon this arcane place of wonders where the inhabitants just up and vanished. The boss for Ep. 2 is also one of the best i've fought in recent memory. It was a great way for the player to show off their knowledge of the mechanics and the tools given to them and it's miles better than Ep. 1's boss.Episode 2, in my honest opinion, felt where the game peaked and then steadily fell off a building with episode 3.Episode 3 is where the fatigue really sets in, the new enemies don't help with this whatsoever alongside the aforementioned length of levels and the level's design.Crucible of souls is a cool level aesthetically, gameplay wise? No, just no. The hub area thing in CoS was not fun to navigate. I really liked using the Ruination Blade to zip around the previous levels but here it felt like a death sentence to use. The rest of the level was fine however if we ignore the weird hub area.I'd reckon my deaths were due to my devil-may-care attitude regarding the Ruination Blade's lunge. However it doesn't change my stance on the matter.Overall, if you really need a game to scratch the boomer shooter itch and you've exhausted all other options, Wrath does a good job for the most part. However if you have other shooters/games you want/need to play you can safely leave Wrath in a play at some point category or get on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game so far, but understand before going in that this is not meant to be Quake in its purist sense. Yes it shares a lot from Quake but it also takes from elements of Turok and other 90's shooters. I remember seeing a developer video that talked about Wrath being its own thing but taking inspiration from said 90's shooters. I bring this up only because I've seen others complain that its not like Quake. For instance it has checkpoints and  limited quick save items instead of infinite saving. Its levels are larger and more open in several areas, feeling a bit more Serious Sam at points. I for one enjoyed these aspects of the game but can understand if others may not. But If you feel fine with these decisions or are indifferent to it then I believe you will find the game to be another great retro modern fps.Though, I do feel that it may be a bit pricey atm for early access, but I was fortunate enough to have it gifted to me. But the price may have held me back from going in on early access if I had to fit the bill myself, though I was defiantly planning on picking it up on its full completion. And I can say it will only become more and more worth the price as they add new content. Ill leave this review with a few final thoughts on the games world and game play.The weapons so far have been very fun to use and all have useful alt fires that had a bit more variety and strategy such as the shotguns alt fire that turns it into a kind of flak cannon. Then there's also a good variety of monsters that all have clear patterns of attack that allow for that kind of old school shooter dance of combat. And then for the level and world design. I found the two levels currently on offer to be well crafted and paced, with only rare moments that felt unfair. Finally there is the atmosphere and music that for me really sold the world. It's no doubt an overused comparison but the atmosphere does feel dark souls like but with a Quake vibe as well. That about wraps it up. If your looking for another 90's inspired fps with a touch of modern influence then you should be very pleased now and likely thrilled by the time the whole game is complete provided it continues in its positive direction.

_childDocuments_.review: I think another reviewer said it best by saying that this is the Quake 2 everyone wanted before id Software took the Quake series into the realm of science fiction. Despite it's obvious source of inspiration, it still feels like own unique game. This isn't to say that in it's it doesn't have it's issues. As an early release, it still needs polish but once the bugs and features are ironed out, this game should be awesome.The overall game is structured similarly to how Hexen was structured. Players progress through the world from a set of hubs. Each hub contains five levels that make up a thematic episode. The levels are massive, taking roughly an hour to an hour an a half each. The completed version of the game is supposed to have 3 hubs with 5 levels each for a total of 15 levels. In it's current state, the game has 1 hub and 2 levels.The weapons are well done and feel powerful. Each one is useful in it's own way depending on the scenario. Ammo at medium difficulty is plentiful with ammo drops being continuous from either fallen enemies or supply drops.The enemies themselves are varied and well designed. One or two are slightly mediocre but every game has those. They're usually the first several enemies encountered and often end up being used as cannon fodder later in the game. That being said, the majority of the enemies are exceptional not only in their aesthetic but their general design. Unfortunately, the AI is extremely lacking and needs a lot of work. Enemies often get stuck on walls or try to track the player through the walls. Not only does this detract from overall quality of the game, it detracts from overall the gameplay as well. I don't know how you would fix this apart from making waypoints  for the enemies to start following after they have lost sight of the player.The general level design and aesthetic is also exceptional but other players have noted that certain areas seem almost completely the same as previous areas of the level. This is partially true, especially on the snow level. I suspect this has a little bit to do with overall size and scope of the levels and the general desire to keep the theme of the level continuous throughout. The best way to combat this would be adding more variety to the rooms possibly through varied architecture but also by adding traps, puzzles, teleporters, slime, lava, etc.The gameplay is difficult but not unfair with the kind of fast movement speed that is typical of a 90s style FPS. Saves are an in-game power-up that is consumable. Some people have a problem with this but I never found it to be an issue. Other power-ups are available and allow the player to do things like steal health from enemies they have just killed.On an older PC, the game can run fairly slowly if the dynamic lighting and certain other features are turned off. Turning them off doesn't make the game look bad (in fact on my computer it didn't make a noticeable difference) and will make the game run smoothly on slower computers.At the moment, there is no in-game controller support. Based on the dev's plan to implement this game on consoles, they will have to tackle that at some point. In the meantime, the darkplaces engine has built in joy stick support which can be turned on in the console. The console can be accessed with shift + esc. The command to enable the joystick is joy_enable 1 and a free program called keysticks can be used to map the keyboard keys you would use to play the game onto the controller. Apart from the annoyance of remapping the keys to your preference, the game will run exactly the same as it would if it had built in controller support.This review will likely change in the future to reflect the future changes. ATM the game is excellent but obviously incomplete, which is expected since it's in early access. All the same, I highly recommend this game, especially to fans of Doom, Hexen, and the original Quake.

_childDocuments_.review: I agree with the sentiment that a good game is buried in here, but I think that game is just the remnants of the original  Quake.  Currently, 'Wrath' is plagued with a myriad of issues---Hitboxes on both items and enemies are WAY too small.  You will find yourself missing items constantly because the game wants you to keep moving at a high speed, but seems to make it so you have to have pixel perfect accuracy to pick up that TINY vial of health.-Save system is really bad.  Classic games were all about save scumming, so this decision is a bit befuddling (I think if the save shrines in the level could be reused this would be a happy medium)-The level design, like Arcane Dimensions before it, is simply a 'look at what we can do!' gimmick.  Brown castle levels are fine, but not when they go on for 1 1/2 hours of copy/pasted corridors.-Enemy placement is abysmal.  Pick up a small vial of health?  Here's ten enemies!  In the same room!  And several of them have a chance to EXPLODE when killed, instakilling you!-Enemies in general feel very cheap.  100% accuracy from across the level and you spawn them a half mile away?  With  splash damage on their projectiles?  Check.  Some of the more common enemies are way too bullet spongy even when compared to Quake's.  The game has too much of a tendency of forcing you into close encounters, when it seems like it just wasn't designed with this in mind, so be prepared to die to very cheap deaths.  A lot.The game has its merits, but I feel this is a case when modders were able to do better with existing game design as opposed to design their own.  If they were to listen to the community, I feel this game could be as well received as Dusk or Prodeus, but given the lack of communication thus far, I'm not holding my breath.

_childDocuments_.review: (preface i am playing on the hardest skill, mostly b/c i assumed there was a hidden nightmare skill opps)Wraith may be the pinnacle of ♥♥♥♥ boomer game design, and i ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ adore it.let me explain with two examples:do you know when you're playing doom3 and you see an oddly accessible large health pack, instantly knowing it will spawn in enough mobs to hopefully detract the exact sum of health given. In wraith you'll pickup a vial worth 10hp totally out of the way and no joke the game will spawn in 8 mid tier in front of you and 2 high tier mobs behind you. _childDocuments_.review: This game is the Quake we never got. An excellent mix of uniquely tenebrous, otherworldly atmosphere and addicting gameplay. Each one of the enemies is a real threat to be reckoned with, and every single weapon you get is an indispensable tool of destruction. - (Note that I've played on hard difficulty for my first playthrough)This game is relentless and will never let you  have something. There's always something, lurking around that corner, behind that door, above the ceiling. And when they do decide to attack you all at once, you better be ready because it won't be one or two of them, no. It'll be an endless stream of enemies, one after another. For enemies themselves, each and every enemy serves a specific purpose in the game's combat. Wretches shoot unending barrage of projectiles, pressuring you from afar, keeping you on your feet. Heretics shoot fairly damaging projectiles, while closing in on you to bite your head off. Oppressors shoot at a relatively slow pace, but their explosive projectiles are powerful and they possess great marksmanship, so if you're not confident enough to bait them, you better keep your distance. I could go on and on and on, but you get the point. The enemies all work together to create interesting combat scenarios. But this raises a question: how do you fight them back?Before anything, I would like to applaud this game for something, which is making the melee weapon(s) actually integral to your survival. The Blade of Ruination and the Mace of Devastation, are absolutely essential,  tools to survive the encounters. The Blade not only deals a lot of damage, but it also doubles as your movement option. You can use it to find secrets, get advantage over your enemies, and escape from tight situations. As for the Mace.... Well, I'll let you figure that out for yourself.For the other weapons, they are also undoubtably amazing. And they all come with useful alt-fire options.With your triple-barrel revolver, you can fire three ricocheting bullets from all your barrels, with your shotgun you can turn your shells into impact frag grenades, and with your Slag Cannon you can turn it into a rocket launcher, and yes, you can rocket jump with it!Even outside of the alt-functions, most weapons are either an unusual twist to the classic formulae, or just plain creative, like the Crystalizer and the Mace. Ammo is surprisingly scarce during early sections of the game, so you'll have to switch between your weapons quite a bit. Which is good, since it encourages you to use variety of weapons at your disposal.But even with these devastating weapons, sometimes the enemies will overwhelm you still. Which is where the items come in to play.I will not get in too in depth for the sake of brevity, but especially during late-game, which is when the game gets REAL, your items will become the crucial factor of life and death. I'll say this much: the adrenaline rush you get from plowing through the enemies with the Flask of Rage  (damage multiplier), or beating each one of them to death with your melee weapon while the Cruel Aegis (invincibility) is active, is unmatched.Some things to note, as, like all other video games, this game isn't without its flaws.First of all, this game is long. LONG. So long that it's almost unreal how long this game is. Each level takes more than an hour to complete, and I clocked in about 29 hours when I finished this game. (Although it is worth noting that I took some time looking for all the secrets that I can find.) So if you prefer games with shorter levels or shorter playtime, you'd have to consider the length of this game before you purchase.Next, the bosses. In the tradition of retro shooters, the bosses in this game are also, in fact, whatever. They're still better than Chthon and Shub-Niggurath, though.Also, I suppose this is a very specific and weird complaint, but this game doesn't have satisfying explosions. The Retcher, your grenade launcher equivalent, does... kinda explode? But it's nowhere near the satisfaction of the quake grenade launcher, which, to be fair, is setting a very high bar, but still. Same goes for the Slag Cannon, your rocket launcher equivalent, which also kind of explodes, and yeah, that's the thing, the few explosive weapons in this game, they only "kind of" explode, and the splash damage and range is just pathetic. It could be the difficulty, but I'm not sure.For another thing, this game is very hard to get 100% kills. The enemies either just not spawn in until you activate a very specific trigger or seemingly get out of bounds. That combined with the MASSIVE level size, could result in a very miserable experience. So if you have a completionist mindset like I do, this might bug you quite a bit. It sure did bug me.And lastly, this game has no end-game / post-game content. There's no new game+, and they don't let you go back to previous areas for remaining secrets and kills. The only thing you get is the Outlander difficulty which is just a harder difficulty for you to play the game in. So unfortunately, I'd say this game has little replay value.But that being said...All around a fantastic experience with captivating gameplay, stunning visuals and atmosphere. Reminds me heavily of Arcane Dimensions, and the best spiritual Quake successor out there. If you like retro shooters, and you like Quake, specifically Arcane Dimensions, I guarantee you that you'll have a great time with this.

_childDocuments_.review: So 1.0 has come out. This game was better in EA.It's still a somewhat fun game running on the Quake engine. Weapons are solid (for the most part) and feel punchy and the enemies are challenging. Levels are huge as well so there's plenty to explore. But some things were better in EA, like the fang-spitter.The fang spitter did not need the nerfs it got. It started out as a weapon that could hold a maximum of 300 fangs and each pickup gave you 30. Granted it was difficult to run out of ammo for the thing but you at least had enough to deal with some of the larger enemies. The alt-fire didn't shoot any more fangs per second than primary-fire but it fired two shots at a time. The benefit was that it did more stun per shot and could stun-lock some of the bigger enemies like the heretic (big blue floaty head monster that rushes you to bite you when it gets mid-distance from you). First nerf took this away. At which point there was literally no reason to use alt-fire. It didn't do any more damage per second than primary-fire and it couldn't stun-lock anything other than the smallest enemies in the game. Second nerf reduced not only it's max ammo by half but all ammo you get from pickups by half. You can now run out with a full stack of fangs within seconds and enemies don't drop enough to maintain it. I know that you have other weapons to use and you absolutely SHOULD use them but I've found myself using the fang spitter much less than the others due to this nerf. Recent BUFF it got was the alt-fire now fires one shot at a time, but twice as fast in a spray pattern. Can mow down a big group of smaller enemies now and put out decent damage against some larger ones. Overall, I feel that the ammo-reduction nerf wasn't necessary because this weapon doesn't do the amount of damage that would warrant it, especially since you can still hold 100 shotgun shells and 100 cysts for the retcher.  more damage potential from a full rack of ammo for those weapons than from the fang spitter.One other problem I've had with this game is that since the levels are massive then you'll see enemy counts around 300-400. The number itself isn't the problem, it's the fact that only 1/4 of them are actually IN the level and the rest will just port in at certain parts of the stages. 3/4s of them are hidden and will just pop in on you and a good number of them are what I call item-punishment mobs. See that box of shells? Wanna pick it up? Sorry, you're gonna be spending half (or in some cases, all) of it just killing the mobs that spawned in on you when you picked it up. Sometimes when they port in there's a slight tell that "hey, something's coming, get ready". Others, it's just BAMF and there's a few stricken (big cyst frogs that explode on death) and a few more heretics to deal with. It gets old really fast.There's a limited save system in the game like Daikatana had, which kinda sucks. UNlike Daikatana, the save system doesn't suck ass and screw you with very minimal saves. There are plenty of Soul Tethers (the manual save item) and a few shrines in stages you can use to save your game. The limited saves shouldn't be an issue here, honestly I'm not sure why they did it that way.Leaving this review as positive as the problems I had may not be problems to others and I'm probably just being a grognard with them. Personally, though I'm just not having fun with the game anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: After so many years waiting for this game, I am happy to say that Wrath did not disappoint! I didn't play early access or watch all the streams and whatnot and waited for an official full release before playing.At first it seemed like your typical shooter. But once I gathered more weapons and got used to how they work, I started to really appreciate how thought out the arsenal is.Unlike some other shooters that literally  the player to swap weapons (I'm looking at you, Hugo Martin!), in Wrath I find myself constantly juggling all the guns mid-combat because . Because it's fun. And because all the weapons are unique and have distinct advantages.Level design reminds me of Turok 2. With sprawling zones with lots of corners and secrets to explore. The game never shuts doors behind the player, so it's always possible to backtrack or even revisit levels.The goal is to collect glyphs and put them into a device in the main hub, to activate it and progress further. Again, reminding of Turok 2.I really like the art style of Wrath. Locations look cool and are very detailed, considering it's made on Quake 1 engine. Sounds are also good. And the music is more of an ambient, complimenting the environments, rather than something that stands out on its own. I have nothing to complain about here.The save system is a bit weird. There are checkpoints, that are rare and far between. But also you get consumable items that act like quicksaves. I don't really see the point, personally. I don't find the game to be particularly difficult, even though I'm playing on hard. So I ended up accumulating a bunch of those saves.Still, I saw people complaining about it during early access, so the devs added an option for unlimited saves in gameplay settings. If you're the type to obessively press F5 after taking down every group of monsters - you can do that.All in all, I'm very happy with Wrath.And I'm glad that after so many setbacks and problems, the developers pulled through in the end and released a good game!

_childDocuments_.review: I played on hard like I do with all boomershooters:It just came out too late. As a game in the boomershooter revival genre, its pretty mediocre and even a bit bad in some spots compared to other games in the genre that came out in the mean time.The guns feel good to shot, but I'm really missing things that explode. Sure the Goo launcher has splash damage, but a splash effect is a lot less fun than a good explosion. The levels are just too large with no real reason to it. They drag on and there are barely any land marks to remember. It sometimes even feels a bit like it was generated. Kind of a scale for scale's sake. In a time of giant openworld burn out, a retro fps that goes for huge levels feels like hit on the title, not a boon. A single level can take longer then an entire chapter of Quake, where every level is memorable. The enemies also spawn in, making it a clusterf%ck of enemy spam at times. There's no real interplay between the enemies and not a single (until now) encounter sticks out. It just feels spam-y. This combined with the lack of ammo makes the gameplay a bit braindead.Also, if you're going to limit saves by making them pick ups, don't put enemies just outside of a door in the corner where they can take 50% of your full health without a single way of you knowing. These 2 designs don't work together. If I cant save, don't make unfair trail and error insta kill stuff. Even more so since the levels are ungodly long.Eh, get it on sale if your thirsty for a classic fps style game and you already played the others. You're not missing out if you're missing this game in your collection. 100% a one and done type of game

"Wrath" could really be a direct successor to Quake 1. So if you are looking for this old-school Quake-Feeling, you´ll have to try this one out. In terms of gameplay, it plays really well and also the level design is good, although I normally prefer shorter levels. Here and there it lacks some variation, maybe some more enemy types or weapons would have been nice. I´m also not sure what to think of the save system "Wrath" uses. It works out well, but I prefer simple quicksave and quickload. But anyway, I can recommend it for fans of classic "Quake". Hopefully they´ll finish it soon...

_childDocuments_.review: Honest review: a solid Quake style shooter with some bad pacing issues. Game is way too long and levels are way too large. After beating the first episode I feel like I have seen everything there is to it and I have no wish to play any further. Even though there are more weapons, more artifacts and more monsters further down the line, I just feel like I'm done. I had fun while it lasted but the nonlinear nature of the hub system kinda killed this game for me. You see - you can play the levels in any order and in theory the difficulty should adapt to you. In practice the game feels more like playing series of disconnected custom levels more than a campaign. Levels have no sense of progression to them as they can be played in any order - this means playing the last one will feel pretty much the same as playing the first. It makes the game stagnant and repetitive. Similar reason why I never finish custom level packs if they are not arranged in a continuous campaign. This might be my personal preference though so you might feel different about it. I believe the game would be much much better if it was half the size and gave you more weapon and artifact variety sooner. Still a good game though.

_childDocuments_.review: So first things first: Wrath just came out in Early Access. As such, you can't reasonably expect anything resembling a serious review since most of the game still isn't here: as of the time of writing this "review", we only have 2 levels and 1 hub (final game is supposed to have 3 hubs with 5 levels each).With out of the way, Wrath is good. Not quite amazing mind you, but good. The visuals, sound and music are all top notch. Levels are big and full of secrets and all enemies have decent designs that you can dispatch with some fantastic guns. The Fang Launcher in particular is fantastic and is great callback to the Nailgun of yore. With that said, there's clearly still a lot of work to be done. Enemy placement is the first two levels isn't particularly inventive and the movement can feel a bit to imprecise at times. Still, the seeds of something great a absolutely here and I for one can't wait to see how the final product turns out.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: I like the game so far and I'm going to keep playing it, but it's not quite worth $25 yet. I would recommend anyone that doesn't already like "Boomer shooters" to instead buy the original Quake and Dusk for the same amount of money, because they're both excellent (and finished) games that are in the vein of this one. If you do like these kinds of games, this one looks promising -- buy it if you want. PROS:- Very, VERY reminiscent of OG Quake (this is objectively a good thing.) Nice to see a weapon that's essentially the Nail Gun in a non-Quake game.- Save system is integrated into the game world in a creative way and makes it (as far as I can tell) impossible to save scum. Really creative.- Movement is delightfully chunky. Encourages the player to move around in interesting ways.- The weapons are very well done. This game's equivalent of the "Super Shotgun" is my current favorite -- the alt-fire rocks. As far as I can tell, all of the guns can be used reliably in most situations.- Atmosphere is pretty good. Not OG Quake good, and not quite as good as Dusk, but much better than Quake 2.CONS:- Enemy AI is still a little wonky. I've only played for a few hours and I've already encountered about a dozen instances of enemies getting caught on the environment in ways that make them easy to cheese. Not sure what's going on with the underwater enemies, either: on several occasions they seem to have inexplicably drowned(??) before I could dispatch them.- (OPINION) Enemy layout doesn't seem quite right at the moment. This is something that's a little difficult to describe, but something about the combination of level design, player movement, and enemy AI usually makes it pretty trivial to handle most situations. I feel like the enemies need to be placed in positions that allow them to play to their strengths (floating enemies that spit projectiles in areas with perilous falls and small platforms, stationery gunners placed on hard-to-reach cliffs behind faster melee enemies, etc.) Just doesn't seem like the environments/enemy placement gel very well yet.- I like the "Cyst" weapon, but the bombs/projectiles it shoots (which can damage the player) look almost exactly like its ammo pickups. If they changed color once they were fired (purple, or something), I think that would be a nice addition. - (OPINION) Andrew Hulshult is a beautiful man and I love him, but I think he's getting overworked. His soundtracks usually grab me right out of the gate, but this one just feels a little uninspired (AT THE MOMENT!!)- The current power-ups (Artifacts) are pretty lame. I'm not saying that this game needs all the standards, but it would be nice to have a few (dual-wielding and quad damage in particular), plus a few more WRATH-specific ones. Maybe a few that are weapon-specific? Anything that helps make the game stand out. Maybe one that temporarily enables Moon-gravity so you can fly around with the Ruination Blade. I dunno.OVERALL: This is a promising game, but I'd hold off on buying it until the kinks are ironed out and it really becomes its own thing.

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty darn good retro shooter. ProsFun! - It's just fun to shoot stuff and explore. Yay!Excellent art direction - I think this is literally the ideal of retro style graphics, everything has just enough polygonal detail and just crusty enough textures.Monsters - Every critter you fight looks cool, is easily recognisable in the heat of battle and has a nicely defined role so they can be combined for varied encounters.Cool setting - As a lover of the OG Quake I have a massive softspot for mystical and eldritch but slightly anachronistic settings. Tying back into the art direction, every level looked fantastic! I'm also impressed with the variety as no two levels have the exact same theme even if they share similarities by hub.MixedArsenal - Overall it's a nicely varied bunch of "guns" but a few of them feel a little weak. The fangspitter in particular feels like it needs too many shots to put down anything and it was the only weapon I felt ammo economy was a problem. Inventory - The items never felt necessary enough to force me to use them. I probably just have a hoarding problem though. Also, I hated the invulnerability powerup knocking you down to 1 health. I used it twice ever.Level design - While most levels are very navigatable I found a few of the later levels too large and winding, with unclear direction. In the 3rd hub levels I got annoyingly lost in almost every level, and in one level in the second it was so bad that I wandered for a good 30 minutes before finding a sequence break I could use to progress. This lead to the latter 3rd of the game dragging a bit.ConsHit feedback - This game is relatively bloodless and I think that actually makes it hard to tell if I'm hitting things sometimes. I'm not saying it should be Prodeus (which overdid it, IMO) but some blood or spark particles I could see outside of point blank range would have been nice. The combat still feels good but I think it is being held back by this.The cacodemon enemy - I grew to hate them. They're too strong for your early arsenal and they constantly get stuck on geometry. They become more tolerable once you get the Lance but the damage was already done!

_childDocuments_.review: Tedious. Mostly just tedious. The weapons are fine; the enemy variety isn't. Shows no additional polish from the pre-release version. The Bestiary is useless, merely consisting of concept art. The story is meh, entirely failing to establish pathos or agency or intrigue of any kind. The "music" is adequate but mostly forgettable ambient tracks that lack a unique creative voice; certainly a symptom of the many, many cost-saving measures 3DRealms hung over the heads of whatever developers got conned into finishing this thing after the originals walked.Wrath was supposed to be a haunting experience; instead, it's merely empty, an echo of what could have been, and wholly bereft of fun. _childDocuments_.review: This retro shooter made in the Quake engine has some potential, but is plagued by too many issues and it's not been updated in years despite having been promised, so for now this is a negative review but would certainly be happy to write a positive one if it gets updated and fixed.The main issues are:1 - The save system is utterly broken (but there's a workaround suggested in the forum to add bindings and use F6 and F9 as per Quake engine's capabilities);2 - There is an unfairly difficult bit at the end of the map "The Gardens" which is source of endless frustrations in the forums and it's probably the only time I have had to enable "God Mode" in decades... and I play a lot of these games;3 - Although the levels themselves are well designed and don't force you to backtrack almost at all, the main map which you use to navigate the various levels is extremely confusing and unless you have a great sense of direction (which unfortunately I don't) you don't understand how to find the next level...4 - Performances seem quite poor, especially compared to other shooters of the same genre;5 - Most importantly, it seems to have been stuck in Early Access for 3 years without notable updates and missing deadlines. I know how difficult it is to develop games, but still, this is far from ideal.An update could easily solve all of this and make this a very decent retro shooter.In the meanwhile, you are much better off playing some of the other gems in this genre - Ion Fury from the same publisher for example is fantastic, then obviously all the usual suspects - Dusk, Amid Evil, Project Warlock, HROT, and so many others.

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely poor level design, full of random enemy spawns that appear right on top of you or worse, behind you. _childDocuments_.review: Diving into "WRATH: Aeon of Ruin" felt like stepping back into the '90s, a period I hold dear for its groundbreaking first-person shooters. From the get-go, I sensed the game's homage to that golden era, powered by the Quake-1 engine, which immediately set the stage for a nostalgic yet fresh experience. The speed at which I moved through the game, the enemies darting around, it all brought a familiar rush, a blend of excitement and challenge that defined my early gaming years​The game's arsenal was a delight to explore. Each weapon, with its unique alternate fire mode, felt like a nod to the creativity of the past, while introducing a strategic layer I hadn't anticipated. However, as I progressed, I found myself yearning for more diversity in my opponents. The thrill of mastering the weapons was somewhat dampened by facing the same enemies repeatedly. It was a bit of a letdown, especially considering the game's potential for variety​Navigating "WRATH's" levels was an exercise in patience and determination. I reveled in the intricacy of its design, the secrets tucked away, waiting to be discovered. Yet, at times, the absence of a map led me to wander aimlessly, second-guessing my path, a stark contrast to the confident strides I took in games of yore. This challenge was compounded by the game's unique save system. While I appreciated the strategic depth it added, deciding when to use my precious save items often pulled me out of the moment, a constant reminder of the stakes at playYet, for all its quirks and challenges, "WRATH: Aeon of Ruin" captured my heart. It was a rollercoaster of nostalgia, frustration, and triumph. The game's dedication to replicating the look, feel, and sound of a bygone era was evident in every pixelated enemy and echoing soundtrack. Despite its flaws, the thrill of the chase, the satisfaction of uncovering hidden treasures, and the adrenaline of combat kept me coming backIn my eyes, "WRATH: Aeon of Ruin" is a polarizing yet captivating journey back in time. It stands as a testament to the enduring appeal of '90s first-person shooters, marrying the essence of the past with the innovations of the present. While not without its frustrations, the game offers a unique blend of nostalgia and challenge, a reminder of why I fell in love with this genre in the first place​.100% recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: I did a quick test on the current version of the game to have some comparison when the full version is released later this month, and I decided to leave a comment about a small piece of the available content.Given all the caveats, I'd say I quite liked what I saw.I believe that among all the new classics inspired by old shooters, Wrath is the one that best revives and expands the most atmospheric aspects of Quake's main campaign.In a strange way, it's like a proposition of the ideal Quake sequel. A kind of spiritual successor, which adds a handful of new mechanics and a renewed sense of spectacle, but retains the core of the original experience, with the same feeling of movement, the same gameplay cadence and the same versatile combat dynamics.We have an interesting gallery of absurd and ridiculous weapons to deal with enemies with cool and cohesive designs, and huge stages, which appear to have a competent design and a fantastic presentation, drenched in a hypnotic atmosphere, strengthened by a dark environmental soundtrack.It is obvious that there is still a certain lack of elegance and polish in the general aspects. From the interface elements, the distribution of resources, the balancing of difficulties, to the lack of synergy between enemy positioning and level design. The game still needs some adjustments to be really good and replayable.And it's exactly these types of things that I hope to see resolved in 1.0.Furthermore, and this is perhaps my biggest fear, is that the large size of the stages means that there is a strong possibility that the game will run out of variety very quickly. And as a result, it can be exhausting and tedious.I only played one entire level. In a calm, methodical way, killing almost 400 enemies and exploring all the secrets. This took me about an hour (Which is the average for all levels). In that same round, I found 5 of the 6 weapons available and faced, i believe, 8 or 9 enemies, out of a gallery of 10 or 11.The truth is that it was possible to get tired and worn out in the second stage.As this is a game with roots in classic designs, I think it's unlikely that the developers will modify the game at each stage in any creative way in order to maintain the freshness of the experience. They are betting on the solidity of the game's core. And this kind of game design is simple and doesn't usually get much more complex beyond what you see in the first few minutes, so...Yes, it could be a problem. I would hate to see a game like this get killed simply because the developers went too far.Anyway, Wrath is what I would like Quake 2 to be, if Quake 2 came out today.I didn't wait for years for the game to be released and I had no expectations other than that it would be an incomplete version of the product. So the fact that it's not the most explosive and well-finished thing at the moment doesn't bother me. It's at least a promising foundation. Post-launch comments:The difficulty appears to have been substantially improved. The game is much better balanced.Weapons seem to deal the appropriate amount of damage now.We have new weapons too, of course.And a narrative? Hmm.The jump received a significant buffer, basically making bunnyhopping much more fluid and accessible.You can jump around like an idiot now, optimally, without fear of being obliterated. I replayed the level I had played the first time and, as far as I could tell, the number of enemies seems to have increased due to larger invasions, better distributed and communicated along the way. That lack of synergy i mentioned before? I think they fixed it.Save items seem more frequent and if that's not enough, there is an option to enable infinite saves.Furthermore, the game seemed better to me, but nothing drastically different from my first visit. My fears remain the same, so I'm going to keep playing to see how successful the developers have been.It looks like a solid buy now.After finishing the first hub and facing the first boss:I must say that these first stages have an incredible design. They are large and very open, but you barely feel the time pass while playing because they don't seem stretched in unnecessary ways.There is a strange predisposition to spawn enemies too far away from you, but each space is purposeful and fits perfectly into the whole in an intuitive way.Overall, the pacing of exploration and combat (AND resource balancing) is impeccable.The only “problem” I saw was precisely the lack of variety that I mentioned before. Since you can do the hub levels in any order you choose, there isn't much room for a gradual escalation of threats. You find almost all enemies and weapons in the first stage and the rest is practically the same in all the others.Which doesn't mean it bothered me (as I thought it would), since everything is very solid. But it's something to point out, since the levels are so big.The first boss was interesting in visual concept, but the fight was as expected: It's just a damage sponge. It's ok, I just missed more intense music.

_childDocuments_.review: I am conflicted about this game. On one hand, the shooting is fun, and the level design is mostly fine aside of tons of platforming because bottomless pits you have to jump over are not fun: I died more often falling down than by being killed by enemies. And if you play the game as intended, it has a limited number of saves, so you can't just spam F5 before each jump.But the main reason I am not recommending Wrath is because it's incredibly repetitive. There are only a dozen different enemy types, and usually the game can't think of anything better than to lock you up in a room and spawn a bunch of monsters around you. This is cheap and was never done in classic 90s shooters so blatantly (even though your memory might tell otherwise). And since the number of enemy types is so limited, the fights quickly become very boring. The whole first episode (realm) that takes 3-4 hours to complete has only ten different enemy types!Moreover, the game uses Quake engine (which is fine), but copies most of its guns, which is not. There's a double barreled shotgun, a nail gun and a super nail gun (shooting spikes, but whatever), a grenade launcher (with goo, still the same thing), a mix of a rocket launcher with plasma gun, and a railgun (ok, that's from Quake 2, but still). There is a unique weapon, but it's pretty boring to use, nothing groundbreaking like shrinking ray in DN3D, BFG 9000 or cannon from Serious Sam. Also, ammo distribution on the levels is rather uneven: sometimes there are tons of boxes, sometimes there's simply nothing so you are forced to use a specific weapon not because it's the best one against a certain type of enemy, but because you are out of ammo for the rest of your arsenal.Then, the boss design is complete garbage. It's obvious they tried to make the fights extraordinary and memorable, and they did: I can hardly remember worst bosses in a first person shooter. Completely unfun to fight, not rewarding to kill, and boss related achievements are badly designed (for instance, kill a boss without taking damage when the said boss spams very fast projectiles in wide patterns, and you also need to avoid lava in the arena).Not only bosses, but AI in general is horrible. Monster are getting stuck in geometry all the time (especially flying ones), but they track you behind walls, and as soon as you strafe from behind a corner, you instantly get a projectile into your face. This is not about getting good, this is about cheating AI which makes the game so not fun.There are a few good things about the game: sometimes it introduces level specific mechanics like flying and changing level geometry, and it makes gameplay a bit less repetitive, but overall it's a drag. Also it has secret chests that require a key to unlock, and the key is also hidden, so looking for secrets is actually fun, but the fights drag the game down. If Wrath was shorter and had more varied encounters, it would be great. Now, I would rather go replay Quake or Doom.P.S. I am puzzled why another retro fps released in February 2024 (Graven) has much lower user score than this. To me that game is superior due to enemy variety (including bosses), more interesting weapons, and better level design (except Act 3 which sux, but thankfully it's the shortest and also has some good moments).P.P.S. Installed Quake after finishing this, and my memory served me right - it is much better than Wrath.
