_childDocuments_.review: Even with just 5 really big levels (there are 10 more that have been promised, but it could be a while), there's a lot of content here and it's a really, really good shooter. Out of all the boomer shooters (of which I've played a ton), Wrath is a definite stand-out. It takes a ton of cues from Quake but manages to do its own thingPROS: * Amazing enemy variety, with a good mix of flying, ambling, and running enemies * Brilliant level design with a ton of verticality. Again, just 5 levels but each one is huge and sprawling * Creative artifact system that mixes up gameplay in a fun way * Challenging combat. Far too many boomer shooters forget that old-timey shooters used to be ♥♥♥♥-kickingly hard, and Wrath does difficulty well * Fun platforming - there's a dash move that you can use to traverse the maps, and it's done very wellCONS: * Overuses some gimmicks; more specifically, it loves spawing enemies *behind* you when you enter a room. * This is relevant to the fact that it's in Early Access, but there are only 4 weapons as it stands, and only one is really good against some of the tougher enemies. Having said all that, it's far and away one of my favorite modern boomer shooters
_childDocuments_.name: WRATH: Aeon of Ruin

_childDocuments_.review: If one thing needs to be praised, its the map design. They're huge, with a lot of verticality, backtracking, secrets, and just very interesting to explore. They're also /mostly/ unique in places that you'd think you don't need a map - but, they're actually so big that I often find myself thinking... was I here before? Do I need to backtrack further?Weapons are, imo, meh. Even if they pack alt-fires, their visuals are the only thing that distinguishes them from shotgun/nailgun/rocket launcher combo. The pistol you get in the beginning, you forget about the moment you get the shotgun. You're never in a situation where you run out of ammo so your first two weapons (melee spike and pistol) are as good as useless.Enemies have good variety to them, both in movement, attacks and silhuettes, so kudos to that too. There's a system like in Heretic/hexen, where you can pickup items (here called artifacts) and then use them when you need them - but its as simple as in those games and I'd love a bit more elaborate system - if anything, then allowing me to STOP using the artifact and have it lose some durability, not have it run its full course.Last, imo, utterly damning thing - but I'll wait until full release:saving system is gamified, meaning, you collect items that you then use to save your game. Now, hold on, this isn't IMMEDIATELY a bad thing, it makes you proceed with a bit of caution and prevents savescumming, and there's also shrines which save your position - but do not restore the game world state, so whatever you killed stays killed.However - pair this gamified saving system with the game that occasionally crashes, and you get a nice frustrating mixture of having to repeat 30-45 minutes of game sometimes. That's not cool at all.All in all.... its an OK game, /probably/ worth the cash, but the most fun I'm having - is exploring the maps. Everything else is, imo, subpar.
_childDocuments_.name: WRATH: Aeon of Ruin

_childDocuments_.review: This review is based on Hard Difficulty because that's where a game either shines or falls.TL;DR:-Bad Design choices almost everywhere-Overwhelming Ranged enemies-Awful Level Design-Horrible Weapon Design-Save Files become obsolete at every Patch-Would not recommend, even at salesWrath takes influences from 90s games and mostly from Quake, especially since it uses a modified version of its engine. So the game ends up looking and feeling a lot like the 90s it tries to take influence from.As someone who loves and grew up with 90s games, and still loves throwback shooters to that era such as DUSK, I did not find myself having a good time playing this game. The gist of it is that there are so many small (and medium) problems here and there that they end up feeling big and making the game unenjoyable.First off, the player's movement speed is too fast. I like high speed. It's what make's games like Doom, Dusk and etc great!But there's a limit to how fast your speed can be, before you start losing control. It also matters how the movement works and how responsive it is to determine how much control you have.Wrath's movement is too fast and sloppy. You don't feel like you're in control. Instead you feel like moving on ice with rocket powered ski boots. So a lot of the time you over-step something.And since this is a modified Quake Engine, your movement goes to sh*t on slopes and you always miss your jumps when trying to jump from one cliff to another.This high speed problem doesn't end here. Part of the fun of games like Quake is the fact that enemies fire projectiles instead of hit-scan bullets. So if you're quick enough to react, you can dodge them.In Wrath, because the player's speed is so high, they had to compensate for it by increasing enemy projectile speeds, which in contrast to a Projectile, turns them so fast that at close range they become hit-scanning weapons and can't be dodged most of the time.The enemies also have 100% accuracy, so they won't fire a burst of 3 bullets at your general direction, hoping it hits. No. All 3 projectiles are fired dead-accurate and WILL hit you.The fact that the player has a giant hitbox bigger than a Shambler does not help. What appeared to have passed by your shoulder has actually hit you. And since some of the projectiles have a small hitbox, they often pass threw slits and small gaps that you didn't think they could. Remember how in CS 1.6 grenades were 1 pixel wide and could be thrown from 1 pixel slits? Yeah, how fun was that!In contrast to what made a lot of the 90s games fun, there majority of enemies are ranged and only two melee enemies exist. One of which is a slow moving zombie that's no challenge, and the other, in stark contrast is a constant charging enemy. Dodging him is not easy because again, they compensated for the player speed so much that it actually became broken. But hey! You only face this guy a handful of times in the entire campaign, so it doesn't even matter to include him here. So let's go back to the bundle of Ranged jerks you're gonna fight.All ranged enemies keep their distance. They don't have a range limit. They can shoot at you from the other end of the map. They won't move closer for a better shot, or even for balancing. They just start shooting as soon as they see you.You've got an enemy that shoots projectiles from its eye at the rate of an MG-42. Accurate as f*ck like the others. Chews down your health, and when you kill him, he drops to the ground, spins around like a fidget spinner and fires around 10 shots in random directions, which can and WILL hit you. So you're forced behind cover even when you've killed him!You got flying enemies which are a copy of Scrags from Quake. They look the same and fire the same projectiles, but again a lot faster with no miss.I could go on for each enemy but they're all the same. They stand back, fire accurately and never get closer unless you break line of sight. Which turns the game into a cover-based shooter. How much? You'll be taking cover as much as you do in Gears of War.Level design is horrible. For a game that requires cover, you're mostly thrown into open fields with none! Either that or you're thrown into claustrophobic corridors.Fighting in the corridors is no better. The whole enemy design and level design forces you to camp at Doorways and peak shot enemies. Trying to run, strafe around or anything that doesn't involve going behind cover means death. And that's not how 90s game used to play out. At least not 24/7.Enemy placement is garbage. Enemies are always placed around corners and such where they can get a cheap shot at you. They even go as far as to spawn a Cacodemon-like enemy behind you at 2 meters so he can chomp off your head without you realizing what the hell just happened.The game has no autosave or quicksave. Instead you find skulls (pickups) which allow you to save your game wherever you want. I went into this mechanic with an open mind but found out it wasn't that good. Limited saves means you can't save as much, and when you can't save as much and there's no autosave, you can die and would go back 20 minutes and have to play it all over again!And at every update, your save files become obsolete so you have to play all over again. How fun! I had to play through the same maps 3 times!Your weapons FEEL and ARE weak (only exception is shotgun). The pistol does piss poor damage even on weak enemies. The fang-spitter (nailgun) is also weak and in contrary to what you might think, it's horrible for crowd control. The Wretcher (Grenade Launcher) has no splash damage. So you end up using a round for each and every enemy, which is a waste since ammo for it is scarce. And it's not even that strong!The only fun, strong and useful gun was the Shotgun. Everything else just felt weak af.Do I recommend this game? No. I cannot recommend this garbage. Not even at sales! Not even to add to your collection of throwback shooters.The problems of this game cannot be fixed from a single patch. You'd have to go back and fix even the most basic things such as the movement.If you want to buy a throwback shooter, there are MUCH better options than this.I'm disappointed in you Gmanlives. This game did not deserve the praise you gave it. You fell for the "old-school" theme and failed to see the game for what it really is. A pile of broken mechanics and bad design choices.

_childDocuments_.review: Many games have tried to capture "old school" ...this is by far the most authentic retro shooter I have seen. The Quake engine never looked so good. The developers have increased the graphical detail and the quality of the visual effects everywhere, without sacrificing the color pallete, the chunky textures, and the glorious gibs that defined the era. Everything feels powerful and destructive whether it's being used by you or the enemy. (Except the pistol. I don't know why the pistol exists.) Adding a basic mobility tool to your arsenal to lets you lunge across gaps is a welcome addition too.Personally though, I would almost say this is more of a Hexen successor than a Quake one.  The overall presentation is more arcane than sci-fi. Where Quake was about abstractly alien factories and warehouses and metal bruatlism, Wrath has snow-covered graveyards, trees, shrines, runes. The light "inventory systerm" that lets you save powerups for when you need them is also more Hexen than Quake.Negatives...   So far, the level design has been kind of uneven. The first map is a maze of largely identical and forgettable tombs. But they seem to be getting better as time goes on, where the later Priory and Gardens have recognizable themes and and central features that tie them together. Also the Coffers feel kind of pointless. The keys and coffers are in seperate locations so you have to spend time figuring out how to open them, only things that come OUT of them are more of what you already find: health and armor. I wouldn't mind more of a lasting and unique benefit to these, like acquiring weapon powerups, or exclusive super good artifacts, to really reward you for matching key and coffee.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate this game (the way the developers intended)TLDR: the limited save mechanic sucks, turn it off and the game is just objectively better, and if the reviewers played the game this way it might have reviewed better than just barely mid.I need to start off this very long review by saying that the game is just objectively worse because of the annoying save mechanic that was almost universally criticized since the first playable demo back in 2019. A lot of time has passed since that demo and the final version. I have more playtime than on steam as i used to have a pirated version of the demo, so its likely I have an excess of 100 hours in the game to legitimize my critic.To explain the save mechanic, you have limited saves, they are a consumable item you have to pick up. Had the developers designed the game with this feature in mind, it might have worked. What they did instead was pull all of the worst design cues from the older retro shooters to make surprise encounters with enemies spawning in 360 degrees around you an occurence every minute. They took the classic John Romero hidden enemy closet trick, and made it the whole game. these encounters were ok when it was done in doom because we had infinite saves and the trial and error of that situation was as easy as spawning back in possibly a few seconds before it happened because you would just save before most suspected enemy encounters. Limited saves are made even worse by the game over reliance on charger type enemies. The skinny thing, the thing that looks like the cacodemon, and then the classic charger type enemy. once you get the the eventide wastes, most large rooms have all of these, and most small rooms have at least one of these. The problem here is that all of them to far too much damage with how frequently used ( most notably the cacodemon looking one).summarizing how the previous two points make the save mechanic ultimately suck is that the game is just designed from the start to be incredibly punishing to messing up for even a split second, and I literally mean split second, holding the W key for half a second too long has gotten me killed on numerous occasions. not being able to reload a recent save to put trial and error directly into action just makes the game a slog to go through.By turning off the limited save mechanic the game just became far more fun because it actually encourages you to play it like a retro shooter game. You're able to make riskier moves, and make better moments to remember the game by. It makes me upset that the developers must have quietly admitted it was a bad mechanic by letting players turn it off in the settings(while keeping achievements btw). This whole thing could have been reworked into a challenge run mode, or had it as an option when you first start a game, and I truly believe that the game would have reviewed far more favorably and got far more attention from the retro shooter crowed. But hey GIT GUD I guess, it's not like there are harder retro shooter games than this that I love and play regularly that did it entirely without a phoned in save gimmick that ruined its reception.

_childDocuments_.review: Tough game to rate!First of all, I played through on hard. Didn't get some achievements and many of the secrets are still secret for me.Wrath visually is really good. Boomer shooter with retro graphics, powered by modern port of Quake 1's engine. The performance is fantastic, my RX 570 didn't have a sweat running it at 1080p 165 fps. Sadly some visual settings are hidden, the engine is capable of more, in console, you can enable lots of things. Weird decision not to put those in the game's options with some decent presets.Maps are large, sometimes confusing, but overall well structured, very nicely detailed, nice lighting, lots of secrets, cool traversal with the Blade of Ruination and thanks to its movement features, backtracking is fast! Some maps look stunning for something that was made for Quake engine. Also since it uses Darkplaces Quake port, you can load other Quake levels in too. Except they won't have that many enemies and lots of things will be broken. But it loads.Guns are fun, all of them has cool secondary attacks, there wasn't any weapons I felt obsolete as I progressed. I used all, was forced to often, in hard, I was sometimes nearly out of bullets, using the melee option was mandatory (but it's powerful, so carefully using it did the job). Artifacts are used for special abilities, VERY useful and again, didn't feel unnecessary, on hard, they were live savers. Enemy variety is a bit lacking and sometimes thematically felt off. There are many different level themes, that should have had their own enemy types or even just reskins would have helped. Such a shame. The game has a few bosses but they aren't that interesting. They all have their gimmicks. The final boss was epic though! Loved it and was satisfying to finish the game.Talking about satisfaction, difficulty and frustration... well, it had all. The save system is limited. You pick up Soul Tethers and save where you want to... One Soul Tether, one save. If you are out of them, you find a Shrine. Survival on hard was hard and I died a lot and was frustrating, but the game offers infinite save option, plus it's a Quake engine game, you can just use console command to save. I didn't use this feature.I have mixed feeling about Wrath. I recommend it, good boomer shooter, has a distinct feel to it, maps are cool, enemies are decent, music is atmospheric, but kinda lacking, length is 15-20 hours. A bit tedious, frustrating and I often felt like, it's a fun game but also wasted potential in many ways. Thankfully as I progressed, I started to enjoy it more and more as I got more weapons and the levels felt better BUT! It could have been way better. WAY BETTER. Also no multiplayer in an engine that supports multiplayer? I mean you can play in multiplayer using console commands. It's gonna be a weird thing, but works!Hmmm... My verdict is a painful 7.7/10. Painful because it has lots of amazing things.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, after final release I have to edit my review which lambasted the game for its seemingly endless delays. But after playing a bit of 1.0, I have to eat my words. This game is fantastic. I'm only one level in so far and I love everything about it. It runs on a modified Quake source port, so if you've played Quake (which you should) you can expect similar gameplay. But instead of a linear level structure, the game opens up in a hub world of sorts where you get to choose which order you tackle the levels in, and the difficulty scales based on that. The first level you pick will be the easiest, and then it scales up from there. There's even secrets to find in the hub world. It's cool. Quicksaves are tied to items you find called Soul Tethers, and each time you quicksave one of those is consumed, but there's plenty of them to find and I have more than I will ever use (and I'm an unapologetic save scummer). And the dark fantasy aesthetic is just *chef's kiss*. I love it. Go on, play Wrath. You know you want to.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE AFTER RELEASE IN 2024:------The new release adds two new fantastic worlds which holds up in quality and art to the first one but with different and new themes. The additional weapons feel great, and the new enemies add some new variation to the encounters.It's great to see Slipgate finally deliver and the fans getting a proper release. Yes, it took too long, but it is a sort of redemption, especially when the final release manages to hold and improve on the quality from early access rather than feeling rushed.I think the pacing and encounters are usually an improvement over the first world, even though the first world has some maps with excellent pacing and setups, but overall I consider it the only real shortcoming of Wrath. The encounter setups are rarely unpredictable or interesting, instead they are usually what you expect and the mirroring of same enemies from left and right happens so often you know what to expect.Beyond that I think its unfortunate that some of the bigger enemies don't traverse the geometry that well because they really add an element of tension. When an executioner shows up you know it's game on, but way too often he doesn't get a fair fight against you. If the pathfinding is a problem for them, they should've been used in areas that are way more friendly to their movements or been improved upon.All in all it's a great package, and you should definitely pick this up if you like the Quake-esc sp games. Make sure to play on the "hard" setting to get the real experience unless you're completely new to fps and arena-shooters. The levels are huge and keep going for probably 35 minutes on average if you play encounters are explore the world.------Wow, If you're the slightest into old school SP, think Quake & Unreal, I urge you to check this out right away. Wrath truly captures the old school feel with fast arena fights, bloody well done gibs, secrets, and a clever ansamble of enemies that compliment each other nicely when the encounters are set up right. Unlike most other retro-shooters that use newer engines to try and replicate the old, Wrath does the opposite and uses older tech in new and interesting ways. To be exact, it's the DarkPlaces source port of the original Quake-code that Wrath leverages to enable less technical limits, larger maps, and the ability to craft a genuine old school experience. It does not go over the top with any of the typical DP-features such as the lightning, instead Wrath has a clear idea of how it wants to look.You are the Outlander, a hunter in a broken world with the goal to cease It's corruption and defeat it's former guardians. Yes, there is a story for thematic purpose, but it is in no way intrusive and entirely up to you if you care. The game has you fragging in no time with little to no handholding, just a short introduction to the blade which is necessary.Speaking of the blade, it is used to primarily build the platforming in the game along with the fast traversal of your character. It might feel a little awkward at first, but after half an hour it felt just as natural as anything skipping around the levels. On to levels then, on your first mission you will have to explore and acquire most of your weapon arsenal, including the likes of Pistol, Shotgun and Nailgun while getting familiar with some of the game's power-ups. These power-ups range from the ability to harness enemy health upon killing them to trading 90% of your health for a short moment of invincibility. It adds a nice strategic layer over the combat to use if you so see fit.Something that quickly sticks out is the save-system. In the old days we used quick-saving, and it's all fine and dandy, but to be fair it allows for easy save-scumming unless you've good discipline. Now instead of entirely removing the ability to save where and when you want, the game allows you to pick up "Soul Tethers" which can be used/consumed to quick save. I thought this system was brilliant, the only gripe is that this should defiantly scale with difficulty. While playing on Outlander (2nd playthrough) and being a decent fps-player I managed to rack up 11 or so quick-saves after just the first level.I'm just gonna briefly touch on the delay here. I've been watching the game for a year or two, but decided I can't hold off anymore. What is here content-wise is not a disappointment, however I get that if you've been in from the beginning you might have a very different feel towards how the project has been handled and communicated.To be fair to Wrath there is a ton of work and passion put into this, and it shows. So for the sake of both players and developers I hope it's going to be seen through to the end.I had a blast!

_childDocuments_.review: Wrath: Aeon of Ruin is a absolute treasure that was worth the wait.  I played some when it entered Early Access, loved it, and put it away until it hit 1.0 so I could take it all in at once.  I admit that for a while I was very worried about the games progress.  However now that I have the game I'm so happy they took the time to finish it properly.Wrath takes inspiration from many of the shooters of the 90's and 00's.  Above all, I see it as a love letter to the Quake 1 mapping community.  The spirit of beautiful, intricate, difficult levels that push the boundary of the old Quake engine is alive in Wrath.  If you enjoy mods such as Copper, Arcane Dimensions, or Alkaline, then you have to dig in to Wrath.  If you enjoy bunny hopping and rocket jumping, then you are in the right place.Wrath is based on a descendant of the original Quake 1 engine.  I believe that in order to capture the feeling of old-school shooters, there is really no other way than to use the actual technology of the time.  And boy, does it come through.  Wrath is such an authentic boomer shooter.  Other games based on Unity or UE just don't match that same authenticity.  Of course Wrath is it's own game, but it  like the sequel to Quake 1 that we never got.Wrath is good.  Very good.  To start with, there is the artwork and graphics.  It is excellent.  I've rarely seen the Quake engine look this good, and it is honestly hard to believe how much mileage they got out of it.  The textures are great, the enemy design is awesome and creepy, even the UI pixel artwork and the journal sketches are beautiful.The sound design is the best I've experienced in a boomer shooter for some time.  Sound effects are crisp, give you plenty of spacial information, and never get tiresome.  The music is very well done, as you'd expect from Andrew Hulshult, and is very much in the tradition of Trent Reznor's seminal Quake score.  The soundscape is tense, creepy, with a sense of unease that typically does not build into the kind of hard-charging metal that we've come to expect in the genre.  No, this one is more subtle, but it's atmosphere is on point.The standout aspect of Wrath is the levels.  My god, these levels.  I'm not sure I've ever seen levels like this.  Amid Evil comes to mind, but even those did not quite match the scale seen here.  Wrath follows from some of the standout examples of the Quake mapping scene.  Just bigger, more intricate, more everything.  I can't believe what they've managed to accomplish with the Quake engine.  Massive trees, ancient ruined complexes that weave from tight corridors to wide open spaces, rocky canyons hiding temples and lakes, organic horrors.  It's crazy.  Honestly the levels are a bit overwhelming at times.  They can be so big, with so much to explore.  There are so many secrets, I didn't even find half of them.  However despite all this, I rarely found myself at a loss for where to go.  There were a few moments of confusion but mostly I was kept moving forward.Without a doubt, the weakest part of Wrath are the enemies.  As I previously stated I really love the designs, however they suffer from a very weak AI.  I believe this is largely a limitation of the game engine, and indeed I could say that the enemies act like they are stuck in the 90's.  Their movement is simple, however the developers seem to have tried to work around that with careful attention to detail in the level design.  The enemy variety is also somewhat limited given the length of the game.  There are literally hundreds of enemies per level, and you meet the main characters very quickly.  There is a lot of repetition.Your arsenal for dealing with the enemies is a fairly standard boomer shooter compliment, centered around a big ole shotgun.  They look good, they sound good, and they mostly have a weighty impact.  Surprisingly there isn't a rocket launcher, but the Slag Cannon's alt-fire is basically the same thing.  My favorite is the Fang Spitter, which is basically your nailgun.  It just feels great to use.The movement in Wrath is very Quake-like, which means there's plenty of movement tech that you can master if you have the skill.  Interestingly, the movement is closely tied with the melee weapon, which gives you a lunge that you can use to get speed quickly.  Using the blade to bounce around and look for secrets is the gameplay that makes up the welcome downtime between firefights.A common complaint among Steam reviews for this game is with the save system.  I honestly quite like it.  Like many games, Wrath autosaves at the beginning of levels, and includes a few checkpoints in each.  However, in addition, you can pick up "Soul Tethers" that function as quicksave spots.  They are a limited resource so you can't save scum, however if you must, that option can be turned on in the settings.  I found that they were far more plentiful than I needed, so it wasn't a problem for me, and also I like that the game has an in-universe explanation for saves.Saves will definitely be needed because the game is HARD.  This is a game for veterans of the genre.  I recommend Normal difficulty for your first playthrough, or Easy if you are a noob to shooters.  The game is long so be warned.  If you think you might get bored with the bang bang, then don't choose a difficulty that will have you dying a lot.Overall, the whole experience is smooth and polished.  They definitely used the extra time to finish this game properly and it shows.  I didn't really have any problems in my playthrough.  How nice to get a well-honed game at launch, it so rarely happens these days.  Another way in which Wrath is authentic to its inspiration.Final verdict: two thumbs up

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic throw-back shooter.Movement and shooting are rock solid with a spread of 9 weapons that are visually and functionally distinct, and are fun to use (though the pistol could do with some stronger impact effects). _childDocuments_.review: Well, it's now April of 2024 and the game is finally out for real. I'm sad to say that the intrigue of this game takes a nosedive after the initial world that was offered in early access. The levels get even bigger and it stops being fun. I finally listened to the advice of others and turned infinite saving on, doing away with the Soul Tether system, and it made getting through the subsequent worlds much more bearable. At some point you just have to give into the conceit that this is the kind of game that is meant to be save scummed. Either have small levels with dense encounters and few saves, or have huge levels and unlimited saves. Not both.It's hard to put my finger on why the subsequent worlds are so much less fun to go through; on the surface, they're very similar to the first world, but in practice, it just becomes a slog. It's way easier to get lost. The lack of enemy and weapon variety gets old quick. You spent a lot of time with not enough ammo. I started the game from the beginning again when I picked this up to play the 1.0 and felt the thrill of the first world come right back, I remembered all the levels and their tricks, it was extremely memorable. But the moment it turned into caves, it just got REALLY boring.I think I'm losing interest in finishing it. There's also some jank in the level geometry that can be tricky to get out of. Maybe I'll come back to it in more distant bursts of time, but I'm bouncing off of the rest of what this game has to offer. That's a real shame. The end result is definitely "buy it on sale" territory.---OLD REVIEW FROM JULY 2020:I was skeptical that the "tiered checkpointing" of this game, one of its most unique mechanics, would not be meaningful enough to come into its own as a meaningful decision, but I am pleased to say I was wrong.There's a unique sense of weight to deciding how far back you'd like to start over from after getting clobbered by a surprise encounter. How many of your previous mistakes do you want to rewind and redo? You've found a Shrine, but do you want to use it yet? Because the level will definitely open up in a such a way later that you'll be back at this location after much progress has been perilously made, so do you want to save now or then? It's really interesting.I find myself having a very different relationship to how often I want to try again versus put the game down and come back to it a little later... my play sessions end up being very long because of it. My Play Time total is really surprising me. Compare this to something like Doom Eternal, where I lose immediately and pretty much just get pissed and turn it off, so making progress is a chore.I had no idea the Quake 1 engine could look this expansive. The use of primitive particle emitters is very tasteful. Just a very very refined game feel from people who clearly have intimate knowledge of the engine. It's very polished and the pacing is really varied. This might be my favorite-playing of all of the 90s FPS renaissance titles that have been coming out. I'd give Amid Evil the best level designs but the ones here are absolutely stellar as well. I really can't recommend this game enough if you're already gobbling up Dusk, Amid Evil, Ion Fury etc. like I am.

_childDocuments_.review: Speaking as someone who has played hours of Quake, both the original and fan content, I can proudly say this one is IT. Sure, there have been several "Quake-likes" to enter the scene, but this one takes the bloody sponge cake.Levels are intricate, enemies are abundant and brutal on Medium skill, and I keep finding myself going, "Just a little further. Just another level." If you are not prepared for massive levels and tough battles, you had better sit this one out. Its an endurance run, in the best way possible for this kind of game.Just thought I would throw down a quick, casual, positive review. You are Outlander. Once adrift upon the Ageless Sea, you now find yourself on the shores of a dying world. From the consuming darkness emerges a figure cloaked in white, the Shepherd of Wayward Souls, who burdens you with the task of hunting down the remaining Guardians of the Old World. You must journey into the vast gloom to explore ancient ruins, discover forgotten secrets and battle the horrors that lurk within.

Fueled by legendary Quake 1 technology, the veins of WRATH pump with the DNA of revered '90s shooters. WRATH embraces the timeless elements of classic titles such as DOOM, QUAKE, DUKE NUKEM 3D, BLOOD, UNREAL and HEXEN and carries them into the 21st century.

Equipped with weapons of exceptional might and an inventory of powerful artifacts, you must traverse ancient crypts, sunken ruins, corrupted temples and howling forests to bring death to your enemies. But do not underestimate your adversaries, for they are great in power and number. Your mind must be as sharp as your blade if you hope to survive the dangers ahead.

_childDocuments_.review: Foregone is very difficult to rate, because it's the platonic ideal of B-tier.I love Dead Cells, and a similar game with a straightforward campaign instead of roguelike structure is very appealing to me. But in execution, it's very medium in every category. * The controls are *mostly* pretty good, I like moving around, but some corner cases (often involving actual corners) can be frustrating. * Most abilities aren't actually very good. Where a lot of builds in Dead Cells are viable and provide different synergies, most of them in Foregone are irrelevant. The direct damage skills do less than your weapons, the healing is quickly overshadowed by leech and overdrive, the skill tree doesn't fundamentally alter the way you play the game.* The enemy design is also ambivalent. There aren't many enemy types, and the elites don't behave any differently. But they do a great job at establishing their types early on, and each level introduces a variant that gets new attacks or behaves differently.I've played through it to the end, played it again on New Game+, then did further grinding by repeating endgame levels to get enough blue gems to finish my skill tree and get all the trophies. Since I got it on sale for 5USD, I'd say I got that amount of fun out of it. But I wouldn't recommend it above other gems of sidescrolling action genre like Dead Cells or Momodora

_childDocuments_.review: Lets begin with the elephant in the room; this game is a 'metroidvania' in the same way that the original DOOM is a 'metroidvania'. Its not at all an interconnected series of areas with a more open-world feel for exploration; no, its just a hub-town that teleport connects to various linear levels. You cannot even re-enter areas that you just came from without first teleporting back to the hub-town. This may seem like a specifically nitpicky point; but we will return to it in a few. Most of the actual level design is fairly uninspired; generally they are long linear areas that wrap around on itself. Shortcuts exist within the level design but 99% of the time you will never use them. The only real reason for them is if you were to die halfway through a level before hitting the next check point; or if you're on New Game+ and you're attempting to tediously farm for Essence. (Entrance waypoint 1 farm; im lookin' at you).That all being said; the artwork is simultaneously amazing and beautiful, while somehow also being incredibly cluttering. Often there's so much clutter on screen between enemies, background objects, foreground objects, parallax background / foreground, doodads, weather effects, etc; that it becomes this weird hodge-podge of beauty and eyesore. At least for me.Enemies are also fairly uninspired and get very; very repetitive. Especially into a second playthrough; which isnt necessarily bad on its own. The enemy types that exist are all fairly well fleshed out and require you to listen to audio cues (teleporting smash attack!) or visual cues to competently defeat them. The audio cues are probably the most fleshed out; as you pretty much just immediately need to dodge any time you hear them. The visual cues... not so much. Visual cue attacks are often very poorly telegraphed due to multiple enemies stacked on each other or background/foreground clutter making it difficult to tell whats going on. Likewise; enemy telegraph attacks tend to happen incredibly quickly (that is to say; there's very little 'wind-up' before the attack happens). This would be less of an issue if the dodge mechanic worked better; but it seems to have practically no invincibility frames attached to the mechanic. Often you will dodge into the three bullets being fired at you only to get hit by all three anyway. Enemy placement can also be a horrific chore to contend with; along with the ledge-physics of the game. Often you will need to immediately rush past and dodge through multiple hostiles to get on the other side of a flame turret (before it one-shots you); except that everything is placed on the edge of a ledge; so when you dodge through to attack from the other side you just fall off repeatedly or get mobbed by the enemies you had to rush through.This leads us to the itemization. Items are honestly fairly lackluster. There's not a huge difference within the weapon types in terms of how they function; yes they do have different move-sets; but ultimately they all just feel kinda clunky. It follows a very uninspired common, magic, rare, epic, legendary (mythic) format we've all seen a hundred times before; and essentially ripped D3's itemization and enchanting system. Ugh; and the enchanting system. Its gated behind speed run events or boss fight events which require you to spend ever increasing amounts of Essence to reroll affixes to try and get a series of bonuses that you want. Nothing is innovated here; and it feels just as frustrating as the iteration that exists in D3. Likewise; you should NOT EVER engage in enchanting until you have a full set of Mythic+ (red text 5th affix) from New Game+ mode. Otherwise you're just wasting Essence.To that end; farming for items, essence, and gold feels very clunky too. You arent really able to increase your drop chances (or drop amount) on any of those things via affixes; so the most you can possibly make is from New Game+ mode anyway. At the beginning I mentioned how not being able to freely enter areas without teleporting back to the hub-town was pretty awful. Well; this is why. The only achievement im missing is the 'max out all skill tree' one; which requires a TON of essence; compared to what you can lucratively farm. Doing the speed runs seems to be good for ~300-400 essence; but you only get the reward once per playthrough. And it takes like 4k+ essence to max out a single skill. Anyway; once you're at end-end-game; and all there's left to do is farm; the level design begins to really drag, since you have to constantly teleport back to town; then back to the area you want to farm / reset. Bosses respawn on New Game+ but they are so undertuned for their gold/essence/item drop rewards that its much quicker (sadly) to instead just repeatedly farm a late game area.All that being said; I'd still recommend it for the price as I still personally had fun with it. And most of my faults with the game / game design are things that can be fixed or updated (outside of linear level design that is). And its certainly not the worst 'metroidvania'-lite game ive ever played.  ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

_childDocuments_.review: is a 2D action platformer with beautiful pixel artwork and a nice and fluid combat system overall. The game features fairly linear gameplay tethered by a core story that I have yet to view to the end, but I imagine that I am about halfway through after playing about 6 hours so far. If you do not want to read too much of my ramblings, please know that this is a very good game and is worth your time. I would refrain from comparing this to any other game mentally, specifically  because these are fundamentally different games, each with its own appeal. My first expectation of this game was upon seeing the "Metroidvania" tag on the store page. I do think this is a bit misleading, as the game does not necessarily feature significant new areas of exploration with branching paths that you can only reach upon obtaining new skills/movement abilities further in the game. Instead the pathing is linear and the story keeps you going forward, with checkpoints along the way that you can use to teleport back to the base at any time, in order to spend your earned currency for upgrades. The new movements and abilities are necessary for progression in this linear style. So I do not consider this game a Metroidvania.The story may become coherent ultimately toward the end of the game, but so far, I haven't seen enough to make complete sense of it. In other words, it's not critical for the overall game. You play as an arbiter, a super soldier, with a task of saving the city of Calagan against the Harrow. There are some voice-acted lines of dialogue, but they are not too many. You will be piecing together the story/lore through random tomes that you find scattered around.Moving around feels fluid, and you are going to be doing plenty of full-area exploration in order to unlock all of the small doors/obstacles that prevent progress. In the beginning, you can run, jump, double jump, and slide. After some time, you will gain other abilities such as air dash, ground strike, etc. These missing pieces do give you a slightly awkward feel, heading into the game, because you half expect them to be there. But the way the game's levels are designed is that you quickly adapt to what you have and there's no trouble moving forward.This game gives you two weapon-based attacking options and also two active combat skills at any time. You can always have one melee and one ranged weapon equipped, and you can easily use them in combination as you see fit. There are quite a few different types of melee weapons that you will get from enemies as randomized loot, and so be on the look out for what you prefer, especially when you are starting  up. The ranged weapon auto-aims when you are close to an enemy, and for controller-players, this is a nice feature for some more annoying enemies. Ammo is recharged by attacking enemies with your melee weapon.Due to the progressive unlocking of movement abilities, some parts of the combat start to feel a bit dry and repetitive before you get enough movements/abilities unlocked to find a set that's suitable for you. Definitely be patient through this section, when you feel that the combat has become a little stale, because it will get better, I promise. I think I am about halfway through the game, and I think everything feels fantastic and smooth.You will find a wide variety of enemies, with some recoloring for enemies marked as elites. Each new zone will introduce some newer enemies and still give you some older ones that you are familiar with. You do not have to worry about. These new enemies each have their own set of attack patterns and will not take you too long to get used to. But when they come at you in groups, even simplistic enemies can be difficult to deal with.Each boss is also unique, you will encounter quite a few along the way in the story, and you will also face boss fights in the side-missions. Don't be too alarmed if you have to die a few times to figure out the specific attack patterns in order to beat them, they are rather well-designed to be fun and not too tedious. I am through 5 bosses so far, and they were all quite fun to deal with.There are no experience-gained or leveling up for your character. Your upgrades come in the form of progressively getting better loot and each piece of equipment is upgradable at the Blacksmith. More rare items will feature additional effects that improve with upgrades. If you do not like any one associated effect, you can visit the Warsmith at the end of side missions in order to reforge any one effect as well.You have 5 different item slots. So aside from a melee and a ranged weapon, you also have a piece of armor, a ring, and an emblem. Each item will be of 5 possible rarities, and with the associated rarity will be increased number of effects and also increased number of upgrade levels.There are two types of currency, gold and blue gems, to be used at the Outpost/base. Gold is used only at the Blacksmith, while the blue gems are used primarily at the Thaumaturge to upgrade your own personal statistics (to a point) and also those new equippable combat skills that you have picked up along the way. The blue gems are also used at the Warsmith after side-missions to reforge equipment.Once you obtain the appropriate "Catalyst" to be able to unlock any specific upgrade tree, you will find yourself deciding to spec your character and skills along 1 of 2 paths in each upgrade tree. You can pay some gold to refund your upgrades later and try out the other potential upgrades, so at least you are not permanently locked in. I wish I could obtain another set of the same catalysts in order to unlock both. After all, I want to see what the character can do fully powered up instead of being capped at 50% potential at full upgrades. Just a matter of personal preference, really.The pixel artwork is beautifully done. A lot of times coming across an enemy for the first time or seeing some stuff in the background, I just sat around and watched the animations for a while. My only minor complaint visually is that there are some background elements that look like in-plane platforms.The game is optimized for controller play, which is good as it's also released on consoles. I would recommend the controller for sure.The background music loops provide an nice ambience for the game. The sound effects work well. The few lines of voice acting is also done rather well.Base price of $19.99 is definitely a good price for the game. Launch week discount of 20% is pretty nice.I recorded the first half hour or so of myself playing, if you want to take a quick peek. is really very fun. I do think it's absolutely worth your attention and money if you are looking for a good action platformer. Don't think too much about the Metroidvania tag too much because it really isn't one. Try also not to compare it with other games, just let this game stand on its own.  features plenty of good aspects to be an entity on its own.From what I have seen, this game is totally worth it. I plan to finish the game and check out other features too.Score 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: I find Foregone difficult to recommend. The animation is very fluid, but it comes at the cost of some seriously wonky physics surrounding ledges and a brutal lack of feedback for when you're taking damage. The sheer linearity of the map would be excusable if the encounters felt more tailored, but my entire play experience was fighting the same varieties of soldiers and bug spawners and beetles that were choking arbitrary corridors and platforms.The loot is probably the least enticing portion of the game. It never felt like a real consideration -- movesets don't have quite enough nuance to make sticking with a lesser weapon worthwhile, while the Diablo-esqe affixes felt more like a cheap way to pad playtime through grinding for an appropriate tier weapon with your desired bonuses.Overall, there's certainly parts of the game that show promise. They are simply choked out by subpar level and enemy design. The levels aren't interesting enough to carry repeat visits and backtracking. The enemies aren't interesting enough to lean in on character action.

_childDocuments_.review: My first impressions video: You can definitely be forgiven for taking a look at Foregone and thinking it's a Dead Cells clone but as someone for whom Dead Cells is my favourite Rogue-lite, I'm telling you it's definitely not that. It's a side scrolling game with amazing 3D pixel art but that's mostly where the similarities end.First and foremost, Foregone is not a Rogue-lite, it's a largely linear, story-based platformer. You'll move forward through different levels to progress the story and when your character dies, you respawn, as opposed to having to start a new run. It's also not a Metroidvania as while there is a hub area you can return to, you're generally constantly advancing and backtracking to previous areas isn't required. Much more of a traditional platformer. At the point I've reached in the game, the story doesn't seem to have evolved much. The character doesn't speak much and has somehwhat flat voice acting when she does. Things might get more interesting down the line but at time of writing, I haven't finished it yet.Where this does share a bit in common with a Rogue-lite is that you do have a skill tree that you will advance as you play and you will pick up look that you'll equip and upgrade as you go. Foregone is much more focused on growing your power through equipment rather than abilities. There isn't quite the diversity in equipment I would have ultimately liked and I some more variety would have definitely been nice but you nonetheless do feel like you're getting more powerful as you go and that the game presents a pretty consistent challenge.I'm a big fan of platformers in this style and though they aren't nearly as common as Rogue-lites and Metroidvanias now, I still think they can be a lot of fun when they're well crafted and this definitely is. Big Blue Bubble is traditionally a mobile and casual game developer so this is quite a departure for them and I think they did a good job. If you want the depth or difficulty of a Rogue-lite or the more advanced exploration of a Metroidvania, you aren't going to find that there. If however, you want a solid linear platformer that plays great and also looks incredible, Foregone is a great buy. I've very much enjoyed my time with it so far and have every intention of finishing it.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a middle rating. Not bad but not great. There's a lot to like but the overall package falls short of similar games. The art style is gorgeous and draws obvious parallels to Dead Cells. The story is forgettable to non existent. The map is incredibly linear with very limited exploration which only lends itself to basic stat upgrades for abilities or a loot drop (I see you and judge you User Tag: Metroidvania) The loot is a cool idea but its hard to utilize it to its full extent without mindlessly grinding areas (which would be fine if the areas weren't very similar with similar enemies), the same goes for the different abilities. I never found the need to switch my abilities because upgrading each ability felt like a waste of resources once i started on a combination that worked for me. At the launch price I'd say the game is fun enough to play but I would have trouble recommending spending $16 on this versus just buying Blasphemous, Hollow Knight, Dead Cells, Hades, Rogue Legacy, Wizard of Legend, Bloodstained, Ori 1 or 2, Iconoclasts, etc. (You get my point) If you have played those games and are looking for a more streamlined action platforming experience with an ARPG loot type of flair then maybe check it out, if not play those instead.

_childDocuments_.review: ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬ is an action-platformer that left the early access limbo and not-so-epic store to enter where it belongs. On paper, there isn’t much that separates it from the norm. In spite of the standard formula, it carves out its own identity through an enjoyable gameplay loop and masterful art design.The story centers around the city of Calagan which is overwhelmed with an all-corrupting evil known as the Harrow. In a world filled with technologies, people band together to create super soldiers known as the Arbiters of whom you play the first, sworn to protect the city at all cost.▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬There isn’t much to the core narrative of . You essentially need to go back and correct mistakes to arrive at a more desirable conclusion. As you move through the Calagan, there are a number of text-based segments which act to partially fill in the missing lore. This is a linear title, so I was expecting they'd do more in terms of narrative delivery but it never really materializes aside from these sparse documents and the occasional verbal context that the protagonist gives. may be tagged as a Metroidvania but in fact, it is a little too linear to be regarded as one. The city is a sprawling, multi-story locale with several locked doors standing between you and your destination. However, most of the essentials are found in your path so there's minimal backtracking. Through this interconnected map, Arbiter can teleport back to a resting place serving as a hub.The main focus is on delivering an impactful action-platformer but succeeds mostly at the former. Arbiter is equipped with one melee and one ranged weapon alongside two active abilities. Using your melee attack is brutal and visceral often feeling quite heavy. Enemies usually go down very quickly but so will your health. While the standard melee chains aren’t particularly complex, the little variety of weapons cover most of the bases for those who differ on prioritizing speed, power, or range. Overall, the main loop that revolves around melee combat is incredibly polished and satisfying—singlehandedly carrying the gameplay.The ranged options are of the fairly standard guns and bows variety, which serves as significant and powerful options. They dispatch enemies with ease and as expected, they hold limited ammo that is only reloaded through doling out melee damage. Aiming is done automatically and is literally hit or miss. The arbiter must be at a certain angle/distance for her to lock on the enemy otherwise, she wastes ammo by randomly shooting somewhere.Earlier I mentioned the platforming aspect of  is subpar to its action, that is where the game takes a hit. The fluidity of character movement and animations is wonderful but often interrupted by narrow pathways and way too many tiny platforms. They are usually occupied by an enemy or two. Surely you want to kill them for coin and essence but it is hard landing on them without getting hit and Arbiter's melee force pushing her back mid-air doesn't help it either.Some enemies are exclusively ranged or melee, while others deal in area/splash damage. Their diversity could be more expansive, but like the available weapons, they do an ok job of keeping things fresh. Enemies in later stages are presented as hard-ass reskins of the previous ones. For the most part, they follow the same attack pattern with little change. Bosses are no exception either as most of them make a return with a strictly new set of moves. Although, I have to admit they provide a great challenge and overall feel epic taking on them.Throughout the levels, there are very few outposts serving as checkpoints as well as a way back to the hub. There you have the Blacksmith to salvage Arbiter's unneeded loot for gold or Thaumaturge to talk about improving her skills. There is a slight issue with the upgrading system and that is the upgrades to your own skills are so insignificant that it never feels like they make a difference. On the other hand, active abilities are redundant. Initial ones, the surge and restoration, are soon so well upgraded and so useful that they render all other abilities trivial. Other people Arbiter meets there is the dispatcher, who gives extra missions and challenges, and the Ferryman, who she can strike a deal with after death. Safely retrieve half of her coin and essence or risk to get all back from where she died.Are a creative feast. Astonishing, dazzling, elegant, meticulous, and so on are only a few of the dozen I could use to describe the art design. Backgrounds are vivid and lush multi-layered scenery packed with extraordinary detail. The characters are rendered every frame in a 3D form which resulted in silky smooth animations that complement the combat. It's just something that not many games share.The overall quality suits the tone. There is a light, exploratory feel to the music for most of the standard levels, while for the battles it elevates to something more bombastic to naturally feel more epic. At first, I thought there isn't much noticeable ambiance rather than only combat-related sounds but when I muted the music,  turned into a relatively new experience that you should play for yourself to understand. Voice acting, albeit very minimal, is surprising and of good quality.▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬In short,  may struggle to define itself within the genre and fails to properly execute some of its mechanics. However, the fluidity of combat works hand in hand with the art design to deliver an aesthetically and technically feels-good-to-play title. For the $20 price tag, buying it at a small discount wouldn't hurt since there isn't much to do in Calagan unless going after NG+ and the extra difficulties (includes perma-death) which are unlocked only after beating the game once.▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of writing  is 4,19€, and my money were completely wasted on this product; the reasons are as follows: is heavily inspired by , all from the enemy design, weapon system, artstyle, to the story being told in the background through enviroments. Unlike  however, this game is put together with the same care and precision of a kamikaze plane in an antique shop.The enemies are all carbon copies from , but their placements have no thought put behind them at all when it comes to the lens of 's mechanics; enemy placements should complement the game's mechanics and utilize the levels to their full potential, but in  the enemies are placed in places that actively strive against the mechanics of the game. Enemies on walls and ceilings are out of reach with your ranged weapon because the auto aim has an incredibly low angle of detection, and it simply can't fire upwards, often you have to jump to be in the same elevation in order to hit anything, and the further into the game you get this becomes harder and harder due to a more heavy use of enviromental hazards, and often enough your only choice is to hit enemies with your melee weapon anyway because of the non-functioning auto aim feature. Your combat capabilities in the air are however extremely limited due to one single unique aerial attack that has a long windup and animation. You can't chain dodgerolls as the dodge has an internal cooldown that the game doesn't tell you about, yet machine gun enemies are placed at the end of long hallways where you have to eat at least a few bullets. There's enemy collision that doesn't cause damage, but their hurtboxes are so extended that you're more often than not knocked off edges since they push you out of their space, so if you're in a platforming section where enemies fire at you and there's a single fat enemy on a small platform - then you can't get past it as you'll be pushed off the edge without being able to line up a jump.You have five melee weapons and four ranged weapons, and their impact on your playstyle doesn't matter in the slightest due to their dps decrepency being so large, so you're always better off just upgrading the newest weapon with the highest base damage. Upgrading itself isn't explained in the slightest, so trying to decipher what an upgrade actually will do for the item is up to trial and error, and even what some stats such as  does is a mystery. Just like in  you have additional item effects such as increased damage to a poisoned enemy, or a certain percent chance to attatch a bomb to your target. The issue with this system however is that no actual synergies exist. I played up to the 9:th area of the 12 available, and there was neither a reason nor enough leniency to upgrade my skill tree in order to unlock  ways of doing specific debuffs. You're heavily encouraged to grind due to having set costs for upgrading items, without it being rare in the slightest, and in order to change your menial synergy you need to beat a speedrun version of a level you've already beaten in order to unlock a merchan that can reroll your modifiers for a cost, and you also get a single item at the end of this challenge level. There is still no reason what so ever to min/max these items as you have to grind to such an extent in order to achieve the synergies you want that you'll just unlock more equipment with better base stats anyway. Even if you were to grind your heart out in order to get all skilltree upgrades so you at least have the  to utilize the synergies, you still can't upgrade a skill before you've found their specific upgrade item that's gated at some point in one of the twelve levels. For nine levels the system didn't matter in the slightest and I hadn't died once, up until enemy damage skyrocketed out of nowhere and the enemies decided to all stand inside each other, chaining their attacks at the same time with their non-telegraphed animations suddenly one shotting me.Your healing is tied to the same Estus style healing everything in the shadow of  has, but instead you only get one charge that refills when you damage enemies; emphasizing aggression and pushing on in order to live. Except that just killing enemies drop healing orbs that immediately heal you, there's skilltree upgrades that give you leech that activates when you kill something, and except for a single enemy type nothing in the game can actually follow you if you run past them, so there's no pressure for survival at all.You still have your bonfire system where you get checkpoints at certain intervals in the levels, except that instead of having the option to upgrade your gear or skilltree, instead it's a teleporter to the hub zone which contains four npcs and nothing else. You will return to the hub zone literally every time you hit a check point as you'll always have enough money for at least some upgrades, and enemies drop loot constantly that you can sell.The bosses are unchallenging, and they all reach their phase two at around 60-75% HP, at which point the entire fight stays the exact same without evolving at all - turning the entire ordeal into a painful slog. All bosses have about three moves that they repeat in the same pattern ad infinitum, and during their phase two they either get upgrades to their existing moves, or get one or two new ones.The artstyle is made from 3D models being pushed through a pixelart filter, where this worked in  due to meticulous care and an eye for detail, in  it looks like a cheap Photoshop plugin that wasn't calibrated properly. Still images may look appealing, but in movement it's jagged and unbelievably sloppy.After the peak of ' popularity it's sadly a fact of life that other games have to try to ape off every aspect of that game without understanding what made it work. ' story is one told by context and world building, through the enemies you fight and the descriptions of items that help piece together the history of this dying world.  has the character spit quippy or asinine dialogue whenever a new landmark is discovered.  In addition to  levels of dialogue there are also of course cryptic npcs that spew random detatched sentences towards you in hope of sounding mysterious, except instead of it being dozens of well crafted, dynamic characters with wants, needs, and goals, instead it's just four merchants that adds nothing. There's also exposition delivered through random text documents strewn across the world that doesn't add anything to the experience.My intent was to 100% this game in order to review it as fairly and accurately as possible, but after eight hours of non-engaging gameplay, bullet sponge bosses, seemingly random enemy placements, incomprehensible systems and menus, asinine dialogue, buggy AI, leap of faith trap placements, and ugly artsyle; it was enough to break me.Not a single part of me can recommend anything about this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Originally released a year ago, Foregone has been an Epic Store exclusive, showing a positive outcome on the platform. Now that the exclusive period has ended, Foregone on Steam is already with a Positive user score, and the work by Big Blue Bubble has proven once again that their action platformer is here to gain even more attention. Calagan was once a flourishing and beautiful city, but such is no more. All are memories with a threat devastating the little that remains. Harrow is their name, and it’s up to you to stop this menace. In a world set by ruins, there is still a little hope, called Rowan. The very first example of resistance, and the creation to bring hope to humanity. A super soldier, or in this case, a class of its own. The first Arbiter, and maybe even the only one it will ever be needed.If you like to discover and unravel lore as you explore, you’ll easily have a good time with Foregone. Discover documents as you progress, and put the pieces together to learn more about the past, present and future. There's quite a big opening to make up your own idea of events, and that in my book is always a major plus.Despite being critically compared to Dead Cells, I genuinely felt Foregone had a lot of things of its own, never really comparing both. Although with similar gameplay, Foregone quickly engages players with its own mechanics.Take no illusions, Foregone is a pure platformer action game, where it could very well take elements of roguelike, with procedural generated areas. Fortunately, it didn’t. I don’t personally have anything against roguelike games, but there’s been so many out there, that I really did enjoy seeing hand-polished scenarios across a fast-paced action game with really good pace such as this.Across the adventure, you’ll be able to unlock, find and upgrade weapons. There are two types of weaponry. The direct hand to hand combat, with swords, spears and many other sharp ones. As well as the long distance ones, either from guns, or bows. Ammo is limited and you need to use melee attacks to refill your ammo, which is a fantastic mechanic, motivating players to be active. Players can and will need to upgrade their armor, weapon and skills, by gathering gold and gems, which can be obtained by slaying enemies, or pretty much anything that can be destroyed in-game. Character and weapon upgrades follow the same pattern, requiring a skill set tree to choose from. In the main hub, players can find a blacksmith, and other NPC's that will help in upgrading equipment as well as proving with extra side-quests to unlock special time based challenges. This is where the main "lootvanian" comes from, since whatever you do in Foregone, it's all about collecting new loot, and defeating those tough enemies.Blacksmith can also boost equipment effects up to three times, so there's a nice mix going, between keeping the old stuff, or just keep looking for those new stats. This mechanic also justifies going back for much earlier challenges to beat your time, or explore deeper an area that was previously a pain-in-the-neck.Aside from secrets, the game is tremendously linear, which is why I can safely say that Foregone is not a Metroindvania, despite some people claiming it to be. You do not need to backtrack in order to progress. In its defense, Foregone it's actually pretty good the way it is. Not every 2D game needs to be a metroidvania, or a roguelike experience.Another top-tier aspect of the gameplay are the Bosses. I really had a good time learning their pattern and gimmick-like behavior. They are well made, with good hit-boxes and like any other enemy, they are consistent. Which now is a good time to mention, how Foregone is fundamentally consistent in its gameplay. Bosses reflect that exceptionally well, but it's actually across the overall game. A solid and outstanding adventure with awesome gameplay.When it comes to visuals, Foregone is simple but easy to navigate and above all, it's not pretentious, which we can all appreciate. There are a handful of scenarios depicting different levels and regions as well as an amazing atmosphere across the ruins of once a beautiful city. I found the art design very likable, and definitely a must if you enjoy 2D designWith a smooth matching soundtrack, Foregone is absolutely a must if you're into a classic 2D action platformer, with tons of delicious loot, enemies, and incredible bosses. The price is on-par with the overall quality, and now that's on Steam, there's no reason not to get it. If you're unsure, wait for sale prices, you won't regret it!

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, I really did. I mean, it's got great pixel graphics, the controls are tight, responsive and intuitive. The environments look amazing and the creature/attack animations are excellent. But the idea to make every mission a timed mission was definitely a bad choice.You start each mission on a two minute timer, if you haven't finished the mission in the allotted time you're teleported back to the player hub and while yes, you get to keep the spoils from your run so you can make upgrades to your skills and gear, it's honestly just really annoying. Enemies have a chance to drop +1 second item, but if you're not close enough to pick it up as it's falling it will often cost you more time to go after it and occasionally through the level there will be a +5 second pickup to grab... but honestly it doesn't really matter. In a "Metroidvania" style game the occasional timed element should be a tool used to heighten tension and add to the story and atmosphere of a game, not a core mechanic. It just feels like a really bad decision on the dev's part and makes the game not fun to play, in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, but it feels like a lot of wasted potential. The story is boring and self-contradicting with some really hammy dialogue and voice acting. The graphics feel like they're in this weird spot between two different pixel counts; meaning they should have increased or decreased the detail to reach a better result. The movement is great, but the combat is lacking. While I like the ammo mechanic, I found most of the weapons' combos to be clunky. The daggers and scythe are the two biggest offenders, getting you caught in a multi hit combo attack from only two or three button presses.The activated abilities were a weak point, I went through the game seeing little reason to switch from surge and heal as by the time you get the others, why would you switch from the skills you've already been leveling? Some of the abilities could have benefited greatly from being a toggled ability instead of one and done activated.The level design is a glaring issue as well. While the artwork for each area had some solid themes that made each feel unique, the actual level was just a simple maze plotted through the area. You feel less like you're assaulting some enemy stronghold and more like you're traveling down a long corridor that keeps switching back on itself. This is likely as much an issue with the map being one big continuous area instead of separate rooms. The design team should have taken a nod from other metroidvanias and had a smaller map designed to be explored.Finally, I take particular issue with the item/upgrade system. Why the need for a hub with a bunch of personality-less characters was needed to make the upgrades, when it could have been done from submenus, I don't know. In such a straightforward game, it's obnoxious to have such a grind to get the equipment you want. First you have to hope the piece at the item level you want drops. Then, if it doesn't have the rolls you want, you have to go through the process of rerolling it off a side mission. There are so many possible item affixes, that you can reroll the same one multiple times and never see the affix you want. Whoever decided that each active ability should have 4-5 affixes dedicated to it, should think long and hard about how much customization a game like this actually needs.If I had the choice of 1-5 stars to give this game, I'd give it two. Parts of the skeleton are good, but the whole beastie needs a lot more love before it becomes worthwhile. As a final note, putting a random gear grind in with a new game+ mode does not make for a game with "good replayability". That's just abusing the Skinner box to get those of us obsessed with bigger/better numbers to play your game more.

_childDocuments_.review: Foregone is a VERY simple metroidvania with a satisfying and fast combat system, that unfortunately has the depth of a sun dried puddle.On the surface, Foregone seems to be a carbon copy of Dead cells, but other then graphics and combat somewhat, its doing its own thing. Its a metroidvania at heart, but dont expect this massive world filled with secrets and goodies, its honestly quite linear. The real meat and bones is the break neck pace of combat and Borderlands style of endless loot being found.Weapons are diverse and plentiful, and each have their own play style. One great thing that i really really like, is how Foregone handles guns. Your ammo is unlimited, but to get more bullets you need to land hits on enemies with your melee weapons. Enemies are fun to kill, bosses are (so far anyways) fun and not annoying to fight. All in all, its a fun system albeit very straight forward.Foregone is nothing amazing, its not a revolutionary, genre defining, must have title, but its a fun game that is open to future DLC and all in all for the price, a great time.
