_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - Foregone is a solid 2D action platformer with a unique art style and engaging combat.One of my big “problems” with how I like to play games is my inability to focus on one game at a time. I like variety and playing different games prevents me from getting bored and abandoning the stories and gameplay mechanics that I otherwise enjoy. My eyes tend to get a little bigger than my gamer stomach can handle though and I usually end up biting off more than I can chew. As much as I dislike it, the current market seems to favor long playtimes, and each new release feels like it takes longer and longer to beat. Don’t misunderstand - I love sinking my teeth into a meaty 40 hour RPG, but as the figurative and literal landscapes of video games continue to grow, I increasingly find myself at a disadvantage because of my gaming habits. The desire to play new releases mixed in with the growing backlog becomes drowned out by the other six games I’m currently playing and that will likely take me 180 hours to finally get through. That’s why Foregone was such a refreshing experience for me. It’s a tight, linear adventure with a beginning, middle, and an end that took me about six hours to roll credits on; and the best part is that it’s a really good time.In Foregone you’ll play as the first Arbiter, a biologically enhanced soldier originally designed to protect the city of Calagan. While I ended up liking the story and its themes, Foregone milks its short playtime for all its worth as it unravels its mysteries and answers your questions. In the opening couple hours I felt lost plot-wise and I had no idea why I was exploring Calagan and its depths and fighting through its hordes of enemies. Eventually everything becomes clear, and the game’s exploration of themes of regret, misplaced good intentions, and the consequences of scientific experimentation gone too far ended up meshing well together. There is a single story choice given to the character at the end of the game, which felt a touch out of place for me, but I was satisfied with the ending I picked.One of the standout features of Foregone is its absolutely stunning pixel art. The backgrounds are a treat to behold and make exploration fun. There’s a mausoleum section level that stood out to me for its huge skeletons and stonework bathed in green light; it invoked so much atmosphere and set such a great mood. There’s a variety of different environments with their own personality and distinctness, from large and elaborate temples to winding and claustrophobic caves. The Arbiter and the myriad of enemy designs are all unique and recognizable and they animate beautifully, and I also like how the 3D pixelated models contrasted with the flat 2D space. This isn’t the only thing that Foregone does well though, and the detailed locations and high-quality animation all work together in service of its excellent combat.In terms of its gameplay, Foregone places most of its emphasis on its combat mechanics. There’s a variety of different weapons to play with including a spear, shortsword, twin daggers, and my personal favorite: gunchucks. In addition to your melee weapon you’ll also have a secondary ranged weapon that recharges ammo as you hit enemies with melee attacks. With every weapon you’ll simply mash the attack button until the combo is complete, with the last hit usually packing extra punch. The challenge and depth of the combat comes from learning enemy attacks and when to dodge to avoid them. You can interrupt your combo at virtually any point to initiate a dodge without losing the combo. This led to some really awesome sequences where I’d be fighting five or six enemies on screen and dodging and jumping and air dashing around while intermingling shotgun shots to stun one enemy while I used the final blow of my combo to eliminate another in one hit all before returning to the first guy I was dealing with. This kind of timing becomes even more paramount in the boss fights, with each having unique movesets and phases and requiring you to utilize new skills you pick up along the way. I think the game falls on the easier side, I only died two or three times outside of the boss fights, but the bosses provide a solid challenge that required multiple attempts to complete, which I was happy to do because of how much fun I was having with the combat.There are some things I would have liked to see and some design decisions I don’t think really work. Foregone uses a Dark Souls inspired mechanic where you lose all your currency when you die. When you respawn at the checkpoint you can choose to regain half of the currency you had accumulated or try and return to the spot you were killed and pick up the entire amount. The game is so easy that this was never really a difficult decision to make, and for this style of 2D action game I’m not sure it adds to the experience. I also think the gear system is completely unnecessary, as you progress through the game you’ll pick up weapons and armor with a gear score and a designated rarity color. Most of the gear you pick up will be salvaged for coins which can be used to upgrade the gear with the highest base number, and you’ll rinse and repeat several times. The problem is I never noticed a difference in any of the weapons I picked up. The buffs felt meaningless and unimpactful and the game may have been better off with a simpler loot system. The platforming doesn’t present much of a challenge, and mistakes you do make have minimal consequences associated with them. I think it would have been very exciting to have some intense and challenging platforming sections to break up the combat and provide a different kind of thrill. With all of the good elements in Foregone, it’s a little disappointing that the game is held back by a few tacked on mechanics that don’t enhance the experience.Despite these flaws though, Foregone is a great experience and definitely worth your time. The campaign is short enough to warrant multiple playthroughs, and the game does offer a New Game + option to encourage you to go again. There are also some timed missions where you’re tasked with killing all the enemies before the clock runs out that are nice to have included. The enjoyable combat, gorgeous art style, and drip-feed plot all work together to provide a short but complete experience. At $20 it’s a competitive price, but is frequently on sale for much less and absolutely worth it. If you find yourself, like me, drowning underneath the weight of multiple giant games, then I recommend you check out Foregone as a refreshing palette cleanser.

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;Dr: It's a good game for a sale, I'd recommend waiting for a sale that knocks it down to $10 or lessI got this game on sale for the 2023 winter sale, and I can say it's pretty good for the sale price. I've seen some reviews talking about the physics being clunky, but I've either gotten used to it by my second playthrough, or it's not that bad. A couple of notes first; I played this game on a Dualshock 4. It has full support for the controller, including glyphs, but I'll be talking about the game from the perspective of that. For keyboard, I can't speak to it. Let's get into the good and bad. Good: It's an easy game to get good at. There's not a ton of mechanics, but once you learn that you should be jumping all the time while using guns, pairing that with the [SKILL] , combat feels so fluid, and I have fun just moving through the levels.Quickly riffing off of that, movement. You get movement skills throughout the game, and they all add to a toolkit that feels natural. My only complaint here is that they didn't do a super-metroid-type-thing, where you have the abilities throughout the whole game, but they just don't tell you about them until later. That's just a small nitpick though, and getting the abilities throughout the game give you a reason to go back through levels, and it feels awesome to plow through older levels with new abilites.Combat is a fantastic part of this game. Clearing levels of enemies is also a ton of fun, as it's a balancing act between using your guns, combat abilities, and melee. Just a quick summation, your guns are mostly better than your melee, and combat abilities trump both. However, you recharge your combat abilities by doing damage with your guns and melee, and you reload your gun by doing damage with your melee. Each weapon plays differently than the others, and having a good loadout for bosses and clearing levels is essential. Bosses are also really good. They test you, and there doesn't feel like a single boss that's a dud. Each one has interesting mechanics, and use your full toolkit. Bad:There's not a ton about this game I didn't like, so this section is gonna be full of a few nitpicks.This is not a long game. Levels are straightforward most of the time, and even though the secrets are well hidden, there's no real incentive to hunt them all out if you're not an achievement hunter like myself. Sure, you get decent weapons and some skill upgrades, but getting a weapon from a secret location kinda feels bad, since you know you're gonna replace it soon anyway. For my personal thoughts, neither good nor badThe story is a bit bare-bones, but it's not terrible. It's a simple tale, and one you can choose to interact with. There are no long, drawn out cut scenes, which I like, but the story doesn't feel too intertwined with the game. A lot of things are just hand-waived away as "you're an arbiter, this is what you can do".Art style is pretty good, i think the pixelated look on the simple models is a pretty good aesthetic, but that's not a big deal to me. All in all, it's pretty good. I'd recommend picking it up in a decent sale.

_childDocuments_.review: 6.5/10Foregone is a very so-so kind of game.On the one hand, the graphics are amazing, and the environments are very well designed. The protagonist is very well voiced, and her animations are stunningly done, even down to how fast she walks depending on how much you move the joystick.However, I felt the gameplay itself was pretty unsatisfying. After playing Dead Cells and Hollow Knight, I found myself disappointed by how my weapons didn't feel like they were bashing monster flesh, but more like smoothly cleaving through butter (while in actuality not doing much damage at all). Also, whenever I got hit by a monster, I would barely notice and then wonder why my health was always so low. Compare this to dead cells or hk, where you get a tiny vibration or sound cue or at least something to indicate your weapon has done a damage.Also, the monster types never really change throughout the game. Sure, they have more health, and sure, they get a new ability every once in a while to shoot fire instead of bullets, but there is very little variety for most of the game.While the lack of stimulating feedback was only a slight letdown, the mechanics were probably the biggest gripe for me.Specifically the dodge, which you would think is a pretty vital and standard mechanic, felt very sloppily done and only a tiny window where you actually wouldn't get hit. On the one hand, this makes you think more creatively about the movement (especially during bosses) and forces you to jump or find cover. On the other hand, it is just frustrating when you can't do what the game says you're supposed to be able to do.I could talk about the weird skill tree system or the strangely done affixes and skills, but other people probably have written better reviews on those.All in all, Foregone is not a bad game, and I appreciated the story, though a little short. However, the lack of satisfying gameplay and variety makes me longing for better titles out there. Also I think it's a bit weird they haven't made a patch or an update since release.All in all, if you keep your expectations where they should be, you'll probably have fun with this game. Just don't expect there to be a super unique part of the genre. Anyway, my opinion is that you should pick up this game if it's on sale or if you've already played all the other good rougelikes and metroidvanias and castlevanias and castlemetroids and vania-metroidlike castles.If you made it this far, thanks for listening through my rant! here's a high five with a gold star on it:,////\(*)''| |ok that honestly looks like trash

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: Foregone is an extremely solid action-platformer with great character building possibilities. The game takes place in a sci-fi world that seems vaguely influenced by ancient Greek/Egyptian culture. You play as a super soldier called an Arbiter. You are tasked with taking down a threat called the Harrow. Although the game generally does a decent job at presenting its story and setting, don't expect to have your mind blown by the its narrative elements. This is an action-platformer first and foremost. The combat is fast, fluid, and satisfying. You can switch between ranged and melee attacks on the fly. Most enemies aren't too spongy, and there's a decent variety, at least early on. The game does reuse enemies quite a bit in later levels, but to its credit the later enemies aren't just simple palette-swaps. They often behave differently than their weaker counterparts eg. firing additional projectiles or adding different status effects. Additionally, most levels add at least one brand new enemy type.Level design is rather basic, but the game does reward keen-eyed players with enough secrets to encourage exploration. Most of these secrets take the form of upgrades for your various special attacks and abilities, but might occasionally toss a powerful weapon or armour piece your way. Where the game truly shines is in the different ways it allows you to customise your character by finding, upgrading, and mixing and matching different skills, special attacks, weapon types, armour and other gear. Things start off simple, but eventually you get to a point where a single weapon attack can start a chain reaction of stuns, slowdowns, and explosions that hop from enemy to enemy. When you find a character build that works the combat is buttery smooth. Beating the game unlocks New Game +, allowing you to continue perfecting your build.In case you weren't sold yet, this game has a type of melee weapon called a Gunchuck. It's a nunchaku made out of two shotguns connected by a chain.  I'd recommend it on that alone.

Foregone has a strong emphasis on random properties for items with the possibility to adjust them some with another random chance. Though, this does not really increase the replay value.Styles to play this game are given through a skill system but it's likely for players to stick to mobility and speed improvements. The random and skill oriented properties of equipment do not support styles however. That dictates a style, when a player gets skill properties for this and that. No matter, the difference has no significant impact, which reduces replay value.The boss fights are entertaining and display some creativity here and there. Other modes of the game stick to 1 life only and 1 life only without "outpost" as ironman mode. The outpost is, where players usually work on their equipment and skill system. Solving the game and sticking to the save file allows to play it again with harder mobs and better equipment drops. It didn't really add some variety but it is okay.Foregone is certainly worth a recommentation for metroidvania fans without too many roguelike elements. Solving it once felt rewarding. Over time, you pick up on the little nuances of more advanced fighting, such as cancel actions, to improve your attack chains.Bosses are quite easy, so the devs ramp up the difficulty by throwing a ton of damage (in New Game+ mode) instead, kinda felt like they took the easy way out on this. As long as you got the mob's (and boss) mechanics figured out, it's just a matter of choosing your most favorite weapons, and effects.Game controls are quite fluid and responsive. However, you need to keep in mind that depending on the equipment, your actions can feel quite cumbersome, so you probably want to finesse it by using jump cancel, or dash cancel, or dash/jump, double jump chains.Still a fun game for the price I paid. Almost 40 hours in and I'm finishing up New Game+.

_childDocuments_.review: Just cleared it. First of all, Foregone is not a Metroidvania since it's very LINEAR. Imagine a single Dead Cells run, but longer. No intensive exploring or backtracking. You only go to the previous stages to go to secret places after you obtain the abilities. The story is just there, nothing interesting.PROS: This game is fun and pretty "short", a single playthrough only need 6-7 hours. Artstyle, great. If you like Dead Cells visual, you will like this one. The combat is really good, alternating between melee and ranged attack feels great The skills are good. I mostly only use 2 of them, the one for buff and healing. The offensive skills are good for farming, but the defensive skills are useless since you can just tank the damage then heal.Character's movement also fluid, dashing around slashing and shooting enemies while jumping all over the place is awesome, EXCEPT one thing.CONS:  The wall jump is clunky. When you press jump while clinging to the wall, the character move a little bit too far to chain the jump at the same wall. You will need to constantly move towards the wall, double jump then dash to grab the wall again. Though combat is great, I don't really like the randomized weapon passive. You will need to equip the strongest one upgrade it, then you found a stronger weapon later on, then change to that, upgrade, and so on. The game is a bit too easy (I played on "normal"). Once you get the right combo, you can go brainless mode, even against bosses, including the last one. Healing is easy since you can do it anywhere at anytime. I only died like 5 times during my playthrough, 2 of them from regular enemies. But then in NG+, its even easier. You get more health, more damage. Even though enemies hits harder, they just died too fast. But again it's still fun just jumping around zooming to the end just to get the last few achievements.Last one, the one thing I hate the most is the grind. If you want to get all of the achievements, you will get to farm a single stage over and over again to upgrade your skills.Overall, this game is good, enjoyable gameplay, but with some annoyance here and there. If its discounted, sure go for it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game, but it's also not that great, either. I'd give it a 6/10.I've played through the whole main story and the side missions and I can say I'm a bit frustrated about it, mostly because of other people's reviews and the tags...Usually I only recommend games I really like and give bad reviews to games which I really think they deserve it... To a game like Foregone, I simply wouldn't give it any review whatsoever, but, since there are so many misunderstandings about this game, I feel like I should write one to help clear things up.Going straight to the point: This is NOT a MetroidVania, it's NOT a Roguelike, and it's NOT a Souls-like. Further details at the end of the review.It is an action-platformer hack'n'slash-esque game, much in the likes of Mega Man X/Zero games, where you can dash and slash through everything and shoot bullets to hit enemies from afar (but the character has auto-aim and so she can fire at angles too, and there's no charged attacks). It has a random loot system (yup, gear with random stats) and it's predominantly linear. You use both a melee and a ranged weapon. Different weapon types comes with different perks. There's a very simple passive skill tree and you also can equip 2 active skills, and each one of them require their own energy in order to use. Their energies are restored as you hit and kill enemies.As I saw a few reviews in which people complain about some mechanics or level design/enemy placement, I'd like to take this opportunity to comment on those as well: the level design isn't something memorable, but it's not bad and in some occasions I've found myself using the terrain to my advantage, like hitting a melee enemy on a lower ground from the edge of a higher ground because the enemy wouldn't jump to hit me or jumping on platforms/hiding behind walls to avoid enemy fire. Enemy placement is actually pretty good, sometimes you need to be quick to dash through a corridor and not get hit by a ranged enemy or simply time your dodge or go back to jump out of the way when it fires at you and shoot from afar (most of the time I was using a shotgun, so usually I had to either get to the enemy first or go back, let it shoot and then dash after it).About the mechanics, my only real problem was with the auto-aim that sometimes would hit a grounded enemy (even when it was not engaged in combat) instead of a flying one, or one in a higher place, that was coming after me, even when I jumped to get closer to it, resulting in some free hits for them/drawing unwanted attention, but no big deal.Other pros and cons:++ I liked the variety of weapons, both melee and ranged, although I got stuck with daggers and shotgun, because they are OP;++ Controls feel pretty good and alternating between sliding and air dashing is fun;+- Unlike Mega Man, enemies don't hurt you upon touching, only when attacking. And you can't pass through them easily, except when dodging, making it easier to hit them with melee attacks. But they can also push you out of platforms because of that. I failed a mission once because I was pushed to a hole from which I couldn't return and the enemy was left alive...+- Tether didn't feel useful for the player to use (but it's ridiculously useful for the enemies, forcing you to stop moving or at least stay near the hook point so you won't take too much damage; in this sense, I liked the idea as it changes the game completely) as the enemies don't move much once engaged, even when having knockback effect on the shotgun, dashing to make the enemy go after you and a +148% damage on break (was pretty useful on Demeter, though); same thing goes for Stasis and Paralysis; the shotgun's stun was pretty useful to interrupt enemies, though;-- Explosive Charge didn't feel useful as well, as most enemies would be dead by the time the bomb triggered and Bulwark, well, I had Barrier so... this leaves only Plague, Leech and Aftershock as viable effects;-- From all the active skills, except Restoration, Barrier was the only one I felt useful, with the Aftershock skill branch along with a bunch of aftershock damage perks from the gear lol.-- Most passive skills feel too costly but pretty useless (for instance, there are these two skills which give you 5% of damage or health at MAX level, but each one of them costs 775 points to reach max level);-- I don't think the random loot system for a linear game like this was a good idea. It only forced me to keep using s***ty equipment to save money for Rarity 5 gear, and they only started dropping near the end, and so I went on the missions only after that so I could reroll their stats for something I'd find useful and then every other drop served no purpose, didn't even bother picking them up.The whole game is linear and separated by levels, instead of being a semi-open-world, but without a clear stage selection screen/menu. Upon completing a level, you go straight to the next one. No results screen. And you can replay levels, even choosing to start mid-stage, so I can see why people easily mistake it with a MetroidVania.You have this hub-like town, the Outpost, in which you can upgrade your gear/skills or go to side missions (which works more like challenges in a modified/reworked level than side quests, pretty much like the Missions from some Sonic games). And you can use the Outpost's transporter to pick a level/checkpoint (the closest you got to a stage select screen). You can access the Outpost whenever you reach a transporter in a level, which works like the game's checkpoints. Your health and skills even are restored whenever you reach one. You cannot, however, use the transporter to go to another transporter, except for the one on the Outpost. You need to go to the Outpost first and then use the one there if you want to go to a different level/transporter.You get new abilities upon defeating some bosses, but you don't really need to backtrack to previous levels to find power-ups or new areas to explore. No health upgrades, no ammo upgrades, no new area/level to unlock with your new ability. There are only secret rooms, and the majority of them are filled with random loot that you can drop anywhere. The minority have minor skill upgrades and lore, but nothing really game-changing, so it feels more like collectibles for the achievement.Simply put, combat is easy and you don't get yourself learning how to deal about specific enemies differently. You don't really need to time your attacks, learn movesets/patterns or stay alert to guard/parry (you can't even guard or parry, just slide-dodge), not even when facing the bosses (I've defeated all of them on the first try, except for the final boss, that I was overconfident I would deal with it without managing my health, like the others lol; but I believe playing on harder difficulty would demand a few pattern memorizations, like one does when doing a Mega Man run without exploiting bosses' weaknesses or no damage runs). You won't die often and I believe you can grind the missions to drop new gear or get money to upgrade your gear if you get stuck in a boss fight.The only Souls-like element it has is the "drop all your money/upgrade currency you got on you upon death but you can grab it all again if you reach your death point".It has some form of environmental storytelling, but I personally don't think that's a Souls-like element, being present in many other games that came before Soulsborne games (Valve's games, for instance).The game is not a dungeon crawler and, like I said on the MetroidVania section, it's linear and separated by levels, and these are not procedurally generated. Dying only costs you your upgrade currency, your progress after the last checkpoint and nothing more and there's no permadeath.

_childDocuments_.review: Forgone is a relatively short game of tight combat and cool visual style that is unfortunately shrouded by the extremely predictable plot and some outdated tropes or retreads of happenings in similar games. I do not have much to say about the sound track. It did not particularly strike me, as it didn't really feel especially connected to what was going on in game, mostly being generic sounding orchestral music in my mind. Maybe that's just me. The best way to describe Forgone is a linear action platformer with elements from a variety of other genres. Dead Cells seems comparable to it in terms of artstyle and some aspects of combat (though the pixel-esque art appears more 3D and alive in Forgone, which is cool). This game has a very similar relationship to the metroidvania genre as Doom 2016/Eternal does (linear upgrade progression with hidden optional upgrades). Weapons and equips are handled like a simplified version of Borderlands (basically you always equip the higher damage item, so no complexity in terms of weapon choice exists, whether you see that as good for pickup and play or boring; I find it a little silly because you pretty much won't want to pick up most equips you come across, but you also won't know how two items of the same colour-tier compare until you pick it up and inevitably take a few minutes to empty your backpack of newly-useless equips after a certain amount of time).You will not want or need to fight most enemies (maybe more in the early game to rack up skill tree stuff, but these trees fill pretty quickly), but you will want optional upgrade pickups. The game forces you to face enemies with keys above their heads to progress through various doors. Good to know which enemies are mandatory, since fighting every enemy would be unnecessarily tedious. There are optional missions, but the first one felt somewhat unbalanced when I first stumbled upon it, so I decided not to do them altogether. There's really nothing to lose from skipping them entirely. I did not use the weapon/equip upgrade station once, I did not feel like it was necessary. Teleporters are convenient in the case of trying to locate upgrades you may have missed, but having to go back and forth between hub and levels just to spend your skill points and/or coins could have been avoided by having the shop keepers between levels like in Dead Cells. Bosses are actually pretty fun, but the tired trope of repeating them was executed here in a disappointing and entirely predictable way. The plot and speech is very surface level and nothing comes as a surprise. I am sure the emphasis was intended to be on incorporating many inspirations into tight gameplay, but I think more could have been done writing wise. There was really no need to bring in the infection/parasite aspect from countless metroidvanias, it's just not adding to anything here. Endings do not really have much bearing on anything, choose the one you think you will be most happy with, and if for some reason you really love the game, get the other ending in new game +. After some research, I see now that BigBlueBubble created the casual MySingingMonsters series and a card combat game called PowerChord. That's three categories of games including Forgone, and six games total. Forgone is the only action platformer so far from the development team, and honestly it is not bad. It is just bare bones in terms of several aspects of what a game of this genre can do to engage a player. Clearly the team is solid, and will probably continue to do great work in the future. Hopefully they take on some more action platformers that take into consideration what makes an action platformer awesome on all fronts.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite having light metroidvania trappings and a visual style similar to Dead Cells, the best way to describe Foregone is as a sidescrolling ARPG in the same vein as Diablo. The level design is very basic, the narrative thin, and the combat and platforming are satisfying but by no means exceptional. Those things don't lie at the heart of Foregone's appeal, however. This is a game about optimising your character build, finding synergies, grinding loot, and rerolling affixes on items until you break the game. There's a heavy incentive to replay levels so that you can gather more gear and currency, all the while playing around with new builds to see what you like and dislike. There's really nothing about the game that breaks the mould - almost everything Foregone does has been seen before in some fashion - but the realisation of the core action-looter concept is very strong. This is the kind of game you can load up knowing exactly what you're getting. Perfect for playing while you have a podcast on. Finding all the secrets, completing all the challenges, and going through the experience again on new game+ even adds a substantial amount of longevity to the playtime.Not one that'll blow your mind if you're looking for something super new and fresh, but a very satisfying action platformer for those who love the punchy combat and loot collection of ARPGs in a side-scrolling format.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: Foregone is about a being called "The Arbiter" who fights to defeat a manifestation of malevolence called "The Harrow" that is slowly consuming all life and mutating it into monstrous enemies. Let's however get this out of the way immediately: The game's art style and fast paced combat is reminiscent to Dead Cells, however that's where the similarities end. It's not a roguelite, and is only meant to be played through at least twice due to two different endings. It's more like the quintessential side scroller adventure game, with a Dead Cells-esque style to complement it.Graphics: 7/10 - Graphics are generally an opinionated deal, but if you like Dead Cells' look, you'll probably like Foregone's. It's an interesting style of pixellation that allows fluid animation. I personally am fine with it, but not everyone is into this style. Gameplay: 7/10 - Combat and traversal are versatile, but at the same time very basic. You have a button for melee and a button for ranged, along with one for dodging and two for abilities you can set. The versatility comes with how many different weapons and abilities you can use. For melee weapons, you have shortsword, greatsword, spear, scythe, daggers, and gunchucks (They sound interesting and pack a punch, but they're basically just nunchucks with explosions). Ranged weapons are bow, pistol, shotgun, automatic rifle, semi-rifle, shock pistol, and probably a few more I've forgotten. When it comes to abilities, there are quite a few and all are viable in their own way. Shields, energy blasts, "overdrive" mode, healing, and so on. Very good and interesting to use, and they allow varied playstyles.Another thing to note is the skill tree. While it won't completely change how you play, there are different skill branches you can go down to get certain boons. You can also reset the skill tree at any time by refunding specific nodes (including Catalyst nodes. Catalysts are find throughout the game and allow you to unlock more branches throughout a skill tree). All abilities also have their own mini-skill trees and catalysts. Lots of options here.However, that's where the versatility ends. With how robust the offerings are weapon/skill/ability-wise, actual combat is a bit overly basic. Your melee attack is only one basic button combo spam and a jump attack. There are no extra button combinations to do different attacks. No dash attack. Nothing. There IS a system in place that allows you to continue your combo in between movement abilities, but that actually can be a hindrance at times so your mileage may vary.Music: 8/10 - While nothing mind-blowing, everything fits well with what's going on in the game. There's a rather melancholy song that plays after boss battles that add a feeling of sadness, for reasons you'll learn throughout the story. Speaking of...Story: 7/10 - I have two reasons for giving it a 7 instead of a 5 or an 8. Let's start with...The Positive: The story is surprisingly intricate, and the lore surrounding everything that's going on is actually quite interesting. From a church cult to a military war to experimentation and to certain things the Arbiter lives to regret - everything was quite interesting and as one who loves a good story, I was intrigued...however... The Negative: The way the story is conveyed is mostly through journals and books strewn throughout the levels. I can understand the need for this, as the game's focus is clearly gameplay. However, due to how you barely learn anything else from any other sources, the story feels disjointed and it can sometimes be hard to tell what exactly it is you're fighting for other than to stop the Harrow. The Arbiter has a few lines to speak during her journey, and she finds a few things that give the story more intrigue, but overall I just feel like there should've been more. Like, there are certain characters just spoken of in one or two lines of dialogue, but they're immensely important to what's going on in the story. Where did they go? Are they dead? Are they alive? We just don't entirely know. The Ending (no spoilers): There are two different endings to get, and if you want the achievement for them, MAKE SURE YOU FINISH THE GAME ON THE SAME SAVE SLOT BOTH TIMES. If you make a new game and get the different ending there, you will not get the achievement. If you'd like to know how to get both endings, well it's insanely simple and you'll see how right at the end of the game.New Game+ kicks in right after you defeat the final boss, and all enemies are harder while also dropping more powerful loot. As for the Ending's story, I'm going to spoiler this even though I will be as vague as possible with my opinion of it. I understand some people can get turned off on a game when someone even mentions how they feel about its ending. So for those who don't mind knowing my opinion, go ahead and read. If you do mind, just skip this: Achievement Hunters: The achievements aren't hard at all to get here. I 100%'d the game without too much problem. Run of the mill "get every upgrade", "find every secret", etc. There's a few tiny curve balls where you have to use a specific ability to get an achievement, but it wasn't hard at all. Nothing is missable, and no achievement is connected to a boss other than those that ask you to defeat them. In New Game+ you can fight the bosses again if you wanted to anyways by just re-visiting their arena after teleporting out of the area.Conclusion: Overall I'd give this game a solid 7/10. It was fun and enjoyable. Had some challenge as well, because enemies DO hit rather hard and certain areas have the perfect mix of enemies to give you a tough time. Sadly its basic combat leaves much to be desired, and I truly wish the story was more robust, as its lore was very interesting. I am not left satisfied thanks to this, but at the very least I enjoyed my time with this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Foregone is a side-scrolling action RPG. Taking place in a fictional city named Calagan, players take on the role of an arbiter, strongest soldier Calagan creates. They must collect items and gears to battle through hordes enemies, fearsome bosses and ultimately, save the crumbling city from corrupting force known as The Harrow. At first glance, Foregone can easily be regarded as a clone of Dead Cells, which is both good and bad. In many ways, both games share similar pros and cons, so the comparison is palpable and will be recurring in this review. If you enjoy Dead Cells, Foregone is a good game to pick up, albeit underwhelming. Nonetheless, I still recommend this game to those who love playing side-scrolling  action games.The similarity begins here. Foregone takes the inspiration from Dead Cells in term of art design by intentionally rendering 3D objects into pixel, which is a great plus if you are in to this kind of art style. However, in contrast to Dead Cells' simple level backgrounds, Foregone goes beyond and adds more details to each level. Doing so not only makes the whole level more vibrant and detailed, it can also tell stories or hint some lore about the places you visit. Take the starting area for example. When you walk out the forest, sun shines upon your face. A vast view of kingdom walls lay before your eyes. You cannot help but wonder what kind of adventure await you on this journey.Kinda like Dead Cells timed gate and perfect kill streak. Activating beacons in each area rewards you with side missions in the hub world. They challenges you with a variety of contest from timed extermination to obstacle courses. This feature adds some depth and skill testaments for players to hone their skills and reflexes. Later side missions even provide some conditions to spice up the difficulties. Moreover, playing these missions is also a good way to farm some gears suitable for the current level.There are six melee weapons and five ranged weapons in Foregone. Each weapon offers different playtime, players are encouraged to mix them up to find the perfect combo or the one that is comfortable their preferred playtime. Ranged weapons are all fun and strong in their ideal situation. Some melee weapons, like Scythe and Falchion(two-handed great sword), are not viable or straight out not fun to use in side missions and later levels. Their movesets are usually slow and outshines by faster weapons in terms of DPS. Guarantee stun effect is a nice bonus, but the levels generally favor faster pace and damage. Either for a sense of achievement and progression or for a test to see how lucky one is, loot-based drop is a simple, great way to reward a player for their efforts. Foregone does it well for the most parts. The drops are rewarding and guaranteed to be better the more you progress. There are two problems for me. The first one is that armors, rings, and emblems should have more variable and unique buffs rather than just health boost. It can give the players more choice and spaces to work out their ideal character builds. The second one is to make certain gears drop from certain enemies or certain levels instead of completely random. It could boost replayability of the previous areas and also give the player's option to farm for their favorite weapons.This is where Dead Cells successfully avoids but Foregone unfortunately suffers. The level design lacks complexities in both game. The reason Dead Cells can overlook this flaw is because the general flow of the game is faster. Players can easily blaze through the levels in seconds. However, Foregone does not have the luxury of it. Big layout of levels accompanied with slower combat makes the problem apparent in the long run. Simple platforming and puzzles of flipping switches do not help the situation at all.Therefore, in my opinion, Foregone can be a better game if the developers lead more towards the metroidvania aspect. The game already has the feature of obtaining abilities that can help you traverse through area that you cannot previously. The developers just need to connect each zone and rearrange some parts of the world to make the linear story experience wider, more rewarding for exploration and more replayability.

_childDocuments_.review: Story:	The usual. 	But one thing I have to call them out on is: Level Design:	Solid.	Exploration is rewarded with secret areas and loot.	The pixel art environments are gorgeous.	A few of the level layouts start to feel reused towards the end of the game. (Ex: The twisty layout that alternates the path you need to take to progress.)Weapons:	I liked the variety, but once you find the late-game weapon that has more stats than all the others, it basically locks you into using that exclusively which sucks.	Pro-tip: Pick the gear with the biggest numbers.Abilities:	I only used 3 the entire game. The others just didn't seem worthwhile (with the exception of Overdrive).	Dash - Because movement in a platformer is paramount.	Heal - Because being not dead is a positive experience.	Bulwark - Because the last 2 bosses were weirdly stronger than all the others and I needed to live and Dash seemed to fall off on damage vs bosses.Controls: 	The controls are surprising smooth for almost* the entire game.	*The  feels really clunky.Bugs: 	Bug?: When jumping + melee + shooting in combination, every once in a while the player ends up facing to the right like the direction the character is facing is being reset to default in the code.		This seemed to happen more frequently in boss fights. 	Bug?: When an enemy is on the edge of a platform that the player is trying to get on,			the player can get "stuck" in a loop:			1. Getting kicked off the ledge by character collision with enemy.			2. Dashing back to the ledge.			3. Go to 1 or kill the enemy with ranged weapon. 			It's a minor complaint, but not unmanageable. 	QoL fix: Make the gold, blue, and time trial clocks that fall out of enemies just magnet towards the player from any distance.			I hate backtracking for anything, especially schmeckles. TL;DR:	Should you play it? Yeah; it isn't groundbreaking, but it feels good to play.	(This is not financial advice.)

What it doesn't take from it are those little ease of use features that go unnoticed when you play DC because they just make things go as you intended. For example, you character turning automatically towards an enemy when you land next to them and attack but for some reason you were facing the other way. It has many annoying little things instead, like most attacks pushing enemies away, but there not being fall damage for them, so you attack them, get them to a sliver of health, they fall from the platform because your attacks pushed them off and now you have to jump behind them to finish them off, in DC they just die from the fall and give you the gold automatically so you can move on. It doesn't handle the space enemies and you occupy very well, if you jump into a platform with an enemy on the edge, since you can't both be on the same place at the same time, it pushes you away, usually off the platform, so you kind of rebound. All these little things add up to a more frustrating and annoying experience than it should be, it doesn't flow as well, it isn't as smooth or as painless as Dead Cells.All that being said, it's not bad. it looks good, it has a simple story but it does the job of giving some context to what you're doing, there is some diversity of builds (more would be nice though), and the overall mechanics and progression are fine. If you want to play a game of this type and you played too much Dead Cells already you might as well give it a shot.

One complain is character sprites can not pass through enemies while walking and it will makes weid collision. _childDocuments_.review: Played this game on epic while it was in beta and I'm so glad It fully released on steam. Its pixelated but at the same time graphically beautiful and the animation is so crisp. The game delivers a soothing soundtrack with a really nice art style that really makes the game nice to explore. While in the begging it seems like there are limited enemies and a set path, as you progress that will change drastically. The vast variety of enemies and their crazy move sets make the game so enjoyable to play. For example one enemy can teleport above your head and pound you to a pulp while another guy is throwing his dual shields at you. later on in the game you will be drifting trough hordes of enemies that will come at you with all kinds of attacks and directions and when taking them all on at once makes you will feel like a God. The weapons are by far some of the coolest I've ever seen in a side scroll-er, like GUNCHUCKS?!?! It's really sad to see that this game isn't getting the recognition it deserves and I hope that people realise this is not some dumb Dead cells copy but a mechanically beautiful game with so much creativity.

_childDocuments_.review: Less than an hour in and /very/ impressed. I'm a sucker for metroidvanian games, and this one looks incredibly promising. Instead of the normal progress-to-get-double-jump-and-dash-etc-etc-etc the game focuses on acquiring powered versions (pretty quickly you get a dash augment that does damage as you pass through enemies), new weapons (and there appear to be a pretty decent number, both melee and ranged), and upgrading weapons through a trade-in-old-stuff-and-upgrade-good-stuff system. There's also a timed side-mission system that I've only tried once. Oh, and a world map with fast travel. The gameplay is very smooth, combat is intuitive and fun, and the variety of ways different weapons interact with enemies is great. It's almost as pretty as Dead Cells (some more dazzling lighting here and there would bring it on par in a hurry). Like I said, I've only just started, but there's tons of potential. It's closer to Dead Cells than Hollow Knight or Ori, but fans of any of those could potentially really get into this -- especially DC. Easily worth the $15 I got it for on sale.Now I'll shut up and get back to playing my new favorite metroidvanian!

name: KUNAI
detailed_description: A traumatic event has shaken the balance of the world. Human life has been almost wiped out by the evil A.I. Lemonkus. Robots roam free across the earth. You take control of Tabby, a killer robot infused with the soul of an ancient warrior. Start out with nothing, progress and increase in strength by killing enemy robots to unlock abilities, weapons and kick-ass ninja tricks. Explore a world filled with secrets, hidden passages and mysterious characters. KUNAI is all about movement and agility. Use your ninja mobility to reach places where no normal robot could ever go. Explore the different pixel-art environments of KUNAI, each with a minimalistic palette, while Tabby makes cute faces. Use a variety of ninja tricks to move around the world and unleash your deadly arsenal of weapons to fight your way through armies of evil machines, rogue androids, and mindless mechs to maximize your badassness. ● Fast-paced action platforming with a grappling twist. ● Silky smooth movement mechanics tuned to the pixel. ● Lots of juicy exploding robots crafted with care (note: screenshake can be turned off at your own leisure). ● Kunai-driven grappling fun with swinging included to amplify those deadly ninja drops. ● A wide variety of places to explore, ranging from a fallen city, floating airships to artificial deserts and more! ● Unique art style, with every area having its own color palette taking you back to the early days of gaming. ● Combat mechanics and weapons in abundance to slice, dice and fire your robotic foes to pieces. ● Friendly and not so friendly robots to meet along the way including Earl, Chief and the evil A.I. Lemonkus. ● Rocking soundtrack with lots of 16-bit references blasting into your ears. ● You are a NINJA TABLET. ‘Nuff said.

short_description: KUNAI is a quirky, fast-paced action platformer. You play as Tabby, a tablet who joins the fight against a robot uprising. Use your kunai and ninja parkour skills to stop Lemonkus, the A.I.-gone-evil that almost wiped out all human life.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the trailer you're going to love the game, period.  I've been looking forward to Kunai for awhile but all my expectations were smashed by the outstanding reality on display.  The most important thing to me in a game like this is always "feel", and my god does Kunai deliver.  The controls are CRISPY.  You get some very early movement upgrades (via the games namesake) and it's just super satisfying zipping around as Tabby.  You actually feel like a ninja.  I would say the movement feels even better than something like The Messenger.  This has more modern controls with jump sensitivity and the ability to attack in all four cardinal directions. Kunai has quite a bit of Hollow Knight influence in the gameplay, but the tone is much less somber and the action is fast-paced.  Highly recommended.  I've only got 3 hours in but I'm so smitten with this game.  Can't wait to sink more time into it.  I DEFINITELY didn't take a day off work to play this on release....

_childDocuments_.review: is a side-scrolling action-packed 2D platformer with a bit of metroidvania mixed in as well. Some hidden rooms with treasures, special weapons, H.A.T.S. you can wear, and more! The fluidity on controller was really exceptional as well, so I’m quite happy with my overall experience playing through it.The premise of the story centers around your controllable character, lovingly called “Tabby”, who escapes a facility, and is then deemed to be the one and only “chosen one” from prophecy, who can set things right and get the world back in order. There’s an evil entity out there, and your job is to power up and stop it! Settings and plot are nice, and while it’s not heavily story-based, the extras you can buy for upgrades along with appearance changes, and the relatively lighter difficulty make this an excellent choice for anyone looking for a game that kind of fits into this kind of a category.  You will make use of your kunai, as the game title hints at, which is kind of like a grappling hook. You can get this enhanced later as you go, acquire a few extra side weapons, and then buy some upgrades to make your life easier as you progress. Don’t forget to check out the map once you get it!  While secret rooms are not on there, it’s still helpful for finding other stuff, and will tell you how many treasures are in each zone.  I wish it were more specific on what each treasure has, or broke down into detail kind of what that zone has left to acquire, but the layout is still pretty decent.Overall not too hard - I did find the final fight a bit frustrating, and without spoiling anything, wasn’t able to perform an action I should have at one point, which was a bit annoying.  Mostly had a good flow with it though, focusing on moving around the map, acquiring new tools to make more progress, and then gradually building up your health/gear/sword powers and so forth.  Definitely a likable game here for me!Controller feels great with this.  Very responsive for the most part.  I had little trouble at any point.  Much smoother than a lot of games with jumping and the timing of various aspects.  Sometimes charge moves didn’t register though, for whatever reason. That’s really the only thing that bugged me with controls as I played.This is not very difficult compared to some metroidvanias and other genres I played. Final battle is a bit challenging, as it took me a handful of tries to get used to, but otherwise not too tough in general. I like that about it… Some games I’ve played will make things too difficult, and I will lose interest if it doesn’t feel like it is worth the effort, so I am glad this one is fairly balanced.  I think most people would fare pretty well overall in this game as they got used to it.Nice little cutscene animations here and there. I liked that. Kept the game interesting having slight change of pace things like that going on in battles, or in the story bits and so forth. Just a few on certain things, but it was mixed in well.The upgrading system was nice for your weapon and also for skills and gear you get. While you don’t have a ton of various items, they are all useful in their own way here and there for random stuff.  Pretty good balancing - making them all fairly functional depending on the situation.Levels were all fun, and I felt the overall layout was good. Music fit the game well, and everything clicked for me. I thought the overall effectiveness of the character, the scenery, other npcs, and bosses was nice. It was not super-immersive story-wise, but it has its charms.It’s a bit convoluted. Like I mention about immersiveness, on the flip-side of the nice settings, the story elements were kind of light. Go here and do this. Now that you have this thing, go over here and do this.  Stuff like that.  Not enough details on why I needed to get things, how they knew about them, and other reasons make me feel the story could be worked on to be more detailed so that it all makes a bit more sense as to why I am doing what I am doing as the game moves along.The price is pretty high for the amount of time I put into the game. I think there should be a lot more content to warrant paying anything near full price for this. Maybe half the price is pretty reasonable though.  Even then it’d be a coin-flip kind of deal for me on half price.Needs more weapons, gadgets, upgrades, and levels, or a lower price tag. It’s just a little under-developed for my liking on all fronts there. Still in and of itself a good game. I just feel like there should have been maybe double the amount of stuff in the game itself on all fronts. Something like that anyway.  Maybe in the future there can be more additional content to balance it out with that asking price.The final boss area has something around the second phase where you have to press a button. This did not show up for me one of the times I tried fighting.  Not sure if anyone else encountered this issue, but it may have just been a one time glitch for me for whatever reason. Still kind of frustrating at the time, especially since the controls were very good throughout the rest of the game overall.While I do recommend playing this just based on the game, I do not suggest paying full price, or anywhere near it. Great fun to be had, but I’d aim for around the halfway mark. Still one I would suggest getting at a good sale, if it drops that low or lower. You will not regret it if you’re into this type of game style. It has a good mix of action and some small RPG-like elements on the upgrades. The metroidvania isn’t too intense, but it’ll make you have to hit up various areas multiple times if you are looking for all the treasures and such.It’s pretty solid, but just needs more content. I recommend this at the right price zone. The grappling is great, the weapons are fun to use, though I mostly used my base sword, and the maps have a lot of secret areas in each zone. Environments clicked, controls are responsive, and it has a nice simplicity to it. Nice little hidden gem though! Put it on your list of games to play, but if you really have an itch to slash up some bad guys, make sure that asking price is “slashed” a bit first. You’ll get at least five or ten hours out of it if you’re an avid explorer, and it doesn’t give you too much trouble along the way. I do not regret playing this one bit. Deserves a bit more attention! Very fun game!Special thanks to  for their support!

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly wish I could recommend this game, especially for younger gamers, but I can't.  Metroidvanias are probably my favourite types of game, aside from the Dark Souls series.  So I'm not averse to difficult games, in fact I enjoy the challenge.This game, however, fails to be a fun challenge, and instead provides nothing but pure irritation.  All the opening areas are far too easy, which is what made me think it was a kids game.  As soon as you get to the Crypto Mines, and then the Mountain, however, you see the game open up to become a completely irritating "challenge" wherein the difficulty comes mainly from the poor controls.  Trying to get pinpoint accuracy with the kunai is far too annoying to actively want to master.  You don't aim at what you want to hit, you just have to hope you've lined yourself up correctly and hit the left or right trigger to shoot them left or right at an approximately 45 degree angle.  It just isn't good enough in my opinion, when you are expected to be jumping over things, dodging fireballs, and hitting a disappearing block from the precisely correct angle and height in order to let go at exactly the correct moment to launch yourself upwards without hitting off something and falling back down.  Think about the grappling hook in the original Worms game, and stick it into an action platformer.  It isn't good enough.By the time I got through the first section of the Mountain boss, only for it to cut to a vertical climbing section where the camera constantly moves, and if you don't make it up quick enough (with no clue where the next climbable point is), using the sub-par controls, you die pissed me off.  When I then died because of the aforementioned issues, only to be spawned back at the start of the fight, facing the first round of extremely irritating climbing and platforming which makes up the "fight", I quit.To make it clear, games I've enjoyed completing in the genre include Hollow Knight, Ori and the Blind Forest, Salt and Sanctuary, Dark Devotion, Unworthy, The Messenger, Axiom Verge, and Guacamele among others.  I haven't given up on this game because of difficulty, but because it is extremely irritating.On the positives for the game:  the art and music, and sound design overall are lovely.  The enemies could do with having a bit more character about them, because they pale in comparison to the player character Tabby.  I don't mean they are in any way bad though, as they are just as lovely as everything else visually.  Tabby is a really endearing character though, and I do think that it could become the star of a series.  The collectable hats were a nice touch, although I'd rather they had fewer hats, but each of them impact the gameplay in some way.If you don't think the irritating factors will annoy you, I totally recommend giving this a go, as I do think there's a worthwhile product in there hampered by poor controls and too many irritating moments from Crypto onwards.  Everything before there was great, if overly easy.   If you think this might make you want to smash your controller though, I'd say avoid it.  If there was a middle thumb button, I'd hit it for this one.  Because there isn't I need to hit the thumbs down.I really wish the devs the best with regards to this game, and I hope it becomes a franchise.  With better level design and a tweaked control system, I think they could be on to a winner with future titles.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely my most favorite robot game! If you liked Cavestory or Metroid I'd give this game a try!Pros:-Great artwork, from splash screens to the sprites. The limited palettes leaves some to the imagination! The music was lovely and enhanced the atmosphere of the environments. The characters are really cute too, I have a weakness for monitorheads hehe... The dialogue was also charming, I had few chuckles!-The areas were fun to climb!-Simple combat, kill to heal. Your sword is pretty much all you need to deal with enemies although the side weapons can make things easier! There's certainly some power progression as you get further along. I really appreciate that you can attack in 4 directions!-Many things to collect! Especially hats which allow customization-The upgrades are all optional and are surprisingly priced so that you could buy all of them by the end of the game if you are looking to 100% complete it-The marker system was handy to keep track of old places where you could use newfound abilities! I appreciate that the markers can be set to different colors-The call function is useful if you forget what you were supposed to do-The bosses felt adequately challenging!-Death is a slap on the back! You don't lose your currency or anything when dying!Cons:-Some areas were narrow so it became less fun to traverse since you couldn't grapple around as much-Combat may feel clunky when trying to weave sidearms and your sword-Lack of a fast travel system, which could make it tiresome to walk from place to place-There are some instakill spots, but save points are plentiful enough that there isn't much of a problem-It may take some getting used to the grapple range before it becomes second nature-Some cutscenes play after every death once you reach a location (but at least you can skip)-Lack of locations where chests have been opened may cause you to backtrack to the same chest more than once-You can't select a different area of the map to look in to see its markers/chests lootedMinor Complains:-Lack of a codex, I'd love to read more about the world and its inhabitants! If only the call function commented on more specific areas too!-The story is a little shallow, but I love it nonetheless!-There was a cutscene that didn't run all the way, causing my game to softlock-There was a hat that is easily missed >:(-One npc blows up but keeps respawning. Hmmm...-One enemy gets stuck on a ledge and keeps making a sound-I feel like the sidearms could be used more against enemies, perhaps some that require you to use a certain one before you can use your sword?I hope this game gets a sequel, it was really well made! It was definitely worth the purchase!

_childDocuments_.review: KUNAI. It is a metrobenia action game produced by TurtleBlaze and published by The Arcade Crew. As you may know,  The Arcade Crew is a relatively new publisher, but some of their staff are from Dotemu, mainly veterans for the arcade videogame industry. The kunai is commonly associated with the ninja, and it could be used as a multi-functional weapon. We can infer that this game is related to such a theme.Gamers have always been looking for a good metroidvania. This game may satisfy your thirst. There are clever movement tricks, interesting battles, and brilliant movements through using KUNAI. With this weird robot made of recycled trash, you will explore the post-apocalyptic world. Maybe this is somewhat similar to a game called Messenger. Nevertheless, there are at least some interesting additions to this game. Slow motion and chain attacks in the air are unique fun to this game. The game experience is great overall, and this is a neat ninja action game.KUNAI. This is a fast paced action game themed on the ninja. Especially if you liked the game of metroidvania, this game can be a good choice. Despite some glitches, the game offers quite neat gameplay. As you begin to adapt to the hardcore ninja tricks, a unique feature of the game, it will ensure consistent fun until the end. If you can afford it, try this game. Recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: KUNAI

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Yes, as long as you don't mind running around as a tablet with a sword and slashing evil computers.It's a platformer, Metroidvania style, with fluid and dynamic movement, medium sized levels, and with save points that bring you back to life when you have died. Your special equipment are two kunais to climb up walls, or you can simply swing on them like Tarzan. Although the levels are not that big, it is sometimes a bit unclear what to do next and you have to backtrack and explore. There are hidden areas with treasure (or new items), your tablet can get new abilities & upgrades. The difficulty is average, even I could kill the first boss in the first try. It does get harder later, of course.Join the revolution of the blue computers fighting the red computers, controlled by an evil AI.The graphic is in pixel art, using only a few colors. Looks good. Gamepad works fine.Retro art platformer with tight controls.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is OK, but doesn't shine when compared to similar gems like Hollow Knight.The game is a joy to control, but none of the platforming pushes the player much at all - this is especially glaring after playing Guacamelee 2, which has stellar platforming sections that are both challenging and fun. Enemy design is another weak spot, with most enemies being entirely forgettable, or in the worst cases frustratingly unfun (the ferro boss and the final boss are particularly egregious with this).The art style is interesting and unique, and everything is generally animated well. The reduced color palette does make the map a little harder to navigate due to the way zones are generally similar in appearance.If you are a metroidvania fanatic this game is probably worth picking up. If you haven't already played Hollow Knight, Ori, Guacamelee 1/2, Timesplitters, Bloodtained, Steamworld dig 2, Axiom Verge, or Environmental Station Alpha... I'd probably recommend those first.
_childDocuments_.name: KUNAI

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game..............but it's not a metroidvania. I really do not like developers calling their completely linear game a metroidvania. If they had called it an Action Platformer then I wouldn't give it a negative review. I like action platformers, but they are charging 16.99 and calling it a Metroidvania? Why? There is literally nothing to gain from backtracking (except health upgrades, but it's a risk to backtrack knowing you might just get a useless hat instead). There is also a hat collecting mechanic that really really wastes your time. Every time you discover a secret or finish an arena expecting some cool lore or an upgrade, you are punished with a stupid hat that HAS NO USE IN GAME. That's right - the hats have no part in the story, progression, or gameplay. I suspect they added the hats because they realized they didn't create any other upgrades besides the ones the game funnels you into that are necessary for progression. The only upgrade you can get by backtracking is health upgrades and you simply don't need them. The charge attack takes all the gameplay away from you by auto-aiming you at every enemy.At first this felt cool, but it became boring very very fast.  It's basically "hold attack and spam" the game. The final boss is a HUGE slog, and I fought the boss once and got really close and then died on my first try, only to discover it wanted me to do ALL OF THAT again (including a 10 part arena? no). Not only is this not a metroidvania....but it's not particularly great as an action platformer. The combat is just boring and repetitive and the charge attack plays the game for you. If you want a robot themed MV, I suggest Haiku (this game was excellent) or Axiom Verge. This game might be appropriate for someone who likes repetitive combat or linear exploration? But it's not a metroidvania.....and I think it's a damn shame. I was rooting for this one to be good.
_childDocuments_.name: KUNAI

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not saying the promotional material is dishonest, but this game, called Kunai, doesn't really seem designed around the Kunai. It's almost like they realized how versatile and powerful it could be half-way through development and tried to limit it's use as much as possible. There are far too many sections that are packed with blocks the Kunai can't attach too and it makes you realize how boring the core combat is without it.
_childDocuments_.name: KUNAI

_childDocuments_.review: Kunai is a nice looking game but is lackluster in the 'fun' department. Tl:dr the game has cool design elements that are poorly implemented and does not hold up to better 'Metroidvania' titles such as Hollow KnightHonestly, the game is like a 6/10 in my opinion. There were too many points while playing where I had no idea where to go next and backtracking through the various sections of the game world is not fun. The in-game music was nice for the fist few minutes but then the tracks just drone on and on while you frequently backtrack through lengthy areas. The combat has potential but is plagued by annoying eccentricities. For instance, your character recoils bakward slightly when striking an enemy with a melee attack. Instead of being able to combo, I'm forced to strike, scootch upward a bit, strike again, and repeat. It makes basic enemies take an unnecessarily long time to dispatch and is counter intuitive to how the attack animation is designed. Another example is the grappling hook / swing mechanic. I'd expect to be zipping along levels and using this mechanic to out-maneuver foes - alas, the fixed 45 degree angles of the kunai ropes and awkward swing motion made this feature clunky (I also found that the grapple was obstructed by too many surface types to be a fun method of travel). I found there were certain areas that seemed like they would be interesting but the game narrative provide little to do in these sections. Similarly, some upgrades seemed like they would be awesome to have at first only for me to realize later how little utility they ultimately had apart from the 'this is how you open certain doors' or 'use this to clear big rocks' types of usage. The final boss is unnecessarily difficult and definitely soured me on ever playing the game again. It's not the worst game in the world but I certainly wouldn't give it another playthrough unless the dev team announced a rework of several primary game mechanics. Since I don't see that happening, I would recommend only picking this one up if it's on sale for a few bucks (and even then I might encourage you to reconsider).

_childDocuments_.review: I love the idea, the mechanics, the art of this game.But the level design feels boring to me. Each level has different things when you arrive there, but from there on is the same thing again and again for the rest of the level.Sometimes I needed a lot of tries to defeat the bosses, but instead of a feeling of accomplishment, I got a feeling of "Finally I'm free of this boring task!".
