_childDocuments_.review: For all the NES fans out there is this a mash up of Metroid, Ninja Gaiden, and Super Mario 3, that ends up being quite a fun ride.  The controls are fantastic, crisp and do exactly what you want.  There are layers of movement machanics so you can go and do exactly what you want... if your fingers are quick enough.  You really do feel like a ninja in a way that few if any other games have ever captured.  You can move exactly how and where you want.Unfortunately when things break down you get hung up on objects, it's rare, but there are a few parts where this becomes problematic.  The chase section in particular is almost impossible to avoid geting hung up and insta killed.  This little section was by far the most frustrating part of the game.  Aside from that the difficulty is a nice fun medium, you will die from time to time, but it wont be so often that you want to quit playing, or so infrequently that you feel invincible.  Boss battles are a bit short and a little on the easy side, I got threw more than half on my first try.  The real missed opportunity with Kunai is the story, there is just enough to structure to the world and nothing more.  You dont need a tune of story in this kind of game, but there are so many characters and funny moments, it would have just been nice if they used them to do a bit more world building.All in all this is a very solid, fun, and addicting game.   I never full out fell in love with it, but I couldn't put it down either.   It wont be an all time classic, but you feel more like a ninja in this game than in any other I've ever played.   The game clearly has flaws but in no way do they outweigh the things it gets right.   I'm not sure I'd be happy paying full retail (currently $17), but if it's on sale for $10 it would be worth every penny, especially if you the idea of being a ninja in a Metrodvana sounds fun to you.
_childDocuments_.name: KUNAI

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the better metroidvania-style games that has released in recent years. I feel like it doesn't get as much attention as it should for as good as it is. The movement is very fluid, it's really fun to zip around using the hook line. Only issue I have with it is there was one point in the game where I just couldn't figure out how to progress, so I stopped playing for a while and came back to it later. Maybe there was some dialogue to tell me where to go next, but I didn't see it. All of that aside, it's a must buy for anyone that's into these style of games

_childDocuments_.review: Kunai is a seriously fun metroidvania/platformer hybrid with unique gameplay and music that sets it apart from its piers. The titular kunai are obtained from the get-go, and are used in increasingly difficult platforming gauntlets throughout the game, which are the most entertaining and unique portions of the game. Accompanying the platforming is the combat, which starts out simple, but over time become more complex with more weapons and upgrades. The combat and platforming are never quite melded together, with enemies only serving as simple obstacles and are easily dealt with. Kunai does have a couple issues, the main thing being the controls, which are very slippery and can occasionally lead to you taking damage. The other is the length, which isn't terribly low, but I would recommend getting this game on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: is a Metroidvania focused around stylish movement and minimalist palettes. You control Tabby, an anthropomorphic tablet capable of swinging around katanas, shooting twin revolvers and moving around very much like Spider Man.The art style is great and helps send the message that this is, in a way, a very minimalist game. The map, combat, enemies and story are as straightforward as possible, without falling into underdeveloped territory. Although the game can be completed in only a few hours, these are fun and thankfully devoid of filler content.The boss battles are more akin to Shadow of the Colossus in the sense that they are not so much a match of strength, but of observation and execution of movement. This took me for a surprise at the beginning, but was a very welcome idea at the end. A good place to spend a few hours, controller recommended 100%.

_childDocuments_.review: The biggest challenge  encounters is competing in the metroidvania space. In the last few years, there's been a lot of solid releases in that genre especially from indie developers. Standing side by side with other titles such as  or  is asking a bit too much from this game.Using a limited colour palette seem to be pretty hit or miss, but it was a total hit for me. However, it's a double-edged sword. Because of the constraints they put on themselves, the different area don't look as distinct from one another as they could've otherwise, which can be a bit confusing. Beside that, I really like the whole "living-tech" concept. The main character, Tabby, is really charismatic. His facial expressions are priceless and reminds me a lot of the way Link was handled in  An expressive main character is pretty refreshing in the genre.When it comes to gameplay, the controls are very responsive and there's a fairly high skill ceiling when it comes to traversal. This is really highlighted in a specific time-trial section, but I do wish the developers challenged their players a bit more. As a whole, the experience  offers is definitely on the easier side of the spectrum. The combat isn't much harder than the platforming, and after a short while you basically obliterate everything in seconds. They implemented some kind of hit recoil similarly to what Team Cherry did in  but it could be toned down a bit. As is, it breaks the combat flow more than anything else and encourages the player to pogo the enemies instead to bypass that.Now, if the visuals are great and the game play is pretty solid, what is holding the game back? I'd say it really comes down to length combined with difficulty level. With basically no real challenging sections, combined with an adequate yet forgivable soundtrack, there's not really any memorable set-piece like the escape sections from  or the incredible boss roster from  The traversals options might be great, but it feels like we barely scratched the surface there. When you really get the hang or the swinging, which is the most unique aspect of the game, you've basically reached the end. The exploration isn't that great either simply because of the fact that nearly everything you get are hats for Tabby. Even then, finding those cosmetics is more tedious than anything else since there's rarely any indications pointing towards hidden rooms. Subsequent playthroughs are the only place where you can really use those skills, but the lack of challenge make them a lot less appealing to me.Overall, I'd still recommend the game to any metroidvanias or platformers fan. It is not one of the greats, but it's still a pretty solid game. It does hit the right niche for me as movement is probably the most important factor to me. Also, feeling like a badass iPad is pretty col. As the first release from  it feels like a success and I can't wait to see what they'll do next. Hopefully, their next release will be a bit more ambitious.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Description:-Kunai is a fun metroidvania w/ a unique monochromatic art style and a focus on fast, crisp, platforming.  Movement feels fluid and well designed, w/ a clear emphasis on speed and verticality.  Although Kunai is a fun and stylish platformer, it feels a bit too linear and doesn't offer enough content to compete w/ the juggernauts of the genre.What's Good:-The main mechanic of the game is the kunai which acts as both a weapon and similar to a grappling hook.  This mechanic works really well and is the foundation for the entire game.  You will use it to traverse the many biomes while taking out enemies, searching for secrets, battling bosses, and completing timed side challenges.  -I really love the art design.  Your character is mostly dark blue, and most of the bad guys are bright red.  All of the background and biome colors are more muted, subtle colors allowing for your eyes to quickly focus on enemies.  I really love this visual design, and it's the main reason I was interested in this game the first trailer that I saw.  Each biome has a distinct theme w/ unique color choices.-This is a fun game w/ a playful sense of humor.  Your character is a tablet and there are tons of references to modern technology like computers, apps, flash drives, etc.  There is a lot of charm in this game and is a major highlight.-Movement, jumping, and platforming feels very fluid and responsive.  There is no delay in anything and everything feels buttery smooth.  Could Use Some Changes:-Kunai feels a bit too linear to compete w/ more well rounded metroidvanias.  You will do quite a bit of backtracking if you are secret hunting, but most of the game proceeds in a very predictable path.  The world doesn't feel quite as organic as better designed games in the genre.-I had a really fun time, but this is a game that could be beaten in about 6-8 hrs pretty easily.  It took me over 9 hrs, but I found most of the secrets and spent almost an hr completing an optional timed challenge.  This is a slightly bigger game than Gato Roboto and Enter Digiton and I think it's comparable in overall fun factor as well.-I would love another game mode or a N+ mode.  This would add some replayability or end game content to the game.Consensus:-Middle of the Road Game (Tier 4 and makes up 25% of my reviews).  Metroidvania fans will likely enjoy this one.  If the art design is not your cup of tea, then wait to snag it on a sale.  I really enjoyed my 9-10 hrs playing this, but I'm not sure how much replayability it has.  So I think this game is very much worth a thumbs up, but there are better games in this genre, so keep that in mind.

_childDocuments_.review: A traumatic event has shaken the balance of the world. Human life has been almost wiped out by the evil A.I. Lemonkus. Robots roam free across the earth. name: Through the Darkest of Times
detailed_description: Dark times mean fear and risks. The risk to be caught by patrolling National Socialists, looking for people who publicly stand against their point of view. The risk of being beaten up or even killed by the German military because we‘re opposing the regime. The risk of losing everything, including our loved ones. This is how we live. This is how we try to survive. Through the darkest of times. You are the leader of a small resistance group in 1933’s Berlin, of ordinary people, from Jews to Catholics and Communists to Patriots who simply can’t stand aside. Your goal is to deal with small blows to the regime – dropping leaflets to spread awareness about what the Nazis are really up to among the people, painting messages on walls, sabotaging, gathering information and recruiting more followers. And all of that while staying undercover – if the regime’s forces learn about your group, the life of each member is in grave danger. Through the Darkest of Times is a historical resistance strategy game, focusing on conveying the somber mood of the period and the very real struggles of average people living in the 3rd Reich. Historical accuracy means that your small group of resistance fighters will not change the outcome of the war, nor will you prevent all of the Nazi’s atrocities, but you can certainly do everything in your power to save as many lives as you can and oppose the fascist system wherever possible. Features: Experience the Darkest of Times in 4 chapters Fight for freedom, weaken the regime and lead your resistance group Plan activities, find collaborators and try not to get caught Feel the weight of responsibility as you make difficult decisions and face the dire consequences Beautifully illustrated expressionistic scenes and events

Few would stand and fight the monstrosity that was the German Reich. Will you? Lead an underground resistance group Through the Darkest of Times.

_childDocuments_.review: Through the Darkest of Times tells a story about small resistance group in 1933’s Berlin. We will lead this group for over 10 years in several chapters of this story.Through the Darkest of Times is a fine example of the game where you've seen all gameplay mechanics elsewhere but it's still absolutely enjoyable to play. There're 2 game modes that are also difficulty choices - one is more hardcore and another is more storytelling oriented one.Up to 5 people can be part of your group and you assign them to missions every in-game week. Successful completion of missions opens new acquaintances and missions, increases the number of your followers and brings important resources, including money that you can spend on various needs of your group.Game is polished really well - I've encountered only one frustrating bug before release though it should be fixed by now. And the narrative part is just great, of course. Visuals are superb, I liked this artstyle. The most explicit negative aspect of gameplay for me were weird transitions between chapters. Your progress resets too much after each chapter so you start from scratch every time. It doesn't matter how good was your economy, what progress you've made and what resourses you saved. Resetting some of those things is reasonable, but almost complete reset is a bit frustrating and you get a feeling that each chapter is too much similar to the previous because of that.Another issue is related to balance/replayability. Each chapter is time(turn) limited and you barely able to complete just one special event (even in Story mode). At the same time there's not enough diversity in gameplay and events to replay game over and over again - even my second playthrough was too similar to the first one, unfortunately (at first, I was sure that there's a great replayability but I was wrong).All in all,  is a fun to play tactical strategy game with a great narrative part. Replayability could've been much better with more possible events and adjusted balance though. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend this game.Story is fine, its actually pretty good. But the gameplay and its loop is terrible. -Choices don't matter -New chapters reset all progress made (Followers, moral and items collected are gone putting you back to square 1) -Major missions offer no incentive or consequences to complete -Items don't really contribute anything (Most of them just increase the danger of the situation and the ones that do help you'll have to do a bunch of missions to get them but it won't matter because you lose them at the end of the chapter) -Getting spot makes no sense half the time (Hiding will still get you spot so whats the point? Also why is talking to a friend or buying paper seen as suspicious?) If your looking for a strategy game pick something else up, because this is really a text adventure with a unfinished strategy game attached to it.

_childDocuments_.review: 'Through The Darkest Of Times' might be one of my favorite games that I've played this year, and it's dedication and passion towards a subject horrific such as the attrocities and rule of Nazi Germany, are portrayed excellently.  It drags you down from the very start, the destruction of Weimar Institution, the triumph of the NSDAP in the Parliamentary elections, the fires in the Reichstag, and the massacres of Köpenick, from there it only escalates into the worst excesses of human deprevation, hatred, and mania. The game isn't afraid to show the full realities of the cruelty and the horrific nature of war, and it does so with full pride in it, such as being void of the portrayal of the Wehrmacht as innocent army-men, who were only serving the fatherland. The news-events are surreal, hopeful, tragic, and everything in between from there; The way they're done are so mundane and casual, that it sets into you how horrific all of it actually is. Overall, a great game on a subject as difficult as the reign of Nazi Germany, would recommend to anyone interested in Historical Strategy.

_childDocuments_.review: Through the Darkest of Times is a lightweight strategy game that takes place in Germany, from 1933 through 1945. It's a historical title that focuses on growing your own resistance movement against Hitler from the time that he gets elected as chancellor, right through to the end of World War II and the fall of the Nazi Reich. At the start, you pick your character by rolling their traits and gender, then outfitting them as you see fit. You can have up to three other people in your party, whom you also choose via an in-game mission, and together you must gain both supporters and marks (currency) in order to keep meddling in SS affairs.The plot starts off strong, be prepared to invest a good portion of your time in this game to reading. Each of the four chapters house several text-driven cutscenes where you make dialogue choices, but about halfway through you'll end up figuring out that no matter what option you pick, nothing really happens; whether you choose to praise or diminish the Reich right in front of obvious Nazi supporters, whether you do or don't trust the American journalists looking for the real story, none of it ends up changing the course of the campaign. Once you realize this, you realize that as long as you keep enough supporters from one chapter to the next, you'll finish the game no matter what.To put it mildly, the gameplay is... confusing. Each chapter has its own predetermined amount of turns, and it's obvious that there are certain end goals to get to; that's not what's confusing, but the manner in which the objectives unfold is what's really unclear. You get an overhead shot of a map with various tasks; talk to members of certain parties and affiliations, buy various supplies to make leaflets or paint signs, go into hiding when you've raised too much attention, and many other things. However, the end goal of a chapter requires certain items to be obtained, and often the tasks to get those items are locked behind other tasks. Sometimes, the beginning line to the end goal doesn't come up until the very last few turns of the chapter, and sometimes you can't even get enough of a certain required item because not enough of the instances appear on the map. I'm honestly not sure if this is all RNG based, but it's incredibly confusing and frustrating, especially given that there is a bare-bones tutorial that explains very little. Despite the effort of throwing in random curve balls, such as a resistance member's wife getting arrested, or needing to hide certain allies from the Reich, the tasks that Through the Darkest of Times sets for the player just feel incredibly shallow and repetitive. If you're not panhandling for money, you're rallying for supporters or buying supplies to gain more awareness. Every now and then you'll do a big task, like raiding a convoy, or spy on the SS for intel, but it's not often or fulfilling. That said, one thing that is done well is the feeling that you're always struggling to just scrape enough resources together to get by. Everything here is bleak, as it should be. From the morose, downtrodden storyline, the tension-filled resistance banter, to the muted sepia-toned graphics. Paintbucket games did a great job capturing the omnipresent feelings of tension, dread, and uncertainty that loomed over the majority of the decade that spanned the rise and fall of Germany.In the end, Through the Darkest of Times has some good ideas, but they're just executed with both too much simplicity and not enough explanation of the game's core mechanics. If it was easier to realize how to trigger certain events to unfold, such as getting testimonies, bombs, or other special resources for end-chapter missions, then players could work whole-heartedly towards a certain goal instead of just mindlessly gather supporters and money. Furthermore, it doesn't seem to matter how high you level your characters, you'll still end up getting caught a ton in the end; not to mention levels are few and far between, and more often than not a resistance member will just up and leave right afterward anyway. The characters would also fair better if they had at least a snippet of background story to them, but everyone, including who you play, is hollow. Even if you're interested in history, with a focus on World War II, you're more than likely to get bored with this title at about the halfway point.The Horror Network  |  Click for Gore

_childDocuments_.review: Really great if you want to experience the atmosphere of the era, and are interested in a detailed look in how the historical events unfolded piece by piece. The first 3-4 hours were fantastic - tense, intriguing and challenging.Beyond that point, the game showed its big flaw - it is not that great as a game. Very shortly, it lacks emotional payoff. Each chapter has three major actions you can aim to complete. However, the time limit makes any one of them feel impossible to pull off. A lot of the events are hidden, and it is unclear how to make them appear. For example, a major event might require 3 of a key item, but the game does not tell you how to acquire them. Randomly completing missions gets you somewhere, but more than likely you'll end up short of any of the requirements. Still, if you don't fall below the morale/support thresholds, the game will tell you your leadership was great and let you progress to the next chapter. In other words, the you do not actually have to do anything to progress in the game, and trying is more likely counterproductive. Trying to optimize the few strategic choices I had made the game feel extremely repetitive at the second and third chapters already.While this sense of danger and futility might be appropriate for the theme and setting, it makes for an unsatisfying game. The slow tempo and buildup needs to reward you with a moment of success at some point. The player's lack of impact in the game world simply gets boring.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm finding Through the Darkest of Times a more engaging history lesson than a game, but the history aspect is amazing so no knock on it.  The main gameplay is managing your small resistance cell (3-5 people), with varying political ideas, employment backgrounds and skill sets through various mission types.  A mission to recruit Catholics supporters may require a character of a certain background while creating propaganda leaflets requires other skill sets.   It's very engaging at first but the missions become repetitive after awhile.   Nevertheless there is a constant tensions between "winning the game" (surviving) and living up to the ideas of the adage "evil prevails when good men do nothing."  Between missions there are cut scenes about real history and the game gives you dialogue choices but it's not apparent that your choices make any difference other than ending the scenes early.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like the game, but have encountered a few bugs and some big historical inaccuracies.The whole idea of cross-party groups is flawed in my opinion. Politics in the Weimar Republic where extremely divided. Communists and Social Democrats hated each other almost as much as they hated the Nazis, and National Conservatives would sooner have collaborated with the Nazis than cooperated with Communists or Social Democrats. I think a better concept would be letting the player play the game as different types of resistance-groups. Communists-groups, Democratic-groups (Social- and Liberal) and Conservative-groups. Mechanics and story-line could change to reflect the difference between these groups.A few bugs I have encountered until now:- One of my group-members disliked another member because the later was a Social Democrat. The problem was, that the person complaining was herself a Social Democrat.- Another member of my group fled to Moscow because he was discovered as being a Communist - but he was a Social Democrat.The game has a lot of potential though :-)

_childDocuments_.review: A historical and informative simulation game where you experience what it is like to be in a regime and are tasked to be in an underground group. It a nice strategy game in which you have to recruit members and gain support like you would have in the past in real life without having to be caught and lay low. You go through each day by planning what your group does such as gathering support, equipment, donations etc where each member of your group specialises in a certain area so they would be more useful in certain tasks. Preparation is key as if this is lacking then you are more likely of being caught and losing a member. Overall, it is an interesting game and history piece, seeing what it is like to be in fear of being ruled.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend for the history, which is well-told, but I can't recommend it as a game.The game systems encourage you to act, but bad things happen when you do. This is presumably supposed to feel like a careful balancing act, but because the risk/reward payoffs aren't well explained it just feels like the game is punishing you. You are given lots of options, none of which appear to be worthwhile. Quite a lot of the time the best course of action seems to be doing nothing. You aren't given much indication what to do or how to do it, and achieving anything requires meeting a very long chain of requirements, which you are very unlikely to do on the first attempt. Missions sometimes appear too late for you to collect the resources to complete them, or disappear with no warning just when you're finally ready to act. Why bother subtly buying paper, setting up a workshop, and printing leaflets, risking arrest the entire time? Well you'll need them for the mission the game gives you two turns to complete at the end of the chapter, but you're not told that until it's too late. If for you 'strategy' means learning the steps which lead to a particular outcome and carrying them out exactly as instructed, you may enjoy this game. Otherwise the game doesn't follow the normal rules of a strategy because you are forced to make decisions without any way of knowing what the payoff will be, if any.The requirements to make some essential missions appear are not explained. The checkpoint system means you can get stuck in an unwinnable position. The game repeatedly resets your progress, which I understand from a narrative point of view, but it means you can never feel like you're building anything.The experience feels pretty arbitrary, aimless and futile as a result. This is probably a pretty accurate depiction of what being a resister was like, but it doesn't make for a good strategy game. If you buy it, do so because you're interested in the history, and play in story mode.

_childDocuments_.review: The line between making a game and making a political statement or educational instrument is extremely thin. Through the Darkest of Times walks that line masterfully. It's one of those projects that puts you into the shoes of a historical place but never forgets that this is a game and ensures that you feel like your choices mattered.You take on the role of a resistance leader during the rise of Hitler. Each turn you will deploy your resistance members to raise funds, motivate new supporters, steal supplies, or conduct action against the Nazis. You need to balance funding, morale, and risks in order to survive each chapter. Your members will develop their skills over time and learning to utilize their personality traits will boost your odds of success. The gameplay itself is not nearly as strategic as it first seems at first glance, but there's enough to feel like a pretty good board game. Mostly, it comes down to keeping your morale high while raising your supporters to a size that they can fund your activities. Random events can occur and require tough choices, but mechanically it's all about balancing those sliders.It doesn't matter whether you're painting a mural, firebombing a military installation, or rescuing prisoners. They all serve as ways to boost your morale mid chapter and require you to collect X materials to perform. At this point you pick operatives that will enhance your success rate while keeping the danger percentage low. Roll the dice and hope for the best, its a game of controlled luck rather than deep strategy.The board game is broken up by "Story Scenes" every few months that work like a choose your own adventure novel. The choices you make will have, potentially long-term, consequences. It ranges from small things like "Do you speak out against things publicly to a friend?" to larger ones like "Do we promise to rescue a trapped family member despite the danger?"The storytelling and choices are excellent on this front. They turn what feels like an abstract board game feel alot more like a personal tale and have you weighing your morals vs. what needs to be done. At least through my first run, there haven't been many easy choices and I like that.The one place I think the game really falls short is the overarching flow of the campaign. As I mentioned before, it feels like a board game but the 4 chapter campaign feels out of place. The way the chapters are structured it feels like they should be separate missions you'd pick from when you start a game.The problem is that your morale, equipment and supporters don't carry across from chapter. You win the chapter, the board is cleared, time passes and you need to start over again.  But if you die or want to try other tactics in a chapter you need to start the entire game over. This lack of reward for doing good, combined with the punishment for failure feels wrong. It really should have been, "Beat one chapter to unlock the next on the main menu" with 2-3 hour games.But overall, this is one of the best games I've played from an edutainment standpoint. It might not have been intended as such but it provides a fantastic way to experience a period in history firsthand. If you want to make a "Serious Game" or "Game for a Cause" it's worth looking at all the things this did right.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me be frank: this is a very good educational experience. But as a game... well, I couldn't bring myself to play it for too long. That said, I invite you to buy this game and check it out purely based on the education factor. Don't expect a fun time though, hence a negative review.I happen to have a connection to Berlin. I know the city. Watching the very real and very historical events that happened there in a game, depicting places I was to 80 years later is chilling in a way that no other game managed to achieve. Then, there's the opportunity to sort-of relive the events of Hitler's rise to power. With the rise of global nationalism these days, it's handy to compare and contrast: which countries are closest to early days of Nazi Germany? If you've been studying history in greater detail, there's probably nothing this game has to teach you. I, however, took quite a bit from it, even if I didn't play for very long.My main gripe with the game is the general feeling of absolute hopelessness and despair. It's like Papers, Please. I like to call this Political Horror. And I am way, way too vulnerable to it; mainly because in this game, well, you know how powerless you are and meaningless your actions will ultimately be. If you don't mind this terrifying feeling, then this game can probably be a much better experience. This game is very antifa, down to its original meaning. Turns out I am way too squeamish to oppose Nazis even in a game, though. If, however, you want to fight the power even if you know you'll ultimately fail then this is probably a pretty good thing.As for the gameplay itself, well... you give your people missions for the week, they execute them, you get results. It's rather bland. Then between missions you get story elements, historical events, what have you. Honestly, maybe if the gameplay itself was better then I'd play this in spite of everything else.It really pains me that I have to give this game a negative review. I'm happy this game exists, maybe someday a better executed version of this concept will surface. Also, this game is a sign that the German government finally considers games to be an art form that can talk about the country's dark history in a meaningful way (fyi - for quite a while any references to Nazism in games were strictly forbidden in games in Germany, but now it's different).Devs - keep fighting the good fight. This is direct action. I'm not refunding the game, what you've done may not be as good as I'd like, but it will certainly be a stepping stone towards greater things.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the story and the way it was interwoven with real history. The novel elements woven in between was fun and I enjoyed reading it. _childDocuments_.review: Through the Darkest of Times sees you play through the events of Hitler's reign from the perspective of a small cell of political dissidents. These may be disgruntled trade unionists seeking to protect the people, or they may be religious conservatives looking to end the persecution of Jews. The gameplay segments are interspaced with visual-novel style narrative sections that see you interacting with scenes of police violence, book burnings and more. The gameplay itself isn't a novel invention, to the point that if you've played similar games about talent-management a tutorial is not needed. Each in game week you can assign your 5 resistance members to missions either alone or in groups with the core stats of these team members impacting their ability to succeed or limit the risk of failure. Some missions are ticking clocks that require immediate action, others will be goals to work towards as opportunities and resources come available. The balancing of the resources in my three hour play session does a good job of reinforcing the despair of being unable to combat the nazi regime on every front. The politics of the game are potent. I had to stop myself at several points to calm down and collect myself before continuing. If you're interested in the game you likely know what to expect here. It's not a spoiler to enter the game knowing what years Hitler entered power and was defeated. Across that decade power was consolidated by Hitler and the nazi party, police authority was strengthened, and dissidents were criminalised.  Perhaps the only criticism I'm willing to put forward here is there are heavy handed comparisons made to current politics. I consider this a good thing when used well, fascism and fascist rhetoric are both threats to current society and it would be negligent for the game to not address them. With that in mind, having Adolf Hitler using the words "fake news" in the same page that Goebbels said "drain the swamp" was on the nose in a way that some people might have their immersion broken and others might reject the comparisons entirely. (edit: Both these sentiments were used by the Nazis, but I'm not a German speaker so I don't know whether these specific phrasings were ever used in that way.) This was however only one moment in a 3 hour play session which was otherwise strictly in tone with the setting. If there are similar moments later in the game I am unaware of them. At the moment I can see only 2 negative reviews unrelated to specific bugs that will hopefully be patched. The first is somebody getting triggered at the (again, singular) comparison to current politics. The second is attempting to spread historical revisionism that the Nazis weren't a right wing conservative party(they were). If you're such a conservative snowflake to be this easily triggered by an indie game you're advised to go somewhere else instead of deliberately tracking down media you know you'll disagree with for the purpose of giving it negative reviews.

_childDocuments_.review: I received this as part of my Humble Bundle monthly subscription. I'm German by descent, studied German for six years, traveled to Germany three times, and visited a concentration camp. I really, really, really wanted to like this game. The story is richly told and the parallels to today's world are both on point and nauseatingly overpowering. The atmosphere is appropriately dreary, but the game is repetitive to a fault. Your crew of randomized minions are unremarkable and easily replaceable. The soundtrack seemingly consists of two songs and three trumpet wails. The graphics are consistently well done, but this strikes me as something that should have stayed as a mobile game. The sequence of events required to get to the major act of sabotage were never clear and, frequently, I'd spend half of the level trying to figure the steps out before running out of time with only one task remaining to finish. Most of my time was spent busking, being in human resources middle management, and public speaking while wondering why the Nazis weren't cracking down on my weekly efforts to collect spare change in front of the Reichstag or other busy area of Berlin.

_childDocuments_.review: Nazi Germany has always been a fascinating topic for me and I was hooked the moment that I saw the Steam store page for Through the Darkest of Times. I was hoping for a strong story and decent enough gameplay to allow it to shine, though the mechanics ended up surprising me with their depth. There’s a strong, historical narrative but there’s also an interesting and immersive layer of strategy thrown into the mix that worked well enough to keep me interested and enjoying this title for its significant gameplay portions as well.Your resistance will have several active members in it, each of which will have a variety of traits and stats, as well as a political leaning and professional identity. The primary stats that all characters share are secrecy, empathy, propaganda, strength, and literacy. Each character has a proficiency in these that represents how talented they are at using it and how effectively they can carry out related missions. The variety of traits is impressive and the selection includes character-defining elements such as athlete, doubtful past, calm, and paranoid, that further distinguish one character from the next. Political identities such as catholic conservative, anarchist, and communist, and professions, like lawyer and metal worker, add further depth with bonuses and penalties to related tasks. The end product is a relatively unique set of randomly generated characters to fill your resistance with plenty of aspects that differentiate them from one another and affect their own stories and commentaries on the world and each other. I decided to go with the first character that was randomly generated for my leader, a communist lawyer, and I was particularly pleased with the passion for the development of this project when he was arrested and beaten for a week before being released without explanation after the burning of the Reichstag.When you first begin, you’ll be able to choose whether you want to play the resistance or story mode. Resistance is an ironman experience that is meant to provide a real challenge, though it may be a tad on the easy side if you’re a strategy veteran looking to have your capabilities tested. On the other hand, the story mode allows those who want to focus on the story to do so without the interference of intense and stressful management of their squad of resisters.Newspapers will arrive at the beginning of each week, notifying you of the events that are taking place around you at the time. The vast majority reinforce the oppressive gloom as the Nazis continue to expand their power and influence while your actions fail to effect any real change. You’ll have your little victories here and there but it often seems as if everyone around you supports the Nazi regime, turns a blind eye to its atrocities, or assumes that the worst of it all will blow over soon.On the other hand, your resistance is attempting to undermine Hitler’s growing authority by recruiting supporters, collecting donations, and eventually, engaging in more aggressive and violent behaviour against the regime to remind it that there are still those who are watching. You’ll determine who does what, but those actions that will hit the regime the hardest are also the ones that will push your strongest supporters to their limits, costing them their freedom and their lives. Fortunately, as they engage in these activities, they’ll rise to the challenge and improve with the experiences that they gain.Through the Darkest of Times places us near the start of Germany’s political transition from the Weimar Republic to Nazi Germany, and does so in a way that is immersive, using history itself to create a fictional story with a realistic and dark setting. It’s clear that Paintbucket Games has read a page or two on the setting as they paint an excellent picture of the era even if there may be a few slight alterations for the sake of a modern audience. The strategy portion is neither the deepest nor the most challenging that we’ve ever seen but it does its part and pairs well with the story being told. All in all, this title is a solid combination of strategy management and storytelling that’s worth giving a shot as long as you don’t mind a touch of commentary on modern politics showing itself on occasion.Original Review:

_childDocuments_.review: Lead a resistance group in Germany from the time when Hitler is appointed chancellor to the end of WWII.You start by hitting a randomize button until you get a political affiliation and job type you like (your stats consisting of empathy, literacy, strength, secrecy, propaganda are not chosen by you) followed by altering your appearance. You view your character and two other random people in a hideout before getting access to the map where you can choose active events to send your characters on missions. Two activities will quickly get you two more characters, with one being chosen from a random pool of three.Your goal is to keep your group active by continuing to gain supporters and maintaining your five members (including yourself) that you send out on activities, ideally while completing the prerequisite activities and collecting the needed items to take on the few big missions included in each of the four chapters. Many activities lead to nothing of value narratively (as the accompanying text amounts to little more than you did thing) or reward wise. You can support labor strikes, hide persecuted people, try to help your neighbors, do events that sound more interesting like passing on information to the press or spies for other countries, etc but all that never really matters as it doesn't lead to anything except maybe some of those spy events being an easier path to collecting an item you need. While there is a lack of information on what can be effecting what in certain scenes, your chances of fighting or hiding from encountered harassers or soldiers, and what some actions even do, there is way to much information on the set events that will lead to your attempted goal.Once you complete an event to talk to a contact, you are shown a full chain of everything that can come from that first event. Hand out books - spy on activities - steal uniform or hand out leaflets - gain access to factory - steal gas. There is nothing interesting or unique that ever happens within the normal gameplay, you just send the best of your mostly random characters that you hope work out for you to do what they are naturally best at, and likely see them constantly continue to arouse suspicion of them until you bring that down through another type of activity. With some events having descriptions like finding a hidden entrance to keep out of sight while the end event text tells you that you were spotted anyway. When attacked, caught by witnesses or police, or when your characters start randomly fighting or having a panic attack you can choose to run, hide, or brute force their way through the job with hide saying it might give you some of the reward and brute force being more dangerous but able to give you everything. Obviously this makes little sense when many missions can't split their reward in half, or when it comes to what hiding for an in group dispute would mean.The actions of your resistance group is almost entirely based around your five characters and you only get to know a little about them through the event that happens at the start of each day. They are never going to be anyone you care about, their actions can seem widely conflicting, and their moods and statements have no relation to what you have been having them do or how you have been doing. Things been really bad and morale is low you might get an event where they thank you for starting the group, things been going good well your best leveled and most useful character (or only useful character in one needed area thanks to them all being random) just left the country or became a traitor. Even events like someone being discovered as a traitor is dull as what happens is that another member just says someone is a spy and you can choose to keep them or kick them out, if you keep them then maybe you get an event later where they don't show up one day and the other person says they were a spy again, if they were it had no effect on the actual gameplay.While good, the story events can be better handled, some might happen based on your political affiliation (on the much worse for you personally side if you are a communist and seeing former friends joining with the Nazis in the others) but your stats and background have no effect on your choice results and nothing done in the scenes effecting your personal life tend to matter. When you are doing the larger group events possible in each chapter you end up getting options with percentage chances to succeed but I never had anything cause me to fail the event, and I didn't know if the percentage changes were only based on my own characters mostly random stats. A general lack of information when it comes to what does what and the effects stats are having on anything outside of mission prep and danger rate (if anything).Short events tend to do a better job showing the growing fascism and gleeful talk of genocide by neighbors and other people you used to or have to associate with, both showing how it really was in Germany at the time and often how people in the US, Israel, Steam's forum posters on this game, etc will happily support genocidal actions and fascism after years of propaganda and being given made up enemies or after finding a government supportive of just being an objectively evil person but the events that showcase historic moments and shifts in power and propaganda are so short and then never really focused on again that the game feels like it is missing out on using historical moments more to tell a better story or to build on your group member's characterization.None of the games mechanics really come together well, a lot of it is going to be based on failing and not being able to do everything, fitting for the setting, but like most games that try that it offers nothing interesting in return. Not succeeding or reaching as many mission events as possible just means that you get less of the writing and art, if someone dies no one cares if someone is captured you get a mission to free them but that's just choosing the people to send and getting them back if you succeed just taking time away from completing your goals for the chapter. Every chapter jumps ahead a few years so you lose anything you did in the previous except for character level ups that allow you to increase one of their stats by one so there isn't even much feel of your group growing or things escalating much when it comes to the majority of your missions and actions.

_childDocuments_.review: A very short game, but also quite worth the price.S, this is a very good CYOA game that involves you leading a resistance group in Berlin between 1933 and 1945. Divided into chapters, there is a clear progression in the way that your group operates, as well as the overall mood. In the beginning, finding contacts, keeping morale up, and getting money is pretty easy. But by the time you get to 1941, your resistance group is struggling with all of those things and having to put itself more at risk just to keep going. By the end game, you are fighting every single turn just to stay alive. There were times in the game when I actually thought '♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, this is it, we're ♥♥♥♥♥♥,' only to be saved by friends or just pure dumb luck. It was definitely a nailbiter. I'm not a big fan of the art style, but YMMV on that point, I'm sure it's appealing to someone. It does do a good job of capture surreal starkness of the period, and communicates a really grim, dystopian setting (which those years undoubtedly were for many people).I actually enjoyed myself a bit in this game,

_childDocuments_.review: This game was received as a gift from a friend. I'm in no way affiliated, sponsored, or supported by the devs.While the core concepts of the game are very solid (coordinating a ragtag team of resistance members in Germany from 1933 to 1945), the game very quickly ducks into safe avenues, waves around atrocities almost for shock value, and hamstrings itself with poor concepts and a lack of respect or understanding of what Europe went through in WW2:-- Each part is limited to very specific turns, and the game will quite quickly meet those deadlines long before you're ready to really make an impact, or just as you're getting ready to pull off a particular mission.-- Many of the item requirements are frustratingly difficult, or literally impossible to meet in the harshly strict turn limit. For example, One of the major missions is getting testimonies together so that a particular SS officer doesn't escape justice. Even when I attempted to literally item grind to get it done, the game only gave me a single testimony, when you need THREE to beat the mission.-- Speaking of item requirements, the game frags your inventory between every part, so even IF you get some fancy Wehrmacht uniform, sorry bucko, it fell through the floor or got used as kindling between chapters. This issue is exacerbated when, in a particular chapter, pamphlets were needed to advance a mission, and at no point in time was I allowed to produce them. Glitch? Maybe. Frustrating? Definitely.-- Roughly halfway into the game, your Protagonist is *told* that they could get the help of the Soviets, British, or French resistance. I tried my damnedest, but not only could I not find any missions that pushed me in one direction or another, it was never brought up again. Never thought I find cut content in an indie game, but there you go.-- The tutorials make it clear that certain missions can unlock others. What it doesn't elaborate on is that these chained missions missions MUST be completed one-after-another, consecutively, otherwise they lock and you have to restart the chain from the beginning. And since you'll be juggling panhandling for marks, rallying support, AND keeping the heat off your team, there's never enough time. The game frequently mistakes "Difficulty" as simply being unfair about timing and item requirements/management.-- The most important thing a game can do in this type of setting is make the player feel like they made a difference. Quite literally, at no point in time did I feel like I'd done anything useful other than get a bunch of money from people, hand out some harshly worded pamphlets, and generally piss off the local police. Flouncing the Wehrmacht or Gestapo never feels like you dodged a bullet, it feels like an arbitrary die roll from a hostile DM.The game doesn't give you the feeling that you're fighting one of the greatest evils of all time from the inside. All of the dark things that your characters learn aren't discovered, it's spoon fed to you through throw away conversations by people you'll never see again, as if to remind you, "Hey, Nazi's are Bad!" Yes, I know Nazis are bad, one of my past times is shooting the grenades on their belts in Sniper Elite, because they thought finding new and creative ways to murder roughly 6 million humans was a "good idea".You never "uncover" anything, you don't become jaded with how aggressively things change, it's all laid out in front of you. The game makes the critical mistake of perceiving the past through a modern lens, and that critically hamstrings the game.By the end of the game, your protagonists don't matter. I didn't feel like I'd save lives, fought Nazis, and lived to tell the tale. I felt like I was reading someone's tie-in fan fiction they were required to write for high school history class.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all... Holy crap.This game takes a historical path and pretty accurately follows the rise and fall of Hitler and his Nazi regime.You play as the leader of a small group of rebels, fighting against the Autocracy. You don't fight back with guns, however. You fight back by pushing for the truth to be known. I personally felt the difficulty wasn't TOO high. _childDocuments_.review: This game is one of those that "it's not about the destination, but the journey". This will take you to a chilling journey of Nazi Germany (from 1933 all the way to the end of WW2). The game has two modes: Resistance mode (which is like an endless mode, without the possibility to save) and the story mode. I've finished the story mode and never really touched the other. Here are my pros and cons:Pros:- chilling story and atmosphere- the setting of playing as a resistance movement against Nazi Germany- likeable characters and interactions with themCons:- there's not a lot of gameplay- the choices you make don't make quite much impact, except for your resources- limited number of members (a maximum of five)- a very limited character customization mechanic (every aspect of the character is being randomized)- while the game shows you that your actions could have serious consequences, 90% of the time a high risk action doesn't wield much consequencesEven though the game seems to have more cons than pros, I would still recommend it for players who just want to experience what the anti-Nazi resistance movement when through. For fans of strategic gameplay with choices that have consequences, please look for a different game.
_childDocuments_.name: Through the Darkest of Times

_childDocuments_.review: This is not just a game, this is an art.Words can't describe how much I love this game. This is a simple game, yes. But what makes this game great is the narrative writing (some event will make you very emotional) and the historical fact that this game give. Also, I need to mention how amazing the art style is.You will spend a lot of time reading text in this game (quite similar to a visual novel). There's many dialogue options that you can choose when the narrative is playing or when some event occured, and your choice will affect the story (I made a really bad decision in my last game and i'm still regret it now). I saw several reviews that stated our choices will have no effect on important historical events. This is indeed true. For anything you did, the Nazi will still be in power until 1945. But I think people who protest this is missing the point. This is a historical game that wants to show the cruelty, terror, and wickedness that resulted from the regime at that time. This message would not have been delivered if, for example, our resistance group succeeded in overthrowing the Nazi in 1942. Also, knowing that you can't alter the big historical event is actually makes this game more thrilling, in my opinion. You know your group is very vulnerable and one fatal mistake will result in your characters being captured, or even killed. I really felt this worry, especially in the last chapter when the Gestapo appeared.As for the gameplay, well, its involve lots of clicking (and reading, like I said). There is no action thing like shooting or punching someone. So, if you only like action game and hate reading lots of text, you may not enjoy this game. But if you, for whatever reason, interested to learn history of WW II, I really recommend you to give this game a chance. To wrap things up, this is a really amazing historical game. Although, I must state that this game is not for everyone. I highly recommend this game to anyone that interested in history (or people who recently want to learn about history). And I think it would be great if a history teacher decided to play this game in class with students when the lesson was discussing about WWII. This is also a short game so you don't need to worry you going to waste lots of time. Just take your time, read the text carefully, and feel it. I bet you going to be very emotional for the victim and disgusted with the regime after you finish this game.Never forget the history. Or we will doomed to repeat it.

_childDocuments_.review: Very enjoyable strategy game that also teaches people things about the regime they may not have known. I don't see why the  character's features and clothing could be manipulated but those other things not. Do we not choose, most times, our occupation and what we believe? That would make the game much more enjoyable to me. Hopefully someone will make a mod/trainer for it if they choose not to do so.

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't the best game, it's an indie turn-based strategy game with some frustrating balance issues. BUT it is the best WW2 game that I can recall playing. Better than Hearts of Iron, better than Call of Duty, because better than anything I have played, it realistically and viscerally connects you to the atrocities and terror of the Nazi regime. It illuminates history and I found myself developing real sympathy for my characters, and ultimately trying to make moral decisions in a nearly hopeless scenario. So perhaps those frustrating balance issues are working as intended. Leading a resistance against the horrors of the Nazis isn't meant to feel easy or fair.. but it's the right thing to do.

_childDocuments_.review: There will be times when the struggle seems impossible. I know this already. Alone, unsure, dwarfed by the scale of the enemy. Remember this. Freedom is a pure idea. It occurs spontaneously and without instruction. Random acts of insurrection are occurring constantly throughout the galaxy. There are whole armies, battalions that have no idea that they've already enlisted in the cause. Remember that the frontier of the Rebellion is everywhere. And even the smallest act of insurrection pushes our lines forward. And then remember this. The Imperial need for control is so desperate because it is so unnatural. Tyranny requires constant effort. It breaks, it leaks. Authority is brittle. Oppression is the mask of fear. And know this, the day will come when all these skirmishes and battles, these moments of defiance will have flooded the banks of the Empire's authority and then there will be one too many. One single thing will break the siege. Remember this. Try.

_childDocuments_.review: A timely, thoughtful antifascist game that serves as a good reminder that resistance is primarily the work of normal, flawed people rather than muscular gun-toting supersoldiersPROS:+ Excellent, evocative writing+ Stylish and striking art direction+ No glorification of fascism or violence+ Randomised yet believable characters+ Minimalistic, yet immersive sound design+ Clever parallels drawn to current political climate+ Mostly historically accurate depiction of Nazi Germany+ Gameplay revolving around direct action rather than mindless violenceCONS:- Very tense and depressing- Over too soon, ironically enough- Very few perceptible consequences from story choices- Both the French and English translations riddled with typos- Character randomisation causing all sorts of visual and textual oddities

_childDocuments_.review: I REALLY like this game!Unfortunately, 2 things pretty much MURDER it:1) The RNG - I think it's a bit heavy-handed, I guess?2) The Bugs - Perhaps it was just me, but I keep running into game-breaking ones (a majority of them)If they fix one of these two issues, I'd consider it to be a pretty good game, if they fixed both, it would be a great one.Also, other's have mentioned it in some of the other reviews, but it suffers from a bit of 21st century tunnel-vision. But, it's a game...so I think it should be given a bit of slack in this department.Finally, the English translation could be a bit better. _childDocuments_.review: Through the Darkest of Times tells the story of an antifascist resistance group in Nazi germany, showing german history between 1933 and 1945 from their perspective.The game consists of two aspects: The gameplay for the most part is coordinating resistance activities from an overworld map, gaining supplies, organizing strikes, sabotaging fascist infrastructure etc. In between gameplay, there are artistically designed choice-based cutscenes that detail the story of the game and show the different facets of germany in this time period.While the game is quite short, the campaign took me less than 5 hours and can be a little repetitive, the story it tells is very atmospheric, haunting and realistic. It makes one of the most destructive and awful periods of human history come to life and forces you to sympathize with the victims of it. So despite the short play time, the experience will stick with you for a long time after that.I definitely recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: The good:+ Historically accurate with great portrayal of Nazi cruelty.+ Great visual/artstyle which emphasize haunting atmosphere.+ Your choices matter. While i understand accomplish something extraordinary is very difficult, i unable to accomplish much even on story mode.* The developer missed opportunity to educate player even further either by showing in-game "booklet" which show more detail about specific piece of history or at least showing player where they could find more about historical information.Overall, Through the Darkest of Times is engaging historical lesson/narrative. But since the game mechanics isn't good, i only can recommend this game to those who want to know a bit more about history during Nazi-time through video game medium on story mode difficulty.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I start, I should mention that I have yet to finish the game, but from what I've seen so far, I'm completely engrossed in the lives of my fellow resistance fighters. The gameplay here is very similar to This is the Police where resource management is the key to a "successful" run. Of course, there are several important differences to set both games apart such as the danger meter and the fact that you'd be wise to keep your people well below the radar of Hitler's many supporters.Intro: (My internet disconnected itself after the intro so here's a separate video for it) Playthrough: (Part 1)Similar to This is the Police, you can recruit new resistance fighters, but unlike the game, there's a maximum limit allowed for your "inner circle". When I was playing the former game, I had like tons of police officers and detectives near the end game, making the game so easy to play, but by restricting the number of "core" resistance fighters that I have, the game essentially ensures that you'll be more careful where you assign your people to. You'll want to especially avoid getting caught since it'll mean that you'll lose access to one of your precious recruitment slots and breaking your imprisoned teammate out isn't that easy of a task either. There's always a risk that you'll end up having more of your people in jail than not.The people you recruit have their own personalities and affiliations as well, and if you've got a good group going, you'll find that you can capitalize on these perks to improve your chances of success for a task. This feature is somewhat present in... again, This is the Police, but I like that this game greatly expanded on it, allowing you to really find ways to maximize what each of member of the group can contribute to the fight. The game also has a meter for both morale and supporters and keeping these two up is crucial since you'll need supporters/allies to to help carry out certain tasks, connect you with new but helpful professionals, and also to rack up sufficient donations to fund your movement. Morale mainly affects your team and it's vital to avoid draining it too much or your team might be disbanded.I know I've mentioned This is a Police a lot here mainly because of the similarities between the two, but as much of a fan that I was, there's one thing I unfortunately dislike about the game - it drags on quite a bit and it can end up feel extremely repetitive (and thus, boring). Through the Darkest Time manages to avoid this by introducing new and more dangerous "events" whenever you complete a previous event for the first time.Due to the shifting Nazi patrols, the danger levels of certain scenarios will shift accordingly as well. In a way, you do feel like you're managing some sort of "guerrilla warfare" operation where you'll try to hit the Nazis in areas they aren't as vigilant in. But of course, as time goes by and the events in Germany escalates, you'll find it harder and harder to get lower-risked events and you might need to send your people into hiding a lot more frequent than before.Not to mention, the game has a time limit as to how long it can progress since it's based on actual historical events and maybe because of this, the game doesn't seem to be overstaying its welcome. + A pretty compact historical lesson all bundled up in an entertaining, "This is the Police"-like game, but unlike often "dry" history books, the game is more interactive and it even puts you into the shoes of the resistance fighters.+ Love the art here. + Strategic gameplay involving resource(and manpower) management - my favorite kind of game!+ The overall atmosphere of the game perfectly reflects the gravity of the situation. The game doesn't try to spin this into a lighthearted game - it's heartbreaking at times and you do feel for the people being unfairly prosecuted in Nazi Germany.+ Your choices matter! At key events in the game, you'll need to make important decisions regarding what your people should do and how will you resolve internal squabbles.+ Impressive storytelling. The game often cuts away into what I call "side stories" where it'll try to illustrate, through words and image, what normal folks in the country feel and experience as Hitler gains power and spread his ideology.+ The price is right, though I'm a bit on the fence about replayability. I'm pretty sure a single playthrough is enough for me. The experience can be even more harrowing and emotionally draining for some, I reckon. - The game doesn't make light of what many would call a black stain in human history (there will be some pretty "graphic" deaths) so it might not be as suitable for kids. You've been warned!Through the Darkest of Times is one of those incredibly rare games that managed to do both things right - educate people about an important period in German/world history and thoroughly gamify the history lesson so that people are actually interested to learn about it. The gamification is so thorough to the point where you can try to feel and experience (without having to resort to a time machine or something sci-fi) what those people back then are going through by putting yourself into their shoes. Definitely a game I would highly recommend if you enjoy learning history while playing games.

_childDocuments_.review: As a few of the critiques already pointed out:This game could've been more fun. And it could've been less linear. Instead the developers focused on historical accuracy; Something many "historical" games seem to miss, especially in regards of this time. So to me it was an interesting and welcome change. The game has what most history books lack dearly: The first-person perspective. This makes it possible to shine light at aspects of the time mostly ignored. For example the sheer political span of resistance fighters. - From Anarchists and Communists to deeply religious Chatholics, Nationalists and Monarchists. What I liked most about it was the chapter-structure of the game, enabling you to witness the shift of lies, persecution and autharianism over the full time of the Nazi reign. From the more "mild" lies of undermining press as "Lügenpresse" (=fake news) to the persecution of minorities; One after the other. >"First they came for the CommunistsAnd I did not speak outBecause I was not a CommunistThen they came for the SocialistsAnd I did not speak outBecause I was not a SocialistThen they came for the trade unionistsAnd I did not speak outBecause I was not a trade unionistThen they came for the JewsAnd I did not speak outBecause I was not a JewThen they came for meAnd there was no one leftTo speak out for me"<~Martin Niemöller, national conservative and former supporter of Hitler
_childDocuments_.name: Through the Darkest of Times

_childDocuments_.review: It is a good game, with enough twists and plot turns to keep it interesting. It has also everything to do with making hard choices. And it confronts you with moral issues. It is easy to say thay you will stand up against injustice living in a free and save country, but what will you do when you're live will depend on it. That is what makes this game so interesting, it is not only fun to play, but the awareness that there where people 100 years ago who really did these things makes it very real.
_childDocuments_.name: Through the Darkest of Times

_childDocuments_.review: It's the first game I can think of off the top of my head that shows what the rise to power of the nazi party was like. Shame the underlying game is so formulaic and boring. Every turn takes place in a week, and every week plays the same. Assign your members to missions that they hopefully have high odds of success in, then rng determines if those missions go well or poorly. It could be a board game, or a cell phone game with how simplistic it is. That is not a problem in and of itself, but it makes the gameplay feel tacked on and out of place.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game as part of the Humble Monthly, and I started out enjoying this game. It fit into my wheelhouse pretty well: a  high-stakes middle management strategy game with a dreary narrative. It's funny how my enjoyment of the game dipped after I figured out how to strategize. Each of the missions a number of turns before it disappears off the map. This includes the major, critical events that you work towards throughout the game. How fast you work through the prep missions is largely controlled by RNG, so instead of pulling 3 of an important item (and hitting the number necessary to go the big mission), you could end up with 2, or even 0 if you're really unlucky. This also determines whether or not you actually unlock the subsequent missions. I found myself stuck, over and over again, trying to do these big missions, only to watch them expire before I could do them. It felt futile, since it seemed to happen whether I hyper focused on the mission or spread myself thin. The difficulty levels don't seem to matter much either with regards to this. Yes, someone could get arrested and you get fewer actions, but you can still make efforts towards your big goals with your remaining people.This isn't inherently bad, but it comes across as unfair. Why the major missions of an act expire before the end of it baffles me. I would end up at the end with a ton of supplies I couldn't use, none of which carry over, so I'd end up having wasted that entire act and having to start from zero, which was never really explained. It never felt like I was actually making progress. In a game about the rise of fascism, having your best efforts inevitably dashed might fit the narrative, but then what is even the point of it being a game?

_childDocuments_.review: This game offers a very unique and intense experience. The game is not without weaknesses. The main gamplay loop, i.e. planning and performing different missons is a bit repetetive and the game at times doesn't explain its mechanics too well. These weaknesses, however, are in my opinion outweight by the games strenghts. The story events in between tell very emotional stories and shed light on aspects of this time that are typically not the main focus in historical documentaries or education. This is further supported by the art design of the game. Overall, the things it does different to other games makes it so good in my opinion. This covers the topic it focuses on, namly resistance of the civil population, and how it does it. I like that it does not let your actions change history, but manages to make you understand why people anyways chose to resist. And this is also well reflected in a main and very important gameplay decision of the developers: there are no extra rewards for completing missions in the game like experience points or loot etc. To beat the game, you "simply" have to keep your resistance group going and survive until the end of the war. It is the player's choice whether you invest scarce recourses to, e.g., provide a hideout to a young man who was called up for military service, but hides from the Wehrmacht. If the weaknesses do not put you off, this game offers a very special and worthwile experience.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing the first hour while covering this game for the Humble Choice Review: Through the Darkest of Times calls itself a historical resistance strategy game, but what it really amounts to is a worker placement game set in 1933 Germany, focused on taking down Hitler.  Let’s just get this out of the way, Hitler is bad and Nazis are bad.  But the problem is that doesn’t make Through the Darkest of Times good. You see Through the Darkest of Times seems to really rest on “It’s a Nazi game” and does very little beyond creating the setting and making up scenes with important backdrops.  Whereas WARSAW adapted the amazing Darkest Dungeon with a Nazi theming, if you remove the Nazi theming from Through the Darkest of Times, you find that there’s not much of a game here.  A little less than half of Through the Darkest of Times is manipulative writing that reinforces “Nazis bad,” but the problem is the story here isn’t particularly interesting or informative other than name-dropping major moments in German history, and making reference to that oh so evil baddie Hitler. The other side of the game, the worker management game where you constantly have to decide what each of your soldiers do on a daily basis isn’t much better.  Much of the game is about gathering money, supporters, or using both of those resources to further your causes, but unlike many worker placement games, the tasks are very rudimentary and just amount to small advances in the game’s plot. There’s a lot of worker management games on the computer, and Through the Darkest of Time isn’t offensive or bad, or even poorly themed.  It’s just uninteresting and personally, I really can’t recommend it when it’s only average at best. If you enjoy this review or it has helped you, consider checking out my video review of the entire Humble Choice bundle, or subscribing to my youtube channel. Relevant video: PS. After posting this review, I got an email from the developer telling me this game is launching on multiple platforms, and if I want a review copy.  Lol.  I doubt they saw my coverage of the game, I just find that funny.

_childDocuments_.review: Through the Darkest of Times is an immersive, story-driven game that gives you a first-person perspective of Germany slowly coming apart by the growing Nazi regime.The gameplay is simple. You start as a tiny resistance movement whose ultimate goal is to reveal the truth of the Nazi government and to help those persecuted by them. Your group grows as you gather supporters, raise funds, gather resources, and recruit more members. Your members can also use their background, affiliation, and traits (Ex: Athletic communist baker, Social democratic lawyer) to their advantage by doing missions that favor their certain trait. In the meantime, you also have to watch your back carefully and to ensure your members heat doesn't go too high, otherwise they might get a knock on their front door from the Gestapo and be arrested.While gameplay wise this sequence can become repetitive, that's not what this game is about. The true purpose of this game is to put you in the shoes of a Germany citizen who can only watch as his/her country slowly falls apart by the nazi party. The graphics are great that blend perfectly for the dark setting, The characters are realistic and likable, and the cutscenes are amazing and can emotionally tear your heart out at certain scenes.While there weren't any problems and bugs that I experienced on my window (at least for me personally), there were only a few things that I wish the developers would add (Not to discredit this amazing game, but just to merely point out). Some of the cutscenes allow you to choose our dialogue, but ultimately lead to the same outcome (unless you do something really stupid like calling a brownshirt fat). Another thing that happens is that there are random events that can affect how your resistance functions (lower morale, raise heat). However, there are also events that can remove your key resistance members no matter what you do. While this can make the gameplay more interesting, it can really screw you up if you were solely depending on him/her to lead the resistance. In one gameplay my resistance spends valuable resources and men to rescue a key member who had just been arrested by the SS. The very next day she returns she suffers a "I CAN'T TAKE IT ANYMORE!!!" moment and leaves without saying a thank you. (At least she stayed true to her unstable trait).But despite these thoughts, they can't change the way I feel about this game. This is one of the most immersive games I have ever played and I applaud the developers at Paintbucket games for creating an amazing game focusing on such a dark subject. I would recommend this game to anyone and I encourage you to try it.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutley love this game! I'm not even ususally a fan of these turn based strategy games, but what makes it so special is the stories that tell themselves. like when you don't have enough money to bail out one of your people's dad and he dies in prison and then someone gets arrested and you muster all your strength to get them out of prison because the last time it didn't go so well and one of your mates was killed in custody. Overall, if you are interested in a good story and history this is a must buy.
