_childDocuments_.review: This is the best that I've seen the WRC series since 4. Granted, WRC 4 is the last one I played for any significant amount of time.I believe that DiRT Rally 2 is this game's main comparison in the market. And  is my review of that. Now you may ask yourself: Why is WRC 8 up and DiRT Rally 2.0 down? —Well, there are a few reasons.  The rest of this review will follow this thought process, so if that doesn't suit your needs, read a different review.KT Racing is still the developer however—Milestone Srl hasn't been the dev since WRC 4. And I have to say this is a huge step up from WRC 7. They are however functional. —“But Space, you said it was a huge step up?!”—Well, it is! Unlike WRC 7 where the cars behaved as though the tires were covered in soap, WRC 8 feels like every track is on a different planet with a slightly smaller mass than Earth.—Let me explain: 90% of the time when your tires are touching the ground it feels good  you keep in mind that everything feels a little floaty. You'll definitely run into situations where you slide too much and then get the car juggled by space-moon creatures as you bounce off of rocks. And there are other times where the car tries to take off as if it merely a hollow paper weight. But , the physics work.In my totally arbitrary and subjective four slot scale. WRC sits in slot 3. If slot 1 is Ridge Racer, slot 4 is Assetto Corsa/BeamNG and in slot 2 is your main DiRT series, Project Gotham Racing, some Need for Speeds and Forza Horizons—WRC and the DiRT Rally side series sit firmly in slot 3. Visually the game is a little underwhelming for a 2019/2020 release. But it's perfectly serviceable.Now, the main DiRT Series has a more robust career than DiRT Rally 2. However, since I'm mainly comparing this to DiRT Rally 2, the career in WRC is very good whereas in DR2, it's essentially non-existent. You'll have to contend with satisfying manufacturers, managing crew members across seasons and have to schedule events, rest days, training, sponsor try-outs. Your crew will get tired and will need to rest or you can replace them with the “B-Team” as you schedule events beyond your means. This effectively means worse repairs during events.As you level within the career you'll unlock R+D points that will improve sponsor relationships, make cars more reliable, among other things.Of course, if that is too much and you just want to drive the damn car, you can just do the quick play mode or even the season mode which is essentially a less involved career mode.WRC 8 does have weekly challenges, but they're nothing close to what DiRT Rally 2 offers for dailies. The co-driver VO is okay. Though, if you're careening off a cliff in Greece in the middle of a storm, your co-driver will still robotically recite the pacenotes as if all was well. But I doubt this will change until some deep learning AI can reproduce a fake voice to do it dynamically. It'd be too costly to record and implement all that dialogue in different inflections.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a sim racer and what matters to you the most is the physics model, don't get WRC8, stay on DiRT Rally or DiRT Rally 2.0 for now, at least until WRC9 comes to steam, if ever.The physics model is off on almost everything except maybe asphalt, it's not horrible, but it's not right, now that this is clear :I like it, it's a good game, not incredible it has its flaws, but hella fun if you're into rally.Career mode is quite good, there is a bit of "management" nothing extra ordinary, but it's nice, there are perks, which give you various bonuses, "historic races" quite explanatory, races with historic cars, or similar, "trainings" which make you gain XP, "Maintenance" which repairs the condition of your car, ultimately these are a good change of pace between intense rallies, and i like it.Tracks are incredible, and very varied, it's probably the best aspect of the game, don't have much to say on that since you really need to experience them to get an idea.Graphically speaking, contrary to what's i've seen in some reviews here, are actually quite good, they're not ground breaking at all, but the game has its touch, subjectively, i like its aesthetic, and no, it doesn't look "like a 360 era game" as i've seen posted here, which is honestly an awful exaggeration.Sounds are ... well they could be better, there is always room for improvements, but they're good, cockpit sounds and engine sounds are rather spot on, environmental sounds are quite satisfying, overall, they're solid, i love the backfire pops and especially how they made it sound in the distance. The weather system is a really nice touch too, it makes the rallies much more interesting due to its impredictability, although as far as i've seen, it's deterministic, if it starts raining in the middle of your rally, it will always do so if you restart.TLDR : WRC 8 is a showoff simulator, if you don't mind getting used to the physics, it's fun and i recommend it for people that are not hardcore rally sim racers, but even then, you could have fun !Now i have to bring WRC9 in this review, for a simple reason, it's literally the same game, with a much much more acurate physics model, UI improvements, and new tracks, i like WRC8, but after trying out WRC9, i can't go back, i would highly suggest waiting for WRC9 to come to Steam if you're interested into the WRC series and if you're searching for a change of pace from DiRT/2.0, it's worth the wait.Just don't support Epig and their disgusting exclusivity practices.♥♥♥♥ you Epic, and ♥♥♥♥ this trash that's called the Epic Games Store.I usually don't post reviews at all, so i probably forgot some things, hopefully this will help you decide if this game is worth your money and your time or not.

_childDocuments_.review: Update 18th March 2021: I was hoping this would grow on me but it hasn't, I was hoping I would get past the problems but I can't. There's too many unfixed issues that have rolled over from the earlier games. The Dev's are not putting enough effort into updating new versions of the WRC games, maybe they think the name is enough to keep sales high and based on so many thumbs up reviews for what I think is a seriously flawed racer it looks like it is, Everything I wrote in the earlier review still stands.Original Review 2nd/3rd March 2021The good & the bad.Bad:The game suffers from constant stuttering where it drops frames for some reason (My guess is that the actual game engine needs updating), In a rally game with lots of tight turns I found myself more often than not having my stage times sabotaged by the juddery experience. The visuals are dated as you can tell by the amount of noise which I think is due to old anti-aliasing techniques, Speaking of noise the British co-driver voice sounds like a WWII Colonel Mainwaring type character, Having spent my 50 years of life in the UK & having not heard anyone talk like that since the disappearance of my Great Grandad's generation I can only surmise that this is some sort of stereotypical joke.Another issue I mentioned in reviews for the older WRC titles is that the cars have no weight & the handling suffers because of it, Good:Dynamic weatherI prefer the Sweden stages better than those used in other rally games.I like the Chile stages/maps.My Conclusion:I think it's sad that the game that holds the official WRC title has been left in their dust by so many other modern rally games, My overall experience hasn't been an enjoyable one so far but if my opinion of the game changes I'll update this review, that said seeing that WRC 9 is now out on another platform it seems unlikely that they'll be coming back to work on this so like previous titles it will likely be left with the bugs it still has today, maybe I should be grateful the audio bug that's still in WRC4 isn't in any of the newer titles. I got this game as part of a Humble bundle, If I'd bought it on release I'd of refunded it as it's not in my opinion an okay game & the fact that it has so many old bug's & issues from previous iterations in the franchise it feels like minimal effort was made, It has real issues that should of never made the release, they're more important than giving the same old tired game a quick spruce up so they can cash in on the branding.WRC 8 has problems, some of which were there as far back as WRC 5, that should tell you all you need to know.

And to be honest if you want a rally game i would go for dirt 2.0 over this, this game feels more like it focuses on the WRC aspect rather than the intensity of the rally itself.

_childDocuments_.review: When I first bought this game I thought it was horrible and didn't play it for months. Few weeks ago I started going thru each setting, literally one click at a time till I found a combination that works really well with a DD2, R300 Podium Wheel and Heusinkveld Pedals. According to Steam I've played DR2 over 1800 hours, and have to say after getting my wheelbase configured properly I have no plans on going back anytime soon. I really like the way the handling changes when you crash the vehicle, the way the dust clouds the front window. I don't have any complaints about the FFB, at times I can even feel the large round circles in the road. Not all, but I do feel some of them. Rally's in Turkey, Chile and Argentina are a blast.I found the Engine, and possibly the Suspension settings to be finicky. Example being, during testing my settings must have been so out of wack because depending on the severity of the crash the wheel would shake to the point I had to quit the rally, and at times exit to the main screen or even exit the game before it stopped vibrating. With everything optimized, now when I crash it hoses my handling proportional to the severity of the crash and gets worse if I crash a second time, will be fixed to a certain degree during repairs, I assume this is by design that it's not fixed completely. When I end the Rally everything is back to normal. Another example if I raise Engine above 79 I start to feel a clunk in the transmission when I shift, along with other odd vibrations. If you enjoy Rally racing I would definitely recommend this game with one important caveat. From my testing and messages I read from others ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ about the game kinda confirm it, you really need to take the time to optimize the settings to your hardware. A couple clicks off either way can have a major impact on the games performance. If you do this you won't be disappointed. I may sound like a fanboy for WRC 8 but I'm not. Up until a few weeks ago I had completely given up on this game and was willing to wait until 2023 for the CM version. When I first bought the game I wrote an email to the developers expressing my displeasure, just want to do the right thing and give credit where it's due. Thanks for developing a really fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: After having played this for almost nine hours in three days, I feel utterly compelled to leave a review. WRC 8 is an honest to God rally racing simulator and it is 100% a simulator, without any doubt. I see a lot of reviews comparing this game unfavourably to Dirt 2.0, and I feel compelled to write what I'll generously claim to be a comparative review. I'll cover the physics, sound, gameplay, and content. I have a wheel (G29 with a shifter) and I've played other rally games, namely Dirt and Dirt 2.0, as well as Richard Burns Rally, the latter of which I consider to be the absolute gold standard of physics quality and fidelity, and to which I will be comparing this game in terms of feel. I am writing this review because, frankly, I think to claim that the physics in WRC 8 are unrealistic or even 'bad' is disingenuous at best and patently false at worst. To start with, the feel of the driving - the difference in surface and traction is vastly more detailed than it is in 2.0, and is about on par with RBR, but comes up short when the damage model comes in. You can feel the difference in tarmac, gravel, snow, and dust very, very clearly, to the point where even the edges of the course are well modelled, something I've not seen since RBR and something which definitely is not the case in 2.0. The actual feel of driving the car in WRC 8 is pretty much spot on, given my experiences in RBR and even 2.0. Honestly, as far as the cars go, the difference between 2.0 and WRC is principally in the core configuration of the vehicles. Unlike 2.0, WRC is licensed, meaning you get WRC 1, 2, and Junior, the official versions, with sequential shifters and AWD on the first two categories. Comparing this to similar - older - AWD and FWD cars in 2.0, the feeling is almost identical, with 2.0 winning by dint of slightly more detailed engine damage. Comparing all this to RBR, they both got it down incredibly well, and I'd be hard pressed to say which is 'better' - both 2.0 and WRC 8 succeed in making the rally car feel like a challenging monster. The sole gripe I have with the physics in WRC is that the cars remain too stable at times and it is too hard to roll them, and all too frequently will a small obstacle cause your car to simply stop dead (with appropriate damage of course). This is a situation of 'closes a door, opens a window' when compared to 2.0, wherein the physics impact on your vehicle seems greatly exaggerated in parts, to the point where rather than stop you, small bits of debris will absolutely send your car FLYING. Whilst I know rally cars are light for obvious reasons, a lot of it seems to come down to jagged track edges in that sim. On the whole, however? RBR remains king, and both of these get close to it really quite well. They get the basic feel of rally down and they're definitely challenging, and with all the assists off in WRC 8, you're going to need just as much skill to get on a podium as you will in 2.0 or RBR. Will it be the same sort of skill? Probably not, but every sim is different. WRC 8 sounds ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing. Honestly, it sounds incredible. RBR had some rather mediocre sounds all things considered, so I won't be using it as a point of comparison, but this game sounds as good as 2.0. The cars feel weighty, meaty, they feel alive, and you can feel the individual clicks of the transmission, the turbo lag, the pebbles hitting the floor plate, tires and suspension buckling under weight transfers...it's all there. I don't know why some people have an issue with the way this game sounds but - whilst I admittedly do not follow IRL rally (yet, I aim to get into it, thanks to this game) - it sounds spot on, and I am entirely capable of shifting the car up and down well (or as well as a noob can) on sound alone. 2.0 does that really well too, so they're about on par there. The only issue I have is that the sound of thunder sounds a bit dodgy from inside the car, often sounding more like a car backfiring, but even the noise of dumping the car into a big puddle and then back out of it is just right. This is where I have to recommed WRC 8 over 2.0. Over the years, 2.0 has turned into a husk of the original Dirt Rally. It's a DLC simulator (I know how rich that sounds coming from the lady with nearly 300 Train Simulator DLC but bear with me), and everything is locked behind a paywall of some kind. I was astounded to see how little I got with 2.0 for the size of a hefty 100+ GB worth of data. It's a BIG game, and that sort of HDD/SSD space needs to be, in my mind, justified by content. And in the case of 2.0, it really isn't. WRC 8? For a tidy 38 GB worth of unpacked data, if even, you get all of the official WRC stages, three different categories of cars, and four special cars, including two historical ones - namely the Fulvia and the Stratos. There's an official career mode, which features team management, and a wholly event-based season mode where you don't need to manage anything other than your basic ability to remain alive. RBR did something similar, too. You got the ability to drive a proper hardcore career from start to finish with a chosen car, and in WRC, you choose a category instead. The stages are varied, challenging, and interesting, and despite how few people seem to like it, I enjoyed the RPG/Management element of the career mode. I like the ability to control the finer points of an experience like that, if even superficially. Is this game worth full price? Given that WRC 9 just came out and has purportedly even better FFB (more on that in a minute), I'd probably go for that one, but the series as a whole is ABSOLUTELY headed in the right direction and I'll definitely pick up the next game - if not WRC 9 then 10. This is the last thing I wanna touch on. Honestly, the performance of WRC 8 is stellar. It runs at a rock solid 60 FPS on my 1060 6 GB with 32 GB of RAM (I know, DCS World is the culprit there), and i5 8600k, but my best mate has an 8 GB RAM old AMD powered PC with a 1660 and it runs just as well as it does on mine. For how good it looks - which isn't perfect, but going as fast as you are, you'll hardly care - it is a crisp and smooth experience. Comparing this to 2.0 feels almost unfair. On that same 32 GB system, 2.0 ran with dips to as low as 30 FPS in places on medium high, with Ultra being a slideshow at times, for...no measurable visual gain? Maybe I'm just blind as a bat, but I could see no difference that would make such a drop in performance valid. Not that it makes a difference, mind you, because as RBR proves, if you get rally right the visuals don't really matter. The force feedback is a weak spot in WRC 8 compared to 2.0 however, and 2.0 definitely has more tightly aliased and filtered FFB. There's less clipping and jagged skipping of gears, it's more solid and robust, and unlike WRC 8, it feels just right - not too light, and not too heavy on my G29. It isn't a top-shelf wheel, far from it, of course, but WRC 8 feels good enough. If 9 improves on the FFB, that'll be my sole major gripe with the game actually fixed. The only additional point of complaint is that Dirt 2.0 supports TrackIR and VR natively, whereas WRC 8 does not support VR and supports TrackIR only through a few external hacks. It does work, however, and I'll have a guide up on my page on how to get it working soon!If you can, and like modern, licensed WRC content, get WRC 9. It's worth the full price. I'd say this is worth the full price, too, if you don't like Epic and don't mind the slight downgrade in FFB. The multiplayer is seamless, the content is vast, the stages are amazing, the DLC is worth the money (especially the RWD Legends pack which is for some reason not listed on the store, Bigben pls fix)

_childDocuments_.review: Requested a refund, reasons for which are quite simple:1. This is not a true simulator, the physics model is not what I had expected. Vehicle handling is not predictable and the throttle/brake mapping (despite the settings) isn't well modulated. Vehicles don't take off / slide properly and you can't feel any kind of connection to the road. It's quite disappointing, given that some 'arcade' titles do a much better job at these simple things. Sometimes you have a lot of grip where you expect less and then vice versa - snow is the worst, which completely ruins the experience. Like some others have mentioned, the physics are just not at a simulator level yet.2. The graphics are not competitive, they're decent, but not at the level that they should be. They fit the style that the developers are going for, but not convincing enough to be likable by sim fans. I expected more photo realism at full resolution. Then again, this is not the selling point of the product.Only buy this if you're looking for something new to pass time, you might like it. If you're expecting a more connected driving experience, I would urge you otherwise.

_childDocuments_.review: After the game suddenly reusing to work after i gave it a thumbs up, and seeing the hypocrisy of asking for a steam awards price for an outdated version of the game, i am giving this game a thumbs down.Oh, also, forget about using the crash reporter. It's trying to send an email to some google-hosted account that no longer exists, with some 401 access denied errors peppered here and there for good meassure.----I am not sure how this review can stand out, for both prospect consumers and the developers themselves, with WRC9 having released somewhere around october outside of Steam.However, here are my two cents on this game after playing this during this weekend.I absolutely dislike the team management bit of this game. It detracts from the overall experience in my opinion. Mind you, there's nothing inherently wrong or flawed with the way it's implemented, but it is not a design element i appreciate. I play racing games to... well, race. The calendar shuffling, keeping the morale of the team up, the RPG skill trees on Research and Development, and so on, are incredibly out of place and they get tiresome real fast. I've spent the last 10 hours or so trying to do the career and i've given up. I am doing random seasons and choosing the individual rally option with a car of my choice.This leads us to our next point, the racing itself. I do like it, it's nice and snappy and everything feels right. I am playing with a controller since i can't get my wheel ATM for testing, but every car feels nippy and responsive. It feels just about right, in the arcade type intuitiveness and straight-to-the-point i like to enjoy. I am slightly confused at this since this labels itself as a simulator, but i am not finding myself bogged down by all the mind boggling statistics and meters and awkwardly heavy and unresponsive controls that seem to plague "simulators" these days. Maybe the simulator bit only applies to the team management aspect, and for that i am graceful. I have yet to try WRC 9, but the driving model in WRC 8 is just about perfect. For reference, i am playing on medium difficulty with cosmetic damage only and no assists. That alone turns the experience into a great driving and playing experience to me.I have one big nitpick to point out however. This game has some serious frame-pacing issues despite my flawed, but over-spec'd computer. There are some real frame pacing issues that makes the physics engine seemingly unhappy. I've phased through walls, launched myself into space, or a small post has sent me pitching forward into my doom. I hit one of the goal posts right at the end of the track and the car went full "my planet needs me" inmediatly after. Unfortunately this happens a lot. It is both hilarious, and frustrating, as i may be having a great run, fly into space, hit restart, and end up quitting an event because afterwards the physics have been wonky and other minor bumps have sent me laterally or in other directions making me restart until emptying out all my tries.This may have been fixed in WRC 9, but if it has not, I'd like for the developers to check out these strange physics issues. The game can behave perfectly at some points but some others are... amusing, to put it into words.I wish valve added a neutral button for reviews because... I like only a subset of the whole package, and i would not recommend it unless it severally discounted ( since, standalone events are like 1/3 of the entire content )Oh, also. This game is prone to crash. Alt-tabbing will cause the game, somehow using a macro to take a screenshot and accidentally pasting it into the game window makes it to crash, the game is allowing user input and inbound/outbound clipboard access. That is baffling, clearly is causing errors, and it could potentially be a security hole at some point.Also the crash reporter is broken. I cannot submit the log file since it just "finishes with errors". So... Yeah. I should have exported that logfile.TL;DR. Get this game under 25 bucks for the deluxe edition if you can. The pricing strategy of the developers here is astonishing. The driving's great but everything else sucks.

Every other graphical setting maxed out delivered smooth frame rates but the game still looks like something from 2011. The co-driver’s voice is absolutely laughable, do the developers think people actually talk like this in the 21st century? He sounds like he’s just been teleported from the Victorian era. Really how much would it have cost to get Nicky Grist or Phil Mills to have done the pace notes? As for the career mode, I don’t want to have to micromanage every aspect of the team, I have no interest in directing the team, I simply want to be the driver without all of the other boring fiddly stuff. Physics wise for me it sits between pure arcade and something like Dirt Rally. I’d say the rally cross handling in Project Cars 2 for example is light years ahead of this and that is only one single discipline in that game, in comparison to this which has the entire game built around that sort of driving. It’s not terrible, but I wouldn’t say it’s very good either. I had some issues with ultrawide support, there's still graphical issues, but doesn't stretch the ui anymore.As others have mentioned, the best part about this game is the physics, but unfortunately it isn't backed up with good forcefeedback. Small cars like the GR Yaris feel nimble and are a blast to drive while lower tier cars like the fwd Ford Focus just feels like an absolute slog to get around a corner. I hate paved courses in DR2.0 but here I'm actually having a decent amount of fun.The sound is disappointing. Engine noises, gravel, tire squeal, straight cut gears, etc, it's all there in theory, but in the same way it was in a game from 2001. The codriver is loud, but the combination of the accent and unclear recordings somehow causes me to miss practically every call. I could give the career management mode a miss, I am much more interested in just getting in and driving instead of trying to figure out the menus. I unfortunately accidentally hit turn off the tutorial and I couldn't find how to turn it back on. Luckily there is another careerish type mode that lets you just hop in and the game puts you straight into the rally.Courses are fun for the most part, but I find myself earning penalties while staying in the middle of the road. Other times I cut corners and get nothing. Overall I'm not sure if I want to keep this game. The physics and courses are great great, but there's just a lot of mediocre elsewhere. _childDocuments_.review: The visual aspect is exceptional, however I would have liked the option for head-tracking. The game play is great in terms of how you progress through single player. (I've not tried online)The audio as with WRC7 is still awful but has mildly improved. The cars just sound rubbish but that said, modern cars do sound like a sewing machine. I would like to have seen more of the classic cars with more "classic events" the weather visuals look great and are more than a little daunting on some of the tracks, specially at nigh. in terms of overall performance the game runs extremely well. Force feedback was very iffy and took tons of mucking about with and is still lacking in any sort of "real feel" and more often than not I lose the car because I can't quite get a feel for when it's stepping out past to the point of control loss. Generally speaking it's very playable with some very challenging courses. I particularly enjoy the free roam area where you can test drive to your hearts content. As far as the free roam area is concerned it blows all other racing/rally games clear off the map.WRC8 has a fabulous level of immersion despite the little things which I don't like about the game. controller setup is a little frustrating but if you've owned multiple racing/rally games you should at least have a basis of what you want your racing experience to "feel" like.side note... it really wouldn't hurt if all wheel/controller manufactures came together and decided on a "standard" for input/output/FFB/configuration and terminology... it would make the life of gamers far less frustrating if, in all the games we owned "*.*" meant and did the same thing across all platforms and games.Despite some obvious short comings this is an extremely enjoyable game and for what it's worth.. as a casual gamer, I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I am going to start with the bad.WARNING: There is no option of Custom Rally/Custom Championship, so if you want to play in WRC category you can do it only in career mode. When you start you have two options Junior WRC or WRC2, go directly to WRC2, there are reports that if you choose Junior WRC you will not be able to reach WRC category. Then there is another problem, WRC2 is divided in three levels (WRC2 Privateer, WRC2 and WRC2 Pro), so always try to improve your reputation with Manufacturers to get Manufacturer Challenges so you can reach WRC Category as soon as possible.Now the general review.WRC5, WRC6 and WRC7 are basically the same, so it is great that we now have a fully updated game with a brand new career mode. In Junior WRC and WRC2 the rallies last for only 2 days instead of 3 days, this is a great improvement as doing 3 day rallies was very tiresome in the past games. The dynamic weather is a brillian addition. Another great improvement was the co-driver indications, in the past games the indications were horrible and robotic, now these sound more natural and clear but still not as good as in DiRT games. Regarding the physics I am not sure what to think, it seems good, but  you get the sensation that the car is weightless and this is very bad particularly during the crashes where the car almost flies away.My main complain is the issue with WRC Category as I explained above, some people have been trapped in WRC2 without being able to advance to WRC, with the game basically wasting the time of the players, the decision to separate WRC2 into three levels is also a waste of time.

_childDocuments_.review: Having owned WRC4-8, somehow WRC8 managed to make a MAJOR step forward without appearing to do so, at least on the surface, by basically HIDING stuff, and that makes it... surprisingly good. It's strange that Kyloton managed to put out its best at the year where they were told they had lost the WRC license (to Codemasters), for this should have been WRC7 (the WRC7 actually released felt like a slightly polished and updated WRC6)WRC8 looks and indeed sounds much like WRC7. Those of you who had WRC7 would recognize a lot of the courses, at least visually. However, the driving model seems to have gotten an upgrade, so the surfaces feel differently now, even on gamepad. Not quite like Dirt Rally 2.0, but feels like an upgrade from WRC7. WRC8 now offers TWO different "career" options... a "driver only" mode called "career", and a "team manager/driver" hybrid campaign called "campaign". Driver mode is same as the previous iterations... win, win some more. Win your division (JWRC, WRC-2, or WRC) rallies for one "season", after which, if you do well, you may be recruited by the next division, or at least, contract renewed. What's surprising is this was hidden on the 2nd menu and may have never been noticed. The campaign added the wrinkle of hiring a crew, gaining XP, leveling up, gaining R&D points, and spending them on areas that can enhance your team and/or your performance. You'll need meteorologist (weather forecast), mechanic (rest area repairs), engineer (reliability), agent (more events, more chance of bonus), physical therapist (crew work longer before needing a break), and financial analyst (reduce costs, increase profits). But some of those had to be unlocked via R&D. Each crew cost money which must be paid from your winnings, and you probably need to hire 2 if one was fatigued out. Every day, you can do training, or special events, unless you have an event to race in. The special events are getting a bit more interesting. So far I've seen historical rally and extreme conditions. Historical rally is simple: take one of the older classic cars, usually something from the 1970's or 1980's, and take it out for a spin through the specified course, going as fast as possible, obviously. I'd say you should take it out a couple times, as it'd be VERY VERY different from the modern AWD or FWD machines you're used to. Extreme conditions is a bit more interesting. Basically, you need to get from A to B, in extremely bad weather (pouring rain, night, fog, hail, etc.) and your vehicle is probably damaged or at least, severely degraded. Can you finish the specified segment of the course in time? Kyloton also learned from Codemasters in that there is now a leaderboard, weekly challenges, and so on. WRC8 is definitely worth buying, esp. if there's a large hiscount.

_childDocuments_.review: Quite the improvement in every way imaginable from the previous WRC games in the franchise. Unlike its predecessors though, this game mainly focuses on simulation rather than being arcadey and it also has this neat team building management feature. However, there are a few things which could've been better such as the objectives. Oftentimes, they are contradicting each other so this means you're bound to fail 1 task unless you decide to change it but this will cost you negative relationship points with the manufacturer (and those are random too so even if you change it, there is a chance you'll get an impossible objective again). The penalties are too punishing, imo. You can take a small shortcut but you'll get a 9 second punishment either way. The vehicle damage and physics are better, that's not to say they are amazing in any way and even if you keep on crashing left, right and center the car will almost look just a little dented and maybe have a spoiler chipped off. And the physics can sometimes behave very strangely when you go off the road. In other words, hardly realistic.Lastly, the game does have minor bugs and a weird glitch, I stumbled upon, where the textures go crazy and the screen goes eventually black, luckily this happened to me only once but it's still infuriating, especially when you're playing on a higher difficulty and you can't restart the stage (this goes for crashes as well).Some may point out there are grindy achievements but as long as you're focusing on the career and playing all the way from junior category and not skipping many races, it's not terrible.Good stuff, I was pleasantly surprised considering the other WRC games from KT Racing are quite lackluster. Many people claim this is the best WRC game in the franchise, I can't say yes or no because I'm yet to play the newer titles but this one was very good.

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to the previous entries, WRC8 recieved an overhaul. Each car really feels like it has its own handling model, there are a bunch of new features added to the Career mode, such as team and calendar management.Unlike all the other games, you will get the opprotunity to try out some iconic cars in career mode between championships, in form of single stages that reward you afterwards.The cars are pretty much the same as the previous game, with the exception of a few special cars.The handling takes a bit to get used to, but I have to admit that 7 had the best and had most fun with the handling there.WRC8 also features a test area, which is effectively a free roam mode, which is nice.Skill points, leveling and perks are introduced.-The Lancia Stratos handles absolutely terrible. I understand the point of simulating an old car plus RWD but not being able to keep the car on the road without spinning out is insane. Had to restart a bunch of times on the Historic Event in Germany. -Rain puddles can lock the car and launch it in a random direction. This is one of the most annoying things in the game, specially when rallying in France. Puddles do not affect a car like that in real life when driving on a straight road. They do not randomly send it like its been "force pushed".-Penalties are way too sensitive. I understand getting one when accidentally going into the spectators or cutting corners but the fact that you get 9 seconds added for roll overs, resets and going off track is beyond frustrating. -For some reason, after you reach lvl 50, you capped the experience points and cannot get the rest of the skills from the R&D tree.

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitely an upgrade over the previous game. The career mode got an overhaul and everything looks much better. You can organise your crew, upgrade your car performance and durability, schedule events throughout the year etc. I like the fact that you need to climb through ranks in order to reach WRC level. Gameplay feels much smoother and even though I'm playing on a ps4 joystick, it actually feels like controlling a car. The surrounding roads aren't rigid as much as in WRC7 though glitches still happen from time to time.Cars sound better and control better. Damages are sometimes bugged, for an instance sometimes you can get damaged just by driving over a flat surrounding road dirt, it feels non-existent and needs some work.Overall, much better work than WRC 7. If you're a newbie in rally games my advice is that you skip all the previous WRC games up to WRC 8. The career makes this game playable over a long time.Since this is the first WRC that got a career overhaul, which transfered to the other games I'll give it 9/10, just because devs really showed some love to it.

_childDocuments_.review: WRC 8 is a official licensed rally game, which was meant to challenge Dirt Rally and later the 2.0 version. Sadly it is lacking a lot comparing to those two.The heart of the game, career mode, starts to repeat itself as soon as you have reached WRC-season after Junior WRC or just WRC2. This is a shame, because every motorsport game nowadays should have a solid career mode, as most people are going to spend a lot of time there.Difficulty can not be choosed by number for example between 50 to 100, there are just a few stock settings which are most of the time either too easy or way too hard. Difficulty also can not be changed in the middle of the season, only when new one is about to start.Driving physics themselves are just okay, nothing too special on wheel in my opinion. Car feels like some kind of empty box floating around and being controlled by the player, the feeling from the surface is lacking. And well, the crashing physics are a big joke.If you are completion-type of guy, it will most likely take you 40 to 50 hours to get all the achievements that are not bugged. And btw, if you are trying to get the perfectionist-achievement, don't even bother, because half of the in game 'objectives' in the career don't work as they are meant to.Sadly one of those games which will not bring me back anymore. Hope that to upcoming TDUSC from basicly the same developers will be a world better!

_childDocuments_.review: After clocking 7 seasons in the game, I can definitely say WRC 8 is a joy to play. If you're coming from Dirt Rally, you will miss some hardcore stuff and the lack of polish might bother you, but stick around and you'll find a game that shines in some other aspects. From the current breed of WRC cars to the variety and length of the stages, there's a lot to enjoy. The game's got all the countries from the real WRC season, which means a LOT of variety in terms of surfaces, landscapes and weather conditions you'll be driving through. The driving model itself could be better, sure, but the game still gave me a run for my money! For the more demanding sim racers, there are plenty of good mods out there!The game's got a ton of little glitches and things that could be better (like the FOV adjustment) but those were all minor things among the lots of fun I had playing WRC8. Sure, the Epic games exclusive thing is a bother, but it's a game by a small studio, you know the kind of pressure these people go through. All in all, this game filled in where Dirt Rally lacked, especially when it comes to racing against AI drivers named after my favorite racers, and in current-gen beasts!

_childDocuments_.review: WRC 8 is an improvement over the last installation of the WRC games. The physics are quite off the real thing, but it continuously improves year over year, especially the tarmac physics are solid. In my opinion it's not quite a competitor to DiRT RALLY 2.0, but it has some positive points (like the better tarmac physics) over DiRT.The stages are well designed (flow wise), but not very enticing visually. What is most developed over DiRT is definitely the career mode, there you can drive a car from the Junior WRC to WRC 2 AM, WRC 2 Pro up to WRC, which is quite nice. During that process of developing your driving skills in faster cars, you have to manage your team and do certain tasks (like test driving, historical events, etc.).Overall I can recommened the game to any person who is interested in the WRC, because it's the only game with the official license to it.

name: SIMULACRA 2
detailed_description: The follow-up to the critically acclaimed SIMULACRA , SIMULACRA 2 expands on the found phone horror format with inventive new apps, a more complex narrative, a larger live-action cast, and a deeper look into the darker side of the internet. A young social media influencer's untimely – and unnatural – death is being ruled as an accident. But Detective Murilo suspects that something is amiss. He recruits your help in investigating the case, and hands you a crucial piece of evidence; the victim’s phone. Using your investigative skills, hacking abilities, and the victim's influencer network, it's up to you to piece together the victim’s past. Game Features Choose whether to be a ruthless investigative journalist or a fresh-faced detective Explore a branching narrative and make tough choices Interact with realistic, flawed characters and uncover their secrets Delve deeper into the SIMULACRA lore from the previous game Be terrified by 4k videos documenting the horror that lurks behind this terrible crime

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I enjoyed the concept of the game, I'm so sad to write that I did not enjoy this game as much as the first one. After playing Simulacra, I immediately bought this one, alas it didn't meet my expectations. The story about social media influencers. You'll play as either a detective or a journalist who'll receive a dead influencer phone and dig into it trying to find any evidance to solve the mystery about her death. Her case was closed, but Detective Murilo suspects that something is amiss and thus he hires you for his job. There are three main characters who you'll have to talk to and learn more about Maya. I loved the quality of the videos, a huge improvement from the first game, but the characters - sadly- are not likable at all. I didn't feel involved and didn't care about any of them, even the dead girl, her personality didn't make me sympathize with her death at all. They added some music tracks and hinting system which is great in case you are stuck trying to contact someone or finding a piece of evidence that'll open different dialogue for you. I liked that they have many ways to end this investigation, a whole tree will open up for you. I didn't find this game scary and there are only a few jumpscares which you can predict, especially the phone calls while you are busy reading text messages. Pros:+Jumpscares.+Around 10 hours of gameplay (single playthrough).+Multiple endings.+Hinting system+Steam achievements.Cons:-The characters are real people with mediocre acting.-Not a very convincing story.I didn't enjoy it as much as the first game. I recommend Simulacra's first game over this one.

_childDocuments_.review: 100% achievement, 3+ playthroughs No. Yes (~23 achievements). No. is the third installment of the  series, which is happening in the same universe as  (). You'll still be able to browse on someone's smartphone to find clues to what was happening on a case, in addition to several new features to enhance your gameplay.- 4 endings with minor story branchings- Hints in case you are stuck- Some information is very hard to find, especially if you want to unlock the good ending- Replaying the game for other endings take time even with a faster chat speedIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650Just like other games in the series,  plays out in the form of a smartphone. The interface looks similar to other smartphones in general while still having a simpler function to make it easy to operate. That being said, there is a notable improvement from the previous game - you can play a video from a certain timestamp now, making it easy to skip video content that you have seen before.As someone who has played the first game, there is nothing new that you can discover. It still revolves around the same concept as the other games in the series, but that's exactly what's bad about it. The game focuses on an investigation task, and there is no element of surprise since I already know what I would expect a few minutes right after I started the game. Imagine having a murder mystery case with you already knowing the perpetrator. It kills off the mysterious vibe that the game was meant to be, especially if the game focuses on the same thing as the first one.On the characters' side, we have three main casts instead of one. They have different personalities which attribute to their career, but there is no sense of attachment to them at all. I couldn't relate to them, especially with their dark secrets that make them sounds more like a jerk than they should be. There is one character that can be considered good, but again, you don't talk to them enough to know on a personal level. On the good side, there are two reoccurring characters from the first game, although you won't be missing out if you haven't played the first game.The story branching is more planned out, but they become overly complicated. You can fall into one of the three bad endings because you chose the wrong choice, and getting the best ending can take you hours of replaying and choosing the right answers if you try to get it on your own. Moreover, there are also some timed decisions and puzzles where you need to type some answers to solve. It takes too much detective work just to unlock the good ending, and the ending doesn't seem too different from the others either, especially if you have played the first game. Furthermore, some dialogues don't seem to flow smoothly if you choose certain options or do things in the "wrong" order.Unlike the first game, this game brings some investigation work into play. You'll still have the same task to discover the truth from someone's phone, but you are doing so in the form of an official investigation. This means that you have an access to government records, allowing you to look up more information that can help you to solve the case. You still need to do the first few investigative works by yourself to figure out the keyword that you need to look up first though.Sometimes, the game will ask you to answer some questions. The answers to these questions can be found by digging through the user's phone, although some information can be too obscure to find. This becomes even worse if you try to aim for a good ending since you need to answer some answers by typing it out, and the hints are way too invisible unless if you look very carefully. Moreover, there are just too many chats and social media posts to read, and finding the info that you need is like looking for a needle in a haystack.Clue-collecting gives some sort of incentive to look through the optional posts. An icon will appear on your bottom right corner whenever there is a clue that can be collected. These clues can be used to either repair broken files or corner someone by giving them a piece of evidence. Unlike the questions, these clues can be easily found - you just need to scroll until the icon comes to capture it. Heck, you don't even need to read the texts at all.I finished the game in 4.9h. I replayed the game several times to get the other endings, which are not that different from each other. There is some hint system that can help you in case you are stuck, but they might not be enough when dealing with those vague questions that require you to investigate people's posts very carefully.The game doesn't have a lot of accessibility options when you are replaying the game for the second time. While it has an option for a faster chat speed, the speed is still too slow for someone who has finished the game before. Moreover, some videos, especially the ones that are played in the ending, are unskippable.Speaking of videos, the game size is unnecessarily big (16 GB) because the developer is trying to support 4k resolution. As someone who doesn't have a 4k monitor, I feel that the size is too much just for a feature that I don't use. I wish there is an option to install the game with lesser video spec.I also encountered one bug when I played the game too fast. Some dialogues will duplicate out of nowhere and you are forced to read the texts twice because of it. Lastly, the game can be hard to read for those who have problems with reading moving texts or seeing bright colors. feels like a step back from the first game. It has more features than its predecessors, but most of these features change the game to be more complicated than it should be. The videos might have more content, but there are way too many audio files that can be explained just fine in texts. Heck, there are even some parts when you have to listen to someone mumbling to himself.The core story is way too similar to . I got a major spoiler just by playing the first game, and I'm not sure if people who are new to the series should start with this game either. While you don't have to play the first game to enjoy this one, the first game explains the universe better than this. Moreover, the simplicity in the first game works better for this type of game. Don't get me wrong though, the game is good, but having nothing new to offer to the table makes it quickly loses its charm.

_childDocuments_.review: Very similar to the first game but with a lot more high quality video footage. Unfortunately, they completely ruined the experience by adding a few ridiculous mechanics that weren't present in the first game like timed replies and a clue processing system similar to that of Orwell. Timed replies: Sometimes during a conversation you will have a limited time to respond to a message but there is no indication that you're in that situation until you click the reply button. If you take the time to read the messages before hitting reply, the timer will already be done by the time you click the button so you missed your chance to even see what the possible responses were. I'm sure I missed a lot of content due to this. Clue processing: Instead of letting you figure things out on your own or by questioning people like the first game did, you have certain clues you have to "discover" before the game will progress. You may have discovered the information yourself, but it doesn't trigger until you click the scan button and then go into the WARDEN software and process the clue. Completely ruins the experience and doesn't let you feel the sense of accomplishment you would have received just by figuring it out on your own.As an example, I watched a video of a crime being committed and then knew who was involved. I went to question them in chat and wasn't able to. In order to progress this, I had to go watch the video again, click the scan button, then go into the WARDEN software on the phone and drag the video into the clue processor. It then told me exactly what I had 'discovered' by watching the video and triggered the chat responses that let me question the individuals involved. This was a completely pointless mechanic that absolutely spoiled the great experience I had with the first game.With this new mechanic, you don't even have to read anything! You can just click through all of the posts and look for the "scan" button to pop up in the bottom point of the screen and click it and it tells you what you should be discovering on your own by reading all the comments or viewing the users posts.. really silly and ruins the whole point of the game. To make it even worse, if you read something ahead of when the game thinks you're supposed to, you won't get the clue, you have to go back and re-read it at a later date just to get the scan button even if you already know the information. Music: This second installment has music which you can play in the media section of the victim's phone. Unfortunately, this is also broken. Once you play the song and pause it, it automatically starts playing any time you hit the back button on the phone and you have to go into media and pause it again to get it to stop. I'm not sure if it was a bug, or if it was supposed to be spooky or what but it was incredibly annoying.All of that being said, I likely would have enjoyed this game a lot if they didn't spoil the experience with these silly additions and hand-holding which tell you exactly where to go and where to look. My advice? Skip this one and play the original.

_childDocuments_.review: I REALLY liked the first Simulacra so I was incredibly excited for this one to drop, despite not really enjoying Pipe Dreams. I have to say, I find it very hard to recommend this game for any reason. I went into this expecting a compelling story that makes you feel like you really have to dig through someone's phone to find details about their life and oddly their death, I expect some level of horror, Instead, I got something that tried to expand in different directions, but the wrong direction across the board. It's also incredibly disappointing to see the template stay pretty much identical from Sara is Missing > Simulacra > Simulacra Pipe Dreams > Simulacra 2. I get Sara is Missing was kind of proof of concept, but really the story elements, the jump scares, they're all horribly reused. Horror - This game lacked a single creepy moment, jump scare, or even cool detail at all. The phone glitches and you literally click to progress the spoops. I  Might as well be a power point presentation. Scares should build atmosphere, jump scares should distract you so much you get focused and suddenly a jump scare knocks you out of your seat, and this game just doesn't check any of those boxes which is a shame considering the first one did it so well. I attribute this to the scare tactics being reused from the first game, but somehow more poorly executed in this one. Story - You kind of see where the story is going an hour into it. The next few hours is just spent waiting for it to unfold. It doesn't subvert your expectation at any point really. The only level of engagement I got from this was like when someone starts to tell you a story and then they trail off. You don't necessarily care about the story, but you kinda just want an ending because you've sat through so much of it. The live action bits in this game are pretty terrible. The acting in this is VERY cringe and even down to the way it's been shot is kind of odd. The first game used live action moments as like a person recording a video in their home or something casual so you're not expecting a performance, but it uses the texts, emails, and phone calls as it's main story telling elements. This game tries to convince you these characters are "influencers" and while they're not necessarily trying to tell you they're good ones, it's just so incredibly cringey to watch, it's not enjoyable. If they just stuck to primarily texts as the delivery, I feel like that could have carried this game further.  TLDR; Reused structure and gameplay from all previous Simulacra related entries, poor acting, bland story, odd cinematography choices, nonexistent horror elements.

_childDocuments_.review: The Simulacra games have been out for a couple of years now, I remember watching various YouTubers play them and being pretty intrigued by the format. You play a game where you're confined to a phone, yet you uncover more information than you could really imagine. This game further expanded on the research aspect of the first one, investigating 3 different colleagues of a murder victim. The story does not change too much with your choices of playing as a Junior Detective or a Journalist, but there are certain moments where the choice does effect your ability to acquire information. The videos and photos of the characters really immerse you into this universe that you're in, especially your interactions with Detective Murilo (who was in Simulacra's first iteration, but had a different actor I believe). The writers did a fantastic job with characterizing each one of them into being fleshed out people. While the dialogue is a little cringe at times especially with how the lines are delivered, most of the content you find really could just be located in someone's phone. Even the side characters that you must access for extra details are well done. Each piece of information (articles, social media posts, previous text threads, police records) is fully written out, which tells me that each piece was carefully attended to during development. There are less typos in this game too, Simulacra originally had a handful of them sprinkled throughout. The atmosphere the game creates while you play is fantastic. I played this both on my own and over call with friends, each time the knocking or breathing catching us completely off guard. The times that the phone malfunctions or becomes sentient are not too close together but happen often enough to keep you on your toes. The visual effects are great.My only complaints involve replayability and the sheer amount of research you have to do if you want every piece of information in the game that will help you get the "true" ending. The game does offer a NG+ that has "fast mode". This does help, greatly in fact, but there are still moments in the game where you have to watch unskippable video content or phone calls. I think if you're in NG+, you should be allowed to skip this content and still maintain the same experience as if you had not.While I mentioned before that every piece of information is well thought out, there is a MESS of things you have to go through to find what you need. Going through each time to acquire posts and photos and numbers to unlock later chat options is extremely tedious, especially when you're trying to get all of the endings. Between what you need there is also a lot of fleshed out nonsense like the promotional Kimera account that posts blurbs from those who took its deal. They serve no purpose other than to clog the feed, same with certain Jabbr posts. If there was going to be extra content gathering in the social media feeds, I think I would have preferred to see a new take on what we experienced in the first game where the main character (in this case the deceased) would make social media comments or posts while you're working to find things out.Lastly, I enjoyed the extra bits of humor inserted into the plot. Murilo's inability to figure out his phone, sending you random videos and butt dialing you. If you yourself comment on things with the character's account and use profanity, you receive an email from IRIS warning you of your language. Even calling emergency services earns you a scathing text from Murilo demanding to know why you'd do such a thing with the victim's phone. It's things like that, that make the game worth playing.Despite the few flaws listed, I really enjoyed the game and have played it through a few times. I only have one ending left to get at the time of writing this review! Would def recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Suffers from a lot of the same problems as the first game. - Designed to be replayed, but is not really replayable (see following notes), because it would require you to play substantially the same game and spend tons and tons of time going through mostly the same motions.- some videos unskippable or un-fast-forward-able- Lots of text conversations are just filler with no good purpose- Have to start over from the beginning if you make one single mistake or want to try a different path- Autosave function serves basically no good purpose; should be supplemented with a manual save option, and more save-game files (not just 3)- Too much tedious searching useless filler fake social media posts for information that you need, but doesn't get saved to your clues (e.g., when cracking a locker combo)- TERRIBLE actors- dumb jump scares being the only attempt at personality, and failingThe idea of gathering info and piecing together information for puzzles is good. _childDocuments_.review: What starts as a simple "found phone"-like murder case quickly gets more and more obscure. The more clues you collect via the phone of Maya, the victim, the more it starts acting hella strange. Ads on social media keep on interacting with you, the phone glitches out and appears to be possessed by Maya, you're discovering creepy video evidence of the night she died and dive into the shallow, superficial world that is "Kimera" and "Jabbr", apps that mirror Instagram and Twitter. (There even is a "tea spill" account and people are getting called out for promoting juice cleanses. LOL.)  Would certain people literally kill someone in exchange for more likes and less ♥♥♥♥ storms? And who is behind the shady engagement boosting service that everyone and their dog seems to use? I won't spoiler the ending (more like: the endings... each of them a total mindf*ck), let me just say - I absolutely recommend playing this. I guess it'll be even more immersive when played on an actual phone.

_childDocuments_.review: The modern FMV game subgenre of adventure isn't huge, and yet it's well-enough populated by games that are worth watching as movies but not so much worth playing as games.  The Bunker, The Infectious Madness, and #WarGames all come to mind.  Sometimes one of these developers will improve the formula, as with The Shapeshifting Detective, but it's still tough to stomach watching every scene and playing out every conversation again with little sense of control while hoping to get a different ending.  For that reason, I think these games should be judged on three questions:If it's a movie, is it worth watching?If it's a game, is it worth playing?Would you really want to watch and play it again?You don't have to have played Simulacra and Pipe Dreams to make sense of this game, but I'd recommend at least playing Simulacra.  At least that will help you determine what the title means.  As movies go, the first game was a series of pieces that made a creepy story about social media personas.  Then they threw seriousness (and any real scares) out the window with the ridiculous free Pipe Dreams, an okay story about micro-transactions and game addiction.  But the developers did one thing in all three games that is supremely clever, no matter how unintentional it might have been: they made the context of the story cover for anything cringe-worthy in the acting.The first game covers for weak voice acting by having the guys be creeps anyway.  The free game covers for it by being silly.  This game tops both by stretching the concept of social media personas even further, to the superficiality of personalities acting as influencers in media culture.  In other words, if the acting seems bad, it's because the characters are fakers!  Right?  I actually was impressed at how well this worked, so that when the songs were awful or the guy was a douche, then wasn't that what they were going for?  Although the movie isn't very scary or even that fun to watch, it is pretty convincing.  You really get to know these four young influencers and each particular brand of facade.Approaching this as a game rather than just a movie, I was even more impressed.  The developers took what worked about the interactivity of the first game and led things off into more branching directions.  You feel more control over what you are choosing to conclude as you work through the mystery you are unraveling.  The game even lets you select from two possible characters at the beginning, although you are an investigator either way.  You can search for pieces of evidence that change your dialog choices based on what you've managed to reveal by the time you have a conversation, and there is even a feeling of real time passing as you are doing a thorough or a poor job of fleshing out what each character was thinking.Most importantly, this is the first FMV interactive movie I've played recently that is complex but still worth playing again.  You don't have to rewatch every video to get the clues, and once you finish the game, it offers you a fast mode to speed up replays.  Once you get an ending, it actually shows you a branching diagram of what you revealed.  It doesn't necessarily tell you where you went off down a particular path, but it certainly gives you an idea of how much more each character might have been hiding.  If only you'd pursued that one sooner, earned her trust, or been more aggressive!I am very hard to please in this aspect of FMV games, and I would encourage more developers to take the approach found here.  My first playthrough took 4-5 hours and earned a third of the achievements, and I would actually play the thing again from the beginning.  Maybe even soon.  Knowing what I'm usually getting with interactive movies, I was pleasantly surprised.  My only significant criticism is that reading social media posts and watching videos by a team of fake bratty web personalities is really no more fun than it sounds, so thank goodness the game works as a game.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the first game and enjoyed it quite a bit - it had an eerie atmosphere within a believable setting.This, however feels like a mockery. It's cringey, it's ridiculously unbelievable - to the point where no suspension of disbelief can help you. Department Of Otherworldly Phenomena is bad enough, then goes the presentation supposedly to show how the detective is not "tech savvy" but it just goes over the top. Your "investigation tool" is ridiculous as well, saying "new clue found" and then restoring the phone bit by bit cause it "repaired" a broken image? I mean,really? If you're into "lost phone" puzzle/investigation games, then you may enjoy this title, but STAY AWAY if you're looking for something within the horror genre. Old episodes of the "Twilight Zone" were more believable and unsettling than this.Even though I bought it dirt cheap due to owning the previous game, I still refunded this, because it only made me feel embarrassed with how nonsensical it is. _childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the simplicity of the first one, but I feel like they over-corrected with feature bloat on this one.My initial impression is that they put too many game systems on top of the found phone premise and it isn't enjoyable anymore. They added hints, but you can ignore them, so I'm fine with those. You can't ignore how the game forces you to "learn" information though. You no longer have to read/view the actual content on the phone; you just wait for the clue trigger to appear and then you process the clue in another app. You never really have to learn/solve anything, you just "pavlov's dog"'d to the answer. If the first game was built with ruby/python with love, this one was ground out of java:EE.I'll probably end up pushing through to the end, but I feel like it would've been a better experience if they leaned more into the "fake-actual-phone" authenticity and keeping the optional layer of hints to help the player if they get stuck / forgot where they left off. I can appreciate the increased production value of this sequel and hopefully they can course correct to a breakout experience for a next installment.

_childDocuments_.review: HOLY JESUS. HOLY MOSES. HOLY MARY MOTHER AND ALL THE ANGELS  IN HEAVEN AND ALL OF THE DEMONS IN HELL THIS IS AN AMAZING GAME!This is the kind of game you NEED to play if you are a freak about horror/scifi games. It dances the line between the two genres more graceful than an olympic diver and I want to say it leans a bit more onto the scifi side but regardless, fans of both genres will find this game amazing!I'm going to try to describe as much as I can without spoiling a single bit of this game because from start to finish its an experience. You play as a reporter/journalist trying to get to the bottom of the mysterious death of an up and coming influencer (I think she was up and coming I have no idea if 100,000 followers is considered big) that was ruled as heart complications which is thought to be a half assed cover up by the police in an effort to improve their reputation and solve cases quickly by your friend/employer/partner in the case the local detective. The detective feels like you might be the only one he can count on and entrusts you with her phone to search for clues. Every part of this game takes place within the phone of the influencer and as you progress you find out about her friends, business connections, and social contacts as you try to reveal the mystery behind her death. You must search through her social media apps, text messages, videos, and phone calls to get to the truth behind the possible murder.I want to give this game a 10/10 because I enjoyed almost every single aspect of it. From the graphics to the gameplay, from the voice acting to the live video acting, every part was just amazing. The only complaint I have is the sound. 95% of the time the sound is fine but no matter how much you adjust the sliders every once in awhile you will get a text or a phone call that is at 10,000% volume and it will blow out your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ear drums. Not to mention, most of the time when this happens the sound that is playing is some loud pitch screeching sound. There was no less than 3 times I had to rip my headset off since the sound was so abrupt and jarring. Because of this I give it a 9.8/10There is so much more I could say. There is so much more I want to say. _childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed Simulacra, and I thought Pipe dreams was an enjoyable (albeit short) experience. I have been looking forward to Simulacra 2, and I began to worry as this project saw multiple delays. I'm not sure the exact reason for the delays, but it doesn't seem like they were used wisely. I don't like writing negative reviews for small, independent projects, but I feel compelled to do so here.So, the core concept here has remained basically the same. Somebody is dead and you need to sort through their phone to find out what happened, and hopefully prevent it from happening again. Great idea, very well executed in the first game. The problem here is that the gameplay seems to have been dumbed down in a very large way. It doesn't really require much critical thinking to progress, and I never once felt a sense of urgency to do so. You very rarely need to dig deep to find the information, and there really isn't very much to read through. You spend a large amount of time in the texting and the police apps. Not much else to look through.Another thing that surprised me was how tame and calm the whole experience felt. In Simulacra, I jumped like a sissy so many times. I didn't even jump one time here. That is a huge bummer, one of the top 2 reasons this game is a hard pass for me. It just isn't scary, not even a little bit. My first (and it will be my only) run took 3.5 hours to complete, and I didn't get even mildly scared one time. I get that you're trying to make this more like a crime drama with horror elements, but I found no horror here.The strangest thing about this game is the dialogue. I understand that the team developing this game may not have English as their first language, but this game could have really benefitted from a native english speaker consult. So much of the dialogue made me wince in discomfort. It took me out of the game for most of my playthrough. I'm guessing this took place in the US, but nobody in the US speaks like that. Even the detective sounded like he just found the English language washed up on the beach and just shoved it in his mouth with no practice. Recommendations if you decide to try making another game:- Get a language/society consult- Stop having your characters send voice memos through texts. Nobody does that. Just have the character send the information through texts.- Stop using phone calls as jump scares. It worked in Simulacra, but it is no longer working. It can be seen coming from a mile away.- If you're going to go in an insane direction with crazy special effects, but are working on a low budget, just skip the weird special effect. It didn't work, it looked campy (in a bad way) and it was not scary.I'm not sure how every part of this game got so much worse, but this should be skipped. Breaks my heart, I thought the first game was amazing, but this series needs to be completely revamped or taken out back and shot.

_childDocuments_.review: I started my journey with the original Simulacra on my PC, and it felt oddly disconnected, attempting to dive into a virtual phone displayed on my TV. When the sequel came out, I decided to do it right, so I played it on my smartphone.Simulacra's first installment had us exploring the phone of a missing person, reconstructing their digital life. It delved into the dark side of dating apps and a demonic virus. It was groundbreaking, birthing numerous imitators. The sequel shifts its focus to a more recent facet of digital culture: influencers and their reliance on algorithms and exposure. This shift breathes fresh life into the series.Graphically, Simulacra 2 is effective without being extraordinary. However, its real strength is in its immersive design, mimicking a phone screen and user interface. This approach ensures a seamless experience, with easy navigation through various apps and files. Though I occasionally missed an inbuilt notepad, having to jot things down on paper felt like a nostalgic nod to the pre-digital age.The audio consists mainly of atmospheric music, setting the mood. Voice acting varies in quality, with some characters coming off as convincing, while others lean towards the cheesier end of the spectrum. Thankfully, given the setting, this doesn't distract significantly.A significant development in Simulacra 2 is the choice of the character you play as, adding replayability. You can experience the game from the perspectives of either a cynical detective or a journalist. While the core narrative remains the same, the two approaches offer distinct experiences, warranting at least a second playthrough. The journalist's viewpoint feels more natural, making interactions with the detective appear organic and spreading critical investigative material throughout the story.Simulacra 2 offers several hours of gameplay, and it's well worth the price. It provides regular autosave points for those who prefer consuming it in shorter sessions. Although I experienced some crashes on my less-than-optimal Android phone, the frequent autosaves prevented any major setbacks. Unfortunately, at the time of the review, there was no scene skip option during replays, making it necessary to retrace familiar steps to explore alternative narrative branches.In summary, Simulacra 2 is a commendable sequel, immersing players in the impact of our digital presence on our identities. The different playable characters offer fresh perspectives, and the flawed suspects keep you guessing about the true culprit. However, the supporting cast doesn't feel as well-focused as in the original. In an interesting parallel to the digital horror in the game, our current shift to virtual interactions adds a relevant layer to the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I will preface this review by saying that the original Simulacra game is one that I enjoyed greatly and I would recommend checking that one out if you like the format. -pros:-Phone feels realistic, some apps even let you make posts and comments.-The Camera quality in the live action segments is very good.--Some of the scares caught me off guard and some of the stuff they do with the phone is unsettling  -cons-Acting is sub-par characters feel unrealistic at best and like exposition spouts at worst. It is impossible to get attached to any of them making dialogue choices feel meaningless and dialogue choices are the majority of the gameplay.-The story is stupid  and most of the plot is just laid out in front of you making it very hard to get immersed. It is a far cry from the compelling mystery of the first game.-There are too many characters to juggle at one time and their stories are surface level.-The critique of modern social media and influencer culture is way too blatant and is shoved in your face every time you use any social media app in game, talk to any of the characters, or interact with the AI that runs the in game phone. -There are way too many attempts at comedy. None of them are funny or subtle. -Most scares are cheap and predictable and use of video effects is unimaginative. TL;DR: play the first game and skip this one.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Bundle for April 2021. If you are interested in the game and it's before May 4th, 2021, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.After an playing an hour of Simulacra and Simulacra 2 to review for the Humble Choice April 2021 Bundle:These are a pair of horror or thriller games.  The first game spooked me with a major opening that has a lot of horror elements in it, but then didn’t do much with the horror aspect in the next 40 minutes.  Instead, it focused more on what life would be like as a woman.Simulacra has you find a woman’s phone and then try to figure out what happened to her.  Though while playing it I noticed how freaking awful it would be to be a woman.  There’s a solid social commentary on how some people spoke to the mystery girl online and it’s done in a very strong way.  This isn’t social commentary being forced in there, but instead a strong point the game makes. The gameplay is mostly about snooping on the phone and has voyeuristic qualities to it.  You can even impersonate her with different people, and it’s quite interesting.  As much as I dislike the horror aspect in the beginning because I’m a scaredy-cat, I found myself wanting to play more as it’s more of a thriller.Simulacra 2 seems to up the production values but presents a very similar experience.  Though I do want to mention there are a few grammar issues that I noticed in both games, and apparently, the team who created the game is from Malaysia, which might explain that.  Nothing that bad, but it can be a bit noticeable. Pick this up if you like horror or thriller, these aren’t long games, but they are unique.  There are some effective and interesting moments, such as hearing a woman’s voice from behind you if you’re playing wearing headphones.
