_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game as much as Simulacra, really I did. I was one of the ones that tried Sara is Missing back when it was still relevant. I was in love with the concept, but the game was downright horrible. However, Kaigan Games did a fantastic job of actually listening to constructive criticism and making their next game - Simulacra - an underground success. It took the few working ideas from Sara is Missing, tossed out everything that was tripe, and crafted an amazing experience as a result. So, I expected Simulacra 2 to basically be an enhanced version of Simulacra as they continued to learn and take advice from their fans. Well, for whatever reason, Simulacra 2 falls flat. It feels bloated with some much inconsequential tripe that it feels a bit more like Sara is Missing than it does a sequel to Simulacra. Don't get me wrong, I don't mind additional, somewhat irrelevant content for the sake of making a game fun or interesting - hence Easter eggs. But Simulacra 2 went overboard. There is so much useless information that doesn't even do a good job of fleshing out the characters or the lore of the story. It just exists to pad out the game and make it look more impressive at an initial glance, but in reality it actually hinders the whole game. And oh boy... the characters. Now I can understand the concept that they are perhaps not supposed to be loved, that you are perhaps supposed to not like them, and that's part of the charm. But I feel the idea of a character you "love to hate" was overshot, and just everyone in the game is instead completely insufferable. I didn't want to solve the mystery of Maya's death or hear the stories of her "friends". They were all insufferable and I would have even been more content if I could have just watched them all suffer Maya's fate and been done with it. All in all, Simulacra 2 is just Simulacra 1 with way too much bloat - content that is irrelevant and bears little-to-no impact on the narrative with completely unlikable characters that you would just as soon watch die rather than try to solve the mystery at hand.

_childDocuments_.review: SPOILER WARNING:I'm not going to bother talking about the gameplay because while the puzzles and logical deductions are more engaging this time around, that's all outweighed by the writing and setup.I really loved the first game. The writing and setup for it was very well done, and the options you had at the end were genuinely compelling, and I genuinely wanted to earn that golden ending to save everyone because I ended up liking both characters involved and wanted them to be ok.Here though? No. Not even slightly. I can't even begin to care what happens to these people as they are all scientifically designed to make me find them irredeemable garbage.I don't care how good friends they ended up being because ALL of them have scammed people. Maya sells fad diets that have caused serious harm to people that tried them seriously (and she is a massive hypocrite). Rex is literally running an MLM and genuinely thinks his victims deserve it, regardless of their situation, just because they were stupid and/or desperate enough to believe him. Mina is tied for most hateable with Rex as she not merely exploits her own tragedy, but its actually someone else's... she is appropriating other peoples' grief for her own gain and pretending to have PTSD. (she claims to have that in her videos and her behavior is so very inconsistent with that issue)Arya is perhaps the least objectionable of the bunch as she just did vapid makeup tutorials and beauty tips, and defrauded a corporation... which.. I can't begin to care about on any level.Sums up this whole game, despite the much better presentation and much more elaborate and interesting puzzles... I just cannot begin to even slightly care what happens to any of the characters involved. Even if the intent was to have  the player pick which one they thought most deserved to die, then there is literally no reason for the player to do anything really, as these vapid, greedy, and at times, downright evil people will surely bring it on themselves later without your or the police's involvement anyway.This was a huge step in the wrong direction.Oh, and just to pre-empt a common assumption based on the above...I'm a millenial, and I hate these kinds of social influencers. They are trash. They can all die in fire.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved SIMULACRA, but this game seems to lack everything that made the first one so good.It really feels like the developers got so caught up in their "influencer fake, phone bad" rhetoric that they forgot how to write an engaging story. All of the characters are one-dimensional charicatures of influencer stereotypes: the depressed musician, the arrogant con-artist, the aging model, etc; and none of them are likeable enough to warrant dealing with them for hours on end. It got to the point where I didn't even WANT to solve the mystery of her death if it meant I had to deal with them any longer. Not to mention that the "monster" had a name so laughable it was impossible to take seriously.Overall, this was a huge disappointment. SIMULACRA could have been a great game series if they hadn't tried to shove their half-baked "deep" message down players' throats and instead focused on recreating the subtlety and brilliance of the original.

_childDocuments_.review: The spark (pun intended) has fizzled out with this one.The original game had great acting, puzzles that actually were fun to solve, and connections between the characters that made me keep coming back for more. I wanted to figure out what happened to Anna.However, the second game did not live up to it's much better predecessor. First, the game seems to be designed for two routes, however, the role you choose initially doesn't change the route you take through the game, just a few dialogue options. I thought maybe it would change the approach you would have to take (i.e. certain files would be easily accessed as a detective, but being stealthy as a reporter would be much easier) but unfortunately it doesn't.I would be able to excuse the cheesy acting, if the characters were actually somewhat likable. While the first also had "hatable" characters, you could still at least connect with them.Next, the saving system. It really didn't improve on the first's "auto checkpoint" style system where it saved after a major plot point (this is fine, considering the frequency of them). The ability to return back to a previous point is useful, however it really only matters during one segment as to where in the original, every interaction mattered.Now that I've mentioned the saving system, the "flowchart" you get at the end of the game hardly makes any sense. In fact, it doesn't really even matter whom you  It would make more sense if it actually mentioned big plot points in order, but it functions moreso like a "flowweb" than anything else.Now, the puzzles. They were much harder than the original's, which is completely fine. However it really doesn't help that some of the clues you need to find are either arbitrary or actually relevant and the game doesn't really tell you about it. The amount of filler on the phone is also an issue that just artificially inflates the difficulty.As much as I want to experience the true ending, the game doesn't give me much of a motivation to actually replay the entire thing.And last but not least, the horror elements. Unfortunately there isn't as good sense of horror. The original had plenty of atmosphere to keep your anxiousness front and center. So, should you buy? No, unless you  want to play the sequel (for credit or otherwise). I promise you though, if you haven't played the original, please buy it instead. It is a much better use of your time.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked this game. It's not a direct sequel to the first game (although there are some references) so you can play this one before the original without being lost. Gameplay is similar to the first game in that you're going through someone's phone and trying to find/restore information while weird things keep happening. Most of the characters are hiding something and it's your job to figure out the truth. Puzzles aren't too hard, but the game has a hint system in place if you're struggling. The characters are better developed than the ones from the first game. The dialogue makes sense and there aren't a lot of spelling and grammar errors apart from the usual "text speak." You can unlock different endings based on your choices  I really liked the music! It matches the atmosphere perfectly. The only downsides to this game (in my opinion) are that you need to play the game at least twice to unlock all the achievements and playing the game multiple times gets annoying because you can't skip or speed up dialogue. The game autosaves, but it only keeps up to three saves, so you can't just jump back and forth throughout the story if you missed something. If you're looking for a mystery game with a creepy twist, you should enjoy this game a lot,

_childDocuments_.review: Let me be clear, I really liked the first game. I think it did most things right and while I wasn't a fan of the jumpscares and it definitely looked like an indie game production wise.This game is a perfect example of how sometimes, less is more.Let me start with my biggest pet peeve of this game, and that's the extreme slowness of it all. The entire plot is not that long, I actually think it might be around the same length as the first game, but it is padded out by how extremely slow it all is. Be it conversations or the extreme amount of stuff you need to click through and scan gets annoying on the second playthrough, if not first.In the first game, your first playthrough was slow, since you had to wait for people to write things out... but after finishing the game once, it unlocked a very fast mode that let you speedrun the game for the other endings and it was awesome.Simulacra 2 has a similiar thing, but it's a gimped version of it. Conversations still take forever to finish, messages load visibly slower than in the first game with this mode on, you are still forced to watch many of the videos and even the credits are unskippable... even though it was possible to skip that in the first game.It makes this game extremely annoying to play more than once and god forbid, try actually going for the good ending without a guide. There is a lot of stuff that needs to be set up and with how annoying it is to replay the game, I would really hate to have to figure it out, only to mess up at one point and have to replay the game again. Then we get to the acting and plot... look, I get what the game was going for, I even think some of the underlying ideas were great. The execution of them, however, was absolutely awful. The characters are unlikable. I can't say I liked even one character in the game. I get that was the point, but by god, I had no desire to help any of these a*****es. Even as an online persona, they all suck.Sure, it shows how incredibly fake social media is and what insane expectations are set upon influencers, but it doesn't make anyone less bad.It also doesn't help that the acting is so bad. I don't know if it is bad direction or if the actors just don't know how to act, but I feel like I saw better acting in pr0n.The first game couldn't win any oscars with its acting, but it all had home feel to it and even the bad acting was so funny, that I think it redeems it a lot.So, TL;DR - worse than the first game in terms of gameplay, making it a chore to play this game more than onceunlikable characters that you don't want to helpgodawful acting, which isn't at least hilarious... it's just bad.Play the first game for the novelty, skip this one unless you like torturing yourself with slow gameplay and bad acting

_childDocuments_.review: Once more with feeling. Story spoilers below The overall production, video quality, physical and voice acting is far better than that of Simulacra 1, if still a bit goofy or maybe cringey at times. but the story is....kinda stupid? 1 felt a lot more grounded (which sounds funny now that I think about it) by having an entity essentially take advantage of people who are lonely/single/craving connections. It felt more believable that someone could fall for it in times of desperation or weakness or just trying to meet the right person. Contrast this with...... Like. Maybe I'm crazy. Maybe it's cause its 2024. But I feel like most people on the planet don't really give a ♥♥♥♥ about likes/follows/engagement on social media anymore. It makes sense to the characters in universe and their motivation to y'know, keep their "job". But I look at it now and its pretty ridiculous. Also the fast forward mode is just worse than Simulacra 1. I miss being able to skip past dialogue/cutscenes that dont change at lightspeed. while it is a lot faster compared to the default speed, it could be better.Puzzles are fine. I do appreciate not having 50 word scrambles, some of which you can only get behind certain dialogue choices, again. What you get is a lot of what there was before, use little pieces of info you're either fed or dig up through social media/the internet/documents, pick apart people's statements and ultimately solve a mystery while trying to figure out how to get that best ending and save everybody/defeat the entity. But also like.....there really isn't much horror to it? The jumpscares there are here are pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ weak compared to Simulacra 1. You really don't get as many times where the phone glitches or acts up. most are mandatory  but the most notable ones don't occur unless you meet certain conditions like That being said, If you liked Simulacra 1, puzzle games in general or lost phone games, odds are you'll find something to like in Simulacra 2. It is pretty short, like the first, you can finish a first playthrough in about 3-4 hours, and full completion took me just under 9. $8 is fine, but consider grabbing it on a sale and trying it

_childDocuments_.review: This game... Wow, it just blew me away. I've never experienced anything like it before. The true ending is incredibly rewarding, the story is captivating, and the choices you make significantly impact what happens next. Initially, I breezed through the game in about three hours and felt disappointed, thinking it was weak and mediocre. But then, it completely blew me away.When you start the game, your objective is to find Maya, the main protagonist. Without giving away too many spoilers, this is what i have to say. Maya is an influencer surrounded by what seem to be "selfish" friends who would do anything for fame through their parody Instagram accounts. Maya is found deceased at the beginning of the game, and it’s your task to explore her mobile phone, uncover secrets, and find the suspect. Initially, you might think you have the right answer, but there are more secrets to uncover. (Have you ever tried being nice to people?)That’s all I’ll say without spoiling anything.10/10 Game. I HIGHLY recommend you play it, but please, don't rush through it. Put yourself in the shoes of a detective and take your time. When you get the "Good" ending, you’ll know it, and it’s incredibly rewarding. That’s why I love this game—it’s more expansive than it seems, and every little breadcrumb should be investigated.Yeah you should play this game (not chatgpt btw)

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who thoroughly enjoyed the original version of this game, I must express my disappointment with this iteration. While there were some redeeming qualities, such as the unique game concept and the unforgettable Rex's song, the overall experience left me dissatisfied. Regrettably, the characters were not as engaging as they were in the previous installment, and the game quickly becomes repetitive. Even in the pursuit of alternative endings, the player must sit through non-skippable cutscenes, which can detract from the replay value. Although the game's price is reasonable, it fails to live up to the high expectations set by its predecessor. In retrospect, had I known what to expect, I would have abstained from purchasing it.

_childDocuments_.review: A definite step up from the first game, which was already pretty solid. Some of the minor problems carry over, such as an American setting made by a distinctly non-American team and cast, leading to some things seeming slightly 'wrong' to an American eye (like occasional British English vocabulary), or shaky faux-American accents.That said, the game tells interesting enough of a story. Some of the characters make some pretty hefty leaps in logic in their conversations, or bring things up in a way that is redundant or brings up dialogue choices that weren't chosen, but the path to the true ending is much less counterintuitive than the first game, with a handy post-credits flowchart, and is different enough (and with good enough production) to actually warrant multiple plays.The irony of a game centered around social media influencers begging for reviews at the end of the game is not lost on me.

_childDocuments_.review: I really really liked Simulacra 1 and I am gradually begrudgingly realizing I do not like the sequel.  The premise alone is so divorced from any reality or relatable idea.  You're handling deliberately leaked evidence in a case regarding someone's death and all of your interactions with clues and law enforcement happen through an app that I guess you can just download in this world.  I haven't played Simulacra 1 in a long time, but I don't remember a mechanic where the game would just notify you immediately when useful info was on the screen.  Games about fake operating systems kind of live and die on the fun of finding info and regurgitating it at the right time, there's no real fun in an icon telling you (before you can even read the information) that you've found crucial data.  I still enjoyed some of the story and the animations in the game but the acting isn't really great no amount of glitch effects can shroud that when all of the actors in the game have interactions on screen together.Honestly I mainly just hate that before you can recognize for yourself that you found a clue, there's a massive icon telegraphing it.  I wish that was reduced or delayed or something.  Maybe if I just read creepypastas at all I would be less disappointed in the direction this series took going way too hard on some kind of lore.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. I loved the original SIMULACRA, and I think with any series it goes without saying that fans worry how the sequels will live up to its predecessor - and SIMULACRA 2 doesn't disappoint. I loved the new additions and expansions that make this game feel more like a real phone. For instance, I was not expecting a music player (so cool!). And being able to choose between two personas for how we go about solving the case gives more room for exploration and makes the game highly replayable. Also, the scanning system reminded me a lot of Sara is Missing, so that was a nice touch. Still, I don't think that this game was better than the original. For one, it wasn't that scary. I was hoping for more subtle noises in the background (not as obvious or silly as Pipe Dreams, but the ones that catch you off guard and make you question if you actually heard them in your own house, as in SIMULACRA 1). And the jumpscares didn't get me like they did in the first game. I would classify this game as more thriller/mystery than horror - or I suppose the psychological horror tag is a little more accurate. But I am still impressed by the murder angle and the creepy paranormal overtones. I really enjoyed this game, and I see myself going back to get the rest of the achievements! Note to the developer: I hope you add a New Game + mode (or fast mode) like from the first game! It would make the second and third and so on playthroughs much better! Also, I hope you keep making games in this universe! Keep bringing the scary!!
_childDocuments_.name: SIMULACRA 2

_childDocuments_.review: The sequel to an extremely neat found-footage horror game, however it can't hold up to its prequel. That's where I'd put this game.Simulacra 2 is a game about searching through a victim's phone, progressing through a decision-driven story, packed into a creepy horror atmosphere. It certainly trumps the first one in complexity and production value which is both a good and a bad thing at once: While it makes the game more realistic and strengthens the immersion while unravelling the story, it also results in overwhelming the player, especially in the beginning of the game where they are literally bombed with data they potentially need to analyse first before proceeding.The Horror aspect in this game felt way too short unfortunately, at least compared to Simulacra 1. Jumpscares are literally predictable and all that creepy stuff that's supposed to give you anxiety just sets the tone for the game's atmosphere instead of dragging you into that terror. And I know that of course these aspects are different from person to person, that's why all "horror" types can't please everyone. However it really is a shame to see it coming so short, especially because Simulacra 1 showed that the devs are able to create an engrossing creepy atmosphere. But don't get me wrong, the tone of this game itself is hit well nonetheless.The story itself is good. I'm honestly surprised that they managed to keep the general plot interesting when the series dropped the nuke in the first game. Characters are ok for the most part, however not as much relateable/connectable as the characters in the first game (potentially because of them all being influencers, while previous characters were literally normal people, I appreachiate Kaigan tried a different route here tho). The decision aspect of the game also is way more complex and besides the 5+ endings there are still subplots to discover.How do I rate this game now? It is definetely a solid found-footage horror experience that has more complexity in story and gameplay, however lacks in a lot of horror aspects and fails to come close to the first game's  amazing atmosphere despite improving on it.If you're into these types of visual novel type of horror games, I'd definetely recommend checking this game out. If not, you may want to look into Simulacra 1 first before deciding if you want to give this game a try or not.
_childDocuments_.name: SIMULACRA 2

_childDocuments_.review: Ease into your chair and prepare yourself for this continuation of the SIMULACRA universe. In this iteration, you will have new advanced tools and a mosaic of widely branching narratives spread across 2 characters that are continually altered by your choices. You will have the choice of playing as a junior detective or a reporter who is recruited by a special department at police headquarters. With only one piece of evidence, you must find the truth of how a young woman & interweb influencer ends up dead on a case that is already closed. Lives and livelihoods are on the line, there is no room for mistakes.Use the tools at hand to unlock the pieces of the puzzle as you discover who is guilty and bring peace to a young lady taken from the world too soon. This is no ordinary mystery; as you begin to discover more about the victim, a seemingly sinister force makes itself known that complicates matters even more. Gather evidence from the victim’s phone that has seemingly been purposely wiped, and use it to reconstruct lost data to build your case. Are you ready to begin your journey for the truth?Released on Jan 30, 2020, by the developer Kaigan Games and published by Another Indie, it is tagged as Indie, Simulation, Psychological Horror; I have added the following tags: Choices Matter, Multiple Endings, Thriller, FMV. It features two playable characters, a detective and a journalist. As an FMV it relies heavily on prerecorded video in full 4K resolution; the acting was excellent in its presentation. The branching narrative depended on the choices you make to unlock your ending for the story. A built-in hint system is available, should you find yourself stuck and needing a little help. Continued lore from the first game about Simulacra. The storyline is entertaining and engaging as you piece together the truth. Exceptional, imaginative mechanics; digging into what makes the game tick was exciting.What an incredible play; I was glued to this one from the start! The more I dug into it, the harder I was hooked. I came into the title with no expectations (as I normally try to do); everything about the title was fantastic, from the narratives and storyline, to the mechanics, to the live video – it was all meticulously designed. I have been interested in the genre for some time, owning just a few assorted titles, and I admit that I was quite excited to have the opportunity to review this one. I do wish I had played the first title beforehand, but no regrets . . . I will get it later. With 11 hours for my first playthrough and possibly many to go, it is great value per hour of play. I look forward to trying the other character when I can take the time to see how that story plays out. In the end, I am rather blown away by the overall quality of the title and look forward to any continuations in the series and/or other releases by the developer. My only real complaint is that I would have liked a manual save or save on exiting for when I wanted to close out the game, so as not to have to redo parts that I had already completed. There is no controller support, but I am not holding it against the title as it is a mouse-use only game.Achievement Hunters will want to note it will require multiple playthroughs to 100% the title. I unlocked 7 out of 27 my first playthrough.Simulacra 2: A Mind-boggling Psychological Thriller; A twisted paranormal mystery to solve in this continuation into the SIMULACRA Universe.9/10 Pro's+ Delightful Live-Action Video in 4K + Exhilarating Story + Imaginative Mechanics + Hint System + Replayability + Steam Achievements Con's - No Steam Trading Cards (at this time)Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: (Received code for review)Coming off of Hypnospace Outlaw around Game of the Year time, I'm always up for a little "fake Internet" sleuthing. This game scratches that itch quite nicely. The live action acting can be a little rough around the edges, and surfing through fake Instagram and Twitter for clues from these "influencers" is as painful as you could imagine it being, but the journey is fun and the puzzles are tricky. The in game hint system is everything I needed it to be, as I got stuck a few times, and it ramps  up how much information it's giving you. I was a little shocked at the end where it shows you a line chart of your decisions through the game and just how much I had NOT uncovered with a single playthrough. Compelling reason to go back and do it again from the other perspective.
_childDocuments_.name: SIMULACRA 2

_childDocuments_.review: Making a sequel to a game like Simulacra was always going to be difficult. It was always going to feel too similar to the first game (this is actually the third game). This game is a bit longer but that only means the cracks are all the more visible. The story does hit an important and topical subject: the world of influencers. I give it props for that. The game has too many weaknesses though. The writing and acting simply isn't up to par. It tries to be funny sometimes but it's either silly or cringy. The acting and writing isn't good enough to deliver enough tension, drama, comedy and definitely not the horror it's going for. It would work for an amateur B-production if I hadn't seen all of it before in the superior predecessor. That's the real reason for my downvote: it's too similar to the first game, there's simply not enough here to warrant a sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: An ungraceful sequel that spends more time spouting its boomer born view that ruined Black Mirror. Let me say I don't disagree with the point its trying to make but rather it delivered it in the worst way possible. In the original game you start off with an innocious phone dropped at your front door and boot it back up. A natural curiosity is born that lets you feed off of who this person was or who they wanted to present themselves at that organically lead you to the game's meditations on identity and personality in light of a world that wants only a perfect but shallow ideal. This was briliant, it was subtle and it fit a growing digital concern that was alive and well but was also fundamentally stupid in all the right ways. That was, of course, until the spooky monster talks to you saying its some monster AI bent on punishing humanity for its woes. That is horrible story telling and shatters the illusion made by the game because it is the creator shouting their thesis at you. You can agree with it like I did but there's just something to be said about the lack of confidence that comes from having to tell your audience what they should be feeling because you weren't sure if it will really come about. luckily this was at the very end.The sequel starts with the equivalent of the game's ending from the very get go, losing the tone, the mystery and doubling down on its new thesis that "influencers are fake and evil." We know that, everyone knows that and the shift in thematic and message away from a larger ensphereing concept to a rapidly becoming dated one as every "influencer" gets involved in more and more scandals cementing the idea that only the very insecure or the very naieve fall for it just seems a  In the end its not horrible but it IS a significant downgrade in several of the aspects that made the first game so amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: Eh. Unlike SIMULACRA, SIMULACRA 2 just made me cringe at all times.It somehow managed to create characters that are so obnoxious to the point where I stopped caring about them and the story altogether. They're not likeable at all - in fact, quite the opposite - and don't even intrigue me at the very least. I could not relate to the entire social media influencer thing going on (I believe that's because it sounded so superficial and shallow, even more so than it is in reality, as if that was the only "depth" the characters had) and the dialogue (both written and spoken) could simply not make me give a damn. Playing this game felt like a chore and, frankly, made me question why was I even doing it instead of spending time with my actual friends. After little over 2 hours of something akin to torture, I uninstalled it with a sigh of relief. I do understand that the creators most likely wanted us to feel uncomfortable with these said influencers, I just wish they'd work more on their writing just to make it so the game doesn't feel, well... annoying to play.Don't get me wrong, I'm a lover of horror literature, movies, documentaries and, more recently, games. The first game was quite scary and made me uncomfortable as well, albeit in a good way. SIMULACRA 2 didn't, though. To me, the interactions and story are forced, uncreative, shallow and bland. The acting is also slightly worse than the first game, with the exception of the main Detective (I really like this dude!).Another thing that bothered me were the dialogue responses I, as a player, had. I decided to play as a junior detective at first; some - if not nearly all - of the dialogue choices available to me were just plain moronic. At times I simply had no better or more logical option to choose from and the cringe moments I mentioned at the start of the review would happen, such as the main detective asking me if I didn't even bother reading the case file (which I had).Ah, man. I really wish this would have worked out because these kinds of Orwellian games are right up my alley. SIMULACRA 2 just couldn't make the cut for me, though.

_childDocuments_.review: Simulacra 2 is more of Simulacra 1: More data to search, more people to hack, more cringe to endure. Another stranger’s phone. Another story tinged with horror and sci fi elements. Another trip into the uncomfortable territory of violating simulated people’s privacy for a good cause. This sequel sticks pretty close to the footsteps of its predecessor. This time, the justification is justice, because the owner of the phone is quite dead, and you might be a cop, or a cop's little journalist helper. That makes the whole endeavour a bit less creepy, even though the characters of the story and the protagonist himself express a whole lot of disapproval of the invasion of privacy aspect of the proceedings. Gameplay-wise, things have been improved and deepened quite a lot. There is now a mechanic where you can store facts that you have discovered as a kind of file on the phone, and use them to confront people with them via chat. The simulations of social hacking have been implemented more gracefully and more challenging. The FMV production values have gone up, the inevitable creepy pasta is quite a bit creepier. So if Simulacra 2 is a whole lot more of Simulacra, and I found Simulacra quite compelling and mostly fun to play, then I must have enjoyed playing Simulacra 2, right? Unfortunately, no, I didn’t. There were a few minor snags: Some of the riddles you have to puzzle out were very obscure, and, to my mind, there was way too much dross to sift through to find the few nuggets of usable information within the timelines of the various social media apps on the phone. But the main reason I felt little enjoyment while playing were the characters. The game’s main four characters are influencers, and as a consequence, they are a bunch of miserable, ♥♥♥♥♥♥, morally compromised people. That's not my framing, that is the inescapable implication of the script. I can’t find a single ounce of sympathy with any of these people even though their life is in danger and the plot tries, unsuccesfully, to redeem them in the end. There is no self-reflection, nothing is learned. Seriously, if I ever want to warn someone away from this career path, I'll have him or her play this game. The cringe is that intense. I admit this might be a me thing, because I look with deepening horror at this business of turning your own life into a product. But I do believe that you can not play this game without developing a distaste for an Influencer's existence. Staring into an abyss can be compelling or even fun, eyeballing these particular depths was not fun for me. Only play this if misery porn is your thing. TLDR: An OK horror story combined with an honest look into one of the creepiest and extensively miserable facets of online existence. This is an acquired taste, and I have failed acquiring it.

_childDocuments_.review: "Simulacra 2" is much better than its predecessor with a far more engaging and (slightly) more complex story. You explore more characters via social media, emails, chat messages, videos, and phone calls (which you can't respond to but it's not a big deal).  The endings for the game aren't very complicated, but the fun lies in HOW you approach suspects with the information you find about them. Based on how you speak to them, and how you address their lies and secrets, you can coax them out of their egos and get them to be cooperative. Or you can anger them and make them turn on each other until someone breaks.Finding the culprit isn't as easy as it may seem. At first, I thought I'd nail it after all the stuff I was finding about the suspects, but then you end up wondering what exactly is the truth. Is it one culprit? Multiple? Maybe there is no culprit? Maybe the victim is the culprit? It's fun trying to figure out the truth, and I got it very wrong on my first playthrough. Again, it all depends on how much information you discover, and how you choose to present it to the suspects. You also have a bonus feature not present in the first game with an app called WARDEN, which lets you look up transcripts, case files, accidents, and blueprints. Granted, there isn't a whole lot to discover, but it still adds to the experience. I also like how you play as a detective or a journalist, and not just a random person who randomly got the victim's phone on their doorstep. At least now, it makes more sense and is more believable. The acting is kind of cheesy and at times bad, but I think there's a certain charm to it. The game is serious to a point but seems to rely on melodrama to lighten the mood. Yes, it's a murder investigation, but you're dealing with a bunch of social media "celebrities." They have massive egos but fluff for brains because, honestly, being a social media star isn't anything special, imo. But again, this sort of ridiculousness adds some amusement to the game. The game has decent replay value, especially if you want to unlock all achievements. You probably have to play it at least twice, and  return to previous saves in order to get all achievements. Plus, you can use replays to experiment with different dialogue options with characters.I do have to wonder why the game has you play as a detective or journalist because there is barely any difference in how the game plays. Some dialogue choices and cutscenes are different, but they have no real impact on the story and events. If there had been some unique experiences for each character type, then it would have made the game even better and even more replayable. Still, "Simulacra 2" is a fun horror-mystery game that features a more in-depth story and more interactions than "Simulacra" had. If you enjoyed the first game, you'll most likely love this one. If you didn't like the first game, give this one a try because I think it's got much more to offer you.

_childDocuments_.review: Good, but very similar to the first game.Simulacra 2 is an interactive "lost phone" experience where you navigate through a missing person's phone and look for information required to determine what happened to her.  It plays the same notes as the first game where the phone glitches out a lot, there are multiple suspects you can blame, and then at the end you deal with the source of the problem and need to get everything right for the good ending.The Positives-Because it's so similar to the first game, the positives of the previous remain the same: fun acting, interesting text conversations trying to figure out what's going on, investigations required to progress in the game, and strange things happening that, if it's your first game, will be eerie but if you played the first will be a repeat.-I did like the multiple suspects element this time.  Specifically, the fact that it was a social media thing was great, and the influencers all had their own personalities and motivations.  I really enjoyed that aspect of it.-There were a lot of insights you could find through your investigation that you could use in your interactions, but it wasn't always just, "You found out this cool thing--use it for greater success."  Sometimes, you were actually worse off if you used the evidence, which I really liked.  You did have to think about how to interact with each character to get the best outcome.  Not all of it seemed to be clear through logic, but people are different and so not always knowing what would set someone off kept you on your toes.-The police officer offered a lot of comic relief and drove urgency to move the plot along.The Negatives-Similarly, because it plays nearly identically as the first game, the game has the same weaknesses as the first.  If you're not a fan of this genre, it will not hold your attention since the only two elements of gameplay are investigation and interaction with the other characters and the information systems you can access.  There are only a handful of puzzles.  The rest is an experience, so there's no real gameplay if you wanted something other than a narrative-driven interactive experience.-In addition to the same weaknesses of the first game, this sequel plays the same notes as the first game so there's nothing new plot-wise.  Same "something bad happened to this person whose phone you're perusing" plot, same "you know something weird's going on while investigating" events, same puzzle types (find information, type it in to solve puzzles, and get everything you need to solve the case), and same kind of interaction with the Simulacra.  So if you've played the first game, it's the same game with new characters and interactions but roughly an identical story and plot.-I liked the ending of the first game better than the ending to the second.  The ending of the first really left me with a positive regard for the game.  This was fine, but it didn't leave as much of a mark for me.  Though, I will say, it kind of played on the dangers of social media, which was cool for the target audience of the game (mobile phone users).Overall, there's nothing new here, but I will say that I enjoyed it, anyway, even though it can't live up to the first game after playing the other one first.  However, if you play this game first for whatever reason, then you might like this one better (I can't say...though I liked the best ending of the first better than the best ending of this one).  The strongest element was the fact that your investigations went through the lives of social media influencers, and that was a fantastic way to make use of this type of game and the perfect plot for the Simulacra gimmick (note: I don't mean "gimmick" as a pejorative).Should you play?  Personally, I recommend trying the first one, though since this is nearly identical and you might have a different opinion about the endings, you will have a near-identical experience playing either one and so can try either.  It's roughly 4-5 hours to play through, and then you can decide whether to play the game over and get different endings (which is how I got over 10 hours of gameplay).  I enjoyed this one nearly as much since I liked the original's formula and ending, but since it was basically the same game it didn't have the same enjoyment as the first experience.  Play if you like the genre or want to try this fun, spooky interactive experience; if you want more gameplay or action from your games, though, this game is not for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Simulacra 2 is a major departure from the first game, and I mean that in both a good way and a bad way. I'll go over why I think this.Firstly, unlike the first game, this one is a lot more dependent on solving the case rather than trying to figure out what is going on. The ending you get is solely dependent on how many clues you find. For example, I got the good ending on my first playthrough of the game, but that's only because I'm super detailed-oriented person. This can be a good thing in my opinion because it is different from the first game and it makes you feel like a detective. On the other hand, one of the things I was slightly disappointed on was the lack of scares. Getting the good ending may be satisfying, but it takes away from the actual "horror" part of the game. When you do the good ending path you don't get a lot of scares, in fact you barley get any. Whereas the first game gave you really good jumpscares no matter what path you were on. If you start getting the bad ending, only then do you get the scares. I would say that's a major oversight considering this is a horror game. Overall, I still think it's a good game. I just wish it was scarier no matter what path you were on.

Its a bunch of friends who want to be influencers even tho none of them have any talent. One of them made a deal with this Simulacra monster and you have to figure out how. This time however it is really hard to even understand what is going in. There is no foreshaddowing at all which makes the game pretty much a spinning wheel without the guide. _childDocuments_.review: So after playing the first SIMULACRA game and unlocking all the endings in that one I decided to play this one and see if it's good as the first one was.I would say you would probably enjoy the first game way more than this one. _childDocuments_.review: Similarly to my review of the first Simulacra game I have to admit that despite some shortcomings this game has, I found it enjoyable.For context, this game is the 2nd in the series, however you don not need to have played the first game to try this one. The developers seem to have taken some of the feedback players gave on the first game and have applied it to this one, so if you enjoyed the first one in the series you will most certainly enjoy this one as much if not more.But let me step back a bit.Simulacra is a pseudo horror detective game which puts you in the seat of a detective/journalist and makes you figure out who the culprit of a murder is via the use of the deceased victims phone.If you are familiar with "A lot of phone" and "Orwell", this game is almost like the child of those two games.The good:*The gameplay loop is generally quite similar to the first game, however has added some new and completely different elements whilst removing some old ones. This is very welcome, especially for an experimental game of this type where new concepts are very welcome.*There's a lot of replay value to this game as there are multiple trails you can follow and get very different results. Whilst replaying over and over might get repetitive after a couple of games, I still think this is a great value add for this game.*The story is quite interesting and also different from the first gameThe bad/nit-picks:*Whilst Kaigan managed to remove the annoying bit of asking me to join their discord every time I finish the game (design choice of the first game) they completely forgot to add skip options for the credits and all of the cinematics in the game. I could understand this when I'm playing for the first time (though I don't think a developer should force you into doing this) but having to watch it for the 4th time because I tried reaching a different ending? It's just a waste of time and ticked me off*Kaigan seems to have listened somewhat to the criticism of their fist game that a save system would be great. So now you have 3 save slots... That get populated automatically, so if you go too far in the game and overwrite those slots, guess what, you have to start the game from scratch and tread through the same interactions again. A proper save system really isn't rocket science and I wish Kaigan implemented this properly.*The choice between an investigator and a journalist in my opinion is completely pointless and was just wasted development time.*21:9 aspect ratio works but video content gets cut off at the top and bottom*Some spelling errors and a game breaking bug where the phone tries to make a call (if you don't allow it to make a call for 15-20 seconds, it will stop trying and you will have to reload your save)*The acting... while not terrible leaves a lot to be desired.Overall, despite the list of negatives being longer than the positives I still recommend Simulacra 2. Whilst it undeniably has some pain points that I wish the developers noticed and remedied before release (or hell even after release) it was still an entertaining game and it also didnt break the bank.Give it a try!

_childDocuments_.review: I love FMV games. I played the first Simulacra and thought it was an interesting, novel, and fun game with cool gameplay mechanics. I am usually skeptical that a sequel will be as good, but Simulacra 2 doesn't disappoint! The story is more engaging than I thought it would be once I found out it was about "Internet Influencers." I have no interest in them in my normal life, but the story about these ended up being very good. I thought the writing was pretty well done. The only negative to the game (IMO) is the vague/obscure ways you need to find your clues and evidence. It's not always clear where you need to go and on the choice tree at the end of my 2 gaming sessions (I've played both the Detective & the Journalist paths), I've not cleared the entire choice tree even once. What a bummer.I appreciate the inclusion of both subtitles and a "fast mode" as it will make subsequent playthroughs much quicker for me. I am not really interested in sitting through all of the fake typing speeds and videos, unless it's new content that I haven't seen in the 9+ hours of the game I've already played. Fast mode is appreciated for sure!And I have to say that a couple of the actors in the game actually did a good job on their performances. Sure, there was a couple who were just CRINGE, but in general...I was pleased with the way they acted their parts. I especially liked Detective Murilo. I thought the actor fit the idea of a grizzled old police detective extremely well. Kudos to him for his good acting!So, in general, I liked the game. I plan to try to play through it a couple more times in hope of finding the dialogue trees I missed, as well as gain the final few achievements I don't have, yet. I definitely recommend this game if you like FMV's and aren't bothered by a few minor jump scares. Personally, I didn't think the game was scary at all, but I've played a ton of horror games, so I'm likely not the best choice for determining the "fear factor" in a game. I'm a bit jaded, I guess, on them. So, if you aren't the type of person who plays a lot of horror games, you might find a few parts of this game to be a little scary. I still doubt it would be terrifying or anything.And I played the game with headphones. It was recommended at the start of the game. Aside from some parts of the music being just WAY TOO LOUD, even after I had turned it down almost to the minimum, it was a good idea overall. I'd recommend using headphones for the experience as well.Oh, and to save you some time backtracking, I'd suggest you take notes on important locations, people's names, case numbers, etc. It will save you some time for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: You're a journalist, you're presented with a phone, to try and solve a case of a... murder? You get to look around the phone, with the few pieces of content there is, so... now what? Well, you try to put the pieces together, to unlock the content that has been corrupted or lost to other means.Bottomline is, this talks about the downsides to influencers and social media as a whole, what lengths these people are willing to go, just to stay relevant and popular in this world. But for you, you need to get behind "enemy lines", to learn what is going on in their world and what has caused this particular event to happen.For me, it was a really rather engaging journey and I got quite invested in it, trying to figure out what to do to unlock more of the phone's content and what has REALLY happened. The hours just flew by, while I was trying to rub my braincells together, to figure out what was the answer to a certain question or where I could find more evidence or whatever it may have been.Certainly recommended - especially considering it can be finished during a rainy afternoon or evening. It's supposed to be a "horror" game, but I didn't find it to be particularly scary and the attempts of "jump scares" were... well, let's just say, not very good. It didn't get to me at all. So should be fine for most people, at least of those that are teenagers and older, I would think.

_childDocuments_.review: Length <3hrs for 1 ending. <7hrs All endings and information.  Straight off the bat, Simulacra 2 feels like a much higher quality than the first game, the phone's UI is cleaner and even the screen saver stands out more. We have a much stronger cast of characters, a deeper story which tries to build a world and background for the Simulacra, and a wider use of apps and interactions.The story of Simulacra 2 is very engrossing if not a little predictable, we are dealing with four influencers and one of them is dead. How she died, and possibly who by, is our mission. As a new agent hired to investigate the incident through her phone, you need to look into her contacts and her friends to find the truth. Simulacra 2 has a lot more focus on interacting with the other characters, as you try to discover what they are hiding you will be digging into their past and their relationship with each other.The cast of Simulacra 2 are solid, some good acting that does feel authentic to mobile communication. There are a few scenes which do come off as staged, but a massive improvement over the first game. At the same time the characters have to be the most unlikable people possible, each one of them has some unsavoury past with a lot of reasoning as to why they justify their actions. The characters being unlikable does not take away from the mystery, it just makes the endings feel a little hollow. I really had no care at any point in the game how any of them ended up.While Simulacra 2 does say it has multiple endings, there is very little difference between them. We have the good ending where everyone is saved and then six bad endings though the variation is who dies and does the detective corp your in get disbanded or keeps working. In total three unique videos and one video should the detective corp get disbanded, while the conversation with the Simulacra is a little different it is not massively significant to the ending. Still decent videos, just saying it’s up to you if you want to spend the time getting to the other endings.Puzzles have been streamlined in the game, most files that you will need to open you just need to witness the correct information. Then you can choose it and place it on the file to unlock the information. You will still be looking through files; it just feels less important. There are still points of needing to find certain information, I just felt overall it was less time consuming and easy to find everything.While being an investigator did make for an interesting change in character perspective and does offer for some great moments with your superior. The video calls are funny and lighthearted, while the actor has to have been the best of the cast. I can’t help but find that at points in the game it really slowed down the progress. As conversations were repeated and you would be interrupted when moving to the next step. I would not say it was bad or good, it just felt like more content was just placed on top, and the only importance being an investigator is it gives reason to your actions.Horror moments are really mixed, while the creepiness of the phone screen is great, it really does unnerve you looking at the images. The Ripper man and the death scenes really feel comical, it looks like a phone effect over a character. It did make me laugh seeing it. Still the game is not overly scare focused and I went into the game for the story.Overall ‘Simulacra 2’ is a good game, with a really interesting mystery to how the Simulacra plays a part in the death of a girl, and the creation of the Simulacra. The dive into what Simulacra are seems deeper, but sort of opens more questions. While the cast of characters feel like stronger actors, the characters all seem unlikable in different ways. Still an overall interesting game, if at times feeling a little bloated.Below you will find my gameplay video, it is really long. _childDocuments_.review: I've only watched a let's play of the first Simulacra game, and decided to buy this one and play through myself this time, as I was intrigued by the story (started watching a let's play for this one). Although, I feel there was a little less horror (and fewer scares), the story feels a little tighter, and the characters feel more fleshed out. (I know people have commented on the acting, but personally, that wasn't a problem for me, as you can clearly tell they're passionate about this project.) I also really enjoyed the commentary about influencers and influencer life, as well as the complexity of human nature and, without spoiling it too much (and at the risk of sounding too cringey), finding the good in people.I will say, the one downside is that the replay-ability is a bit mind-numbing when you can't skip some cut scenes/videos that you've already seen. It would be kind of nice to be able to skip anything you've already logged as watched when it comes to the non-skippable cut scenes and videos. Otherwise, the option to speed up the game after your first play through is super nice.I'm excited to try and get all the achievements, and unlock all the branching pathways. _childDocuments_.review: Great game, and in my opinion the best game in the series! It's not reliant on the story from the first game either, despite it being a sequel. Overall I enjoyed the story a lot! It also adds in a lot more detail about things present in the first game. If I had to raise any complaints, the main one would be the difficulty in replay-ability of this game. There is a "fast mode" that you unlock after completing the game once, which speeds up the dialogue. However it doesn't feel as convenient as how it was in the first game, where I believe you could sort-of fast forward at various points in the game. You're still forced to watch through certain videos from start to finish on the phone, and while the dialogue is speed up a little bit it still feels rather slow and makes it a bit of a chore to really replay the game.Of course, I feel a lot of that could be tied to the the limitation of the game's design and programming. Understandably this game had a LOT of content and work put into it, so I understand the desire to not allow the player to be able to skip certain things. Still a fast forward button or changing the fast mode to allow you to skip cut-scenes/videos would help with replay-ability and would  be nice to have added to the game. Still, it's a 10 out of 10 story and was worth playing until the end!

_childDocuments_.review: I got the game for $8. I don't think it was worth $8 to me but I can definitely see how others see the appeal. I went in excited but honestly I was let down by the ending. But I can see how they justify the price... high production value, high quality videos, the actors were mostly okay but Rex was a bit much for me.Worst part of the game for me is that it's so centered around social media, instagram type stuff. That wouldn't have been so bad but I didn't like digging through fake fashion histories and fake popularity for research... but you gotta do what you gotta do. _childDocuments_.review: Sequels are almost never as good as the original.  While there were some interesting moments, it did have some flaws.The Cons:--Characters were introduced too quickly, and the women were too similar, so it was much more difficult to keep their identities straight.  All three of them were petite, vain, social media "influencers", and two of them had names beginning with M.  They weren't distinct enough right off the bat to keep them mentally separate, and I didn't really get them mentally sorted out until the the game was almost over.--Most of the characters were pretty unlikable.  Too greedy and self-absorbed for me to make a connection with them.  I did end up bonding well with Mina, by the end, and the cop was funny, but the rest were douchebags.  The woman who went missing might have been more relatable, but we didn't learn enough about her to really make a connection.  These characters didn't draw me in as much as those in the original game did.The Pros:--The acting was better.  In the first game, a few of the secondary characters were a bit amateur.  This time round, even the characters who had very few lines were sharp and professional in their delivery.--The detective role was an interesting take.  It did make the game a little bit less personal than the first one, but it was neat to have the police resources at my disposal to look up information for use in conversations.Overall, it's worth a playthrough, and if you get it on sale then the price is definitely right.

_childDocuments_.review: Hesitantly played this game after finding the original to be incredibly disappointing. TLDR review of the first: Lot of promise, then linear, silly plot, choices don't really matter. Text misspellings, lazy and mispronounced voice-overs. Mediocre visual novel with a nonsensical plot, very little character development, and an overall feeling of "wow, what a waste of time."I was hoping the sequel would offer a bit more and, at first, I was pleasantly surprised. Great UI improvement and smoother control, high definition full-motion video, better character development... But then it dipped right back into the nonsensical dialogue with vague answers to questions that you can't retract or expand upon that might change the ending completely. At one point, you're forced into dialogue where you have to respond with "sunny" or "stormy" responses or be served with good or bad plot development. Too bad the responses you're presented with are so ambiguous you have no clue how the characters will reply. Then the finale where you're faced with even MORE incoherent babble and have to respond exactly how the game wants you to in order to get the "good" ending.Again, like the first in the series, the game suffers from terribly vague dialogue choices that have way too much affect on such a linear plot, then an ending that leaves way too much unanswered and sets the stage for yet another disappointing sequel. These found phone/device games always have so much promise, but are always such utter disappointments.

_childDocuments_.review: In the Simulacra games, you’re put into the role of a person who gets in possession of a mobile phone, and you have to solve puzzles in order to figure out what happened to its original owner. I’m lumping these two games together because even though their narratives aren’t connected to any great degree, the overall concept and gameplay is identical for both games.In general, the Simulacra games remind me a lot of how the Orwell games work, in the sense that much of what you do is rifle through personal data. What’s different is that in these games you’re an active participant and not just an observer, so you get to talk to various characters directly, instead of just listening into their conversations.Now just finding a phone and looking through its contents isn’t that interesting, most people in general aren’t interesting. But both games start with video messages from the original owners that indicate that something sinister is going on, and that’s where the FMV sequences come into play. For what it’s worth, these sequences aren’t played out of some misguided, ironic attempt at nostalgia like many other FMV games. It’s more just a representation of how we use our phones in real life. Video isn’t just a gimmick here, it’s part of what the games need to have in order to tell their stories.Unfortunately, the acting during these FMV sequences isn’t that great. The first game does come off a bit better because it’s mostly centered around online dating, so there are only a few videos or instances of video calls that happen, but the second game targets influencer culture, where video plays a much bigger role. And there are also video sequences that happen outside of the context of the phone, because this is a sequel and I guess that’s a way of telling your customers that it’s worth buying another one because it has more stuff than the previous one. As a result, the unconvincing acting takes up much more runtime.And I do have to say that the second game really hams it up a notch. It’s difficult to tell if the acting quality is intentional, since the second game is a rather scathing takedown of influencer culture, it could also be a jab at the terrible acting influencers employ during their fake drama.The writing is pretty decent for the most part. I mean, these are cheesy horror games mostly about millennials, so you’re not really expecting F. Scott Fitzgerald quality stuff here, but it still manages to convey a sense of personality, even to some of the characters whose voices you never get to hear. Though I have to say that the second game has this weird idea of making every single character you have to investigate a complete asshole. I guess this comes with the territory for professional influencers. But if you, like me, watch cheesy 80’s slasher movies in order to see smug teenagers die in creative ways without having to empathize with them, it’s weird for the game to then turn around and give you a bad ending for wanting to punish these self-centered jerks. To get the good ending and also not miss out on a bunch of actual puzzles and therefore content, you have to stroke their egos quite a bit and metaphorically appeal to the power of friendship to solve the mystery.Overall I like the gameplay of the second game more, because it offers a broader set of mechanics, but I liked the more nuanced characters in the first game better because not everyone there is just a despicable manipulative asshole. But in general, they’re nice time killers and they’re fully intended to be played through multiple times to get to see everything. And the nice thing is that the developers even implemented a fast-forward feature for repeat playthroughs so you can get through the text conversations faster, which was much appreciated. So yeah, if you want a modern example of how an FMV game can work and you can stomach some stilted acting and don’t mind the presence of generally dislikable characters, I’d recommend these games, they’re a fun little distraction.

_childDocuments_.review: This one's close, honestly. I love all of the previous Simulacra stuff, including Sara is Missing and other unrelated "lost phone games" like Replica. This one's campier than ever and it's no longer fiddling with the mystery of "paranormal or real life". Instead we're after a demon and it's made clear very quickly. The FMV sections are filmed well. The 4K footage is so well done, the lighting's generally good to great and the physical acting ranges from decent (lead detective) to pretty bad (any of the influencers). The voice acting is also just bad. You can get through it. The quality of the audio itself is alright, but the acting abilities are non-existent. The story is also not too interesting until the last third of the game, when all of a sudden some drama kicks up and in the beginning 10 minutes, where the mystery's getting you interested. The text conversations are the worst yet with being forced to be very sloppy with your work (you can always ask like 1/3 of the questions since you can't return to the previous choices for no reason) and with never really getting a clear answer to anything. There's multiple endings though and so maybe things clear up. However in my ending, I basically got lines that are the classic vague lines of any paranormal mystery. "You have no idea", "the wheels are in motion" and all that crap. So why do I recommend it? I still enjoyed my time and still thought of the game after I finished it. There are no games like this really either. A Normal Lost Phone doesn't even feel like a phone and the story is so milktoast that it's just absolutely dull. Replica was fun, but there's only so much you can do with a drawn phone still. Simulacra's making the right decision with FMV and it's really entertaining and more immersive that the other games in the genre. This is the best series you'll get in this genre and this is just another hit until something better finally surfaces.

_childDocuments_.review: If you played Simulacra, which you should before playing its sequel, you will like this game.  However, this is one of those cases where some of the eagerness to "add" to a sequel also took from it a little bit.   The best elements are there; the creepy atmosphere, the sense of being watched, the occasional jumpy surprise and the realistic phone content.  However, there are some things about the game that changed that I can't really say added quality so much as subtracted from the tension.  In Simulacra 2 you are no longer 'you', but instead you are either a tabloid reporter or a detective that gets roped into helping an aging police officer who is in charge of a rather...unbelievable police force department that specializes in potentially paranormal activity. I know, right?  Why not a paranormal investigations team?  It would change the plot a little, but it might make more sense...Anyway, the police officer is there to muddle who you are helping vs harming and to give you a special app that is made to repair corrupted data and search police records.  While I'm not a huge fan of the "click an icon that pops up to tell you that you see a clue you can save" idea, it's almost necessary to sort through the mountains of text that come from the victims/culprits/etc.   That's because they're all .  That's right, you're investigating  awful people on the internet.  Honestly, there was a point where i was considering  just to rid the game world of some toxic people,  I'm not sure the goal was to make me root for  I enjoyed the game very much, overall, but the atmosphere became less isolated and eerie by including a police contact and hack tools.  I also miss the ambiguity of the Player's identity; choosing to be a reporter or a detective was less immersive than just being some guy who is holding someone else's phone. The suspense and terror are still there, and investigating a murder does change the pacing for the positive.   Instead of a race against time to track someone down, many puzzles give you time to work and find replete clues.   The timed elements are all when texting with someone or solving a timed puzzle, and a failure doesn't necessarily doom anything unless you fail a bunch of times in a row.  At least one even just lets you start over. Overall, this is a pretty solid sequel, but the devs should be careful not to continue to make the game series to be more like Orwell, because that doesn't suit the subject matter here.

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10An interesting experience with some creepy moments, but that could have been better if it took more risks and didn't play as safe as it did.Simulacra 2 is like the first game, but with a better production value, including some high quality videos. You play as either a detective or a journalist and investigate the strange death of an influencer, working alongside a veteran detective while interrogating 3 suspects, all while using the victim's phone. As the story unfolds, creepy things happen involving the phone.The game has some interesting developments throughout the story and has plenty of choices on the way that can lead the story towards a specific direction, with multiple possible endings - the game even shows a "decision tree" at the end to show the decisions the player took and how many decisions they could have made instead at each point of the game.The acting is pretty decent. It feels a little over-the-top at times, but it's by far not bad and it certainly shows the investment that was put into the game, which is cool.The main problem of the game here is that, much like the first game, it still plays too safe. I won't go into details to avoid spoilers, but mostly everything in the game follows a pattern and even the creepy moments could be creepier - I don't necessarely mean they should be jumpscares, but they're still somewhat predictable and they could have been more disturbing. Also like the first game, you can see the scenery around the phone, but nothing actually creepy ever happens in the scenery, which is a huge missed opportunity.Also, while the game is mostly straightforward, there are a few parts (one or two, not many - again, most of the game is prety straightforward) that are needlessly convoluted and hard to figure out.What would have been better for the game would be something that allows the player to more freely investigate things and involves less patterns to be followed - some people are hiding things, others aren't... Some clues are relevant, others aren't... Etc.Still, Simulacra 2 is still a fun, creepy experience with some replayability, easily worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: Changed to thumbs up after the second playthrough, update at the end.You know, the first game has its charm, even though it's not perfect, esp. regarding presentation and handling. But still there was enough depth to it to be able to connect with the people portrayed. They mostly felt like believable human beings.This one on the other side is technically better made, looks more professional in comparison, but the writing doesn't fly with me as well, because of one reason: *Warning: Spoilers may be ahead* Those kids you're dealing with, including the victim, are portrayed to be pretentious f*cks that only care for themselfs and their online "success". They are as shallow and cliché as it gets. That makes it hard to have any positive connection to or even the slightest interest in them. I even caught myself thinking that I don't care what really happened, because the way they are portrayed, they kind of deserved it. That's not really a good premise for feeling like a detective (or reporter) that tries to find out what happened. I'm not finished with the game yet and I'll play it through anyways, maybe there's some surprise waiting. But right now, my hopes are not that high.Update: So after finishing the first time playing as detective - which was really not rewarding - I gave it a second try and played as reporter. Turns out it really makes a difference, because if you take your role serious (and I do because I'm a passionate roleplayer), you apply a different mindset. As a detective, you dig up as much dirt as you can naturally, as a reporter you try to be more balanced, which resulted in more character depth and even led me to the good ending, which felt much more rewarding in turn. Boy, this is a mixed bag. Anyhow, I still changed to thumbs up, because 50% rewarding isn't too bad and others may not be that deep into it all like I am. So my suggestion for a possible third game would be to either focus on a single role to play  or - like in the first game - no predefined player role at all,  to make the experience more straightforward and thus more rewarding. In this case, putting a role on the player maybe wasn't the best design decission. But that's just my two cents.

name: Knuckle Sandwich
detailed_description: About Guide a young man through his first day in Bright City – a bustling island paradise with a horrible secret. Find a new job, make new friends, and attempt to solve a mystery revolving around a ludicrous gang and a fanatical cult. In this RPG, you defeat enemies in turn-based battles by completing minigames unique to the foe you're facing. These minigames are made up of a variety of challenges, including rhythm games, shoot-em'-ups, memory puzzles, and quick-time events. Features: An offbeat and personal story with a focus on humor. Over 100 fast-paced minigames specific to each enemy and playable character. Vibrant city locations to explore on a fictional Australian island. A massive cast of characters, including several partners to join you along the way. A huge soundtrack with music by Nelward, Lizzy, Gyms, Barchboi, and pngsequence.
