_childDocuments_.review: I originally left a review before completing the game. I've incorporated those thoughts into this more cohesive review now that I've finished it.Reviewing Knuckle Sandwich feels incredibly complicated in a way that's hard to understand unless you've played it. I will start by saying I genuinely enjoy the game and would recommend it to almost any of my friends. It is clearly a project with a deep amount of care poured into it. The writing is enjoyable, the art style is incredible, the music is amazing, and the microgames are fun. Anything good about the game is fantastic, and it's an aesthetic gem because of it. Knuckle Sandwich's curse, though, is that the opposite is just as true.Though they're comparatively infrequent, this game features some of the most bafflingly horrible design choices I've seen in such a passionately-made project. The inventory management is the one you'll have to deal with most often; it is outright bizarre that players are only guaranteed eight slots of storage space, including key items and worn items. Though it's amended somewhat when you gain new party members with their own inventories, none of them remain with you permanently. Once you finish a given area, you will have to carefully swap items and be whittled down to the default eight slots again. In theory, this encourages you to use consumable items more liberally, but in practice, it's just incredibly frustrating.The quality of the WarioWare-like minigames for dodging and countering enemy attacks are similarly bipolar. To begin with the good: most are implemented cleverly and feel like a genuine test of skill. There are plenty of similar control schemes between them, so they feel intuitive to play next to each other. The way the bullet-hell-type attacks were taught especially stuck out to me. The player-controlled ships all have a mechanic that lowers their fire rate the longer the shoot button is held down, and this mechanic is subtly taught (without any dialogue) through a section in chapter 1 that's disconnected entirely from the battle system.This type of game design is incredible, especially considering that players might not even realize it's there. It's perfect in its invisibility, being masked behind what initially seems to just be a quirky minigame before the main story begins. It feels all the more painful, then, when the worst of the worst microgames are introduced alongside it.Though they're small in number, some attacks can only be avoided with luck. I'm convinced the microgame in which you must catch falling scoops of ice cream in a cone, for example, is entirely impossible if said scoops spawn too far from each other. This small handful of bad apples bogs down the quality of certain sections of the game by a lot, as each enemy type only utilizes a few attacks. You'll run into the same enemy a lot in any given area, meaning you'll be greeted with the same few microgames repeatedly until you move on to a new piece of the game.This questionable gameplay extends into the overworld puzzles as well, arguably more often than not. The first few, mostly being based around hitting colored buttons to open and close off areas of the map, feel genuinely enjoyable to figure out. They are rewarding in a way that suggests the developer clearly understands the medium. Very quickly, though, these puzzles shift from requiring careful consideration and planning to bashing your head against them until you happen across the solution.The Pokemon-style ice puzzles specifically are frustrating even in their most basic form, as they seem designed around pure trial-and-error. The camera makes no effort to actually show you what you're hurdling towards until you're locked into a path, meaning there is absolutely no way to plan out your next move until making the wrong one. This becomes downright unacceptable towards the end of the game, where you will be repeatedly thrown back onto one of these puzzles after already completing it. (Specifically, this happens every time you fail another puzzle that is similarly designed around trial-and-error.)I've used "baffling" to describe some of these choices already, but designing puzzles like this is, in the truest sense of the word, completely baffling to me. The gameplay is not just bad. In fact, I quite enjoyed most of my time with it, and it's clear that the dev genuinely cared about making it fun. But I cannot fathom a universe in which these late-game puzzles are enjoyable to anyone. They are designed to be frustrating, as if to taunt the player by saying "Yeah, this sucks, but you already sunk eight hours into this. What are you gonna do, NOT see where the hell this is going?"And, of course, by "this," I mean the primary reason Knuckle Sandwich's demo garnered so much intrigue in the first place: the story.Backers and casual fans, myself included, all waited nearly five years to see how the unsettling twist at the end of Chapter One would progress, and what other gory, 90s-slasher-inspired story beats would be introduced. In the time between then and now, I enrolled in and graduated from college, the Knuckle Sandwich demo always in the back of my mind. The absolute last thing I expected was for all of the aesthetic and narrative sensibilities promised by the demo to be pulverized and promptly thrown into the garbage disposal.The shift in the style and substance of the story isn't necessarily a bad one, even if it's not what was originally promised. The three main characters you play alongside are charming and surprisingly down-to-earth. It's fascinating to see quirky characters like this react realistically to realizing they're in way over their heads as they become involved in a major, magic-filled conspiracy. The game also leans a bit more into the themes of gentrification and class divide that inadvertently caused the events of the demo in the first place. The weight of what happens in the demo doesn't leave the protagonist's head, and this is shown mostly through subtle character actions and expressions. These are all very interesting narrative elements, and incredibly unique for such an otherwise quirky, colorful RPG.Unfortunately, a lack of overall direction considerably dampens the narrative. Plot points and characters are introduced and discarded seemingly at random. Though Knuckle Sandwich does a good job at tying most of these elements together by the end, many didn't seem developed enough to warrant their inclusion at all.It wants to make social commentary on billionaires, but it's clear from early on that the only billionaire in the game is ignorant rather than malicious. It wants a cool reality-bending glitch effect to carry narrative weight, but the effect feels unimportant because it was already used at the very beginning of the game. The protagonist's actions in Chapter One continually weigh on him but otherwise become completely irrelevant; there's never even any risk of his new friends finding out about it. Busdriver's characterization as a powerful being carrying immense guilt is incredibly interesting, but every other aspect of his existence is so vague that it just feels unsatisfying. The protagonist's boss is a fascinatingly repulsive character but is mostly completely absent. The big twist villain carries about as much weight as Zootopia's.Basically, everything is neat, but I just wanted—and expected—a bit more. I wanted a tighter narrative, I wanted the disturbing tone of the demo to persist throughout the rest of the game, I wanted a better explanation of the mythical elements of the plot, I wanted a deeper social commentary, and I definitely wanted a more satisfying ending. But I only wanted so much more of any of this because I genuinely enjoyed the sprinkles that were already there.All in all, this game is worth experiencing at least once. I might not care to start a new save file and painstakingly search for every secret I missed, but I'm satisfied with what I played for $20

_childDocuments_.review: Before I say anything, I would just like to say that I've followed this game fairly actively since around 2015 when gameplay was really starting to pop up, I was beyond excited for this game and I was more than happy to donate when the Kickstarter happened in 2018. An RPG with a unique artstyle that's combat is heavily inspired by WarioWare microgames and Mario & Luigi Superstar Saga? Count me in! ...What I wasn't expecting was while this game loves to boast it's WarioWare roots, it somehow completely fumbles the novelty of WarioWare, and what makes it such an easy series to revisit. The battles start out pretty fun, but quickly begin to wear thin when you realize how much health enemies have and how battles constantly put you at a disadvantage because the game wants to ensure that you see every microgame the enemies have to offer (which vary in variety, mind you. There are many reskins of microgames that are either just longer or have slightly altered attack patterns). Enemies have so much health and you feel like you're getting nowhere because, even if you have the best equipment available, you are consistently hitting around 1-2 HP of damage per hit, and when you are constantly having to replay microgames that last up to 10-15 seconds PER ENEMY TURN, it just gets exhausting. There was some controversy when the game was revealed to have a skip battle option, but honestly? I probably wouldn't have finished the game without it. There were so many instances throughout my playthrough where there was a room full of enemies and I did not want to interact with any of them because I knew I would be stuck in a battle for 5+ minutes at a time just trying to take out 2-3 enemies that aren't even gonna give me enough EXP to get even a quarter of a level. Boss battles aren't much better, flat out awful pacing. Most of the boss battles are just stalling and surviving long microgames while your attacks do miniscule damage in order to pad out the fight long enough for the enemy to cycle through all of their dialogue, they charge and use a big move, all of their stats drop, and they die. Rinse and repeat. Dungeon exploration is just as bad if not worse in regards to just feeling sluggish and not fun. During development, there was so much emphasis being put on by Andrew Brophy about how much he wants to make a game without all of the bad parts that usually make RPGs drag such as long dungeons, annoying block puzzles, etc. It amazes me that Knuckle Sandwich somehow manages to do the exact opposite of this. This game has some of the most obnoxious dungeons that I have ever experienced in a video game and it's not even because they're necessarily hard, there is just a very clear lack of direction for what the game wants you to do and the puzzles are just downright bad. This game has it all, annoying switch puzzles, annoying ice sliding puzzles, you name it, it's probably there in some form. It only gets worse when you experience this game's inventory system which is downright abysmal. You have 8 spaces of inventory that are taken up by equipment and key items while constantly coming across new healing items that you just never get to use because your inventory is always full.The other major issue I have with this game is the story, the game starts with a great hook that I don't want to spoil if you never played the demo, but then proceeds to do next to nothing with that plot point, it's barely even brought up again after the first chapter, which is very disappointing because it was such an interesting premise that I was so excited to see explored more. Instead Knuckle Sandwich offers a plot that is not only extremely poorly paced, but it is just flat out boring. The plot twists are predictable and uninteresting and there is little to no character development after the game really tried to advertise how big of a role your party members would seemingly play. This could have been easily forgiven if the dialogue did the heavy lifting, but even the writing shifts after the first couple of chapters and  most (not all) jokes ends up falling flat or ends up getting overused (this game loves running gags). This aspect is especially surprising to me considering how much I loved the dialogue in the demo, it was very witty and was one of the best things about revisiting it. To say I'm disappointed with Knuckle Sandwich would be an understatement, I backed around $100 for this game in 2018 when the Kickstarter launched, and as if my experience couldn't have been worse, they forgot to include my name, along with other backers in the Kickstarter credits at the end of the game. Knuckle Sandwich feels like a prime example of what happens when a developer gets their dopamine rush from having their game successfully funded (3 separate times) and quickly run out of steam to actually finish the project they set out to complete in the first place and I can't stress enough just how disappointed I am with this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: Knuckle Sandwich sells itself as one of those quirky jrpgs with a strange battle system that promises to be innovative, but slips a bit on the delivery. The first 20 minutes of gameplay are in form of a very fun prologue with a lot of passion on its making and it instantly got me hooked because I'm a dinosaur, a jaded caveman that have been playing videogames ever since the Atari era so I'm always looking for a new experience in this oversaturated videogame market. Screw the nostalgia glasses. I know fellows that religiously play FF7 and Chrono Trigger every single year and will parrot that they need nothing but to replay those over and over until their deathbeds, but I'd rather go look for something new.But boy, oh boy, once those 20 minutes were over, my excitement slowly and begrudgingly melted away into a puddle of disappointment. Clocking 16 hours to completion, all that Knuckle Sandwich did for me was to make me appreciate Undertale and the work Toby Fox even more than I already did.The initial premise set in the prologue of Knuckle Sandwich (a REALLY bizarre reveal as to why the game got this name) never went anywhere, in fact, once the Chapter 1 started, it got immediately kicked into a curb to give way for another bizarre premise. Okay. Fine. I had tried to not consider this a bait-and-switch and think of it as just one more eccentricity, but unfortunately the story turned out to be merely wacky for the sake of being wacky, lacking that so called je-ne-sois-quoi to become special in any manner. To be frank, maybe the prologue had a bit of a morbid premise, but it was a funny one, nevertheless.The plot and narrative are just so, very, very average. Something-something burgers made of human flesh, but lets ditch that. Hey mate I'm a blue vampire and I need help. Spirit energy making things go gagaaa. Goblins. So CRAZY! Insert a groan here. There was no attempt to build a world, have an actual lore backing all of its absurdity, or to be memorable in any manner. The characters are sorta... funny, but lacking any form of development, backstory or personality to make me actually care. The whole schtick of one of them is that he's just a guy... with nothing much to say, so it's moot to try to talk to him, since... he'll always say that he got not idea of what to talk about. Ha ha. Ho ho. Heh.Yet, it was the kind of average that hooked me enough to keep playing to see if there was anything going on, but then --- wait a second, I just looked at my save file and at 15 hours I'm at 97% completion? What? Is the game about to end? Where's the big reveal --- WAIT, THIS IS THE BIG REVEAL? So in the last 10 minutes the game tries to tie all the strings together with the premise that I thought to be trashed and forgotten. Gosh, this is just so.... incredibly mid. Why the HELL the final boss looks like that? So, alright. Huhhh huhnn, and and and and....Huh. The credits are rolling.What. What? WHAT???Underneath its (initially) fun minigames, Knuckle Sandwich has very simplistic, if not barebones, battle and jrpg systems. Status values and weapons barely seem to make much of a difference since balance is all over the place, damage values oftenly made no sense, there's only a handful of weapons and accessories to be found around the world and by around 8 hours or so you simply stop finding anything new. I feel that at this point of the game's development, the dev shrugged, decided to gave up on this aspect of the game and moved on. I'll skip the dungeons, those are simply cookie cutter with sliding and switch puzzles that have no right to waste your time. I felt I was back to the 90's, but not in a good way. All of this wouldn't be so bad if the battles weren't repetitive. But they are. Enemies are loaded with a tad bit too much HP to pad their lenght and force you to play the minigames. This is actually made worse by the fact that enemies constantly get an extra turn at the start of the battle and attack you, then you get to have a turn, but they are faster than you, so you play the minigames AGAIN before finally attacking. If you are REALLY great at hitting the very tiny critical bars, or creating multiple combos in the ring gauge, you can get to beat some enemies in one go, but good luck at that. Some special skills have mediocre damage, others can blow away an entire enemy team, so you are better off just spamming those and cheesing the game  healing to full by backtracking to vending machines.Would I recommend the game? Maybe. Sorta. I've got mixed feelings and the review section on steam only got thumbs going up or down. Despite of its flaws, there's actual passion on the creation of this game and the battle system with warioware minigames might be really interesting for some, it's just not groundbreaking or genre-redefining.Knuckle Sandwich is also a quite short experience, so all those flaws might end up being not so much of a big deal. I was actually more disappointed this year for playing FFXVI since that game had no right to last beyond 80 hours and was 20 times more repetitive with its battles and boring sidequests. A 6.8 score from me, a valiant attempt from an indie developer. It's just a shame that it sorta missed the mark of some the aspects that games like Undertale and others managed to understand so much better. Dear Andy, I hope you can take this ounce of criticism. Keep making games and improving as a developer.Cheers!
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, this game really makes me wish there was a meh option to pick when rating games. At the end of the day, I can tell Andy had his heart in the right place and I can't even imagine what it's like to spend 5 whole years of your life working on one single project. However, I can't recommend this game to anyone. I feel a lot of the issues that are present in this game stem simply from the problem of having one guy making all of the decisions without anyone else to come in and tell him, "Hey, just because it's a trope to have tedious puzzles in a final dungeon to extend the length of it, doesn't mean you should put that in the game (even if you're making a joke about it, it doesn't make it funny)." This game suffers heavily from the time it came out. Earthbound Indie RPGs are now a meme and Deltarune chapters 1-2 have come out which I feel that game hits so much better at doing everything this game wishes. Better comedy, better characters, better combat. I know it's not fair to compare the two but all I kept thinking as I was dragging through late-game fights was how much I appreciated the combat system in Deltarune over this game. Even ignoring the comparisons, I feel like the game still falls short in just about every aspect.Warioware minigames? They're annoying and repetitive, you will find yourself doing the same galaga minigame over and over again in EVERY chapter.Enemies? They're alright until you hit the end and you start just fighting reskins of the same enemies with the same minigames.Combat? Even to this day, after multiple updates, still doesn't make any sense to me. Some enemies you'll stomp in two hits. Others? Even with the OP goblin summons, sometimes they'll do only like 3 damage. Straight up it feels like your damage is capped in certain fights because the dev doesn't want you to go to fast or else you'll miss some of the dialogue.Speaking of the goblins, it would have been cool if, rather than just being some big damage dealing attack, it would have been worth finding them all if each goblin did something different. Like, other than for achievements, there's no reason to get the other goblins because they ALL do the same exact freaking thing.More than anything else though, the characters piss me off the most. It's not that I found them to be annoying but I was more annoyed by how nothing their involvement is! When we first go to your co-workers apartment, there are some interesting things of note about Thea and Echo that are you find out about them but it never amounts to anything. Thea built her own computer and has a collection of anime figures/collectibles and yet we never learn anything about her. In fact, her story, whatever small meaningless story that is, is about her getting caught up trying to be a hero. Echo has a heavy connection to sports but the most you get out of her when it comes to asking about it is that she used to play it in high school but doesn't now because she gets fatigued easily. This is a worthless point that goes nowhere and the 2 special scenes I had with her amounted to nothing being added to her character. I'm not going to even bother talking about Dolus, ♥♥♥♥ Dolus, worthless nothing character that, if you picked him to be your co-worker, you wasted a pick!Brightfangs? I feel nothing towards them. I liked the first two fights but the final two just ending on stupid microgames that were at best not fun and at worse, confusing on how to play, terrible idea!Mr. Apricot? I feel nothing towards him because we don't get enough time see his 'arc' flesh out, like he says he wanted to make bright city a better place but is also shown as being a 'I'm better than everyone' rich type character so honestly, I would have just preferred for it to be that he really was just the villan or more over have him be punished for his ignorance .Which I guess I should talk about the story so spoliers for the ending the game: And also another warning for a major MAJOR spoiler, reader discretion is advised: A lot of people have complained about some of the jrpg tropes that are in the game but honestly a lot of my complaints are with the things that aren't included in the game. This game feels like a turn based rpg made by a person who is not a turned based jrpg fan and only has an outsider view of them. There's jokes about the power of friendship yet at the end of the game, we've pretty much made friends with all of the enemies that we fought along the way,   The problem with all of this is that, in a jrpg, we would have spent so much time with all of the characters that we'd know more about them, we'd feel the weight of their words when they say they love bright city and want to protect it. I see so many people now trying to 'fix' RPGs by turning them into something they're not and makes me sad to see the growing death of the genre because it was great. It still is great! But the people who are trying to trim off the fat are slicing through the meat and cutting into the bone. This game feels hollow and soulless even though it is pouring over with soul and it's because the person making the game (from my own viewpoint) doesn't have a TRUE passion for the games he's replicating.5/10 game with 10/10 graphics and music. Wouldn't recommend you play this, not even on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: I started playing this game without any prior knowledge, just stumbled upon it on Steam and thought, 'Why not?' I can confidently say that I wasn't disappointed, and .The combat in the game is enjoyable, thanks to engaging mini-games that add a fun twist. There's a good variety of enemies and bosses, keeping the game-play fresh throughout. The dialogue is well-written and presented in an enjoyable way. The game draws heavily from its inspirations but never wears out its welcome, often evoking a sense of nostalgia. Bright City is filled with secrets, adding an offbeat and mysterious vibe. The music, sound design and visuals are fantastic, really adding to the overall experience.The game offers good accessibility options and lets you fine-tune the difficulty to your liking.I love it!Before diving into the negatives, I want to touch on some aspects that may not be great, but personally, I find enjoyment in their flaws.First off, the close-knit, no-hope friend circle is bland. Surprisingly, this makes the group feel oddly realistic and relatable to regular people. I appreciate the fact that, in a world filled with over-the-top personalities, the group I'm left with seems mundane. This enhances the bizarre nature of Bright City and makes the kid more relatable.I adored the trial-and-error puzzles; they gave me a nostalgic feeling, like being a kid playing Pokemon on my Game Boy in the back seat of the car, banging my head against the window, wondering why these puzzles were in the game. The frustration was oddly enjoyable. The puzzles have been tweaked and are not as convoluted as when I first played, but I still found them enjoyable.Some of the mini-games seem luck-based, but personally, it didn't bother me. The overall combat was easy enough that the only times I took damage were during the 'luck-based' mini-games. Without those, I honestly wouldn't have needed any recovery items. To be clear, even though a bit of luck could make those mini-games easier, they still felt skill-based.While the overall story is fun and engaging, it feels like it ends abruptly. The final boss didn't have the epic feel I was expecting, and the epilogue felt unnecessary. Without spoilers, it's challenging to explain in more detail, but overall, I found the conclusion unsatisfying.The limited inventory was annoying; the game attempts to make you strike a balance between gear, supplies, and key/quest items. Overall, I felt like the system fell short due to the nature of the game. Tight inventory management like this is better suited for a survival-horror game where scarce supplies add tension.Despite its shortcomings and annoyances, I would still recommend this game. The overall experience isn't perfect, but some flaws contribute to the overall charm, making it a memorable and unique adventure.In short, this game . .
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: Waited patiently and expectantly for this one. The expectations people have for indie games have changed since the demo released in 2018, and I am no exception. Nice things first, this game is a labor of love. A lot of detail was crammed in, I think the developer slam dunked on the ticket of creating a professional product. I got about 15 hours out of the game, which was more than In expected. There were a lot of micro games, and a lot of little secrets and references to giggle at. I applaud this game for having a cast of likable and relatable characters without dating itself with references, keeping the narrative sort of "timeless" while still being quirky. The music is quirky, punchy, lively, bright, and just absolutely phenomenal if you're into weirdo stuff. Also hats off to the sprite work, there are SO MANY unique characters in this game, and the look is uniform and natural. Some of the art in the game is more "amateur", but it plays into the game's charmThe bad. Gosh, the over world puzzles lack creativity and are just not fun, and the combat just isn't right. I was annoyed with how much of this game is being thrown around from screen to screen, getting talked at, then sent to another screen. I just want wanted to explore! A lot of characters felt underutilized, the story is... frankly not assembled very well, and none of the characters have real depth. If you're coming in from the 2018 demo, then you will likely be disappointed because the actual mood of this game is not at all like what was set up there. Back to the combat, the microgames have intuitive-enough controls, but tend to be a bit slippery. In some cases, you'll be trying to dodge bullets with a body that is just too big and too slow. The RPG mechanics are scuffed, and honestly irrelevant. A couple spells are insanely strong, and most of them are so bad that they're a complete waste to use, even if you perfect the microgame.I think overall, this game is worth the $20 if you're into weirdo RPGs, but it pales in comparison to the games it is trying to emulate, and is overshadowed by the other indie RPG releases of the last five years. That being said, my hat is off to the developer - well done
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: I was really looking forward to this game for years, backed it on Kickstarter, etc. but my interest kind of faded over time and I was anxious to see if it would hold up to my past expectations. I was even holding out for the game to just be "okay," and I was honestly still crushed. On the quirky indie RPG spectrum, I'd probably place Knuckle Sandwich somewhere between YIIK and Ikenfell.Knuckle Sandwich really feels like someone's first RPG that they spent 7 years making. Not because it's that polished, but because the game was way too ambitious in scope, and none of that ambition pays off because the whole thing is mired by a bunch of really basic design issues. I liked the music, but... yeah.The tone is going for wacky and chaotic but everything feels lethargic and understated, random events happen but nothing matters, the pacing is awful, and the story is boring and keeps dropping plot beats on their head. All this time I've been wondering what the deal is with the bus driver, why he's so significant, etc. But it turns out he's just kind of... there. There was a dream sequence early on where he started unironically explaining midichlorians to me, and it was at this point that I realized the game had no idea what the ♥♥♥♥ it was going for.The gameplay has learned zero lessons from its predecessors. The combat suffers from the same problems as YIIK; there's so much emphasis on minigames and QTEs (and so much padding between them) that they end up making the battles more tedious instead of less. It makes the same mistake as Ikenfell where action commands matter by an order of magnitude, so everything hinges on unreasonable attack QTEs and feeling out poorly telegraphed enemy attacks. The game also falls into the typical RPG trap of giving you a myriad of granular stats, and some of them (e.g. damage and speed) don't even seem to do anything.The first boss I fought was just a huge damage sponge. I did more damage to him by winning against his minigame attacks than I did by hitting him, and his telegraphed attack has a sound cue that arbitrarily changes halfway through the battle. He also has zero plot significance and shows up out of nowhere. That's basically the whole game right there.The dungeons are just huge enemy mosh pits with "puzzles" interspersed between them. The puzzles themselves are tedious and obtuse; from what I've heard they only get worse, or devolve into pure backtracking.TLDR: Knuckle Sandwich, more like, Nothing Burger.
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: If you're here because you thought this game's story was influenced by "Fargo, The Big Sleep and American Psycho..." then I would recommend that you don't buy this game.In fact, I'm sorry to say that pretty much everything on the original Kickstarter is disregarded in the finished product. Every RPG trope the creator sites as aggravating, this game falls into--almost deliberately so. The game plays its darkest card almost immediately, and never returns to that point afterwards, seemingly taking every possible moment to undermine not only any plot points that could add additional grit or maturity to the story, but even anything that could allow a player to take this world seriously for more than fifteen seconds.Humor clearly was the forefront in this game's writing, but when those comedic aspects also fall short, it leaves the characters and world borderline hollow, tired "quirky RPG" caricatures, going from "wacky" location to the next without any sense of direction, until it all culminates in a finale that tries to replicate Earthbound/Mother 3, failing to replicate any of the heart, social commentary or emotional gravity.As someone who has been following this game since 2018, and eagerly anticipating its release as more and more excellent indie games are finally seeing the light of day, I am truly, sincerely sorry to say any of this. But everything this game takes inspiration from, I know firsthand that those sources already did them better. The best parts of this game are the soundtrack and the mini games, and even the latter becomes tiring after having to repeatedly input the same commands and watch the same animations over the runtime of a turn based RPG (even if it is a short one), topped off with seemingly inconsistent damage dealt for failure/success.In closing... I hold nothing against Andrew Brophy as a person, and I wish him and his team the best in their future endeavors. And I especially hope people will support and look into the music artists, their work for this project was incredible. But this game could have really been something special, and being released at the tail end of the era of "quirky Earthbound RPGs," I was hoping for more than just another name in the pile.
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: This is a true passion project.For SO many years Knuckle Sandwich has been in development, and that wait has truly paid off. I'm only 4 hours in and it's already shaping up to be one of my favorite RPGs ever. With the wackiness of the MOTHER/Earthbound series, Warioware like combat minigames (which are genuinely more unique and enjoyable than the combat of Undertale), several amazing artstyles, an AWESOME soundtrack, and so much heart put into it, Knuckle sandwich is 100% WORTH IT!Show Andy and all of the other people involved some love, because they've truly brought a gem to life.
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: I backed this game on Kickstarter when the campaign was running. The game looked promising and I was very interested in the "Knuckle Sandwich" angle for the story, the unique art, the groovy music, and the battle system for the game. The only thing that came through for this game was the art and the music. Everything else is either "lol xD random", not funny, or straight-up bad. This game abandons its namesake and instead opts for a nonsensical story that feels like it has no real purpose. The game is about 10 hours long, but the story is more around 2 hours long, maybe less. A lot of nothing happens in this game. Usually, the developers of great indie RPGs have something to say, but I genuinely do not think Andy Brophy had anything to say. The game is a mess. The story sucks. The battle system gets stale quick. The characters are weak and forgettable. The pacing is horrible. Yet, I think this game's biggest flaw is that its frustrating and it seems to have been designed that way on purpose. If this game was supposed to be a hit piece on how RPGs suck, it's not a good one.
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: Beware an over-promising demo and good art direction. The game's mini games quickly wear out their welcome, the story bogs down with half-baked absurd-ism, the thin RPG veneer falls off and you are left with an overly long series of corridors, seen-it-before puzzles and scripted boss fights. Before long you will have realized that special skills are useless, that Warioware was wise to keep its microgames short, that quirkiness without heart is tedious and inoffensive.Don't let the (great) music fool you. Knuckle Sandwich is all gloss and no taste- the marzipan of Earthbound-likes.
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: I'll hand it to Andy Brophy. The visuals, music, and overall vibe of this game are top notch. You can tell this was a passion project for him considering the time that went into it. While I enjoyed those aspects of the game, the story was a huge mess and super underwhelming, especially the last hour or so where all the big revelations come in to play. The gameplay starts to get monotonous over time as enemy encounters are way too frequent and last way too long. Even putting in only about 10 hours on the game, it felt like it dragged to get to the finish line. Can't recommend, but it was still worth supporting indie creators.
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to say it, but this game was disappointing. It has charm with lots of things from it's art style to it's gameplay to it's cast. Unfortunately, the story and gameplay mechanics flat pretty quickly. The story has little cohesion. The protagonist is boring and leaves a lot to be desired. The supporting cast, while cute, felt very two-dimensional and barely had any characterization.The mini-games of the battle system are a clever spin, but battles quickly become tedious. Limited capacity of items isn't so much of a challenge as it is a bother.What I think absolutely hold strong are the art and music. Incredible all-around from start to end.I genuinely wanted to love this game since I had backed it after having played the demo and being hooked by what I thought would be a colorful game with dark, gruesome elements, but the mediocre narrative and the mechanics really do it in for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: Knuckle Sandwich has a solid start; it's wacky and a mix of Undertale and WarioWare. My problem with it resides in that it overstays its welcome and it cannot hold its energy for as long as the game lasts. The last hour or two of my 5 hours with it ended up being a chore and I quit the game because I was tired of navigating the in-game menus and a boring level design. The minigames and the vibe of Knuckle Sandwich are fantastic but I think it should have been more streamlined for it flew too close to the sun in what it was trying to do. 3/5 - Ask yourself whether an average experience is worth 12 hours of your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: For the passive and uninitiated, Knuckle Sandwich offers a safe familiar taste of the subversive scene- though without any of the ingenuity or innovation of its predecessors and peers. The game places all its confidence into irony and inspiration rather than itself, leaving only the vacant frame of an RPG beneath.The plot meanders from one inconsequential event to another, attempting to subsist itself on flat characters lacking any chemistry with one another. The dated quirky tone is void of any real wit or clever writing, and now reads better as satire of the saturated scene of “subversive” indies rather than the receded genre it supposedly parodies. The only thing Knuckle Sandwich remains firm upon is the fact it has absolutely nothing to say, best exemplified by the game itself:“I have nothing to say about anything that is happening right at the moment”.Wacky chaotic combat is what remains of the game’s identity, deriving its formula of micro-games from the Warioware and Rhythm Heaven series. Yet despite an underwhelming ~12 hours of playtime the gameplay quickly grates on the player, as enemy variety is small and they often recycle their abstract micro-games between each other. Even boss fights begin to lack unique attacks as the final chapters approach, and those that are easily overstay their welcome. Nothing about combat is fast or dynamic, as despite claiming to “create an RPG that doesn’t feature the things I dislike the genre” it falls into the familiar time-wasting tedium with intrusive encounters and an obnoxiously small inventory system to manage.Knuckle Sandwich should’ve had its time spent back in the oven rather than under a rock as, despite the long six years of development, the game is immediately out-of-touch with the scene around it.TL;DR 5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: So much of the proceedings of this game feel like a cruel joke made at my expense.  I can take a good joke, but Knuckle Sandwich is the equivalent of getting the "made you look" treatment for 8 hours except it's "made you wait" and "made you backtrack" and "made you think your timed hits were going to make a difference in this boss fight but actually you just have to wait some specified number of turns before it's allowed to die."  A joke like that can be funny once, twice, maybe even thrice- maybe especially three times!  Knuckle Sandwich only has this one joke, embedded so deep in its DNA it infects the inventory system with "made you pick up a thing but your pockets are full."Nothing about this game respects my agency, my time, my intelligence, none of it.  It is a relentless barrage of cruel pranks, a real suckerpunch, a knuckle sandwich to my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ teeth.  Some basic stat manipulation via cheat engine revealed to me rather late in the game that most of the RPG mechanics are just for show.  You will be heavily sandbagged for most boss fights, and perhaps the only important stats are the ones that let you survive mistakes (HP and defense), while your attacks are only useful in standard enemy encounters.  I can't tell if it's intentional, but the speed stat appears to do nothing at the time of writing, so enemies will almost always act before you.  While this is inconvenient and annoying, fixing it wouldn't save Knuckle Sandwich for me.  I won't get too deep into the weeds about the specifics of the writing, I think it starts out strong and falls off very quickly.  A review that long would be above my pay grade (0 dollars) and I already had enough unpaid chores for one evening.Knuckle Sandwich is a cautionary tale in being too friendly with your playtesters.  Make some enemies and have them  judge the early builds of your next game, Mr. Brophy, I mean this sincerely.  Hop into someone's dms, call them a little ♥♥♥♥♥, then be like "hey I'm working on something you wanna give me some feedback, ♥♥♥♥♥?"  It'll change your life, I promise- and hey, I do hope there will be a next game, because there was a strong hook at the start that made me believe in the payoff that never came, so you've got half of a winning formula and good taste in music.Better luck next time.
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: Knuckle Sandwich is a good experience. Is it a good ? Not reeeally... I would give Knuckle Sandwich a big "Yes, BUT". To make a long story short, almost everything this game does it does with style and flourish and then fails to stick the landing. The style and flourish is really impressive! I finished the game in its entirety, and I'm always going to recommend a game that I actually decided to see through to the end. BUT. If the opening hour of the game fails to grab you, put it down. It will not get better.To make a long story long, the single largest caveat to enjoying this game is the combat. It's bad. There's not really any two ways about it. Microgame combat, as a concept, is an interesting idea. It feels nice when succeeding the microgame for an enemy attack not only prevents damage, but also hurts the opponent. In concept, it adds extra incentive to learn the microgames to give yourself an additional edge in combat and keep things moving.In practice, the amount of damage that is dealt is entirely trivial and almost never meaningfully shortens a fight. Microgames also vary wildly in difficulty, even for the more 'please grind me' overworld encounters. Some are entirely based on luck, some felt wildly impossible, and some had execution schemes that the game seemed to expect you to use a d-pad for but could be completely trivialized by using a stick.Enemy health pools is the second biggest problem. Enemies in this game have too much health, and I consistently felt like I did entirely too little damage. It felt like I was supposed to be doing the traditional RPG 'buff stats and deal status effects to manage the enemy' but I had no tools to afflict status effects or change my stats for half the game, and the incredibly restrictive inventory didn't allow for me to effectively use items in battle. Then Thea, one of the party members, learns Heat Wave and the entire game completely falls apart. When my standard attacks were doing somewhere between 30-70 damage (thanks wildly inconsistent microgame damage ranges!), a max damage heat wave (which targets all enemies on screen) would do . I was never able to tell what moves or attacks would do what kind of damage to what enemies in the game. There was some kind of elemental resistance / weakness system??? Some abilities did like, lightning, or ice, or fire damage, and it never made sense to me.Eventually, I turned on the option to enable a skip combat button in most fights, and I just did that instead of actually slogging through it. Unfortunately, enabling the accessibility helpers also disables achievements, so uh. Sure. (EDIT: maybe just a bug that cropped up at the same time? I've seen some other people mention it.)How about all the things that aren't the combat? Well, they're better on the whole but still a bit wonky. The music is unconditionally good. Bangers all around, for sure. But there's also no place to purchase the soundtrack in its entirety in a single spot...? Odd. The art is gorgeous and helped cement the world the game takes place in.The writing was... hit or miss. Mostly hits for sure, but I feel like it doesn't reach the highs of the opening couple hours and the ending was sort of a wet fart. It felt... like it just didn't come together. The people who eventually make up the 'hero's party' never felt very fleshed out, and while each party member got a 'focus' chapter, Dolus especially never felt like anything more than 'a party member', and I don't really know how to articulate that further.The darkly comedic tone of the opening is quickly replaced with a lighter tone of quirky absurdism that was funny but eventually wore thin. A few encounters in the game sort of happen, get brushed aside with a 'well  was weird', and then you move on. Who is supposed to be the actual antagonist of the game isn't really clear until the end of the game, and then you just sort of hit it with a rock and game over. There's an epilogue chapter, but it felt more like a 'I am out of time to make more game and must wrap up loose ends / cram in story ideas I had but couldn't execute fully'. Enjoyable, entertaining, but ultimately unpolished and incomplete.Final verdict- enjoyable but ROUGH. I recommend enabling combat skip from the start and simply ignoring all fights (still gives XP and rewards) that aren't clearly bosses. It'll save you some time, for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: A very charming game in the line up of wacky earthbound inspired RPGs even if I personally think that is a very loosely defined genre. I loved it, it's a pretty solid game with a really fun story. Artwork / Graphics are solid, especially as the style changes for certain segments. The music is fantastic as well!What I liked: The story is my favorite part, it is a very character driven silly adventure that isn't too complicated and is simply "fun". The ending bit was great and reminds me of something you'd see from Space Dandy. The variety in game play is a nice touch, I've seen comments saying that the mini games can get too stale after a while which I can understand, maybe if they weren't as frequent, but the combat is still far more entertaining than most back and forth RPGs. The setting is also really nice, and it's cool to see an Australian game where the local culture seeps into the characters.What I disliked: This is not really a criticism, because I don't personally see it as a bad thing, but the only thing I can say here is that this game feels like a first time project. That's super unfair though, because its clear a lot of work was put into it and for a first big game by a solo dev the amount of content here is crazy. But as nicely as I can put it, there are some spots that feel rough around the edges.I genuinely believe Andy has a ton of potential here, and that should he decide to continue game dev, he could seriously go on to do some really fun things. I implore anyone interested to give this game a try! <3
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: This review contains multiple spoilers throughout it. Please avoid reading if you want to avoid being spoiled!I'm not terribly great at writing down my thoughts, but I felt compelled enough here to try.This is incredibly heartbreaking for me to recommend against. I am an absolute sucker for "quirky more-than-meets-the-eye RPG" experiences and I'm a longtime WarioWare fan, so this game seemed like it would really appeal to me. Unfortunately, the game seems to have faceplanted the landing that it was anticipated to stick with ease.Starting with what I appreciated, I absolutely adore the game's visual presentation and soundtrack. Seriously, the game is an absolute treat to look at and listen to. The game's tracks are nothing but back-to-back hits, all whilst accompanying a comfy, contemporary aesthetic rooted simultaneously in the familiar and foreign. I think the game really shines in those aspects, which adds to the pain of my mixed feelings about it. This is just about where my praise for the game ends.The first major plot hook is pretty well done. By the time that the game namedrops itself, I found myself excited to see what the rest of the game had in store. However, it really feels like the game immediately forgot what it wanted to be and opted for an over-the-top "haha lol so random" and "you have no idea what's going on, huh?" approach to the rest of its story, cast, and locations. This isn't an inherently bad thing at all, but for multiple reasons it really detracts from the overall experience in this case. I can't overstate how much of a personal disappointment it was to be yanked away from the first couple of chapters' developments in favor of purely contrived meandering where the game is practically constantly jumping the shark in favor of another, funnier-looking shark soon after.There were multiple moments that had me legitimately laughing to myself in the absurdity of it all, or admiring genuinely clever bits of writing. However, more often than not, the gags and the "omg so silly right?" moments really overstayed their welcome. Abruptly meeting strange new characters and enduring their shenanigans is only amusing for a short while, but the majority of the story is littered with these moments. I found myself fatigued and not looking forward to progressing things because of it all.The moment-to-moment battles are close to being great, but they almost always feel tedious and obtuse. The enemies' attacks and minigames themselves are pretty fun despite a couple of stinkers. The actual gameplay problems arise with the RPG side of things. Your stats feel like they rarely have any meaning at all, despite being introduced early on and explained. I was constantly questioning if leveling up had any meaningful changes in combat outside of HP, EP, and the occasional new skill. I was constantly fearing that I was underleveled, so without any clear scale of power I would take on every fight I could find for XP. Basic attacks feel incredibly weak, usually hitting for 1-3 damage per instance. That's despite the addictive skill-based timings and theoretically-infinite scaling if you're good enough. Then, out of the blue, you'll land a skill that hits for hundreds if not thousands of damage for seemingly no reason at all. Assuming that the game encourages you to use skills, it's very easy to burn all of your EP. Defending restores 1 EP per turn, which is incredibly slow given the pace of each turn. Even if you're loaded up on EP and breezing through enemies, you still usually have to wait for their turn before you can attack, which brings me to the next portion of this criticism. Enemies tend to go first in combat no matter how high your speed is, resulting in almost every battle forcing you to endure 2 waves of attacks before getting to do anything. This would normally be fine if every encounter was limited to a single enemy, but in encounters with 2+ enemies, the pace is brought to a crawl. Next comes the common-as-of-now complaint of enemy density. Screens are frequently littered with enemies with no real rhyme or reason. I'm by no means a combat-skipper at all, but I couldn't help but feel like the game could do with a few less of them in each area to avoid getting stale. This is compounded by the fact that you never really get to the point where you go first in combat and are able to clean up encounters quickly after over-leveling a bit.Starting with the chapter taking place on a cruise, the boss fights or "significant enemy" encounters take a turn for the worse. Nearly every major fight clocked in at 10+ minutes for me. I don't know if I was doing something wrong, but I don't think I was underleveled since I took on every encounter I feasibly could. What's even worse, is that most of these fights are seemingly scripted to be as such. The initial fight with Brightside takes an extraordinary amount of time. The novelty of his character and the situation itself almost immediately grew old and annoying. Then came the fight against the purple-haired Brightfang (I forgot their name, sorry!). Their second phase took an enormous amount of turns to complete. Thirdly, the boxing-arena-match thing lasts for a minimum of 12 rounds of combat, which felt awful despite how much fun the gimmick initially was. The frequent dialogue from the reporters in that fight didn't help the pacing either.My last major area of critique comes from the game's item and inventory system. You're limited to a handful of inventory slots per character in your party. Usually, you have 2 characters to work with, but often times you're stuck with only the main character's slots. This wouldn't be much of an issue if it wasn't for the fact that equipped items still take up space in your inventory. With 2 slots for weapons, and 1 slot for an accessory, I found myself constantly hurting for space. The game is pretty generous with item capsules found around each map. They usually contain restoratives or debuff cleansers. This, however, further drags the issue into the spotlight since you'll be forced to juggle your existing items and the new one. What's even worse,is that the game treats certain key items the same as regular ones. Important key items will be vying for your inventory space all the same. This combination resulted in me feeling borderline-stressed out over what to keep, what to toss, and what to store in the PCs, assuming I would even remember they're there later on. New weapons found in the overworld give no indication as to whether or not they're worth keeping until you actually get them into your inventory. At that point, you've probably tossed something in favor of the new item, frequently resulting in bad trades or wasted items. This doesn't even begin to include the dozens of "flavor text items" that may or may not have any purpose later on. I eventually gave up and tossed anything that wasn't obviously useful to keep, but I kept wondering if I was going to regret doing so. It's a seemingly-easy place to tune the game up a bit, but I can't help but feel like this was strictly intentional somehow.I haven't played more since finishing the lost forest + cave area, as I've started to grow tired of the game's shortcomings and over-indulgence of nonsense. Again, to reiterate, I don't think 'nonsense' or non sequitur humor is inherently a bad thing, I just don't feel like it was executed very well here. I know that my review doesn't truly matter since I haven't completed the game, but frankly I don't think I can put up with the game enough anymore to do so. What could've potentially been a massive sleeper hit and unique diamond in the rough unfortunately suffers from a slightly-overly-ambitious scope and haphazard sense of direction. For a solo dev's efforts, I think respect and slack must be given. The game is by no means "bad" by any sense of the word, but I just can't bring myself to call it "good" either.

_childDocuments_.review: Knuckle Sandwich is made with heart, and I wish I could recommend it. But the game simply isn't fun to play. It's strategic elements are light to non-existent. It's real time tactical elements are enough of a mixed bag that they can't make up for it. The story, while not a mess, feels badly paced, and manages it's plot points badly. The music is fine, the art is well made, but those things don't make the rest of the game fun. There's too much to take apart here, so here's a short example of what I mean by badly designed for certain systems. Lets just look at items. Characters have 3 slots, a left hand, a right hand and an accessory. I only saw about 3 weapons total throughout the entire game. Two were knives and one was a pair of scissors. There were also several pairs of gloves that boosted defense, but since they took up both the left and right hand slot, didn't feel worth using. The strategic options are again, incredibly limited. More annoyingly, equipped items take up inventory slots. This would be tolerable except each character can only carry eight items. This means if a character has three items equipped, they can only carry five other items. This isn't helped by the fact that key items have to go into your inventory. So if you find a key needed to open a door, you either have to toss items out, or backtrack to an item storage PC. There are lots of things in games that subjective and up for debate. The item limit in Knuckle Sandwich is not one of them. It's a bad system. It punishes equipping items, it punishes exploring for extra items that the player can't carry, it punishes carrying quest or bonus items with the player in case they have a fun interaction or might be useful later. I hate it.On the flip side, at least Knuckle Sandwich was made by someone who cares. I don't know that I'd purchase another Andy Brophy game day one, but I'd at least look at it.

_childDocuments_.review: NOTE: Spoilers ahead!Knuckle Sandwich is... an okay game, thanks to a few post-launch updates. I was one of the people who followed this game long before the Kickstarter launched. Back then, the most we had to go off of were some carefully cherry-picked scenes from (now unlisted) trailers and a GameSpot playthrough of what would end up being more or less the demo we got to play.GAMEPLAYInitially, many of Knuckle Sandwich's overworld areas and puzzles were ridiculously annoying. Most were neutered in later patches, which I can somewhat appreciate.The battle system feels awesome at first, though some bosses either end up having way too much health or feel completely arbitrary and scripted. Many skills feel useless and you are doing single-digit damage for most turns during the entire game.The inventory system was very unpleasant to use when the game launched but was improved upon a lot with the introduction of the 8 additional "pocket" slots, more item storage locations, and increased item storage capacity.STORYThe story from the Prologue to the end of Chapter 1 is great, and that's more or less only what was shown to people for years leading up to the game's release. Most of the game's dialogue is very funny and smartly written.Very quickly after the end of Chapter 1, the game devolves into complete nonsense that has very little to do with the diner or the titular "Knuckle Sandwich". What seemed like a simple start to a story that could go anywhere became muddied by many forgettable plot points and parties that appear and disappear at random. I can appreciate games being nonsensical within reason, but it definitely felt like some parts took it a bit too far.The diner comes back at the end and the twist revelation is interesting, but feels like a complete cop-out, with the Boss not appearing for 90% of the game. You don't really find out who the actual "enemy" of the game is until the very end, and it feels completely random and unearned. The final boss feels unfitting and anticlimactic, and the story gets tied up in a confusing and vague way.OTHER NOTESThe game launched in a state I was pretty unhappy with. There were lots of bugs and crashes, annoying gameplay elements, missing Kickstarter backer credits, and a whole lot more. After taking several years and funding from 3 (three!) different sources, I was really hoping the game would have released in a much more polished state. Thanks to Andy's vigilance, nearly all of these issues have since been fixed. That's something I can respect a whole lot.Something that struck me as really weird and uncomfortable were a handful of self-inserts. The cruise ship, originally named the S.S. Darby, was renamed the S.S. Andy at some point during development. In the second half of the game, you also fight two of Andy's self-inserts. Their introduction has some of the most blindsidingly post-ironic dialogue in the game and it uses the popular "Vine boom" sound, which makes that part of the game feel instantly dated. Overall, the self-inserts feel narcissistic and rub me the wrong way.After being shown the same cherry-picked parts of the game for 6+ years, it was really disorienting to see what the bulk of the game ended up being. I didn't feel 'betrayed' or like I didn't get my money's worth or anything, but it was a hard feeling to let go of with how much prominence the demo content had in what was shown leading up to the game's release. The game felt less like "Knuckle Sandwich" and more like "Andy Brophy's Goblin Minigame RPG". That's totally cool, but I really wish there was a little more transparency there.FINAL THOUGHTSDespite all of the problems I personally had with the game, I enjoyed many parts of what I played, and I see where a lot of the love went into it over the years. I'm sure many people will enjoy the game and like it for what it is. As for me, I can't help but lament the missed potential.

_childDocuments_.review: I backed this game back in the summer of 2018 on Kickstarter. I was very involved with the community ARG in getting the demo released. I'm a little disappointed that it took three different types of funding and five years to get this game out (Film Victoria Australia, Kickstarter, and SuperHot Games all contributed money to this game; Brophy told Kickstarter he could complete the game within a year), but that's beside the point.. Its presentation, with its art style and music, is still one of the best, but the game itself falls short when compared to others of this type.The combat, in particular, is what really bogs this game down. I remember not finding it difficult or time-consuming during the demo (probably because there were only a couple of fights), but by the time you reach the second chapter early in the game, it becomes apparent just how long every single battle is. Microgames are meant to be quick, but Knuckle Sandwich manages to make them last far too long for each move. This makes the majority of battles drawn out, tedious, and, most importantly, not fun. It's probably the reason why the game offers ways to make the combat easier or even remove it altogether from the game. But even outside of combat, the dungeons are filled with some of the genre's worst elements. I can't understand how anyone thought having the final dungeon be a series of guesswork puzzles would be enjoyable, or how teleporter mazes and sliding ice puzzles are fun. And don't even get me started on the horrendous inventory space. I'm sure you'll see that mentioned a lot in other reviews.The game emphasized accessibility for players regarding combat and making it easier. While this was a welcome addition to avoid repetitive fights, the game still lacks some fundamental features. For example, there's no way to quickly save and quit outside of designated save points, and accessing the accessibility settings requires you to return to the title screen. At launch, the game also failed to include options for colorblind players. It's puzzling how much attention was given to accessibility during development yet basic necessities like these were overlooked, all while the game remained buggy.Finally, the biggest disappointment for me was the plot. What was promised in the demo to be a funny but dark game became one that feels unfocused and inattentive to what made it special. You could cut out about 7-10 hours' worth of content, and nothing of value would be lost. Even the characters cannot salvage what remains, as they do not experience any kind of growth or resolution; they remain one-dimensional and only serve to act as random nobodies. Finally, the ending was so out-of-touch and had so little relevance to the scenario presented at the start that I was anxious just to get to the credits so I could see if there was some punchline and it would go back to being good again, but that moment never came.This hideous amalgamation of traits is why I've backpedaled on recommending it.

_childDocuments_.review: knuckle sandwich is a very good game. It's got tons of soul and a slappity soundtrack, and is clearly built with love and passion.however!!If you've only played the demo, you might be expecting a somewhat different kind of experience.so let's be clear about this!knuckle sandwich is not really a game about working at a cannibal food joint. what it really is, is a tribute to the older, classic rpgs, where things often happen for seemingly no good reason, and the overall plot is mostly there to keep you scratching your head, while you bounce between set pieces. it reminds me of how it felt to play videogames when I was a child, and not really understanding what was going on, but being into it for the cool battles, music, and everything else.there's only a sparse few fights in the demo, but the classic rpg inspiration really becomes obvious with the amount of fighting you'll be doing in the full game itself. expect a lot of combat encounters, and expect it to often take a while. sometimes you'll spend a minute bashing one enemy in, only for the next to ambush you before you really have any time to think. whether you'll really have a good time with this, comes down to your enjoyment of the combat minigames themselves, but for the record, the game comes with a ton of customization options in the settings, and some of the minigames can be disabled altogether, if they're not really your kind of thing.also following the classic rpg inspiration, expect there to be a lot of pretty basic, but sometimes time confusing puzzles. flipping switches, sliding across ice, conveyor belts, that sort of thing. it might be a little jarring after being lured in by the otherwise modern humor and presentation, and you might think to yourself the puzzle design is a little outdated and not very exciting, but it does make sense when you look at the game as a love letter to the rpg genre as a whole. it's worth pointing out, that a lot of the puzzles people initially took issue with, have been smoothed out with patches after release.all in all, I have to give this game a lot of credit. it does a lot of things right, and you really get the sense that andy brophy made exactly the game he wanted to make, with little compromise. it's humorous, it's intriguing, and your party members and friends are shockingly relatable. the personalities of your party members aren't deliberately stereotypical or overblown, and it really helps to create a sense that you're just ordinary everyday guys who unwittingly ended up in the middle of something incomprehensible. there's secrets, and hidden depth in places you might not otherwise expect.tl;dr the amount of knuckle sandwiches you actually end up serving is a lot lower than you might expect, but it's still a great game, and a worthwhile thing to experience. it's truly the world's most authentic knuckle sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: This game is straight up bad in so many ways, but I think it's because it bit way more off than it could chew. Looking at the other comments it seems it's one of the many Kickstarter games that maaaybe didn't have the understanding on what it would take to get their product to completion. I mean, they only missed the release date by 4.5 years, c'mon guys. The story, characters, level design, economy, move sets, and inventory are all completely nonsensical. Strong "did it for the lulz" energy. The first hour of the game or so is actually very promising, but then there is a steep fall off and never recovers. HOWEVER, easily the best part of the game is the minigames that happen during each battle. I love WarioWare and implementing that play style into an RPG like this is so fun and keeps things so fresh. Even just regular attacks having a lite minigame to keep you engaged - it really feels like the next evolution of the timed button presses you see in many other RPGs. Overall, though I didn't like this game, I would like to see the devs take this idea and give it another shot. Make it more stable and slightly more traditional. The in-battle minigame idea is just too good to abandon.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been trying to figure out what to say here because most positive and negative reviews alike are from passionate fans who do have valid criticism and positive qualities to share.  I would like to initially say that I loved this game and it lives up to many of my expectations I had back when I started waiting in 2018, subsequently playing a half-hour of chapter 3 at the DreamHack convention in 2020, and then playing the new demo in 2022.I think what most people are saying here is right, yes the demo promises a very different game on a narrative and emotional level, you could argue the story is a little all over the place.  I think for me the moment they (ch2 spoiler) , I was keenly aware that the story was going to move in a more of a goofy disjointed fantasy direction and readjusted my narrative expectations a little.  Nonetheless, I still think I was subconsciously waiting for a moment or a big twist that gave sense to all the wackiness that never came, so do with that info as you will.More importantly, I think we should talk about the game that's actually there rather than what it's not, so let me begin by jumping right back into story and saying- the story is pretty dang fun! Everything I said in the previous paragraph is true but also I feel bad for anyone who can't let themselves have fun without seamless cohesion.  There's so many fun ideas and I felt consistently entertained throughout the whole game whether it was the impressive visuals or the funny gags or the charming cast of characters.  The weirdness of this game is so in your face, there's never a slow moment.The combat system is just awesome! I don't think there was a single mechanic when fighting that I felt went underutilized, in fact I went out of my way to fight every single enemy I could find in the game just cause I loved the gameplay loop so much, it never once felt like a grind.  Despite that fact, my main issues for combat are less about the exciting and fun mechanics of it, and more about the damage output.  It was very frustrating that the three different basic attack mechanics have extremely unequal damage output.  The first one you use is by far my favorite and also feels like the hardest to pull off critical damage, but ironically you get rewarded the least for that despite it having the smaller window for "big damage" and the most variation between attacks with the bomb placement and attack window starting positions.  The circle attack despite being fun is the same every time and by the end of the game just feels like the worse version of the bar that slides up and down because i consistently only get half as much damage out of it.  But I think the worst offender here the Protagonists "Beat Down" move.  Towards the later half of the game, the move became objectively the best and easiest way to end any encounter in one move no matter how many enemies.  Now I'm very happy that in the accessibility options you can choose to instantly win any fight, I'm sure that appeals to a lot of people and I'm glad they had that option, but as someone who was excited for fun turn based combat, I certainly did not expect mashing the arrow-keys be a "win battle" move, and I didn't enjoy that fact.  I think this move would be more interesting if there was a trade off, as in you choose to attack all enemies in the match with the understanding that you will do less damage then a regular attack.  I'm not thinking critically about my next move when the best attack available also damages everything on screen.tldr: lame-playing becomes the optimal way of ending any fightOk there's no getting around this one, the inventory management is really bad.  Funnily enough this doesn't actually affect the experience that much because I rarely (almost never actually?) had to use healing or energy items.  This isn't a brag, there was almost always a vending machine right next to you so there was no reason to expend a limited resource when infinite healing and energy restoration was at your disposal.  I think five very easily adjustable things would pretty much instantly fix every issue I had here:- way less vending machines (health and energy res)- more washing machines (saving)- way more computers (item storage)- weapons and accessories (equippables) don't take up and inventory slot only after they're held- inventory slots increases from 8 to 12This may sound like it makes management easier... and you'd be right.  I don't want difficulty deciding what to keep or get rid of when this dilemma doesn't actually serve any purpose towards the other facets of the gameplay.99% of the mini-games for defending are fun, probably my favorite aspect of fighting right alongside timing your basic attacks.  Throughout the whole game you can almost always be sure that your going to play some new mini-games that you've never seen before when you encounter a new enemy, which makes it really fun to actually seek out new enemies.  I don't think there's a single enemy attack in the game that isn't interesting to defend against, even the basic timed defense has so much variation in how the enemies attack you that it feels different every time. Also it is imperative that you know how good this game looks, Knuckle Sandwich has this amazing way of animating everything so that it looks so alive and present.  A lot of the game seems to be using subpixel animation, squashing and stretching in order to convey both subtle movements like bouncing and head bobs right alongside super exaggerated poses and jumps.  I recently read a joke Andrew made about going through so much effort to avoid animating walk cycles for most characters, and the way they accomplish this is hilarious and is something that needs to be seen for yourself.I'd also like to say that Andrew has been releasing patches this game from from day 1 of release so I don't know how much will be fixed or changed but this is based on the playthrough of the game I already had.  I am excited for the future where much of what I'm saying here is outdated because of how on top of everything this developer has been with giving you the best experience of this game.  This is a very special game that had so much heart and soul put into it and should be experienced for that alone.Anyways point being I loved it!

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game; I've been super excited for it since the original trailer and demo years ago to the point where it's consistently been in my top 3 most anticipated indie titles period.Upon playing it, it's both exhausting and lackluster.I'll start with the pros: it's very clearly taking inspiration from GBA titles like Mario & Luigi and Mother 3, and I really appreciate it's wacky, surreal nature. The art is fantastic, the writing and humor is pretty funny, and overall it's quite appealing to look at.The story is unfocused and uninteresting beyond the first couple of chapters, and it was hard to stay interested when it seems to forget it's primary plot point. It tends to jump all over the place, but in a particularly uninteresting manner.The combat is fun and interesting at first, but it feels extremely unbalanced and inconsistent. Your primary method of attacking changes randomly without reason, and the minigames get samey and repetitive. What's worse is that, no matter how well I did with certain special attacks, they seem to barely do any damage, which led me to just using the normal attack 90% of the time while fighting (which is a huge bummer, because it feels like I'm being punished for wanting to try out the special attack minigames). What also gets exhausting is the sheer amount of enemies you'll encounter in any given area; for instance, in the cold dungeon, it feels like there are literal swarms of enemies in every room that you can't avoid. Fighting begins to feel like a chore and resource drain, and it never feels like you get substantially more powerful. It's one thing to have like, 4 enemies in a room, but I was frequently running into 8 or so anytime I left and came back into an area. The biggest issue, however, and the main reason I won't be playing it again unless it gets updated, is the inventory system. A character can only hold 8 items each, total, including equippables and consumables. 8. Inventory management is absolutely miserable in this game. Unless you're able to run constantly back and forth to a PC to dump your items, you're going to have to drop or use things randomly to make room for whatever you find, or just give up completely on picking up new items. I couldn't even be excited to pick up simple key items because I knew I'd have to get rid of something to make space for it, which is not fun. I understand that it's taking inspiration from Earthbound's horrible inventory system (I love the Mother series btw), but somehow this feels like a satire of it that only exists to stress the player out. My breaking point was when I found a keycard to a gym or something on the floor, but once again, I didn't have space to hold it.One minor grip but, with the game's artstyle and gameplay, it BEGS to have controller support of some kind. It's been a long time since I've had to play a game with the arrow keys, which is fine, but this is definitely a d-pad/buttons kind of game at heart.I wanna like this game. I waited five years for it. But it needs some serious overhauls before I'll play it again, namely the inventory system and enemy balancing.
