_childDocuments_.review: I've waited 5 years for this, and I absolutely love it. The gameplay, story, characters, etc. are fantastic. Absolutely amazing.Unfortunately, the game has an undying love for bad puzzles. Seemingly every 5 minutes there's a boring, trial-and-error filler puzzle. They are never engaging and always the most tedious tasks conceivable. During the final area, the game throws multiple of them back to back. And if you make an error (on any of the TRIAL AND ERROR PUZZLES) you have to restart the entire sequence. Every single puzzle in this game is complete and utter dog and brings the game down considerably from its potential. I love this game so much but the puzzles are so bad and obnoxious I just had to stop.There are two puzzles in particular this game loves:1. Colored button puzzles. The game will present you with a very large room, with colored walls and buttons placed around. Pressing a button toggles the walls of its color. You must navigate and find the correct sequence of buttons to reach the end. They're tedious, but for the most part fine early game - but the game uses these SO MANY TIMES it gets incredibly exhausting.2. Ice sliding puzzles. The kind of puzzle with a large section of ice and safe areas, where you must find the correct path to reach the end. I used to think I liked these puzzles, but whew boy. The ice puzzles are much larger than the screen, requiring you to make mistakes to see certain safe areas. The safe area is smaller than it looks, resulting in many accidental slides. When failed, they bring you down to a lower area where you must walk all the way back to the puzzle. Later puzzles require you to re-do other puzzles to get back. Fun!This game would easily be a 10/10 without the terrible puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s almost the end of the year and, well, I have to get in another RPG game in. Especially when it’s a game that I played the demo for, twice, and liked it both times. It’s finally time to dive into Knuckle Sandwich’s weird world.In Knuckle Sandwich, you play as a down-on-his-luck guy who is moving to Bright City. A lot happens, but to make a long story short after failing to get a job from the Job Center (due to be unfairly fired from most), you end up working at a burger place called Gorilla Burger. Except the boss is terrible and he turns to the cannibal burger business after trying human meat burgers made from a gangster that tried to kill you. Business boomed after that, which gets him to hire new employees (and your future teammates) Thea, Echo, and Dolus. However, the boss disappears afterwards and you four try to find out where he went and what he was up to after finding out a dark secret. Though, you guys get a bit sidetracked after running into the Brightfangs being suspicious with a suspicious weapon and suspiciously going after the mayor. Suspicious…too suspicious to not investigate.There’s also a B plot alongside this where you and Busdriver (who *gasp* isn’t a bus driver but a goblin that tracks anomalies) team up. While Busdriver can’t be in the human world for long, you act as his proxy to find out where the huge spike in Spirit Cells are so it can be taken care of before something weird happens. Luckily, this ends up coinciding with the A plot, so our deadpan guy can just go with the waves.While the story is a bit hard to really grasp at first, I enjoyed it. It’s a crazy ride for sure and I’m sure the intention was for you to get sidetracked alongside the characters, which worked for me. I also really enjoyed the writing for the whole game. The characters are written well, the meta/fourth wall breaks were sparse and used for quick jokes, and I guess I had the perfect sense of humor for this game as the jokes did land for me. There were also a couple last minute plot twists to tie up the loose ends and while one or two had foreshadowing, I don’t know how to feel about it. Though, it didn’t really bother me much which I feel is due to the random, wacky nature of the game helping me to just roll with it (since you do that for the whole game anyway). I also did like the characters, all the other team members were nice to hang around with and I did like how you did a dungeon with each of them alone before you all travel together. Also, my favorite character was definitely Dolus. Dolus is the best and never failed to make me laugh with his silly pose.I’m still a bit sad that the opening of the game, where your boss cooks up the guy you killed and loves the taste, was just a way to get you there and get that knuckle sandwich line in for the title card rather than it being a big part of the plot like it seemed.Well, let’s get into the gameplay. You’ll be traveling in the overworld a lot and Knuckle Sandwich does exploration really well. Aside from wishing you can change default movement to run, I liked how all the different areas looked and that it does give you a reason to explore with all the hidden items you can find or do. The dungeons (well they’re not dungeons in the traditional sense) were also unique from one another with unique enemies and puzzles (which some are annoying, but the ones in Chapter 7 have been patched to be easier).Though, there is an annoyance with the inventory. Your inventory is limited by eight slots, but your equipped items and key items will take up spots. Which is annoying as you can be out three slots always. I do understand the reasoning, but I do wish either equipped items or key items didn’t count. It does get better late game, when you’re traveling with everyone, but still it’s going to be a problem for most of the game.It’s only a matter of time before you run into an enemy and get pulled into combat. Combat here is the expected turn-based combat, but there is a twist. It employs minigames for your attacks and dodges. A simple one for regular attacks and dodges, and Warioware-esque minigames for skills that you do and dodge. Your regular attacks have a few variations, with half being a one hit with a critical hard-to-hit spot and half being one you can build up a combo with as you can do it until you mess up. Dodging regular attacks will just have you learn an enemy’s tell and pressing dodge right before it attacks. There was only one enemy early on where the tell was seemingly nonexistent, with all the others being obvious. For skills, you’ll need to do a Warioware-esque minigame. There are a lot of these and they’re specific to the enemies and characters. For you, it’ll affect how effective your attack will be. Early on, it does seem the skills are useless, but they do get more powerful the more you level up. When it’s the enemy doing a skill, you’ll need to perfectly do the minigame to not only dodge it, but also send the damage back to them. These even get harder the more successful dodges you do. There will obviously be a few duds, but a lot of them are good. You can also summon your baby goblin(s) which deal major damage once you charge up the summon bar. You can even find more baby goblins which seems to make this move more powerful. The best aspect of this is that your character does a little pose with the goblin.The only attacks you can’t dodge are the special attacks, which are the ones that can put status effects on your parties. Your luck stat determines the chance of your characters dodging this, but I only saw it happen once early on. Granted though, the status effects can be tolerated. There are two that affect your regular attack minigames, but you can get used to it enough where you can raise the combo a bit.I do want to mention the boss battles. I don’t want to spoil all of them, but the game does a great job with the boss battles. All of them manages to be unique, even if it starts out like a regular boss fight. The art style can change, how you win can change, and the genre can just change. It was fun, including the difficulty spike in Chapter 5, and you never know what a boss battle will hold. Not to mention that the way Knuckle Sandwich handles the boss battles make them feel different from regular encounters.There were some instances where I felt the battles did go for a bit too long, whether it was intentional or not. Though, I never did end up changing any of my settings.I feel your enjoyment with Knuckle Sandwich will depend on how much you can tolerate. If you can tolerate randomness where the connecting lines aren’t obvious until later and like playing minigames in combat for your attacks and dodges, you very well may enjoy this game. It also helps that it looks like the demo is here to stay, which is a decent indicator of what you should expect from the rest of the game. Personally, I ended up enjoying the game more than I thought. There are a few annoying aspects, like the inventory, some battles did feel too long, and some plot points being dropped until the end, but the game is honestly really charming, the music is great, the combat was fun, boss battles were all unique, and I loved the colorful art style and how it changed sometimes. It may take a couple hours, but Knuckle Sandwich really comes into its own once the real plot comes in full force. If this game interests you, and even better you liked the demo, I do recommend picking it up.

_childDocuments_.review: I think I can solidly say that the game's plot was all over the place and even by the end it didn't feel like quite a built-up conclusion. It felt like such a long way from what was, kind of the game's original premise.The combat's balance is kind of all over the place, it feels like doing the mini-game specific moves sometimes is always the right or wrong choice, stats are kind of inconsistent and it really feels like stats don't matter in the end.That being said, music is pretty fantastic and a lot of work went into making everything super reactionary to what you do in battle such as the background wobbling with how powerful of a hit you do, to characters reacting to getting hit, enemies reacting, tons of unique sprite work.Honestly if there would be a sequel to this, somehow, I'd honestly still check it out. This game doesn't quite live up to the Warioware RPG premise, but I honestly think there's still potential to really ring out a few more fortune rocks from this thing. This is unrefined gold, I just know it.Edit: I've changed my review from Negative to Positive after mulling over my own thoughts on this game for a bit. A lot of my opinion remains the same, but the one thing that keeps me coming back is the sound design and the combat. The combat being heavily mini-game based can make some encounters absolute slogs but I really did like the idea. Some mini games are absolutely perfectly paced where as others take way too long.UNREFINED GOLD, AAAAAAAHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH

_childDocuments_.review: I beat the game last night, I was hyped about this game since it was on kickstarter so many years back. Before I begin to describe my thoughts, let me give an overall rating.Story: 3/10Gameplay: 3/10Battles: 9/10Overall I give this game a 3 star rating.The boss battles are phenomenal, they are so fun and I never once was bored while playing one, but the game play was extraordinary repetitive, after the ghost fight in the cooler room, say hello to "Puzzle Sandwich" because the rest of the game is just puzzles. Towards the end of the game, it's no longer even puzzles, but genuine IQ tests lol. There's a lot of moments in the game where it gives you the illusion of choice as well. Where you think you can make different decisions than the intended story, but nope, it'll eventually just force you to do the choice it wants you to. Now for my biggest gripe and why Knuckle Sandwich disappointed me the most... the story. The game forgot what it wanted to be. The name "Knuckle Sandwich" has no meaning in this game. The first 20% of the game is 9/10 in all 3 of my categories, this is where the plot is that your looking for a job, accidentally commit a murder, and your boss gets a taste of human meat and wants to serve it. I thought that the plot would be what happens and you stay working for him trying to prevent the cops + public from finding out your feeding human meat. But after the cooler mission, the game forgets about gorilla burger completely until the end where he turns into a fricken dragon. The story goes in like 6 different directions and the whole game feels like, "then this happens, then this happens, and then this happens..." it doesn't have a coherent connection. I loved the music and the vibe, but it became so random. I apologize Mr. Brophy, but I wanted the game that the kickstarter advertised to me, the demo is genuinely perfect I wished it continued the route it was going. Mr. Brophy, if someone asked you, "why is this game called Knuckle Sandwich?" How would you even respond, because only the first 20% is actually "Knuckle Sandwich" the other 80% is "Goblin Puzzle Adventure!" I apologize to leave a bad review on such a young game, but that's the point of criticism, is to improve it.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really looking forward to this game given its promising initial display and flair it had. The first chapter was clearly the main highlight of the game aswell as the ost (Shoutout to Lizzy and Nelward contributing to it). But after that it was just a whole lotta nothing burger and it soured my opinion to this game. Most of the fun kinda got sucked out and thrown out the window immediately after the chapter 1 conclusion and maybe a bit of the 2nd chapter. If they stuck around with the initial plot that was shown off in the demo and such, I would have enjoyed this a lot more. Didn't expect to buy a very hollow and boring rpg and felt like a rushed clunky mess of a game.After the first chapter hook to reel you into the story and see what it will unveil, it really doesn't do that until they cram it to the end of the game. Even then the ending felt extremely rushed and just dissatisfying just like the rest of the story. It suffers a lot of pacing issues and going back and forth for pointless and one-off encounters that don't matter. Your party members don't really get any character development growth or feel natural to the group, they are just there to exist for gameplay purposes in terms of having a party system. From going to an interesting greasy shady burger diner, we go off to a resort and a cruise ship that drags on that it ends up being filler. They had a deltarune lancer like character except this one was extremely insufferable and not funny at all, while there was a few chuckles upon its first encounter with them, they continued to throw him back into the games several chapters just to extend the non existent story. We go through these so called "reoccuring villains" that are extremely bland and not really memorable given their short time they are displayed. Sure we get some flashbacks but even then they barely do anything with it afterwards. The twists are really obvious and not really well written. It felt like we were constantly jumping all over the place and not focusing on the main plot point at all. Going from having a great session at the start to wanting to get this slog over with in the end. Even the ending to the game was a spit to the face with it's "It's over guys! back to the title screen now" fakeout and the epilogue felt like nothing but a gut punch to the people who bought and/or kickstarted this mess of a game.Another major selling point of this game was its usage of WarioWares Microgames into combat. Whether you are using skills or the enemies do their special attack. You will be doing a variety of interesting but simple microgames. Some of them are really fun but others are just not fun at all especially the Car dodging the incoming UFOs one. While other ones are fun for the first time, a lot of them are just cookie cutter "Shoot em up!" microgames that drag on the combat a lot. Speaking of combat, it seems like its very random in terms of your initial attack, sometimes you get the two bar attack which is a one time hit and very useless, to getting the gamebreaking circle timing window one if you're really good at it you can clear enemies in no time which can be rewarding but the battles get repetitive and lose its charm really fast. Bosses are a really big slog slowly wittling its hp down or having to watch it do its same gimmick 5 turns in a row just to keep the fight going on for another 10 minutes, and I myself go through every enemy encounter I see just incase I'm not underleveled and get stomped. The only rare difficulty spike was the cruise ship boss which I only game over'd once which was weird when I was clearing everything beforehand and after that boss like it was nothing. The inventory is another can of worms where key items aren't held within its own section or a void inventory but are managed in your actual inventory which means you have to leave up a slot for a key items sometimes if you are holding a bunch of healing/Energy consumables, this isn't a survival game, just give us a stackable inventory system instead of this clunky one where you're deciding what to deposit/withdraw often and what your dull party members should carry. You are also given a select choices of skills via leveling up or having these ROMS when most of the time you can just spam "beat down" and mash your keyboard to win almost all encounters and bosses, all the other skills are extremely useless and deal little to no damage even if you perfect them. Pretty sure the speed stat doesn't work as how almost every enemy will always attack first no matter what. It's so inconsistent and unbalanced where half the time I just run away from fights near the end of the game just to get it over with.This RPG's point of interest and areas you explore are just plastered with pointless npcs and the places you do run around and see are just small and empty. Most of the shops don't matter knowing how unbalanced the stats are to combat and the most items you can sell or buy don't really matter in the end unless you're really struggling with microgames and dodging obvious enemy cues. Speaking of level designs, most of them are riddled with annoying mazes or unneccessary backtracking for zero plot purposes and on top of that, we heard you like ice sliding puzzles and warp pads traversing. You will spend a solid 15+ minutes dealing with its horrible padding of a map just so they have the game be seen as a longer rpg. They often reuse some of the puzzles later on just to further more halt the player from continuing just to do another obstacle later on.  but no if we took all of that out, my hours on the game would have been halved. I would have still had the same opinion on this game whether it was short or not. In the end I can commend the developer who tried their hardest to deliver this game to the kickstarters and new people who stumbled across this game via from demos or just similar rpg interests. I can tell they put some effort, but It should have been in the oven for a lot longer to fix up a lot of its issues including the story itself. $20 for this is a skip for most people when there are other rpgs/games you can get for cheaper and have a better enjoyment outta of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Can't say I'd recommend this game to anyone who's played the demo, It builds expectations and instantly fails to meet them. For a long time the demo was the only thing people had of this game, with an intriguing hook and a fun intro you can't NOT know what happens next. Without spoiling, the plot of the demo is immediately dropped after CHAPTER 1 for some Pokemon evil team plot! Honestly, I felt tricked, but I wouldn't say I was scammed.The game has its charm, the art, character, and scenes especially. Although I wish the characters were expanded on more, I'd argue that they're the best part of the game. The WarioWare-esc battle style is a very fun concept, although they re-use a good chunk very often and it gets dull after a while. Personally I ended up skipping battles after I've fought the enemies once and rushed straight to the next boss. Which by the way, shines in this style of battle mechanic! Final boss was pretty disappointing, lots of build up just for a very repetitive fight with a VERY dull design.The music though? There's a few bops but its mostly just the battle themes for me. Most of it was made by hyperpop artists, who are very talented musicians. That's it.TLDR; This game leaves a lot to be desired, especially after such a good intro! I can't recommend it in good conscious though. 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: The video essay you'll find one day will be called: "Style without Substance: A Lesson in Tedium"The developers have created an RPG that is absolutely upsetting to play for no good reason.It has all the things that RPG players hate! Backtracking... Horrible inventory management... Poorly organized maps that implore you to explore and reward with you with nothing!I love the combat minigames! Even speeding them up with the combat speed settings make every battle an absolute slog. So much so, that there's a convenient "skip" button for those who are impatient! However, you won't get comfortable with that because after every combat is an unskippable 15 seconds of watching your money winnings physically roll across the floor. For completionists who grind out all the limited enemies, it's a major waste of time. Backtracking is a waste as you will find nothing returning to previous zones, such as disappearing merchant NPCs by the Job center or the fishing man once you find some got dang BAIT for the minigame!!!My lowest point was several hours in when a fishing minigame was introduced. I got the tutorial and was told to find bait and return. I get bait 20 minutes later, and walk all the way back to do some fishing... but the NPC is GONE! I was devastated yet again.

_childDocuments_.review: My feelings on this game are complicated. I really like a lot of what is here, and ultimately came away with a positive impression. I do have some issues though.The game really slogs midway with some of the combat minigames. When the minigames are short they are really fun, but when they get longer and with more enemies it feels like a drag.The story starts really interesting, but then decides it wants to be something else partway through. Admittedly it actually turns out to be pretty interesting, but I long for what was promised.I feel like your party didn't really get as fleshed out as they could have been. They kind of just show up out of nowhere and the interactions you have with them are pretty basic. Inventory management is really rough, and not in a particularly fun way. It feels like something from a game 20 years ago. All that said, this game still does pretty some great things. The soundtrack is dope, the minigames are mostly fun and silly, and it has genuine moments that had my jaw on the floor from the absurdity.I will continue to champion quirky RPGs like this because I love them and their weird ideas. Hell, this game has you playing Beyblade as an attack at some point, and it gave me the widest smile. I just wish I liked this game a bit more than I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Knuckle Sandwich is a game worth playing to see it's interesting (at first) battle mechanics, and amazing art style. The game switches to a 3D polygonal style for some cutscenes and has well crafted pixel art for gameplay. The game was always was very engaging visually. As for battle mechanics, each enemy has usually one or two unique attacks that makes battles interesting and varied, as well as your own attacks having 3 different varieties of basic attack, and each party member has their individual unique special skills.Knuckle Sandwich's weak point is hands down the storytelling. It is inconsistent, especially at the beginning, and will often have the player experience a TON of story in about 15 minutes, but the story vanishes for the rest of the dungeon/area aside from small flavor text which more often is a quip or gag about the current situation or surrounding area. The game often chooses these small jokes over any world building or character development, and the characters suffer as a result. Characters can be extremely one note, almost the entire game, with the standout exception being one wannabe thief character who has self doubt issues. Goals often are reduced to "We want to save the city!" which is an angle completely out of left field when compared to how the game starts, and the goal itself doesn't have much meat to back it up.While combat is extremely diverse, with each enemy having at least one unique attack, this diversity is squashed by having each attack in the game do very minimal damage, both when it comes to dealing and receiving damage. Even with an attack buff accessory and one of the strongest weapons in the game (Big Scrib), I was often doing 1 damage increments for the majority of basic attack patterns until successfully hitting the time command 5-8 times, where it would begin to do 2 or 3 damage each further successful hit. This is damning because:1. You have to land a lot of attacks! Even my special moves would only do slightly more damage than a good 8+ combo basic attack. If I messed up an action input early on in the attack, I would do 1 or 2 damage only. 2.  The enemy attacks A LOT. Even with each unique enemy attack, and the 3 levels of difficulty their attacks have, it is not enough to offset the amount of times you see each attack. Enemies often attack 2-3 times a turn, which has you replaying the same battle mini games again and again, and if you are successful in these mini-games then you deal a small amount of damage back, however if not the damage you receive is relatively small.These two things slow the battles down to a crawl if you miss the action command for your attack and get hurt by failing the enemy mini-games. In boss battles, it was hard to tell if i was waiting for a scripted attack, or if they just had that much health. The last few bosses in the game had fun mechanics of their own, but most bosses have the player wailing on a punching bag of a boss with 1-3 damage per attack, even after using all of my special attacks and super goblin move. Despite these issues, I found Knuckle Sandwich to be a flawed but enjoyable game, and I think the developer should be proud at what they created, but this game seriously lacked story planning, almost as if it was making it up as it went along, and the game suffers from it a TON. Somehow, the ending was satisfying, though it also felt completely out of left field. It's clear the game doesn't have many players sticking it through to the end though, with a 15% achievement rate for the "beat the game" achievement, only approx 3/20 players beat the game as of the posting of this review.If the battle mechanics and art for this game look like something you would enjoy, give it a shot! If you are going in expecting an amazing story however, it might be best to look elsewhere. 20 bucks isn't too big of an ask for a game like this, so I would recommend it as long as you are aware of it's shortcomings. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: I thought it was Pretty Good for the most part. Some segments I'd even say are "Just fine".It's worth your time if you weren't attached to every chapter having the undercurrent of the incident in chapter 1.There were some issues I had but I'm not mad at it. Some people are saying chapter 1 and the final chapter were more interesting than everything between them, and I'd agree, but I wouldn't say the rest of it was bad necessarily. Just not very impactful. And you typically want something to have that impact.I think Andy would have done better to be looser about bosses.  The way you fight them, you're never really surprised that you made it because you know that he tuned it specifically for you to be stuck in a kind of specific pace.You have to listen to all of the dialogue no matter what. You will hit a No Damage message, the RPG mechanics are not consistent for those encounters because it will literally stop you from overperforming. That kind of hurts your soul to encounter, in every other game it's incentivized for you to really crush the objective. But you're not allowed to here.I understand what people mean when they say they were betrayed but I also wasn't entirely attached to it as something with any real emotional impact or interesting story. There were a few cool surprises and it played well for the most part, though there were some microgames that I would have just thrown away and maybe he could have added others in places.One part of the final boss I also would have thrown away or truncated."I liked it and the whole aesthetic package is amazing, but the gameplay itself wasn't" I guess is how I'd conclude it.Please keep making games, Andy, and Actually Play Earthbound past Onett (his words not mine)- that annoying guy from the discord that fought cry n shame for 8 days until he hit the no damage message

_childDocuments_.review: Do I recommend this game? Yes. But not without some warnings, first!I'm someone who followed this game's development all the way back from 2017. I was excited to play the game finally and I *did* enjoy my time with it. But unfortunately, my experience was severely hindered by aspects of the game completely unrelated to the actual game's content.Let's start with the most severe issue: I played almost the entirety of Knuckle Sandwich at what I'd estimate to be about 60% of the game's full speed. This has, according to my friends, been an issue ever since the demo of the game, and it has never been fixed. I only noticed this was the case near the very end of the game when for some reason I noticed that the game was running faster for a few seconds, and then I started to become more aware that certain mini-game attacks would slow down the game even further.Let me be clear: I don't have a bad computer. My PC is perfectly capable of running this game. I have a good graphics card & a CPU that is more than capable of running a game like this. So this is not an issue with my specs.Anyway, once I noticed this, I became curious. I tried to mess around with settings like enabling/disabling v-sync, changing the screen performance settings, etc, or even trying to see if alt-tabbing the game was the cause. None of these ended up being the case.In the end, I don't know what the issue is, but I did find a fix to make the game run at full speed that worked semi-reliably: Every time I'd launch the game, I'd go into the screen settings and restore them to default. This would, for some reason, un-full-screen my game. Then, I'd full-screen it again with the option in the other title screen settings menu. After this, I had to make sure not to alt-tab from the game at any point. If I did, the game would return to running at the low speed, which let me remind you, is what I'd estimate to be an inconsistent 60%-ish or so of the game's intended speed. If I didn't alt tab, I'd be able to play the game at full speed like normal.You might think to yourself, "Well, that really sucks. It sounds like it'd make the game tedious." And the answer is yes, it did. It hindered my enjoyment of the game so much that it became a chore to play it. Because when this game is running at that speed, EVERYTHING feels worse and unpolished.As for the other issue that negatively impacted my game, it was the result of a sub-optimal wording of an option you are given when starting the game. When you launch the game, you are asked if you want the mini-games to be "default, harder, or hardest". I had heard from friends that a common complaint with the game was that it was too easy, and I had also heard that the game's creator had said that the game was on the easier side. As someone experienced with both RPGs and micro-games alike, I naturally decided to switch this setting to "harder", hoping it'd improve my experience. I was wrong.Because you are given this option before even playing the game, you lack the full context of what it means, as it is not explained well enough on the settings page in my opinion. In Knuckle Sandwich, enemies have 3 tiers of enemy mini-game difficulties. Once you clear one, the next difficulty will be used the next time you see that attack. When I set this mode, I ended up unknowingly making it so that the game would have no difficulty scaling at all for these attacks - I'd see only very basic forms of the mini-games - ones that were very easy to beat, and unchanging. This severely messed with the game's balance for me, and made things mind-numbingly uninteresting and easy, especially when coupled with the lower-speed I was unknowingly playing at.Additionally, even though I chose "harder", I swear that I only ever saw the easiest difficulty for the mini-games, as once I (thankfully) midway through the game realized something had to be wrong and set it back to "default", I started getting what were clearly meant to be the upgraded difficulty mini-games I was meant to be seeing all along, which made the game much more fun. I recommend that this option be clearly explained on the settings screen so that nobody else runs into what I did here. Playing without the mini-game difficulties scaling properly completely ruins the fun of them and makes them feel like padding for the battles instead of a worthwhile addition.With that out of the way, let me get into why running into these two issues was the perfect storm of ruining my first-time experience with the game:- Mini-games take too long and become too easy. The mini-game timer essentially became irrelevant for my own attacks, because there was no way I wasn't going to be able to perfect them with the extended time I was given from this issue. Enemy mini-games also became easier as a result, because their attacks were slower and their difficulties were static and unchanging. Mini-games themselves felt worse to play, particularly ones with the tile-based movement.- Because of this, battles were a tremendous slog. The slow down made it so that battles that should've taken mere seconds took at least roughly twice as long. The door enemies in particular were one of the worst things that came out of this. Their high health coupled with the slowdown on my game made it so battles that should've been maybe a minute max took 2-3 minutes each. And there are segments where these enemies are thrown about constantly. Attacking enemies was made easier because I had more time to react, and the same went for dodging attacks. I was never in danger at any point before I fixed the speed and mini-game difficulty issue. Once I did, I had party members KO'd a handful of times, and even lost once during the final boss.- Scene directing was sometimes mistimed. Songs would end too soon. Certain SFX were mistimed, especially during battles. This extended to the credits and made them take an absurdly long time to finish, as I guess despite me fixing the issue for that final play session, it came back for the very final moments for some reason.- Moving around in the game felt really not good. The run button barely felt like it did anything, and the normal walking speed felt stupidly slow.- Finally, I wish that changing options on the title screen saved them right there, and you didn't have to enter the game and save afterwards for them to stick. At one point I tried to set my battle speed higher, and didn't save after switching it. Because of that, I was playing on normal speed still, and just thought that I couldn't notice a difference because the game With all of these in mind, the first maybe 70% of my play through felt really bad. At one point I was genuinely thinking that despite loving the game's aesthetic and vibe, it was the worst RPG I had ever played. The game play in how I experienced it was, simply put, extremely un-fun.THANKFULLY, I know now that is not the case. Once I figured out a reliable way to get the game to run at full speed, and fixed the mini-game difficulty issue by restoring the setting to "default", and made sure that I was on the fastest battle speed, I was astonished. The game felt so, so much better. Almost all of the unpolished feelings that I was getting from the game disappeared. I am glad that I figured out how to fix these issues in the end, but the fact that they made over half of the game feel terrible to play is extremely unfortunate, and I wish that I could have known earlier, or never had to deal with these issues in the first place.Because genuinely, I think my only real complaint with the game beyond all of this is that the way that weapons and the inventory are utilized make it feel pointless to experiment and lacking in options for the player to try out.So, I'm going to recommend this game, but I'd strongly advise Andrew Brophy to fix these issues - ESPECIALLY the slowdown issue. If these are fixed, I will update this review to positive and edit it.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally a S tier quirky Earthbound Inspired RPG in 2023!!!This is my fav indie game of 2023The story goes wild - from , to teaming up with some dimensional goblin to investigate on what's causing all the anomalous activity in the world.You have all these wario ware mini game battles with all these quirky enemies. Each enemy with their own mini games. You have your normal attacks where you have to use different sliders to time your hit button and you have your special attacks that each are on their own a mini game. The normal attacks can get affected by debuffs so attacking will be more challenging.The game's visuals are super good - pixel art with a lot of ingame engine visuals, shaders, there's also some 3D cutscenes and sprites.Soundtrack is awesome! It even has my favorite quirky earthbound inspired musician Nelward compose the soundtrack for it! You'll hear some bangers on this game.The minuses I had with the game:Running doesn't feel fast enough;There could be more various soundtracks for regular enemies, it can be somewhat tiring to hear the same thing.Also a feedback I must include:I noticed some games had a call/talk button feature in the menu (undertale, undertale yellow, knuckle sandwich, deltarune) for when you are in different areas and it has been bothering me that there is no feature which can auto trigger it or have a reminder about it that once pressed you can check the call/talk dialogue. Without the reminder it's hard to remember to check the talk/call feature. This feedback needs to spread, so do share this in a game review that has the similar call/talk feature.

_childDocuments_.review: 12/24/2023 Edit: A buncha updates adding a new "other pocket" for your inventory and making balance changes have happened since this review, so this is outdated as of the moment. Not sure when I'll take the time to play the game again to update this review, but I hope everyone's enjoying the updates.I'm honestly not exactly sure how to review this game but seeing the other reviews, I think they say pretty much everything I had in mind throughout the game, so I'll just make this as simple as I can, just to get those thoughts out anyways. Starting off with the gameplay, the inventory feels tight, even with one other party member to carry your items with (This becomes less of a problem once you have a full team moving around.) You have to at least use up three of the spaces in each character's inventory to have a fully equipped loadout with one-handed weapons for each hand and an accessory, and two spaces if you use a two-handed weapon. The fights you'll be having are pretty entertaining though. Lots of skill are put into the minigames, especially if you use the harder difficulty (which is the one I used for my playthrough, which I thought brought a pretty good and balanced challenge), and they all use the same controls, so you won't be left confused for the most part. Some minigames, however, do feel like you have to be pretty lucky to successfully avoid. The damage done by your whole party can feel pretty inconsistent too. Sometimes you'll do pretty good damage, sometimes you do barely. Special attacks seem especially guilty of not doing as much damage as you expect to, so you might end up just going for normal attacks most of the time. The stat boosts that weapons and accessories give you might even feel completely unnecessary after a while with the damage you'll do later on. In contrast, enemy attacks hurt you pretty good if you fail to dodge them (some are entirely undodgeable) and some ESPECIALLY can hurt you a LOT, possibly even one-shotting you. Another thing is the normal attack minigames. From my attempts at each one of the three, there's only really one you'll probably doing the most damage with, so even getting the right normal attack minigame to do a lot of damage with is kind of RNG.Story-wise, it's definitely not what I expected for the most part from the demo. If you finished it, you probably thought it'd be a darker story, having presented itself with themes of ridiculous murder and a not-so-ordinary job you'll be doing in a wacky world. You don't really get that same feeling beyond Chapter 1 though, mainly because it abandons most of that right afterwards. Without spoiling it, the rest of the story feels like a weird adventure with your brand new friends of sorts, trying to save the world. You know, an experience and a story you might have felt before. Speaking of, the world itself is full of interesting mysteries and characters. Character designs are pretty unique and quirky enough and I don't think they ever get overwhelming and you certainly won't have a hard time recognizing anyone. With all that said though, I just really wish we could have explored this dark part of our story more. It caught my interest that way, but now I've been sucked into a ride that I wasn't exactly looking for, yet I think I enjoyed it. It's also pretty funny at times, and overall, is pretty entertaining when it really wants to be. Whether or not it'll keep your interest for the whole time you'll be playing it is another thing though.Overall, I like Knuckle Sandwich, but it felt like it was missing something. I definitely like the amount of work that Andy put into this game and I don't regret spending my money on it, but maybe this isn't the most knuckle I could have gotten from my sandwich.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been watching this game since the original Kickstarter teaser, and I am finally glad it's out! It didn't quite live up to my expectations, but it was still a great time! There's a lot of things to love in this game, such as the music, the visuals, and the humor. Although I enjoyed all of those things, some stuff in the game didn't resonate with me as well. The story felt a little empty until the end of the game, which made it a big of a slog to keep going. I also had issues with the balance of battles, as some either felt way too easy, or like my equipment meant nothing in the battle and I just had to slog through. Another complaint with the battles were the minigames; most were great! but the few that weren't really drug down my enjoyment. The dev is actively patching the game as I write this, so these might not be issues in the future. In the end, I still really enjoyed my time with Knuckle Sandwich, but I'd recommend going in with not so high of expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game! I have a few issues, like some of the overall pacing, the game balance around chapters 6-7, and the fact that you can't zoom out to see the whole room whenever you come across one of those ice sliding puzzles. I had to power through the whole game on my laptop even though I wanted to switch to my main PC partway through, and attempting to manually import my save file to my PC just caused error pop-ups upon opening the game. Overall though, I waited about five and a half years for this game, and I can easily say that it was worth the wait. Congrats on the release!

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, so here's the deal.I've beaten the game and I'm left with a really strange feeling. What I played isn't at all what I expected or even wanted. After following this game for about 7 years, part of me hates that dissonance, and another part of me wants to celebrate it as some kind of victory for artistic expression.This review is marked Negative, but I still believe the game is worth playing. Read further, it's complicated. lolVisually and musically, this game is an absolute triumph. I have no notes there. It's absolute eye and ear candy all the way through.For a while, the story didn't hook me at all. It completely drops the intrigue set up by the opening in favor of an entirely unrelated plot. For a while, I found myself resenting this direction, but towards the end (and I mean the VERY end) this new direction started to actually interest me. Even so, its so just bizarre that the game's namesake has little to do with the story it ends up telling. Sorta gives off the vibe that some major story restructuring happened after the game was successfully crowdfunded.And the gameplay. Oh my, the gameplay.The bare fundamentals of combat are great, another thing I have no notes on. The minigames are super fun. Combat can occasionally overstay its welcome, and when that happens, the game drags A LOT. But man, there are some bigger issues in other places.Inventory management is the big thing you're gonna hear a lot of people complaining about. Each party member only has 8 item slots, and these slots get taken up by equipped and key items. This is an archaic system that deserved to be left in the 90s.The game's level design is also just bad. In the bigger areas, I would be wandering around aimlessly for just slightly too long. And don't even get me started on the game's "puzzles" (trial-and-error guesswork implemented ONLY to bloat playtime).Clearly the time spent on playtesting was only used for finding bugs, not refining the player experience.By the end though, I was left with this really weird feeling. There was a lot of the game I hated, but I couldn't be mad at it. It's in this limbo state between incredible artistic expression and meaningless schlop.No one will truly understand what I mean by this, but that's okay: I can draw a lot of parallels between this and YIIK.Development went on for so long that the tastes of the developer seem to have changed. The core vision seems to have morphed throughout development, resulting in a confused final product. It's just so fascinating to think about.I say "seem to have" because there's no way of knowing for certain. The creative process is complicated. Maybe this was all the plan from the very beginning, and we were none the wiser? I don't know.There are secrets in this game I haven't seen yet, and I don't think I can give a fully informed opinion without first seeing it all. So, take my words for what they're worth. I've just beaten the game.If there's anything you get out of reading this, let it be this (TL;DR): Knuckle Sandwich is worth playing.I signed up for "Andrew Brophy's macabre cannibalism RPG" but I got "Andy Brophy's WarioWare goblin RPG"I want people to see what I see here. Dive into the mind of Andy Brophy and pick away at the layers, try to see what happened here. It's all just really fascinating.I was missing from the Kickstarter Backer credits, but that's since been fixed.I updated my review after beating the game. The original review is under the line_____________leaving an early positive review for the algorithm boost cuz it's deservedthe visuals+music+combat absolutely live up to the hypethe story is mostly boring so far (8.8 hours in, halfway through chapter 5)inventory management is a total pain in the ass (only 8 inventory slots per character. equipped items + key items take up those slots. party members take items with them when they leave the party (there's an option to "swap" inventories when they leave ??? what does this mean??))there are questionable level design decisions including really brutal enemy placementsso its honestly a great game with a lot of great moments, but the negative bits just bring the overall package down a lot.right now i'd put it at like a 6.5/10. this may raise if the story manages to wow me or if it pulls something insane that ties it all together

_childDocuments_.review: I finished the game a few days after release and have been sitting on my thoughts for a bit. I honestly feel a little misled from what I saw of the game leading up to release through the years. The hook from end of the demo having hardly anything to do with the full game was a little disappointing. The first couple chapters of the game are a blast and I love them to death, but it feels like the game's direction kind of lost focus midway through. Most puzzles in the game felt like trial and error/walking around until you happen upon the solution. _childDocuments_.review: I wrote a review of this game when I was about halfway through it, with a promise to review the full game positively if it ended up addressing my numerous issues with it in later chapters. I thought the game showed promise and had a lot of charm, and genuinely wanted to give it a chance. However, after reaching the credits of this train wreck, most of my previous goodwill is now gone. The game had a genuinely promising demo, which promised a quirky indie RPG with an insane darkly comedic story premise and fun combat that mixed together warioware-style minigames, Paper Mario-inspired timing challenges and standard RPG mechanics. The rest of the game is mostly disconnected from the first two chapters showcased in the demo, other than some extremely weak payoffs that happen too late or are otherwise unsatisfying.The RPG combat and world exploration starts out fun, but is slowly dragged down by this game consistently having some of the worst game design decisions I have had the displeasure of encountering. Expect everything from tedious inventory management (this received a slight fix in the form of a "magic pocket", but your key items will still take up space and the weapon you are holding still takes a slot in your pockets for some reason, at this point they should just do what UTY did and make the magic pocket have infinite slots), puzzles inspired by gen 1 Pokemon gym puzzles no one liked, walking through big mazes filled with enemies that constantly ambush you while you do boring color switch puzzles, animations and sound effects that are unskippable and break the flow of combat, most special attacks being either worthless () or instant wins in regular battles (), enemies with attacks you can't dodge (there's one particularly tedious instance of these where every enemy in one area does one before you can even act), ambush/surprise round mechanics that are extremely unclear and seem to happen at random with some enemies, status effects that barely matter, an attitude that shifts between introducing interesting ideas and not caring about exploring said ideas, and that's without even getting into the biggest issue the combat has; the game is seemingly allergic towards using its own combat system.For whatever reason, almost every boss in the game has an ungodly amount of defense, to the point your basic attacks will only deal 1 point of damage. I assume this is to make sure they get to monologue at you or do some kind of comedic bit, which works for a few of them but this happens so damn often that by chapter 4 I stopped trying to strategize or have fun and just used basic attacks the first few turns so I could be sure I wasn't wasting time and special attacks on a boss that only dies when it feels like it. Most bosses have a second phase that features some kind of gimmick, which is usually completely unrelated to the standard combat mechanics. These range from decently fun to awful but the main point here is the game refuses to use its central mechanics in the encounters that could have utilized them to their full potential. There's a couple of rare bosses where the second phase gimmick involves a twist on the normal combat mechanics, which end up being some of the only fights I genuinely enjoyed.And that is perhaps the worst part of Knuckle Sandwich. It very briefly achieves its full potential. A bit after the midpoint of the game, you play through a chapter that features a party member with enough damage output to pierce the stupid amount of defense many enemies have, some good comedic bits, and also a boss fight that recontextualizes your character's move set in a genuinely fun gimmick fight that also happens to have the best boss theme in the game! After that chapter I had some hope for this mess, only for the next chapter to take an almost immediate nosedive and double down on every terrible game design decision from earlier chapters.Outside of the fact the first 2 or 3 chapters arguably don't matter for the most part, the game has a lot of other issues when it comes to the story and writing. Your party members mostly talk about your current goal and have one or maybe two character traits that are generic and mostly left unexplored, and their combat abilities don't feel connected to them as characters (). As a result I don't really care about any of them, which makes some later emotional moments not really land at all. I don't think I've ever played an RPG where your party has so little to contribute to scenes they are in, despite each of them getting a whole chapter to shine by themselves.The overarching narrative seems to be more concerned with trolling the player, wasting your time, adding too many characters and not giving you enough information instead of telling a cohesive story that has an actually satisfying payoff to anything. The game pretends early on it will explore themes of guilt, death and trying to fit in society yet being rejected by it, only to toss the emotional crux of chapters 1-3 away in favor of a needlessly complicated plot featuring characters you don't care about and that ultimately remembers the first third of the game at the last minute and struggles to quickly resolve everything in the most unsatisfying way imaginable.I've noticed people have been getting increasingly tired of and annoyed by the numerous quirky earthbound-like indie RPGs, reducing most of them to shallow imitators with nothing of value to say that hide their lack of point behind their wackiness and trippy visuals. I always thought this critique was unfair, and even with games like YIIK I at the very least could tell the creator was trying to say something. But with weak gameplay, terrible puzzles and exploration, characters I don't care about, themes that aren't properly explored and a nonsensical story, what else is even left if not the quirky aesthetics? Knuckle Sandwich is a truly hollow, frustrating experience, that is still considered decent by most who played it purely due to its visuals, charm and music tricking you into believing you are playing something better. There's an epilogue/new game+ or something after the credits, but frankly I've given this game enough chances already.Your time is better spent elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Knuckle Sandwich

_childDocuments_.review: Good mixed with bad.Recently a patch was released that seemed to correct a major issue which was stats. Even in maxing out attack at every chance, I was doing 1 damage per attack, whether ATK was 80 or 110, which I think was mistake by the designer. This seems fixed, but it still colored my experience.To the game as a whole, in a way I want people to experience it, but on the other hand I think they'll have a similar experience to me.I kickstarted the game based on the premise. The creator communicated well and didn't seem to expand his scope such that the project would never be complete--which is good.However, the game also feels very hollow.For an RPG and rpg world, it is incredibly small and empty. The characters have no character, which makes the endgame feel very bland. Your supporting cast have no arcs, nor do they really interact together. The villains are disjointed guests to the story. The opening set such a bizarre, dark tone that is just abandoned instantly.Nothing in the story amounts to anything. The ending is kind of a kick in the balls.Items are basically useless and the number of equipable items are so small it may as well be nothing. Having 8 slots, even for key items, is an odd restriction when most items are barely useful in combat, and equipping weapons or CDs don't open a slot for you.The main character has this sad-disinterested look on his face the whole game which isn't endearing or helps you connect. I'd rather have some resolution to his trauma midgame that helps him overcome the ending. Just an annoyance, and maybe just my opinion.The level design is also basic and mostly boring, which is a shame given the long development time. I avoided plenty of combat and still maxed my level (which is 30, btw).There's little sense of progression and you gain only a few paltry skills. Odd choice for an rpg.That was the bad, now the good:Visuals are wonderful with little surprises the whole game.The minigames are mostly fun, though I could have seen them used more sparringly to speed combat up a bit.The boss fights were mostly fun, despite some high HP, and had decent attack variety. Certainly the highlight of combat.The minor enemies were fine, now that the game is patched.The music is lovely.Overall, I'm left a little empty after almost 6 years of waiting. There's lot of potential, but not a lot pays off.I appreciate AB and all the work he did--making a game seems like it would be a slow, awful mess, and he stuck with it. For that, I'm glad I supported the project. There's a lot of creativity on display, but I feel a little more collaboration would have made the game more fun and memorable.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the all-time greats. This game is so special. I feel like a lot of games these days can describe themselves as "this is an rpg but ___" and you definitely can describe knuckle sandwich saying it's an RPG mixed with WarioWare. But i feel like knuckle sandwich really stands on its own. I've really never seen a game attempt a battle system in this way. The amount of quality put into every single minigame that the battles throw at you makes me expect to see a lot of repetition. But I kept being surprised with new kinds of minigames up until the final battle. Every single special move in the game, either your own, or your enemies, is accompanied by a WarioWare styled microgame. All of these games have multiple difficulty levels, and enough variation to keep you on your toes. Something I really loved about this game was that, in lots of different microgames, you control a little sprite of the character that's being targeted by the enemy. There are so many different sets of sprites depending on the microgame, like probably at least 6? and all of those artstyles have unique sprites for every playable character. Even characters who stay in your party for a relatively short amount of time. It's an attention to detail that i really admire. This game is filled to the brim with secrets. Heaps. After beating the game, i immediately started a new playthrough just looking for new things to do, and it almost felt like a different game! Special moves you can unlock by helping out certain npcs, rare items to decorate your house, a mysterious npc i keep seeing that ive HEARD is a secret boss but i still havent figured out how to fight. Goblins. This one dog that rolls around that i can probably talk to. I think what really shows how much is hidden in this game is that, after beating it, with my file showing 100% completion, i only had 4 of 32 achievements. In my second playthrough, im around 2/3 of the way through and have 14/32. It kind of does feel special to discover a lot of these secrets on my own, since online discussion of this game has been pretty scarce, at least where im looking. While it is nice to have that sense of mystery from the game being a little less known, it deserves a MUCH bigger audience. I haven't been able to put this game down. Its world is small but so intricately crafted.From my limited knowledge on the game before i played it, i really didnt think i would care much for the story. Not that i thought the story would be bad, but i thought it would be the kind of game where the story is more of an afterthought to get you from scene to scene. But Knuckle Sandwich had a genuinely intriguing and thought provoking story with a ton of great characters. Theyre still silly and goofy at heart, but all the main characters feel like real people.  The game's writing is also really good. Games don't often make me laugh out loud, but some of the jokes in this one really got me. Another facet of the writing that really speaks to me is just, how kind you can be to some of the npcs. Like, in a really genuine way. Like you can ask them about their lives, if theyre happy with what they do, and they really appreciate you caring about them. Putting a smlie on a characters face fills me with a warm happy feeling. tl:dr its an rpg but like warioware

_childDocuments_.review: Knuckle Sandwich is a fun game to play, and a joy to listen to.  The graphics are also overall very good, nothing to complain about there.The microgames in battles make for a fun little twist on the turn based RPG formula, spicing up the combat.  Sometimes battles can drag on though since every enemy that attacks triggers a microgame in its turn if it uses a non-standard attack (which happens more often than not), and this especially becomes noticeable when the enemies "ambush" you and get a free turn at the start.  And if they have higher speed than you then they get to go first right after that, so you can end up doing 6+ microgames before you've even had a chance to attack.  I think Undertale handled this thing a little better where it would combine multiple enemies attacks into a single attack round, thus making it so that the time playing the "defending" minigame didn't scale up with the number of enemies linearly.  It's still a fun system overall though, and battles go by faster if you do well enough in the microgames since doing one perfectly does counter-damage to the enemy instead of hurting the player.  Annoyingly though, for some enemies this counter damage is a much higher source of damage than your normal attacks, which can lead to very long battles if you're not performing well in the microgames.As others have mentioned, the limited inventory system is a bit annoying at times, although in a recent patch they added another "pocket" which basically doubles your standard inventory from 8 slots to 16 slots, so that helps a lot.  I think the game expects the player to use items more than they actually do though, in which I think there's some balance issues with how items and healing works overall in this game.  There's often vending machines near savepoints that will fully heal your party, so if you can hold out until one of these (or are willing to backtrack a little) then it is often optimal to just hold on to healing items.  However this doesn't mesh well with the limited inventory size, which seems to expect you to be going through consumables rather liberally.  I think if the game dropped the full heal stations (the vending machines), then using items would be more encouraged and the smaller inventory size would make more sense.  There's also some items that remove status effects like "curse" and "sick", but these status effects normally go away after a few turns and don't persist between battles so I personally found these items not very useful, especially since using them would take away a turn that I could be doing an attack with.One minor thing that always bugged me throughout my playthrough was how I could not run diagonally.  You can walk diagonally, but not run diagonally for some reason.  I was really confused for a while as to why I could only move diagonally in some rooms until I realized that these were rooms where I was just not allowed to run.I also did a playthrough on the game's "challenge mode", which is definitely a challenging difficulty.  However the balancing in the difficulty felt a bit all over the place sometimes, with some enemies just 1-hit KOing you if you didn't perfectly perform a microgame.  There's one boss in particular on the cruise ship that just feels impossible to defeat unless you know to use a specific item on him that has a random chance to insta-kill him.  But then by the end of the game, the final boss was doing less than 10% of my total HP per attack (like 6 damage), and it felt laughably easy compared to earlier parts of the run, although I had been using the Sturdy Charm to max out my character's defense on level-ups so normal monsters would stop 1-hit KOing me when I didn't play microgames perfectly.  I think this mode in particular could use a bit more fine-tuning in its difficulty, in regards to damage values done by the monsters at least.Knuckle Sandwich's story is overall what I'd say was the most disappointing part of the game for me.  To preface this, I'd just like to say that I never actually played the demo before the game released (or after), so I didn't have any expectations from that coming into the game.  Knuckle Sandwich has a lot of interesting ideas that it presents but it never really focuses on one long enough to let it develop into something interesting.  Probably the best part of the game story-wise is the first few chapters where the game feels like it's going in a focused direction on a specific, interesting plot point.  After chapter 3 or so the game decides that it's instead going to explore some other things, and never really properly loops back to what it was setting up in the beginning, despite it being where the game gets its name from.  There are still some good moments in the story, in particular the boss fight in the cruise chapter is a standout moment, but they're mostly good just on their own and not in a way that builds upon the main plot.  The game also reveals some "twists" near the end too but they don't feel properly foreshadowed or built up to to be satisfying, and some feel inconsequential to the plot as a whole.Overall I still enjoyed my time with Knuckle Sandwich, enough to do a second run on the game's "challenge mode" as well.  And I've bought the OST since that's still my favorite part of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I think purely based off visuals, design, and music, Knuckle Sandwich is a must have game. It is an incredibly fun RPG with a flavorful aesthetic, quirky humor, and a unique soundtrack that no doubt has been inspired by  that we all know and love.However, while I adore this game for everything mentioned above, I was a bit disappointed to find out that the story is a bit lackluster. It doesn't really seem to know what it wants to do or where it wants to go, so you find yourself experiencing a discombobulated story with no real direction. For an RPG especially, it's important to have a somewhat grounded story for your audience to digest.I still highly recommend playing this game, because even though it may be disjointed with it's story, it's still really fun with it's battle mechanics, and a joy to experience with it's quirky dialogue.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun and good game. But I feel like almost every positive comes with a caveatGame play Is immaculate, the mini games for combat are a great idea, and **almost** always felt challenging and fair, as far as game play goes I don't think I've played another turn based RPG this active, not even Undertale made me feel this engaged with the combat.Which is why the over-world puzzle design is so confusing to me. without spoiling any specifics multiple overworld puzzles feel like deliberate attempts to pad the game with the sheer amount of trial and error required to solve them. Some of the minigames were also luck-based, even beyond the joke one that was literally luck based, and for some reason you have no control over the "minigames" which just apply status effects (this can be crippling if you get unlucky in one section I won't spoil)The inventory system is interesting, It's incredible small, only 8 slots which you also need to fit your equipment in, however there are also PC's placed around that can store an infinite amount of your items. I would of complained more about this however the dev has been adding more and more of these PC's around the game where things like having to drop irreplaceable items or leave them behind has become less of an issue, so instead I'll just say that this whole system seems unnecessary, the dev could have just forced any item you found when you didn't have room to your PC instead of not letting you get it at all, but It works well enough, especially when you get more party members.The writing is good... for what it is. If you were expecting a crazy RPG experience contrasted with a relatively realistic dark plot you won't be getting that after where the demo ends. but you also kinda will, it's tough to explain but essentially the plot goes in a *completely* different direction than where the demo implied to the point where honestly the demo is in no way a good representation of this game's story, as far as gameplay goes it's relatively good at showing what it will be like.While others complain about them I actually like the character writing a lot, It's a lot of the time goofy or kind of awkward, but it feels more real than a lot of other RPG's, even the ones trying to make their NPC's feel "real" characters don't speak like they are in a movie (most of the time) they speak like they are actually having a conversation, this contrasts really well with the rest of the world when it works, it *doesn't* work when they are spoofing common RPG tropes, but it's hard to get into that without spoilers so all I'll say is is that lampshading works a lot better when you don't actually make me do the mundane things you are lampshading.Music ranges from exceptional to forgettable, the main battle theme and a few other tracks stuck out to me, but some really important scenes and fights can be bogged down by music that just doesn't sound appropriate, despite being from multiple composers every track I feel fits the style of the game, but it's like the style of the game doesn't agree with some of the encounters it makes me have while playing it. This can be subjective though so you'll have to decide yourself how the music is, like everything else it feels very polished good or forgettable.Art is incredible, it feels like the only positive without a "but". everything is beautiful and vibrant, while also having a cool movement to it, not to mention how many different art styles they have that they manage to make work together. if anything "clashes" it does so in a good way. Probably the best looking RPG I've playedThe story itself without spoiling it is also weird, like I mentioned previously the game just sorta... pivots.. from where the demo seemed to be heading to a completely different direction, and it sucks because I'm not sure if this was intentional or not. but if it *was* the story they were building up in the demo genuinely seemed more interesting, if not at least more unique. Whats there is enjoyable, but **especially** if all you remember from this game was the demo, you will constantly be waiting for the game to "pick back up" the multiple plot elements it dropped. (which to be fair, it does, eventually)I still recommend knuckle sandwich, I enjoyed it a lot and again the minigame gameplay stuck out to me a ton, if you've played a lot of RPGs and are looking for one that's really unique and yet somehow at the same time pretty standard fare as far as RPG's go, play knuckle sandwich(also a lot of this was made by one guy, and for that, it's definitely worth playing)

_childDocuments_.review: played this game for something around 50 hours. currently in my fourth playthrough, and i still couldnt reccomend the experience enough. its so good. even with its flaws and the bugs. its one of my favorite games and it was made by mostly one guy! wow! if you've been following it's development for a while, the direction it took with its plot will surprise you, no doubt. maybe for the better or worse, but i do think that direction led to a way more interesting final product than what people predicted. there's a lot of things mixed in here, genres, themes, inspirations. if you are a fan of any of the things this games takes from, you will probably go like "ah. i know that! i like that! i like how it is implemented in here!" i also think it's great that this game is so Australian, it's like a small peek into its culture.and. well, the gameplay. oh golly. i love it. all of the microgame attacks of the enemies are fun to learn and beat, the art that accompanies them might change its style, but that makes it even more varied and vibrant. even if a bunch of the microgames are reused, theyre usually given a change of look and a twist in its mechanic to fit the enemy better. and your special attacks, skills, are also little games! one of them lets you see a specific sprite of the enemy you are using it against! you can use it with like tons of enemies! and all of them have unique sprites for that one attack! what! and, yeah, one of the issues people are talking about its the inventory limit, which is 8 items, including key ones. i think its fun to manage your inventory, i learned through the game a fairly good strategy for it. also, you can deposit up to 128 items to have them saved for later! _childDocuments_.review: Lots of great dialogue, gags, surprises and a good combat system, but the actual narrative leaves plenty to be desired.Important characters are left by the wayside for hours, a whole lot of nothing happens between pivotal plot points and it commits the cardinal sin of sloppily lore dumping not once but twice in the span of less than probably 30 minutes towards the end-game. Basically, Knuckle Sandwich was a good comedian, bad storyteller.Without spoiling much, what especially perplexed me was the incident behind Gorilla Burger(?) weighing so heavily on the MC. It's brought up two or three other times throughout like the developer wanted it to matter more than it did, but I didn't sense any tension or significance between the incident and the grander story outside it merely being what sets off certain events at the beginning. They try to establish a loose connection at the very very end, however I couldn't bring myself to exude any enthusiasm over it by then.Great dialogue aside, the game's flavor text is mostly in service of the comedy rather than fleshing out the characters you meet. By the end of my not so super short runtime, I hardly knew Thea or Echo or Dolus. Dolus might be the only character I could see myself connecting with, as what depth was there was expressed mostly, appropriately, without speaking. He's clearly socially awkward, so his abrupt dialogue, quick exits and that one dorky facial expression he makes as if out of nervousness endeared me to him. Unfortunately, he and maybe B-Side were the only characters I got anything out of outside their comedy factor.On the whole, however, the gameplay and humor remained fresh enough throughout that I felt obliged to finish the journey I started.What I'll mostly remember are the audio and visuals, which did a considerable amount of heavy lifting. Great mixing of colors, fun special effects, incredibly well-polished combat animations, and the music... OOOOOH it's so good! It's not quite your Undertales or Personas in that respect, but it's fairly close. The makeup of some tracks feels uniquely Knuckle Sandwich, with the others being generally awesome in their own right (my favorite track is probably the "coolroom" dungeon track).It's a fun ride for about 80% of said ride, but the latter couple chapters really soured my impressions of the story and the gameplay did lax at points due to a lack of evolution in the combat by the 7-8+ hour mark.I'd likely rate this a 7.5/10, but, like, a passionate 7.5! There's a whole ton of love and polish put to this project and it oozes out of every hole, especially initially. I can confidently say I'll be occasionally thinking of this game as the years wane. Whilst it may not be as good as other indie RPG's, not many of them are nearly as memorable.If you can gel with an irreverent tone not unlike WarioWare (which, btw, was a direct inspiration and they nailed it 110%) and don't mind mixing loads of giggles with your JRPG's, you could do far worse than this.

_childDocuments_.review: Its decent. Art style and overall vibe is pretty charming, really nails the GBA style. Game is absolutely held back by the story and strange combat balancing. You'll go from doing 500 damage normal attacks on one enemy with 3000, then you'll do 50 to an enemy with 300 health immediately after. I don't know if "Dolus Ball" is broken or working as intended, but it one shot every enemy i used it on, including bosses. The story has a really great start, but the intrigue fizzles out within an hour. The ending positively surprised me, but it did seem very quick and brief, especially in comparison to the way the game drags out nearly every section. I would genuinely recommend the game for the decent variety of mini-games that makes up the combat system, as well as the general art style and humor. Overall, it was a good game, that could've been great with some minor tweaks and a overhaul of the story in the mid section of the game. I'd give it a 6-7 out of 10.
