_childDocuments_.review: More middling than outright good or bad.A beautiful world and enchanting soundtrack let down only by the core gameplay being a little too simple for its own good. I feel inclined to be nicer to it since it's a solid effort for a solo developed project and I'd like to see it expanded or iterated upon, but what's here right now is a very rudimentary 3D collectathon platformer for better or worse.The jumping and special moves can be a little clunky and unsatisfying at times, many of the tasks required to earn the primary McGuffin "Sources of Earth" are copy-pasted over the three main areas, the puzzle dungeons have challenges ranging from okay to asinine, there's no hazards or enemies to speak of so traversal is your only real challenge, the GUI looks very cheap, the map screens leave much to be desired, and what little story and character motivation is here is very barebones. I enjoyed the airship sections since it controlled pretty well and soaring over the gorgeous environments was pure eye-candy, but they comprise very little of the game and aren't available until after finishing the meat of the game.I still enjoyed my time with it enough to 100% finish it since I'm a crazy magpie person who can wander around a big world collecting shiny objects for hours, but this project feels more like a proof of concept than a full game. I'll happily check out what Orbital Express does next if they have more of a budget to work with, but for the time being I can only recommend this if it's on sale or you really like the idea of vegging out for a few hours running around collecting things.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Tasomachi is a short story of a lone traveler named Yukumo on the way to To-en, eastern continent. Unfortunately, the twilight fog causes serious damage to her airship as she is forced to land on nearby town. She is requested by feline-like inhabitant to search for “Source of Earth” to recover the town and repair her airship.The game sets into the oriental fantasy world influenced by traditional eastern architecture and modern machinery elements. From Japanese Torii gate to modern machineryan, I was slowly captivated by beautiful and complex day/night eastern environment as it hints how the whole city was much alive before migration. On the other hand, it also gives strong aesthetic sense of self-exploration and isolation. It oddly feels relaxing and relieved, but demands a bit of your imagination to invest into the world.I always fascinate in eastern fantasy design (both environment and character appearance) and it’s probably strongest point of this game. The plot is pretty straightforward and self-contained presented in text dialogue, but quite engaging toward the end. However, I personally wish the game provide more background of protagonist and culture of townspeople aside from twilight incident and sacred tree topics.You’ll spend most of the time on town exploration and platforming in both town and sanctuary. This is basically how gameplay loop works:- You freely wander in town and collect Source of Earth spreading thought out the area.- Unlock the sanctuary gate and complete the trial (puzzle / platforming)- Unlock the second part of area; collect more sources to meet the requirement- Complete another sanctuary and obtain new ability, allows Yukumo to reach new area- Revisit town to witness the change and process to the next districtGameplay is simple and similar to old adventure games like Zelda franchise where you revisit and perform unlocked action to collect the rest of relics. Some are well-hidden or inside breakable environment. Three main districts offer distinct surrounding environment and breathtaking landmarks, but share its consistent design.Once you dispel the fog, the visual becomes clear and lively as you witness the changes in town. You will meet some Nezu tribe members that offers short quest that involves collecting stuffs in specific area. Completing quest first time will grant Source of Earth as reward. Some quests in late game can be bit tricky to fine or require airship to complete (which features airborne exploration). The game keeps track of your collectables via visual sign. However, it doesn’t have hand-holding and mostly rely on player’s sense and memorization.Moreover, coin is a common drop and randomly respawned each time you revisit area. You can repeat NPC quest to obtain extra coin. Coin is simply used to exchange decoration, outfits, or complete quests which are optional, but necessary for 100% trophies.The twilight fog is featured as a main environmental threat; you don’t expect any combat or monster like most common platformers. In fact, your reflex and 3D platforming skill will be tested in sanctuary. Each sanctuary contains set of platforming stage ranged from simple jumping over moving pad to the combination of timed-based gimmick and boosting pad. The goal is to collect Source of Earth at the end of each room.One thing I want to mention or you first experience Yukumo’s control is floaty movement type. It’s sort of low-gravity that you can switch action or trajectory in midair (something like to 2D Sonic, Rayman, LittleBigPlanet). It can be double-edge sword that benefits experienced player or accidentally punishes by its imprecision. Moreover, you sometimes need to run-n-jump combination on jump pad to boost vertical momentum.Each stage has option to skip stage using in-game coins, but I recommend it feel more rewarding to overcome trial by yourself.On the late game, you will revisit to collect more sources, but all stages are changed to advanced levels. Some are challenge and can be very frustrating, because it requires you pull off precision landing and movement from floaty controls. In old version, difficulty curve is high even player who familiar with platforming, but they are significantly toned down to be more accessible for casual player which I’m appreciated the game direction.Tasomachi tends to focus on aesthetic design as it features “Photo Mode” by pressing V. Even it doesn’t offer editing options, it still quite welcome for screenshot lover.Note: Your screenshot will be saved in: "%USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\tasomachi\Saved\Screenshots\WindowsNoEditor"There are some nitpickings where Yukumo’s clothes act weirdly in Photo Mode and you can also push your Airship out of bound during collision in Photo Mode.In-game audio is quite good and some give solid feedback when pickup or interact. My only gripe is jumping pad has weird choice of sound effect and lack of responding voiceline from Yukumo and feline NPCs.Soundtracks are composed by Keitaro Ujiie or well-known “Snail’s House” which is oddly interesting choice to put electronic music into traditional setting. It’s complicated genre that involve different synthesizers of electronic sound and instrument (such as future bass, picopop, wonky music, etc.). Each area and day/night cycle features different tracks that fit well either being cheerful melodies, arcade or daydream feels. Overall, it’s personally refreshing for me and Ujico’s work is always impressive.The game is powered by Unreal Engine 4. The world is polished and crafted by original assets. They have simple and clean textures to keep its theme as original concept.My desktop specs are above minimum requirements and can run on highest settings with 1080p resolution without lagging and any crashes in total playtime. There are few noticeable frame drops when instantly turning camera with particle effects. I also suggest for specific graphical option and key binding. Overall, it provides solid performance with decent optimization.My major complain aside from mentioned issue is lack of Yukumo’s facial expression and some transition during interaction. I think having her rigged face to support expression would make character livelier and feel like she’s part of game world.Tasomachi is a game of embracing the sense of wandering and self-exploration without relying on action. I personally consider as an experience by inspiration rather than rich-feature game. Is it worth a full price? It depends on your expectation and value single-man project. For me, it’s similar to supporting artist printing / painting from Pixiv fanbox (or other art community). I hope to see more works from nocras either digital art or maybe the continue of Yukumo’s journey.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is beautiful but looks only get it so far... While people might be deliberating on movement and camera smoothness... all of that could be forgiven if the game felt more thought out.   Repeated animations and repetitive jumping/platforming makes such a beautiful game feel dull.  The sacred tree scenes don't really deliver any satisfaction or explanation for why they're important.   Every element of the game feels stuck at 70% development.  I was looking forward  to this game for a long time ... but I think I can only recommend it on sale, for players who have low expectations and want nothing more than a stunning environment to jump around in.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: For me, Tasomachi was originally just a comfy 1-2 afternoon 3D platformer with plenty to collect and explore. Taking the time after initially beating the game to really delve into the interactions between each unlockable abilities and all the different mechanics in the game truly made me feel more joy and satisfaction with movement than most other games that I've played. I will mention that the bunny hopping plus there being no speed cap has some impact on this, whether those were intentional or not, but I think it adds to the experience for the better. Even without using them the game and it's movement can be enjoyed fully. The pure sense of place to place movement is incredible and something I haven't really experienced from any other 2D or 3D platformer.Music and atmosphere are really special as well, where I think the game shines the most as a piece of art. Very interesting worlds to wander around and the music is a pure vibe. Also, knocking over the cat people is an underrated feature no one seems to mention about this game.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think the game is completely bad, it has a lot of potential to be a great game. This game is really just a jumping game with cosmetic upgrades essentially, good for people who like to do jumping puzzles like in FFXIV (my bias). The issue with this game is that it should be early access at a lower price imo.My biggest issue is the camera control, as it is not as snappy as you think it should be. The problem is that your character moves with the camera, and there is a small movement delay after stopping your camera. This makes moving your character very awkward, as you are fighting with your camera the entire time. Even after the latest patch to the slow camera movement, it is still slow. No idea why the devs thought it was a brilliant idea to make a 3D platformer with momentum attached to the camera controls.As other people mentioned, the character animations are very stiff and weird at times, several clipping issues, and even hardware issues. There are a lot of other small issues that I think should have been taken care of at the very beginning of development, but listing them would make this review go on for too long.It's really a shame to see this game not doing so well, because I think a lot of the problems could have been avoided with more player testing and actually implementing concerns that are repeated often from the community. I will keep an eye on updates to see if my review will need some editing, but I cannot justify recommending this game for $20 when the most basic features were not tested well enough and needing to be patched on the 2nd day of non-early access release.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: What the game makes up for in beauty, it lacks in gameplay and overall dialogue. There is some initial charm, but it quickly starts to fall off when you notice the repetitive fetch quests and sanctuary trials. Towards the end, it just becomes a tedious and quite frankly annoying grind to finish off those last few achievements. The game has a good, somewhat unique soundtrack, although there are only a handful of tracks which loop throughout the entire game. In the rich and colourful environment, a lot of the NPC dialogue tells a sorrowful and quite depressing story; one which I feel is an unfitting juxtaposition.I know that this type of game has an audience, but if you’re like me and just want it for the pretty atmosphere, you might wanna consider the gameplay before buying.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Simply put it's a sightseeing platformer. The most rewarding thing is to explore and collect items in several large towns. As the trailer shows, the platforming physics and animations aren't AAA quality but they're decent for an indie and definitely good enough for me.The gameplay starts very easy then gets more challenging and interesting once you have to boost then immediately ground pound from a bouncy net onto a moving platform; that part could have used instructions. I'm far from done the game so I have yet to see how it will get more challenging.I've been taking it slow since I love using the ingame photo mode. Finally exploring Nocras' art from the inside is awesome.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Tasomachi is perhaps not what one would expect based on the trailers for the game. This is not a mystery or a puzzle game, this is a platformer and a low budget game where you explore to collect items and money in order to progress to new areas. The game's artstyle is very beautiful and oozes atmosphere, and the soundtrack is calming and catchy. It's a good game if you just want something simple to do and are in a relaxing kind of mood. One downside is that the jumping animation looks a bit rough and can make the platforming aspect feel a little bit floaty. It's still controls responsive enough I feel, though, it's more the animations that needed work than anything. Overall I've enjoyed my time with the game so far and would like to see more from this developer in the future.Update: I noticed since the latest patch with the character you play as in game her landing animation is smoother now. It's not perfect or Uncharted level of animation here, but it suffices for what platforming you do in game now I would say. After putting more hours in I'm still enjoying the game. I would say if anyone has played the Crackdown games and enjoyed exploring the worlds to collect the orbs scattered around in that game, then this game you may also enjoy. It's a simple but relaxing and pretty looking collectathon game where you collect primarily through exploration, platforming, and unlocking a few new abilities.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: The things I like about this game, I really like. It just feels like it needs a couple months of QA and polish. If it was technically early access, I'd probably recommend it- but since this is treated like a full release I just don't feel comfortable doing so.The pros: -I love the design of our protagonist and the lil fluffy friends she encounters. -The landscapes are pretty and the ship is really fun to drive. -If you're a fan of classic platforming and collectables (I totally am) then the gameplay will suit you too. The concept and design of every element is great, they just don't quite feel finished.-The difficulty increase of platform puzzles feels very naturalThe cons:Major issues:-Glitches. I got stuck in the slow-mo phase after picking up a collectable and had to reload. Not ideal when there's no auto-save-The expository text screens disappear too fast for me to read them, so I'm not following all of the limited story that there is-The music in general is great, but feels totally off to me in the temple areas. It's this serene, slightly desolate, empty place and yet the music is this hyper jazzy-funk mix that just feels totally out of place.Smaller issues:-A lot of objects aren't collidable, so your character just phases through them. Doesn't affect gameplay, but makes it feel really unpolished and takes you out of the world.-Some of the puzzles feel a bit untested, for example in puzzles with spinning wheels you can just use the characters jump to pass them by completely. Sometimes the reverse happens and your jump is too long for the distance between platforms.-The map. There was a map added recently to the menu screen, and maybe it's just me but I find it very unhelpful with no way to know where your character currently is. Since the map exists, is a little minimap out of the question? -A more general follow on from the last point- it's really hard to know where you've already explored in an area as well as where you are in general. If you want all the items, there's going to be a LOT of backtracking and going in circles.-It's a little lonely. I'm not sure how this could be fixed, maybe if the game played into that isolation a little more it might be better? The music sets up a kind of holly-jolly romp around, but apart from the occasional animal creature that has one line of dialogue, you're only really interacting with signs. It feels like there's something missing.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: CAUTION: THIS IS A VERY VERY OLD-SCHOOL JAPANESE INDIE GAMEBy saying this, I mean the graphics, 3D modelling and texture are fantastic - they came from the famous Nocras, who has drawn numerous art for huge games like Zelda BotW and Pokemon Sword/Shield.However, despite the artistic concept and execution being very much perfect, the game feels uncompleted in a lot other aspects.With that, I mean almost every aspect expect those above-mentioned - control, smoothness, plot, puzzle, music and sound effect, dialog, UI, and so on.But I would still recommend for the artistic aspect, a walking-simulator-ish game like this.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a meditative feel to it. You explore (mostly) empty cities and collect items while electronic ambient music by Sail's House bops you along. I think the bad reviews are from players who will expect to have every second of a game filled with action and storytelling. While each gamer has their preferences, if you don't like slower, pensive games this isn't for you. It's a pick-your-own-pace platformer for those that don't always need an objective or finish line to have fun.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Basically, I would recommend the game without any restrictions, if it weren't for the airship levels.++++I like the design a lot, even if the protagonist just never blinks. The puzzles are fair and really manageable, even if some certainly need some practice (especially regarding timing). A cozy really very beautifully designed world - it's a pleasure to discover it.----What I absolutely don't like about the game - are all the levels that have to be completed purely with the airship. For as comfortable as the game is during the "normal" levels, it probably has a special "challenge" here. Too bad these levels kill the coziness of the game for me and after the main game (the last level being the worst of all), I uninstalled the game directly. There are certainly people who like it, I am not one of them.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: This is a complicated but albeit so so recommendation.Do you like relatively simple puzzles with collectibles?  Lots of repetition, story left to imagination, and an atmosphere that leans towards solemn but ultimately bright?Like others I would say this game wasn't what I expected from the trailer.  It feels like a tech demo, and it feels like it could have a lot of potential, and perhaps that's what's most frustrating.  Rather than a bad game, it's just in the middle.  I wasn't sure I'd finish the game upon starting, but low and behold I wanted to get everything.  If that sounds like you, you'll probably enjoy it.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Less of a 3D platformer than an exploration game with a jump button and a couple of mobility upgrades besides, Tasomachi is one of the most pleasant and relaxing games I've played in recent memory. There's nearly no story to speak of, the main character Yukumo is stranded in a strange foggy valley shortly after leaving home on an airship adventure. She must travel the fog, collect lanterns, and reawaken sacred trees to bring the sunshine back. It's the sort of game that ends with a giant blank screen that simply says THE END.But it's very pretty, the jumping is precise enough if not terribly inspired, and the music is delightful. A good game to spend a lazy weekend on.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game, purely because I have been listening to the soundtrack on Spotify. I decided to search the title of the album on a whim and the 1st result was the Steam page.I looked it up the exact same time as the Winter Sale started, so I considered that a sign and bought it.With that said, he's my impressions of the game:For anyone reasonably decent at platformers, there's about 5 hours of actual content spread across 3 open world levels and 7 challenge areas. Plus a little time trial area. There isn't really a huge amount of backtracking, you only have to visit each level and each shrine twice to get all the collectibles.Saying that, there is a pretty huge grind for the coins if you want , to buy decorations, concept art and costumes for the main character. The final outfit you get for gathering all the collectibles is 150 coins, which is more than the amount of coins I managed to gather throughout the entire game. It will take a really long time to get the few thousand required when you can only pick up 1~3 at a time.The game world has a very unique aesthetic, the movement is basic, but serviceable enough once you unlock all the moves that backtracking to the levels and exploring them again felt really nice. If you can get a boost jump chain going onto a launch pad you can really get moving, it feels great to pull off combos like that because the levels have got so much verticality. And you can shortcut the hell out of some of the shrines too.They are empty, though. There isn't a lot going on in them. You'll see a lot of the same asset re-used across levels like those safety mirrors they put at intersections just scattered everywhere. Even though there's zero cars.And fire hydrants. Right next to the water.Flying the airship around is also great, but I wish it was a bit faster. There's a challenge area that opens up after beating the game with some airship time trials and they have boosters in them and I wish stuff like that existed in the normal levels.The soundtrack is amazing. You can listen to it without having to buy the game, which I highly recommend doing. It doesn't quite fit the game perfectly, there are some tracks which play in the shrines which were way more intense than what I felt was happening on screen. But it works best when you're just bumbling around in your blimp looking for shiny things to gobble up.The main character Yukumo doesn't actually have a lot of character. No sounds, no idle animations, not even any facial animations. The game constantly reminds you about a photo mode but didn't seem to put much care in making the player character photogenic, aside from the option to cycle through her animations with a button. Which is a bummer considering your reward for 100% collecting everything is an outfit.There are some really annoying puzzles in the shrines that just don't work properly. Mainly the memory puzzles, where the buttons just seem to turn themselves on and off randomly. Not sure if that was just a me thing, since I'm playing this game at a pretty high FPS. But it is really weird and annoying.The other annoying thing is, despite there being a checklist for all the collectibles, there isn't one for the lore scrolls. And there's no way to read them after you collect them. Which is a real shame, because they're scattered across all the levels in multiple parts, so there's no way you'd be able to remember them all.Overall, I recommend it. It is a relatively short, inoffensive game with a fantastic soundtrack and some cool environments to jump around in. Great if you have some really younger kids that might not be able to grasp some of the more demanding 3D platformers, or if you just want to chill out and explore some really interesting little towns putting along in an airship.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Slightly janky. Not particularly deep. Bit rough around the edges. Pretty easy overall. No real story to speak of.Plays more like an interactive art piece than a game, and I still kinda love it. The vistas are gorgeous. Combined with the calm-ass soundtrack, it's just really damn nice little experience.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Great exploration collectathon. Music absolutely was a joy to listen to, though the intro song is probably the best one. Puzzles were very enjoyable and fun. Airship stuff was fine, sometimes it was annoying, but the views it gave were worth it. Overall very relaxing game, definitely enjoyed my time spent.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyed this, comfy exploration.It took me about 20 hrs of casual play to 100% it.Outfit's super cute too, and Ujico* on bgm's a pleasant surprise. UI's rather basic, has that doujin feel, but I adore the atmosphere and art direction.They've since updated the game to vsync enabled with 120 fps cap, so the gpu issue should be abated.Regarding the jumps being floaty: they are, somewhat. They seem to have a fixed time-in-air, which is less great for jumps right next to each other, rather than distance ones, but, at least on controller, the precision of the jumps feels okay. You're able to change direction midair, and while you hover at the peak of the jump a bit long (the floaty part), there's none of that weird acceleration or momentum - your feet glue to the ground on landing, which makes for good precision imo. It's precise enough that I've been able to jump my way on top of the map, but just when I thought I made it oob, the devs put a coin there.Rebinding would be nice at some point, I'm not a fan of the jp-style O (or B if xbox) to confirm, and I'd like to swap left / right triggers, but minor gripes. All in all I enjoyed it - so much that I skipped out on the new PoE league to finish it - but I tend to like exploration / walking sim types, so if you're looking for a platformer with more action or interactible thingies, maybe wait for a sale or just skip this.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: The game is kind of short, but a chill and calm experience. It's probably around 5-6 hours. Game is receiving some QoL updates from time to time which make it even better.The physics and movement are kind of weird at first but you can get used to them. Some times you wont reach jumps that seem really easy to do, and falling on some platforms feel kinda clunky at certain points (there are really weird interactions when falling through a platform). The platforming has been balanced a lot and it does feel much better by now, but it might still require a little bit of polish.  The music is top notch, it literally makes the game a entire new experience. It conveys each area's feeling in a really interesting way. If you didn't hear the soundtrack yet, give yourself a huge listen because its phenomenal. Really memorable.The graphics and the world building are really cute and nice. The cities, specially, have a unique feeling to them; this accompanied to the great music and the day-night system offer really good moods.I have mixed feelings about the story. I find it interesting how you can discover the lore through the world, but some of the extra lore feels kind of simple, and nonsense. It still works, I guess. The main story fills its purpose.To sum, fun game, short, but quite good. Hopefully there will be more stuff on the future.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Tasomachi is a charming 3D platforming and exploration game where you complete challenges and look for collectibles to restore life to a series of towns. The gameplay is fairly easy and straightforward, and there is a lot of extra content to complete after finishing the story, such as a timed challenge and races in your airship. This is a game for relaxation and pretty visuals, not challenging gameplay or a complex narrative.The game's strongest feature is its beautiful level design, which is very nicely stylised and has a gorgeous East Asian aesthetic. It is a fairly straightforward collectathon, with the items hidden or spread around the maps in a variety of ways. Many of them are locked to story progress; you are meant to return to the locations multiple times. The music is also fairly good and reminded me of some of the tracks in Muse Dash.The platforming sections are pretty easy and suitable for beginners. The jump is a bit floaty as other people have said, but it's easy to get used to. You unlock new platforming moves with each new area. I recommend playing with a controller.The English translation is a bit clunky, even in the main menu, which led me to accidentally delete my save after finishing the story for the first time ("Format Save" = RESET PROGRESS!!! Not chapter select, to my great misfortune). So ignoring my Steam playtime, 100% can be done in 7-8 hours. The achievements are a bit grindy, particularly for customisation collectables, which require you to run around collecting money that spawns randomly, but none are missable.Tasomachi is relaxing and pretty, and I enjoyed my time with it. The game isn't overly unique or particularly memorable, but it's fun for what it is. If you like the thought of playing as a cute girl helping towns of chibi anthropomorphic cats through jumping about and collecting things, then you'll enjoy yourself.Overall: 7.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't as bad as people say, is it anything groundbreaking? absolutely not. This game, to put it simply, is a collectathon. You basically collect this source of the earth to fix your ship, You fix your ship literally with 5 minutes but as it can take you to the multiple cities your go to, the ship is really badly damaged, more likely won't be able to go anywhere to far, this is where your collect 90 of these earth fragments is what ill call them. The city is covered in this weird fog, in each city you'll have to go to a sacred tree in each city, usually two sacred trees per city. To undo the fog you have to do go to each tree via by the doing trails. The trials are pretty easy, some are harder, but not to bad, just take it slow. I saw this is another comment about combat. I repeat there is NO COMBAT in this game, i haven't beat the game but i am in the 4th, city which is about 3 hours in, with 70 earth fragments collected. Haven't experienced any combat at all, another thing is the games movement does feel clunky and floated but within 30 minutes, you get pretty used to it. overall, this game is the biggest thing out there, there was some lore you can get via finding books. but i dont know to much either, The game is that bad, could it be better? absolutely, is it a good relaxing game? Definitely, i think you should play this game, it's not that bad, its a pretty okay game, and i've been enjoying my playthrough of it.Heres a playthrough of it that im uploading everyday on my channel right now
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: I read some negative feedback on this game as of story and puzzle difficulty, but honestly, this game is a gem. I know that every single game made may reach a larger audience and some others will stay on a reduce target but if you are one of those gatherers, collectors and need a relaxing game, this is the one. Sometimes those games full of dialogues, NPCs and rich in stories may work for the tags of puzzles and platformers but Tasomachi is perfect the way it is. In fact, devs, I need to do a request which I'm sure I'm not the only one thinking of it: Please, PLEASE remove the Format Save option or implement save slots. I dedicated a significant amount of hours and I, willing to break the game, selected Format Save by mistake. On my defense English is not my native language. Still, I think some of us curious gamers may hit that option unintendedly.Thanks!

Need to move around to actually pick up the coins even though I was standing right where it indicated. - Repetitive controls overall- Glitches at certain angles and when taking picturesOverall, the game has great potential if there's more story.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a collecting game dressed up as a platformer. If that's what you're looking for, it's great fun. There's a story, but it feels like more of an afterthought and definitely isn't essential for gameplay. _childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Hey everybody, the only reason why I'm writing this review, is i think that people are giving this game unfair negative feedback. Firstly, I would like to address  the most popular complaint, "the music doesn't fit the game". I would like to say, that i understand what people mean by this, the game definitely has a unique soundtrack, but i don't think that it doesn't fit in. The soundtrack in my personal opinion, is actually an enjoyable listen, it's funky and ambient to the right extent. I also think that the soundtrack is well made, and just getting an unfair amount of hate. the majority of the negative reviews are written with under an hour of playtime, which in itself is stupid, so please just ignore them.As for the actual gameplay, I think the game is enjoyable. Let me start of by saying that there are many un-natural feeling mechanics, as well as fidgety bugs, and glitchy spot's, but nothing game breaking or anything worth directly complaining about. As fir the story and challenges, i don't think this game requires a lot of thinking, nor skill, but it's a great casual play, and towards the later part of the game, finding all the lanterns and collecting everything can pose a challenge. The only major probleme with the gameplay is the somewhat inconsistent frame rates, i find my game feeling slow and laggy, and then seconds later feeling great, which can be a little annoying at times. I Think i've covered everything i wanted to, and i hope anybody who was curious about the game can benefit from it, thanks!
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: May not be the super polished AAA platformer, but for $20 (or less during sales), it is definitely a recommendation for those who only have 20 to 30 minutes to play and just want to collect items. Also a good game to play in the background while chatting. Soundtrack is also really good and helps prevent you from getting too heated during the last few items.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, my only complaints about this game is that it feels very unfinished. The jump mechanics and ship controls are pretty dismal and I think they need to be tweaked just a bit. The puzzles in this game are true to 3D platformers and if you like these types of games and love Japanese style/aesthetic then buy this game. I give it a 6/10.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Buy this if you want a chill  game, don't if you want a .As an exploration game,  is really great and fantastic. I wish I hadn't let myself be deterred by negative reviews from people I now see were expecting a 3D platformer because the game is miscategorized under that label. If I had wanted a platformer I too would have been disappointed, but as a relaxing exploration game? This is one of my new favorites.Except for an optional & timed end-game challenge, I found it almost perfect. Collect things at my own pace, pick up coins one-at-a-time to buy fancy outfits, unlock furniture for my house. The miniature animal NPCs (even the one who politely begged me not to come back) and constant motion of swirling leaves, seas, and canals make the game world feel vibrant and alive from daytime through the night.Each zone slowly evolves as new moves are unlocked and previously blocked off areas become accessible. New NPCs and mini quests are added with each step, so each of the three main areas feels fresh as you continue to explore them. The so-called platforming element to advance each stage and unlock new moves are remedial challenges of escalating difficulty (that can each be skipped for a small in-game fee). These consist of walking on slowly spinning wheels, short memory games, and jumping between wide square platforms.There are brief lore scrolls scattered around that give names and clues about the towns and characters, but as with other dedicated exploration games I love like  the actual story is left pretty open to your imagination. I don't count that as a demerit, but it's worth mentioning.The game world is beautiful and I actually gasped the first time I saw the lanterns come on. There's a dedicated photo mode to take incredible screenshots, and the game world is filled with benches and stools to sit on and admire the view or look around for any collectibles you missed. Maps marked with collectible locations are available for sale in each zone (paired with a menu showing specifically what you've missed) as well as lightable lanterns you can use to visually chart your progress.Definitely pick this up, on sale or off its reasonable $20 list price, if you can tell from the trailer that this looks like a world you'd like to spend some time in -- to explore!
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: The towns are amazing and very relaxing but everything else, especially the ruins just feel rushed and out of place. The OST is nice and I listen to it sometimes but some of the tracks don't really fit with the theme.Overall it's a nice chill game but it feels like they just wanted to get over with publishing the game instead of polishing it and finishing some of the mechanics. I would suggest waiting for a sale if you want to pick it up.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: A game to feel good. Exploration and platforming is about 95% of you're doing but even after journeying through the same map 10 or 15 times to find the collectibles, it didn't really bother me because the game is simply stress-free. The different towns/maps (4, not counting the special maps) are both easy to maneuver in and filled with secret paths, shortcuts and collectibles. Every time I do another round of the map, I find stuff that I missed.The entire game is based around collecting lanterns by exploring or completing simple puzzles to progress through the game. The more lanterns you have, the more areas you unlock. You can also collect coins to buy outfits or objects to customize your base. Maps are somewhat small but the level is design is compact and vertical. There never are parts of the maps that are empty or lacking details. The fact that you can (and are encouraged) to climb buildings often means that you discover secret paths or can parkour nicely from building to building.After 1h or so of playing, you unlock the airship, letting you fly around the same maps that you were on foot earlier on. This changes the feel of the game greatly as you can't go through the same paths to explore and there are also puzzles and secrets to unlock with the airship.Graphically, the game is gorgeous. Not particularly in the technical or high-fidelity aspects but the design works extremely well all around. The towns are foggy and mysterious when you first reach them but become colorful and full of life later on. The water is really beautiful and reflects all details of the towns while the light changes depending on the time of the day. The night gives a different feel to all maps and also highlights the collectibles that you might have missed.It is somewhat disappointing that the game is so short (around 3 hours for me to finish the story ; probably 5-6 to get everything) but it fits well as a walking simulator and nothing is really urgent in the game so you can take your time :)
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: I don't usually write reviews, but I really enjoyed this game. It's a simple collectathon easy for beginners to get into. Movement took a little bit to get used to, but by the midpoint of the game I felt it was very smooth to get around, especially after unlocking all of the movement skills. I was able to complete the game in about 8 hours with no need for a guide. The main downsides I saw were you can only have a single save file and there wasn't any celebration for completing the game (no "thanks" or anything).Graphics: 9/10. It's a very pretty and colorful game. Just don't look too closely at the protagonist's face.Music: 8/10. I enjoyed most of what I heard, though some tunes didn't seem to match the environment.Difficulty: 3/10. I didn't struggle much on anything.Overall enjoyability: 8/10. I expect I'll play it again at some point.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a potential to be really good, i found out about the game by accident on youtube, the soundtrack is one of the best ones i have ever heard.I have only played it for 40 minutes but you can tell a lot about this game just from playing it for a few minutes, it does feel unfihished, it needs lots of tweaks to make it feel good, i would love it if characters were speaking/had a voiced dialoge  to make the game feel more lively.Going up to the signs in order to learn about the game, this is your only tutorial for the game which is a minus.Level design and character design seems really amazing, the mechanics on the other hands could use a huge change, such us soundtrack activation in some spots, this could use some kind of transition.The animation of picking something up feel as if character teleported to the thing you wanted to pick up which feels off, jumping animation is also way too slow.In other words i absolutely love where the game could end up being if it was fully finished, it is cheap so it's worth the money.I wouldn't mind paying more if the game would be perfectly playable.This is neither a negative nor a positive review from me, as i know a small studio worked on it and tried their best on doing the game.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: I think if they had only rebranded Tasomachi as a 'relaxing 3D hidden objects platformer', it would get much better reviews, because in essence that's what it is. If you find yourself wanting to keep playing it, it will probably be because you have an itch to run and jump around and try to find more Sources of Earth, not because of the 'mystery' and 'adventure' that's promoted in its description. Because it just does not deliver on either of those things. =/ I still reccommend it, but first I want to address its glaring issues (Spoiler warning...I guess? There's not a lot to spoil, tbh)The thing that makes 'mystery' intriguing is the idea of solving it...like, you expect to eventually be given some information that answers your questions, or at least lends them context. But you don't get that in this game. I haven't found all the 'information scrolls' yet (and there aren't even that many), but so far their contents have been vague at best and kind of trivial at worst. I have no reason to expect that the ones that remain will reveal anything interesting about this world.As for 'adventure'...when it comes to games, adventure usually implies stakes? Like, a reason that compels you/the MC to continue their journey? But again, you don't get that in this game.You have to fix your airship, yes...but the game insists that your adventure isn't just about you; you're also trying to save this mysterious town. Any context given for your actions usually has more to do with the state of the town than the state of your airship (case in point: you end up fixing your airship before beating the game).The problem is that the game gives you very little reason to be invested in the state of the town. 99% of its inhabitants don't speak outside of giving you directions or simple sidequests. You barely learn anything about its history or its culture (there is NOTHING TO READ IN THE LIBRARY-- huge worldbuilding red flag for me).And worst of all, your little animal friend just...gives you orders. Half his dialogue is literally "I want you to do X" and...that's it. Like, he's the only important NPC in the whole game; you think they'd try a little harder to make him sound like a friend or someone who really needs your help. And it's a shame, because he really is cute...if only he were an actually endearing character, I'd be more than willing to beat the game just to make him happy. ^^;Basically, if you don't have any completionist impulses you may find yourself very bored with the lack of substance in this game (I didn't mention the sanctuaries, but honestly they feel so tacked on and irrelevant that they're easy to forget. Personally, I paid to skip through about half of them ^^;).BUT, if you are a bit of a completionist (I am) or if you just like the idea of searching for things and putting your hand-eye coordination to the test to retrieve shiny objects, then I think you won't regret buying it (I don't ^^).The visuals are BEAUTIFUL. The first time night fell in Shiokaze Pier it took my breath away...I love how the moon just glows like a huge ghostly lantern in the sky; it's not realistic but it looks incredible and it works for the game.I also like the music a lot...people have said it doesn't match the aesthetic (especially in the sanctuaries) and I guess they're not wrong, but I got over that pretty fast. ^^; The BGM for exploring the towns fits perfectly fine, though, and it's very soothing.The contemporary-meets-ancient design of the towns is nice, the controls are nothing special but they work fine, the game runs well with no lagging or glitching, I WISH THE MAPS WERE ACTUALLY HELPFUL but that's more of a pet-peeve than anything else...and best of all, the game doesn't punish you for anything. ^^ You can rotate through areas to collect as many coins as you want; there are no lives to keep track of, not even in the sanctuaries; you can pay with the coins you collect to skip the sanctuary challenges if they annoy you (and the price is always the same); there's no fall damage or reset mechanism if you land in the water (like, you respawn back at the pier but you keep anything you managed to collect before you fell)...the only thing you need to worry about is making sure you save your progress. TL;DR Tasomachi actually does a GREAT job of being a cute, relaxing, stress-free game (even if it's not particularly interesting), and if that sounds good to you go ahead and buy it. I think you'll enjoy it.

Some of the controls are indeed finicky, but with some patience it will be fine (as of this review I have minimally cleared zone 4, and picked up <110 lanterns.) I bought the game blindly so I had no expectations, but so far I'm enjoying it. I feel a little bad running over some of the cat avatars. _childDocuments_.review: This is a game of great graphical enjoyment but yet it's doesn't reach that pure beauty state which is much of a cliff hanger on the quality itself. The creator of the game is no doubt has the skill and artistic sense to make a game of 100% pure art and beauty but he has chosen the wrong tool and wrong dimension for it imo...This game feels a lot like the Treasure hunt pulled right out of Second Life (A virtual social game), and the quality of it stays at that amateur level. Yes, clearly the game creator doesn't have a lot of 3D modeling experience and he have to "work around" a lot of stuffs due to lack of skill, if he has chosen to make a game in a much more 2D environment with a fixed frame for view, something like the Trine series for example... then this will be a much perfect game that will 100% shine with his current art skills. But by choosing the wrong game dimension and landed on a territory he's not too used to making, the whole 360 3D dimension reveal flaws in the art work, like bare bone outskirts and bare looking water body, which if he'd chosen to do these on a much packed scenery, will create immerse art... so yeah the wrong dimension choice resulted in the whole amateur and "unfinished" feel of the game... While in the old Second Life, players have gotten used to the bare sims and have learn how to pretend the outskirt of the 3D isn't there, and role-play the whole part out and only focus on seeing the good stuffs, but this isn't Second Life out here, so the rules doesn't apply at all to normal gamers... That's also a reason why even as a snapshot maniac, i don't find the urge to take a ton of snapshots in this game despite the beautiful graphic scenery, not many places can form a good art piece unless viewed from a special angle... maybe that's why the game require the fly cam, like Second Life, we need to choose the sweet spot for our snapshots to look great. And since this is clearly the treasure hunt concept from Second Life, which isn't really meant to be played alone, it's more like an event that's used for creating social topics among friends and getting some traffic for the SIM owners (in Second Life that is). Yes, they can be fun and gotten some obsession from some of the participants, but like i said, it's not really for single player and those hunts are short and not repetitive unlike this game design here. Stretching out too long in the token finding make this game a grind, and  lost its fun and enjoyment the longer we play... So at its current state, this game doesn't really meet the requirement of a professional game and only landed somewhere near an amateur work, and it plays like the treasure hunt events in Second Life and very much getting the same experience... we get to see nice scenery and explore while we hunt for the tokens, and that's just about it. Even though there's collectibles like outfits and such but the outfit and their rigging system is soo outdated, like those stiff clothing items in Second Life 10+ years ago... yeah, for someone who played Second Life before, they might be able to accept such things, but this is a game of 2021... so no, this isn't a quality that we accept nowadays. So those being the final rewards in collecting the tokens makes it a big lack luster... And those "furniture" items that conveniently place themselves in the starting house area... Just because the players can't do anything with them, makes them ain't attractive at all as a reward... at least make these furnishing items that we can decorate that house with, a housing system of sort, then it might be more worthy of collecting them. Remember that, something that's been accepted in a VR world a decade ago doesn't really live up to standard for nowadays game, the game creator has the skill and talent to make some great artistic games like Gris or Trine, that much credit i can give him, but he's chosen a wrong tool that doesn't fit his skills and lead to this disappointment. If you are making another game, and plan to go full on artistic design... since you got a musician in your team already.. I'll suggest you to go for pure music and art enjoyment 2D platformer (like Gris), you will get a much better hit there. But this one, is simply half baked and showed how unskillful you are in 3D modelling, especially the rigging part. You guys do have the skills to make a great game, just not this dimension and angle of view imo.Putting those major stuffs aside, there's a lot of minor flaws in the game too, for example:[1] The inability to remap our own key binding can cause frustration especially on a precision game like a platformer.[2] Require another separate key/button to do double jump is just silly and make the whole control awkward. Why can't we push the jump button twice to trigger it? Like a proper double jump?[3] Some (not all) of the background music doesn't fit the game design theme at all, the artist and the musician need serious communication and not doing their own stuffs the way they like it then put everything together and call it a day. Yes the musics are great by themselves, and the artworks are great, but they are like puzzle pieces made by 2 completely different person without communication in between and expecting the puzzles will fit on the final puzzle board. Note to Dev: "Take Gris for example and you should learn a lot from it on how to make the artwork and music goes in harmony, and hopefully improve a lot in your next game."[4] Seems like the game devs themselves hated the platforming part and added a shortcut to by pass the whole game play, if you can't love your creation, don't expect your players to love it. Why choose a genre you can't love to create in the first place? Just wanting to show off the art skill you have like those artist in Second Life? Then yeah, this isn't a bad approach but you made a few bad choice, dimension and genre that you can't like/handle to begin with.[5] Every Area is a repeat of the previous area with different positioning on stuffs and npc only, if you don't want to be creative in the game play part, don't make it this long. Not trying to be harsh but being realistic here, a shorter version of everything without repeating will certainly make this game a lot more love-able.[6] The skills we can unlock at each area needs more usage, not just there to fetch a few hard to get or far positioned tokens. There's more creative way to make them fun. And at current state these skills have their potential wasted.[7] There's certain area that the character can get stuck, and there's no way to get out of those situation other than return to title and lost progress... wish they will have a way to get out of those situation, maybe by adding a restart from checkpoint option in the menu. That will helps a lot of frustration and avoid the lost of progression.[8] Why can't your NPC look straight at the character during a conversation? What's the purpose of pushing them down when we walk close to them? Isn't there better ways to create the dialog box and make them more easier to read? The current dialog system makes me want to skip through the lore session and npc dialog... [9] Nauseating Alert! Can't turn off motion blur in game!So yeah, in overall, this game is not even close to any indie standard, more like a hobbyist circle/doujin work on new toy/experiment. Can't really be recommending it at its full price, and some might even find the discounted price way too much to pay for this content. So it's gonna be a thumbs down from me until they somehow improves those flaws and make this game better. But if you love Second Life and enjoyed those treasure hunt events, this is still a game for you, because there's a lot to "hunt" for.

_childDocuments_.review: Video review - When I think of indie platformers, more often than not it’s the tough as nails 2D offerings. Dustforce is one of my favorites, I owe my career to the anger-inducing levels in Super Meat Boy, and more recently Celeste has cemented itself as the gold standard for the genre.But now we’re in this weird nostalgia phase, where developers are calling back to the 90s with varying degrees of success. Blue Flame came out earlier this year, with slick combat and a gothic touch. Balan Wonderland is … well …. a thing. Now we have Tasomachi: Behind the Twilight, a stunning 3D exploration platformer from a solo developer who just so happened to be an artist on Xenoblade Chornicles 2, various Final Fantasy projects, and The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild.Tasomachi is an exploration-based 3D platformer, set in an absolutely stunning East-Asian inspired world. You play as Yukumo, a traveler who loses control of her airship when a mysterious force pulses through the world, covering the land in fog. Arriving at a mostly abandoned town Yukumo crosses paths with a member of the local Nezu Tribe; adorable cat-like creatures who are blighted by the mysterious force that has plunged their world into darkness. Thankfully there is a mutually beneficial solution to this problem; restoring power to the Source Trees of each town in the region, dissipating the fog, and freeing the villagers who can fix Yukumo’s airship. A convenient plot for sure, but it provides just enough of a reason to set the game in motion.Tasomachi has three major villages to explore and much like the modern 3D Mario games, your progress is hindered by the need to collect Source of the Earth, powerful lanterns hidden throughout the villages in hard to reach places. Your job is to roll into each village, collect enough lanterns to unlock access to the Source Tree Sanctuary, complete a series of platforming challenges to restore life to the Source Tree, and dissipate the darkness. All up, you can expect to take a leisurely 4-5 hours to get through what Tasomachi has to offer.When arriving at a village for the first time, darkness and barriers will surround you, keeping you confined to a certain part of the town. However, you are free to just roam, poke, and prod at the world as you search for lanterns. I immediately fell in love with the fact that there were no threats, no time limits, no enemies, and no death. It was just me, this gorgeous abandoned world, and the phenomenal soundtrack.Once you have collected the required number of lanterns, you can unlock the Source Tree Sactuary which harbors a number of platforming challenges to be completed. Aside from the art, this is where I could really pull direct inspiration from Breath of the Wild. Each of these challenges just has the same vibe as one of the many Shrines in that game. Sure, less of the puzzle and physics elements, but it’s very much a “you’re in this space, make it to the end” kind of vibe, and I really enjoyed that.Yet the beginning of Tasomachi is actually a little rough. Yukumo’s jump feels really floaty, yet doesn’t get as much height or distance as you want. The momentum of everything just feels a little … weird. Keeping in mind that I play a tonne of platformers, I’m used to precise and pixel perfect control, and Tasomachi definitely is not on that level. However, I won’t say that it is bad. The game is designed well to fit into Yukumo’s movements, and by the end of my time with the game, I felt just as comfortable here as I do playing the dark worlds in Super Meat Boy.When you complete each challenge, and rekindle the power of the Source Tree, a portion of the fog is dissipated from the village. You can now access areas that you couldn’t before, but you’ll need to collect more lanterns, unlock the second Source Tree Sanctuary. Occasionally you will unlock new abilities such as a butt stomp, an air dash, and eventually a mid-air platform jump. Much like the aforementioned movement concerns, these powers all feel a little lackluster at first. Yet by the final challenges I was able to reliably combo air dashes and mid-jump platforms to increase my movement tenfold, so once again I wouldn’t necessarily say it’s bad, just not top tier.As the darkness is completely lifted, the entire village is ready for exploration. The Nezu residents will return, new paths will be available, challenges will appear, and a general sense of accomplishment is immediately served up. I loved seeing life return to these places, and exploring the town I just helped to liberate became a zen-like experience for me.From there it’s a rinse and repeat pattern. Collect enough lanterns to unlock the next village. Go to next village, lift the darkness by collecting lanterns and restoring the source trees. Explore the liberated village to collect more lanterns, and move on.I’m not going to spoil the ending areas, but when all is said and done you do gain access to your airship, which allows you to then explore other areas of each village you were unable to before. Life has well and truly returned to each location by now, and I just cannot stress enough how chill the vibes were as I saw society return.But perhaps the biggest issue with Tasomachi. It never breaks from its formula. Each village has two Sacred Trees to restore. Each village will have the same chores to complete in order to find all of the lanterns. Each village has a store that will sell you clothing and furniture for your home base. Each of the Nezu will say the same things to you, depending on which extra task they give you in order to get all the lanterns. It’s a very rinse and repeat game, and depending what you are looking for, that could be an issue for you.Personally for me, Tasomachi is the exact game that I needed right now. A beautiful world, with a bare bones narrative, that just let me soak in the atmosphere and enjoy my time there. To give you an idea of what kind of world this is- you can sit. Literally just sit on the benches, and let time melt away. This a a stop and smell the roses game. A take your time and just collect the things game. This is Breath of the Mild, a time to relax.But I also cannot discount the areas where it fails. It’s presentation is definitely lacking, with a menu and UI that just screams placeholder. The movement and weight of jumps and the powers don’t feel great. I learned to control them, and for what it’s worth I don’t think they’re as terrible as I thought in my first hour with the game, but they are certainly not great.While I really believe that each village has its own quirks and vibe, the challenge areas are a little more hit and miss. Take for instance this maze. This just wasn’t fun. Neither was the guess the random teleporter challenge. Once again, not the worst thing I’ve seen, but also nowhere near the best.That’s Tasomachi in a nutshell. I can see why people would bounce off it, saying that there are a dozen other platformers out there that do it better. But I don’t care. Tasomachi is doing something interesting here, creating a chilled collect-a-thon that calls back a hit of nostalgia, but takes the edge off at the same time. Also, this is made by a solo developer. Art. Design. Programming. Narrative. All one person. Taking that into consideration, this is a phenomenal debut.But would I recommend Tasomachi? Maybe. If you are looking at this and can imagine yourself cozied up with a controller in hand, a cup of tea by your side, and just switch your brain off and enjoy the vibes, then I’d say this might have something for you.It’s like Kraft Mac n Cheese. I know it’s not great, but I love it anyway. Tasomachi isn’t a bad game, it’s just not a phenomenal one. That’s totally okay, because I love it for what it is, 4-5 hours of platforming goodness, with nothing but good vibes.
