_childDocuments_.review: TASOMACHI: Behind The Twilight is a 3D platformer developed by Orbital Express and published by PLAYISM.  Orbital Express is led by veteran industry artist, nocras, who has worked on hits such as Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn, The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, and Pokémon Sword and Shield. The music is composed by popular Japanese artist, Ujico*, who has over 200 million views on YouTube. TASOMACHI: Behind The Twilight follows the story of Yukumo, a young girl whose airship becomes damaged at the beginning of the game.  She arrives at a seemingly abandoned town covered in deep, dark fog and must search the town for both parts to repair her airship and to help free the town from the darkness. TASOMACHI: Behind The Twilight is a beautifully crafted game that combines smooth and simple gameplay with a stellar soundtrack and delightful settings.   Beauty: Hitting above its Weight When booting the game up for the first time, the player is presented with only a few options: load/start a game, format a save, settings and quit the game.  Let’s start with the settings.  Settings are pretty barebones, although it contains everything one would expect from a game’s settings.  Graphics range from “lowest” to “highest”, rather than using resolution.  I suspect that the way the game calculates “lowest” and “highest” is based on a render scale.  SFX and Music volume sliders are important, especially since the majority, if not all that you will be hearing in TASOMACHI: Behind The Twilight will be the music and sound effects.  There is nary a dialogue in sight.  There are some control and camera settings. I played with my mouse and keyboard but TASOMACHI: Behind The Twilight also has controller support.  The controls themselves are pretty simple and intuitive although the camera control on a mouse is a bit too fast.  The last major set of settings are the languages, with only a limited number of languages available.  The game is astoundingly beautiful.  It looks like it was pulled from a Studio Ghibli movie.  The colors are bright and vibrant, the shadows are moody and intense.  If you’ve played Breath of the Wild, you’ll definitely feel an urge to go back and play after seeing this game.  This game’s aesthetic just screams character and I love it.  You don’t need realistic photogrammetry to create a beautiful game and TASOMACHI: Behind The Twilight is a great example of that.   However, beautiful graphics does come with its costs so heed this warning!  Make sure your graphics card can handle this game!  It is incredibly GPU intensive and playing this game on anything lower than high settings takes away one of the most unique aspects of TASOMACHI: Behind The Twilight.   The music is also great and unique, and it fits this style of game with a mix of more orchestral, smooth swaying tracks and more modern synth style music as well.  Like the general art style of TASOMACHI: Behind The Twilight, there are aspects of traditional and modern in the soundtrack and I hope Ujico* releases some of the tracks in this game on YouTube.  I am in need of some new study music.   The game for the most part, runs smoothly; I rarely experienced any texture pop ins and loading screens are short.  Moving your camera around quickly and certain actions can result in relatively harsh frame drops but I found my game still ran relatively well even on the highest resolution.  If you’re not a fan of motion blur though, I’d be careful and adjust your camera sensitivity settings as needed.  I did find myself feeling a little sick after swinging the camera around quickly to test out the frame drops.   3D Platforming, Stress Free The gameplay is similar to most other 3rd person platformers (think Crash Bandicoot or even something like Knack).  The bulk of the gameplay will rely on your movement, utilizing the standard jumps or the various movement abilities you unlock to beat each Sanctuary.  The goal of the game is to collect enough parts and Sources of Earth to repair your ship as well as uncover the mystery of the town you are exploring.  Money can be picked up throughout the locations you visit and can be used to skip sections of the Sanctuaries.  But what are Sanctuaries? Sanctuaries act as small parkour dungeons where Yukumo must reach the end of a jumping puzzle to claim a Source of Earth as well as unlock the Sanctuary.  The more Sanctuaries a player clears, the more the light will return to the town.  These dungeons have a variety of challenging jump mechanics that, although simple to understand and solve, will require a bit of finessing, especially for someone like me who isn’t as proficient at platformers.  Something else that initially worried me was that there was no auto-saving!  Saving is done by praying t a shrine, marked by a yellow-green swirl effect.  Thankfully, there are plenty of shrines scattered through the sanctuaries and the town.  There is a light checkpoint mechanic in place after you complete certain objectives so even if you fail a jump after clearing a section of a Sanctuary, not all of your progress will be lost.  The lack of an auto-save is not the punishing handicap that other games exploit to increase difficulty.  Instead, it acts as a way for you to regain your spot, so that when you fail the moving platforms section for the 5th time (as I did), you can just return to the start, rather than at the shrine one door away. My critique of TASOMACHI: Behind The Twilight’s gameplay isn’t really an analysis of the mechanics itself but more a reflection of what kind of gamer would be interested in this kind of game.  The levels are relatively simple and most of the game is dependent on exploration through platforming. There is no combat, no life bars, no stamina bars, no rarities, nothing of the sort.  The game is designed to not be a stressful boss murdering enemy slaying high octane game but instead a low-stress, almost Zen-like experience.  It reminds me of Journey or Ori to a certain extent.  A beautiful game with easy to grasp mechanics that exists to wrap the player in its beautiful world like a big warm hug.  A Gamer’s NirvanaTASOMACHI: Behind The Twilight is almost inviting you to simply take in the sights and sounds of its world at your pace.  Imagine most popular video games as a 100-meter sprint at the Olympics. TASOMACHI: Behind The Twilight is that nice stroll through the park as the spring breeze gently blows past you, the sounds of birds chirping in the air and flowers starting to bloom.  If this is something you are not interested in, this is just not the game for you.  However, for fans of platformers, for fans of the art style of nocras, for fans of the music (trust me, after a few sessions with TASOMACHI: Behind The Twilight, you will be) or for people who just want to take a break and play a nice, relaxing game: TASOMACHI: Behind The Twilight is worth picking up.It honestly might be worth picking up just for the visuals alone, walking through a section that you’ve restored to the light and basking in its beauty may be worth the price of admission.  No YouTube video or Twitch stream of this game will do it justice, and this was just on my 1080p monitor.  I can only imagine how crisp and glorious the art style would be in 4K.   TASOMACHI: Behind The Twilight is not a demanding game.  It doesn’t ask a lot of the players.  There aren’t any boss fight patterns to memorize, team plays to execute, loot boxes to grind or any of the flashy features of most modern games.  Instead, this game is a meditation, the gamer’s Zen garden.  If a peaceful game is what you’re looking for, TASOMACHI: Behind The Twilight is the game for you.  10/10
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Tasomachi: Behind the Twilight is an absolute triumph, showing that open world games don’t have to be bloated messes more concerned with “player retention” than actually providing an enjoyable, compelling experience. It keeps things deliberately simple from a mechanical and narrative perspective, but provides more than enough substance to keep you coming back for more — plus a few stiff challenges for those brave enough to take them on.This is the sort of experience open-world games should be aspiring to provide: not endless checklists of pointless busywork, but incentives for players to explore these intricately crafted environments. You should come away from an open-world experience at the very least feeling like you know your way around — and in more picturesque examples, having a strong desire to visit those places if only they were real.That’s exactly how I feel about Tasomachi: Behind the Twilight. My time with the game has felt like a holiday to a beautiful, idyllic location with no pesky other humans to interrupt or disturb me. And heaven knows I suspect we all need a holiday right now.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight is a charming and visually captivating indie game that stands out for its serene atmosphere and unique aesthetic. Developed by the Japanese studio Orbital Express, the game combines exploration, platforming, and puzzle-solving in a beautifully crafted world.One of the most striking aspects of TASOMACHI is its art style. The game features a distinctive blend of cel-shaded graphics and traditional Japanese art influences, creating a vivid and enchanting world. The environments are lush and vibrant, with each area meticulously designed to evoke a sense of wonder and tranquility. The game’s use of color and light is particularly impressive, contributing to a dreamlike ambiance that draws players in.At its core, TASOMACHI is an exploration-focused platformer. Players control Yukumo, a young girl searching for lost parts of her airship in a mysterious and magical land. The platforming mechanics are smooth and responsive, allowing for fluid movement and precise jumps. The game encourages exploration with its wide variety of levels and hidden secrets. The puzzles are generally well-designed, offering a satisfying challenge without becoming overly frustrating.The narrative of TASOMACHI is understated but engaging. The story unfolds gradually as players explore the world, uncovering fragments of lore and interacting with whimsical characters. The setting is reminiscent of classic Japanese fantasy, with its floating islands, ancient ruins, and enchanting landscapes. While the story may not be the primary focus, it complements the gameplay and adds depth to the exploration experience.The soundtrack of TASOMACHI is another highlight. The music is soothing and atmospheric, perfectly matching the game's visual style and enhancing the overall immersion. The sound design is subtle yet effective, with ambient sounds and gentle melodies contributing to the game’s calming and reflective tone.TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight is a delightful experience for players who appreciate beautiful art, thoughtful exploration, and relaxing gameplay. Its unique aesthetic, combined with smooth platforming and a tranquil atmosphere, makes it a standout title in the indie game scene. While it may not offer intense action or deep narrative complexity, it excels in providing a serene and visually stunning adventure that is both enjoyable and memorable.- Gorgeous and unique art style- Smooth and enjoyable platforming mechanics- Relaxing and atmospheric soundtrack- Engaging exploration and puzzles- Story may feel minimal for some players= Limited in terms of challenging gameplayOverall, TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight is a hidden gem that offers a peaceful and visually enchanting journey. It's a must-play for fans of atmospheric platformers and those who appreciate artful design and tranquil exploration.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: A cute, relaxing little platformer collectathon with lovely scenery that makes for a fine palate cleanser from more intense or violent games.  Speaking of violence, the extent of it is launching the occasional firework at stationary, glowing lanterns or the odd big rock. The platforming and puzzles are forgiving and there's no penalty for failure. There are no enemies (unless said stationary, harmless lanterns count), there is no health or fall damage, you can't die, the worst the game will do is teleport you to the start of the area with nothing lost.  It'd be a fine game for young kids to wander around the pretty locations, collect shinies and get used to 3D platforming in general.There is some notable jank though. The jumping is very floaty, the mid-jump movement skills don't have any animations (although they do have a particle effect and they work if you consider them like a gust of wind to push you), Yumeko's face doesn't animate or change expression ever, the English is not great, the controls are kind of weird and not remappable and the menus are only passable. None of that is deal-breaker stuff and it's a chill game so it's all easily overlooked. I'm usually a mouse and keyboard kind of person but the controls were so odd that I went controller this time. The game felt just fine on controller so I'd strongly recommend playing with one of those.There are a few little quibbles that frankly are more amusing than actual problems too.  Like, you can buy furniture for the sizable house you stay in but it all gets shoved in this one little corner while 90% of the place doesn't change. It's weird. I get that the purpose of the place is to show the collectible tallies for the different areas and allow changing outfits but the furniture is done so strangely it makes one wonder why bother.  Some of the lore notes are the same deal. I'm fine with things not being explained but if you're going to do that, just don't say anything. Don't, for example, have a note that says that it's unclear, a mystery and nobody knows. Why'd you take the time to tell me nothing I didn't already not know? The game's also bizarrely lantern-centric. Harmless and I may be missing a cultural reference somewhere but it's still quite noticeable how almost everything somehow is or involves a lantern.Don't let any of that dissuade you though. It doesn't detract from the overall experience. The environments are quite striking and have a refreshing aesthetic so just wandering around is pleasant. The camera's smooth and you have full control, I've never had any troubles with it. The airship, once repaired, is a genuine joy to fly around as well. I'd love to have one myself, with matching hat of course!  Grab it on sale if you're looking for something different to relax with or if you want something you can safely let a young kid play.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: As an amateur Unreal developer, this is basically the kind of game I've always wanted to make, but never had the patience nor the skillset to complete.  Yes, I notice the little Unreal-specific quirks present in the game such as the basic UI and the imprecise trigger boxes.  But these are nothing compared to the wonderful level design, a true artistic vision lovingly transferred from 2D to 3D.  I'm just a sucker for fantasy vertically-designed environments with overkill architecture.  This is such a relaxing game to play.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: I'm thoroughly surprised with how much fun I had with this short little game. The platforming is simple and the missions are basic. The environment is breathtaking to soak in, especially when flying around in the airship. The game does an acceptable job at keeping you invested in collecting the Sources of Earth, that are the main focus of the game, with rewards such as outfits and decorations for your main hub of operations. The puzzles can be a bit tiring at times, however if you push on through you're lucky not bombarded with them one after the other. Allowing the pacing of the game to be a little more varied at times. Tasomachi's soundtrack is no slouch either. Music by Ujico/Snail's House does a wonderful job capturing the aesthetic of each location and activities in the moment. Tasomachi is a fun experience when you want to have a more peaceful and relaxing time to just kick back a play something simple. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: it looks cool and cute but the game is not fully developed or polished. has so much potential as story or game play even interactions. But the game play is way too simple and boring. all you do is just get into a map, do a bit of walking around and solve jumping puzzles to get coins or some achievements. Honestly might say waist of money :<
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: A light platformer collect-a-thon game. It's greatest strength is reveling in the aesthetics of the world. Relax, listen to the music, and wander around in a beautiful townscape.Controls can be clunky. story is fairly light. Movement felt off until completion of the main game, at which point all abilities were finally unlocked. It was at that point did the game really feel fun exploring the 3D space.If you want to experience the beautiful world and chill to some Ujico* then this is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty and chill platforming game, with some puzzles and a lot to collect.It only took me about 3 hours to get to the end, and it recycles a lot of assets and puzzles, so be aware.I was left missing some voice acting or at least some cute sounds for the fox-people as they were speaking. Wasn't a fan of just silent text lines on a 3D-game.Get it if you want to just chill, listen to the funky music and explore the different towns. =P
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Beautifully designed with a simple concept and execution.  Needs a lot of refinement but it has the potential to be a very fun game.  It will never be accused of hand-holding you because there is very little explanation of what's going on or what you need to do next but the visuals make you want to explore it all to fine out.  The Map is useless.  Add a compass and zoom feature to it and you'd have a navigation system that could be useful. It'd also be nice to know what the things in the shops are that I'm spending coins on, and to have a confirm or cancel transaction feature.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: A nice plataformer / collectathon game with beautiful scenery. The game has no combat, very little dialogue and no mystery or plot to solve, so this might not be the game for you if you are looking for a more engaging experience. However, it is perfect to switch off your brain and relax for a while, as you run around exploring the maps and enjoying the views. The game is somewhat short (I completed 100% in 12 hours) and its relatively easy. You have multiple locations (3 main areas, and several other smaller maps) that you can revisit at anytime to keep exploring and collecting more items. You progress through the game by conquering challenges in temples, which are usually simple platform puzzles. Conquering a temple will in turn unblock other areas of the map, or give you more skills to reach places that were out of reach before.If you are looking for something to relax and pass the time, give it a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a mid/sideways thumb option because despite my issues with it I like it more than I don't. Mostly it's far too expensive for what it is, I would only reccommend with a STEEP discount.If you think of it like a playable soundtrack, something to enjoy the chill vibes in short sessions here and there to unwind, you'll probably dig this.If you're like me and you prefer bingeing and going for full completion, there's not enough polish or variety to justify what it asks of you in that regard, so just grab the OST [which is bangin] and look elsewhere for something with more meat to it.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Platforming and exploring a beautiful world with no-combat is what's on offer in Tasomachi and if you like collecting things then you're in for a treat. The lack of combat doesn't hinder the gameplay at all and as your character uncovers more areas, more traversal abilities are unlocked that let you uncover more and more of the map. Although you can finish the game in a decent amount of time there's much more you can explore after you see the credits roll. The joy of this game is in figuring out how to get the macguffins that push the journey forward so if searching out hidden items in games is not your cup of tea then you may not gain as much enjoyment as I did. The soundtrack is especially good and as someone who quite often turns music volume down in games, this is one soundtrack I wanted to listen to.This game offers a great sense of achievement as you uncover all the varied ways in which to get that 100% and it never feels unfair or overly frustrating.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Story: Barely there, and very light on lore. But I don't think the point of the game was to get invested in a deep story. It's more just there to give a setting and a motive to progress.Then again, I haven't finished it yet. Maybe more goes on, but I don't see that happening. Will update when finished.Gameplay: An open world collectathon, that works sorta like Mario Odyssey, though less creative. Does the job well still, and the animations/sounds don't get annoying.Platforming is a little too floaty for me, with how your character sorta drifts a little, and lack of jump height control. So dungeons are a mixed bag since they're either platforming or guessing. Decent challenge, though a little annoying.Music and Visuals: Incredible! Music helps create a mood/vibe to help you relax and just enjoy, and the art direction is fantastic with its colors and atmosphere. And it goes the extra mile with the photo-mode and day/night cycle in these decently sized and dense maps.This game starts off really weak and not promising. But once you get to the first world, especially when you first clear all the fog, the game REALLY shines its magic! While it clearly had a restricted budget, it does really well with what it gives you.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Visually, the towns are beautiful and charming. Ujico/Snail's House composed the soundtrack which is how I found out about this game. I added it to my wish list and got it on sale. The team that made the game was incredibly small and this is definitely an indie title.There are plenty of areas to fix. There is no voice acting so all of the story is presented in writing, the only NPCs you interact with are the cats that stand around the 3 towns, the difficulty scaling for certain puzzles and challenges is a little unbalanced, and to 100% the game you will need to spend time farming in game currency for shop Items. There are parts of the gameplay that shine through including some of the challenges with how they interact with the map and the balloon portions towards the end.The positives: good soundtrack, beautiful environment, low stress/investment.The negatives, short, little story, repetitive gameplay. All things considered, It is worth the purchase if you can get it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay is fine, but the visual/graphic is very nice and beautiful, music is ok-ish.But sadly this game UI really need lots of polishing. I feel like I'm playing some kind of low end unreal engine/unity game because of the UI look and feel.If you don't mind the bland UI, this game will be nice to enjoy play.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Extra casual and slightly clumsy to control, the music is nice and so are the visuals. Rare case when an aspect of them being simplified works and looks like a style instead of a shortcut taken.Bit expensive, I got it on sale, maybe I should have waited for the price to go even lower, but I'm having fun anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: If you like fanciful anime pictures of magical Asian cityscapes and the cozy beats of Ujico*/Snail's House, then this casual game is for you. I’ve never before played anything that captures this feeling so well. It’s quite lovely, calming, and dreamlike. The dialogue from the cute little cat people is always simple and sweet, as are the tidbits of lore scattered throughout. The levels are beautiful, and there’s a photo mode so you can get the most out of them. The platforming gameplay is easy, and you can honestly finish the game in under 4 or 5 hours, but if you want to be a completionist and really savor everything, the more advanced challenges will take you about twice as long to complete.I’d happily play another short and charming game by this person, Nocras, with music by someone like Ujico* or Mamomo. However, I’d really love to see these feelings and aesthetics flushed out even further in a full-length game that requires players to complete more challenging feats in order to advance the story (rather than being entirely optional). Keep up the good work, Nocras!
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful jaunt through a pretty, concise, nostalgic game.By far the most enticing part of  is the elegant storybook visuals. Although I never used the photo mode, the game is picturesque in nearly every moment that is played. While beautiful to look at in still, some of the animations of our main character are clunky, particularly when jumping.Speaking of jumping,  has a surprisingly robust movement system - intended or not. After obtaining all upgrades, the player can simulate bunny-hopping by chaining jumps. Especially when going back through collected everything after beating the main story, the tools given to the player allows for gross exploitation beyond the expected paths of many objectives.The gameplay is good, but often confusing. Without knowing what collectibles are left, (description is only populated after collection,) using one of the steam guides is recommended for a 100% playthrough. Particularly with some of the trials (of which there are 24), the "challenge" isn't testing the skill of the player, but sometimes patience. It is almost impossible to "fail" a maze unless you eventually give up.Story is almost non-existent, but for a short, sweet game like this, I don't mind the story. Some of the in-game found dialogue regarding the main girl is interesting to think about, and adds an air of child-like wonder that I also loved in the  games.Overall I would say that most of the game is a 9/10 in enjoyment with a few low points that bring the final rating to an . If you don't care about visuals I think your enjoyment will be less than that.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun game once you get into it.Feels a little rough in the first few minutes, but can promise you it picks up from there.Overall the platforming puzzles are a lot of fun and each one is a little different which helps keep things fresh. If you feel like going back for completion each puzzle also has a more advanced version.I did hope to fully complete the game but after a bit over 4 hours it was starting to wear on me a little...Overall the music is amazing, but after a few repeats it can get a bit monotonous.The puzzles and seeking every last item is fun, but again after a while it becomes a bit of a drag.Will I go back? Yes, I think I will... I won't play the full game again but think the puzzles and seeking are refreshing enough to warrant another session.If I have one piece of advice, don't binge the game, rather play it across two or three session instead.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Charming 3D platformer in gameplay style of Spyro the Dragon, but on a budget. You play as a lil girl called Yukomo which likes to buy useless trinkets for her home and clothes. I swapped the music for Astral Throb Synthwave mixes from youtube. It was a very relaxing experience as the game is pretty easy. Good for sunday relax days.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Its a nice map 3-D platform jumping simulator but too quiet. Map - Feels great, almost matches the cover-art. Some music fit nicely to the map especially at night. Jumping around at different height feels fresh. The NPC are too basic, it always idle at their spot and their number makes the map feels abandoned. It needs extra NPC walking around. The last airship mission are great fun, dev should add more of such stages.Puzzles stage- Relatively easy and straight-forward, it needs to be more bold, creative and fun. I love to see the puzzle take to some crazy height like the 3 maps offered. Sometime it needs a hint for harder stage instead of just offering a payment of 20 coins to skip.Collectables - You can buy items from shop and it goes to your 'trophy' room where you can see all progress and change skin. It's a nice feature but not good enough. Even after i bought everything from every shop, the room barely have any noticeable changes from the start. Apart from the nice skins, i want to see more stuff like furniture, ornaments and decoration to make it lively. Overall, it's a good game to enjoy and waste some time. Lot's of potential for the devs and i hope they succeed what they started, the map is too good and the game is incomplete without improvement. I will visit the game again in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10I had a lot of fun playing this game, I think it suited me a lot.It was very relaxing to walk around the towns and help the kitties. The atmosphere was beautiful and it grabbed my attention quite often. It was always nice to sit down somewhere and drink tea IRL. Unlike in a lot of games that are fast pace, this one gave you lots to do in each environment which gives you time to soak in your surroundings for a bit longer.The puzzles were somewhat challenging but they didn't take long which was nice. For an indie game I thought there was enough content. The music was absolutely perfect. Ujico did an amazing job as he always does with music (BTW I remember your artwork from Wonderworld).Anyways, thanks for this lovely experience!!
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice and relaxing 3D platformer with a great look and soundtrack to it. Reminds me of early 00's platformers in a good way, but far less punishing that those. Most of the game is basically about navigating the world, wondering if something might be at the top of a building, or hidden somewhere, and working out how to get to there. The "dungeons" are more focused platforming challenges that can get a little tricky at times, but are also all fairly short with little consequence if you fail. If you're struggling or just want to progress to the next area you can skip them all together by paying some coins too.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Tasomatchi is a platform game with no enemies to take down if you expect some action to go away; here we are entitled to series of puzzles, platform and collectible objects that allow us to advance the story. It imprints this magical side that can be found in Ghibli studios but unfortunately the missions are the same in each city and a certain weariness is felt at the end (I took 11 hours slowly to make all the successes). I would have liked more life in the cities for a deeper immersion but we must not forget the work of the dev 'and the music which is very pleasant to listen to. I encourage the studio to continue to this path and move forward and give their best.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: A quiet, chill platformer/collect-a-thon. I've greatly enjoyed the few hours I've put in so far. I've completed the first two areas, and three "dungeons". The moveset is limited so far, mainly just a jump, but abilities appear to unlock over time. I just unlocked a drop move. All abilities play in to the platforming and exploration. If Genshin Impact was "anime BOTW", then this is "anime Mario Odyssey". It's a very quiet game, - no enemies, health bar, stamina management, etc. Towns are empty until you complete dungeons to "restore" them, and only then do they unlock their platforming challenges and a few NPCs waiting to give you hints or mini quests. BTW, the NPCs are cute cats. This is a really enjoyable game if you meet it on it's own terms, and can forgive a few short comings with animations and controls. Relax, unwind, enjoy the beautiful scenery and BGM. Soak up the ambience and complete some basic and not overly challenging platforming and exploration.
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

_childDocuments_.review: Yukumo is a young girl traversing the world in her beloved airship. Upon arriving at a certain town, her airship breaks down. She decides to explore the town to search for parts for repair; however, the town has fallen silent, with no trace of its inhabitants...
_childDocuments_.name: TASOMACHI: Behind the Twilight

name: Welcome to Elk
detailed_description: Feature List They've Gotta Learn Sometime - Frigg, a young carpenter from the big city, needs to adjust to their new small time life, rife with gossip and drama. True Stories and Tall Tales - Every story in Welcome to Elk blends the tall tale with the tragic truth of everyday living just off the beaten path. Tragic Comedy - Just as much heart as humor. Life may be hard, love and death might go hand-in-hand, but laughter always follows. Imaginative Minigames - Every game in Elk is uniquely tailored to the stories and moods underlying Elk's intricate web of narrative. A Good Storyteller - Nothing is more important than a good storyteller on Elk. That's why you'll meet them as you play. About the Game True stories told by real people. Frigg has a lot to learn in the small town of Elk after life in the big city! An apprenticeship as a carpenter, a group of new, complicated friends, and a town predisposed to all kinds of difficult relationships. But they're going to find their way just like all the other off-beat immigrants to the island of Elk. It's how life is across the water. And just as they have fun exploring all the little nooks and crannies of an old, storied island and its old, storied people, Frigg will face some tough decisions, some heartwrenching situations and a the kind of heartbreak that sits with you forever. Whether it's playing cards for candy, getting their feet wet at the beach or just sitting down to listen to a story well-told, Elk will be an adventure that Frigg will cherish for the rest of their days. The stories in Welcome to Elk are told by the people who we know and/or were there when the events took place. All are told from memory. The way they are used both on our webpage and in the game is true to the core story but everything like names, locations and other details are changed, renamed and often re-framed to protect the real people behind them, therefore, we call them tall tales. The stories are not one-to-one like you would experience in true crime for example. They are rewritten and combined to one linear narrative. Characters may play a role in one story where they were not a part of it originally and only us who designed it will ever know – or come close to the real truth of the stories. Welcome to Elk might look like a “fun” game but it’s about telling stories – some are filled with humour, others are dark, but they go hand in hand.

short_description: True stories told by real people. Welcome to Elk transforms the weird, wonderful, dark and desperate tales of the road less-traveled into an inventive, biographical adventure. This is an island like no other where drama, trauma, love and laughter hide around every corner.

_childDocuments_.review: So, it took me a little while to get into this game. I thought it was kinda quirky at first, also wasn't really sure where this game was heading. The game takes you through many different stories, some are funny, leave you feeling good, some are sad, leave you pondering. After the first story which was told with a video, like actual footage of a person just telling their story, I got more absorbed in the game. I wanted to find the other stories. You can tell the developers put a lot of themselves in this game. It makes it feel somehow personal.I found a phone number in-game, which of course I called out of curiosity. I was expecting a pre-recorded message easteregg thing. Instead it was Simon who answered the phone. It really caught me off guard!! It was funny and slightly awkward haha.  I think he is one of the developers (?) I thought I saw Simon again in one of the story videos as well. If you read this Simon, thanks for fixing the pinball machine! ;)Anyway. This game is about stories. There are  no choices to stray from the story path. You just sit back and walk them. If you like this sort of thing, buy it! I definitely enjoyed it a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Welcome to Elk

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to Elk follows a woman named Frigg who has left their life in the city to take up a carpentry apprenticeship in a small town named Elk located on an island. Upon accepting this apprenticeship position, she expects this part of her life to be calm and boring, however this is not the case. It’s not long after she arrives that she learns that this small community has its own problems, colorful characters, and stories to tell. For better or for worse, she gets quickly involved like she always lived there.Taking place a little bit over a week, you’ll be traveling across the island, exploring everything Elk has to offer, hanging out with and getting to know your new neighbors, and totally not doing carpentry despite a boat being in the progress of being built. As Elk is hand-drawn with many things hanging out in the open, the developers have luckily predicted that there will be players looking for any and all interactive items. Thus, all the characters and items that Frigg can interact with will be colored in to contrast all the black and white outlined items and scenery. Which certainly helps as some will switch between interactive and not. Every day you’ll run into a story being played out and a minigame. The minigames here were pretty good though some of them did leave me wanting to play them more. Minigames can help lighten the mood, like the dance competition you have at the beginning, playing golf, or even building your own contraption. Though, there are also minigames that brings us right back to the horrible reality and compliments the story it’s with. Like trying to help Anders remember his parents by pasting facial features on balloons ransom note style or beautifully sending off a man that newly died.If you somehow missed the main selling point, the stories told in Welcome to Elk are true stories that happened to the people that the team knows or were somehow involved. To fit into the game alongside others, each story is rewritten to better fit, but the impact is still there. The themes range from death and alcoholism to uncomfortable situations. Depending on what story that is being incorporated, it can be a brief mention, part of a character, and/or gets a spotlight as the featured story that day.At the end of the day, Frigg returns to her new home and sleeps to have some strange dreams on a boat and wakes up to a new message in a bottle sitting on her living room table. Who is leaving these and why is unknown. Once your curiosity gets the best of you, it turns out that they contain stories that strangely somewhat correlates with what happened days before. In addition, Frigg is sometimes visited by strangers (well, strangers in a sense that they don’t live at Elk) that once she walks up to them, we’re treated to an actual person being recorded telling a story that they experienced. Making it more charged than it would have been if you were just reading or quickly scanning the story.Before going in, the game does autosave your game only with no option to save your game manually. Since Welcome to Elk silently saves, meaning it doesn’t give a sign saying it’s saving like other games, I don’t doubt some people will be wondering what’s up. This game can honestly be completed in one go and you may not even want to stop (like me which told myself I would to savour this game, but I didn’t end up doing it). If you do need to step away, try to exit the game after Frigg wakes up or try to guess where the game would autosave. However, this also means that the game autosaves right at the credits which isn’t bad unless you want to go back and read the stories placed on Frigg’s table.Though, there is good news in regards to this. If you want to read all of the stories the developers gathered without playing the game again, or just don’t want to open the game just to read one, the developers have listed all of them on the game’s website ready for anyone to read (though it seems that two only appear in the game during the fmv style retellings). There is also a bonus story, called “Lauge and the Diamond Smugglers” that didn’t end up fitting into the game.I will also like to mention that I appreciate how the missable achievements are easy to find. They all become available at different times, and some can only be caught during that day, but the game puts you on a path that will have you right there or pass right by it. Considering that interactable items are colored in as well, you can easily spot them too. There is only one achievement that is hard to figure out, but there is a hint on the game’s website.Welcome to Elk is truly like no other game and I highly recommend picking this gem up. Even if you’re someone that takes a while to connect and sympathize with characters, this is written in a way that encourages you to. Everyone will connect with at least one of these stories and feel for those that had to experience the others (or for one particular story impressed). I also love how the developers didn’t shy away from topics such as death no matter how difficult it will be, but rest assured that they are handled with care. With this all packaged with a lovely art direction and great music that both gives you a feel on Elk and matches whatever scenario Frigg finds herself in at the same time makes this a game you shouldn’t pass on.
_childDocuments_.name: Welcome to Elk

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to Elk was a must-play for me, and is actually the only game I've bought (so far) in the 2020 Steam Winter Sale. Unfortunately, I didn't find the game particularly appealing. While I found some of the stories contained in the game to be intriguing and I thought the mini-games were creative, the game never came together for me into any sort of cohesive whole.It reminded me a little of the 1999 film American Beauty, where so much dysfunction is contained within a single block of the suburbs. Elk Island, in the same way, has so many issues spread across it's few inhabitants. However, the isolation of Elk Island makes the resolution of any of its issues a more complicated matter. A raging alcoholic, who hides beers around the island, seems to be enabled by her friends. The game actually has a repeated joke about her alcoholism, which I found a little questionable. At the same time, a man who clearly seems mentally ill is left unsupervised with a child in a cave (that he actually lives in). If these two weren't isolated on an island, there might be more resources for support.The game also reminds me a bit of the "magical realism" literary movement, which seems almost like a modernist offshoot. I loved reading Gabriel Garcia-Marquez ("One Hundred Years of Solitude," "Love in the Time of Cholera") growing up, witnessing as grounded reality became more fantastical. However, It seemed to me that "What Remains of Edith Finch" better struck this balance within the form of a game.It's hard to say why the game didn't click with me. Perhaps if it were completely grounded or completely fantastic and metaphorical, it would've resonated more clearly? As it was, though, it just seemed muddled. I felt more numb and confused than moved.
_childDocuments_.name: Welcome to Elk

_childDocuments_.review: Not as affecting or memorable as I had hoped, but it's always great to find idiosyncratic games that execute well on doing their thing. An interesting one thematically. To me the game quickly felt upfront about what it's doing - even seemingly telling you at points, And I actually felt accommodated, treated like a guest through the journey and its serious topics. Worth knowing not to expect a self-contained fictional world, nor anything especially outlandish, as this can be rather mundane (in a nice way).
_childDocuments_.name: Welcome to Elk

_childDocuments_.review: They each have other-worldly, idiosyncratic art styles and superb soundtracks. Each in their own way captures the drama, poverty, and tragedy that can strike small, tight-knit communities. Presenting these biographical stories and interweaving them into a single fictional narrative is the core of the experience. Without spoiling too much, suggestions throughout that there's a great twist or reframing on the horizon are red herrings. This is about using narrative as an experimental vehicle for true stories. And it works! Although, it falls short for me of truly committing it all to one narrative. The true stories (or tall tales - they are not 1:1) are often told thrice. Once within the thread of the main story with the characters you're familiar with, then once more with real FMV of their retelling, then one final time within bottles as first-hand textual accounts.  By intruding various real world elements into the game world, they undermine the verisimilitude of the characters and place you're trying to get invested in. The story becomes about the meta interruptions on top of the interruptions of tragedy to the protagonist Frigg's life. At one point when Frigg says she has to work one of the characters outright tells her "you know that's not going to happen" as a wink to the player.  Whilst switching the means of telling these stories very cleverly draws attention to the central question of the ethics of telling stories, the details lost in retelling, what we gain from stories, how invented stories are themselves real in a way, how fundamentally stories are all we have in the end yet don't have to define us, etc; it feels in doing so it reduces Elk to just answering this question. A mixed blessing perhaps. It's certainly not unambitious for it.The stories themselves are engaging and thought-provoking,  It's packed with astonishing moments. I love the subtleties in its world-building most of all, as they uniquely capture the hardship of island life. Aspects like one resident having to live off squirrels they catch capture the sheer poverty on the post-industry island. The bottles hidden in every corner and the way every day somehow ends with Frigg at the pub just to cope with the day's events shows the rampant alcohol abuse that can occur in such communities. The anarchism with the main antagonist acting with impunity speaks to how an island can be its own separate world to the mainland. The stories as they're told within the main narrative thread strike the perfect tone -  The activities you engage with all the residents in and the incredibly varied minigames that accompany them As with the aforementioned games, Elk has a beautiful aesthetic. It's designed for readability with only interactables and people infused with colour, but it also nicely reflects the sadness of Elk. Its cartoon appearance allows the seriousness of its subject matters to throw you off, much like you might be in real life. Death, alcohol addiction, suicide, and threatened rape have to meet a world wherein a penguin pops its head out of a barrel.
_childDocuments_.name: Welcome to Elk

_childDocuments_.review: I marked this as "Informational" on Senscape.This is such an interesting game. So many story telling techniques are utilized. You arrive on an island called Elk. Elk is an island of the dead you are told. You may be a cartoon character dancing one minute, helping to carry a body the next. You will hear the stories of how they died. Real people that submitted stories contributed to this and are shown telling the stories.This is not a family friendly game because of language and adult themes. There are a few easy mini games that are quick to get through. We found ourselves wanting to skip them and get on with the story. A good amount of the game is watching the game unfold, be it in a dream, or on a drunken evening…If you are looking for action or a quick moving game, this is not it.There is no mouse support. You will be using the spacebar or enter key to progress the dialogue. We recommend using a controller if you have one. Movement is WASD or arrow keys.There is an autosave function only. Do not quit playing unless you’ve accomplished something, or you will be replaying portions of the game.Playtime thus far is around three hours. I would guess this is at least four hours of game play for many. It depends on how many times you wander around instead of doing your quest.It can get boring, but I keep playing. At this point, I am curious see if I am dead; I guess I will have to report back after more play.I would really encourage the devs to add mouse support.
_childDocuments_.name: Welcome to Elk

_childDocuments_.review: The game focuses on the darker sides of the human experience, but remains truly human in the care taken to represent these true stories. That being said, Welcome to Elk did not feel like a cohesive game, but more of a disjointed mishmash of those stories which only serves to give them a platform to be told, heard, until they're lost in the madness of life. 4/10
_childDocuments_.name: Welcome to Elk

_childDocuments_.review: It’s not often I come across a game I feel the urge to replay immediately after finishing it, but that’s exactly what happenned to me with Welcome to Elk. It has a captivating aura that makes you want to be part of its special place and then spread the word about it, and I think that is exactly what its creators intended.Without giving away too much (I think it’s best to approach WtE knowing as little as possible about it), this is a game about storytelling in which different real-life stories are gathered and unified to be told through the fictionalization of the village of Elk.During our playthrough, Frigg (the main character) will receive messages in a bottle containing texts that are always related in some way to the events of the game. What’s special about those bottled texts is that they are actually telling us the true events that inspired the project, events we have been playing up until then adapted into the gameplay’s context. They are messages for Frigg, who is in turn acting as the direct link between game and player by handling those stories to us using the videogame as the media. The creators even go as far as to include some personal stories of their own, but I won’t be spoiling that content in this review.Since conversations are the core feature of the game, it is worth noting that the writing used in the dialogues has a really good execution. The characters speak in a very informal and natural manner and each one of them have their own personal way of talking that expresses their personality through a very carefully designed selection of words and idioms. They have very expressive facial animations, too, which make them more relatable as well.Gameplay-wise this is a simple and humble game, but with a remarkable amount of different minigames, each one with its own set of rules and controls and with a high level of polish; they usually have a touch of absurdity that adds originality and freshness to those little moments, and some of them are really emotional and are conceived to leave an imprint on the player through their mechanics, which they achieve with a surprising amount of rawness that reminds us that we haven’t arrived at Elk just to have fun.Regarding other key aspects, the visual style has a very interesting approach that leaves the background environments in a secondary position by not coloring them, and saves the colours for the most important elements (mostly characters). That way, the scenery serves as the symbolic canvas in which all the different stories are displayed to us. Also, since we will spend quite some time wandering through the isle of Elk, the creators put a lot of effort in the characters’ movement by making it very smooth and pleasant, with a really charming and distinctive animation style. The game’s atmosphere is completed by a soundtrack that’s heavily influenced by danish folk and creates a comfy and cozy setting to play in.In the end, the core essence of Welcome to Elk is to express the will of its creators to turn the game into a story-spreading device conveniently built around the town’s bar, meeting point of oral transmission where words flow like the beer that gives life to the people of the village.See you in the second afterlife.
_childDocuments_.name: Welcome to Elk

_childDocuments_.review: provides players with a uniquely whimsical and touching experience. The stark juxtaposition of the comically twee styling and silly mini-games with the heartbreaking nature of the stories creates a whiplash-inducing emotional rollercoaster.The various accounts sometimes addresses incredibly sensitive subject matter such as death, alcohol abuse and violence; this is done sensitively despite the more jovial aspects of the game and manages to feel authentic and touching rather than distasteful in any way.My more detailed review of Welcome to Elk and lots of other games can be found on .

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game mainly for the characters' cute appearance and funny way of walking, and looking for some stories. I got what I expected but differently.You play as a girl visiting an island and greet the people, hearing their stories. There's no main story but each day you hear a (weird) standalone story and have a related (weirder) dream in sleep. Some stories have real people talk about their experience like a memoir.I can't say I like this game or not, it is one of a kind I can't expect any story in the next day - story told includes Picking up a way to  They don't give answers just left players in wander. If you care there are more in the drifting bottles, including the story about a lady hitting a bottle .I'm confused by the end but I believe it contains suicide contents and made peaceful, be aware.
