_childDocuments_.review: Back in March, I was able to try out one of the many Beta tests that were announced for West of Dead.  In the short period of gameplay, I enjoyed what was presented: crisp, punchy gunplay with a beautiful cel-shaded palette and a mountain of possibility.  Fast forward two months, and West of Dead presents its completed take on a rogue-like spaghetti western with paranormal tendencies.  How does it go?  South.  Very south.Much of what I touched upon in terms of plot has not changed since the Beta, so hop over  for a refresher on what Purgatory has to offer for William Mason.  West of Dead's saving graces fall solely upon its gameplay, weapon selection, and sound design.  Purgatory, Wyoming spans ten different areas, 6 main stages and 4 side stages, procedurally generated so no map will play out exactly the same.  Each stage is filled to the brim with an assortment of enemies: gun-wielding rangers, to demonic dogs, cleaver throwing giants, and murders of crows to name a few.  The fighting areas are tight and compact, with breakable cover to keep Mason on his toes, timing perfect dodges to avoid bullets and explosions and always staying close enough to see the lights of his enemy's eyes.  The cel-shaded, overly saturated style beams life into the desolate, dreary environments Mason will be see over and over again.  From crypts to farms, churches and mines, it is a nice blend of different areas to battle in, especially with some of the environmental hazards some of the stages sneak in.While relying heavily on tested titles like Dead Cells, the twin stick shooter's weapons are delightfully chunky and powerful.  The weapon selection is numerous among its four categories: Revolver, Pistol, Shotgun, and Rifle.  Collected Sin from fallen enemies can be traded with a mysterious Witch to unlock your arsenal, each displaying different variations to suit almost every style.  Mason can also hold two secondary items, which range from hard-hitting offensive items like axes and dynamite, to defensive items like shields and lanterns.  Rounding out a completed build are charms that can add passive abilities such as extra HP from healing items, or regaining lost health by hiding behind cover or inflicting damage on enemies.When all these pieces come together, the sound of a fast-paced battlefield is electric.  Rapid reloading, which is done automatically after not shooting for a short period of time, projects little noises of bullets filling their slots, the sound of an old time-y cash register pinning open after each enemy falls, the 5 note tune from an acoustic guitar signifying an emptied battlefield and a job well done: Upstream Arcade absolutely hit the nail on the head with making Purgatory, Wyoming feel as Wild West as it possibly could.While Purgatory is considered an avenue in the afterlife where one stays before judgment, West of Dead could've used a lot more time before finding its way out.  There are a ton of bugs and polish issues scattered throughout.  One of the biggest offenders is the game's auto-aim assist.  Aiming is not a precise objective, but more of a suggested idea, as long as enemies are within sight, guns will snap onto a target.  This can range from working as intended, to exploitative, to run-killing.  Longer ranged rifles can hit enemies off-camera so long as they are illuminated in light, but will also take precedence over enemies who are anywhere in the darkness.  Many times Mason will have an enemy barreling towards him, be just enough in the darkness, and Mason will snap to another enemy across the screen and maintain firing presence with that enemy.  Normally this wouldn't be an issue, since a quick flick of your aiming reticle would keep the closer target in line; but the auto-aim will always take the enemy in light over an enemy that is technically hidden in darkness, and won't peel off said enemy until they've been dispersed of.  It's an unnecessary inclusion of difficulty, as many runs have been tarnished by this mechanic, and the fact that auto-aim assist is an option that cannot be turned off is maddening.West of Dead's AI also finds itself riddled with issues.  You will constantly find enemies that won't engage in combat, even as Mason plugs holes into them, which makes some rooms disappointingly easy.  Outlaws, randomized mini-bosses that play a role in Mason's past life, can get stuck on collision after a slide over cover, and never fire another bullet, allowing Mason to casually drain their life bar and complete what would've been a tough fire fight.  This same problem happened with the first two main bosses in the game: they took one slide into cover, got stuck, and immediately went passive.  If you were interested in the difficulty of those main bosses, I literally could not tell you.But the biggest offender is the structure in which West of Dead handles its story telling.  Mason's life is shrouded in mystery, and can be slowly pieced together by eliminating outlaws, and accepting the burden of weary souls trapped within Purgatory.  Accepting burdens will reward Mason with a piece of his memory back, alongside able chunks of Sin, Iron, and weaponry to help in his journey, but each burden comes with a price.  Burdens will curse Mason, requiring him to kill a number of enemies before getting hit, with one hit while curse being an instant kill.  These do provide a tense atmosphere while demanding cautious traveling, but these moments play opposite of what West of Dead does well, which is delivering a fast-paced shootout.  Add on top the issues with auto-aim, and more deaths from accepting burdens will feel unfair than justified.Memories can be given to the Witch, which give a small chunk into how Mason got to where he is.  While these are interesting tidbits of plot, and more reasons to use Ron Perlman's voice acting, there's no way to look back and replay past memories, and with two different recollections happening between which memories you pull, it can be unnecessarily convoluted.Collecting all these memories and burdens will procure the chance for Mason to face the final boss.  Now, I understand the novelty of the “show, don't tell” style of story telling, letting the environment and actions tell the overarching story instead of slapping you in the face with it.  But the way West of Dead handles its unlocking of the True Ending is so needlessly concealed, that it absolutely kills any momentum in finishing its story.  After accepting three specific burdens needed to acquire the True Ending, the secondary objective while killing the final boss is never alluded to or represented in a way where the player would find out unless by sheer dumb luck.  While finishing my 2nd run, I had three friends watch the entire run, and none of us had any idea of what I missed to truly finish the game.  If you miss the secret objective and defeat the boss before completing it, your run is finished, and you go back to the very beginning, to do it all over again.  There's absolutely no excuse for not giving a hint, or just not having it in general, since there is already a prerequisite that needs to be accomplished before getting to the final boss for the True Ending.  It's just bad design, and a disappointing end to my 18 hours of game time.So with that, my time with William Mason is over, and the town of Purgatory, Wyoming is now behind me.  I started on this trail with a 30 minute demo that intrigued me enough to continue down its soon to be completed path, but when I got to the end of this road, I realized that the dirt road I was traveling on felt a lot like the state of West of Dead: usable at times, deemed effective by some, but ultimately incomplete by today's standards.What a shame.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic presentation. Very cool cover-based shooting. The overall game feel is great.I really  want a well executed version of this game to exist. I'd say the game really isn't that good, yet I still played it for about 7 well-enjoyed hours. So it definitely has something to it between the charm, presentation, and core ideas.Sadly it comes off as janky and oddly generic.There's an amount of jank to this game that continually surprised me throughout my few hours of game time.  I often found myself sticking to the same weapons more or less, because they just work well in most scenarios. I found the rogue-lite elements to be typical rehashes, and didn't offer many interesting choices to consider.If anyone can recommend a game that has this game's core mechanics, please let me know. It really is fun to play, but I cannot wholly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: places you firmly in the boots of William Mason, a lawman in a previous life now stuck in purgatory and seeking vengeance. A third-person rogue-lite shooter where every run assembles your shattered memories from 1888 Wyoming,  wishes he was this cool.The Steam store does this game justice.  was exactly what I wanted and exactly what I got. _childDocuments_.review: This is a game with many strong points. Great art and music. Satisfying combat at times. The loot feels varied and the meta-game progression doesn't feel all too micro transaction style grindy like in some other roguelites that use it. Ron Pearlman as the voice of the narrator is of course a joy to hear. You feel really sluggish because you have to wait for each animation before doing something else, no combining dodge rolls and attacks for example.Transitions between things take way too much time.Another thing that makes you feel like you've transformed into a slug is that every time you go near an object you can take cover behind you automatically take cover, very good when you want to take cover of course, but when you try to move out of an enemys way it can cause problems. But worse than that is that you still take cover even out of combat.Dialog repeats and it's again too slow to skip dialog and it often feels like the keypress to skip it doesn't register. "There it was, a way out of this place." Yeah come on,  just let me exit the damn floor, I've heard you say this a million times, if you need a loading screen just give me that and stop wasting my time with repetition. And along those lines, there's some messages I can only describe as tutorial popup's that happen every time you do some things. Like the lost souls whose burden you can overtake has a bunch of tutorial text along with whatever dialog they give each and every time.Having the mines be the starting level each and every run kinda sucks, it's by far the most generic environment in the game, in fact the only generic environment of those that I've seen so far, and they could have been in any random fantasy game, nothing about it shouts the wild west.The camera is sometimes very unhelpful and this in combination with the lock-on features adds a fair bit of artificial difficulty to the game.The keybindings for mouse and keyboard is kind of crud, and some of them can't be changed in the menus. As an example you navigate the menus while in game with 1 and 2 rather than the keys you have set to left and right.While the darkness is a part of the charm of the art style, it's sometimes just way too dark and it just feels like you're running through corridors with black painted walls.

_childDocuments_.review: The makings of a very good game are all in place, but unless you are highly tolerant of bugs and unintuitive controls, I would wait for the game to be patched.  Menu navigation, PC movement, NPC interaction, and aiming feel "off" to differing degrees.  Some may enjoy the drawn out, unskippable, and (in my opinion) overly frequent cutscenes and NPC animations, but personally, they just feel like they break the pacing of the game and waste time unnecessarily.  Do I want to wait 30 seconds after an outlaw battle to hear that the witch might be relevant to the "memories" dropped by the outlaw?  Sure, and maybe the first 3-4 times it feels immersive.  But after awhile, it's just like, damn, let me play the game, please?West of dead was recently moved out of beta, and I don't think that gives potential buyers an honest indication of the polish this game currently lacks.  Should be moved back to beta or otherwise be indicated that West of Dead is in a pretty janky state presently.

_childDocuments_.review: Very buggy. Forces you into taking damage at times which no roguelike should ever do, for example I've had kamikaze enemies sit at the top or bottom of ladders unmoving, there's no other way past and all I can do is climb up, which is painfully slow by the way, and wait for the canned animation to finish while the guy just blows up on me, potentially killing me outright if I have a burden I can't get rid of as that means you die in one hit.UI/UX is painful some (most?) of the time, for example there's no reason the aiming reticule should be constrained in the way it is if the user isn't using a controller. It leaves me frustrated the same way it does when the cursor drifts onto my second monitor in a poorly made FPS game. The UI was obviously built for consoles, scrolling menus with the mouse is absurdly slow to the point where you need to use WASD to scroll down it, and accidentally nudging the mouse while doing this sends you back to the top of the list. Combat sometimes feels quite nice, but the canned animations make it feel very clunky at times, for example when I'm trying to pull away from cover but instead he just slowly crouches down and walks around it, or the aforementioned ladders being so slow and the guy apparently needs to straighten his poncho or some ♥♥♥♥ when he reaches the top. The fast travel portal animation is just stupidly slow as well which when combined with the so incredibly obtuse fast travel selection screen means it's often quicker, or at least less frustrating to just walk. There's barely any mouse control on the fast travel screen at all, you can select a point, but if the point you want is off screen you need to manually click your way along the list until you can see it and hope you don't accidentally double click or it'll lock you into the silly animation again.Please, if I'm not in combat just disable the cover system. Jesus christ, I spend thirty seconds walking for every ten second fight, fights do not last a long time at all so let's give traversal a little love shall we? Especially if we're intent on the fast travel system being nauseating to use.A list of points I'd love to see improved:• Let me move the fast travel map by clicking and dragging it around. Simple, but would vastly improve the experience.• Disable locking into cover outside of combat or just make taking cover automatically a toggle so when I need to enter "cover mode" I just hit a button and bam. But when I'm out of combat I'm not struggling to navigate the world.• Please for ♥♥♥♥ sake, just let me scroll the list of stuff in the Witch Store with the mouse wheel, technically you can but it would take forever to actually get to the bottom of the list. Make it scroll at a reasonable speed, or make it so holding W or S scrolls it properly, and the selection option doesn't reset when you move the mouse. • Unconstrain the cursor when playing with mouse. Or make that an option in the menu, whatever. It makes sense for analog sticks, I get that, but in a PC release mouse and keyboard are the standard and this game plays better with a mouse and keyboard anyway, movement aside.In short, the game's very pretty and has some good ideas but even the best idea can be made frustrating by poorly polished UI/UX mechanics and clunky animations that prevent you from responding to things you otherwise would have. It just feels like no one on the dev team played this game with a mouse and keyboard for more than five minutes. Feels early access. Even though I'm giving it a negative review, I do think the game can be fun so I won't be refunding it. I just can't recommend a game that feels frustrating to play much of the time, even though this feeling stems from what should be relatively minor problems to fix. I hope they are, and if they are I'll be happy to swap this review to a positive one.

_childDocuments_.review: West Of Dead is a roguelite shooter. Players take on the role of a nameless flaming-skull cowboy, fighting through hordes of enemies in order to recover his memories, his true identity, and a way out of this grim Purgatory. This game is easily one of the unique entries in the genre in terms of combat. The flow of gameplay offers a different approach to the speedy, combat-heavy peers. However, outside of gameplay, the game feels flawed. Many inconveniences and technical issues can easily push the players away from it. The game as a whole is functional and playable, mind you. I just have a feeling that this game should be advertised as an almost-finished-early-access product  because of the lack of polishing. Still, I would recommend West Of Dead since it provides ample enjoyment to play through."Slower Enter The Gungeon, but with no bullet hell and limited dodge." is the simple way to describe this game. Most of the time rougelite shooters are easily connected with bullet hell, which often leads to the testament of players' reflexes and their characters' maneuver. West Of Dead does this feature the opposite way. The game encourages you to take your cover, take your aim, and take your shot during every combat encounter. The slow pace might throw you off guard in the beginning if you are used to faster shooters. Once you are familiar with the flow of the hunt, it is actually quite relaxing and rewarding. The game does throw in some agile enemies to shift the pace, but like in bullet hell, you only need to observe your surroundings to quickly position yourself to a safer cover and resume to your "target practice". The "Dodge" ability functions more like a last resort for avoiding damage since there is a recovery time before the next dodge attempt. If you grow tired of the fast-paced roguelite games, West Of Dead is a nice change of pace.There are adequate amount of weapons in West Of Dead. The player's arsenal is divided into two parts: guns and abilities. Guns, for sure are your main damage resource and each gun provides a different playstyle. A consistent and reliable six shooter that offers critical hit every five shots, a shotgun which encourages you to shoot from cover, or even rifles that inflict status effect and stun your enemies. Different guns offer different strategies. It is vital to choose the guns that fit your appetite. Abilities, on the other hand, serve more as crowd control and utility. Daggers are great interruption for melee-focus enemies. Various emblems give you different buffs to your character. Bombs and Lantern help you control the field, turning the tide to your favor. My favorite build is Freezer and Escalator, Axe and Lantern. Freezer slows tough enemies which offer easier chance to take advantage of increasing damage from the Escalator. When things get dicey, throwing axe to deter the closest enemy and throwing down lantern to stun all the enemies in proximity. This combination gives me sufficient information to decide whether to retrieve or take my shot.Very inconsistently, each level has a chance to not spawn an exit or having the exit locked behind a rune-gated room, which requires specific rune that function as permanent power such as break down metal door or receive zero fall damage. This problem almost ruined my enjoyment for the game. Out of ten playthroughs there were four runs I was forced to restart because the exit and even the boss room were locked behind a metal door. In order to break the metal doors I needed to find and defeat Boss B. What's even worse was that the area of Boss B was locked behind a teleport sigil, which requires me to defeat Boss A, aka the boss in the area I was stuck. How does exit and boss room not being set as guaranteed access and important room spawn is beyond me. Luckily in later runs I never encountered the problem again, but this is still a concerning issue in an emergency to be fixed.I don't how exactly I did to make them stuck in place or looping that one vault-through-cover animation but it is a constant phenomenon which needs to be addressed. The one reason I can think of is throwing abilities at them in rapid succession while they perform specific action. For my experiences, throwing Axe and Dynamite when they are vaulting often force the outlaws to showcase their majestic stamina, vaulting over cover constantly without breaking a sweat. This bug breaks my showdown immersion with these bosses.→Pause menu can only be controlled with keyboards, but the main menu and upgrade menu can be controlled with both.→The upgrade menu cannot be scrolled down with wheel.→The mouse and keyboard in menu respond a bit slowly.→Option to refresh shop items.→Items and guns should be sold separately. I am tired of seeing three items in the shop when I need a better gun.→Rooms should be locked once combat begins. It is easy to run out of enemies' aggro range and shoot them safely.→Contexts display weirdly. Often the dialogue often start anew mid-sentence.→Corridors between rooms are still too long.

_childDocuments_.review: West of Dead will be very familiar to people who've played games like Dead Cells or Curse of the Dead Gods.A lot of the mechanics are incredibily similar, but what makes the game unique is its atmosphere & combat.You play as a cowboy in purgatory, where light is your friend.Once you enter a room, you need to scout it, hopefully without being spotted. You take quite a decent amount of damage per hit, so it's highly recommended to take cover. Now instead of you taking damage, your cover will. However, it'll eventually be destroyed, which forces you to switch.You can not aim at enemies in darkness, which means you have to try and find a way to illuminate them. The most common way is to run up to an unlit lantern, and light it. Yes, you will expose yourself out of cover, which is what makes the rush so exciting. But if you manage to do it before getting shot, it will blind enemies nearby, which then rewards your risk.You can hold two primary guns at once. Shotguns, rifles, revolvers, pistols all control slightly differently in terms of range, hold or tap to shoot etc. They also can come with random traits like bleeding, pushback etc.You also have two alternate "gadgets". This can be a long cooldown axe that does massive damage, which can save you in a sticky situation. Or it could be a Sherrif's badge that reduces your damage.As you explore the randomly generated area, you will find different paths. Some contain shops, some contain upgrade stations where you can choose if you want to improve your health, gun damage, or gadget damage.Quite early on, you will earn the ability to teleport back and forth between some portals that allows you to fully explore the map if you choose to.You can also choose which exit you'd like to take, which will determine what next area you'll end up in, as you progress through the game.There is also a permanent progression system. Between levels, you come to a witch where you can spend your sin. You can not leave the room until you have spent it all, on brand new weapons and tools that can now be found in your playthroughs.After the witch, you can fill up a healing flask, which can be used during your battles in emergencies.Although the combat is great, it can get a bit samey after a while. I'm hoping that as I play more, I'll see a bit more variety when it comes to the extra gadgets. I'll confirm either way in this review, when that time comes.So to those that have played games like Dead Cells, you'll no doubt catch all the inspirations this game took, but I don't think it's a bad thing at all. The formula is fun in the end, and the combat is really fresh and intense.Switching between cover, and your guns, lighting up torches and barely dodging out of the way of an attack can be incredibly overwhelming, but rewarding when done right.I think the world and story is intriguing, and the atmosphere is done very well.Recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: West of Dead

_childDocuments_.review: West of Dead is a twin-stick roguelite shooter where you play as an undead gunslinger regaining his memories as he navigates the darkened labyrinths of an Old West-styled Underworld. But design, controls, and technical issues bog down what is otherwise a game with top-notch presentation.The gameplay consists of navigating through various mazes, going room by room and finding enemies, gun boxes, or upgrade shrines. There's an emphasis placed on the dark and light in the game. Enemies that are shrouded in the dark obviously can't be seen, but in addition, it's very difficult to target them. You can counteract this by running up to lanterns and lighting them up, which stuns enemies in its light radius and allows you to lock onto them. A heavy emphasis is put on staying in cover, as enemies chunk your health with each shot. You're able to carry two firearms, each with their own respective ammunition count. Reloading is performed automatically, chamber by chamber, whenever you're not firing. Weapons are about what you'd expect from the Old West. The majority fall into one of the three categories: pistols, shotguns, and rifles. As you play the game, you unlock weapons with on-hit effects, such as the Razorshot rifle, causing bullets to also put a bleed DoT on your target. Equipment is similar. You also have two slots, but all equipment has a cooldown, which can be shortened through equipment level and by upgrading your equipment CD reduction. You can find equipment like hand-held lanterns, which you can toss to stun enemies in an area or there's also equipment which can damage enemies, like axes, dynamite, and throwing daggers.Progression is fairly straightforward. As you kill enemies, you gather Sin. You can spend Sin at the end of each level by talking to the Witch, where you can unlock new weapons, passives, and equipment. As you go through each level, you'll discover weapon chests and upgrade shrines. Weapon chests contain upgraded weapons to pick up. At upgrade shrines you can upgrade one of three stats: Health (Higher HP, Higher melee damage), Perception (Firearm damage), and Equipment (Higher equipment damage and CD reduction). These stats do  carry over to new runs if you die.You play an undead gunslinger, going through a cel-shaded Old West underworld in search of who you were in life. The main character is voiced by Ron Perlman, who nails every single line given to him. Guns feel good to shoot, and the levels are varied. Expect to explore areas like an abandoned mine; a rotting cornfield; and even a dark, murky swamp. When you die, you're sent to a dreary saloon, bartender included. You can speak to various characters in the game, but five and a half hours in, I didn't find any other characters that were voice-acted. It feels like the main character single-handedly carries the game forward. The NPC's aren't particularly interesting nor have any depth, going only by their profession: Bartender, Trader, Witch-Woman, etc. When you speak to them, they don't have a lot to say. Maybe one or two sentences at most.Here's the elephant in the room. I'll preface this by saying I played WoD on mouse and keyboard. The mouse works  of the time, key word 'most.' Most of the time you'll see your bullets shooting your intended target, but sometimes, especially for enemies in the dark, it's like the game purposefully tilts your aim off as if you're not supposed to hit that target. You'll either hit another enemy off to the side or miss entirely.This is also often the case with using equipment. For example, I had the throwing axe at one point. It stuns whoever it hits and deals a chunk of damage. Approaching a room, I can see a ranged enemy and a melee one at both sides of the door. My plan was to axe the ranged enemy to stun it, kill it before it had the chance to shoot me, and kite the melee before finishing it off. Simple, right? Instead of throwing the axe at the ranged enemy, the axe instead flung itself off to the side, hitting a distant enemy that wasn't even on the screen despite me aiming at my intended target the entire time. The lanterns are another example of this. When you want to chuck a lantern to stun an enemy five feet away from you, you instead throw the lantern out over the enemy's head.This isn't just limited to attacking enemies or using equipment; this is also the case with dodging attacks or entering cover. The way you enter cover is you simply approach it and you'll hide behind it. You can slide into cover with the Dodge button or you can vault over cover with the same button. Dodge and Vault being on the same button means that sometimes when you want to slide into cover, you instead vault over it and put yourself in plain view of enemies, promptly turning to swiss cheese and dying.The problem with entering or exiting cover not being a dedicated, separate keybind and instead being proximity-based means that you'll also die because you're fighting with the cover system. For example, you often have to dodge AoE attacks, like the dynamite explosions. An enemy chucks dynamite at you, and you're running to avoid it. However, you run by cover, and you get magnetically locked to it, slowing your speed to a snail's pace and causing you eat the explosion you intended to avoid. This is also the case when shooting enemies when you're also trying to enter cover. You get locked into the shooting animation and you'll just stand there, walking against the cover instead of entering it and eating a bullet because of it.Dying is expected in a roguelite, but dying because the controls aren't doing what you want is extremely frustrating. I can confidently say the majority of my deaths five and a half hours in were because of the controls. It genuinely feels like you're fighting with them, and it's actively trying to screw you over at times.Some design choices really make me scratch my head, especially for a game that's on PC. You often can't use the mouse to interact with the Esc menus. You instead have to slowly scroll through the menu tabs with the keys. This is most apparent when you're spending Sin to unlock stuff. You can't mouseover unlocks, and because of that, you can't see the descriptions of what you're buying unless you use the keyboard to slowly scroll through every single item on the list and get to the one you want.In addition, you can't rebind keys. I found this especially frustrating because the UI reverses the buttons on the screen. Your right click button is on the left and your left click is on the right. This is also a problem with the two equipment slots; The left equipment slot is R, and the right equipment slot is E. Because the buttons are reversed and you're unable to rebind them, you'll often use the wrong tool for the job, shooting your shotgun when you intended to use your rifle or using a knife and hitting air instead of chucking dynamite at that enemy in the distance you intended to hit.There are also technical issues. When you speak to NPC's, the UI disappears, and a letter box shrinks the screen. Normally, this would add to immersion and remove distractions. But there's a bug with the game, wherein sometimes when you're skipping through the cutscene dialogue after you visit the trader or skipping through any NPC's dialogue, the UI won't appear again and the letterbox stays on the screen. To my knowledge, there isn't a fix other than just hitting Esc, going to the main menu, and going back to where you were.I really wanted to like this game. The cel-shaded Old Western underworld setting is extremely unique and compelling. And Ron Perlman's voice work is top-notch. He nails the main character, and Ron really gives him personality. But I can't recommend this game due to the above issues, where you're fighting the controls and there's a lack of basic options such as rebindable keys.

_childDocuments_.review: Seeing some baffling reviews and actually for once feel compelled to weigh in as the Only Person Who Is Ever Right about Anything:1: IS IT ROOTIN'?Cowboys. Wyoming. The afterlife. The texture is gritty but not pretentious - it feels mature and tasteful at every step. I'd qualify it by saying that I want... A Little MORE of that texture - I've found that after only a few hours I seem to have exhausted new dialogue, including dialogue from the man in the saloon whose sole purpose appears to be to provide dialogue. Regardless - the lone gunslinger sheriff feel is on point. The visuals too execute extremely well on the abstraction - and this is in a game under 230 MB in size - around a quarter of the size of its own OST. Also Ron Perlman no seriously did you guys sell your souls or-- Ok no I actually do want to elaborate on that by stressing that I find Mason's narration equal parts amusing and pathetic (in the like, literary sense, as in it-- nevermind i'm just going to move on) and it portrays a great sheriff-turned-phantom. Also maybe I'm crazy but those subtle nods to primal myths native to the american west are cool (its been forever since i was in a fun college class let me have this)2: IS IT TOOTIN'?Yes. The music is beautiful and dynamic, understated but diverse and flavorful. The game can feel a tad quiet from time to time, even with the volume sliders all the way up, but in fairness it keeps the dynamics punchy and the sound effects pointed. The little dings and bangs of play are all great (with the sole exception, as far as i've progressed, of the upgraded melee sound effect). Fights end with these little musical stings that make me literally want to go "yeah.... I'm the sheriff baby." I kind of get the sense that the entire voice budget was spent on Ron Perlman though. Maybe it's more artistic than I'm giving it credit for.3: BY GOD, IS IT SHOOTIN'?Ok I have a lot to say here. Firstly, though, I think it's important to give some context to the gameplay for someone looking at potentially buying this game: It is a twin stick shooter and a roguelike, in a sense. The game focuses heavily on strategy, where you never know what situation exactly you'll find yourself in but attacks and moves are highly predictable and can always be outsmarted on their own terms or, sometimes, yours. Enemies are only visible and targetable in the light, so lighting lanterns or finding other light sources is essential to your survival. Find guns and support items on each floor, make multiple runs to unlock more advanced rewards, unravel a story - fight the odd boss, use cover. I've seen the criticism leveled at this that the twin stick controls are really built around the auto-aim, and, yes, I agree, they are. I also think it's very very in keeping with the more strategic spirit of the game. If anything, the circumstances where you are meant to be dependent on manual aim serve more to punish you for not controlling the lighting in a room. I can't think of a lot of games I've played that are so fast paced while all gunshots are essentially certain hits - if you fire on an enemy in the light and have a clear line of sight, it Will connect, and the same is true for them, so it's less about being good at clicking on bad guys and more about knowing when and where to move so that you can make your attack before they make one on you.The game has its share of minor bugs - I've gotten frozen after a boss once (though restarting the game fixed it without ending my run, thankfully) and on one occasion I had some kind of encounter with a respawning piece of cover that deleted my body but very much allowed enemies to attack me. These really haven't diminished my enjoyment of the game, and they're rare enough that you needn't consider them an inevitability.4: BUT MOST OF ALL, IS IT KIND?Yeah it's pretty nice.

_childDocuments_.review: I definitely don't hate the game, but I'm having a hard time loving it either.I think the style is fantastic, makes for a very visually striking game.The gameplay is seriously lacking though.From inconsistent/unreliable controls, to janky or awkward interactions, the game is just kinda hard to play for all the wrong reasons.The cover mechanics are nice, but annoyingly aggressive/magnetic. It can be annoying trying to fight enemies or avoid attacks when your character is basically stuck to cover against your will, especially since they move much slower in cover as well. Which wouldn't be so bad if it was deliberately my choice to get into cover in the first place.Not to mention the game seems heavily reliant on you being in cover since most rooms and fights are littered with it and the game buffs your reload speed for being in it.Which on the topic of reloading, since all guns reload automatically and only one bullet at a time, it can be slightly annoying trying to keep track of how much ammo you have left, or even when you're actually reloading. Since the only way you can deliberately reload is to just stop doing anything, up to and including avoiding being shot/whacked. Though you can still move of course.But also coupled with awkward reload and cover mechanics is awkward shooting mechanics as well. While pistols and shotguns feel well enough with not having any sort of 'wind up/aiming' time, rifles are cumbersome to use and deal '' damage. Especially since your 'crosshair' is tethered to your character with less range than a shotgun combined with the sort of isometric and ever-changing camera position, it can be really frustrating and annoying even trying to line up accurate shots especially at even slightly longer ranges. Even more than that though the game also suffers from the same problem almost all top-down 'isometic' style shoots suffer from which is depth perception. Which is to say it can be hard to tell where various in-world elements are (crosshair, projectiles, enemies, AOE effects, etc) in relation to other things in space. So ultimately the game effectively forces you to always play as close to the enemies as possible, but also wants you to keep your distance which can be hard to do either with all the jank you have to deal with. So I have no clue how the game expects players to play.The in-run upgrades are pretty disappointing too. The earlier level of these upgrades give significant improvements but give exponentially worse improvements at higher levels. While I understand this is likely to encourage players to diversify in their upgrades, it also actively punishes specialization and is still ultimately bad even for people who  diversify since at some point the upgrades become effectively pointless regardless of what you choose.Speaking of which enemy scaling seems like it needs more work as well since between levels, enemy stats increase at such a rate where you really  better/higher level guns between each stage. Which even that only takes you so far since the only stat that seems to increase with a guns level is its base damage, and only by a bit. A Level 5 gun is significantly better than a level 1, but a level 2 is only marginally better than a level 1.Even the abilities didn't get much use out of me since they're either too situational/didn't work half the time, or just generally a bit ineffective.But I dunno, maybe it gets better if you  invest your time into it, and like I said I certainly don't hate it.However I just can't really see myself coming back to this game any time soon, or at all for that matter.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this. It's oozing with style, Ron Perlman does excellent VA work, but it just doesn't come together gameplay-wise. A few rapid-fire complaints:- Animations like warping between waypoints and jumping down ledges take way too long given how often it happens- Weapon unlocks are largely meh, which is made worse by the fact that the meh weapons will bloat the loot pool and you can't always tell how good a weapon is prior to unlocking.- Dialogue is hard to skip, which wouldn't be a problem if a) gameplay wasn't halted during almost all dialogue and b) the lines weren't so repetitive. I have sympathy for the latter, as I'm sure Perlman didn't come cheap, but it should still be easier to bypass.- Instability. In under ten hours I had a run broken when I tried to continue it and couldn't progress through a hallway without falling into a void, and a softlock right before an Outlaw encounter that required quitting out of the game. Not a banner performance.And perhaps my biggest issue: Tying in with the animation complaint, the game just feels very slow to play in many ways. A lot of time is spent lightly jogging through samey corridors and busting open boarded doorways for no good reason. You're encouraged to hide behind cover by appreciably quicker reload speeds, so uninspired defensive shootouts are often the norm. Your character snaps to cover when available and takes a second to break free of it, giving even less incentive to leave cover and making it feel like flypaper you're struggling to escape. Enemy HP can massively outweigh your DPS if you don't get good upgrades, making for tiresome magdumps either sitting behind cover or kiting.The novelty of the game and its presentation allayed most of these issues for the first couple hours as I got to new areas and heard new voice lines, but for the past 3 or so I've been persisting trying to get the "Righteous Path" ending as one last hurrah, but instead finding much annoyance whenever I fail and find myself back at the start of a Sisyphean, molasses-wading run. I just can't do it.This might still be worth it if you REALLY dig the presentation, grab it on sale, and don't have the same gripes with the gameplay as I do, but make sure to tap out when you find yourself not having fun - if you get to that point, it probably isn't going to get better.

_childDocuments_.review: If I could put a neutral review, I would. But for multiple factors, I can't recommend it, especially at full price. The pros:-art style and general atmosphere (as others have pointed out) is very Mike Mignola Hellboy reminiscient, its really cool-music/SFX are great-Just the presence of Ron Perlman is a W-upgrade system is nice and simple-the shooting itself is fun as is learning how each weapon works-game isn't super RNG dependent, you can usually scrape by on the stuff you find/buy and its pretty easy to unlock and try new stuff often-runes are nice when you get them. beat a boss, find a rune adding something new to your kit so youre more likely to find upgrades/items in the future. tho it does suck to initially have so many paths you can't take because "you need something to get across this"Cons (Pretty much all gameplay):-I'm ok with the fixed camera angles but they are so unhelpful at times and you can do nothing about it-getting into/exiting/moving around cover is so sluggish and feels like ass, how does this happen when its a core ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mechanic of the game-I also felt that aiming with the mouse was sort of sluggish too but ymmv on that tbh-i swear enemies with guns have autoaim if you're not in cover. you can dodge one shot from the same enemy just to get smacked by a second or third and it feels ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awful. this is particularly egregious in the  fights. -there are some enemies that are melee only and a smaller subset that you have to let get closer to you to even be able to shoot them. and then you have a 0.5s reaction window to dodge or try to kill them or get ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. WHY. -theres a whole mechanic built around light. turn on a light, nearby enemies get stunned, you can actually see in a small-ish area around it. this is fine. what is not fine is feeling like you're pinned down by gunfire that you can't see where its coming from exactly and have to either blindfire or risk taking lead because hee hoo, you dont get to see in this room and you really want to even be able to shoot, find cover and generally exist-speaking of stun, the stun mechanic isn't really explained well if at all. almost all, if not all, enemies have a white bar and a green bar, white for stun, green for health. white bar goes down, enemy gets stunned for a while. different guns have different stun damage. but the game never explains any of this to you, or if it did it was easily overlooked.I had one very successful run where I got through Chapter 1 and 2, two  encounters and what I believe to be a final boss, died because I made a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ weapon swap and asked myself if I wanted to go through two sections of 3 levels again just to fight this cancerous boss again. I don't. So I gave up. If you like roguelikes with small roguelite and RPG elements, consider playing West of Dead. but dont get it full price and know how rough the core gameplay experience feels

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to like this game even despite the weird camera and slow paced combat, but it quickly falls short as a roguelike. Every weapon feels the same, every outlaw (boss) encounter feels the same, and every generic encounter feels the same. Even as you unlock new weapons and abilities, they don't really change the gameplay. You get the same rifles, shotguns, and pistols, but with different rate of fire, magazine size and damage. The most unorthodox weapon is flame gun which also illuminates the area around it's projectile, and this is important since many enemies are hidden in the dark.Alas, West of Dead fails to implement this "illuminate the location to see enemies" mechanic properly. Either you switch on the lamps scattered around room, or you can't see enemies at all (with the exception of flame gun). This is incredibly primitive and quickly gets so boring. And it feels like the game is unfinished, because similar concept with darkness in Curse of the Dead Gods is implemented so much better. There, you have a torch, but you can't use it with weapons, so you have to decide when to attack and when to use the torch to light up the fires or illiminate the area around you. What, there're no lamps or torches in the Wild West?The same goes to other features of the game that feel raw and unfinished. Collecting memories which unlock boring (and unskippable!) scenes, hunting for items/upgrades to reach new areas (a-la metroidvania), unlocking meta-progression items with only one currency and only a small selection of items to unlock at once (staple roguelites like Hades have several currencies to progress in several types of unlocks simultaneously, which is way more fun). Everything about this games screams mediocre and/or unfinished.So why waste time on this when there are tons of great rogulikes with much more interesting combat and progression?

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like we've been getting a lot of these stylized action roguelikes lately, and for the most part they've been pretty good. West of Dead is yet another game trying to tackle the genre, but with some cool twists of its own.So starting with what is most obvious about the game: its aesthetic. West of Dead is a very dark game, and I mean that quite literally. There's not a lot light to go around and the sheer amount of shadowing emphasizes what little you can see. The color choices are even muted to help further this look, with most of the levels being constructed almost entirely out of darker colors. Of course, this makes enemies and such harder to see, but that's the point.This is why light plays such an important role in combat. There are a number of lanterns scattered around that, once lit, briefly stun enemies in the same room and allow the use of your gun's lock on feature, which is disabled when shooting into darkness. It's a simple mechanic, but it's a cool way to tie the gameplay into the visuals. The audio that goes along with them isn't that bad either.It plays pretty much like any other roguelike. Gameplay sessions are divided into runs in which you traverse a series of levels and upgrade your stuff along the way, losing everything once you die. The core gameplay loop here is very defined — you enter a cycle of "enter room, kill enemies, pick up loot, and move on". That's not necessarily a bad thing, as other mechanics can shake things up, but I found the variety here to be pretty underwhelming.It doesn't take long before you start running into the same room layouts with the same enemies and little in the way of differentiating them. One thing the game is sorely lacking in are special rooms, kinda like The Binding of Isaac's secret rooms, sacrifice rooms, etc. With West of Dead, you pretty much just get your shop and upgrade rooms, that's it. The core gameplay loop may be solid, but the lack of anything to really shake it up does bring down the experience a bit.What really brings the game down though are the numerous design and technical issues. The most notable of these is unfortunately one of the game's core mechanics: its lock on feature. As you are only able to lock on to enemies in the light, this makes aiming when there are multiple enemies a bit difficult. It wasn't uncommon for me to try to be aiming at one enemy, only for the game to direct all of my shots just to the left or right of him, hitting an enemy farther back in the room.You can even completely exit a room and still be forced to lock on to an enemy in that room, rather than the enemy that followed you out of it and is now about to damage you. It is an utterly flawed mechanic and has caused me numerous unfair hits and even deaths. It would be different if this was something that could be toggled, but that is not the case here. It is forced on the player on all methods of control, even keyboard and mouse (which cannot even be remapped, but that's another issue entirely).That's not the only issue though, there's also the lack of a dedicated melee button, the wonky game camera that can sometimes make enemies hard to see around corners, and the fact that it's difficult to hit enemies that are right in front of you. Although that last one is likely a design choice, it doesn't make it any less annoying, especially given how dodgy the melee can be.Ladders are also an issue, as you are unable to change the elevation of your shots. If an enemy is right at the top of that ladder, you will be forced to slowly climb up to meet it, oftentimes eating an attack as a result. The game's cover system has also gotten me a few times. There's no dedicated "take cover" button, you automatically magnet to cover when next to it. This not only decreases your movement speed, but makes it difficult to wrap corners without exiting cover first. The amount of times I found myself taking shots because I accidentally got too close to cover was much higher than it should be.And then there's the more blatant technical issues, such as the time I got stuck on a ledge and took damage until I died or the numerous instances where I activated a portal and nothing happened. It's not fun having to close and re-open to fix these issues, so hopefully these are something that can be patched with time.With all of that said though, I cannot recommend West of Dead. Although the core gameplay is solid, the lack of variety and numerous technical issues really bring down the experience. From the many design flaws to the actual bugs, there are quite a few issues plaguing an otherwise decent game. Perhaps this will be a game that I may recommend in the future, but as it stands, I cannot in good faith do so.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: I'll cut it to the quick and say BUY ON SALE.Why? For one, I beat the game on my second try. Which made things a little awkward because there were many mentions of stuff I would've been doing with various NPC's prior to beating the game. Maybe I'm lucky, or maybe I'm just good but I have better reasons.The game has a lot of small but slow frustrating sections. I'm not talking about combat. I mean teleporting to various locations around the map, talking with NPCs, and buying upgrades take just way too long. Again not like they take minutes, but they're seconds upon seconds of time with dialogue skips that don't do a whole lot and forced interactions. By that I mean you talk with an NPC, they say their lines and this takes a bit and then you accept the quest or whatever and they say another thing. Just some wasted time, why there needs to be a big change of perspective for something so small, and something so frequent, is frustrating. Secondly, some enemies kind of lag behind or bug out, and I wouldn't mention it unless it was so frequent. These stone golems are constantly fidgeting and the final boss would slide on his feet multiple times. Granted, the gun play was fun and the idea of using cover is something unexplored in other roguelites I've played. The guns all feel satisfying to use, but it's also frustrating that because of the reload on many of them, some guns just feel un-viable at higher level floors or against certain bosses.Ron Perlmans voice acting is great, and I can tell he cared about what he was doing, putting some real emotion behind the lines that required it. But after only about 6 hours of play (in a roguelite, where you're supposed to play over and over), lines would come up again and again over and over. It got annoying. Sort of like that "I can't go in this room yet" or "This door is locked from the other side" sort of frustrations.Now you could turn the voice down to zero, I imagine, I haven't checked. But even then you'd be missing out on the cutscenes and memories which add some compelling layers to the story, which was the only reason I continued to play. Overall, it is fun and provides and interesting story and fun gameplay. However, the repetition of voice lines, and the frequent micro-cutscenes such as NPC interactions, sign reading, and laddering climbing add a lot of forced dull time. I would recommend it, but not for $20.

_childDocuments_.review: First things first, I am normally not into 'roguelike' games but I picked this up cheap due to the overall art style, setting and, of course, Ron Perlman's voice work. Let's just say this has been a very pleasant and addictive surprise for me!I've been playing this with a controller on PC and find it snappy to understand/use. The cover mechanic, which sometimes gets lambasted as being 'too sticky', takes some getting used to but never caused me any major issues. _childDocuments_.review: West of Dead is one of those games where I'd give it a sideways thumb. I don't necessarily recommend it, but I don't think its a bad game outright. The cover based shooting is fun and the perfectly timed dodges are satisfying, but ultimately the game is just ~okay~ which is fine. Not every game can be the next Chrono Trigger, Super Mario World, or Halo 2. The first 8~12 hours were a lot of fun, learning the mechanics and enemy patterns and such, but after that, and after having to beat the game 3 times because the game doesn't even remotely hint at what to do for the "secret" ending, other than "help your friends," it started to get old. The achievements are unnecessarily stretched out to pad the game with "content," namely the achievements for helping 50 Lost Souls and killing 50 Outlaws. This could easily be cut in half and many people would get it naturally just by playing the game the way it is intended, instead of having to reset for a proper RNG room number to spend a few hours grinding with no other purpose in the game. Using a guide I was able to see my numbers of Outlaws and Lost Souls that I had helped (which the game doesn't tell you by itself, another quality of life update that would have gone a long way) and at the 17 hour mark I was at roughly 24 for each, and I don't even typically play this genre of game. Cutting these numbers down would have been completely fine, turning these achievements into something most people might naturally pick up along the way instead of having to commit a few extra hours to grinding. West of Dead is also a game riddled with bugs. I can not tell you how many times Mason would be talking about the Outlaw, and then the game just stops working. It doesn't freeze, things are still going on, but the pause menu doesn't work, you can't move, you can't shoot, just an infinitely long stare-down between Mason and the enemy Outlaw. Thankfully the game has autosaves so it's not that big of a deal in the grand scheme, but this is only one of a handful of bugs I encountered. If you're rolling near some cover that is in the middle of respawning, you can just clip through the floor, or more commonly, you can become invisible and invincible. This would be neat and funny, except that while invisible you also can't shoot at anything so you just can't play the game and are once again forced to reset. When you clip through the floor or fall off the edge, enemies can and will still swarm and attack you during the game's animation of bringing you back up to the floor, which has cost me more than a few of my runs. Again, autosaves save your life here, but its still kind of bizarre that a company that could get Ron Pearlman as the voice actor for their leading role somehow couldn't patch out some relatively basic game bugs, especially in a game built like it could probably run on a PlayStation 2.I outright do not recommend the DLC though. It takes everything that the base game pushes you to do and just throws it out the window. It consists of trench-like hallways, and you climb and descend ladders to get into each room for actual combat. This is fine and all, except that the new DLC enemies that spawn have Mortar guns, which fire bursts of 6 at a time, arcing upward and thus can go around any of the cover you're behind, and destroy any destructible cover in 1 or 2 shots. The game also loves to spawn two of that particular enemy instead of one, as well as a few little guys who just run at you either way to flush you out and keep you in harm's way. These things compiled on top of the face that you can't reload your guns within a certain time limit between dodging makes the DLC level very frustrating to get through, also considering that the damage from both enemy's mortars can overlap and render your dodge roll useless, allowing you to dodge one but not the other because they're clustered together but spaced out enough to ignore your i-frames. You can call it a "skill issue" on my end because as I said I don't normally play these types of games, but when nearly every source of help online and even in the guides section here on Steam tells you to "just stand outside the doorway and fire your guns in, just cheese it bro" then there's something wrong with the fundamentals of the way the DLC is designed. You shouldn't have to completely alter your playstyle in order to continue playing the game in the way it was originally designed. I tried and tried to play the level the legitimate way, but after 6 or 7 times I finally had to cheese it because it is just so unforgiving overall (any of the ricochet guns and the buzzsaw are life savers here). I wanted to love this game. I remember seeing the trailer revealed a few years ago and thinking to myself that it looks really cool and interesting, I thought it was awesome that Ron Pearlman was in it, the setting is really cool, and I really liked the art style. But between my completionist nature for games with low achievement counts, the bugs, the overall lack of story to be told and the irrelevance of your friends despite the strange narrative push with them, and the unbalanced DLC, I can only say that I liked it, and only really in the first half of my playtime. Pick it up on sale if you really want to try it out, or play it free on Xbox Game Pass, but I can't recommend this game for anything more than like $10.

_childDocuments_.review: When I originally reviewed this, I received a beta build and it was just prior to the release. After playing the 1.0, there are some things to point out. First off, I want this game to take off because at its core, I love it. I also want to encourage more games to be in this gritty styling and era. BUT there are some things that currently push me more toward being "On the Fence" of this game than a "Yes". Pros:- I love the simple dark gritty graphic novel-esque environmental design. It gives such cool vibes and works well with what they are trying to create with the overall game. - I think Ron Perlman does a simple but engaging job with the VO. It works for the character, for the vibe the devs seem to want to portray. I like it! - The animations from sliding across cover, doing a rolling dive, to flipping your gun around and into the holster are very well done. It's really enjoyable and brings more life to the mechanics you do / interactions you have in the game. - I really enjoy the variety of enemies and the design for them. They are familiar, in a way concerning the archetype of enemies we tend to come across in games, while also bringing something a bit different. I WANT this game to be epic and do incredibly well just from the above BUT...Cons:- The game is meant for controller use and yet there are glaring issues with the aiming in the game (especially when enemies are in shadows - an element purposefully placed in the first place to hide enemies and to create more dynamic fight interactions.) Playing the game with mouse and keyboard can assist against some of the bad aim assisting in the game but the game isn't meant for mouse and keyboard, so you'll have a much clunkier experience overall (in menus etc). - Though the aim/targeting in the game has clear issues for players, the AI has impeccable aim/targeting (whether you are in shadows or not and without even needing line-of-sight of you) -  There are times where you will find an enemy on higher ground than you and you have to climb a ladder to get to them. I like this playing of verticality in a game like this BUT enemies can still hit you on the ladder when you are not at the same plane as they are. Also, they will just stand right at the ladder, giving them (What feels like) a very cheap hit on you (which is even more frustrating in a game with limited healing). - Enemies will often get "stuck" in corners and doorways. You can then just get a good angle on them and shoot them dead or they will suddenly spin on you and strike you. The Cons, overall, just come down to core mechanics not feeling up to snuff with a 1.0 release. Beta, yes, but 1.0 release, no. You can tell A LOT of time and energy was put into this game and to tell this specific story but it feels like you have to try to find too many "loopholes" in the gameplay to make it work.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Bundle for September 2021. If you are interested in the game and it's before October 4th, 2021, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.When I think of West of Dead, I think of a cowboy crossed with Ghost Rider.  Players take on a dead soul, trying to escape from purgatory, and ignoring the rather obvious link to Hades, it’s a good concept. West of Dead’s gameplay is focused on lighting.  If enemies are in the shadows, players can’t damage them.  If the players ignite torches it will blind the enemies, but enemies of course will shoot at the player, causing them to have to dodge out and ignite the light to illuminate the area.  There’s also a strong cover-based system and a rather solid weapon selection here.  I found a lot that made me hopeful for the title. But I also have seen some not-so-flattering opinions, it sounds like this is a love-it or hate-it game, and it may be a little light on content, which could be a problem.  However, for the hour I played it, I started to enjoy myself and had a pretty fun time.  But I also wouldn’t put it high on my growing list of rogue-lites, it’s good, not great. Pick this up if you like cowboys, the wild west, or rogue-lites and need a new one.  Also, the main character is voiced by Ron Perlman, so his fans might want to check it out.  The cover-based shooting was rather strong here, and I already found a couple of weapons that felt very powerful, so it might be worth picking up just for that. _childDocuments_.review: So intones the recently deceased William Mason upon finding himself in purgatory and not…where, exactly? Collectively, we’ve lots of ideas on what the afterlife – should there be one – has in store for us. But we don’t . It’s what makes this mortal plane of ours such a terrifying thrill.Not so with video-games. We  know where death leads us: back to the last checkpoint or a swift return to the previous quick save. Death is a momentary impediment to progress, which is just as well because there’s often a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of baddies determined to scrub us from existence.Weep for William Mason, then, who certainly didn’t bank on the afterlife being chock full of gun-toting ghouls and monsters. But then he probably hadn’t expected to look like a stylish cross between Ghost Rider and  McCree, either. You could do worse. Swings and roundabouts ‘an all that.Slipping into Mason’s dusty boots I push my way into an empty saloon, which serves as the gateway to purgatory: a waiting room within a waiting room. I’ve little idea of what’s in store for me. I came here for  striking cel-shaded aesthetics, which create a world that often feels like a thick layer of ash caught in a time loop – forever frittering away without losing an inch. There’s farms and mines and towns, but in the words of one of our latter day cowboys, they’re more like someone’s faded memory of farms and mines and towns.And that’s it as far as my knowledge is concerned. I was just excited to play something new.The saloon’s sole occupant, the barman, doesn’t give any hints. He might have said “roguelike” and provided a definition, but instead seemed merely content to muse there’s east and there’s west.East for the good souls. West for the bad. Of course. I’ll be going west, then.I enter my first arena with a pistol and shotgun. There’s a ghostly Confederate lurking in the dark, rooting us in time but belying the republic’s unity; far from expunged, we know this particular evil only grows in shadow. I fire off a few clumsy shots, but the darkness keeps my opponent safe. If I want to stand a chance of taking him down I’m gonna need to light the torches hanging from the ceiling – an apt metaphor if there ever was one. Once lit they cause the ghoul to momentarily flinch and I skid behind cover – a coffin, natch – to try and acquaint myself with the twin-stick controls. I’m new to this, so I miss a bunch, but the control scheme seems fluid enough that I figure I’ll get the hang of it eventually. The ghoul goes down.‘Eventually’ is not the third or fourth arena, where, encountering lumbering zombies that want to GET IN MY FACE, I experience death within death. I’m zapped back to the beginning and reborn once more. That makes sense. I didn’t remember hitting a checkpoint.The saloon again. The barman winks, or I think he does. Onward.‘Eventually’ is the fifth try. I’m more confident with the controls, able to slip and slide between cover easily, dispatching ghouls with relative ease and familiar now with the upgrade path that suits me best (maximising health seems to do the trick). Before long I’m on the second level and beset by new challenges, but I’m pretty confident I’ve got this. I take more risks, not getting too anxious whenever I see my health take a knock.Hubris. An ill-timed dodge sends me into the path of some kinda hell-hound, ending my run. I’m okay with it and look forward to my next try, which is right away. Pretty fun this shooting malarkey.The mountains. Here we go.Only it’s not the mountains. It’s the mine. By way of the saloon. I’ve gone right back to the beginning. All my weapons, all my upgrades – gone. Snapped away in an instant. There’s no checkpoint – which I had imagined triggering in the passage from one level to the next – to speak of.Okay, this is  how death is supposed to be. Welcome to the roguelike, Ross. Where dead is dead.The real question is how I could possibly be so ignorant of an entire subgenre. I don’t rightly know. It’s not like I hadn’t heard the term “roguelike / rogue-lite” before. I’d just never shown an interest in that kind of game, so the finer points, or the fundamentals, were lost to me. There’s the argument that I probably ought to do my research before jumping into something new for the first time, but then I can’t think of a better introduction to the genre than this. Swings and roundabouts an’ all that.Onward. From the beginning.This time I’m sure the barman winks. I want to send him west, but then I can’t very well blame  because I picked a new title to review based on aesthetic preferences, you know? Besides, he seems like a decent sort. Too bad he has little of interest to say.I’m better at it, that much is certain.  is a ton of fun when you’ve got the mechanics down; clearing arenas of enemies by dodging, skidding, and shooting from cover becomes a slick, graceful exercise in repetition that thankfully doesn’t get stale. When I inevitably die, I’m prepared to submit myself to the ordeal all over again.It helps, I think, that the ‘sin’ you spend – acquired within missions – on new items, such as health potions, and new weapons, carries over from run to run, so each time you’re coming back better equipped with a broader range of choices. It’s only the upgrade stations (amount of health, damage, etc.) that are reset.The levels are procedurally generated, meaning the many runs you’ll make shake-up your route and enemy placement. Ostensibly that’s a welcome relief when there’s such a heavy emphasis on repetition, but the maps are super basic: there’ll be pillars, cover, torches, and enemies, and the procedural generation just changes where they all are.During the first few repetitions you might notice the tweaks, but it won’t be long before it all blends into one. I found they just weren’t distinctive enough to ever feel like fresh arenas; the mine was the mine, the mountains the mountains. Sure, a sense of brevity will come to the first couple levels, scaled according to players’ growing skill. But inevitably the environments will start to grind even when the gameplay remains engaging.There’s the outline of a story in here, told through the acquisition of memories dropped by different bosses, but I don’t much rate it. It’s by-the-numbers stuff, unfolding slowly and with little spark, expressed in tired Western cliches – "cold empty skies", "thick as molasses"…you get the idea. Even the mighty Ron Perlman, who voices Mason, can’t spice them up.My original point of contention was how buggy the game arrived, but the developers seem to be on top of that now. For instance, I had an issue where if you happened to roll onto a piece of cover that’s magically reconstructing itself there was a good chance that model would disappear and the game would either crash or require a reboot. In such instances I was at least be able to return to a mid-run save point (applicable only if you do not die), but it still felt sloppy. Enemy path-finding can be very sketchy, too, especially if you lure them into prior arenas. I haven't played since the latest patch, so perhaps these issues have now been ironed out.I’ll definitely return to . The roguelike isn’t necessarily my go-to kinda game, but its relative simplicity and compelling combat won me over. Given you’re certainly not as ignorant as me, you’ll know whether or not this sort of game is for you. Is it a good roguelike? I really can’t say – you’d have to ask the genre aficionados. Perhaps if I were to dig a little deeper into the genre,  might end up feeling like someone’s faded memory of a roguelike. Is it, from my meagre vantage point, a good introduction? Yeah, I’d say so.And it does look awful pretty.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game because of the art style, the music and the voice acting. As a rogue-lite it's a pretty new player entry to the genre. Think Dead Souls or Hades. It'll starts you off with an easier difficulty curve that allows players to adjust and learn as they do. However unlike those two it offers much more methodical in the combat with the cover based shooting mechanic. Whilst you don't need to use cover (shout out to the double shotty style) it's best used if you want to preserve health and make it further in runs. I recommend those who want to try rogue-lites but find the others too hectic.For experienced players this game has it's issues. The main ones I found were controls and character behaviour. I tried playing this both on Keyboard and Mouse and, PS4 controller. In general there are fundamental issues I personally have. Gunfire and standard melee attacks are combined the same buttons. This looks like a great idea until I am in an enemies face and I'm trying to melee but instead my character is trying to fire an empty gun. Please let us remap melee to something else. Health potion and Interact - They are also the same button. I understand why they did this. There's a delay on drinking the health potion. A mechanic where you can't just activate for instant heal. You have to strategically use it. But why not just have the button remappable too? They don't need to be the same button.Controller - There is no option remap any button. You just have to get use to it or don't play with controller. A quality of life change would be allowing players to swap the icon mapped shown between xbox/sony/nintendo/generic. Not an issue for me personally but for people who're trying to play on PC but with a Switch Pro or PS4/5 controller it's not obvious what button is what to them.Game/System options - There's no on screen button prompts at all. Unless you know "Esc" key is back or "B" is back you don't know how to leave the menu. Another issue here is that the bars for difficulty, shadows, aim assist etc have no clear indicator or box that shows up when selecting. If you are on keyboard and mouse you are left to blindly click left/right of where you clicked to get the right setting for you. A bug I encountered a few times was the combat music kept playing after clearing a room. It was only when I used the teleport pad that it reset. Not a big issue but something that had me wandering around wondering if I had an enemy following me when I had cleared the floor.TL;DR Worth getting for new players to the genre but for experienced players wait for a sale or try it on gamepass if it's still on there.

_childDocuments_.review: I hesitated for a long time because of the lukewarm reviews, but I absolutely don't regret my purchase. It's a fun game with a strong personality that isn't just its beautiful aesthetic.  Unlike most popular rogue-likes, it is intentionally not designed as a very fast-paced action game, it's not a bullet hell, you don't enter a room to clean it mindlessly with OP items and synergies. That's the opposite of that. Each room is like a dynamic, unscripted puzzle where you need to master your positioning, the pathing of the action, the threats and particularly the reloading of your guns. The controls are a bit strange at first (I strongly recommend a controller) but once you understand the philosophy of the gameplay (for instance: you reload faster behind a cover), it feels so great, badass and cinematographic. The enjoyment you get from this game is not in the quantity of toys you can play with, it's in the pure and core satisfying gameplay and gamefeel.These are the only negative points I found so far:- I'm not fan of the Dead Cells-like progression system for the weapons and items. The strange aspect of this is that you can manipulate the odds of your run by not unlocking the items/guns that you think would be bad. - The camera can be a bit annoying because it doesn't always show you the full room or what you want to see. I solve this problem by watching the aim indicator that is colored when there's a remaining enemy off-screen.- I have no particular interest for the characters and the story, but I admit I don't play those games for that. Even the monologues of Ron Perlman do nothing for me.- It doesn't seem to be built as a game that you will play for 200h like the other popular rogue-likes, but that's not a problem IMO. If I ignore all the possible items and weapons to unlock, I think I'm progressing very fast through the game and chapters. I might be wrong, but I feel that I can finish the game without unlocking 75% of the stuff, which is actually a plus for me!Negative update: I'll rewrite my review one day, but until then I wanted to insist on a big flaw of this game: the meta progression and unlockable items/weapons are terribly balanced. Many are factually bad and still expensive to unlock. While unlocking those ♥♥♥♥♥♥ guns/items, you also make the game more difficult and random. You can't even reroll when you meet the merchant during your run... To give you an example of a terribly designed item (items are not spammable), there's one expensive knife that can lifesteal. Sounds good right? Actually, that knife only heals 10 HP. Yes. Read it again. Ten health points. No matter the level of that weapon, it will only heal 10 HP per successful hit, even when you reach the mid-late game where you health bar is 300+ HP and where you lose 25% hp when you take one hit. Take into account that using a knife has a long cooldown (on average you can use it 1-2 times per room) and take into account that the maneuver is risky, and now you can imagine how bad the design of this item is.Complaints about the game balance are not new, but the devs are silent  99% of the time.They didn't acknowledge this problem in the last updates and the rare moments they make an effort to communicate it's to ask their players to write game reviews because it helps them... No shame. It really feels like they only care about selling their game, not supporting it.
