_childDocuments_.review: BottomLine at the Top:  What this was, was good. But it could have been so much more.  Ultimately recommended to aficionados of the p&c and cyberpunk genres, but go in with tempered expectations.  Except for the music and art, that's as good as the trailers made it seem.-------------------------------------Pros--------------------------------------The visual style.  Really fantastic pixel art.  There is a link in the menu to the artists tumblr feed and his work is excellent and exemplifies not pixel graphics but pixel art.-In the same vein, the music.  On par with the great pixel art the music in this game sets the tone for the whole story.  Again there is a link in the games menu to the Blood Music website if you are interested in more of their music. Apparently they are a publisher but I thought they were a band or an individual artist.  Still not super clear on that.  Regardless their work on this game was top notch.-Very stable game (take this with the caveat that it took me a while to play thru this due to school/side projects/global pandemic/oncoming apocalypse.  There were some issues apparently when it first came out but the developer was pretty rapid in how they addressed them and I do not have any major complaints about its stability.  Alt-tabing out caused no crashing and there was no setup nonsense or resolution headaches.-This game evoked several of my favorite movies and games in an indirect way.  Its got a kind of Johnny Nemonic/2001:A Space Odyssey/Ready Player One/Loom/Beneath a steel sky/Space Quest 6/They Live vibe to it which i totally dig.-I like the AVR mechanic.  -Cyberpunk adventure game with sweet freakin music, I mean you're going to check it out for that reason alone.-------------------------------------Meh.--------------------------------------I was never sold on the dialogue color option.  Choosing to have white text for every character talking had some kind of aesthetic value i guess but from a practical perspective it could be hard to keep track of who was talking.  In my head all the characters ended up sounding the same at times and i think in some psychological way this contributed to that.-no fast travel option-only 9 save slots-No voice work.  Given the issues with dialogue I'll discuss later I am still undecided if this was a good choice or a bad one.-Has steam achievements but from what i can tell no badges.  Not a big issue for me but I might have rocked a profile background from this game.-------------------------------------Cons--------------------------------------So before i get into this games overarching main con, I want to talk about the main character.  I take notes when i play these games and I'm going to write one of them here: "3.5 hours into this game and I feel like i still don't know anything about the character I am playing.  It doesn't feel like an actual character, instead more like a writer pretending to be a character.....that probably doesn't make much sense but I guess I'm just having difficulty identifying with this guy.  Like what is his personality exactly?  The story is compelling in that the setting is so interesting but the character development, thus far, feels...not lacking but its missing some kind of Je ne sais quoi..."I can say that 6 hours later at the end of the game that feeling is never resolved.  I played this whole game with an awesome looking character, in an awesome looking setting, with an awesome background music, and yet I never felt invested in this character.  -Which i think is a good transition into the games main con which is its lacking dialogue combined with a scattershot story. Despite my quote at the start of the con list, for the first 50-75% of the game it felt like there was still maybe a chance that this could all get tied together nicely with some crazy crescendo in the final act with an epic conclusion, but that just never materialized.  Without giving spoilers Ill just say that what we are left with nearly bumped this game into the total fail zone.  Ignoring other gamers varying tastes in music (I super enjoyed it but maybe its not for everyone and could feel looping) I think this aspect of the game is what really made some players hesitate with hitting that recommend button.-I think the tragedy of these two cons listed above is that they both stem from a common issue I have seen in p&c games whose developers primary language is not English and that is that if they had a better proofreader it could potentially have negated these issues to a degree.  a proofreader is not a miracle worker, but a good one could clean up stiff dialogue and incoherent story lines to a degree.  But if you have weaker interpersonal dialogue between underdeveloped characters in a story that doesn't stick to the path its chosen and combine that with a proofreader who is mediocre....well you get this situation and for someone who loves cyberpunk and literally organized a popular steam P&C group it is an incredibly frustrating situation.-I touched on this in the last bullet point but i wanted to emphasize the "Stiff" dialogue.  I've seen this phenomenon in the translations of Japanese movies sometimes and its what made me point to proofreading as a main issue.  It was too matter of fact and forced.  To clarify, the nuts and bolts translation is fine there's is no broken English or anything like that but the dialogue between characters just makes it hard to connect with them.  Its disconnects you from all the world building that the design and music has built up.  How can I connect with these characters when they don't sound like they connect with each other.  The main character and his girlfriend displayed zero chemistry and its to be expected when their conversations have an emotional range on par with an ikea table's instruction manual.-And finally game flow and pixel hunting.  At times things seemed like a great balance, its tough to find that perfect point of challenging but not boring in p&c games.  But when you get stuck you get really stuck and it gets boring which is the worst sin a p&c can make.    Final Thoughts:I mean, for a certain kind of gamer (i.e. me) this title's hype pushed all the right buttons.  I started our p&c fan group the  right around when I first saw previews for this game and it is by far one of the titles I had been most looking forward too.  It didn't disappoint, but it didn't completely fulfill my expectations either.I usually don't try to give games grades or percentages, but i will say that several reviews give this in the low 80's or B range.  I know my cons seemed longer and more detailed but don't let the amount a wrote per section detract from the pros list.  To me that 80's/B range is pretty accurate its music and artwork really are excellent for the feel this game was trying to achieve but the dialogue and mess of a story are responsible for that lack of 20 more points. At the end of the day if you are a cyberpunk fan and a point and click aficionado this is a must play.  Since you made the excellent choice of reading my review ;)  when you go to buy it you'll be fully prepared for cons and hopefully you can focus on that great design and try your best to immerse yourself in the game world.These cyberpunk P&C games really get you hyped up for Cyberpunk 2077 and since every gamer on the planet will be playing that for months after it comes out you best pick this one up now and give it a go!
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: I'm torn between leaving a positive review and a negative review but at time of writing the reviews are 100% positive, so I'll be mean. It's not terrible, many of the puzzles are satisfying to solve although there were some moon logic/guide dang it puzzles, and the game has a solid sense of humor. The game's biggest problem in my opinion is the writing of the protagonist, who is a great example of why, if the developer includes a self-insert, it should not be the protagonist.The visuals are great, and the toggleable AR glasses are used to good effect, but it lessens the effect of the well-done creepy AR adverts when the protagonist explains every chance he gets, "well that's creepy, maybe technology has enabled capitalism to go too far". The protagonist is so heavy-handed with his explaining the game's message that the moment meant to be the incitement where it's revealed that the system might actually be sinister fell flat because the protagonist had been waxing philosophical about exactly what the dire warning predicted since he tumbled out of bed.In the end it gives the effect of a cyberpunk title that doesn't trust the viewer to understand the point.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: A huge miss for me personally.  I'd normally quantify a game like this being as firmly in my wheelhouse as a game could possibly be:  I have an enormous boner for cyberpunk/outrun aesthetics, and I like old-school point and click adventure games, but found this to be a pretty big let-down.It's definitely a tremendous homage to the point-and-clicks of the early 90's, but it does so to a fault and reminds me why this style of game fell out of favor as hard as it did:  Puzzles with unintuitive, ridiculous solutions.  Tons of red herring items that lead to a clogged inventory full of useless junk.  The only trope I thought it missed was the pixel hunt, but they throw in a minor one right at the end of the game to hit the trifecta.The first chunk of the game is relatively enjoyable and challenging in a good way.  Everything  is where VirtuaVerse drew my ire.  I'll forgive a handful of instances in games like these where I have to check a walkthrough because I'm helplessly stuck, even more so if I think to myself "Oh, I should've figured that out" after looking up the answer.  VV got to the point where I'd be confronted with a puzzle and be like "I don't even want to guess. I'm positive the solution is some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Rube Goldberg machine nonsense."  I was often correct to assume so.The story starts alright but gets progressively worse and in my personal opinion has a terrible ending.  If I had to compare this game to anything, it would be DreamWeb.  That's not a compliment.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: If you're into point&click adventures, cyberpunk settings, pixel art and synthwave, VirtuaVerse might be one of the best games you'll ever play.If aforementioned things mean nothing to you, you probably won't feel the game is something to write home about.Mechanically it's a classic point&click adventure game and does nothing out of the ordinary. If you're familiar with the genre you know the drill... you point and you click (surprising, I know) and solve puzzles (inventory puzzles and the occasional logic puzzle) to advance the story. Puzzle design comes with a common problem of many adventures of old and is not always the most intuitive.Storywise VirtuaVerse is not among the most memorable games (although the ending is pretty surprising). What made it great for me was its beautifully immersive dystopian high tech low life cyberpunk setting.The audiovisual aesthetics are outstanding, the pixelated retro inspired graphics are among the most beautiful things I've ever seen and the soundtrack by Master Boot Record is a straight up banger.It might be a case of "style over substance" but VirtuaVerse made it into my top 5 all time favourite adventure games instantly.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: is a point-and-click adventure game released on 12th May 2020 and developed by Theta Division. It is both a love letter for the 90s and early 2000s cracking scenes and LucasArts classic adventure games. As a fan of point-and-click genre, it is almost a perfect fanservice to relive those good old days. For those who have no quite particular attachment to the genre, there might be some barriers between you and the game due how puzzle heavy the game is compared to similar but more contemporary entries of this genre. In my opinion,  never makes an astronomical leap in its logical puzzle-solving process like its older predecessors so this game can still be enjoyed by newcomers of the genre.  uses item-based and inventory-based puzzles. You click on various objects in the world and Nathan, the main protagonist will interact with it. These objects can be looked at, where Nathan will give opinions about what he thinks of the particular item or interact with them. Puzzles can be solved by either using the various knick-knacks Nathan has plundered over the course of the game or through the dialogue. For the most part, the puzzles are logical. There is maybe only one instance where I had to consult a guide. Basically a solution requires you to go to another part of the world without prior hints regarding the solution. It is definitely more puzzle heavy than your average modern adventure games like  or . The amount of junks in your inventory can reach 2 dozens by the end of the game. While it sounds daunting, the game never felt frustrating to play. In the end, the difficulty depends on how familiar you are to LucasArts type games. While I don’t mind more focus on puzzles, but it lacks some modern features like item highlight and instant travel. I have never got stuck because of pixel hunting and finding items in the map because the graphics are clean and interactable objects are designed to be as obvious as possible. The lack of instant travel though is irritating as the game requires Nathan to walk all over the place. Sometimes you will spend time watching him walks through 3 screens just to get to your objective. The game ran flawlessly and its minimum recommended spec is pretty low and should run in most computers with modern OS. Never encountered any bug and it never froze or crashed in my entire playthrough. The game is very polished out of the box. The story takes place in a far future where people are implanted with “Permanent Reality” Chip inside their heads. It allows them to see augmented reality programs from within their own eyes. The protagonist, Nathan is a retro tech geek who refused to have chips implanted inside him. One day he wakes up with his girlfriend missing and only leaves a cryptic message on the mirror. Nathan starts following her trails to discover the truth behind her disappearance. The game has nice ideas and concepts for the world, but fails in utilizing it to execute a gripping plotline and fill it with well-written and memorable casts. A lot of the characters are one note and never really get developed beyond their purposes in gameplay. The story only provides context for the puzzles you do. If you only judge the story by that measure, it works but not more. What the game does well is the humor that plays directly into the puzzle solutions. Nathan can be ruthless in achieving his goals and he achieves them by being the ultimate jerk to the NPCs.  executes most of its absurd, cartoony dark humor well. While players can’t really sympathize with these one dimensional NPCs, you still can have fun chuckling at their misfortunes caused by Nathan’s actions. is one of the best looking pixel art I have ever played. Every screen in the game oozes atmosphere. There are a sheer variety of locations to visit and each have vastly different atmospheres. The little animations put in these scenes bring them out to life. Raindrops will reflect the colors of surrounding neon lights, advertisement hologram flickering in and out and so on.It is a shame that the game isn’t voiced at all. Decent voice acting would make the delivery of the jokes much stronger. The overall soundscape of the game isn’t bad. It doesn't have much production value, but each location has distinct ambient sound effects that fit in their environment. The music is excellent. There are a good amount of variety of synthwave songs and catchy chiptunes that they can fill early 2000s electronic band’s albums. I find myself bobbing to the rhythm of the background music sometimes.  presents most of its aspects very well, except its story that fell short.  is worth it if you are looking for a puzzle-oriented adventure game with an amazing presentation and banging soundtrack. If you are looking for deep story and complex characters, you won’t find it here.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: visually impresses and it is apparent that a lot of work has gone into making this game look and feel as retro as possible. Characters, environments and objects are rendered superbly and it always amazes me how beautiful a pixel world can look if it is done right.The story has one of the most boring tales I have experienced in a point and click game. After nine hours of playing this game the story had not developed at all. I remember thinking to myself that nothing had happened. The story picks up slightly towards the end but at no point was I intrigued, excited or motivated to finish the game. It just felt like a chore. No characters in the game are developed. We don’t get to know any of them apart from superficial banter and the odd humorous quip here and there. I suppose this harkens back to the old days of adventuring and perhaps this was done intentionally but just be aware that you won’t be able to bond with any characters emotionally. They are just puppets designed to tell a tale, unfortunately the tale is monotonous. The amount of backtracking and walking you have to do in this game borders on infuriating. Just thinking about it makes me angry. No double click to exit a screen, and screens wrap constantly, meaning you’ll be walking a double screen to get to one location, and rinse and repeat. No map. No fast travel. It kills your enjoyment. In the first half of the game there is a semblance of a fast travel mechanism but you still have to watch a cut scene followed by a long walk to your destination. To make things even worse, you have to left click the mouse to continue walking when you reach the end of the current screen but the cursor strays onto objects or people, initiating a comment or conversation you had already seen. Puzzles are really not logical at all. I have never been so stuck in a point and click adventure game as much as this one. I was constantly using walkthroughs. I think this was partly caused by a lack of motivation due to the boring nature of the game but even after learning the solution, I would often think to myself “Really!?”One artificial intelligence has prevailed over all others and society has embraced a virtual reality led existence. Nathan, the protagonist of the story, is a loner and a rebel. He sells modded hardware and cracked software and refuses to comply to the new system. Using his skills, Nathan has developed a custom headset which gives him the ability to turn reality on or off and he can see things that the majority of the population cannot. One day, Nathan awakes in his apartment to find a cryptic message scrawled on his mirror. His girlfriend Jay has gone without warning. Nathan sets about finding his girlfriend in the neon-soaked streets full of hackers and digital merchants.The first half of the game involves Nathan trying to find his girlfriend. It took around ten hours to find her and during that time nothing happened apart from me asking her whereabouts and solving puzzles to get to her. Once found the story moved on a little but it never really accelerated and chugged along to its conclusion. It really wasn’t very exciting. There is no character development at all and you just don’t care what happens because you are frustrated by the game mechanics. There is a bit of welcome humour throughout the game and some of the characters are amusing but never memorable.  I don’t understand the thinking behind not including some sort of fast travel. Just a quick exit would have been suitable. As it is, you will constantly be walking from point A to point B and back again over and over again.Puzzles are not very logical in my opinion. I started writing down the inconsistencies as they were occurring so often. For example, in one puzzle you need to get a fruit of a tree. You have a grappling hook but even though it is a good idea, the game says so, it won’t allow it because the fruit could drop and break. I spent ages trying to find something to break its fall etc. but in the end the answer was to blow the tree to smithereens. Another example was that you needed to make a hole in the ground bigger. I’ll use my spade I thought. No not allowed. I kept getting told I didn’t need to make the whole bigger. In the end I made the hole bigger using something else.The game will only let you use the solutions it has programmed in and although that is not unusual in an adventure game, other games don’t give you so many perfectly reasonable and logical alternatives that you aren’t allowed to use. The puzzles just don’t seem very well thought out in this sense.Also, you may have all the tools present to solve a puzzle or turn on a piece of equipment etc. but you won’t be able to until you have fulfilled something else. The game is terribly linear.You can accrue a lot of items within the game. Some you will never use. Some you will use, but they don’t get discarded after you’ve finished with them. They just stay in your inventory cluttering up the interface.  There are times when you have to combine up to four items together to make a new item. With all these erroneous items it can become tedious trying different combinations. Undoubtedly the game looks amazing and it easily the highlight of the experience. I was impressed by the amount of detail a pixel game can convey, with subtle suggestions leaving your imagination to fill in. It ranks up there with the best games of this genre I have played for detailed characters and environments.I found the music annoying. The same tune would constantly loop and be fixed to one screen. I turned the music off. Special effect sounds were very good however. It is worth noting there is no voice acting. Curator Info: This game was received for free through curator connect.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: This MBR Album is everything from the Golden era of point and click story adventure games from the Lucasfilm classics, to the Sierra legends, infused with more Cyberpunk Gibson hacking action than even Technobabylon or the legendary Blade Runner story adventure game itself, and that was a hell of a game! This Cyberpunk retro-futurism inspired adventure is also a non-stop ride of nostalgia, inside jokes nerdy trivia, and even MODE 7 GRAPHICS! Remember that hype train?There's a level of CRAFTING that's tangible with this game, which makes it stand out with the greats like Monkey Island or Space Quest. First off the graphics got me, where had I seen this art style before? Holy ♥♥♥♥ Valenberg painted this game. So going in I already knew the scene leader MASTER BOOT RECORD did the music for this, but now I'm also seeing Valenberg at the helm of design. Wow. That leads me to the music. I knew MBR's sound, so I expected more of that, right? What I didn't expect was a level of sound design that showcases the painstaking work that went in for what, four years of development? The music grows with your playthrough, it is crafted to enhance the mood and what's going on in-game, and at no point does it feel like a standard soundtrack just looping in the background. I even noticed audio cues when walking around the various locations in the game, which clearly showed they cared to make things perfect. Which leads me to the journey, from all the advertising, and certainly the cyberpunk genre itself, I expected more of the same: neon rain and tech. Yeah, there's definitely a lot of that, which as a fan of the genre, I absolutely love - however at the core of a point and click adventure game is the ADVENTURE: we follow our hero to all sorts of exciting places. It felt like we only stay in the locations long enough to get to know them, but not long enough. If there's a sequel, it would be great to revisit some of these places. The gameplay is a complete point and click story adventure masterclass that I'm sure even Ron Gilbert would enjoy. It definitely makes you pay attention to solve logic puzzles, in a way that games often don't nowadays in the era of twitchspeed plays and constant fps k/drs, etc. The way it's been created really made me want to play through it to see what the authors put into it and why. Also, it's a really good example of the devil's in the details. Whenever I got stuck, eventually it would be the answer that's so obvious you slap yourself on the forehead, or occasionally so silly you'll find yourself laughing about it later. The dialogue and writing is fun, hilarious at times - gripping at others, and most importantlt inherently human in a story about what it means to be human. There's a sense of seeking community amongst the outcasts, strength in unity. There's a lot of really strong messages in the game, that made it really fun to keep traveling along on this crazy journey.  I am looking forward to more from Theta Division for sure. If this indie crew could pull off something so big in scale, scope, synergy, imagine what they could make next. Bigger and better. Git Gud. I guess I'm really feeling like shilling this game because it made me care about it, a lot. The story stood out as something new and different, whilst also being familiar. The characters, even the fandoms, all had so much to them, and all felt like I could run into them on any night out.  And with that rolling MBR soundtrack, the game in itself is a party, especially considering how locked in most of us are right now. What a perfect time for this game. It's been hard not to spoil in this review. There are so many things I wanna talk about. I can't wait to read how others enjoy things.Anyhow, best album I've played in a long time. Plus there's a Wilhelm scream in there if you pay attention! With a bike so 7331 that it would make KANEDA jealous, the only thing that's missing are more tentacles! Here's hoping they do more with this fantastic world.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: VirtuaVerse is an authentic homage to adventure games of old. An ode to retro hardware, entwined with the underground scene that helped birth it. The game feigns all forms of hand-holding, and while challenging, manages to be intensely humorous and enjoyable. Subtle, and not so subtle references abound with some of the most nerdy trivia you're likely to find in a game.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: I played through a good chunk of the game, then couldn't bring myself to finish it.The puzzle difficulty comes from arbitrary and random restrictions and ends up feeling tedious. Oftentimes there is a perfectly good solution, the game will even tell you it's a good solution, but you have to do something else because... well, because that's what the game wants you to do. It gets tiresome.The main character is thoroughly unlikeable. The game has you commit at least one murder (indirectly), but it's treated as no big deal, a necessary barely evil act to get what you want. Most of the NPCs are kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as well. That also gets tiresome.The overall story is complicated and after a while I completely lost track of why exactly I was solving all these puzzles. There's a self-conscious retro esthetic and ethos. Listen, yeah I spent the 90s listening to my modem whine and screech, but we don't have to spend the entire game pretending that all computing was great then and evil now, or that ASCII was the all time pinnacle of art and communication.I feel like I gave the game a really good chance to be good and entertaining, but in the end I can't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: Meh.If you're a super fan of Master Boot Record it's probably going to be worth buying just for the music, but if not... you should look before you leap.Short summary: a retro point-and-click adventure game with a cyberpunk pixel art aesthetic and music by Master Boot Record.The music is great (as expected), the art is great, but the game... is not, with flawed puzzles and writing. Once again I find myself wishing for a "meh" review option on Steam.The game is presented in a style intended to invoke the golden age of adventure games, with art that ranges between good and absolutely gorgeous. The interface is your standard point-and-click affair, with two verbs - "look" and a combined "use"/"pick up" - and of course an inventory in which you can combine items. A bit later in the game you also get an icon to switch between viewing reality as it is, or viewing an augmented reality version which is how most people in the setting see the world.Most of the puzzles are OK I guess, but there are some  bad ones in there that drag down the game as a whole. Even the best adventure games tend to have a few puzzles that rely on Crazy Moon Logic, and this game has more than a few of them - but here they are not in fact the worst offenders. The really bad puzzles in this game are ones where progress is completely opaque to the player: something you do unlocks a dialogue option in a character somewhere, with no indication that the game state has progressed in any way, or that you should ever interact with that character again.And speaking of going back to talk to characters again, there is a lot of backtracking - most of which does not serve to advance the story in any way. You solve a puzzle, and then you have to go to back to some far-off previous location just to tell a character "I solved the puzzle!" to unlock the next step... and then immediately go back to where you just were. It serves to pad out the play time, but not to improve the game experience.To cap things off, there are some annoying pixel hunts as well. Not many, but enough to be frustrating.The game also does the Monkey Island 2 thing of casual cruelty in puzzles, but not even doing it for comedy. You outright , and it is only acknowledged in a single line of dialogue by one of the man's compatriots and then completely forgotten about.That leads us to the next point: the writing. If I had to describe it in one word it would be "sophomoric".It's a dystopian setting, and the new augmented reality technology is bad. How do we know this? . This game's writing is sorely in need of the old adage of "show, don't tell".This is what a typical conversation in this game might look like (paraphrased):"This augmented reality technology is really bad.""Yes, it's letting corporations cover up bad things.""Agreed. Capitalism is a bad thing. Maybe technology has gone too far.""Yes. Exploitation sure is bad. We shouldn't rely so much on technology."Basically, heavy-handed monologues that are for some reason written for two characters - two characters sharing a voice and agreeing with each other.There are also a few moments in the story that I think are supposed to be big twists, but they fall flat. Either because they are just more of the sort of stuff that the protagonist has been ranting about all game long, or because they are about something we don't actually know anything about, so there's no reason to expect anything else.All in all I don't regret the purchase: it's not an awful game - it's just not very good.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: The pixel art is phenomenal. Really hits those cyberpunk vibes. Will run on mostly anything built after 2000.This is where the game fails miserably. It's a pixel hunt nightmare where you must scan each environment for items because if you miss something, you'll inevitably get stuck. Sometimes it's a tiny thing that you'd normally gloss over. Other times its something that game says you don't need right now and won't let you grab it only to unlock the option once the story progresses. Meaning you have to backtrack hoping you remembered the item existed. The other thing that really got on my nerves was that items persist in your inventory even after they are pointless. The screwdriver you get in the beginning of the game has maybe two uses but throughout the game you'll be trying it on everything because why not? It's a screwdriver. Having generic items like this or a knife and not removing it from inventory means you'll be continuously using it on everything. The credits say they had playtesters but they all must have been masochists. I love point and click adventure games but this one has the worst gameplay I've experienced. Really could do with a hint system to help guide players if they miss that one tiny object or some of the non obvious puzzle solutions.The soundtrack by Master Boot Record is top notch cyberpunk. Very synthy and retro. No voice-over dialog.Visually and audibly this game knocks it out of the park oozing that dystopian cyberpunk atmosphere. It's a shame the gameplay and story didn't match in quality. The story is pretty lame and doesn't really pull you in. Character development is non existent. It feels like a bunch of fetch quests with tons of "your princess is in another castle". Gameplay, as stated above, is more a chore than pleasant experience. Around the middle part of the game, I basically gave up and used a walkthrough guide because I was fed up with getting stuck due to missing tiny items.1 thumb down.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: Visually stunning, "Tears in rain" beatiful retro cyberpunk adventure goodness with a stupendous soundtrack. Unfortunately, it tries to be old school very hard and turns into a complete pile of old school junk that it celebrates in-game, but that serves no purpose in 2020 and it's mostly nonsensical and completely devoid of logic. This was the original sentence, "It's still going to be a grudging recommendation, but with a very, very large caveat." I've changed my mind while writing the review. It doesn't get a pass. Use a walkthrough unless you particularly like banging your head with a hammer. Sure, it's pleasant when you stop.A lot of "puzzles" in this game are mostly absurd. Day of the Tentacle absurd, outside the box with a heavily skewed logic, requiring you to think like a cartoon character, not as a player or an inhabitant of that world. And for some of them the game does exactly zero to give you a hint or point you in the right direction. The puzzles may appear logical when you read them in a walkthrough, but are nowhere near that in-game. I was reduced to actually clicking everything with everything and doing completely random things to progress because I never use a walkthrough on first playthroughs, hence the 15 hour play time. This seriously looks like retro just for retro's sake. Complete with a lot of useless items you can pick up that don't have any use. I wonder how the playtesting for that went. I wouldn't exactly call this good gameplay mechanics and feedback systems from the game. There's a lot of retro adventure games that do this a whole lot better. Just take a peek at , , ,  and the Blackwell series or anything by Dave Gilbert and . But hey, I'll take into consideration that I'm just Homer Simpson sloooooow. Duh.The main character is a somewhat annoying, bland piece of cardboard without a face that casually destroys other people's lives searching for his girlfriend and getting entangled in something bigger. Most of the characters are actually underwhelming and slightly uninspired, making the world much blander than the visuals, writing and music present. And the puns and jokes the main character has sometimes clash with the seriousness of the situation you're in, making the moments feel like something from Monthy Python and the Holy Grail.The world is masterfully crafted, packed with tons of details. The screens are a joy to look at and the ambience is absurdly good. Huge props for the visuals and even more huge props for the soundtrack. It's incredibly good, so good that I actually just stood on some screens listening to the music because it's actually better than the gameplay (yes, I will repeat a few times that gameplay sucks more than your little daughter spilling her chocolate milk on your PC case while you're clutch winning DOTA 2 Internationals).The story and writing is competent. It's a typical cyberpunk, AI, virtual reality fare and it does a good job. It slightly takes a nose dive about halfway through, but still manages a solid ending. And the game features a few noteworthy messages, if you look around hard enough.It's very obvious that Theta Division put a ton of work into this game, but the puzzles really scrub over everything the visuals, writing, atmosphere and music bring and it makes gameplay a needlessly frustrating experience. I'm hoping that if they make another game, they'll take a few cues from some other books instead of replicating the annoyances of 90's adventure games.Take a peek inside the newly opened  if you like to walk off the beaten path and only sometimes return to the main roads. You might find something worth exploring. And if you do, thank you for the visit.: 4 missable achievements, the rest are story.

_childDocuments_.review: A really pretty game that falls into the trap of vague, non-sequitur puzzle design. There's nothing suggesting to the player what they should do next to progress in the game short of trying everything out and being absolutely certain not to miss clicking on the right pixel. The age-old point-and-click problem. There's also a glitch in the first area that prevents me (and a bunch of players, apparently) from progressing at all.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: A love letter to point-n-click genre and to an entire computing era, made with sincere passion. Retro, but never in a useless or meaningless way (as some easy indie cash-ins do). Cyberpunk, but not only in aesthetics and as a mere neon-fest with rain. Just play it ASAP if you even remotely liked Indiana Jones: Fate of Atlantis and you like Cyberpunk sci-fi, and BUY IT NOW if you ever got an Amiga 500.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: AverageClear Time: 5+ Hours100% Time: 5+ HoursSummary: A point & click adventure/puzzle game whose great soundtrack and visual design is unfortunately marred by a boring, generic story. Frustrating and nonsensical puzzles, frequent backtracking and numerous pixel hunts only further exacerbate what could have been an actually good successor to the Lucasarts of old.A point & click adventure. You pick up items and use them on other items so that they hopefully combine and solve a puzzle. You play as Nathan, who wakes up one morning only to find his girlfriend missing. Accidently breaking his AR/Permanent Reality goggles, Nathan becomes embroiled in a much larger plot involving strange techno cults, underground gangs and what could possibly be far more than he can chew.It's a game with a cyberpunk aesthetic so naturally both the soundtrack and the visual design are fantastic. Fixing the AR Goggles allows to to swap between "permanent reality" (the reality that almost the entire world lives in that they see through their goggles) and actual reality, which only those who haven't been implanted or live technology free can see (such as yourself). It's unfortunate that this mechanic is not utilised enough to warrant even having but when it works it's a great feature. The NPC's all have cool personalities and outfits and the world fills expansive.Gameplay wise, it's just frustrating. While early game is ok, mid to late game puzzles become frustrating because of how one track the puzzles are. Even if you have an item you think could solve the puzzle, until you have the actual correct item (which alot of the time has no relevance) you can't progress. Sometimes that correct item involves spending minutes backtracking to an NPC who may have unlocked a single dialogue option that you need to click in order to progress for no reason other than padding. There's also alot of red herrings: There's one character early on who explicitly states she likes a certain kind of drink and she'd open a bit a more to talk. Giving her this drink does nothing. The character next to her (and not connected at all) is a character you actually need to get drunk to get an item, yet not once does any conversation option ever mention alcohol or anything related. It's just guesswork. If you only fed him one drink nothing will happen, and Nathan doesn't even remark anything on it. You have to somehow know to keep feeding him drinks. It was about this time I thought "yeah, this is going to suck".Otherwise it features numerous negatives. Nathan is a VERY unlikeable character; super arrogant, self absorbed with no character development. He directly causes the deaths of multiple people in order to find his girlfriend with no remorse and the people that die aren't at all bad people. The cyberpunk world looks cool but is super generic. The story is barebones, uninteresting and been done a million times before.Get rid of the pixel hunting and backtracking and it would have made this a more bearable game. Let some of the puzzles be open ended so you can experiment. Rewrite Nathan to not be a total jerkoff.I don't know I thought this would be good, I don't even like these games. I'm not good at them either so alot of the puzzles I found frustrating may have been solved alot more easily by people who like this genre. I wouldn't take my review all that seriously knowing this and instead find reviews by people more experienced in this genre.Luckily very easy. You'll get 29/33 just by beating the story and the other 4 are gotten in the first 1/3 of the game by using certain items on certain things. Use a guide for those 4.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: VirtuaVerse is a cyberpunk point-and-click adventure. Do you like 90s point and click games? This game is for you then. Modern game in a retro style with a good, humorous story.Humanity enslaved in a virtual reality world. What you can see is not always real. Your reality is bombarded with ads, and an AI control everything.Our protagonist waking up in the morning, and his girlfriend is missing. Your mission to find her slowly changing to another mission about freeing the whole of humanity.-The story is very good and entertaining. While ingame the AI influence the thinking of the humans, it is comparable to our modern age when the independent press no longer exists and every single one trying to influence our thinking based on the interest of business or political groups standing behind them. This means that the story is actual, as fighting against suppression is, and was, always an important part of human history.-The game has decent music. Worth to buy alone for that.-Retro point and click game. Miss the old days when it was hard to figure out the next step? Well, there are still guides, videos nowadays, but you can make it hard and challenging to yourself if you avoid using those. This is not a regular straightforward game.-Visuals. It might be retro and pixelated, but still, some parts of the game just nice.There is only one thing I disliked in this game. Executing a double click on a zoning area not execute fast travel to the next area. This existed already ages ago on point and click games. You need to wait until your protagonist walks there.I really loved this game. Decent music, excellent story, and the atmosphere of the 90s point of click games.Story: 9/10Atmosphere: 7/10. Cyberpunk game, but only the first part of the game fits the atmosphere and visuals expected for this style.Visuals: 9/10 in the retro style genre. Virtuaverse is sticking to it during the whole game.Gameplay mechanics: 7/10.Music/Sound effects: 10/10. I never muted the game. The music is just awesome.Voice acting/Narration: 1/10 No voice acting.Game difficulty: 7/10, sometimes very hard to progress without hints or a guide.Perfection time: 10-15h. Of course, it could be less with a guide. 4 achievements missable, but all those are during the first part of the game. There arent any after you escaping the Club. Worth to save during the Club Scene so you can return easily for missed achievements.Please keep in mind that there are few reports, that achievements not working on this game if you using old steam library. It might be fixed in future and developers shows willingness to fix the issue.Follow my curator if you like to see achievement-related information on the store page of the games: completion times, MP-DLC achievement requirements, useful information.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to , a future cyberpunk adventure where companies spam advertising 24/7 and virtual reality has become an almost permanent tool. Hardware and software are equally regularized and freedom to think and create is entirely compromised. Our main character, Nathan, still fights to hold on to the last big remaining of the human condition and together with his girlfriend they hack and modify their way into survival.One day, though, everything changes as his partner goes missing, leaving behind an encrypted message. Nathan will traverse the city and search for his significant other, but what mysteries lie ahead? More importantly, what is Jay involved in, that made her leave so suddenly?When comes to the world and consequently, its story,  is packed with details and references to provide a fantastic placement of characters. The main story is intriguing and remarkably captivating, even for non cyberpunk enthusiasts. Featuring iconic humor, hardware and software references which many of us can quickly pick on. It’s clear  was developed by software enthusiasts, which is a major positive point!Following a traditional gameplay style of Point & Clickers, Nathan can look and interact with objects, each with its different dialogue. As players progress in the game, picking up items and combining them becomes available, but there’s more to the gameplay, a lot more. Nathan can use different apps in terminals, complete mini-games in order to progress and even interact with other NPC’s to complete objectives.The puzzles are not repetitive, nor is any feature included in the game, as everything feels unique and progression leaves a print of slowly walking towards the truth. The expected pace can be compared to other classics of this genre, and looking for small clues may prove useful, even though sometimes lacking attention can delay your progress. Like with many other similar games,  will require your complete attention, to take on even the small hints.There are some interesting gameplay details that will catch your attention, such as the good amount of scripted messages when incorrectly using items, which is always funny and somehow pleasant to see. Clearly an adventure up and beyond 10 hours of gameplay, especially with plenty of dialogue and details surrounding each area of the game.The pixel art suits really well the retro futuristic vibe and it’s extremely well designed, with impressive reflections and little details such as rain and characters distinctive behavior. Simple but complete, or more specifically, with a soul. Colors are vibrant, in both the advertising neons all around the city, but also in the dark alleys hiding all the hackers illegal activities.With a fantastic soundtrack by ,  is filled with an 80’s atmospheric wave of futuristic ranging vibes, immediately associated with a cyberpunk universe, matching the game entirely. You can listen and purchase the soundtrack , and I personally found the music highly suiting each scene, giving a much needed touch since the game isn’t voiced over. is a fantastic and highly recommended Point & Click, with a good and sharp sense of humor, featuring a desolated cyberpunk vision, one where freedom is fought true hacking and hardware manipulation. A smart, engaging and overall, fresh approach over the genre. Impressive dedication from the developers, a game developed with care and love.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: I am old and grew up playing the adventure games which clearly inspired VirtuaVerse. As such I was prepared to love it with all my heart. However, in addition to borrowing the look of older games, it also borrowed one of their more egregious shortcomings: rigid, single-path problem solving.Several times in the first hour-and-a-half I found myself frustrated -- not because I couldn't see any possible solutions to a problem, but because the solutions I came up with (given inventory, world, and text clues) was not the one the developer chose as "the right answer".To be fair, none of the solutions are as bad as the completely arbitrary moon logic that Sierra was sometimes (in)famous for, but the end result is still a beautifully done game with exactly one path through it. And that ends up punishing players who don't have the exact thought process that the designer did.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: I'm generally a fan of point-and-click adventure puzzle games, but this one really just didn't work for me.  The dual layers of reality were fun to play with and explore, but there were too many times where I knew exactly what I needed to do, but had to look at a walkthrough to figure out how to make the character actually do it.  Frequently, it was because I hadn't tried-and-failed to do something else first, even if it would have made sense without that.The most painful was a point you get completely stuck unless you examine a specific spot on a character's clothes.  There's no indication when examining the rest of the character that those specific pixels are significant, when every other character's clothes are just part of their design - nothing like "he's wearing a cool jacket" when you examine him in general, just the same brief description that any other character gets.Some of this could be forgivable if the story was engaging, but while the world was intriguing, the actual story was pretty meh.  I won't spoil the specifics, but the ending felt like it was building up to something, then swerved in a totally different direction and left a whole bunch of things hanging.  That was probably the intent, but it meant that the ending didn't make up for the slog to get there.I don't really  the time I spent playing this, but I definitely would have enjoyed playing something else more.  There was also way too much slogging back and forth between different areas - the quicktravel (which is totally not mentioned anywhere - hit M) worked pretty well for the first few sections, but some of the later ones just required crossing several long screens repeatedly, back and forth, back and forth...
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: I'm honestly on the fence about this one, but my ultimate answer has to be a non-recommendation.VirtuaVerse is a cyberpunk adventure game that gives no real specific information about the history of the world the story takes place in. It's just the future and everything is kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥. You play as Nathan, a hardware engineer and retro technology enthusiast who wakes up one morning to find his girlfriend gone with only a lipstick message on the mirror to clue him in to her location. Going out to look for her, he winds up getting swept up in a typical conspiracy plot.The primary positive that I can say about this game is that it looks and sounds amazing. The pixel art is crisp and highly detailed, the dark environments are lit with luscious neon and later lovely natural lighting, and the design of the backgrounds and characters are great for establishing the type of environment and world you're in. The soundtrack is similarly extremely well done with a great mix of synth rock, ambient, and world rhythms for the non-urban environments. The presentation absolutely sold me on the game and was the reason I bought it.The puzzles are where things start to break down. Now, I actually don't think most of the puzzles were that bad. It was actually much simpler than expected to get a grasp of what you're supposed to do, even on the 'Classic' difficulty. I was surprised considering that this game was advertised on hearkening back to classic adventure games which had awful puzzle design. Now, the problem is that they still managed to screw up the puzzles in different ways. You know what you have to do and often have a ton of items that you could reasonably accomplish your objective with, but the game still expects only one response from you. So, there's a lot of fiddling around with different items, only interacting with certain items in a certain way, pixel-hunting since even now we still have games coming out that don't make interactibles reasonably distinct from the environment around them, back-tracking to older areas for new items or to talk to people you'd previously exhausted all dialogue options with, etc. About 40% of the time the puzzles are a bastard to solve and not in a fun way; in a way where you have to comb over the map 15 times, talk to everyone, and use every item on everything else. It's just tedious.I might still recommend it if the story was any good, but it's pretty bland and forgettable. It's typical cyberpunkian corporations overstepping their boundaries and rogue AIs and what not. Outside of the final twist, there's not many interesting developments, and the final twist leaves the story narratively unsatisfying anyway since it kind of comes out of nowhere. No real special care was taken with world-building or incorporating world-building with the story, so the game's ultimate message rings rather hollow and progression feels random throughout. Also, the game leans way too far into the adventure game protagonist being an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ trope. A lot of adventure game protagonists are ♥♥♥♥♥, but this might have surpassed Mystery of the Druids because at least Halligan never got somebody killed in the context of the game. Nathan is thoroughly unlikable for how he uses people and their property as he pleases without repercussion. The ending of the game feels appropriate in this way but just makes everything worse.VirtuaVerse was a disappointment. It looks glossy on the surface, but when you dig beneath it all, it just winds up being mediocre more than anything. I don't know, if you want some decent atmosphere and alright puzzles maybe go for it. If you want a good story and a good adventure, go elsewhere. Play Technobabylon instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Music and specially graphics are fantastic. The aesthetics, animations, cutscenes... are of a sublime level. However, the dialogues are boring, most characters have no personality whatsoever, or just plain stupid. The story starts well, with plenty of programming/computing references but quickly becomes convoluted with lack of proper explanations, attempting a to be grandiose, sarcastic, self-guessing the future etc.BUT, and it's a big but, the worst part of the game are the puzzles/mechanics. A lot of pixel hunting, not logical solutions and VERY SLOWLY walking between locations that are very far away.

_childDocuments_.review: is clearly a love letter to point & click adventure games of the 90's, not only in its engine, animations, and interface, but also in some of its puzzle design. The pixel art is a masterpiece, the soundtrack is memorable, and the adventure is captivating. However, the price of fidelity brings with it some of the elements that made old games frustrating, such as lazy direction, useless inventory items, pixel hunts, and baffling riddles that are sure to prevent completion in one session. Thus, it's difficult to accurately appraise  as a yes/no recommendation, because it largely depends on your threshold for games that don't lead you by the hand. ✅ Pixel perfect art. The real magic happens once you enable AVR overlays (a game specific event)✅ Wide ranging OST. Also, incorporates environmental effects for immersion✅ Simple "look" and "use" interface, no clutter of icons and options.✅ Roughly a dozen locations to visit, though not all accessible throughout the game✅ Serious story but not without (sometimes dark) humor. A complete ending, though it does allow for a sequel.✅ Simple achievements for collectors. Only two missable, but not hard to find.❌ No branching decisions. Nathan takes actions you cannot control (ie, indirectly kills a character)❌ Lack of direction. In many instances, figuring out what to do is the puzzle. This leads to brute forcing.❌ Limited world building. Almost no character development. Plot dumps dampen the climax and reveals.❌ Useless inventory items. Many have limited use, and stay with you to the end of the game.❌ No fast travel. Backtracking is mandatory. Expect to spend a lot of time wandering between screens.❌ No voice acting. Silent characters from start to finish.❌ Extremely linear. A one-way trip, with no alternatives. Limited replay value. is centered on Nathan, a hardware engineer who wakes up to find his girlfriend missing. In a quest to locate her, he gets wrapped up in a conspiracy of global proportions. You'll travel from seedy city streets to underground metros, desert junkyards, frozen caves, and even outer space. The dystopian future portrayed is a familiar one, but explored from an AVR perspective where everyone is jacked in from birth.The game wears its LucasArts and Sierra inspirations on its sleeve, mimicking both the best and worst aspects of them. It nails the art, atmosphere, and audio superbly, no qualms there. But it brings with it many frustrations that plagued early point & click games, ranging from red herring inventory items, invisible flags to earn new dialogue options, and of course, puzzles with solutions that aren't hinted or explained clearly. Granted, crafting hints without giving away the solution is a very difficult task in and of itself, but  is stingy on explanations for what you need to do.This issue extends to the writing as well. Nathan is a fairly one-dimensional character, who acts like the hapless victim in the game's chain of events. But is he really? As the player, you don't have agency over how to solve the obstacles in Nathan's way. Every objective is about doing something to advance Nathan's cause, however he sees fit, and he's not very forthcoming about what he has in mind. This creates a rift between him and the player, which is widened when Nathan's actions cause other character deaths. While probably intended to be dark humor, it's hard not to judge Nathan's actions because his story is framed from the perspective of an onlooker. Classic games did have protagonists whose actions ruined other people's days, but they also did a better job of putting you in the character's shoes, so that you feel complicit in the consequences. For , it culminates into an ending that isn't quite positive for Nathan, but at the same time, may please some players as karmic justice for his misdeeds.The world of  is compelling, but not fully fleshed out. The reveal of the big bad comes by way of plot dump, which is overwhelming and requires suspension of disbelief. Characters we meet never really grow or change over the course of the game, including Nathan. It's hard to feel any chemistry between the couple when Nathan finally does find Jay.If it sounds like I'm bashing the game, that isn't the intention. If anything,  is a welcome addition to the point & click genre that feels increasingly niche among mainstream titles. But rather than simply emulating its inspirations, it misses the opportunity to improve upon them and become something even better. If  earns a sequel, which I sincerely hope it does, it would be nice to explore more character depth, and involve us in the decision making. The puzzles could be complimented by character commentary, as well as unique feedback for incorrect item combinations, or item use attempts on environmental objects. And why not consider multiple routes? What made the original  game great was the ability to play simultaneously from two perspectives, and to alter the ending by your choices. That inclusion would have certainly taken  to the next level.Fans of retro point & click classics will no doubt enjoy this nostalgic adventure. For the uncertain, watch a bit of the early gameplay to see if it's right for you. Thankfully, you can now refer to player-made walkthroughs if you need help, so getting stuck is no longer an issue. Humanity's future is in your hands.: Story based achievements with 4 missables. If you want to play without looking at solutions, simply save at each new location you arrive in after an event. This will allow you to quickly reload and replay the section you need. With guide, maybe ~3hrs to 100%

_childDocuments_.review: I'm convinced not a single person beat this game without a guide. A good Point-and-click game has intuitive puzzles, this does not. Most periods of this game you'll be walking around with 25+ disjointed trash items in your inventory with no explanation where to go or what to do. What do you call a game that is impossible without a guide? A bad game. Art style and music is irrelevant and its positives are wasted when the meat of the game is rotten. Waste of time and money.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun adventure with great chiptunes and pretty pixels. I might have liked the writing as a kid, but it's not going to win any Pulitzers. The puzzles are generally fair, maybe sometimes too obtuse for the age group the writing aims for.You do, however, get to play as one of the bigger douchebags ever tasked with saving humanity. Among other misdeeds, the protagonist goes on dating websites under his girlfriend's ID, gets her a criminal record, acts indignant upon being lightly reprimanded for killing her team mate, and harasses an innocent black mechanic.This is a lukewarm recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: I know some may find the puzzle part of the game difficult and annoying,but once you find the rules of this game its actually more special than other point&click games.I think maybe its bcuz we're use to focusing on how to use it right after finding it,thats why I was stuck for so long at beginning.but dont,at least dont waste as much time as i did before.However,i dont want to spoil your game experience by shortening your thinking time with my tips so i wont say too much but what i can say is that there are maps in the game~and yeah i was that dumb to miss it.Other aspects of the game are also great, like the soundtrack and the story.I usually don't like playing male characters as a female, bcuz there're some certain feelings that i cant relate to.But this game was an immersive experience for me,not to mention how beautiful its cyberpunk world is.The only thing I didn't particularly like was the language translation of this game,i know it has nothing to do with the game but still, i want to mention it in passing. i do REALLY appreciate the translators,but i'd appreciate it more if you didnt translate with your own personality. Bcuz Nathan sounds like a street punk in Chinese.Anyway,i'll play it again in English.All in all, thanks to the team that made this game, its very special!
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: You know, there are so many good things i want to say about this game but I will keep this short.The story is great and it points to a lot of contemporary things we deal with today. It's thought through and engaging. Definitely a story that could be made for a movie. The puzzles are difficult, granted, but not impossible. Most of the times i was stuck because i did not have a particular item which i found only after hours of scanning screens or that when i forgot to check everything again as there are so many variables at certain points in the game. What i absolute love is all the little references to old PC hardware and the WAREZ scene. Or the Scene. I am an older gamer myself so i recognize all these little references. It put a smile to my face and the devs are definitely of the oldskool i think :) The graphics or pixelart is beautiful and it really adds to the great atmosphere in the game.The only thing that would make this game even better is voice acting. I know old point and clickers dont have this, but it will definitely add something extra to the game. Perhaps a director's cut like Disco Elysium?
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: VirtuaVerse has its moments but it lacks polish to captivate anyone but hardcore point&click fanatics. While visuals are usually passable and often stunning from time to time there's a character or animation that's plain ugly which, compared to the main protagonist, makes it look like an afterthought drafted day before deadline (e.g. his girlfriend's walk animation). It's still solid 7/10.Music is acceptable, at least for a while, but I've found myself gradually lowering the volume during the first hour or two and finally ended up muting it checking for few minutes only when I got to the next area. Almost same mood and bit throughout entire game, one set of instruments, very similar tracks, becomes repetitive quickly. SFX saves it just a tad but not without its own quirks - some of the sounds are too loud, some too quiet. General audio experience reeks of somebody willing to spend more money on a pair of designer headphones than decent audio mastering courses - 4/10.Finally, let's get to the meat of the genre - story. While it touches upon some interesting subjects, man, does it lack in execution! Dialogues suffer the American movie approach of stating the obvious and explaining what happens as it happens making every character sound artificial. Game world is littered with nerd's wet dreams like winning a drone race with circuit jumpers, becoming a hacking group member by getting a tattoo or having a cool girlfriend who's not only an ex rock star but also a secret agent slash hacker. If that wasn't enough, every few minutes the player gets Wikipedia-level-of-detail schooled on 80's hacking community lingo and hardware - it's neither fun to read nor needed for the plot but it's there with all its inaccuracies and bollocks - I am an 80's hacker, trust me when I say nobody wants to go back. I played in English but can't shake the feeling the original script wasn't in English... My guess is Hindi or Mandarin. I'd rate the story higher if it wasn't for small bugs here and there that can skip whole dialogue when actions aren't completed in specific order. Plot gets 6/10.Did I enjoy it despite? Somewhat, yes. Enough to recommend the game? To all point&click and pixel art fans - probably maybe. Overall: 6/10.I should add I've encountered zero technical issues on my Linux machine.

_childDocuments_.review: This game, while visually pleasing, was a pretty terrible game.  I've played many point and click games, and unfortunately this has got to be one of the worst.  You get so many items and it's not even clear which ones are used for which... Also there are plenty of times where you can't even be sure of what to click on, so you kind of just have to click on everything until you find which is interactive.   For me personally, if guides weren't available online, this would be unbeatable.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has beautiful pixel art cyberpunk visuals, that's actually why I bought it. Also, soundtrack is not bad.At the beginning, you can choose between "easy" and "hard" version of the game, which is a nice feature.I didn't finish the hard version, I switched to easy one because I got stuck and frustrated quite early.However, even in the easy version I had to use a trial and error approach on some "puzzles" and they were just stupid.The story seemed rather childish to me. I was expecting something more dark and mature.Overall, the negative feeling prevailed, mainly because of the story and the "puzzles".
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. A LOT of hard work, creativity and love went into making this game and it seems to have all been fuelled by a single passion: 80's / 90's nostalgia. This game is pure distilled 80's nostalgia, the game design, puzzles, art, environment, story, dialogue and characters are all thoroughly steeped in it. It feels believable and immersive because it is just so consistent in delivering on this single theme.If you're into classic point and click adventures like Space Quest and Monkey Island and find yourself wishing someone would make more games like those then you're in luck, you've found it!As with anything so purely distilled it can come on a bit strong though, like eating something super sweet and then suddenly feeling overwhelmed and nauseous, which is my only issue with the game, but we'll get to that.In classic 80's style VirtuaVerse brings you both the best and the worst parts of those old 80's point and click adventures. It delivers a large variety of environments to explore and characters to interact with, especially when compared to most other modern point and clicks. You travel to various different settings and climates during the game making it feel large and immersive. The environments and characters are in beautifully crafted pixel art animation. Probably the best I've seen to date. As always the most important thing about a point and click is the story and the game really delivers there. It tells a tale of a dystopian cyber punk future where the main character goes from just trying to achieve a simple goal to suddenly finding himself on a mission to save the world. The story, in true 80's fashion is also quite long compared to most modern point and clicks making it good value for money.Unfortunately the game also brings you some of the more frustrating elements of 80's point and clicks. Convoluted / moon logic puzzles. They're not entirely "scare a cat past some tape to make a fake moustache" (GK3) levels of crazy but it definitely left me hopelessly stuck a couple of times and reaching for a walk through (space fruit pixel hunt, I'm looking at you). To be fair, this was probably to be expected when I chose to play the game in "Old School" mode.Another down side of its 80's style was that it doesn't contain any of the newer innovations in point and clicks that one has come to expect, like the ability to hold down a key and see everything you can interact with in the environment or other mechanics outside of the classic inventory system.Now for my biggest gripe. Nostalgia is, lets be honest, stupid. The idea that everything was better when we were kids, teens and tweens is mostly just the product of over hyped memories of a time when we were more care free. Objectively though, especially when it comes to technology, the past was rarely a better time. I'm not trying to yuck anyone's yum though, I myself, like a naughty child reaching into the cookie jar, indulge in the 80's / 90's nostalgia of my youth from time to time. It's partly why I was exited to pick up this game. But I'm aware that nostalgia is basically just mental masturbation. Nostalgia, when you engage with it, should always be done tongue in cheek, ironically and with a large dose of self awareness.Contrary to this, VirtuaVerse has a very serious tone. Railing against how modern technology is turning people into zombies, and holding up the 80's as an example of when technology was still "pure" by contrast. It seems to want to send a message, not be light hearted like Full Throttle or Leasure Suit Larry that does similar thematic / nostalgic trips. All the characters, especially the main character, seem to seriously believe that everything about the 80's was just plain better, especially, get this, the computer hardware! At one point his girlfriend while looking at an LCD monitor even says, totally unironically, "As Nathan always says 60Hz CRT or bust". A statement so unhinged and baffling that it totally breaks the immersion of the game. Now I can still roll with this to some degree, fine, these guys have a serious fetish for 80's hardware and this plays well with the theme. Cool. What annoyed me the most about the characters was just that they seemed so very proud of how steeped in their delusions they are. Around every corner you find references to what an elite bunch they are because they, for example, know how to code pixel animations that by today's standards are completely obsolete, primitive and underwhelming to look at. This makes the characters in the game come across as a totally out of touch circle jerk of douche bags who pat each other on the back for having achieved the ability to crawl in a world full of people who are running on a regular basis. A classic nostalgic confusion that because something was hard to do in the past it is still worthy of praise today. When dealing with a bunch like this it's very hard to take the message of the game seriously, however hard it may have tried to push its narrative.In short, my biggest gripe with the game was that I found the characters unlikable and immersion breaking.Over all though, this game is a cut above most other modern point and clicks. If you're into point and clicks this is definitely a must play. 8/10
