_childDocuments_.review: The music and graphics were excellent; however, the story and main character's actions just didn't do it for me. They might be fine for you though.About halfway through the game I considered uninstalling, not out of frustration with one of the difficult puzzles, but out of exhaustion from the main character being very unlikable.After completing the game, I can say while I liked many of the puzzles and characters, they were not enough to overcome my distaste for the character I was playing.If that sounds fine to you, and you're just in it for great cyberpunk music and art, you'll probably like it!
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: I agree with what most of the other reviewers have said:Art is top-notch. Music is great. Storyline is awesome. Character design is great.The game is just really *really* freaking hard. If you don't plan on looking at cheats, expect to spend whole days just systematically clicking every single item on every other item or point of interest, and going back and forth in scenes (which you can't shortcut through). Some of these solutions have no logical connection, yet have to be combined in specific ways to solve puzzles. I was scratching my head for a few of them.It's well worth the money for the experience, it's fun to play, and for the most part enjoyable. But saying it isn't frustrating would be a lie. I'm familiar with MBR and how he "advertises" his music... very much steeped in the hacker ethos. I get that. But man, sometimes this feels more like an extended intelligence/sanity test than a fun video game. If you can finish the game without cheating and with your sanity intact, you're a better person than I.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: I would totally recommend this to anyone who enjoyed LucasArts point and click games in the past, read Neuromancer, and digs synthwave. If I had any gripes at all it would be that our protagonist Nathan is a bit of an irritating man-child, but it never bothered me to the point I wanted to stop playing. The dialog can be periodically clunky, but again, never to the point that it detracts from the overall fun of this game. I didn't expect VirtuaVerse to be as big and sprawling as it is, but there are plenty of environments, puzzles, and cut scenes to make this feel like a triple-A effort from the heyday of point-n-clicks. And with a score by Master Boot Record, obviously the soundtrack rips. Honestly, I'd say it's worth the full purchase price.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: A cyberpunk adventure with story and music by Master Boot Record; published by darksynth/metal label Blood Music, which itself bears the name of a 1980s sci-fi novel. What a way to come full circle!This game does an exceptional job of being what it wants to be. Would it work for most people, though? Probably not. VirtuaVerse is slow, bold, and unnerving at times. It requires pixel-hunting, backtracking, and solving complex puzzles without much room for improvisation. Critical reception seems to reflect that "imperfection." And yet, that is all part of the game's strategy: no compromise! Well, almost. If you don't accept the challenge, there is still Story Mode. But if you do, get ready to beat it the old way, with frustration and fury at "stupid puzzles."VirtuaVerse has very detailed, colorful pixel graphics. That makes pixel-hunting more interesting than it usually is. Every scene boasts tons of intractable objects. Glaring screens and neon lights, tiny buttons and giant mechanisms, movie posters and sticky notes: not everything bears a meaning, but every detail complements the atmosphere still. Add augmented reality that puts even more detail into the environment, and you have an informational overload neatly tied to the narrative, which, by the way, is written by Vittorio D'Amore, also known as Master Boot Record, a synth-metal artist from Rome, Italy. Vittorio wrote both the story and music for the game. It might even look like the protagonist is based on Vittorio himself, judging by "breaking the fifth wall" remarks. While some might say it is a generic cyberpunk story, I would argue that it is cyberpunk in a way that is more true to the genre than most other stories, even prose-wise. It has that boldness and vision of classic 1980s science fiction imprinted on the name of the publisher, Blood Music — originally a Finnish darksynth/metal label that has already dissolved since expanding to game publishing.Let me sum it up: pixel graphics, atmosphere, story, setting, music, and overall vision are fantastic! Puzzles are demanding and often not logical within the limited scope of options, but that is how developers wanted them to be. Love it or hate it, I guess. Even though it took me around 16 hours to beat the game with no guides except for the Pill Street progression that established the necessity of backtracking and paying attention to the smallest details, I enjoyed solving it. My pace was one level a day: it required just enough focus to give without too much struggle.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: Do not pay full price for this game. After the first act, the "difficulty" of the puzzles relies entirely on completely random and arbitrary leaps of logic that you would never make without scanning every pixel of every screen multiple times. Often the solution to a puzzle is found and discarded because you haven't clicked the right spot at the right time in the right order, in spite of the fact that you (the player) have already solved the puzzle. This happens OFTEN. You will solve the puzzle in your head, and find you are unable to carry out the solution, causing you to discard the correct solution and begin an endless hunt. In some cases, new dialog options will appear with literally no indication that a character would have anything new to say.  There are a few sad attempts at "red herring" fake puzzle solutions that only serve to irritate you. Often, the real world logical solution to a puzzle is dangled in game, only for the actual solution to be some completely insane thing that makes little to no sense.  The game looks great and has an amazing soundtrack, but it plays like Quest For Glory 1.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: The good1)	Nice artwork in the first ½ of the gameThe Bad1)	The music isn’t for everyone, and is grating at numerous points, especially in the latter portion of the game.2)	The art drops off dramatically during the last 1/3rd of the game, and in the middle is only passable at best. The game literally goes from a scenic cyberpunk dystopia to rectangles by the end.3)	Character design is rather poor, apart from one notable exception during the ice cave area. The main character looks alright at first, but quickly as you see others you realise that he only looks good in comparison to the other abysmal artwork on display.4)	Areas at the end of the game are uninspired and lacklustre in terms of creativity, especially when you consider this game is a homage to 90’s point and clicks like Monkey island, which created a host of funny events and a main character you wanted to explore with, whereas by the end of this game I simply wanted the main character to shut up, drop dead and rot away.  – Neuromancer has a similar ending in regards to the location and the idea, and pulls this off far better, and whist Neuromancer ending felt amazing, this ending felt like a cop out.5)	The host of characters are totally unlikeable. Whilst this wouldn’t be a problem if our main character wasn’t portrayed as holier than thou, they are. Nathan believes he is not god’s gift to earth, but god himself. He walks around, ruining lives for sometimes no reason, and never once does he question his own motivations. His objective at the beginning, as he searches for his girlfriend, is derailed near instantly as he struggles to be a decent human being to just about anyone around him. Whilst some characters in game seem to deserve this attitude, there are others such as the homeless man at the beginning who we just act rather condescendingly towards, or better yet as an example a young gang member, who because Nathan simply cannot wait twenty minutes, has murdered for no reason, and he never once seems to understand the ramification of this even when directly confronted by the gang leader and his girlfriend about it, do not. A personal favourite of this absolutely horrific display of sheer apathy to any other sentient creature is observed in the junkyard, wherein after murdering an A.I that physically cannot move to hurt him, and only attempts to defend itself as he approaches, instead of being granted an option to perhaps converse with the creature, he instead makes it kill itself. After which, he gloats over his victory, saying this is what A.I get for trying to be people, which is ironic because Nathan is the least human character in the game. This is oddly juxtaposed by the way he treats another A.I in the graveyard, treating the dying machine with respect… until he tears off its arm from the then fresh corpse. Whilst granted he was doing this is help another machine, the odd manner in which he demonstrates his inner twisted morality is horrifying as a player to have to witness, and apart from the gang leader moment he is never questioned on it once, not to mention the time he cheated on his girlfriend with three pleasure bots, and had the audacity to accuse her of cheating on him for the pure reason she has male friends. If our character was designed as unlikeable, it would be interesting, but he is continuously displayed as the true hero in all of this, which leaves a sour taste in my mouth.6)	There are a few places in the story where the A.I wars are alluded too, a seemingly extremely important event that has coloured most of humanities perception of A.I ever since. However, very few details are ever given on the A.I wars themselves, making to impossible for the player to sympathise with the A.I hostility, especially when they demonstrate they are often kinder and more humane then our main characters. 7)	The game completely jumps the shark at the end, or should that be jumps the giant squid. It feels like playing a completely different game due to the tonal shift form gritty cyberpunk to pirate to A Space Odyssey watered down. This again makes it really hard to follow what the characters motivations are anymore, as what they are trying to stop is not only already happening, they also all seem to enjoy using it and our main character even after trying to say that the VR is bad, gets annoyed in a town where he can’t access it, and goes out of his way to do so. 8)	The puzzles in game are unintuitive and illogical to the extreme. Problems are solved via sheer arbitrary guess work, and sometimes you have to have looked at some tiny pixel before you can make the solution that you figured out ten minutes ago actually work. By the halfway mark, I was already using a walkthrough because I simply could not be bothered anymore. The back tracking to previous areas was novel about twice. It’s a shame then that this was in the mid-late game near mandatory for every, single, puzzle. Calling them puzzles is perhaps too nice, as really they are all riddles, with every riddle being ‘what is the writer thinking now?’.9)	Speaking of the writers, there a ton of funny haha epic references to the early nineties computing scene. This was charming at first, however it quickly becomes obvious that the writers are doing nothing more than slapping their own backs. There is what is likely meant to be a funny sequence when a demo disc is played, and the side characters all talk about how hard it could be to code things that. Gee whizz developers, thank you for my computing lesson in my point and click cyberpunk game. Secondarily, they speak of the IRC network for a while, in an odd tone that would imply ‘only 90’s kids would remember this’ – this not only means that the reference would be lost on the average player, but as someone who knows what this is and uses it, was embarrassing to see at best and insulting at worst, as it implies the service they speak off is dead – which it simply isn’t. 10)	In conclusion, don’t play this. If you like point and click games, find one that has escaped the trouble they faced in the 90’s. If you like Cyberpunk, play The Red Strings Club or Va-11 Hall-A, which are both more interesting and have much better executions and exploration of the topics discussed in this game.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: An old-school hardcore Adventure in a cyberpunk setting - what can possibly go wrong? A lot of things, it turns out. It has some clever puzzles and witty gags, and the art is gorgeous, but the whole experience is extremely uneven in both narrative and gameplay. Narrative-wise, the game tries to balance humorous and serious beats, but only succeeds with the former. Jokes are good, and oftentimes made me laugh out loud. Serious bits, on the other hands, are fifty shades of awkward. The protagonist is prone to long preachy monologues on the evils of modern tech and the shallowness of modern culture as opposed to cosy and virtuous retro-scene. That would be bad enough, but then the "main quest" so to speak (introduced around the mid-point) is an extension of this "philosophy" and literally has to do with saving people from themselves as they "get alienated in their own realities" by way of AR tech. All of this is extremely inelegant and groan-worthy - Black Mirror this game is not. And speaking of Black Mirror, the game commits probably the worst ludonarrative sin - it utterly fails its worldbuilding. The setting of VirtuaVerse is extremely vague and unspecific, just some cyberpunk tropes glued together by nostalgia and resentment of modernity.Then comes the gameplay. The game gets points for aiming for a higher level of challenge than most modern adventures, and some puzzles, as I mentioned earlier, are very cleverly designed. An extensive inventory that makes it harder to "bruteforce" puzzles is also a good touch. Unfortunately, all of this goodwill becomes undone by it being extremely slow and backtrack-heavy. The former aspect is the most aggravating. Locations are sprawling and uniformly zoomed in, while walking speed is slow and there is no "double-click to exit immediately" feature. It makes backtracking something you're going to dread. And you're going to do a lot of backtracking, because, on the one hand, there is no hotspot highlighting, so important spots are easy to miss; and on the other hand, some actions and dialog options are locked behind plot triggers. So each time you get stuck in a puzzle you have perform a sweep of all the available locations to check if you missed a hotspot or a new dialog has opened up - at snail's speed. It just sucks the enjoyment out of harder puzzles completely.All in all, if Steam reviews provided an "uneven" or "neutral" option, I'd rate VirtuaVerse that. But unfortunately the system is binary and I'm too frustrated with the game to recommend it in good heart.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy point and click adventure games, SKIP THIS ONE.I played and beat Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis before the internet and walkthroughs/guides/hints were available, but that game had strong logic to its puzzles.　THIS GAME is incredibly obtuse and has the worst case of moon logic puzzle that I've played yet.  Goals SEEM simple enough, however how to go about it will make no sense and you have zero prompting or direction from the game as to how/why you would accomplish your goal.Sure you can do the old process of elimination and try and every single combination that exists, but that's not using logic, following a pattern, or using your noggin, that's just going by rote.  The person who created the puzzles for this game needed to go back and think through the puzzles and have it work by logic and not because the creator already knew the end goal and worked in reverse via God mode.The other bad part is it's difficult at times to see who is speaking to whom.  There is little differentiation from any character, no VOICES for a game in 2022 when games made in the 90's had them, and not even a difference in FONT or COLOR to differentiate the characters.Save your money and buy a BETTER point and click adventure game, there are actually a handful of them on Steam!

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful setting and a theme that resonates--an examination of how far we're willing to delude ourselves into thinking our creativity can solve any problem. I don't want to spoil anything, but there's some really good subtle story telling--like how the one character off-handedly mentions he was forced to get the permanent reality chip installed while in prison--that helps build the world. The art is beautiful, the music pulses and the writing tackles powerful themes while also imparting a lot of history around the origins of computer technology. Gameplay wise, I would say it's actually quite hard for an adventure game because it commits a few "sins" that most video games don't--for example, it may expect you to use an item twice in a row or talk to someone you'd exhausted dialogue options with earlier through an intuition that now they may have new dialogue based on something you'd encountered. Definitely give it a try if the art design appeals to you--we live in an age where you don't need to spend longer than you want to on any given puzzle and the music, visuals, and themes are really excellent and convey very contemporary concerns, despite being set in the future. Well worth playing through to the end.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: This is  decent cyber punk themed game.  I liked parts of it, particularly the middle.  The main character is... not that likeable.  A lot of the game is just trying to ruin things for the npcs, to attain some personal goal.  Around the middle this changes to ruining things for a collective and worthy goal but all the same it doesn't feel great walking around as this sort of creep.  The settings are interesting particularly as the game moves on from a generic cyberpunk city to several other locales.I played through the first time on the story mode and didn't feel that I could review it fairly, s the devs recommend playing the original version.  I played partway through the original version and did enjoy it more, but not enough to want to complete the main storyline for a second time.One of the better cyberpunk pixel games around.  The world-building is there and the level of detail great.  Just feels like viewing this world from the perspective of a jaded hipster.  The 'humor' is mostly mean or just not there.  This doesn't bother everybody so there's a good chance of any cyberpunk fan enjoying the game.

Everything. I would recommend it to everyone.I love the artwork, i love the sound/Music, i love the story and the humour.5/5 from me.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a few months since I played this game. I thought I had already reviewed it. I was actually just listening to the soundtrack, which is some of the best chiptune music around. Mainly because it stays true to the origins of chiptune music, which is the Amiga cracktro scene. I really thought I had already reviewed it, and I actually just wanted to update my review. But apparently there is no review to update. What I wanted to say is that I've been thinking about this game a lot. I finished probably around 4 point and click adventure games each week, for several months straight. Most of them I don't really remember, even if they were good. But Virtuaverse keeps hanging around in my memory. I realize that this game is actually really good. There's quite a lot of friction in the puzzle design, but out of the 30+ adventure games I played, this one is a winner. They are all trying to capture the experience we had playing these games in the past, and VirtuaVerse is the only one that succeeded for me.The graphics are better than any old school adventure out there. It's the best of both worlds, because you get pixel graphics that move at 144fps/sec. The smoothness is just perfectI would say there are some design flaws in the inventory navigation systems. The contextual menu doesn't really feel like it's better than a left/right click systemThe environments in the game feel alive, and are well populated with various NPCs. Each location is its own self-contained universe.The length of the game is at a sweet spot. Some games are too short, and others are so long that they feel like a chore to complete and you lose interest in the story.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: VirtuaVerse is a big game, developed by a small team. Visually, it is in the style of the old Sierra adventures with pixels and lower resolution. However, Theta Division accomplishes an amazing amount of detail with this artform and the environments vary from urban, to desert, to snow, to undersea, and finally to space. Nathan, the main character, is out to save the world and journeys through multiple locations completing MANY subtasks in order to achieve his final goal. The music was excellent, although I did find it wearing after many hours and ended up turning the volume down. The dialog is extensive, but not overwhelming, and the absence of voice-overs was a plus. Overall, it is a good game that I would recommend with one caveat. You need a lot of patience to work through complicated multi-step and (sometimes) obtuse solutions.  Perhaps I do not have the stamina that I had 'back in the day,' but during several periods of being 'stuck,' I resorted to peeking at the text Guide posted on Steam to get myself moving forward again. I spent quite a few hours with this game and at times, it wore me out! It is definitely worth playing all the way through, as the ending was quite a surprise...
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? It's a classic point and click adventure taking place in a slightly dystopian future. A polluted environement, acid rain all day long, plastic plants, augmented virtual reality everywhere... a nice cocktail of Blade Runner and Neuromancer. You play a small-time criminal trading with illegal hard- and software, looking for his girlfriend who left him overhasty in the morning. Those things happen, no idea why he is trying to find her... The first thing you have to do is to repair your damaged AVR glasses, though. Finding a new lens for them isn't so easy, you have to poison a guy, blackmail another, have one getting fired from his boss and send a fourth one on a drug trip he won't forget too soon... all completely logical in a point and click adventure. Once you are able to use your AVR again, all locations suddenly become much more colorful with ads (or illegal graffiti) everywhere. You can turn your AVR off again, something that most of the other characters can't do.The controls work fine, you can basically look at/use a bunch of hotspots and your inventory. Trying everything with everything would take some time, because there are quite a few locations and inventory items. You talk to characters in Monkey Island style, seems you cannot make wrong choices and can just go through every available option. The item descriptions are ok, while the dialogues are often a bit subpar. Important to-dos are automatically written into your journal, so you don't forget the main story while trying to solve small problems.The game is drawn in pixel art straight out of the early 90s. Lucas Arts couldn't have done it better. Really cool! The synthwave soundtrack is not extremely bad, but I did turn the volume down soon because I got a headache from it. This doesn't matter very much, because all the dialogues are not voiced. No ultrawidescreen resolution or gamepad support.Classic pnc adventure in a cyberpunk world. Pixelated graphics and a good story full of typical item-oriented puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: The game managed to win my sympathy very quickly and could be an ideal cyberpunk adventure if it had not ignored certain things that make any point'n'click quest better. As I often say, the genre of adventure games is evolving for a reason, cutting off unnecessary things from itself, and highlighting the right ones. And here, if you look with a general look, then the game is just great. The pixel art is incredible, the plot is quite worthy - in some places humorous, in some places cynical, the music is beautiful, most of the puzzles are complex but interesting. The gameplay itself is built quite competently, but then what I mentioned above comes into play. Some puzzles are not just complex, they defy logical explanation. And if, for example, I can accept a riddle with a tattoo (yes, it turns out you need to find out information from one of the random people walking along the street with this puzzle,  which will become your key knowledge for solving), then in some places the solution to the riddle will be, for example, the key phrase that appeared on the character at the other end of the map after you performed some action.  You have no idea that this phrase appeared, continuing to run through a huge number of locations and trying to figure out something with a bunch of surrounding objects. And even this can be understood if the developers tried to intentionally complicate their game, but why simple things are not executed. For example, trashy inventory, why items that we will never use in the future, do not disappear from it? Ideally, if you have a large number of locations, then all the interaction points that are not needed for passing should cease to be active after the first acquaintance with them. It may seem that I didn’t like the game, but it’s completely not so, I got great pleasure from it most of the time (and its duration is quite serious). It's just that when you like something so much, you obviously want it to be even better. It is difficult not to note the inspiration that the creators had, the enormous amount of labor invested in every aspect of the game. This is a full-fledged fascinating adventure for fans of the genre, made in the best traditions of old-school games. And it seems to me that the problem with some puzzles arose precisely because the adventure is very large-scale, so there should be a lot of diverse content, and this can lead to the fact that some things will not be entirely successful. Perhaps a flexible hint system (not necessarily straightforward, but giving at least a direction vector), cleaning inventory from useless things would not hurt the game. Point changes can make the game even better, especially since all the fundamental things in it are already done at an excellent level. I am glad that there are more and more new teams in the genre offering their unique vision, I will wait for the next projects from these talented creators.

_childDocuments_.review: I rate this game 10/10 and here is why:10/10 Support:I issued a bug, they answered immediately and fixed the bug with todays update.10/10 graphic:I like pixel art and it fits the cyberpunk setting.10/10 music:The music is great and fits to the setup. sometimes i was wondering if the game was made inspired by the music or the other way around.and finally, the game remind me on the lucas arts adventure games and has native support for linux :).

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. I grew up playing the old Infocom, LucasArts, and Sierra games so I went into this with a pretty good idea of what to expect.  Had this game been released back in the late 90s, I probably would have given it a great review.However, I no longer have the patience to deal with pixel hunting for objects hidden in the environment,  excessive backtracking for no reason other than to artificially extend the length of the game, or with having to click on the same spot over and over again trying to trigger a specific dialog option before I can do what I already know needs to be done.  Oh, and there are no autosaves so yea, welcome to 1990.Even worse, there is one point where you have to do some translating but the text doesn't pause so you can write down the code. Instead, it scrolls quickly by forcing you to re-trigger the dialog over and over.  You even have the answer key in your inventory, but your character is too stupid to use it.  No, they make you flip back and forth between the dialog and your key, one letter at a time, until you get it figured out.  Yes, I liked the artstyle, the story, and even the music although it felt a bit repetitive. As to the game itself though, I really wish I would have skipped it. There are far too many other really good games in this genre such as Unavowed or the Blackwell series to spend time playing this one.Oh, and it also crashed on me right as the final cutscene started and my last save was about 2 hours back.  At that point I gave up,  uninstalled, and tagged it with "probably never going to play again.".
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: If you like point and click adventure games, then you should give this one a try on sale.If you like cyberpunk, you should give this game a try on sale.If you like great pixel art and great music, you might want to give this game a try on sale.If you like all of these things, it *might* be worth full price, but probably not.It's an above average game that will give you about 8 hrs of fun.  There are the usual point and click game logic brain farts, and the game could sorely use some quality of life upgrades like speed walking or a better fast travel system.  But all in all, I recommend it if you can get it for cheap.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: Played through this game and enjoyed it, recommended if you are a point and click fan and enjoy the cyberpunk theme but with some caveats. Also if you were interested in this game but avoided it due to all the mentions of the difficulty then it's the perfect time to try it out with the addition of the easier mode. I played through both and the pixel hunting and tedium is substantially reduced. The whole thing feels much less clunky I would say. Anyway the visuals are probably the first thing that you noticed and of course they are fantastic. Dark and moody atmosphere, buildings and streets washed in neon lights, unique character designs. Soundtrack is also awesome, chiptune and synth that fit the atmosphere well. Story is alright and is probably the most hit or miss part since it has a lot of old tech references and themes that some may not care for. Plot goes a bit off the rails near the end imo. Overall though I did enjoy playing through this and I think it's worth trying out now more than ever.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Beautiful cyberpunk point-and-click adventure game with a few hard puzzles and a messy story- Really pretty cyberpunk style pixel art.- Rich synthwave/electronic soundtrack- Decent game length. You should get at least 11 hours of play time without a walkthrough.- Intriguing characters and events kept me playing to discover more.- Clever thoughtful puzzles. (For the most part. See next section)- Certain puzzles are artifically hard. Among these puzzles, some are caused by not unlocking expected character dialogues until a certain unobvious event is triggered. Also there is a riddle section that requires extreme lateral thinking. Even the main character remarks that it is hard and a little silly.- Pixel hunting is required and a few objects can be hard to see or have multiple hotspots.- No voice acting or different text colors to differentiate who is talking- Overarching story feels far fetched and messy. The dialogue didn't feel authentic and there's too much focus on 80s/90s technology.Worth a purchase if you're a fan of point-and-click adventure games, especially classic LucasArts ones.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: Note/ TL;DR: If you like 90s cyberpunk nostalgia and very-challenging adventure games, I DO recommend this. I'm thinking that the majority of people won't, and this is a fiendishly hard game.I was as excited for this game to come out as I have been for any adventure game since the 90s. I really, really wanted to like it, and I actually enjoyed this game overall, for the most part. I've been a fan of cyberpunk since reading Neuromancer in the early 90s, was big into the BBS scene, the whole "hacker" scene of the 90s - and was big into adventure games as well. So this really pressed all of the right buttons for me, in that respect. That part I absolutely loved, although it becomes less and less cyberpunk as the game progresses.I had seen a couple of reviews before I started playing that talked about moon logic, but I was really pleasantly surprised by the first third of the game. I loved the aesthetic, the pixel art, the music. The puzzles seemed hard, but not rising to the level of what I'd call "moon logic". I was absolutely loving it. Then I get to the middle third (or so) of the game. The difficulty ramps up by an order of magnitude, and some puzzles I would definitely classify as requiring moon logic. Don't get me wrong - I enjoy a difficult adventure game. The issue to me is just that this section of the game is just so dense with very difficult puzzles that the plot grinds to an absolute halt, and you find yourself frustratingly backtracking, randomly trying every inventory object you have on things in the environment, repeatedly talking to the same people over and over again to see if new dialog options have opened up, etc. When you manage to figure something out, you rarely get any satisfaction, because the plot doesn't advance and you are just immediately presented with another puzzle. It really took me out of the mode of enjoying the game and made me feel more like I was doing chores.  A few things really added to the frustration. One of my major pet peeves in adventure games is pixel hunting, and there was a fair amount of it here, some so obscure that I had difficulty finding even with a walkthrough. At several places in the game, you have to talk to a certain character about something in order to progress, however the dialog option that is required does not appear until you perform some obscure sequence of actions, even though in many cases it is readily apparent that you need help from a specific character. The messages that you get when trying various actions could certainly be more helpful as well - sometimes something won't work, but you're on the right track - the message you get will likely just be the default "that's a dumb idea" message, or whatever, with no clue as to WHY that didn't work, or what you need to do to fix it.With all of that being said, the last third of the game lets up on the difficulty a bit, and is way more enjoyable for it. The ending, well....I won't spoil it, but I *really* hated it.Overall, the pixel art is awesome, the music is awesome, and the plot is....serviceable. I'd say that if you're not into adventure games AND 90s cyperpunk nostalgia, give this one a pass. If you are, it's worth a shot. Even with its flaws, I'm glad that I bought it and played it, and hope that the devs take the criticism in the constructive spirit that it was intended and do even better with their next release.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I'll keep this short and to the point. The story is fairly solid and kept me interested. The actual puzzles relied on way too much backtracking and moon logic. If you have a walk through handy when you get stuck, it might be worth a spin if you are a fan of the genre; although I thought the game became increasingly less cyberpunk as things went on so beware.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: VirtuaVerse – this is a very well-done game, and a must-play for any fan of the cyberpunk genre. While playing this game you will experience inventory object puzzles and philosophical dilemmas, all while being serenaded with beautiful (yes, truly beautiful) pixel art and well-placed music. Yet, this game is not without faults, and I simply cannot review it fairly without distinguishing an imperative boundary: a ‘before’ and ‘after’.  (the beginning of the game to discovering Jay’s involvement with The Blade) - VirtuaVerse has an absolute superstar kickoff. When entering the game you are immersed into a world that is both surreal and strange enough to evoke curiosity while also being real enough to make navigation sensible and understandable. I find that quite often games struggle with this aspect, and VirtuaVerse pulls it off in spades during the beginning. The facts of the matter are delusional enough to keep you wrapped up in the mystery and willing to press on and investigate. The puzzles during this time also make enough sense to a mildly experienced adventure gamer. They are challenging enough that they take a bit of thought, but do not wander off into infuriating Sierra-style moon logic. The puzzles also do the game justice, as they require wandering around the city and engrossing yourself into the environment. The Pill Merchant puzzle, the Beggar puzzle, the Pi nerd puzzle, the Bouncer puzzle…these are excellent, and require interaction with the surrounding environment in order to solve. They are realistic enough to be solvable, while also being challenging enough to be interesting and require adaptation to the beautiful environment. One critical feature I really appreciated about this part of the game was how well it highlighted a critical feature of cyberpunk dystopias – that of a  existence. The resulting vast divide between the wealthy and the poor creates a powerful story-telling dynamic that resonates with people today because we can look around us and see it coming to fruition. Life imitates art, art imitates life.Unfortunately, with the concept of a cyberpunk dystopia becoming increasingly more popular, especially with the infamous release of the long-awaited Cyberpunk 2077, we are running the risk of losing the essence of what makes cyberpunk so powerful as a genre. Too often we are being fed cyberpunk-style content by those who would be on the ‘wealthy’ side of the divide, painting a picture of what cyberpunk “should” look like without the ability to grasp, and therefore portray, the resulting loneliness, entropy, decay, hopelessness, anger, and vitriol felt by those on the ‘poor’ side of the divide. Cyberpunk is truly a populist genre. Perhaps the best way to sum up what I enjoyed so much about VirtuaVerse was how elegantly and accurately it grasped the cyberpunk dystopia. We play as Nathan, a desolate and hungry protagonist – ‘hungry’ not necessarily for food, but that which makes life worth living. All the essential needs are met in a cyberpunk dystopia, but all aspects that allow us to thrive are cut off and require extremely hard work and sometimes breaking the law (Nathan’s desperate attempt to protect his privacy, the space and nutrition needed to be healthy, etc.). This is why Nathan’s search for Jay is so pertinent and why I found it so easy so get invested in the game at the start – she’s clearly the one true piece of joy and contentment that he has in this brutal environment. I felt compassion for him and see him as a true Everyman.  (discovering Jay’s involvement with The Blade until the conclusion of the game) – Once Jay is located and she confirms her involvement with The Blade, the game takes a noticeable downturn. I did not want this to be the case, as I was completely engrossed in the game up until this point. Jay has ceased to be this enigmatic ‘dark angel’ of sorts and is now just a mouthy “cool hacker girl”.The problem is not necessarily with the dilemma that Nathan faces, but in how it is portrayed. Strangely, it almost feels as if this half of the game was written and created by an entirely different group of people. The story is not bad (I actually enjoyed the concept of the Technomancers and the threat of everyone being locked into separate realities), but what is bad is how the characters seemingly stagnate and the puzzles shift from interesting and challenging to just plain terrible. Nathan stops being an interesting, hardworking, clever, and relatable protagonist to being an obnoxious and jealous boyfriend (I’m not sure if the creators were projecting their own emotions into the game whenever Ramirez is involved or were simply trying too hard, but I have my assumptions) tasked with the heavy virtuous burden of contacting the Technomancers and saving the world. Jay becomes a snarky Mary Sue, a secret genius hacker who is also a talented AVR graffiti artist with a seemingly low opinion of Nathan. In short, once we reach this part of the game, characters go from being dynamic and interesting to one-dimensional stereotypes. The puzzles in the second half were, to be completely blunt, some of the worst that I’ve ever experienced in an adventure game. While it could be stated that the devs were trying to pay homage to the Sierra-style adventure games of the past, frankly it is impossible to do this effectively because of the current gaming climate. Sierra, the scapegoat for this argument, could get away with such creations back in the day because the market was not as mature. Today, people have experienced plenty of adventure games with better and more challenging puzzle mechanics and can do one of two things if they get frustrated with a game’s puzzle: 1) look up a walkthrough in seconds, 2) quit the game and play something with better puzzles. Sierra was able to bleed every drop of life out of their games both because they needed a way to draw out gameplay while also not needing to address the options available to gamers today. One example of a good puzzle in the second half of the game is the altar puzzle in the hut in the Nuwaka jungle that requires use of the ASCII chart. This puzzle is grounded in logic and can be reasoned out. In contrast, use of the ASCII chart for the Satnajoskull riddles is ridiculous and has little to no grounding in logic to allow the player to reason the numerical intent – it simply came across as if the devs tried too hard to make it hard. Nearly all puzzles in this half of the game follow this pattern, including the nearly-impossible Technomancer Rune puzzle, and the Octopus bait puzzle (Jay’s entire sequence in the boat and Missile Command Center is clearly a filler and so clunky from a gameplay standpoint that it may as well require the use of dumb cursors). As a whole this is a good game, yet I would recommend use of a walkthrough for the second half because you will be wasting your time without some guidance. I would recommend not using a walkthrough for the first half so as to better absorb the environment and overall atmosphere of the game (it is likely that a walkthrough will not be needed at this time anyway). I hope that the creators of this game work on more projects in the future and follow a pattern similar to the pristine one followed at the beginning of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: not terrible but also really not great , so iI will give a thumbs downI will give some positives first: The pixel art graphics are really great for the most part and still pretty good the rest of the game. Music is also pretty good.The puzzles are good for the most part, but there are some pretty contrived ones. I had multiple ones where I hit a wall for while. Prepared to get stuck a lot. This is not necessarily bad. I think the developers tried to go for a oldschool style adventure.For example there are multiple items with no use clogging up your inventory the whole game. Decide for yourself if that is up your alley.Now to the bad parts:  I read some reviews that warned about the story/writing aspect of the game and boy were they right. They went full throttle on all the clichés and tropes and it is most of the time more annoying than funny or interesting.The biggest problem is that the story and the characters are very bland. Also doesn't help that the main character is the biggest ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and does mean ♥♥♥♥ to everyone he meets. I get it that it is a trope in adventure games that you crazy stuff to solve a puzzle, but here it is just too much. Yes you actually a have to kill a guy and the characters in the game kind of gloss over that fact.Some redeeming aspects are some of the later areas, which are varied enough in style to keep you grinding through the hard puzzles and bland story. I think the last area was pretty neat.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. It has a lot of positives. I adore the soundtrack and art design for this game. It drips cyberpunk and if you don’t love the cyberpunk aesthetic you are a crazy person! I do dislike these pixel style adventure games, I feel this retro style needs to end. The resolution of this game is at the limit of what I would accept in a pixel style game.  I would prefer it was smoothed out like “Unavowed.” However, each environment is very well crafted and full of detail, so I can forgive it.I also think the plot is quite well done in this game. The idea that everyone is so focused on their VR lives that they don’t even realize that reality itself is being distorted is delightful and your quest to stop this from happening is a great cyberpunk plot…now if only it had involved a murder mystery. I believe all adventure games should be murder mysteries as this style of game is best suited to that.  So the fact this isn’t a murder mystery is pretty disappointing.  However, it’s quite a very serviceable cyberpunk story.  The characters are a problem.  The only character developed in anyway is Nathan and he is a real pos.  He is responsible for some pretty egregious stuff in this game and his attempts to justify it to himself are insane.  I would find this a massive problem…if I didn’t think the developers purposely made him a pos for narrative purposes Despite the fact I enjoy the soundtrack immensely, the art direction, and the plot of the game…the puzzles are so horrifically bad that I can’t recommend it.  I had to use a walkthrough for almost the entirety of the game…I’ve been playing adventure games for the last 30 years and I could not solve basically any puzzle.  That’s a problem, I feel the developers could not have possibly play tested this game.  I can’t even think of an adventure game where the logic in literally every single puzzle is so divorced from the solution.  The Dig and Monkey Island 2 have some pretty absurdly difficult puzzles…but not every puzzle.  While old Lucasarts games had issues with the absurdity of what items you combined to get the solution which made them very difficult…the problem with this game is far more egregious.In this game it’s not just the fact that the combination of items sometimes is absurd…it’s that the player can’t even comprehend what the game is even asking of you.  In most adventure games you are given a goal and then you have to search for items in the environment to accomplish that goal…but here the solution never seems connected to that goal even remotely.  I’m only going to give one example so as not to spoil every puzzle, but just know literally every puzzle is this absurd.  So at one point you need to talk to the Cypher Master.  A guy is using the only computer that has internet access so you need to get rid of him.  There are no hints given on how to accomplish this task, you can try giving him items, but that doesn’t work.  Leaving that building and walking around the town  reveals a cat sitting on a roof and a dog in another building. To get the guy off the internet, you need to first knock the roof of the building next to the one the cat is on to knock the cat off the building, disturb the dog in the other building and unleash him, so the dog and cat start a fight in the street.  Doing that causes the dog and cat to then eventually make their way to the building where the guy is on the internet and he runs away?  It’s a real problem in game design.There is absolutely no way to have guessed that was somehow the solution and the chain of puzzles that lead to you accomplishing getting that dog and cat into a fight is equally ridiculous.  So you basically have like an hour long string of other puzzles to ultimately lead to getting this dog and cat into a fight (it’s not as simple as knocking the roof of the building…I’m not even going to go into the absurd smaller puzzles that allow you to even accomplish that goal) which (1) there are no hints to even lead you to believe this chain of smaller puzzles would cause the dog and cat to fight (2) no hints exist that to get this guy to stop using the internet you need to start a dog and cat fight.  Every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ puzzle is this way.  It’s difficult for me to comprehend that anyone can solve these puzzles and win this game without a walkthrough.  Even if you told me, well I won the game without a walkthrough, I would simple never believe that you accomplished that through logic.  Instead I would assume you would have managed it by simply clicking on everything and trying everything with no concept of why you were doing these things or what you were even attempting to accomplish by doing it…basically you would have to brute force this entire adventure game.  Read any walkthrough for the game and it immediately becomes comical how devoid from logic any of these puzzles are.  I can’t recommend such a poorly designed adventure, it’s a real shame.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of old school point and click adventures, cyberpunk and synthwave I thought I would really enjoy this game. That however, was not the case. Even as someone who has developed their own point and click adventure game, I found navigating the world and solving puzzles to feel clunky and unintuitive. The game has you solve a puzzle just to leave your apartment at the very beginning. Rather than have the plot unfold organically, you again have to solve a puzzle just to get to each new step in the narrative. Leave your apartment? Puzzle. Contact your girlfriend? Puzzle. Open a door? Puzzle. At no point do you just flow with the story and feel steeped in the game world because you're constantly banging your head against the wall trying to figure out how to even progress the game alone by baby steps. The game often contradicts itself. For example, you can buy a set of screwdrivers, which the player says contain proprietary screwdrivers, yet you can't use them on a cell phone because it requires "proprietary screwdrivers". It has you solve puzzles multiple times in really bizarre ways, then makes you backtrack to solve the puzzle again in a different way. It is just not straight forward at all. Often the puzzles seem random with no context or subtle hints given. The game also allows you to solve a puzzle in a wrong way, which makes you have to do it over again. This is a big mistake in point and click games that only causes frustration. For example, at one point there are 8 options of items you can get from a vending machine, which you need to use on an object that has at least 4 interactive variations. But only one combination works and you have to keep trying each one until you get the right one. I encountered a game breaking bug early on when a pizza delivery drone froze the character and itself in place at the apartment. This resulted in my having to reload and do several tasks again, which felt even more punishing considering I didn't even know *why* I was ordering a pizza or if that were what I needed to do to progress the story. Unfortunately the game really lacks plot hooks or traditional plot elements. Instead you're just dropped in and expected to know what to do or why to care about doing it.I've made it about 3 hours into this game and there are no interesting characters, in fact there really isn't a cast of characters at all. There is no plot other than "find your girlfriend". If a game can't interest you in 3 hours, with at least some kind of plot hook, what is the point?The graphics are great. The music is great. Unfortunately the story, controls, gameplay, world building and characters are completely lacking. This game could be much better if the developers had focused on telling a good story with good flow rather than constantly tripping over bad gameplay. It's all style and no substance.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: I so badly wanted to love this game, but I just can't. Once I start a game or book, I  to finish it--here, I stopped after just a few hours. The style is very attractive, the music is good, and the story overall is interesting. The element of turning on and off the VR had a lot of promise as well. You play as a cynical dbag hipster whose dialogue is pretty cringy but has a lot of fair ideas about data privacy and technology. I thought I could move past this until a few hours in when you link up with more dbag hipsters and it's just painful. The issues raised about technology overrun, uses of data, privacy, and our interconnected future are really interesting and critical to discuss, but the presentation absolutely kneecaps the impact. The self-congratulatory dialogue became unbearable. Additionally, some of the puzzles are super cryptic--I'm no expert, but I would NEVER think to do some of the things they ask you to do, and the prompts are really minimal. Between the dialogue and having to look at walkthroughs way too much, I decided to spare myself and just read the synopsis somewhere else.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful graphics, bad writing.The gorgeous and moody art and good music and sound immediately drew us into this game but unfortunately bad writing and game design ruined our stay. Dialogues are heavy-handed and unrewarding and for half of the puzzles the player is left to flail randomly with zero clues, making the game practically unplayable without a hints book. The author tried to recreate the self-deprecating humor of the point-and-click classics and to imbue the game with nostalgia for old tech and failed at both.There are some great ideas in the game design like the augmented reality elements but they aren't used to their full potential.It's a real pity. With better writing, this game could have become a new classic.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: If you love point and click game, Blade Runner movies plus cyberpunk vibe, this is the right one specially made for you.The gameplay is quite easy and can be so chillaxin'. The pixels' graphics and retro-ish sounds make the city and its environments feels so realistically vibrant and alive.But most of all, the story is one of the well-written around that is so rare and enjoyable to follow from start to the end.Thank you for making an excellent game, Theta Division and Blood Music!We'll be expecting more like this in the upcoming future.b(^_^)d
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: Gorgeous pixel art and animations. Unfortunately, the visuals are the only thing this game has going for it. Poor writing, unlikeable characters, nonsensical puzzle solutions, endless backtracking, and basic music/sound design bog down what could have been an at least okay experience. Ultimately Virtuaverse ends up feeling like a painful-to-play waste of time.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: This game is AMAZING!!! If you love the old-school Sierra games, then you are in for a real treat! It's everything you love about the Sierra games, but has that gorgeous cyberpunk world. The art is incredible, some of the best art I've seen in years! Plus, the soundtrack is fantastic. This game is a must-have for every gamer!
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: It took me a while to decide whether to recommend this one or not.The music is amazing.The art style is great.The story is ok.It's just the flow of the puzzles and the jumps of logic that makes this game less enjoyable than it could be.    Yay, progress?  Nope!  No satisfaction for you because that still won't work.  Or how about ?  Simples!  Er, nope.  Generic failure messages when you try, no explanation why.Story-wise, it's got some really nice ideas.  Although, again, there are bits where the execution falls a little flat.  One point near the start where your actions have some pretty severe repercussions and your character barely bats an eyelid.  Points to be pointed and clicks to be clicked, dontchaknow.So I will recommend this, but with a big BUT hanging over it.  It will probably get frustrating in places.  Expect to get stuck, expect to walk miles back and forth through screens that don't really add anything while trying to find out what you've missed.  And, hey, there's no playing hunt the pixel like with Full Throttle!
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: I love the visuals. Looks amazing (bought it without knowing anything else, and in that front it doesn't disappoint).It has no voice acting, witch is a bummer, but not a deal-breaker.The problem is that puzzle design is really bad, and as an adventure game, this is catastrophic. I've been playing Adventure Games since the early days (King's Quest I), and this game's puzzles reminded me of the "moon logic" of those times. I had to visit walkthroughs more times than I'm comfortable with.  Normally, when I do that, I slap my head saying “What a dummy. How didn't I see that!” With his game, every time I read the answer, my response was that I would have never arrived at the solution organically. Made me want to quit more than once. For instance:  As far as I can tell, this is a game by a small team, and --again-- it looks amazing. Hope they get better puzzle design in their future projects, because there are a lot of things to like. But in adventure games, puzzles are EVERYTHING.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: If I were to review only the first part of this game, I would definitely recommend it. It has a godly setting, decent graphics, good music, intriguing story and quite interesting puzzles. The writing is weak enough, but I can forgive that because of how hilarious it is how Nathan ruins everybody's lives and doesn't even feel guilty about it.Then, after a few hours, you meet Jay and receive a new mission. From this point onwards the game feels like it wasn't getting as much love from the developers. The main mission itself is very maximalist and kind of lame, graphics look cheaper overall and some animations like Jay's walk are just painful to look at. Musical accompaniment becomes more bland, puzzles become less interesting and have more moon logic in them.Only near the end, the good parts outweigh again as Nathan discovers the secret of VirtuaVerse. Music and visuals unite to create an outstanding atmosphere once again. I like how the mechanic of switching between real and AVR worlds gets some attention here, it's a shame it was almost forgotten the rest of the time. But after that, the story is just cut off, I guess, the writer was just too lazy to give this game a proper ending.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: The pixel art and the music (ESPECIALLY THE MUSIC!!!) are absolutely perfect!Played the demo and needed more of this. God, the music is SO damn great!However, story and character-wise, I found this game was lacking a lot!The main character is one of those "back in my days" and "kids and their technology nowadays" people. At first, I thought it was meant to be satirical but the more often he dropped comments on that, the less I believed it. He doesn't go on a journey that helps him grow or learn anything. And once we find the missing girlfriend,  , the story becomes too convoluted.The puzzle design needs an overhaul ( ) and you can't even leave a screen per double click, a feature that makes your life easier in almost every modern adventure game.The bleak ending made me also wonder what message this game actually wants to send us. It's both too on the nose and not saying anything at all at the same time.I doubt I will go back to revisit VirtuaVerse but I will definitely listen to its soundtrack over and over again. It's SUCH GOOD MUSIC!!!
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: The music, graphics and storyline in this 'game' are great. The controls are pretty good. The puzzles are awful. We're all used to getting stuck, having to make leaps of logic and occasionally having to just "try everything" to break through some poorly clued puzzle. But for this game you will HAVE to use a walkthrough guide at several stages. So, it's worth it for the look and feel and the story. But be prepared to treat it like an interactive graphic novel rather than a game you can 'win.'
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: VirtuaVerse is a decent entry in the Cyberpunk genre.If you have seen the "Perturbator - Sentient" music video, you will recognize the art style made by the same pixel artist Valenberg.Valenberg's pixel art and animations are detailed and charming.The music and writing are excellent as well.VirtuaVerse asks the usual Cyberpunk questions of transcending humanity and abuse of technology.For a point & click, VirtuaVerse is nothing new or outstanding. Overall a pretty intuitive and enjoyable experience.Except the backtracking and moon logic elements plaguing the genre.Backtracking is a staple of the genre and can be somewhat forgiven, except when you are forced to jump back and forth long distances between locations just to trigger a single dialogue option.(Lucky if you even manage to figure it out on your own)   Justified and Righteous RANT incoming:Some puzzles were too silly, I hate mindless moon logic. The worst was the ridiculous over-the-top Rune puzzle !After going through 2 entire zones full of riddles (hours of gameplay!!),you naturally forget some fleeting symbols on a video you watched only once 2-4 hours AGO!First of all, you don't know the significance of these runes to even write them down.Also the video is full of moving pictures and other nonsense, once again,why should the player pay attention to THESE symbols in particular, at THAT time?After HOURS of gameplay, going through 2 large zones, the 3rd zone asks you for SOME Runes?!?It is a miracle if you even remember seeing the symbols on that video.There are no hints, you can't ask the characters in-game, your inventory items aren't helping either.How and why would you think of going back and re-watching the video that has ALREADY served its purpose.Also the symbols are so fast to disappear that you might have missed them the first time.How would you know where to even look?!?!??!?!Is the game expecting the player to cheat and look up a guide? Because that's what I did !!!Sense of accomplishment GONE. Even if I figured it SOMEHOW on my own, I would not be elated or feel smart,I would be frustrated at the silly game design.And you know what is the WORST!?!Once the riddle is solved and you can finally talk to the new NPC, there is a dialogue option where they discuss the idiocy of that last riddle!So the devs knew it was trash! Acknowledging the bad game design does not make it good!Don't put it in the game in the first place!!What an amateur game design mistake. How conceited are the developers?!?That Rune riddle alone was almost enough for me to drop the game and become biased.But I managed to stay open-minded and judge it as a whole:Decent (enough) product.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: This is an "old-school" point-n-click. The set of this one is some cyber-techno-scif-ish fantasy, patch-work like. You get a ton of the "related keywords" in there.The genre of the game implies significant presence of back-and-forth and severe "moon" logic with the intent to be funny. It means that, very probably, you will be "blocked" several times: you will have to bail out and read a guide, or engage in some serious brute force effort trying all combinations (inventory/chat), scanning all screen pixels (static/dynamic)... you can try to sleep on it too, but do not wait too much or you will forget too many details to salvage your run. Yes, you can get into other runs trying all the other branch paths. I even wonder if there are alternate endings.Let's be clear, this is not a problem of this specific game: this is a problem of the genre of the game. I knew in what I was throwing myself into. And I was not disappointed, this is why I sincerely do recommend this game. I may have grown tired of this genre though. But there is one puzzle, specific to this game, which is imho over the top.I was an amiga 500 coder in my teenage years: the related techno blah blah, sounds, visuals are all real. No wonder since the main coder is from the c64 scene.This is not appropriate for a young audience. It ran perfectly on my custom lean gnu/linux distro (x11/GL/vulkan) within the steam runtime.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: As a raw work of creative passion, I'll give this one several hearty slaps on the back . . . though my expression while doing so is a little tight and solemn, a little tinged with regret.  One, it's a crazy, neverending gallery of quality pixel art; "Surely this Lite Brite gravy train is going to end after all  wild business!" you think, but  just keeps on poppin' up with fresh environments and lore-rich objects, with new scenarios that are  fascinating.  Two, the synthwave soundtrack sets a highly stuzzy cyberpunk mood (disaffected yet melancholic, baby).  Three, the world building -- for roughly eighty-five percent of the experience -- works pretty well, and most of the conceptual  matches up in a satisfying way.  Four, the puzzles!  They are many, they are challenging, and seldom are they stupid . . .However, the , which the game promotes as a front-and-center part, has a few, sometimes  off-putting aspects, like a case of manslaughter in the early game that doesn't dovetail at all with the semi-serious tone.  Talk about disrupting the Feng Shui of your conceptual background furniture!  )  The ending especially soils the sheets:  what starts as an interesting thought experiment winds up with a big zoomed-out reveal that does not coincide  with what you've seen throughout your lengthy adventure.  These things leave a bitterish taste in my mouth.(Other adventure games are jumbled, dreamy wonderlands full of jokey fun-times and weird puzzles; they are presented as such, do not disappoint by going outside the lines . . . and often manage to delight anyway with a story that kinda hangs together.  But when you're trying to go for something serious, you have to play it more carefully.)Okay!  Disappointing story aside, the puzzles in the game are  tough, and save for one or two out of  (the clickable quests just keep on keepin' on!), they are cleverly designed and well-integrated, always advancing the world building by a few bricks.  The part that spanks you more than any other is the mulit-leg AVR goggle repair quest at the outset.  Now that's on  mode; I have utterly no clue as to how  mode is supposed to play and I don't  to know, since my good ol' bro and I wrung quite a meaty, bittersweet experience out of this sucker after the surely intended fashion.  Not a bad item for  all in all, and I'll tell you:   has got meat, son, it's got meat on its meat -- like those pop-up Matroyshka muscles Popeye has in the old 'toons.  Hey that  is all right, y'know?  He's a lopsided beast, but he's got about enough heft to kick a hole through the wall of your hillbilly trailer.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game because of the retro cyberpunk style. I basically can't resist.It starts bad and the puzzles kill it. A visual novel might work out better, but instead this click and point gives little story nor instruction nor highlighted items, as a result I had to stay in one place waving my mouse and test everything for a solution,The worst part is: the puzzle is easy, like distracting a guard at the club so you could enter, but the solution part is difficult - you need to order the right kind of pizza among all the pizzas, learn the street name which I've entered hundred of times, then delivery it to the club and NOT to your house even you have easy access to a motorcycle. So basically it is not about solving the problem that matters, it is about all the other trifles.To make it worse I do not know what I've missed to proceed. There's no hints given so I had to watch a walkthrough, many came without sense. The design is not good, like if you failed to discover the credit card you can still leave the apartment but you can't proceed without it so soon or later you will wonder where this mystery credit card is and how to get it, which could totally lead you in the wrong direction.I can't recommend this game. Not even for the love of pixel graphics.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: Yeccch, I really want to like this. Aesthetically, it's fantastic. But it houses all of the things I hated about early point-and-click games: difficulty finding necessary items and dumb solutions to puzzles, with a very specific clickpath. It made me end up using a guide, but I started to notice a pattern where ALL of the puzzles were so stupid that I just couldn't be bothered having to just keep looking back and forth between guide and game... It'd also help to have a button that highlights interactables in the environment.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: Everything I wanted it to be. Bit of a sudden start compared to things such as Monkey Island or Simon the Sorcerer but that's not a bad thing. If you like Classic Retro styled point and clicks I think this is a must for any fan. I'm only an hour in and its got me hooked. Also its great to be able to be "Stuck" on a P&C and knowing I cant cheat myself and look up a guide yet! XD-----------------AFTER COMPLETING IT------------------I did enjoy this game a lot, a couple of puzzles went from super easy to extremely difficult at times but I managed to fumble my way through. The music is great and I really started enjoying the characters towards the end, but I wish it was just a bit more.*spoilers*My negative issue was story related. Overall I had a good experience playing this game and would do again at a later date.After all - Its the journey :)
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: Better than Cyberpunk 2077 - No, really!Even though I really enjoy point-click adventure games, I very seldomly play titles that require me to read my own dialogue. In this type of genre I usually prefer games like Gemini Rue, Techno Babylon or Primordia. I would've never guessed that I would actually like VirtuaVerse. Surprisingly the direction, execution and story delivery works so well that I ended up going through everything on my screen and it left me curious for more. I would say that the majority of this game is very well designed and interesting. They really did an outstanding job with relatively simplistic tools and delivered something simply - refreshing. I ended up buying this game as a bit of a joke to wait for the release of Cyberpunk only to end up enjoying it more than that game. The puzzles are fairly straightforward, but they do get a lot harder towards the end, I even got myself stuck in one part and had to look at a guide! ♥♥♥♥... To conclude VirtuaVerse is a pretty cool game,with a beautiful design and setting, well worth a try when sales come around! Don't be afraid to give this a go, it's really a unique experience. Don't worry about computer specs (laugh) or be scared away by the graphics, the low quality is intended and deliberate for the aesthetic of the game.Thumbs up from me!
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: I liked it because of the use of theme in this game. Didn't quite like the puzzles tho, they're kinda boring and not so rewarding, when you reach a certain point you get so bored that you don't even want to learn the rest of the story because of them. Story isn't that good either, but give it a shot.Edit: I've just forced myself to finish the game, and i did. Ending wasn't that bad but, honestly this is just a mediocre game, cyberpunk theme and the music are the only pros of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: VirtuaVerse

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly quite boring to me though the visuals of the game are cool. Borderline unplayable without a walkthrough because there are steps that I really cant imagine anyone could figure out on their own, theres just lack of information and combinations of things would take forever to think of. _childDocuments_.review: The story was great, only the ending bothered me a lil bit. And the dialogues were somehow different, difficult to describe. Only my opinion.I love pixel style and the cyberpunk style just fantasticallyLove the soundtrack, matching the style of the gameGameplay was ok, could have been more modern15 € for 15 h is ok, in Sale in any caseAverage 10 h, I needed 15 h, made up achievements, for a PnC ok

_childDocuments_.review: i'm a huge fan of master boot records, who i've also seen live, and that's the main reason i bought this, but i also really like adventure games and the cyberpunk setting. this game is dreadfully generic! it seems to just tick all the checkboxes that someone may expect in some retro cyberpunk universe like all these generic modern jrpgs that cash in on nostalgia of secret of mana or chrono trigger. virtuaverse is so freakin boring in both art and gameplay.
