_childDocuments_.review: After playing for >100 hours, completing the campaign, and finishing +16 sandbox with all factions, i can say that this game is, for the better parts :- Stable/Playable (I encountered no game crash, nor errors, with the "worst" bug being solved by simply surrendering the fighting in which i was stuck.) (Played on an Acer Nitro N50-600, I5-8400 CPU 2.8GHz, NVIDIA GTX 1060 6GB, 8G RAM)- Enjoyable (Some part of the campaign may be more difficult than others but taken on the right angle, they become easier.)- I liked the display of creativity and the choices in the graphic design of the game. To be able to create something "new" from an over used thematic such as the Vampire thematic is something to be recognized. Be it the design of the units, the artworks of the cards, or the "cheap" but effective cinematics, all are proof of the creativity put into the development of the game.- On the same tone, like the graphic design, the campaign story / world building, while weak on some aspects also show some creative strokes which would have transform the campaign into something better on many aspects if correctly used/refined. The ideas are present for a good scenario, but unfortunately, they were not used to their full potential. (Nota Bene : I speak of the underlying scenario, not the dialogues between the characters, which are sometimes...good....or can be very cartoony if not very bad on other times...sometimes it is 8/10, other times it is 2/10.^^)- The OSTs are great and the sound design fit the thematic. But on the other hand, some units sounds are not that great sometimes, i think that it could be improved for some units. Overall, it is good.- The three main Vampires factions are all playable and are complete. (There is a fourth faction, human faction, with models, cards, nearly everything to make it playable, even specific lords, but isn't playable...certainly because they did not had the time to finish it for the release date unfortunately.)Now regarding the bad parts of the game :- Repetitive actions. FORTUNATLY, you will not experience it that much during the campaign, but if you play three or more sandbox map, you will feel it and it even get worse depending of the difficulty.- Lords are too powerful. While usefull and thematic for the campaign, they easily becomes a one man army, which tend to degrade the strategic aspect of the game, most notably when you play a sandbox map.- The recurrent cards and the repetitive operations to trow them out of your card hand. Most notably while playing a sandbox as Dracul, if you max the card rewards, you will end up after each victory to choose two cards out of three, and to make it worse, the cards are for an unknown and certainly buggy reason, the same for every victory, they are not even random.-  Some cards are not very usefull if not useless, with the Sabotage and Clairvoyance being the top ones.- The Ruling choices are a good idea, but the Ruling cards should come with perhaps special objectives and should be linked to a specific quest, linking the Ruling and the Quest choices, making it simplier.To end my review of the game i can say that i like the game, and that i do not regret my investisment, even if it isn't totally finished (with notably the human faction missing from the factions available) and the game can still be improved on many aspects.Palindrome Interactive managed to create an honorable first title, as well as creating an original IP (Immortal Realms : Vampire Wars) full of potential for the company future.I recommend playing it if you like the Vampire thematic and strategy games. And while it is a good game, in its current state it is not at its full potential, and thus fail to achieve greatness.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately cannot recommend. The game isnt bad but mediocre. The early game is pretty interesting but mid-game and end-game is tedious and boring:1. You start with a vamp hero that improves abilities over the first 5 or so levels but after that nothing. Your heroes get stronger but no new abilities or improving of abilities.2. The RNG for hero generation is quite bad. Example: You play the Moroia who cannot regen mana. When you recruit a new vamp hero it will give you heroes where half their abilities are about mana regen, so... useless.3. The tier 3 units are very easily reached which removes your chance of actually using most tier 1 and 2 creatures. With the massive power gap between tier 2 and 3 there is no way you can keep your tier 1 and 2 creatures so that leaves you with only a handful of battles to play with them before you replace them all with tier 3. This ends up making the battling quite a bit boring.4. There is no real penalty when you lose a hero vamp. This adds some futility to destroying enemy armies unless you take over their keeps afterwards. 5. The auto-battle is pretty bad to use. I can do a battle and get out of it pretty unscathed but auto battle will cause me to either lose units or everyone be heavily damaged.6. The AI in tactical combat is not great. They are not completely stupid, but not very tactical. You will find yourself out powered by a great margin (it will even tell you that your defeat is written in stone) and then you still win.7. There is only like 5 maps. 5! 5!!!!! I personally dont really like campaigns for these games (although I did try playing this one's campaign) so I mostly play sandbox. 5!!!!!!!!!8. The sandbox customization leaves a lot to desire for. You can basically just set your clan. You cant specify the amount of enemies, their AI level or really anything. You just select your clan and the % of boost or handicap you want to give the AI's (all 9000 of them) on things like blood gain or xp gain. 9. Tactical Gripe: There is this mechanic in the battle that drives me nuts. If a creature (enemy or ally) has had their turn already in the round then it is pointless to cast any  positive or negative effect on them since the round will be deducted from the amount of turns it is active but you will not gain the benefit. *facepalm*I pre-purchased this game so I guess the disappointment hits harder.. but if none of the above bothers you then you will like the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but the longer I played it the harder that was. The problems with this game are really basic, to my point of view, and can be summed up in a few bullet points.1) The UI. The UI in this game is pretty bad.. Okay, maybe not just bad but actually terrible. Here's how:    -You can't hover over the stats on unit cards to get details on what they mean. You kind have to guess from the icon.    -When you're fighting a boss with a lot of abilities you cant select him and scroll down to read all his abilities, the game slowly autoscrolls down from the top to the bottom and then back to the top.    -The game provides you with with a grid function to help plan out your unit's route. When you click one of your own units you can see all the available routes it can go, but when you click an enemy unit nothing happens and you have to count the squares manually if you want to plan ahead.    -The game does a terrible job of highlighting what you're currently focused on, especially units.    -When you're in big fights (10+ units) you can't tell the order of movement because you can't scroll through the initiative bar.    - When you equip items to a hero it doesn't show up until you deselect it, select something else, then select the hero again. Not a big deal but it makes the game feel unfinished.2. Ranged units can't move and attack on the same turn. I've played other games in this genre before and this was a shock. It crippled archer units for me and made them deeply unsatisfying to play.3. The maps are too small. When you're fighting on one of these maps you'll often bottleneck your own units because there are so few routes they can travel that they all end up taking the same one, possibly 2 routes. This is especially bad if because you can't scroll through the initiative bar during the planning phase.4. Unit's don't come with any sort of backstory or descriptor, at least not one I've found, and feel vague and uninteresting after a while. Putting thin blood in front of a one dimensional spearman unit does not make it interesting. On the flip side, the hero seemed really interesting to play, especially in combination with all the hero specific spells. 5. Some people pointed out that the voice acting was bad, but it's more of a mixed bag. The heroes and cut scenes  were voiced well enough but the actual base units didn't sound like what you'd expect gothic vampires to sound like.6. Bugs. I only encountered one but it ruined the game for me. Basically, I auto-resolved a fight I thought I'd win easily and lost 3 units. Afterwards, the game showed me as owning the area but I was unhappy with the unit loss so I reloaded from  the last autosave. It turns out it was autosaved for AFTER the fight and now I'm still missing 3 units, but the area is no longer under my control and can't be claimed.Overall, it's not a terrible game, but I wouldn't call it good either.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is based on 130 hours in Beta and a couple in the "finished" game.I'd give it a strong "neutral" rating, but there is no such.  Initially,  I was pleasantly surprised to see that the game has lots of potential and is a good start. I see it as a nice combination between Warlords II Deluxe and the Heroes of Might and Magic series games. It is substantially different from both, however, so it feels new and I like it.- It is not fatal to lose heroes, which adds a welcome additional layer of strategy- armies and capped in size, like in Warlords II, making it impossible to make indefeatable deathballs.- the card system is neat and adds a special flavor- once you figure out how things work and that losing and recapturing castles is not a big deal, the challenge becomes similar to that of chopping wood and trying to avoid a splinterCurrently there are 12 missions and 4 Sandbox maps. This feels too little for a full game. Provided that the units and assets are already designed, it will take little investment to make a few dozen terrains for Sandbox, some more open, other more closed and sheltered, some with more AI players, others with less.Larger number of maps to choose from is more important that larger number of playable races.A usable map editor is strongly recommended. Players will donate thousands and thousands of hours for free to make the game richer by designing and uploading maps. A map folder, recognizable by the game, that contains custom maps should be considered.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? No, it is a streamlined 4x strategy game with an underdeveloped enemy AI, which hurts in a single player game. Expand your kingdom conquering neigbouring provinces. Defeat your enemies in turn-based battles. Use cards for special effects. Not too complicated, but all the core aspects are working fine, the lore is fantastic and the visuals are gorgeous.In the lands of Nemire, Vampires rule the land. They are the protectors of their lands, keep the humans safe... as long as they pay their blood tax. Fitting for a vampire game, there is no gold, but blood as the main ressource used for buying everything. On the main map you manage your provines - move your armies, claim cities to gain a constant supply of blood, recruit new army units or generals, heal your armies, develop your provinces by constructing buildings and a few more things. Additionally you can interact with the game using action cards, which you will receive every four turns (or on special occasions). There is also a large upgrade tree for your clan which can be developed spending Legacy Points. When two rival armies meet in a province, combat occurs. You can either auto-resolve it or play it in turn-based combat. Your armies are lead by Vampire Lords. Turn suitable humans into Vampire Lords if you need more generals. Armies without leaders fight much worse. Lords can equip items to improve their stats or learn new spells with enough experience. The turn-based combat works fine. Nothing complicated, move your armies, attack, flank, cast spells, occupy shrines to gain their benefits. Maybe a bit too simple for die-hard strategy buffs.The game is single-player only, and it's core feature is the campaign. Three clans fight for supremacy (the brutal sewer sulking Moroia are my favorite), and there are four missions for each of the clans. The narrative is really cool, told during the missions and in cinematic sequences. Other game modes are the sandbox (long game that allows you to select your clan, land and win condition) and skirmish (just a battle where you select the participating units) modes. I am highly impressed by the aesthetics. The beautiful map of the dark fantasy lands scrolls softly, there is a zoom option to take a closer look, and a turn option to see the map from all sides. Very polished.  It is also clear that a lot of work went not only in the artwork but also into the lore and story of the game. The soundtrack is high quality as well. Gorgeous single-player 4x strategy game in a Vampire realm.

_childDocuments_.review: Palindrome Interactive enters the vampire realm with their isometric strategic entry that both appeals and frustrates. My first impressions of the game has some nice positives and of course room for improvement. What My first impression of the game wasPassion: Clearly the developer has a great passion of games of the past. Heroes of Might and Magic, Total War, Card Game classics that have a nice mixture of territorial conquest, campaign story progression, and various game modes to a nice start here.Mood: It has a Gothic mood to it with good use of colors and presentation that works. Dark, but clear in its map and card creations. It's all about the blood, so caution for those who do not like blood in games, but it fits the over all aesthetics of the game nicely.Navigation: Easy movement choices with straight forward army placement. They have learned well from past games. Army leveling, different army units, and plenty to do in game that is not hard to grasp.Base: A nice solid base game that they can build on. Each faction is represented well in its theme, simplicity, and research.Camera: You can zoom in and rotate to the vantage point you wish to play at. Its dark risk, its civilization, and you can control the different viewpoints. Isometric is a tired mechanic, but it does the job in Vampire Wars.What needs to improve:Eye Impaired: One thing that bothered were the little things in battles and other parts were the AI choices and AI camera angles were way too small. Enemy cards, movements and overall everything was so small that you gave up reading it. Making the cards large and readable is a good thing. Third person perspective would have been a better choice that isometric. Small bad, big good.Animation: Some of the sequences were inconstant and bulky in their appearance that does not match the in game content at times. The gorgeous cards do not match the animated bulky style that takes away from the overall presentation. One is more Gothic and stylized. The other too cartoon quality that had two different visions contradict each other.  May not bother others, but it did me. Nothing new: Isometric, Capped Armies, Repetitive limited card and army base (which could change with expansions), straight forward progression and story telling, lack of pvp, and unfinished ideas need to be done to warrant the cost. This hurts replay.PVP: The game feels like a board game with no player vs player options. For now, but still a negative. My thoughts on Immortal Realms is that turn base lovers may see too many redundant game play mechanics and themes that they may pass on it for the price. It is just another game on a long list that has flooded the turn base genre without bringing in anything new or inventive. After time one game looks like another with the exception of its theme. If you love Gothic Dark Vampire genre games, this game maybe right up your alley. Vampire Wars has a lot of passion, some nice beauty to it, and does more right than wrong. It will all come down to what's next in additions to expand on its base. I would see the 'game play' in action in the Video section on the top of discussion before purchasing. Wait for a sale. It has potential but as is needs work. My score 3.0 out of 5

_childDocuments_.review: Vampires seem to be an even bigger hit in recent months than they usually are. Maybe it’s the smell of Bloodlines 2 in the air, or maybe we’re just shifting our focus from zombies for a bit. Either way, like zombies, vampires can be great if done well but, like many genres, an utter disaster if done poorly. I, for one, am happy to see the recent explosion in blood-sucking titles especially when they’re adding something new that we haven’t seen before.Immortal Realms: Vampire Wars manages to be both familiar and new. Although not particularly complex, it covers its bases by incorporating a strategic map with plenty of locations to keep it interesting, tactical combat that has enough depth to keep even a veteran of the genre entertained, and faction progression that will keep your forces improving from the start of a scenario to its end. I won’t complain about the three playable vampiric factions and their campaigns either.Immortal Realms: Vampire Wars has you taking command over a faction of vampires as they lash out at the world around them to subdue it under their will. Though there are plenty of vampiric factions to contend with, those pesky humans are consistently a thorn in your side. Don’t underestimate them though; peasants may offer little threat to your superhuman forces, but a squad of trained knights is a different scenario entirely.There are three key vampire clans available to play: the Dracul, the Nosfernus, and the Moroia. The Dracul clan claims to be the only one that maintains a pure bloodline and they rule over their subjects more or less like a human lord might save for the blood tax, of course. The Nosfernus like to play around with the dead and pack their armies full of skeletons, zombies, and ghosts as opposed to the half and thin-blood human-like forces of the Dracul. Finally, the Moroia go a third way and focus entirely on the arcane, using magic to summon and create forces composed of gargoyles, mages, and automatons. These clans are immediately available to be played in both skirmish and sandbox modes, but they must be unlocked in a specific order for the campaign.The strategic map is not an unfamiliar one, though it does have its touches of innovation that give it a unique feel. It’s divided up into provinces that often contain locations such as keeps, forests, caves, blacksmiths, wishing stones, and so on that each offer unique benefits to those that claim and upgrade them. For example, a populated city will provide a reliable income of blood, a third-tier keep may give the holder the capability to recruit some of their elite core units, while a blacksmith allows them to spend some of their accumulated blood to craft new pieces of equipment for their lords to benefit from.As territory is claimed and battles are won, you’ll gain experience for both your units and your clan as a whole. Clan upgrades are faction-wide skill trees that improve just about every aspect of your armies and territories. Depending on how you specialize, you can have incredibly powerful lords, units that are recruited with several levels of experience, improved blood income, and more. The wide variety of focuses for you to dabble in offer even more of a choice by often having several tiers, allowing you to really hone in on a specific area if you so choose.Cards play a significant role on the strategy map as well (the combat map too, but we’ll get to that later). Cards are granted by being victorious in battle, purchasing them with blood from libraries, and by the passage of time. Your own preferences will determine which you find the most use with, but like the upgrade tree, there are plenty to get your hands on. Some are simple and will grant you bonus blood while most others will cost you some amount of that resource to grant an immediately consumed benefit, like healing the units in an army or acquiring magic items cheaply.Combat in Immortal Realms: Vampire Wars is grid-based and will remind veterans of other games in the genre like Heroes of Might & Magic. It’s straightforward and to the point, which makes it easy to quickly get into playing, but also makes it so that frequent battles may start to lose their luster. This is made worse by a lack of variety, particularly when seeing the same maps again and again. I found the variety of units to be a strong point, particularly since each is not only made up of attributes but also abilities (mostly passive, some active) that made it so that each was unique. Though they’re all categorized as archers, warriors, tanks, or assassins, one unit may be noticeably different from another in the same grouping even if they fill a similar role.A different set of cards is used in combat as opposed to the strategy layer. These cards act less like general events and much more closely represent magical spells, dealing damage, healing and protecting allies, and so on. They drain your lord’s mana reserves which often take several turns to replenish as they recover quite slowly. As your lord levels, you can choose which of these to improve from three options, each providing different benefits to improve on the original card.The AI itself is acceptable, though I often found myself wondering why my enemies hadn’t taken advantage of a vulnerability that they had opened up in my forces. Although I never had my heart broken that one of my units hadn’t been wiped out, it was common that I would win battles that were determined to be evenly matched without losing a single unit while wiping out the enemy forces entirely. For the most hardcore of gamers, where the challenge is everything, this may be a deal-breaker, though I found that other areas of the title made up for it even if it was a bit on the easy side.My only real complaint here is concerning the ease of gathering information. It’s almost impossible to see what card an enemy plays against you as it is particularly tiny and burns away as you’re attempting to pull out your magnifying glass. Any status effects that are on units must also be viewed in the slowly scrolling card that appears as you hover over them. It would be a vast improvement if more info was readily available to the player at all times.Immortal Realms: Vampire Wars is a solid addition to the genre. Its setting stands out as a unique one to me and although there’s certainly plenty of inspiration taken from the legends we’ve heard in the past, Palindrome Interactive made it their own. The interlocking systems of the strategic map and tactical combat are designed well and offer plenty of opportunities to customize your clan as you progress through a scenario. I’d recommend that tactical strategy fans give this one a go at some point, even if they’re on the fence. It may not be the most challenging title that they’ve ever played, but most of its other aspects more than make up for its shortcomings.

_childDocuments_.review: If I were to describe this game in one sentence it would be as follows: A game with strong foundation, but a lot of underutilized or wasted potential. But let's not get ahead of ourselves and look at its strengths and weaknesses.STRENGHTS:-  ART. Immortal Realms: Vampire Wars features very high quality art that is best represented on Cards. I can't praise art of this game enough. Everything is very detailed, atmospheric, diverse and just a pleasure to look at.- ATMOSPHERE. This one is a bit subtle but at its core this game makes you feel like a vampire ruler who is playing a deadly game of influence and warfare. The fact that game represents quite a few things with cards certainly adds to this feeling.- DISTINCTIVENESS. All factions in this game look, feel and play very differently and this is very noticeable in everything about them. Never have I felt that there were too many similarities that were to this game's detriment.- THEME. As the name implies, Immortal Realms: Vampire Wars is a game about vampires. All playable factions are vampires. Everything oozes with vampirism. It is very nice to see that the game just grabs this theme with both hands and sticks to it."SO-SO" ELEMENTS:- SOUNDTRACK. While by no means bad (I quite enjoy it myself), it does feel that there could have been a few more tacks. Music is very thematic and fits the game like a glove, but perhaps a few more tracks would be nice.-  STORY. The writing in this game is a bit on the meh side and while perfectly passable, it is very clear that there is a lot that could have been done better. As a writer myself, I did notice this and it does bug me about this game. But it doesn't really detract from it that much either.WEAKNESSES:- REPETITIVENESS. This game is very VERY Repetitive. Early in the game it is not noticeable as player is highly encouraged to approach every situation with careful consideration and thus it is actually fairly entertaining, but as the game progresses and player becomes stronger, many of these elements fall sideways and it becomes rather repetitive because at the end you are just doing the same thing over and over again or just auto resolve battles, which doesn't help. This point does fit into ATMOSPHERE of the game - you are very powerful and simply can't be bothered with dealing with menial small battles anymore - but it still makes game repetitive and rather dull at times.- BALANCING. Immortal Realms: Vampire Wars has SEVERE issues with balancing and this is VERY noticeable. Story missions have random scalings in difficulty with one in particular being VERY grueling slog. Many units feel very underpowered and thus player is always resorting to other options. Faction economy is not made equal and thus suffers from balancing issues. Many more examples can be found unfortunately.- LACK OF CONTENT. It is very clear that this game has a lot of potential for MORE. More, more, more. More scenarios for story, more sandbox maps and victory conditions, more units, more customization options, more keywords. Don't get me wrong - what is there IS GOOD overall, but more is needed. It feels like a dish half-full.CONCLUSION: Immortal Realms: Vampire Wars is not perfect and most likely never will be as it doesn't seem like there will be more content for this game (Which is a big big shame), but still it is fairly solid game that does what it does and at worst does passable job. I don't think this game is for everyone, bit still I think it is enjoyable and has right to exist.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good. Not great but good. The core gameplay loop is repetitive but solid, and easily pulled me in for hours. The Art style is great as well. So if you play this game just on the skirmish maps or in multiplayer, you'll have a fun, if shallow experience.Now for my criticisms, which only really apply if you played and cared about the campaigns, which I assume everyone does since they serve as a good introduction to the different factions and their style while in-game.The game's world has much more lore and history than it lets you in on, and while you can piece it together, it's difficult and not very intuitive. There are tons of things that don't make sense in the story as a result, the motivations of characters, timelines etc. If the Campaign missions were longer or more numerous and also better paced, providing more information to the player, then it wouldn't be as glaring.Lastly, the voice acting. God almighty, the voice acting. Now the people they got to voice the characters do a good job, they really are trying, but I get the sense that they aren't native English speakers, and as such the developers should have done more to help them out. The voice acting is stilted, awkward and jarring. It can really pull you away from enjoying the game, but like I said, the voice actors themselves were pretty competent, and there were rare moments where their performances were serviceable.I just feel like they didn't have enough direction and that in a lot of scenes where two or more characters are speaking, it's obvious that the actors were just responding to written sentences, and not playing off each other. If anyone here has ever played the game Bound by Flame, which is also a great game with good game-play and an amazing world that is marred by it's terrible voice acting, you know what I'm talking about.Other than that, the game is fun, and worth a buy. There is a distinct lack of content to break up the monotony of the card game-play and battle game-play loop, but like I said earlier, those are solid enough on their own. It'd be good to see some DLC to flesh out the games mechanics though.

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of writing this review, the overall score for Immortal Realms: Vampire Wars sits at "Mixed". I'd like to throw my review in the mix and say that I really disagree with this. The game is perfectly playable and there is nothing wrong with it  that a few good patches can't fix. Most notably the UI could be a bit more clear and informative.The TL;DR is this: Even if the game wasn't about vampires, the game mechanics are unique and interesting enough that it would be an instant recommend for me.IM:VW takes inspiration from the classics of the genre, most notably HOMM and Disciples, and arguably some aspects are reminiscent of the Total War franchise.The first and most immediate difference is that provinces cannot be interacted with directly. In order to do anything - be it recruitment, building or other interactions - you need to have a Lord present. Each Lord can perform 3 moves or actions per turn, so making the most of each turn is the name of the game. Further complexity is added by the fact that many province-unique buildings can only be used once every 4-turn year, so Lords cannot camp a single province but must stay mobile for maximum efficiency.On top of this you have your Action cards, of which you draw 3 at the start of each year but can gain more through various in-game actions. These cards represent blood rituals, decrees to your mortal followers and orders for your armies. Crucially, despite the name Action cards does not actually cost actions to play, and so playing the right card at the right time is an important skill to master. Cards, however, cost Blood to play.Blood is the final mechanic that makes the campaign map come together. IR:VW is a single-resource game. Everything from unit upkeep to province upgrades to the aforementioned cards comes from the same resource pool. Your main way to increase blood income is to claim the fealty of the mortal villages and cities that dot the campaign map. Human settlements will grow each year, increasing passive blood gain... but there are other ways to obtain blood. With a Lord present in a settlement (yours or the enemys!) you can use an action point to cull all available population for a large one-off Blood boost. It is efficient to perform this action once your own settlements have reached maximum capacity so yearly growth is not wasted.If the gameplay described above sounds appealing, you are correct. Moving on to battles.Battles are turn-based and rely on an initiative stat for each piece to take it's turn one at a time. The combat grid is square-based with only some units able to attack diagonally, making positioning key. In cramped ruins and graveyards, spearmen and other tanks race for control of vital chokepoints. In open fields, cavalry and wolves swarm isolated units and quickly flank them to death. A balanced army will serve you well.Taking a page from Disciples 3, battlefields always have a few altars that generate special squares around them. Units standing in these squares gain bonuses ranging from situational and strong to universally useful, like a straight +20% attack power.Damage is percentage based and to the eternal credit of the game, hovering over an enemy will display all relevant modifiers for the attack and the retaliation strike, if any. I am pleasantly surprised how balanced this aspect of the game is. In the 12 hours I have played so far, I have yet to encounter an enemy that feels too strong or tough. The same goes for my units, the a.i. will not hesitate to gang up on a wounded, overexposed strong unit. Even a tier 3 unit can be taken down by a group of tier 1 units using good tactics, flanking, and clever use of spells.Spells are unique to each Lord based on what schools of magic they have access to. They are similar to Action cards in that they exist outside of the action economy. As long as your Lord has mana to spare and Spells off cooldown, they can be spammed several at once, as long as it is your turn. Just like in early HOMM games, spells can be cast on ANY of your units turns, you do NOT need to wait for your Lord to come up in the turn order. Note, however, that each spell has a range calculated from your Lord's current square, so keeping him or her in a central position is a basic strategy. Even more interesting, very few Spells are fireball-type instant win buttons, but require finesse and understanding of the game to get your mana's worth out of them. This makes it very satisfying when you maneuver your Lord into the perfect position and devastate a bunch of enemies with a Bloodstorm PBAO.Conclusion: Without a doubt, this game needs some tough love. The clunky UI no doubt turn a lot of people away, and the combat AI have some areas it could improve. Most notably, the AI have issues using buff spells correctly, often wasting them on nonsensical targets. At the end of the day though, the gameplay of Immortal Realms feels fresh and engaging, and for a veteran of turn-based strategy games like me, that is really all that matters. If you have any interest at all in this genre, my advise is to not sleep on this game. I predict that a few patches down the line, you won't need this review to explain to you why the game works. I have zero regrets buying it at full prize.

_childDocuments_.review: What an absolute hidden gem this game is. I played this a bunch in alpha and beta way back prior to it's release and it's a game that has so much potential and delivers on some of that potential.The good:- Asymmetrical vampire factions. The factions are very unique and very fun. From the honorable Dracul with their militaristic approach, to the occult Nosfernus who make use of necromancy and demonic pacts, to the Moroia - high arcane vampires that go full out on the magic approach.- Unique and engaging unit rosters. The units of each faction and the neutral factions are fantastic and very different from one another. There is a lot of depth in how you can play with the units and the army compositions you can make. Werewolves, bats, golems, zombies, knights and so much more.- Tactical combat. The combat is actually very tactical - you need to make use of positioning, ranks and files, abilities and keywords all to really perform your best in the combat. And the magic the lords add to the combat is fantastic.- Magic. And on that topic - the combat magic is fantastic here. You have faction based magic and you have schools of magic in addition. You could have a Dracul hero with half dracul magic and half shadow magic from the school of shadow - combining blood magic with shadowy teleports and debuffs. And there are a lot of magic school options - allowing amazing feats of magic like earthquakes, lightning storms, fire, shadow, ice, essence, etc. - a lot to explore here!- Sandbox conquest mode. This can be hit and miss for people. You move armies across the world map and lay claim to territories. These territories can be upgrades and developed, but can very easily be stolen if you don't protect them. I think it's fun- you might not.- Actions and cards on the world map. Each army has action points that you use to move, claim, upgrade, recruit, feed, heal, and so much more. If the army is lead by a lord you get 3 action points, and if not the army gets 2 action points and becomes limited to moving and attacking. In addition to these action points you can interact with the world through cards - and these cards are a mix of generic and faction specific - and there is a lot of fun to be done with them.The bad:- The AI. No beating around the bush with this one. The AI is decent on it's best moments, but mostly below average. You can easily predict what it will do.- Conquest sandbox. I added this as a possitive and a negative because - it's just not for everyone. It plays like a boardgame and either it works for you or it doesn't.- Not enough terrain modifiers in combat. The combat maps have chokepoints and shrines, but beyond that it's pretty limited. No bushes to slow down movement, no elevations to give height advantage, etc. It's pretty basic on this front.TL;DR: I honestly think this is a great game and I'd rank it a 7 out of 10. If you are into tactical combat, card games, board games and a pretty vibing vampire setting - I'd be happy to recommend this to you.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s beautiful. Not beautiful in the sense of photorealistic high-end graphics, but beautiful in the far rarer sense of good and evocative design that gives all four factions (the fourth being the unplayable humans) a unique theme and fits them well into the four different realms. The map buildings update to reflect who controls them and which upgrades they have unlocked. There is no need to open new windows to see what upgrades any building has. All units are displayed within their army in the world map.I like how the gameplay on the world map has been simplified. You only interact trough anything either with a lord or with a card. You can own buildings, and some provide passive bonuses, but all actions are orders that can only given by a present lord or via playing a card.The best part is that despite there being only one resource, the resource management is different between the three playable factions. The classical vampire lords of the Dracul govern their human cattle most efficiently, leading to more population growth to be passively taxed and, when a vampire lord comes by, killed for their blood. The undead Nosfernus do not require upkeep to sustain themselves, but are too inhuman to get the villagers within their realm to pay the blood tax, leaving visiting villages to feed on them as their only source of income. The vampiric witches of the Moroia collect the blood tax from villages in their domain and can eat villagers but their main source of income are not the human villages but their own castles in which their lords can simply create blood using alchemy.The key to victory however is winning battles without losing units. You are surrounded by other factions at all times and there is absolutely no diplomacy within this game. The only way to security is killing the first invader without being weakened so much that a second would get you. The battles are definitely the meat of the game strategically speaking, but they are also the boring part. It’s not that they are worse than the battles in HoMM, it’s just that they aren’t anything new. The more cluttered terrain allows for choke points and spells can only be cast in range of the lord. But moving unit by unit is rather tedious, especially given how well the actions on the world map have been simplified and streamlined.I’m aware the strategic depth of the combat is necessary to allow the player to triumph over the A.I. But a faster and simpler combat system like in Disciples 2 would fit the streamlined world map far better. I think it breaks the flow of the game when the battles take so many more clicks than the management of the realm on the world map.

_childDocuments_.review: I like it despite all the following things I am about to say:Needs to be cheaper considering the lack of diversity in the game, though if the amount and diversity of units, maps, cards, etc is increased than the price could be justified.Need to be able to hover over stats and abilities to see what they are/do, particularly when its an enemy unit or card. More diversity in well everything, cards, units, maps, etc. That way you can really specialise your plan, army and lord. Maybe make it that each black smith or library makes different things so you have to find more instead of only really needing one, e.g. some make rings, some make armour, others weapons, or maybe some make mana buffs, others specific to your lord, some boost your whole army. Make them somewhat speciailised. That way you need to find more to really improve your army, plus the find could have an impact on your game plan. As you can tell my main problem is lack of diversity and specialisation. Need to make it that your choices of units and cards and upgrades matter more, maybe make it that you choose one of the other for upgrades, e.g. village growth could be increased or village total pop allowed, maybe when you choose a new lord you get a buff and a debuff for your nation, so you can use lord choices to tailor your nation towards you plan. I would also like maybe if you could put a lord to work? like instead of each lord being an army some could be put into a region and give it a perm buff, sort of like a governor. E.g. a lord in a city or village greatly increases blood income or pop growth or pop limit.I know I have said a lot of things I would change but I still do like the game just either needs more or cost less.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this on a whim due to the vampire setting and some nostalgia of my turn based strategy times of old. I'll never regret thechoice. _childDocuments_.review: Play time is a bit low only because I spent most of my time playing in the beta.I'll start off by saying this game has a lot of potential and there is quite a bit of room to improve, but it is a good game.+ Unique takes on Vampire factions. You have the Nightmarish Aristocracy of the Dracul, the cursed undead lineage of the Nosfernus, and the arcane savants of the Moroia. Each with their own strengths, weaknesses and unique mechanics.- The factions are in need of balancing. The Dracul struggle without an economy to support their expensive units unless you plan on drowning your enemies in Thinbloods. The Moroia are glass cannons who really struggle to stay alive if someone so much as breathes on their units (except for their constructs). I would say the Nosfernus are in a good spot which inherently makes them the best of the three once you know how to use them.+ The OST is amazing- The gameplay loop is repetitive and a bit lack luster+ The campaign is hard, but fun to play and has a really well thought out story- The voice acting ranges from incredible (such is the case for each of the faction leaders) to cartoonish/derpy (like the vast majority of unit dialogue, which you will be hearing A LOT)+The setting and world building has had a lot of thought put into it and makes me want to immerse myself in it- The game has a very unfinished feel to it where in most aspects I can think of, things are *almost* goodThere are a plethora of unique mechanics in the Keyword system which is a system that works in an RTS like Total War Warhammer but doesn't really work in a turn based game on a chess board like this. If they took an approach like XCOM and had bigger maps with differing elevations to add some variety to combat, that would work a lot better to break up the repetition. Having a ton of keywords and special abilities works for a RTS game because there is constant chaos and units will slap into each other and duke it out. On a small flat map with a turn order, almost every unit needs baby sitting our you'll find yourself flanked and losing units regardless of any special abilities they may have, which then reinforces the feeling that many keywords don't matter and the gameplay loop becomes farming out doomstacks of the best units until you steamroll the whole map.The game takes a lot of inspiration from other games and tries to blend them in a satisfying way, but because combat is so unbalanced and repetitive it takes away from the experience.I am recommending the game because I can see the potential and hopefully things can turn around and improve. No Man's Sky managed to turn around from one of the worst launches in history and if that disaster could be saved, then I have hope that this game can live up to the potential I see it has

_childDocuments_.review: A well balanced mix of cards and turn based strategy, with a strong connection between both the world map and the battle system.  Beautifully presented with a demanding resource management format that never gets in the way of the combat driven story.  It's great to play the bad guys and so far has remained true to form, with loving nods to the Coppola production of Bram Stoker's Dracula, though the lead voice actors could have done much better (the supporting actors are superb, though, chewing ALL the scenery).I recognise the needs and benefits of an optimised use of in-game graphics for the cut scenes, which clearly aren't a driving force for this title, but it was a shame not to see something a little more suited, as the blocky graphics look extremely dated when you zoom in well beyond an optimal distance.  Combined with some stilted acting, this does take you out of the moment.  Also, in game character models are great but, although I'm only partway through the Dracul leg of the campaign, it already feels as though there's a distinct lack of female voice acting and representation in character models with the one female character beyond Dracul's wife (a vampire beast-mistress, ruling over the wolves) having no notable lines beyond her brief intro and a character model that was basically a giant male thug on a horse, which feels a little lazy and again conspires to break immersion, which is otherwise awesome.These are minor gripes, though, for a game that has no performance issues that I've noted, a beautifully well balanced system that challenges without ever overwhelming and an atmosphere I haven't found in a game for a very long time.  If you like well produced Gothic horror and enjoy turn based strategy, this is a must buy.

_childDocuments_.review: On the main menu screen, you’ll find Tutorial, Campaign Menu, Sandbox, Load Sandbox, Skirmish, Options, Credits and Quit. Selecting the Tutorial, it will then welcome you to Immortal Realms and explains that the tutorial will teach you everything you need to know to play and explore in the world of Nemire. There are three campaigns Dracul, Nosfernus and Moroia, each with four chapters. To begin with there is only the Dracul campaign available to you, you’ll have to unlock the other campaigns. The first Act in the Dracul campaign is A Night to Remember. “A storm is brewing in the northeastern reaches of Warmont, and the night sky is tainted blood-red by flames on the horizon. Whispered rumours have reached the rulers of the Dracul clan, Vlad and Cecilia, that something strange is happening at the border of their realm. They have sent out one of their minions to investigate...” The tutorial hints are displayed in the top left corner along with the Win Conditions, Quests and Event Cards. The top right corner displays a mini map of your current area and those areas under your control. There are also icons on the map indicating your armies and the enemies., These will detail some information on the current army selected such as, Threat level, Army Size, Mana and Action Points. Above the mini map there’s Toggle Full Screen Map, Toggle Game Speed, Toggle Army Overview, Toggle Mini Map and Main Menu. Looking down the world your controlled areas are outlined in red while other areas not under your control are outlined in white. You start with your first area which contains your Keep and your current army indicated by a banner above the army. Your Keep is your base and should your Keep fall it will be game over, the same goes if all your armies are defeated. Selecting your Keep will detail some information about it and your units in the bottom left corner of the screen.  Blood is your main resource in the game, without it you won’t be able to recruit new units, upgrade buildings and playing cards. Your armies will also start to lose health if you run out of blood. You can top up your blood stocks by claiming villages and cities which will give you varying amounts of blood each turn. In the top centre of the screen is your Blood Pool, this will tell you how much blood you currently have along with the amount of blood you’ll gain each turn.   Clicking on a village or city on the world map will give you some information on it such as Growth, Population and Income. Growth will increase your population per year. Population provides one blood income per turn, depending on the size of the village or city will determine the maximum size of the population. Income is the amount of blood per turn you’ll receive. Sending your army into a province which isn’t under your control will allow you to Claim that area using the Claim Army Action button. Any resources from this province contains will then be applied to your overall resources your next turn. Using the Claim Army Action will require one action point. Once you have a province under your control, you’ll have some options available to you such as, Feed, Split and Construction. Feed will allow you to consume all available population for extra Blood points. This will give you three Blood Points per population, consuming all the population and this will cost you One Action point. Spilt allows you to split your army into two armies, this also costs One Action point. Construction allows you to upgrade the province to increase its effectiveness. After you’ve used up your action points the next thing to do is end your current turn. This will then replenish your action points and give you any blood resources from provinces under your control.  Every four turns you’ll draw some Action cards, these will cost you Blood Points to activate them. You can collect new cards through unique clan actions or buy them from the Library build. Playing as the Dracul clan will grant you new cards after you’ve spanked some botty in combat. These cards can give you bonuses such as Sacrifice will give you Gain +15 Blood Points or Target Village or City Gains +2 Population. You’ll be able to recruit new units to your army by visiting the province with Dracul’s Keep or other recruitment buildings. Upon arriving at the Keep selecting the Recruit Army Action will display the recruits that you can add to your army. There are different Classes for the army units, this will determine the base stats of the units. Tanks have high health and armour but don’t hit very hard. Assassins deal high damage but their health and armour stats are low. Warriors are a good balance between the Tanks and Assassins.  Some units will have extra bonuses which gives them extra effects like Ranged Attacks, so pay attention to your units and use their bonuses to your advantage. Another way you can recruit units is to play a Recruit Action card on any recruitment building under your control. This will then show you the available units you can choose from, although not all units are available to you so you’ll have to unlock them as you progress. Not only will these units cost more to unlock and add to your army, but their upkeep will cost more. There are other places in which you can recruit units to your army so keep a mince pie out for them. You can move across multiple provinces however you can’t take control of a province if it doesn’t share a border with the provinces under your control. If there is a Keep then you can claim that province even if it doesn’t border with your provinces. Some provinces are hidden under Fog of War and won’t reveal themselves until you visit that province. You will also find Special Buildings such as Wishing Stones or Library, Wishing Stones allows you to draw a card which can grant your army more Action Points, or they can gain +1 Veterancy Rank or replenish your Lords mana or other bonuses. At the Library you’ll be able to purchase new cards for blood. Like the Action Cards which are drawn every four turns, you can choose one of three Rulings. The Ruling can offer your clan powerful boosts depending on how you proceed over your next turns. If your intention is to conquer everything in the near future then you may be best to choose the Ruling Elites Focus which will offer you a reduced cost in new units and gains blood after combat. Take Up Arms will offer you reduced Blacksmith card costs although Library cards will cost 100% more. You will have the choice of three Rulings each four turns. As your clan gains experience, they’ll level up and they’ll receive One Legacy Points. This can be used in the Legacy Tree where you’ll upgrade your clan. These will give you bonuses to your Buildings, Units, Lords and unlock new building upgrades.   Positives + Multiple clans/stories + Multiple game modes + Looks and runs very well + Has achievements + Has cards Negatives - Frustrating at times As leader of one of three vampire clans, descend into a dark vampiric world in turmoil in this turn-based strategy game … Immortal Realms: Vampire Wars.   8/10

_childDocuments_.review: 1.5 hours is quite a short time to properly play the game with its campaign and sandbox, however, it is more than enough to get the feeling of it. And, in my opinion, the game is not as bad as people make it to be. It has its problems, like junky animations, annoying ambient sounds, and easy combat, but overall the game is decent.The main problem that I had with it was the combat, as it is rather boring. What makes it boring is the unintelligent enemy AI and unbalanced level design. Enemies just rush you like a kamikaze, with some of them just going right in the centre of your army and dying in there. They lack any tactics and can easily be beaten with minimal fighting force. All you need is a little bit of intelligence and a good eye for unbalanced level design. For example, while playing the campaign I found myself fighting my first human lord. The combat started and while looking at the map I found a weird spot at the right half of the map, where buildings and other map boundaries created a perfect spot for an ambush in a shape of a + sign. There all units placed on the sides of + would be protected from all attacks, besides the attacks from the front and the unit in the centre would be just gang-banged. So I used one of my units as bait and lurked enemy minions into the trap. I think I do not need to state that they were butchered. I mean bad AI is a problem on its own but combined with questionable level design, they turn into a disaster. And what makes it worse is the fact that most of the maps in the game are unbalanced and can easily be abused. It is somewhat similar to checkers, where getting your units on the boundaries of the field is pretty advantageous, as it makes them immune to attacks. The problem is that, different from checkers, the whole game is full of these spots that turn even the weakest units into unkillable machines.Besides the combat, the only other major problem that I had was the unfinished feeling to the game. Most of the animations are quite junky, and so are the ambient sounds. I believe that not much explanation is needed when it comes to junky animations, as you can just google "TF2 SFM" and get the feeling of what I mean by it (I understand that most of the TF2 stuff is made junky on purpose as a part of the joke and enjoy these kinds of videos. Just could not think of any other example). When it comes to ambient sounds, I just found it annoying. For example, when pressing on different places of the map you can hear the local ambient noises, like insects in the forest, creepy sounds on the graveyard, and so on. The problem is their implementations. Instead of them smoothly taking over the music, as it is done in most of the games, you can feel the mp3 file blasting your headphones. I mean it is like listening to an ASMR and getting a random noisy ad playing in the middle of it. It is just annoying and destroys the experience. Besides these points, I did not have any problems with the game. Would I recommend buying it? Not in its current state. The game is unfinished and feels more like a beta test than a proper game. However, it has a lot of potential to it and, if not for the problems listed above, I would have probably enjoyed it. So, if you like vampire-themed games or turn-based strategies, I would recommend adding this game to your wishlist and checking on it from time to time. Maybe the developers will be able to address the issues that the game currently has and turn it into something that you would enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend this game in its current state. There's really 3 big reasons:1.) The UI is kind of a mess. The game gives me cards I can't even use. I started out with 5 recruitment discount cards in a mission that doesn't allow recruitment. 3.) Thinbloods are useless garbage, I honestly wouldn't even bother. If vampires are immortal these guys are definitely not. vampires. It just doesn't make sense to me, I'll come back to this in a couple of months and see if this problem is fixed or not. Once your armies are equipped the opposition is weak, making it just a walk in the park to complete the mission. _childDocuments_.review: Update: I uninstalled this and asked for a refund. Further comments below.Original post:I'm marking this as "No" as a "no for now/wouldn't recommend it at full price," with love.The Good: I love Territory Control/Resource Management/Strategy games. If you can see the games I own and play, the horror and/or vampire genre is one of my faves, too. I learned about this from a V:tM:B2 fan group, so I figured this would be a good way to scratch that itch for a bit. Anyway, blood should matter in vampire stories. I really like how the mechanics around blood feel for the the Dracul Clan. (I haven't played the Moroia at this time). As you capture towns and cities, you get a steady stream of blood, which you then spend to do basically anything, but also to keep your units from starving. That feels awesome and intuitive. You can also devour the "surplus" population in a place for a whole lot of blood right now, but also dropping your passive blood "income" until they have a chance to bounce back. The Dracul treat humans something like pre-industrial farmers treated their livestock: "Most nights we drink milk. Sometimes we eat steak." That feels the right kind of creepy. Bravo there. OH! I also love the art and music. Did you get the latter from Vampyr?The Bad: This game cannot be called "finished" in its present state. There're bugs everywhere. I've had cards whose effects got reversed. Last night, I saved at an earlier spot, then had the game load the auto-save when I tried to revert back to that earlier one. When I turn my monitor off while running this game, the screen always gets scrunched when I turn it back on again. It also cuts off the "Save" button, so there's that, too. The "Cancel" button on the options screen really ought to be "Back," as "Cancel" means "undo the changes I've made." I could go on. With love. I got this game in beta and expected more polish for their full release this last Friday. I expect they'll fix at least some of these bugs. Oh hey, my machine isn't the newest, but I stick new parts in it every year or two, so it's not a fossil. Running this at the settings that default to "Ultra" every time you turn the game on crashs my game, every time. I've been running it at low every time the last couple of days. I'll try higher settings later this week. Still, guys, graphics like these shouldn't break on a machine like mine. I think you've got some serious refactoring to do. Manage your tech debt, people.The Ugly: <<Spoilers Ahead>> I bought this game, having just watched a play-through with the Dracul. Thinking that would generally be the experience, I thought it looked great. I really hate the Nosfernus. I hate their campaign mode leader (he hits notes that remind me of a certain politician I really hope gets voted out of the White House right now. He's also petty and overall obnoxious). I hate how their powers and spell cards work. I hate that I have to slog through their content before I get to play the Moroia in the campaign. I really hate their experience of blood. If the Dracul are to humans what we think old farmers were to their animals, the Nosfernus are basically PETA's view of industrial animal processing. It feels creepy and gross in ways I don't feel like I signed up to play. Further, since they don't get passive blood income, that results in a whole lot of back-tracking to go eat towns and cities you've already conquered. (Right now, I use Grandpa Nosfernus to do that, while I use the two sidekick characters to do the creeping). Frankly, I think a better experience, more in-line with this "zombie apocalypse incarnate" thing would be to just devour towns and cities once, getting a huge amount of blood, and leaving an empty tile. Why do people keep coming back to these towns? Maybe that's why they keep going back to Dracul territory: at least it's better than the Nosfernus. In the story, these "vampires" leave the lands they claim as lifeless wastelands, so yeah, consuming villages entirely makes sense here.Finally, let's talk about gender representation. [As stated before, I haven't played the Moroia content yet]. The RTS genre is known for its white-dude lens. True, it's mostly looking at European-inspired scenarios, and units are usually just copies of one another. But if fantasy/horror-based game makers can imagine elves and dwarves, or zombies and gargoyles, respectively, they can imagine People of Color, and women in reasonable armor. Let's also talk about Cecelia Dracul (significant spoilers ahead). It's cool that your first level in Campaign mode is from her perspective. What's not cool is that she gets Fridged at the end of the second mission, then undeadified in the Nosfernus campaign *just* to get under Vlad's skin. People, it's 2020. I know the vampire genre frequently uses the trope of friends being turned into enemies, but the gender treatment here is unconscionable. It feels extra-gross that I had to play the faction that was doing all this (the guy who killedher the first time, and the guy who's violating her body and soul just for lols). Again, I haven't played the Moroia, so I can't speak to how Elizabeth feels. From the written material, I'm kind of nervous it's going to fall into the "women are irrational," "women are just sex objects," "women are manipulative/decadent," "women will break your heart and steal your soul" tropes. I'll reserve full judgement until I actually play that part though. Unfortunately, though, I have to play through two more missions of buggy, squicky Nosfernus content to do that. That's why I can't recommend this game, though I'm clearly going to keep playing it. Thanks for reading.

Pick it up on sale and eat some hummies.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a neutral opinion to put on this game, because after about an hour I have some very mixed feelings about it.Positives:Art style is awesome in my opinion, soundtrack is good(Kind of a mix between Total War Warhammer and Darkest Dungeon in my opinion), at it's core has interesting mechanics. Card system doesn't need much explaining and makes sense quickly(at least for someone who has played MtG and StS).It has vampires, which is an auto plus on my end.Negatives:Voice acting is inconsistent on quality, and in general I do not think it is very good. The way buildings are upgraded and the way units are recruited is not the best in my opinion, I find having to have a lord dedicated to the task of building upgrades very odd. Ingame cutscenes, while making good use of the assets they have, I think would have been better done in an art-scene style. Archers feel clunky, very, very clunky, in my opinion.Overall: I love the vision this game has, I love the art, I like the music, and the core combat mechanics are good. Where it falls short is in it's campaign-map mechanics, and some awkward VOs. I do enjoy the game as of an hour in, but I would also say to wait for a sale, and enjoy it then.

_childDocuments_.review: I started playing this in Beta so all my hours aren't shown, but I've really enjoyed myself more than I thought I would. The setting is a nice break from standard fantasy strategy/4x games. The world map is fun to interact with, having to make key decisions about where to move my armies, what buildings to upgrade, how to manage my blood income, and a lot more. I only wish/hope to see more map variety on the strategic level going forward.Tactical combat is more engaging than I thought it would be at first. I was worried the maps would be too small or boring, but there is enough variety there with different bonuses to try to fight for control of to keep me interested. I will say the AI could use some work as I've been able to win battles I had no business winning, but I can't complain too much about that since I do enjoy winning a fight against long odds with an army half the size of the enemy.Playing through the campaign now and I must say this was a big draw for me. So few strategy games bother to focus on a story-driven campaign and instead commit everything to sandbox mode. I like a good sandbox playthrough as much as anyone else, but whenever a game offers a story-driven campaign like this one does I'm immediately drawn to it more.In short, there are certainly places for improvement in UI, AI, and other things you'll see in other reviews, but overall I'm quite happy with my purchase and I enjoy the time I've already put it.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitly a nice game, if you, like me, like Total War and turn based strategy, like age of wonders and xcomThe fullprice of 40 euro may be a little bit too much in my opinion (the ~34 euro i paid in pre-order is reasonable).But ofc its not a aaa title or a xcom 2: revenge of the undead (....damit now I want a vampire dlc for xcom 2...) which you shouldnt except from smaller studios, but here are a few things that would be nice if they could be added into the game (I will further update this List as I play further):1. Loading screens: Before and after each battle comes a short loading screen during the campaign. It takes about 15-20 sec for me, but I get bored pretty quickly so I always take a short look at my smartphone during that. Unfortunatly the loading screen doesn't close automaticly, so that I always waste a few seconds before I realize, that it finished. Just a small change but yeah would be nice.2. Different campaign difficulties: I know balancing different difficulties can be difficult (haha) but for me replaying games on a higher difficultie is often one of the most important factor for replaying campaign mode in games. An relatily easy adjustment could be: normal =how the game is right now. hard= all enemy units have+20% health. very hard=all enemy units have +50% health. Boosting health would be much better then damage in my opinion, since boosting dmg would result in much quicker deaths and most player probably prefer to not lose any unit (don't ask me how often I had to reload my legendery xcom2 campagin to get through it without a single death....).3. Level of units: With level I mean the experience level and not the tier of the unit (just so that is clear). Unfortunatley how the level of a unit is displayed is is nearly 100% identical to total war: warhammer 2 and could be done much better like for example use for the level dots of blood. So for example lvl 2 means 2 yellow dots, level 4 one orange and lvl 9 3 dark red dots. Additionally a ranked up unit doesn't really feel much stronger then a freshly produced lvl 1 unit, so it would be nice if most units could gain, for example a new ability upon reachin level 6 or 9.4. Battle maps: It kinda saddens me that nearly all maps have similar size and all have 3 shrins. A more diversified list of maps would greatly improve the game quality and would keep the players playing. So maps with 2,1 or even 0 shrins, maps who are extemly thin or whide, maps without anythin on them, so a complete open map.

_childDocuments_.review:
For as long as historians can remember, the ancient Dracul bloodline has ruled over the mysterious lands of Warmont -- Realm of the Bloodthrone. Inside the secluded borders of this land, an unholy court of vampires feast on the blood of their human subjects. And, as long as they give it willingly, a vicious peace between mortal and immortal is kept alive under the watchful eye of the vampiric rulers -- Vlad and Cecilia Dracul, forever bound by eternal love.

To the east, a cold wind blows over the desolate planes of Mourterra -- The Land of the Dead. No humans live on this barren and cursed soil, and yet the land is far from deserted. Horrifying remnants of the ancient and corrupt Nosfernus bloodline stalk here in silence, patiently waiting for their chance to once again plague the lands of the living.

Meanwhile, in Esain -- The Frozen North, another bloodline of vampires resides in solitude and isolation from the world. For the mystical clan of the Moroia, magic is blood, and blood is magic... and it runs thick in their cold, blue veins. No being -- living or dead -- dares interrupt their dark rituals and bloody soirees.

Tonight, the smell of blood is strong on the wind, and a red moon lights up the dark sky. A new vampire war is imminent, and none will be spared from the coming horrors.

Immortal Realms: Vampire Wars is an engaging strategy game set in a dark vampire world in turmoil, that combines empire management and turn-based combat with unique card-game elements. Descend into a mythical world filled with horrors and legends -- and hurl yourself into a compelling gothic epos paired with a challenging game experience.

Feature List Choose from four colonial powerhouses: England , France , Spain and the Netherlands , each providing different benefits and unique gameplay styles Take on four extensive single player campaigns following each nation on their path to supremacy. Appoint a leader for your adventure from four different character classes: the Explorer , the Merchant , the Buccaneer and the Pirate – each providing their own advantages and disadvantages Establish and manage trade with 60 Caribbean cities in a huge 3D game world. In ‘ Port Royale 4 ’ you will take control of a colony as a young and ambitious governor who is eager to learn what it takes to manage and grow his small settlement into a bustling trader city. Develop production chains connecting multiple islands and create complex trade routes across the Caribbean, covering the ever-growing needs of the respective cities. Make use of the detailed sea map to avoid stormy weather regions, cliffs or shallow waters. Fulfill tasks for your nation’s viceroy, earning more fame to unlock town buildings, ships and more. Conquer the cities of rival nations or hunt down their fleets with a letter of marque while also keeping a keen eye out for pirates and other privateers. For the first time in the series, naval battles will be turn-based, with up to 8 ships battling at one time and tactical captain maneuvers that can turn the tide in even the most hopeless of situations for a glorious victory.

name: The Alliance Alive HD Remastered
detailed_description: The Alliance Alive HD Remastered marks the glorious rebirth of the acclaimed RPG brought to you by FURYU Corporation. Uniting the talents of writer Yoshitaka Murayama, designer Kyouji Koizumi, art director Masayo Asano, and composer Masashi Hamauzu, this epic adventure comes to life with innovative gameplay on a backdrop of vibrant visuals and a classic tale. Players can develop their party’s skills through combat-based character progression, immerse themselves in the game’s lush world via dynamic vehicle-centric exploration, and form alliances with various guilds and factions. Venture further into the world to discover new vehicles to traverse in, magic to wield, places to visit, and more to experience! STORY Humanity has been shattered and enslaved by Daemons invading from another realm. The Dark Current, a cataclysmic event caused by the Daemons’ emergence, has decimated the population and divided the land into separate regions, leaving the survivors to be subjugated by Daemonic overlords. A thousand years have passed since that fateful event, and mankind will remain silent no longer. To reclaim their homes and free their people, an unlikely fellowship of heroes will band together to spark a fiery revolution. They must form alliances with the remnants of the resistance throughout the world to make a united stand against the legions of Daemons. If they fail, humanity as they know it will remain forever stifled by the darkness… KEY FEATURES A Vivid World : From lava-covered wastes to snowy mountains, the numerous themed realms around the world offer their own unique experiences and challenges. Navigate each diverse environment by utilizing a variety of different vehicles, including ships, rideable beasts, and flying machines. Forged in Battle : The ferocity and strife of combat can draw forth your inner reserves of power. Build up determination to enter a state of Ignition, which allows you to execute devastating critical attacks. Repeated use of weapons and Ignition attacks also has the chance to “awaken” a new skill for your characters mid-battle. Stand Together : You cannot challenge the Daemons alone. Form alliances with Guilds and factions to mobilize the strength of warriors and scholars all across the land to confront terrifying foes. Allying with Guilds also grants you the ability to call upon them to aid you in battle, among many useful other perks. You're going to need every last bit of help you can get.
