_childDocuments_.review: After The Alliance Alive’s 3DS release back then in 2018, we finally got the HD Remastered version on Steam. As someone who loves more old-school JRPGs, this game just seemed right my ally and I have to say that it contains a few interesting and refreshing features that I didn’t see before in this genre. Although I didn’t play the original game, I could immediately tell that the appearance greatly improved with the HD Remastered version and thus, I was especially eager to give it a try. Plus, there are even playable characters with animal ears and tail, so I couldn’t resist. A huge plus here is that the premise is so unique in The Alliance Alive as you have more than one hero to save the world together.The Alliance Alive takes place in a world where humans were invaded by Daemons. Due to that incident, a barrier got created that caused climate changes and thus, the so-called Dark Current arose that reduced the population and divided the land into separate sections, which ended up creating different zones where the survivors were ruled by the firm grip of the Daemonic Overloards. However, thousands of years passed and finally, humanity decided to free themselves and get their home back. Different heroes band together to raise a revolution although if they fail, humanity will remain forever in the darkness.First of all, as aforementioned, there are multiple heroes, nine in total, in The Alliance Alive. After being a while into the game, it switches the character’s perspective and you find yourself with another playable character that has no relation to the story of the previous ones before – at least for now. As you’re playing through the different stories, they get merged later on. This was a feature that I really liked as it’s like a prologue where you’re going to see what the characters were up to or what happened to them before they meet up and start to fight together. It’s also a nice change when you not only have one side of the story and get a change once in a while so you’re not stuck with the same one. On the other side, this means when you don’t really like certain characters you will be stuck with them for a while.I have to admit the gameplay is on the simpler side. I quickly just selected the strongest attack every time and put the x4 speed on in battles. I skipped through the battles, so to say. This happened due to the gameplay being quite easy and the HP refilled after every fight anyway, but at least the SP only filled up very slowly after using it up. However, The Alliance Alive has some pretty nice features when it comes to the gameplay that I never experienced in a JRPG before. For instance, characters don’t level up here per se but either their HP or SP gauge gets extended as a reward. Arts you’ve used, on the other hand, do level up and get stronger the more you use them. During battles, it’s possible to randomly acquire a new skill as well the player can use afterward. On the other hand, while most enemies are easy to beat, a few mobs were incredibly difficult to fight that are meant to make the player stay away from certain items until they get stronger.To be honest, the directions were a little bit confusing for me in The Alliance Alive. Although I easily know what I was supposed to do next, it’s not possible to look up what you actually have to do. While there is a quest log in the menu available to reread, it’s kept rather on the short side and doesn’t give proper instructions on what the player has to do but only a summary of the story. However, when I paid attention to the dialogue, the next task was always clear, but this also meant that after saving and quitting the game, I forgot the instructions and had to guess how to advance. Luckily, there are a lot of cut scenes so when I moved in the right direction I could tell that I was on the accurate path so I just had to advance. Sometimes, it’s not even possible to leave a building before completing the main story’s task, which greatly helps with not getting lost.There are even puzzles available in The Alliance Alive, so you don’t go through a dungeon only beating enemies but have to interact with objects as well to advance. Of course, there are traps hidden too where you have to fight an enemy when getting tricked and sadly, curiosity always got the best of me so I couldn’t resist examining everything. Although that just means that I loved exploring the world of The Alliance Alive even with the risks – you see, this game is just beautiful through and through. Although the dungeons do look pretty like in a usual JRPG, I especially loved the design of the world map of it. Sure, detailed graphics aren’t really visible here, but I liked the different terrains during walking to the next destination. The player can interact with the map as well and use a glider to get on higher positions although you can’t technically fly around here.The Alliance Alive is a JRPG that made me feel nostalgic while it managed to implement a lot of interesting and new features. Although most of the gameplay being on the more easy side, the battles were entertaining and fun, to say the least. The grinding works differently here and instead of leveling up, your maximum HP and SP get extended. I have to admit, exploring the world of The Alliance Alive was the most entertaining aspect of this game for me, as the environment is so beautiful. The terrain isn’t very detailed, but the player can interact with it by using a glider, plus the HD Remastered version has sharp character sprites that made them even more pretty. An interesting premise is the constant switching between the perspective of different characters that had a refreshing change. Overall, The Alliance Alive is a great JRPG that made me feel nostalgic, even implemented puzzles, and ended up being a great experience.

_childDocuments_.review: A good RPG except for several brick wall bosses, once you hit them you'll just get walled until RNG lines up perfectly or you grind out a solution. Some would advise using very specific strategies that require you to completely spoil mechanics and story for a first time run, which I did not, thus resulting in my play through hitting these walls.To go further in on said bosses, they have AOE skills as their primary damage sources. One of these bosses does so much damage with theirs a team wipe is expected and the game has you go through three parties to 'maybe' finish the fight as a result. In the other instance, it is a three phase boss that ends with them spamming confusion and death status moves on your party that will often result in a wipe if you don't win the DPS race. If you lose this fight you are forced into a 'bad ending' that takes roughly 4 minutes to sit through if you skip text and does not lead into new game+ but instead forces you back into a pre-fight state with LESS resources, thus punishing you.An overall good game marred by several honestly confusing choices for major bosses makes this one where I just can't advise someone get it, especially if you have limited time to play games.

_childDocuments_.review: is a remastered version of the original 3DS JRPG game with turn-based combat. Overall it follows a pretty classic JRPG formula and offers a good story, interesting combat mechanics, and plenty of hours of fun with vivid visuals. It will be plenty of hours of furn for the right player, and I am glad that this remastered was done for the PC. Please be aware that a controller is required for this game, there is no support for keyboard or mouse.Daemons have won the war against the humans. As a result, the beastfolk control the humans and also see them as inferior beings. You will lead a resistance team of humans against the beastfolk. The story is very interesting and will definitely keep the player engaged. It also tracks multiple characters, each with unique stories and interesting development.The world is wide open in this game, so you will need to pay attention to where you are going. Otherwise it's actually pretty easy to randomly wander and get lost. You will need to read what other characters are saying to know where you should go. There's a nice internal guide where you can look things up when you are playing, should you get confused about something.There are a total of 9 characters, and you can have up to 5 teammates in a party at once. The combat is turn-based. You can actually choose to auto-play the combat if you want to auto-grind, especially for lower level enemies that do not take much through. You can also play out the combat at 4x speed. All of the enemies are visible while you are moving about, so you can outrun most if you don't want to fight them as well. Leveling up is not through the traditional way. Through use, your weapons will level up and you will unlock new moves. It's a bit like the  series. If you win the battle, you will be fully healed. But if you have one character die in battle, they will have less HP the following fight. Sleeping will restore them. But if you lose a few fights in a row, then it will be game over. Luckily you can find golden gems to retry a fight, so that the game over will not be permanent.There is no manual save, which is a pity. Fortunately there are many save points, but I still would prefer manual saves.The graphics are very nice, and the color choices remind me of watercolours.The music is great too. Unfortunately there's no voice-over for the dialogues at all. For a €39.99 it seems like a blatant omission. I understand that it's a remastered version of a 3DS game, but would have been a nice addition when made for PC. can only be played with a controller. There is no support for keyboard or mouse.The pricing is perhaps a bit steep at €39.99. But it's totally worth it, in my opinion. It's such a good game.Thinking about this game as a whole, I can say that it's a very good JRPG with a good story, nice combat, and plenty of hours of fun. The music is memorable though I really miss any kind of a spoken dialogue. I think I am about halfway done and I have not had any moment of boredom. I can only hope there will be more remastered version of 3DS games coming to PC, as there were some solid JRPGs on that system.  is certainly a gem that might be easily overlooked.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is a nice mid-tier JRPG that I played because Yoshitaka Murayama, the director of two of my favorite games, Suikoden and Suikoden II, worked Scenario on this project. His influence is apparent as there is a system in the game that lets you recruit a ton of NPCs, though compared to the Suikoden games, it's much more limited and basic. I liked the lighthearted and playfulness of the cast, and a couple of emotional story beats.Unfortunately I didn't find much need to dive too deep into the battle engine. Setting up an attack for each character and turning on autoplay was sufficient for almost every fight in the game, and I was very grateful for the 4x battle speed option to skip through most of the encounters at top speed. Especially in the last dungeon of the game, in which each combat encounter is exhaustively long. There are really only two points in the game that combat is any less than trivial, once at the game's midpoint when you have to divide your characters into multiple parties, and again in the game's final few chapters. All and all, I consider this a good palette cleanser game. Something nice to play in between those big AAA releases to relax with and enjoy. It's definitely not essential, but still good enough to recommend casually.

_childDocuments_.review: The Alliance Alive. It's a polished JRPG made by FURYU & published by NIS America. It was originally released in 2017 on the Nintendo 3DS platform. This new launch title is the HD Remastered version which enhances its original. It's welcome that the game, which received a lot of positive reviews at the time of release, can be upgraded for new platforms. The Alliance Alive is a outstanding JRPG title released in 3DS twilight era, and many talented creators had participated on the production for it. For example, Writer Yoshitaka Murayama, Designer Kyouji Koizumi, Art Director Masayo Asano, and Composer Masashi Hamauzu. Thanks to them, The Alliance Alive comes to be an epic adventure featuring classical fantasy world narratives, unique anime graphics, and innovative gameplay systems.The world of Alliance Alive is set to the fantasy world in which humanity is troubled by the invasion of demons. With their strong offensive, humanity is divided into several regions and some are enslaved. However, most of the survivors were subjugated by demon overlords. Such dark ages have lasted for a thousand years, but finally 9 heroes have come to save humanity. To get back their home grounds and free their people, these heroes with different fellowships gradually make bands to spark the flame of revolution. The player must make alliances with the resistance remnants around the world and unite them to face the demon forces. As you know, if the player fails this world will remain forever lost to the dark.In this game you become each of the 9 main characters and play each separate story. The battle style is a turn based system that forms a party of up to 5 members. The game follows the rules of the classic JRPG, but also includes unique systems. Unlike other RPG games, your characters will not level up in this game. Instead, your characters gain stat boosts randomly after the battle. Players can wear their favorite weapons and armors, but to improve certain skills and proficiency, the equipment must be used in combat. Above all, the combat formation is at the core of the game mechanics. Depending on your position, such as attack, defense, and support, it will have an effect on your skills and abilities. It reminds me of Square Enix's SaGa series somewhat. Of course, these features make the unique vibe of this game even more impressive.Really enjoyed The Alliance Alive so far. This game has a lot of interesting elements for JRPG fans. Attractive characters, interesting combat systems, intense soundtracks, unique anime artworks, and an epic story where each narrative links to a huge adventure. There are some grinding elements, but exploring the world of The Alliance Alive is a great pleasure. It's pity that character voices are not supported in some JRPG games, but this does not ruin this fantasy world and characters. If you are looking for a classic JRPG with unique modernity, The Alliance Alive HD Remastered will be a good choice. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: + Interesting take on the usual JRPG story+ Cool combat mechanics+ Great gameplay/story pacing+ Helpful quality of life features- Nonexistent difficulty scaling- Subpar graphics for a remaster- PC port issuesStarting off 2020 with a new JRPG, this time for an HD remaster of a 2018 3DS game. The developer is FuRyu, the same studio behind The Caligula Effect. When I reviewed that one last year I didn’t come away too impressed, so it’s time to see if they’ve improved.TAA is what I would call your average JRPG. It does some things well, but falters elsewhere, not really shining too much in one given area. The combat, for example, is pretty well-done, but is ultimately brought down by the game’s complete lack of difficulty scaling. The story, while providing a different take on the usual JRPG formula, isn’t anything too special beyond that one change. And of course, the HD remaster itself still suffers from some issues, both with regards to its graphics and PC port. Given all of that, I cannot say that I recommend the game unless if you’re really digging for another JRPG to play.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: I can definitely recommend the game itself, but the quality of this port is terrible. If you decide to play the game, consider playing it on Switch or PS4.The game's progression is truly unique, while formations offer a slightly different take on generic turn based combat. Emulators do a better job of both.I wasted an hour trying to get a controller working, as no input worked on Title screen. I am still puzzled why there's no keyboard + mouse support. Anyways, I have no clue what happened because I haven't played the game before (couldn't screw anything up yet) and reinstalling it fixed the issue (implying something WAS screwed up on my side).If you have an ultrawide monitor you will be forced to play windowed mode or suffer this dialog bug.I'll spare you the details, but I wasted almost an hour trying to get rid of that bug, with only partial success. Workaround: Switch to windowed (not borderless) with the resolution you want and restart the game (yes, this brilliant port is unable to process resolution change without a restart).Some generic battle text still ends up partially off-screen. Didn't find a way to fix that.The issue is only partially fixed and I am forced to play in windowed mode.

_childDocuments_.review: Sigh... I really wanted to like this game.The hand-drawn art style is beautiful and unique. The OST by Masashi Hamauzu gave me strong FFX vibes, and considering that's my favorite OST of all time, I had high hopes. With a story written by Yoshitaka Murayama of Suikoden fame, I was pretty sure I was in for a treat.And for the most part, I was.The game has a slow, very slow, and rough start. The first 10 hours feel more like a tutorial than anything else, and 10 hours to get into the real meat of the game is a lot, especially for a 35-45 hour game. By the 10-hour mark, I had reached chapter 20, and to my knowledge, the game has 20 more chapters to go. So, half the chapters of the game feel (to me at least) like a tutorial.After the 10-hour mark, the game opens up and turns into a somewhat open-world RPG. You have gathered most of your team members and can build your group as you see fit, travel the world, gather NPCs to fortify and level up your five guilds (which are reminiscent of your castle in Suikoden games), and traverse the sea to learn more about the world and the antagonists of the story.But here lie the issues I had with the game. First of all, I could not get invested in the plot. I don't know why, but it just didn't grab me. I wasn't interested in the world and its problems, I didn't hate the antagonists enough, and overall, the story felt slow to me.The second issue was with the progression system, both for the guilds and the units. To level up the guilds, you have to recruit NPCs from around the world. While this gave me strong Suikoden vibes (I love the Suikoden games), it required a lot of legwork. I had to travel back to places I had already visited countless times, mostly on foot, and frankly, I didn't find the NPCs all that interesting. Furthermore, the NPCs cannot join your party to fight alongside you, and they don't even contribute to the guilds by providing new services; they are just fodder for guild XP.Your units do not traditionally level up; instead, their weapons improve. They RANDOMLY learn new moves for the weapons they use most, and those moves RADOMLY level up...Overall, I enjoyed the art style, characters, and OST. I saw some really interesting ideas in the tactical combat, weapon progression, and guild systems. However, I also found my time with the game boring. I felt some enthusiasm when I gathered the whole group, when the world opened up, and when all the guilds came together. For about 5-10 hours, I enjoyed gathering new guild members, leveling up my guilds, and building the right tactics for party combats. But, at the same time, the game felt grindy, slow, and convoluted to me.While I don't usually focus on voice acting in RPGs, and it's rarely an issue for me whether it's present, absent, or even if it's not great, for some reason, the lack of voice acting in this game was oddly noticeable. Especially during cutscenes, the direction was such that I expected to hear the characters talking. I understand that many games, especially on portable consoles, struggle with voice acting quality, but this game felt barren without it.Lastly, I played the HD Remastered version on Steam, and I experienced at least 4 hard crashes during my 23 hours of gameplay. This prompted me to use the quicksave button frequently and made me anxious about my progress.All in all, I don't believe The Alliance Alive to be a bad game; it's just not the game for me. Despite loving the art style, soundtrack, and many aspects of the gameplay, I might consider returning to it with a guide. However, if I have to play a game following a guide, it begs the question: am I truly enjoying the game?I retired at Chapter 24, 23 hours into the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a hell of a ride, it has the soul of a classic jrpg of the past while adding some interesting concepts like formations and an unique way to level up and unlock skills.The game draws inspiration from two main sources: Bravely Default and the SaGa games. From the first one, you can see the similarities in the character design, the world map, and even the music, to an extent. And from the latter, the inspiration comes from the way you level up (or rather, you don't), because after each battle, there's a random chance you will gain some HP and/or SP. But also during battle, you can learn new skills by using the ones you already know, which makes the battle system so fun while playing casually, and frustrating while playing for completion.But after all is said and done, even good games have problems, this one suffers from a couple of unsolved game crashes and freezes in the early game (I only encountered one), some unexpected difficulty spikes and even game walls, that will test your party composition and progression, and understanding of the game mechanics... so be prepared for THAT kind of boss walls.

_childDocuments_.review: The Alliance Alive is a great RPG that I hadn't heard about until recently and was a heck of a lot better than I had expected. It has Saga-like combat, allowing you to use whatever weapons you'd like and gradually learning new abilities with them as you go. You constantly upgrade existing abilities or gain minor stat boosts along the way when facing challenging opponents rather than using a strict leveling system. There is also an editable positioning system with a number of choices to make in setting up specific roles and party members.The story is solid if unobtrusive and includes heavy recruitment of townspeople into various guilds of your choosing, allowing you to select which types of upgrades you would prefer to use. There is plenty of optional exploration and three side characters to recruit, all of whom are quite interesting. Essentially, it borrows heavily from a lot of great JRPG games and packages them together very smoothly in one great experience.

You usually attack with your strongest skill or preserve MP.Some battles are just too easy, and your decisions don't matter.Among the hard ones, some are fine, and you can have a strategy works for that, but most are hard in a RNG kind of way.Battles are very repetitive. Even though this is a common problem among JRPG's, the good ones manage it somehow. This one did not.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game don't get me wrong, but once you hit chapter 25 or so the difficulty spikes out of nowhere to where your motivation to continue playing is completely gone. The character interactions and characters are pretty enjoyable, the graphics are nice, and I enjoy the combat system and music. There are so many good things about this game that I absolutely love.But the last 15 chapters or so are not only a slog, you hit these awful walls of bosses that suck out the fun in the game. Either you spend time grinding more (which sometimes won't even help you out) or you pray that the RNG will be nice to you. If you want to try this out go ahead! But from chapter 25 onward if it's too difficult just look up a playthrough and watch the ending instead of putting yourself through torture. You'll keep your sanity.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a real shame that at the time of me writing this review this little gem has only 27 reviews. Alliance Alive is a traditional-style JRPG apparently made by a small dev team on a limited budget - hence it's completely missing any voiceover - however it retains the classic JRPG charm and remains very enjoyable to play, with adorable character designs, interesting lore and a fresh look on a turn-based combat system. _childDocuments_.review: It's a 3D JRPG with a world map! Haven't seen one of those in almost 20 years. There are interactive elements on the world map, and there are no random battles anywhere: instead you have enemy icons you can avoid. Each type of enemy icon has a specific movement pattern, and there are perks you can buy to make avoiding them easier.The combat elements resemble those of the SaGa games, specifically SaGa Frontier 2 or Romancing SaGa Minstrel Song. You have technique sparking, tech(nique)s level up as you use them, there are formations, attack/defense/trickery modes. No combos though.Gameplay is very linear, you switch between different teams for a while, then they all unite and you can pick your party like a Final Fantasy game.The combat can get a bit grindy if you are trying to powerlevel.There are multiple new game plus modes, I recommend you read up on them before you choose one. There's also NG+ mode extra content for each mode.All in all, a solid 85/100 if you're looking for a JRPG fix, or a 9/10 if you want a SaGa-ish gaiden game.

_childDocuments_.review: As far as I've played, this is surprisingly fun. Surprisingly, because with the name Furyu involved, I can't help but be doubtful. And after playing some more, it sure is Furyu. But oh well.This game works a little like Saga games, but takes your hand for quite some while, so you get to learn about the world, before it lets you go wild. There are no scaling enemies, so you don't have to worry about Saga typical issues, and things.. work out pretty well, really. Lot's of exploration, actually reasonably nice dungeons with their own little somethings going on. Not a revolutionary game by any means, but fun, if you like classic jrpgs. (i.e. dragon quest, or older Final Fantasy games) Given how those start to really die out, I can definitely recommend this game. If you do have a controller, this game functions without a hitch. (using a DS4 simply with Steam, and no other program)edit: After playing to chapter 20, it looks like the game kills itself. There's so much bad game design going on, that combined with the biggest weakness of the game, the way too slow growth system, spirals out of control. It's fun until then, but that's not worth full-price at least. I know I don't feel like grinding for hours try to roll way too low chances and getting the money for the equipment you need. For way too many characters, too.In the end Furyu will be Furyu. As fun as the games can be for a while, and this one lasts longer than most other games by them, eventually it's all for nothing, because someone thinks you need to stretch the game more and more and more. In this case, with really terrible grind.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay... those who have played NIS published games should know that all their games are up to the "great fun" level, and "create with love" by their developers/studios... But here on steam there's been some hiccups on the releases of some of their games, because there's no love in the porting work, and that spoiled quite a lot of fun for those who wanted to play these games on the PC. Alliance Alive here is yet another one of those great games that suffers a lazy port job from NISA... As a PC game, it doesn't support keyboard and mouse. So unless you have a controller, you won't be able to play this game. (Who doesn't have controller these day you ask? Well... there's still the preference thingy, you know, pc race isn't the same as console race... lol!) Anyway, other than the PC port that comes without keyboard support, the rest of the game is as good as the old version, although it says it's a HD remaster, those hand drawn masterpieces didn't get a "re-draw" by their artists, but simply gets... "enlarged", so, you can expect to see a lot of blur when it zooms in... but when it zooms out, it's still pretty eye candy.The game itself, is a masterpiece made of love and details. Although the game play is something a veteran rpg gamer might have experienced before somewhere... we can still easily tell how much love and care is put into the making of this game. Short example of how detail it can be, normally in other rpg games, when we found hidden characters, they often are just background, and will never participate in the main story dialog or cutscene, here, in Alliance Alive, every hidden characters partake in the story like they are part of it. Another good example is, when we are forced to buy something or reject a trade offer by story, normally those games will assume that we don't have enough money and proceed the game dialog with that, but here in Alliance, it checks if you have enough money, and the line changes according to that even though it still force us to reject the trade with other reason saying "We have that money, but that sum is outrageous!", we don't get that feeling of "hey i got enough money, why do you say i don't?" thingy... this is how carefully their dialog is planned. The graphic, well, the original graphic is a real beauty. Hand drawn texture that makes the 3D models look like 2D art paintings. But the HD remaster didn't do it justice, everything is simply stretched and it can be quite blurry when the game camera zooms in. But like all 3D, when the game camera zooms out, the details become pretty like it used to. So... there's still beautiful scenery and artwork to enjoy, just that the zoomed in part can be ugly.Story wise, well, like i mentioned above, it's made with love, they have all the details taken care of in the dialog. And even went all the way to take care of the "What if" situation by giving us 2 more endings.. What if we defeat the boss at the beginning of the game? What if we can't beat the last boss? These all are answered. Which makes new game+ worthy.Gameplay wise, this is an rpg game with turn based battle, and with skill awakened mechanism, which means we get our skills and stats randomly from battle. Like good-old NIS rpg/tactic games... it's pretty grindy.Completionist wise, the collectible here is those rng skills we learn in the battle, and it can take some time to collect. There's a guild system we get to build towers and hire npcs to join our guilds, and hiring and finding all those npc is part of the collection. So there's plenty of things to do, and makes it really fun to explore every corner of the world to get those done.In short, really recommend this game if you have a controller and don't mind playing a pc game using a controller. In fact, go get yourself a controller just to play this game, it's worth it! :3

_childDocuments_.review: The Alliance Alive will probably not be the best JRPG you've ever played, but it's definitely an adventure you will have found memories of. I had a very good time playing this game and would recommend it to every JRPG lover out there! If you want a great 30 to 50 hours adventure with an endearing group of characters, then you should definitely give The Alliance Alive a chance!Pros:+ Charming characters+ Lovely artstyle+ Striking character design, especially main antagonists+ A battle system that is simple yet effective+ Art awakening is fun and satisfying, and gives you an enjoyable progression despite the lack of a traditionnal leveling system+ As far as I could tell during my playthrough, every character is usable and will be useful as long as you know how to take advantage of their strengths (Yes, even Renzo, which ended up being the one hitting the hardest in my team)+ Accessible and thorough manual with tutorials and useful tips (what does what stat, clear explanations about specific game mechanics, etc...)Neutral:+/-  The game is easy. The only way you're susceptible to wipe is in very specific locations that are a high risk high reward kind of deal and can be your doom if you're too greedy, especially early game+/-  The story is good, probably not the best you can find out there, but still good+/-  Music is good, but except two or three tracks, not especially memorable+/-  The game doesn't take you by the hand and there is no quest logs or indicators. Like old times, you will have to talk to a lot of NPCs and figure things out yourself for most of the side quests stuff (which I don't dislike, personally) Cons:- No character voices, even in cutscenes, which I'm very sad about. The characters are already endearing and having voices would've made them all the more interesting.- Bestiary is very limited and newer, stronger monsters are pretty much all recolors with better stats- Treasure chests contents are honestly VERY underwhelming most of the time- There is a ton of recruitable NPCs and it can be tedious to go back and forth cities you've already visited to be sure you haven't missed anyone, the tower system is interesting though (albeit a bit OP considering how easy the game is already)- The Max HP loss on death/escape is interesting, but you will never die enough for it to actually have an impactOverall a very nice game, and you should definitely try it out if you're looking for a nice little adventure!

I'll post more reviews as I go along in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Dam visually this looks like Bravely Default, I wonder if it's any good+The gameplay is fun. You just use your arts per character and everyone (well almost everyone) has a choice of two weapons. It's also a plus that theres an autobattle button and a 4x speed button for battles.+With the two weapon system, you can build anyone however you want to. This allows anyone to play their favorite characters (unless their favorite characters are Tiggy and Robbins) with whatever weapon they want.+The level-up system is unique in the sense that there is no level-up system. After every battle, your characters have a chance of increasing hp or sp and that's it. You can unlock arts by hitting enemies with weapons and that is also by chance. After every battle you get talent points and using this, you can upgrade your talents for your characters. This may seem like a negative but really you will not feel like you aren't strong enough unless you are skipping out on weapon/armor upgrades. These are important as since your hp and sp are the only things increasing per level, better gear is what will up your damage and defense.+I had so much fun with the loop that in some areas, I would grind all 11 characters until each and everyone of them rarely upgraded hp and sp already. Unique level-up system and I honestly expected not to want to grind but I just found it really fun just waiting to see if my hp or sp will increase as unlike other grinding games, just one fight is all you need for the 'level-up'.+There is a lot to explore and a lot of side stuff which rewards the players for exploring. I love being able to recruit the npcs to my guilds. Kind of reminiscent of increasing your friends list in Radiata Stories but not really since you don't play them. It is oddly satisfying to assign many people to guilds.+The world is really really fun to explore. There is so much to find in the different islands in each of the different realms. This becomes more apparent when you unlock things like the airship as there are things you can finally go to in places you're always in. Besides recruitables, challenges like the different water dens are always welcome.+Robbins is such a cute character. If you don't use Robbins, what are you doing.+You can name your ship many things. I chose ♥♥♥♥♥EATER for this game.+The soundtrack is a vibe. The strings just go hard on the tracks. I am a big fan of the main theme and dam the guild theme. Sometimes I just went into guild towers just to hear the dam guild theme. It may seem odd for most and it was odd for me but I was a fan of the fact that the field theme didn't transition to a battle theme when entering a fight. A very strange design choice but I wasn't unhappy with it honestly.+The plot may not be the most engaging but it was fairly funny for the most part. Surprisingly enough this game does tackle some dark topics like racism and classism and of course those are always a plus. The story didn't really butcher those topics and really touched them well in addition to the comedic scenes.+The way the characters develop with one another and maybe they are just the basic tropes of characters in JRPGs but they are all individually unique and they just mesh with each other really well.-This game is not voiced at all. Even in the cutscenes, we just see mouths opening and dialogue popping up but no voice acting.-I mentioned how the gameplay is fun. It is fun in a therapeutic way where you can sit back and relax and watch the autobattle while grinding. It is fun to see big numbers. But despite this the gameplay is a bit too simple. Yes it's nice to see many weapons and all but we aren't afflicting status effects or debuffs or buffs for the most part. The battles are just use your strongest move over and over again. Occasionally heal.-Not only is the gameplay too simple. It is too easy. Your health literally regenerates after every battle (unless its a chain battle/ water den battle). Sometimes I did want a challenge. This game did not offer one. The biggest hurdle might be a part where you have to play everyone, but I do grind every character I own for most JRPGs I play, so I didn't feel any difficulty spike.-For a remaster, it doesn't look that amazing.Overall it was a fun experience, I didn't find any of these cons to overpower the pros and I would still recommend this to people who enjoy the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: The art style is wonderful, the world music is kind of forgettable but the battle theme (especially Ignition) is fantastic, the story is okay nothing too crazy, there's some surprising bits here and there though.The combat is saga-esque, which is to say you use a move and sometimes you'll unlock a new move from the tree of skills (magic and sorcery excluded--although you can learn sorcery spells by breaking items [that are repaired when you sleep so break away and roll the dice].It doesn't have traditional "beat monster gain level gain stats", you gain HP and SP (MP) from battling; the stronger the monster the higher the chance the numbers go up. It's rather fun to fight challenging monsters to raise your HP/SP quicker.There are guilds, which can be used for a myriad of purposes from crafting gear to unlocking new spells to debuffing enemies/buffing you, to additional damage in battle, which adds a bit of flavor to replayability.The game is by my accounts pretty easy if you grind or learn what moves are good to use for whatever character. That said there's a place in a realm that snows and if you're not ready for it (and honestly, even if you are..) it can be a complete and total softlock, so if you play this game make sure you save a second time there in a different slot.The game has NG+ as well as three endings (one of which you have to really go out of your way for, the second being the "you beat the game" ending, while the third is a NG+ ending), and NG+ unlocks some additional dialogue, world building, and NPCs for the guilds so there's reasons to replay.There admittedly is a lot of characters but most of them (really all of them) are likable or at least not annoying (to me) and all but one of them is usable in some fashion for your gameplay style.I love and still love this game. I played it on 3ds and beat it multiple times and when it came to steam i bought it to give my support. I wish it'd get a (good) sequel but alas; none so far.A few other things to add, the game doesn't support mouse and keyboard as of this review. While I can't defend the choice or explain it, I used both a PS4 controller (with a jay2king's DS4tools; I'm unsure if i needed them or not; I never tested without it since i just use it for controller games by default so i can remap) and with an Xbox controller (this had no problems being detected natively without the program.)There is a 4k texture pack if you have the space and the internet speed for it. It can be found in the discussions of the game.I've also read reports that the game crashes but I've left it open for hours and hours as well as tabbed out many many many times and played for very long play sessions and I never experienced this. My setup as of this review however is a very high end and top of the line windows 10 computer with a lot of extra ram, so that may have something to do with it.

_childDocuments_.review: Purchased this on a complete whim and I am rather happy with the decision. It has been probably almost five years since I've picked up a traditional turn-based JRPG but with games like FFVII Remake reminding me what I don't want to see from the RPGS I used to adore I found myself more drawn to the prospect of picking up one of several games that seemed to fit the bill.For whatever reason I decided to go with The Alliance Alive over some of the more popular alternatives and thankfully it is just what I was looking for. Nice world map reminiscent of every good JRPG you've ever played. The encounters seem to primarily operate under Chrono Trigger rules (as far as entering engagements is concerned anyway) where as 9/10 times the enemy will be displayed on the field map and you have the ability to evade/ escape them a good majority of the time from what I can tell.The combat is turnbased but moves quite quickly, further aided by the ability to increase to 2x or 4x  with the tap of a button should you so desire. Each character (I only have the initial two) appears to be able to equip any type of weapon and upgrade said weapon skills accordingly. I tend to favor having more focused, class type characters though so I am specializing in Sword and Shield for the male protagonist, and staff and bow for the female lead.You gain new weapon skills at a fairly reasonable clip, and this can be increased by purchasing abilities that reduce skill cost/ or increase the frequency at which new skills are obtained. I've honestly just been roaming the map and really only completed the first objective so I can't speak for the main story. The primary two characters however seem quite well adjusted and likeable enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Occasionally a JRPG comes out that feels like a deliberate attempt to be as "JRPG" as possible, and this is one of those games. The story and characters are very basic and best described as "fine," the art and presentation are a little cheap, and the game technically runs very well. However, it's the mechanics that are a mess, and the bulk of the game's content, and I want to explain how annoying this game is to actually play. Combat itself is a pretty basic round-based combat system. Nothing really to remark on fundamentally. But let's discuss what you can actually do besides use equipped items to buff/heal, and that's arts. Arts are every spell and attack, from free ones to the most expensive. There is no "attack" or "defend" option, just arts. Using them is just clicking on them, but how they work is a mess. Someone on Steam edited their characters' stats to test out what they actually do, and it turns out, every art works off different stats, with absolutely no in-game mention of this. The result is some very frustrating outcomes, like the guy who starts with a bow and has high agility but is terrible with bows, for example, that would lead the average person to just keep using bows with him, having no luck, and assuming he just sucks or bows suck. You can guess some things accurately, but others are a mystery, meaning 95% of people who have ever played this game have played it "wrong." What about learning arts? Seems entirely based on RNG and fighting the strongest monsters you can; it's nice to be less of a mess than SaGa Frontier, which is sort of feels like, but also sort of lame when the game just refuses to let a character learn something simple for hours on end and there's nothing you can do about it. Oh, and spells are mostly purchased, but frustratingly it's one spell here, one there, two over here, and so it's hard to look at all your options and make an informed choice.How about leveling? Well, you can't--there are no levels. Stats are locked in from the beginning of the game for each character. All you can increase is HP and SP (SP is used for arts), and this is, again, RNG, though it seems to improve against tougher enemies, while also having a built-in limiter to plateau them against any specific enemy strength. So grinding in this game ultimately is sort of required but also frustratingly unrewarding and just stops working after a while, until you go to the next area.Then there are talents. You earn talent points from every fight, and you spend them on talents; most talents pertain to making arts cheaper to use or learning them faster or leveling them up. But there are several other useful talents as well, like cheaper prices at stores. What's annoying about talents is that it further locks you into your playstyle; after you've unlocked multiple talents and arts with swords, you're just punishing yourself if you dare try to change. There's no real reason for this besides "it's a thing you do in RPGs." There's also formation. This is an interesting system, where you can assign characters "positions" that are basically stat changes, and then also change their actual formation on the grid to boost the strength of certain arts or draw/avoid aggro. Using a given art in a given position will also strengthen the art when used in that position, which is a weird choice that seems to just punish you for experimentation. It's just sort of finicky to set up and there aren't really enough options to it, but it's a nice idea.What about gear? Gear is surprisingly sparse in this game, with 7-8 of each weapon type only. 1-2 of those will be starter strength, so there's very little to look forward to. Very little non-starter gear is easy to simply purchase at a store as well, yet the difference between different levels of gear are substantial, considering your base stats are locked in. So you're constantly looking for gear to outfit your large team (and don't neglect team mates or you'll regret when the game forces you to use them), but always feel behind, as you'll only have, say, 1 good bow but 3 bow-users. Alot of the gear in the game is unique, outside of research, so you will inevitably feel like you're just under-equipped constantly, which matters alot when enemies are 1-shotting you over it.So let's talk about the guilds and research. There are 5 guilds in the game, which each can offer alot to the player...not that you'd know that. The game gives you very little information on what the guilds can really DO for you, so you have to just level them up to find out. Except, there are a limited number of "recruits" available to you, meaning a limit to how much guild upgrading you can do. This is very frustrating when you realize the best positions, the best gear, the best spells, and numerous other bonuses, are all locked behind the guilds. You're basically making choices that will have heavy late-game impacts without any way of knowing what's what without referring to like the one detailed guide on the internet, and really, you should be able to unlock ALL of them eventually, but too bad.Speaking of choices, let's talk about side-questing. There really isn't that much of it, it's mostly just either extra fights and dungeons, or recruiting people. But the game can be annoying about it; you often do have choices in these quests, with often unforeseeable consequences. Some people might like that, but I find it annoying; you're already limited on recruits for guilds, but you can easily limit yourself even more with a bad choice you had no knowledge of, or you can miss out on gear in exchange for...nothing, because some choices have no positive outcomes.Since there is a character limit, I can't write an entire novel on the mechanics, but I've hopefully made my point--the game is frustrating. It tells you how things work, but it doesn't really tell you how things work. There isn't a satisfying gameplay loop, there isn't a clear understanding of how everything is supposed to fit together in a cohesive vision--it feels more like mechanics for the sake of mechanics, with insufficient information being given to the player to navigate all these different systems. It's the sort of game that I imagine the experts really like, because they know it backwards and forwards, but for a new player just trying to have a good experience, it's very frustrating--you don't know where to spend points, what gear to use, what formation or position to use, what guilds to upgrade, how to handle sidequests, even where to go in some of the main quests. It's an okay game for the first act but then it really falls apart, and begins to feel either like homework or like beating your head against the wall to progress, since you can't even just grind levels to overcome any weaknesses. I can only recommend this game for people who like learning lots of arbitrary rules and systems just for the sake of it.

_childDocuments_.review: This remake from the 3DS was one that many weren't expecting to get another chance to shine, but it's come to Steam with a brilliant remaster. The world of Alliance Alive has many different environments for you to view, such as a beautiful rain filled realm or a fiery hot volcanic realm, while showing off a fun cast of characters from various walks of life. You won't grow tired of seeing each and every of the main characters, as they're easily the draw with this game. With that said, this game operates on a different axis compared to standard RPGs, in some methods to it's benefit and some to it's detriment. With this review, I'll focus on what I liked, and what I found to be concerns for any potential buyers. - The artists for this game clearly put in the effort to make this game look spectacular with a charming chibi style, beautiful visuals for each various land you go to, fun enemy design, and impressive attack animations for what was effectively a 3ds game. The music isn't a slouch either, you'll have a great time listening to the music as you explore each area. - With how the game operates, you have a revolving cast from various parts of the world that are initially all seperated, and for the first third of the game, the main focus is uniting everyone, while also learning what makes each of them tick and what they want. As you play through the early story, you'll see an event from one character's perspective and see in a later chapter a different character's perspective. It's not something I've often seen in RPGs, and I would say that the game does this well. The main part of the game, from Chapters 1 to 33~ are what I would consider the better aspects of the game. - The game is quite generous when it comes to recovering you after combat. You'll always refresh to your current max HP after combat is over, so long as you're not in a series of battles, i.e "chain battles". Furthermore, status effects are removed at end of combat, so as long as you win or run away, you'll be back to full. No need to worry about buying Revives or Potions since you'll simply recover. Even if a character is knocked out, they will revive back to their current max HP at end of combat, though max HP is lowered each time they're KO'd. - The game heavily encourages you to put actual thought in how you form your team. If you put everyone in attack, you'd certainly deal decent damage, but you'll find yourself falling apart rather easily. Instead, the game wants you to learn how to make team formations and understand what the combat asks from you. Having a good tank and/or a good healer is paramount to doing well past the first third of the game, as when enemies are dealing more and more damage, the ability to have one character sit and tank aggro while the others shred the enemies is quite nice, and similarly having a healer is important to keep your characters up during tough fights. - Equipment does feel a little odd, the best way to get items is to pretend the shops don't exist for the most part and simply scavenge the various areas you can go to for good items, such as the later game Water Devil dens where you run in, grab what you can, and leave. The shops are useful later on, but only when you can properly grind money. - It's hard to place whether I would consider this a positive or a negative. The game has a unique leveling system that I feel isn't explained as well as it could be. If it were explained properly in game, I would argue that this would be a positive, but alas you are mostly left on your own to research this yourself. To put it plainly, . Essentially, you never directly level up your Strength, Agility, etc, but instead simply get tankier, gain the ability to use more special moves, and unlock those special moves.For those who want an easy way to understand how this works, the game's leveling/awakening system works as follows.The game wants you to get better abilities/stats as you fight better enemies. For example, a common wolf isn't really a challenge after the first five minutes of the game, so you won't get anything from battling it after a certain point. However, if you were to battle a larger boss wolf, such as the one directly outside the first town at the ledge, you will have a higher chance to level up your HP/SP or get new moves. Namely, . Towards the later end of the game, to unlock the "final" skills for a given weapon, the consistent ways to unlock it is to simply find a very strong end-game enemy and spamming the basic attacks until it unlocks. There technically is, certain weapon skills have a higher chance to unlock related higher level skills, i.e: A bow skill that does "All Enemy" attacks have a higher chance to unlock the more damaging variant of the attack, and a weak counter used against a strong enemy may unlock the stronger version of the counter.  - Unfortunately, the game does feel a little rushed towards the last quarter of the game, with many things happening far too quickly, and certain important story elements quickly inserted in without time to simmer. Considering how beautiful the story building had been up to that point, I do unfortunately have to knock a point off for this. I will note that I still found it enjoyable, and it had a lot of very enjoyable ideas that were enhanced in this last chunk of the game, but it is still worth noting that it may concern others, especially as certain story parts aren't fully explored or explained. - While I do think at the end of the day the "unlocking new attack" version of leveling up is quite interesting, but most of the combat feels unexplained or useless. It isn't told what stats matter for what weapons, and the only attacks that really matter are the strongest AOE attack, and stronger single target attack you have on a non-tank/healer character, and for those the best defense/heal you have. Status Effects you can do feel useless, and boosts/demerits are cute, but not useful unless you're dealing good damage while getting them.I did enjoy the game, I'd recommend it. It feels like a breath of fresh air and I loved the world it told, and it left a lot of questions that I'd love explored in a new game, but I would warn new buyers to understand that they're in for a unique experience. This game's a work of art, and sometimes not everyone can fully appreciate what the game wants to show.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game a lot. It scratches the old-school JRPG itch for sure. The story, while a little cliche, is decent and the characters are likable. The combat is both my biggest gripe and the best aspect of The Alliance Alive. The player is given a lot of leeway to build the characters in a way that they see fit. I'm all about the unarmed combat - there's something about punching monsters in the face that's really refreshing. So if you want to basically raise a team of D&D style monks, you can.The flip side is that for all of the freedom of character building and formations and other game mechanics that aren't exactly spelled out during your time with the game, you're never really forced to use any of it in a meaningful way. I would argue that the game is wide as an ocean and deep as a puddle when it comes to combat. The rumors are true: you can just go in with your most useful/damaging skills and progress with a clear conscience. I haven't beaten the game yet, but I've had a few boss encounters where I'm forced to think about what I'm doing. These encounters, however, are few and far between. You'll deal with mooks for the most part and will probably run on autopilot for a goodly portion of the adventure. I recommend the game but only if it's during a sale. The Alliance Alive is worth your time, but there are better JRPGs that are probably more compelling than this one. I give it a 6/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing game that reminds me of when the first experimentation was being moved forward with exploration in RPGs (ie romancing saga series), which ended up turning into some ridiculous action game genre that doesn't resemble RPGs at all. There was a lot of love put into this game from the art designers.This is a SPECTACULAR RPG and it is well worth the price. I know people are into what they are into, but this game resembles the very turn of the genre that happened around the late 90s. While it is beautiful, it still lacks some "traditional RPG" elements. There is still turn based combat, but there is a numbering system that has been simplified.Skills are enhanced by using them and they are not linear. This helps customize the experience but does not follow traditional RPG roles. This game reminds me of the first movement into cheapening and "dumbing down" the RPG genre, but it is still 10000000000000000000000000% better than any RPG released today in my humble opinion.I recommend it 100% over any of the garbage released today with DLC "costumes"  objectifying women to sell crappy programmed games that lack any depth.While it isn't the most "fun" game, this game has traditional deep RPG roots with a great story and I love it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so dull. After 14 hours, I can't do any more.The gameplay is SaGa-like, but immensely slower. With no Battle Rank to scale up enemy levels, the game is way too easy and you almost never gain HP/SP or Awaken new abilities. As much as I dislike Battle Rank in the SaGa series, this game's lack of it makes me realize the important role it plays to keep challenging the player.The story is fine. It's more linear than most SaGa games, but opens up around Chapter 20, at which point it's almost more directionless than a SaGa.The music is fine, but music is too low in the mix. And the light exploration music rarely changes to a battle theme. The music helps present the game as dull, boring, and barely worth your attention.Movement speed is slow. Just walking around maps is tedious, fighting enemies is unrewarding, and there's little to discover.Bosses are fine, I guess. Shield talents are basically mandatory to avoid taking damage, and then the bosses can barely do anything to your party, while characters  have a chance to Awaken some new abilities.There's just not enough here to make playing this game compelling or interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: Alliance Alive (AA) is a tiny, traditional-JRPG with a fantasy story that does not take itself too seriously. Nine characters are slowly introduced, each a rough trope, however everyone is likable. The art direction is fantastic, especially the environments--with each map feeling really different. Sounds are classic-rpg and the music fits the fantasy theme, but the lack of voice acting is noticeable.Fans of SaGa games will quickly pick up the combat with characters randomly learning abilities during battle, with the addition that battlefield placement plays a role. Battles are quick, and there is a chance for small stat boosts after combat. Battle animations are vivid, fitting the rest of the art direction.AA feels like a budget-title done well although it lacks the charm and polish of other JRPGs. If you have cleared your backlog, grab AA to get lost in a fantasy world for 30 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: Preface: Just barely recommending this game. Alliance Alive HD is a slightly above average RPG with cutesy chibi graphics, although it suffers from some pretty major inopportune difficulty spikes.  At one point in the game, after you've absolutely stomped every enemy until then, you slam into a boss that will totally obliterate you if you aren't over-geared and haven't been grinding. Doesn't sound too bad, right? I mean, just go level some more! Well, therein lay the heart of the issue -- you can't leave the zone to find enemies to grind. That's right, without warning, suddenly you just can't turn back. If you don't have a backup save, and find yourself unable to defeat this boss, well, you're sorta stuck. Time-wise, this falls somewhere around the middle of your play through. Had I not made a backup save to another slot an hour prior, I likely would have hit the uninstall button. Now, some of you might think I'm exaggerating about the difficulty of this boss, but I can say without a doubt, that it is more difficult than anything else you'll tackle in the game for the next 7 hours or so. To top it off, you fight this same boss again later on, and oddly enough, that one is a cake walk (and I didn't even grind, I was just plowing through the game). I feel like they got the stats backwards for which fight was which. Beyond this horrendous oversight, game balance and difficulty is pretty fair for the most part. Regular enemies in the final dungeon might be a bit on the strong side though, but at least in that scenario you have an area you can go back to so you can rest, level, repeat. In the end, if it wasn't for the boss that shall not be named, I'd give this game a solid 8/10. With that said, such an oversight really grinds my gears, so I'm giving it a 7/10. It's a serviceable RPG with a decent story, and features interesting combat mechanics and a unique "leveling" system. If they made a sequel, I'd play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, before I start ripping into this game, I might as well start off with the good. The graphics are really nice and the cinematic cut scenes are really well done. The character interactions and the story are decent during the first half of the game. However, once the characters finally group up, everything sort of falls apart.The Combat difficulty spikes dramatically for no good reason, and the necessity of grinding is pretty bad. The combat system was trying something clever with the use of tactical positioning and weapon breaking to do great damage, but I don't think it worked out very well. Also, after chapter 25 or even 20, the character interactions and story end up dropping in quality. There are optional party members, most of which really don't feel like they should be optional, and the characters really don't develop past that point either. Also, those cinematic cut scenes really don't feel right without voice acting, but I can see why they didn't.Overall, I had higher hopes for this game near the beginning that very quickly fell apart and became a slog of trying to get it over with.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a charming game, with an interesting story, colorful characters, and beautiful artwork. Perhaps a bit silly at times, but that's JRPGs.Having played several more conventional RPGs, how this game does stats and leveling is quite different. There's a lot of randomness involved. Maybe a bit  much. However, it wasn't so bad that it actively got in the way of enjoying the game, and it was definitely refreshing. Instead of collecting experience, leveling up, and gaining moves and stat increases at set intervals, you collect 'talent' to unlock useful perks, and based on the strength of the enemy your HP/SP randomly increase and you randomly unlock moves. Stats are more-or-less controlled entirely through equipment.The overall combat balance of the game is a bit wacky - it's really easy for the first half of the story, but then as the world opens up in the second half it becomes way more difficult. Thankfully, there's also enough optional content to do at that point that clearing the difficulty spike doesn't feel like grinding - and once you can clear it, battles become engaging enough to keep you on your toes. Team composition and formations become really important.Apart from those minor nitpicks, the game was plenty enjoyable, and I'd definitely recommend it if you're into JRPGs.(N.B.: The moment you have all nine main characters (i.e. the halfway point), you really,  want to make sure that before you proceed with the main story you spend time getting training and speccing all of them so you can split the party into three self-contained teams (each with attacker, tank, and healer). Because you  end up doing just that, and it's going to be hard, and you won't be able to rectify it easily once you realise the situation you're in.)

_childDocuments_.review: Originally a 3DS game, this is a relatively short rpg made by the scenario writer for suikoden. There are achievements for speed running the game. The game also includes modern QoL improvements such as the ability to fast forward and automate battles (which just keeps repeating your commands until cancelled).  This might make it sound like the combat is brainless but it isn't. Some regular enemies can be quite challenging.The game starts off simply which I think might have been a mistake as the game really shines once you get to the halfway point of the game. That may seen like a long time but it's 10 or 15 hours. Once you get the ability to recruit people to form your guild, the game gets a lot more interesting. The game also has "hidden" party members which is rare in modern games.Combat: First, you have rows like in suikoden which affects things like speed/healing boost, defense increase and attack increase. The combat is more like the SaGa games where you get inspiration in battle and you learn new moves and moves have a chance of getting more powerful every time you use them.  You can also customize formations if you choose to focus on that aspect. There are no levels. Your stats only change with gear and your hp and sp may go up after battle. The chance increases with more difficult enemies. Gear is the most important. Any character can equip any 2 weapon but some weapons are better for certain characters. There is no "defend" command unless you equip a shield which can also be used offensively. You also get talent points which every character, even those you haven't recruited yet, collects at the same speed. This allows you to change things like the chance of gaining hp, lowering skill cost or increasing threat when using a certain weapon. Getting downed in battle lowers max hp until you rest.Missable recruits? Yes, in the sense that you can make choices that lead you to not being able to recruit a character. If a character is named be careful on how you interact with them. Unlike suikoden, the mass majority of people you recruit do not fight. However, every recruit can be assigned to one of 5 guilds which powers up the services/power offered by that guild. Certain super recruits allow the construction of towers which have the additional benefit of providing battle effects within range. You have a base where you can talk to your recruits and they occasionally chat in a mobile like chat program within the game.Cons: The game has cutscenes but the game is not voiced -at all-. It didn't bother me but it was weird to have unvoiced cutscenes. In conclusion a great game to play.For more Japanese games look  at "Japanese Games on PC at

_childDocuments_.review: I like RPGs. When I came upon this game, I thought "generic throwback RPG ported to Steam? Where do I sign?", and within only a few hours I can see there is a lot of good quality in this game. So then I played a few more and realized how shallow this rabbit hole was. While no pun was intended by that, if you foolishly play through this game, you will see a rabbit's butthole. Seriously, this is not a joke, but I do find it hilarious.Exploration:This is the one acceptable parts of the entire game, and it ain't even that good. Sure, world map stuff is a welcome old love of mine, but this type of content usually only enhances an already good game. Putting good exploration into an otherwise awful game is like putting icing on feces and telling people that it is chocolate cake.Characters: Remember Chrono Cross's unusual party recruits? I wish Alliance Alive had half of Chrono Cross's party quality. Chrono Cross knew how to make deep and meaningful characters even when they were wacky folks who you can grab help from. Alliance Alive does not know how to make deep and meaningful characters, and mostly fails by making only boring characters and lackluster oddballs.Story:Remember when some Japanese guy said "hero and villain team up" and made Maoyuu? Yeah, that guy at least put effort in and made a decent product. On the other hand, Alliance Alive gives up in almost every attempt to make good story. At no point do I care about the stakes or have any belief that the heroes could lose, because they never push any emotional investment. What little emotional investment is forced drama that tests my patience. In this game, someone is blinded during a story moment. Did it affect combat for that character? No, because common sense does not matter in forced narrative convenience. It only adds a blindfold to their eyes and gives up. Battle Gameplay: Oh, this is where it gets really bad. First, and most importantly, stat increases occur randomly, and are not naturally determined via a reasonable method. This single fundamental issue turns what could be a unique and enjoyable battle system into FF2 but far worse. So.... at first if you play, you won't think much of the battles, but the longer you play the worse the battle system gets. Fights are either too hard or too easy with nothing in between thanks to the imbalances caused by the random level ups, but this imbalance still occurs thanks to the complete and utter lack of polish when it comes to encounters. When a party member gets knocked out, their maximum health decreases until the party rests. This stacks until a character becomes useless in battle, and only serves to drag out exploration by making it an issue of stamina. This is atop the generic MP system and level up mechanics that simply doll out stat increases based on use. You will be forced to get the growth ability if you want to actually finish the game, as otherwise you will not up your stats fast enough. Even though I figured out these challenges, this game's battle system kept getting worse, until it became completely unacceptable in the final areas, where the random encounters with common enemies were actually more difficult than the final boss due to the massive amount of damage four or five common monsters could cause in a single turn while the final boss rarely does enough damage to warrant any defensive actions or healing. Go play Octopath Traveler or the Bravely Default series. Alliance Alive had some moments, but I really cannot recommend this game. If this game was $15 or less, then it might be a fair deal, but it ain't. Playing Alliance Alive only makes you need booze to survive the stress, which appropriately and comedically means that playing AA leads to AA meetings.

name: 30XX
detailed_description: Join us on Discord! Come and keep up to date on the latest in 30XX developments! About the Game The Year is... 30XX combines the crisp controls and fluid movement you love from action platformers like Mega Man X , the replayability of a modern Roguelike ( Binding of Isaac, Enter the Gungeon, Dead Cells , etc) and co-op play into a single gorgeous package. Awaken a thousand years after 20XX to realize the world that needed you is gone, changed irreversibly by the advent of the Synthetic Mind and a human race that's lost the will to reach for the stars. Explore the lush, verdant prison our world has become, and fight to save what remains. Rise. Fight. Fall. Adapt. There's a sublime meaning in this endless cycle, somewhere, buried deep. Features: Pulse-pounding action, precise platforming, and beautiful spritework Characters with fully distinct playstyles - master Ace's swift, combo-friendly Techniques and Nina's intricate Power Fusion system for even more replayability A fresh new set of levels, items, and powers every time you play - 30XX is never the same game twice! Roguelike-style progression that lets you tune the game's systems and difficulty as you play, even after you win A robust level editor - the same tools the developers use! - that lets you build single level chunks or entire custom campaigns Local and online multiplayer, so you can enjoy 30XX with a friend

name: Sniper Elite 5
detailed_description: Season Pass Two Roadmap Season Pass One Roadmap Deluxe Edition includes Season Pass One Join Us On Discord About the Game The latest instalment in the award-winning series, Sniper Elite 5 offers unparalleled sniping, tactical third-person combat and an enhanced kill cam. Fight your way across the most immersive maps yet, with many real-world locations captured in stunning detail, and an improved traversal system that lets you explore more of them than ever before. France, 1944 – As part of a covert US Rangers operation to weaken the Atlantikwall fortifications along the coast of Brittany, elite marksman Karl Fairburne makes contact with the French Resistance. Soon they uncover a secret Nazi project that threatens to end the war before the Allies can even invade Europe: Operation Kraken. EXPANSIVE CAMPAIGN Many real-world locations have been captured using photogrammetry to recreate a living, immersive environment, and multiple infiltration and extraction points and kill list targets provide a whole new perspective on each mission. Take on the Nazi plot solo or work with a partner, with improved co-op mechanics allowing you to share ammo and items, give orders and heal each other. ADVANCED GUNPLAY PHYSICS AND TRAVERSAL Use ziplines, slide down slopes and shimmy along ledges to reach the perfect vantage point, or to sneak past a sharp-eyed lookout. Factor in rifle stock and barrel options along with gravity, wind and heart rate while you line up your sights on the target. HIGH CALIBRE CUSTOMISATION Use workbenches to customise and upgrade virtually every aspect of your weapon – change scopes, stocks, barrels, magazines and more. Rifles, secondaries and pistols all have a huge variety of options. On top of that you can select the ammo to suit your target, from armour-piercing right down to non-lethal. INVASION MODE – CAMPAIGN DROP IN PvP AND CO-OP Invade another player’s Campaign as an Axis sniper and engage in a deadly game of cat and mouse, providing a new dimension to the challenge as you stalk your prey. Alternatively, as Karl you can call for assistance and have a second sniper drop in to help you out of a tricky situation. TENSE ADVERSARIAL MULTIPLAYER Customise your character and loadout and earn XP, medals and ribbons as you take on intensely competitive 16 player battles that will really test your sharpshooting skills. If co-op’s more your style, you can team up with up to 3 other players against waves of enemies in Survival mode. ENHANCED KILL CAM More realistic and grisly than ever, the trademark X-ray kill cam returns, showing you the true destructive power of each shot. Bones deflect bullets unpredictably, ripping a new path through enemy bodies. SMGs and pistols can also trigger kill cams, including multiple shots in dramatic slow motion.

_childDocuments_.review: Although i have not finished the game at the time of writing this review i can still confidently say that Sniper elite 5 is amazing.Sniper elite as a franchise is one of the most underrated video games out there and the 5th instalment is no different.Its set in 1944 France (personally fav setting and period of ww2) the graphics are absolutely beautiful running the game at 4k upscaled all ultra at 100+ frames the engine is also well optimised too my friend who has a weaker system (2060) was able to run the game at high with no issues gunplay like previous instalments is satisfying and snappy.Level design however kinda disappointed me most fights are super close quarters so i found myself using my pistol more then the actual rifle itself (more kills on it at this current time)however i also wanted to keep the game historically accurate (not using suppressors on snipers)so it only made sense to use my pistol i think the same old factory level gets boring(basically the same premise as the one in Sniper Elite 4) i expected a lot more interesting locations considering the game is set in France which had some of the most important battles of the second world war the missions set in the city however where amazing reminded me of the original Sniper Elite and that scary feeling long range sniping in this game is kinda not a thing but even still i had my fair share of fun for now this will be my fav game in the franchise simply due to those city levels overall a solid 9.4/10 a lot of re play value with different modes and collectables.The difficulty itself was not super difficult (i played on hard) however not seeing enemies on the mini map is a awesome design change to make it more challenging.
