_childDocuments_.review: Mafia: The Definitive Edition is a remaster of a game from 2002, and a game that tried really hard to stop me from playing it.You play as Thomas “Tommy” Angelo, a cab driver working in the city of Lost Heaven during the 1930s. One day, Tommy is doing work on his taxi on the side of the road when two men being chased by a mob of other men commandeer both him and his cab as a getaway driver.  The two introduce themselves as Sam and Paulie, and after being attacked by the men he drove away from, Tommy goes to them for help, and ends up leaving his life as a cab driver behind and working for the Salieri crime family.Okay so, the biggest problem with this game is 2K’s launcher, this putrid little program and decides, like a false god, if you can play your games or not, or if you can mod your games or not, depending on what 2K game you’re actually playing. I almost had to refund this game because it would just crash on the main menu. After consorting with the Witches (The internet), I found the fix.Using the "mafiadefinitiveedition" %command%”  line in the Steam advanced launcher options allowed me to skip 2Ks launcher in general, and another file I got from the PC gaming Wiki let me skip the unskippable intro video. Don’t ask me HOW this fixed my game, but it actually let me play the game from start to finish with 0 issues afterwards.Okay so. How is the game? Mafia: The -Other- Version is the first time I’ve played the first game from start to finish. I played Mafia (2002) back in 2006 for maybe two or so hours before kind of putting it down, so I don’t really have a frame of reference between the two. So I’m just going to be talking about THIS one, and going back to the original in the future.Mafia is mostly a third person shooter, with segments for story and driving. The game presents itself as an open world game, and yeah, you can go anywhere in between mission segments, but there really isn’t anything to do in Lost Heaven, at least in the story mode. Most buildings except for the really important ones are just set dressing, and you can’t enter any of them. However, it is really nice set dressing, like a dinner table sheet you haven’t spilled beef on yet. Lost Heaven exists as a kind of character, it’s basically just there so the place Tommy and Pal’s exist in feels like a real space, and not just a segment of warehouses, apartment, and business buildings. You CAN actually turn off the driving segments, save for the most important ones. But I didn’t do this, and I felt like just driving around and listening to the radio or chatting with whoever was in the car with Tommy was reward enough.I like Tommy, he’s a fun guy. Also, before you ask. The race took me three tries.  It might have taken me two or one, but I reloaded a checkpoint when I messed up too bad. Shooting in the game actually caught me off guard. At first it felt weird to me, but getting use to the weapons let me appreciate the punch and crunch you get from using them. Mafia DE uses rag dolls, but only AFTER the guy is dead dead. Its been a long time for me since a game actually had death animations that wasn’t just a guy scrunching over like he had to poop before falling on his face. Guys you shoot react to the world around them. Getting a shot to the head just drops them like a sack of potatoes going down stairs. Shooting them in the chest until they go down has them clutching their wounds, taking out a guys legs will have them crawl around for a bit. If there’s a wall behind them, they’ll slide down the wall, if it’s a car they’ll crumple over the vehicle. Lamp posts and fences do the same thing. Its nice, made me feel like I was playing an older Max Payne game. You don’t have MANY weapons to play with, but you have one for job. Several pistols, a Tommy Gun (Its a Thompson, not a gun that shoots Tommy’s), a shotgun to turn people into shredded paper, and a rifle for “I want to kill you, but at a comfortable distance”. They all sound nice and have nice animations to them. But Tommy will ♥♥♥♥ the shotgun or pull the slide back no matter if you had ammo in the chamber or not. So that’ irked me. Looks nice, though. Driving works, Its not special or crazy, but it’s nowhere near as awful as some games make it. You won’t just magically lose control of your car for hitting a bump, and they all feel nice and weighty, like a car made entirely out of steel and iron should. Lost Heaven in general is nice and detailed. A lot of work was put into the city to make it feel alive and real. Tommy will greet people that greet him on the street, your car has a fuel gauge that you can refill at a gas station, although no one comes out to do it for you like they should in that time period. You can get pulled over for speeding, your car radio will scramble when you go through tunnels, environments explode and shatter during gun fights. Its all very pretty, makes me feel like a princess that smuggles hooch. The story is probably Mafia’s strongest point. Its crazy that I never heard all that much about it outside of big Mafia fans. Everyone is voice acted well, and they either had some dude working in a slave pit, or used really good motion capture for the faces and bodies. Everyone moves so natural and realistically in a way that most Triple A games can’t even manage. Everything from the eye movement, to the way Paulie purses his lips, to the points in the game where someone will just put out a cigarette, and then absent minded put a new one in his mouth a minute later. really helped immerse me in the world of Mafia. Mafia also has one of the sweeter love stories I’ve seen in a video game. No gratuitous sex scenes, or weird forced drama, they just sort of fall in love and get married over the course of the story. This was also the first time in a very long time that I was actually heart broken from the events of a video game. It is nuts to me how much mileage a story can get out of Italian dudes doing crime. Sony’s Sad Dad games can have all the characters crying on screen they want, but “I’m sorry ___, I have to go.” Made me pause the game and take a minute. I -really- liked Mafia: DE. Its a great story carried by pretty good gameplay. There is also a Free Ride mode where you can just explore Lost Heaven and do some quests to get secret Cars, but the game relies almost entirely on it’s story mode.I’m actually sort of afraid of going back and playing the Original now, not that it sours my opinion on the remaster. Because everything I’ve heard of Mafia 2002 is that it’s the better version. But for now, I highly recommend the game. Even with 2K doing everything in their power to stop me from playing it. Mafia: Definitive Edition gets 8 smoked cigarettes out of 10. I now have lung problems. It’s crazy how little they use the ♥♥♥♥ word in this game when the sequel actually has the record for it being used.

_childDocuments_.review: So, what can I say.I played the original Mafia back in 2002 and boy I wasn't prepared for the journey it took me on. I was 12 years old (and probably shouldn't have played it, but what can you do?) and I had never experienced anything like it. A couple of years later Mafia 2 came out and I played it, but the tone was different and while I still liked it, it never gave me the sensation and the feels of the first one, but I liked it and I will never forget the moment I realized I was about to kill Tommy in that one mission.Fast forward to the Mafia: Definitive Edition. I was excited when it was first announced, but became sceptical when I heard Hangar 13 was going to do the rework. Those were the guys who did Mafia 3 which had about nothing in common with the Mafia I loved. It was buggy, generic but most importantly it had not the slightest bit of the mood, the characters or the atmosphere of Mafia 1. So could they do it?Hell yes! The Definitive Edition is great! They kept to the strengths of the original, while tending to some of the weaknesses like the melee combat or the shooter mechanics. I will get to this in a bit. The game looks amazing. Anyone who has a soft spot for old cars will spend quite some time admiring just the beauty of the cars. The city itself also got an upgrade and really sells you the 30s, BUT it is little more than a nice backdrop for the story. Compared to modern Opern Worlds it is empty and meaningless, but it used to be this way in the original so I'd consider this neither a pro nor a con. After all it won't distract you from living your own personal gangster epos.The driving is something you have to get used to and a bit of a matter of taste. The cars behave in a sluggish way and really feel heavy. They make you believe you're in a world without all these little technical helpers that make driving so much easier today. I prefer it this way, cause it adds to my immersion, but you can turn it to a more casual mode if you dont like it. Of course I have to talk about the infamous race you do quite early in the game. For my taste it's way easier. On my first try I ended up second place, took me three tries in total do complete the mission.Melee combat in the original was hilarious. You were flailing aimlessly trying to knock down your enemy. In the remake, melee combat is still not great, but they implemented a quick time counter based combat which does the job.Gun Play: So for the gun play they implemented a new cover mechanic similar to Mafia 3. I think it adds to the game in a good way, though making it a bit easy from time to time. You stay in cover while enemies shoot, pop out when they stop and as soon as the stick up their head again you kill them.The guns themselves are a bit weird. The crosshair is a circle and the spray is somewhat horrible especially with the Thompson machine gun. This is kind of sad since it is such an iconic weapon for the setting. The shotguns do not enough damage for my taste. I would have prefered them to be one shot kill up to a medium distance, but you have to land a headshot for this. I ended up using the Colt 1911 like 90% of the time only switching it up when I ran out of ammo, which hardly happened since you can almost always land a headshot with your first shot at short or medium range.SummaryOverall I am very happy with how the Definitive Edition turned out. It enables you to relive one of the best singleplayer story games I have ever played in modern graphics and you will most likely enjoy every minute of the story, but keep in mind, that it is an almost 20 years old game in its core. It's definitly worth the 40 bucks, but if you are unsure, grab it in a sale with 50 percent off, but make sure you play this masterpiece!

_childDocuments_.review: A cinematic, "airtight" open-world experience that prioritizes a shorter, but more memorable story and missions within it rather than a bloated game with meaningless quests.Yes for an open-world game it is extremely short, clocking in at about 10 or so hours to get through the main game. But the approach here is all killer, and no filler. I can't even think of a bad mission in this game. Yes there were some that were a little bit better than others, but all in all every single mission was extremely memorable.So many open-world games suffer from bloat, meaningless missions/quests, and artificial time-wasters that it was so refreshing playing a game that had an immersive open-world, but also a very memorable story that hooked you from beginning to end.The only thing that weighs this game down for me was the fact that it definitely needed just a little more polish before it released, driving doesn't feel great, the gunplay is so-so on mouse and keyboard, and there are numerous glitches and bugs within it (not to mention it requires a beefy PC to run well), but all in all I very much enjoyed my time with this game, and am really looking forward to Mafia II.

_childDocuments_.review: I count the original Mafia among the best of my gaming experiences, and have replayed it the last time somewhere in 2019. This remake captures the same atmosphere as the original and is a great remake of the original story from a game/filmistic view point. Only for that, I recommend it. It's fun, nostalgic, a good (quick - rather old-fashioned) game on its own even if you didn't play the original. (And if you think the acting and animations are not up to standards... eh, they're at least better than in 2002.)However, there are few downsides compared to the original:- No Django Reinhardt (that I heard so far) in the sound track (understandable if copy right issues);- No wheel support (driving on PC with the wheel is something is still plug and play in the 2002 version), which is a bummer for those really liking the realistic side of things. A good point here is that the realistic driving settings are still quite good for a non-car game and the gearbox can still be operated manually.- The animations of pedestrians in particular repeat a lot. This is the most common example of where the game apparently cut some corners in the remake to speed up production. It's very atmospherical, but don't expect RDR2 level of detail (not that every game should reach that standard, but still, this one is noticable).Overall though, happy to have bought. Not a replacement for the original, but a reinterpretation that I enjoy playing through.

_childDocuments_.review: I´m too old for thisI am proud owner of the original Mafia Special Edition in a white box back from the days where games still had boxes and you were proud to had one that was supposed to be limited to 5000. It was one of my first games that featured a realistic environment game world and I had to buy it twice for patching my german version to the english spoken language. Back in those days the term Open World was limited to a city you could drive freely within your car. You found small easter eggs here and there and all you collected was cars, sweet old cars from the 30s. You lived in this city and it was fun to drive around with your rare cars. Even after the thrilling story you could drive around for hours and you were even prouder of your collected cars in free roam extreme. I don’t know what I had expected when I heard that this wonderful game get a remake. I think I was dreaming of reliving the good old days and imagined to see everything just in much better graphics. I was deep disappointed as finally played the new first mission. Not because it was a little different with the new road blocker feature, no that wasn’t it. Simply one and only one thing turned down all my fun. It had names and it looked not only different but right out wrong. You guessed it folks, Paulie & Sam. I don’t know who is the poor guy that Paulie is modeled after, but he has my deeply compassion that he was forced to stand model for a once nice guy that now is almost the new personification of "the Joker" from Batman. Sam looks a little better but was not even close to the original too. It took me a few minutes more and then an afternoon that I had booked out to play this game turned into one disappointment after another. -	No free game world, no free roaming after or in missions-	poor remake of old and loved chars, best worst example is Paulie: Once a nice guy with humor now is a freakish looking bastard (just see the first time you met Ralphie). When he laughs you want to call Commissioner Gordon to summon Batman because this face has to be the Joker.-	Some cut scenes just feel wrong, e.g. why would a Don recruit someone right of the street (who just wants to get revenge on someone who wrecked his car) to his trusted members of the family. In the original it looked more like Tommy would have at least get a little background checked before he entered the meeting room and he don’t demand to get his revenge on Morello’s men. Imagine, the other guys have to stand outside the door while the new guy is part of the meeting just because he was chased by Morello’s men and is recruited right away.-	no use of the cable cars-	collecting of magazines just to keep you busy to search for something-	cars are not really collectible (no, just unlocking theme in every type by sitting in one of it for a few seconds does not count)-	once rare cars now standing and driving everywhere-	the whole city feels wrong, I don’t know why but the 30s then (Mafia Classic) felt never like the 60s like here-	Missions are just that, Missions. The whole story is parted in tiny short missions and after everyone you have to press next, you almost wait for the statistics how long you have needed, how poorly you have aimed and how bad your score is in comparison to other players.-	Everyone looks a lot younger than in Mafia Classic, it seems now only young guys can have experience with cars, guns and crime. And that was just a few things to mention.For the good parts (Yes I have good things to tell too):-	Some side chars look and feel very good. Morello and Frank couldn’t be casted better-	The city feels a little bigger, has more roads and alleys and looks very good (but still don’t feels like the 30s of Mafia Classic)-	Some of the Cut scenes feel more appropriate and believable For someone that never played Mafia Classic I would recommend it to play this game and never play the original so you don’t know what you miss. For someone my age that had played classic 2002 I would only recommend to buy it on a cheaper price, you will be disappointed to some degree here and you will wish to forget how great Classic where.I know, everyone has his own opinion, that’s mine and I don’t like to discuss it here, if you agree, that’s fine if you disagree then write your own opinion and don’t  pick up on mine :) Thank you!

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is best described as 30's era Grand Theft Auto if you could only play the main story missions and there was nothing else to do in the game.  I see why people were so frustrated with it when the original version came out.  They built a big, huge open world and then didn't actually use any of it.  The city is huge but there's no reason to go anywhere other than the mission objective, the driving around is just to burn time between the set piece scenes. And the driving and combat are both kind of clunky.  You can tell from the dialogue that there was intended to be more.  They drop hints about side missions to steal cars... places to customize your look... lots of the stuff that was in GTA, but if it's there I sure didn't see any evidence of it after 5 hours.  Just go chapter to chapter of set piece scenes, and they just weren't good enough to carry the game in my opinion.I never played the original so I can't make a comparison.  Looking at this version in 2022 I will say the production values and voice acting are really good and there is some beautiful scenery in this game.  It's pretty to look at and the story was kind of interesting, but not interesting enough for me to finish it.  I love the old 30's era cars and the main character feels like a cool person to be, but it wasn't enough for me to call this a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game runs like hot garbage. I assume all the "definitive edition" trilogy games run like hot garbage, since they all use the same private engine developed by Hangar 13 / 2K Czech. It seems to be related to the scripting calls, because it'll run fine for a long time when you have nothing going on, and then suddenly when scripted events start to trigger, performance becomes potato and the game has a seizure. The music/voiceover (but not ambient sound) is always the first to desynchronize, and the video will halt or skip repeatedly to wait for the audio to catch up.Hangar 13 shouldn't try to reinvent the wheel when they clearly don't understand how wheels work, or I guess how to release fixes post-release either. Given the terrible development history of Mafia III, I'm betting nobody still works at Hangar 13 who knows how this engine works, and thus it hasn't been fixed because they can't fix it.

_childDocuments_.review: I never played the original Mafia although I have played Mafia II and Mafia III; Mafia 2 being my preferred experience and III being a little too purposely fictionally racially driven but had a decent amount of side quests. With that being said, this is a new Mafia experience for me. The story starts off really quick, by mission 2 you're already "in the family", I had a laugh at that. Not a single ounce of actual build up, just a taxi driver that is quickly thrusted into this position willy nilly, but I moved on. The story mode does not allow you to roam around the world, which I find very odd. There's a separate mode for that but the only things you can do is drive cars and 2 types of motorcycles, collect collectibles and I guess enjoy the scenery and kill people as you wish. I didn't think this would be a big deal but playing the game, several times I wanted a break from the main story that was almost copy/paste of the previous mission. Several times I quit the game, roamed around for 5-10 minutes after realizing there's literally nothing to do in the world. There are no side quests at all, no random events, no shops, no money system, no player housing...nothing. It makes for an extremely limited experience making me feel like I'm not a part of the world, I'm just participating in an interactive show that won't be renewed for Season 2. Many times I felt like they missed an opportunity to incorporate events in the game for the player to feel like this is their home, this is their job and my actions affect the world around me. For instance, after the race, the mechanic comes up to you and thanks you for winning the race, citing he wouldn't be able to make rent and would be homeless if Tommy (you the player) lost. That's a big deal. He then states to come by his shop, he's got something for you. You never go back to the shop, you never see that character ever again in the story. You're lucky to just pass his shop every once in awhile as you do the same copy/paste missions for the story. Missed opportunity. What Hangar 13 did remarkably though, is that they built a beautiful world filled with amazing detail. Bravo. Seriously, I think that's why I'm so upset with the story and lack of features. They created this gorgeous, detailed, semi-lively world and you're forced into a linear story that doesn't let you appreciate all they have built. The scale of Lost Heaven is vast but I feel like it could have been bigger, but only if they decided to add features that actually let you explore it. They have an entire airport you think you can explore but you can't because it's locked up, even in free roam I couldn't get in to check out the hangers and the planes, wasted potential. The second thing Hangar 13 did great was mocap and voice acting. Although Paulie sounded like a 12 year old most of the time, the lip syncing and acting was spot on. The character details were perfect, all the way down to the abundance of pores on Tommy's nose. I'm giving this a NO recommendation because it's so limited. You will play it, notice you've played a game with a pretty mediocre story with your typical mobster tropes. You will be wanting side quests, you will be wanting to free roam and do what you want within the world like you could with past Mafia games and notice that you can't. You'll be left feeling unsatisfied and wondering who exactly decided to build such a beautifully detailed world and not let you, the player, the consumer, explore it to its full potential. Get it on sale. The most I would spend on this title is $10.00.

_childDocuments_.review: I initially dismissed the Mafia series as yet another open-world 'GTA clone', but it appears I've been missing out.Whilst there is an "open world" in Mafia: Definitive Edition, it is only there in service of the story. It is there when you travel to the mission objective, but it isn't full of icons for things you need to cross off the list. You undertake a series of missions, mostly involving driving around, shooting things, very much like a GTA game, but aside from collecting a few cards and magazine covers, you just do the missions and enjoy the story. Think LA Noir, but on the other side of the law.From the opening cut scene, you are led from one mission to the next, often skipping the usual trudge back to the next mission marker on the map. Once you complete a mission, the next scene begins. Whilst it is possible to go out and roam the streets, this is a separate mode called Free Ride. You  just do the missions and walk away. I really,  appreciate that in my advancing years (lol). The story is beautifully told. Set during the depression/prohibition era in the US just as the spectre of WW2 was appearing on the horizon. The world you inhabit during missions is full of atmosphere and period radio stations, classic architecture and classic cars. It takes around 11 hours to complete the story, but it was one of the few games I've played recently that really gripped me. Like a good book I just couldn't put it down.With this being the "definitive edition', I've not played the original, but the definitive edition looks better than some newer games. With its "optimal" graphics setting it pushes my RTX 3070Ti quite hard at 4K, but it sure is pretty.I wholeheartedly recommend this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Mafia: Definitive Edition

_childDocuments_.review: Mafia: Definitive Edition is equal parts brilliant and also incredibly frustrating.The amount of sheer detail that went into recreating this PC classic is admirable. You can tell the developers really care for the source material to have rendered Lost Heaven as beautifully as they did.HOWEVER, and this is a BIG HOWEVER: This game shows its AGE.But before I get to that, let's talk about the story:I love how authentic it feels (at times). As an Italian American, who grew up with Scorsese and the Sopranos every Sunday, I appreciate the realistic dialogue, and the attention paid to the culture. However, there's some choices that are made here in order to make the game feel like a Hollywood Blockbuster---choices that definitely ruin the grounded nature of the narrative. One moment you're a cab driver breaking into the crew, and shortly after you're shooting down an escaping plane on the tarmac. Is it a game about the Mafia? Sure. But it's also a cover based shooter that makes its bones with set piece after set piece. And that's where the game falls incredibly short: When you actually have to play it.The shooting has obviously been reworked from the original, but that doesn't mean it's fun. In fact, it's not. Every mission turns into a gallery style exercise in frustration. You'll find yourself restarting from checkpoints over and over again, without understanding why the hell you got killed in the first place. And don't get me started on the forced stealth sequences. They're TERRIBLE. While the game looks modern, and the details are gorgeous, the game design is painfully stuck in the past. There's also a major issue with variety; there is none. You'll drive to a mission, shoot up the entire room indiscriminately, drive back to wherever, and then wait for the next bit of story. That's the entire game. Sure, there's a free ride mode (and some useless collectibles), but it's unfortunate that it couldn't have been worked into the main narrative. Overall, it's hard to recommend Mafia: Definitive Edition. There's genius in the story, but there's also this heavy catering to incessant video game tropes that often clash with the narrative. (You kill cops and politicians like no tomorrow, but the Don has a major issue with you robbing a bank?)I can't say the game is "fun" either. Maybe we're spoiled by modernity, but the loop of shooting a room full of guys and then driving doesn't really do it for me in 2022. All in all, the only reason to play Mafia: Definitive Edition is to experience gaming history, albeit with a much prettier coat of paint.

_childDocuments_.review: This is often described as the best of the three Mafia games, which is setting a surprisingly low bar. Technically, it's riddled with bugs. Audio that decides to just not play, pop-ins and pop-outs, inconsistent ally/enemy AI, occasional game-breaking loading screen locks. Pushing past this is pretty much not worth it.In terms of aesthetics, it's OK. The remaster has helped it a lot, but the distance textures look almost like they haven't fully loaded in, and the higher quality comes at a cost of being poorly optimised. The cars are probably the biggest standout, and they do look and sound good. However, the radio is dull as dishwater, the buildings lack personality, and the character models are competing with themselves to emote purely using eyebrows and flat, stoic expressions.Gameplay... Is just all-round mediocre. Despite being explicitly a wheelman, the car driving is just so-so. It's not as horrendous as some people say, but it's certainly not the focus, which feels odd considering it's a quasi-open-world. The gunplay is intensely flat, with a mediocre selection of poorly-handling guns that pack a varied and unsatisfying punch. You will inevitably not get to use the more interesting weapons anyway, and end up hoovering up ammo from the fallen. Worse, the mediocre story - told in a series of vignettes with brief interludes - has flat characters, a poor sense of threat, boring worldbuilding, and feels entirely irrelevant. We never see the major events in the hero's life that'd give him more personal stakes. We never see any of the side stories come to fruition. Instead, we have individual levels which show off one aspect of the game and don't impress. Two full stealth missions, one full race mission, and a whole lot of padding which involves you shooting either a 1911 or a Tommy Gun at guys hiding behind crates. Even with bugs, 12 hours to be done with it on the medium difficulty. The gameplay doesn't motivate me to revisit.LA Noire tells a better gritty crime story, and you're a cop in that one. This feels like someone tore out all the pleasurable context that makes the story missions of a GTA game pop, and instead went through a checklist of requirements to be a 'third person open-world game' and then gave up.Not recommended.Edit: Also, the "fox" noise when you find a collectable? It's a hyena's laugh. Really? Finnegan disapproves.

_childDocuments_.review: It's everything I've ever wanted. I love it.I fell in love with the original Mafia for being realistic and immersive. It was everything Grand Theft Auto wasn't. It was subtle, believable, and HARD. Driving was hard, but rewarding. Shooting was hard, but rewarding. I loved that.This is EVERYTHING the original Mafia was, but better. I'm still playing through (on Classic difficulty, with Simulation driving) and it's been a blast. It's just *slightly* different to be refreshing yet not so much that it changes any major plot points or missions. It's a worthy replacement of the original.Oh, and Fair Play. That racing mission. It was JUST as head-bashingly hard as it was originally (on Classic difficulty anyway) and I loved that. This game doesn't hold your hand. It throws you into a 1932 Grand Prix and says "Win it." I wasn't even sure if I could beat it at all in the first 6 attempts, until I learned to master my racing line and braking.As a side note; I got the game pre-ordered, so I got the V12 FWD car. It's amazingly fun as well, being reasonably quick and nimble with a low center of mass; and being the only FWD in the game so far (the cars change as the years pass) it actually feels pretty unique to drive. Defo worth it. Probably my favorite car in the game (so far).

Overall, this game is beautiful and is pleasure to play. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Paid for this from my own money, around 40 euros at the time of purchase for a 'masterpiece' (as others claim it is) published last year in September. With 2 hours spent in its 'free ride' mode. It is the worst game created. Sure, sure; story is interesting but also feels far too quick with all these years passing by from 1930 to 1951. You barely feel like you get to know the characters if you're indeed new to the franchise. Animations are wonky, driving is utter garbage and most important of all the fighting is horrid. This game is so cheap that its developers couldn't even add interactive buildings and people. Overall it was fun and all but not worth the price. _childDocuments_.review: A solid 7/10 game. The story is excellent and you feel like your watching an interactive movie about Tommy Angelo a cabby turned gangster. The atmosphere of the city and the environments are also very nicely crafted + the occasional radio broadcast gives nice tone to the era. However some of the gameplay parts are in my opinion not very well done and not so smooth that i would play the game just to repeat those. _childDocuments_.review: When I reviewed Mafia on 13 August I wasn't expecting to play the DE as soon as I did. Truth be told, it wasn't even in my library at the time, but a fortuitously timed sale led to me playing largely the same story in a story-driven game twice in the space of two months.The story is THAT GOOD. I will join with others who suggest that the (minor) narrative changes made for the DE make the story very slightly less interesting, the characters less refined, and overall feeling like a very good mafia film rather than an all-timer. However, for those who like to play video games like a film with gameplay, this has to be very high on the list.The most important difference though is that the DE takes almost every one of my criticisms of the base game and fixes it. Admittedly, most of those criticisms were relics of their time, but taking functional systems for third-person shooting and driving (while still making it clear, handling-wise, that the game wants you to feel a degree of realism for the 1930s), as well as modern graphics, and slapping them on top of Mafia makes this into a great game. It's admittedly a little bit less immersive when you're not enabling a speed limit to cap your driving to 40mph to avoid getting a ticket (though this is an option in the settings!), but to my mind the quality of life difference is more than worth it. Likewise the modern approach to checkpointing, where almost any meaningful progress results in another checkpoint: again, to some degree a matter of taste, but I don't have time to slog through bits of a level I can beat 8 times to get to the one bit I can't yet. Indeed, this checkpointing approach really allows the cinematic finale, The Death of Art, to shine through as one of the single best set pieces I've encountered in games generally.To my mind the answer between the two, assuming all else remains the same, is fairly clear: play the DE ahead of the original. The original is a very good game, and benefits from a better story and slightly better immersion, but the gameplay in the DE is something you can enjoy, rather than something you put up with. At 10 hours for my full-story playthrough (without gathering all collectibles), at full price the DE feels a bit steep, but on any kind of sale it's well worth it.8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: is an amazing way to do a remaster. It's very faithful to the original game. It's easy to play, graphically and musically stunning. An amazing journey awaits with this game!✅ Amazing story✅ A variety of difficulties✅ Amazing Soundtrack✅ Fun gameplay⛔️ There are some technical glitches with cutscenes and audio⛔️ An occasional graphical artifact appearedThe gameplay involves a lot of different elements. Driving, Stealth and Combat are three of the major elements in there.The driving isn’t going to be the easiest for racers in this game. The majority of the vehicles in this game are 1930’s based. Many of the vehicles are big, bulky, and not meant for speed. However, there are bonus vehicles inside of the game as well. By having the entire trilogy, it’s possible to gain a 1960’s sports car as well. It’s fun to drive but does take a bit of the realism out of it. Still, driving throughout this Chicago based city, the vehicles work well.  They fit perfectly with the background.The stealth only appears in a few portions of the game. It is optional to use but it can make things a whole lot easier. At one portion, using it saves time from doing a huge shootout and makes getting to the objective 10x easier. While this might not be seen as a Mafia method, it was a fun alternative to the usual run and gun style.The combat is basically what is expected of the other games. There is a lot of cover based shooting. Objects and people will be destroyed as the story keeps going.  In one stage, it’s possible to destroy the power to a building and set a service station on fire. Seeing all of the wanton destruction was a nice touch.  The guns handle pretty decently. The reticule gives a basic idea if it will be a direct hit.  There is enough gunfire to keep busy. Depending on the mode, it will increase or decrease in difficulty. Playing in Classic mode also affects the difficulty of the situation.   The graphics are just as good as the other two Definitive Editions. It really was impressive to see the various effects during the daytime and nighttime. The inside of the buildings were beautiful and period appropriate. Seeing all of the neon lights at night was really spectacular. A lot of care and consideration has been taken to make the city its own entity. Also, the rain effects were not only beautiful, but they also added a unique touch to certain scenarios. Remember to not just go through the world, but to experience this world as well. Try and get a feel for the environment and times that are going on. It’s an experience worth treasuring.  The music in this game, both radio and official soundtrack has been amazing to listen to. It’s fun to go between both radio stations to hear the different types of music playing.  The music is period appropriate and helps to set the mood. However, the official soundtrack is just as amazing. One particular song, Sarah, evoked all sorts of emotions when it was played.  One scene in particular shows a unique plot point coming life with the help of this amazing song.  The sounds of the city and people are consistent. There are countless conversations, street noise and things going on in the background that helped to cement the 1930’s city.🔹 This review was completed on a Desktop PC. The specs for this unit are as followed. 🔹 CPU: Intel I9-9900K🔹 RAM: 64GB DDR4-3200 Kingston🔹 SSD: 1TB Samsung 970 EVO M.2🔹 Graphics Card EVGA GeForce RTX 2080 GAMING, 08G-P4-2080-KR, 8GB GDDR6, RGB LED:The game does have a few cosmetic glitches inside.  There were cutscenes that don’t show properly until the game was reset. Also, at one point the sound for the vehicles completely disappeared during gameplay.  Finally, some artifacts appeared here and there during the game. Otherwise, the game handled decently; there were no crashes that occurred like in most modern games.  The framerate has been fairly consistent and it has been a decent experience.  has been an experience worth waiting for. All of the elements mentioned such as the soundtrack, the gameplay and the graphics make it a thought provoking and moving experience. While there are technical glitches inside of the game, this doesn’t distract much from the overall experience. It is a worthy remake of this great game and an amazing addition to new and old fans alike.

_childDocuments_.review: I somewhat recommend the game. Not fully. While the graphics and combat are better than the original, the story is B- grade. In this game the main protagonist wants to be in the mob and seems to enjoy it, while in the original game he was forced by events to join the mob and was never that much into it. I like the Tommy from the first game, in this remake I am ambivalent towards the main character at best, just like with Vito in Mafia 2. These are not great characters. The reason why everybody is sad about what happens to Tommy in the first game is because he was a moral person with a lot on internal monologues. This Tommy has none of that. And nowhere is it more obvious than in the Hotel missions where in the original he has an internal monologue, while in the second one it's not existent since they changed the mission.Another complaint is Sarah. In the first one she was a quiet, more subtle presence, in this one she's been beaten with the feminist stick, where she's all "empowered". Makes her less enjoyable than the original.Maybe I am biased for the original, but the characters in the remake have less personality than in the original.Now, for the stinky parts, not related to the story.The game is very "Hollywood"-ized. It's very flashy and in your face. The dialogues contain a lot of "♥♥♥♥", "sheet" and all that. That's not offensive, it's just cheap. The original kept the swearing to a minimum, which is more in tone with the times. People didn't randomly swear all the time. It's not that they are swearing, it's that they are swearing so much it is unrealistic. Just like Mafia 2, check out the Youtube compilation to see how many times they say "♥♥♥♥" in Mafia 2. It's funny, but like a fart joke, not like a good joke.The campaign is alright, I see they changed some of the details and the missions are slightly different. The race is just as hard as it was on "Classic difficulty" and I struggled for 2 days to get it done. On Easy is so simple I did it in the first try on a second replay.The map is fine, the country side is huge, but the fact that you can no longer interact with the the subway is just bad game design. In the first one you could ride the subway. I don't remember if you could ride the trams tho. Neither in this one. A shame and a missed opportunity. The city detail is good, it looks like a real place. That is fine.The cars are okay and feel mostly fine. The slower ones seem better, but anything with any power is terrible because they constantly skid and drift. This was not an issue in the original. The cars were always slow and terrible to drive, but that was fine and it felt like a car had weight and wasn't just a GTA V mockery of a car, where every car feels made out of polystyrene.The music is alright, but they left out the most iconic song out of all Mafia: "Django Reinhardt - Belleville". That song is so iconic that even my wife knows that when she hears that song I'm playing Mafia, she even hums to the song. Why they skipped this one, I don't know, but just seems like a mistake. Some other songs are missing, like "The Mills Brothers - Chinatown, My Chinatown" and a few others, but that's a minor complaint.Now, the worst part, the achievements.The Classic difficulty trophy makes you work for it. It is HARD and I mean HARD to do. This achievement is not the worst tho and I don't really dislike it.However, the side missions are really bad.First of all, the challenges suffer from that classic issue, lack of imagination and originality replaced by TIMED CHALLENGES. This is the cheapest way to make something challenging and it is lazy. Everything is timed. And you gotta do stuff precisely or you don't get to do the achievements.Example 1:Smith car mission - timer is a cheap way to make a mission, but the car bugs out. You gotta refuel frequently but when it is time to start the car again, 50% of the time the car does not move. Nice design, developers, a real stinker mission, I tried for 2 days to get it done.Example 2:Bike mission - bike handles like garbage. It is the worst vehicle in the series. Uncontrollable pile of sheet that you cannot control and have to do a jump with. I was so frustrated with this one. And of course, timed, because why not?Example 3:Alien mission - the car respawned as a taxi. Yep, I was driving something else, then failed, because the whole missing is so bad you can only beat it by memorizing where the ufo spawns and gradually progress every time. But I started the mission with another car, failed and on one of the attempts I got respawned with a taxi instead of the car I started. Bugs like these are so annoying because they make you waste time going back to get your car and travel to the mission again.Other bugs I encountered were visual, like on the main street, next to the Bertone's garage there is a hole missing but the steam is coming out of the ground in the middle of the street. I mean, come on guys, it's minor but it is so obvious, where is the QA team to check this stuff? You can find it by driving on the main street next to the water and going south from the big bridge, it's in the middle of the road, between the lanes. It's a small bug, but it is so obvious, I wonder if the QA team really earned their money. I say this as someone who has done QA in the past for games. This would not fly past the teams I worked with.Anyways, I rambled enough, do I recommend the game? I'd say yes, for casuals it is better and easier than the original. The original has the "hard" difficulty of the 2000's, while newer games have that "Call Of Duty" difficulty, which make it easier for the unskilled to play. However, the first one is better due to the story, but is lacking in graphics and combat system.I'd say, if you're not good at video games, this is great for you, and you're going to enjoy this one more than the original. If you're a sweaty nerd that likes a good story and are willing to get passed the shortcomings of the era, the original is a better pick. I guarantee that you will like the original story more than the new one.I give it 6/10 on the hardest difficulty, 8/10 on easy and this is probably what casuals should stick with.

You're Don Salieris goon and do jobs, rivaling with Don Morello in town Mafia 3 is much better in every aspect.The struggle and rise of the black Mafia, FBI agent Donovan who was in Vietnam war with Lincoln, white politicians that had to arrange with and accept a black Don and the countless real-life references such as the emerging of Las Vegas make for a far more interesting story that's also dynamic and evolving. (Las Vegas was a nowhere town before the Mafia started to construct casino hotels there as a legal mainstay because gambling is legal in Nevada. Frank Sinatra and other entertainers that came to Las Vegas in the following are known to have been part of the Mafia. The Murder Inc. is also a famous organisation from then.)All-in-all I did not regret playing it however, short and forgettible, but by no means bad.

The original dialogue and narrative at the end of "Just for Relaxation." All the other mission titles that you blunder-screwed up to the high heavens, The driving mechanics (no mafia DE does not have the same driving physics, they are GOOD but not the same, way to sensitive) Having captured cars placed in the Salieri Garage, The driving segments at the beginning and end and middle of almost every mission (we actually LIKE the driving, hence the desire for the return of the same driving physics).  AND also cutting out my hopes and dreams of a free roam mode with currency and shops and stores and all that good stuff. That's too much to ask to keep in the game right?But the graphics, and the gunplay are so much fun. I can't lie, this gunplay (despite the Tommy Gun changing just a little)  is soooo cool. playing on the hardest difficulty and mode is a navigable challenge that will have you conserving every round, and dying to find the next health box, just like the old game. Shooting from cars is somewhat less stressful than the og. The reflections int he water on the street and everywhere else are fantastic. I can't believe it, the Euros actually made it. A game that balances my distaste for ruining things while trying to fix them when they aren't broken and my love for Theme-appropriate graphics, amazing graphics at that, and creating a great game that I'm sure will satisfy series new-comers.Remember 2002 fans, It's not fans of the original that get the spotlight anymore. _childDocuments_.review: Mafia definitive edition is like a glass of your favorite beverage, it’s good when your tongue first touches the liquid and it’s still good when your try to get the last drop. But, since it’s only one glass, the pleasure doesn’t last very long, but a glass full of enjoyment is better than a full bottle that only contain a quarter of enjoyment.  I never played the original Mafia, but the sequel Mafia II is one of my favourite games of all time, so I was pretty excited to play the first installment of this beautiful franchise and I wasn’t disappointed. The story and its characters are bot excellent and well developed, bringing you a tale of friendship and the beautiful but tragic descent into hell of Tommy Angelo. The musical score and the voice acting are on point to bring to life this wonderful recreation of a Chicago-like city during the troublesome years of the great depression and the prohibition. The visual are great, the original game, from what I’ve seen, is not the most pleasing to the eye, but this definitive edition looks fantastic, from the model of characters to the one of the cars and from the lighting to the textures. It’s a beautiful game that should hold is ground for the coming years. The gameplay is also excellent, the shooting feels good and the driving is grounded and a lot of fun. Mafia definitive edition renew my love for this franchise and got me playing Mafia II again. I hope that this remaster will help Hangar 13 create a better future for the Mafia franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: Mafia Def EditionsBrought on steam sale, and an absolute bargain.Getting to play all three games has provided an interesting insight to how game development has changed over the years.First off we have the fully remade classic Mafia def 2020.  This is without doubt a masterpiece triple AAA gold standard and actually shows how a focused story plot with simple but effective game mechanics work so well especially when we start to compare it with the more open world of Mafia 3.  Mafia Def edition is more than a video game, it is a library standard holodeck example of urban 1930’s and would provide future generations an insight into how folk lived in that time period.  Unlike literature it propels the observer into a world of nostalgia and provides an insight into life in the 30’s.  Mafia Def has a fantastic story to tell and it tells it well.  Plenty of top quality cut scenes and the cars don’t get me started on those old cars fully detailed and yep slow to drive but what a ride.  Voice acting and cinematic is top notch.  Game play cover and shoot is passable and to be honest satisfying in its simplistic way.  It does everything well that it needs to do.  Rain soaked city streets and depressed people give this game a cyberpunk feel, neon’s lights and retro cars would have been a good place for cyberpunk 2077 to start off from.  I could imagine these streets forming the ground urban city rising upwards into mega complexes with flying cars and steam punk trains and airships...  getting a bit off track but you get the idea.  Mafia 2 remastered, well almost.The second game 2010 moved the series into a semi open world across multiple timelines.  It’s good to play with a reasonable story to tell.  After playing the first game the quality of the remaster is not up to the standard of the first then it is not a fully rebuilt game like its predecessor.  That aside it plays well and has the same nostalgia with good cover and shoot game play.  Mafia 3This is a fully open world with all its repetitive side quests.Good game yet it provides an insight into why open world games have fallen flat.  Story is sacrificed in favour of repetitive game play associated with open world environments, plenty to do yet almost intimidating in how to play through it all.  The quests are numerous yet the same.  Get used to the same smuck face being lured from the pack so you can stick a knife in his throat as he says “The devils made his presence known, I’d better go a check that out.”  Then he saunters over to his death without a care in the world.  Yes the stealth is great and works.  The gunplay is good, very good at times.  Cover system and animations are great.  It plays well but lacks that story focused narrative that makes the first one stand out as a cinematic masterpiece of storytelling.  SummationIt’s not size that matters, a smaller map but a great story and city environments propel Mafia Def as the best of the three, personal opinion.  Cohesive story telling the player where to go and what to do draws the player into its world like most open worlds don’t nowadays.  This is the crux immersion.  If Chief O’Brian was on the Enterprise and punched in 1930’s America into the holodeck then he would not find a better world to escape into.Great games with nostalgic vibe, fully worth a bye for all three, but if in doubt at least do yourself a favour and get Mafia Def Edition.  Just awesome, going to play it again.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent remake of a game that so desperately needed one. Hangar 13 made a lot of smart decisions in the game to appeal to both fans of the original and players new to the series. There have been a lot of changes from the original, and I think they made for a better experience overall. Remember that removing elements can be as impactful as adding them. The original voice acting was rather flat, and the new cast does an excellent job. Moving the optional car collection missions to outside the main story was a smart choice, as those tended to severely interrupt the pacing of the story. Turning every mission into an escort mission was a very bad idea in hindsight, so the need to manage the health of your companions is removed. Some of the missions were thankfully shortened, such as in the second mission reducing the number of objectives from 5 to 3, and the longest mission near the end is about half the length now, so it doesn't feel like a chore by the end. Most importantly, I think, the extremely long commute between objectives in the second-last mission, without a doubt the biggest pace-killer in the story that turned what should have been an exciting climax into the most boring mission in the game, is now completely removed. The ungodly amount of time spent driving in the original has been massively cut down, and you can still skip unnecessary drives if you want. The combat has been upgraded from "basically unplayable" to "functional." There's little to say on it, except that it works and doesn't feel like an obstacle between you and the story. The game is now no longer so crushingly difficult that it feels nearly impossible to get through. Not that there's anything wrong with a good fair challenge, but Mafia didn't feel fair in the slightest, and the extremely stop-and-start feel of the missions being routinely interrupted by token combat sections, with sporadic checkpoints to boot, made the story feel like it was continuously being gated off from you to force you into combat. The story itself is alright, by the way, even if it is just a copy of Goodfellas.The open world has been improved too. You will no longer be interrupted by raised bridges blocking your path, and the public transport system absent from Mafia 3 has gracefully returned to the series. The fact that you can't enter the trams or trains has been a point of contention for fans of the original, and I've heard it said, to excess, that this ruins the game. But it is in no way a deal breaker, since these systems are still there, and do their job of making the world feel more alive. If you could use them, you would still prefer to go by car 99% of the time. This was probably the logic of Hangar 13, that it's more interesting from a gameplay standpoint to go by car instead of waiting around for a train or tram and then waiting again to reach your destination. Whatever. Like I said, it doesn't matter. Being able to use public transport can't save the life of a bad game (like Watch Dogs, for example) and not being able to makes no difference to a game's actual quality. It really doesn't matter. And Mafia: Definitive Edition is more of a linear game anyway, where the open world is simply a backdrop to the main missions. Don't go into this expecting Grand Theft Auto, because if you do you will be sorely disappointed at the lack of stuff in the open world. But I can definitely recommend Mafia: Definitive Edition to old fans and new. Even if you just wanted to ride trains all day. Andonce you get into modding it becomes even better.

_childDocuments_.review: Never played the original, so this is a review of the remastered edition clear from any nostalgia bias: 'Mafia: DE is a third person FPS set in "Lost Heaven". You play as Tommy Angelo, a cab driver who works his way up in the Salieri mafia family, in the process doing exactly what you would expect a mafioso to do. I'm about 3/4 of the way through the story and the game is compelling enough to finish. Here's the pros and cons: 1. Voice acting, graphics, and story are all pretty good and do serve to keep you invested. However, the story  is 100% on the rails so outside of some afterthought collectibles replayability is zero. I'm not sure what the point of having an open or semi-open world is without any side missions or branching paths.2. Gun play is pretty good, although the game is very stingy with ammo (something i absolutely hate in games) and there are only three handguns and three long guns; more variety would have been nice. 3. The driving is actually pretty well done even with mouse/keyboard. I didn't find the race mission or any of the driving portions excessively difficult and you can skip a lot of the tedious point to point driving if you want. Overall Mafia: DE is a good ~30 hour experience and worth playing if you like third person shooters and atmospheric single player mafia themed games. It does have its flaws though and is a remake of an old game after all, so I would only buy this one on sale in the $10-20 USD range. Definitely not worth the full $40 asking price.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pleasure writing about Mafia: Definitive Edition since this is one of the finest remakes I ever played on Steam and it's also addressing a gaming franchise I'm very fond of. Developer Hangar 13 handled the remake and I have to agree that they are almost absolved of all “sins” regarding the narrative dumpster fire also known as “Mafia III”. It just so happens that 2022 marks two decades for this series, so the timing seems perfect to me. I played the original Mafia that kickstarted all of this, right around its initial release. Young as I was, the game left a strong impression and like many others at the time, I just had to compare it to GTA III,  then fresh template for 3D crime tales set within open worlds. 2002's Mafia was vastly superior in some aspects (such as the vehicles & story), yet distinctively limited as far as the exploration itself was concerned.Nowadays I know better than to compare apples to oranges, of course. The Mafia series uses its maps as set pieces, not playgrounds. The arcade elements are reserved for activities outside the game's storyline altogether. And for the most part, Mafia games have a clear cut ending which leaves little room for debates or maneuver. Collectibles might require subsequent playthroughs.Mafia: Definitive Edition does an excellent job at retelling the gripping story of its initial version from two decades ago. It avoids retconning (imposing different interpretation on previously described events) while actually developing the side characters and offering them believable personalities. I know there was some short-lived backlash over not remastering the initial character models or their original voices, yet I was pleased to notice that those visual and audio changes are integral to the remake and they did not prevent me from thoroughly enjoying my time spent in the new Lost Heaven. This fictional mash-up between New York and Chicago is the perfect setting for our tale.The protagonist is a taxi driver turned mobster and it would make a classic rags to riches trope if not for the many plot twists which I shall obviously not spoil. Like any good movie of this particular organized crime subgenre (think Martin Scorsese or Francis Ford Coppola), accountability eventually catches up with the characters. It's not a lifestyle worthy of praise even if it keeps us glued to the screens of our TVs or monitors. If you want “happy endings”, look elsewhere, as the Mafia series succeeds in mimicking the grim reality and the usually inevitable conclusions of its real life counterparts that inspired those fictional characters.Facing the consequences of your actions is only a matter of time. Mafia: Definitive Edition remakes all the missions I experienced several times in the 2002 version. Even the more annoying ones, such as the notoriously wonky racing section. Still tough as nails and requiring several mission restarts until you “get it right”. But it's part of the charm. Otherwise, driving from point A to B still remains the main role of the map, even if it was extended to incorporate the city outskirts which can now be explored at any given time. Rural areas as well, those will be cleverly used for chase sequences.Ironically, Mafia III  does share one positive trait with the remake I'm reviewing: the Illusion Engine is powering both, though it received some well-deserved updates over the years. Proprietary engine and an obvious nod to Illusion Softworks, the creators of the 2002 Mafia. Game looks gorgeous and ran without any issues, not even frame rate drops, nevermind any game breaking bugs or crashes to desktop. At least in my book, those vintage vehicles are the main stars of the show, but the character models are equally convincing. I did not mind it for a second that all of them look entirely different from the the initial Mafia version. A remake should be allowed more creative freedom. It's the clear distinction between that and a remaster. Also, I cannot pass the chance to praise the integrated, minimal HUD which can be further disabled to allow proper screenshots. To say that I used the option frequently, would be an understatement. And you can play the entire game in Black & White too. It's as close as you can get to a Photo Mode, though the inclusion of additional filters would have been most welcome.For Mafia veteran players it may feel kinda weird to not hear Django Reinhardt's Minor Swing every 10 minutes or so while in-game, but the new soundtrack is adequate and it complements the excellent voice acting. The accents are top notch, never cartoonish though some jokes are still present. I am glad that Sarah was given a more prominent role in the remake. A sassy performance, just as I expected. Overall, the entire cast is more fleshed out with the help of the overhauled dialogue, random banter or on-point.You can't have organized crime without having to "whack" certain individuals, right? At least in Mafia: Definitive Edition you now have cover-based shooting mechanics which weren't a thing back in 2002. Just another aspect I am glad they dispensed with in the remake. Simply crouching or peaking around corners and hoping to not get one-shot by a shotgun blast, didn't make the original version any more endearing to me. The Tommy Gun still has one helluva recoil though. "Spray and pray" will only get you so far, concentrate the fire in short bursts.You have to keep in mind the timeframe for this game. Of course the cars will handle like "refrigerators on wheels" when compared to present-day cars. And guess what, you can make the driving even more challenging by switching between arcade and simulation modes while also playing on the Classic difficulty setting. Learn to anticipate braking, consider it bus driving even when you'll control a sedan. Easier said than done during a high speed chase. The inclusion of various collectibles does encourage exploration of various parts of the map you'll otherwise rarely visit during the story. At least you're taking in the sights, there's plenty to see and admire though far less to do in terms of side activities and hustles. It may even feel like an empty city if you will just compare it to Ubisoft or Rockstar open worlds. From one end of the spectrum to the other, I reckon. Having too much stuff to do and clutter that mini-map can be equally daunting.Without a doubt, this is one of the finer video game stories out there. Once you overlook Mafia: Definitive Edition's open world shortcomings and simply focus on the missions, you will realize the cinematic feel of those scripted events. It should speak by itself, the fact that I reached 100% of the game's Steam Achievements, something I rarely strive to since I usually lack the spare time.The direct (remastered) sequel holds up well and is also worth diving into. Then you can skip Mafia III and (im)patiently await for the prequel we'll be able to enjoy in a year or two. While I have my key from a bundle, I am certain that Mafia: Definitive Edition deserves to be bought even outside Steam Sales. Talking about offers you can't refuse. + Steam Achievements.+ Gorgeous graphics and sounds.+ Superb storyline and cast of characters.+ Replay value through side missions & collectibles.- No Steam Trading Cards.

_childDocuments_.review: This was my original review after a few hours of playing:(Love the og. The remake is pretty good, but: remove the fps cap, and please give us the option to turn off certain HUD elements. I respect what you did in terms of accessibility, but it would be nice to have the option in the menu to remove objective markers and the mini map (fom missions like "Happy Birthday"). Otherwise, great game)After finishing it, I will not change the thumbs up. I believe everyone should experience this story. It is less flushed out, the characters are a little weaker than in the original, but the performances are amazing. When it comes to the game's performance however, I am severely disappointed. Just like in Mafia III, the lighting is incomprehensible when you change locations. It got me killed so many times, when I'm in cover at the door aiming at the exterior and I can't see anything. Just really bright white light, as if someone has put two through my head. AI is erratic and unpredictable (not in a good way). Animation glitches and pathfinding always ruin the experience. Playing on classic difficulty does not reflect the original's trial and error structure, but it's still annoying when you die from a bullet of an enemy that's either zipping around cove like it's gears of war, or dying from not being able to see through doors and windows.I also disliked how the game ran on my 3900x/2080ti machine -- 60fps lock unless you go borderless (just as bad as mafia III). The game looks stunning when it stands still, but start moving or running away from cops and you'll be watching an artifact cancan. White halos over every object and character, along with horrible object pop-in that's prevalent in Mafia II Definitive Edition. But when it comes to texture streaming and decals -- it looks immaculate. Not even in Red Dead 2 can you see such high definition decals for posters and ads, it's very impressive. Along with the graphics, the sound design is hit or miss. It definitely hits the bullsye in the atmosphere department: I remember visiting a bar under the metro track, and when the train passed all the glasses and pictures on the wall started clacking and moving. It felt real. Where it misses, is in places like dialogue: in the beginning of the game I could not hear a thing Sam and Paulie were saying. It sucks when you have to read the subtitles while evading the police. Overall, I liked the game. I loved re-living this life again, with all it's ups and downs. I want to go back into that world, but something stops me. For every amazing memory, I have three negative ones. I hope that Hangar 13 implements some changes into the engine and their AI, because these fixes would make the game and actual Definitive edition of the Mafia. Foe now, I recommend that everyone who loves old mob or Scorseze movies checks this story out. This series deserves recognition and respect.

_childDocuments_.review: I regret not having played the original version. I tried a few years ago, before they announced the remake, because I had played Mafia 2 at the time and it quickly became one of my favorite titles, mainly because of the storyline. So, I tried playing the first part to learn more about its world and characters, but I couldn't; it had aged too bad. To my surprise, a few years later, they announced the remake, and I was very excited. Finally, I could close the complete arc that I had liked so much. Now, regarding the game itself: Graphically, it is beautiful; the vehicles, environments, and characters are sublime. Every detail is carefully crafted. Unfortunately, it's just a pretty picture to admire because gameplay-wise, the title is very weak. They could have taken advantage of the remake to add more variety, something else to do in the open world, perhaps a shop to customize our character, some mini-games, anything that would make exploring the city enjoyable instead of a chore. Once you finish the story, there's nothing else to do. The game could easily be a linear video game since the open world is empty and lacks activities. I think that's the worst part because, in other aspects, like the plot, the game is brilliant. There are also some issues with the animations, a bit clunky, but I've just finished playing Red Dead Redemption 2, and there's no comparison; maybe I just need to get used to it. To give it a rating, I would give it a well-deserved 7 out of 10, mainly for how gripping the story is, which, for me, is the fundamental pillar in any video game.

Most of the time the player character doesn't snap to cover when pressing the button, you have to try several times when in combat. The AI shoots through walls and cover objects. Repetitive missions where cover based shooting is required...-Can't stand the dead eyes on every character. -Lot's of visual glitches and gameplay bugs happening on every mission. -Really bad checkpoints where you have to listen to dialouge over and over if you die and have to reload.-Why do I have to press ENTER again after i've chosen to reload a checkpoint? (And oooonly the ENTER button...)-Character movement feels floaty AF. Runs into objects and other stuff when when navigating in tight areas such as small rooms and corridors.-Control scheme is just a mess. Cumbersome and doesn't make sense (M&KB).-After a certain amount of tries on a mission I set the difficulty to EASY, just to be able to skip that part faster (so I thought)... _childDocuments_.review: After completing the story for this game in 14 hours I can give Mafia definitive edition the thumbs up. I hadn't previously played the original Mafia coming into the definitive edition, so the story, characters and world was completely new to me. Some people have complained about the cover system and the combat in general. I find it lacking in some places, especially when it comes to molotov's and grenades they just don't feel powerful enough to me and are only really useful against a group of enemies or cars. Overall I find the combat to be adequate, nothing really to point out, the only criticism I have is that sometimes ammunition can feel limited or in some missions you realise that you brought the wrong gun for the mission, due to the proximity of enemies in some areas. As for the story, I really enjoyed it, the rise and fall of Tommy Angelo's life of crime is believable and you sympathise with Tom, Paulie, Sam, Don Salieri and the rest of the gang. I advise not turning on the Skip Unnecessary Drive option as taking a good, regular drive through Lost Heaven really immerses you into the setting and time period of the game. TL;DRMafia definitive edition is a good game and if you haven't played through Mafia's story yet, you REALLY should.

_childDocuments_.review: Should you play it? Yes.Should you play it on Classic? That's a different question.Considering I played and finished [only] Classic difficulty I believe it suffers from a lot of problems that needs to be reviewed.Checkpoint system is rather bad, the way it switches objects (enemies, players etc) around without any regard to where they originally were.Driving on gamepad is a must, while most of the times you need keyboard+mouse for shooting parts. You'll have to accept gamepad hotkeys on UI that won't switch on the fly (like most modern games do).Ammunition is so low that it requires you to only go for headshots unless you wish to run around trying to collect some ammo.AI is ok, I guess, but they have rather fast reaction time, so it gets frustrating eventually. Besides that they barely do anything even if sometimes they try to maneuver around.Weapon sound design is boring and bland, sadly.Visually it's fine, on the level with Mafia 2, city could've been prettier.Shooting enemies is not fun as there are only so many times when you can finally spray and pray for awhile. It feels like this system probably has been inherited from Mafia 3.As promised you don't have much health and you don't regenerate much health, so in prolonged fighting you can sometimes reload after death to be almost immediately killed.I can't recall much of the original Mafia story, but overall this interpretation is fine. Voice acting is good but plot itself is lacking additional depth. By the end of the game plot gets a little annoying at times. To be honest Mafia 2 overall felt better by the end of the game.Sandbox - non existent and it's best to just skip all the useless driving around or better yet, listen to dialogues and then skip it.It's a linear mission based game (which is fine) so open world only exists for you to hide and run away from cops but also to driver around between missions.Stealth missions in general are rather primitive and are nothing more than a time sink.Overall I kind of liked it and it had also frustrated the hell out of me by questionable gameplay decisions and implementations.

_childDocuments_.review: Mafia DE is unfortunately one of those games that you want to like - really, really want to like - and then it does everything in its power to try and stop you.First, the good. It's gorgeous - absolutely gorgeous. Every game in the Mafia series has so far been one of the best looking games of its time, and DE is no different. From the mist of rain hitting the overhead rails to the distortion of the lighting through windows and headlights, the almost excruciating amount of detail in character's skin - and even the movement visible in the neck when characters are talking. The cars and city themselves are all looking spectacular from every which angle you care to look.The story and atmosphere are very nearly as good as the aesthetic. It's not quite the same story as before, but it's close enough that it plays out the same. Sadly I don't feel like it's as well scripted as the original, causing some parts to just not fit together or character attitudes being out of place, though the voice acting is better without question. In any case the game just feels alive, rather than being a forced situation as is so often the case.The driving won't be to everyone's taste. Anyone used to driving aides or even modern conveniences is going to have a bad time - the game reasonably accurately simulates what it would feel like to drive a period-accurate, low revving, high-torque, two tonne behemoth around with bicycle wheels for traction. Even the ability to pull off a "one wheel peel" is maintained. It is also fair to say that the actual road rules are only followed when it's inconvenient and the concept of "give way" is foreign to everyone.All of the above culminates in a spectacular start to the game, and as soon as that music hits (the same intro track to the original game) you're ready for a good time. The first three missions, being that they're mostly driving and some running, play extremely well to those strengths. You're set up for what looks on the surface to be a pretty amazing ride and you can't wait to see where it's going or how it's going to get there.But then you watch the cop car that just rammed you disappear. You drive into a small bush in the countryside that's tougher than any bollard known to man. You watch an enemy suddenly decide he wants to be on the opposite side of what should be a solid wall and pass through it. You fire a gun with the reticle completely over the target and somehow still miss. And you immediately realise that the same level of care and polish that went into the previously mentioned points just wasn't applied equally.Gun play is where the game really falls down, which represents a huge issue as this is a fairly significant portion of the game. Accuracy and strategy are basically foreign concepts. It is possible to land a headshot, killing your target in one hit, but it isn't reliable by any stretch of the imagination. You can also make the enemies flinch if you hit them properly but most times their intelligence will just "reset" and they'll immediately shoot you again (re-fire rate be damned). And you can forget about the car combat from the original where you can shoot out tyres (doesn't work), puncture or explode gas tanks (also doesn't work), or even take out the driver (possible, but only by accident) - just pummel the enemy until you see smoke.Even the "Extras" aren't particularly enjoyable. There's a timed side mission which is outright impossible to clear until about the fifth time due to a moving target and an overly restrictive time limit. Most of the collectables are only marked on the mini-map when in extremely close proximity, which makes walking the best way to search in a game centred around driving for transport. And there are achievement-related collectables which are only even suggested to exist if you approach from the right angle. Guides will make all of this easier (or even possible), but they don't make it fun.Of course, you can somewhat make your peace with all of this. You remember that it's a videogame and it's going to have limits, and maybe some of the above is just a design choice that you don't agree with (like the very-slightly-non-standard controls). But just as you're coming to terms with it all, the game will close on you. It doesn't even necessarily crash - it's just suddenly gone, right in the middle of what you were doing, and now you have to start over from a poorly placed checkpoint with a weapon and car load-out that was inexplicably saved at a different time to your location.Having completed 100% of what's on offer, I'm not sure where to go from here in terms of replay. If you could combine the best of this re-imagining with the best of the original you'd have an absolutely brilliant game, but as it is you have to really pick your poison when it comes to what you want to sacrifice to play through the story. And, for my money at least, I just feel like the original offers a better overall experience - especially if you have the original music to go with it.
