_childDocuments_.review: A Seductive Descent into the Forbidden - "Lust from Beyond" ReviewOverall Rating: 9/10"Lust from Beyond" is an ambitious and controversial game that explores the darker side of human desire, blending elements of psychological horror, surrealism, and eroticism. Developed by Movie Games Lunarium, this title ventures into uncharted territory with its provocative themes and unsettling visuals, creating a divisive gaming experience that pushes boundaries.Storyline (8/10):The game revolves around Victor Holloway, a protagonist who becomes entangled in a secret cult obsessed with carnal pleasures and otherworldly realms. As you navigate this disturbing narrative, you'll uncover a web of eroticism and horror, often challenging your comfort zone. The storyline, while intriguing and original, often struggles to find the right balance between storytelling and the explicit content it attempts to depict.Gameplay (7/10):"Lust from Beyond" combines first-person exploration with puzzle-solving and occasional combat sequences. The puzzles can be engaging, but they often feel secondary to the game's thematic focus, making them feel disjointed at times. Combat is clunky and unrefined, detracting from the overall experience. The game also occasionally suffers from performance issues and bugs that break immersion.Graphics and Atmosphere (8.5/10):Where "Lust from Beyond" truly shines is in its visual presentation and atmosphere. The game's environments are meticulously crafted, and the attention to detail in its erotic and grotesque elements is both disturbing and captivating. The unsettling, otherworldly landscapes and haunting soundtrack contribute to an immersive and unsettling experience that keeps you engaged.Erotic and Horror Elements (9/10):The game's explicit sexual content and disturbing imagery are central to its identity, making it an experience not suitable for all players. It explores themes of desire, pleasure, and pain in a provocative and often shocking manner. While these elements contribute to the game's unique appeal, they can also be off-putting or alienating to some players, resulting in a mixed reception.Conclusion (9/10):"Lust from Beyond" is a daring experiment in combining eroticism and horror, offering a unique experience for those who seek unconventional narratives and themes in gaming. It excels in its visual design and atmosphere but falls short in terms of gameplay, storytelling execution, and technical performance. The explicit content and challenging themes may polarize players, making it a game for a niche audience who can appreciate its audacious approach to storytelling. _childDocuments_.review: Victor Holloway is a generic video game protagonist with a boring job at an antique store and an indie musician girlfriend who finds himself plagued by dreams FROM BEYOND. An unlikely trip to the City of Dreams finds our hapless protagonist tossed like a salad into the trippy psychosexual world of Lusst'gha in search of carnal pleasures and a desperately-needed personality transplant. Will he finally become cool? YOU DECIDE!The arc of the story was enough to keep me going through its roughly 7-8 hours of gameplay. It doesn't find itself getting bogged down too often to tedious exposition and its world actually hangs together pretty well as far as Lovecraftian worlds go. Could you find beauty in H.R. Giger's fever dream? Much like the Amazon, it's as beautiful as it is dangerous. The Unity engine shows its limitations here and there, but the environments, from the town of Bleakmoor to the twisting tunnels of Lusst'gha are very well realized.Progressing through the game unlocks the orgy environments and character models. Good for what there is, just wish there was a bit more of it.While the plot-related writing gets the job done, it's not exactly full of surprises for those savvy with this genre. It doesn't help that Victor is not exactly the sharpest tack in the drawer, which comes through in his dialogue especially. In fact, most of the characters are pretty flat. Wouldn't have minded a couple more hours of gameplay to really flesh them out; backstory is unceremoniously shoved into infodump letters throughout the game.It's easy to get lost in Lusst'gha. One mucus-covered vaginal passageway looks a lot like the others. Knowing what to do and where to go can become very frustrating very fast. It helps to have the walkthrough guide handy if you get stuck.Quick time events are the bane of any gamer. Lazy, obnoxious, just takes players out of the immersion. This game is full of them. Thankfully, there's few penalties for failing and generous time.Autosaves only. Would have been nice to have been able to save at certain points, particularly for Achievement and collectable hunting.You're a lover, not a fighter. And it shows.If you're into this kind of thing, go for it. It's one of the best I've seen for what it is. The weaknesses are really all in the gameplay; the scripted parts feel like heaven compared to janky combat and quick-time events. Once you've beaten it, enjoy the Chamber of Pleasures.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get this out of the way right off the bat: this game is NFSL. I have never played such a depraved game in my entire life. I saw things that I will never unsee. And I loved it. The lore and worldbuilding is right on the money in its inspiration from HP Lovecraft and the design of the other dimension looks like textbook HR Giger. Throw in lore about the chaos god Slaanesh from Warhammer 40,000 and you've got Lust from Beyond on your hands--hands which are now sticky and smell like a combination of ozone, sulfur, and wet mushrooms.  But really, this was a very good game that I thoroughly enjoyed. I found the overall setting and story engrossing and its got plenty of collectibles that provide more background into the circumstances your character finds themselves in. There is an option to blur sexual content but this is inadvisable, since it will do little to protect you and you should have a completely unfiltered view of all the bloody, filthy, debaucherous sights the game has to show you. I found the puzzle elements of the game to be at a good level of challenge, where some of the trickier ones might take a little time but you can figure them out without totally derailing your play session. Even for the ones where I eventually had to look up a part of the solution it would just wind up being something I felt foolish for overlooking. Stealth is necessary for a fair part of the game and generally I hate stealth in games, but it didn't ever feel unfairly difficult or that the AI was broken in its ability to spot you. Once you have a weapon it tends to become more a matter of making progress easier rather than 'get caught and you're dead' anyway.  And speaking of weapons, I would describe the combat as adequate. Like many story-driven/exploration horror games, combat mechanics tend to get less polish. For general fights there really isn't much of an issue aside from your character reloading the revolver in a calm, gingerly fashion when there are sadomasochistic murderers actively trying to stab/club you to death. The 'boss fights' (I use that term lightly) are pretty mediocre but not particularly difficult, so while its arguable whether they should even be in this game or games like it, they don't wind up being too much of a stumbling block once you figure out what you need to do. All in all, Lust from Beyond was kickass and I recommend it to anyone who loves cosmic horror and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up horror content in general, so long as they can handle sexual situations that might compel them to take multiple showers afterwards.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a sequel to Lust for Darkness and while I feel it did a lot of things BETTER than it's predecessor, it also did a lot of things worse.It feels a lot more like a game than the last one, the character models feel more alive and the world feels way more alive than the last game. In terms of setting and ambiance, I would certainly say it is WAY better than the last game. The town of Bleakmoore is a really good starting level and it really has a wicked Silent Hill vibe to it, but once you're back in Lusst'gha, or the Mansion, the world just feels cramped and repetitive again. I felt like they did a damn good job making the visuals prettier and in some cases, more grotesque, so in that department the game is really good.Voice direction got a LOT better this time too, the characters feel a lot less awkward reading their lines and conversations feel more real this time around. But it still runs into some really hokey borderline porno lines at times (A dude literally says "WOW, Chosen One! You're so lucky! Our master only sucks off a few chosen!" I mean, come on...)The sexual aspect of it this time around feels like a step in the wrong direction though.These interactive sex scenes where you do ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Dead by Daylight skill checks to ♥♥♥♥ someone are justSo needless and stupid. It feels so ♥♥♥♥♥♥ awkward and out of place doing SKILL CHECKS to have sex with someone. A lot of the sex this time around just feels in your face and overdone too. The first game did a pretty good job of blending the sexual aspect of the game into the rest of the world to the point of it feeling artistic and in tempo with the tone they were trying to set, but this time the "Click the mouse button to ♥♥♥♥ the monster" ♥♥♥♥ just felt so off and forced. The blend of sexuality and grotesque is just completely lost in favor of going the more porny and "shock factor" route. After several rooms of the same 3 desiccated corpses copy pasted around the entire level it just starts to make you numb to it all and that's NOT what you want from a game like this.They added dialogue choices now, which was. . .a step in the right direction. . .except some of them just don't feel right. The story as a whole just kinda trips over itself several times and the characters all flip flop so many times you can't really find yourself sympathetic to any of them. The story tries several times to make you feel sorry for one character or another or to feel forgiveness for someone and yet between the mountains of terrible things they've done or the sheer lack of remorse in your characters' voice, having your character suddenly go "You're right. Go! Be free!" is just SO jarring.They tried to flesh out the "Lore" of the other world and the sex god and. . .there's something about trying to make this intricate backstory about all that ♥♥♥♥ that just highlights all the WRONG things about this game and I feel like that was a bad choice on their part.And then we get to the gameplay as a whole and - if you compare it to the last game, they took the critiques about said gameplay and rather than push the game towards like a walking simulator, they instead tried to make the game feel even MORE like a game and that made the game feel more "natural" but boss fights? I have magic now? It all just kinda kills the feeling of the game as an erotic survival horror. Like it feels like they tried to make the game MORE of a game as if that would make it better. Does it make this one more fun to PLAY than the last game? Sure, but it doesn't necessarily make the game BETTER. Also, the same click the left mouse button to pick this up, press E to pocket it is still there which now feels incredibly more clunky and jarring when you're in the heat of a "run away from the bad guy" scene and then get stuck fumbling to pick up an item. And lastly, the last leg of the game just feels like unnecessary padding. They even toss you a gun halfway through that one-shots all these guys you were supposed to be running from as if even they recognized the game was running on too long. The last game clocks in at about 3 hours all things considered and this one full on lingers into the 11 hours and the last leg of the game just kinda drags on. The shift in your character's personality coupled with all the other random plot twists all just feel unneeded and serve as a reminder that "longer" does not always mean "better".Last game, even though I thumbs downed the game, I still recommended it as an experience for those who wanted to witness the mix of grotesqueness and eroticism as an artistic experience but in this case I can't even do that. This game strayed way too far away from the mix of grotesque and sexual in favor of trying to make it more "video gamey" and while I feel like it made this game LOOK better, it actually made it worse for what it is.We went from a mediocre game with a strangely fascinating experience as an art project to an average video game with a tasteless over-saturation of blood and sex and, honestly? _childDocuments_.review: With a name like "Lust from Beyond", you would be forgiven for thinking this is going to be some hump filled eroge or VN. After viewing the screen shots, you might be forgiven for thinking its a quick game with a little scary or gross imagery with plenty of scenes of boot knockin'. But its not. At least, not primarily. The first chapter has a bit of smutty fluff but you rather quickly get the idea that things are not all straight up debauchery. One of the characters in the group whom you meet first is a man with two heads (Three? Technically?) and it sets a dark and disturbing tone from the first few minutes. You start your journey in Lusst'ghaa (pronounced LOO-st-GAH) saving? harvesting? stealing? a critter from a rather provocative orifice. All of Lusst'ghaa is a wet organic world of grown structures that very much reminds one of Geiger and Lovecraft. Shapes in the walls and ceiling when seen from the corner of the eye evoke thoughts of the shape of bodies but when you turn to look closer you doubt what you saw. I'm certain this was intentional, as it continues each time you return to Lusst'ghaa. Nearly all of the creatures you encounter in Lusst'ghaa bear a passing touch on the human shape, but twisted. The second chapter introduces our hero. A rather average seeming man named Victor. He's an antiquarian. His second quest is to get a romantic evening set up for his girlfriend. It seems simple, not overly contrived and like you're going to spend some time getting lucky. Indeed, you START to do so, but then it goes sideways.  Victor promises he will get help for what happens, and after trying several professionals, settles on one in Bleakmoore. A cutscene later and you're in Bleakmoore, which will be one of the three major settings for the rest of the game. You will move back and forth from Bleakmoore, Lusst'ghaa, and the Mansion your first chapter took place in. After your introduction to Bleakmoore the game settles into its stride as a horror survival game. When it finally gets going, it feels very much like the Amnesia series. You have health and sanity, which you can mend or drug back to full. There is no weapons at first, meaning your only option is to run and hide. If your sanity drops to zero, you still get to play but things get harder and more interesting. The loss of direct control of the player character was slightly annoying but played into the whole "going mad" theme. (Your directional controls wind up inverted randomly as you move.)I'm pretty hard on games about plot. There is ALWAYS a point at which I mentally throw up my hands in disgust because "Why the hell would this person DO that?" or "The ONLY reason this is happening is to cause the plot to happen." All too often in modern games they hammer you into choices that anyone with an ounce of intellect would avoid like the plague. I didn't have that moment with Lust from Beyond. There were some questionable choices made by Victor, but they all felt genuine. Like the character had his reasons for what he was doing. Most of it is at gunpoint, but it makes sense, and the slow descent into more and more questionable choices and madness is something you can actually see happening. All of the game is dark. Its all in darker areas with poorer lighting and its a little bit before you get a lantern to see around you better. The hero even makes a snarky quip about getting a lantern instead of a flashlight to the character who gives it to you and gets a little sass back. The stealth element of the game is loose but serviceable. If you're sneaky, you can avoid fighting nearly all of the enemies. There are a few unavoidable fights. Your health starts at four pips and there is an option fairly early in the game to increase it to five, but I HIGHLY recommend taking the stealth speed increase instead of the health or sanity increase. It really helps with moving about. You'll find that enemies who are already hitting you are going to probably kill you. You run faster than every enemy in the game, but if you've angered a couple they will converge and all clip a pip pretty quick unless you can break line of sight and shake them. Some enemies do two damage or more. The name of the game is don't get caught, don't get hit. It reminds you several times, RUN don't fight. You eventually get a knife (and can upgrade it later for finding enough hidden statues in the level where you can get the knife) and you CAN kill most of your enemies but they are going to make it hurt. Really, just run and stealth. Until you can't. Near the end you acquire a revolver and there is a more traditional boss fight almost directly after. Poor Tim. The game gives you audio clues about if you can be seen or not, or if an enemy is behind you. Listen to the music and you'll have an easier time with it.As you begin the end, you wind up with all the ammo you can ever fire (literally a box that provides infinite) and a couple of more traditional fights, including one three part fight with different puzzle elements to it, but that's at the very end.There are about a half dozen(?) puzzles in the game but they are all of a much easier nature. Finding the missing part/key, organizing paintings, turning lock dials, etc. There are always enough clues to solve the puzzles with a little trial and error. You'll find the Lusst'ghaa puzzles more challenging. The first time you're really solving puzzles there gave me a hard time mostly because while I found the three key parts, I kept running right past the bloody door.There are several sex scenes in the game. One you can entirely skip (Just leave and confirm you want to leave) and several you don't have an option to skip. None of them are very long and require QTE style clicking to advance. But having sex, romancing the other characters, getting it on, is not the main objective. If the sex bothers you, there is a censorship option to blur things out while you play. (if the sex is why you're here, there isn't really enough to keep you "entertained".)My biggest complaint with the game is the jarring narrative split between the first "act" and the second "act". In the first act, you are dealing with one major enemy and in the second you start off not really knowing there is a second major enemy. It feels more like an extended denouement, or maybe an overdrawn epilogue. There are a few short chapters and then you get a clue that there is something more going on. I was frustrated, because this felt at first so tacked on, so forced. As though the Dev's were looking for a way to stretch out the game longer. I feel like there should have been more threads in the first "act" of the game, things that give you a better sense of it not being at all what you think is going on if they are going to go the direction they did with the second "act". I would have also liked to see a chapter select. I'd love to go back and further explore some of the stages in the game that I accidentally advanced because I didn't realize that an action would start the next chapter. Now, I have to see if I feel like replaying the game just to see if I want to explore those areas again. The latter is minor, the former is larger. I DO appreciate that there are relatively few jump scares. They relied more on atmosphere, tone, and actual content to scare and freak you out than just throwing a flash in front of the screen. Three of the jumps got me really good. I'd have to say they were all in appropriate places. None of them in the middle of a touching scene or anything.If you can look past the plot device of sex for the sex god, everything revolving around lust (at first) in the "religion", you'll actually have a really good time with a tense stealth survival game and a plot that does not go at all like you think it will. Fans of the Amnesia series and the Hellraiser movies will definitely find those itches scratched here. I definitely recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid sequel that improves on every aspect of the game with more mature adult content and themes, but still has some jank.I played this entirely on Steam Deck and was able to complete the game from start to finish. I did not complete all the side content though. This game, like the first, did not seem to be well optimized. I used Proton Experimental, 40hz refresh and 40fps in game, and a low medium mix on graphics. The game struggled to keep 40fps even in areas with little going on. However, the game was still playable, just not ideal.The story of this game picks up a year after the first. We have a few returning characters along with a whole host of new one's. You play as an antiques dealer who has struggled with his sexual appetites and seeks a psychologist who can help. Without spoiling anything for the story there are a lot of, somewhat predictable, twists and turns throughout the story. It is a satisfying experience overall though. You find yourself trying to get free of another cult that rose up after the events of the first game, while assisting the remnants of the Cult of Ecstasy from the first game. The game ramps up the adult content and makes it feel more mature this time around, but still doesn't quite nail it. The fear factor is also ramped up and not just jump scares. You feel the tension and anxiety in a lot of situations. The story is about three to four times longer than the first game as well.The world is even more disturbing than the first one. There are four "zones" in the game as you progress. You start in our protagonist's antique shop/apartment for the intro. We then travel to the city of Bleakmoore which has two "sub-zones". We then travel to the Yelverton Mansions, from the first game. Lastly we return the Lusst'ghaa, where we get to see more of the twisted dimension and learn more of it's secrets. The H.R. Geiger inspiration is still the strongest in my opinion. The world in this game felt very lived in and sinister. It was a joy to explore all of the creepy, disturbing, over the top environments and it kind of just worked.The gameplay was much more refined than the first, but still simple overall. You have weapons this time around, the puzzles are not overly simplistic, and object interactions mostly served a purpose. They did add quick time events for sexual encounters which was interesting, and didn't feel too out of place either. It is still best to sneak around but you do have to fight and or kill quite a few enemies. Most of them are not difficult and you can outrun all of them if choose. It was still janky, and hit boxes were not great, but I had fun.The game improved on the foundation of the first; made a longer, more detailed and engaging story; brought us a more detailed and interesting world to explore; and a drastically improved gameplay experience. If you are looking for a solid psychological horror game with very adult themes that aren't just about sex, then I definitely recommend it.

But it's all empty text, an introduction to something that never arrives, and remains lines after lines of expectations... all to nothing. But the constant flow of these uninspired, meaningless sentences about gods, universes, alien lust gets so monotonous like rain that kinda becomes poeticNow for the adventure itself: the main puzzles are all easy, and they're in the end repetitive. They don't offer any challenge whatsoever. They're blocks to be pushed, stones to be picked up and placed on pedestals to open doors. Second, there's also the other type of puzzles, the connect dots puzzles, the mosaics, the rotate a drawing puzzle, those kinds (i remember one of the founders of these is an old game called 7th guest). They're also obviously very very very easy, and for good reasons.What else? There's collectibles! I failed at one of those, they're quite hard, it's your standard item hunting, one set for each of the main parts of the story. They are frustrating, but it's no doubt where the real challenge is. It's definitely the best part of this game because it's the most diffcult one. You collect all of them, place em in a contraption, they release a special item that's completely optional, has nothing to do with game completion, or the story, the characters don't even notice them! And that's arguably a problem when the best part of the game has nothing to do with "the game". But hey, a challenge is a challenge, for a player. He decides how he takes on his game, what's important for him/her.The last part is scattered choices! They're not that bad. There are nomore than 2 or 3, one for the ending, but it's ok. I don't like these kinds of choices which in the end are kill/don't kill, but generally speaking i like any game or book or movie that offers a sort of sundry parcel of elements each distinct from the other. Like a theatre act that stops for a dance, a sports duel, a juggler skit. I like it, it's good design. I liked it ever since Monkey Island broke the puzzles streaks for the insults part, as we all know. A good game or book breaks its own pace, defies its own design, the player doesn't get bored and is entertained..So these are the parts that structure the game. None is really good! They're old mechanics, in short standard modern game tropes. The only things that would have made the game stand out are the hardcore scenes.And that part is no doubt, unarguably, the WORST part of Lust from Beyond. Like seriously poor.What professional reviewers write first I leave for last: the story. I'm not going to sum it up entirely, what's the point? It's videogame journalism trope and common reviewers tend to copy it. That's where writing and reading is not about informing, but only vain showboating for writers and simple pleasure for readers. But one decides whether to buy a game or not, so its story is just not important. Suffice to say this game's story purpose is to serve the gameplay in having the protagonist jump many times over between the real world and the alien world of "Lust'ghaa" with its main "rulers" seen as deities, hence uuuuh the main character is in a sect of worshippers which opposes the competing sect, both bent on controlling the potential power of this alien world, turning Earth into a sort of branch of Lust'ghaa, with the prospect of a "lust apocalypse" on Earth. See? You probably didn't even need to know it. Standard videogame and B-movie story.This game is not worth buying, then, because the "sexual content" is nothing but bait. It worked for me, it's good marketing, they did their job, who can blame them, but at least you may not fall for it! Must a bait always be fake, though? Not at all.Bye!

_childDocuments_.review: I found the story, the characters (even those only mentioned) and background history to be very interesting, interconnected  and detailed, with enough mystery to get me thinking for hours in and out-of-game. The immature "please mark me as funny" reviews aren't helping. If you click "more like this" on the store page it won't list horror adventure/walking sims, it'll list dating games with explicit content for the sake of explicit content, and even South Park which is known for jokes about excrement, genitals and homosexuality. That is so off. The description alone reads psychological horror, Lovecraft, Giger, nudity and quick coitus-time events with a seemingly unconnected protagonist.Many psychological horror games rely on suggestive creepiness and one pop element like abuse and trauma.Normally Lovecraftian inspiration alone makes a boring unoriginal game about collective visions and names that are difficult to spell and pronounce. But Lust from Beyond focused on Earth characters and their history of confusion and manipulation. They're not hooded cultists with fundamental malice, they're morally ambiguous and relatable. This sequel is reusing a lot of from the more open-ended Lust for Darkness while still being able to stand on its own (you don't need to have played Lust for Darkness to get immersed entirely in the story/timeline).Only negative is the audio tracks that are mixed a bit unevenly. _childDocuments_.review: Now that I've finished playing Lust From Beyond completely through - twice - I'm updating my review. While not perfect (is any game?) I really REALLY enjoyed this! I hate over use of words like "fantastic" but this game was. My vocabulary is too small to properly express exactly what I feel about this game.I would highly recommend you play them in order. The first in the series is right here: I have to say it's not quite as good as this one, but it's part of the story and is good enough! There are two very short free games after that before Lust From Beyond. The game took ~16 hrs for my first play through and eight hours for the second (having figured out all the puzzles and half the collectibles the first time around). Now that that is out of the way, here's the rest of the review! + The Story. It's really good! I didn't care too much about it in the previous games, but with this one, that changed. Can't really say why... I guess this game made the characters more important to me than the games before. + The audio is decently good. The music is very VERY good! There were times when it really made the characters come alive to me where they might not have otherwise. My only complaint on the audio is that sometimes things that should have been quiet were too loud. A man walking on the floor above you in a hotel shouldn't be "Bang! Bang! Bang!" When he's half a building away you really shouldn't hear him at all. A few times I was startled by foot steps sounding like they were right next to me when they were not. + The writing/dialog was pretty good. Especially knowing the creators were (probably) not native English speakers. The few mis-spellings and such that I noticed in the sub titles were fixed in a patch right after launch. + The graphic quality gets a + too, if only barely, and with a couple of caveats listed below. I'm not sure the Unity engine showed this game as good as, say, Unreal might have, but I'm sure the devs had their reasons. The Anti-alliasing is pretty poorly implemented. I don't know if that's the graphics engine or not - but I've never seen a stunning 3D game in Unity (comparatively speaking here.) + The Art was fantastic! I feel any time the graphics failed, it was probably a failure of the Unity engine.+ All achievements trigger/work properly. + The art pack was included for free, something few developers do!+ Multiple endings done really well. Not just a few lines of dialog different like some games. +/- The voice over wasn't the best, but it was adequate. - I noticed some texture issues with a few corpses. Notable texture lines making it look like a leg was two pieces stuck together. It's not common, but it did happen repeatedly. Some corpses were seemingly very low texture quality as well. I don't know if this was done purposefully to lesson the impact of a dead/mutilated person or for other reasons - either way, I found it distracting, unreal and would have preferred for it to NOT stand out as a poorly textured surface.- The AI was a little too predictable making the game overly easy and took away a little bit of the fear factor. I almost gave the graphics a negative because of the anti alliasing and the fact that... it could have been better - but I did enjoy the game SO MUCH that I felt that was overly picky. While I left an honest opinion, I think most players will realize there is no game that's perfect. If there's something that turns you away from playing this game, it shouldn't be that! Some things to keep in mind: This is not a sex game. This is erotic horror. There are some very disturbing images. There are a small handful of jump scares. Overall I did not find this game to be particularly scary most of the time. The AI is not particularly bright which makes it very predictable.Also, there are few games I have finished that I actually WANTED to replay immediately. I have rarely finished up a game and experienced such a distinct feeling of... disappointment! realizing it will be probably be years before I get to experience another game like this._____________________________________________________________My Original review:I'm only 2 hrs in but loving it so far! Hate that I have to sleep now! So far it's all I expected and more. If I finish and the game tanks, I'll update this - in fact I'll probably update it either way, but wanted to get another positive review out there for the launch. The devs are fantastic - keeping up with questions on the forum etc. I really don't expect the game to somehow turn around from what I've seen. The only disappointment is that now I'll have to wait a long time for another sequel :c

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty decent Lovecraftian horror game, not for the faint-hearted or prudish, but if you made it far enough to read reviews for this game, you probably know that already. I won't say too much on the story or events of the game to avoid spoilers, but there is a deeper story and more character development than I was expecting. Some of the horror of game does fade somewhat due to overexposure. The "Beyond" realm as mentioned in the title of the game is just used too much. It has a nice design, but you simply visit it too many times. The gameplay is ok at best. It's more than a walking simulator, but not much more. You get some items for combat, but for most of the game you're better off avoiding enemies rather than fighting them. There is a sanity and health system similar to other Lovecraftian games, but there are so few sources of sanity-draining and combat is rare. The game gives you loads of healing items for health and sanity, which removes much of the challenge. This is a good thing, because the game does feel a bit clunky. It is at its best when you're exploring, looking for items, enjoying the spooky locations, not when you're fighting or sneaking.The graphics and sound design for the game are decent but not amazing. The voice acting is a mixed bag but the characters who get the most dialogue are generally played by the most talented actors. The art direction is good but the graphics are satisfactory rather than amazing.The worst aspect of the game is, without question, the performance. The game regularly stutters and has an unstable framerate even when it is only targeting 60fps. It also causes my GPU temp to shoot up and in some areas it will tank frames down into single figures. In other areas, it runs fine. The performance doesn't seem to be linked the complexity of the area, some of the most simple areas in the game are those that run the worst. Anything with fog tends to run really badly. Unfortunate, the game just needs better optimisation. Unity engine games rarely seem to be great for optimisation, but this one is pretty bad.Overall, I'd say it's a 7/10. It's worth playing as it is a fairly unusual horror experience and there is more care and craft to it than I initially thought it would have.

_childDocuments_.review: After revisting this title, I felt it only fair to update my review somewhat. I purchased this game close to day 1 and on release I had a difficult time getting the game to run properly. It does seem that the devs have quickly patched the game to perform much better. All in all, the game is something of a mixed bag. But I'd like to give a tentative recommendation here if you're a fan of other indie horror titles like Amnesia or Outlast. The controls and combat can be a little janky in places; but this is outweighed in my mind by a fairly unique experience. I also can't help but enjoy this game for being what it wanted to be - violent, sexual and a little bit depraved in places. While the game has some rough spots across the board, you can tell that there is a not insignificant amount of creative vision here. Calling this game a 'sex game' definitely sells short the overall experience - a erotic thriller with stealth elements and some light puzzle solving. The game boasts multiple endings and a fair amount of collectibles, easter eggs and secrets tucked away. My first playthrough took between 6 and 7 hours. I'm a newcomer to the series, and for what the story is, I didn't feel lost along the way. Also included is a little bit of readable lore that filled me in on the foggy bits. As a standalone story, I'd say this works fine on it's own.Again, I'd give a tentative recommendation here. It's a little bit messy in places, but offers something a little unique in a landscape of similar games that pull a lot more punches.Looking forward to future works from the developers. But I'd love to see the next one leave the gate with another coat of polish.

_childDocuments_.review: First things first, despite the tags, don't go into this one expecting pr0n. It's still NSFW, it has some scenes, but that's clearly not the focus.TLDR, a decent NSFW survival horror tackling some extreme themes with a lot more sweat put into it than most NSFW games but not as great of a story and systems as other AAA survival horror games out there, but it doesn't cost as much as those other AAA survival horror, so it evens out nicely.This is, first and foremost, a survival horror adventure set in a lovecraftian world with a decent portion of gore on the side. You alternate between 3 distinct locations, a blood, gore and dismembered body parts aplenty cultist base, a calmer (though a bit unsettling) pleasure cult mansion and a lovecraftian dream world with statues of disfigured humanoids doing pleasure things everywhere and anxiety inducing walls.The story is...ok. It's marginally better than some lower budget horror games out there, and a lot better than most NSFW games. The graphics and mechanics are incredible. Opening and closing things is very satisfying, the UI is great since it's contextual and hides itself when not in use. It even has reflections.Stealth is a bit wonky. It works, but feels like a hastily added sort of system, missing features and all, though those missing features also serve to make it more realistic. This is made worse by the fact that, for the first action mission, stealth is all you have.Sound is great, it's contextual, high quality, and varied. The only problem I have with it is its surround capabilities, which aren't that great. Nothing that impacts gameplay, but that's mostly on account the rooms are small enough you'll be using your eyes a lot more than your ears.

_childDocuments_.review: Having really enjoyed Lust For Darkness, I was highly anticipating the release of this game. Sadly it does not deliver for me. I was looking forward to playing another horror game where the fear is atmospheric and thought-provoking. What I got was a game with fairly steady jump-scares, random enemies in places that feel unnatural, and (as of right now) one stressful chase sequence that feels like Outlast without the fluid controls.I'd hate to only mention the negative aspects of Lust From Beyond, so to be fair I will say that the beginning is very strong and shows exactly where the last game shined. There are just so many things in this that feel shoehorned in from other series, which would be fine if they were executed well. This game also has some of the most inconsistent voice-acting that I have ever heard.These developers are great at telling stories, as proven by Lust For Darkness. I hope in the future they focus on telling interesting stories with good atmosphere instead of adding layers that strip immersion from players just to make it feel like a traditional horror game.

_childDocuments_.review: I play a ton of horror games and have come to realize that you can easily divide the genre into “great” games and “garbage” games, with little in-between. So, while Lust from Beyond may have erotic themes, it is still a horror game at its core – and therefore must fall into one of the two categories.Put simply, yeah, this game has a lot of the ero stuff – both in its setting and as a story device. Whether that be the naked NPCs everywhere, the walls being made of certain organs, or just the random cult activities that you get to take part in – the game goes all out on making sure it gets that AO rating. Now, I won’t deny that a lot of the content is gratuitous and simply there for shock value, but I can at least respect the effort put into making the experience as depraved as possible, enough so that I couldn't even show some of the scenes in my video review even when censored. So yeah, the game has that part on lock for those that just want to play it for that.For those that want an actual game, well, Lust from Beyond might not be the best option. This is one of those first-person horror adventure games where the gameplay is almost entirely just you walking around, examining objects, moving things to and from, and solving some very basic puzzles. It is not a straight-up walking sim, but the gameplay that is there is dead simple.Like, most of the objectives simply have you searching the environment for an item or two before then having you repeat that in the next area and so on. Because there are tons of doors, drawers, and other spots to look through, the gameplay can come off as padding at times and a good chunk of my playtime was this aimless wandering around hoping to come across the item that allows me to progress. The puzzle design is just as bad, as the vast majority of them simply require you to take a piece of paper or some other bit of information and apply it elsewhere.And of course, you have all the usual horror game fluff on top of that. The random jump scares, the forced stealth sections, and the clunky combat too. That last one is especially bad here – you can’t tell if your hit is doing damage as there’s no indicator or other feedback, it’s like your swinging at air. Granted, combat is considered a last resort in this game, but when you do have to use it, it’s definitely not a fun time.Lust from Beyond is the second game in the Lust trilogy, but is a standalone story, so you don’t need any prior knowledge. The problem is that the story is... not good. For one, it’s got some really wonky pacing. The first ten chapters felt like it could have been its own game – and honestly, it would have been better off – but it just kept going.The next several chapters it goes overboard, ramping the pacing up to the max and subjecting you to a ton of dialogue info-dumping. And no, it doesn’t help that a lot the important names and places are stuff like Ac’mlale, Lauv’abrarc, Ughro’eccna, and Xu’thrar. I mean, it was already pretty hard to keep track of towards the beginning, so you can imagine how the last several chapters went. It was like the devs had to wrap up everything quickly in order to stay on schedule, resulting in a shorter and more rushed game (it took me seven hours to beat).The story also has some really poorly executed twists – the kind where you can 100% tell they are coming and it ruins any sort of impact they were going for. The game drops the most obvious hints leading up to them, so it would honestly be a bit surprising if someone didn’t get where it was going.Those two issues pale in comparison to the game’s dialogue and voice acting – which are easily some of the worst I’ve been subjected to in any horror game. Robotic conversations, unnecessarily exaggerated lines, overly wordy sentences, it’s all there and had me wondering “what kind of humans actually talk like this?” And I don’t mean to slam the voice actors, but let’s just say that they at least tried.As a whole, the graphics aren't that bad. I mean, it’s nothing too spectacular, but it’s not completely bare and lifeless like others in the gerne. A lot of thought went into constructing the world in a way to further the game’s erotic themes – so credit is due there. The sound and music are not quite as good, but again, not entirely bad. It’s mostly atmospheric stuff, so you don’t really notice it to begin with.I’ll preface this by saying that I am still on a 1070 Ti, as I’ve been unable to get my hands on a 3080 yet. However, this card is above the recommended specs, along with my 3700x for CPU. Despite this though, I ran into countless issues with frame drops, stuttering, and just a general mess on the performance front. For example, a lot of the time I would be well above 60 fps, but still have this slight stutter effect when moving around, like the camera is jittering a bit. This makes the movement look choppy and forced me to enable motion blur just to mask the issue.That’s before the fps drops though, which are plentiful depending on the area. The alien dimension, for example, dunked my fps from 120 down to like 40. I found that the shadow setting was the main culprit there, as turning that from medium to low gained me 50 fps alone. It became this fun mini-game where I would have to constantly change my shadow settings when swapping between that realm and the real world, as keeping shadows on low in the real world just does not look good.Lust from Beyond is not a good game. There are elements of a good game hidden in there, but the overall package just doesn’t cut it. From the tedious gameplay to the story full of some of the worst dialogue in the genre, it really isn’t worth the time if you’re looking for anything more than just a bunch of erotic content stringed together as a video game. And that’s even before you consider the performance issues. Maybe those can be fixed up with patches, but I don’t think the underlying game can be saved.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: The forth game in the series brings the same level of disappointment as the previous instalments. I guess giving it a chance was another mistake, the forth one in a row.Let's see: it's still a chore of a game that features unlikable one-dimensional characters, outright vulgar erotic scenes that in fact are not hot or enthralling at all, boring puzzles and non-existent stealth, reused assets and repeatable animations, cheap jump scares and a number of unsuccessful attempts to create a really shocking content that would still pass the censorship. The writing is just bad. From time to time the game's plot gets so predictable that it seriously borders absurd or a parody. The dialogues are mostly cringy at best. The lore is there, but if you skip it you won't miss much.And the end of the protagonist's story, well, it was more than just a subtle foreshadowing as the outcome was painfully obvious from the very beginning. Why? Because all the previous games from the series went along the exactly same plotline with the same dark ending. Boring, disappointing, unfulfilling.The game lacks everything, especially originality and the real depth, but at least sex scenes are not strictly heterosexual anymore and thus not entirely dull, however this small brave step made by developers are definitely not enough to make this game really worthy of attention.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is best described like this;-walk around and find items -solve simples puzzles-solve puzzles with items in your inventory-run away from monsters whom you can't kill and wait for 2 min each time you die for the game to reload entirely...yeah...fun.I have played Lust for Darkness and i really enjoyed its mysteries and overall playtime.  I wished it was a little more interactive, but it was a great experience.This time, the game try to be darker, by incorporating a lot of 'Giger'esque textures, and giving you a more 'personal contact' with the 'underworld'.  Simply said, you will pass more time into that weird and gory place than before...It is all good, yes! but...But there is also some problems here...  For some of you, those will be minors, for other people, they will be major problems.In 2021, we should not see games that don't realize how bad it is, to make the player wait an entire reloading of the entire program, each time you die from a 'running away from something' section that you failed.  That is just torturing your players...and make for a very frustrating game.  Espacially for casual players like me, crushing my left mouse button because i don't see the 'hand' icon appear quickly enough to climb that echelon, is not something 'fun'.  it is getting old very quickly and remind us of old 'vampire games' that was incredibly hard because they rely on quick fingers instead of good gameplay. I actually stop playing the game at that point and i am now wondering,'am I gonna go back to it anytime soon?'...do i have that amount of time to lose running away from 'monsters' when i could play something else and enjoy better, more interresting gameplay?...  I don'T know.  I guess it depends on what type of player you are...  But, if you play walking sims  like this type of game, do you really enjoy running away from monsters that appear out of nowhere, and beat the hell out of you for you don't have a clue why?...Well it worked in Silent Hill, yes?So yeah, although i love the world of this game, i wish there would be less 'running away from things' and more 'explore and discover what's out there...'It all end up knowing what you are getting into...  If you came here thinking it is a sexual game, you are wrong.  it is a horror game way more alike to Silent Hill than Acting Lessons.Anyway, don't get me wrong,... that is a great game, as Lust for Darkness was, but it really depends who you are as a player. It is not for everybody.  if you are easily frustrated, it may be hassardous to your health (or your mouse health) to play this one...Still play the game, but give the controler to your partner...  ;)Oh, also, about the requirement, my computer only has a 1030 GT with 2mbDDR5 and it works well, although i have to lower the video settings a bit.  I encounter no bug as i played the game so far, so that is great!  ;)

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty decent game, with huge Call of Cuthulu vibes, unique art direction and interesting story.Unfortunately the game runs horrendous on a RTX 3070 it stutters frequently, in terms of problems with the actual game the main character is one of the most pretentious and unlikeable people, some of the lines cause constant eye-rolling and some holes in the story direction directly tied to the characters choices.(For example you need to use a payphone to contact an important character but you don't have any coins on you??? So you need to use a coin you are selling for a high amount instead. This was alright until you go into a hotel that has a payphone which requires no payment, this is about 20 seconds later btw)There is a good shock factor and the immersion is nice but the cons far outweigh the pros, if you like a nice mystery solver with survival horror elements you will like this, I thought I would but the dialogue is mediocre at best, reminiscent of a game you would find for Xbox 360 pre-owned in a bargain bin.The price does not warrant the early stages of the game which provides more boredom than anything, especially once you reach the "Giger-esque" areas that are long-winded and empty. _childDocuments_.review: It's time for another after dark special of weird creature sexcults and B-movie horror, oh yes, it's Lust from Beyond time!  For my money LFB is light years better than Lust for Darkness which for me fell into the "I'd barely recommend this to someone," category.  I liked the lore, story, graphics and will to be weird of the predecessor but it just wasn't that fun to play with boring stealth sequences that felt random, terrible chases where getting stuck on the environment was your worst enemy and just generally mediocre gameplay that failed to engage me.  It did have a mansion to explore and I tend to always rate positively games where I'm rummaging around mansions, so it might have gotten extra points for that, I don't know.  LFB still isn't perfect.  I wouldn't recommend it to Splinter Cell fans or war shooter nuts but if that's all you play, what the hell are you doing here anyway?  As for your garden variety horror maniac like me; I enjoyed this one quite a bit.  You'll meet characters new and old in LFB as you fill the penis pump shoes of Victor who heads off to the town of Bleakmoor to see a head specialist.  It seems Victor has been turning into a violent sexbeast in bed and his girl Lily has had enough of his antics.  Upon arriving in Bleakmoor you're greeted with this begotten, desolate town that's straight out of Silent Hill or COC: Dark Corners of the Earth.  Those Dark Corners' vibes are fully enforced after getting put up in a rundown hotel for the night only to be woken up from a pleasant though disgusting wet dream (that takes place in the altered realm of Lust G'ghaa) and chased across the rooftops by the less than sane members of the Scarlet Lodge sexcult.  That early part of the game in Bleakmoor is some of the strongest stuff here, that isolation aura of the best horror movies and horror games coming into play as you search the town and try to find the doctor.  You are searching for clues in environments that are fairly interactive; digging up notes, grabbing collectibles (some of which unlock hidden caches of items) and generally receiving some bonus reward or feeling of progression for snooping around.  The graphics are great for an indie in most all aspects in these early scenes (aside from some ugly textures here and there) and ambient sounds flicker in your ears that always have you looking over your shoulder to see nothing (but one time I DID see something...).The game's first big action set-pieces take place in the hotel, where you'll be introduced to the puzzle and monster evasion bits of Lust G'haa and then a much more frenetic chase throughout the hotel itself.  Stealth won't win any awards but I found that if I was generally out of sight, I was generally out of sight and didn't get cheaply killed.  It's basic stuff without light or noise meters in play but it worked.  I enjoyed the puzzles in Lust G'haa in the first game and they are fairly engaging here without ever becoming frustrating.  Instead of getting a mask that enables you to see paths and solutions that you couldn't see LFD, Victor later unlocks an essence power that is sort of a telekinesis that can open up new paths or enable him to lead friendly, disgusting NPC creatures into helping him unlock the way forward.  Generally, I found the new additions to Lust G'haa satisfying for opening up more gameplay in the squishy, not for the squeamish world.  You'll find shrines that allow you to level up abilities (I focused mainly on health since I knew there was combat later on) and although at first you can't bring your Earthly possessions into the forbidden realm, later on you can haul your pistol, knife, healing items and much more into play.  Unlike the first game where the general idea was, "An inventory?  Inventories are for virgin losers," LFB has you keeping track of ammunition, health, sanity and essence.  Essence is charged throughout Lust G'haa and easy to find when needed.  Health and sanity are managed by various bandages, potions and elixirs.  You'll be watching health the most as even when my sanity hit the skids, I never did manage to get that achievement where Victor says, "So long cruel world!"  You'll see some disturbing imagery and start getting that shroom trip come-up vision, but other than that sanity could be better utilized.  I still would refill when down to 2 points because stumbling drunk vision isn't the best for drawing a bead on enemies with your revolver or finding that one activation point in the environment.  Speaking of drawing a bead there's both regular combat and boss battles in LFB.  Though it won't win an award for innovation, it works.  It's not as terrible as the combat in Today is my Birthday, Follia, Back in 1995 or numerous other B-movie thrillers with the worst combat imaginable.  When the word was out that LFB has terrible combat and then I finally played the game myself...I was thinking, "Jesus H, these people never played Follia: Dear Father, did they?"  Seriously, that game had an attack and defend function and I was killed nearly every time I chose to fight anything because there's exactly 1 monster out of about 8 types that can actually be killed with your weapons.  That to me is bad combat.  With sneaking hit or miss, I used my knife or gun at every chance I could and usually defeated my foes.  Charging up the knife swing and readying the revolver is a bit of a pain but I got used to it.  It's a piecemeal system but I'm kinda glad it's in the game since the stealth is about breaking the line of sight and nothing else.  Combat helps break up the action even though it's very basic.  There's 3 boss battles in the game and I actually enjoyed them.  The first against a tyrant like stalker in a gimp mask was satisfying since there's a lead up to actually fighting him.  He gets mentioned in the story throughout until you finally have to face him after dealing with an entire level of him stalking you beneath the theater.  The theater underground was the game at its best to me; mixing sneaking and combat with puzzle solving, lots of exploration and lore discovery with a boss battle on top.  The puzzles in the game range from the same ol' same ol' to some more innovative designs and were generally fun to solve.  I never felt that the controls held me back either.  I experienced no input delay, inventory management is smooth, QTE events worked (there's QTE sex in this, oh boy!), running is somewhat slow but Victor's not an Olympian and the interface was intuitive for the puzzles as well.  One of the coolest new additions to the game are some choices that will definitely change your ending and even change how some characters will treat you in the storyline.  As the game progresses you spend half your time in the mansion from the first game mixing with your fellow sexcult friends while spending the rest of the game in hostile zones taking on the Scarlet Lodge or exploring the bonerland of Lust G'haa.  I enjoyed this split in the gameplay which almost lends an open world feel to the experience.  There is a few sidequests added this time around and the more you explore and uncover, the more supplies you'll find.  I think the safe hub respite helps makes the tense bits of the game even more white-knuckle.  Graphics were pretty good as in the first game though it seems that darker textures or the rendering of certain "ugly" landscapes are where they become the muddiest.  I also thought the sound design was fantastic with only the general performance of some of dialogue lacking.  That was more on the actors than the sound itself, though I generally enjoyed the dialogue.  It's a B-horror world focused on sex and violence, if you're expecting Shakespeare, again I must ask, what the hell are you doing here?All in all, Lust from Beyond did exactly what a sequel should do. It's light years better than the first game and even won someone over who wasn't that into Lust for Darkness.

_childDocuments_.review: Played "Lust From Beyond" yesterday and it is the only game so far, that caused me a literal headache. Nothing serious, nothing strong, but still.Even with disabled head-bob (which I normally do not disable), camera was constantly swiveling even when I was just standing still (for example during "cutscenes"), when walking (and especially running) the camera seemed to change field of view or maybe it just changed zoom or something, but the point is the view was "stretching out". But even worse, it felt over-sharpened. Which was made extra worse in some scenes, which had lots of glares. And the "other" world had excessive glares, let me tell you.Thankfully, the game was not that good in other aspects, too. Which surprised me, because I played both the "Prologue" and "Scarlet" chapters which were released long before the full game and I liked them. I do not think they had any of the issues already described, maybe except for some glares in the "other" world in "Prologue". And somehow they felt more polished, even though they were technically "demos".The story in the main game does not feel... "real". It's too abrupt and edgy, quite a few little things do not make sense even. And not in a sense of "oh, I'm in a bizarre situation, and I am going insane", which was the case for the demos (maybe that's why it worked there). I can't relate to any parts of it. And to be honest, dialogues make it even worse, even though voice acting itself is ok.Furthermore somehow it felt the atmosphere, I felt in the demos. Especially the 3rd chapter, which meant to present a spooky town, where all people are cultists, but there were [almost] no people and the town looked outright abandoned. Resident Evil series was able to do much-much better job in similar areas.The "other" world also felt... Plastic? Visually, if you are a fan of H.R. Giger's art - you most likely will like it as well. It's similar combination of body-horror with some bio-tech sprinkled by Lovecraftian motives. But, again it had those annoying glares everywhere and did not feel as "alive" as I remember it from the demos. Still better than "Agony" (or "Succubus" from the same devs), though.It was not an easy decision, but I did decide to drop it after all. Maybe I was expecting too much, maybe my memory of the demos was too good, or I ignored some things for the demos, because they were demos. But I just did not feel it, and it definitely was not good enough to ignore the headache.Oh, and to those who wonder: yes, there is sex in the game. Even some QTEs during some scenes. But it's not like you see it every minute, the scenes are rather "strategically placed" and they do make total sense, considering the circumstances of the game. Don't think people would be watching those for pleasure, though. But either way, if you do not want to see those, there is a "censored" version of the game, too. They even dropped 1 steamy achievement from it. Not like I would recommend the game either way, unless you are a huge fan of Giger.

_childDocuments_.review: Lust from Beyond is a game that I have been waiting to play for a long while, and I've finally been able to get my deviant hands all over it.Whilst this is a positive review, the game has one glaring issue that needs to be addressed, and I will come to that shortly.The Lust series is a love child of Lovecraft and Giger, and it couldn't be more perfect when it comes to the setting and the atmosphere, the walls of Lusst'ghaa make you feel as if you're walking around the very artwork of H.R. Giger in 3D, whilst you immerse yourself in the story that could come from the very mind of H.P. Lovecraft himself.I was a massive fan of the original game itself, based in a mansion that is torn apart by the actions of a man craving for power, whilst this game broadens the area of the world map, I won't go into too much detail, but it's a massive step for the devs, and they pulled it off relatively well.I was immersed in the story from the get go, even if it does use a couple of the same set ups reminiscent of first game, the level of detail in the area's in which you explore is rarely seen even in the triple A industry and I have to commend the devs for that, just purely amazing.However the one area that lets this game down is the combat and enemy encounter system, by far some of the most infuriating and downright keyboard slamming moments of gameplay I've felt in the longest of times, and trust me I play Darkest Dungeons, that combat system is downright cruel, but rewarding when you finally get it right.This however, Lets just say I have not felt the urge to just Alt F4 so hard in a game in a longtime until I played the Combat or Running sections of this game, recall when I talked about the Giger walls, imagine running through a Xenomorph hive getting chased by some creature you can barely fight, whilst in pitch darkness with just a lantern that lights up just a couple of feet in front of you, whilst having pulsating red edges closing in on you because you're low on health, whilst... yes I know another whilst, whilst your camera zooms in and out and wobbles from side to side because you're also losing you mind because of all the horrors you've seen.It is nauseating and it just completely takes you away from the game, personally I would have gutted the combat system and removed it completely, especially when it comes to the boss battles, they're unimaginative and just poor level design, it does unfortunately take away from the amazing detail and thought that went into the levels otherwise.So why leave a positive review? Because the story and the lore is amazing, the writing is top notch, even if the delivery from the voice actors is a tad bit uncanny valley.This is a top notch game, where it explores the erotic-horror that fans of Giger (Alien) and Lovecraft have been hoping for on a media that has been incredibly slow on the uptake, whilst films and even recent TV Media such as Lovecraft Country have been taking advantage of.This is a good game, but what lets it down is the combat, and because the combat has such a large roll in the game itself, I have to give the game a 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give this game an "Ehhh" rating, because that's what it deserves. A game with potential, but unfortunately didn't quite hit the notes I was looking for. It reminded me a bit of a poor man's Outlast II, except with more H.R. Giger flesh walls. I am uncertain if I wanted more because the game really was lacking a lot, or because I've been around the block and have read and seen quite a bit of smut to know where a pretty neat idea like this could go. When it comes to games like this, if it feels too indulgent, then it means you're on the right track. That's what I wanted. Hell, I could've even gone for more of . Just go nuts. I know this will make me sound like a lecher, but I wished they had really leaned into the sex angle. Lust For Darkness felt more sex-packed than this, oddly enough.The voice acting was hit or miss. Victor's VA was convincing when the script called for tears but the "sarcastic straight man" got a bit old fast. There’s also no save slots or cloud saving so that was very inconvenient when I wanted to play on my pc and then play on the steam deck. The game has some performance issues on the deck related to the shadows and anything set higher than low would hit the performance so bad it would tank the frame rate to 20fps. _childDocuments_.review: Veni Vedi VeniWell I finally finished the game. PROS- Graphics look amazing on a 4k monitor-The game doesn't pull any punches with shock content. I found it refreshing actually that they just did all the outlandish things they wanted. It's not something you see all too often in most if any games. -Sound design and art design was fantastic. Very nice homages to lovecraft, giger, and beksinski with clear influences readily visable from each artist. -I like the additional content bits where you can view character models, animations, etc-I enjoyed being able to interact with environments and make decisions that impacted the ending-Some decent jumpscares that really got me-The erotic content was fun while constantly towing the line of either gratuitously shocking or just horrifically absurd. This bullet point might be a con for a different person than myself. CONS-The writing. Oh sweet slumbering eldritch gods the writing. Horrendous. Dialogue is stiff, clumsy, amateur, unnatural, and awkward. Multiple times during this game I groaned in agony at how abominable the writing felt to play through. If the writers were more adept in their art and each voice actor was up to par with Dr. Austerlitz then the game would feel much more AAA. The plot was heavily contrived and each loading screen was littered with nonsensical metaphysical prose that just barely (if not at all) made sense within the lore of the world. Just to give you a sense of what it feels like I am going to spend 1 minute making up my own example to give you a taste. "In the pools of infinity the unknown becomes knowable. The essence of misery lies in each corner of the world. We offer solace to the madness behind our eyes."  - Voice acting was terrible for every character aside from the conjoined twins, Victor, Mabel, Dr. Austerlitz and theodore. Amanda was particularly bad in my opinion. They should have switched the voice actors for Mabel and Amanda as Mabel was much better at emoting and line reading. -Facial animations are not great which is why I think a majority of the humans in this game wear masks.-Navigation was frustrating and sometimes utterly tedious-Game dragged on in the last hour or two. I would have liked to spend more time in the mansion fleshing out each character and their backstories rather than navigating countless nearly identical gigeresque hallways and solving half baked puzzles and fetch quests. -This last critique is more of a personal preference but I feel that this game should have leaned slightly more into the humorous side of its essence rather than the sadistic side. The former is much more charming and memorable. All in all I give the game a 5.5/10. It is far from a masterpiece and I would hesitate to say that it is a good game. That said, I enjoyed playing it and don't regret buying it. If the developers were to make another I would likely buy it and play it because at the end of the day it's still (somehow) fun.

_childDocuments_.review: *Warning 18+*Lust from Beyond is a lovecraftian horror game filled with gore and sex, and more sex. It's a sequel to Lust for Darkness, and the other two Lust from Beyond prequel games that ties the whole story together. This game really nails the horror atmosphere, like a "sexy" Amnesia. You play as Victor, a antiquarian who has visions of another world and on recommendation from his girlfriend goes to see a doctor. After that everything goes down hill pretty quickly. The characters are also very memorable. So if you're into Lovecraft, Giger, and/or Beksiński, and don't mind a bit of sex and guts then boy howdy you're going to love this game just as much as I do. And I give this a 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing this game through to the end was the epitome of the sunk cost fallacy.I enjoyed the first game (Lust for Darkness). Despite its corniness at times, it was an entertaining experience that knew its limits and didn't overstay its welcome.Lust from Beyond, on the other hand, is an experience that edges on insulting. So many sequences of this game are absolutely painful to trudge through; from stupid arbitrary fetch-quests that pad game time, to quarter-baked "combat" mechanics that'll drive a teetotaler to alcoholism from how touchy they are. Anything remotely meaningful in the story/horror department is muddied and marred by the "game" that encapsulates it. The story (interesting at times) could have been explained adequately in a game not much longer than Lust for Darkness. And the sexual body-horror the game is supposed to pride itself on was, honestly, fairly tame and underwhelming compared to other works with H.R. Giger's flavor.I wish I could extract more positive things to say (and to be fair there probably are), but the game just had way too much painful slog and padding to allow redemption. I canceled my cult membership the moment the game was over (i.e. hit the "uninstall" button).

_childDocuments_.review: I always hate writing poor reviews on indie games. Especially when I can obviously tell that a lot of effort was put into the game graphically. Truly this game is a masterpiece at times visually. However, sparse moments of gorgeous graphics and the very rare well thought out scare is not enough to save this game.To preface- I am an avid enjoyer of psycho sexual horror, when I first found this game I was incredibly excited because it seemed like the perfect game for me. I'm not coming at this from the view of the content being too shocking because I just... found it boring. The horror of bdsm and satanic orgies portrayed in this game feel akin to missionary in the dark, I was not titillated, nor was I disgusted, I was completely blank the entire way through. The writing is also incredibly poor, for a game that wears its lovecraftian inspiration on its sleeve things are overexplained and the plot is quite frankly boring at best and mind numbing at worst. I don't care for any of the characters, I am not motivated by the plot, I am simply moving from point to point, being yapped at, and then being slapped across the face with a dildo. Not to mention the game is just... not fun to play. There's very little direction a lot of the time, and it can end up with long moments of not really knowing what to do. The puzzles are fun! I'll give the game that, but even then half of the challenge is sometimes just understanding your objective, something that's especially hard when your interaction icon is tiny and very hard to miss. Also the inclusion of skill checks just feels... weird? Very out of place to be completely honest.Look, I still have a lot of issues with this game, but the baseline is that even after dragging my feet to the near end in hopes things would get better, I just can't find it in me to care about it. Which is truly a shame because the art of this game is honestly gorgeous. Overall, I personally wouldn't recommend wasting your money or time on this game, however I also can't stop you.(Oh also I continuously got violently nauseous while playing this game even after turning the motion blur/head bobbing off which really didn't add to my already crappy experience)

_childDocuments_.review: There are a number of things that I think this game does well, and a number that I think could have been removed or re-tuned but overall, I think the game is enjoyable and is worth the money you spent. I think it's an interesting game because it's trying to do multiple things, including adding combat - which I think is a bit of a rarity.PROS- It's basically a game where you get to play as a Slaaneshi cultist. That's probably an overdone joke, but I think it's still appropriate. I half expected a Grey Knight strike team to teleport in and purge us. Joking aside; it had great little snippets of lore dotted about the place that helped build the universe, even if some of them are placed in puzzles. Why would you hide a letter in a puzzle?- It's called an 'Erotic Horror' but honestly I think it's more of a horror game with some erotic elements. I think it's tastefully done for the most part (other than the Scarlett Lodge sections, but I also think that's precisely the point of the Scarlett Lodge)- Technically it works, in thanks in large part to using the Unity engine. I didn't have any instability or other technical problems at all during gameplay.- The Essence 'magic' system. Interesting magic, but kinda wanted to make use of it more.- Combat. While I would say that it's execution needs a bit of a work, I would also like to point out that I appreciate that it is there.- Doesn't feel short. CONS- Combat. There is a section of the game early on that I think I would be unable to pass because the bad guy summons peoples to literally club you. On the way to get out an enemy spawns basically just behind a door that you need to pass by to reach the exit. I only passed by exploiting crouching through combat, because for whatever reason the enemy only seems to attack someone from the chest upwards, missing you. - Tied to above; literally unkillable monsters. I am willing to accept such handwavery magic from the lusstgha realm, but not from humans. - Mentality/Instability. Very cool idea; but overused. It makes sense seeing something like a 'bin' box made up of body parts, but when statues start to test your 'sanity' while being in lusstgha, I think it is detrimental to explore the area, which I wanted to do (even though the area is very linear). When you start losing mentality when you kill people who are actively trying to kill you, I also think it kinda misses the point of 'flight or fight'.This game isn't going to light the world on fire due to innovative gameplay or whatever, but I do think it will keep you interested and engaged for its duration.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has very limited gameplay mechanics, which at times didn't bother me because I took it as more of a story & art-focused game. Sadly the art is not always that good. Lustgha (or however its spelled...) looks more or less the same everywhere; its creepy, but otherwise really boring.As for the story... well it sucks. This is a case of where the mystery is far more compelling until it is revealed.  It's mostly predictable, and forgettable. It's sometimes shocking but only for a moment and then quickly goes back to underwhelming. The ending had no emotional impact for me and it did not strike me as inspired or interesting. There are very many snippets and references to lore scattered throughout the game, but damn are they boring... I tried to read all the documents, notes, etc. in order to immerse myself more into the world of the game, but I can hardly remember any of it; it always felt so overglorified because just like the quotes that display over the loading screen, they sound poetic/philosophical but are actually shallow and non-sensical when you think about them even for a second. It gives the illusion of depth, but no real substance when you break it all down semantically/philosophically. Lastly the horror is bland. I don't hate jumpscares, but on their own they aren't enough. The atmosphere is only tense because you don't know when the next jumpscare is coming. The nasty body-horror is disturbing, but so what? It ceases to be shocking and just becomes unpleasant to look at after a while which ultimately leads to an unpleasant overall experience.Honestly as somebody who loves both horror and eroticism I expected to love this game, but ultimately I was really underwhelmed, bored and overall disappointed. If you're like me, you won't be able to resist this game out of curiousity, but do yourself a favour and lower your expectations, whatever they are.
