_childDocuments_.review: I don't feel like going trying to encapsulate this entire game in a single review, so I'll just focus in on one thing that makes this game unique. The whole appeal of roguelikes is that the randomization doesn't allow you to commit levels to memory, forcing you to master the underlying mechanics rather than just memorizing things in order. However, it is also true that there are almost always certain patterns that you start relying on after a while. Things like the order you do certain bosses, whether you clear out levels before moving on or try to bumrush the boss, etc. This is the only roguelite I've found that forces me to adjust not just my playstyle, but also my underlying strategy every time I enter the Breach. Do you grab the Altar of Blood as soon as you find it, or wait until the end? Well that depends upon how much health you have after beating the first mini boss. Do you get a weapon right away in the first world, or wait until later? That depends on how many rooms you had to clear before you discovered the boss. I've never played another roguelike that forces me to reevaluate the fundamentals on every run quite like Scourgebringer, so if that's what your looking for I cannot recommend this enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Every single aspect of this game is fine-tuned to be as satisfyingly badass as possible. _childDocuments_.review: This is a roguelike game where you cannot get Op throughout your playthrough, it is skill dependent and this is what makes it enjoyable. It is incredibly fast-paced, but that does not mean you blindly run through and smash the attack button as fast as you can, you will get destroyed. It's all about quickly and efficiently positioning yourself and pushing enemies into places on the map where you can reduce the likely-hood of getting hit by the other enemies. You have a gun, a sword with a light attack and a heavy attack for deflecting bullets and stunning enemies. There is also the dash ability, it does not have any i-frames but I find that better, touching enemies does not harm you, you only get harmed from bullets or other attacks, you can get an upgrade that allows you to dash and deflect bullets at the same time but with a 4 second cool down.Tips to combat some criticismGuns not being useful: Dashing, slashing and shooting consecutively into an enemy or group of enemies is fast, efficient and allows you to better manage ammunition and deal lots of damage.attacking moving character around too much: There is a hold button which allows you to lock in your position whether in the air or on the ground to prevent you from moving somewhere while attacking you do not want to.inescapable bullet sprays: Do not deflect towards enemies or boss in cases like this because of course you will get hit, you need to git gud and learn to out maneuver it and use the deflect to open room to escape not deflect back at enemy.
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fluid. It's not the Celeste-Dead Cells mix you're advertised, but I wasn't looking for that. If you want a easy-to-learn, hard-to-master arena roguelike with a focus on movement, combos, juking the AI, and making multiple tactical decisions within actual seconds, you will LOVE THIS GAME. Again, This game is FLUID AS HELL. You have a rock solid set of controls that are simple in execution, but already lend so much depth to how you get around the map. Each movement option can come before or after another one in quick succession.Next, the skill tree allows you to take the depth of the game slowly, easing you into it until you're a pro.You're eased into the combat, and for a good while, world 1 is a good enough challenge! You will die to not having enough awareness of the map, or stray projectiles, and so on. Yes, I'm dedicating a section to just one move, but THIS MOVE IS THE BEST IN THE ENTIRE GAME.It starts simple. You smash a vulnerable enemy (with an exclamation mark above it,) and then it's stunned. Then, you realize you can bait the enemy into becoming vulnerable by smashing it while it's  vulnerable. Next, you learn that the hitbox on this thing is probably the most janky thing in the entire game, and extends so far forward that you can almost throw it out before you're ready, and still make plays. Then, you unlock Lethal Club, which acts as a reflector, so you can clear out bullets that previously gave you trouble. THEN, YOU UNLOCK STRIKING SMASH, WHICH REALLY OPENS UP THE GAME. Wanna stun an enemy that's about to laser you from across the map? LITERALLY PLAY POOL WITH YOUR ENEMIES. Finally, you unlock Dragon Punch, which takes the unsafe timing the Smash already had and basically negates it, allowing you to extend the ALREADY BROKEN hitbox even further. I can go on forever about this move. It's really good.All of this in one move. If you can pack this much functionality into ONE MOVE in your game, you know what you're doing.IT IS SO ACCESSIBLE TO PEOPLE WITH ADHD! Its pick-up and play nature, combined with a fast travel system that would make Enter the Gungeon cry, and MANY accessibility options that can make the game  for players with ADHD. Similarly to Celeste, the Accessibility menu adds features like adjustable game speed, more hp drops, complete invincibility, auto-slash, and even a subtle reminder that your health is low.THIS GAME IS REALLY GOOD. PLAY IT. It's not celeste x dead cells, but it's still more than worth it

_childDocuments_.review: This game gets compared a lot to , but while both share a similar degree of mobility and fluidity, a more apt comparison otherwise would be  and . The latter in particular seems to inform much of 's art style, focus on speed and aggressiveness, and general structure (down to such things as enemy mechanics, stat upgrades, item rooms, etc). And that is certainly not a bad thing at all, as 's minimalist but tight design are a great source to take inspiration from. What it does need now however, aside from the obvious missing content, is something that rivals 's synergistic weapon system, because at the moment you only have a single primary melee weapon and accompanying move set for the entire game, with no ways to change it other than upgrading your raw damage. You can get different guns (which closely resemble their counterpart in ), but those are more situational in use. Even with its current limitations however,  already has a lot to offer, and there is most certainly more goodness to come.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to like it but in its current state I don't feel compelled to play more. It has a ton of potential but it's not fun. Still, I recommend it with the hope that with some tweaks it could become a great game. Pros:- Character movement - I love constantly being in the air - Satisfying attack animations and sounds - Interesting and beautiful environmentCons:- Dash has no i-frames. This feels so unnatural that the developers need to tell you it doesn't in the tutorial. On top of that there's no real dedicated dodge option when the enemy design is largely based on spamming projectiles. This means that if you miss the stun on an enemy, your options are to use the slow and unsatisfying deflect (more about that below) or run around like a headless chicken. I don't like being forced to run, I want an option where I can still move in and attack. If that option exists, it wasn't communicated to me and after an hour and a half I gave up trying to figure it out. -The combat seems to rely on the slow heavy attack to stun enemies or deflect. Now, I know it's not objectively slow, it's just slower than everything else the character does, so using it breaks the flow of combat. You feel forced to stop in place for a fraction of a second, which would've been fine if you had to use it every once in a while. But you have to use it All. The. Time. In every stage and multiple times on a single enemy or group of enemies. Dead Cells had more slow and deliberate weapons, which added variety and some people probably liked those more, but it also had options where you could stun enemies with a bomb that is fast and you only need to use once, then move through and finish them off while dodging, attacking, and shooting in one fluid unbroken sequence. This made combat feel fun, intuitive, and you forgot about your end goal while having such a blast playing in the moment. The fun and intuitiveness are just not in this game, yet, and the most frustrating thing is that it's just short of achieving it, so you keep playing, trying to "get it", until you have to accept it's just not there, not for you. - The game is marketed as a mash-up between Dead Cells and Celeste but they completely fail to mention Hyperlight Drifter, when the entire art style and much of the gameplay seem heavily inspired by Hyperlight Drifter. That's not a bad thing in itself, I loved the style of Hyperlight Drifter and it's great to see it being developed further, but I wish they had communicated this more clearly, because actually playing Hyperlight Drifter wasn't quite as fun as Dead Cells or Celeste. It had the exact same feel of having to dash around a lot while being shot at, and while many will enjoy that, I didn't. They either need to provide more varied combat options or simply communicate better their influences, so that I know up front that the intended way to play is just not for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Initially, I gave a negative review, but I would like to amend this to a more neutral review, as I am currently at the final boss in the new updateI said the following previously:"The rooms (all of them) are extremely repetitive and the bonuses that are given in the tree should be toggleable. The shopkeeper is usually too expensive for what it's worth, while the charming artstyle is enjoyable but hampered down in repetitiveness. Not a huge roguelike person so don't know how others who play the genre feel, but the drops don't really affect the gameplay meaningfully to me."I stand by this assessment, but the third and fourth floors do something I feel is necessary to gameplay, and that is, punish you for acting too impulsively (dashspamming), or hinder the ability to dodge behind crevasses and walls, which alters the dynamic decently. _childDocuments_.review: I LOVE this game. I first got an early demo as a part of a bundle and I've loved it ever since.I'm not usually too keen on roguelikes or intense fast combat, but the mechanics are just too fun! It's simple but because it's so fast paced it doesn't get too stale (especially as you gradually progress to find new enemies), and I feel like I'm getting better on every run. I've been playing for about 6 hours and I just made it to the fourth area. I get the impression it's a short game but I haven't reached the ending yet, I prefer to play it in small bursts as to not get burnt out, but it's still in early access so it could easily get longer! Who knows?Speaking of early access, it's currently an option to be able to submit feedback inside of the game which I really love. I'm assuming that'll disappear when early access is over but it's still a great addition.The art style and aesthetic in general is BEAUTIFUL. Pixel art on its own is nothing original but the style is really nice, everything is really pleasing to look at and the base dark purple makes it way more appealing that standard black.Even in early access, it's a really good game that I really recommend if you like roguelikes or intense combat, but keep in mind that I feel it's pretty short, especially if it's taken me so long to get to the fourth area because I'm just not used to these kinds of games. _childDocuments_.review: Take that positive review with an asterisk next to it. This game is actually really, really fun. But theres a few things that can really break the experience. The combat it fluid and chaotic and just makes you feel like a badass every time you finish a room. and this is further emphasized when you get new abilities from the skill tree. The thing is, this game can feel unfair at times. It was fine in the older updates, but with some of the newest updates, the game has become too chaotic and stressful. An example is how with in the older versions, each room only had one to two waves of enemies to deal with. Two waves was perfect, gave a good difficulty, and didn't need to be changed. With the newer updates, there can be up to 3 waves. So when you think you are done, have only 2 or 3 heal left, and then another wave of enemies are trying to rip you apart, it just feels unfair. It's worse with the number of enemies that can spawn in a room at once. The worst offender of this is the second area, were this is very little to maneuver on (this being a game about mobility, that is horrible) and there is 15 to 18 enemies coming at you at once. Again, in the older versions, this wasn't much of a problem. It feels like it's upping the difficulty where it doesn't need to.The last thing is the difficulty spike. The first area is difficult but manageable. But then the second area pops in and now your getting riddled in bullet holes. They really need to balance it out betterThe game is still in early access, so these problems with probably get ironed out, but right now it's just crazy. I still recommend it because of how fun most of the game is. Theres around 4 areas right now, each with there own theme and enemies. As long as you can get past the 2nd area, everything else is amazing other than what's listed above.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, this is not a metroidvania, nor a roguevania. This is just a roguelite game with a map that you can backtrack within the same level. A metroidvania has a persistent world that you can explore at your leisure, and upgrades that change your movement and access to that world. A roguevania is the same as metroidvania, except with procedural generation.I hate just about every single last thing about this game. The music and art are great, love it. Everything else? No.Your movement is floaty, and you don't even really ever need to touch the ground, so you never get any sense of playing a platformer, with physics, and having to time your movement and jumps to avoid enemies.... which is you know, most of what a platformer is. Your attacks makes you automatically glom onto whatever enemy your attack, randomly flitting about them, pushing you into other enemies and hazards all the time, because you can't just jump and hit a guy, you have to float on top of him, mashing attack. This feels *awful*, all the time. It's automatically a dealbreaker for me, right there, because you no longer feel like your position matters. It's only "you're inside the enemy" or "outside the enemy".Any feeling of speed you might ever get from having so much movement capability is ground to a screeching halt when every single room you enter is a very tiny one room arena. And you can't even just blast through the enemies quickly and move onto a new area, and possibly feel any kind of momentum, because in every single last room of the game, a second set of enemies will warp in after you beat the first set. I hate this so much. When you make a game where you have very fast movement and can fluidly hop and dash around, don't immediately then lock the player into tiny claustrophobic rooms, every single room of the game. There should have been varied sizes, and larger areas to actually utilize this kind of semi-flying movement style. Your movement speed and maneuverability is completely wasted in this game.The entire game boils down to glom onto enemy, mash, mash, mash, disengage, smash to reflect projectiles, glom onto another enemy (or, the same one, since many enemies are stupidly tanky to the point where I'm literally passing out from boredom while trying to play this supposedly fast-paced game), repeat ad nauseum.Also.... your dash/dodge doesn't have i-frames. AHHHHHHHH

_childDocuments_.review: I think there is a great game here for people who might enjoy it. I personally couldn't get into it despite enjoying my first 2 runs. I just don't have the motivation to continue past the point I am at but I am also not a huge fan of 2d games with floaty movement mechanics. So, if you like 2-d roguelites AND you like some more floaty feeling movement this game should be right up your alley. I think it should be good. I just didn't get enthralled.
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: This game scratches that itch of a roguelite with supremely good combat and movement (can feel weird at first, but it's worth it when you adjust).  It's all so well tuned and polished that I picked it up in 30 mins, and went on to be amazed at how challenging it can get.  I got as far as level 3, not sure what's past that, but I'll be playing to find out.
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very fast paced. You spend most of your time flitting around in the air and swinging your sword attacking enemies. It's more offensive than trying to dodge or defend. Getting shot at? Do a heavy swing your sword to block/reflect. Going to get hit? Attack them first. There are much better roguelites out there. While this one isn't bad, I can't recommend it at this price point.
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: roguelikes are at their best when the upgrades you get during a run changes completely your playstyle, have great synergies and make every run feel unique.This game isn't the best at that, the upgrades you get are stuff like "+30% damage with the gun if you are in the air while holding your breath and looking away from the screen" which is underwhelming af, if not useless.However the combat and the mobility is awesome. I also love the speed modifier. It's fun to play the game at 150% speed
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: I reckon this game is pretty fun. This is more of a personal review, as opposed to a mass audience type of thing.I suffer from Diabetic Neuropathy in my left eye since about 4 months ago, so my opinion is a little skewed, "Why would a half blind guy play a game with bullet hell elements?" Yeah, I know.The pacing starts out fine for a game of this type, but you get butchered (A LOT) restarting is fast, and you don't really feel like the game is 'too punishing' or unfair, you just gotta git good, learn the different enemy types and use the lightning fast movement and potentially infinite 'double' jump to your advantage.There are minimal invincibility frames here, usually just after you get hit, which makes the dodge feel kinda bad at first. You can still be hurt mid dodge, in fact, it isn't really a dodge at all, much more of a means to close the distance between enemies rapidly, but try telling your brain that. I was dashing into projectiles and taking hits for a long while before I grasped that I was 'doing it wrong'Next is the gun... (Blast.32 iirc), this is your ranged weapon, which I still find I don't use nearly enough. I am forever leaving ammo refills on the ground to come back for later because I don't need them at the time. It does feel a little underwhelming, but like I said, I probably just need to use it more, at least there is that option.The game seems to kinda drip feed in elements that I feel should be available from the start, such as the combo meter. You are encouraged to play fast to keep the combo growing, so you can earn more Blood (Currency) This keeps the action moving, and feels good. I just don't really understand why it is something you have to unlock, since it fundamentally changes the way you played the game before you had access to it.I'm not really sure what this is, not really a review, just a little ranting/opinions. The pacing feels awesome, and the game is fun to play, I think with my lame vision, I just struggle a bit.I'd recommend it, I think it is cool, gonna keep playing to see if I can win. 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: I love a lot of things about this game, but ultimately for me it was just too hard. I tend to play hard roguelikes, so I was a little surprised that I've stopped the enjoying the game before I got good enough to regularly progress to the 3rd level. So, I guess I'd have to recommend that you pass on it.
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough one; so much style, but I can't give it a thumbs up. The music, aesthetic, movement and quality are all great, with some super cool boss designs, but there just isn't enough of anything for the price, or to make the gameplay loop satisfying.I've played through this entirely off steam, and found that after a handful of runs, I'd made it to the final biome and purchased all of the upgrades, with very little motivating me to continue. The lore is outlined so minimally that it errs on the side of redundant, the NPCs have barely any interaction (the base one literally sleeps unless you find something new for the first time, so about a dozen interactions in total), and while the rooms and enemies are random each time, there are a couple of minibosses per biome (literally a couple) with a single recurring final boss per stage.I know they've add modding capability now so I can see the playtime increasing from the community, but as it stands, I'd suggest instead looking to something like Hades or Binding of Isaac, which have a ginormous amount more content for the price and effort.
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: As it's been a while since I first reviewed the game I decided that I should update my opinion on the it. Previously, I did not recommend the game as I felt that it was too easy and not worth the 15 buck I paid. I will leave the original review because I think it still holds some merit but I believe that the game has improved a good deal since. The addition of 3 more bosses and challenging environments as well as the trials you unlock after first beating the game have added a lot more replay value to the game than its initial release offered as well as a more difficult and rewarding experience. There are also more guns that can be used and mods that can be added to them so your build can vary slightly (although not very much and imo assault rifle is kinda op). The game is still the same in terms of combat as my original review (i.e. spam everything you got until it dies) but the addition of 3 more floors makes you have to be more cautious with preserving life so you don't run out and die. One big problem I have is that some of the alter choices feel like they provide no value while others are almost necessary to win the run which coupled with the same combat mechanics makes the game grow boring pretty quickly but the fast pace action can make up for it.I think that if you want to play a quick paced, challenging game and have some loose change, the with all the additional content plus the addition of in game challenges have made the current iteration of the game is now worth the 15 dollars I originally paid.Original review:(I want to preface that I still enjoyed the game and have high hopes for its future because the game's core mechanics are pretty fun and It looks awesome. The problem for me it there is not much diversity to game play and the advanced technique of spamming dash, gun, sword, and that stunning attack is enough to kill all bosses in a matter of seconds. It took me 3 hours to beat the game (to it's current point) and while it was fun during that time I don't think it's worth the 15 bucks as it currently is. That said, this is what i think could be improved off the top of my head:- implement different types of melee weapons (because I'm getting bored of the stabby sword)   that have different attack speeds, ranges, and effects.- make it more penalizing to spam all your abilities at the same time.- improvement to the items that drop and the totem buff things because I'll be honest, it   doesn't feel any different to play the game if you have 20 buffs or having none.- add in a hard mode)
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: Celeste came of age and had a baby with Doom Slayer.  The combat is smoother than Olive Garden's fettuccine alfredo.  The overall experience is as cohesive as an Isaac Asimov novel.At the time of writing this review, the learning curve is quite steep; I'd expect the game to be extremely frustrating, maybe even inaccessible, to someone without experience on a fast-paced precision action game, like 90's Mario/Sonic, Celeste, or Hotline Miami.  That might change when the game comes out of early access, and is understandable since it would be unfortunate to have carefully-crafted learning/tutorial levels invalidated by a change in the mechanic.
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: I've been keeping an eye on this game since 2018 or so, and wanted to give it some shine since it came out. here is my update since my first 50 minutes:+ PHENOMENAL combat. it's exhilarating to dash between enemies, slashing and shooting and maneuvering for the perfect hit that gets you to avoid taking damage.+ INCREDIBLE pixel art and animations. Has a unique vibe with terrific art design that keeps it from looking generic. the closest comparison visually is Hyper Light Drifter (a game I am coincidentally trying out now), but even that has a wildly more neon style to it that sets it far apart from ScourgeBringer.+ great music. really gets you goin'.+ has a fun, snarky sense of humor that I wasn't expecting at all.+ upgrades so far seem to have real weight to them.+ cool worldbuilding.+ getting back into the fray is super quick and easy, making the "just one more go" itch endemic to roguelites such as this incredibly easy to scratch.ScourgeBringer has only improved since its Early Access phase, I adore it and it's been an essential part of my downtime regiment. when you're doing great, you feel like an absolute god/goddess. highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: I have played a lot of games, and with 2 exeptions, it usually was kill time more than to have fun.But this game is one of those exeptions.The controls are tight, the soundtrack is great, and if you havent noticed this game is beatiful.For starters, this game is more combat based with platforming elemants than platforming based with combat elementsThe combat feels great, its fluid and has a  high skill ceiling.This game has a pretty solid enemy diversity already and the bosses feel very unique compared to other games. It has the boon of the entire room fitting into the screen which makes the combat close quarters and overall more fair.Something that concerned me at first is that usually with heavy combat focused games like this, if the pacing focuses only on combat it can end up stale. But this is an exeption, the platforming elements smoothly (again, tight controls) diverse the pacing (unlike in Dead Cells where the platforming is absolute cancer, dont worry about that).Of course, being an early access game, content is still on its way. But know this, I have 24 hours on the closed alpha, which Ill say had around 14% of the content you will be getting from the current version (mind you, not the full game)
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: For a game in alpha, this rougelike has already built an addictive, fast-paced, and extremely mobile combat system that on its own is near worth the price of this game. Not to mention the wide move set that adds subtle intricacies and expands into more fun gameplay options as you progress through the skill tree. The only negatives I really have is the repetition of rooms and a lack of realms, but again this game is in alpha and the developers have already been consistently releasing updates with more scheduled, so this is really a non-issue. If you are a fan of action based rougelikes or are a fan of fluid and dynamic combat, this game is a steal.
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty great game, combat feels smooth as ♥♥♥♥ and it's really fun to dash around the room like a meth addicted squirrel shooting and slicing through everything, perfect mix between mindless button mashing and quick thinking and precision. graphics are alright, simple style and some cool designs here and there. Soundtrack really gets you pumped when you enter a new combat room and then the idle track which is great so you can backtrack without having your ears blown out. As a rougelite it is lacking a few areas such as the progression is so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ grindy, Honestly my main gripe with the game is that it's a grindfest of smashing your head against the wall forever all for some really uninteresting upgrades and then eventually getting the important ones after going through the others, There is no variety in your runs as the guns and perk shrine give you ♥♥♥♥ that is so interchangeable that I legit don't even pick them up sometimes cause they don't do ♥♥♥♥. Still a real fun and great game that I recommend, If you don't think it's for you then maybe get it on sale?
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: My complaint about this game is that there is no variety. Made it to act 4, and all the enemies are recolors of the act 1 enemies. _childDocuments_.review: Should have been a rogueLIKE with a slightly tighter movement system and it was perfect.A beautiful and frantic game wasted on poor design decisions that just make it frustrating to play.Basically, a total lack of fair healing and some weird out of control auto-moves like when you attack, or sometimes slightly off auto-aimed dashes, or even some moves with unclear recovery, makes taking damage kind of unfair.Add to that some enemies that are just WAY too fast to correctly react and predict with your slow heavy attack to parry (if they even have a "charging" animation at all).And of course the LITE element of unlocking the means to actually play the game, however still on quickly repetitive layouts and items that don't add to the experience.All of that sadly put me off.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the most initially exciting games and most disappointing games I've ever played. The perfect example of wasted potential. It just shouldn't have been a roguelite.Every single run is the exact same. You use the exact same mechanics to fight the exact same enemies in the exact same rooms over and over again in rooms that look the same in a map that is mostly the same because it has 0 thought put into it.With such a snappy movement and combat system, this game would've been an amazing metroidvania, slowly unlocking all the mechanics the devs just dump on you as soon as you start. Or at the very least, there could be some interesting unlocks (new weapons, new areas etc.) or satisfying unlocks (just more damage or health to start with, not just 2 initial health upgrades you buy immediately). It's crazy how quickly I got bored of the game once I realized this was all that it offers.Hopefully this team makes something with the same gamefeel quality, but better overall design in their next project.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game, if it wasn't a roguelite. There is almost none run to run variation. Most of the things are small bumps on stats, there are altars that matter a bit when it happens but it's still not impactful. The biggest impact would be the gun but not enough for me to think the game is different enough. The first and second level maps are pretty boring with the third having a nice environmental change. _childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game for what it is, the combat is pretty fun in short bursts, it's just not fun for dozens upon dozens of  nearly identical rooms. This is basically the same problem I had with Monolith/ Star of Providence. A really neat idea for a game, but the execution doesn't have enough visual depth or gameplay variety to avoid going stale faster than McDonald's fries.  Worse, so many of the things which would make this game really fun are hidden behind "upgrade" currency.  It just disguises a very simple game as a grind which isn't an upgrade.

_childDocuments_.review: I just feel a little disappointed by this game honestly. _childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, I can't recommend this one. I've had fun when it started. It was fluid, fast paced, the graphics weren't too much of an eye sore, the music was pumping ... but after a few attempts it's become painfully obvious that the game doesn't have any long-term fun for me.The meta-progression unlockables don't feel all that interesting imho, the in run upgrades don't either. The gun is extremely underwhelming and hard to use in such a fast paced game, when you play with a controller.The rooms and enemies are extremely repetitive. You will face the same 3 to 4 enemies in EVERY room in the 1st world. Then the 2nd world adds a few more, but the time until you get there is just ... too much.I've had about 20 or so runs and each and every one of them has been almost identical. From the way I fight to what I fight to where I fight.Even the music is the same for EVERY fight. Then you get a new combat track in the next world, which you get to hear for another 15 minutes until you reach the next world, etc.Finally beaten the first boss after tuning down the difficulty a bit (accessibility options are a plus here, but can actually make it harder instead of easier ...) Almost beaten the second boss, but I just don't feel like continuing to eventually beat the remaining 5 bosses in what must be hours and hours of mindless grinding.It almost feels like it was designed for mobile. Hop in, do a room or two, then hop out again, but then again, controlling this on a mobile device seems ... horrible. But wouldn't you know it? It IS a mobile game. Go figure.Take other rogue-lites, for example. Like Neon Abyss or Dead Cells, or even Hades ... all of which just have so much more to offer, where every run feels different, has different levels, weapons, power ups, etc.Here, you have a sword. And a gun you can use intermittenly. And that's it. You can unlock a few more moves through progression, yeah, but ultimately ... it's lackluster. Then again, for a mobile game it's probably pretty good.
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: Basic game loop is nice and fast, controls are responsive, but there is little else going on. After the introduction, there is very little progression of characters or story. You can grind a while to unlock all skills from the skill tree, but these feel barely noteworthy. There are some more to unlock, but I would have to beat the level 5 boss when I can barely reach level 3. When there are no interesting rooms or events to find, the grind alone will not convince me to keep playing.
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: As a person who pretty much grew up in the rogue-like genre's birth (Binding of Isaac, Spelunky, etc.) this game takes that concept to what I would consider it's perfection. As many people say, it's like the combination of Celeste and most rogue-likes, which I would agree on. The controls are extremely tight and responsive, and the gameplay is challenging, but not unforgiving; every time I lose a life, it felt like my fault, and even on ones that I think was accidental, I look back and realize that it was quite the contrary.While I don't have many hours on this game (yet) I feel that it's going to be a good mainstay for the quick game session before work, or just after getting up to get my reflexes in check, it's a great trainer for on the go planning and execution, and I love that about it, to me I like Isaac, but that game is too slow paced for what I'm in there for, this hits the perfect balance of being quick, but not feeling like it's rushing me to complete every stage, and the completion of the game doesn't feel impossible either, not easy, but not at all impossible.This game is something interesting, and I hope that it gets more traction from those in the rogue-like community. A solid [9.5/10]
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: I've conquered the true ending in Dead Cells, escaped hell in Hades on 30+ heat many times, and bested the 5th pantheon in Hollow Knight. I'm confident I've played about 80% of the games in this genre, but never before have I felt such rage at poor game design. At first glance, this game appears to be a well-crafted indie gem with flawless, flashy combat that you hope will satisfy that familiar roguelike itch. However, every built-in system has some quirk that makes it unfun:Not many times after I lost a run felt, "okay, this was my fault, I'll try to get better next time" because beneath the flashy combat, the whole game just feels like a hot mess.  5/10

_childDocuments_.review: The procedural generation in this game compliments its action-heavy nature by creating a 'hack n' slash' in which the player can be both stylish, and self expressive. The game could use a bit more variety that I'm happy to see the developers implementing with constant updates. I highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys the free expression of Devil May Cry, with the procedural generation of a game like DeadCell, and the visual art of Celeste.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game the other day after hearing about it online. Scourgebringer is extremely enjoyable, even with it being in Early Access. Game is super fun and challenging. _childDocuments_.review: honestly so far my experience has been kind of just okay. i feel that the inability to cancel sword combos into other attacks makes you feel like you have way less control over the fast gameplay than you should have. also the fact that its so easy to accidentally miss a point-blank heavy attack is a bit of a fun-ender for no reasonthere are also *too* many types of attacks. you've got a main attack, a heavy attack, a dash attack, a fury attack which just is a full-screen AoE, and a gun which i forget is even there. also there's too many movement options, i also forget there even is a wall running ability because it's so unnecessary with the dash, double jump and everything. i often feel like i confuse buttons with other buttons because they all kinda mesh into one single spam of buttons.also the battle music is a bit obnoxiously intense, like calm the ♥♥♥♥ down, it's so unfitting lol. this game has a crappy edgyness to it that's annoying and badthat's also reflected in some of the enemy designs which are a bit obnoxious aswell, and kind of bring the whole experience down. a game like this should have a health system like Hades, which allows for more leniency, instead of a system where small hits and BIG hits deal the same damage, and thus you're punished for the tiniest of slip-ups the same as you would be for a terrible misplay in a bossfightlet me talk about the movement aswell. it feels strangely slippery. not nearly tight or consistent enough for the types of situations the game throws at me. the dashes can also lead you into an enemy while missing their hitbox, leaving you open for a hit somehow. which is just very stinky.at the end of my experience, i found myself just wanting to close the game because i wasn't enjoying it

_childDocuments_.review: Legitimately one of the best combat systems out of any roguelite I've played. Once you get a feel for staying in the air as much as possible it becomes incredibly satisfying. _childDocuments_.review: Interesting idea, but the movement concepts present suck. Getting stuck in the air while attacking and getting constantly stuck to walls is more obnoxious than intersting and having attacks shift you all around enemies (and probably into enemy fire) is also obnoxious. Dashing slashes carrying larger enemies with you instead of moving you through them is an equally stupid decision since it typically invites damage. That's my core issue-the things you do in game are typically more risk than reward and leads to frustrating hits where you feel like you have no control. Also, why is this a rogue-like? Having tighter designed levels and set character increases makes more sense than random bad rooms and uninteresting stat boosts would be far more interesting than yet another ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ taco rogue like.

The gun is underwhelming. I think it barely does damage for all of the work that you do to make it reload. It takes 2 hits to kill a floor 1 enemy. Bad.- The smash' hitbox is just  big enough to hit the 3 demons' projectiles. You will mistime it. A lot. This is a floor 1 enemy by the way! There might be an skill tree upgrade to make it bigger, but I honestly don't really enjoy the grind. At least there are in-run upgrades to increase the range of it at least. Oh, but I can't really control what i get to drop, now can I?! Expensive shops. Yeah.- The game doesn't feel hard because you didn't master the mechanics yet, but because you have to grind out the (quite literally) skill tree.- "Adaptive difficulty", yet no option to actually change the difficulty manually from what I could find in the settings. Why do I have to pretend to be at a certain skill level to change the difficulty the way I want it to be? Oh, and what does this "adaptive difficulty" even change? I don't understand...Now, I don't hate the game. This is a cool game. But the negatives put a damper on my personal experience. Yes, I probably will continue to play it, but I would like to have my concerns addressed.(P.S: Now that I know you read the review, you have been blessed with the knowledge that the comment section is open! Feel free to leave some comments and I will gladly read through them.)

_childDocuments_.review: So, what is ScourgeBringer? Short answer: "Thanks, I hate it."Long Answer: It's a pixel platformer with a kickin' soundtrack and great controls. However, It's not a rogue-like or rogue-lite. It may say it on the box, but it's a punishing platformer with a poor attempt at "rogue" mechanics. It relies more on player twitch reflexes than crafting a working build out of the available parts. However, the parts that are rogue inspired are all rusted and dull, providing very little positive value to a run success. It doesn't help that the enemies are one-note and only get hard when there are tons on screen and all firing projectiles in your general direction. However, you are woefully inadequate to combat bullets at the beginning with no real counter outside of a bullet reflect perk gained by the "progression macguffins" obtained after every sub/main level boss which are the only thing carried over after death. Nothing changes between runs except the perks you come equipped with and only add a sprinkle of flavor to an otherwise bland chance at success.That being said it's not my cup of rogue tea. Get it on sale if you really want it, but don't go into the game thinking Dead Cells level of build crafting. However, definitely expect to die and repeat the same process over and over again (Look ma! I found the Rogue-like).
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: There's multiple small issues that build on each other and make the game unenjoyable.This will be repeated throughout the game and it does not change. This would be fine if the enemies were interesting, but so far, I haven't found any difference between level 1 fodder and level 2 fodder, and mini bosses don't require much though either.This makes combat even more shallow. So far, I've only seen buffs to base stats, nothing that would change how your run plays out. You will be slashing, shooting, and smashing the same way as the first level, just with more efficiency. The repetitiveness of the combat is made worse by the gun being unviable. The bullets are too weak and don't have much utility since ranged enemies are not an issue. I mostly found myself spamming the shoot button while slashing, which ignores the point of a ranged weapon. However, there's not enough ammo in the gun and reloads takes too long to make this a viable way of killing enemies faster.This only impacts controller users and cannot be turned off in the menu. When dashing, the game will correct the direction of the dash, making it so if you were trying to dash past an attack and be in range to counter, you'll jut go head first into damage. This is compounded by the a lot of attacks requiring precise movements to avoid and the fact that dash has no invulnerability frames, making it annoying to deal with.There are some minor elements that don't seem to work well together. The game want's you to be aggressive, so it gives to a dash attack and the smash to countering attacks and stun enemies and reflect bullets. However,All of this builds upon itself making the game generally unenjoyable for me. It's a hard game but there's not much else going on aside from it being hard. If repetitiveness doesn't bother you and some of these issues don't sound deal breaking, the game can be fun.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is extremely fun and aggravating at the same time. The controls are wonderful and the fighting feels great! A floating Head's gameplay: I just don't think I'm that skilled enough to play through an entire map perfectly, take minimum damage and then survive a boss battle at half-health. Then do it all over again when I die. This game is the epitome of "get good". That said: all this coupled with the fantastic controls and fluid movement; it's balanced perfectly to challenge the most skilled platforming gamers.I'd recommend this for those players that want a challenging experience with great controls and movement.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I start I do recommend this game. However, it does not make a super great first impression. Look at most of the negative reviews' play time and that should become apparent.  I was frustrated at first, and there is a really big difficulty spike in the 3rd level because the first level fails to teach you how to play, just how to stun lock enemies around the room.Then I started to figure it out, and it started getting really fun.  Its fast, a little frantic, the controls are as precise as you make them, and the added challenges in the later levels make things interesting and challenging.My advice, remember to stay calm. The first hour or two I'd get my blood up a bit and start making more mistakes and enter a death spiral of sorts.  Just chill, take a break. Try a run with some of the accessibility options to learn enemy and boss patterns.  Then, turn them off and try again, or don't. Its definitely not an easy game but its a fun game to learn and get better at. If you like Sekiro in the way that it makes you get really good at one type  of gameplay then you'll probably like getting good at this one too.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun, fast, arcade rogue-lite, with a accessible game loop. This game has changed a bunch since it's early access.On its 1.0 version (release out of early access), they changed the game to allow players to have way more tools.The game feels fluid, easy to pickup and intimidate to master.You can unlocked and then disable/enable abilities and passives to learn everything in the game as well as to gain achievements.Each biome has good feeling difficult progression, they don't feel unique but different enough.Each complete run through is about 15 to 30 minutes long, so it's considerably fast paced. And they reward you for going fast.The only thing I wish was in the game was a wishing well of sorts where you can gamble away judge blood (meta rewards) to gain random rewards or to spawn random enemies for blood. I have racked up 500 judge blood and haven't progressed far enough to spend it else where. It would be nice to have a random thing feature to spend it on.Could definitely see them creating another main character with a completely different play-style.There's so much that could be done.Love the lore of the world and arena you're battling in.I just need more.Like maybe alternative routes with a different main and mini-bosses.I play this game for 30 minutes to an hour each day.

_childDocuments_.review: ScourgeBringer seems really promising and is actually a lot of fun, however, it's simply way too difficult to be enjoyable for long because it's hard to make much progress. I've played for several hours and the farthest I've made it is a room into level three. It would be awesome if the game had a difficulty starting with something a bit more forgivable and progressing up to what it is now. I like the use of the concept of starting back at the beginning, like in Dead Cells, but this game is far too brutal that it ends up feeling frustrating rather than fun.One other thing thats a bit annoying is frequent music changes which are bit harsh. The quick switches between ambient and hardcore music is distracting. Why does the music need to change when fighting ordinary mobs? Seems like it should be reserved for the mini bosses and judges. The regular background music is nice and I think the aesthetic of the game would be improved if it played out most of the time.If these aspects of the game were improved, I'd give it a thumbs up. It loads of fun to play and I'd like to be able to play it to completion.

_childDocuments_.review: The game could be fun, but the controls are just abysmal. Your character sticks to every wall, suspends in the air during the attack, basically she does everything to reduce the mobility and get shot.There's no need in wall climbing during fights. A separete button could be used to perform the action. Or even a better idea -  just scrap the whole mechanic altogether and not design the levels with wallclimbing in mind. _childDocuments_.review: I know it is a subjective thing to say, but this game is hard af. One minute I've got all my hearts with just a couple more rooms to clear before I get to the boss, and then BOOM I am down to 3 hearts and now gotta fight the boss. Booooo.I have been playing the game a lot recently..... almost have my entire skill tree filled up. I have noticed a slight improvement. I am able to get to the 3rd biome now, and I think I might have reached the mini boss, but I don't remember because I was loaded up on ambien. I think the game is very fun, very addicting, very frustrating, very colorful and well designed characters, and I like that I am able to turn down the speed of the enemy bullets. But its still just too hard. I've learned how to control it now, but there are tiny flaws in the game that constantly throw wrenches in my game... such as not being able to attack a room boss on the ground when its standing on hidden spikes because I trigger the spikes. Or the swiping motion of the sword missing a bullet because the bullets were too close together. Tiny things like this will drain your life fast. I'm really look forward to the full release, and I hope that there will be more health to acquire throughout the runs. Also, there needs to be some identification on some of the buttons and weapons and store things, for us gamers that don't know what everything is. Other than that, dope ass game!!

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Got to stage 4 with nearly max hp. When I entered the portal to the next level the game crashed and I lost all progress, so switching from recommend to not. Getting to the later levels is difficult enough without that added possibility.You know that feeling when you are playing DMC or a similar slash-em-up like Hyperlight Drifter, or Hades, and you stylishly clear an entire room of mobs without getting a scratch? It's missing from this game most of the time for some reason. It LOOKS really good when you watching it, but that feeling is missing.Urrrrhg. I'm leaning towards not recommending, but I keep turning the game back on for more punishment so I guess I like it?And like... I could change the difficulty, but my pride won't allow it so I guess I'll just suffer or get good. _childDocuments_.review: When I was reading the info about this game, I was just thinking "Let this not be just another randomly generated map game", reason to be, the maps in those kinds of games get to be very generic and the game itself very monotone.Many people say that every run feels the same, and I think that argument requires some context. It wouldn't be bad to repeat the same level in a game where you progress throughout an specific dungeon, like in Celeste where you move through a map and if you fail you will repeat the same map. In Celeste it works because the tone changes constantly. This game feels the same the whole run, it gets repetitive and the enemies get very uninteresting quickly.The over punishing mechanics don't make this any of it forgivable, not even the music, despite been good makes up for the repetitiveness experience.The mechanics are very punishing and is very little incentive to retry after you fail. I really hope the game improves, I really do hope I have reasons to come back and change this review, so please take this comments in a constructive way.

_childDocuments_.review: ScourgeBringer : By Triple F"ScourgeBringer," developed by Flying Oak Games and released in 2020, is a fast-paced roguelite platformer that combines fluid combat mechanics with challenging procedurally generated levels. Set in a post-apocalyptic world where a mysterious entity called the Scourge has devastated humanity, players take control of Kyhra, a skilled warrior tasked with venturing into the ever-shifting depths of an ancient machine to save what remains of her world. With its pixel art style, intense soundtrack, and focus on fast reflexes, "ScourgeBringer" has been praised for its addictive gameplay and tight controls, drawing comparisons to titles like Celeste and Dead Cells while establishing its own unique identity.Combat mechanics are at the heart of "ScourgeBringer," designed to keep players constantly on the move. Kyhra can perform a range of actions, slashes, dashes, wall jumps, and gun attacks all of which flow seamlessly together, allowing for highly mobile combat. The game’s signature “smash” move interrupts enemy attacks and plays a key role in combos, letting players chain together moves without touching the ground. This results in a thrilling, aerial combat style that rewards precision and timing, creating a sense of rhythm where players are both attacking and evading in rapid succession. This combination of speed and skill makes every fight feel dynamic and responsive, with the control scheme allowing even beginners to pull off advanced maneuvers after a bit of practice.Level design in "ScourgeBringer" is procedurally generated, featuring rooms that vary in layout, enemy types, and hazards on each run. The levels are split into distinct biomes, each with its own unique aesthetic and enemy set. Players must clear rooms filled with enemies and traps to advance, collecting upgrades and items along the way. Each area culminates in a challenging boss fight, testing the skills acquired throughout the run. The randomness of each room’s layout and content keeps gameplay fresh, as players are forced to adapt to new configurations and enemy placements. This element of unpredictability reinforces the roguelite structure, giving each run a unique flavor while encouraging players to refine their approach with each attempt.Progression and upgrades are integral to the roguelite experience, and "ScourgeBringer" handles this aspect with a blend of permanent and temporary upgrades. During each run, players collect “Judge Blood,” a currency that can be spent on permanent upgrades in the skill tree. These upgrades range from increased health and improved weaponry to new abilities like double jumps or faster dashes, giving players more tools for future attempts. Additionally, temporary boosts and items, like increased attack speed or health regen, can be found within each run, adding a strategic layer to progression. This dual progression system gives players a sense of accomplishment, as even failed runs contribute to long-term growth, making each attempt feel worthwhile and encouraging persistence.The boss fights in "ScourgeBringer" are a standout feature, providing a marked increase in difficulty and testing players’ mastery of movement and combat mechanics. Each boss, called a “Judge,” has unique attack patterns and abilities that force players to adjust their tactics and think critically about timing and positioning. These fights require fast reflexes, as players must dodge projectiles, counter attacks, and strike back with precision. The boss encounters are intense, demanding both memorization of attack patterns and adaptability, and each victory feels hard-earned and rewarding. These climactic battles serve as skill checks, challenging players to make use of everything they’ve learned so far in order to progress.Art and sound design work in harmony to create an atmosphere that is both gritty and energetic, perfectly suiting the game’s fast-paced action. "ScourgeBringer" uses a pixel art style with intricate animations, capturing the fluidity and intensity of combat while lending each enemy and environment a distinct look. The visual design is enhanced by a pulsing electronic soundtrack by composer Joonas Turner, whose music brings a sense of urgency to every encounter. Sound effects are sharp and impactful, reinforcing the visceral feel of each hit and dash. Together, the art and sound create a cohesive experience that amplifies the game’s sense of momentum, keeping players engaged as they dash and slice through each room.Difficulty and learning curve are important aspects of the "ScourgeBringer" experience, as the game is unapologetically challenging from the start. The fast-paced combat, coupled with the requirement for precision and timing, can be overwhelming for new players. However, the learning curve is balanced by the game’s tight controls and responsive mechanics, which allow players to feel that improvement is always within reach. Each run feels like a chance to get better, and the incremental upgrades make it possible to progress further with each attempt. The challenge is demanding, but the game’s feedback loop keeps players motivated, making each failure feel like a stepping stone toward eventual success.All in all, "ScourgeBringer" is a masterfully crafted roguelite that shines through its fast-paced combat, fluid controls, and immersive atmosphere. It successfully blends challenging gameplay with satisfying progression, making each run feel like a meaningful part of the journey. While the difficulty may be daunting, the game rewards perseverance and skill, creating an addictive loop of action, growth, and discovery. The art style, music, and overall presentation elevate the experience, making "ScourgeBringer" a standout title in the roguelite genre. For fans of intense, skill-driven games that prioritize movement and combat, "ScourgeBringer" offers an exhilarating adventure that is as rewarding as it is punishing.

_childDocuments_.review: Here’s my first impression review of this game. Responsive controls, good art design, great pixel art including the animations. Taking damage is very easy. No guaranteed recovery during gameplay. Not before boss fights and not after boss fights either. In order to progress you need to play FLAWLESSLY. In order to even practise boss fights you have to play from the start again to the point you were and hope that you won’t get wrecked in the process. Environment hazards tend to occasionally blend in which makes taking damage even easier. Repetitive music, which frequently oscillates between calm and aggressive, gets annoying rather fast. Fortunately the music can be configured to be less dynamic. I like difficult action oriented games which can serve even an insane level of challenge when it’s done at a piece meal sized segments. They still offer a fair challenge which can be easily practised as the segments are short and can be repeated quickly. This kind of difficulty can be found from games like Super Meat Boy, Celeste and Rex Rocket.I really don’t like the endurance type of difficulty where instead of mastering tight challenges you are expected to perform less demanding actions perfectly over longer periods of time. The trope “No recovery before a boss fight” is really hitting my nerve and not in a good way: this has soured even otherwise great games like FTL for me.Here the difficulty is based on a simple concept: Do not ever expect recovery. Playing through a level is like running 5 km and then a boss fight without recovery is like doing a 200 m sprint after that. And then once you get past the first boss the game drops into the next harder stage… without ANY recovery.The combat mechanics drive you really fast at the enemies and it feels like the gamepad controls even lock in. While it makes doing damage easier, the opposite is also true. What makes this unbearable is that dodging ranged attacks is very difficult and the expected invulnerability frames during dodge movement just don’t seem to be present at all. So you’ll take damage very easily in a game which basically has the one hit life system instead of energy.This kind of difficulty was also present in many arcade games like Metal Slug series, but in these games you can pop in more credits to continue in case you want to see what the game has to offer for a price. As this game does not allow even that I have a suspicion that there’s not a whole lot of actual content.

_childDocuments_.review: Always wanted a Dead Cells that plays with the crazy fluidity of Celeste's jump'n'dash?What, you didn't even think about it?Then think about it... it's a quite good combination.To not give the wrong impression, both Dead Cells and Celeste are quite larger games than this one, with more depth. But this game is done... ; what it delivers, hits the spot. It is fantastically fluid, tight, and fast-paced. You're totally all over the screen with the incessant jump'n'dash while making split-second decisions.Although it has less depth than Dead Cells, its playthroughs are quicker and they feel lighter, which is a good reason to get into it, especially if you don't have much time and need a small mental break. When I start playing Dead Cells, it takes like 20 or 60 minutes until the game inevitably hands my ass back to me. ScourgeBringer hands me back my ass in four or five times less time. With that, the loss feels less annoying. Also, it's a game you can easily start if all you have is five or fifteen minutes, and prefer them to be intense. You start it, and that's just what you get; unlike with Dead Cells, which you're reluctant to start because you know that if you do, you'll disappear for an hour.And this is truly by design; one of the earliest unlocks is to be shown the direct quickest way to the level's miniboss and then the boss, so you can skip through most of the lower level areas that you're already comfortable with, and rapidly reach the higher levels that you're not.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. Tough but exceptionally fair, given you can slow the game down until you are comfortable.Your first instinct will be to keep up the frantic pace you can move and attack with. Slow down. This is a roguelike in the hard sense. Health is your most important resource and it doesn't rain down on you. You will get SOME health drops, but being reckless will not get you to the end. You need to learn enemy timings, and attack patterns. You need to know how to best take apart a room of enemies by prioritising. Every new level you are going to have to observe as it keeps switching things up. There are bosses that are best fought almost entirely by deflecting their shots back at them.This is also not a game of crazy combos. You are never going to get overpowered, just generally stronger. Your main decisions are around your choice of gun and your choice of blessing which still won't radically alter your gameplay.Finally the game has roguelite elements in the form of a permanent upgrade tree. It will make the game a bit easier, and I think the health upgrades are pretty well essential, but are also the lowest priced on the tree so you won't go without for long.Wholeheartedly recommended. Keep in mind the play-time is fairly short, unless you want to achievement hunt and increase the difficulty once you've beaten it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game had a tonne of heart poured into it. Great, but some flaws. DNF for the time being (you'll see why below), but I'm certain I'll get a hankering to fire it up and beat it proper at some point.Pros:+ Very satisfying, free-flowing movement.+ Gorgeous pixel art, animation, and art direction.+ Tense combat encounters with tough but well designed enemies: you need to make use of all of your abilities, prioritise enemies, and think on your feet. Heavy attacks can stagger enemies in vulnerable wind-ups as well as deflect enemy projectiles, and the dash is an oh so satisfying gap closer. + Good level design; effective use of terrain and new hazards to make you evaluate each situation a little differently. It plays a huge role in enemy prioritisation.+ Heavy OST+ Customisable game speed and difficulty in the options (you'll see a number of reviews call this game too hard: just enable additional pickups and turn the bullet speed way down, should be easier then :) )+ Some fun guns + Interesting boss fights+ Decent meta-progression- Besides the early-game meta-progression, the roguelite aspects very lacking; stats and perks feel very inconsequential at the end of the day. Some perks genuinely feel as if they're nearly completely useless. I can see the original intent in their design, but they're so ill-applicable for most situations, or so generic that you'll always end up with them. Stat increases are cool, but so minor that you barely feel the impact. It's there for sure, and does make a difference, but it is very minor. - This lack of variety makes the game a bit tedious to revisit in later runs, as . No wacky builds and so on. Pair this with larger maps more suited to the roguelite formula a la Isaac, Synthetik 1 and Gungeon. Traversing rooms with arena combat after arena combat. It really starts to drag after the first few hours.Overall, I recommend this game, despite the issues I've had. If you aren't the best with action games that require fast thinking and fast reflexes, just tweak the difficulty in the settings right at the start, rather than fumbling around too much.Looking forward to whatever else these guys make!

_childDocuments_.review: A solid, brutally unforgiving roguelike.ScourgeBringer has quite an innovative gameplay, and the constant dashing makes for very nervous gameplay, with barely any downtime. There's a respectable bestiary, with lots of fun patterns and great artwork, and the overall design is really consistent. Given what the premises are, this could have been a game that rewards you for just ramming into stuff and getting away with just a lot of mashing.Instead, it requires a lot of method and deep understanding of enemy patterns to beat.Just as importantly, the "peripherical" stuff is handled very well. Maps in each world are just the right size. They don't get absurdly large as you progress, and as a result, exploring to make the most out of each act doesn't feel tedious.The game also doesn't punish for trying to go fast. Indeed, you get some stuff for finishing each world under a certain time, which can make up for what you missed by skipping some rooms. Additionally, it's mostly just your stats that change over the course of a run, and while of course it helps to have bigger stats, everything is very approachable if you play well, regardless of how mediocrely you've been doing collecting items.The absence of actually game-changing weapons, crazy synergies and stuff like that might seem like a downside to some people, but the way I see it, the base gameplay is already so rich that it's not a problem, and the game successfully puts the emphasis on that.Now I usually most enjoy games that require you to make perfect use of a couple mechanics to progress. In SB though, it's clearly not enough. You have quite a large moveset, and you do need to incorporate every move in it to maximize your damage, and generally keep doing relevant stuff in every situation. We're not looking at a fighting game level of complexity, but it's not an average shooter/hack n' slash/whatever you want to call it either.As a result, I didn't find myself willing to engage with hard mode after beating it a couple times, but some people certainly will. If you're the kind of person that didn't choose to ignore the style mechanics when playing Devil May Cry, you'll probably enjoy it very much.

_childDocuments_.review: Fast paced, challenging, and you might even break your mouse.  This game REALLY tests your reflexes and pushes them to the limit.  There is always something to focus on, and if you ignore that tiny enemy in the corner that you think isn't a threat, the game will absolutely punish you for it in time.  Wouldn't recommend for anyone that isn't very interested in games with high intensity, but otherwise pick it up.  This game is heavily underrated and deserves some attention.Not everything about the game is great however, the progression for upgrades is fairly meh, you'll get through all the initial upgrades rather fast if you have a high skill level with games like this, but the most of the upgrades don't give you a simple passive perk, most require skill to use properly, and the game rewards you for thinking quickly and making strategic decisions on the fly to make the most out of what it offers.  Otherwise the upgrades give little to no additional benefits.  Move fast, attack fast, hit hard.  At the same time know when to back off, and don't let yourself get greedy.

_childDocuments_.review: For what it's worth, ScourgeBringer is a great, snappy roguelite. It just feels fun to control and makes you feel powerful from the very beginning. The music and sound design are a highlight here: it's all varied and cohesive at the same time. And, sure, some of the enemy types are shared from room to room, but each level has you approaching the fights differently.The only big gripe I have with the game and why I'm bouncing off of it is the difficulty curve. it's a punishing game and I can appreciate that, but I wish that there were more opportunities to recover health, maybe by pulling off difficult technical elements or by defeating enemies in quick succession or clearing rooms without taking damage. It often feels like the game is giving me tools to do really cool and stylish things but punishing me pretty aggressively when I miss once or twice, since the level of bullet hell this game reaches can lead to losing a third of your health pretty quickly. This leads me to play a little more conservatively, which feels less fun.I'd say it's worth full price for the time you get enjoying the game, but I'd definitely pick it up on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic gem of a game. Really unique combat system that feels extremely tactical: you enter a room, have to analyze the threat of every enemy, then plan and execute a route through a room at blazing fast speeds.My two main problems:- Health feels very RNG-dependent. As a newer player you're constantly taking chips of damage and praying for health drops because it can be very punishing. And as a more experienced player you're praying for a shop where items cost health because otherwise all the health drops are useless. Not the worst system but I feel like it could be a lot better.- No build variety. There are occasional upgrades you will get in a run (and some permanent bonuses) but they are all in service of the jack-of-all trades playstyle that requires you to learn and use everything at your disposal all at once. Not really much of a negative IMO because the combat is absolutely superb and the skill ceiling/difficulty makes it very replayable but there aren't different characters or anything to radically change the playstyle.

_childDocuments_.review: Super tight controls that feel amazingly good. The pixel artwork and color palette is delightfully minimal, and evokes a bit of an 8-bit nostalgia, but the game loop has modern rogue-lite progression system not unlike that of Dead Cells. The music is great too! I also really enjoy that a whole game session may be only 10 ~ 15 minutes long, and you can even save and quit any time you're not in combat, then resume the run later. Overall, it's super enjoyable to play, and with the short sessions, it's a perfect game to play on a quick break.My one complaint is that it's a bit more difficult than I would like. I suppose that with enough practice, I might eventually beat that 3rd world... but I worry that I may never be able to. It kinda sucks that I've played through worlds 1 and 2 enough times to collect enough of the persistence currency to unlock almost all of the abilities in the skill tree, but it seems that I need to beat the boss of the 3rd world before the top branch of abilities even becomes available - and I may never have the reflexes to get that far.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly wasn't sure if I'd ever beat this game after I unlocked the full skill tree and still struggled to keep up with the later stages, but I pulled through and I think it's quite solid with a few things that feel a bit off. The only reasonable way I've found to have anywhere near enough health left for the 5th zone bosses is to get the one powerup that restores all health. I think instead there should be the ability to reroll guns and mods in the shop to healing items seeing as I always have plenty of blood for it. _childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: If you want a fast paced, stylish action game, I fully recommend ScourgeBringer.It's so statisfying to go full Unga Bunga and mash buttons in this game. Not that the gameplay is mindless (you get shredded pretty quickly in later levels if you don't play efficiently), just that your aggression feels well rewarded and visceral.Other reviews mention a lack of content, and I'd say that's a fair criticism; you'll notice it. I think what is there, ends up being enough, but your mileage may vary. Overall, the focus is more on you getting better as a player, rather than your character getting stronger from a skill tree.The other criticism I'm seeing has to do with how the game controls (your dash doesn't make you invincible, you can't block, etc.), I think it comes down to how much effort you're willing to put in. Once you get used to the tools the game gives you, you'll figure out how to handle seemingly unfair encounters. It's so satisfying to plow through enemies/environments that used to seem overpowered; but yeah, until you get over those hurdles, it can be frustrating.All in all, I hope to see more games like this, with their foot fully on the accelerator.
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer

_childDocuments_.review: The game is really good, fast, furious, and very skill-based.My only issue goes to controls which could've been a bit more polished. For example, if you're "glued" hitting one enemy, you can't easily peel off to attack another one. Sometimes with mid-bosses, you keep attacking them after they're dead, and it happened I couldn't unglue fast enough to get to the next enemy that was preparing a shot.Your basic sword slashing overrides any other input you might want - including the smash which is the only way to deflect bullets or stun enemies, and including the dash. in the gist of a massive fight, when you stop counting the hits and start almost button mashing - this makes you glued to an enemy that you don't care about at all, instead of letting you switch over to another target easily.Finally, the dashing, being so important and all - is bind to your mouse cursor rather than your directional keys. This means that if you're shooting an enemy and want to dash into the one behind you - you have to move your mouse across the screen. Similarly, if you aim up and jump to hit an enemy - sometimes you'll jump over your cursor, and then if you dash - you'll slam to the ground rather than pinning this enemy against the ceiling.These little details may not seem like much - but in a fast paced game like this, they're pretty frustrating. It feels like you have a good plan and what often messes me up, is that I didn't position my cursor perfectly so I hit the edge of the platform with my head. In the chaos of the battle, my eyes are already looking for next targets, because I'm assuming I'm attacking the one I dashed towards to - but instead, I'm stuck in some unplanned place and it really destroys the flow of the battle when this happens.Despite this - its all probably solvable with painful upskilling and getting good. If you have time to learn to fight input that doesn't help you, you'll love this game. Otherwise, if you like action roguelikes - you'll probably just like it.
_childDocuments_.name: ScourgeBringer
