_childDocuments_.review: Dandy Ace is a rogue-lite experience that takes so much from existing rogue-lite games and is so afraid of trying something on its own that the result is soulless and artifical. It is like a machine analysed existing rogue-lite games and then was tasked with creating a new rogue-lite game from the collected data. Take features and systems from Transistor, Hades and Dead Cells, slap Persona as a style on it and you got Dandy Ace.What is unique in Dandy Ace? You play as Good Magician who gets trapped by Bad Magician in a mirror and has to use his magic cards to fight through groups of enemies, jumping from area to area while drinking tea and eating cupcakes to restore his health. That's where the uniqueness ends and the copying from other games starts. Now don't get the wrong idea, I am not  recommending this game because it copies from other games, but because it doesn't bring anything new to the table aside from copying stuff. Nowadays, creating a truly unique rogue-lite or even rogue-like experience is difficult, as there are so many games that are already doing it before you. However, this game deliberately takes from other games without even trying something on its own and that's why the resulting experience is not one that I would recommend.In Dandy Ace, you enter a strange world in the mirror, fighting Wonderland-esque enemies using your magic cards. The  is one of the reasons why I bought this game, as it copies the skill system from Transistor by Supergiant Games. At the beginning of a run and throughout it, you get magic cards that you can equip to get skills, but you can also attach a card to an already equipped card to add a secondary effect to the skill of the equipped card instead. Throwing cards barely pokes enemies? Attach bubbles to them and watch your cards turn into a powerful crowd control. Got that nice bomb skill with a good area of effect, but don't care about the Charm that it applies? Attach a card that turns the Charm into Stun. There are some good build varieties and synergies that keep things fresh. I would say that the skill system is one of the most positive things about Dandy Ace.However, cards and thus skills have , which means that after a while, the damage output of your skill becomes obsolete and you are forced to change it with another one. Found your favorite skill during a run? Well, don't get too excited because an area later, you will have to replace it to deal enough damage to be able to keep up with enemy scaling. Yet even if you deal enough damage, there is a lot of kiting in this game. See,  works always the same. You enter a "room", which is a slightly larger area in what is otherwise a hallway simulator and you can more or less predict when and where enemies will spawn. Quickly, you will find out that staying in the middle of a group of enemies is a bad idea, there are forks dashing at you, fireballs burning, lightning orbs rotating, it is almost a bullet hell, but with enemy shenanigans instead of bullets. So you run back (unless they lock you into the area), kiting some enemies out of their spawning areas, repeat that until every single one is dead. For a rogue-lite game, this is an utterly annoying and tedious gameplay loop.What do you say? There is  in this game, so just evade enemy attacks instead of running away? Yes, one kind of cards gives you movement abilities. Reminiscient of Hades by Supergiant Games at first, you will quickly learn that most if not all dodge/dash/move abilities do not have iframes. This means even if you dodge at the right time, enemies are still able to hit you. Now in itself, this wouldn't be the worst, but most enemies have some sort of ability that has an area of effect or shoot projectiles at you. The perfect example is an enemy introduced in the third area. It is a caster that creates a wave spell that slowly moves towards you while expanding in size. Now since dodging doesn't have iframes, you cannot dodge through this wave to reach the enemy. You have to dodge to the side or run back to where you came from. Since this game has tight areas, mostly being a hallway, dodging to the sides is often not an option and you are forced into an awkward dance running away from the wave, waiting for it to expire, then quickly dash back to the enemy to hit it before it casts the wave again. Oh, have I mentioned that most areas have doodads that you cannot dash over as well as gaps that you cannot, you guessed it, dash over? You will constantly collide with environmental doodads or gaps that you cannot pass over, making evading enemies even more annoying. It doesn't help that all non-stationary enemies swarm you like you are the light and they are the moths, no matter what skills they are actually using.Last but not least,  will constantly keep you tipping on your toes. There is no auto-attack or default skill that you can always use and more often than not, you will end up in situations when all your skills, even when used wisely, are on cooldown, requiring you to literally do nothing but watch the enemy for almost a second. It is a constant pace breaker.What is most important in a rogue-lite game? Progression that keeps you engaged, unlocking new shinies and adding more variety to the game. Dandy Ace copies Dead Cells here, you get  in an area and unless you finish the area and reach the end, they are lost. Successfully reaching the end allows you to spend Shards to unlock new cards as well as other small utilities and QoL stuff, and additionally choosing a trinket similar to how you choose a Mutation in Dead Cells. This works, yet most stuff isn't quite exciting, for example most trinkets are of the style of "#% less damage from ranged attacks" and "#% increased movement speed if you haven't been hit recently", adding or better, changing little in your overall gameplay loop and only providing small bonuses.Areas are big, with many many small fights that all feel the same and play out the same. There are no surprises within an area aside from small optional paths that end up in a small treasure chest giving you a card as well as the occasional little shop that does nothing but sells you three cards with a reroll option. Else, it is just one big hallway followed by another hallway in another area and so on.There are multiple areas and in the beginning you can take only exactly one path. Finding keys later unlocks new paths, although aside from swapping out environmental doodads and re-arranging them a little bit as well as slapping a new enemy type in there, there seems to be no difference in choosing one area over another as one knows it from games like Slay the Spire and Curse of the Dead Gods. Areas themselves don't stand out much, there is not much difference in colour and it feels like doodads are just swapped out when you enter a new area, which adds to the already monotone gameplay loop in combat situations. You feel like you are doing the same thing constantly again, over and over, not only area after area, but run after run. The variety is too little to keep you excited or engaged enough to look over other flaws.Dandy Ace does not excel in anything, most of its systems and features are copied, in equal or worse quality, from other games and thus it ends up being a hollow, soulless experience. I would say that if you are absolutely starved for a "new" rogue-lite experience, if you have burned through all other (popular) games of the genre, my gosh, then go ahead and buy it on sale or even for full price. The time that Steam gives you before you lose your right on a refund is more than enough to experience all the flaws that I have listed and make a decision for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: Hesitant recc, here.This game has a lot of potential, and beyond that it's already pretty great. However I think warnings are in order:(1) This ain't Hades. The characters and design is absolutely wonderful, but don't buy or play this for story. You'll be disappointed, understandably Hades' dialogue system can't be matched but as it is, dialogue here isn't trying to use Hades' system or any meaningful one whatsoever. Expect lots of repeated dialogue as you play, expect- well don't expect anything for story. Wonderful charming characters, but it's repetitive.(2) Early game is a slog. I've not actually gotten out of the slog yet in fact. Progress is slow and you have far less movement options (customizable however) than many other games of this genre, and outside of rare RNG cupcake drop, and a cup of tea you bring along (starts off with 1 cup, can be refreshed moving between areas) there seems to be no options for actual sustain. The card system is fun and unique, but at the end of the day slow, cautious and honestly kinda tedious traversal wins out when you have extremely limited heals and cupcake RNG seems to be incredibly low. There doesn't seem to be any item that increases the likelihood of cupcake drops, and if there's any meaningful upgrades/options for sustains it's still very stingy. Perhaps this fits- you're a magician and a dandy, not a brawler. The slower pace, combined with repetitiveness is currently a detriment though, one that the card system and general charm of the game makes up for, but I'm hesitant to recc as a result.If the devs are reading reviews- what's here can be great. Just needs some tweaking and a few additions, really, and it'd be confidently recommended. Give some healing options, maybe with a risk/reward sort of gambit. Or give a bit of a shielding/dodging option other than the current (eh, alright) fairy summon and dashing. Perhaps a decoy illusion?The dialogue is probably fine if the game's slog is minimized at least a bit (for instance through either healing or damage avoidance... that isn't just "stay far away from enemies"). More would be wonderful, though.Maybe I'm missing out on the condition-affecting item, but if not there should be one that increases duration a fair bit. The debuffs and buffs ones (+5s) are nice already but when damage is so costly and movement options limited by the number of card slots- well, something to incentivize or at least make viable more "brave" playstyles would be nice.

_childDocuments_.review: So i picked this game up in a sale and thought i'd give another rougelite a try, the game is an isometric rougelite with a magician themed story and visuals to match.The gameplay plays exactly like hades, but just terribly more clunky and without the fluidity of the game, the cards you get are usable in different slots and can be upgraded based on what you pair them with, this mechanic sounds cool but just comes across as overly complex for no real reason, its hard to tell what effect im getting and whether its any good or not, so half the time i was just shuffling cards in my deck like a complete buffoon having no idea what im doing, also the game completely lacks a solid tutorial so you're left to try and figure stuff out, but there's too much to figure out.The combat is fine, but the dash you have to dodge just is far too ineffective and i found myself getting cheap-shotted a lot because the visuals are quite cluttered, some solid colour contrast between projectiles and foreground would've helped that and albeit i do like how flashy and vibrant the theme and look of the game is, it just doesn't work when there's a lot of emphasis on dodging projectiles.Music and voice acting is fine, didn't have it on for long since i slapped my own music on so hard for me to comment on them, but the bits i heard sounded solid.Overall, hades styled game that just didn't execute as well as it gameplay and design wise, has some unique and quirky elements that others may completely enjoy, however i did not.

_childDocuments_.review: Dandy Ace is an isometric action roguelite game. As Dandy Ace, players need to guide the great magician through the palace created by the self-proclaimed nemesis using the power of the cursed mirror. With powerful foes in the way, players must utilize Ace's tricks up his sleeves, magic cards, to their potential. At first glance, Dandy Ace can easily be regarded as Hades clone. I agree. The similarity is palpable. However, the game has done itself justice with interesting combat system and dazzling artstyle. Is it the next Hades? No, not even close. Flawed it may be, Dandy Ace is still a good roguelite game to pick up.Arguably the best part of the game. In Dandy Ace, player's arsenal is presented as magic cards. There are three types of cards: blue cards for evasive maneuver, pink cards for damage, and yellow cards for crowd control. Players are also given 4 main slots and 4 sub slots, where things get more interesting. All magic cards have two abilities, one for the actual power, the other for upgrades. For example. The starting pink card "Wild Cards" let you shoot 5 waves of cards, but it can also function as an upgrade for other cards which shoots out more cards when you damage an enemies. This system opens up a lot of creativity for build variety. The optimal build is blue, pink, and two yellow, in this order. It is a basic build to get you through the run, but you can definitely have carrier combo. My favorite one so far, is what I called "Condition Build" with two Wild Cards upgraded with poison and bleed, a blue card upgraded with Hex or Curse, and a yellow card to bind or slow down any foes. This build helps me melt through the dungeon with ease.→Artstyle is vibrant and cheerful.→Bosses are creative.→Many Magic Cards to choose.There are four ways to explain this problem.→ The only place the story is relevant is the opening cutscene, which is a brief introduction to how everyone is stuck in the cursed mirror. The game doesn't explain how the cursed mirror was created and how bosses came to be. The ending isn't done properly either. The cursed mirror doesn't react to Lele's defeat and the troop escape, even on Nightmare mode completion.→ There are only like four NPCs to interact. Two are the assistants for your trinkets and unlockables, one is for your "guidance" allegedly, and one is for overall upgrade. I think the game needs more NPCs to either make the dungeons more interesting to explore and also shed some light on the lore.→ Commentating on each enemies encounters is a double-edged sword. The dialogue needs to be rich to bearable. Sadly it is severely lacking in both Lele and bosses parts, making the  repeated comments annoying. And the fact our protagonist does not respond with his optimistic character is disappointing.→ I don't think putting late game enemies in the beginning area is a good idea of difficulty increase. I would rather to have old enemies have new movesets or more elements of surprise.→Walls don't block projectile.→Bosses need to have their bullet-hell attack reduced a little.→It is easy to get visual and auditory fatigue with repeated runs.

_childDocuments_.review: Dandy Ace is a really fun roguelite, with amazing visuals, great humor and a deeply customizable ability system, with lots of stuff to unlock.Although short, it features various features that encourage replayability without getting boring.The best part is finding a combination of cards that really go well together and tweaking your kit until achieving an unstoppable combo and obliterating your enemies!Disclaimer:Even though it looks similar, this is not a Hades-like, so don't go into it expecting the same game! It distinguishes itself with unique systems and game feel, and deserves a lot of credit for that!

_childDocuments_.review: Although the game gets many things right, there are a few major flaws which are a deal breaker to me.First I really like a few mechanics I recognise from Transistor and Dead Cells, which I really like. For example every card has an effect as an ability and a different one as modifier, or the flask that gets less refills as the difficulty level rises.Now for the things I don't like.. the game is isometric but the map isn't aligned with the moving direction!! Also the dash/dodge will stop any actions queued and while dashing you can't queue any actions. The interactions are a little unpredictable at times. Also the map is very narrow with a lot of obstacles that are almost impossible to dodge (let me remind you that the movement is not aligned with the map..).I like the concept and design of the game, but the described issues bring me to not recommend the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to try my best to say this without coming across as an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Bear with me.Dandy Ace is a game that looked at several other roguelites and dared to ask the question: what if that, but it's about goofy stage-magician-wizards?It is that, and nothing more. Dandy Ace does not bring anything new to the genre whatsoever. The aesthetic is fun, the writing amusing, but after 7 hours I can only conclude it's just not for me. The sad reality is that Dandy Ace is a game on the same store as Hades and Enter the Gungeon and Dead Cells and all three of those games are just better than it at everything it's doing.Dandy Ace is not a bad game. It might even be worth the time if you can get it for cheap! But ultimately it's a game that struggles to reach beyond the pile of its contemporaries that far outshine it.I look forward to Mad Mimic's future projects to see what they do with their talents, because I think the thing the game is lacking is polish and personality outside its fun aesthetic. Movement feels a little too stiff, animation quality varies. But mixing and matching abilities to complement each other is still there from other roguelites, and still feels good. The depth is good, but not exceptional. The music is okay, but not amazing. The voice acting suffers from a case of 'there desperately needed to be more recorded lines', but thankfully the options menu includes the ability to turn off the narration.Unfortunately the very existence of that toggle tells you that it's just not going to live up to the standard set by something like Hades, but not everyone can hire Logan Cunningham and I don't faul Mad Mimic for that.I believe the point of a 10-point scale is that a 5 is dead-middle average, and on that scale this game is very much a 6/10. It doesn't stand out as especially good or especially bad, and I don't ever think I'm going to go back to it, but I can't say I actively don't recommend the game.

_childDocuments_.review: AHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH!This game is a breath of roguelite air. It's got a little of everythign from all the heavy hittersWizard of legend style cards-as-moves, only in Dandy Ace you can combine your cards for various sub attack effects, stats, status attacks, and so on.It does the slay the spire map progression ( although you aren't given a direct path choice, you can just see what the map has to offer - and find the proper exists on your own ) It does the dead cells refillable health pot at breaks between levels, and also collect-currency-to-unlcok-more-skills-and-itemsit does The Hades action of precise timing and usage of your moves, and the manipulation of your cards is sort of like god boons - combining them in just the right way can really change your loadout - the gameplay loop is fun, and it's challenging at times too ( it gets easier as you earn more cards to appear in your pool ) you can set cards to any of your four face buttons on a controller, and then setup a secondary spell card under it -which can add raw power to the main card, add a status effect, or change the attack ( liek adding addiotnal damaging bullets upon impact ) it's a fun system, and as you gain more and more cards, it really starts to get fun ( there's even a muda muda move ) the graphical style is pleasant, but iot IS motion tween paper doll style animation ( all special effects are done typical post processing ) it's not a bad style, but for ppl into hand animated frames, they might say it  looks janky as a result. Which is fine, bc thankfully Dandy controls well - you do NOT use R-stick to aim your attacks, it is NOT a twin stick shooter. you aim where you face, so keep this in mind. bosses aren't random - but you can choose which one you wanna fight ( once you get the keys to open the levels up, that is ) Highly recommend this game, it's fast paced past the intro level, harder than you expect at tims and it has an addicting gameplay loop of " just one more run  "

_childDocuments_.review: Okay.  I do not write reviews too often, but I felt like this game needed to be talked about in comparison to other rogue-lite games I played and my own personal experience with it.So, you may be thinking to yourself "This game looks fun.  Oooh, it's a rogue-lite, and I love those.  I played Hades and absolutely loved that game.  This is just another one but with a magician.  Sounds amazing." For the most part you would be correct.  Some of the strongest positive aspects of this game are its theme.  I would even say the theme and some of the characters are even on par with some of the characters from Hades in terms of fun yet distinct personalities.  For a general summary, here are some pros and cons with this game.** Pros------ Great character and theme with a minor story setup that is amazing------ The diversity of cards and the amazing effects associated with them------ The complexity of choosing card combos------ Decent music for the inevitable amount of grinding ahead** Cons ------ The card layout for those card combos------ Pretty much just two main pathsAs you can see, I am enjoying the game.  However, there could be a couple of tweaks to make it either better or improve on their next game in the series.For me personally, a rogue-lite has a few elements that I look forward to and want emulated in the games I enjoy. A rogue-lite must have a great story/theme, music, streamlined mechanics, and lots of re-playability for various achievements, awards, etc.  Obvious top-tier examples of this include slay the spire and hades.  In both games, the have: a tailored theme, good music for the long hours of grind, extremely succinct mechanics that makes gameplay streamlined and quick, and lots of either post-game content or achievements. When I look at any rogue-lites, this is the criteria I use. That is why games like Void bastards and Griftlands are good games but not top-tier games, since they fall short in one of these categories for me.Dandy Ace is a good game for me.  The unfortunate place it falls short in is the card layout of your card combos.  This mechanic has essentially four main slots for your abilities that you will acquire as you progress, with additional cards supplementing or improving those abilities.  In theory, there is near infinite possibilities since one main ability could become a supplementary ability of another. This complexity would seem great for allowing for awesome combos.  And indeed, some are truly great like a blackhole and stun for massive damage, or five-of a kind with elemental damage for massive debuffs. Yet, in terms of mobility and layout for best progression, I automatically use a certain layout. Since I use a controller, my a button was always a default for a blink/movement ability, my x for a main/quick attack, my y for a long range attack, and my b for a control/big damage attack. You could have all control ability slots or damages for your four main slots but then you suffer in movement and then die.  In comparison to other rogue-lites like Hades, they already have a layout based on the weapon you choose.  Other powers and upgrades later acquired already improve or minorly change your layout.  Since one is always acquiring/swapping out new cards, your playstyle constantly changes.  If you don’t, you become severely underpowered for future battles.t Ultimately, the complexity that initially is very exciting proves to very tedious in trying to think out the best combos for your cards.  Since each card has a level that corresponds to its power, it is very easy to think to always choose the most powerful cards.  Yet, some cards abilities may play to a specific playstyle that changes every time you incorporate new cards.  As a result, one is constantly pausing their screen, comparing stats, choosing stats and musical chair-swapping cards to increase your power as you progress through the game.  I often felt that about at least 10% of my run time was devoted to card management.  As you can imagine, this card management/constant swapping becomes very tiresome.  To have a snappier (and enjoyable gameplay), I think it would have been easier on the developers to have a cards with a supplement ability already attached to them.  Have the game procedurally generate these cards to make it quicker and more fun to go along the run. Limiting the cards in this way not only entirely limits the tediousness but also allows the player to still choose a layout for their own personal playstyle. You could keep the levels attached to the cards for some way to quickly judge damage/power for the needed situation and offering more cards with these already supplemented abilities available to cater to various playstyles.  This would drastically improve gameplay quality and want me coming back for more hours, rather than feeling utterly exhausted after one run. Overall, do I still recommend the game?  Absolutely.  However, this main issue is what personally prevents me from enjoying the gameplay atmosphere like I did in Hades.PS For additional ways to control for card choice, the bunny wagon guy could offer to exchange a card you have and offer some choices that reflect the manual switching out of abilities (ie puts in five of a kind with poison into a magic hat and then offers five of a kind with burn, a rocket with poison, or five-of a kind with stun).

_childDocuments_.review: Dandy Ace is an extremely solid roguelite that has an awesome card combo mechanic that really brings the game to the next level.So Dandy Ace is an action roguelite that plays similarly to Hades or Curse of the Dead Gods.You have 4 different ability slots in the game that hold different cards you find. And there is a huge variety in these cards and they are mainly categorized by color.So you have purple cards that tend to be different attack abilities, you have blue cards that tend to be movement abilities, and then you have yellow cards that tend to be crowd control type abilities. And every ability is completely different and they all have their own cooldowns and everything and so you use the cards you find as your main abilities to kill enemies in the game.And at first I am not going to lie I was a little skeptical about the game because the core combat and gameplay tends to be a lot less tight and responsive then games like Hades or Curse of the Dead Gods. However once I discovered how deep the card mechanics actually went I was instantly impressed. Because not only do you find cards in the game that you use as your 4 main abilities but you also can upgrade every single one of your abilities with any other card allowing you to create a seemingly infinite amount of ability combos. Also there is even more depth in some card combos as you can have cards that do different things depending on what type of card your upgrading. So there could be a card that adds stun to yellow and blue cards but if you attach it to a purple card it will apply something else.So every single run feels completely different as you are trying to create these super interesting combos to make some amazing builds. And unlike other roguelites where you just keep getting more passive items that automatically create synergies with each other like Binding of Isaac it is really refreshing to have a game that allows you to fully decide how your cards you get are going to synergize with each other. It really makes you feel like a genius when you get a nice combo going because you are the one that put it together.And so you go through each map and use your abilities to kill enemies and find new cards. And after you kind of master the gameplay it makes sense why the game feels a little looser than other games in the genre. The game is giving you a kind of sandbox to play with in terms of the abilities you use and combine and when you get the hang of it it starts to feel really solid.One slight complaint I have with the game is that every time you walk into a new part of the map it will spawn enemies but only after you walk in a bit and you can’t see where they are going to spawn until they actually start spawning. So it led to me just in every area I could I would walk in to trigger the enemies spawning and then instantly dash back from where I came in order to train them and make them easier to kill.I personally prefer when roguelites already have enemies spawned so I know how I want to approach them instead of having to just barely trigger the spawning and then running away so I don't get surrounded by a million enemies spawning around me.In between each floor there's some tents where your assistants are at where you can spend shards you get from killing enemies to permanently unlock new cards, abilities, and charms. And the charms you can equip one each time you get to this area until eventually you hit a soft cap around 3. You can refresh the charms you have selected but it keeps costing more and more money to do so, so you definitely want to pick the charms you want that run but it gives you a little flexibility to be like, "okay I'm about to fight a boss so let me switch out some of my charms for more defensive ones."There are also keys you can find that once you find are permanently unlocked that allow you to go into new areas and even pathways on the map.And I will say I have put several hours in this game to get a good grasp on the mechanics and progression but like a lot of roguelites I cover I have not even scratched the surface of everything the game has to offer. I think there is a ton of replayibily in this game and a ton of stuff that makes me want to keep playing the game and that's definitely a good thing.Also the presentation of the game is spectacular. I love the super stylized art style, and all the characters have full voice acting which is pretty uncommon for roguelites. I also love the main character you play, Dandy Ace, as he is so cocky like all the time. So I think that Dandy Ace is an absolutely solid fast-paced action roguelite that has an amazing gimmick of the card combo system that makes each run feel completely different. I don’t think this game is one of the games you could put hundreds of hours in but I truly think that the card system and the highly stylized presentation makes the game more then worth it for its asking price.And if you love Roguelikes and Deckbuilders as much as me then follow my  for more reviews and videos about them.

_childDocuments_.review: I've beaten the first difficulty and I wanna write down my thoughts/impressions so far. I may update this review as I play more.Dancy Ace is a bit of a mixed bag. On one side, the goofy mood and graphics of the game deceptively hide the punishing difficulty. This game is pretty challenging. I've played hundreds of hours of Dead Cells and Hades, so I have a fair bit of roguelike experience. Dandy Ace has no parry, no i-frames on the dodge, no deflect, no block. The only way to defend yourself is by crowd control effects (with a very short duration) and by timing your dodges with the attack pattern of the enemies. Every skill, including dodging, has a cooldown, you can't spam it. You need to time it right.However, the lack of defensive tools does mean that the game forces you into a caster/ranged build all the time. I've tried melee builds with stun and etc, but getting into melee range of enemies (and possibly surrounded by them) is just way too punishing. You lose too much health trying to get in range to do damage. Dashing into enemies just means you take damage from their attacks, even if your dash does damage. There are a few skills that can help, like a shield that blocks one ranged hit, invincibility, and invisibility. Overall though, a ranged/caster build is just way easier. I do wish there was more build variation. I enjoy variety, but some builds/combinations are just so much better than others, it kinda forces me into becoming an OTP because I need the highest damage output. Visual exhaustion/overwhelm is definitely a thing. After a few hours of Dandy Ace, the amount of things that happen on the screen is just too much. Projectiles from all directions. Harmful surfaces on the ground. Your own skills creating more flashes of light and colour. Cards popping up on the screen when the cooldown is done. Some toggles in the setting to disable certain visuals, such as the cards popping up, would help a lot in terms of visibility. There are not a lot of audio cues that help with combat, something that Hades and Dead Cells for example do really well, you can use your ears when your eyes are overwhelmed by the amount of stuff happening. Twitch integration is great. Viewers can choose your card rewards rather than the player just getting a random one from the chest. They can give you buffs and heals. They choose the path you take through your run. What bosses you will face. They can even temporarily become a boss. However, it tends to clutter the screen with more windows, ongoing vote timers, a game that already has so much going on, having another 25% of your screen hidden because of 3 ongoing viewer votes, is a bit much. I had to disable the Lele mode because it was just crowding the screen too much. An option to hide the vote window in-game and make it appear as a text message in chat instead would be greatly appreciated. In return for handing your "control" to your viewers, the buffs and heals you get from the Twitch Assist make the game a whole lot easier. It's a fun experience handing the reigns of your game to the whims of your chat. The only downside being the extra visual clutter on a game that is already troubled by it. I would also like to see more enemy variation, especially in terms of attack patterns. Higher difficulties just increase the enemy damage and health, while reducing the amount of heals the player gets, but it doesn't actually make combat more varied, just takes longer and taking damage is more punishing. This makes increasing the difficulty less exciting because you already know what to expect. I enjoy the game a lot, it's fun, it's goofy, the graphics are both funny and adorable. The amount of cards and the possible combinations is insane. The dialogue is cringe as ♥♥♥♥, but in a good way. But these small things that just, could've been done better, takes away the potential the game has. I hope the developers will be polishing the game more after release, as a bit more polish could turn this into a true gem. Despite it's flaws, I still recommend it. It's a fun game, far from perfect, but fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Looks like Hades, doesn't it? Looks can be deceiving. It's pedigree is almost entirely from Dead Cells, down to the teleporters, branching paths, droppable heals, and trading "cells" for permanent upgrades. On that foundation it builds its own thing, and does it reasonably well.You have four card slots, for every face button on the controller. You can assign any card to any slot. There are three types of cards: blue (dodges), yellow (long cooldown special attacks) and pink (spammable attacks). There are no restrictions on how many of each you have; you'll probably want to have one of each, and use the fourth slot for whatever you want.And then there's four additional upgrade slots; you can use cards as upgrades to other cards. And this is where it gets fun, as creating powerful and explosive combo effects is what the game is actually about. For example, there is your regular "throw cards" attack. If you use it to power up another card, then that card's attack causes cards to fly on hit. So if you pair it with an attack that has a lot of projectiles... there's going to be a lot of cards.The cards have tiers, which forces you to constantly on the lookout for new ones. Enemies get stronger (and different) in every area, so you'll have to find cards of higher tier. But be careful - having your card effects work well together is just as important, if not more. What's the point of picking up a "teleport-to-enemy" skill, if all your attacks are long range projectiles? But you gotta keep those cards circulating, or you'll be outmatched. Tough choice! You gotta improvise, and that's the main appeal of the game.If you want to play this for the story, don't - there's not much of it. It could have no dialogue whatsoever and it wouldn't hurt the game. The aesthetic and character design are another matter, they shine bright even without any given story context. The main antagonist, Lele, serves as the game's narrator, and he's nothing special - but not annoying either. You can turn off the narration if you think you've heard too much of it. Oh and one final note: the game is clearly designed with casters in mind. I mean, you're a magician, what would you expect? So the combat style from Hades simply doesn't work too well here. You gotta keep your distance, consider your crowd control effects (there are SO many), and only approach when it's relatively safe. So grab your cards and your top hat, and shine bright!

_childDocuments_.review: It feels like this game wants to be a skill-based action roguelike in the vein of Hades or Curse of the Dead Gods or Dead Cells, etc. But it seems that they missed the memo on the 'skill' part. There are a lot of little things I could quibble about, but the big glaring elephant in the room is that there are no i-frames on the dodge. It's just a 'briefly move fast' button. And there's not a parry or anything else to avoid incoming damage (which is telegraphed poorly, with enemies briefly blinking white in the middle of the multicolored confetti that is basically every battle), so you can either play slowly and defensively, hitting enemies a couple of times and then dashing away, waiting for their attack, then repeating, or you can just face tank a bunch of hits and die. And to add insult to injury, there's a snide narrator constantly commenting on everything you do. (This can be turned off, at least) So if you want a game that will repeatedly kill you unless you play like a frightened rabbit, and will then mock you for dying, this one is for you!Skimming the forums, it looks like the game may get better later on. My advice to the developers would be to make a better first impression.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent little challenge, doesn't particularly have the gripping longevity of some other roguelites but it's still an alright experience to fill some time with.The base system of using excess spells to modify held spells does add some nice customization to combat. There's a fine amount of variety to the spells but nothing major. Players can equip trinkets but most of them aren't very interesting, the fact that players simply choose one from the list of those they've unlocked means that there's not much randomness or variety to the process. And players can only even have three at a time.Otherwise there's not really any customization. Similarly there's not many random special encounters players can have in an area apart from finding a shop or chest. Players can unlock alternate paths but it doesn't take long to do, there's only two main routes overall; and they eventually all lead to the same central path anyways. It's hard to really tell if there's much variety to the rooms since they all blend together so easily, although the enemy variety does start to ramp up throughout the higher difficulty modes.The music and art are both nice, the English voice acting for the antagonist is pretty fun; although it sucks that turning the audio off also disables the subtitles; so random narration dialogue can't be discerned anymore. The narration commentary also happens too often in general, which causes it to get stale relatively quickly. The dynamic between the protagonist and the antagonist is actually quite interesting, so while the overall world and motivation for the journey isn't especially engaging; seeing the relationship between the protagonist and antagonist develop is fairly intriguing. Although past the second difficulty mode the game doesn't have any new dialogue for meeting each boss; nor does there actually seem to be a conclusive end to the story after players finish all the modes.The game manages to keep up a relatively decent amount of challenge even on the lowest difficulty; but the upper thresholds of that challenge most comes from clutter. Often times the game will wait until players are at the centre of a room to spawn all the enemies in, which immediately surrounds the player with danger. This combined with how comparatively little space there is in many rooms leads to players simply having no safe place to go sometimes. In quite a few areas the border of each room is surrounded in traps; which punishes players for trying to dodge away from threats because their dodge moves them so far that it forces them into a bordering trap. In these situations there's literally no safe option; players either dodge out of one attack and towards an enemy who immediately hits them or they dodge away from the enemies and end up in a trap that hits them anyways. The bosses in the later difficulties are similarly spammy in a way that results in players having no safe place to go sometimes.Lacks the systematic variety and substance that gives most roguelites a lot of longevity, and the strangely unfinished end half of the story is very disappointing. But still provides enough of a decent challenge to be worth trying during some spare time.If you're interested in finding more games like this I've probably reviewed quite a few on my curator page .

_childDocuments_.review: This game is phenomenal! I took an interest in it after loving Hades and trying to find similar games and this is one of the few games I bought as soon as it came out. You get different cards throughout your runs that are essentially your fighting abilities and they're all completely different from each other and you can kinda combine two to give your main card different effects. You can have 4 active ability cards and can assign another card to each of those but you are not limited to the first 8 that you pick up. Throughout your dungeon run you can find more cards at higher levels and swap them out or sell them. There are passive permanent upgrades to the cards levels, unlockable trinkets to further boost Dandy during your runs, and a lot of other things to boost you as you increase the difficulty, as well as a lot of other components to the game. Voice overs are great and campy, the whole game is just a great concept with even better execution. If you stream then there is also a twitch mode that lets your viewers interact with and change the game as you're playing. Definitely worth the full price, if you're on the fence then wishlist it and wait for a sale, you won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: A weak recommendation.Combat is above average in the genre, but the game locks the fun behind grind.I appreciate a cool beverage on hot summer days, but not when I have to go out of my way to go to a store in the day's heat for a single bottle. That's how I feel about this game. It has me make a separate run for every small bottle, and it's not REALLY good enough to justify the work.In terms of gameplay it's the closest thing I have seen to Dead Cells in a top-down perspective game. Mechanically weapons(cards in this game, which also function as upgrades), progression, gameplay and difficulty seem to be remarkably close to that of Dead Cells. This game shares nothing with Hades other than top-down perspective.This game does only one thing, but it does it well. That thing is combat.Now the big question is how long will you stay before just 1 thing turns monotonous. Movement speeds are balanced perfectly. When I saw a threat I could always see a path to avoid it (provided there was one). This brings me to 2 problems, but every attack I had so far had something unique about it. The same cards also function function as passive upgrades for another active card. These upgrades vary from card to card, but broadly speaking they either trigger another attack, or a debuff. You can freely swap all cards as you like (swap places, swap upgrades, or swap active and upgrade), which adds a layer of control, I would love more roguelikes to have.  After each stage you get a choice of relic, which seem to have the same pool each time. These are more damage after not taking damage, more damage after taking damage, less damage taken, etc. In my opinion all of these are boring and don't add anything to the game. You go to a room, defeat enemies that just spawned and then go to next room. Keep doing that until you find a portal to next area and then then do it again. It gets repetitive as soon as you're done experimenting with cards. Since I'm comparing it to Dead Cells, I feel like I have to mention how much of that game hangs on relatively good exploration. Exploration is non-existent in this game.Much like in Dead Cells you bring blueprints to checkpoints and spend collected currency there to actually unlock the item. The actual upgrades are also very similar (starting gold, recycling, recycling upgrades, healing potions, and ofcourse cards through blueprints). The major difference areIt's good, but monotony outpaces progression, which downgrades it to "okay".

_childDocuments_.review: although I only played for a short time, I can't recommend this game for a couple of issues I ran into while playing,First, let me give credit where it's due; the card system is awesome. There's a lot of opportunity for synergies here. I ended up with a build that let me deal damage over time to enemies and when the died they would explode, and the enemies that they killed would explode killing other enemies and so on and so forth. That was great.Now on to the problem that I felt outweighed the cool card mechanics: the jank.Hitboxes were a big problem in my time with the game. Enemies attacks that were visually missing me were counting as hits. Ace's hitbox was bigger than his character model, leading to a lot of frustrating situations where I was taking damage from projectiles that should have flown past me. Another aspect of how janky this game feels is the dodge. A lot of the time, the dodge didn't feel as responsive as it needed to be considering how many enemies this game throws at you at once. It's just not as fluid as it should be, especially compared to other games like Hades.Good games make you feel like each of your deaths or failures are your fault. That is not the case here. I felt like my death, and each hit before it, was unfairly earned. There were other things that weren't my thing, like the dialog, but in the end that isn't a big deal and in a more fun game could be dealt with. Don't get this game if you are looking for a tight, fluid experience. Do get this game if you have more patience for rough edges than me I guess.These issues are something that can be worked on by the dev's, and I hope they do. I could see the hard work they put into designing this game, so hopefully one day this review with be outdated.

_childDocuments_.review: The strong point of dandy Ace and what separates it from other rogues is the card system, each card can be used as such or as a modifier to other cards, giving you a chance of fun experimentation combining effects and debuffs. Also the art is pretty nice. Outside of that, is a very competent, fun roguelite.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey everyone, if you enjoy a good fun ARPG with roguelite elements, funny dialogue, and a wonderful art style you need to check out Dandy Ace. Let's go into what you have to look forward to:Dandy Ace is an 2.5D Action RPG game where you take the role of Dandy Ace, the world's greatest magician, who is trapped in a cursed mirror world by his unbeknownst greatest rival, Lele the Green Eyed Illusionist. Sent to this world with only your assistantts Jenny Jenny and Jolly Jolly, you use your deck of powerful card tricks and trinkets to make your way through this mirror world and find a way to escape. Along the way you battle various minions monsters and even find help from Nnif a bunny who is out to turn a profit. Will Ace be able to escape this mirror world?Combat in the game is using 3 various types of Card Types;Pink Cards: Combat cards which have various attacks such as 5 of a Kind (5 Card Cone Attack), Dancing Wands (Single Target attack that bounces to nearby enemies) or Titan's Punch (Melee range stunning fist attack).Yellow Cards: Utility Cards which have various offensive or defensive attacks and CC (Crowd Control) effects. These vary from combat effects stun, charm, weaken, and more effects and also various defensive effects such as barriers, invulnerability and shields.Blue Cards: Movement Cards which give you either a dash or blink movement ability. These abilities also have various secondary effects from ground effects, CC, and damage effects. Using these various cards you use them to create Primary and Secondary card type combos. Primary Cards use the ability of the specific card and Secondary Cards add effects to primary card attacks. For example; Dancing Wands throws a wand which hits a target then bounces to nearby targets. Attach Toxic Spray to make these wands do poison damage or attach Bubble Trouble to add exploding bubble damage on all your wands. With so many cards there are a large amount of combinations to give people various ways to play.Replay Value: The main story-line plays through the story of ace, but once you find your way out of the mirror world on the normal setting, the game includes various difficulties for Hard, Very Hard, and Nightmare mode. So you can get hours upon hours of fun so the replay value is high.Twitch Mode: The game also includes a twitch mode which allows audience participation in twitch chat. Your audience takes control of Lele and can cause various effects which make the game more difficult by summoning additional enemies, using card tricks, or even giving you a special cupcake. You can also add a twitch assist mode to have your non lele players help you by giving you additional healing cupcakes or random buffs. They can choose maps and cards for you as well, which can make your game easier or feel like Houdini's upside down water escape (very hard and deadly ;) )Game Ratings: Rating of 1-5 (lowest to hightest) Tophat! The game is overall a great experience, more elements could be added but considering it was an indie game, its well made and polished quite well. But if the game adds more features in the future such as public leaderboards or in-game challenges then it would easily be a 5/5! Love the artstyle and vibrant colors. I also especially enjoy the non-gorey combat which is common in many other ARPGs. Only thing that would make it a 5 would be graphics settings to accommodate people with lower system builds. The background music is fun and is enjoyable to listen to while playing. The voice overwork is really well made and the voice actor for Lele (who also did many of the other male voices) really gave the characters a personality of their own. You can play this game for hours and hours. For a $20 price tag, you get a lot of value for this game. If you equate the value of a game to time playing, then this game would be worth thousands of dollars.So yes, this game is really great, I was a tester for the game and did receive a copy for free, however I would easily have purchased this game regardless. But I played this game for many hours before release and since have been enjoying the full release with all in-game elements. I recommend this game for people who love fun fast paced action type games and want something less bloody and dark and more Dandy.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ll be blunt. Dandy Ace is not a bad game, it just is plagued by the weaknesses of the roguelike genre and succumbs to them. It is a game with a lot of charm, nice animations, nice music, and an interesting approach to weapons. But it is in the moment to moment gameplay where it becomes far too situational to recommend to a wide audience.TLDR:  If you have NOT played all of the aforementioned games and/or you are likewise not a roguelike addict, ehhhh this becomes much harder to recommend.What Dandy Ace does well:Dandy Ace’s primary inspiration is Dead Cells. You collect blueprints which unlock items you can equip from the start on future runs, runs start with a random assortment of cards (as long as you upgrade this properly), and there are (limited) branching paths you can take to complete the game. It draws some inspiration from Hades from the camera perspective, although it is less smooth because of an awkward angling placement.The artwork is charming, and the voice acting is mainly passable. The enemies are pretty creative and are well designed. I really like the upgrade system, where you could slot in other cards you find to power up the weapons you’re actually using and you can do this on the dime. This was the most creative innovation in Dandy Ace, and I really think more games of the genre could learn from this. In most roguelikes, you tend to have to toe a fine line between psychopathy and safety, such that you generally have to play close, tight, and fast to weave in and out of enemies. In Dandy Ace, you’re rewarded by playing more like a ranged character that can basically lure enemies out of their rooms in small groups and pick them apart from the edge, kiting backwards. If you want to die in this game, run headfirst into a room and try to fight from the middle. The game does a good job placing you in locked arenas where you have to do this, although they tend to be larger and give you more room to maneuver than the average room.And now, what Dandy Ace does poorly.First and foremost, the story is… asinine. You have such a bizarre relationship between Lele and Dandy Ace, such that Lele is like the average Twitch fanboy who trapped his favorite streamer into an alternate reality where he finally gets to force a 1v1. You have a weird power dynamic where Lele is “helping you” get to the final boss and Dandy Ace is too mentally challenged to put two and two together. There is this entire world that supposedly exists inside this magical mirror, but you never escape? You just win and then Lele says “I’ve retrapped you in a harder mode?” And when you beat Nightmare mode you don’t even have an end cutscene that is like “we definitely left the mirror?” What the ♥♥♥♥ is this writing.Now, I could overlook this except for the fact that:  Enemies spawned in? Voiceline. You killed enemies? Voiceline. Cupcake dropped? Voiceline. You stop moving for 15 seconds? Lele complains. So you can’t ignore the story, because Lele is constantly talking to you as a reminder that you are, in fact, trapped in this magical mirror and these are his minions doing his bidding. There are like maybe 4 voice lines that he has that are funny, but after 11.5 hours of listening to the same 10 voicelines, I’m about ready to Gangplank Q to cranium. You can’t access any menus from the pause screen, and even then I don’t think there is an option to turn him off. Then you have the single biggest pitfall plaguing any roguelike game, Dead Cells included: unlocks that downgrade you. What I mean by this is that as you unlock more cards, you come to realize that the vast majority of them are troll cards. Remember how you’re supposed to play this game as a ranged mage? Well good luck, because 60+ percent of all the cards you can unlock in this game are melee cards. This means that the more you unlock, the worse chance you have of being able to complete your build. So after a certain point, you realize that you’ve trolled yourself, because now it’s near impossible to complete the higher difficulty because you can never get any cards which are actually good.Now before any of you say “skill diff,” let me explain why ranged cards are  to beat the game: the bosses are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. They are mongo ass to play against. In most roguelikes, you get your ass kicked because you either didn’t understand the boss’ attack pattern, or because you ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up and got filtered by your reflexes. You know how in most roguelikes, hell even in Dark Souls, most bosses have momentary windows of opportunity for you to attack them in between rounds of their BS? Or in bullet hells like ROTMG and Enter the Gungeon you can attack while moving in a different direction? Or that, if you’re good enough, you can complete the boss taking 0 damage?  Good, because in this game you can do neither. Not only do the bosses never give you a breather, but you must be facing the boss to attack them. So what you will do for the majority of the fight is run around away from the boss and the hundreds of AOE environmental hazards or attacks and pray you get to hit them. Both Scissorella and Axolangelo have attacks that lock onto you  meaning that the only way to dodge them is to dash EXACTLY at the time they fire the attack. God forbid you do it half a second too early, because their aiming reticle will snap onto you. They have auto aim installed, apparently.  Lele in particular is a stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fight.So the only way to beat the bosses is to abuse damage over time abilities. DOTs are so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ op, they are necessary to winning the fight, and you can basically stack them as much as you can. The ideal build is using the 5 card fan attack (like Twisted Fate Q) with either poison, burn, or bleed buff because each individual card stacks one tick of DOT. So in the rare window you have, you can dash right at the boss, spam the ability, hit all your cards, and stack 30 DOT stacks on the boss, which will do at least 1/3rd of their HP while you’re dodging. If you can find them, run Twin Daggers also with DOT (or alternatively vulnerability, but this is less DPS overall). My favorite card to round it out is Event Horizon with vulnerability, as it gives an AOE slow necessary for clearing rooms of minions. Once you get to Lele, swap for Fairy Lights, as you need some protection against projectiles for his BS. I’ve tried to beat the bosses without DOTs, and it’s impossible. This is why unlocking upgrades is a direct detriment to your experience: the more cards you have unlocked, the harder it is to find the cards necessary to stack DOT builds. Other builds can be more effective than DOTs with normal enemies, but you’ll inevitably get filtered by the bosses. So you’re really not rewarded for experimenting.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent Game that gives me more of that craving for Hades. This roguelite dungeon crawling action game is top notch when it comes to punishing you with death loops until you discover more cards, more powers, more passive more buffs and so on, addicting and full of surprises as you progress your way to the Evil LeLe palace.The graphics, voice and storyline are all fun, goofy and loveable. The main importance is the gameplay. It will remind you of Hades but completely switches up the style with the way customization of skills and upgrade works out. The death loop is addicting enough that you will come back for more, and more and more. Everytime you discover something you want to unlock it and see what it does, you get a new card, you combine different card elements and cater to your own style. Most of the cards revolves around attacking, controls, and dash cards with different buffs by matching the card with another card you can match up with each card up to 4 cards while carrying some passive itemsYou will start off a bit easy thinking you are Hot Stuff until you get pummeled in the mirror world by the enemies in this game until you learn their patterns. Don't go in playing this game like a melee character because you are a caster so you want to play like a caster, Kite and run you fool! Highly recommend this game if you like getting shredded by candles and small merman things.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely a must-buy if you're a fan of games from Supergiant. Lele in particular has a Mark Hamill as Joker vibe to him in a really great way.I streamed this game for 2 hours and I usually take on a developer tone noting what's good and bad about a game as I go. For this 2 hours, I couldn't find a single thing to change. No extra features, no missing features, and 1 bug that let me cheese a pack of enemies for a few seconds. The game's built by a smart team who did fantastic QA. This is a properly polished product and worth your time!

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun roguelike/-lite/whatever you want to call it, especially if you like the art style and general theme.It starts off a little slow, which might turn some people off. _childDocuments_.review: I came into rougelikes/lites through Hades, so keep that in mind as I discuss this, but I honestly feel like Dandy Ace is a top tier example of that style of games. The gameplay is rapid, and it moves very smoothly. It's relatively intuitive, but the mechanics still have a lot of depth to them. And by nature of the way the systems are designed, there's tons of customization available.The weakest point of Dandy Ace, I would say, is the story. That's a common problem that plagues roguelikes, so it's not much of a hit against it. But if you're coming here looking for an expansive narrative to suck you in, this isn't the best place to turn. The story is functional enough to get you into the meat of the gameplay.The art style is going to be a subjective matter, but I personally really enjoy it. All the character models look good, the bosses in particular.There is a pretty steep learning curve to the way combat works in Dandy Ace. You can get the basics, but the basics are not enough to go very far. Due to the high level of customization, and the high level of variability, there's a lot to get control over. I mention this because there's definitely potential for someone to get frustrated early on. It took me a few hours of play to really latch onto how everything works, how to maneuver, how to combine your abilities, etc. And so much of that is down to finding how you personally like your setup to be. A few hours may not seem like a lot, but when each area takes 3-5 minutes to clear, that's many runs. Definitely not a game one should expect to pick up and immediately crush.All in all, I think this is an example of a roguelike/lite that hasn't gotten nearly the love it deserves. As long as you're willing to put some time into learning how things function, I would highly recommend snagging it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not bad but not as good as it could be. It has a hades look, and a lot of abilities as well as cards you can add as secondary modifiers, so there is variety in that sense. Some of the abilities just suck, and melee is terrible so you are somewhat limited in that sense. So most of the game you use the same abilities with the same modifiers because others are too situational. Combat is limited, just hitting x, y, and b as soon as the cooldown while youre spamming blink. Later on between the large amount of enemies, small areas to fight in, and traps, theres wayyy too much on screen and too many enemies. This means the game becomes "blink and kite simulator" which ends of being somewhat boring and repetitive. The maps and levels are super repetitive, have no variety or identity, and all seem the same. There is decent enemy variety but you do feel you are fighting the same enemies, on the same looking maps, with the same few cards just spamming attack. None of the depth of hades. A lot of the trinkets are positive/negative which is dumb and you mostly won't use them so you'll stick to the few best ones. Theres only like 4 total bosses including all the routes, and the keys just mostly open up more areas to loot chests. The problem is as people say, as you unlock more items you just get more useless trash you won't use from chests. After beating the game once since theres no new characters or enough variety I didn't feel the need to continue. Game isn't bad but gets somewhat boring and repetitive fast. 7.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: MIXEDThe game has some very cool ideas and is fun when it's fair, but that fun is hindered by very questionable design decisions. Reading the Steam forum, they seem intentional, which makes them all the more puzzling. Why would you make your game LESS fun on purpose?Dash have no invincibility, so they are a positioning tool and nothing more. That would be ok, if positioning would be strategic, but it doesn't due to the VERY SMALL arenas you are forced to fight in, with plenty of traps all around you in every direction, a magnitude of on and off-screen projectiles and spawning enemies literally around and on you. Some attacks are easy to discern and dash away from, while other animations have an active hitbox before they are even on the screen. Other effects blend in with your own or the surrounding, so you are hit and don't even realize by what.Balance is also a big issue, with many of the unlocks being terrible and you have no way to disable them. (There is also definitely something wrong with the RNG seed for me, since there are multiple bosses, but I've only seen another boss a single time and otherwise the Rose lady over and over and over again)If the dev's would actually listen to feedback, it would be a great little gem, but as it stands, it's very frustrating in many parts, which ultimately made this tip more towards "not recommend" - there are other games worth your while more.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not too big on Roguelike games. I think there's definitely potential in them to be more approachable, and this game feels to have delivered on that for me. There's deeper layers to this than I play as casual player on normal level for sure, but that's perfectly fine for me when I am not forced to go so deep into it all but just give it couple of seconds to figure out card combinations etc.I'm enjoying this. I just made it to the final boss for the first time (I think it can be done in an hour casually once you know what you're doing), however died as I got greedy. As it should be. I'm not sure of the replayability for someone who isn't crazy about the genre, but I definitely feel like getting all the keys and paths done could add to it - which doesn't necessarily add much to the game itself, but gives you bit different feel with different enemies.Very worth it at -25% sale at the very least.

_childDocuments_.review: Another game where I wish there was a "Meh" vote. The game itself isn't terrible, and in a world where Hades didn't exist, I might have been tempted to give it a positive vote. Unfortunately for Dandy Ace, Hades *does* exist and is a much *much* more polished version of the same game, to the point where Dandy Ace feels woefully under-performing and unfinished in comparison. It's basically a version of Hades with clumsier less versatile weapons that forces you to always play from a long-distance caster perspective, because even the weakest enemy can murder you up close. This would be fine, if the game realized this up front and always made sure you had at least one long-range weapon by default, but more than half the available offensive abilities are only useful up close or are so hard to aim or take so long to recharge between shots that they're only worthwhile as secondary weapons... It's like making a bullet-hell game where 3/4 of the available weapons are punch or shotgun range attacks. With a few refinements, it could have been more fun. Alas, I discovered pretty early on that the only secondary effect worth a damn is stun (and a lesser extent, push). That's it. You need Five-Card that you can spam, with fire, poison, or some other DOT effect attached, and every other power should be a ranged or mine effect with stun on it, that you toggle back and forth between while you wait for then to recharge in the vague hope that you can stop enemies in their tracks for a few seconds and snipe them from a distance with your DOT while staying out of range of their projectiles. That's it. That's the entire strategy to playing this game, other than trying to mitigate the bad cards you're given as rewards until you luck into getting a higher tiered version of one of the more useful ones. Rinse and repeat.

Good thing I didn't die on my nightmare run because replaying would have been torture.Other reviews mention dead cells and hades ... why? _childDocuments_.review: So take Hades, swap out the main character for a magician, and replace the underworld with a magical shifting palace and you’ll get something like Dandy Ace – the latest action roguelike to grace Steam.And yes, I’m going to begin by addressing the Hades comparison – as I’m sure a LOT of people are going to make it. Yes, this game plays very similarly and even has that same isometric view. However, it also has a TON of differences setting itself apart, not just from Hades, but from the roguelike crowd in general. So no, this isn’t just some straight restyled rip, it’s actually pretty unique in some ways.In this game, all of your attacks and abilities are tied to these magical cards that you find throughout the palace. Four of them can be equipped at once and the real magic lies in the fact that each card has a separate, passive ability that you can tag on to any of your primary four cards – effectively allowing you to hold eight cards at once. This is where the synergy comes into play, as your primary may just be a simple ranged attack, but the secondary effect can be anything from poison damage, to explosion upon death, or even wild cards spreading everywhere upon impact.You’re not locked into keeping a card upon picking it up, it’s a very customizable experience and encourages you to experiment as much as possible to find those optimal card combos. It’s a nice breath of fresh air from other roguelikes where it feels like you’re tied down by RNG and have to stick with what you get – it’s a much more freeform experience in Dandy Ace and it’s very fun trying out the different combos.Movement feels fluid, the visual and audio feedback are sufficient, and I didn’t notice any funky hitboxes or other such annoyances. This is good because this is a very fast-paced game and even the slightest hiccup hinder the experience, but I didn’t have any such issues here. Sure, it can be a bit overwhelming when there’s like ten enemies on-screen, but if anything that can make your optimal card combos shine that much more.Aside from the unique weapon system, the roguelike elements are pretty basic. The random map generation is there, permadeath is there, and there’s also the permanent upgrades you can unlock in-between runs to strengthen your next – all the usuals we get from such games. The game has some replayability in that there are a bunch of new cards, trinkets, and other upgrades to unlock, but nothing I could see myself spending dozens of hours on, even if I do enjoy the gameplay.That’ll lead me to the game’s biggest flaw: its lack of content. All those card synergies are neat, but you have to go through quite the grind in order to complete your collection and the level variety isn’t exactly helping there. There’s little in the way of special rooms, it’s mostly just the same web of connected battle rooms with nothing really breaking it up other than the occasional shop room and the actual transition between levels. Even across multiple runs, there is a bit of a branching path early on, but it’s not enough to really set each area apart from one another – they all blend together by the end of it. Each area does at least look nice (the game as a whole has some solid visuals) – it just could really use some more variety.1440p, 144 fps, no bugs, no crashes, no stutters, nothing. It ran flawlessly and controls well on both controller and keyboard and mouse, with the latter being fully rebindable. The controller even has an auto-aim option, which makes the more precise cards a lot easier to use.So, would I recommend Dandy Ace? Yeah, it’s a fun enough experience to warrant recommendation. It might not have the depth of something like Hades, but I don’t regret my time with it. The core gameplay is polished, the card system is some really unique stuff, and the visuals and music aren’t bad either. Still, the level design and overall variety could use some work. As it stands, it’s much more fun as a one-and-done kinda experience than one I would see myself returning to – which is something I know a lot of people look to this genre for, so that’s something to keep in mind for those interested in it.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: I think Hades was pretty much the first proper rogue-like game I played. I hadn’t really thought about the concept ever before but found I enjoyed it greatly, so I looked for more similar games. Dandy Ace was one of the games I ended up with.A couple of things to consider here. I enjoyed playing Dandy Ace. I like the concept with the cards you unlock, how you best combine your weapons. Gameplay-wise it is a lot of fun. My achievement hoarding dragon brain rejoiced at all the things to collect and unlock and I spent a good amount of time making my way through all the levels. Although there are quite some things to get, it’s not a complicated game to figure out. You’ll soon have down what to pick and what to combine.The design is very cute. It feels a little bit like Alice in Wonderland on crack and I am very much here for it. The enemies look cool and unique enough, I think this game has a very succinct and recognizable color palate that makes it easy to remember. I did get occasionally frustrated but a) that is the nature of roguelike games and b) I insisted on going through all difficulty levels to get all the achievements which obviously made my life unnecessarily hard.So, while I had a great time playing this, I uninstalled it once I had everything done and never felt like revisiting the game. Replayability in games is pretty important to me, especially when I look at the price point of the game. Sure, I put a good amount of hours into it but I feel like I got my money’s worth more with other (similar) games that cost way less than this one. I would definitely wait for it to go on sale because otherwise, the price point is too high for me. Or, on the other end of the price spectrum, if I think of, for example, Hades, which costs a bit more but had me revisit the game time and time again, I really feel the cost of Dandy Ace at full price would not be worth it for me.I don’t really have any big complaints about the gameplay or any of the mechanics. It’s very much what you would expect and want from a rogue-like, so we’re good in that department. I enjoyed playing it. But it’s not my favorite game of this type. There are others that intrigued me more and especially motivated me to come back for more time and time again. So, all in all, I would recommend the game, but I would only get it if it’s on sale. Otherwise, you can get somewhat more value for money from other similar games.
