_childDocuments_.review: is an action rogue-like in the truest sense of the word. When you die you are dead and you start back at the beginning. There are no extra lives and no continues. This is an isometric action game where the four controller buttons are bound to different movesets.The sheer number of movesets in this game is astonishing. While they are categorized as combat, support, and movement-based skills, within each of those categories is an enormous number of different skills. It would be impossible to list them all here, and in fact unlocking them in game will take hours.These movesets are collected in the form of “cards”. You bind any card to the Y, B, X, or A button, and within each slot you can bind a second card that will also form as a passive enhancer of the first card. This means each one of the cards has both an active ability in the main slot but can provide a passive ability in the second slot for any one of the cards you combine it with. That leads to a huge number of combinations to play with to find a collection of eight cards that work the best .And in addition to these movesets you can also equip trinkets that act as passives. These don't change any major fundamentals, but they again provide another variation to the already huge number of combinations. I've heard this game be compared to Hades, not that I would know I've never played it. But it is very similar to a game called Transistor which had a similar mechanic of swapping in and out different abilities into actives, active-buffers, or passives.Like any good rogue-like there is a sense of progression as certain collectibles can be used to buy permanent upgrades that will help you with subsequent runs through the dungeon. This means no matter what the outcome of a particular run might involve, you will be working towards some improvement in your overall game state, either literally in the form of permanent upgrades or just through practicing the game itself. Failure does not go unrewarded.Maneuvering through each dungeon is very straightforward. There are no mazes, platforming sections, puzzles, or anything outside of either open and closed combat arenas. This is a game that is purely focusing on its combat which fortunately is the game's greatest strength. Just make sure you understand that that's  this game offers. There is no grand overarching story, big character choices to make, or any other distractions from the constant fighting that is going to take place. And the fighting is mostly good. It's fast and dynamic, but not without its faults. Healing is hard to come by, which makes damage avoidance paramount. This means you'll be dodging frequently and only taking pot-shots when there's an opening. In the open areas of the map, the safest strategy is always to back track the way you came and kill enemies as they funnel toward you, which seems antithetical to the game's design philosophy. The closed areas will force you to fight without an option to retreat. Most enemy attacks are clearly telegraphed. However, some boss abilities will change the direction of their charge/throw  you've dodged and you’ll still get hit. This feels very unfair. Also, on a widescreen monitor enemies above (and sometimes below) are hidden, but their projectiles and attacks will still activate leaving you no visual indicator of the incoming attack. Otherwise, the gameplay is solid. is a nice looking game. Despite its low budget it's easy on the eyes. The enemy variety is lovely, and you'll be fighting creatures you won't see in other video games. There are angry teapots, evil dilettantes, a fat man with a paintbrush, and the infamous cuckoo clock. Everything is animated well, and even though the fights can get very chaotic you can usually tell what's going on.Outside of the in-game graphics, there isn't much to see here. There are some small animated cutscenes but this is not the focus of the game. Voice acting is very hit or miss. The villain is ludicrously silly, and the voice acting of  in particular is quite weak. That said, given that the story is an afterthought here anyway, and some of the voices can be disabled, you're not missing out on much.The story is incredibly threadbare and not even worth speaking about. There is about a 30 second opening cutscene and you're essentially immediately thrown into the procedurally generated dungeon. They're only a handful of characters and none of them are at all developed.With four different difficulty settings and an innumerable number of combat combinations there's a lot of replayability here. I generally try to avoid rogue-likes but I had a good time with  and I can certainly recommend it as long as the combat would interest you.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a fun rogue-lite where the clever twist is that every single move you can make (dashing and attacking) is decided by cards (representing the magic tricks of the titular magician) you find in each run. There's also card blueprints you can find that you can give to one of your assistants in the hub area, if you get her enough mirror shards (currency that you can spend between zones but not runs) she can unlock cards and additional passive perks which you can find in future runs.The game is rather easy to beat in normal mode but that unlocks hard mode where it's more challenging, adds some new mechanics and some new unlocks.The story is quite simple and whimsical where a "great" magician has trapped Dandy Ace and his two assistants in a magical mirror world where he's basically king. The characters are rather charming in their simplicity with the likeable himbo Dandy Ace, the adorably incompetent Lele (the antagonist), the hypercompetent done-with-this-crap Jolly Jolly and bubbly little sister Jenny Jenny. It's a saturday morning cartoon story, nothing deep but lovely and wears it's heart on it's sleeve.My only gripe is that there's not that much variety in zones and the screen can get rather hectic with the particles of the enemy attacks when there's large crowds. I only wish it had more map variety and maybe some invincibility frames when dashing but other than that, a lovely indie gem that every fan of the genre should try.TL;DR: Lovely and whimsical action rogue-lite with a great variety of moves that allows for a lot of interesting and fun builds, a saturday morning cartoon story, great aesthetic but that could use a bit more zones to add variety. Would recommend to any fan of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Did you like Hades? This game has many things in common with it, with one key innovation. Like many other roguelikes, you have a procedurally-generated maze filled with random enemy spawns and you get random weapons (cards) as you progress. The more you play, the more cards and passives (trinkets) you unlock. While weapons drops are random, selected from a pool of unlocked weapons, trinkets can be selected. There are eight card slots and three trinket slots that you can use to create your builds, with two catches, but more on that later. The levels feature two different (short routes), each with its respective boss, and then a linear sequence with another boss and a final boss. Nothing so far seems new, if you've played other games in the genre. But Dandy Ace has two distinctive features: card damage doesn't scale with enemy health, so you're forced to adapt your build pretty often. While you sometimes can just upgrade the rank of your card to make it deal more damage, very often you'll have to make do with a higher-rank card that doesn't fit that well into your build (or deal with dealing little damage, your call). The other interesting feature is that four card slots are for spells, while the other four are augmentations for each spell. You can put any card in any slot, and it will do something. This means that, for example, I can use a card that casts two daggers and deals bleeding damage, or I can augment another card (my dash, my stun, or a damage-dealing card) and add bleeding damage to that card. Interestingly, while you don't want lower rank (low damage) cards in active slots, a level one card has the same passive effect as a level eleven.  Since there are 60 cards in the game, you have a lot of options to choose from.What this means is that, while in Hades you would choose a weapon, and then gradually build up towards your preferred build, in Dandy Ace you find a few cards that work together, you squish enemies for a while, and then notice that you're not dealing quite enough damage, so you look at the weapon drops and come up with something else, rinse and repeat.Most builds are similar: one dash card (blue), one low cooldown damage dealing card (pink) and two utility/crowd control/high-damage-and-cooldown/survivavility cards (yellow), but there's a lot of room for tinkering and for improvisation.9/10 would easily recommend to any fan of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable enough. At face value (see what I did there?) it has enough polish and the card combination system makes you feel like you're really making impactful decisions. I'm not sure I was making impactful decisions. Granted, I have not unlocked all of the cards yet but so far it seems like you pretty much *have* to take a dash/blink. The gameplay pattern as you progress is dash/blink, then spam your cards in the general direction of the enemy, then dash/blink away and repeat. There are some cards that indicate you could try a more bruiser-y style gameplay pattern with high damage+low range and defensive cards... I... Maybe I just suck but I'd really like to see somebody beat the game on super mega death difficulty doing anything besides kiting and throwing abilities from afar. Still, the game is fun to play and at the end of the day that's what I care about. It's a yes from me.
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good! Obvious Hades influences, but it's its own game. You can't just run into a group of enemies face first and expect to survive. You have to play a lot more tactically and patiently, isolating big foes and taking them out one at a time in a prioritized order, while you do some AOE damage to the rest of the mobs. Needs more cards!
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: This one is really fun;  the art style really carries the lighthearted tone, and the narrator/villain really hits that sweet spot in humor of being so comedic levels of petty and pathetic. The real hook; the mechanic that I feel makes things stand out is what I've been calling mix-and-match magic; any combat ability you get can either be equipped to one of the four combat slots, or, appended to an already equipped card to add damage, or apply a buff yourself/a debuff to anyone it hits, so this allows for a quick change up of tactics when need be, like, heavy emphasis on crowd control attacks for  rooms of enemies, then swap cards around for heavy focus on single target damage when up against a boss.
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game, but only just. It's fun while it lasts, and there are some cool synergies to play around with using the card system, but overall, there's just not that much content to experience. There's only 4 bosses in the game, and for the first couple of hours, it feels as though you are kinda just using the same cards over and over again. It also doesn't help that the melee abilities just aren't all that useful - they're far too punishing to use in comparison to all of the ranged attacks. So suddenly your options for creating a nice build become even more limited.Regardless, I had fun for the hours I spent with the game, but I wouldn't recommend paying more than like £5 for it at absolute most.
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: I managed to beat the final boss on my 3rd run after learning what the game is during my first 2 runs. Took me 40 minutes to learn it and 40 minutes to beat it.I mention this because I love that you can be strong early if you play your cards right without having to invest hours just to get permanent upgrades to even have a fighting chance like many other roguelitesSuch a fun game. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: Tight controls? Check Cool spells and weapons ?   CheckReplay value for Roguelite with different builds and difficulties + Unlockables ? Check. The _ONLY_ thing this game is missing is a bit more content.  I would gladly pay for a DLC of extra levels. If you like Roguelites ( Hades,  DreamScaper, Going Under) you owe it to yourself to pickup this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: Doomed to a lifetime of Hades and Dead Cells withdrawal, I'm always looking for more similar games. Dandy Ace is clearly influenced by these two, but in a more fun, light-hearted setting. The card crafting system evokes Transistor, with cards that can serve as either an ability or an upgrade, providing plenty of interesting decisions. Polished, responsive controls. Challenging but not punishing. Not as much depth or replay value as its inspirations, but still provided quality entertainment for a few days.Developers please note: I got a spinning beach ball of death when I tried to open this on a Mac. Works fine on Windows though.
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: There's not a lot to this game, but what is there is well executed. The art, voice acting, and gameplay are enjoyable. The run format and progression borrows several ideas from Dead Cells. The cards mechanic is unique and is definitely the best part of the game. I most appreciate that the cards you've selected aren't locked and you can easily rearrange them at any time. One thing that bothers me in other roguelites is the more weapons you unlock, the less likely you are to get the one you actually want on a run. In Dandy Ace, so many new cards get dropped on runs, that you'll definitely come across the ones you like.I also appreciated the difficulty curve of this game. In a saturated market of "tough as nails" roguelites, I enjoyed a game that I was able to beat in about 8 hours. New difficulty levels are unlocked after beating the game for players who are looking for an additional challenge.The one area where this game falls flat for me is the music. Given the theme, there was opportunity to have something resembling creepy carnival music. Instead the game provides generic electronic music. I found the music boring, repetitive, and mismatched with the rest of the experience.Overall, this probably isn't one of the best roguelites out there, but if you like the genre and you like the magician theme, it's worth picking up.
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: An incredibly entertaining roguelite with a fresh setting, a fun combat system, fantastic voice actors and a good pinch of humor. You can unlock many active and passive skills that can be combined with one another in a variety of ways. Everyone can create the perfect setup according to their preferences. I play a lot of roguelikes and -lites and Dandy Ace is definitely one of the most entertaining. Clear recommendation!
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: Despite this game being a challenge to play through due to it's ever increasing difficulty, I still think it's a fun game. Just remember to take breaks every now and then. Some of the hit boxes can really get you if you aren't looking for a second (and you gotta choose between obtaining a card upgrade or a healing upgrade each stage, if I recall correctly. Haven't played in quite a while)
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with decent graphics. It's really enjoyable mix of few games.What is Dandy Ace? In one sentence it  would be:Pick  and mix it with From :+ camera perspective+ general idea of gameat this point worth to mention i also do own Hades and this game wasn't anything special to me. Like... Hades, gameplay-wise, does not offer anything new, it's also same copy-paste from other gamesFrom :+ a little bit scrolls-like system, not necessery stats-wise, but cards/weapons drops, works best with twitch integration+ items unlocking and collecting+ huge fully explorable maps instead of small arenas of hades, + twitch integration
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: A very tentative "no" review, because this game is quite fun for about 3 hours which is pretty good for the price, and I can see some people getting even more out of it, but it really lacked a lot of the replayability and variety that roguelikes should have. You only 3 buffs a run which you collect quite early, and your scaling just comes from leveling up your cards which doesn't change the gameplay enough or feel very satisfying once you get used to what the combos are, which doesn't take long. Otherwise, the game is snappy and fun and I've played much worse.
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game. Just bought for myself, but played enough at my friend's PC that I now am confident to write a review.Disclaimer: I'm not a hardcore rogue-like player, but I do like skill based systems and hard games. So my perspective may be different than yours.Things I like - the game is really hard, but not UNFAIR hard. There's a learning curve to be sure, and it feels good when you feel you are getting better at the game, the more you play it. The humor is very tongue-in-cheek, which I like, and the game never really takes itself too seriously. The skill system is very robust, with a mix of League of Legends meet Guild Wars vibe. I like that each card has its own strategy, place, etc. Which helps to vary the game play. Things I wish could be better: I wish there could be more variety in cards at the beginning. Eventually you get more cards to choose from, with more control, sure. But a wider variety at the star should be considered. Also the music, while good, could have been more explored.All in all, highly recommended, even for non hardcore gamers such as I
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: It took me 7 hours to beat the game on Normal Difficulty. Then you have several higher difficulties to try. Pretty fun, but gets quite repetitive after some time.It's clearly inspired by Dead Cells in terms of unlocking system - investing shards (cells) to unlock cards (weapons), trinkets (mutations) and permanent upgrades (The Blacksmith). There's also a synergy system between cards, most likely inspired by Transistor, which is pretty good.Definitely can recommend on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: Great simple Action roguelike. Not many new concepts but still fun to play. My only complaint is that the ending after beating nightmare is none-existent. No admission of defeat or whatever from Lele, kind of bland. One suggestion i would have would be for the "true final boss" be a dark mirror version of Dandy Ace that Lele created out of accident when he trapped them in the realm, so you have to beat your clone to truly escape. Although it would still be kind of cliche, it would be a fun challenge and feel like a more proper, satisfying end to the game, rather than just seeing the credits roll once again. Devs - I hope you read this and consider implementing :)
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: While I haven't put a ton of hours into this game so far, I can say it's one of the better Roguelike on the market.I've seen complains about comparisons but this day and age, that's a pretty half-assed gripe if you ask me; 99% of inventions are the results of taking two things that were already invented. If you're going to bash this game for being similar to games like it on the market, then you should chastise the "originals" (Dead Dells, Hades, etc.) for being too similar to the games of the 80's and 90's that forced you to start all the way over from the beginning, each time you died.Rant aside, here's the good, fun aspects of the games:- The combat feels pretty good, smooth fast, not super long CDs on any of the skills I've come across which adds to the fast-paced feel.- Very unique in most, if not all of the combat cards you get in the game. They're all very original in many aspects and fun to experiment with.- Speaking of experimentation, you can utilize the various and numerous cards you get by throwing one skill on another and augmenting its affects. (Think, Transistor)The cons?- If there is one big thing I'd like to see changed IMMEDIATELY, it would be the clutter in the maps. The areas you fight in are too small to have That. Much. CLUTTER. I already can't count the number of times, in just the small amount of time I've put into this game that Ace has gotten caught on the superfluous amount of unnecessary environmental obstructions. Just reduce it by 50%, at least, that's all I ask.- The only other big negative I can think of at this time is the narrator. Great VA, don't get me wrong, but I have it on low and the dude still insists on commenting at least twice in every room.
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game with many combinations of mechanics, although the combinations of cards left a little to be desired - only adding extra damage to abilities or increasing stun duration etc. I beat the final boss in the 8.4 hours I've played and have no desire to replay the game now. It's good fun while it lasts!
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, good mechanics. Similar to other top down/isometric perspective Roguelites such as Enter the Gungeon, Hades, Transistor etc. but has it's own identity.If there is one shortcoming to this game, it is that there are a multitude of skills at your disposal (once you unlock them), but there are specific primary/support combos which are clearly superior to anything else... And, these particular skill combos make even the hardest difficulty somewhat trivial, once you get skilled at the game and understand enemy patterns.Still, it is well made, has good voice acting, and a good (but very strange) story/premise. Well... the story is somewhat juvenile and isn't particularly deep or compelling like Hades, but It works and is a very fun experience, so don't let that deter you. The devs also say they have plans for additional content/missions in the future, making it a good buy in my opinion.I would recommend to anyone who is a fan of the rouguelite genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really good game :D Have been following it since 2019 and I'm super happy that it came out eventually!I would give it 8/10 <3The combat feels really engaging, which is one of the things I like the most about it.A few suggestions coming from my experience of the game:> The resources lost between stages are a bit high, you can only carry shards after reaching the next stage. Especially in the beginning, you get around 10-20 each stage and 20 for unlocking one feature and losing 15 stage on the stage where you cant beat through yet seems a bit high.> The commentator is a bit too annoying in terms of frequency, it's good that it can be turn down a bit in the settings menu, but even on Low it is still quite frequent in commenting everything I do :(> It would be nice if there are more cards :D> I personally find Portuguese Voice Over much more engaging than English Voice Over, and to be honest the characteristic of Dandy is a bit too self centred at times. It was much more immersive in Alpha/Beta when there wasn't too much dialogue from the main character, so that the player can feel themselves immersed as the first person point of view more
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent mashup of Hades, Dead Cells and Wizard of Legend with a unique and addictive card system. The game allows you to craft your own play style and tweak it as you discover more of the toys the game has for the player to experiment with. For fans of the Roguelite genre, Dandy Ace is not a title to sleep on
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: So I've played about two hours. And will play a bit more.Hands down. This is a good game. Not revolutionary or groundbreaking, but good. Hades set the milestone for action-rpg rouge-lites when it came out. The gameplay was crisp, there was a story, it had fantastic voice acting, and there was a sense of progression in the unlocks.Dandy Ace is all of that just... less.TL;DR: It's a pretty good game that doesn't push any boundaries nor introduces any new concepts. Fans of the rogue-lite genre will find that it borrows a lot from a ton of other games. But overall it's a fun game and does what it does well. If you've played Hades and have run out of content then this is a good second place. If you haven't played Hades yet, get that instead. Good Things First:1: Items and RandomizationYou don't gain upgrades like you do in other rogue-lites where they stay with you for the duration of the run. Instead your entire moveset and ability list is determined by the cards you pick up. As you progress further into the mirror the cards you can find become higher tiered and do more damage. So each run you are constantly switching playstyles in order to be as deadly as possible. You have four card slots, to mirror the three different types of cards. You have Movement cards, Attack cards, and Power Attack cards (that have a longer cooldown but do more damage). What makes it interesting is that each card you pick up can be attached to one of your active cards to add an effect. Stuff like adding poison, slowing the enemy, making the enemy weaker, adding a burning effect, ect.  It's honestly a lot of fun. I had a run when I doubled down on poison so that every action I took resulted in an enemy getting another few stacks of poison. I had a run when I just picked up movement techniques and added damaging elements to each of them, so I flitted around the battlefield, letting my passives wear enemies down while I was untouchable. This is the best part of the game. Knowing that when you open up a chest and get a new card that your entire playstyle could change, and that you're excited about it. 2: CombatThere have been a few points where I've shouted that the hit that killed me was "absolute Bullsh*t" But overall it seems to be a very fair game. It's hard and the bosses are interesting, in a good way, to fight. It has a good selection of enemies. As you progress further it's the same enemies but they have a new quirk so you know how they act but have to deal with a slight change in how they act. E.G. Early level towers shoot 1 fireball, later they shoot 3. Additionally. While it is compared to Hades, I'd say the combat is completely different. In Hades you're trying to avoid attacks and then get up in your enemies face and deal as much damage before getting away. In Dandy you're flitting around the edges of the battlefield. Doing as much damage as you can before the enemy gets too close. It's an easier game (imo) but at the same time you're also much more of a glass cannon than in Hades. The Okay:1: The InspirationThis game borrows heavily from other rogue-lites. And that's neither good nor bad. It has a teleportation system that reminds me of Gungeon. It is an isometric action game like Hades. It has a progression system like Dead Cells. It's narration style is in the form of Hades. You can run from room to room (outside of gauntlet rooms) like dead cells, you're completely free to skip some enemies. Heck, it even has the exact same sort of healing as Dead Cells does. You get a certain number of heals per floor depending on how many you've unlocked and occasionally enemies will drop healing items that you can use. There's probably a few other similarities that I could mention. But overall, if you play rogue-lites, you've already seen everything this game is offering. 2: MusicIt always feels appropriate but I don't think I'd listen to any of the songs outside of playing the game. 3: Level ProgressionI enjoy games where you have an objective to work towards. Dandy Ace does that. Except... it's meh. It's the same sort of progression that Dead Cells has. I am ambivalent about it. It does give you the feeling that each run is important and you can take a step to empower yourself just a bit more, but at the same time it feels like artificial gatekeeping in regards to beating the game. It's very similar to Dead Cells. You can find 'blueprints' to new abilities that you can unlock as you progress through the game. You can buy things that increase your survivability and can make your runs easier. If you like a bit of a grind you'll like this aspect, if you like games that rely purely on skill or knowledge of the enemies then you'll find it annoying. 4: Enemy DesignEvery attack is well telegraphed. Honed to the point that once you see it you know how to avoid it but you still have to be fast. I'd say that the enemy diversity equals Hades (if I haven't compared this game enough to it). Further more, as you delve deeper into the mirror you fight the same enemies but they are more powerful. A melee fighter who just thrust a spear at you may thrust at you in the same way, but slightly faster and the attack has 3 hitboxes instead of one.The Bad:1: ArtstyleI kinda like the artstyle of Dandy Ace. But... it just doesn't flow. The character models all look great. The background looks great. But they just don't... mesh. Taking a second to look at the cards offered in stores the character models just stick out. They don't feel like they belong in the same game. That is subjective though.2: StoryThere is a feeble attempts at a story in the game. A failed wizard traps a successful magician in a cursed mirror for the price of his soul. Maybe there's more to it but that's about as much plot as I've uncovered and I doubt theres more. I got mildly excited when I first started playing when it went into Hades styled plot (you walk up to a character and talk to them) but after my 3rd run I realized that characters just went back to saying the same thing they said last time. For a rogue-lite it's a decent effort. But it is sorely dissapointing after Hades. Especially since the game seems to take inspiration from Hades and has the same sort of Visual Novel stylized representation of each character talking to each other. 3: Narration The story is decent. A fun idea that some narration could be built of, but it gets tedious even two hours in. Your 'nemesis' constantly talks or taunts you at the beginning or end of every room you enter. When an enemy drops a healing item he exclaims how they shouldn't have done that. What might have been humorous lines when I first heard them have been ground to comedic dust by how often they are repeated. At this point they are more annoying than anything. If there were a wider variety of lines it may have been a bit more okay. With the current situation I just want an option to turn him off unless he says something new.Your sidekicks are also copy paste examples of anime girls. It could work, but at the same time they barely have personalities outside of their tropes, and as far as I'm aware there isn't much story development for either of them. 4: Level DesignThis is much more nitpicky than my other complaints. But I have some problem with the level design. It's structured as a rogue-lite where each room you enter contains enemies. There's some rooms you can just run through and some rooms where you're stuck until you kill everything. There isn't any indication that a room is done or that there's an enemy left in the room or not if you're not in a gauntlet room. More than once I found myself wondering if there was another thing I needed to kill before scampering around the room to find the turret in the corner that I hadn't dealt with yet. 8/10 Good but it misses greatness by a long shot. Get Hades before you get this game. It's worth it but there's a much better game on the market.
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: Only a few runs in so far; but am enjoying it a lot more than I thought I would.Definitely more like Curse of the Dead Gods or Slay the Spire than Hades; other than the angle not sure where people are getting it from who have played it. Unlike Hades which is very melee focused, Dandy Ace is extremely movement based. The iframes don't seem to be present or as easily utilized as Hades but honestly if they were the game would be too easy. With the AOE and combinations you can already do, the combat in Dandy Ace is kite and position focused than anything else.Only downside is Lele can get kind of annoying with all the voice bits. Why can't we get some more voice acting from the assistants instead ;o;
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun game. If you've played Hades, this game is similar, but with a different feel and atmosphere. If I had to summarize it, I like this game's gameplay better than Hades --> it gives you more control over your moves. Hades has a deeper and longer metagame though, and there's a bit more variety in the stage layouts. If Dandy Ace adds a metagame system akin to Hades post-end game, then it could reach greater heights. The game's art and atmosphere is also great.
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: Like many said, this is very similar of Hades, isometric action roguelike with different build option, with similar upgrade like in Dead cells (gather some material and can only spend in specific area).The game itself is fine and have a different enough themeEven thought it doesnt feel to have much to propose and may not feel outstanding or unique enoughSadly the "unlocks" feel way too grindy and doesnt add anything but just doing 532 runs for the permenant unlockI note this 6.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

_childDocuments_.review: Dandy Ace is an over the top fast-paced roguelike experience that follows a fabulous magician seeking to combine and use his magical cards while fighting and looting his way to defeat the Green-Eyed Illusionist, Lele, who has imprisoned him in a cursed mirror. While battling your way through Lele’s ever changing palace, combine different cards with more than a thousand possibilities, each with their own playstyles and powers. Every run provides new challenges and combinations for players to explore as they progress closer to Lele.
_childDocuments_.name: Dandy Ace

name: DIRT 5
detailed_description: Join Our Discord! New DLC Available Continue your Career in the DIRT Off-Road Series with the Wild Spirits Content Pack - with new cars, Career events, sponsors and customisation items! Available to purchase now on Store or included as an entitlement for Amplified Edition and Year One Upgrade/Edition owners. Included as part of the latest game update, DIRT 5’s selection of tracks is expanded with a pair of brand new Stampede events in Morocco, and five more real-world liveries added to a quintet of cars! AVAILABLE NOW - Year One Edition About the Game DIRT 5 is a fun, amplified, off-road arcade racing experience created by Codemasters. Blaze a trail on routes across the world, covering gravel, ice, snow and sand, with a roster of cars ranging from rally icons to trucks, to GT heroes. With a star-studded Career, four-player split-screen, innovative online modes, livery editor and more new features, DIRT 5 is the next generation of extreme racing. Let Loose Whilst respecting the heritage and retaining the DNA of the franchise, DIRT 5 writes a new chapter in the legacy of DIRT – bolder and braver than ever before. New features, new innovations and a fresh approach make DIRT 5 a hub of off-road racing, style and culture, where you can constantly create highlight-reel moments. Blaze a Trail Across the Globe Take a trip around the world to and race on over 70+ unique routes across 10 different global locations in stunning, dynamic environments. From racing on the frozen East River in New York, to under the Christ the Redeemer in Brazil, to shining by the Northern Lights at Norway, take on opponents, the terrain and extreme, everchanging conditions. Push The Limits with Incredible Cars Get behind the wheel of an eclectic and exciting roster of cars. Conquer the toughest of terrain with boulder-beating machines, take iconic rally cars to new locations, or feel the power of 900bhp sprint cars. Rallycross, GT, trophy trucks, buggies muscle cars complete the ultimate off-road garage. Own the Spotlight in a Star-Studded Career Under the tutelage of an icon, all eyes are on you to become the new star of an amplified world of off-road racing. Earn sponsorships and unique rewards, conquer all locations, and take on a fierce rival in our biggest ever Career. Compete or Co-Operate in Off-Road Action Local split-screen up to four players on offline modes, including Career, makes DIRT 5 the perfect couch multiplayer racing game as you battle for position with your friends. Online, throw down in curated race playlists for up to 12 players and compete in innovative objective-based modes. Create and Capture with New Features Capture your biggest jumps and best moves with a detailed Photo Mode, and show your creative flair with DIRT’s deepest-ever livery editor for all cars. Plus, more brand new features that allow all players to create and play in DIRT like never before.

_childDocuments_.review: An offroad racing game. The graphics are great and I loved the sound design which really adds to the feel of the races. The controls were more arcade than simulation which is fine by me since I'm more of a casual racing game player, but the races themselves were really easy and became repetitive and stale after a bit.
_childDocuments_.name: DIRT 5

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: It's OK. Easy AI. Could be better with graphic improvements and more tracks.The Rally titles are for the sim players. The numbered titles are the for the arcade players.I enjoyed DiRT 2 and 3 so much - and still do. 4 was a departure from the numbered titles arcade feel. It tried to be both. Met with critical acclaim but mixed reviews from players. It was the black sheep but still delivered that quality we are all used to from Codemasters. 5 appears to have brought the numbered series back to its arcade roots. Just focused on fun. While it does do that to a degree, this is a turd.The textures. Oh the textures. Have we not made any progress? Almost feel like they've been ripped right from the 10 year old previous installments (being 2 and 3). I loaded into a race on tarmac that looked like the textures were still loading. Everything was on Ultra High at 1080p. Compare that to textures from Rally, Rally 2.0, and even 4, this game is a step back in quality. Can't help but think the glitz and glam, bright distracting colors are there to cover up the quality regression. The cars are OK. Maybe that doesn't matter when you're ripping past at 80mph. But still, it's nice to stop and look at what the art team have done. I just can't do that with 5. It's appalling. Do not let any of these photos fool you.The AI is largely a piece of cake on Very Hard. The only real challenge I had was with RWD cars on technical tracks, and the ridiculous things you slide around an oval track. Those, quite frankly, are not fun. It's NASCAR on dirt. MAKE A LEFT TURN! Furthermore, you can't be clean. Even if you want to, you can't. You have to shove and push in every event. Because the AI will do that to you. In my first few hours of play, I was shunted more times than I care to count. If you try and race ~90% clean, by avoiding as much contact as possible, you will not win. You'll be at the back while watching the AI shove each other. Once you manage to slip past, it's a no brainer. You win. On some tracks you can get first by turn one. The absolutely ride on rails.There is a small selection of tracks. Forward of reverse of each one. It's limited. More tracks would vastly improve variety.The car selection covers iconic rally, 'murican trucks, to modern day beasts and EVs! Granted the list is short compared to something like Forza, but the ones you want are there. There is zero tuning or upgrades to be had. You get what you get... and that's it. This leaves many cars relegated to the garage because no on will ever drive them. Thinking "too slow" or "handles like crap". In turn it's a full on meta roster. Previous installments in the series, in fact all of them, offer tuning on a basic level. No, not talking upgrades, *just* tuning. Brake Balance, LSD, Camber, Toe, pressure, aero, etc. In very simple terms too. Honestly, just give me something please.The music gets repetitive fast. After 5 hours of play, I turned it off. In most games I turn it all off anyway unless it's something without lyrics; like World of Warcraft music.The playground thing is another copy and paste from Trackmania. Which is what GTA V and Forza have done. This means you now get the same people who post playgrounds or tracks you can't complete unless you know the secret, spend 30 minutes trying to get past a certain section, or just straight up crawl along to figure it out. None of that is my idea of fun. I can't blame CM for that. That's player issues. But makes part of the game less appealing to me. I have to weed through dozens of playgrounds to find one I can just blast around in.It's extremely repetitive.After having dragged this game through the mud, I'm going to completely confuse you. I like this game. Granted it's not their best work. In the short time I've played it I have grown to like it. The ability to blast around a track without much effort is what makes it fun. Much like DiRT 2 did all those years ago. The game that really started it all for me. Despite its issues it's got an appeal to it. That glitz and glam I ragged about is what gives this game a great aesthetic. The bright colors, grabbing graphics and positive soundtrack. It feels like an event when you're playing. As usual, I still support Codemasters by buying their games. At least for now. EA is involved now and that just spells doom.

_childDocuments_.review: Apparently I was able to launch the game and play it a day early (even with the Amp'd Edition). Anyway, first impressions of ex-Evo's DiRT, it's not Motorstorm, but it's pretty damn close with a lot of extras. Played through some of the the Career mixed with online/Playgrounds and I gotta say, I'm thoroughly impressed with what I see from a gameplay perspective. I'll just list out my impressions:- Performance. Let's just get this out of the way: it's not good. I'm noticing now it has Denuvo Anit-Tamper, which, while offline play is hugely appreciated, is likely the largest contributing factor to performance loss. No crashes at least, but an i7 3770 GTX1650 16GB/DDR3 pulls 55FPS at low with about 5-10FPS variation, and that's with adaptive resolution off. DiRT 5, thankfully, is one of those games that looks pretty even on low settings, but good god it chugs. Optimization needs to be a priority before content starts rolling in because if history is anything to go by, more content will make bad performance worse. For the purposes of what I expected though, clear pretty 55FPS is much better than motion-blurred 30FPS in Motorstorm Pacific Rift on my old PS3, but that's far from a good standard. - Lots of progression make races meaningful: Career progression has a lot of variety. From what I can see, you progress through several races until you're able to "throwdown" in a 1v1 with a named racer; inconsequential in the scheme of things, but a nice touch nonetheless. Races earn you experience, cash, and rep for your sponsor of choice, all of which ties into...- Customization: Cars can be customized! A wide selection of patterns, colors, paint types (glossy, matte, "special finish," etc), all paid with cash earned in game. None of it is performance related (I'm looking at you Ghost NFS's), so unlocks are purely for stylish bragging rights. Stickers are fun, they can be plastered anywhere on the car at any size with any orientation with the editor. - Tracks: Very pretty, lots of locales, and with  of variety. Tracks can range from tight circuits where clean racing is a must to absolutely chaotic offroad racing with hazards (read: fun) everywhere; a bunch of different and unique modes to boot. Not as much verticality and absurdity as something like Motorstorm Pacific Rift with cliffs and lava, but it's easily made up for with one feature: Dynamic weather. Race conditions can do a 180 as time passes: Tracks can transition from grippy and clean to snow-clogged and slippery, bright afternoon tracks can fade into night by the end, it really works wonders for keeping things interesting. I haven't even gotten to the Gymkhana/technical races yet, but I have good expectations.- Sound/Music: Sounds are clean and crisp, as would be expected of a AAA racer, but there's some cool effects. The soundtrack (which is great btw, The Chemical Brothers, The Prodigy, you can see the influence) plays continuously, but as you transition from menus to races the music will instead play out of speakers around the track, allowing you to still listen to the music without it playing on top of everything else. - Playground: It's cool and has the potential of spawning infinite content. There are some drawbacks, limited assets, small arenas, etc, but I find it to be very novel, occupying a space really only Trackmania filled otherwise. I enjoy the "puzzle racing" aspect of it, where setting the best time isn't reliant on just your racing skill, but also how well you can navigate really tight corners, jumps, and otherwise convoluted track designs. My only serious complaint is the lack of a "History" tab; the only way you can go back and check the leaderboards is to pin/favorite the track and come back to it later. Otherwise, very neat addition. Conclusion: Motorstorm is dead and not on PC, god bless, but this more than makes up for the Motorstorm-shaped hole in my heart with lots of cool features to boot. Frankly, that's good enough for me.

_childDocuments_.review: CodeMasters make all sorts of driving games. From the arcade to the simulator, they've produced games all across the spectrum for people from the sweatiest Asetto tryhard to the most casual Burnout fan. Dirt 5 has been met with a great deal of controversy, because many people feel CM missed the mark and produced a game too light on the simulation side and too heavy on the arcade side. I won't dispute that this game is unabashedly arcadey, it just is. But that doesn't mean it isn't a blast to play. It harkens back to the days of Need For Speed Hot Pursuit 2, or Flatout Ultimate Carnage, when racing games were no more complex than getting to make sick looking cars vroom real fast. It has a few issues, online performance has been a sticking point for some and it's a monster to run on high settings. But I've been hungry for an arcadey goofy racing game I can play with my non-racing fan friends, and Dirt 5 is just the remedy to what ails me. It's flashy, it's loud, and it's a polished arcade driving game that simply doesn't have a substitute of it's quality on the market today. I don't want all CM games to be like this. But i'm sure as hell glad this one is.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: With the recent updates to the game, it has made great improvements. It finally fixed my issues with my controller, and gave us more controller options for deadzones and sensitivity settings. However, the game still needs work when it comes to optimization, physics, and difficult curve before I can recommend it.DiRT 5 is a mixed bag. Essentially, the best way I can describe it is that it's a more grounded, watered down version of their previous game, ONRUSH. (Codemasters Cheshire, who made DiRT 5, was originally named Codemasters EVO, who made ONRUSH 2+ years ago) However, it fails at what I wanted from a more arcade styled DiRT game.Firstly, the driving physics and handling aren’t great. They feel somewhat floaty, and the handling is way too easy. I turned off all the assists, and I had an easier time controlling these vehicles than other, more arcady racers, like Gas Guzzlers Extreme. I’m talking about on keyboard too, which I’ll mention why I’m using it over controller in a later section. I honestly rather have an arcade racer like this challenge me with vehicle physics and handling rather than with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ rubber banding AI...Secondly, the crashing physics suck. They got them right in ONRUSH, but yet in DiRT 5, hitting other vehicles feels like bumper cars. I’m not talking about ‘takedowns’ in ONRUSH, but it generally felt better bumping and hitting cars in that game. I know this ain’t a vehicular combat racer, but I want it to feel good for those rare times I end up smashing into players, or hell, they end up smashing into me.Thirdly, the 3rd person camera is terrible. Again, they got in right in ONRUSH, yet in this game it jerks around at every little hit & bump. Also, it tends to clip on objects if they fly past it, causing the camera to jerk into the car. Could we just have the great 3rd person camera from ONRUSH, please?Fourthly, what I didn't mention originally was the difficultly. Its weird, because some events can be really easy, yet others, like the Sprint ones, are really hard on the same difficultly setting. I turned it up multiple times, and I'm still really pulling out ahead in standard races but falling behind in others. I don't get what's wrong with the difficulty.Another reason why I’m still giving this game a negative review is because it's plagued with some of bad technical issues. I don’t care that it's a ‘live service’ model game, or that it is being worked on for current gen, next gen, and PC. We are paying $60 USD or more for a game that should have been released in a polished state. Let's start with the PC issues:•No window options (Windowed, Borderless, Exclusive Fullscreen, etc): You got to use ALT + ENTER to get into fullscreen, but it seems the game only runs in a borderless windowed fullscreen, so you don’t even get the performance boost of running in exclusive fullscreen.•Forced TAA anti-aliasing: The worst anti-aliasing method ever, which makes the game look blurry AF and causes ghosting on the vehicles. It boggles my mind there is NO WAY to turn this off, or atleast, use a different AA method...•Terrible optimization & pitiful graphics: My system is 5 years old (my specs are on my Steam profile), so I don’t expect it to be able to handle high settings, but I can’t even maintain a locked 60fps on all medium settings with the resolution settings all on 1080p. On all ultra low settings, I couldn’t even get a stable 60fps in a Gymkhana event in the Cape Town Stadium! For ♥♥♥♥ sakes guys! This game ain’t even that graphically impressing! ONRUSH looked not only better than DiRT 5, but also ran better than this on the PS4 Pro...Like I said in the edit, while some of the issues that I originally listed were solved, but this game still needs more work before it can be really good. Its just still just too average mechanically and gameplay wise...

_childDocuments_.review: Do not buy this game. At the time of posting this, the game is four months old and already 50% off, and I don't think that's enough. I played the whole thing on a free weekend and I still want a refund. I am 100% confident that this is the worst racing game Codemasters has developed by far. After my first hour, I was bored out of my mind and sightly mad. After five hours, I felt dead and empty inside. I don't have a single positive thing to say about it.It's in the title, you race on dirt, so why do these cars have so much grip  that it feels like a slightly damp road in a road racing game? It's genuinely faster 90% of the time to drive as though you're on asphalt in this game. Even water does nothing, you can drive through a veritable lake on the track and not notice. Interestingly, RWD cars seem to have  grip than anything else, until they don't, because their traction works like a light switch. In every other situation though, these cars are so grippy that I often can't drift at all when I want to, . Also, the AI are brain dead immovable objects that can block you for whole laps on narrow tracks, and even on the hardest difficulty they drive so slow that - provided you get past them before they pile up and block you - it's nearly impossible to lose first place, let alone fall off the podium, unless you specifically choose the slowest cars available... which sometimes you have to specifically buy, because the starting car is sometimes pretty good. That doesn't matter either though, because even a dead last finish still gets you a stamp and still allows you to progress. What's the point? Listen, I appreciate that racing games have finally begun to move past the idea that you must take first place to progress, but LAST should be a LOSS.Speaking of pointless things, money. I don't understand why that's even a mechanic, because you earn so much money from every race you're guaranteed to earn a million before you finish the game, even if you take the shortest route to the credits like I did. That route is five (5) hours long. Five hours to beat the game and it still feels like it was padded for time. Add to that the fact that everything to add value to a career mode is gone (sponsors are meaningless afterthoughts, no teams at all, no sense of progression whatsoever, no rhyme nor reason to anything,) and you have one of the most shallow big budget racing games ever to hit the market. Not just shallow, but lifeless in every way. There is no personality to this game, so they hired some YouTube "personalities" to carry the whole game on their shoulders... and whether or not that's a good thing depends on whether or not you enjoy Donut media. The cars are lifeless, they all feel the same, and the the extent of customization available to you is three presets, four sponsor decals that are just for looks, and one sticker. Woo. Even the graphics are lifeless, with this game looking so amazingly dull that if it wasn't for the sheer abundance of particle effects and bloomy lighting, it could be two console generations older than it is and probably look nearly the same. I'm not one to prioritize graphics either, but when your game has nothing else going for it...Who is AJ? Who is Bruno? Why do I care? Why were they some of the easiest races in the game despite being the final ones? What's the point of secondary objectives when they're all stupidly easy and do nothing of value? Why does the camera look up and down with the right stick instead of look behind and either zoom in or raise the angle? Why does the weather and even the time of day change between two opposite extremes in five seconds or less? Why does the game take five entire minutes to launch? What am I doing here? Why is pathfinder so mindbogglingly stupid? Why is any of this? What even are the throwdowns? Whatever they are, they're important enough to get their own dedicated tab on the career screen, not only did I never get an explanation from the game about what they are, they're all optional.This whole game is optional, and the right choice is to choose any other option.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: DiRT 5 shouldn't have been called DiRT 5. It feels more like a spinoff dirt game, more so than DiRT Rally series. It's way too experimental to be a mainline DiRT game where fans expect something specific instead of something experimental, at least as much experimental as DiRT 5. It's a good arcade game with good design, eye-watering graphics and floaty but generally great driving physics. I'd say give it a shot if you're looking for something to play in short bursts or you want to try something different in arcade racing genre.Firstly; DiRT has never been a simulation game. It was always a mishmash of frantic and andrenaline pumping races, sugarcoated with pretty UI, sparkled with great alternative/rock soundtrack to accompany you through your dirt and mud filled journey. Sountrack and UI stayed thankfully, but compared to the rest of the game, they just feel like a nod to the old times when DiRT 2 was the real deal. UI and sountrack is heavily inspired by DiRT 2; and it shows.Graphics are the best the series has ever been, with incredible dynamic weather system, beutiful lighting engine and combined with all the confetti, sparkles and good map design gives a great feeling of craftsmanship and talent codies still have. As it's being a mainline DiRT game, meaning it's an arcade game, handling physics also have been adjusted from DiRT 4 and DR accordingly. Due to fans splitting up on DiRT4's handling modes and general feel, codies have decided to ditch the realism aspect of the handling and went all arcade. As with soundtrack and UI, handling takes a lot of inspiration from DiRT 2, trying to feel fast paced and adrenaline filled. For the most part it succeeds; if you don't count some of the cars feeling extremely unpredictable and uncontrollable (I'm looking at you rock crawling) and when you put that fast paced handling model on slow cars, some vehicles feel like a drag, a chore to drive. It all vanishes when you get into an Aston Martin or anything with more than 300HP really. Once you get the hang of it, it's really fun and unexpectedly engaging.Soundtrack and menu now. Soundtrack... where do I start? Codies have always been great at fitting their games with their music and I'm glad to announce that it has not changed. In fact, dare I say, it's better than ever; better than DiRT 4, almost side by side with DiRT 2. Grungy tunes accompanying you in menu and loading screens, high-tempo alternative music and some rock/country sparkled in between in races create a great atmosphere; capturing what made DiRT 2 so special. Menu is also extremely inspired by DiRT 2,using extremely similar fonts, artwork etc. but it falls a bit short of it's predecessor. It's nothing bad, in fact UI is pretty good; but if you've played DiRT2, you'll see the flatness and lack of extra depth in UI design.Car list. It's absolutely briliiant. Seriously. This is where "spinoff" feel comes from the most in my opinion. Older dirt games always had "dirt"-special vehicles in their car list. But in DiRT 5, you can race in a freakin' Aston Martin, a BMW M2 or if you fancy yourself a classic 911,Fastback Mustang, or even an offroad EV. This is an offroad game mind you, this bold choice of cars is a nice welcome in my opinion. Models are extremely detailed as well.What it has in those aspects, it falls short in story and attention to detail. It's not that DiRT 5 lack any neat details; it's just you have to specifically look for them to notice it. Story is... well... almost non existent. Although it's nice to see Donut Media in the game, they (or any other character in the story for that matter) don't really do anything. Even what you are doing is not really clear; even the game is self aware of it by mentioning how or why even you're racing in the first place. Because of that, it's really hard to get any kind of motivation to play and experience what the game has to offer. What it offers is not much either, sadly. There is no traditional rally, which has always been a part of DiRT series. Instead, there are some vague, "different" type of events which feels almost the same, except with different vehicles. Most are fun, but some are just... bad: rock crawling for example, as I mentioned before. This is another reason why it shouldn't  have been a mainline entry imo; as it creates a false expectation in players.All in all, it's a fun arcade racer if you give it a chance and try to enjoy it. It's not for everyone, especially not for hardcore sim racers. But it's really obvious Codemasters really wanted to try something new with DiRT 5 and because of that I believe it deserves a chance, more than what it got. All you have to do is look at it from a different angle.

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't recommend this game to people who played Dirt 2-3-4 or the Dirt Rally-games and are looking for simcade. This is an arcadegame in my opinion. The visuals are great, everything looks great, but thats where the positives end for me. - This game's physics feel odd: when on the throttle, the steering is VERY sensitive. If you're not braking or applying throttle, the cars don't want to steer into a corner. And if you steer and apply throttle, snap-oversteer isn't uncommon.- If you have the driver-aids off, they seemingly still do interfere in certain places, making the cars very unpredictable. I actually got frustrated sometimes with the way the cars handle. If you are racing, you want predicatability.- There are alot of different cars, but the different stats on those don't really matter for the races. two-wheel drive (front or rear) and 4-wheeldrive don't matter in ways of terrain, driving style, speed or cornering. - The AI either falls all the way back during a race, or get rubberbanded right up on your rear or past you. And don't get me started that the AI has the ability to brake mid-air and actually slow down.- Different terrains also don't feel al that different. Tarmac isn't that much grippier than dirt, snow or ice, ice feels the more like tarmac than the tarmac does.- There is a weathermechanic that doesn't do anything other than inhibit visibility. You would think that rain on a dirt-track will make you slide more to which you have to alter your driving style, but alas.*Edit*: I finished the main campaign now, and it felt like a slog to get through. Little variation in types of races, scenery or cars available. So i understand the low % of people who finished the main campaign- You can't change anything in the setup of the cars, so if you don't like the feel of the cars: tough luck.All-in-all: Dirt 2 and 3 felt more realistic than this game does, and those games are 13-15 years older respectively.
_childDocuments_.name: DIRT 5

_childDocuments_.review: Finally a proper Dirt game, in the spirit of playful arcade games like Dirt 2 & Dirt 3. The visuals also much better than what is shown in youtube videos, most likely because of the compression in youtube videos. Also the kind of tracks & visual details in Dirt 5 seems to be very sensitive to less AA & image compression artifact.Unfortunately to long time Codies fans, the new (non-EGO) engine used in Dirt 5 is less optimized than the old and trusted Ego engine, resulted in less stable frame rates compared to e.g  Dirt Rally 2.0 or Grid (2019). But I still managed to get (mostly) stable frame rates between 40-60 FPS on an GTX 1050 Ti by specifically lowering most details (the Auto settings are stupid, it's unlike in FH4 where you can specify the target FPS), but it still looks quite flashy compared to Dirt Rally 2.0, which while looks really good, start showing the old age of the EGO engine due to the visual style.But my biggest gripe with Dirt 5 is the content. Compared to previous Dirt games (including the not so arcade Dirt 4), the car classes in Dirt 5 seems to be very lacking, or maybe because it just doesn't fit my taste. They have 90's rally cars, but I can't see 2000's rally cars, only modern ones, which leave a big gap in the car list. Also unlike Dirt 3 which have 60's, 70's, 80's, 90's, Open Rally, and Pro Rally categories, in Dirt 5 you only have Classic Rally, 90's Rally, and Modern Rally, which means a lot less cars in general.This is very similar situation with Grid (2019), in which not only the base game is very thin on content, even the complete game is still thin on content. Which make it a very bad proposition of value, because you can do similar Rally Cross or Cross Country event on Forza Horizon 4, albeit with a rather generic looking tracks (because it just off road parts of the map), but in turns you can do it with a lot of car choices which makes the events more varied.Also, I don't really mind with the Donut Media involvement, because I also regularly watch their contents on youtube. But if the lack of content (partially) also due to the development budget spent quite significantly elsewhere, I'd rather have more content than familiar commentary.And the Playground it just not fun enough, I kinda like the weirdness of it, but creating a tracks / routes with great flow isn't easy, and with the generic backdrop of Playground mode, it makes Playground feels like a chore to play. The various spectacles of the mode doesn't really add much to the generic backdrop. Some tracks in Playground admittedly looks fun to play though, but after testing it for real, I think the fun tracks in Playground mode is just a drop of water in a vast sea of boring stuff.TLDR; I welcome the return of the playful DiRT series, but the lack of content really kills it. Wait for it to really drops in price, or until new significant amount of content (locations & cars) are added.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really glad this game came on for a free weekend; after looking at all the gorgeous videos, even watching some of the behind-the-scenes stuff, I was excited to see the Dirt franchise return to heavily stylized racing a la Dirt 3. There's no doubting there's a certain exuberance in this game that I haven't felt in the Dirt games in a while. I've been a big CM fan since Grid, then played Dirt 3, Dirt Rally, Dirt 4, and Dirt Rally 2.0 totaling a couple hundred hours. This game does feel very flashy, exciting, and loaded with interesting ideas. For instance, I can't remember if of all the racing games I've played, I've played one that natively had player-made maps. There are some really interesting details here!However, the game was a total disappointment. Although I love the gorgeous track environments, the beautiful lighting, the sexy-looking menus, and the return of music from actual major artists, this game fails  where it matters most: the racing.The new handling model sucks. You almost can't tell the difference between different driving surfaces, because the cars barely drive differently between them. Drive through a giant patch of standing water? No effect on the car whatsoever. Cars that are flipping in midair seem to right themselves without touching anything. You can barrel into a turn and start turning without any concern as to weight transfer, and the car responds. If you ever need to brake, the brakes have tremendous stopping power no matter what's going on. Also, as has been mentioned elsewhere, it appears as though there's no real car damage. None at all. Not even as an option. Yikes!Also, ugh, the track design. Of the ~8 or so tracks I tried, all but one were thoroughly so wide that you never had to go below 45mph to make it around the track. Perhaps this is just due to the fact the game is exclusively centered around racing in large packs, but designs like this make the tracks booooooring as helllllll.The progression of cars seems... non-existent. As far as I could tell, there's no upgrading cars, there's no tuning, and really the only thing you can change on a car is the paint job. Maybe DLC will change this, but I didn't get the vibe there are even that many cars to choose from. Plus all the ones I tried drove really similarly. Not to mention, after only about an hour of playing the career mode, I already had the money to buy the highest car in more than one class. WTF?The graphics, while in some cases absolutely stunning, also had surprising gaps in quality. Drive through that patch of water I mentioned earlier? The splashed water is straight-up 2D as far as I could tell. Looked like something out of a proper 90s arcade game. This is running on bleeding-edge hardware (Zen 3 Ryzen 7 and an RTX 3070) and maxed-out settings, so I don't see this getting better.The sound is shockingly bad; the car motors sound distant and unconvincing, even when you're using inside cameras. The in-game music also sounds heavily filtered, as though it were played through a small radio. I don't get why.There's also random other quibbles I have with the game, like when I was in a head-to-head race and one of the goals it gave me was to "Jump + Trade Paint". Ok, I get it, hit the other car while in mid-air. But this track . The completionist in me is deeply frustrated by this >_>.Also, despite a clear focus on the visuals, this game doesn't support VR. Dirt Rally 2.0 did, and looked damn good in it, which makes this all the more disappointing.A bunch of reviews have joked that CM made a Need for Speed game here; there may be some truth to that, but I can think of at least 6 (relatively old now, and mostly available legally online for free) NFS games I've played a lot, whose overall experiences were more coherent and ultimately more fun than this.To me, this game seems like someone designed a literal arcade game with today's tech. It's flashy, gorgeous, exuberant, and loud. But it's also shallow, unsatisfying, and self-limited. I'd feel happy about it if I paid $1 to play this in a movie theater (rip lol) for 10 minutes and then walked away forever. Maybe it'll get better with future releases, but I fully expect to never want to buy this game, despite being a  racing fan and a big CM fan to boot. I'd probably download and play through Need For Speed: Underground 2 again first. That game had customization, tuning, decent driving, and a real story, to go along with having a strong sense of aesthetics.

_childDocuments_.review: A completely different genre to Dirt 4 and not particularly good at it. Dirt 4 was by no means a perfect game but it was an interesting and challenging rally game with procedural stages and physics that could be challenging (if not top notch "simulation"). 5 has thrown all that out the window to be an arcade wheel to wheel off road racer without any rally at all. I'm not set against that idea but to my taste it doesn't do it particularly well and it's up against much better competition in this genre in my opinion.Performance is an issue for me, it looks pretty on high settings but runs very bad so I have to turn down the settings to the point where it looks worse than Dirt 4/Dirt Rally 2 and the frames still bog down when there's a lot happening on screen in front of me. The career races are all short, no qualifying and start from the back so they all turn into a frantic dash of bumper cars to try and overtake all the AI before the end. Even on the hardest difficulty I'm lapping much faster than the AI most of the time and that's how it has to be so that you can win in this format. The driving physics just feel over simplified to me, even turning all the assists of and driving manual I don't feel a proper sense of weight or tire grip. In comparison, Forza Horizon 4 manages to have fun, easy to drive, arcade physics while still giving the cars feeling to me.A few other miscellaneous gripes:- No car upgrading or tuning- Very limited decal customisation/paint options- Relatively short car list- Constantly shows me adverts for it's DLC trying to direct me to the store- No mouse support in menus- Podcasts? - Troy Baker keeps trying to coach me in the menusThe good points? - Good car/environment sounds- Cool tracks and environment designs, a lot of variety and attention to detail- Great soundtrackNot sure if it's intentional but I find it quite funny that the main two main voiced character rivals are Troy Baker and Nolan North.In conclusion, while this isn't the direction I hoped for with Dirt 5 it certainly has potential but sadly to me it falls short of really delivering. If you're interested in arcade offroad racing I'd instead recommend checking out Forza Horizon 4 or Wreckfest. Horizon in comparison has a multiplayer open world, massive car list, upgrades and tuning and full decal editor. Wreckfest combines old school arcade racing feel with soft body physics and awesome destruction to properly lean into the bumper car match these games end up becoming anyway. Both run much, much smoother on my system too. It feels to me that they're trying to mimic the success for the Forza Horizon series and I think it falls quite short of competing with FH4 and in the process they're lost the things special to the Dirt series. I picked it up cheap in a bundle and in that context it's a bit of fun but I wouldn't buy it specifically, certainly not for full price.

_childDocuments_.review: IF you are looking for a rally sim, do not buy this game. This is not for you.Whilst this title reminds of the old DiRT 2&3 games, it still lacks some jazz. It feels like it's missing something that made the previous DiRT games full of life.Overall the good parts are:+ The arcade racing action+ Good driving experience and handling, suited to anyone+ Diverse racing modes and tracks combined with a decent variety of cars, about just enough to fill everyone's needs+ Good weather effects, especially thunderstorms+ Graphics are overall good, with a few parts on certain areas that look unpolished+ Donut media+ Good soundtrack, decent car sounds. At the time of this review I have only played ~3hrs and got to drive 4 different cars.Some negative parts:- Minor bugs in graphics and physics, weird particles in certain moments- No technical tuning for vehicles, limited player customization- The overall performance of the game. I'm running the game on a Ryzen 5 3600, 16 gb of ram 3200mhz and a 5700XT card on very high and I barely reach 65-70 fps overall (1920x1080).- I'm experiencing random crashes about 30 mins into the game. Might be from the game or not, I've still yet to determine- Few graphic settings. Missing AA & Fullscreen options.This is a fun game nonetheless, so if you want to have some fun for a couple of hours per day, it's a good arcade experience with enough variety to keep you entertained. However, because of the issues this game currently has, especially performance, I'd say that you either wait for more patches before paying full price for it, or get it with a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to leave this positive review despite some issues that the game has. Here's why I think you should give it a chance if you're looking for an arcade racer to enjoy on a couch with a controller:1) Fun arcade physics, which are honestly quite good, even though they do act strangely if you flip your car or bump into large obstacles2) Playgrounds which are a very important feature of this game, devs gave us quite a  large variety of objects to make tracks with and they honestly are a lot of fun, do not look at this as a gimmick, it's a big feature of the game.3) Some very interesting and fun vehicles that offer decent variety, including both historic (Porsche 959, Lancia Stratos) and interesting concept cars (An electric Audi AI: Trail Quattro is great).4) Decent mode variety that I would break down to: gymkhana, racing in a circuit, racing on a point to point road, racing an oval and racing on ice and path finder. In combination with playgrounds this provides enough variety.5) Fun atmosphere of a festival, which I sorely missed in dirt 4.*6) I have greatly enjoyed my time with this game, just crank the difficulty up to provide a good level of challenge.Issues that I have with the game include:1) Impossible to disable TAA, use sharpening in your control panel for now.2) Graphics are actually quite decent, despite many people lying about dirt 2 looking better, but some assets and texture work could definitely use improvement.3) Performance is mediocre, considering the picture quality the game provides. I expect an improvement on this part, but it is by no means terrible.4) Physics can behave "glitchy" sometimes as mentioned above*5) Sometimes invisible walls can make tracks feel too restrictive, track design could use a bit more freedom and interactive physical objects.If you still have your doubts about this game, I recommend waiting for a sale, this game is worth 30$, while full price might be a bit too much.* - added after completing the game
