_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr An improvement on the original in almost every perceivable respect, with the "almost" there only being that the execution of the game involves a lateral move in mechanics. It is not simply an improved Curious Expedition 1, but a different take altogether, which uses many lessons from the first game to create a much better product. Whether you like this different take is up to personal preference, but from a design and quality of play perspective, it is an objective improvement. 8.5 / 10Curious Expedition 2 follows the adventures of a team led by a lead explorer, who is under the loose employ of one Victoria Malin, a woman obsessed with a mysterious and powerful technology she stumbled upon on one of her own expeditions. The game is not devoted to this storyline, though, as you complete many expeditions in between 'story missions' that are more similar to the first Curious Expedition.Maybe that is a good place to go next...Curious Expedition 1 involved a pure rogue-like experience, with each 'run' standing alone, comprising of six expeditions of procedurally generated regions of a handful of types. By finishing (and, importantly, not necessarily *winning*) runs you would unlock new expedition leaders, who came with a unique perk, unique starting party and unique starting equipment. My pursuit in the game was always to try to complete runs with a variety of these teams, though I very seldom succeeded (feel free to throw your obligatory 'git guds' in here...). The only real reward for doing so, though, was that in the character selection screen, expedition leaders portraits would have more fancy frames (silver or gold, I think, instead of plain wood) ... so really just your own private bragging rights. Still, I was drawn into the original by its nice-if-trendy pixel graphics, awesome music, and infinite variety of gameplay experiences. While you would frequently encounter similar situations, how you handled them was always modulated by your circumstances, and no run (even with the same party) was even the same, even if many of the parts were the same. Now, how does #2 compare? It improves in almost every way, while deciding to build the game differently. Instead of a true rogue-like experience, with each run being fresh from one another, CE2 starts you out in a Story Campaign that takes place over a much longer play session. Your characters can have items equipped directly to them now (one 'hand' item, and one 'body' item), which opens up worlds of possibilities. The experience system is more gradual and long-term, with smaller points adding to pools of larger needed amounts to gain levels, where the original had this somewhat awkward "star" system that capped out fairly quickly, and could not be used to level animal companions in CE1, where the new exp system lets you level animals to great effect similar (or greater, even) than humanoid allies. Between expeditions, your performance earns you rank progress with one of three expedition sponsor guilds, who each have their own special abilities and unique available items based on your progress with them. Further, you gain "Expo tickets" which can be used to purchase a variety of beneficial items, upgrades and services between expeditions. I could go on in terms of the 'weeds' of their improvements but instead I'll focus on one last *huge* improvement / change in my opinion...combat. They completely overhauled how health, injuries and combat work in CE2 versus CE1. CE1 had a rather unique dice-based combat system that had its charm...but it was very RNG heavy and incredibly mercurial - two of the same combat encounters could go wildly differently depending on the dice, from winning without injury, to a full run wipe. CE2 is far more forgiving, giving the player many more tools to deal with combat creatively, and reducing the brutal power of enemies, animals and monsters overall. The amount of times I wiped due to a single combat in CE1 during a run that had been going swimmingly until then...I can't count. In CE2, playing on normal difficulty (as I always did in CE1), I completed the entire campaign with only *one* lost companion, who wasn't even lost in combat but rather a random world event that I didn't anticipate. In CE1, you often end up going through travelling companions like water in the desert. I was so much happier, relaxed and satisfied playing CE2 because of this change alone, and all the others just added up to a much more pleasant experience.So, was CE1 bad? No. It was a starting point, and a unique experiment, and honestly I still think its a good, fun game in a lot of ways. It just suffered from taking away control or options, or making you feel like you were being punished for playing, where CE2 very rarely does so - if something bad happens, you usually *could* have avoided it by taking a different path, preparing differently, or just taking less risky choices. In CE1, sometimes your hands were tied and you were led to a place of destruction by pure randomness and bad luck. Giving players agency, options and respecting their time and effort by giving them second or even third chances is something I have grown to value more and more in games, and CE2's developers clearly seem to have learned a similar lesson between their games. It has a demo, so if you are unsure if its your cup of tea, just try it out! Its a unique (and, for me at least, pretty chill) experience  and I definitely recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the Alpha of Curious Expedition 1 on the dev's website, and bought it from them before it was even listed on Steam. The game currently has lots of things that aren't finished. That's fine. It has tons of improvements over the original game: different types of expeditions, factions to support, custom explorers, a merger between the combat environment and the exploration environment, just to name some of the biggies. This game is fantastic fun, and as more and more effort continues to be poured into it, this game will both grow and gain polish. Buy now, or buy later, but it's a winner for sure, and don't be concerned by the fact that it's still under construction.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the first one. I instantly bought the second as soon as it was available because the first one was done so well. The combat is worse than the first one, especially the combat animations, which in the version I played could not be sped up and looked mostly terrible.  When it was pixel graphics, the developers could get away with bad animations as it just added to the charm. Now it would literally be better with no combat animations. The character selection is minimal and nothing compared to the first one. The first game had a seemingly endless supply of explorers to play and unlock. Each character seemed to make the game different to play and were unique, and also were named after real explorers which was really cool.They added these house mechanics, events at home, and hats which were pretty cool at first, but were entirely unneeded. _childDocuments_.review: In its current condition CE2 is an inferior game to CE1. With early access games, that is to be expected: they usually have a strong foundation, but limited content. Unfortunately, CE2 has major issues at its core, since almost all of its main mechanics are sluggish and simply less fun when compared to its predecessor.The only upside is the art, which is gorgeous for the locations you visit. At the same time, art direction on the world map is in conflict with the rest of the game at the moment. Map tiles look messy and hard to read compared to CE1, but this will hopefully be updated in the upcoming releases.All in all, CE1 also came a long way since its launch and Maschinen-Mensch worked hard on improving it to become the fantastic game it is today. With the same commitment CE2 could potentially become a fun game later down the road as well.Edit 1: As of September 2020, the combat has improved and is definitely not a deal-breaker anymore. The world map is still less intuitive, and the game still feels sluggish though. I ran a small test: resting at a waterfall in CE1 took me around 15 seconds (with some events happening), while in CE2 it took almost 30 seconds due to extra fade to black transitions. This makes the whole experience less enjoyable compared to CE1. At the end of the day, if you play these games for the atmosphere and storytelling then CE2 is fine, but if you prefer a roguelike with snappy mechanics then CE1 is still the superior game.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: When taken on its own, a decent little game. When compared with its predecessor, utter rubbish. CE2, along with CE1, is a tile exploring game where you control a party of adventurers in a strange land with a mission of some kind, usually find the doodad. Rather than a sequel, CE2 feels like the same game rebuilt, either in a reimagining or to be closer to the original vision of the game. As a whole it contains a huge number of improvements and QoL upgrades which make the game much smoother, more transparent, and entertaining to play. However, it also completely overhauls the base mechanics. This alters the core gameplay loop, robbing the game of almost all of the charm, charisma, and . For all the improvements, everything that made CE1 great has been either stripped out and thrown away, or changed for the worse. For example, there is now a long lasting campaign and story, removing the quick game feeling and slowing the feeling of progression significantly. The inventory and provision changes also significantly alter the game for the worse, making the entire campaign feel locked in with equipment. And the addition of a story with some kind of mentor and rivalry is just uninteresting and feels antithetical to what made CE compelling and fun. There is also a change in art style, which wasn’t to my taste but is in no way bad. Anyhow let’s take a look at a few of the main ups and downs.  I do recommend this as a game of its own. I do not recommend this as a sequel to CE1. If you loved the first, then I suspect you’ll find this a simplistic and boring, but prettier and smoother, downgrade.If you found the first game too ‘unfair/unforgiving’ or too short and lacking depth, then you’ll really enjoy this.I don’t really want this to have a downward thumb, but Steam has no neutral option, and while decent, it isn’t the sequel I was hoping it would be.

_childDocuments_.review: It's about a thumbs neutral game. The first game had an openness and balance to it that this one doesn't. It feels like, well, just over.If you are new to the franchise, buy the first one not this one.  The first one understands it's a light game with some rogue-like elements- this one tries to feel more weighty and fails as a result. Combat can get too long and slogging when you have tons of dice- the underlying combat system isn't that fun that I wanted more of it. And losing your supplies you bought after the expedition? Urgh.... I get it was for balance but the previous game balanced keeping your stuff very well.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a fan of the first Curious Expedition. Although the first iteration was by default much more brutal so I definitely appreciate the difficulty choice and scaling this time around.I will start by saying this. If you are a fan of rogue-likes then you should purchase this game. You basically explore island regions for various landmarks, treasure, ruins, villages/natives, and exploit your environment and findings all the while trying to complete various story driven quests and quests provided by village chiefs. Once the primary mission is accomplished you sail back home and upgrade your crew or recruit new crew members in preparation for the next expedition run. This is done ad infinitum, and is a hell of a lot of fun. This is a definite 10/10 rating for me for the following reasons:1. Its only 20 bucks or less2. You can replay the game multiple ways (campaign or director mode), and replaying the campaign is actually fun because locations and events are procedurally generated. The core events will remain the same or change depending on the choices you make.3. The game has actual replay value after playing 40 hrs.4. The game has multiple play styles (be friendly to natives, hunt, plunder, treasure hunt, survey, collect items)5. There is a wide repertoire (classes) of main characters and secondary characters to choose.6. Each expedition you pass leaves you feeling with an overall sense of accomplishment.Why people don't like this game:1. It can be challenging, things can go wrong quickly but this is part of the learning process.2. There are minor bugs when playing with a controller.3. There are elements of luck involved in all aspects of game play.I enjoy both skill based games and luck based games. This game requires solid strategy and luck. But this is what adds to the replay value. Things aren't always going to go in your favor and you need to adapt to survive. Curious Expedition 2 now allows you to make some sizable upgrades during expedition intermissions which is a welcomed addition. The graphics are much more aesthetic this time around, and I found that because of this I was pulled further into the lore of the game and had more genuine enjoyment. You probably won't find this game fun if you are a kid. The critical thinking required demands a more developed mind. I really appreciate the game guys/gals, I am looking forward to your switch release too. Keep up the good work and make more games like this, I will be watching and buying. I will be playing this game for at least another 60 hrs.BestJeremy M

_childDocuments_.review: Had a great time in my first playthrough. Solid game. For any roguelike lovers and 19th century enthusiasts a must buy, I'd say. There are quite some missed opportunities imho, actually too many to list here but they would be all a bonus and not essential to the core gameplay, hence I am not counting them as negative points.Anyway, some things I'd like to see:x Character customization. Seems totally doable as the "regenerate" button mixes up basically every possible combination. Why not just let us choose instead of clicking regenerate a 100 times?x Longer Campaign/Open end. At the end of the final Mission it is kinda disappointing to just lose the party you cared so much for. It feels like I should be able to experience many more adventures with them but sadly, nox more stuff to do in Paris. I guess I kinda miss the Darkest Dungeon-ish part here of being able to not only make you party stronger but also your headquarters. A house in Paris where your party stays in between expeditions and which you can upgrade in several ways to give you advantages would be awesome.x more tooltips on many things. It feels like a lot of tiny game mechanics aren't properly explained in the game. Like the "danger meter" (since there is no official term for it. The Skull + Number when you hover over an enemy party) for enemies for example. In a game where there is no way back and every move is set in stone, it is quite essential to know what symbols and numbers mean, imo.Like I said, there is potential for many more things but in the end, it is a really fun game and worth the small price.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? No, it is still in Early Access, and while it was great fun to play, it is still unpolished. I had no crashes, but sometimes the text was in a different language or sometimes strange things happened... not sure if this was intended or a bug. The game oozes charm, when it is finished and bug-free, it might be a masterpiece. Have you ever dreamed to be an explorer in the 19th century, when airplanes were not yet invented and large parts of the world map were still more or less unknown? Then this is the right game for you! It is set around 1897, but whole islands appear suddenly out of nowhere, and so it doesn't matter that someone found the sources of the Nile already and most known lands are more or less mapped. You can still explore those islands!First you have to select who funds your expeditions, but since you are a well-known explorer this is easy. Just select which of the three societies (noble Englishmen, capitalist Americans or zen-like Japanese) should hand over their money. All come with their little perks, so select well. Spend their money to buy some things you might need, like food or bandages. Also choose your companions, because you don't want to go out alone. Your expeditions are tiny and consist only of a few people, though. And then you are on your way to one of those mysterious islands, to plunder its treasures. You move your party around the randomly generated island and interact with its natives or things you encounter. There is a lot to find, like animals, plants or other explorers, shipwrecks, shrines and other large buildings made by gods. Or aliens. Who knows?While exploring the islands you have to manage your party and keep them sane, preferably with whiskey or chocolate. Various encounters require you to make decisions, and you can barter with natives for goods. Sometimes you have to fight animals, monsters or natives. Combat is decided by rolling the dice, like the success or failure of many of your actions. Native villages are a good place to rest a few days, or for hiring a local party member to join the expedition. And the next one, if he survives. Most of the time when you enter a sacred temple, you destroy it and large parts of the island as well. Plundering temples often leads to natural disasters, I was responsible for volcanoes spitting lava, gigantic cave ins, island-engulfing poisonous clouds... good thing you can always run back to your ship and leave the natives alone.Home in Paris you can plan your next expedition, visit the pub or the societies, buy new special equipment for your party members or hire new companions - and start the next expedition.Lead an expedition into unknown islands and plunder its treasures, but don't get eaten.

_childDocuments_.review: Sort of fills that Renowned Explorers void I have, similar in premise but very different in terms of gameplay. They are both completely different games, and I respect that. However, I am not completely wowed by CE2, nor do I hate it. I suppose I can list out a few personal pros and cons.Pros: 19th century expeditionary settings and trappings we know and love.Surprisingly difficult, and the learning curve isn't too steep.Resource management and terrain types to account for during exploration.Barter system with variable factors keeps things interesting.Different expedition goal type missions. Things you can unlock to make crews more specialized and/or diverse. Cons: Combat in general? Easily my least favorite thing about the game. Not too sure if the enemy has to roll on their actions, but it can really suck when you roll blank die or fight an enemy that retaliates on rerolls. Locale people hate it when you attack everything in sight, I get that, but why do they dislike me protecting myself from panthers, scorpions, and the like when they attack me? Story missions cap the end of each year, and while the maps and side goals may be different, the story is the same. While I don't dislike the story, it kind of takes away from the roguelike nature of the rest of the game. A luke-warm recommendation, but not in all out negative way. What I really want is RE:IS 2, and while not very similar CE2 fills the void with being a new game and having many things to learn and uncover.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not nearly as fun as the original Curious Expedition. Some complaints:- The competition with other explorers from CE1 is gone. So you no longer have to balance the competing priorities of rushing to the pyramid as quickly as possible, versus moving carefully, resting, and exploring the whole map. This removes a HUGE component of what made CE1 exciting, challenging, and fun. - Ironically, even though you now have as much time as you want to explore the whole map, it's pointless to do so, because all your gear disappears between expeditions. So you might as well rush for the pyramid; don't bother exploring. In a game that's supposed to be about exploration...- Combat is so, so much worse compared to CE1. The animations are slow. The dice combos are useless and unsatisfying. I don't understand why they chose to keep the dice combat system while removing all interesting dice combos; they should've just replaced the dice system entirely if that's the direction they wanted to take. Because there are no interesting dice combos, fighting with your hands and feet is inexplicably just as effective as shooting a gun. Remember how exciting it was in CE1 to get trade for some guns and combat items, get some lucky dice rolls, and defeat a whole slaver camp? You'll never get that feeling playing CE2. - The art is worse. I appreciate the hard work of the artist(s) who made CE2, but I'm sorry to say it's an objective downgrade from the pixel art of CE1. And I think 99.9% of players agree about this. A core part of the Curious Expedition gameplay loop is destroying the land and looting treasure from native peoples. This is a transgressive premise for a game! But the pixelated graphics gave CE1 an arcade game-y feel that made it okay, like it was all part of the game. Adopting a more realistic art style for CE2 makes it feel less like an arcade game, and I don't think that works well when the core gameplay loop is so transgressive. Imagine if they released a Postal game with hyper-realistic graphics -- it would be less fun decapitating people when everyone looks like a real human being. And so too it's less fun looting treasure from natives when they don't look like pixels in an arcade game. Separately, and I apologize if this feedback sounds harsh, but I just have to say, I simply don't like the art and animation style of CE2 in general. It looks and feels like a low-budget cartoon for children. - Speaking of making a game for children, they nerfed the difficulty. CE2 is way too easy compared to CE1.- Campaign mode. Why is there a campaign at all? This game is supposed to be a roguelike. It makes no sense to shunt players into campaign mode when they thought they were playing a roguelike. Nobody asked for this, nobody wanted this, I don't understand why they did this.tl;dr CE2 is a downgrade from CE1 in pretty much every way. I've got 10 times more hours in Curious Expedition 1. That's the one I recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Full disclosure, I was a passionate fan of the first game from the moment it became available on Steam and watched it go from a quirky addictive mess to a fascinating powerhouse that consumed many an afternoon in my home. Sadly, the sequel isn't even the fun mess that the first one began as. It's polished, sure, with an art-style that feels ripped from "Tintin" or "Rupert," but it's also weirdly soulless. They shoehorn 21st century Western identity politics into this 19th century-set game at random nonsensical intervals; the joy of selecting from and unlocking numerous historical figures is gone (be prepared for bland cookie-cutter fictional no-names); there's no mystery because everything is flat-out explained to you with every step (over an hour in and I was still getting tutorial tips); and instead of pursuing your own fame and glory you're now a lackey working to enhance the reputation of the game's anachronistic Mary Sue mascot. So, instead of the joy of guiding Harriet Tubman, her pet riding-tortoise, her cannibalistic mutant sidekick, and her team of dino-warriors in the quest to have a statue of Tubman erected in London...you get to watch your fictional no-name running errands for the fictional Mary Sue back in Paris, but hey, at least the salamander people use "xe/xir" pronouns! All of this absolutely kills the replayability, the very feature that was a hallmark of CE1. Let me reiterate, the tutorial takes FOREVER and relentlessly hammers home just how "important" the Mary Sue is. Instead of competing with other explorers to become the explorer par excellence, you're now racing to beat an artificially-generated ticking-clock in the form of a purple fog that the Mary Sue unleashed. And instead of discovering weird and wonderful things on your own, the game forcibly drags you into them and leers at you as it yells about their importance over and over. You could play multiple games of CE1 and never once encounter dinosaurs, lizard-men, abominations, etc. but never fear! CE2 forces you to meet aliens, salamander-people, mole-men, etc. over and over and over till they feel less like momentous discoveries and more like simple window-dressing in your typical urban-fantasy game.Shiny? Yes. But worth the money? No.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright. A full campaign run of **Curious Expedition 2** is done and dusted. You might think that is *curious* phrasing, but I say it that way because there is a ton of replay value and for the cheevo focused gamer, there are a lot of challenges to complete beyond the variety of characters available to play through the campaign with. I initially chose our favorite *SteamWorld* captain, but eventually switched over to the *Naturalist* for a full run. Anyway, **Curious Expedition 2** was even *curiouser* than **Curious Expedition**, and well suits a proper sequel. If you haven't played the first, I'd recommend doing so even if it's not specifically necessary for playing the sequel.I mentioned that I switched from the Robot to the Naturalist. Why? Because you start out with a Yeti companion, lol. And because I found the animal companions to be more reliable, and since it's ideal to try to adventure with a full party, and animals are less prone to negative quirks, it seemed advantageous. I ended up actually firing the yeti and sticking with a party consisting of an elephant, a red elk, and a ridable land jellyfish. That was an excellent combo. The occasional addition of a mercenary or story companion and we were good to go.Companions do have passive abilities and their own unique combat abilities. For example, people live the red elk, and so it passively boosts your relationship with the various islander tribes. In combat, the jellyfish could electrocute and set enemies on fire. Having some party skill diversity is important.Although RPGish, the RPG elements are mostly in how you spend fame cards and cash, how you organize your inventory, and a few story/side quest choices. Fame helps you unlock new companions, items, and opportunities. Cash is what you use to purchase your expedition goods. Once you're on an expedition, however, bartering replaces cash. Any goods you return to Paris (your hub) with is converted to cash and fame. However, if you are forced to retreat from an expedition before completing your objective, you get nothing. You do select a sponsor, and they will always at least partially fund every expedition.Expedition objectives range from mapping new islands to finding lost missionaries to validating the existence of legendary monsters, raiding fabled pyramids, and so on. There isn't a huge variety, but they have variable difficulties and size to keep them interesting. Finish enough of these and you'll go on a main story expedition, which are much longer and with several chapters each. Completing a final main story expedition completes an Act and moves the story forward.This game takes its inspiration from adventure classics like Indiana Jones, The Goonies, Tomb Raider; and mixes in aspects of classic CRPGs to spruce up the experience. It never takes itself very seriously on one hand, and yet always manages to respect itself as a game.The artistic design is in every way quite perfect for how the game represents itself. There are several different types of biomes and a vast amount of races, animals, and so on, all created with detail and a loving hand, so to speak. This is a very eye catching and yet completely indie looking game. The audio is all sound effects and music. I thought it was quite well down, never intrusive, but always present. A warm blanket of sorts.I will note that you can change difficulty before every expedition, and after having my ass handed to me on the very final story missions, I dropped the difficulty down. Combat itself is pretty fun but easy on all difficulties, but where the different difficulties truly factor in is with exploration and situational RNG. All if which is resolved with action dice which is a cool system you'll learn to become very familiar and comfortable with. The interplay of dice and buffs ends up being quite a compelling system. Also...if you do end up dying, you're basically rescued and brought back to Paris where you can then choose to do it all over again, probably with new tactics lol.I played on the *Steam Deck*. There were zero issues and I didn't have to make any adjustments at all. Additionally, it's generous with battery life. I was able to play for about four hours on one charge.All in all, I had a very *curious* time with **Curious Expedition 2**, and this is one of the few games where the DLC is all practical and can impact the base game experience in a completely positive way (by increasing the biome and character variety and expanding QoL options). I'd consider getting the entire package if you intend to play through it. Very highly recommended at the asking price.

_childDocuments_.review: I might be spoiled by the CE 1 but somehow the new dice system is not as satisfying as it used to be. I played the multiplayer part of CE 1 for hundreds of hours (even got to the damn pyramid in the end) and every run lasted just a bit longer because I unlocked some new stuff (guns, yeti, ...) and figured out new dice combos that seemed much more powerful.Here, I bought a rifle and wait? It deals less damage than my bloody club? Sure, it deals a point or two more if boosted, but I kinda expected more than that. Also I don't see a great use for re-rolling except hoping to get better roll on the blank ones.Also, there's little to no choice on the events. You can choose who partakes in the event, but you still roll every dice, so it does not really matter who you send in. About the graphics - I like the static parts, some good work there, but as others have stated, the animations look like a 20 year old Flash game.If the devs want my advice, scrap this game, go back to CE1  and add some DLC's to that instead. I'd buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a decent sequel to the first Curious Expedition. If you liked the first one, even if you were hooked simply on the pixel graphical aesthetic like I was, you'll probably like Curious Expedition 2. There are a critical lack of Age of Discovery games out there, and this captures the wonder inherent with the era very well.Lacks some polish in some areas as the first one did, and the direction you're supposed to take after finishing the campaign isn't as clear as it was in the first game. I'd really like a retro style cold open gamemode a la the first Curious Expedition; no clubs, a set number of shop items, and five islands escalating in difficulty. Simply my preference.I admit, I had my doubts about the game when I initially saw the art style when Maschinen-Mensch released the first early access alpha, but as I played the campaign it grew on me a lot. I still think I prefer the pixel graphics of the first, but this isn't bad at all.I'd say get it on sale. It's great fun, but not for twenty USD. A bit overpriced.One more thing: the aesthetic of the "thematic" islands is fantastic. I never thought I would see a tech wizard mole shoot a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gun at me until it hit me in the face and scorched my party to dust. The prehistoric island is, of course, a classic, and the Corrupted World (with a literal Outer God just walking around) is my personal favorite. Very Lovecraftian. Here's to hoping that they'll release an Arctic setting, as they did in the first Curious Expedition.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Tentative thumbs-up here. I played a lot of the first game and basically it's about doing whatever you have to do in order to bulk up on sanity and dice. Once you get ahead, it's hard to fall behind if you know what you're doing. Still totally fun to play for a few hours and I'd recommend the game to anyone who hasn't touched the series.The sequel brought with it a, let's say, moralistic streak to the narrative that for me was a bit tedious compared to the earnest (and disquieting) colonialism of the first game.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I love the first Curious Expedition game, and I've been excited for the sequel. Curious Expedition 2 is still early access, so a bit of jankiness is to be expected. All the hiccups in the character animation, mechanics, and balance... That's fine. Even the slightly unintuitive new interface is something that will probably change and get refined in time. Everything in the game feels very slow and "sticky". Combat animations take ages. Changing scenes takes ages. Cut scenes take ages. Anything happening on the world map takes ages. Rolling combat dice takes ages. There are no real dice combos now, so assigning every single combat die takes ages. The gameplay is just not as quick and snappy as the first game, and it makes everything drag. It's part of normal early access woes, so I'm confident it's just a matter of it getting tweaked and updated and polished over time. All of that would be fine.....if it weren't for the lag. Dear god, the LAG. Even on low graphical settings, the game is practically a slideshow at times. I can deal with all the other early access issues, but the crippling lag is the breaking point that makes it unplayable and made me request a refund. I'm still eager to play this game, so I'll definitely be purchasing it again when it's a bit more polished! There's lots of potential, and it's well on its way to being a great sequel to Curious Expedition. I just can't recommend it until the lag issues are resolved.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: (Played 25-30 hours on Switch, which was a review copy. Bought a PC copy to support the developer.)CE1 and CE2 are both good games, and I recommend both. Which game is "better" depends on your taste -- especially in terms of art style, length, and difficulty. CE2 is much longer but provides easier difficulty options. My first playthrough of CE2's Campaign Mode took ~15 hours on Easy difficulty,  whereas CE1 runs can be finished in 2-3 hours (though it took 10-15 hours for me to beat CE1 on Medium difficulty). CE1 is a pure roguelike. So if you want a more casual experience, go for CE2. You can change the difficulty in Campaign Mode to let you restart an expedition upon dying, instead of restarting the whole game.CE2's other mode (Director Mode) is also fun and good for experienced players. I like the challenge of difficulty modifiers. The system for combat and playable characters has changed. I find the new combat system more time-consuming but also a bit more interesting. You're no longer choosing a historical explorer but a character class. Rivals from CE1 are mostly absent. I've yet to try enough classes to say much. But basically the classes are geared towards different ways of gaining Fame.Other things: I was glad to see more positive interactions with native groups in CE2. The new tribes, creatures, enemies, items, weapons, gear, etc. are cool! Explorer Clubs change things up, especially for available shop items in Director Mode. Weekly online club competitions are a nice addition too.And I dig the new art style! I wasn't keen at first, but it really grew on me. I wouldn't play the CE games just for the procedural storytelling. But I love the board-gamey aspects of strategy, survival, and resource management. I only wish CE2 weren't so long, especially story missions. I'd rather have shorter runs and more time to experiment with different playstyles. Still, I find the formula addictive enough to keep playing. Too many nights past my bedtime...Overall, CE2 is worth trying if you're a fan of the first game. While the general formula is the same, CE2 has a lot of fun new content and enough variation from CE1 to provide a fresh experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: There are those reviewers who claim the graphics in this one are much worse than the first, despite their update.Those reviewers are right, the paper doll physics of the characters look terrible, it was a bad move.  Despite this, the gameplay is engaging and addictive, the combat is pretty decent, and the story is enough to keep you going.  Get pet dinosaur, ride a jellyfish, fall in love with a monster.  I enjoyed it, worth the $20 (maybe even better on sale).
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best boardgame-ish games I have played. Plays kind of like Darkest Dungeon combined with Talisman, but with more options that you get as as a player, including avoiding combat in many different ways if you wish. It also has a lot of replay value with different modes and unlockable player characters with different specializations. Very nice, hope even more DLC will come with time.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished the campaign for the first time and, wow, what an improvement over the original. The original was a decent game but the characters eventually reach their full potential and you either play until they die or start a new run. Curious Expedition 2 would be worth buying just for the campaign but everything else is done so much better in this game. Juggling inventory, changing equipment during expeditions, learning new skills, and party management are much more engaging and immersive. The fantasy races and islands are great. Plus, if you miss the endless adventure, it's still here once you finish the campaign.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: This rogue-like has a fresh and cozy feel to it even in the hard mode, where you'll also find the level of challenge I enjoy. It's got a "one more turn" level of addiction to it.EDIT: As with the previous game, the developers continue to produce new and updated content for free. You can feel the love.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: this game is criminally underrecgonized. it is the tintin roguelike you never knew you needed. a fun and evocative visual style masks very deep mechanics and difficult (but not unfair) gameplay. the progression system and quick play time means you don't feel cheated if a run goes sideways - and bad runs create good stories.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I adore this game. To me, Curious Expedition 2 is a game of recruiting a rag-tag group of adventurers and critters to explore the mysterious disappearing islands. The gameplay, much like in the first game, is a race against time as you try to survive on the islands with your few resources without resorting to eating your friends.The game has plenty of NPCs you can recruit with their own individual abilities and traits. You can create a diverse cast of adventurers or you can be like me and play 90% of the game as the Naturalist (Robots of Lux DLC, 6€), and befriend a bunch of dinosaurs (even the T-Rex! but you cannot ride it...)!The island-expeditions themselves are very fun, but can get slightly repetitive for an achievement-hunter like myself. There are many points of interests scattered around the map for you to investigate and decide if you want to have morals or just pillage and loot whatever you come across. Personally I had a tough time being mean to the pixels on my screen.I've heard people having issues with the art-style, which honestly baffles me. To me its very charming and suits the mood of the game perfectly. I personally ended up buying the Highlands of Avalon DLC just to meet the cool looking sea serpent and befriend the Clydesdale draft-horses, which are absolutely friend-shaped.As with each indie game, there were some visual bugs and whatnot, but I found nothing that impacted my gameplay (aside from when my T-Rex was injured and she kept playing the "taking damage" animation constantly and was rather loud about it. But honestly I think she was just being dramatic.)I had slight issues with the enemy aggro-system, in which if an enemy is chasing you and you turn to approach them, they sometimes get a surprise round anyway. This might purely be a skill-issue on my part however.All in all, I highly recommend trying this game and supporting the developers, who even released a new, FREE cultist update this summer, 4 years after the game came out. <3
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sad, dude.I eagerly awaited this sequel, and i can't recommend it like I would the first game. Everything good about Curious Expedition is lost here.The combat is dumbed down. Say goodbye to dice combos- now you just roll for the best option on each die and "enhance" it with another die of the same color. Good Lord, the animations in combat are atrocious, too. Not only are they barely serviceable for what they're trying to show, you will surely get tired of having to wait to see your unit swing his fist in the general direction of a hyena. On the topic of wait times, there is now an extended animation for almost everything. For some reason you have to check your full inventory instead of it simply being displayed on the screen at all times, which requires a 4 second animation to bring up and another 4 second animation to dismiss. The music is, on average, worse. Not much else to say.Filler content. Why are there three 3 explorer factions to level up? You unlock new units, sure, cool. But what purpose does this serve?No more timer. There is no longer a time constraint. This was one of the major factors that drove decision-making beforehand. Now you have no reason NOT to waste a full week resting up if you can. On the topic of missing content, why do i CARE about fame in this game? In my 70 minutes as of writing this review, there hasn't yet been any competition im against like there was before. Furthermore, I don't retain supply items between expeditions, so I have no idea why I should care about doing anything besides going directly for the primary objective on each island and then leaving instantly.The spritework is worse??? Maybe I'm crazy, but the sprites for the items somehow aren't as distinguishable or charming as before.Do not buy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting game.  Very enjoyable at times, and very frustrating at times.  The frustration mostly being due to the plethora and severity of negative events.A few examples:1.  Party member just randomly developed alcoholism, even though I made it a point to never carry alcohol.  Due to the alcoholism and I may lack of alcohol supplies, she became extremely angry, argued with me, and left the party (even though we were lovers).2.  Had tea with a local shaman who asked me to select a party member.  Selected party member left, never to return.3.  Was asked to participate in a contest.  When dice selection window appeared, it said it was impossible for me to win.  Why did it even bother to ask me?Despite all that, I would have rated it a 6/10, but the lack of a proper save system forced me to lower my rating to 4/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Curious Expedition 2, by Maschinen-Mensch, is a sequel to the 2016 roguelite exploration simulator Curious Expedition. In it you play one of several explorers searching newly revealed islands for the purpose of finding treasures and completing objectives at the behest of one of three explorer societies. Curious Expedition 2 starts with an introduction to the overall plot of the game. Victoria Malin leads a small team of explorers through an island that should not be there and is surrounded by a mysterious fog and equally mysterious natives. This discovery leads to a new age of exploration and you, the one who Malin has personally selected to help uncover the mystery of the islands, joins in. You can read the full review here: Curious Expedition 2 is a very enjoyable game. It is deep without being complicated, and offers plenty of non-trivial decisions whether you are approaching it from a narrative perspective or have a taste for min-maxing. It also feels distinct. While there are other games that focus on exploration (such as Renowned Explorers) no other game, except the predecessor in the series, is doing anything remotely like Curious Expeditions 2. If the game or theme interests you at all, I definitely recommend getting it.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Party went insane looking for my ship and a malaria-ridden monk that was afraid of butterflies ate my corgi and later ran away with my treasures.Some fun to be had, love many of the rogue-lite aspects but probably not quite enough variety of events and systems to keep me as motivated as Renowned Explorers managed to.  Lots of fun though, especially once you level a couple of characters & weapons and rolls start going your way.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like this type of game, there's a much much better one you should play instead - Renowned Explorers: International Edition. Very similar in that both are tactical RPGs where you play colonial era explorers exploring (and looting) exotic lands. Except that one is much less repetitive, much more humorous, with more satisfying combat and character progression, and a tongue in cheek tone that is much more befitting of the premise of these games.This is not a bad game, but it gets really repetitive. I've played for 10 hrs but it feels like I've played for 40 whereas in other games I play for 40 hrs and feel like I've played 10. I've dragged myself along playing the game hoping that it would complete by Act 3, but it's now Act 4 and I don't know if I have the endurance to continue - and that's after only 10 hrs.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I got CE1 first because I was charmed by the pixel art and enjoyed it well enough to decide to get CE2, and honestly 2 is such a better experience, at least for me. I like the artwork more than I thought I would, the combat is tons better, and I enjoyed the story mode quite a lot.I only have two gripes that aren't really about the game itself, just things that bugged me: first the party size limit got annoying after a while, because there were so many cool looking characters and animals I wanted to take with me. Understandable however, since I imagine any more than what's default will make the game far too easy. Secondly if you have an animal-only party and get the sanity event where your main explorer has to eat one to stay alive, you can't choose which one to sacrifice, the game makes the decision for you, which really sucks. I had a bonded turtle that I had for pretty much the entire story and then while struggling in the final expedition, the game made me eat the turtle instead of letting me pick something else that I wasn't so attached to. I feel like it should give you the choice if you have more than one animal.Anyway besides those two things, great game and very enjoyable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Curious Expedition 2 is a game where you take the mantle of an explorer and sail to discover mysterious islands in an alternate 19th century. While exploring you can play a role of an anthropologist, big game hunter, or a tomb rider, each with different goals and tasks to fulfill and have an entourage consisting of simple cooks and feathered dinosaurs, shooting energy beams from eye sockets of Obsidian Skull carved from a fallen meteorite.CE2 provides a lot of replayability with events, items, characters and companions, famous explorers, and by luck or lack thereof in dice rolls. With a mixture of the above, each game you play can be different and exciting. Creators put a lot of effort into systems that support emergent gameplay and story, there is also a lot of extra emergent fun possible if you place some additional limitations on your campaign (which I encourage you to) like "pacifist run" or "animals only campaign" etc.There is a good amount of content that you won't be able to see all of it in the first couple runs, every so often there is a small content update bundled with minor fixes.The game does have some problems; imbalance between combat and exploration difficulty or occasional bugs (which devs can fix as quickly as within an hour), but that was nothing that would ruin the fun from the game.Overall, a great game worth buying made by a company worth supporting 👍
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game rules. I played it for a university class on rogue-likes and wound up playing for almost 23 hours in one week. I may have popped a blood vessel in my eye because I forgot to blink during some long play sessions. I am sure I'll keep coming back to play it again and again throughout the years. The designers have done a fantastic job at making you feel that you are constantly on the brink of disaster while still having some hope of success. Astoundingly, the hand-crafted narrative of the base campaign does not detract from the emergent storytelling I loved in Curious Expedition 1. Instead, even more so than the original, curious Expedition 2 is a player story generator. I could write out around a dozen fun anecdotes about my first explorer, Harold Malcolm's adventures. I could write even more about the adventures which followed him! Those stories all happened because of interesting decisions that CE2's beautifully interconnected systems forced me to make. But I won't write those stories here. I don't want to spoil all the wild stuff waiting in CE2. If you are worried about the colonialist vibe of being an explorer "discovering" new lands, hunting local wildlife for fame, and stealing sacred artifacts from indigenous people, you may still love this game. The devs take several opportunities to take the piss out of Euro-centrism and the racism of Europe around the turn of the 19th century. Moreover, this game is so alt-history/fantastic that it becomes absurd in a very fun way. That said, the scoring conditions on CE2 incentivize being an absolute monster. I wound up back in Paris with whole ecosystems of "trophies" to parade through the city for fame and fortune. Harold Malcolm left islands devastated and devoid of life. The absurdism of a British big game hunter punching his way through every wildlife encounter significantly alleviated any ruminations on the horror of who my player character was. That may not be enough to wash the awful taste away for you, so if that is the case, I'd give this a pass. Buy this game. Then, when you love it, buy the DLC too. Support these devs. This is one of the most elegant mergings of a game's systems with its narrative I've ever played.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: A cute game that appeals to people who like exploring, strategy and creative story telling. The game offers you multiple ways to go through it depending on your play style and personality which creates an immersive experience. The Discord channel they have set up creates a good community and atmosphere around the game too.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sorry to have to say it but as sequels go, this one just doesn't cut it. The first Curious Expedition was a tight, clear, quick-moving unique adventure. The second one is an attempt at doing massive graphical improvements, while sacrificing the momentum that was built into the gameplay that the first game was excellent for.Punching giant spiders, and having it actually work out favorably, was too silly to take seriously, but the game continues as such, your main weapons being fists and kicks. The battle system as a whole is so slow, clunky, and silly, I can't believe they actually went with it. It is a sad regression from the first game.Most of the game is exactly the same as the first one. Just not as smooth. There are a few interesting additions worth checking out.Between the added complexity and the wild attempt at better graphics, it just doesn't hold a candle to the first game.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Liked the style and the premise, but it feels horribly overcomplicated. There is an absolute mountain of systems (characters/dice/combat/inventory/supplies/sanity/sponsors/unlocks/stores/traversal/locals/rewards/etc/etc/etc) and game makes no effort to explain any or even make a case why should you care about it. Did they make it for fans of the previous game or something? Feels underdesigned and impenetrable for a fresh player.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played CE1 so I am going to write up my experience based of CE2. From what I leaned and saw, CE2 is basically everything thats CE1 but improved and added more stuff, while changing the art style and animations to match of those french comic books.After doing a showcase for Curious Expedition 2, I got sucked into this feeling of exploration with a game where decisions truly matter and you can play with True Ironman enabled(Permadeath, No save-scumming), not many games do that option these days, and I want to make the focus on the wording "decisions truly matter" because that's one of the strongest factors of this game in my opinion.Party building/resource management mechanics are similar to Darkest Dungeon. On top of that, you add flavor of exploring maps like in strategy games, which have randomly generated locations/events based on biomes you explore, every single time you start an expedition. Combats in CE2 are quite unique. You use dices that get generated from each characters skills / equipment as potential action in battle. Dices split into 3 colors and same color dice side can be used to boost another dice of same color. Or you might roll a dice side with nothing on it which means empty action if dice have blanks(example: a shotgun gear of level 3 gives you dice with 3 Red sides for 1st skill, 1 Red side for 2nd skill and remaining 2/6 sides are blank). It does sound a lot of RNG, but trust me, it's all controllable. Plenty of ways to reroll dices, get extra dices, upgrade them, use better gear, level your characters etc.Speaking of progression, game have a lot of replay value and unlockables. Not to mention 8 different main character classes that you select at start of the game, which drastically change the playstyle of your campaign.Resource management is truly fun aspect as you try to min-max every barter/trade with locals/merchants and try to figure out what to take or leave since your inventory space is limited, especially without mule animals or equipment items that give you extra inventory slots. People who like to make profits/"scam" is going to enjoy this process in CE2.I could talk a lot more about all mechanics, details and story related missions, but I want to leave some surprises for you and enjoy the discovery part of the game. There are a lot of trial and error things you would need to do, but once you get the hang of expedition generation rules/mechanics, you will never blame luck or RNG because everything in this game is generated within specific rules which doesn't cheat on you (exceptions are rare bugs, but those gets reported quickly on game's active Discord server btw).Curious Expedition 2 could be one of the wackiest Ironman games of 2021 and I totally recommend it!Devs also promised more new content later down the line, so that's pretty hype (even though in my opinion, game feels like a complete package already).Hopefully my review was helpful!You can also check my showcase stream/video to see the game in action from pespective of a new player:
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's almost a completely different game from its predecessor.Expedition 1 is an arcade-y, board-game-y exploit-em-up where every voyage is the 1800s aristocratic equivalent of a smash-and-grab. You loot, murder, and leave, or you fall behind in the score chart.Expedition 2 is basically an rpg with heavy resource management and board game elements. Some knowledge from 1 is portable, but overall the game is more forgiving, makes more information available to the player, and allows playstyles other than outright desecration and thievery.However.Expedition 1 is more accessible, plays quicker, and is lighter in tone. So I can completely see people bouncing off this and preferring the first game.Also, there's a chance that 8 hours in the campaign map that gets generated for you is bugged and unwinnable (one of the ship part locations doesn't spawn,) and on normal that means your whole party wipes and you start from scratch.It happened to me, and I couldn't be bothered to restart the multi-hour process of getting back to where I was.Assuming you caveat emptor, this is otherwise a pretty solid variation on the mechanics and themes of the first game.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is a reluctant thumb up. I'll write in 2 sections: for those who've come to this fresh and those who've played the first one.1) If you're freshThis game is a charming rogue-lite-ish survival turn-base board game with clear objectives and now there is storyline. It's fun to learn, fun to combat, but the campaign mode is not the most enjoyable experience, luckily, there is a thing called the Director Mode that let you play more freely. 2) If you've played the first gameIt's just the first game with a lot better combat, and non-pixelated art, also it now has a story. You can now engage in combat without the fear of losing everything. I'm not a fan of the newly added story progression, though you can ignore it by playing the director mode.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Not a bad game. Suffers form some design choice. You lose most of the gear you accumulate during an expedition it gets trade for tickets that don't have a good value compare to the barter you could have done in expedition, The games rely so heavily on the Sanity gauge, that any other aspect of the game are irrelevant since you constantly need to keep this bar fill. Impossible to predict when a companion will quit or be mad since their are no trackers for those other than a sad little face you never know how bad things are. Some characters for example will regain trust if they drink alcohol, but you can't give them any from your inventory. You need to have a event triggering drinking at a camp or something. The art is by far one of the best, feels like a living comic book. The difficulty forces you to speed through missions, and you can't explore with side missions, you are forced to follow the 2-3 mission pattern per act. I was under the impression this is supposed to be a rogue type game but usually in a rogue you can redo missions and you grow stronger overtime, this is not the case, if you die you go back to the beginning either of the mission or the whole game. either way you are back to your weak self not really able to progress much more.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: They should churn out more game content for this now, I'd 100% buy it. I'd easily pay more money for more scenarios/stories.They put a lot of systems in that are great for a thought-provoking, choices-are-important game. They implemented these choices in very simple, but very powerful ways. For instance, when you are camping, your companions can bond with each other. I ran into a situation where I needed to get rid of one of them. The other one freaked out and begged me not to get rid of his buddy. He said he'd leave, too, if I got rid of his friend.I had the follwing options:   - backing off  - convincing the person to stay and let their friend go   - or getting rid of them bothFor fun, I first tried backing off. The person who was begging me was so thankful, they burst into tearsThen, shortly after I chose the option of getting rid of the first one and convincing the second to stay. I had to make a roll, and I made it. The character stayed while the other left. He took a morale hit and I felt like a serious jerk.Lots of great, system-based choices like that in this game. Made it a very interesting and engaging play. My own game, , struggles hard to implement systems like these. These developers do it so elegantly, my hat is off to them, 100%. It's an inspiration.Def made me want to play it in new game plus mode, to make different kinds of decisions, build different kinds of teams.Other stuff:- They removed the old "race" system for competing with other adventurers for reknown, which is both good and bad. I didn't feel like a crummy imperialist trodding all over other cultures just for my own statue. But there also wasn't the intense pressure to play to "win", which is good. But boy, did it feel good to win, in the rare cases I did in the original.- That's another point, this game is a whole lot easier than the first one. It has just enough danger to be enjoyable, but it doesn't beat you to a pulp and rob you of all hope.- I loved the art of the first game, but I'd say I love this style even better. Kind of reminds me of Where's Waldo. Tons of cool detail and vibrant colors.- I like the combat system a lot better, they worked in a whole bunch more choices and modifiers, which helped to soften things up a bit. Combat in the first game was unrelentingly brutal and just kind of sapped the fun out of it. We get it, you guys are tough and wins should be earned. Sometimes, it's just fun to have fun in a game though! I appreciated the changes.100% solid recommend, y'all should buy this. Give these people money! Encourage them to do more great things!
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is still a very early review as I am only in Year 2 of the game. But I feel like I can put in my early thoughts, as the game does deserve more positive feedback.At it's core it is still the same gameplay loop as the first Curious Expedition, but it seems like the Devs truly wanted to make the sequel a bit more different. Which I actually think is good, as that means the first game is still a valid choice to play, if you find that certain choices are not for you. The combat for example is more accessible and streamlined. That doesn't mean it isn't less tactical and later expeditions will feature quite hard fights. But the times of printing out spreadsheets for combos are over and I do not miss it at all.The other thing that immediately is a big chance is the art style. And yes, the ligne claire style is probably not one for everyone, but I adore it. The characters are striking and the backgrounds are gorgeous. That every event always has the right background for it, even when you simply make a small camp or have a short cutscene is great. And I would assume that they will built upon it in future updates. The Pixel Art in the first one was beautiful of course, and it had it's own charm, but this artwork really works for me.Another big chance is the focus on a narrative and more character interaction. In the first one you simply tried to be the best explorer(and it only had one mission goal all the time), in this one you have several normal expeditions(with varied mission goals) per year and one special story mission. It creates a fun interesting mystery that connects all the expeditions you are doing. Working towards something is rather nice. And now characters can create friendship, fall in love, tell stories to each other and so on. You will feel attched to your trek and that is very important to me. I don't want anybody to die, and I will try my best to keep them free from any mental problems.Also all the expeditions you do, you do for a sponsor. There are three different societies that will give you money for any of your trips. Whenever you bring treasure back, your standing with that group rises and unlocks various specific options, be it a new recruit or some special weapon or gear. They will also offer services, for example the Royal Avalon Society will treat any mental illness from a character in your trek. Just as long as you can pay for it.It is noticeable still in clear early access, some animations and art are placeholder, some eventlogic still seems to be a bit weird and there are some bigger and smaller bugs. You pay for early access and you get early access. They have a discord server that is the place to report all the bugs, there is no ingame feature for it(there is a button that will lead to their server though).Right now I would recommend the game for anyone who has no problem with it being in early access. The rest can wait until it is more polished and they will a great game. I am certain of it.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Go buy this game if you don't mind playing early-access.After avoiding the game for a while because of a bunch of negative reviews, I bought CE2 at last. Although I would have preferred the art style of CE1, I am in love with this gem. This being said, I am not sure how I feel about the linear progression and the story missions. I'm not sure if it's good for the game's replayability. I am also missing some features from CE1, such as  harbor sidequests and more choice at character creation, but I am very confident that the developers will add those (and much more) down the line.In any case, I can recommend this game to anyone who liked the first part or really just anybody who likes FTL-style games, because this is one of the finer examples of the genre.If the devs read this, vielen Dank und weiter so!

_childDocuments_.review: Curious Expedition 2 is very fun, light hearted, cheerful, turn based adventure game perfect to play for example while eating dinner or to relax for a moment. It revolves around completing simple objectives on procedurally generated maps while exploring, managing resources, party members, fighting and dealing with random events. I found gameplay loop not too complex, neither difficult, but surely  fun and engaging. Truth be told, game leaves a loot of room for you to shape the experience you're looking for; there are 3 general difficulty levels and 3 failure repercussion you can customize at will, varying difficulty of missions you choose from, and also you have freedom to rush through them relatively safe, or take risk and explore thoroughly with resources dwindling and ailments/ negative events piling up, so in summary you can turn rather trivial expeditions into very challenging but rewarding if you choose so, and that's praiseworthy!What else i like about this game is it's beautiful, colorful, diverse artstyle, cute, charming, funny characters design and animations, and music.Combat is based on dice, has some depth to it, I generally like it, although by the end of campaign it felt so repetitive I started actively avoiding it...Similar thing I have to say about random events, encounters and banter. At first when everything is new, it feels fun and exciting, but some hours in it starts to feel very repetitive and generic, even to the point that I started skipping through them without reading...  I can't shake off impression that the game maybe lacks a little of variety in terms of map objects and really interesting random events, but nonetheless it has enough of them to be fun and engaging for long hours, and it's definitely worth recommending!

_childDocuments_.review: I've really enjoyed this sequel. I see a lot of criticism about bugs, art direction, and combat. Here's my take on it:Bugs:Yeah it's buggy, but it's to be expected right now since it's in early access. I was able to play the game all the way through. Some tips on impassable bugs I encountered: DON'T RUN OUT OF SANITY. When you do, you'll get a tutorial popup telling you to rest/eat consumables, but you won't be able to exit the screen. Instant game over and restart. Try and be diligent and stock up on lots of consumables so you never have to deal with that.(EDIT): I was able to counteract this bug by getting my sanity to 0 in the tutorial level. If you get this bug, make SURE you do this every game Art Direction:I like the art style, it's storybook-like and well crafted. Did I like the pixel graphics from the first game? Yes. Not gonna lie, I expected the sequel to follow suit to it's predecessor, but I'm not mad at the new style. The anatomy and shading look good in their stylized format. I see a lot of criticisms on the animations, but considering the pixel art style from the first game, the animations were way more limited in CE1 (You can't really add a ton of complexity when your characters are like, 4 rectangles tall lol. HOWEVER the simple animations they did have were good, including the effects). CE2 has taken a lot more care into adding MORE animation overall, and I can respect that. HERE IS WHAT I WILL SAY THOUGH: Since they aren't doing pixel graphics anymore, that means they have chosen to add complexity to their characters that they didn't have in their first game. Since the new characters have clearer facial features, bone/limb structure, and other things like hands, they should take advantage of it. Clearly they are animating using puppet rigs and are trying to go for a cut-out storybook style, BUT I think some improvements should include more hand and head positions for characters.  Combat: I didn't encounter any bugs here personally. There are some things I like and dislike.I like that it's simple and straight to the point. Dice gets rolled, attack is done. New Nurse character that has healing dice. YES. No more scourging to find a shaman that can only be found on expeditions. Getting damaged in CE1 was brutal due to the high infection rate. CE2 is more forgiving New character types have more unique types of dice and different effects. Instead of the combo system in CE1 where multiple dice were combined, CE2 gets rid of that. Now everyone has special dice with special moves, and you can't combine. This might be considered good or bad depending on your preference, but I like it. There is added strategy to choosing characters and buffing before attacking, etc. It would be cool if they took the best of both games and included combos with the new dice typesI don't like how they don't have auto enemy targeting. I have to click the dice, click the enemy, click the dice, click the enemy, over and over for each person. It gets oldOTHER IMPROVEMENTS:Less brutal sanity costSanity consumables have their failure chance listed in their description. The failure chance is also greatly lowered compared to CE1More events, more things to do, new questsVillage interaction has expandedNow you can visit your city and purchase cool stuff from sponsors like weapons, upgrades, elite party members, etcTL;DRAvoid getting sanity to 0 at all costs, you might come across a dead-end bug. I think the new art style is fine but the animations have room for improvement. Combat doesn't use combos, it's replaced with new characters having unique dice. CE2 has more events, party members, and locations than CE1. The game is also less harsh on sanity cost and infection

_childDocuments_.review: Curious Expedition 2 ranks among my favorite games of all time.  In a series of distinct expeditions, you must lead a team of explorers across procedurally-generated maps, overcoming obstacles (from combat to dehydration) that require you to make the most of each party member's special talents.  Each further expedition poses greater risk while also yielding more opportunity for rewards – and your goal is to seek out the technology that could bring peace and prosperity to the world!What makes Curious Expedition 2 so special and so replayable is its variety of classes.  There are the basic human classes (cook, missionary, field nurse), the more specialized human classes (Taoist monk, kinematographer, Grail knight), the non-human classes (salamander sea priest, mole tinkerer, shaman peacock), and so very many pack animals and pets (treasure corgi, donkey, red panda).  Your companions come and go – when playing on difficult settings, expect crew members to die, transform, depart, etc. – and it is the player's job, both during and between expeditions, to maintain a crew that can both survive and thrive in expeditions harmoniously while scooping up as many treasures as possible.Although you control a team of up to five, one serves as leader, and belongs to one of several leader-exclusive classes.  These classes determine gameplay, allowing for enormous replayability. These leader classes shape your whole gameplay; as an anthropologist, you'll want to devote time to interacting with the indigenous people of each island you visit on your expeditions, while as a pirate, you have no strong incentives to avoid antagonizing (up to a certain point) each island's native population.  Looting a temple and killing game cause distrust, but if you're playing a leader class that doesn't much care about popularity among the indigenous, you have all the talents you need to avoid the villagers, anyway.What Curious Expedition 2 isn't is a game about combat.  Even while playing as Big Game Hunter, the most combat-friendly leader class, you have strong disincentives (other than your time, of course!) not to fight everything you meet.  One of the biggest mistakes I made was thinking that I had to fight every enemy – fight selectively, because combat yields a few bonuses but (usually) far more disadvantages.My recommendations to new players?  Keep your crew happy; cure your crew of any debilitating mental illnesses (such as alcoholism); be sure to keep a lantern for caves and wading-boots for swamps; and don't take the loss of a crew member (even a beloved one) as insurmountable.  It will happen, and you'll sometimes find new friends in unexpected places.  Above all, be willing to experiment.  Happen across a mysterious portal?  Investigate!  Receive a chance to take on a yet-unknown quest from a village headwoman?  Leap at the opportunity!  The game rewards risk-taking.  After over 273 hours of gameplay, I know a lot of the payouts – but the game continues to surprise me with all of its combinations and permutations of advantages, disadvantages, and challenges.This game is at its most fun at its hardest, and, once you feel as if you've learned the basics, I strongly recommend ironman mode on lunatic difficulty.  I recommend in the highest terms – and I hope that Maschinen-Mensch will continue to develop such enjoyable games of strategy and exploration!

_childDocuments_.review: I would give this game a 9/10.I really want to give it a 10/10, but sadly it is currently severely lacking in incentive for replayability.Honestly, the main gripe I have with it is Maschinen-Mensch's stance on modding.You see, the first game was almost laughably easy to edit and mod, and has spawned a pretty strong community doing so.But TCE2 is entirely closed off, everything is encryped and locked. TCE2 is objectively better than TCE1 in almost every way, and Maschinen-Mensch did a tremendous and increidble job at making such a fantastic roguelike game. The formula works, and is executed to perfection.But once you've finished it once, it begins to become stale.There's still things to learn and discover, so you finish it twice.By the third time, you've likely got every explorer unlocked, but no intention to ever use any of them, because you're done with the game.Now TCE may, as I said, be objectively worse in nearly every aspect, but if I come back to it in 6 months and look at the steam workshop and there's new fascinating things to play with? I might just sink another 20 hours into it. The same can not be said about TCE2. I really cannot wait for the game to open up to some of the most passionate people in gaming : Modders.Doing so would likely make this one of the, if not the best roguelike of it's entire generation. Perhaps more.Ramble end.
