_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure what to expect with this game and just hoped for some nice adventure, and I really got it and enjoyed myself for nearly 30 hours for my first run, with a fighting party whose members were animal only (likely the easiest setup). I'd have likely done a second run to test a diplomacy party if I hadn't a backlog full of games.The game rules aren't much realistic though and lower a bit the immersion : your main resource to manage is Sanity. Every time you move, you lose some depending on how unfriendly the terrain is (eg: swamps make you lose more Sanity than grass).You can get back Sanity by eating food, resting, or special items or events. So unlike survival games, food isn't that important. It feels a bit weird, but this allows the game to focus on other things.The 2 other core elements that put pressure on your expedition are :- to stop you from resting too often, there's a fog coming closer to the island more and more with the passing days ; once on the island, that fog prevents you from seeing tiles and raises the Sanity cost- several actions will lower your reputation with the local tribesAnd of course, there are combats. They require enough tactics to keep my interest along the run, without being overly complicated.The story is nothing exceptional but it did the job of keeping me interested and giving me a purpose.Thus said, I'd have not enjoyed the game if I didn't save scum. Normally, at best, if you die you should restart the current island expedition. That'd have frustrated me too much, especially as some horrible things can happen more or less unexpectedly while you learn the game ropes.Also, the humans are pretty annoying to manage, and I quickly ended up with my sweet animal companions. 🙂Lastly, the game lacks a bit of depth, except maybe for the min/max lovers or master strategists who don't mind party wipes, but for me, it was fine.I enjoyed the visuals and I'm glad they took that style instead of the 1st Curious Expedition pixel art (which prevented me from playing it). However, the backgrounds in the city feel a bit flat, but we don't see them a lot.- A taste of adventure- Really sweet atmosphere, between 1889 Paris and exotic & mysterious islands- Original mechanisms- Many little parts that fit well together, preventing the game from being too repetitive- Very good replayability, despite a small lack of depth in the gameplay mechanisms- Lots of gear with interesting perks- The game just got extra free content, more than 3 years after release !- Gameplay rules aren't much realistic, lowering the immersion a bit- Too much guesswork on the consequences of our actions at 1st- Luck often matters a lot- The more you lose, the more chances to lose more (and vice versa), which makes the previous 2 points even more painful- Inventory management is painful : you quickly get too many items and constantly throw useful stuff away ; some of it being very small items (although the smallest ones take no space)- Gear evolution is pretty limited after less than half of the run- It doesn't feel like a rogue-like in the sense that the randomization almost doesn't affect the gameplay ; ie: all my expeditions felt more or less the same, and I didn't feel like I had to adapt to the circumstances, only to the island type
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I've played this and the Alpha for around 10-20 hours and Curious Expedition is a pretty good History-Roguelite with Squad Management and tactical elements. I have experienced no bugs yet (but according to the forums there are still some in, though none gamebreaking) - so the early access is SOLID, mainly seeking feedback from customers, expanding the game still a bit and weeding out last, but not big bugs. Can recommend, why?What can you expect? History in the late 19th century setting, the late age of explorers where the most remote and weird places on earth would be discovered. Everything revolves around the Paris World Exhibition, where you can find people to recruit and sponsors (factions) to support you on your expedition, unlocking special benefits as you progress doing quests for them. Surprises, things going wrong, for every risk you can take, there is a high reward, for every high reward, weird and dangerous things can happen. Historical, mythic, mystic, outright weird "von Däniken style" events - it's all there, in a simplistic gameplay of you exploring a fun little map, meeting people, dangerous animals, finding forgotten temples, native tribes and weird travelers.There is strategy and tactics to it. You can synergize your team by picking the right people together.. for example a cook, a native and a hunting dog as your supporting characters make you well-fed all the time, preventing bad events from low sanity (your walking points on the exploration map are called sanity, and if they are below 50 of 100, bad events start to fire - you mainly recover them by eating or resting, but you cannot rest everywhere).For equipment and weapons for your team you acquire items that change your dice. A lot revolves around dice that you can combine to get more powerful effects or to find bonus treasure in the ancient temples you discover. A little thinking here, a little pondering there and if you like probability or mathematics you can totally optimize your dice rolls, too, but it's not really necessary - rule of thumb is enough.So, a game that is really not to be pressed into one category, with a nice graphic novel style graphics. But how does it differ from its predecessor?1. Different Graphics (Curious Expedition 1 had Pixel Style, this is Graphic Novel style)2. More story elements (CE1 was revolving around procedural generation and randomness, this has some red thread underlying story elements as you explore).3. Factions and unlocking advantages with them.4. A historical story hub / starting point with the gameplay revolving around the World Exhibition in ParisIt is a DIFFERENT game to its predecessor, even when it shares some of the gameplay elements with it, you can play both as they are different experiences, the first one more anarchic, random, chaotic - this one more beautiful, story-based, with deeper tactical and strategic options. It is not just different graphics and a 2 put to it, it's a different game altogether, and a good one (for me) to boot! What can I say.. I like both games and can recommend both :-)Of course I made a video about it, a long walkthrough through the first TWO missions with all the tips you will need to proceed even further without any problem - you can click around in it to see different parts of the game, and the different elements. If you watch it completely you will get an introduction into all gameplay mechanics and advanced strategies and tactics that will be a big advantage for a beginner in this game, you can find it here:All the best, yourImmanuel Can

_childDocuments_.review: This game improves on its predecessor in many ways, and the prior game is one of my very favorite games - a title of exceptional quality. The CE series are unique games. Though there are 'curious' things like sandworms, cultists, and dinos in this game, the uniqueness comes from its map-based resource management game play.At core this is a route planning & risk management game. Route A will cost you fewer resources to travel than Route B, but there are higher dangers affected by the particular group of party members in your trek (think Darkest Dungeon RE: party members). If one of your characters is a pyromaniac, then every time your group pauses he may set the forest on fire and you have to FLEE the flames! Did you prepare to clear his mind with a mushroom, or are you stuck possibly dismissing your dear pyro, weighing the risk of fiery death against whatever skills that character has?This is not RNG, it's calculated risk; that character is a pyro - you knew it and you kept him in your group. You sprained your ankle because you DECIDED to climb up the tower even though you could clearly see the dice you had vs the roll you needed.What this is NOT is a power fantasy. The graphics are bright, but the design is not meant to be a mollycoddling sandbox; this is a roguelike where if you make the wrong decision - if you repeatedly take a 35% chance-of-success dice roll and you LOSE - you can and will die. You have to PREPARE with a tactical approach that can create resilience to the small failures.You are faced with a fight you can't handle; you must stock up on extra one-time-use combat items ahead of time, or use an item that can distract the enemy so you can sneak around them, or understand that you have to RUN AWAY.IS THIS GAME BETTER THAN CE1? Yes and no; this game is better in some ways and not in others. There is a lot more varied content here, including equipment and simply more of everything. This means the experience is quite a bit more varied than in CE1. The game does significantly more to explore the full potential of its EXCEPTIONAL map-based resource management game play, including some truly inspired features like caverns with fog-of-war and light management, and the extremely hazardous corrupted areas. CE1 remains better in terms of overall framing and pacing, with the 6 expedition story arc a bit more clear-eyed in putting clear pressure on the player in terms of winning a race by a particular deadline. CE2, by contrast, has improved gameplay but muddled framing; the story arcs just don't have the clear call-to-action motivation that CE1 has.The gameplay is a significant improvement over CE1, however, and this is what I'm playing now over CE1. I expect the brilliant developer will eventually fix the weak framing, and in the meantime simply making these islands and then not showing the island outline is a design master stroke that flips CE1 on its head.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game.  A lot has been changed and improved from the first game.  It is a really fun challenge.  I completed four complete campaigns and got all of the achievements in 145 hours of playtime.  The value for the price is fantastic.You begin by choosing a leader.  As you progress in the game, additional leaders become available that you can use in future playthroughs.  I changed my mind on my favorite leader a couple of times, so there are definitely options for everyone with vastly different strengths.  The leader makes a big difference in the best way to approach specific expeditions, but it isn't limiting options - you can still generally play how you choose with whichever leader you pick.There are a lot of characters and animals that you can take in your party.  Depending on your play style, everyone will have different favorites because they all have different advantages and disadvantages.  One of my favorite things was the emergent storylines that developed between the teammates in my party.  Friendship, love, hate, special bonds with animals - it really added a lot to the experience.  It made for very difficult decisions on whether to replace one of the characters with another one that might be more useful for my play style.There are three groups in the game that you can work for.  As you work for them, you gain access to additional party members you can recruit, special items that you can keep and use for every expedition, and items that can show up for individual expeditions.  All three groups have useful contributions, so it makes sense to eventually work for all three groups.I liked the options in the dice combat system a lot.  I could do something useful with any set of dice that was rolled and it was nice to be able to choose what was the best way to use a particular roll.  Even with the same characters against the same enemies, the strategy varied a lot from roll to roll.  There was a lot of depth in terms of order of using dice to act, too.  I also appreciated how character growth or item improvement added additional die faces and was a really valuable way to affect combat strategy.The achievements offer a nice range of accomplishment levels.  Some are very easy, some just take time, and some are very challenging but still fair to obtain.  It is probably one of the most balanced sets of achievements that I have seen.  I really had a good time going for them - something I don't do in most games I play.The graphics have a quality to them that really grew on me over time.  They are well done and very distinctive from other games.  They also add appropriate amounts of humor or cuteness to certain events.The game was very stable.  I encountered a few small bugs - most of which have already been fixed.  There have been frequent bug-fixing updates so far, so it is likely that any remaining bugs will be fixed quickly.My only real complaint was the physics of dice re-rolls.  The initial rolls seem fine.  But when re-rolling dice they frequently seem like they are just lifted and dropped.  They don't roll and stay in the same position with the same die face showing.  As I grew more experienced in the game, this issue went down in importance, but it would still be nice to see it changed in the future.Overall it was a really great experience and I'm looking forward to seeing the additional content the developers are already working on.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is "pretty good".  Plus: I like a lot of different exploration games; I never played CE1, but I liked Expeditions: Conquistador and Reknowned Explorers.  All these three are very similar.  Minus: definitely check out a let's play video to see what you think of the animation style.  The overland map is fine, it's kind of lo-fideilty but cute, and clear enough.  The CYA sections have characters with stick-figure animation that takes some getting used to.  Maybe it will be better after early access, but it's definitely not for everybody.There are basically three levels of play: the exploration map, tactical combat, and the strategic layer between missions.  For the exploration map, there is good variety for EA, and I assume more variants of the missions will be added as EA progresses.  For example, if your sanity drops to zero, the only event that seems to happen is "fire ants attack".  That gets a little repetitive.  It's pretty easy to get the hang of it, and there are nice tradeoffs around stretching to get one more shrine, and managing your relationship level with the local tribes.For tactical combat, it is pretty simple.  It isn't really "tactical".  Each turn, each character gets 1-2 maneuvers selected from a small deck.  These are usually attacks but there are some other options.  You can quickly organize the maneuvers for maximum effect; compared to other tactical games, this is pretty simplistic.The strategic level is actually the most interesting of the three.  It isn't anything unique, but in between missions, there is a good variety of upgrades from vendors, and three sets of  reasonably interesting looking unlocks from different expedition investors.  For example, if you do multiple missions for Edi-Bot, you can unlock a nice stun-wand which does damage to both the wielder and one enemy; and later you can unlock an improvement which prevents the self-damage.  It will be interesting to replay at least three times to experiment with the different investors.

_childDocuments_.review: Quite the gem we have right here! :) It might need some polish, but the shape is there!For new players:This is an expedition simulator par excellence, building upon the ideas of the first game and pushing them further!You will have to assemble a crew, choose their equipment wisely, and then trek out into the wilds! Its pretty hard sometimes, and it can be distressing to lose all of your companions. It definitely teaches you, to sometimes just give up and head home in shame.There's so many great new ideas in this one! I especially love the fact, that it seems much more viable to just be nice and friendly with the natives. Using the kinematographer is my foremost joy, and paired with an antrophologist or cartographer you have a lot of ways to gain fame without stealing anything from the locals! I for one am also just in love with the artstyle. Yes i get it, the 2d animations are a little stickfigurelike sometimes. But that can be polished and i think the detail on both the characters and backgrounds make up for it easily. also..i mean just look at those little people on the map. they are the most adorable.Yes, there are bugs and yes i have experienced some gamebreaking ones (All fine after alt+f4 and a reload though). But the devs are hard at work and do actually take every bug report seriously. Join their discord server and be a part of this extremely active community, with bug reports being stored and answered by the minute!Now for some critique:I am still getting to grips with the new dice system. While this one gives more weight to who you have in the party, with most characters using kind of special dice with special moves, I miss the combinatory stuff of the last game. It was a lot of fun to discover awesome combinations. HOWEVER I get that it wasn't very accesible. To get any meaningful progress in CE1 I eventually looked up dicecombinations, because you have to know what your aiming for before you choose what to reroll. In CE2 that doesn't happen. All the info is right there. I would still love to see boosts with different colorcombinations, though that probably gets really complex really quickly.Can wholeheartedly recommend already and am really eager to see where this is going!

_childDocuments_.review: Curious expedition 2, developed by Maschinen-Mensch and published by Thunderful Publishing, is a turn-based dice-rolling adventure game available on Steam for PC.  The player is thrown into randomly generated islands tasked with different missions ranging from surveying islands to killing your own groupmate turned-zombie due to their inattentive infection.The game is set in 1800 Paris where you find yourself first learning about the purple fog. On the first mission you see the fog take over the island you are on and after a close escape to your boat you look back to see the fog has cleared but there is no island to be seen. You are then taken to the exhibition grounds where you can go recruit new team members at the tavern and build your team.  Along the way you gather expo tickets which can be spent on items, equipment, or recruits through the different sponsors’ headquarters. Curious expedition 2 revolves around your sanity, and if that is not your first priority then wish your quest goodbye. Sanity is what keeps your team together and prevents insanity events from occurring. Insanity events occur when your sanity reaches zero. Sanity is what gives your team the ability to move across the island and serves as a somewhat “stamina” for the team.  Every time you travel with your team through the island it will cost a certain amount of sanity. You can regain sanity by eating food or drinking your favorite alcohol or sleeping at camp sites or villages you find along the way. Towards the end of quests, you find yourself fighting off insanity events and praying to come across any place to rest.The next staple of Curious expedition 2 is the dice rolling. Whenever you are faced with an obstacle such as combat or success/failure of looting a temple; the game presents you with your dice to roll. Each color of the dyes-side is associated with something different.  Red is combat related, or green is related to looting. For example, if you try to steal from one of the villages, the game will ask you to roll the dice and if you do not roll at least two green dye, then you will get caught. Depending on the team member, their dice will have different colors on them. If you choose a British soldier for your team, both soldiers’ dice are all red, but if you pick a chef, their dye will have some blue sides and some green. This forces you to diversify your team, so you do not only have all one color of dye. If you mainly focus on red sided dice and a very combat-heavy team, then you will have a much higher chance when required to roll x number of red but an awful and possibly impossible chance when asked to roll a certain number of blue or green dice.  Good vs. Evil  - With all these different events and choices to make, you can choose to be the good explorer who gets along with the natives; or the pillaging thief who decides to steal from their temples and take all their offerings. I chose to be the devil's advocate during my playthrough and steal all the treasure and loot I could find. In doing so, the natives turned on me very quickly and attacked me on the island instead of offering goods or services. The tribe encounters get very repetitive as you can only really trade with them, recruit a new team member, or interact with their leader for quests or information. I also felt the tribes trading prices were very steep, and if I wanted something good, I would have to trade some of my loot for it, which made me think, “hmm, do I really NEED to eat, or keep the golden llama?”Your Team -  The relationships you develop with your team members can be quite short if things go wrong, and the conversations start to become repetitive and uninteresting. They can also develop a variety of different illnesses that if not treated will slowly but surely ruin that character and result in tragedy such as death or turning into an eight-foot zombie who you must now kill to survive.  While there is a huge variety of character appearances and different character traits; I never felt connected with any of the team members or a bond to any due to uninteresting relationships and the fact that it seemed I would lose at least one team member every quest, so our times together were cut short.  Equipment and tickets - I also had a hard time buying equipment with my hard-earned expo-tickets (earned from completing quests) because it seemed I would cash out on equipment for a team member through the shady dealer and the very next quest he decides to leave our group because he lost all his “loyalty” to me. The equipment does have a lot of variety and you can create several various builds for any scenario or quest you are about to head out on.  Repetitive Loot - The looting seems to be one of the highlights of Curious expedition 2 but can quickly go bad if you decide to travel too far and do not have enough sanity to return. The loot also does not have a lot of variety as it seemed whichever islands I went to it was the same couple loot items at the various locations. The locations have texture variety depending on what area you are exploring, but you can always expect the same village, temple, etc. just with a different look. Conclusion - Curious expedition 2 is an overall well-developed game but does share its number of bugs and glitches. The story line is easy to follow and has a seemingly loose structure, which is not as interesting to follow as the game progressed. Sanity has become my life's goal when I play this game and nothing else matters when trying to find a campsite once you run out of items to help regain sanity. The dice component is well managed and very entertaining when you are trying to steal from a tribe and not get caught. It is well thought-out and plays a major role in the game and your success while exploring the islands. I enjoyed playing but did not build any relationships with the CPU nor did I really care due to the lack of interesting conversations or want to build a loyal team. I am going to give this game a 7.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. Well-presented graphics, whimsical tone, and it really gives you a chance to write your own story. This game grips you with every journey, the planning, speculating, and tension will keep you up hours past when you should have gone to sleep.Jungle opera is a genre of fiction dating back to the Belle Epoque, but it is rare these days, probably because people might find the aesthetic archaic or problematic. This game does a great job of addressing that problem. You can indeed be the swashbuckling Victorian big-game hunter that leaves a trail of death and destruction...but you can also be an Arabic cartographer, a Chinese folk herbalist, a Nahua spiritualist, etc...and select teammates from around the world too!

_childDocuments_.review: I got the first iteration of CE in a bundle a while back, and I just got around to playing it. Within a few hours of playtime, I realized that I'd severely underpaid. I found the sequel and DLC on Steam, and it doesn't disappoint! CE is a difficult roguelike game that forces you to learn its mechanics fast. I appreciate the beginner mode to teach you the ropes. Beginner is still difficult and engaging though! It took me tens of hours to beat the main plot. I believe in CE1 dying in combat killed you completely and restarted your campaign, so I like that this one's a little more forgiving: it erases your party and a few past expeditions and you don't lose all your progress.In typical roguelike text-based fashion, they just drop you into gameplay, but if you actually read the text instead of clicking through, you get tons of hints! Combat dice are simplified and boosted by color. This makes it easy enough for newbies, but as challenges get harder, the details and complexities become more vital. Auto-generated islands in 5(?) different landscapes with different questlines and integrated online tournaments means that it never gets dull. Often when I beat a game like this, I'll set it aside, but the sheer amount of content has me hooked. I'm trying to work up to getting all the negative traits in Director's Mode, and the difficulty has been scaling so well that I'm glued to my seat. Haven't tried Lunatic (the hardest difficulty) yet, so we'll see if I get there! Thank you, devs, for the thorough descriptions, snarky voice, and fun surprises throughout the game! I'm spreading the word to everyone I know!

_childDocuments_.review: Curious expedition 2 is a pretty fine exploration game featuring adventures and explorers in their search for glory and unravelling mysteries. It has a rather vintage and steampunk vibe into it, also it features a board game-like style play mode.This game is awesome generally speaking, it has some minor bugs in some of the adventures, but the whole experience compensates.This is a rather simple game to play but at the same time, you can spend a lot of time fulfilling your missions or having a brutal trip all the way, but that's precisely how it gets more exciting.I strongly recommend this game for those people who would like to experience a different kind of strategy or board game.The art is also very cool and you'll find out some of the locations and their inhabitants to be very particular and interesting :3.  Overall, good and entertaining.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommendation with reservationsThe randomness factor in the game can be punishing. The game puts the player against two fairly merciless clocks - sanity and the ever-approaching purple fog. If the player cannot find the objective in time - and some objectives are only revealed halfway through the expedition - this easily results in a loss. Resources (sanity restoration, medical kits, etc) are usually scarce, and the end-of-year storyline expeditions have multiple stages and failure in the last stage means you have to start over (only at the easiest setting that allows restarting individual expeditions).Pros:- Timeless cartoon graphics (if this is an art style you like)- Exploration atmosphere- Many viable party compositions- Persistent progressionCons:- Randomness can be quite punishing- Race against not just one, but two clocks- There is very little time for backtracking; chose your path wisely

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite games, I have also played for many hours on switch and also played CE1. Definitely recommend it if you like strategy, roguelike, or exploration games. Easily worth full price.  Pros: Great story telling that fits well with the gameplay and randomly generated maps/eventsFeels well balanced with difficulty, with multiple difficulty customization optionsGood variety between different explorers, there are several different strategies you can go for that feel balanced to meDLC is fun and it complements core game wellThe progress that stays between a runs adds new items and character that keeps the game feeling fresh, and I like that you can choose which unlocks you are working towardsCons:A bit of a steep learning curve at first, this is the type of game where you have all the tools from the beginning and you have to learn what works as you go (which I really enjoy personally)I now that I have played more I wish there were some more intense and unique challenges that aren’t as easy to plan for.Progress between the 3 societies seems a little too slow, I don’t think most people will play for long enough to unlock a lot of it

_childDocuments_.review: Curious Expedition 2 ReviewCurious Expedition 2 is a game where you take a ship on an expedition, you get some gold to buy stuff like shovels and medical kits. Then you explore ruins. You also build a team of fellow explorers. The actual gameplay is clicking on stuff and the combat is based on rolling dice.Pros+ You can fill out your party with some cool characters, such as a dog, a horse, a parasaur, and more. You can also bring other explorers with you like sailors and chefs that bring unique skills to the table.+ It's something different than what I'm used to. It's kind of like a point-and-click Indiana Jones game.+ I didn't run into any glitches. It's pretty straight forward to play this game. The first level is a tutorial.Cons- It's too harsh. During your exploring, random events happen, which is cool, but most of these random events suck. For example, sometimes a character will just get mad at you and "run away" and you can't go after them. I found a Yeti and brought it with me, gave it food, was nice to it, and then it got addicted to alcohol and abandoned my party. One of the worst events was when the forest set on fire out of nowhere and it said my dog was dead. Super annoying to lose my dog that I'd been putting all of my promotions into and exploring with since the start of the game (the first time this happened I went to a previous save, the second time my dog died was literally on the last mission of the story mode so I just said screw it). I was playing on the easier difficulty, and yet these random events will just pop up and totally destroy the squad you just spent hours putting together.- To explore the map, you lose "sanity". If that hits zero, your squad goes mad. They eat the dog, run away, get lost forever, just a bunch of crazy stuff. I think on easier difficulty you should have higher sanity. It's annoying because sometimes the game doesn't let you bring a tent with you, so then you just keep losing sanity and you can't sleep on the ground without a tent. So then, you can go ask a villager to sleep in their village, but they get mad at you and you have to trade them treasures. And the villagers don't even let you sleep until you're recovered, you regain like 25% sanity, so if it was really low, you have to trade them even more of your treasure. These systems kind of feel more like an annoyance.- Party size is too small. You can only have 5 party members, and you can't store them! I would have liked to keep my parasaur and my elk in a stable or something so I can choose which one I bring on specific missions. There was a part in the game where I had a full party, then found a baby raptor. The game forced me to choose if I want to keep the raptor and send away one of my current party members forever, or to permanently send away the raptor. I didn't like having to choose, I wanted to keep them all.Bonus ContentThe DLCs for the game are fine, they're more of the same. My only dislike here is that on the "Taishi Shore" map, you are forced to use teleporters to traverse, and they are only one-way teleporters. So basically you get farther and farther from the ship, and the game screws you over because everyone in your party gets cranky and starts whining and there's no way to get back to the ship quickly so it's like the longer you are on the island the more annoying the gameplay gets.Final VerdictThat's pretty much it. The game is like a 6.5/10 or a 7/10, so just barely passing for me. If you want to explore some islands for about 10 hours, have at it. After completing the story you can do more expeditions in Director Mode, but for all the cons I stated I don't know if I want to go to the trouble. The game would be improved if on lower difficulties it was more relaxing, and if there was more of an emphasis on collecting and keeping wild creatures.

_childDocuments_.review: Really interesting game that incorporates many of the concepts introduced by Darkest Dungeon (sanity meter, having to assemble a preparatory stockpile of usable equipment that even includes shovels and torches while keeping in mind leaving space to store goodies). The art style is pretty unique. I like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice balance of strategy, planning, and risk vs reward at the beginning of the game.Once you get to the larger maps however... is where the game falls apart. Horrible mess of ideas/execution of the game and challenges versus difficulty balancing. Lag becomes more noticable as the challenges keep piling on.RNG. Freaking RNG, There's a chance that you could start a game where everything was made to lose, on top of that the room for error is very small, one bad roll could end the entire run. RNG dice rolls gets ridiculous at late game where you cannot keep up, and it gets to a point where you can't get any more dice or fudge the rolls in anyway you start to plan for losing rolls instead.Everything tries to kill you; animals, people, teammates, infection. And it is almost impossible to prepare for these scenarios on the longer maps. I've had a run where all my team mates got an infection after one fight, and only brought 2 med kits... with no means to get more healing (no traders, prehistoric map). You can also make a mistake and lose the map because you run out of ways to find sanity/food.Leveling up become irrelevant after a while, dice don't scale well in late game. Starting resources/gold/food does not grow well late game either. The scarcity gets worse later on.Maps become more challenging, but also more frustrating; more dead ends, too many tiles effects that even the auto-pathing becomes unreliable. Larger maps = larger mistakes. Your inventory is too tiny to prepare for every predictable challenge.I faced all of this... on easy mode... Yeah this game is HARD~In both good, but overall in my opinion, mostly bad ways.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been here a while.  I don't know how long...let's just say 'a while'.  I wish I could say I keep returning to these strange islands, but the tiles that make them up are so drenched in randomness and opportunity that I can't really be sure I actually left.  I think I return to town, gain a new expedition member, catch up on the world's news, though even it always relates to these disappearing isles where I spend months without end trying keep my sanity up as I carefully pillage treasures from the ruins of the natives without angering them too much.My clearest moments are when I am turning in tickets at this bizarre worlds fair, using them like a second currency to buy equipment, improvements to equipment, helpful perks and sometimes expedition members before setting out again to gain more treasure, only to ultimately return and trade the treasure for tickets.  The cycle repeats, but the expedition is never the same.  All the while I grow stronger, gain abilities, become more adept at my own particular way of expeditioning, and most importantly I come closer to understanding those strange creations and their creators.  Those artifacts that seem to either be some sort of technology or magic.  I can't tell which, but every time I chase down a legend they are there, the footsteps of that vanished people and the often broken things they left behind.  Things that can probably bend or change reality.If I am being honest then I have to say that I don't know if my sanity is still with me at all.  I have had expedition members squabble over non-sense, natives ask me questions and look askance at my answers, mole-people I have never met before determine me a threat and also a friend though never at the same time.  I have watched an egg become a dinosaur and felt all kinds of anger and regret at having to eat one of my best expedition members, one I tamed from the wild myself who ferried me over countless miles of so many islands.  I use wands to flatten mountains and trade the skins of chitinous horrors for good will and supplies.In the nights I wonder where I will find my end, in Paris comfortable in a bed or upon one of the isles drowning in madness's own fog?

_childDocuments_.review: First time I've had a chance to play this series, not being a big fan of pixel art. And so far I'm loving it. The graphics are more to my taste, the balance between exploring and combat are tons of fun. Its the type of game where it pays to be well supplied before disembarking on your expedition, yet knowing what to take is a gamble, including the type of crew you recruit in your hub of Paris. I have only played a little over half an hour and I am having a blast. Considering its early access im very impressed and I recommend it wholeheartedly....so give it a try and if you are into roguelike adventure games I am sure you will enjoy it as much as I am.I wanted to add something to my review...Some people are complaining about things they have either not noticed, or have YET to notice. I read a review where one person gave a negative review because they no longer have a time restraint, which makes resting for a week an option that has no consequence. Not true. Missions do have a time restraint, but will only warn you when you get close to losing. Something this person clearly has not experienced. The same person made a comment on how combat is dumbed down cause you can buff a certain color dice with a different color dice. No idea what he means. There are ways to add new color dice rolls with potions you must buy, and you can buff a character with buffs from other crew members. But im still confused on how he means that. So just be wary and take some of these reviews with a grain of salt.

_childDocuments_.review: It plays a lot like the first game, but with better graphics, better combat, a much longer campaign and quite a lot of balance changes.Combats are more interesting than before, different opponents use different strategies. Wolves focus fire, panthers make it hard to reroll dice, snakes stun and poison you.  You don't have to remember obscure combinations anymore, instead dice can boost other dice so its much easier to see what your different strategies are for a given rice roll.Fame is now the main currency between expeditions, it's not just for keeping score.  All items are automatically sold for fame, except equipment which you can keep for the next expedition.  You use fame to level up at the different factions.  Fame also generates tickets which can be used to buy equipment.Equipment now has to be put in equipment slots for it to have an effect, but equipment slots don't count towards inventory.  Which means you'll have a lot more equipment than in the last game.  Equipment also has levels, a level 4 rifle has better dice than a level 1 rifle.The combination of your main character class, which faction you choose, what party members you choose, and what equipment you choose makes for a lot of different strategies, and provides a lot of replay value.  Even within a campaign the strategies will change as party members are lost and replaced, or you swap out e.g. a low level axe with a high level rifle.

_childDocuments_.review: Curious Expedition 2 is an extremely unique roguelike where you go on insanely fun expeditions to random islands that keep popping that can have anything from natives to fish people and crazy places to discover like pyramids, caves, and weird alien technology.I absolutely love when a completely new, one of a kind roguelike comes out and that's what Curious Expedition 2 is. I played the original game and absolutely loved it and thought it was so unique so when I saw the sequel officially came out I knew I needed to play it.The game takes places in the 1880s in Paris and there are tons of adventurers that are going on expeditions to strange islands to find treasures, discover wonders, and get all the fame and glory!And so you pick your adventurer, get a crew together, and set off on your expedition. You can choose how difficult of a challenge you want which will get you more rewards but it also comes with more danger. And on the normal difficulty which I played on if you die your crew and your characters are dead forever. And your characters can level up in the game and get new gear and stuff so its a pretty big deal. You have to get a new crew together and everything.There is an easier mode where your crew doesn't actually permanently die when you lose and there is a harder ironman mode that wipes your campaign if you lose. In my opinion the game is best at the normal difficulty where you can lose your crew because that’s what makes the roguelike aspect of the game work the best. And thematically it makes sense for time to pass in the world and new adventurers step up to the plate.But enough with all that! What is the main gameplay like?The main gameplay when you are exploring these islands is a kind of hexa grid map that you can travel on. And traveling takes up your sanity. So as you explore you need to make sure you have enough resources. You need enough food or other items to regain sanity, you need healing items, tools like climbing gear for mountains or extra water in deserts.And this sounds like a lot but it really isn’t. And that is coming from a guy that hates survival games because of all the meters and chores you have to do but this game has a simplified but effective version of all that. It’s important in the game but it never feels annoying, instead it’s just an actually crucial and thematically fun mechanic.And so you travel and discover more and more of the island and you will start to find random things like native villages, shrines, caves, chambers, graveyards, waterfalls, magical technology and more. And this is honestly one of the best parts about the game. Every time you get to one of these you get an extremely unique and surprisingly deep events that have this gorgeous artwork and lore. So you might find an elephant graveyard that you can search through and if you roll well enough you can find loot.You could also find a native village which would allow you to trade with the locals, or rest there as long as they aren’t hostile and you aren’t overstaying your welcome, or you could even meet with a village elder if they have one and get quests or learn things about the island.And every time you are on an expedition you have a goal. It might be to find a specific magic gate or find a lost explorer. And sometimes you will have a somewhat of a guide like a compass that is very inaccurate but gets better the closer you are to them.There are also things roaming the islands which could be anything from traders, to natives that can be hostile or not sometimes depending on how you’ve treated them, or enemies like wolves or even sentient mole rats.And combat in this game is very fun as well. Every single character has their own dice with unique attacks and abilities. And so on your turn you roll your dice and you have one re-roll where you can re-roll any amount of dice. And if the dice landed on one of their attacks or abilities you can use it and sometimes you can boost dice with other dice of that same type to make them even more powerful.And also there are tons of weapons and items you can find in the game to equip to your characters that give you more and unique dice as well.Overall the combat is actually pretty solid and has a lot of depth to it. Also having different dice colors is pretty smart. And on top of combat you will also be using those dice in other situations like trying not to fall in traps or if you need to persuade someone.And so when you complete your objective you sometimes you will have to return back to your ship and sometimes you just instantly win. Obviously a lot easier said than done as the game is decently challenging and really makes you think and plan things ahead. Also there are some things you can do that can completely wipe out the entire island with stuff like poison gas.But when you do hopefully win you go back to Paris and get showered with fame and attention for your grand adventures. You also get expo tickets as rewards for bringing treasures back. And another cool thing about Paris is there are three different companies that can sponsor your adventures. So you pledge yourself to one sponsor and all your experience you get goes to that faction which will unlock new faction specific weapons, items, and even people that you can purchase with those expo tickets which is really awesome.And something really cool that I have not seen a roguelike do is there are weekly online competitions between which faction will bring in the most treasures each week and the winning team wins unique rewards. I haven’t played enough to see if it is always just one sided like some of these types of competitions go but I am very intrigued by this mechanic.And the last thing I really want to touch on is the story. The game is a roguelike but it kind of does something similarly to Hades where it has a story that is somehow tells even though the game is a roguelite. And the worlds, missions, and events are still randomized but there is a story that progresses even if your characters die as long as you aren't in ironman mode and that's really awesome.And so overall I would highly recommend Curious Expedition 2 to any roguelike fan. It is so unique and even if you aren’t the biggest fan of the turn based resource and party driven gameplay, the theme and presentation are absolutely a joy to experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Curious Expedition 2:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Victoria Malin is considered one of the greatest explorers in 1880. Her latest expedition saw her discovering the fascinating South American country of Peru. The expedition itself was a total success. However, on the way back to her headquarters in Paris, she came across a storm of such ferocity that many of her crew were thrown overboard into the extremely agitated ocean. Her vessel miraculously seemed to cope with wave after gigantic wave crashing into it. Despite being thrown around like being inside a washing machine, Victoria managed to see land and decided to head towards it. As her ship approached the Island, the sea became calmer, and she safely reached shore. Interestingly, this particular island isn't mentioned in any available maps. After exploring the island and talking to the natives, Victoria sees a strange, possibly ancient structure, and after studying it for a while, she decides to touch it. Instantly, a purple storm erupts from it, and the only way to escape is to go back to her ship and hope for the best!  Thankfully, she makes it back to Paris, but her new role of Director of the Expedition Universelle restricts participation in any new expeditions. So, you are the next biggest explorers in line. Are you ready for the next extraordinary adventures, helping Victoria to find this invisible Island?Curious Expedition 2 is a rogue-like turn-based combat strategy game developed by Maschinen-Mensch and published by Thunderful Publishing on 28th January 2021 on the Steam platform. The game will become available for Nintendo Switch, Playstation and Xbox platforms later on in 2021. As you start your first playthrough, you'll be playing Victoria Malin when she lands on the mysterious Island after the massive storm. This first Island is basically a very good tutorial. Then, when you are back in Paris, you'll have to choose who will become the leader of your next expedition and in which level of difficulty you'll be playing it: Traveller, Adventurer or Lunatic. After all that, your adventures will start in beautiful downtown Paris in 1886, where you'll plan your first and all subsequent expeditions.Each year, you'll be able to go on three expeditions. The first two will be to earn fame and experience, and the third one will be a part of the overall story. One thing you'll have to do before going on your next expedition is to go to the famous Boussole Cassee Pub, where you can recruit new crew members and ask for financial help if you have enough expo tickets. You'll receive expo tickets when you successfully complete an expedition and return with most of your goods and treasures. The maximum number crew members who can accompany you in your travels is four; five including you. You'll also be able to visit three houses/sponsors in Paris. At the start of the game, you won’t be able to do much when you visit them, but as your playthrough progresses, you'll unlock items, characters and use specific abilities to upgrade items, train or heal your characters. Of course, if you have enough expo tickets.Each Island you visit will be procedurally-generated, and each of them will have different dangers and places to visits. As you land, you'll see a little bit of the top-down relief map; the rest of it will be in a fog. You'll be allocated a certain number of sanity or movement points which you'll use to move your party around the Island. As the environment of each island varies, the cost of movements might differ as well. For example, it will cost you more points to travel through dense forests or swamps than on a flat surface. You'll come across areas with mosquitos and dangerous plants, which can give give one or more of your characters a serious illness.  You can also come across areas full of tar which will penalise your movement too. So, you need to make sure you have enough Sanity points at any given time. If you were wise enough to buy plenty of whiskey, chocolate and tins of tuna, for example, you could use them to revitalise your sanity points in the map view. You’ll also want to find a place to rest. Places like missionary churches or local tribe villages can offer you a resting place overnight and revitalise your sanity points, but you mostly need to trade to be able to rest. However, if you find an Oasis, waterfalls or spring water sites, you can rest for free. As you move around each island, you'll find sites to visit, such as shrines, shipwrecks, caves and deserted camps.  When you find one of these sites, you'll have to choose what to do, and the dice mechanism will be implemented. As you know, a conventional dice has 6 faces. When you start the game, all the characters in your group will have four faces of the dice covered with actions and colours. The action will be available during a fight, but the colour will determine a specific action's outcome.  For instance, when you want to search the deserted camp you might need to have a minimum of two green faces to be successful. If you have a total of 3 characters with each, you will have 3 green dice faces. Well, you might think that you have a great chance to roll at least three green faces. But it might be totally the opposite, and you might use a cunning tonic which is green and will add another dice before the roll, which can improve your chances of success. But bear in mind that most of these items can also be use in turn-based combat, so be wise about when to use them.You'll also come across traders, villagers and dangerous animals. Dangerous animals will trigger the combat phase, but you can also have the native tribes after you if they disapprove of your actions on their Island. The combat phase also uses the dice mechanism, but you can re-roll any dice (actions) once before starting the fight in this instance. Remember that most of your characters will start with four actions/colours per dice, so each dice will have two blank faces. You might be very unlucky and get only blank faces. So the re-roll is always good to have.  From then on, it is conventional turn-based combat using the action from the dice. You can upgrade your characters during an expedition as you earn experience points that can be used every time you discover a location. You'll need 10 XP to upgrade a character to level 2 and 20 XP to level 3 etc. At the end of your successful expedition, you'll receive fame points and expo tickets, but that will depend on returning home with treasures. You'll also receive experience points from your sponsor and unlock items and other goodies.Positives:~~~~~~~ +	Fabulous artworks+	Procedurally generated levels+	Fun story+	Every expedition is different+	Good turn-based combat+	Great replayability+	Achievements and trading cardsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	I don't have any!Curious Expedition 2: Embark to the most curious and daring exploration of all time and become the crème de la crème of explorer in the 1880's.  9/10 Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed a game called "Invisible, Inc.", chances are you will like this game as well.Curious Expedition 2 and Invisible, Inc. throw you into maps full of shortcuts, loot, enemies, objectives, secrets and challenges. The catch is that you start without any information, and it is game-over if you waste too much time on exploring.To win these games, you must gather information by venturing into the unknown. You don't know where to start, move out and finish. The only way to know it is to keep moving and complete the map which was a huge blank in the beginning. Gathering information in Curious Expedition 2 is vital to your success, and it manages to create expectations, suspense, and curiosity (yes, an intended pun) to keep you motivated in the process.Players playing CE2 will get a little excited and nervous when they are just starting out an expedition. Players will also feel relieved whenever they find a campsite at the brink of insanity.Players will smile when they earn a small fortune, or a powerful weapon.Players will be concerned when they encounter a formidable foe.And finally, they will be wiping off their sweat when they managed to escape before the fog consumed their party.The other significant aspect of CE2 is dices. Dices are rolled to determine success and failure of Events, and your available actions in Combat. Some may not like the idea that the game is heavily reliant on luck, since game of luck tends to be out of player's control. To circumvent this issue, there are many smaller mechanics and content that support building your own plan.Dices don't have numbers, but instead have skill icons painted red, green or blue on each side.Dices with the same color can be merged for maximum effect of a skill. So even if a dice seems to lack powerful skills, they can still be used for buffing other skills with the same color.You can choose which skills and colors you want to own by choosing certain characters and items. This encourages planning, and also forces you to choose whether you want to focus on a single color, or remain balanced for all colors.You can get more dices by expanding your party size and equipping items, You can upgrade your dices by spending resource to upgrade characters and items.There are also consumables that temporarily gives more dices.The developers thought a lot about implementing randomness into the game. They could have gone with generic XCOM percentages or traditional dices, but instead they tried a different approach to reinforce strategy, tactical and unique aspects of the gameplay. I would say that they succeeded in this regard as well.The art direction is also solid. Because not only it aligns with the game's goal and vision, it is unique enough to stand out from its competitors, and is also familiar to everyone. Everyone has read a fairy tale book full of illustrations before, but bringing those drawings into a game to bring back old memories is something not many developers have tried before. Violence is contained, so it is also easy to recommend this game to children and female gamers.Those three points are why I believe Curious Expedition 2 is worth your money. You feel you are a part of the expedition, dice mechanics can be mastered to support your plans, and the way this game is drawn is appealing and familiar at the same time I can definitely gift the game to my young cousin and my friends who love board games.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like a pot of sweet honey gameplay, completely ruined by the campaign mechanics. Its just one of the worst gamedesign I've ever encountered.The expedisions themselves are great: vivid, misterious, with a lot of sites to explore and fairly interesting balance - you can plunder, loot and hunt, but this will decreace natives affection. Eventually they start to hate you and the hunter will turn the hunted - endless hunting parties will spawn and drag you down, no matter how good you are. This mechanic is well-balanced so you wont struggle to keep the affection. However, affection decrease not only when you attack but when you are attacked as well - and this is odd, considering the fact that monsters track and chase you through out entire isle. Yet you can stop them with traps and drop off your tail without fighting so its not that big of a deal.BUT THE CAMPAIGN IS JUST HORRIBLE.Campaign mission consist of several expeditions (usually 3) - and those expeditions are as big and hard as the regular ones, sometimes even harder. But:1. You have no idea what biome you are going to land into. Only the 1st mission is known, the latter are unknown. You dont know what gear to bring or even what trek to build. 2. Provisions are provided only to the first mission. Yes, you have to stretch those medkits for 3 expeditions cause there are no good substitues to treat wounds in the wild. Same with food, same with torches, SAME WITH WATER cause who knows what comes next?3. Mission goals can do a 360*. Lets say, on 1st mission you need to find your fellow explorer and you assemble the exploring trek, bringing relevant provisions. Suddenly on 2nd mission your goal is to beat up a 350hp Guardian! You're just ill-equipped for that kind of goal. Some items might help but you didn't knew such a fight would emerge and even if you did this would come with a price of making 1st mission harder.4. Quest items. Obviously, campaign expeditions have a certain unique mission and a lot of them require some quest item. Thats okay for the 1st mission, but on the 3rd you might end with a ton of those items - and they reserve inventory slots! It is hard to keep all the companions alive by the 3rd exp, some will die, reducing those precious inventory to a bare minimum - and even that might get overburdened by the quest items.All those problems makes me wonder: why in the seven hells would I want to go campaign missions? They're extremely dangerous, provisions are heavily limited, my trek member WILL die. This sounds like a high risk - high reward formula, right?But no, the actual rewards are minimal because I cannot extract any treasures, my priority becomes just SURVIVING the encounter. Why would I want to embark on such a rogue-like quest that offers only losses?I tell you why. Because they're mandatory.

_childDocuments_.review: This won't be a very in-depth review I'm not the biggest fan of Roguelikes/lites. That said, I did enjoy Curious Expedition for its charm, originality and theme. I like things with a Lovecraftian or otherworldly vibe, with strange worlds and just plain weird ideas. Being set in "our world" but having a Velociraptor as a teammate and trying to find a golden pyramid in really strange lands? Very immersive and enjoyable for myself, I kind of get lost in the world and I enjoy myself, even if I kind of suck at these games.I'll be honest, when CE2 was first announced, I did jump to conclusions. I saw a picture or two and thought to myself; "here we go, the same game, with a new art design! I'm no fool!!". I also didn't really catch on to the art style, which is extremely ironic, considering what I will explain later.After watching a few early access videos from a couple Youtubers I enjoy watching; I was glad to see that there were changes in the game, some pretty decent ones too. I won't go over them very much, or discuss technical details. Many Youtube videos would do it justice way better than I could.I will, however, say that as soon as I tried the game for myself, I fell in love with the art style. It was ironic, because I'm a big fan of the Franco-Belgian comic book art style. Tintin, Asterix, Lucky Luke.. just to name the popular ones. I have a good collection of them.Honestly, the art design in CE2 is incredible and really goes to elevate the experience! I did not hate the pixel art, but it felt a little bit generic. The art design here just really brings me down to those comic books I was talking about. Detailed, crisp lines and incredible backdrops... wow, I am blown away!New art style, with new and revamped game mechanics really make this an easy game to recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: I gave Curious Expedition  a shot, a few years ago, and refunded it after 1.6 hours. It was very shallow, the economy was unbalanced, you had to rush everything, there was nothing to do with what you gained from your expeditions. In Curious Expedition , they fixed  that.  is what I expected from the first game, and I'm glad I gave it a shot, despite my previous experience with the franchise. This one is good.- There is combat. It's dice-based, and it's pretty cool. It works very well;- You can have a party of 5 characters, and even more, as you can temporarily get some that do not occupy a "party spot;"- You can equip two items on each party member, which may improve your navigation, preserve sanity, add extra combat dices, etc.;- You can ride a mount;- There is an actual campaign in place. In total, it is comprised of 20 expeditions, so one playthrough is  longer and more interesting, now;- Besides unlocking new starting parties when reaching certain milestones, now you can also unlock a bunch of new hireable characters, gear items and usable ones in ;- There are 3 such clubs: Avalon, Lux and Taishi. Whenever you go out on an expedition, you pick one of them to be your sponsor and, when you return, all the fame you earned will go towards increasing your reputation with the chosen sponsor, unlocking new stuff;- In clubs, you can also upgrade your items, cure ailments and train characters;- You characters level up. You do not get to choose , about them, to upgrade -- they just get a little more HP and better dices. But it's something;- After each expedition, based on how much fame you earned, you'll gain  that are used to purchase items, upgrades, etc. in town;- There are community events. If you join in, and do certain activities during your explorations, you get points and, after the event ends... well, I assume you get the reward shown, but I haven't actually seen how it goes yet, as they last for a few days and I have just finished my first campaign;- Competitors are . You no longer need to rush your expeditions -- you can actually  them, now;- Sanity felt a lot more manageable to me, compared to CE1. Only once did I verge on insanity. I was able to do 150+ days expeditions without inconveniences;- (That does not mean you can roam around forever; after a rather long while,  does start to push you forward. But there are items to manage that as well;)- There are more events than in CE1, more tribes, more types of islands, new terrain difficulties, etc.;CE2 is much,  better than the first. Exploring is now a pleasant and rewarding experience, rather than an annoying one with no payoffs. Congratulations to the developers for realizing and implementing exactly what the game needed, on this second installment. I don't remember seeing anyone else nailing this before, completely fixing and greatly improving a game to what it really should be, in one shot. one, I recommend. I'm guessing it costs around $15 in the US and EU, so I'd say CE2 is totally worth full price for people in those regions.P.S: the game is slightly . Any character may fall in love with any other, as if homosexuality was something as natural as heterosexuality. Love triangles may form, and no party involved is bothered in the slightest. There's an "asexual" tribal race whose members are adressed to as "Xir," "Hir" and other pronouns of the sort, which is ridiculous.Also, the developers censored a guy for complaining about the first issue I just mentioned in the forums. He asked for an option to have heterosexual couples only, or for the odds of these showing up to increase, to match reality, and they immediately locked his thread.So, the game  good, but you may not want to encourage this type of behavior with your money.

_childDocuments_.review: Curious Expedition Original was great fun, a little old school, a bit hardcore and definitely roguelike with total wipes due to little else than bad lack and unfortunate roles. Curious Expedition 2 retains some of that live or die approach... if you want it. This is due to difficulty levels, and I think this is great. The difficultly settings really let you choose how much of a punishment you are wanting to take. I took the easier approach to learn the game, experiment with the various companions and leaders and definitely checking out the DLC fantasy lands. They're fun. I moved to the normal difficulty, and oh boy, what a difference that makes. Poor decisions and gambles, hurt. The forced story elements are brutal but if you make logical decisions, have at least some luck, or just good supplies, you can probably make it. The mysteries, surprises, the joy of being lucky or just, you know, greedy combined with finding a great adventuring group really does relive the original experience with the added bonus of upgraded graphics and a steady approach. If I have one complaint, it's going to be those story adventures, the ones that can be difficult and multi stepped which means if you gorged on resources in leg one, two and three... oh boy. If this is your first go or your a fan of the original, give it a go. You can get an Island done in a relatively short period of time which also makes this game a I have some time, can I feel like I did something tonight. Yes! And rreplayability is good due to the leader and just some random events you don't always see. It's great fun!

_childDocuments_.review: After 13 hours i finally beat my first run of this game. When i was a kid i play the stuff out of the oregon trail and this game really hits a similar spot for me. Its an interesting little game in that all in all 13 hours is pretty short to complete a run, granted i was going a bit fast but if youre a min maxer or otherwise enjoy taking your time with decision making in games you could get a lot more hours in a single run. And i really like the fact that each time you play the maps are laid out differently each time including the main story ones so every time you do a run because of that and the way random events and other random stuff happens, you may be experiencing the same story but the runs themselves will all play out completely different. expecially when trying new main character classes.honestly if you like dice rolling and a bit of role play similar to dnd, if you like the oregon trail or the concept of that game, if you like the sound exploring islands with procedural generation and inventory management this is an easy pick up. especially on a sale. _childDocuments_.review: This one is unique. I just finished a campaign and a good bit of a director run.It feels like a hybrid of a simple adventure style game, with a randomizer feature and a dice battler.Note: You WILL lose people, you WILL NOT have a perfect run. ***Do not strive and reset over and over for a perfect run.*** Go for fun. Experiment. Pick things you might not want to, or even try to roleplay your character! Are you a big game hunter? Go ahead and skin some animals. Raider? Yeah, take that obviously cursed artifact. This game rewards risk vs reward decently well with a couple small exceptions.Pros:++Simple, easy to learn.++You can go combat or non-combat++Various ways to play the game with focusing on a bunch of features.+With some strategy, you can recover from a near party wipe (eg. with only your leader alive). I'm a bit torn if I really like this, I was going to put this as a bit of a downside, but I do like the fact you do NOT have to play perfectly or bring someone from the start of the game to the end to have a super powerful person.+An *interesting* sanity system. You will have both really funny and really horrifying events. Bring brain bleach. Some of these are just scary to mention.+With a DLC you can tame a T-REX, and from my experiences, almost every creature you encounter.Neutral~Some DLC items make the game a bit easy...? Sake and Field Kitchen mainly.~Characters feel somewhat disposable. You use someone for a while, and then ditch them when something better comes along. When you do it it feels just... I dunno some of the dismissals are kind-of sad. With the DLC you CAN freeze someone for later at the least.~5 person team limit: too many good options sometimes makes you have to make difficult decisions. This is probably the toughest part of the game, picking up another person or creature. You want to experiment with some new people or you find a creature hatches from an egg, etc. I know the reason why this is so: so that you don't just bring an army and just trounce all combats and dice events. But I would like the option to bring people back to the ship or... I dunno... just "something" to do with em instead of just "Get lost!". As I said above, the DLC has a cryo chamber to store one person, but it's in town, and when you find interesting things on a trek, and you want to mess around... it's a difficult choice. However this is not a con because I like the fact that if someone perishes or leaves while on the trip, you can reliably find a replacement on the trek.Also some creatures take up two slots of your team O_O;;;; ~Some items should be weightless for obvious reasons, but aren't due to gameplay reasons... I'm looking at you "earplugs"... just how heavy are these damn things? XD, likewise some items that seem heavy are weightless, like a bunch of skinned quails that you can cook.Cons-(Cosmetic) No renaming characters o_O;? Not even the starting character(s).-Some options feel a little harsh. Example: I have a sick person and I'm resting at the boat (which takes you to and from the island). I can't tell the crew to "keep my infected/sick person who is losing HP each day here while I finish the mission". Nope. I have to bring them along and force them to join in combat and more than likely get worse.-Islanders always are upset about the death of ANYTHING on their island. This one is just weird cause I understand if you kill one of their creatures, or if the natives are pacifists... but if you are on an island with warriors and they love battle and such and there's a band of evil skeleton pirates roaming around and you kill those pirates they get angry...? I know why this system is here but it feels awkward.-Director mode deficit that adds a junk character to your team is just... ugh to me.-Director mode does need a few new deficits. With the way it is, it feels like endless mode with a few tweaks. You CAN however, skip the deficits.

_childDocuments_.review: This game captures the goofy magic of CE1 and extends it to new, strange worlds. It is a fantastic sequel that extends the old game in exciting ways. Particularly of note are the new combat system (dice based but more dynamic choices), animated character/environmental scenes, and beautiful world map. The Expo does its job as a meta-world that you can slowly upgrade with each expedition and across expeditions. There are some beautiful scenery and moments tucked away in each of the worlds, encouraging you to explore widely for (sometimes literal) hidden gems. The temple disasters are improved and feel more balanced while still obscenely threatening. Little touches like the 'night before the expedition' and various social interaction scenes in the wild drive home the character relationships. Beautiful and well-made sequel!
