_childDocuments_.review: So, I came back to edit my review because something didn't sit quite right with me. Initially I loved this game, I liked the inventory system much more, I liked a lot of the new interesting events or character types, but once I hit a wall I began to realize the horrible truth. CE2 is just mediocre compared to CE1. Lets start of with the most noticeable change, the . Without a doubt, the cut-scenes seem to be much more vibrant and full of detail, but it seems like the character animation were ripped from an early 2000s flash game, and all the people no longer have any semblence of human, and look more like automatons. It's really upsetting because they genuinely could have made it much much better. Even the sprites and the worlds feel cheaper, with the map you walk around on somehow feeling less pretty and more like a mediocre voxel games procedural generation. Next, lets talk the . This point may not matter for everyone equally, but the differences in music and the quality of sounds between CE2 and CE1 is astonishingly sad, The first game has a wide variety of unique and cool sounding music reels, sounds, event and noises that make the game really pop, making the entire expedition feel unique, with biomes even having their own dynamic soundtracks for events and such. CE2 has an awful soundtrack. The music is mediocre and forgettable, the character sounds and voices are actually so badly done, that the Skeletons just use the default female sound, and most characters don't have any unique sounds at all, rendering the idea that characters have voice or noises useless. The biome soundtracks are bad, far worse than the previous game and completely forgettable. This whole game screams forgettable compared to the first one. Now, Combat. One of the things I actually do like about this game is the revamped inventory and item system, allowing characters to equip a weapon and 2 supporting items is a genuine improvement, however it comes in contrast to a very slow and boring combat system that is basically the first games system but dumbed down. The dice rolls and combinations feel cumbersome and the combat feels mundane. All the damage and health numbers have gone up tenfold, and so most items and their damages feel much less "punchy" where getting a 12 damage hit in the first game was extremely good and very rare, in this game its a mediocre shot. Really sad to see that because I wanted it to be much cooler.And finally, the game itself. This game actually somehow has less variation seemingly than the first one, sure the 2 DLC world types balance it out but overall this game feels extremely cheap. In Curious Expedition 1, Dinosaurs were seen in extremely late game worlds, or rarely through other events, and so getting one was difficult and uncommon, and rewarding as well. Special niche characters or weird natives were very uncommon, and so their interactions felt cool, and interesting. Also, for some reason this game outright removed the Arctic biome, which is just dumb. The highlands are cool I guess but for a game about dangerous expeditions, removing one of the coolest places to do that is just stupid. Not to mention character dynamics are also worse and just silly now. Are you really going to try to tell me my Catholic Priest fell in love with a native warrior and had a gay relationship in the middle of the 1880s, or that my main character and a lizard monster who goes by (Xe/Xer) and yes that is real they use neo pronouns in this game unironically, fall in love out of nowhere and offer almost nothing to the game or dynamic itself? This game feels soulless. I was willing to entertain the idea of making a no-name into a reputable hero, but the game doesn't care enough anyways because Marin, the games poster-girl explorer, who is a massive, egotistical narcissict who causes the main problems of the game, is for some reason the best and most well loved character no matter what, and so you basically play the entire game as a side character with no real value or end goal, unlike the original which had you questing as a real world person in a vivid fictional world to rise to heights unseen before.TLDR; Music is worse, graphics are mediocre, characters are far worse, and the gameplay is boring.Buy Curious Expedition 1 for the actual full experience for what this game is trying to mimic and fails doing so.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Curious Expedition 2 suffers from some of the same frustrations that plague all games with any level of procedural generation, but, overall, it is a fun romp filled with adventure and mystery. The structured story missions that frame the side quests provide a much-welcomed story to the game, and the myriad of characters, items, and gameplay options kept each mission fresh. Much like the mysterious islands you will explore and conquer, Curious Expedition 2 is worth checking out ;-)
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with loads of replayability. The rough formula for the first game is back with slight differences but Curious Expedition 2 improves it in many ways. CE2 has QOL features, more events, villagers, maps, equipment and items.Main additions the devs should add are probably more tooltips, adventurers and a setting for faster combat. Tooltips because sometimes you have no idea what the mechanics are without going to the wiki since there are a ton of stat modifiers in the game. Also, the first game had insane replayability partly because of the sheer number of "secret adventurers" which have widely different playstyles. This game has only 8 leader classes so Im hoping they have a dlc which adds more or even a leader customisation function so you can design different leaders.But overall its a very good game and a rougelite hidden gem.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent sequel. Don't pass it up if you were a fan of the first game. :) Updated graphics, (though I can understand the love for the original game's 8bit artwork) a new story line, new characters and items, lots of fun new content! I really loved the first game and was kinda hesitant to purchase CE2, I think the price was what got to me. But I'm so glad I finally picked it up. Love the whole overarching story in the campaign and the clubs were also a cool addition.  The game also feels really balanced. Just the right amount of good and bad dice rolls to keep me engaged, but also not cursing the rng gods every other roll. Sure, I guess you could say it's just a cleaner, slightly improved repackaging of the first game? But idk. I really love it and think it has a ton to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I've always loved Adventure, since I was a small kid pretending to be Indiana Jones. This game has  everything want in an adventure story. Explorers,dinosaurs,lost cities, and treasures! The setting of the game reminds me of a Jules Verne novel, oddly enough he's in this. The lore is very lovecraftian in nature which makes me want to keep exploring while knowing this may end very badly, but the mystery of the unknown is what keeps me going. And now I hear that there is a DLC that takes place in Avalon! If they make a Norse ice level DLC then this is game goes from 100 to 1000.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't really expecting much when i got this game, it looked interesting and it was on sale so i decided to try it and honestly it's really fun, the visuals are pretty unique and there's enough diversity to not make the islands boring and i definitely recommend if you like this kinda game. The only issues i have is the tribes feel pretty repetitive even if they look different and it would be really cool if you could steal treasures after an expedition. Other than that though pretty solid 7/10
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Aah, man. I am as frustrated for this game as I was by this game. Curious Expedition 2 just went on that bit too long for me, and pushed my gaming experience from excitement to tedium. Such a shame, because if I had reviewed this at 10 hours then it would read very differently. That said, I did still stick with it to the end, and my overall gaming experience was positive. I haven't played the first installment, so there's no comparison here. I believe some reviews slate reduced content by comparison. For my part I was initially very impressed with the procedural maps, the islanders to meet, the points of interest to visit, and the encounters in the wild, but there weren't enough of them to take me from the start of the campaign to the end without the repeats getting dull. The graphics worked for me (except for when characters spin their arms around their elbow joint like Jack the f'n Pumpkin King) and I found the bright colours and cartoony style very visually pleasing. Combat uses a dice system to determine whether or not you can use one or both of your characters abilities. I thought this was a pretty cool idea, and I had fun with it. It was especially nice when playing a build that wasn't combat focused, so that you actually look forward to getting surprise attacked by a bunch of angry mole-men. On levels with lots of forced encounters the combat did swiftly become a chore though, and the added threat of losing a character if they finish the battle with so much as a scratch did not contribute to my joy joy feelings.The item and character unlocks are a big perk here, and I enjoyed recruiting randos into my party, including the indigenous locals. The only problem is that, as this is a procedurally generated game, you occasionally just get dealt a bad map and party wipe. That's not really a negative in itself, seeing as that's kind of the nature of exploring, but what I did find was that I was very fond of my first two parties, and I honestly can't even remember who or what I ended up actually winning with.  It's starting to sound a lot like I didn't enjoy the game, which is not the case. It's just that at one stage I really was looking forward to getting home for work so I could play it for a couple of hours, and it's a pity to see that excitement wither. I will still remember this one fondly though, and I think there is a lot of fun to be had for anyone who likes turn based RPGs and exploration games.NB - Playtime is inaccurate as I was busy watching Knightfall (recommend) whilst playing the latter half of this. I would imagine the campaign is around 15 hours long.Hi there! If you like my review, please feel free to check out our curator page! For more full reviews, you can check out my personal page:
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended over 100 %To be entirely honest, this game is hard, but very rewarding.the difficulty of the basic 'easy' mode is already  challenging, the higher difficulty modes are suicide ( for now i guess ).Yet this game has a lot to offer, and finishing a complete expedition is very satisfying. **Every wrong move can lead to complete anihilation of your crew and efforts, so beware every step along the way, as there is no save in the campain mode. fun word, campain : set your CAMP in the bush, and have some PAIN coming out of there alive Let the safari begin! unleash the wrath of good ol' colonialism, or just visit new worlds, fun time guaranteed;
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game forces decisions onto you quite badly. Like the fact that my character ate the raptor they had raised from an egg and had kept for many adventures. I can only applaud the originality and creative writing the team put into that game, it's truly inspiring. I just wished it was less needlessly punishing.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: At first I was turned off by the change in graphics from the first game, but I took the plunge anyway and absolutely fell in love with this game. It's a perfect sequel and the constant updates is wonderful. This is how more games should be, fully finished by release with added content and constant dev support post release. Too many games these days are unfinished and abandoned. Compared to the first game, I feel like the varying level of difficulties are balanced and appropriate. I have successfully completed the game many times, it can be a challange, but not impossible. I hope they add in some winter tundra areas in a future update.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: A lot like the original, but different enough to keep me entertained. If you enjoyed the first game, you'll likely enjoy this one. The graphics are a little better, if you like the cartoon-y style. The game play is all that really matters to me, and it is just as good (maybe even better) than the first game. If you haven't played the first one, pick up a copy and play it. If you enjoy it, grab this one, too. Or, do whatever you want. I'm not your mom.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: A great game with IMMENSE replay value, you don't get 2 of the same adventures, and even if you get close to it, small elements will change your experience from one playthrough to the next. There is humour, some more serious moments, and it takes a strategic mind to win combat sometimes. The devs are also very reactive and most problems you can encounter (if you do encounter them) are fixed within several weeks, great job !
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Huge improvement over the original! New graphics are much more pleasing and this is a better rogue-like now that promotes multiple runs and expeditions .. just one more -feeling is very strong in this one. The repetition is not an issue as you change the explorer type and approach the situations fresh: sometimes you want to explore the map, sometimes you befriend the locals, other times you loot everything or kill everything etc.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I am absolutely delighted by this game, it has a unique mood full of adventure, a stunning soundtrack and is just an all-around fun experience. I'm had grown rather fond of the pixel art style of the first one, but after playing this I realise that the art style they went with (likely inspired by comics like Tin-Tin that deal with similar subject matter) fits perfectly. If I were to nitpick for flaws I can present 3 minor issues: 1. finishing a campaign deletes your save and leaves no trace of its existance, one could argue for a new game plus or endless mode but I think a simple hall of fame would be the most elegant solution for a game that is tied to your fame/accomplishments/legacy as explorers. 2. The curse mechanic is downright cruel, and although I'm fine with that, i don't think it is as fun as it could be ( a text that reads something along the lines of: oh btw your favorite character is dead, run over by a horse, accidents happen) Some warning signs between missions or having it play out in a more spectacular manner would likely remedy this, as it stands encountering it is not particularly fun or mysterious, but rather anticlimactic.3. I experienced some issues with the combat animations, defeated/downed opponents will often return to their idle/alive animation state when they are not supposed to. This is slightly emersion breaking,  a very minor bug.other then that, 1.Brilliant.2.A labor of love.3.I definitely recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the first game, you're sure to enjoy this one too. It takes everything great from the first game and adds on top. The new combat system is much more expanded with things like status effects and weapons for each party member. There's a story campaign now too that I didn't expect but loved it all the same, it makes the expeditions have more meaning than the first game, where fame was the only goal. I've only played through one campaign but I can't wait to get plenty more under my belt! Happy exploring!
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game has adventure elements like exploration, mission stance, supply, and trade; and mixes this with decision factors that are all about survival.  It's like Pathway and Darkest Dungeon, but I personally prefer C.E. 2 of the three brands.  The events of the first act take place in the late 19th century, so that makes it a VIctorian Age questing, adventure and looting strategy game.  Lick the frog and maintain your sanity!
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the first and blindly went into this sequel without much research. My logic was that even a simple expansion on the Curious Expedition 1 would likely keep my attention long enough to justify the ~20€ price tag. I probably would have been satisfied with an incremental step.This game delivers far more than what I was hoping for, and being really addicted to playing for the first week of purchasing was truly a surprise. It's great fun.My only complaint is that the gameplay is feeling a bit linear on my second run-through. A mode separated from Malin's storyline would be welcomed, or better yet other "campaign" like stories could freshen things up.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: What if someone made a boardgame based around combining colonial adventure comics, roguelikes and JRPGs? You'd get this, and it's pretty great. The game is centered around performing expeditions with a party. It starts off with preparation: securing funding, provisions, and supplies. Next, you it's off to a randomly generated map, populated by indigenous tribes as well as flora and fauna of varying hostility, in search of a randomly generated objective. Throughout all this, random events will grant your party boons or present them with obstacles. Every few successful expeditions, a story mission will become available which plays identically to normal expeditions but progresses the story surrounding specific recurring characters. The whole thing works really well, and there's a steady reveal of new elements or situations that keeps it from getting repetitive. Works really well as a game to play while listening to something else. The UI isn't the most straightforward and takes a bit of getting used to, and some of the mechanics aren't entirely clear, but nothing insurmountable. If you think it looks interesting, there's a good chance you'll enjoy it.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very good game. I am playing it in early access and it became way better with time, the released game should be even better.For those who never played CE1, you play as an explorer, manage your trek with different kinds of companions, manage your gear (lots of fun objects to try and combine), explore mysterious lands, pick up treasures, fight monsters and win fame!For those who did play CE1, the biggest narrative difference is that there is actually a scenario: every 3 or 4 expeditions is part of a scenario. The graphics are quite different, as you can see, but it grows on you :)There are a few tweaks to combat mechanics, many new characters, monsters and items, so it's a new discovery every time!The game is about 12-15h long to complete it a first time, if you're not used to it, I'd say.I highly recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: LOVE, LOVE, LOVE this game!! It still has a few bugs, but it is in alpha still. I loved the first one, and can't wait for this to be fully finished. The new game mechanic's are nice, but not so different from the last game, which i really enjoy. The art is awesome, fun, and interactive. The new clubs are a great addition too.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Hardcore rules, procedurally generated content, a pet parrot and a pet turtle, a cook that always seems to fall madly in love with me, for seriously you guys this game is a good time for as long or as short of a time as you want to give it. I never knew how much I wanted a game to take away my ability to load until I had to actually think about all my decisions.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: So far my first play through, when I had no idea what I was doing for the first few missions, was my best play though. I survived several years and then got overconfident and lost everyone in the howling wilderness. This is a fun game, already more enjoyable than their first version. I love pulp adventures and this is probably my favorite to date. Yeah, it's a bit gamey and silly and sci-fi, but it's still fun. I'd love it if the devs' next project was maybe more serious and more realistic... like maybe race the Nazis to various treasures or something. Too Indiana Jones, maybe...?
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: With all due respect, i cannot figure out, for alpha 11 preview being available, why are the developer so fascinated with changing the degree of difficulty and rejected to design a customizable difficulty system. What the CE series truly attract us players, in my opinion, is that a sense of triumph of collecting a variety of treasures rather than being stuck in frustration helplessly

_childDocuments_.review: Even in its current alpha state I'm enjoying this almost as much as the first. _childDocuments_.review: My ship disappeared！I am in the task of looking for orchids. After I found Orchid, I needed to go back to my boat.But then I remembered that my ship was not displayed when the mission first started.I think the ship disappeared when the mission first started, but I didn’t think it was a big problem at the time.When I return to the position of my ship, I can still see the background of the character on the ship while resting，but I can’t do anything.In the end I can only be swallowed by the purple fog in despair.I tried to submit bugs many times, but all failed.This serious bug really affects my gaming experience. My few hours of hard work were all in vain.I hope the production team can fix this bug as soon as possible and give feedback.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like playing as a settler in a civ game. Only that you get to experience what they would, if they encounter an unknown civilization. I enjoy uncovering the fog of war to reveal the next encounter while I fear if my supplies and my sanity will suffice, hoping for a campsite.I found out about myself that I would steal every damn relic I see, not because of greed, but because I want to see what the consequences are. And boy, are there consequences!And then there is the dice rolling mechanic, used for combat and risky actions. As the colors stand for different traits, and characters have different strengths, while lacking certain traits, it is a really elegant mechanic that makes for meaningful choices. Don't fight wolves with humanistic anthropologists. Wolves don't negotiate! I do feel though, that the core gameplay is kinda tough, as I seem to always have insufficient supplies. But as astroneer taught me, that I would be a s**t astronaut in a fun way. This game showed me that I would be a terrible explorer in a fun way.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I love the new illustrations and color palettes! Overall, it feels more detailed and with more content than the first game, with a bigger and more complex story, several expedition objectives, a diversity of crew members you can pick from, working with expedition sponsors...Can't wait to play more soon!
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Curious Expedition 1 is a great "one more turn..." game like Civilization. The mechanics are easy to learn after a few failures, with some hidden features and RNG that keeps multiple playthroughs unique. The introduction of modding support refreshed the game further, with modders allowing you to fine tune for an easier, harder, or wackier experience.CE2 is still in early access, so reviews are premature. But this developer has already released one fantastic game, and CE2 is shaping up to be an iterative, if not evolutionary, game.HOWEVER, I would only recommend jumping into the Early Access if you love CE1 and trust the devs to deliver a fantastic sequel; the alpha access is lacking many features. Fun, but obviously a demonstration of ideas - not a product for people new to the series and looking for a complete experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of CE1, and I was on the fence about CE2, but I'm glad I gave it a shot. It's still in Early Access, and despite the bugs (I luckily haven't encountered too many game breaking ones yet), it's still really fun, although very different from CE1. Developers are very communicative and are actively working on fixing problems, which is really good to see. I'm very optimistic about the future of this game :>I think the biggest problem I have with the game so far, is the lag (even with the lowest settings), as it also affects my entire computer.(Also, go Taishi!)
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: A very encouraging start! I enjoyed the first Curious Expedition, but didn't play all that much because of the punishing difficulty curve - some might want that from a roguelike but for me I was so focused on trying and failing to just keep my party alive the actual objective of the expedition came a distant second in priority, and the exploration and discovery aspect was more of a wishful dream. Now the more generous allowance of how far you can travel with the sanity available means I've actually got realistic choices to make, and the progression of the party members makes it feel deeper.The art style is growing on me: I was a fan of the pixel art of CE1 but the maps give you more information and with some polish the character models will be good replacements. I hope it can stay more reminiscent of the Tintin books that the Steam banner picture evokes. Still a bit rough, but the clubs, the Paris Expo setting and the bar hint at a more fleshed out experience to come.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Played on the Discord Beta and then since Early Access launch, and still loving it : Huge replayability, beautiful Ligne Claire/Tintin & Herge style, lots of great improvements since CE1.And the devs, already from the first opus on, seems to always be very active on the game, its community, and launch & post launch support.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'm having a great time with this game! It's a really cool exploration & story-generating machine with good procedural world generation, interesting risk/reward decisions and beautiful visuals. I also like the meta-game of getting tickets for successful missions and building and retaining a crew over time. This creates high stakes for every expedition.The turn-to-turn gameplay is all about assessing risks, planning ahead, and learning the rules of the world and the game.As clearly stated in the game's description there are some early-access typical bugs, but they didn't hinder my enjoyment of the game in any way.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I was so hyped to get the chance to play this game on Early Access and it hasn't disappointed me!The difference in the art style from the first game gives it a refreshing new feel, while still retaining the delightful premise from the first game. It feels familiar but new at the same time. I love that when you travel across the map you now get the little doll-like representation of your characters plodding along. I don't think I'll ever get bored of it! So cute!They've also expanded the kinds of expedition you do now. Rather than just always going for a Golden Pyramid, you get a choice of a few quests and it displays the difficulty. I like having the choice, and I'm (slowly) learning that different strategies are needed for each one which makes for different gameplay each go round! There are also a wider range of interactions while on expeditions which I like.Everything is so much more detailed: you can clearly see the stats of your companions, your standing with the natives, the next attack move from enemies-it's just a lot of nice touches and improvements from the first game.I've seen a couple of reviews critiquing the combat, but I've honestly had no problems with it. It feels more like a turn-based RPG style, with the added difficulty of having to get a good roll of the dice. Honestly, in this style it feels like it would be a great board game (developers *wink* *wink*) and it's enjoyable to play. It's different to the original, yes, but it's a new game! I'm glad they tried something different with it, and it works nicely.I will admit that the different sponsors/factions confused me a little when I started playing, since there isn't much/any explanation as to what they do. I would maybe recommend there be some kind of text at the beginning to explain what they do, but since the game is still in early access I can understand this not being the case yet.For a sequel to Curious Expedition, I'm thrilled to bits with it. For an early access game, it's really impressed me. Yes, I've experienced a few bugs (one which killed my party sadly) but the bulk of the content is there and it's really fun to play! The developers are obviously super passionate about this project and are also really nice to boot, which is the perfect combination to make a game as charming as this.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Have only just embarked on my expedition, but loved the original and there's a lot of that same excitement and potential lying just beyond the map. We hadn't played story mode before, but it's intriguing and promising so far. I've noticed combat is a bit simplified without losing complexity and interactions with characters on the field and between your party is more nuanced. I loved the original's pixel art characters but in Curious Expedition 2, characters and backgrounds are fully inked in a sort of Herge (Tintin) ligne claire style which I absolutely love. Can't wait to explore more.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely game made by a bunch of lovely people <3 I really like the new art style , the whole setting now reminds me of the Tintin comic books. The interaction with the indigenous people are much more nuanced, and all your travel companions have much more character also the turn based combat was refreshed and is now a more tactical and just feels better.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Love the game, the series, and the dev support! Can't wait to see where this goes. The new style of missions is great for me. I like not having to compete against npc's. Having different objectives suited to your explorer type is really fun. Only con right now is that sometimes the animations and dialogue seem slow.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I like:-The graphical style, it's charming even if some animations (like dancing) look a bit awkward.-The soundtrack and ambient sound effects are great.-It's relatively faithful to the original game and the expanded mechanics between expeditions are a definite improvement in my opinion.I dislike:-The removal of combat dice combos from the first game, they were such a fun mechanic. As it is now the dice dont interact with eachother and the effects of some can merely be boosted. I dont understand how that's supposed to be an improvement over the original, combat seems underdeveloped and simplistic without them.-The game can be somewhat buggy at the moment.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the introduction bit! I'm not a fan of roguelites at all, but this was really fun so far and I wanna play more :DI was afraid the writing would be too long, but they kept it quite short and I actually read through everything, when I expected to skip through most of the dialogue.Haven't encountered any bugs either. I really don't understand some of the complaints... Someone was saying the inventory takes too long to open?? Really? It literally opens instantly? But then I haven't played the first Curious Expedition, so who knows on what insanely amazing inventory UI I'm missing out on.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Isn't it awsome when the new game is out 30 Minutes and there are already two negative Reviews by people who haven't played the (closed) alpha nor reached the depth of the early access game? No?Okay. Seriously. Here is some detailed review. I try not to spoil so you will see for yourself. Because I think this is/will be a great replayable game for a fair price. # ContextI've played the alpha for three months now. It takes the main aspects of curious expedition (one) and adds a lot new things.And I love it, for it is not too much "more of the same". Because of the generous modding capabilities of "One" there was no way to have a version 1.5. that would justify to pay again.# Gameplay (so far)Storytelling in "rogue"-likes is not easy. If you keep it to the bare minimum (and with that I think of moria or rogue with ascii output), then "its all in your head". Which is great till you want to see more, then it becomes complex like "does a dragon have the same amount of space (1x1 char) compared to an imp?", what color does a ray from a wand, ... but I digress.First: CE2 has a new storytelling mechanism - and different missions so you are not stuck finding the pyramid again and again and gain. This the right amount of innovation, because it adds some kind of freedom and also some complexity. But not too  much so you end up civilization like micromanaging everything.Second: The design makes things different. And that is for the bette without outdating the first versionr: This is more physical, more goofy and to some extent displayed different that you might feel alienated/frustrated. Example: The dices. I find them too detailed and hard to read. And for some reasons, the reactions to a dice feel random when the dice are rolled (and I knew the chances) so I wish (Hello developers!) CE2 had a "I don't want to know" mode that except for battles you would not see the dice and just been told the results. (Rationale: If I can't change the outcome, I'll do it anyway.)If you are a lifelong reader of tintins adventures (and still like it sans the contextual racism and views based on it's creation time and societal mood) this feels like new adventures of that very era with characters that are interesting, diverse and well drawn. So I am all in on the style.Third: One needs to adapt. With CE Rivals I learned a new playstile because I was stuck in a routine from one (and how to beat it on "easy" ... well, try to beat it) - and that was great because the competition showed my ways that I had not considered. Its the same here: There are a lot of similarities, but if you keep your style, you will miss a lot and might not even get to "win". I'll write more when the game gets there. So far I like it and it feels like money well spent.
_childDocuments_.name: Curious Expedition 2

_childDocuments_.review: Curious Expedition 2 is the follow-up to the award-winning 19th century expedition simulation. Join the legendary Explorer Clubs and venture on unprecedented expeditions to regions never explored before for fame, science and treasures.

name: Dreamscaper
detailed_description: DREAM. DIE. WAKE. REPEAT. Dreamscaper is an endlessly replayable Action Roguelike with a waking/dreaming gameplay cycle. By night, delve deep into your subconscious, facing nightmares in an ever-changing world filled with unique items, abilities, and challenges. By day, explore the city of Redhaven, build relationships and unlock permanent upgrades in order to take on the next dream stronger than ever. Features Lean into the nightmares and make the rush of permadeath your ally. Use lucid powers to manipulate the elements, warp space, and even control time itself. _childDocuments_.review: This game feels like the halfway point between Hades and The Binding of Isaac. The game is tight with enough item variation to keep it fresh (not to mention some decent combat). However, the waking world gameplay could've been fleshed out a bit more; as it stands it feels like running through a checklist of talking to folks and picking up items before diving back into the dreamworld. Maybe if it went into more depth a la Persona it would feel more gratifying to connect with people in game.Regardless, I'm enjoying it. A solid game to play while catching up on podcasts.

The story is great and I personally love the combat of the game, with some of the weapons being absolutely AMAZING to look at while fighting. The animations are amazing and by playing you can definitely see just how much work and *love* went into this game. _childDocuments_.review: Bought this game due to the Hades comparisons, but wouldn't say that 'if you liked Hades, you'll like Dreamscaper'; it's best to consider it on its own merit. It's an introspective game with not much to go in the way of narrative, but I enjoyed it greatly.General:- Very beautiful level designs and OST- Huge variety of weapons/skills with entertaining descriptions- Poignant settingsThings I enjoyed but might not have universal appeal:- Puzzle rooms- Characters were unvoiced/had no faces- Revisiting memories in dreams and chatting to others in the waking world- RNG in build across runs- Difficulty spikes in mob rooms between levels after the first twoThings I was mixed on at the start but grew on me, given the game's context of Cassidy fighting her nightmares:- Combat is slower than Hades. However, abilities/dodge/ranged/melee all play a healthy mix in a good run. I chose to ignore parrying in favour of a shield that allows you to take a free hit every 15 seconds.- Animation lock for some ability casts- Increasingly claustrophobic rooms with many traps- (at least for the first few times you hit a new level, past the first two) the challenge was in fighting through mob rooms to get to the boss alive; the mechanics on the boss fights themselves are beatable blindMinor things that caused some frustration:- Targeting can be a bit wonky- Have (very rarely) gotten trapped dodging into an out-of-bounds area in Level 3 (effectively run-ending)- It's a bit difficult to see in mob rooms in Level 4Overall, a beautiful rogue-like with largely solid combat and unique setting - would recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: i played 8 hours of this game the first day I received it. Was able to get through three of the bosses and unlocked about half of the gifts to give to the NPCs. Pretty fun game, definitely worth a play if you are into roguelikes. The Combat isn't super complex but once you get the dodging and parrying down, it goes a long way to making combat interesting.There are quit a few weapons already in the game with variations effects that they can trigger. You will definitely find that you enjoy certain weapon fighting styles over others and I greatly enjoyed having to master weapons through use/killing enemies.On controller the ranged attack is a bit annoying to aim at some times but overall not bad and the abilities you can find really changes things with mixing in all the pieces into each combat. I did find I got animation locked while using the abilities, but you can account for this once learn the different enemies' fighting styles.Overall a good Roguelike and really enjoyed the interplay of emotions and interpersonal skill building with the NPCs.

_childDocuments_.review: This game. GOTY contender right here. If Hades can have their GOTY nominations, Dreamscaper is very, very worthy of the same noms.This game is a roguelike-topdown-soulslike action game, and yeah there are a lot of the same games in the market already. Dreamscaper did not do anything that so groundbreaking or visionary, but they did a lot of things uniquely and charming.We have the combat system that felt really smooth and really weighed in on each and every move you make. The combat system is simple: a basic melee attack, a basic ranged attack, 2 special skills in the form of Lucid skills, a dodge attack and a parry mechanism. An "ultimate" which is to stop time to make your character pretty much invincible in a short time. Simple, right? Well, the game gave you a lot of freedom in customization, you can pre-set a build that you so choose in order to complete a certain run of your choice. Also, this feels really much like Persona in the sense that you can buff your character and combat experience by interacting with other inhabitants in the town, give them gifts, socialize with them and hear their story. In turn those will be your "inspiration" that you brought into your own Dream - the main levels of this game, the entire gameplay was just the dream of your character.Which to me, seems to be a very good way to tell a story about someone who is insecure and is pretty much a stranger in a big city, to slowly open up her heart and interacting with people, hear their stories, then brought those desires and hopes into her own creation. We can witness the character growth in real time, with us as the main driving force - each and every one of the playthroughs are unique. You can build Dual kunais with flame trail dodge and run blades rain on Lucid, or run freezing skills in synergy with parry skills to go for a tanky approach, The gameplay is hand-in-hand with the character story, and i think that's the beauty of this game.I haven't played through enough of this game to have a full & complete opinion on Dreamscaper, but based solely on what i saw so far, this game is a must buy. A charming, small yet fullfilling experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: As advertised, in Dreamscaper you caper through dreams. They're rather uninteresting dreams; they're more like memories. They're still uninteresting as memories. She's helped along by her friends -- they're profoundly uninteresting friends. Even despite this, Dreamscaper isn't ashamed to ask you to care about its characters' vapid babble more than you care for your actual real-life friends; and to traverse hundreds of rooms when just a dozen shows you all the depth the game can muster; and to read fifty-two 'memories' about nothing more than eating burgers and driving around.In other words, Dreamscaper is using the grammar of the rogue-lite to make you  like you care about progressing deeper through your dreams and relationships, because of how much time you spend reaching the end. Except, it's a lie: the substance of both 'progressions' is better suited to an action-platformer-esque game of, let's say, only four or five hours' length. (That would have probably better suited the small dev-team, too.) I'm quite close to finishing the game, but I was done with it a long time ago, my interest kept on life-support by those gimmicks common to the rogue-lite genre. At this point, all I accomplish from finishing Dreamscaper is to insult those games which were worth every minute spent within, and yet I've played for an equal or lesser number of hours than this one.Capering through the commonplace concerns, collections, and recollections of an unexceptional lady and her really very boring friends, you can't help but remember that there's another rogue-lite that plays better than this where you're fighting out of an Ancient Greek underworld built from beautiful hand-drawn environments. It might not be on sale as often, or for as cheap, as Dreamscaper -- but sometimes money does actually signify value.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: A  "Hades-like", although  significantly more boring.  If you haven't played Hades (y tho?), skip Dreamscaper until you have.The ludonarrative integration of the rougelite loop is very well done and on par with Hades (if not better). I quite enjoyed the setting: during the night you're battling deeper through your dreams and subconscious, confronting your traumata and childhood memories - where all the progress resets once you die/wake up. At day, you strengthen your relationship with former strangers, meditate, daydream - all to build up resilience permanently (aka stat upgrades, new items etc.) to make the next night more fruitful.The story is relatable, and all the characters are very well fleshed out, and I enjoyed learning more about all seven (+ the main character). The writing is also good, as is the art style, and all that's missing is some quality voice acting to make the whole game perfect storywise.My major grievance is the combat: although basic and versatile (two base attacks, two spells, one ulti, dodge, parry), it's not as crispy as Hades. Many weapons and spells, but all feel very samey, and it get's boring quite fast. Due to perspective and flashyness (esp. the more upgrades you have) the screen becomes stuffed quite fast, making it impossible to see what's going on at all. The ratio between enemies/damage and available healing gets very imbalanced in the second half, and even with a good build you die fast.Most (day-)upgrades are miniscule and only incremental percentages, making out of run progression boringly slow.Nonetheless, worth to try out for yourself, especially on sale.Bonus points for how you level up your friendships: by learning more about the character of the seven NPCs (be it through inbetween the lines during dialogue or the game just straightforwardly telling ypu), you try to choose handmade gifts out of an everexpanding list, trying to figure out which type of gift would excite which NPC the most (and therefore netting more "friendshipXP")
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Edit 3: Devs haven't addressed the issues. After playing through it more and more, I can't recommend it. The story really lost me, and the combat is way too clunky and slow.Edit 2: Dev reached out to me about my issues and genuinely took them into account and made me feel like the considerations might make it into future patches. He also edited my save file to remove my grievance in the immediate so I could keep playing.I want to like the game, but it asks you to waste too much time. It's guilty of a plague on this genre where you have to grind and grind and grind to get anywhere. Huge chunks of map generation are hidden behind 'upgrades'. The core game is fun for 10-15 hours, and would be an amazing 10-15 hour experience. The problem is that the grinding makes it a 50+ hour slog. The 'progression' is just far too slow to be enjoyable for longer than a few hours.Edit: The most direct thing I can mention is that the map doesn't fully generate until at least 10 hours of XP grinding (and only if you can do well without those upgrades) just to allow the maps to generate all the way. It's such a clear and blatant waste of the player's time.

_childDocuments_.review: Great mechanics, great graphics, great gameplay, great controls, but only an ok story. Plus the amount of damage you take from enemies only 1 level apart can get a bit stupid sometimes. You'll be holding your own just fine, getting good gear/weapons/powers, having fun kicking ass, beat the boss with a bit of a challenge but got through it ok, then you descend to the next level and all of a sudden you have single enemies hitting you for huge chunks of HP. Or you enter a "room" with like 4 enemies and 3 turrets and ♥♥♥♥ is just flying all around you and your dodge can only work against 1 thing at a time and you kinda slow down when you dodge(some graphic bullet speed thing) so the next hit or couple hits automatically land b/c there was no way of getting out of it. Or your dodge is a long dash across the ground and you either get pinned into a corner or behind an obstacle or dash into a trap or environmental hazard. So, the game is fun, but you'll get into a few sticky situations that are clearly unbalanced then walk into the next room and it's just one guy that you take out like nothing. It's stuff like that that just makes me tilt my head and go WTF? There's not much consistency there.My biggest complain, though, is the story. O...M...G is this girl a pathetic SJW mess. I've known depressed/suicidal people(been one myself) and never knew anybody that was like constantly self berating and "Oh woe is me" ALL THE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ TIME. I get it, there was a big tragedy and she feels bad and moved to have a new beginning. I really get it. But ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with all the 1 note characters and NEVER hear anybody referred to as He/Him/Her/She ever unless she's talking about her mom or sister. This game is set in like if hipsters were to create their wet dream of a city. Cafe's, vinyl record store, hole in the wall coffee shop that's obviously not as "corporate" as Starshmuck's, beaten down book store with a few couches, etc filled with stereotypical hipster denizens like a dude wearing loafers with calf high polka dot socks in shorts with a long sleeve shirt/sweater tucked in the shorts with glasses and some fedora looking ♥♥♥♥(I'm a big nerd and technically a millennial b/c of my birth year but ♥♥♥♥ those pretentious hipsters). And there's a few more, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, man really? Fortunately, though, those interactions only last short times so it's not a big deal, just a great annoyance. The dialogue is a bit clunky too. And not really believable to me. Everybody she/you talk to are so 1 note characters. Almost as if the whole "new" city and people you meet are really all in her mind or aspects of herself (since getting to know them increases your skills, damage, and resistances) and the fighting you do in the "dreamscape" is just a deeper level of psychosis. I have no idea how far I am through the game since it's a roguelite so I can't say if that's a spoiler or not b/c I've only gotten so far story wise even though I've made it all the way through the dreamscape and just repeat the levels again and again. Also, either there are a crap ton of people I have yet to meet b/c the gift/craft list has placeholders of those who'd enjoy receiving them and I've discovered a bunch of recipes for stuff but with quite a few of those placeholders still empty, while the ones that do have icons for the people I know are only 2 or 3 of them. Out of like 65 I think. How long til I meet more people?! Only upsetting b/c you only meet people/places after you've been through the dreamscape either by winning or dying so it's a slog through levels to go back into the city, have a handful of interactions that don't move things along a lot, then you have to go back through playing the levels before the story will go further. Bit of a slog sometimes.All in all it's a fun game with an expansive array of play styles, weapons, abilities, and gear. Great mechanics, gameplay, graphics, sound, and combat. Only drawback for me is the SJW-ish theme of a bunch of pathetic intellectual types only being nice b/c of social justice/contracts formality. I could be way off and will change my mind by the end of the story and if so I'll change my review. I'll still give it a thumbs up b/c it really is a fun game with a variety of items to keep it from getting boring. The story part is just a big eye roll for me sometimes. Maybe it's my military background b/c this kind of wimpiness is either overcome or you don't cut it and go back home b/c it was just "too hard". This game would be even a better deal if you got it on sale. Then yes definitely get it.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok so what if you made Binding of Isaac in a Post-Hades world, and then also gave it like, a Life is Strange-y aesthetic?Idk that's mostly a joke. Dreamscaper is a neat roguelite; if you've played roguelites before, you have a good idea of the basic moment to moment gameplay. The between-run layer involves going to different locations in your hometown(?) to spend between-run currencies on buffs, new rooms to show up during runs, etc. etc. etc. roguelite stuff.I'm only an hour in, and while I'm enjoying it, I will say that so far the between-run stuff lacks some of the character and panache that the runs themselves have. I assume, based on some of what I've seen, there'll be more of that later? But I wouldn't expect a full on Hades-esque meta-narrative (would love to be pleasantly surprised though). Idk, Dreamscaper is good, the gameplay is good, the items/weapons are unique (although I wish they were a little flashier), and so far the bossfights are really cool and unique. I feel like it's missing some character, but maybe either 1. I'm spoiled by Hades, as we all are by now, or 2. it'll show up more later.tldr: would recommend if you like Roguelites and want a roguelite to roguelike!

_childDocuments_.review: more fun than i remember. minor nitpicks that could improve some quality of life (being able to drop any equipped item when you only need that little bit more to purchase the item in the shop, usually to replace it/ and the health fountains not giving anything when you heal at full hp, bit of a wasted room in early floors) and multi ability overlap clarity when you chain attacks and multiple enemies are also firing, its hard to dodge and see. and minor combat clunk of the windup of certain attacks from enemies could be improved. the basic mobs get ranged checked a lot, so our short ranged attacks really suck in comparison. and being able to run in the park to get to the other side to pick up a new recipe would be nice since that map is a bit too large for the slow paced walking. but overall positive. very fun game. although also wish you could save a run mid-way though clearing a floor. if you gotta go randomly or power outage or something, is mildly annoying. also an explanation of what putting more points into the ?/6 health fountain/puzzle room does. i assume it makes it more frequent to show up as a room, but kinda weird those enhances dont say anything when the other ones that say +1% are shown. you would show a 1% increase in text, but not a brief explanation of lucid pool 2/6. could just say: "increases chance to appear during run" dont even need to put a percentage increase. but it doesnt even say what putting points into it does. minor stuff really. mild confusion etc. 7/10 - charming and fun. we do be gaming.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, definitely a must-play if you enjoy the rougelike genre.Pros-1. Very nice aesthetic2. Smooth gameplay, easy to learn, but with plenty of benefits to mastering it (Perfect hit system + using critical extinguishes).3. Well-written storyline.  The characters you bond with are interesting, and the pieces of backstory are given to you at a nice pace.  Some very fun dialogues.4. Great Symbolism.  I really appreciated this, though this kind of falls under the category of the 1st/3rd points.  The boss cinematics (especially the last one) really fit well.5.) Solid difficulty scaling.  There are training wheels options & options to make the game very challenging.  Shouldn't be too hard to find where you stand + increase it when you get more familiar with the game.Cons-1.) Minor nitpick here, but I would definitely appreciate an active display on the hud for your actual damage.  The game gives you a nice stat modifier window/inventory, but only shows base effects/damage on any weapon you have or will pick up.  It would be cool to see your trinket that modifies base damage by 20% or other modifiers actually show when mousing over the weapon, or when comparing weapons to pick up.2.) I keep getting an odd glitch where a blurring effect occurs whenever certain particle effects happen.  Luckily, this doesn't happen during actual gameplay, as the particle effects are in certain rooms or in the "real world".  Just a small inconvenience that I'm sure will get fixed at some point.Overall-This is an indie rougelike with a lot of passion and a message, the kind of life I love seeing in a game.  If you like the core gameplay loop, definitely give it a try, it's worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: Preface, I tend to not be good at Roguelite/likes yet managed to beat this one on normal (I enjoy them sometimes, phases of game type likes, weird I know).  Now, I didnt use the super easy mode available (its an option you can turn on/off to make the game easier at any time) but my so far singular clear is on normal.About how the difficulty works.  You have bog standard normal, then at some point (think after second boss) it unlocks to allow you to pick Normal or upgrade intensity via 4 different variables.  1. Map sizes, more rooms, more loot, more mobs to die to.  2. Mob density and setup within the floor AND rooms3. Mob damage4. Boss HP+DMG +50%And there is a setting for each of these 4 that is set at Hard (Again, not sure when it unlocks, think after you beat 2nd boss) and Nightmare, which unlocks when you clear the game once.  The higher the intensity, the more rewards you get as well as challenge.  Also gives a visual indicator via upgrading Cassidy's room.So people looking for a head+wall experience might want to shy away unless you feel you suck at roguelite/likes but I feel it is worth the money for most people if you are looking for something to sink some time into.

_childDocuments_.review: I see a lot of people comparing this game to Hades and I think that's not a good bar to set with this game. Yes it holds similar dungeon crawling elements, but I quite like this game more. What this game lacks in complexity adds to how flawlessly its elements works. "Keep it simple stupid no?"Honestly, I wasn't too into the story because I cared more about the "dungeon crawling" elements of the game. The mastery system for each melee weapon, ranged weapon, shield, and lucid attack was a great touch. It gave me a reason to try out every weapon and grind them to complete mastery. Granted, I found myself trying to build an optimal set for each run, but unfortunately RNG prevented that at times. I went into the final boss fight with a less than ideal lineup and was forced to really play safe in order to clear the run. Add in Dream intensity to this mix and the challenge became greater and more fun to try and master.This game really doesn't have a weak link in my opinion. Everything may not be perfect, but a jack of all trades is better than a master of just one. I highly recommend this game as one of the better dungeon crawlers I've ever played. (If not one of top 5.)

Some have tells and give a warning flash while others don't, and some versions of enemies can be stun-locked while others can't are some examples. The runs are enjoyable and the main loop is smooth. The unlocks available are deep and interesting from multitude of weapons to various expansions for each run. Again, I really like this game and the only issues i have with it center around combat.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to be careful about what I say because I don't want to turn off anyone who would enjoy this game from playing it. This game is wonderful, and I'll explain why, but something I should get out of the way is, if you are looking for the next game to consume all of your time for countless months with a seemingly endless plethora of secrets to discover, this probably isn't it. After about 20 hours, I've completed a full run and nearly a second, yes there is still a lot of difficulty scaling, character progression, and even a couple dozen ability & equiment unlocks to wade through - and it seems I haven't even truly completed the game yet, as is common with the genre...but at this point I feel like I've seen most of what the game is going to throw at me, maybe minus a couple of things, a few cool abilities, and I can see myself quickly going from playing this every chance I get, to maybe just doing a run or two on the weekend, then playing something else. It's a Roguelite....the whole point is repetition. But when I've got over 100 hours in Rogue Legacy 2 and still haven't seen or unlocked everything or fought every boss, it feels less than good that seemingly just about the only thing left in Dreamscaper is the infinite stat scaling/NG+ after just 20 hours. I guess I just wish there was a little more meat on its bones. But I can appreciate it as the small, indie game it is, made by 3 people. Just know that is definitely what you're buying.And honestly, for $25, I don't think it's unreasonable. But I got it on sale and I think most people would find themselves happier if they did as well. I've definitely gotten more than $15 worth out of this game already and expect to continue to play it a lot more. Despite the repetition, it just feels good to play. Even at this point, I still find myself saying "I'll save after this floor....okay maybe I'll just do one more....actually I'll do this one too..." and I basically have to force myself to stop. And I think there's something to be said about a game that is continually playable, not because of the expectation of seeing or experiencing something new or unexpected, but because they designed something that is so mechanically satisfying to play, you don't even care if it's just the same thing over and over. I would say that's a big part of why Hades was so successful, and this is very much in the same vein, though there are definitely some differences, and I think some who like one game will not like the other, so allow me to explain in more detail...Dreamscaper has dozens of melee and ranged weapons, and there are modifiers that can make the same weapon feel different on different runs, particularly the ranged ones. There are also dozens of targeted spells, mostly AOEs and skillshots, like what you'd expect to see in a MOBA or ARPG. Pretty much all of them are REALLY fun, beautifully animated, you really feel their impact. Spellcasting is my favorite part of games with this type of combat, and was one of the key things that had me interested in this game, and it has REALLY delivered. The combat is a little slower and more methodical than Hades, and I was concerned at first about that resulting in it feeling clunky - but while it did take a little getting used to, I've been surprised at just how SMOOTH the combat feels....dodging between projectiles, sniping enemies with a 3 pronged ranged attack, then dashing in for the shotgun kill. It's just amazing. There is so much polish. It would be fair to say this isn't a game that reinvents the wheel, it just aims to give you one of the nicest wheels you've ever seen.The meta progression in the waking world is pretty identical to Hades, between the ways you upgrade the dungeons and your character's stats and perks. It has some added layers of complexity though (different gifts for different characters). Also, the floor progression is much more Binding of Isaac style, on a grid with bombs, keys, and even hidden rooms, and you can freely traverse a floor until you descend to the next. I find that more satisfying to "solve" than just the pure linear progression of Hades, but it can slow it down a little for people who want to just get to the point.Something else notably different in this game, relative to Hades, is the tonal difference of the narrative, characters, and dialogue. Hades' dialogue and characters are witty, sassy, and charming, and it's understandably one of the things people admire most about the game. I'll admit that I don't really CARE about the characters in Dreamscaper, except the protagonist and a couple of her relationships, and the dialogue isn't always delivered in the most impactful manner even when it's good - but at the same time, I like what they've done. There are actual conversations between you and characters sometimes, and they seem charmingly realistic, but I also enjoy when the game actually just says a line describing an implied conversation you had with someone. It sort of gets to the point without wasting your time, and leaves more to your imagination.THAT BEING SAID - the actual STORY being told....I absolutely love. If Hades is like some anime that everyone talked about at school, Dreamscaper is more like Pixar, specifically Inside Out (if Pixar had a really dry, snarky sense of humor). I haven't finished the game quite yet, but I've really enjoyed the way it has delivered the story of this girl's life with vague hints, memories, and lavish metaphors. I was actually holding back tears one night as I made it further than I had before and uncovered something new about the story, and found it incredibly relatable. It wasn't even blatantly tugging at my heartstrings with really obvious dramatic story beats - just with the things I was piecing together, and the things in my own life it made me think about, it really resonated with me. It's probably not for everyone, but the nice thing is, if you don't care about this game's story and/or it doesn't mean anything to you, it doesn't shove it down your throat or force you to listen to what it has to say. The pieces are there for players who care, without bogging down the experience for those who don't.IN SUMMARY:On one hand, I feel like this is just generic enough of a Roguelite that any fan of the genre who likes the look of the combat and the graphics could probably enjoy it as one of the more competent new entries in the genre, regardless of what they think about any of the details. This is a prime example of a modern dungeon-crawling Roguelite being made masterfully, without breaking new ground, although I would say the spell variety and combat mechanics might just be my favorite in any game in this style. There are things Dreamscaper does that I can't just go to another game to experience, that I would like to see more of. But probably the biggest difference between it being just another Roguelite and something special is whether or not the details resonate with you. I find the themes of childhood reminiscence, interpersonal relationships, depression, mental health, family dynamics, etc. to be interesting and unique, and nice to see approached in this medium. It's not something you see a lot in games. But I can fully understand how there are people in the world who couldn't care less and would probably even think it pretentious, especially with how vaguely symbolic it can be at times. I really don't think the game is full of itself....but it's definitely not for everyone. If you are still on the fence, I would maybe skim through the negative reviews and hear what people didn't like. Many of the complaints people have are valid and fair, but many of the things people don't like, are actually the things I like. So if you think you wouldn't like it for the same reasons they didn't, maybe it isn't for you. But if you feel like the things they're complaining about wouldn't be important to you, there might be more that you'll love than hate.

_childDocuments_.review: Hades meets Persona in this procedurally-generated rouge-like centered on dreams, memories, and fears. The cozy vibes are immaculate, the music is perfect, the cast of characters is small, but distinctive. There's a friendship meter and gift-giving system for each one, with short conversation scenes granted for each Rank Up. Our protagonist is named and not silent, she does speak to characterize herself in these scenes, and the narration she gives about her Memories. The complete lack of voice-acting (even voice-grunting a la Spiritfarer) is a bit of a let-down, but it fits thematically with the somewhat off-putting decision to render no human faces. In the dream runs, this makes total sense, to save effort for a small model barely seen in detail, but some of the individual scenes get REALLY CLOSE to the painterly, well-shaded, smooth, rounded heads, which is truly a bit disturbing. Fuzzy or blurry divots for the eyes, and lumps for the nose/mouth on the head, I would have found much LESS disturbing. The complete lack, i don't understand. Does the protagonist Cassidy have face-blindness (prosopagnosia)? Every NPC, including Cassidy herself, has distinct hair and clothes, even glasses and mustaches, but no eyes, nose, mouth, or ears. They look like those peg-head pose-able artist mannequins. Body language animations in conversations helps make their tone of voice mostly clear, but not always. It really has the effect of making you feel like you don't fit in, like you're one layer removed from the characters, or that you're missing some information when you talk to them.The protagonist Cassidy has some sort of grown-up job, but we never see her at work. We see her haunting various public spaces, doing completely unproductive, mentally-healthy things like - Meditating in the Park, Sketching at the Cafe, Daydreaming at the bar. The importance of Third Places and rest on full display. A new city isn't really your home until you have a Third Place (not home or work) to frequent. The plot centers on Cassidy battling her nightmares to approach more and more distressing memories around some nebulous family-related trauma - we only get hints from the Memories she can find in the dream world. The combat is DEEP, highly fleshed out, with a large array of stats, stat-boosting gear and upgrades, a use-to-master system, several flavors of status effects and elemental magic, many types of weapons and dodge and super-skills, as well as bonuses related to timing parry and attack windows that differ by weapon! I feel like it's on par with Neir Automata, personally!One negative I noticed - the farther you go into the game, there is a lack of tutorials for the new content that gets unlocked, such as the Forge, Challenge Rooms, and Puzzle Rooms. I specifically struggled to understand the win-state for the Dot Puzzle Room, which I thought was like 2048, but was actually Minesweeper. I had to go looking on Steam Community to find that explanation. If the replay-able tutorial level DOES give that info, it was not clear that I SHOULD go back there to find it after unlocking new room types in the main game.

_childDocuments_.review: let me start by saying that this is an early access game, and you should understand that more will be added to this before they consider the game finished.When I loaded up the game for the first time, I was really intrigued by the style of gameplay.  A 3D roguelike with interesting puzzles, elegant combat with rewarding complexity, and music that made me want stop everything I am doing and just listen.  For the launch price of 14.99, this game it delivers so much more than you pay for.  Your dreams are the rogue like action game, and when you awake, you venture out into the town, fostering friendships with the townspeople.  Giving them small gifts, and talking about life.  You will gain new abilities/weapons to find in your future dream travels to go even further.This is a nice twist on a classic game-style that has become ever so popular.  I will be coming back to this game regularity and intend on buying the soundtrack as soon as it releases.Don't sleep on this one, but dream within the game playing Dreamscaper.

_childDocuments_.review: I just started, but this is a very, very lovely game!Gameplay seems like a mashup of Isaac, Gungeon, Diablo and a... hmmm... walking simulator, I guess?The main action happens while you dream, and you go from one randomly generated room to another, picking up loot, solving puzzles and fighting "monsters". Fighting is fun and easy to get into - but it also has high skill ceiling because of sheer amount options available.First, there's you main close range weapon, which you can chain into a combo (3-5 attacks depending on the weapon). Like in Batman: Arkham games, trigger the chain at the right moment and you get extra damage.Second, there's your ranged attack. Charged attacks (like a bow) have a perfect 'moment' when you should release a charge, to get extra damage. Not all ranged attacks are charging, in my short play, I also got a beam attack.Third, there's a shield. It removes some damage, but trigger it at the right moment - and you parry, stunning the opponent.Fourth, there's dodge. There's even equipment for dodging - shoes! There's a familiar 'chain NOW' flash when dodge ends, and if you dodge at the perfect moment, you get a short slow-mo action going, so all of this means something, but I don't know what yet.Fifth, you have your "lucid powers", which are two skills you can equip, that spend your "lucid" bar, basically a a rechargeable superpower stat.Sixth, you have 'bullet time' which you can trigger at times.Seventh, you have bombs which act just like in Isaac - place and they go boom for a lot of damage or environmental destruction.On top of this, you have keys, sand (dream currency), and waking world currency that is used to upgrade you.Waking world is the walking simulator section, but I mean - you can just teleport via map wherever you want. This is how you attain upgrades, and what's very interesting - is that it isn't just a silly old "Purchase upgrades" option. Your avatar basically goes to meditate in the park and "work on her mental health", which gives you - you guessed it - health in the dreamworld. You can go to a bar, sit and "daydream", to unlock special rooms in the dreamworld (like, puzzle rooms, shops, etc).The coolest thing are 'ideas', a thing you pickup in the dream, which is a 'blueprint' for an item. Then, with an idea, and few Inspiration Points (also pickupable), you go to Sketch Cafe, and you 'sketch' yourself an item to use in the dream.All in all - gameplay wise, it is nothing you haven't seen before, but it is done so well that it clearly shows - it doesn't matter to be the _first_ to do something, it matters to do it well.The whole game is wrapped into the theme, everything is related to dreaming in some way or another, and this is what's so great about it.Music is mindblowing, graphics are amazing, and environments are beautifully crafted.If there's a roguelike worth your money (after Isaac and Gungeon), then this is it, 100%. I really, really can't upvote it enough.There's one thing that annoys me about the game, and that is consistent usage of 'they' to refer to NPCs.It took me more than 40 minutes to realize that dialogue is NOT referring to PC and NPC doing something TOGETHER, but is instead referring to an NPC in a gender-neutral way.This is first confusing, then annoying, especially when during an actual dialogue, your character refers to an NPC as a 'dude' and similar.Game introduces an NPC as stranger, and next thing you read is about how this NPC is "telling Cassidy about the concert they attended this weekend."

_childDocuments_.review: Looked like great fun, the upgrade system sounded promising and the combat looked fun. BUT! The upgrade system slowed down way too hard, the combat is way too clunky and you often die to being spawned in a horrible room and 6 ranged folks simultaneously hitting you with 6 different attacks which you can't just spam dodge yourself out of. The game becomes way to repetitive and the rate at which you collect resources is way too slow, even with the "2x if you don't take damage" and all the difficulty bonuses.And the worst thing is ... you are basically forced to swap abilities/weapons all the time in order to keep up with the enemy scaling, but 80% of abilities/weapons are basically useless compared to others which turns your run into an RNG fest and makes losing late to bad RNG way too frustrating. You pre determine your build from the start with favors and chosen upgrades etc. but with bad RNG you just might not get anything to upgrade it further and basically have to ditch the run and get basically nothing in return for wasted time. A fun idea, but it feels like the developers just gave up half way through and went the "lets just add some maths to boost play time" path.

_childDocuments_.review: This game reminded me why you should always support Indie developers. Dreamscaper is an Action Rougelike with a beautiful art style, relatable story, and masterful gameplay. I hate to compare all Action Rougelikes to Hades, but it is hard to deny the similarities in the progression system. Once you finish a run, you go around and talk among the locals and build relationships with them, gaining benefits along the way. Although this is not a bad thing in Dreamscaper as I personally really enjoyed the way it was executed. As far as the gameplay goes, there are a plethora of primary melee weapons and range weapons. As well as lucid attacks which are your abilities. All the weapons felt unique, and had their own weaknesses and strengths. With my time, I never truly found an "OP" build that I always tried to get, since every build was viable in my experience. Every run felt fresh because of this aspect. The gameplay is more slow and methodical, similarly to games I have played like Curse of the Dead Gods, and not fast paced like Hades. You have to be mindful of when to attack, block, or parry or you will be greatly punished. I am relatively new to Action Rougelikes, so it took some time for me to get used to the challenge but it was rewarding to feel myself improving. As far as difficulties go, there are difficulty modifiers that you can choose that can make your run more challenging. I also really admired the story. If you or someone you know has struggled with mental illness, then you will be able to relate to the story and connect with Cassidy. In my experience, this was the first game I have played that dealt with this type of narrative and it was beautifully written.Overall, I would recommend Dreamscaper to any Action Rougelike fan, and if you are unsure about purchasing it full price, wait for a Steam sale. It is worth it, and It is even out Xbox Game Pass now!If you are reading this Devs, thank you for a beautiful gaming experience, and my personal GOTY for 2021! I am looking forward to see what you produce next.
