_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - A true knockout hit of an action roguelite. Worth it at full price for any fan of the genre or anyone looking to get in to it. Just an incredible action roguelite that hits all the right notes. Unique art style, gorgeous soundtrack, excellent gameplay, and a "present but not overbearing" story that doesn't feel tacked on.Combat has a great flow to it, and you'll find yourself mixing things up between rooms depending on the enemies present. Every melee and ranged weapon has a "Perfect Attack" window that rewards timing over button mashing, and there's a surprising amount of variety in the movesets. Everything from your standard baseball bat, to a long-range spear, to a large anime sword are all present (plus some more wacky weapons like a fishing rod and yo-yos), and as far as I can tell not a single moveset is shared across the dozens of melee weapons. Ranged weapons mostly differ on timing and what their "implicit modifier", i.e. the mod that's always present on the item, is, but they still play quite differently from one another too.Even your dodges are different, allowing you to decide between one of seven choices, including: a short-ranged roll so you can dance around attacks without losing DPS uptime, a long-range dash to get out of range of AOEs, and even some that serve as "openers" for some offense. Shields again are more similar to ranged weapons in that their variety lies in the implicit modifiers, such as "the shield that's good for parrying" and "can't parry but blocks all around you".On top of all this equipment variety, there are Diablo-like modifiers and rarity levels which improve the number of modifiers a weapon can have. These can range from just ok (+20% duration to a 2s slow) to quite powerful (e.g. max health). That being said, rerolling these can be quite expensive and isn't something you're going to be spamming in a run without some serious loss of currency. It wouldn't be a roguelite without passive items, and there are plenty here. I never felt like they contributed a significant amount to a "god run", aside from one that gives all attacks leech, but they do nonetheless contribute to your power and make for some fun builds utilizing various elemental synergies. Arguably the main factor that sets this apart as a -lite and not a -like is the meta progression, which comes in three major forms and one minor form. First come character upgrades, then "room" upgrades, and lastly are unique passives that you get from befriending characters between runs. The character and room upgrades are quite powerful, but personally I felt the progression was a bit slow for how important some of the upgrades can be. Befriending characters grants you a nice bonus to specific playstyles (e.g. one grants bonuses to ranged attacks, one to spells, etc) and can be changed between floors, so if you find yourself getting a lot of items geared towards one playstyle you don't have to feel like you're entirely wasting the passive. The rest of the game falls on presentation, and the game delivers on this front. The art style is beautiful, and as you progress in the dream world, devolves in to a more twisted and nightmarish depiction of reality. The calm, ambient piano music is a treat to listen to between runs or while deciding if you really want to swap those items out between rooms (vinyl pressing when?). There's something here for everyone who even remotely enjoys the genre, with adjustable difficulty ranging from "normal, take less damage each time you die" to "nightmare, everything does 2x damage, has 2x health, new enemies, new attack patterns, new boss moves". Overall, a truly wonderful game and an excellent showing by the developers for what has clearly been a passion project. Hope to see more from them in the future, and I feel this game is well worth it at full price. (seriously though, vinyl pressing of the OST when?)E: It took a little over 2 years, but we -did- eventually get that vinyl pressing. Thank you, devs and Dale North!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is beautiful, and is an amazing experience. But does it really fulfill a roguelike player?The boss battles are amazingly designed, but the average enemies in the game feel really stale and clunky. Unlike industry staples of similar price points like Dead Cells and Hades, the combat does not feel fluid, swift, and snappy. Instead, it feels clunky, difficult to grasp, and genuinely unintuitive.Essentially when I play Im just speed running through fights mashing left click until I get to bosses, because that is the highlight of the experience, where as in Hades Im taking my time in every room because the entire experience is fun and rewarding. Also, becoming better at the combat barely helps you in boss fights because its more learning their patterns than combat mastery, again, making learning the combat feel useless.On top of all this, the developers gave the story a more prominent position in this game than I would have liked. I prefer story telling like Hades, or Dead Cells, where I can learn the story at my own pace while being immersed in gameplay. Instead, I find myself standing still watching dialogue and (admittedly beautiful) cutscenes play.Its a real shame, I just don't see this being a good roguelike.This game seems like an RPG, made by people who play RPGs, that they decided to make a roguelike after the recent success of many indie roguelike staples. There are too many instances of "Oh heres a roguelike mechanic" with almost no depth, as if it was an afterthought.

_childDocuments_.review: I have no idea how and when this game got on my wishlist, but when I randomly got an email saying it was released, I decided to give it a shot. I also have no idea how to structure this review, so let me just start by saying the biggest draw for me was the visuals and art style. This game is absolutely beautiful. This game has one of the most creative settings I've ever gotten the chance to experience. Both the nightmare world and real worlds are well thought out with interesting details that tie into Cassidy's story. I can't say more on how immersive these worlds feel. Not to mention the music feels perfectly made for this game. This is a roguelite game so each run essentially starts over once losing, but there is still progress made towards future runs. After having played only a few games in this genre, I have found that my favorite part of roguelites is its variety in each run. It's important to me that each run feels different and good to play. In Dreamscaper, I love that no matter what items I am dealt with in the beginning I am still interested in pushing it as far as I can. I am given the option to create some starting items before new runs, but I personally liked keeping it random and trying to experience a different playstyles each time. Unlocking new items and weapons for the future runs is done more creatively than in other roguelites. Unlocking them is done by building relationships with people in the real world and that feels fun at first...but I can see how other people will find it a chore later on. It builds quite slow and finding the right gift can sometimes take some trial and error. I don't personally mind it, but I certainly have a higher tolerance to grind these sorts of things in games. Though, I wouldn't mind knowing what gift I've already tried giving to someone. Now on to some pros and cons.Pros:+Visually stunning to look at and play through. All the lucid attacks are so pretty and animations are smooth.+Music feels right for the game and doesn't feel boring even after 14 hours of gameplay. +Story and setting is light, yet engaging. The vignettes between characters and memories are thoughtful enough that it gives Cassidy a personality. Not to mention it is done in a way that feels so unique.+The Combat. The combat is challenging and engaging on a technical level. The controls feel tight and each hit feels so heavy. There's timing involved with the melee weapons, dodging, and parrying. All of it is so rewarding once you've gotten better at executing them. Being able to parry and or dodge at any time feels so good. +Variety of weapons, items, and abilities to use. There are seriously so many options at your disposal that it keeps runs fresh. Whether you choose to use your water gun to start an engagement or maybe you want to call down a meteor or maybe you want to challenge them to breakdancing. I would never have thought using a set of yo-yos would be fun, but here we are. All of it feels viable and such a joy to use. I do wish somewhere in the description that it distinguished what the item actually is (eg. melee weapon, lucid ability, ranged weapon, etc.)+Skipping the Boss fights. Though I loved the two boss fights I was able to experience. I think once might have been enough, especially seeing as the 2nd boss was challenging enough to end a lot of my runs. Having the option is nice. +Challenge Rooms. These were rooms that had a combat challenge tied to them and completing them awarded you with an item. I thought that the challenges were tough and a nice addition to create some additional room variety. +Teleporting to other rooms. Being able to teleport to different rooms on a level is so convenient and makes traversing/exploring an entire level feel worth it and not as much of a chore. Also the item distinction in each room made it easy to revisit rooms if you left a hp pot there and wanted to save it for later. Genius. +For an early access game, there is plenty of content to explore. I've played early access games with far less to offer in terms of actual content. Cons:-Enemy types lack variety. Currently there are only a few enemy types, but that's understandable. I do like that each type gains new abilities as you progress into the next level. -Enemies are quite tanky. Especially because once I've gotten one stun-locked or juggled it's over, but it seems to take longer than I'd want it to take. They felt like combo sponges after getting an enemy in the air.-Too many projectiles on later levels feels a little silly. Taking any damage on the last level is lethal and getting taken out by a stray projectile because of dodging another attack feels bad. -Puzzles don't feel rewarding. It feels like most of the time i'm just turning the item I get into sand since it's not better than what I have currently. Though, I honestly love a game of minesweeper from time to time. -Unlocking new abilities or items may be too grindyEven though I have yet to complete the final boss, I can't wait to see more content for this game. For early access and with such a small studio, I am so incredibly impressed that I am 100% invested in seeing this game get to the full release!

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper has a fairly soft personal sadness story wrapped around a very good action roguelike game. I often see it compared to Hades, and if you're looking for Hades, then this is not it. It is, however, a different game and worth playing for its own sake. It has good abilities and items, clean and comfortable combat controls, and a reasonable selection of situations and enemies. There are a good selection of unlocks and gradual power-ups, and perfectly pleasant artistic content. The bosses and enemies all have a second set of behaviors you can unlock with the difficulty modifiers so once you think you've mastered the first set, go ahead and turn the dials up and try the next ones. Well worth a complete play-through.

_childDocuments_.review: I tend to like Roguelite games, and while this one looks pretty at first glance, mechanically it doesn't work as well, it's a case of Narita Boy, lots of flash, almost no substance. People praise it because they like to sound edgy, to like something different, but different doesn't mean good, nor polished. 1. - It's not like Hades etc where you jump in, lose and jumps in again. Here you die, and go back to the real world, then slowly visit a different location with snail-like walking pace, just to upgrade things, then visit to another place, to upgrade another thing. 2.  - Many weapons have long wind up animations while the enemies will just hit you straight away. There is a technique called perfect attack, it which you time your presses/combo when Cass flashes white, but the timing is ridiculous, it's like 0.1 secs fast. If you see the white flash, it's already too late, so you gotta feel and predict it. I can guarantee you that you'll almost never execute a perfect attack combo. Else you can also upgrade it to increase to the perfect attack timing by 5% increments at a time, at a max 25% iirc, which is about 0.25 secs probably lol.3. - Knowing how sluggish your movements are, even with the fastest weapons, some mobs have "snap" like attacks, that without knowing what they can do before hand, you will definitely get hit while you are approaching them. Going on later stage, some mobs have total hyper armor, requiring you to hit it afar or hit once dodge once, it's so tiresome. The same looking enemies can then attack with range blast, or their attacks have another range wave. You don't get good with this game, you simply win by trial and error. Because the same enemy that you've beaten before now suddenly attack with a new blast at a further range that you didn't anticipate before. The mobs are harder to deal than bosses.4.  - Know the difference, it's not ugly, it's messy. There's a skill where you call in a tornado, and it covers almost half a screen, with your character in the middle, and you can see anything. An explosion of light, a big orb, where you lose sight of your characters too. Then when you move on the top of the screen, due to perspective, your character gets so tiny that it's hard to see her. Enemies can be small and just a glowy thing, you won't even realize it while fighting other enemies with everything looking so small and your skills covering your screen. You will die plenty of times, not because the enemies are difficult, but because you can't see anything, sometimes you are trying to dodge, then you can't dodge, because you realize there is a barrier/tree/box, but the graphic is "fade away" because you are near it. Then enemies also attack off screen, there's a red arrow pointing when they do, but it will get chaotic the moment there's 2 of them. 5.  - Lots of weird things to upgrade and a 5% pace each, with very little resources every time. The puzzle are pace breaking.6.  - There's some puzzles, but you don't know what you are supposed to do, do you make a path? Do you make all blue, or all red? There's also secret rooms, but almost 0 indication, perhaps one day you'll discover it by accident. Again, another trial and error. Trial and error mechanics in a rogue-lite game is garbage mechanics. 7.  - Really, there's no sense in the story, just random parts about remembering her past, and talking random stuffs with random people. You also randomly pick up random memories on the stages. Sometimes it's there, sometimes it isn't. And ALL of the people, including YOU, is faceless.If you are looking for a slow experience, this is it. But if you are looking for engaging Roguelite, You can get Hades or Devil Slayer Raksasi, this one doesn't compare at all. Then you can return to this one and appreciate how well polished the other Roguelites are.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played Dreamscaper too much not to write a review of it. It was kind of an impulse purchase, after browsing through the Steam store page, reading user reviews, and watching Youtube reviews of the game. I plopped down the $22 for both the game and the soundtrack, and it was love at first sight.	The game plays like Hades, and feels like Celeste. Your character, Cassidy, has just moved to Redhaven from the podunk town of Backhill, and is working through mental health struggles stemming from an as-yet hinted-at trauma from her past (I’m only 25% of the way through the game, according to my save data). 	During the day, Cassidy will walk around the city of Redhaven talking to the other  inhabitants, making friends, learning about their hobbies, and even forming deeper bonds with them. Cassidy can craft gifts to give her newfound friends to advance her relationship with them, in order to keep them in mind when she goes to sleep, which gives her different buffs when she enters her dreams.	Also during the day, she can meditate to increase her personal stats, and each new ability is something she can work on. For example, “Don’t let my demons get to me” gives her a +5% damage boost against floor bosses. She can also go to the bar to daydream, where she can think about her dreams and spawn new challenge rooms, increase the merchant inventory, among other additions.	Furthermore, Cassidy can think of new equipment to bring into her dreams. These Ideas, once collected, can be sketched in her sketchbook, which requires Spark points (Sparks of Inspiration!) to unlock. Once unlocked, these items will appear in later runs, much like how the unlocks work in Enter the Gungeon or Dead Cells.  I absolutely love how many permanent upgrades and unlockables Dreamscaper gives the player. 	By day, Cassidy works on herself and tries to overcome her challenges. By night, Cassidy enters her dreams and battles her demons. The game plays very similarly to Hades, except that she won’t be petitioning Zeus to help her. Instead, she will find weapons, shields, dodge rolls, and keepsakes to help her. The keepsakes act as universal buffs, and can affect Cassidy’s weapons or provide support. Maybe she collects a keepsake that adds poison damage to her attacks, or one that makes her ranged weapon pierce enemies (the Sewing Needle!). 	The combat in this game is quite smooth, and is fairly easy for me: So much so, that I increased boss difficulty and still didn’t have much of a problem. Then again, I played Enter the Gungeon  and Hades, so what’s easy for me might be more difficult for someone else.	There is only one criticism I have against Dreamscaper. I think the game needs greater boss variety. Most other roguelikes I’ve played have a random assortment of bosses per floor. The Binding of Isaac randomizes its floor bosses, and Enter the Gungeon has a few bosses per floor that it might throw at you: Either the Bullet King or the Gatling Gull on floor 1, and the Gorgun or Beholster on Floor 2, for example. Dreamscaper, however, only has one boss per floor, and, while it does give the player the option to skip a boss if they have defeated it previously, there is no incentive to do so because it deprives the player of a boss-only keepsake (a massive health boost and possible damage increase) and important resources.	I am extremely happy that I purchased this game. Dreamscaper is a delightful roguelike with a wealth of permanent unlockables, and I appreciate that it’s on the easier side. I love the theme of the game and how every aspect of the game fits into it. Dreamscaper is a delightful game that I would heartily recommend to anyone who either currently enjoys roguelikes, or has never played a roguelike before.

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite roguelites ever, but its unorthodox design and art philosophy may turn off some folks who aren't used to or expecting it. It bears similarities to Hades, but going in expecting the exact same gamefeel is a mistake and will not mesh well with Dreamscaper's unique direction.Pros:+ Gorgeous artstyle. People will not like the bloom and dream aesthetic. That's a personal thing, but not objectively bad, and plenty of people will love it too ( as I do).+ Varied items. Hit enemies with boxing gloves, an umbrella, or just summon dozens of phantasmal knives to rain down on enemies from afar!+ Control over your runs: you can select unlocked items to start with, and difficulty options are available from 1st boot-up.+ Responsible depictions of mental health, and dialogue is extremely well-written. + Permanent upgrades are unique; while the classics of more HP and money gain are here, so are more unique ones like new types of rooms to vary your runs, and starting with a little companion friend.+ You can teleport anywhere you've been on the map at any time. Praise be.+ Discourages spamming with a "perfect attack" combo window.Cons: - Stable overall, but with a couple of hiccups in mechanics or item interactions etc. (there are some antisynergies, and none of them ruin a run but they can be unsatisfying).-Dreamscaper has a lot of hidden mechanics and interactions that can be hard to grasp at first. 1.1 helped with new UI and interface upgrades that convey more info to the player. Still, other things like how health recovery affects leech (it does), items not critical extinguishing with themselves, what a critical extinguish is, etc. could go unbeknownst to a player for many hours or even their entire playtime.-Can get grindy if you're a completionist or trying to ace the hardest difficulties.TLDR: Know what you're getting into here. Dreamscaper can be frantic, but it is much more methodical and dream-like than for example Hades or Undermine. It weaves optional puzzles into the roguelite formula of pure combat, it has an artstyle that is unique and foreign to the genre, ergo gamers should be aware of this because they generally don't actually like change.If you can get yourself into the mindset the game encourages (it's not difficult to do) you will have a fantastic time, and as you can see from my hours, it is more than worth the price. Most importantly, the dev team are sweethearts and have poured themselves into this project for 3 years and have been very attuned to the audience's desires in that time to make the best product possible. See y'all in the Dreamscape.

_childDocuments_.review: Satisfying. Good messages.This game takes a bit to get going and I honestly wasn't hooked on it at first, or so I thought, but I found myself thinking, "well, I've got 30min before I gotta leave.....I can get in a few levels or a round" and then would be playing....and playing....and playing. The dialogue in the real world can be a bit forced/lame at times but it is also an example of how people should properly interact and hold conversations about difficult and sensitive topics. I did find myself reading every word and enjoying the development of the relationships and the development of the protagonist and the overall story. I found myself wanting to get deeper in the nightmares not to beat the dreams but to gather resources because I was interested in developing the relationships. I will recommend having a guide open on which gifts to give to which character. If your goal is to 100% the list and max out everyone's relationships you'll want to do this. Some of the gifts require a fair amount of resources to craft and if you get it wrong, you just blew a lot of time for, essentially, nothing. Using a guide did not diminish the gameplay experience, in fact I found it made it more relaxing and enjoyable because I didn't have to stress over blowing resources on the wrong person. You will probably already have to run the nightmares multiple times so it doesn't diminish the gameplay experience (especially if you are looking to 100% every weapon then you will be doing the levels A LOT). I appreciate that so many builds work well and I often found myself surprised by skill combos that worked well together. As a player you do need to be a bit more flexible in your builds and goals because there are so many items to randomly sift through. It's a repetitive game by nature but it was soothing and familiar to run the gauntlet and adjust the difficulty that when I quit playing I felt a little sad because it had become part of the daily routine to run a few rounds. Overall, if you're new to this genre of game, this is a good entry level game. Well built, relatively satisfying, responsive controls, connection to real world issues and maybe will help you through a tough time.

_childDocuments_.review: Faded memories, everyday scenes, and faraway sounds. There’s something familiar about this place, but you don’t have time to focus, especially not when there’s somewhere to be; something to find. When you find it, everything should make sense. Right? As you search area after area, looking for that something that will answer your questions, you realize how dangerously low your health has dipped. When the monsters finally overcome you, the world disappears, and you suddenly wake up. Developed by AfterBurner Studios and co-published by Freedom!Games and Maple Whispering Limited, you play as the dreamy heroine, Cassidy, in the roguelite game, Dreamscaper. By day, she is a down-to-earth and spunky gal, just trying to find her place in the world and in her town of Red Haven. By night, she is a fearless fighter in the realm of sleep and the subconscious. Join her in both her daytime adventures and night battles as she tries to uncover the truth and her own insecurities.  Instead of beginning with a long and exploratory exposition, in Dreamscaper, you begin in the middle of Cassidy’s narrative and must work outward to find the beginning and the end of her story. At first, her daily interactions with the citizens of Red Haven are certainly odd and a little off-putting. Between their reactions and conversations with her, prior events had occurred, unknown to the player, that will require further conversing to discover what had happened. The more you speak and gift the people of Red Haven, the friendlier the people are with Cassidy. This will, in turn, benefit Cassidy in her dreams as this unlocks better upgrades, weapons, and abilities. The biggest hurdle for players is the threat of Permadeath. If defeated in the dreams by an enemy, Cassidy is forcefully awakened and her previously gained advantages that were obtained throughout the levels will be removed. This game mechanic can be difficult to get through as one wrong move and players are forced to restart from the beginning and can only hope that the weapons and lucid powers found are the same, if not better from the ones previously obtained.  Dreamscaper is a unique combination of being both relaxing and challenging to play. This action game does a fantastic job at capturing the surreal ambience of the dreamworld. The game play is smooth, the music is lovely, and the atmosphere and design are beautiful. Much like how alluring dreams can really be, there is something magical about how Dreamscaper captures one’s attentions and imaginations. Just be careful of dying as waking from a nightmare is never fun for anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Review of Dreamscaper.  Verdict: thumbs up, but with reluctance.  This review has two parts: (1) what this game does new, (2) the macro of what this game's like.(1).  Clearly, the appeal of this game is the theme/mood.  Defeat your nightmares?  You'll need a healthy state of mind first!  How well they delivered on this potential leaves a bit to be desired.  The powerups are things like "Meditate: be okay asking for help" and such.  These messages are nice - they're in the right place.  However, the big 'miss' here is the conversations in the awake world.  It's mostly "Herp derp, have mundane conversations with the people in the city to become their friends and then get the buffs that come from that."  There are several good tidbits of wisdom in the script.  What would have made this game a truly emphatic thumbs-up: if the awake world conversations had more 'substance' of that kind, and if they really reflected how a person can go from an unhealthy mind state to a healthy one.  If they had done that, they would have smashed the unique theme of the game, and really delivered on the potential they found.(2).  This is a 40-hour game if you're putting it down after you beat the last boss.  The progressions are like Vampire Survivors, the level layouts and rounds are like Isaac, and the micro is third-person action combat.  In the first 6 hours you'll be unlocking the mechanisms of the game.  Between hours 6 and 10 there's a dip.  The combat will seem grindy, repetitive, and lacking nuance ("K, I keep playing Snowy Village and Dark City, and most of the time I'm just running away from the baddies and letting my ranged attacks recharge").  You'll be wondering if the rest of the levels don't get more interesting ("Is there gonna be a real variety of baddies on the later levels?").  The assortment of weapons and items will seem thrown together and arbitrary.  But after about 12 hours, you'll see that the combat becomes rich and challenging, and the set of weapons and items in this game really does hang together.  This game is excellently packaged, tuned, balanced, and paced, if a 40-hour game is what you're down for.  There's nothing smashingly new in the game mechanics, but it does a good job of combining game design aspects into one.  However, you might find, if you're bigbrained, "K, this is complex enough that a smallbrain wouldn't be able to figure out the good strats, in several different ways, but I can pretty much see the end from the middle."Overall, do recommend.  But I do wonder what a better job of this game would have been like.  It's a hecking shame that the development of this game is over.  If they had done an ambitious version 2.0, and you can tell they were smart enough, this game could have been truly one of the greats.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I tried out this game sooner - it's a simple yet great experience even though it's only in early access. * If you prefer a video review (with ultrawide footage), check the link  at the bottom * - It has a hauntingly beautiful style with music that matches the gameplay. Characters, mobs and the scenery are all "drawn" with a dream-like feel in mind. Outside of combat the music is a mixture of melancholy and subdued cheerfulness. Combat visual and sound effects are flashy but are still matched to the general theme of the game. - The plot matches the simple graphics and audio style but it is very personal for the main character - Cass. It is delivered through your frequent runs in the dream or nightmare world. In that reality you build your memories from the "wins" you get before starting  over. NPC characters in the world not only help you to get stronger but also flesh out the world of Cass. - Gameplay for Dreamscape is great. The outside world works similar to other RPGs. You meet people and converse with them to improve relationships (You can also give them gifts you craft). Improved relationships benefits you through passive buffs and items you can obtain for Cass' dreams.Combat has the feel of Hades (another rogue-lite) or Diablo 3. _childDocuments_.review: The game can be described in one word."Grindy."That's not a bad thing if you like spending 2-3 runs unlocking the ability to wear shoes, (Dramatisation) but what's important to note is the game thrives off of incremental increases based entirely on how well you do during actual game-play loops. The only difference between it and several other roguelikes is that in 13 hours of playing, I unlocked maybe a quarter of the options I'd eventually have.Another thing to note is that if the game is tampered with, it'll wipe the entire save of everything. No notepad edits or EheatCngine here, you're in for the long haul. As to what it does well, if you enjoyed Persona like relationship-building games, then you'll be crafting your little heart out making breadboards and postcards for your new friends to have them upgrade their sweet sweet skills. The battles feel hard, but not overwhelming, but the RNG is absolutely unforgiving. If you roll bad weapons, you have almost no options to rectify such that I had unlocked in the 13 hours I played. I hope you like bullet hell, because this game is a bit like Dark Souls 3 for speed of combat with the added benefit of having to be -very- careful where you stand lest it become fire when you're not looking. You can parry as well, which makes a lot of the ranged unpleasantness bearable. The game severely punishes poor reaction time and environmental unawareness, but the art style is one of the best parts of the game. Everything is done to the same unique art style, and it was a joy to see deeper levels as you play out the Character's life-inspired nightmares and resolve them.Overall, I don't have the time or energy to grind everything, but if you do the game won't disappoint.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is a fun psychological rouge game that sets the player on a quest to help the main protagonist conquer her personal fears brought on by certain traumatic events  experienced through out her life. And by doing so causes potential questions about the emotional stability of One's own life! Some of these emotions are Regret, Fear and Remembrance.  These are emotions (and many others) all of us as human beings must endure, accept and learn to control. All of the main emotions are represented as bosses that one must defeat leading to the eventual spiritual enlightenment the character needs to fulfill and manifest her own destiny.It's a really nice premise that you can  tell the developers were enthusiastic to create It's music is soothing and thought provoking and the graphics (while not stellar) are more than adequate in a kids appropriate kind of way. Combat for the most part is fine with lots of weapons and support mechanisms to help you with the journey ahead. Although later in the game they seem a bit too under powered for what they represent especially after grinding your way though out the game to make your favorite builds only to realize the latter enemies need more and more hit points to defeat.While the game admirably tries to help with this by letting the player bypass already defeated bosses and lets you acquire heath and special abilities prior to the next stage, The ability to keep one current (upgraded weapons build) even at restart  of a mission would have helped greatly with the grind and repetitive aspect of Dreamscaper. And I know that this a rouge game which Dreamscaper represents  but even after mastering weapons to 100% I'm still not sure why I should be required to level up those weapons again.. say a sword to level V when I have already done so 6 times previously.With all that being said, Some casual confusing camera angles, Annoying slow down of (some) Lucid attacks  hold back Dreamscaper from being a must have thought provoking game for the $30 mark but for the $9.99 mark it's really worth  the price for admission for this thought - provoking journey though one own potential emotional state.

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is a competent rougelike with a lot of unlockables and a decent combat system.Did I finish it? Absolutely not. ...but it was fun for some time.It's a nice little game to spend a 30 minutes on every once a while.The game is about going into your dreams and fighting until you wake up. There are bosses between stages and the enemy variety is decent. Later levels raise the difficulty and introduce new hazards. They also increase the enemy size which is an issue because the particle system and flashy vfx makes it really difficult to see what's happening on screen when enemies attack. Levels are also wierdly designed as I got stuck on geometry multiple times. The combat is quite good, there multiple attacks, parrys you will never need to use, special attacks I kept forgeting about and dodges that are sometimes so slow they literally get you killed. All these depend on RNG, so if by chance you end up with a better dodge or a special attack you can make it quite far.There is also an other game in Dreamscaper. Once you are awake you can go around a town and make friends on a visual novel-esque game. These friends provide additional buffs to combat or certain abilities, once you "fully upgrade" them. You do that Sims style, by making them gifts and talking to them. The combat focused dreams and the melancholic visual novel are quite a bad mix. Perhaps this narrative should have been told differently, because right now it just breaks the flow of the game. There isn't really a story, the talks with NPCs felt more like a series of small talks. They don't complement the combat gameplay, they just make it more tedious, because you have to go through them to acquire their buffs. Thankfully, these are completely skippable and you can ignore this aspect of the game for the most part.There is so much stuff to unlock and master, so the game does get grindy, but the combat and weapon variety make up for it, even though stunlocking enemies is basically the best strategy even in late game areas.The combat does have its issues, namely scaling. Between stages your weapons more or less need to do double damage to remain viable. That means you have to pray to the RNG gods to drop you a better weapon a soon as you enter a new stage, otherwise you'll be hitting bullet sponge enemies endlessly. This means it's impossible to focus a build, because switching your weapons as soon as you find a new one is unavoidable. So why is there even a class system that focuses on specific playstyles?

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: 8/10A really accessible fast-paced action RPG roguelike that anyone can play. You explore dreams and nightmares. There are 6 floors that are procedurally generated (dungeon crawler layout) with each of them a boss level. Choose and improve your equipment on the way to overcome the enemies you encounter. Strong visuals, strong combat and high replayability. The story and the enemy variety are for me however a bit lacking.~ GAMEPLAY ~Responsive and crisp combat. Discover room per room as you progress through each of the 6 procedurally generated floors. Keep your eye out for a secret room and resources that can help you. Find or buy items to make your character stronger. Each unknown room (blank square on the minimap) can hold a small variety of enemies.Before going to the dungeon, you can improve your character by spending resources to discover or improve new skills. This is also where you meet and develop relationships with residents of your town.Gameplay is very accessible. There is even an option (lucid dreaming) to ease your progress for each run. It gives you additional defense each time you die and need to restart.☐ Bad☐ Not special✅ Good☐ Beautiful~ GRAPHICS ~The dungeon crawler rooms and the combat action effects are beautiful. Impressive for an indie game.☐ Bad☐ Not special☐ Good✅ Beautiful~ AUDIO ~The dynamic soundtrack is on point. It’s cozy and lively, depending on the situation you’re in. It suits the game.☐ Bad☐ Not special☐ Good✅ Beautiful~ WORTH BUYING ~☐ No☐ Wait for sale✅ Yes

_childDocuments_.review: Short Review: 2 thumbs way up for me. Incredible gameplay, UI, and design polish with very immersive concepts that marry the gameplay and story, much like Hades, and has an excellent, accessible combat system in the vein of Wizard of Legend and Mana Spark without sacrificing the ability to provide yourself with challengesIt's been awhile since i played a great Rogue Like on the same level combat-wise as Wizard of Legend and Mana Spark. Every hit is tactile and weighty, and the variety of combat options and styles is boundless. Story wise, this works a lot like Hades, which is a positive. People looking for similarities will find this game will satiate their need, though to what degree will depend on the player's preferences. _childDocuments_.review: Can I, in good conscience, recommend a game I never finished? Goodness, that one sentence could probably be this whole review but stick with me here, I do have a point to make.It's worth mentioning that I am a huge fan of games like Gris and Manifold garden so Dreamscaper was definitely rubbing me up the right way from the word go. That being said, it's also the first in that category of Thinky Art Games that I couldn't finish and I don't fully know why. I never finished a play sesh thinking "well that's enough of that!" I just... stopped.Anywho, here's the boring technical part where I say things like "good sounds for your ear holes, good graphics for your eye holes, and good writing... well, writing certainly. Quite a lot of writing."That could be a part of the problem actually. While the characters are, on the surface, interesting and well rounded, I find I tire of them quickly. Brings to mind conversations I used to have with my writers' group about character voice. You could take a sentence out of any conversation in Dreamscaper and without visual clues, I would have no idea who said it. That is what we academics call a major whoopsie doodle, if you'll forgive the dense jargon. It pulls me out of the fiction and makes it feel like every character is an author insert trying to make a point that the author personally cares about. This is where a writer needs to hone the ability to allow their own opinions to shape their characters, but not define them. Ultimately the characters you write should be allowed to express opinions that you don't agree with or care about things that you don't.For all my whinging, there is a fun game to be played here. I enjoyed the dungeon crawling and the combat which is smooth, visceral and varied etc etc, but at the end of the day, this feels very much like a game where the gameplay is intended to serve the story, not vice versa. I felt like the game was punishing me for just wanting to focus on the core gameplay loop and not invest in the world or story. I guess that's fair, and if I carefully wrote a book for someone to read, I would be a bit upset if all they wanted to do was pick it up and whack people on the head with it.Look, I do recommend Dreamscaper, I just can't say it's as exceptional as I first thought it might be. After all, how good can a game be if you lose interest and stop just befo

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that deserved more attention than it got.  It's a solid roguelite with a good story underpinning it.  It definitely has its flaws, but offers features rarely seen in roguelites.  You get a bevy of melee, ranged, special attacks, dodges, and blocks that can all be upgraded and changed throughout each run.  The options truly are endless and it keeps each run very interesting.  I also loved the ability to perfect time blocks to reflect projectiles or off balance tough opponents for a follow up melee beat down.  Each attack/block felt tactical and purposeful (e.g., making sure to combine elements for additional damage).  Button mashing will not help you in this game.The main reason you may not want to try this game is that it's hard - very hard.  I just beat the game on 0 level difficulty (all bosses without skipping any) and only ~9% of players have ever done this.  Even on difficulty 3/8, only 3.9% of players have done the same thing.  The enemies in the later levels frequently require special attacks/ranged options because they are aggressive, coordinated, and unrelenting.   Some of this is artificially inflated by the camera angle and some of the optional skills being not very useful in actual combat (e.g., long casting time, small attack range).  Also, some mechanics are fairly useless in the late game like perfect timing melee attacks.  You just don't have time to wait for the visual cues for a little bit more damage when staying put might end up with you dead.Overall, it's a very enjoyable experience that despite its flaws, will be a good find for anyone who likes the harder side of games like Hades, Cult of the Lamb, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: I came across Dreamscaper after playing 200 hours of Hades. I was looking for similar games that could recapture some of the magic of discovery and progression that made Hades such a delightful experience.Dreamscaper is not Hades. There probably isn't any game that can measure up to the experience of playing Hades, and there probably won't be for a long while. But a lot of the same elements are there, and I did really enjoy Dreamscaper for what it was.The "story" in Dreamscaper is more of a personal journey. There aren't really "events occurring" so much as a character working through her issues. The supporting characters are fairly interesting, though not quite on par with the literally larger-than-life dynamic personalities of Hades. But to be fair, the characters in Dreamscaper are ordinary folks, not mythological deities.The overall atmosphere of the game is "nostalgic." It's an exploration of the protagonist's childhood memories, so that makes sense. There is a very different energy here than Hades' cheeky and horny angst. It's more sad and calm.In terms of the feel of playing the game, Dreamscaper has a lot of similarities to Hades. There is a varied arsenal of different weapons and abilities, progression through randomized levels with boss fights, a wide selection of permanent character upgrades to purchase using resources gathered during runs, a relationship system to grow closer with the characters, etc. Unlike Hades, every aspect of your loadout can change throughout a run: you can swap out weapons and abilities as you encounter new and better ones along the way. It's both more flexible than Hades and less; you're not locked in to one weapon for the entire run, and there are many more weapons and abilities (and combinations thereof); but with more randomness comes less control, so it's a lot harder to craft and hone a particular build in Dreamscaper than in Hades. A lot of the "builds" are elemental damage modifiers, in which all you're trying to do is find a bunch of gear that (say) deals Lightning damage or increases your Lightning damage dealt. The upgrades are largely "number get bigger," and while it can be satisfying to get a bunch of cool multipliers, it does feel less "combo"y or "breakable" than Hades (though there are certainly some very powerful and broken-feeling builds you can end up with).The gameplay is challenging, like Hades, though perhaps slightly less. Like Hades, a lot of your ability to clear rooms and defeat bosses effectively comes from learning their attack patterns and timings. I do wish there were more variety to the enemies, as many of them are just "the guy from the last level but he is stronger and has more abilities now" (though that criticism applies to Hades as well). The boss fights are by and large much easier once you learn their patterns, though there are still a few that can be tough for certain builds. The "hard version" of bosses are definitely a force to be reckoned with, though.The art and music are attractive and inviting. It's much more The Sims than Guilty Gear, but in a way that fits the atmosphere nicely. It's stylized in a very different way than Hades, but it works in its own way.The developers are also very community-oriented and are responsive to community input through their Discord. The Hades developers probably are too, but I have no direct experience interacting with them.So in conclusion, if you liked Hades because of its horny angst, badass metal riffs, mythological themes, and bloody humor, you may not have much interest in Dreamscaper. But if you liked Hades because of its randomized runs, variety of weapons and builds, feeling of progression, challenging boss fights, and dynamic cast of characters with complicated relationships, then you should absolutely pick up Dreamscaper. And if you didn't like Hades, then you probably stopped reading this review after the first paragraph.

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is a new Early Access action RPG with both rogue-like and rogue-lite aspects, and to be quite frank, it’s rather beautiful! There are two general areas in Dreamscaper. The first is the dreamworld, where you progress through various levels and memories, battling your inner demons along the way. The second is the waking world, where you talk to your friends and colleagues, and craft gifts to increase your relationship with each of them. You get introduced to both worlds during the tutorial, along with the different gameplay aspects of each; combat, crafting, talking, etc.The first thing that grabbed my attention was the style of graphics. Dreamscaper is simply beautiful. The different dreamworld levels, waking world locations, characters, and enemies all look incredible! None of the characters have faces, or at least, no facial features, they’re simply eyeless, noseless, mouthless, expressionless folk. I thought this a little creepy to begin with, but the creepiness quickly subsided with each conversation. It’s pretty amazing how well feelings can be portrayed without facial expressions!That brings me onto the waking world. You wake up, crafts some gifts, and go to the different locations to talk to the other characters and give them gifts to increase your relationships, unlocking new conversations, equipment, abilities, and influences/perks along the way. Each character has their own unique personality, and prefer different gifts, but the in game notes help a lot when it comes to figuring out who would like which gift the most! Does somebody like cycling? Maybe I’ll give them a cycling helmet! There are some less obvious ones though. That may sound a little boring or repetitive, and I thought the same at first, but that didn't last long, and you'll see why in a moment!The crafting is basic but effective, with only three different materials. The catch is that each material can be have one of six different levels or qualities; poor, common/+1, uncommon/+2, rare/+3, epic/+4, and legendary/+5. Nothing really out of the ordinary for an RPG. There are, however, quite a few different gifts to be crafted, and you won’t be finding too many materials too quickly. There’s also a loadout window where you can craft weapons and equipment to start out with on your next run, rather than leaving it up to the RNG Gods. At the moment they appear to be one-time use weapons, meaning there’s not much incentive to craft anything other than gifts until you’ve maxed out all of the relationships. Their most recent patch has hugely improved this for the poor quality weapons, making those free to craft, so now everybody can start with their favourite weapons! There are still some player convenience and quality of life improvements that could be done here, and I have no doubt the devs will be introducing those in a future early access update.What surprised me the most about Dreamscaper were the conversations. I thought the most gripping part would have been the dreamworld and the combat, but after a few discussions with different characters, I started to become more and more invested in the waking world. What struck me the most was how real and relatable the conversations were. Cassidy’s (your character) side of the conversations, in particular, really resonated with me! I was actually pretty gutted once I’d maxed every character relationship and there were no more conversations.While I really loved the conversations, the dreamworld was also good fun, and certainly challenging! The first level and boss worked as a pretty nice intro into the world, and gave more of an idea of what to expect on later levels, but the difficulty ramps up pretty quick. It doesn’t help that I completely suck, but I like to think it’s difficult too, and it's not just that I suck! The fact that each weapon has a different range, each dodge has a different style and stride, and there are often several different enemy types, traps, and red pits that all cause damage, makes the gameplay and combination of equipment both exciting and difficult to master! The tagline “Dream. Die. Wake. Repeat” (from the Steam description snippet) definitely makes sense, and fits perfectly with my experience. Their most recent update lowers the difficulty somewhat, so there may be a little less dying involved now. I managed to reach the final level prior to the patch, but only beat the final boss after the difficulty was lowered.While you may think that a game with six levels wouldn’t take long to beat, or couldn’t have much variation in it, you’d be completely wrong! The procedural maps, different enemies, weapons, dodges, shields, abilities, influences, and keepsakes, combined with the different qualities and random modifiers, make for a very different experience with every run! I loved unlocking and discovering everything! My favourite melee weapons turned out to be the Koregan/trident and Mallory/scythe, mainly due to their range, but they also looked awesome, and I absolutely loved the thunder step dodge!I usually wouldn’t go for this kind of game, generally because I’m not a fan of replaying the same thing over and over again, but it didn’t feel that way with Dreamscaper! Every run was different and posed new challenges, and trying to find the right balance/build for my playstyle was fun and exciting! It’s only two weeks into early access, but you could almost mistake it for a fully released game! The realism of the waking world content was incredible! How they got me tearing up over a conversation about ice-cream, I don’t know! I feel all it’s missing at the moment are boss fights at the end of every level (only active on three levels at the moment), and some end game waking world content, both of which the developers have mentioned are on the way, along with a few quality of life improvements. It’s also awesome to see developers getting so involved with community feedback (through Steam discussions and Dreamscaper Discord) and implementing suggestions into the game without ruining what's already there! Hats off to you, Afterburner Studios! You’ve created a truly amazing game, and I look forward to seeing more story progression and additional content and improvements throughout early access, and into the full release!

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty enjoyable roguelite here. It's got a somewhat different tone and pacing than your bog-standard affair, but if you've played any games with Binding of Isaac style mechanics, this should slip on like a nice glove after you dream a few times.game is two-fold : main chunk is you going through randomly created dungeons ( aka, lucid dream mode ) you start with random melee wep, random ranged wep - and you can in typcial rogelite fashion: obtain new weps in the runs themselves along with skills to use, stat boosts - and memories - more on those later.the second portion of the game is your Waking hours - here you are given a few places you can visit, each with a time it takes to travel there, each location tends to have different NPCs depending on when you arrive, and the goal of the waking hours is to converse with npcs to build relationships, or gift them items; these in turn provide you with more items to add to your drop pool in the runs themselves, and oftentimes you're given some insight into our MC's world.The flow feels pretty good, you have a dark souls-esque dodge roll, and shield parry move - which are vital to beating the bosses. I defeated the very first boss, and it was actually fun finally getting it's patterns down to the point where I was anticipating it's moves to be on the attack. game looks amazing, it's a very beautiful game, imo - and it runs rather well.controls are tight and responsive - it's your standard twin stick formula here - deflecting works as it should, dodging is fine, all the mechanics ( including how your ranged shots do have ammo ) work fine, it's a decent system.SO back to memories - in the lucid dream sections, you sometimes find a sprkyl green shimmer - these unlock memories for the character - you get some lore, ( which is typed out on the bottom of the screen, you don't even need to stay in the area you triggered it in )  and these unlock yet more things for you to find and play with in th runs.I get worried whenever  dev makes a game with a clear art style in mind, and a certain presentation - I'm pretty sure ppl will label this as " pretentious " especially after they see nobody has a face. BUt it's not. SO far, I have been enjoying the mysterious lilworld built here, and the odd characters inside it.COmbat is fun, the dungoens mix up events enough to not feel stale, even after you get your butt whooped by the same boss a few times, and repeat the dream to try again.It's in early access, nearly feature-complete, but the devs want to give it more spit and polish ; more weps, more levels, more events, more interactivity between dreams - and what you have right now is a very decent chunk with obvious love and attention being given.I would highly recommend this game if you're as into roguelites as I am - perhaps not if you are a diehard, ETG on turbo without being hit once, and no damage on all bosses clear - sort of person. this game will challenge you in a vein closer to dark souls, not super fast hyperkinetic combat, but practical and planned purposeful combat.

_childDocuments_.review: A roguelike action game with very fluid controls and a smorgasbord of weapons, magic spells, evasive maneuvers, and other cool tricks to play with.  The game feels very nice with a controller and is even passable with keyboard and mouse.  Gameplay has a nice difficulty curve and is challenging, with an option to turn down the difficulty if necessary.  Would be nice to have one to turn it up as well in the future.It tells a story of a yuppie in the big city, and while it hits many relatable notes with people of similar age, the story is still a bit barebones.  It feels like going through the motions with no cohesive main plot.  Maybe that's just how life is though.  There are constantly updates to the game though, so I expect that to be filled out later.Overall the game is very solid and fun to play, but the story that is told feels somewhat empty, like a lot of separate dialogues with no connecting threads.  Good for fans of roguelikes, which often have an extremely shallow or no story at all, but the game seems to be teasing a deeper story without following through.

_childDocuments_.review: The basic gameplay seems like very standard ARPG + Roguelike at first, but the waking and dream aspects of the game constantly enhancing one another keeps the game constantly fresh and fun. It always feels like you're making progress, even when you're losing to the same boss over and over. The game switches between the ARPG dungeon crawl mode and the waking-life social interaction mode frequently enough that neither becomes frustrating before the other offers a change of pace. The difficulty curve also increases at a comfortable level that gradually puts on pressure. There are also a lot of nice quality of life features like quick-travel to previously explored rooms that make the game have little filler or downtime. The main character's backstory is also revealed gradually, through item descriptions, conversations, and memories recovered from her dreams. There's definitely some specific traumas she's dealing with that I haven't fully learned about yet, but a lot of the background details of her life feel very relevant and relatable for anyone who is going through or has gone through a quarter-life crisis within the past 10ish years. Also, the music is beautiful and got stuck in my head within 2 hours of starting the game. Dreamscaper is a lot of fun to play and every time I start the game, I lose track of how long has passed in my own world while I am busy exploring Cassidy's two lives. Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: It's nice to look at for a bit, and the dream world and real world premise is a neat one for a roguelite. Unfortunately, there's nothing else I can really say positive about this title. The first map can be a little challenging as you learn the ropes, but eventually, it becomes a cakewalk, while the second map is a chore with a boss that's exponentially harder than the first. While I like difficulty to ramp up, it's too steep, and - more importantly - you have to play through the first area each time, which is incredibly boring. Since the first map is so easy and you have to keep playing through it, I would get obliterated in the second map, then had to suffer through the yawn-inducing first map again and again. It's like mastering a Mega Man map, but not knowing the boss' attack patterns and only having one life on every single run, which would make for a pretty miserable Mega Man experience, wrecking the map and then getting frustrated when the boss of the map is the only moment of interest, and it's fleeting.I didn't experience any satisfying sense of progression unlocks, the real world feels like "the Seattle experience" of coffee shops, libraries, parks, and other hangouts for emo millenials to feel pretentious and deep in, while the "characters" around town are essentially silhouettes who say one or two uninteresting lines, and want gifts on an incredibly gamey, point-based system (yes, I realize this IS a game, but all immersion and characterization is ruined, while the game takes itself so seriously that there's no winking parody feel like in Dead Estate).It's not a terrible game, but I wouldn't go so far as to call it a good one. Each attempted run made me dislike the game more than the prior one, which is the antithesis of what a good roguelite should do. Neon Chrome, Rogue Legacy, Dead Estate...those games taught me things through the gameplay which made me get better, there were little rewards/unlocks or pieces of knowledge which made the next attempt(s) more interesting or fun, and I just had to finish them. I just scowl when I look at Dreamscaper on my games list now, and I'm going to feel a sense of relief and satisfaction when I uninstall it. Get those other games I mentioned instead. They're far more worth your time than this sub-par roguelite.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played quite a number of rogue-lites recently, but  is different than most. By including the social aspects of a Persona game, it's more story-driven than other games of its genre. But does this unprecedented spin on the genre work, or is it better left untouched?It's been ten years since it happened. Cassidy hasn't been able to keep it off her mind since. The tragic moment still lingers in her memories and has led her down a path of loneliness and depression. Seeking a new life, Cassidy moves half-way across the country to Redhaven. The crowded streets are a shift from the quiet hometown of Backhill, and she struggles to fit in with the way of society.The sad news is that life doesn't always go the way you want it.Instead of pursuing her dreams as an artist, Cassidy becomes yet another link in the chain of daily life. A dull job at a boring office. Haunted by nightmares, she's met with unrest at every turn, even in her slumbers. But why did these nightmares begin, and can she stop them? While not the focal point of the game, her tale is still concise and engaging to follow. is divided into two modes. During the day, Cassidy can socialize with people she encounters, forging new bonds. In the style of , relationships bestow new powers. When asleep, she will find herself in so-called Dreamscapes - darkened versions of places she holds dear. Invaded by fearsome creatures, they are not a safe place to stay, and Cassidy will have to face her fears when venturing forward.There are six Dreamscapes, four of which are unique, the other two being harder versions of previous areas. Each consists of a multitude of connected rooms holding treasures, enemies, and alike. Various loot can be picked up and equipped, making way for multiple playstyles. Suit yourself! At the end awaits a challenge, either in the form of a boss battle or a hardened enemy. I would guess that the latter are temporary placeholders.Despite the procedural generation threshold,  managed to craft many memorable locations. The snowy landscapes and cozy homes of Backhill stand apart from the neon-lit nightlife of Redhaven. Various buildings can be interacted with, giving the player an idea of their surroundings and what meanings they held for Cassidy. 's locations feel more personal than those of any other rogue-lite experience, and it's one of the game's many strengths.Fundamentally, combat is quite simple. You've got your standard array of attacks: a quick attack and a slower, more powerful one. Your ranged weapon is useful for attacking enemies you don't dare approach. Additionally, various tools are in your aid. Bombs offer a destructive way of combat, but can also remove obstacles. I preferred to utilize lucid attacks (special abilities on a cooldown) to take down enemies one by one. You can also slow down time -style, but keep in mind that this will drain your Lucid meter. There's an array of weapons to choose from: slugger bats, water guns and katanas are only a few examples!I found combining these to be extra satisfying, and I'd encourage you to do as well. Enemies can feel like damage sponges if all you do is slash away at them. Utilize everything at your disposal, and you'll dispose of enemies faster than you can say the game's title. You'll have to be precise about your movement. Otherwise, the situation can quickly turn dire. Actions such as parrying are of utmost importance, as they can deal a crushing blow to the enemy. The bottom line is that 's combat is fun and simple to learn, an ideal combination if I do say so myself.As touched on briefly earlier, Cassidy can socialize with various personalities found throughout Redhaven. Currently, there are six in total, although I expect more to be added. When approaching someone, you can choose between talking to them or gifting them an item. Both increase your status with them. When your friendship reaches a new level, you'll unlock new gear.Cassidy can craft gifts with resources found through exploring her dreams. It's a good idea to keep a person's preferences in mind when doing so, as giving them a gift they love will further your bonds even more. The more you get to know a person, the more interests of theirs will become clear. If socializing ain't your thing, you can also spend these resources on customizing your starting loadout, picking whatever weapons you prefer.The story is told mainly through conversations with your friends. The problem here is that these stories don't run parallel due to how the friendship systems work. Cassidy can be depressed when talking to one person, and upbeat when conversing with another. I don't know how they could've avoided this issue, but it doesn't make it less apparent. I also ran into situations where a character would marvel over my appearance, shouting, "It's been months" despite chatting with them the day before.Indie games often make up for their lower budgets with more personality across the board, something which can also be applied to ! The game uses a soothing art style to express itself. I can't put my finger on how to describe it. I've included a picture below to illustrate what I mean. A picture is worth a thousand words, as they say.Accompanied by a beautiful soundtrack, the game truly is exceptional to look at and listen to. I can only wait in excitement for what is next for  after  is complete. Suffice to say, they have a lot of skill and passion, and it shines through every aspect of this game.  is not only a good rogue-lite, but it also comes with a touching story about dealing with depression. It's an unusual combination for sure, but it works quite well. Although the game has a few problems, it didn't ruin my enjoyment. I can only recommend the game. | 1920x1080

Well-varied, in Ranged, Melee and Special attacks, plus a variety of passive and not-so-passive additions.Story is something that resonates with anyone who has experience in mental health. _childDocuments_.review: This is a must-try game.  The way pieces of the past slowly get filled in, while the game itself sticks to pretty familiar action roguelike elements, was very unique and interesting.  So was the personification of the emotions behind them.  As a labor of love from a small studio, the experience is worth way more than the price.Minor gripes, in case anyone somehow reads this drivel:** The balancing isn't bad, but it's a bit too up-and-down from trivially easy to "what just happened" (for me, at least), then your whole run restarts. I know it comes with the genre, but the slog it takes to get to the later levels just to get used to the different enemies is a bit demoralizing.** Please make the damage numbers bigger, ideally an option to change the size.  Only criticals I land seem to pop up big.  When I get crushed by a huge hit, it shows up in 6pt font in the midst of battle effects, and there doesn't seem to be any other feedback.  Random hits like this happen a lot, too, and damage goes quickly in this game.** Parrying is a mandatory skill it seems, but the game engine doesn't make it work very well IMO.  It's a fixed camera angle, and parrying is direction-sensitive to hit.  So you have bullets coming from angles that are very hard to gauge - including when the bullet is actually behind your character during the timing window - which creates unnecessary frustration.** I know it was an intentional art style, but the no faces is super creepy.Those are only observations by an old man in the gaming world.  Thanks for creating such a great game experience!

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper's every bit as cool as I'd hoped it be from the promotional material I saw.  It's one of only a hand full of roguelites that adds some real story and gravitas to the game external to just the moment to moment combat.  What I was surprised by was just how well a lot of the theme comes through in the game play and character interactions. I found myself almost always leaving the house, even though they just let you run back to back dreams if you'd like.  I did this because...I felt like it was the best for Cassidy.  There's no real consequence to choosing to just sleep immediately when you get back from work, but the game's a lot about just...finding ways to get along in the world, and I felt like just sleeping all the time to escape wasn't the play.  I'm not usually the type to let characters get in the way of efficiency in games like this, so this was a pretty cool departure  for me.Everything you do is pretty well contextualized as well, from the "spells" (which are called Lucid Attacks) to the names and characteristics of the bosses, to the flavor text on some of the items.  It's just a very cohesive game, and I've enjoyed all of my time in it so far drawing parallels from Cassidy's struggles in her dreams to things in real life we all deal with.Regarding the combat portion of the game itself, it's an alright level of challenge. I'd put it on the easier side of top down 3d action roguelites I've played.  I hope to see some rebalancing around stuff like the Lucid Attacks because they in can often invalidate some of the other combat options due to their sheer power and infinite usage.  This makes hit and run/kiting styles not only incredibly strong, but also often simply the best way to play given some of the best mob-clearing lucid attacks are on a very low cool down and still have moderate range.  I have played a lot of roguelites of this style, however, so it's possible I'm just used to how they typically play out.Overall, I recommend the game and I'm excited to see what comes next.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. It has a very nice art style, it's easy to get into and understand, but the combat deepens as you play it. It's just right, taking skill and concentration but not being just some insane enemy or projectile spam that's hard to react to. When you die, you are aware of why, it's a fair game with opportunities for you to hone your skill as you play. The loop is very satisfying, I really enjoy how after doing a run, there's always these cool down activities to do to mix up the pace. The story bits woven into the game are satisfying too, it's interesting without bogging the game down with super long cutscenes or some kind of exposition dump that that feels shoehorned. Interesting enemy and boss designs, I just haven't had a game I found just plain fun like this in a while.I did have some occasional hitching. Might be just because of how old my machine is, def I would follow the dev's recommendation and try to close out anything running in the background. I think if there was any genuine criticism I have other than those rare performance issues I had, the treasures you pick up in dungeons can look similar sometimes, they're all glowing orb-looking things, but you're going to grab everything anyway, so it's not a huge deal. Keys for example though look the most "unique" of all the objects, I wish they were just a little more differentiated like that.But overall, this is a fun game, it's way too easy to just get sucked in for hours going from dungeons, to managing and upgrading things in the waking world, to doing another dungeon run. And then you look at the clock and realize you've how long you've been playing the game, and it only gets better and more engaging the more time you invest in it.You should but this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've put 10 hours into the game and still keep going back for more. I picked up the game because I thought the combat system looked cool. I always like games that reward skill and timing instead of just button mashing. What I like about Dreamscaper is that each weapon has a unique rhythm to it. As I played I got to experience more weapons and have found several that I enjoy using because the rhythm feels great.I also like the amount of variability in abilities, from the way you block, to the way you dodge, to the "magic" you get to use. I have found favorites that let me customize play style or change it up. I'm particularly fond of "BAMF" dodging.As for the story, the system for unlocking and discovering the story feel a little slow, but at the same time I've had some great "Oh Wow" moments with parts of the story, so it is engaging. One big hope is that they develop more music variety for the game. The background music is "dreamy" and gives that ambiance of being in a dream, but some rooms are nightmares and I'd love for the room music to vary depending on the challenges. I hope this is in the pipeline.Overall, I'd give a recommendation to anyone who likes ARPG combat that is customizable and enjoys a challenge. The dreams get progressively harder so the challenge continues to build until you fail and you do it again. There is enough variation in dreams that I keep coming back and I look forward to seeing this developed more.

Speaking of those relationships, they are your permanent upgrades to make runs easier, along with spending certain currencies not lost upon death.  Overall, I can't find one thing to complain about with this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool weapons.  The game is playable with mouse and keyboard, though you may need to reconfigure the controls a great deal.Blocking and hitting are greatly complicated because the main character doesn't seem to want to face toward the enemy.  They could do a lot better with the character automatically correcting facing when the block or attack keys are triggered.  This is 2021.  Let the character move an inch to the left and the shield 20 degrees over.Waking world progression is slow, full of awkward, cringey dialogue, and provides minimal benefits for combat in the dream world.  Even with the game being a roguelite, I felt frustrated with the lack of progression I felt when repeatedly losing to the boss.  I can't really save up resources to grow stronger the way I want.  I also had trouble fighting the boss at full health because of the character repeatedly facing the wrong way while blocking against mediocre mooks.Ranged attacks are very slow, which greatly complicates the battle against Fear.  You are in a pool of water and attacked by a shark (which represents Fear).  You need to hit the mines in the water to do damage and stun him. It's also a struggle to reach fear while he's stunned, lay in some follow up blows before he recovers and starts swimming away again.Oh yeah.  And no one in this world has a face.

_childDocuments_.review: For what it is, this game is a beautiful piece of art that clearly had a lot of love poured into it. Unfortunately, it feels more like an interactive art piece than a game. The concept of the gameplay being split between waking-world interactions and dream battles is an interesting one, but functionally it feels like two different games - neither of which were compelling enough to make me want to play more. Even at two hours, I was already forcing myself to continue on.  Now at 3.8 hours I am confident nothing will change that will make me enjoy this game, and I have requested a refund.The dream world is where the "dungeon-crawling" takes place, and in between runs, the player is returned to the waking world where they must travel to various sites within a city to level-up the character by visiting various sites, speaking to and building relationships with NPCs, and interacting with multiple locations to access the leveling menus. For someone who enjoys slowly unraveling a story over time by interacting with NPCs and revisiting the same sites repeatedly to get new interactions, this game may be appealing. My problem is that I do not enjoy such mechanics. Unfortunately, in order to level the character, it takes 5+ minutes in between each run to visit the various waking world sites, interact with NPCs, and level up attributes. It is incredibly grindy and not what I want to do in-between dungeon runs.As far as the combat and interactions go within the dream world, the enemies all feel very one dimensional and same-y. The rooms look beautifully designed and are visually interesting, lending to the somberness of the story, but it feels as though the gameplay loop took a back seat to telling a story and creating an otherwise immersive piece of art. Nothing about the battle gameplay had me wanting to come back for more. Every loop kinda felt like: "oh I died? Huh. Didn't realize I was out of health, Oh well. I guess I gotta go talk to some NPCs now..."In the end, it felt kinda like going to an arcade to play a pinball machine that is supposed to be really good, but then you find out you have to walk through the wing of an art gallery and read the plaques on all the paintings to appreciate the art before you get to play any pinball....and then it turns out that the pinball machine only has the flippers and bumpers on a flat plane...no ramps, no loop-de-loops, no multi-ball combos, in other words: not that exciting.... And then it turns out that every time you lose a ball, you have to go back through the art gallery to read more plaques.... So then you're like, "well maybe I don't really want to play pinball after all".That was my experience anyway. On another note, I think it's weird that anyone would compare this to the wildly successful rogue-like that takes place in the underworld. It's nothing like that game and is misleading to even make the comparison (which is why I won't name that other game here). I had high hopes based on the game trailer and the pictures that this would be a very different but fun game, but it turns out what was here just wasn't enough to keep me entertained.
