_childDocuments_.review: One of the best roguelites I've played in recent memory. Key touchpoints:* The world is beautifully designed, both graphically and narratively.* The rogue-lite elements are fantastically implemented, leading to a wide swath of build variation and a purposeful feeling of progression.* The variation in well-implemented and diverse weapon/movesets, skills, and attributes leads to incredibly diverse gameplay.* The skill curve with perfect strikes really amps up the feeling of accomplishment and raises the ceiling for mechanical skill progression.All in all, great game with elements of Dead Cells, Hades, BPM - Bullets Per Minute, Wizard of Legend, etc. Highly recommended to sink a few dozen hours into.My plea to the developer -- please, if this game reaches a level of commercial success that permits it, add co-operative play. The community would explode and propel this game to new levels of recognition. If it's not in the cards for Dreamscaper, then perhaps for a sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: Originally, I had given this game a thumbs-up. But a lot of the annoyances have caused it to wear out its welcome. This has to do with two major issues that cause the experience to sour after a while. My pros list still stands. The game has buckets of style, and frankly that's what makes it such a disappointment. Many of my issues could be instantly fixed by the developer simply admitting that the game's universe is too small to warrant the grind, removing the mind-numbing repetition (especially the puzzles) and speeding up overall progression.The biggest problem is grind. The Minesweeper and "line up the pipes" minigames were fun perhaps the first 5 times. They were tolerable the next 20 or 30 times. After 50 or so, I have really started to dread seeing them. You can't skip them because you need the rewards to have a chance in hell of surviving the late game. Your chance of solving the puzzles is 100%. So it's basically just a chore, like cleaning a toilet, that has to be done. Then there's the ability, presented as a bonus, that allows you to gain double resources until you're hit for the first time in a run. I now see that as a disingenuously positive spin on "if you get hit, you get half resources for the rest of the game." Getting hit even once means, if you're trying to get unlocks, that you should probably quit the game immediately and start over. Which doubles down on the grind.The second problem is there's just not enough content or variety to warrant the sheer volume of replay necessary to get completion. The same couple enemies, same few locations, the same few bosses -- these are all tiresome long before you get more than 50% game completion. When a run ends, I don't say "I want to go again!" I say, "I don't feel like seeing all of  again right away." I don't want to do more Minesweeper. I don't want to fight the same three enemies only to miss a dodge after 5 minutes in and have to restart so I don't lose half my resource collection., an action Roguelite, is a game that has a lot of love in it. As an art piece, it's beautiful, with a consistent stylization that serves the surreal theme of the mechanics. While it has some serious shortcomings, its overall thematic and artistic verve help shore up the repetitive gameplay.The game reminds me in some ways of . The gameplay is entirely different. The connection is that both have a very deliberate and carefully executed visual and auditory style that works with the gameplay without getting in its way. Indeed, there's a heavy sword in the game that I'm fairly certain is an homage to Red's blade-dragging trek across the abstract landscape of .Persistent character development comes between runs in the form of the main character's budding friendships in a city to where she has recently moved. Learning their tastes, bringing them thoughtful gifts, and taking time for self-care frame the stat improvements as self actualization. It could easily have been an eye-rolling pop psychology self-satire, but it comes off as sincere.In addition,  has a lot of quality-of-life features for an indie game. Combat proceeds from room to room, like many roguelikes of the past, but this is the first I've seen that has fast travel built in. There is a definite sense that the game is meant to be playable and there's an unmistakable attention to detail in the UI.That's not to say I don't have criticisms. I have a lot of them:For me, the most obnoxious thing in the game by far was the way the characters develop their relationships through stilted conversation that is cut up into incomprehensible sentence fragments. Imagine trying to read this review if it was written like this, with each line appearing on its own, one by one:This is how the characters interact. I think we're supposed to imagine them speaking naturally, and natural dialogue style is fine, . You can't spoon feed us two or three words at a time like this. The way to create the illusion of natural speech is to give us an entire comprehensible text and let our brains turn them into lifelike interactions. I was constantly losing the thread of the conversation. There's a famous meme that demonstrates how you can udernsantd a sntenece eevn if the lteters are scbrmlad as long as the first and last letters stay put. This is about how the brain works with written language. We use those starting and ending boundaries to make sense of words. Not to get too deeply into it, but this also somewhat applies to sentences. We perceive boundaries (which are indicated in English with lots of punctuation), and our brains do a trick that stitches things together into meaningful segments. You can't split a sentence up at random and trickle it out. This game ignores that. You're constantly trying to remember during the 8th or 9th spoon-fed pair of words what the sentence was about. This is hideously destructive to the emotional resonance that could be created with these characters.The game's biggest gameplay weakness is a lack of variety and a thoroughgoing repetition in playthroughs. While you get to change weapons, they don't feel much different. Whether you get synergy with their damage types and the items you find is down to luck. With the random selection of equipment through the game, you very rarely get to establish an actual build, so builds come to feel more cosmetically different rather than usefully unique. You can elect to use a specific type of passive in your playthrough, such as "increased lightning damage" or "increased ranged damage", but since you're liable to quickly encounter a weapon that doesn't match your choice but outperforms it by double, you quickly learn that the only good choices are the most generally applicable, nullifying the apparent choice.Collecting resources that are used in the waking world, which is the part of the game that persists, is a definite grind. You can complete the game many times over long before you unlock your real-life friendships, self-improvement, and inspirations. Which brings me to something else -- this "waking world" looks and feels just as dreamlike as the action part of the game, so it fails to act as an anchor in the way it should. The NPCs that you befriend do little more than mill about with smudges for faces, passively waiting for you to chit-chat or deliver unsolicited gifts, and I found myself unable to appreciate them as interesting characters. Instead, it quickly became a grind of obtaining crafting mats in the action portion, then making guesses based on vague backstories about who would like what. And I wasn't sure why I was bothering, since the main result is to improve those passives I already said aren't mostly very useful.All that said, I still think it's a worthwhile experience. In many ways it's a bizarro-world , except that instead of the gross-out retro horrorscape with over-the-top items, it's a thoughtful, almost touching dream with subtle abilities.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, I'd recommend Dreamscaper to any fan of the roguelite genre.I'm sure you've heard Dreamscaper being compared to Hades and...it's a really good comparison, yet it still continues to shine and set itself apart. But what does being "like Hades" even mean? Well, as with any roguelite, the progression system and looping are essential to lasting success and Hades created a spectacular system. Dreamscaper lends it's own interpretation of a similar system. You have your character upgrades, world upgrades, relationships, and unlockables, as Hades had with the mirror, the hall upgrades, relationships, and your weapons. Let's put a check next to progression systems. Looping is one of the things I think is toughest to nail with the vast amount of roguelites being released nowadays. In Hades, when your run ends, you'd likely take a peak at all the new upgrades you could now gets with the rewards that you made it out with. After visiting the mirror, purchasing a new ball for Cerberus, and maybe unlocking a new weapon, you sit there before leaving for your next run, before you put down the controller. Thoughts run through your head, "What time is it? I just got these fists...I want to try them out so bad! Plus I got the healing fountain unlocked in Asphodel. I gotta see how far I can get, or at least how these fists work." And like Sisyphus, we are bound to the runs, lost to enter into one again and again. Dreamscaper does this exactly, and I'd beg to say better. There's a mastery system that rewards choosing new and less-preferred weapons to start your run with. Who knows, your least favorite might become your favorite weapon (*cough cough* fingergun for me *cough cough*).One last similarity is the relationships. I'm not going to speak to these as I didn't experience the story as I would have liked. I skipped past one too many conversations and it became a skipping bonanza. I know that there is one there, but unfortunately, I'm not much of a reader and this is one thing Hades definitely outdid with everything being voice-acted. But, I think the relationship system is a great way to hide a story and I love the mechanic. Definitely wish more roguelites threw this mechanic in.What's different? - Room selection and fast travel, you can explore as much as you want. - Loot Loot and Loot: you're constantly getting new gear and upgrading within a run.- Brings me to my next point, flexibility. If you like never knowing where a run will end up and having fun with whatever weapon drops, this is it. Whether it's you blowing chunks out of a boss with a fingergun or wrapping him up with yo-yos.- The game HEAVILY rewards learning and observation. You'll get farther in the game by not taking hits, not by upgrading stats. Upgrading stats is a safety blanket and is there to aid you in your progress so you can see more of the game (i.e. If you have all of the health upgrades, but still are taking a lot of hits, you're gonna have a bad time). Also little quirks like your bombs don't hurt you and actually standing in them when they explode can reveal hidden doors. (I think it requires that you stand in them. I've been testing this)- Most of the bosses and enemies seem very fair with their attacks and windows. Nothing I noticed was overtly the games fault for my deaths. Either my overconfidence and haste, paired with some precarious trap and red floor placement, met me with a cruel fate.Current Cons:- Weapon Scaling. Weapons don't upgrade or scale on their own. Although this lends to flexibility, you can get jerbaited into taking items you usually wouldn't just for the stats. Either enchantment rooms need to be guaranteed or scaling needs to be introduced somehow.- How slow Cassidy walks in the waking world. Really small grievance, but a grievance enough.- Maybe it's just me, but I often find myself forgetting the time-freezing mechanic. Not sure what to do with it, but I'm also not sure if others use it frequently or not.

_childDocuments_.review: Re-Review Incoming.This game has changed a lot since I last reviewed it and even then I kept it short and sweet. For those wondering about this game, it is an action roguelike/lite rpg. You're gonna find a lot of things familiar here and to me that's a good thing but there's also enough to set it apart from it's comparisons that I'd rather you discover for yourself. Do you like the dungeon/level design of Binding of Isaac? Then you'll love exploring and looting. Do you like the action combat style of Hades? Then you'll love fighting every single enemy and boss in the game over and over and over again.Other than the action and roguelike/lite elements of the game the two standouts to me are the music and art style of characters and levels. It feels and sounds like a dream (pun intended?). Speaking of sound, there's so much variety here ranging from sound queues from enemy attacks or Cassidy's many many many weapon choices, so I suggest playing with headphones if you want your senses to tingle.Last but certainly not least, the dev team here are amazing. Before closing the game they invite you to their discord channel which you should definitely join. They love seeing new people pour in and gush about their game, and most importantly they love talking about the game and giving advice about what to do if you're having trouble with something. They've also done a wonderful job including the community in the many changes it's gone through while in Early Access.Overall this game gets a will continue playing out of 10, and then another highly suggest checking it out yourself out of 100.

_childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly compelling storyline for a roguelite and a solid gameplay loop.The basic gameplay is room by room arena fights and treasure rooms. The layout is random but that doesn't add much until you are in danger and hoping to find the shop or a healing font. There is also a secret room every floor.What hooked me was the character growth and story. You get benefits by cultivating relationships in the real world, as well as purchase-able upgrades. You get resources to do so by dreaming-including inspiration to make gifts for your friends, which improve your relationships. Memories found in dreams give resources and help tell the story. Ideas found in dreams must be unlocked by sketching them in the real world. Meanwhile, every weapon, lucid attack, dodge and shield can be mastered by having it equipped while dreaming. Picking up new-found items in the dream lets you start with them in future runs.As a whole it's a slightly slow progression loop, but that keeps it from being too easy too quick.It also had me re-evaluating my play-style constantly. Normally you can kind of peg your build early on, but that wasn't the case here. Weapons have different attack rhythms and you do extra damage from "perfect" timing of your button presses that differ wildly by weapon. Inflicting multiple elemental conditions results in extra damage so you start using more varied ranged and lucid attacks. Enemy variety also starts requiring more movement, range, and alternate attacks.Highly recommended.My criticism is the game does feel a bit slow in terms of progression and even transition between rooms. Lucid attacks are on a timer so I found myself idling in a room for them to refresh, which seems unnecessary when your lucid meter instantly refills when no enemies are in the room. Enemy variety is low, with the same enemies just getting new moves in later levels. Finally some gameplay information is only given to you in the new level hint boxes

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting rogue-like by a very talented team. If the combat is tripping you up, make sure to zoom in all the way. Fingers crossed someone is able to mod in support to make the PC walk faster in the daytime scenes. It gets pretty brutal watching her crawl across town.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is cute and charming. The dream concept is interesting and allows for a lot of creativity with the genre. The story became more compelling than the core gameplay, it was sad and in some ways relatable. I wish there was a dialogue history as it's easy to blink and miss something that was said. You can fast travel between dungeon rooms which is cool and never seen in the genre. There was a lot of neat weapons and fun references in the game. Despite all that I dreaded making progress after the first few hours due to how painful it is. The lack of variety in the enemies and levels makes it feel kind of empty. Grindiest grind of any roguelite I've seen. Little gains, extremely high costs. It's basically the most important aspect of the genre, so it doesn't matter how good the rest is when that aspect feels like a slog.

_childDocuments_.review: I love it. The way they managed to make a Roguelite relaxing. One of the most rare things and at the same time one I value a lot: you can skip boss fights once you killed them. (If you are farming or whatever and want to skip it, you can) The way you unlock things every single run and having so many options to target whatever makes most sense to the player... love it!
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Positives:- It's very pretty and the amount of care and detail in the dungeon rooms makes this game special. It's not just random square room layouts, but camping areas and playgrounds and cities and volcanos. Even shops and treasure rooms look better than they need to when you just go in and out quicky.- The visible progress bar gives you a clear overall goal (instead of guessing how many levels there are). During a run, the minimap makes it very clear what things can still be collected in a room and the teleport function makes it super easy to explore in multiple directions and play strategically without wasting time.- There is an option to skip bosses which makes it easier to explore later levels.- Puzzle and challenge rooms, as well as the friendship overworld quests, are good additions since they add a bit of variety to the gameplay. There is always a thing or two to grab after a run.Neural:- A story about overcoming depression, yeah, blah blah blah, been there done that, onto the pile with you next to the other 5000 games that have the exact same hook. At least you can skip all the dialog.Negatives:- There are a ton of weapons, skills and items, and it takes way to long to unlock them all ... but even then, unlocks make the game worse because you will most likely get an offering for some random weapon that you don't know or like but has higher damage, and you would rather want you current one upgraded instead.-  Melee weapons are a joke (all of them). Spells deal the most damage by far. Parrying one-shots everything. Ranged weapons use mana but the shield does as well (?!?!?!), so you fire 2 arrows and then you can't defend yourself and it takes f****ng ages to refill. If you use the dash with fire trail, you can cheese every boss if you just run away for long enough. Enemy damage numbers feel pretty much random. The simplest enemies on floor 4-6 take longer to beat than the first boss.- The numbers for stat increases don't feel great at all. I don't want to take out my calculator to see if that 10% increase on a 20% damage boost that happens for 3 seconds with a 25% probabililty after a perfect attack makes that one weapon better than the other one. Or how overworld upgrades give like 6% more this or 2% better that.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR - Fluid, fast-paced gameplay, beautiful Last Of Us-esque environment that lays underneath a genuinely soothing soundtrack was a much-needed respite when society has mostly devolved into pretending to be a bunch of beans. Can't wait for Face DLCI'll be honest, I was pretty high when I bought this. Actually thought it was a full game, because it felt like one. Like a fast-paced top-down Dead Cells with a Persona-style driven story where inbetween dungeoning, you go socialize with people around town to unlock stuff by talking to them or doing activities which take up time before you have to go back home and go to sleep, which is where the dungeoning happens. (As of yet the main character seems to sleep for roughly 21 hours a day?)Took me a while to realize I had absolutely no idea what was going on, story-wise; the game is just fun to play. Definitely better with a controller. Definitely check it out.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is gorgeous; while challenging its still relaxing. If you enjoy rogue likes this is a perfect game. Even in early access it feels fleshed out. Each weapon is a unique story line that helps you pick up the story over time. Theres some story if you want it but doesn't shove it down your throat. Outside the dream world can get boring but its a good escape from the combat. Overall its cute and the music is breathtaking.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper struck a chord with me where Hades, one of its main competitors in the genre, failed, and that's saying something. I found myself vibing so hard when playing it. Maybe it's because I love dreaming, and this game managed to capture the feel of my dreamscapes. It feels like I'm having a fun dream, and like one of the other reviewers said - if lo-fi roguelikes were a genre, this would be it. No stress or anxiety, just vibing.Here are some things I noted so far in my short time playing the game.+ interesting and refreshing leveling and progression system  + well-designed, cool abilities (where else can you obliterate nightmares with a laser?)+ simple controls but a variety of ways to go about defeating enemies (see point above)+ gorgeous! simply gorgeous art that heals my artistic soul+ clean and beautiful level design+ pleasant, fitting bgm and sound effectsIf the reason Dreamscaper caught your eye is the idea behind it, like it was for me - trust me, it's absolutely worth trying!

_childDocuments_.review: I was pleasantly surprised after rebuying the game years after I refunded it in Early Access, even though the game has a just few big problems.I am a big fan of Roguelikes and Roguelights. There is something that always triggers me to go for another run because the only thing that keeps me from winning is me (and in the case of Roguelights some Meta-Farming). I had this exact feeling most of the time with Dreamscaper too, yet being a Roguelight I think it is important to get this out of the way first: The metagameprogression in Dreamscaper is . After finishing the game for the first time after about 20 attempts in 18 hours I only finished the game to 40 % - so if you wanna go for the 100 % get ready to grind. But let's go through the game step by step.Dreamscaper does good what a good Roguelight has to do right: High pace gameplay, rooms with traps, damage pools, items galore, bombs, keys, secret rooms, special rooms, some Danmaku and quick deaths. If you have played Isaac, Hades or about any other Rogue you have heard of all of this and Dreamscaper doesn't really innovate in most of the parts.What is special though is the loadout you get: You get a Meele Attack, a Range Attack, two Spells (Lucid Attacks) and a Shield. Attacks either deal normal or elemental damage, wherein elemental damage can explode in a lethal combo. Using your Shield or your Range Attack depletes an (lucid) energy bar, so playing defensiv and only doing ranged attacks will lead to you going in for the long run and leaving you open to enemy attacks - at least thats the idea they are trying to go with, more on that later. Also you can level up each active item once which feels like useless grind for most of them, and do have the ability to parry with most of the shields, which is nice, until you realise the camera... more on that later. Interesting was the concept of attacks with a short period of time where reusing the attack would lead in a stronger, faster attack.The special rooms are pretty basic but give you some time to breathe and some well needed Item-Ups (on each stage the items get better, so you have to regulary switch your items through), the enemies are good designed, yet after some time you will have mastered the about 7+ designs that exist and will quickly realise, that in higher levels the enemies just get upscaled with speed, range and sometimes a new attack. This however leads to the good feeling of being able to master the game, a basic premise for every Rogue. At the end of every stage is a boss. What is special here is that you can skip bosses once you beat them, but you'll miss out on the very good item they drop. The boss items were underwhelming in my experience, as they all served the purpose to boost your HP and one more stat. The bosses were challenging, some more than others, and I died to almost every one of them.After finishing six floors and beating the final boss you get the ending which I can just assume is the bad, or rather "placeholder" ending until you finished the metagame. Each floor increases the difficulty quite a bit so when reaching the last floor I almost instantly died in the next room due to the enemies bombarding me all of a sudden and yet it didn't feel unfair. A good run to the end can last around 45 minutes depending on your playstyle.The second big part is the awoken world, after you woke up from the dungeonpart. Here you will meet new characters in the city that your protagonist just moved too. You will befriend people, level up many, many, many stats, unlock new items and more opportunites for the dungeon. This part is much more fleshed out then Hades world and the game emphazises the story and the friendships you build with many . All of the characters you meet feel alive and all have their own topics they are passionate about, as well as their problems and sorrows. While you don't have to expect an RPG here, no choices or dialogue options, the NPCs are excellent for a Rogue and with it the story. The story plays through to the dungeonpart where you fight your own troubled past, no spoilers here, and the theme is fitting and very well executed. However this part also suffers under a massive inflation - after seeing everything the dungeons had to offfer, most of it quite a few times, I only finished 40 % of the game and a massive part is the many many many layers of metagame progression. The game features four different metagame currencies and while it is normal to earn a few hundreds of some of them in a long run there also are upgrades that cost up to 1.000 currency. The rest of the game will be a massive grind and to get to the real ending I can only assume that I have to befriend everyone to a maximum - no ending in sight yet.One of the three biggest problems (metagrind, balancing plus one more) is the balancing part of the game. Many of the passive items feel similiar and some stand out so much that you can barely live without them. Out of all of my runs that went  the farthest, including my first victory, I was relying on the single Item that gives you lifesteal. Being able to constantly regain health after a mistake is the single most important item you will find. Period.The rest wasn't much better: There is one shield that takes away the option to parry but gives you the ability to ignore one hit every 20 seconds. Period. There are so many weapons with way too short range that you don't want to use and weapons with elemental damage are much, much better than the ones without. If you make an elemental explosion you can deal up to 500+ damage in the late game with your weapon itself only dealing 50. The Lucid Attacks are even worse.: Either stamp in an absurd low range on the ground or let a dragon roar about half of the screen dealing massive AOE. In my first won attempt I had a low-CD aimed grab over the whole screen and a good AOE-Damage, with a combo of both I could perma-cc most normal enemies. Running away and spaming your lucid attacks is a viable combo.Still the game felt fair on most runs - enemies don't randomly one-shot you, even the bosses, enemies are no bullet sponge and attacks felt dodgable.The music is very well and supports the theme of the game. Sadly the game lacks any kind of voice acting, which could have really helped with the immersion. I only ever had one crash and one hardlock where I jumped in a road-sign right at the beginning of a dungeon. The tutorial is  overloaded. Many nice QoL things.The graphic in the dungeons is superb. The graphic in the real world... let's just say it is an interesting concept to not give the characters faces, but still I felt like it fit the game. It feels like a design choice and not like money saving, so yes, I actually enjoyed the graphic.However, here comes the third big problem: The camera. Oh boy, the camera. I can't desribe how bad the camera sometimes feels. Since it has a fix point and kind of gives a 2.5d vibe, trying to parry enemy projectiles or sometimes even trying to figure out if a slow moving projectile would hit you standing absolutely still became a very, very frustrating task. This also lead to the before mentioned supreme reign of the one-hit shield. Yes, after around 15 hours of concentrating I learned to read the camera, but this shouldn't  be necassary!Dreamscaper is a good Roguelight that delivers on its premise and surpasses itself in it's story, graphics and music. While sometimes being frustrating in the bad way and having some bad issues with balancing, the game still was fun and is definetly worth checking out, if you are searching for the next Rogue. Just don't expect a masterpiece like Isaac.

_childDocuments_.review: okay so i had previously written a review but im changing it now because of the awakening update.This update gave a new vibe to the game. i espesicially like the city shown when moving from place to place in the waking world. The game also became mor difficult because of the fact that not everything(eg altars, challenges etc) is available at the start of the game. More progression systems were inroduced(eg daydreaming) which actually reward the player for playing. Previously i had unlocked almost allthe equipment so when i played it felt like i was grinding to finally beat the last stage(i didnt). Lastly the fact that you can have up to three saves is nice as you can grind a certain weapon with one to become able to beat more stages. It is also possible that more than one person plays the game as there are 3 saves.Generally: The game has both an interesting story and fun gameplay. The dialogues are actually interesting(pretty rare for me to find dialogues that interesting). Additionally the levels are neither easy nor difficult. There is a sense of satisfaction afyter beating a difficult stage.There is a variety of weapons,. shields lucid attacks etc which adds evenmore to the gameplayAs for negatives there aren't a lot. Personally i would have prefer the had not changed some things and would have just left them as they were. I am not a fun of the fact that ranged weapons consume lucid and dodnt have projectiles you can pick up anymore. i think it takes away the difficult decision whether ot not to use your ramged weapon(before the phoenix update where this was changed there was always shorthage of projectiles and you had to be careful not to waste them). Lastly instead of lucid being use for the "Clock"( I dont remember what it's called I'm talking abou the thing that slows down time) you know have to wait three rooms or immediately skip the cooldown using a lucid altar. In my opinion this renders the ability kind of useless as it can be used rarely and it also takes away your ability to use your ranged weapon(it consumes lucid and it's duration is till your lucid runs out or till you manually disable it, which still caused it tpo have a 3-room cooldown). Also let'sbe honst here. it was not all that good even before the phoenix updateScore:9/10

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very good. It has many of the tried and true mechanics that make up Roguelites. The art style is also amazing, very inspired and quite unique. Levels really feel dreamlike.That said, I think it can improve in several areas. Currently, the "level up" system for the special rooms feels a bit odd, since you have to go unlocking the different special rooms outside of your dreams. _childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is an artistic gem with very satisfying gameplay. The main character is a huge nerd and her interests find their way into the gameplay by inspiring the weapons and skills you use to approach combat. From wielding giant buster swords like Cloud to earth-bending like Toph, lightning dashing like Sasuke just to name a few, it's really impressive how many popular fantasies this game incorporates. The artstyle has this gorgeous, homey feel that's really uplifted by the sentimental music. If you're a fan of video-games and pop culture and you enjoy challenging and pretty rogue-like action you should definitely give this a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little roguelike with most of what we've seen in other roguelikes but now with some Persona mixed in. Fight in your dreams using a shockingly massive selection of diverse weapons. abilities, dodge moves, and customization to really tailor make your runs. Outside of dreams you explore various areas to spend materials you gained in your dreams, and also talk to various characters and learn their stories as you get more friendly with them. Its all very stylish and well crafted, each environment is diverse and adds the surreal vibes you would get in a dream.No complaints really, its a solid experience with a decent story (if you decide to pay attention, i didn't). $25 is A LOT for a game of this nature though. I understand the effort and design, but Hades is a tough game to beat at this price. On sale for anything less than 20, 100% a recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I highly recommend this game if you're looking for a 3D roguelite! Beautiful aesthetic, rewarding gameplay, tons of replayability, and just an overall really fun experience. _childDocuments_.review: A great Hades-inspired rogue-like. Lots of variability in abilities and weapons. Many possible gameplay styles. The story doesn´t get in the way, I would be very surprised if someone actually felt all the stuff it wants you to feel. Had fun, finished it. _childDocuments_.review: This review has minor spoilers (like the number of bosses), but they involve mechanics instead of plot.  I will give my thoughts below, both good and bad, on various topics related to the game:As a disclaimer, I mostly played on normal difficulty since the rewards for playing on higher difficulties were pretty underwhelming (20% drop bonus for all options hard and 40% for all options nightmare).  I will probably revisit the higher difficulties later just for the added challenge.Well, to begin with, I have had a blast playing this game.  I found the controls fairly tight and responsive.  The abilities were pretty neat too with some really unique options.  Melee weapons were distinct enough in their timing, range, and attack vectors to be fun.  Ranged was understandably gated, but boiled down to mostly burst attacks at shorter range or single attacks at longer range.  Weapons (melee and ranged) and several abilities can spawn with elements, but it was too random to make consistent use of it.  Armors were sadly pretty much the same, even after mastering all of them.  There were a couple outliers that had neat effects, but the tradeoffs were too massive to functionally use them beyond the first level or two.As for itemization, they had a TON of it for this type of game.  I was very impressed to say the least.  However, I do wish that you could pick a weapon/ability and stick with it throughout your playthrough.  You can choose your initial gear, but keeping the same items or abilities became exceedingly difficult since the cost of upgrading was high and not every floor had a forge.  Not only that, but by the time you get to the second floor, your starting gear is objectively outclassed.  Many times, I got stuck having to choose raw power over usability or elemental complements due to the above issues and the randomness of spawns in loot rooms and the shop.Regarding the Story, be warned that it is pretty depressing.  I haven't finished it (even though I've beaten the game a few times) because my relationships are still not maxed out.The most fun I have had in this game is the tough fights that require good timing and high mobility.  There are some issues with a few things like Shadow Step has way too much time before follow-up actions allowed, weave's range was too short to avoid the majority of attacks, and two or three of the melee weapons had such short range that I would practically have to collide sprites to connect attacks.  Otherwise, it was really neat getting different combinations that were strong enough to win against bosses before your health ran out.Challenges were entertaining and you had a pipeline minigame and a minesweeper minigame.  I did run into one issue with the "dodge 2 attacks or projectiles at the last moment" challenge.  I was on the second floor fighting the dude with lance weaponry.  And yes, I do realize that the timing required is obnoxiously tight - probably around 1 or 2 tenths of a second based off of how I did it against ranged weapons, but I just could not get it to register even after taking multiple hits (including the majority of my hp) using trial and error to adjust the timing.As for the six bosses...I have to say that the first two bosses are very well made.  The third and fourth boss start to discourage melee because you don't know when they will attack.  There are some patterns to it, but the window you have DPS before they whip around and chain-smack you is something you have to time very carefully.  This often means missing out on a lot of damage and needlessly dragging the fights out.  The rest of those two fights are just running around like a headless chicken.  The fifth boss is the hardest boss in the game.  If you do not time your attacks correctly, it will whip around and chunk a quarter of your health before you realize what happened (and yes, I do have maxed health and reasonable armor).  That wouldn't be a problem if the time between attacks was consistent, but it is not.  6th boss is just annoying.  Being invulnerable half the time while using melee attacks and sweeping ranged attacks means you would have to be a hardcore massochist to choose melee.  If that's not bad enough, you lose your weapons!  I used a melee focused build the first time I got to the boss and did 0 damage whenever I finally reached it.  Later, I learned (through trial and error) that this was because of the invulnerability that the boss uses when it's not attacking...which is about half of the fight.Overall, it has been a pretty good experience.  I would definitely say that I got my money's worth out of it.  I'll probably play it some more when I have the time, but almost 40 hours isn't too bad for an indie game in this price range (especially on sale).  Devs seem cool too from what little interaction I have had with them.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, I have to say, I absolutely hate the whole Roguelite / Roguelike mechanism.I suck at it and I hate to start over and over and over and over again.This game is no exception.But I still kinda enjoy(ed) it, since I didn't even realize that I already played longer than 2 hours.• The gameplay feels fluid and the weapons and items really feel different, I really like it.• The world itself is somewhat procedually and well and detailed designed. I would wish for a little more monster-variety though. The graphics are also special and neat.• The Soundtrack is very fitting and lovely composed. Reminds me a little to some Final Fantasy OST.• My personal highlight are the Sound Effects. It's just a pleasure to hear all the animations, pickups, transitions and so on. 10/10, great work here. :)• Besides the Roguelike-aspect, I like the progression-system itself very much. It's not getting boring and the little small talk with all the people in the game is really refreshing.• Overall this is a very well done game and worth the money, give it a try, even if you hate Roguelike like me.You can just jump in for a quick session of 10-20 minutes, this is exactly what I need at the moment, no time for MMO-like grinding.I really can feel that the whole team put heart and love in this game, it feels very polished overall.And just as a side note: I can even play it on my old Lenovo T540p Notebook with Geforce GT 730M (on low settings of course).8/10 (would be a 10, if I was a fan of Roguelike games. ^^)

_childDocuments_.review: I was initially drawn seeing compariosns to Hades, which was a roguelike that I enjoyed a lot.TLDR this game is NOT Hades and imo to expect Hades-like polish to it would be expecting too much of Dreamscaper, but it does have it own charms that may make it attractive to you if you are looking for a game you can play casually at a slower pace with some "life advice" sprinkled into the game, but for it's asking price of $25USD, I can't see myself giving this game as my next recommendation to someone looking for a game to commit to.Reasons to like the game- Cassidy and the people she becomes friends with grow on you. Through the interactions and events, you see more of Cassidy's growth as a character struggling through life and all its problems- Scenery in this game rivals that of Hades and other beautiful games in my opinion. Not so much that its "ultra-HD" but it has a wilderness aesthetic that you can really appreciate- The real life lessons that Cassidy's friends give you. As you have more conversations with the real world characters, they share their thoughts and feelings that I think a lot of young adults can feel these days. How to motivate oneself in work, life as well as dealing with ones personal issues. In that sense, the games immerses you into a sense of knowing you aren't the only person out there just trying to live out life, and that's one thing that really makes the character/story development become a positive pointReasons I didn't end up liking the game in the end- Combat feels too slow. I found myself fighting with the game inputs, always feeling like I was never reacting as fast as I'd like too. The best way to describe it is you feel "heavy" even with some of the fastest weapons equipped. After a certain point when I felt like there wasn't much left to discover, combat started to feel boring.- The story starts off slow. The first 4 hours of the game didn't really draw me in. Cassidy comes off initially as immature and unlikeable, and I considered dropping the game quicker but in my experience with other games that start slow I change my mind down the line, so I kept going, and eventually changing my opinion in this respect. But if you can't see yourself playing a game that doesn't pick up fast, then you may feel disappointed- The levels can feel pretty repetitive and boring at times. When I would plateau through the deeper levels in 5 and 6, I would feel too drained in wanting to continue a run as the time in between runs can run almost 45 minutes before dying because I explore as much as possible in every level to min/max my stats. The pacing just gets a bit slow and the desire to commit to a run is a something I struggled to do at times, making my runs become more like a slog to try and finish rather than a joy to make it through a complete run- Although there are a lot of weapons and abilities in the game, once you find the ones that you like to use, it becomes more beneficial to turn off the ones that you just don't like. I found myself going for the same builds that work for me, because the ones that didn't work for me just REALLY didn't work. It felt discouraging to go for various builds because the gameplay feels too bias towards forcing me to pick only the ones that work. This was one thing I felt was really unpolished vs a game like Hades, where nearly all the weapon aspects feel great to use, and encourage builds that I wouldn't always pick
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: I kind of love this game. The combat is a bit clunky and it has some rough edges, but it deserves praise for not just cloning every other isaac-style roguelight game out there.The "game" world takes place in the dreams of the MC, a woman who is somewhat withdrawn from society. In the game world you do all the expected things. You pick up keys, bombs, sand (money), manage your health and unlock floors room-by-room through puzzles and combat. I really like the art style, but this by itself would leave me thinking this game was competent but merely ok gameplay wise.The waking world is what really makes this game feel different. It's the equivalent of the castle in Rogue Legacy, but the combination of incremental unlocks and Persona-ish social system add a ton of heart. It might just be a case of "right place right time" but art, style, and even music paint a picture of a person in their middle years trying to learn how to be a social person again while dealing with feelings of loss, regret, and the wistful remembrances of childhood memories. I'm a middle aged man and these things are all deeply relevant to me, and really support the framework of the dungeons and combat.Combat itself is somewhat souls-like, emphasizing timing, dodging, and blocking. It's paced and considered. Button mashing and being endlessly aggressive will just end with you dead.As a whole, this game is wonderful, if not as a game, then as art.

_childDocuments_.review: I've completed the EA content so far, but feel confident recommending this game as my recommendation is based primarily on the gameplay mechanics, which I doubt will be changed fundamentally.There are 3 core reasons I find the combat very enjoyable:1. Satisfying impact. Hit stop, sound effects and slow down during parry/dodge make the game feel really good to play. The special abilities are also appropriately 'bigger' in visual and sound effects, making them feel badass and worthwhile.2. The weapon selection is large, surprising and innovative. I looked at the available unlocks early on and thought:"Why the hell would I want to unlock a yoyo as melee weapon?" Turns out, the devs figured out how to make a whole lot of unconventional weapons fun to play. The yoyo, boxing gloves and water gun feel every bit as viable as the sword, daggers or flamethrower. It's actually really fun to get more options than your usual rpg weapons. There's even a fairly large selection of dodge types from rolling to teleporting to acrobatic spins.3. This one is highly specific and may not matter to most people, but I am so fluffing glad they put just frame comboes in the game. It's a mechanic that I've long held more action games should be using, ever since I encountered it in Oneechanbara: Bikini Samurai Squad way back in 2009. The just frame mechanic is mostly seen in fighting games, but it adds a lot to action games as well and Dreamscaper implements it really well. Your character will flash white briefly to signify when you should press attack again to do bonus damage. The sound and visual indicator when you do it right are unambiguous and satisfying. The best part is that the white flash is rhythmically consistent with the attack animations. In other words, if your attack is a double slash, the timing will be: animation start, beat, slash 1, beat, slash 2, beat, just frame. This makes it possible to use the just frame mechanic even when you can't see your character clearly by paying attention to the wind-up animation once you hit the button and the short time between doing multiple attacks. It's effectively part rhythm game.In short, if just feels really damn good to play and that's the most important part of an action game to me.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Just... zero challenge. The combat needs a lot of work despite being described as "souls-lite". Yes, every weapon has a combo; you can block, you can dodge and so forth, but it's just slow and lumbering instead of technical and strategic. I can understand a slow attack speed with something like a hammer, but a pair of knuckledusters? Also, would you choose, you can just cancel attack animations with the dodge, making the slowness of the combat pointless.Here's a list of things encountered within the hour:- 100% health recovery items are common drops. This is generally speaking a cardinal sin in games of this type.- If the above weren't enough, all shops i encountered offered 100% or 50% life recovery for very little money- All combat against minor enemies boils down to "stunlock enemy and mash button to kill" to win. - The camera ends up being your worst enemy. While it works most of the time, if the play area is slightly larger like in some cases of the forested area, enemies that are farther away that use projectiles can get in cheapshots when you go in and kill them solely because the camera stays very far away highlighting areas where the player isn't.- I shouldn't get to 4th level out of 6 within the first hour of playing with solely using normal attack and block, opting never to use things like dodge, slowdown time, overpowered magic attacks et.c. which would make the game significantly easier. I also used ranged attacks very sparingly, as it is extremely overpowered as well.- "Use gamepad to play", yeah, no. I bet it would be slightly more challenging with a worse control scheme, however.- The weapon's usefulness is determined by its attack speed, which is marked in no way when given the choice to pick up the weapon. A weapon with slow attack speed but twice the claimed DPS often ends up being worse. - The ranged weapon's usefulness is determined by its attack type and range, but these are not listed anywhere- Apart from special effects, the only things all weapons let you know of themselves is a nebulous DPS stat. They don't show you things that would interest you like the attack range, attack speed, per-attack damage, special combo finishers (such as AOE) and so on. There's plenty of space in the dialog, but it's not used.- The "waking world" permabuff roguelite thing is... theoretically interesting, but the dialogue is so poor it resembles the average soap opera. The characters simply aren't characters, and there's little done in making them interesting. The hollow shells they push as characters feel like "this is the character's job, gender and age, that means the character acts like this". The tutorial bartender you're told to talk to is the most grating of all the ones i managed to talk to, starting by mouthing off at her customer, you in mid-conversation. "There's nobody here at this hour", gee, i do wonder why?- The whole "go around and talk to uninteresting people" also feels like orange juice mixed with toothpaste. There's very little reason given to knowing the people. Supposedly the idea is  their experiences skew your worldview, but this is brought forward quite poorly. The makers of this game really need to play Persona to understand how to do similar things correctly.- It also seems to be very random where a person you would actually want to talk to is, so long they're not running the short list of locations, making obtaining the permanent buffs a bit of a crapshoot.

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper largely follows all the formulas of Hades. In the few places that it departs from them, it departs for the better. Dead Cells is often being mentioned, because many of those differences do appear in Dead Cells; but to be clear, Dreamscaper is a Hades-kind of game, not a Dead Cells-kind of game.The tone of the game is different, for sure. Hades is a game for troubled and socially awkward geeks seeking to escape into the world of majestic heroes of Greek antiquity, endowed with fabulous martial skills, and fighting to Break Free from the Oppression of the Father, who keeps imposing Demands, Duties and so forth. Dreamscaper, in contrast, is for gamers seeking to escape  the world of a troubled and socially awkward geek, who is endowed with fabulous martial skills - in her dreams at least - and is fighting to break free from her  demons, such as Fear, Isolation, Resentment, and so forth.While the premise of Hades will obviously be the more popular one, I find myself kindly nodding to the premise of Dreamscaper. I might even miss "The Father Hades", in his quiet despair at his prodigal solipsistic son, yet unwaveringly determined to put some sense and some responsibility into the young lad's head. But the parents in Dreamscaper are not present, and the one who must bring some order into your head is you.Gameplay-wise, Dreamscaper is largely like Hades, except for some differences which, as I mentioned, I do like. The first one is that it doesn't bind you to  fighting style throughout your run, based on the weapon you pick at the start of Hades. At all times you have options available for melee, ranged, "magic"/ultimate attack and parry/block. You can encounter and exchange a variety of weapons in each of those subcategories during the run, but they all remain available throughout, and you can quickly adapt to use the appropriate one for the situation.The fighting is tight and fluid. Two specific aspects are based on precise timing: parrying and criticals. I find the parrying quite satisfying. The penalty for missing it increases the deeper you go in your run, while the consequence of hitting it right always remains devastating for the enemies. And getting the parry timing right always feels intuitive; I never missed a parry while feeling that it wasn't my fault.I have some mixed feelings about the timing of the criticals. Your basic melee combos are 1-2-3, and for the critical you must hit the very exact timing for the 2 and the 3. The thing is that those timings ; for one weapon they will be like +0.4s +1.2s, while for another they will be like +0.6s +0.2s. They are not "spelled out" like that, nor are they anyhow "intuitive" (as the parry is). Rather, the character "flashes" at the expected time for that weapon, but you are not given even a fraction of a second to  to the flash itself, you must hit at the exact time of the flash. Meaning that you must pre-practice the timing after seeing what it is. And you can freely practice that when there's no enemies around (there's good audio feedback), but it's quite hard to keep this ad-hoc timing in the heat of a battle, especially when any weapon change means those timings will change as well.It's not impossible but it's frustrating, as opposed to the parry, which is always satisfying. This is not a  minus; if you're good at all the other aspects, you can quite well win even without landing criticals.You can "recycle" any rejected weapons, or newly-offered weapons that you prefer to not take, into "sand", the money that is valid during a run. You can also fast-travel to any already-uncovered area of the current stage before you proceed to the next stage. Not only to return to a shop at will once you've gathered the necessary amount, but also to return to a screen where you've left a health refill that you didn't need back then but do need now. There are secret areas with boons. The weapons have secondary effects, and you can aim for loadouts that reinforce particular styles of play. All those aspects are present in Dead Cells, but not (quite) in Hades, and Dreamscaper is all the better for incorporating them.Another quality-of-life boon that seems unique to Dreamscaper is that, once that you had defeated an end-stage boss, that fight becomes  in all the ensuing runs. You get his drops only if you fight him, of course, but you still need to  the boss of that level. (I mostly choose to fight them, because the fights are good, but whenever I arrive quite low on health, it's good to be able to skip them and try to recover a bit on the next stage, rather than ending the run there)On the artworks side, it doesn't hold up to Hades. Well, hardly anything does; Hades is a ludicrously high bar to reach in terms of artwork. I also dislike the artistic decision to make all the people faceless; that is not anyhow original, nor good, it's just lazy and somewhat off-putting. But having said that, the in-game graphics are really very nice. I especially like the snowy suburban landscapes in the first stage, and the other stages are quite good as well. The music is nice and pleasant. The animations feel kinetic, natural and smooth.If you like to play Hades, give this a try. Hades surely drew you in with its outright incredible artwork. Dreamscaper still has very good artwork and music, and a gameplay which I ended up enjoying even more than that of Hades.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: I have yet to complete the game, but playing it for the first time kept me up for 12 hours straight. Never have I played a rogue-lite game that made me feel so much, especially with characters that don't even have a face. There is just so much to this game, I gotta split it up. The Combat:Man, this feels good. Being able to change the way you dodge with different "shoes", change your range attacks with different weapons and the whole main melee thing. But that has been done. What makes combat great in my opinion, is that instead of swarming you with mobs and having a bullet hell style of fighting, the combat in this game draws you in. The timing system where you deal more damage when your character flashes gives incentive for not button mashing, and this doesn't just apply to melee, but to range and magic too. This gives the movements in the game a certain weight and connection to the player, and brings the whole sense of immersion to the next level.The Puzzles:Man, I thought that it was just simple line connection or surround the dot, and I thought it would be a pain, but boy was I wrong. Puzzle stages are some of the most looked forward to for me. Nothing is explained, and you are left to intuition. Being a visual person, the line connection puzzles came easy, but it took me a good 30 minutes to figure out at the later stages that I'm not trying to surround the dot for the other kind of puzzle. Without spoiling anything, the moment it finally clicked and hit me, it just felt so good. The pacing of it being once per stage helps take a break from combat and really gives the game balance. The Story:Man, no other rogue-lite has given me more of a sense of loss in the first 10 minutes than this game. The writing is amazing, and everything seems so real. I cried, I laughed, and I felt a hole inside me that still never closed. tl;dr, this game is amazing. The story and writing brings validation to our everyday pains and struggles and the combat is intuitive and immersive. To the writers, creators, designers and all staff who brought this game to reality, thank you for the tears, you wonderful bastards.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Visually this game is great, but the gameplay is too slow for my taste. The weird combo timing system isn't particularly fun to engage with, the first few bosses aren't really interesting to fight against, and while I appreciate having a bunch of different weapons and items, none of them were very interesting or did anything to change up my play style at all. If you're here for the gameplay, you're going to be disappointed.The environmental art in this game is gorgeous, but the character art is lacking. The character art issues are most prevalent in the daytime sections, where you'll talk to a handful of other characters around the city but the lack of faces make it tough to engage with them. The lack of animation or voice acting (or even pseudo voice acting a la the Ace Attorney series) in these scenes make it even harder for me to engage with them.  A lot of other reviewers have compared this to Hades, and I get the comparison but Supergiant put a ton into the game's audio and visuals. While that game's talking scenes lack substantial animation, it compensates with some beautiful character portraits and some top notch voice acting. Dreamscaper does not have any of that, and it suffers for it.Oh yeah, the story. I didn't even notice it through my handful of runs. It might be good, it might get good, but from what I saw it was practically nonexistant, and it doesn't do much to create a compelling atmosphere to compensate for it. Might pick it up again later if it's on a big sale, but for the time being I'm refunding this.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely fantastic roguelite with an endearing story,beautiful music and great visuals. The combat flow Is great and looks and feels really satisfying.If you have any interest in roguelites I would definitely recommend giving this one a shot. _childDocuments_.review: I think this is a great rogue-like game. The difficulty isn't too crazy even when using the modifiers to crank it up a bit, I feel like I'm making progress even when I wind up doing the same content over and over, and the atmosphere of the game, both in the dreamscape and the real world, is fantastic.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: I can only recommend this, over and over again..!My, what a joy this game is to play! The atmosphere, the storytelling(so far) and the subjects it touches, is just phenomenal! It really reminds me of what I wanted in the games 'Hades' and 'Curse of the Dead Gods'. It deserves praise.The combat in this game is very simple, but feels so good and fluent, when you nail those timings on a weapon - and even so, if you spam the combo, it still doesn't take away from the fluedity and fun this combat system gives you. The animations and visuals are so perfect and so well done, that I can't get enough of looking at it.I have yet to even finish the third level, but I am enjoying the feel of waking up, getting any new unlocks done and then select "random" on melee/ranged weapon, power, dodge and shield and going back into the dreamworld to try out a random newly discovered setup, that just looks fantastic. You can get a 'Fingergun'.. A LITTERAL FINGER, POINTING AND SHOOTING, and I couldn't help but laugh and love that ranged weapon after I saw it for the first time.This game blew me away, and I am only 5 hours in. So much more to discover and I am here for it!
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing addition to the action rogue like genre. I was initially put off a bit by what seemed like simple art (character designs spefficially) but I'm glad I picked this up. These guys have played games and know exactly how to add QOL, ease of use gameplay and elements Roguelites - gaming done well, examples:- You can fast travel from the beginning at all times, for great flow- You can select your starting loadout, fully, from the beginning as you unlock more items (versus only much later, or only one or two types for a payment)- You can deselect whatever unlocked weapon/item you unlocked from the beginning (No 1 at a time, no bloated rng drops you don't want) - You can choose to either re-fight previously defeated bosses, or skip them for somewhat less rewards. No either having zero re-playable bosses ( The miner roguelite game ) or always having to re-fight them (most roguelikes)- Ease of use, fast dashing into portals that seamlessly take you to the next room, very impactful fast combat and freedom. - Earlier levels and shops always still feel useful to clear, if not only for the keepsakes you can stack- Well done progression system/unlocks + A ton of items to unlock - Small QOL things like higher starting loadout rarity, ability to enchant it so you keep that loadout regardless of newer loot etcMix that in with a deep, somewhat dark heartfelt story, as pieces are laid around as you go. Tackling trauma, mental issues, loss. I relate very much to that concept, the idea of lucid dreaming, confronting your past, the story told. Improvements:- Resource grinding: It is a bit grindy, especially later stages. I also feel like the other difficulty options don't really seem worth it. 5% increase in resources for 50% harder fights feels like a trap. I feel more customization can be done in that aspect ala hades pacts. - Skip boss cutscenes, for some reason the holding button feels slower than it should be
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Played before official release and I like how much fun it was and still is. The improvements over time were nice to see and made the game a lot smoother and felt better over time.Gameplay is great - easy to learn but kinda hard to master especially with so many different weapons. Personally I skipped most of the conversations, but that's just me; I think the story is nice if you're into that.Overall great roguelike!
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun roguelite reminiscent of Children of Morta in terms of being more story focused. Doesn't lack in interesting gameplay with compelling items and stats. Sufficiently addictive and fun. It's a very feel good happy game without lacking any challenge. I have yet to beat the third level but I can totally recommend it as is! Like Risk of Rain 2, the state it's in now is a perfectly playable and complete-feeling game, and it's only going to get more content and polish from here. Not a perfect game of course but very very well worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice game and first early access that didn't disapoint me.Every update go in the good direction for the game and improve it for real, not just adding content, but IMPROVE it.I don't know if the artistic style suit every taste but feel very good to me. Feel like you fight dream ghost in some important place of your memory.I would enjoy some lo-fi music for this game.Just buy it if you like roge-like game with inspired artstyle
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what a fantastic game. The visuals, music, story, dialogue, weapon variety, progression system, and combat are all top notch. No complaints about anything so far.I rarely leave reviews on games, but this is fantastic. The only game I can compare this to (not the gameplay, just the FEELZ) are the Ori games. Simply beautiful.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: A great roguelite experience.I loved every second of it, the gameplay is smooth and satisfying with most weapons, the soundtrack is beautiful and enriches the game a lot.The great art direction and hard-hitting yet elegant storytelling tie everything together.This is one of my absolute favourites, what a fun time!
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun, challenging and atmospheric game!A great variety of Melee & Ranged weapons as well as abilities (you can flip enemies with a giant frying pan. It's amazing.) and passive items make trying out builds a rewarding and flexible experience, the combat is satisfying with a perfect attack and parry mechanic that raises skill ceiling a little. Getting to know the various NPCs and crafting gifts for them is interesting, and guessing who'd prefer what gift (especially early on) is also enjoyable. Backstory is good as well, and small lore bits deliver new bits of it with a nice simplicity. Boss battles and their aesthetics are great too, with some mechanics that can be figured out by paying attention.The only negative point would be the relatively small variety of enemies, although encounters are kept spicy with enemy placement, bonus challenges and environmental hazards. In later stages you mostly fight upgraded versions of earlier enemies. This fact did not impact me negatively personally, but I can see why some would not like it as much.Over all, this game captures the feeling of that whacky super hero dream you may or may not have had some years ago, and combines it with important topics that impact many lives nowadays. The dialogues are nicely written and feel honest. Also, the VFX and environments are super pretty. If this looks interesting to you, no need to wait on a sale. If you like it after playing for 2 hours, chances are you'll like it 'til you're finished.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely well paced, excellent writing, and great artistic style.  The gameplay variety is large and the challenge is adjustable along multiple facets (resistance, damage, amount, etc.).  Controls are good and combat is engaging without being punishing or overwhelming.  If there is any downside, it is that some things are not clearly explained or defined - although you'll never be penalized for not figuring it out.  An excellent "one more run" game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: My initial impression was: Curse of the Dead Gods x Life Is Strange, neither game I like very much. However, after a few more hours, I've found myself coming back for more. The first half of the game is tough. You're low in power, some of the nuances aren't explained so you get hit more than you like, but after you get familiar with some of the items, and get some upgrades it starts to feel more fun. The story, which felt a bit too real for me, plays a large role, and I was glad to have the option to skip the dialogue. Lots of weapons and abilities, combat is fun, very challenging.4/5Bonus for the devs, who are super cognizant of any issues that arise and work to fix them quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played through and beaten the first two areas (there appears to be 5 or 6 total.The combat feels slow and incredibly clunky. Your character often gets of the camera for seeing enemies. It's not clear which enemies are "permanent" (i.e. map obstacles) and which aren't.There are just too many abilities and weapons, the variation of which doesn't feel impactful. If weapons synergized and combo'd together it would feel better.The bosses feel very very slow and not challenging.The UI is really unclear about swapping items, which items you have equipped, and your stats are sort of buried on the side. Every room transition is the same wipe in/wipe out instead of dynamic for different rooms. It makes the game feel tedious transitioning between rooms.The fact that aiming and movement are separate sticks on the controller is super weird to me. It means that if I use the right stick to aim, then I HAVE to use a bumper button on the controller (e.g. RT or RB) instead of a regular thumb button. Since the aiming has no throttling to it (i.e. you don't pull down a weapon button slower when you use less force on the trigger), it doesn't feel impactful to use the trigger buttons. Aiming should just have you be stationary and use the left stick to aim, or have an option for it.This game has a lot of unrealized potential. I'm sad I can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: A bit rough around the edges. When they say early access, it's not really missing features, it means that it's not really technically sound. Compared to the Demo/Prologue version they put out I've experienced a lot of bugs, but it's a small team of three very dedicated guys and they've done a great job listening to the community feedback and expanding upon the game. Once this game gets patched up, it's going to be a must-have. QUICK 2nd EDIT: Just throwing this in because I think it's important: devs have already addressed a lot of the big issues like getting stuck on some of the new props in the map and a few other bugs. These guys are on one and it's impossible not to root for them and support them with this game.Everything about this game is executed exceptionally well. The art is nothing short of gorgeous, and there are lots of different 'biomes' that showcase different color pallets in the environment and all of them are so thematically on point yet remain in the background and let you focus on the gameplay when you need to. The same thing goes for props in the environment. There are different types of rooms and the full release included new waterfalls in the puzzle rooms and new amazing lily blossom loot rooms (they were they before, now they just look amazing) and they serve as a nice change of pace from the combat.The story and progression of this game are tied together yet the story is completely optional. There are NPC characters in different places in the hub world, a cozy cafe, a dimly lit park, a small, quiet, and cluttered bookstore, etc. Talking to these characters and gifting them items you craft via resources gathered in the levels is how you unlock new items, abilities, etc. The characters talk about a lot of real-life and sometimes sensitive and emotionally compromising topics and it allows you to connect with the different characters while also giving nice exposition and background info on the protagonist. Or not (Press F to pay disrespects and skip all the dialogue and get back to punching monsters). The more you learn about them, the more tools you have at your fingertips to kick some butt,  That's all I really need to say about it, but going a bit further, with dodging, blocking and parrying, strong, regular, and ranged attacks, lucid attacks (special abilities) and dozens of options for each, there's just so many ways to keep combat interesting each time you pick it back up.If the word 'crafting' scared you earlier, a lot of the mechanics in this game have enough depth to them but overall are pretty simple. My dog figured it out and has done most of my crafting. The crafting is really fun, because you have to find out which characters would enjoy which gift based on clues about their interests. It's a lot of process and elimination and a fun little mystery as you go along. You can max out all characters and unlock all abilities without finding out all the perfect matches, they just help you progress faster. Once you've maxed out all the characters and have all the abilities, you can now use these resources to craft loadouts you want in each run and hand-pick all your favorite <everything>. This is all done in the 'Dream Journal.' The other tabs in this journal are really only useful in the beginning of the game when you're still trying to figure out what characters like and see where you are in unlocking everything. There's an Unlocks, Characters, etc.All this and more to come! There are currently 6 levels/stages on the current release, a boss every other level, and I think they're supposed to have 5 or 6 bosses in the end so this purchase will probably keep on giving in the passing months as these three are locked in the coding dungeon by their publisher. Best of luck with your game guys!e-  spelling

_childDocuments_.review: So, here's the thing - I really don't like giving indie games negative reviews, especially when there's clear dedication and effort behind them. I wish the devs of this game all the best, and I hope that they continue to make art that they're passionate about. That said, I just could not get through this game. I gave it a fair shot-- two fair shots, actually. I bounced off it initially after only an hour or two and then came back a few months later and put a little more time in. And despite really wanting to like it and see the best in it, it pretty quickly outstayed its welcome and I had to put it down.There's a lot to like here, to be fair. The framing device is unique, and the art is absolutely gorgeous. I'm most disappointed in the fact that I did not make it far enough to see all the levels, because each was visually stunning in its own way. There's a vast amount of abilities to choose from, each with their own distinct feel. And the fast travel mechanic between rooms is genuinely such a simple but nice feature in a roguelike. It feels satisfying to be able to clear out a level without the frustration of constant backtracking. Here's where the flaws begin to show, though, because the game's pace makes for fairly slow and methodical runs, encouraging you to visit and clear all rooms and secrets before progressing. But the core loop of the game depends upon you doing many, many of these before you will get enough of an edge to progress through a full level, and the progression outside of the dream world is similarly incremental. This makes for an experience that simply drags way more than necessary, and seeing the long list of tasks to take care of and unlockables that remained was more disheartening than motivating. Combat does not feel particularly snappy or engaging either. Many of the abilities, especially the dodges, feel sluggish and difficult to time properly, and the sheer number of different items conflicts with the mastery mechanic, which encourages you to stick to the ones you use most. All of the permanent upgrades you get are so minute that you barely feel the difference between runs, and even the lucid mode toggle did not particularly help. And the relationship building with the NPCs outside of the dreamworld goes similarly slowly, with a gift-giving mechanic that feels more gamey than genuine, and conversations that meander without coming to any meaningful point. Ultimately, I am disappointed more than anything, because it felt like there was a lot of potential here, and maybe this game wasn't quite right for me, but would be for some. Buy it on sale if you want to give it a chance, because I think it does deserve at least that.

_childDocuments_.review: Even though it is still in early access, what is here is brilliant. The gameplay is pretty damn good that can be compared to something like binding of issac but more melee focused, the story is realistic and relatable as it deals with and discusses real human scenarios and emotions, and it even has a social link system akin to the Persona series where as you build up relations and get to know more of the supporting cast then you get more items added to the loot pool. The graphics are simple yet colourful and somewhat complex, on closer inspection there are a lot of solid colours and a few rough edges but given that the game takes place in a dream it is understandable, plus on the whole it is beautiful. The animations tend to have a stop and go flow to them (such as when you dodge or attack) which adds weight to the movement.If this game was in EA the same time as Hades was and had the same amount of time put into it and released about the same time, then I think it would tie first with Hades for game of the year, as for now though it is currently in the running for best EA game of the year (it'll be a tusstle between it and Baldur's Gate 3).I cannot think of any personal complaints but no game is perfect and I'm sure people will have different opinions on the matter but from me it gets a 9/10.
