_childDocuments_.review: This is an indie game and it shows in places. That said I just had an amazing 50+ hours with it and would love to dive into it again once they get some details ironed out. The closest comparable game I can point to is Hades. Same basic level up and talk to people > take a run > level up and talk to people loop.The good:- Crisp top down action game play (think Hades), with lots of builds- Amazing visuals and sound (the backgrounds are incredible, and while it does reuse assets it re-skins them in a way that keeps it from feeling samey) - Unique game play presentation and way it addresses mental health- nostalgia - I won't ruin anything but if you were a kid in the 90's there's gonna be references that make you smile and little touches that take you back.The Bad (Mostly constructive criticism that I'd like to see addressed so I can throw another 50 hours at it)- Melee feels underwhelming (there are a load of buffs that you can get to ranged weapons including tracking and x3 projectiles that make ranged obviously superior. Melee damage just doesn't ramp up the same way. This won't stop people from beating the lower difficulty's with mostly melee, but means at nightmare 8 ranged is king)-Auto-Recycling after the end of each area seems to be broken, although it wasn't when I started playing. Getting that back up and including objects other than potions in auto-recycle would be a nice quality of life bump. - There's a lack of communication about how some of the mechanics work, I still don't know how elemental extinguish crits work, or how many i frames each different dash gives you. (hopefully the short ones give you more cause I can't figure out why anyone would use most of them otherwise)- Ranged weapons have a few that lag behind, thrown weapons often fly over their target at higher ranges and short range weapons like the super soaker knock off and the flame thrower make it hard to see enemies and know when to dodge out, their decreased range also makes them less viable. Giving these weapons (and melee weapons) some additional buffs through additional relics that are tuned towards them would make more build options feel viable. (things like damage ramping up the longer you hold a flamthrower/supersoaker on a target, ways to make melee stagger bosses, ways to combo from dodging/parrying/blocking into melee giving bonus damage or openings, better melee boosts from your friends)If you're into Hades, Dandy ace, or Wizards of legend you're probably gonna like this one. Personally I'd love to see this company do well to see what else they can make!

_childDocuments_.review: I really love this game but it is held back by some major flaws.Pros:- A lot of fun weapons and spells (or lucid attacks in-game).- Amazing atmosphere.- Interesting socializing mechanism outside of combat.- Combat can be fun.- Right game length if you want to clear the game once with a bad ending.Cons:- The camera is really bad. Some rooms are vertically long and your character as well as the enemies are barely visible when standing at the top, making it nearly impossible to dodge in many attack instances in late levels.- The color palette in level 4 made me want to drop the game. I spent a minute looking for a health potion because it has the same color as the lava floor (pit).- Most of the cool items and weapons are locked behind progression. The starting collection of weapons/item/spells are okay but they feel very samey which makes the game boring very quick. I'm glad I stick with it.- The most important mechanic to deal damage (other than crit), is called critical extinguishes. This mechanic is not very well explained in-game. Had to google why I couldn't deal any damage and saw a thread on reddit telling people to try this.- The progession for the good ending is VERY slow. Essentially you need to befriend with 8 NPCs in your real life to achieve this. I understand what the devs are going for. But it takes forever just to be kindred spirit with one NPC. The dialogues are cute but honestly completing 6-7 runs just to max out your relationship wih 1 NPC seems way too slow.Overall the game is a very decent rogue like with fun combats but it takes some time until you can get to a more enjoyable state.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really creative roguelike with an interesting premise. In addition to the combat  (which was great due to the variety of weapons/combat styles) there are some nice quality of life mechanisms, like being able to teleport to any room you've been to in a level. _childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is your typical action roguelike, you go in defeat a bunch of monsters and bosses and after you die you upgrade yourself and do it all over again. The best part of the game is the writing and the character design. While the general plot of depression and struggling with your role in society is pretty generic and overdone the conversations of the characters are great. A lot of the dialogues feel like they could actually happen, the game isn’t afraid to meander and talk about nothing. At the end of the day it is still a game and the end of the story amounts to the power of friendship trope but it is good until it reaches that point.The game has a lot of meta-progression you are not really meant to win for a while. Once you are strong enough to win the game is kinda easy and I ended up with big winstreaks despite increasing the difficulty after each win. The game gives you too much choice to the point where you can end up with the same build on each run.The core combat system of this game is focused around elemental combos. They are cool and confusing at the same time. Even after 40 hours I still can’t tell how much damage a combo will do without trying it out, even if I have the same lucid skills they may do next to no damage on one run and kill a boss in 3 hits in the next. In general the game has a lot of filler stats that don’t really matter but clutter up your stat screens. Comparing items and figuring out which one is better is a chore and items without an element are usually a nonstarter.The game gives players bad incentives for example you get bonus resources until you get hit for the first time. Because of that you should use the crystal shield as much as possible to get the most resources. The issue is that the game rewards players for doing the same boring thing over and over and tries to band-aid fix that by having achievements for using bad items.Parrying isn’t great in this game, the camera is different all the time which makes judging the timing difficult. A parry oneshots ranged enemies but so does every decent lucid combo without any risk. There really isn’t a good reason to parry other than farming parrys for the grindy achievement. Speaking about achievements this game has a lot of achievements that are grindy and annoying for no good reason.I have a pretty mixed opinion about this game, it is fun for a while but it has a lot of things that are poorly designed and it is hard not to think of this game as a worse version of hades in every way so I can’t recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is a top-down ARPG Roguelite game where you play as Cassidy, a woman who you don't really know much about at the beginning of the game. You seem to have moved into a new apartment as there are boxes everywhere, and your space is very cluttered. The "overworld", which is just Cassidy's waking life, allows you to explore an ever-expanding list of places in the city where you live. These spaces have a finite (so far) list of NPCs that you can interact with. I'll get back to that later. When you're done exploring the overworld and seeing the various things you can do there, the last thing for you to do is sleep. Sleep and dream. In her dreams, Cass is a badass. The dream is separated into layers, each one being from a memory, initially, you seem to be at your childhood home in a suburban neighborhood, when you descend a layer, it's in a city presumably near your home from your youth. Another layer is a woodsy vacation spot and so on and so forth. As you battle nightmares through the levels, you will find memories that will hint to parts of Cass' past life and give you ideas that tie into the game's crafting system. You also find that the bosses at the end of each level are named for things that Cassidy battles in her actual life such as Fear, Loss, Isolation, Negativity, etc. When you are killed in the dream, you wake up. As you advance further in the dream, waking up will cause new parts of the city to become unlocked, new items to be available for crafting, and new opportunities to strengthen Cassidy in the dream.In terms of combat mechanics, I think this game is one of the best I've played. Each weapon plays a little bit differently, but in general, you will have a 2-4 hit combo that is more effective if you time it well. When you push your attack button, Cassidy will perform the attack and her sprite will flash to indicate when to press the button again. There are many items in the game that increase the timing window, so if you're bad at this at first (I'm still terrible at it) it does get easier. Blocking works pretty much the same, holding the block button will hold a shield out, which tapping it at the right time will parry an attack or knock a projectile back at whatever threw it at you. There is just enough timing that it's not too distracting, but also feels very rewarding when you time your combos just right or manage to parry a projectile. Cass can also dodge, an action boosted by equippable objects that can turn your dodge into a fire dash, or a ground pound, or a dozen other things that can change how you fight. Finally, there are lucid powers that you can use while  dreaming. You have access to two at a time, and there are dozens of them to cover. They are basically spells - but the effects are quite literally a blast. One of them will freeze the entire room you're in, one of them will shield you with a giant static field, one of them will drop a fire bomb at your location that fires a directional blast of fire at anything near it. I haven't even seen half of them yet. Once you've delved into the dream a few times, you start to get a feel for which weapons, shields, dashes, and lucid powers you like, and then you can start mastering them, which allows you to start the dream with more and more powerful versions of them. Which brings me to crafting.Dreamscaper doesn't have a terribly unique crafting system - in fact, it's quite simple. In the dream, you'll find ideas. These ideas translate into items that you can sketch in your sketchbook. Items sketched in your sketchbook are items that, once sketched, will be able to randomly appear in the dream. They can be any of the aforementioned weapons, shields, dodges, or lucid powers. Ideas cost a resource called Inspiration that you collect in the dream. Better ideas cost more Inspiration. In the overworld, you will also find items that are basically recipes for things you can craft in your home at your desk. Items that you craft at home can be given to NPCs as gifts to increase your relationship with them and open new dialogue and story options. The more you get to know an NPC, the stronger their influence on you has in the dream. For instance, there's an old man who, if you choose him as your influence, will increase your crit stat in the dream. The more you get to know him, the better this bonus is and the more stats bonuses you will unlock. Each NPC as a specific stat or element that they increase, so you can target the NPC that has what you want.Improving Cassidy in the dream also comes in the form of daydreaming at the bar or meditating in the park. Both of these actions are basically just a unique and creative way to imitate a store. When you meditate, you open a list of improvements that cost a resource you collect in the dream. You can increase Cassidy's HP, Lucid power, etc. Daydreaming is very much the same, except that it costs a different resource (also collected in the dream) and allows you to add things to each layer to make your runs easier and more rewarding as you progress. You can increase item drop rates, add puzzle rooms, add health or lucid power rooms, etc. I'm going to finish here by talking about what literally forced me to keep playing Dreamscaper, the hook for me was the visuals and the music. This game is graphically gorgeous. The scenes, the characters, the abilities...it's art. It's beautifully done and I could honestly look at it all day and not get bored. Right down to each minor character animation, you can tell how much painstaking work they put into making this game LOOK amazing. Not surprisingly, the music is also incredibly done. These two elements are very integral to the immersive feeling I get when I play this game. If you're interested in roguelite titles but never could get into one, I definitely recommend this game. I spent a lot of time trying to like this style of game until I found Dreamscaper and I highly recommend it. I spent the first three hours just ogling at the artwork and music while dying over and over again trying to figure out which items to use. If you do pick it up, do yourself a favor and play it with a controller.

So much great potential but mired by lackluster design and production quality. I consider this more of a draft and less of a full game. Maybe another year in development and I might re-purchase this, but as it stands now it's just not worth even the discount. Great effort, but too little o justify purchase.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: I had had the demo for this game for a while. Tried playing with the keyboard and gave up. Then I received the game in bundle and it sat in my library for a bit. Just started playing it, this time with a controller, and I love it. I like rogue-likes well enough, but there is usually no depth to them story wise, which is ok. Rogue-likes should be fast  paced and difficult. This game has a slower pace to it, yet it doesn't take away from the fun. The weapons and abilities are fun to discover. Every time I started a new run, it was interesting to check my layout. The weapons and abilities are creative. The activities in the waking world are never boring, I actually care about the protagonist and want to see her build the relationships with the other characters, and not just for the abilities (influences). Nice game. You can see the love which went to making it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Just getting started with this game but already really enjoy it. Like many action games it's a little clunky with the keyboard but it's fantastic with a controller and the action has a really good level of difficulty to stay challenging without being too frustrating. The arts style and music is also great and it runs very well on a low-spec laptop. The mechanics of weapon-equipping and upgrading are a little confusing but I love the relationship building and the central gameplay loop is very addictive.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Game's pretty wonderful. Its hard not to compare this to Hades for obvious reasons, and it holds up. Variety in the form of weapons, lucid attacks, and keepsakes is a little less exciting than Hades Boons, and there's definitely less depth in builds. On the other hand, the meta-progression mechanics are more compelling than Hades' for me. Music, tone, writing all hit the spot for me but I can see how it would be a miss for some. Combat I wouldn't say is as crisp as it could be from a camera and movement perspective, but animations, attacks and spells are all incredibly satisfying. 26 hours in I'm perplexed by the difficulty. Some of the bosses are underwhelming and are easily defeated on the first try, whereas others (5th and final boss) are a massive leap in difficulty. Still haven't beaten the last boss. If you enjoyed Hades a lot but are getting tired of it, this is a must-grab and an entirely comparable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: ok I havent played the game much but i can say for absolute certain that this game is very good. sure my opinion could change because I've only beaten the first boss, but this appears to be a story about self betterment wrapped in a rogue-lite package. There a lot of really unique ideas here and honestly i already love this game. Also, please name another game where i can hit people with a blackhole, drop a fireball on them and then hit em with my buster sword? ok probably a few other games let you do that but listen this game is dope go buy it whoever made it deserves monetary compensation for this absolute gem
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: I have played most if not all Roguelites and games like this, this one really does it very well.  A great breath of fresh air in art, music, design, even the out of game world relationship building at first I thought was silly and unnecessary but I grew to like it, although I wish after all that hard work building relationships the perks you get from them were more, kinda seems really off balance.BUT, great weapon selections and animations, great variety of ways to do damage from abillites, melee and ranged.  Keeps it fresh.  Took me 20 hours to beat it for the first time.. I also think the difficulty settings unlocked should yield more rewards.  Make the game WAY harder and longer each run but only get what, max 20% more out of battle rewards? So instead of 300 i get 360? doesnt seem like its worth it, like the realtionship perks.  I feel those should be rebalanced too. BUT aside from those comments, the game is truly fantastic and a joy to play.  Most roguelikes just fill content with useless perks and upgrades and things like that but everything feels well polished and balanced in terms of rewards IN GAME.  The added bonus of the developers story really makes me want you all to play it even more.  Respect to the developers for their journey and their vision, they did create something truly special here...
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game for what it is, but the over use of bloom effects to create a "dream-like" effect is very annoying - everything being out of focus is cute for cut scenes but this is not what you want in the middle of action.  Combat is good with lots of weapon effects and synergies, but overall for an ARPG played over maps that look identical from room to room (it's a dream), it gets old after a while.  It's also hard to parry shots if you move around a bit since the game is played from inconsistent angles - it's an isometric or even top down affair that has a fixed camera angle on most fights that is way too low.I suppose if the depression/recovery story speaks to you, it might have a deeper connection.  For me, I eventually just felt it was tiresome.  As other reviewers have said, Hades is a far tighter experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: I helped kickstart this game. Normally throwing 50$ or more at a kickstarter campaign thats a video game is very rare for me because they can hit or miss. this particular game however is a bit special.I met the devs at DreamHack and played their demo (a little unhealthly to a point they had to kick me off a couple times, don't blame them at all lol).  they told me about their pre alpha, stuck around for that and all the other extra projects till release.Every single update has always been a challenge that always feels so rewarding.The combat I never expected it to be so deep at all. but there is so much too it that helps so much from the parries to the elemental bonuses and extinguishes.The gameplay is where it shines a lot.there are things that the game doesn't tell you but its one of those old school functions where discovery is rewarded.Story aspect can be difficult to grab a hold of mainly because its all text and no voice/action. but it does tell a story through visual metaphors and everyday conversations with the people you bond with. even the weapons and levels have much to add to the story.Just go into it with an open artistic mind and it'll make sense in the long run.Highly recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is a game that does many things right. The core mechanics are solid enough, the soundtrack would deserve a separate essay detailing how incredible it is, and the basic gameplay loop of whacking monsters around within vividly designed dreamscapes while using cool dream powers provides for neat, bite-sized bits of action-RPG fun. But for me, this was all hampered by the inherently repetitive nature of the game’s roguelike elements, the occasional messiness of the combat mechanics, and the lack of an immediately engaging narrative to make me want to come back for more. At the end of the day, I still think Dreamscaper is a decent little game (hence the thumbs up) – but I’m probably not going to stay up all night thinking about it.For more honest indie game reviews, check out our Curator page:

_childDocuments_.review: Great rouge-like with fun weapons and amazing concepts. Love the way it ties the waking world with the dream world. Love the bosses and the character development. Its a perfect mix between story and action and probably one of the only games that I play that i am genuinely interested in the back story of the character. 10/10 would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun entry to the rogue-like genre. The combat is great, and there is a large variety of different weapons, dashes, magic abilities, etc.The way that everything is tied together with the theme of dreams, relationships, and different emotional issues is also well-done, and drives the player to continue playing and exploring.Very much recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give this a mixed rating.If you're like me, and you saw this game and thought it looked like Hades, and Hades was amazing, and Hades 2 isn't out yet...well I have good news and bad news.Good news, it is indeed like Hades. Very very much so. You run through escalating levels, moving from combat room to combat room with occasional divergences. Combat is melee, range, dodge, but this game adds two spells and a block/parry mechanic. Then you die and return to an overworld where you upgrade your character, expand the content of the levels, and form bonds with a cast of characters.Bad news, it is a worse version of Hades. In every single way.The combat has none of Hades' polish, and you will quickly lose patience with it. The depth simply isn't there, as you constantly switch out your gear for something with better numbers and realise that the many many gear pickups are all shallow to the point you will stop caring about them after about two rooms of using them. The upgrade system is perhaps the one area where this game should shine, but instead it runs headfirst into the biggest failing, which is the plot being utterly generic and uninteresting, with a cast of characters so dull that after almost six hours in this game I still can't keep their names straight in my head.The writing here is just...it's really bad. Which is a big problem because the lore here is that everything you are doing is just a metaphorical battle for the main character to overcome her trauma and find her better self...except none of that comes across in any of the writing, and none of the characters have any interesting relationship with her, and honestly she's so dull that I can't actually remember her name for sure. Cass something I think.Part of this is surely that it lacks the phenomenal voice acting of Hades, or any voice acting...but I believe even just reading Hades dialogue would have made me care about Zagreus' quest. Care about whether he mended his relationship with Thanatos, or helped Achilles to find his lover again. I cannot imagine caring about any of the characters in this game, even if they had an all star cast to croon each insipid line in my ear.I feel bad about not reccomending this game, because it's clear that real love and effort went into it...but having attempted to copy an all time great, they have only showed off how poor a substitute they could create.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: There are many things I like about this game, but combat feels weird (slow, stiff, clunky). It looks like a quick flashy action game, but it feels like a slow, deliberate souls-like if you examine your character movements and enemy attack patterns.If combat felt the way as fluid and powerful as it looks on videos it would be 9/10 along with the nice variety of weapons/skills the game offers. It doesn't. A good chunk of weapons lack any weight to their attacks and combat pace resembles dark souls games (slow and deliberate). You get locked into attack animations and dodging locks you out of dodging again for a short time."Perfect Attack" mechanic allows you to time followup attacks for bonus damage. Great system in theory. Too bad the games triggers a slowdown effect after successful hit/evasion, which delays the timing for a perfect attack.No attacks are technically unavoidable, but some of them are difficult to learn and react to simply because there's no way to practice against specific enemies and some enemies are difficult to read. You essentially have to learn the timing, because animations are too fast. I found Bosses to be the easiest enemies to read and react to, which is a problem IMO. It's grindy and mostly boring. Later ranks might unlock something more exciting, but where I am at right now I get boring stuff, like minor stat boosts (e.g. 5 MaxHP/5 MaxMP/2% MP regen), item unlocks (item pool), random event room unlocks and upgrades for event rooms.The biggest positive I can say about this game's progression is you can control your starting gear, which gives value to having larger item pool. You usually get random gear with better stats within first 2 minutes of each run, but  this gives you some sense of progression and also it allows you to pick your dodge skill/animation, which doesn't rely in stats as much and can improve the feel of the game a bit.I wouldn't recommend this to anybody I know.With that said I do recommend trying it, because I feel people who like souls-like combat might like this game too. Just...set yourself a 110min timer, so you can refund it in case you don't like it.If you don't like souls-likes, Hades has a similar price and top-down action combat, but is superior in terms of gameplay mechanics. I'm not a fan of grind in Hades, but I would recommend it over Dreamscaper any day. Combat feels more fair, progression is more rewarding and you actually have a better chance of beating the game without grinding meta-progression.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game with quite a few layers. While dealing with depression and loss, it also shows how relationships can be a great help in dealing with real world challenges. This also doubles as part of the game's dynamic in which building those relationships helps the protagonist overcome challenges and learns new abilities to take into the dream world to defeat her inner demons. Very engaging and always a joy to come back to every now and again.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game. Somewhat repetitive, as the difficulty ramps up significantly, so you will probably repeat the earlier levels many times, but I feel like that's to be expected. It's a good feeling when you can breeze through a level you initially struggled on, primarily because you've mastered the mechanics of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: So far I must say the game makes me feel underwhelmed and overwhelmed at the same time. I bought it with expectations of getting a fairly dynamic slasher but this is not it. However, pacing is not the only issue and I wanted to appreciate the game as it is, still. But I feel incredibly unimmersed because of the artificial boundaries and lack of continuity in moving around the map and the game overall. Levels meaning a single dream feel clunky and too fragmented. Cutscene transitions are not fluid at all either, it breaks the immersion even more. Upgrades and other overworld mechanics feel kind of cryptic and not very easily understandable. It just feels quite messy. There's not that much in-level variety either - I had three same-looking burger place rooms in level 1. They feel very unlively and bland, there's just nothing in them. Nothing to add to the atmosphere, really. No voice acting or any kind of emphasizing the text just makes the story part of the game really just go quite unnoticed. It's all just making this game feel really dismissable and forgetful. And I mean, maybe the game gets better later on, as the story progresses. I'll play more and see. But so far I'm sadly just disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: DREAMSCAPERYou play as beautiful Cassidy, during the day you learn about her life, make friends and build relationships. While sleeping she becomes a powerful heroine that battles room after room filled with nightmares, she makes it to the bosses which are traits of her personality she must overcome.Honestly this is one of the first roguelite I actually enjoyed, the die, level up and repeat function feels varied enough that it never gets boring or to hard.The combat is solid, I love the different weapons and skills you can find, everything feels fluid and fun to play.The music is also incredible! Really no complaints of any kind, the story seems sad but beautiful so far.Check it out!9/10

_childDocuments_.review: the game is really beautiful in terms of graphic and the music really fit in with the game since it just give a good atmosphere all around the gameplay, i thuoght i would quit the game once i beated it but i still play it because of how stunning and unique the idea of the game really is, the key points:-The game runs really smoothly and the tracking of the mouse/gamepad is really nice and easy.-Gameplay has a LOT of deep, the weapon, the shields, everything is just to vast and really fit the rogue-like item amount.-Free updates & content added constantly and did i say again ALL FREE?.-The music of the game is really good, keeps you calm and comfy at all times and the fighting song also fit in.-The Combat system is unique because not a single run so far had been the same and the enemies are worthy adversary even in later runs.-The story of the game also has a lot of indepth on it and keeps you wondering what will one of the "in-game friends" tells you.-The discord of this game really is active and they devs listen to their community for hotfix,problems,bugs, or ideas which is something REALLY good.Overall this game is a hidden gem and hopefully this review can help you give it a go to see what happens, trust me once you see the game idea and the animation graphich (specially when you go to dreamland oh mama) you won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Its an interesting disconnect from the otherwise gritty and dark rougelikes (rougelite?? whatever) that you yourself enjoy. Instead of a doomed world, its some faceless lass in Oregon. Or Washington. Slaying all manner of nondescript blobs in the name of facing otherwise metaphorical (but real for you) monsters. All the common vestiges of the rougelike are here, but its merely laid out before you in a soft manner. I'm trying to mean this as genuinely as I can. The internet really loves ruining common words but anything else I could use would just synonyms. The game is comfortable. There. How about that. As an example: Instead of going to a blacksmith for weapons since they're not real, you sketch 'em out. Merely giving you the 'concept' of a knife, or whatever. Then they might just show up in the world later on. They have a lovely theme, and they stick with it eloquently, without having to beat you over the head with it. It boasts a deeper combat system than Dead Cells (in that you have a combo system), and it has a nice plush mystery for you explore if you are so inclined. Its filled with a non-existent, yet visceral nostalgia; being just vague enough to remain relatable, but detailed enough to take its own direction. Much like the lass you play as.I wish I had played this before I went ahead and delved into Dead Cells as deeply as I did because I'd love this game if I wasn't so burnt out on rougelikes. Its tone is so dramatically different and refreshing from anything else going on. Highly recommend on that alone.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: While I hate this genre, this game is very good. Its a typical rogue lite, but has some nice upgrade systems, and a cool double world, where when youre awake, you power up your character, by visiting, and unlocking more places in your town. Meet new people, unlock, "ideas", that power you up. You can also craft gifts for the friends you make, and the give you different passive abilities. Weapons are cool, different, and unique. The powers you have, and get, are also all pretty cool. When you sleep, you enter the game world where you do your fighting, and eventual dying. You can skip beaten bosses, but will miss out on upgrade supplies, power ups, and it has something to do with final score upon death i believe, i havent skipped any yet, but noticed a skip bosses counter, so fact check me on that one. The bosses arent too hard, as the game isnt. Its a good difficulty level, which makes it actually fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: I want to first off say thanks to my friend for giving me this game! >w<; So far what I have played of the game;I've had the game randomly crash on me two times - both being fatal errors (will change numbers of things over time if it continues)I really enjoy the music it's super relaxing and I love it.The mechanic where if you die you basically have to start over was annoying at first but it also makes complete sense because if you go through and die for example to the first boss of the game then come back through with your best gear and full health it would make everything a lot easier but would probably be unfair in a sense.The visual novel aspect and building relationships with the characters is kind of cool and different well at least to me - though as you progress with the characters some of them feel like they talk more than others lol.Anyways I've liked this game so far and look forward to experiencing more of it xD long as I don't get wedged between two boss mobs and literally can't escape REEEEEEEEEEEE.

_childDocuments_.review: At first I dived into this game pretty much blind, thinking it's another rogue-like that I'd enjoy slashing my way through.But then the story got to me, and it actually got really deep and some interactions with other characters really make you think about some things..Definitely worth picking up at the normal price, if it's in sale and you like roguelikes with a wee bit of story, a must have
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: First Steam review ever.This game is really well done. The combat is great, the pacing is phenomenal, the minimalist but touching 'Persona'-esque town conversations are wonderful. I've read some reviews of people disparaging this game because it has a female protagonist. Ridiculous! The central character could be any gender, there are no romances. Instead this game tackles deeper, social/psychological issues like depression, imposter syndrome, struggling to fit in, being a fish out of water, insert metaphor here that the vast majority of us will immediately feel connected to.The combat is stellar, and I can confidently say that after 20+ hours in and unlocking *all* the social unlocks I have yet to complete the game entirely. The sense of progression is wonderfully paced, the gameplay loop is extraordinary.I'm excited for what these devs continue to produce.  If only for the writing alone, I truly applaud this piece of art.  The combat is just icing on the cake. If you like roguelikes and character building please, please try this.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: A fun game so far. It feels a little slow compared to some other Rogue-like games, but does have the option to save between floors if you need to step away which is nice.A full run for me right now (not completing all floors, only 4-5) takes 30-45 minutes, whereas a full-clear in something like Hades is about 30 minutes total. So it's a little harder for me to jump into quickly when I have a moment to myself, knowing it will need a longer stretch of time to really enjoy.The story is interesting enough, and has a Skip option for those character interactions you just can't stand. I would love to see the cinematic skip-option a little more responsive. It takes like 2-3 seconds to cancel the boss animation, and there's only so many times I care to watch the first 1-3 boss animations before it's just stale.Edit: Found the setting for skipping cinematics, definitely a nice quality of life improvement there. Also, beat the game for the first time(15hr or so in?), definitely a fun challenge and will be back for more!
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Really great variety of weapons / spells / passives and combos. There is a lot to unlock and discover which makes each run different, took me 14h to beat last boss on standard difficulty and there are 2 more difficulty levels. I'm not even close to have everything unlocked / mastered. Game also looks nice, has its own unique graphic style and some spells can be really flashy. Devs are patching up the game and everyone can give their feedback on official discord, nice to see that it's not just dump and take money project but actually something they are willing to continue working on. The only thing i don't like is the way this game tries to tell the story, most of the time it's just a plain text on the screen or just feels forced.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Great game so far its a rogue lite similar to Hades with a touch of diablo.This game throws lots of abilities and weapons at you to play with.You are kinda forced to take new abilities or weapons since they don’t scale and the ones you find are better, this keeps the run fresh in my opinion.The game has some very nice visuals, the music fits the tone.In the overworld you follow around Cass and learn about her past while making friends with people and learning about them, you also get permanent upgrades for your runs.Funnily enough the visuals are also my biggest annoyance with the game almost all abilities have spectacular graphics which sadly obstruct the view of what’s happening. This has cost me the run multiple times because the enemy in a big explosion might not be stunned and hit you anyway or you don’t see the visual cues for attacks or sometimes you even lose track of your character.Another smaller problem are obstacles like trees etc you can easily get stuck between the side/corner of the arena which essentially is a invisible wall since and enemies.Anyway lovely game I am very interested in seeing it finished.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to leave a negative review for a small development studio, but the combat just isn't doing it for me. The range of weapons is nice and unique, but the combat itself doesn't feel fluid and to echo what another reviewer said it just feels...heavy. All of the weapons feel slow like your swinging them through the water and I personally despise the "perfect timing in order to get a crit" system implemented. The environments, enemies, etc are all really well done...but I just can't get over the combat itself. I'll try the game again sometime in the future after a few major updates to see if it's improved, but for now I'm just not enjoying my time with it.Edit: Decided to give this another go after the 1.1 update went out and spend a lot more time with the game, going an additional 4 hours on top of the ~2 I did at my initial review. Unfortunately for the most part what I said remains the same to me. There are some weapons that do not feel slow, but overall I still do not enjoy the combat. I still despise the "timing attacks" system. I was wrong about it being used for crits, but it is used for bonus damage and slightly faster attacks and crits are handled by a separate RNG system. I would much rather a system be implemented where how you attack an enemy (from behind, knocked into a wall/barrier, on the third strike, after a certain sequence of button presses, etc) dealt bonus damage. Even if the bonus damage wasn't an issue, there are still some things about the combat I don't enjoy, like the slowdown of time on certain strikes or counters as it takes away from the rhythm and has caused me to take damage as I hit the dodge button or parry button too early from an incoming attack. What I do enjoy about the game is the same as above - environments, enemies, etc. One thing I missed in the first game that I found I enjoyed the second time around is the upgrade system, though there are some aspects of it I think could be improved.I think if you're someone who wouldn't mind the timing aspect of attacks or the slowdowns after parries/certain strikes then you probably would enjoy the game. For me though it is just far too distracting and annoying for me to continue playing what is otherwise a good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is beautiful, fun, and addictive. I just beat the final boss for the first time and don't feel like putting the game down any time soon! The combat is fluid, fast-paced, colorful, and just plain fun, especially on the later levels. There's a varity of weapon types that are truly unique and fit the dream setting well - from finger guns and paper airplanes to tridents and my personal favorite, the primal scream. The only flaw I could find is that some of the "lucid abilities" (spells) make it momentarily hard or even impossible to see what is going on. Design-wise, the game is absolutely gorgeous. The different levels all have a very unique feel & atmosphere, which is helped by the fantastic music. Every level is a pleasure to look at and immerse yourself in. My main gripe with the levels themselves is that I never seem to have enough items to unlock all the rooms despite having leveled this up, which can be frustrating.The "waking world" offers a nice little break from exploring & fighting while you make friends and level up your character. There's a good sense of progression with your character becoming stronger and your loadout becoming more powerful over time as you invest your earned currencies.The game has a "lucid mode" that makes your character more resistant with every death, which makes it more accessible for those who haven't played this type of game before. There are other accessibility options as well (e.g., aim assist).Overall, this is a gem of a game. It has some very minor flaws that don't distract from the overall experience. I highly recommend giving it a try!

_childDocuments_.review: You sit down at your computer and lament: "Man, why does Binding of Isaac have to be about ridiculous gross things and domestic violence?" You slide closed yet another message from a Redditor telling you to get therapy and wonder when there will finally be a roguelike that is themed around your own screwed-up-ness. (Un?)fortunately, I am either pleased or sorry to inform you that today is the day!Dreamscaper is a top-down action roguelike based on taking mundane items and using them to fight your inner monsters. It was created by a team of three visually identical game developers who became self-aware of how garbo the industry is and opened a time rift to perpetually exist three years out from leaving their old jobs. Overall, the gameplay is pretty traditional; go through doors to explore a map. Rooms lock you into them until all enemies are defeated. Some rooms contain time-wasting puzzles which yield items, some are treasure rooms with items already in them, and some require you to abide certain combat conditions to receive a reward.You can have a melee weapon, a ranged weapon, and up to two magic attacks. You can also pick up passive items, companions, and orbitals, and potentially a shield you can block or parry with. The range of items is wide enough that you can easily determine your own preferences, things to be on the lookout for or things to set out with. What you have less control over is how good those starting items will be, whether you will find sufficient resources to upgrade them over time, or if you will be forced to trade them out by fortune or necessity to survive. I've seen a number of negative reviews for this game that really criticise this point, but I'm not wholly sure that it could be considered a roguelike if you weren't forced to make value judgements based on random dice rolls like this. There will be runs where you can take your trusty pool cue through the entire game and buff it up into a super weapon, there will be times where you'll need to trade it out. Whatever the circumstance, you need to figure out a way to survive based on what life gives you. The game is pretty difficult -- good items go a long way, but 90% of what's carrying you is your own dexterity, situational awareness, and timing. It's totally understandable to get frustrated by the difficulty, but it's the nature of the game and delivers a kind of triumphant fun that you're either here for or you're not. I'm pretty much all here for it.Lacking is definitely the area of the overworld and meta-progression. Items, abilities, and stat upgrades are unlocked through a series of menus in buildings around town. These take the thematic form of meditating in the park, writing in a journal at the coffee shop, and such like that. I understand that the theme is relatively appropriate, but navigating to them is more awkward and time consuming than it has to be. You can take a buff with you to the dream state from each one of the NPCs around town, but you need to have conversations with them, or bribe them to acquire and level up those buffs. Each level-up guarantees a 100,000% cringe auto-playing dialogue between your character and the NPC.Fortunately, these interactions are a minuscule amount of the game, since the bulk of what you'll be doing is descending through the assorted levels of your mind palace and the bosses along the way. As far as this goes, I find it enjoyable and will continue to play this game into the future for that reason. Therefore my recommendation is positive.

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is a quintessential roguelite character action game, with minor RPG elements and simple but well-written character story moments that are evocative of the Persona series of games. Over its development, Dreamscaper has changed a lot, and I daresay predominantly for the better. Many aspects have been refined and expanded since I first played it, and I can absolutely recommend it.The (very) extensive selection of weapons, abilities and gear have made every one of my runs enjoyable thus far. Perhaps moreso, they have very much made me think and adjust on my feet, often adapting my playstyle mid-run to account for the new dynamics. The challenge feels unique, and quite welcome.As is almost necessary of games of the roguelite genre, the desire for "one more run" is an element this game certainly has in spades, and I have found myself awake at strange hours of the morning playing it more than once.Conversations between the characters in the Waking World are well-written, and despite the lack of voice acting, I found myself very attached to them before long. There is something to the stories, simple and small, that makes them compelling. Perhaps it is because that makes them more real.I should mention that the music is (without hyperbole) some of the best I have heard in an independently produced game for quite some time. My compliments go to Dale North for the excellent score. Every piece fits the world and moods perfectly, and are beautiful in their own right. Of course, the game is not perfect. I find myself wishing that there could be deeper, more regular and more organic interactions with the characters met in the Waking World. The game could benefit from greater enemy variety, late game activities/options for more varied and challenging runs, and a little more time fleshing out narrative aspects of the dream world. But there  something special about it, as an immersive experience - a realisation I found surprising when it came to me. The pieces may not come together seamlessly - but they come together well. And the game as a whole evokes a strange nostalgia. Thinking about it feels like the remnants of a half-remembered dream, that I wish I could go back to. And lately, I often do.To put it another way:Hades (by Supergiant Games) was my Game of the Year when it arrived on the scene.Dreamscaper is not Hades. And perhaps it would be foolish to expect that it would be. But if you were to ask me if Dreamscaper is worth your time, and money? I would say: "Absolutely. Without a doubt."PS: A quick note on combat that I would have appreciated knowing, going in. The combat system can be fast, but above all, it is . That is to say: unlike many character action games that focus heavily on pure mechanical timing and execution at a maximised pace, Dreamscaper rewards mechanical and strategic consideration in equal measure. Managing positioning, engagement distances and being mindful of gear synergies and dis-synergies are just as important as perfect dodges, parries and attacks. Deciding when you will  attack can be just as important as deciding when you do.I have come to the conclusion that Dreamscaper's combat is about timing, patience, forethought and precision. Coming from a long history with the Devil May Cry franchise, this threw me for a loop when I first jumped in. But once I acclimatised, I was enjoying myself immensely.

_childDocuments_.review: Sitting squarely in the dime-a-dozen roguelite genre, Dreamscaper makes a name for itself by taking nods from the best of fellow roguelites like Hades, Dead Cells, and Isaac, and then adding a coat of its own incredibly unique flair. The roguelite "run" occurs in the dreams of Cassidy (the player). On death, Cassidy wakes from her nightmare but instead of immediately beginning another run, she has the option to venture out into the "Waking World" to interact with different people around town (in a series of social-sim style interactions). These interactions drive progression in both item unlocks and bonuses for future runs in the dreamworld as well as furthering Cassidy's story (which, and I cannot stress this enough, is some of the most compelling and relatable dialogue I've experienced in a game. It's a wonderfully pleasant surprise that makes Cassidy a character worth emotional investment).The gameplay is terrific. Not ground-breaking, but wildly satisfying nonetheless. Melee weapons have the right amount of heft, ranged weapons are varied and unique, shielding and landing parries feel awesome, and powers feel powerful. Exciting synergies don't tend to matter until the latter half of the game, but after several runs the first couple stages can be rushed pretty quickly to get to the juicier encounters. I've seen several complaints about enemies being damage-sponges that become button-mash-fests when you get the stun-lock on them, but this "issue" really only matters in the first stage. It also tells me that players aren't upgrading stuff as they progress or they're just stuck in the early-game, since face-tanking single enemies loses viability pretty quick when you need to manage 4+ enemies in the late stages with projectiles flying every which way.Presentation and performance are standouts. I'm not going to say something someone else hasn't already said about the art and music - they're delightful. Performance-wise, it wouldn't surprise me if someone told me this was the most polished Early Access title they've ever played; it's that good.Content availability is above par for what to expect from an EA roguelite, there's enough here that you could 100% the current offering in a couple dozen hours.Couldn't be more thrilled to support the devs working on this game, they've got something special here and have set the bar exceptionally high for themselves.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: From it’s opening moments, Dreamscaper invokes a feeling of a strikingly polished Early Access game with fantastic visuals, hauntingly beautiful music, satisfying and fluid combat, a heart-warming and engaging story and an addicting roguelite loop born from the dreams of Cassidy, the main character.It’s an immensely satisfying mash up of a roguelite with randomized dungeons pulled from Cassidy’s subconscious, ARPG style combat and loot combined with waking world narrative and Persona influenced relationship building. Persona games are proof that it works and Afterburner Studios used the formula very creatively and successfully. You play as Cassidy, a young girl suffering from depression who’s moved to a quaint little town of Redhaven. She spends her nights in lucid dreams fighting figments and projections from her fears and insecurities and her days hanging around town trying to awkwardly establish some human connections. A story most of us have surely felt and experienced.The visuals are incredibly well crafted. From the distorted amalgams of Cassidy’s dreams and nightmares that form the dungeons you traverse in your sleep to the waking world’s parks, libraries and shops you and your co-workers frequent, the amount of details and attention put into them flows from every scene. Even Cassidy’s journal, encyclopedia, in-game icons and loot drops are phenomenally well done and fit into the dreamlike state of the entire game sublimely.The relationships you form during the day through conversations and gifts unlock items and grant new powers that you can find and use in Dreamscapes. As your relationship level increases, so does the strength of the powers or influences, as they’re called in-game. Just as in life, having strong human connections makes each of the individuals stronger. When you reach certain levels you also get a short conversation cutscene. They aren’t voiced, but they are well written and shine a spotlight on each individual’s likes, dislikes and quirks, including Cassidy’s. And they’re so human, so every one of us, it’s marvelously touching.There are 7 characters since the Reflection update and there may be more to come in further updates. Every move to a new location and chit-chat advances time in the waking world. Depending how well you did in your last Dreamscape, the more time you have before Cassidy needs to go home, which is always 9PM. The gifts you can give are crafted from materials collected from nightmares that carry the words of emotions, like bliss and solace, representing the meaning, comfort and familiarity those objects bring to the people you give them to.When Cassidy succumbs to sleep, it’s time to enter her lucid dreams conveyed into randomly generated dungeons full of her negative emotions personified as monsters, aberrations and traps. I absolutely love the transition and falling into sleep. Her dreams play out as a fast paced, beautifully fluid, isometric dungeon crawler with varying rooms. You’ll encounter enemies, puzzles, challenges, shops, upgrade rooms and occasionally Cassidy’s memories presented as will-o’-the-wisps. You can pick up the memories and get a small glimpse of her life. There’s even a fast travel system in dungeons where you can easily teleport to any room you’ve already visited.A brilliant tutorial will introduce you to all the mechanics you need to know. Combat consists of normal, heavy and ranged attacks, dodges, blocks, parries and lucid attacks. And it works wonderfully. You can cancel your attacks with a dodge, which is an excellent thing. It also includes a slow time ability. If you chain your combos correctly, with Cassidy flashing when you need to attack, you’ll get bonus damage. Items, weapons, modifiers and abilities are plentiful and can be upgraded by using the game’s currency called Sand. A fitting name for a game about dreams. They are unlocked by forging the relationships in the waking world and can then be found in dungeons or bought from shops.All items have stats, great comments and descriptions and you can also check all your stats on the character screen. Items you collect in a single run stay with you until you die and wake up. You lose everything upon death, but can set up your starting equipment by using the same materials you use to craft gifts. Or leave it random and hope for the best on your next run. One incredibly awesome thing is that you can skip bosses you’ve already defeated which makes repeated runs much faster. You get a random item even if you skip the boss.There’s something really worth mentioning in the game options. A checkbox next to something called Lucid Mode. I cannot express how happy I was when I saw that. If you turn it on, every time you die, your lucid resistance increases, making your subsequent runs easier. I really wish more roguelite, soulslike and similar games did something like this. I believe a larger audience would have a chance to enjoy them. I’m aware that many fans of those games will not agree with me because the challenge is the point. Kudos to the developers for implementing something like this. Another great thing is that the game includes color vision deficiency options, three of them, and a slider for severity.I really like what Afterburner Studios has crafted. It’s still an Early Access, small bugs remain, nothing major and things will surely change as the game continues development. But it’s already a great indie gem. There’s a lot of very quality content and it works very smoothly. I’ve gushed enough, but not to make everything sound like sunshine and rainbows, there are a couple of things some may find questionable.Relationship building and gift giving may seem a needless grind to pad out the game and acquire better abilities that could’ve been avoided or reduced. Free your mind and take it from a different perspective, besides purely mechanical. Consider a meditative, dreamlike loop of establishing strong connections with your fellow human beings that don’t happen in a heartbeat. That fits very well with the game’s overarching story. Even the conversations that may seem out of context or in the wrong order sometimes, depending how your relationships progress, follow the patterns of dreams which are anything but ordered.Dreamscaper brings a lot of personality, heart and a very relatable story to the table, but further ups the ante with good mechanics and very solid combat. No small feat for a small studio and an indie publisher, but an unreachable height for any AAA soulless husks churning out $70 garbage cans. The love and time invested into the game are very obvious and that’s what good indie games are known for. Dreamscaper is one worthy of your time.Take a peek inside the  if you like to walk off the beaten path and only sometimes return to the main roads. You might find something worth exploring.: Very straightforward achievements. Loaded achievement requires collecting 6000 Sand in one run.

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is an action-focused roguelite that combines a lot of great mechanics that all come together to offer a lot of variety in moment to moment gameplay.While the combat focuses mainly on using your melee and ranged weaponry, you also have 2 slots for special abilities, a shield which let's you block and parry enemy attacks and projectiles and different types of dodges.There's also a pretty large amount of different items for each of these slots, with lots more to unlock throughout the game.It may feel a little overwhelming at first, since there quite a lot of abilities and attacks you as a player get, but once it clicks, each is a very valuable asset in keeping yourself alive and decimating enemies.Enemy types are also quite varied, with different attack patterns and strategies.On the other hand the floors and bosses are always the same, both of which there are 6.The story follows Cassidy, a girl that recently moved from a small town into the big city and focuses mainly on how she deals with her anxiety and depression, trying to connect to the new people around her.This unfurls mainly through dialogue with other characters roaming around the city and improving your relationships with them.Dreamscaper also looks very pretty.The different areas you visit all have a distinct look, despite many of them being reimagined versions of themselves and always are a joy to wander through.Character animations and ability effects also are a spectacle to behold - however, oftentimes i found them to be too good even.Sometimes there will be so many effects and particles around your character, you won't be able to see enemies anymore and may get hit by an otherwise easily dodged attack.Hades had a similar issue in Early Access, where it's effects were simply too overhwlming until they dialed them back a bit.Maybe an option to decrease these effects could be useful to some.Overall it took  about 35 hours to finish the story and another 5 or so hours achievement hunting.There's still lots of unlockables left for me to try out however, so for those interested, the game may offer still more playability.

It's challenging but permits steady progression. It's graphically very nice and the story/combat flows at a good pace. I would highly recommend this game if you play games in short bursts. _childDocuments_.review: This game is earnest and creative in just the way you hope for from an indie game. The visual style is gorgeous, the characters are relatable, and the gameplay has a unique blend of ‘slice-of-life’ RPG and roguelite elements that feels completely natural yet quite unusual. I quite like how a big part of the game is just getting out of the house, chatting to people, and doing peaceful, real-world things to level up your character, while the other part of the game is fighting for your life with all sorts of fantasy weapons and abilities. Oh, and it's nice that they break up the action a bit within a run with some puzzle minigames, just to give you a bit of a rest between battles.It's not perfect though, and there are a couple of things though that I dislike—things that I often dislike about roguelites: one is that there isn't as much random variation as I'd like, which can make the levels feel a bit repetitive; another is that to me the difficulty ramps up too quickly (I think roguelites do this so that you really feel the benefit from leveling up between runs, but sometimes I just feel like I can't do anything to survive). Oh, and I feel like there's a bit too much up-front information, but I'm bad at paying attention, so pretty much any upfront information is too much for me...Having said that, I think if you like roguelites, this is definitely worth giving a go.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to recommend this game. I'm not great at this game, nor was I very good at Hades or anything else in the genre. It took me twenty hours to finally clear the dungeon, and the reward is a punch in the face. You get a bait and switch final boss with a bait and switch ending if you clear the game before maxing out your social links, a process that involves hours and hours of grinding materials. _childDocuments_.review: Been playing Dreamscaper for a while now and I'm going to recommend it. Honestly though, it's more of a lukewarm, play it if you've finished Hades and grown tired of other games like Rogue Legacy 1 & 2. I would recommend this over both Cuisineer and Dead Cells, though, but that's propably a preference.It has a "Die and get stronger," mode, which I love, because I suck and its awesome to actually - eventually - finish this game.It's hard being mean or overly critical of this game because the studio is obviously small, and Dreamscaper is a labour of love. Mechanically, I'm pretty damn dumb, so I played hyper agressively, rarely using my shield. Still managed to beat normal difficulty and I'm working my way up. Played this for, like, an hour, maybe an hour and a half over the course of two weeks and I'm left feeling split on how well this game would work in more intense sessions.Your resource gain is borderline painfully slow. Like, there's a lot of upgrades, and picking any feels like picking the least worst instead of something cool and different. There's also a friend system, but it lacks any of Hades charm. Ironically, Cassy was making friends while I was skipping dialouge by the end and only cared about what those people could give me. So, for a game about mental health, not, uh, not a great message. All of the dialouge is also with these low res people with no faces. I get its a small studio, but that seems like a really dumb move, considering facial expressions and emotions tend to make for better bonding with fictional characters - rather than static text popping up above them.But, I'm critiquing that stuff because I'm bothered by the fact that I really like it. So, yeah. If you already played the better Hades, then try this out, but lower your expectations by quite a lot.

_childDocuments_.review: So this game is pretty good.  I prefer Hades a bit more than this one, but this is a nice change of pace to Hades.  There are a couple noteworthy differences to mention:1., There is no voice acting in Dreamscaper.  +1 for Hades... oh well.2. Dreamscaper lets you skip boss fights once you beat them.  (I never did though since I always wanted the loot so don't know what that's really like).  Unfortunately, boss fights also seem less varied than Hades.  I'd say ... +0.1 for Hades... so we'll just call it a draw.3. Dreamscaper has a map so each area is almost like a puzzle.  And you can teleport between rooms that you've explored to get around faster.  Since Hades is about the action, it's just a playstyle difference, so will call this one a draw too.4. Dreamscaper had some puzzle rooms so it wasn't all about combat.  I wouldn't have minded seeing something like this in Hades.  +1 Dreamscaper.5. Dreamscaper's weapon and equipment system is a little more advanced it some ways than other action rogue-likes I've seen.  The ones I saw that had a lot of weapons and equipment limited to you 2 or 3 slots worth of stuff.  Dreamscaper has 6 (or 7?) slots, plus keepsakes (which are permanent buffs for the run in addition to your equipment).  There's also an equipment mastery system which ... seems underwhelming from the little I saw of it.  You just run around with the item and it slowly fills to 100%.  Once there, you unlock a notable upgrade.  But here's the thing... just cause you set an item as part of your starting loadout, doesn't mean it'll be the weapon you end up with at the end of the run cause it's about the buffs on the weapons that fit your playstyle too.  It's hard to compare this to Hades cause they are based on different game styles.  Both are appealing though, and I look forward into digging into this more.6. I found the story to be less interesting in Dreamscaper than in Hades, but I didn't get far into it either.  The dialogue bits I did run into just didn't seem to have a purpose to something grander and to me, just seemed like filler to say "Hey... you're getting to know this person better."  Maybe it gets more interesting later on.There are lots of other differences, of course, but most the other stuff are differences you would expect within a action rogue-like genre game.  In short, I'd say... if you haven't played Hades, that's the game to get.  But if you have and are looking for something new in the same genre, then this one is definitely worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Visually Dreamscaper to me is very beautiful. It has a handcrafted aesthetic that reminds me of watercolors. They decided to portray emotions more through body language and memories you find scattered within the various levels. The music is somber, haunting but turns to more upbeat melodies during boss fights. The game is hard, you will die. But each time you return to the waking world you have access to more areas of the map and you can sketch and daydream too (and meditate) to obtain new abilities and powers that will help you when you go back into the dream world.The game can also be a grind at times and is definitely demanding. But if you like me you don't mind the grind so much but I am only a couple hours in so that might change depending on how much it gets. I used to not like rouge games but find small developers and companies since Hades emerged making more and more excellent, creative games in this genre and Dreamscaper is right up there with a fantastic experience. So kudos to Afterburner Studios for putting forth a game filled with love, passion and creativity! Look forward to future games! ❤️

_childDocuments_.review: A very fresh take on the rouge like series. This sets in the modern world. Basically you meet friends in day time to enhance your abilities, unlock gear and power ups etc. There is story and character development as your main character make friends in the day. When you sleep, the fun begins. Dreamscaper is about you conquering your nightmares while remembering details about your past. Combat is fluid and creative, just like your dreams, there can be weapons/gears/accessories that won't normally occur in any roguelike game, for example, you have the traditional sword and magic stuff, but you also have stuff like yo-yo, a finger gun, or a guitar. Don't want to spoil too much as part of the fun comes from discovering these stuff yourself. This game also offers you alot of tools to destroy and survive like perfect attack timing, parrying, dodging, a shield, a range weapon, shoes, relics, two "active skills" and even a slow time emergency button that recharges every 3 rooms... this makes this game easier than other entries in the genre. That said this game can still be challenging as the HP is quite low and the MP is also shared between a lot of things which forces you to choose carefully what to use in which situation.Some notes below that are not really pros or cons:- Characters have no faces- There are no voice-overs- Some mechanics are not explained (e.g. puzzles in dungeons, but they are easy enough to figure out)- The camera depth is a bit strange that it is hard to gauge the vertical position of your character (like it is hard to run to a projectile in the middle of its flight path and parry it)All in all this is definitely recommended solely for its unique setting. This game is a light roguelike which you character slowly improves across each playthroughs, they even order an "easy" mode which grant you buffs each time you die. If you are new to the action roguelike genre this game is a very good entry title.

_childDocuments_.review: I've bounced off this quite a few times but decided to keep it in the end for the gorgeous but lifeless art, and a useful lesson in game design.  To cut to the chase its a very beautiful but ultimately dull game.  I can imagine the designers are frustrated as they feel they have ticked lots of game design check boxes, and yet it isn't the success they would expect from doing so.They have achieved something that I have never seen so perfectly done before - by walking an impossible tight rope along everything functionally and qualitatively good and producing something that is in aggregate so inert, inoffensive, bland, and is incapable of activating emotional game play.  It should be used as a case study in game design courses, and yet it is the type of game I expect the pinnacle of their students would produce.  The difference between 'my parents paid for me to go to game design school' vs 'I have lived and breathed gaming, dropped out of school, and made something cool with an edge my soul was always driving me to make'.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: There are better roguelike action RPGs *cough Hades cough*. This really didn't grip me in these first few hours.  See below for breakdowns after beating final boss + 35 hours.The biggest issues is that it already feels tedious. It's tedious to smash every thing in a room to get every possible reward in the room. You are marked if you don't hit 100% in your report card after each floor.  It's tedious to kill certain mobs, especially since one of them auto-targets after you dash instantly, which, ok, i could play around that but it doesn't feel fluid.  Ranged attacks on controller kinda sucks. After 22 hours Ranged attacks on controller sucks less, and I've gotten much better/faster at finding secret rooms, but the learning curve for neither difficult nor fun, but tedious.  Some dashes still suck at 100% mastery. Perhaps if I take the movement speed buff it'd be different, but Bruce gives me crit and Tamal gives me more fire, and those are fun stats.Once you got a damage build going, bosses are insanely easy. The hardest part of this game is navigating around Red Waste (lava) protecting ranged units and your wonky-ass dash. Fast travel is nice. Loads are fast.Boss design is... fine. Some arenas/models are pretty. Mechanically, except for boss 2, is intuitive and pretty easy to figure out. (Boss 2 just has tells that took me very long to learn the timings, esp with jank dashes.) Final boss has a gimmick, and that gimmick is visually told to you is poorly. A bunch of runes appear below your feet (and I was very, very far from the boss after a knockback/dash), yet the key information is on the boss itself with a small icon appearing on him. There was no indication what that gimmick did when you inadvertently interacted with it, indeed literally nothing happens, making you wonder if a DIFFERENT gimmick is in effect. (This is difficult to describe w/o spoilers). Suffice to say, I died quickly and was like, 'oh.' Again, another time I died to something simple that I felt like a instance of poor game communication/visualization, and not because I couldn't play around it. (Other times include were enemies immune to CC hitting me through blinding Lucid Attacks.) Second time I got to boss ez pz. Music has been unimpressive. This is a game where you would turn it off and play your own. Edit: This game is pretty chill if you do listen to music, youtube, audiobooks, w/e. Also, I get that it's trying to do, but the 3 ways the upgrade are represented: sketch, daydream, and mediate just seemed a bit too similar to each other. (Crafting did seem different enough.) Like mechanically it's fine, but thematically it's a bit... Girl, do you spend 2/3 of your day just sitting quietly? The Dialog is uninteresting.  After 35 hours and defeating the final boss, and reaching friendship level 5-7 out of 8 for the characters. It's still boring. It's a lot of small talk, and several conversations are similar to each other. Main character's depression, unsurprisingly and perhaps kinda tragically, makes these conversations more grating and annoying. I don't feel rewarded unlocking more dialog. I feel rewarded getting the in-game inspiration upgrade. This is supposed to be "story rich" but that seems more like marketing than truth.I know it's a dreamlike/surreal game, but the fact that the main char works in marketing but never goes to work bothers me.  EDIT: Turns out she recently lost her job, but her old boss is willing to write her a letter of rec for her new one, but she doesn't even want to apply for a job. what is this /r/antiwork lmaooo. The entire premise of this game is self-care/working on yourself, developing a support network, and all the other stuff you need to do while depressed, but then she doesn't try to find a new job... She'll spend 1000 mediation points at the park and daydream for hours at a pub to center herself mentally, bur now when a person tries to help her career she immediately regresses. It's like... why are we doing these self improvements. Why are we conquering her fear, negativity, regret, etc if she literally just gets worse. Depression Quest was better at dealing with these themes.Animations are sometimes a bit wonky to me, and the art design is not as gripping as I had expected it to be.All in all, you may find a build that you are comfy with (crystal armor + Wind attack + Boostie Fuego + fire dash + 2 Lucid attacks that can proc crits/elemental combos for me), and then you can just boost those abilities in the forge every floor. Then you, have the tedious work to just get as much sand as possible to boost your abilities and then quickly burst the bosses down. Even if the boss encounters are kinda fun b/c you have a lot of space to do combos, dodge stuff, parry stuff, etc, you spend most of your time boringly hunting down for sand and trying to 100% rooms for that one achievement. On that note Vampire Fangs is OP. I turned off so many trinkets just to up the odds I get them.The game begins tediously with jank. You upgrade rooms, yourself, etc to make it less jank. You find a build that fits you, and go through tedious room after tedious room to do tedious sand farm to boost that build. When you finally get to the bosses you just faceroll. And when you finally beat that final boss... nothing. You gotta continue tedious conversations with dull companions with poor, uneventful, wordy dialog.
