_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't say it's a bad game, but it definitely could have used a bit more time in the oven imo. Since there is no mixed option, my tendency is more towards a negative review. It's an alright roguelike if you're tired of playing Hades and Isaac and just want some mindless action grind. It's definitely not on the same level as  these two, but it has some similarities (mostly with Hades) and some similar enemies.The positive:- Huge weapon and skill variety- Extra difficulty options- Good roguelike gameplay with many mechanics such as perfect attacks and parries to master- The bosses are all very different from each other. Imo the third (and maybe fourth) boss is where the game peaks. They're fun to beat repeatedly, don't become trivial too quickly and have no big gimmick - Plays pretty well even on mouse and keyboard- The game runs smoothly with no lags or other issuesNeutral: - Lots of things to unlock outside of the dungeon (which does make the game more grindy)- The story is... alright. It's mostly just in the background. There are no big reveals, the metaphors are very straight-forward and overall there is nothing big going onNegative:- Not much enemy and room variety. You will encounter the same enemies across the entire game, with only one or two new enemies added for every floor. It's nice to learn their patterns better, but for a roguelike I got bored of the repetitiveness very quickly- My biggest issue is the balancing of the game: Every floor the enemy damage and HP just rack up massively. Especially around the 4th level those huge difficulty spikes become very obvious. You can have a build that makes all enemies and even the boss feel completely trivial on one floor, then die in 4 hits on the next- Overall it feels like the game wants you to grind a lot. Repeat the same floors with the same rooms, enemies and bosses over and over again, then buy upgrades outside until the earlier floors become a cakewalk and the last floors become.. doable- Most unlockables are just there to stretch the game more. You really need to unlock the healing fountain, upgrade shop, challenge rooms and even puzzles for every single floor separately. - It's hard to have a consistent build when you have to replace your entire gear essentially every floor. Your main weapons often double in strength from one floor to the next, so it's hard to plan ahead for a full run from start to finish. Upgrade rooms and item choices appear randomly, so there is no guarantee that you will even get the same weapon type or element. Due to how spongy enemies become, not replacing your weapons is just frustrating as well- Just as an example: My last run before quitting I had a skill that did 750 to 1300 damage (on a crit). Ranged, usable every 3 seconds. This was NOT enough to oneshot regular enemies on the final floor of the game on normal difficulty, btw. All my other weapons and skills (which I acquired on the same floor) did 200 damage at most and were all close ranged or had longer cooldowns. It's absurd how the HP of enemies scales in this game, while your weapons do pathetic amounts of damage even on the highest levels and rarities. You rely on getting lucky and finding that one skill with busted damage or cheesing the game with status ailments like freeze. - For how much the game wants you to grind, it just doesn't offer much outside of running the same dungeons with the same bosses over and over again. The dialogue outside of the game is so bland, it's really difficult to care about these characters for anything other than the skills they give you.- Lastly, talking about the other characters: It feels like every dialogue starts in the middle of a conversation. Almost like starting a movie in the middle of its run. You will meet a person for the first time and the dialogue is "I'm sorry for spilling coffee on your pants last time we met". I don't even know the name of this person, but apparently we have a whole history? Other dialogues start with lines like "Wow, I can't believe you have such a tradition in your hometown!". I assume this was done on purpose to make the dialogue feel more "real", but it's a very odd choice.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the better Roguelike's i've played. Also the game that solely got me into the genre as well. I'm writing this review way after I bought it and came back to it after playing so many other games in the same genre. And this one just hits different. It feels the most polished out of all the other ones i've played so far. The controls feel responsive and there's a certain weight to the movement in the game that feels good. Not to mention the tons of variety in spells, ranged, melee, and dodges. And there's also the passives as well. The social aspect of the game is also part of its unique charm. and having passive stats being linked to it not only makes it important to actually pursue but the small stories are nice as well. They have the same cozy feeling as some of the stand out narrative games. Right when I felt that i was getting used to the repetitive nature of the game I tried the other difficulties. And was pleasantly surprised that it actually gave more variety to enemy types as well as attacks. There's a ton of completionist type stuff in the game. Mastering each type of item to get that special unlockable passive, maxing out relationship stats to get extra stats that also go along with any type of specific build you're going for, etc. All, in all, I can't recommend this game enough and a shame that this game set the bar so high for me straight out the gate. because, now, it's hard to find other games in the genre to come up to this expectation. So far i've seen 2 other games that have given me the same joy in gameplay as this one. Good job devs!

You will not be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Game progression has a great sense of momentum and a reasonable difficulty/skill curve. I usually bounce off of roguelike progression, but the sand system helps a soft player like myself acclimate pretty well. The variety of play styles afforded by equipment combinations makes for good replay value while the way the stat progression of drops are structured sort of forces me to want to get better at using even my least favorite weapons when I know that I need a DPS upgrade. All in all, I love how you can just pick up the game and go,  satisfying all those RPG cravings in a single dungeon. Also, keeping all of the menu crawling in the waking world and doing all of your dreamworld resource management on the map instead of diving into menus (i.e., strategically leaving equipment, potions and bomb-rocks in case you might need them later) keeps the pace nice and snappy.This is great so far. Looking forward to how things develop!

_childDocuments_.review: I think I just don't enjoy roguelikes. Also my pc specs are mid so I played on low quality 60 fps.The resolving emotions theme is what intrigued me, but right after yet another frustrating failure in unforgiving reflex-heavy combat is not a good time to be reading such nuanced dialogue. You witness the protagonist making meaningful connections & resolving issues while you are having your anxiety cranked up to 11.On the roguelike gameplay (I cleared all to-dos apart from 1+ intensity ones):- With such a vast variety of equips and passives, it feels very hard to achieve any sense of synergy. There are a handful of passive items that make everything OP, and then the rest is narrow and underwhelming* considering how hard it is to build around. (*I guess this isn't valid since I never picked up those [element] damage +20% passives... maybe they are amazing)- I hate rarity tiers everywhere I see them, and I wish that was entirely left out. I think the success of Hades was greatly overblown by it being a red text slot machine, and although I appreciate how low-impact rarity is in this game, a set number of lines for everything (maybe 4 or 5) would have been far nicer. Just my marginal opinion.Other minor stuff:- Puzzle rooms are a chore. I made a no puzzles save and never went back. Don't unlock puzzles.- There are 3 separate things called lucid something. The meter & its burst time, the specials, and the easy mode setting. You would expect lucid attacks to consume lucid meter, but no, these specials are free with a cooldown.- Critical extinguish carries, but I only know how that works from a MS paint image on the wiki. There is no in-game graphic that shows which element explodes with which elemental debuff.This review has been mostly criticism but I do like the game enough to give a thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: I was torn between a positive and a negative review, but I will settle for a positive primarily because this is a small game made by only three people and clearly there is a lot of work put into it. Too much I would argue - it would have been better without the very dull dialogues and I'll touch on that in a minute.One important point is that from a consumer/gamer point of view, this game is priced around the same price of much better games such as Hades (and I guess Hades 2, haven't played that one yet), and curse of the dead gods. If you haven't played them, they are significantly better so do that first. And once you have done that, stick the olympus mod on top of Hades and play it again.Also, I'd suggest getting this game when regularly discounted at -75% off unless you have a reason to support this indie team.The game is OK, playable, but quite uninspired. The initial feeling is that it seems a bit a mobile game, but the more you play and the more you get past that and see that there's a competent game, it's just very average in most of his aspects.There are also some odd design choices. To level up you have to build relationship with characters in the city areas, which I found quite boring due to the very generic writing. It's like speaking with an early-AI character so I just ended up skipping all of it.There are a lot of items to equip, but some don't really make sense. I don't see why we need so many variations of dodge. Give us a few, hell one even, but well done. Not stuff like you go zig-zag and you don't end up in a straight line; or a dodge so small, that you can't get past some of the traps or the lava.The balance is quite off, but with this kind of game it is somewhat understandable and it's OK that some runs will be better due to luck. However, it seems a bit excessive that I beat it in 9 hours compared to 14 in howlongtobeat, and it's because I happened to get some OP build where I was leeching too much HP back, and a good combination of power ups. Previous to that I only beat the 3rd monster, and with that build I just finished the game (6 or 7 levels - haven't counted). To be fair I was glad since I was getting quite bored.There are some minor optimization issues where sometimes the framerate lags a bit with no noticeable culprit, but this is not a big deal 99% of the time the game runs smooth.In later levels the game gets a bit chaotic and not always clear what's going on, and what's worse, it doesn't get "difficult" in that way - you just know where you have to end up dodging to avoid enemy attacks, far from enemies and spam your stronger area attacks. In better designed games, escaping won't grant you victory.In a nutshell: if you are a fan of the genre and have already played the classics, you might have some fun with this one.If you are not a fan of the genre, I think this could appeal to a more causal kind of gamer, as it's more luck-based than others.

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is a game true to its promise: At night you battle difficult emotions you've accrued after the death of your sister, and in the day you grow your friendships with different citizens around the city. In the 'dreamworld,' the more you fight off your inner-angst, the more inspiration, resolve, and energy you have to tackle the day, allowing you to grow your relationships more quickly, as well as meditate, daydream, and sketch in your sketchbook -- all of which help you when you fall back asleep. A great relationship exists between both worlds, and together they tell a story of personal growth through reflection, and friendship. I'm happy to say too that neither world becomes tiring or monotonous -- at least, this game does better than most rougelikes at keeping things rolling and changing. In the daytime city, you unlock new dialogue with your friends every time you grow in a relationship level. I'm impressed by how relatable this dialogue is, and also by how different and enjoyable each friend was written to be. In the 'dreamworld,' you can vary up your run by choosing from new weapons (ranged and melee), shields, shoes, abilities, and items -- you can also scale up or down the difficulty if you get irritated, or bored, haha. One last thing I'd like to comment on: the art style of this game is something I've never seen before. Particularly the color-scheme, so vibrant and immersive, and the character art, which gives everything an appropriately dreamlike, surreal quality. Just a great game.

There's also a HUGE variety of weapons, both melee/ranged of which you get to use at the same time, and there's also 2 utility buttons, similar to the God abilities from Hades that you can have on at one time.There's just SO much content in this Roguelite. _childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is, simply, a wonderful game.It has a unique art and music style that I find nothing less than captivating.The plot is revealed as you play.It's an action Roguelite and a Relationship Sim at the same time.You play one to advance the other, and somehow it all works, and works well.For all its' fast paced, often chaotic, action, the game always feels actually somewhat soothing rather than stressful.I have 62.4 hour total at this point, and 3 hrs since launch.Even in the Early Release I never saw a but, or had a crash, something I have not seen in a Triple A title on release (much less an Indy Game) in nearly 20 years, and in an Early Release never.This may just be my favorite game since the original Secret World.

_childDocuments_.review: Not terribly far in yet, but far enough to evaluate it per its genre.Pros: *Music is nice and sets the tone.*Pleasant minimalistic art style and coloring.*Good diversity in paths, but also enough ability to play how you want to enforce progression (in particular, you can pick your starting items each run, though these are often outclassed by floor 3 without upgrades).*'Waking world' gameplay is distinct and helps set it apart from peers enough to feel novel.Cons: *Competing against real giants like Hades and Isaac for a niche. I think it does so successfully, but would play Hades before this game if I've never experienced either.*Visual noise becomes a problem, like many entries in this genre. In particular some lucid attacks can block view of enemies and set you up to be hit without being able to react.*Ground Hazards are more invasive than in most other genre entries and many of the dodge animations aren't sufficient to bridge ones you 'have' to cross.Overall based on 4 hours in, I would give it a 7 or 7.5 out of 10. As an example, I would personally rate Hades 8.5 and Isaac 8, so not far off from those entries, but clearly hasn't been in the running as long as either. Solid game.

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is an ARPG with roguelite progression and hack'n'slash combat. There're 2 major parts in the game - dreams where all action is happening, and real world where you can interact with some characters and get some bonuses for your future battles in your dreams.An overall quality of the game is quite amazing and there's a lot of cool features:+ Great combat system. It's challenging and rewarding - well timed attacks are way better than button mashing. There's also a decent amount of different weapons that are suitable for different playstyles.+ Well designed enemies. There's not that many of them, but each of those feels unique and requires a different approach.+ Simple but entertaining puzzles. Solving a puzzle will reward you with equipment.+ Very nice music in the game.+- Real world part feels more like a tool (for roguelite progression) and wasn't really interesting for me. Luckily it's skippable and doesn't take much time.Currently I believe there's enough content for ~15 hours. It's not a game that you'd want to replay over and over again after completing it, but there should be more content added later on and it's still a lot of a quality playtime.Dreamscaper is very polished for an Early Access release and it's really fun to play. An easy recommendation for fans of ARPGs/roguelikes. 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is a rogue-lite that I feel can be compared to Hades. They're both "combo" focused rogue-lites that encourage the use of multiple attacks while at the same time dodging enemy attacks. You can also customize your beginning loadout of abilities such that you can have a fairly consistent experience in each run. If Hades is an 8/10, then Dreamscaper is just slightly worse at a 7/10, which still means it's a good game.In Dreamscaper, you have a melee attack, a ranged attack, and 2 "Lucid" attacks which are basically magic attacks that can do a wide variety of different things, but are limited by a cooldown. You also have a shield that you can use to block & parry attacks and a dodge. Fairly standard stuff. A unique thing that Dreamscaper throws into the mix is that your attacks can have different "elements" that provide various debuffs. E.g. Fire causes burn damage over time, Lightning causes shock damage over time, Water slows, Wind increases critical strike chance, etc… Furthermore, if an enemy is inflicted by an elemental debuff and you hit an enemy with an element that "reacts" to that element, the 2nd attack will hit for around 130% more than normal. This fairly simple mechanic is pretty fun to master, not only because it's a core mechanic of the game, but also because it's fun to see high damage numbers on your screen :).Throughout my time playing Dreamscaper, I was constantly thinking of ways to improve my chances of beating runs. This is because you can pick what starting weapon loadout you'll have in Dreamscaper. While all of these starting weapons will be Level 1 (you can find up to level 8 weapons throughout your run) and therefore will do minimal damage by the end of a run, the nature of the element system means they can still be useful. After all, it's the 2nd elemental hit that gets the 130% damage increase. Therefore, it's OK if the weapon that causes the 1st elemental debuff isn't all that strong, since no matter the strength of a weapon, it'll inflict the same elemental debuff. I started the game having my entire build focused around increasing my melee weapon's damage (i.e. a dodge that leaves a fire trail behind causing constant fire damage and a lucid attack that deals wind damage to everyone around you over and over again. Combine with a Water weapon and each hit will do 130% more damage). By the end of the game, I completely changed my thinking and my entire build focused around increase my lucid attack/ranged attack damage (i.e. a dodge that leaves a fire trail behind causing constant fire damage and a wind melee weapon. Allows for the flexibility for a large amount of ranged and lucid attacks to do major damage). There is a surprising amount of depth to this system!In addition to the great elemental system, Dreamscaper simply has solid combat. There is a decent variety of enemies and they're all telegraphed really well. You have to respect any enemy that you face because health is scarce and you taking even a few hits can doom your run. The bosses are another highlight in this game. While there's only 6 bosses in the game, they're all vastly different from each other in terms of both looks and the way they fight. What's great is that the game encourages you to mix all your weapons together. This is not only because of the elemental system, but because of how the ranged and lucid attacks work. Ideally, you'd want to kill every single enemy from ranged since that's the safest option. However, ranged attacks cost mana which refills very slowly over time (refills to max upon room completion). Lucid attacks, like I mentioned, have a cooldown. Whenever you enter a room with enemies, it's unlikely that you'll be able to sit back and kite all of the enemies from range (unless you get lucky and create an OP build). Also, there's no limit to how enemies attack (e.g. there's no "Arkham-style" system where only up to 2 enemies can attack at once). Therefore, it's a good idea to be on the offensive and kill as many enemies as possible as fast as possible before they get a chance to swarm you. So you want to be able to quickly analyze a room, think about which enemies you want to kite and which you want to attack from melee, and deal with them quickly according to your plan. The main negative to the game is that it isn't "fast" enough. Fundamentally, the combat in this game is combo focused where you want to string multiple attacks together. However, the actual flow of combat is relatively "slow" for a combo focused game. It's not really fast like Hades or Devil May Cry. The speed is more similar to Dark Souls. While a combo focused Dark Souls would be perfectly fine (I mean, look at Nioh), this game isn't all that difficult to justify sacrificing the speed. This is because your dodge roll can cover a LOT of distance, such that you don't really need to worry about timing a dodge to take advantage of the invulnerability frames. Pretty much as soon as you see an enemy attack, you can dodge roll whenever and in whatever direction, and you'll likely be far enough so that the enemy's attack won't hit you. I think if this game was faster or more difficult, it would be a lot more fun.The progression system within a run primarily involves finding higher level weapons and various "relics" that provide passive benefits. A flaw with the relics is that apart from a select few (like…..less than 10 I think), most of them provide fairly uninteresting benefits. For example, +20% melee damage or +20% ice damage. Not very interesting and so you're usually not all that excited to find relics in your run.The permanent progression system is a lot better. During a run, you'll find various currency that you can spend after the end of a run to provide yourself with permanent benefits. There a are a lot of different permanent benefits that you can get that can seriously improve your chances of winning, so it's usually exciting to spend the currency you've earned. Furthermore, you can craft gifts and give them to people in order to improve your relationship with them. As their relationship with you increases, you can equip a passive item that can provide some major benefits.One thing I didn't like is that in order to get the true ending, you need to maximize the relationship of ALL people you can meet to maximum…..this is a bit too much. This would involve beating the game like 8-10 times in order to accumulate the currency necessary to craft all the gifts (you also can also increase the relationship level only once between each run. The maximum relationship level is 8, so at a minimum you're looking at 8 runs). I don't like when rogue-like games set a really high bar for the true ending, because it can get repetitive.This game is trying to tell a story about Cassidy, the character you play as. The whole game is basically about her battling her negative emotions (Fear, Regret, Negativity, etc…) which take the shape of the bosses. As you defeat the bosses, Cassidy is seemingly overcoming her trauma. She also overcomes her trauma by talking to people around the city in the "real" world. I honestly didn't care too much about this. This is because I guessed what happened as soon as I saw the opening cutscene, so I wasn't that invested into "unravelling" what happened. Furthermore, Cassidy doesn't really say anything during a run / when you beat bosses, so I don't really feel that she's overcoming these negative emotions (also because…. You know…..I keep fighting them over and over again in a run). Finally, during the talks that she has with NPC's in order to improve relationship levels, the talks are often about fairly mundane things. Like a character's interest in history, or music, or general workplace random chit chat, etc…. It's simply not all that interesting.Overall, Dreamscaper is a fairly good Rogue-like with solid combat and a unique elemental system that you'll enjoy mastering. It could stand to be more fast-paced and/or more diff

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty solid Roguelike. I have 2 major complaints though. First, once you've died a few times doing things in RedHaven gets pretty bland and samey. Also, can they please remove the notification "!" for areas with nothing new? I understand that after I've woken up I have materials to upgrade my dreams. That isn't worth telling me I need to visit an area.The second, the combat is waayyyy too slow. If I get hit, it is almost definetly because it takes forever to complete any action in this game. The combat isn't as smooth as it could be because of this. The majority of weapons have almost a full second between the parts of a combo. Similarly, most of the evade tools are so slow it looks like Cassidy is entering bullet time while everything else moves at regular speed. Just about every action could be sped up 1.5x and the game would feel infinitely better. Especially when it comes to using abilities. The cast time is totally unreasonable and you have to be a mile away from the enemies to complete the cast.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, so I've spent around 100 hours with this game if you count my time with the prologue, though I'm not sure you should, as this game has been in flux until it's release. These guys spent around a year in early access, and honestly, at every step the game felt done to me, but they just kept improving it, adding things, changing how systems work. Adding customization options. Polishing things. And adding buttloads of content. I paid for the supporters edition with the prologue, I bought the soundtrack. This is probably my favorite game. There are some folks that gripe that the combat is too basic because enemies have a tendency to get stunned locked. That's not wrong, but what I think it ignores is that is your reward for either hyper aggression, or playing smart and methodical, because if you don't stun lock the enemies, then they are a problem. Also, as you get farther along, they get harder to just bum rush and stun locked. Some enemies straight up can't be.The way the developers have stayed connected and active with their community is a big reason why they were able to take a game that felt done at every step and keep making it better. For all the buzz it's gotten, I don't think it's enough, this game needs to reach more hands.

_childDocuments_.review: Very promising game! At the time of this being written, the game is still early-release and not completely finished, but what has been put out so far is excelllent and very enjoyable. Games structured around dreams are a very promising venue for bridging the gap between out-there, high-fantasy gameplay (in the dreamworld) with the often-conflicting need to ground the narrative and the protagonist in a way that is not too unrelatable and not too far removed from conflicts and issues we recognize from our own day-to-day existences (in the daylight-world sequences between dreams). Dreamscaper is a prime example of a game that successfully lets the player have his cake and eat it too in this regard. By making the gameplay a back-and-forth dynamic between classic, roguelike action-rpg capers in the dreamworld and alternating waking-world sequences of relationship-building and dialogue-based probing of the protagonist's psychology, Dreamscaper hits a very enjoyable balance that is already great fun and likely to become even more so once the game's development is brought full circle. Thumbs up for the great game that this already is, and fingers crossed for it to become even better as the final touches are added to its development.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue-likes are super common right now, and while there are some *amazing* entries in the genre, they can start to feel a bit boilerplate-y since they all share a lot of the same features. While Dreamscaper *does* include a lot of features that will be familiar to fans of the genre, they're cleverly utilized and worked into the game in an incredibly unique way. The duality of the dream being the "combat" portion of the game where the rogue-like permadeath and loot-finding and RNG elements come into play and the waking world being where Cassidy focuses herself through mediation, sketching out new ideas, and improving her connections with other people, is both amazingly unique and extremely clever in the context of the game's lore.It's early access, so of course there are a few things that need more polish, but I think I have already found a new favorite rogue-like in Dreamscaper.

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty good. Sometimes great. Mostly ok.Dreamscaper is very creative and that's the biggest plus I can give it. Variety of interesting weapons, perks, designs and lucid abilities. Combat is alright, fairly simple overall but gets the job done.The biggest weakness is the story, at least long term. At first it's quite interesting because of how things unfold with the snippets of memories found and opening up social interactions.The problem is because of its disjointed nature, you don't really get attached or invested in anything. The system reminds me of Persona 4, but completely detached and confused. Persona had a masterful pacing to it which managed social interactions, time and the dungeon gameplay perfectly. It continued to progress.In Dreamscaper, it tends to be a stop and go deal, because it depends on how far you get in a run. This becomes an exponential curve in requirement too, because to unlock more story stuff for characters when crossing past level 4 and beyond in their relationships, you need a lot more resources.Essentially it becomes a grind, and I hate grinds.Ultimately I'm a little bored by it. Weapon variety is good but combat is fundamentally the same - doesn't feel very different. I don't care about the character stuff anymore and while I really appreciate the thematics ie. subconscious exploration, working through grief, etc, I find it's a little too scattered to get much engagement out of it.Huge credit to the art and soundtrack though. _childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of attributes and I am hoping to expand on all of them as accurately as possible. Thank you to the publishers freedom games for providing me with the key.Curator Page:+Gameplay+Progression+Unlockables+Replayability+Sound design+Aesthetics+Difficulty scale-Reused rooms-Lack of visual optionsDreamscape has you travelling deeper into stages of sleep, in order to discover yourself and finally find peace. Every time your character goes to sleep, you fight through randomly generated rooms, equip better gear, defeat bosses, and ultimately repeat after inevitably dying. At the end of each level you must face a boss in order to proceed. You are given the choice to skip that boss fight if you have already beaten it in order to reach your previous state quicker.The progression is made satisfying by often picking up new items to improve your damage, resistance and mobility. The map layout and enemies are also randomly generated each time so you never play the same map. There are a lot of items for you to unlock and find throughout your adventure. You will get the chance to also unlock more items to find in the world, as well as unique rooms and how frequently they will  appear in your adventure. When you are awake, you must travel between various places in the world and strengthen your character in all sorts of ways. You will also meet unique characters that will give you improved boosts in battle, the more you get to know them. Of course all of this happens by simply playing the game.The audio design is simply tremendous. The music is absolutely adorable and a pleasantry to listen to. The sound effects are mellow and at the same time pack the necessary heat to emphasise what is going on.Following that note, the aesthetics are a treat to look at as well. Lacking some complex details such as faces, the way those details are designed to be lacking adds to the overall quality of the fidelity. The difficulty scaling is adequate to say the least. The game definitely requires a few playthroughs in order to unlock more items and strengthen your character further. Without such upgrades, it will be extremely challenging to be effective in progressing through the levels, and in turn the story.My main complaints with the game thus far is that there are no visual options besides one, and that some rooms are carbon copies that are reused throughout the world. This would not had been such a big deal, but the levels themselves are not consistent of more than 10 or so rooms. The developers should focus on designing more rooms for further variety. This is a game that needs to be replayed a lot of times to reach the end. This results in the user having to see the same rooms over and over again. I would prefer to see those rooms in separate playthroughs, rather than the same stage.Overall, this early access title is very well put together. There is already plenty of content to be had. With some work on adding more variety to the world, I am eager to see what else the developers have in store for us. So far, it is absolutely worth your attention.#dreamscaper#overview#earlyaccess

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like I should like this game, on paper it ticks all the boxes for me. There are however design problems at its core that mar the experience.The music sounds like it was composed by a gay pianist with clinical depression. The sad, sentimental soundtrack plays continuously, even during combat sections where it feels out of place. After a few runs I had to mute it for my sanity.The visuals are distinct and quaint in their minimalism, but style shouldn't come at the expense of gameplay. The camera angle, along with the lighting effects often make it difficult to perceive depth. This means at times you won't know whether or not you are in the path of an oncoming projectile. This is unacceptable in a game with bullet-hell elements.Speaking of gameplay, there is a mechanic where if you press the attack button when your weapon flashes, you deal additional damage. However the window to execute this move is way too short; it would require inhuman reflexes to achieve consistently. The fact that each weapon has its own distinct timing further compounds this problem, making a novel mechanic mostly luck based.Progression between runs feels grindy and artificially inflated, with three different currencies each responsible for different unlocks.  In addition It requires your character to fast travel to different locations, and have wooden conversations with NPCs. The dialogue has the vibe of awkward elevator small talk, and the accompanying relief when it ends. This portion of the game could have been cut out and replaced with a single menu screen, and it would have been better for it.The boss battles are by far the highlight of the experience, they are well designed mechanically and thematically, each representing an emotion in the protagonist's subconscious. But in order to reach them, you have to put up with the aforementioned tedium, and I personally don't think it's worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Amazing roguelike with great atmosphere and design, an almost serene, soothing experience to play through, while simultaneously providing challenging gameplay that keeps you craving more. Dreamscaper is a game that I've been looking forward to for a long time. I was a backer during the kickstarter campaign, the early alpha demo they showed us then already looked so promising, and I'm happy to say that the final product did deliver. I can't recommend it enough. You play the game as Cassidy, a girl suffering from depression, facing her nightmares/dreams at night and meeting people and building relationships during the day. First up, the graphics are beautiful, they are simplistic yet surreal, and very effective. Especially the dream world is a joy to look at, and the various maps/levels of the dream world all have a very distinct look and feel to them.The audio is also well done, though the tracks can get a bit repetitive over time, especially during the waking world.The combat is fluid and satisfying, and very rewarding. The difficulty curve can be steep, especially as you progress through the levels, it really ramps up, new enemy types are constantly introduced and existing enemy types also gain new attacks and abilities. Especially the big boss fights are very exciting and rewarding, as they should be.There are so many different types of equipment and abilities, all of which have a distinct playstyle. If I had to name a con, it would be that when you pick an item there's no way to "preview" the attack or ability, so I've picked up items that I ended up hating and regretted picking up. Related to what I've written above, the difficulty curve is steep, and while this is not neccesarily a bad thing, because of the permadeath there is not really the room to test out new items to see if you like the feel of them. I pick up a new item that I've never used before, I try to figure out the feel of it but I don't really get the chance to do so because the difficulty ramps up quickly as you progress and I end up dying as a result. However, I would not say the difficulty curve is a bad thing. The game is immensely satisfying to play and has this "one more try" feel that keeps you coming back. While exploring the dream world over and over again, you can see your improvement, and it has this high risk high reward kinda feel to it that keeps you craving more.Whenever I close the game I'm immediately looking forward to the next time I get to play it, and that is a feeling I have not experienced in a long time. At first I thought the waking world would feel like a bit of a chore, but I quickly started to like the characters and every one of them felt relatable and real. Your first conversation with them is awkward and clunky, and as you get to know them you can speak more easily, they all have their very distinct interests and traits, and at the start it can feel a bit like a mechanic. Learn interests, craft the right gifts, build up your relationships to get better stats, but I quickly found myself enjoying the conversations almost as much as the roguelike part of the game. As you get to know the people around you and get closer to them, the conversations also become more intense, and the feelings really hit home. Subjects like death, depression and burn-out are handled maturely and feel relatable and real. Expect to be hit in the feels more than once.I do have one gripe with this section of the game, first up, as I've said before, the soundtrack during the waking world seems to be rather lacking, and you find yourself listening to the same tracks all the time. Similarly, the text-based "chats" are also quite repetitive, aside from the "big" conversations (cutscenes) you get occasionally, the small chit-chat bits you get to have just seem to be an endless repetition of the same sentences. It reminds me a bit of Geralt's "Damn you're ugly" or "How do you like that silver" combat dialogue, while entertaining at first, the lack of variety quickly becomes apparent as you play more of the game. I hope the developers will expand on the text and dialogue in this game. I also really think this game would benefit from voice-acting, to really add to the feel even more. Not for all of the text, but maybe the longer dialogue "cutscenes" and also Cassidy's memories, just to add that little bit of extra emotional attachment and immersion to getting to know more about both Cassidy and the people around her.I would like to add that despite all of that, I am in awe at the fact that such a promising game was made by a studio consisting of just three people. Despite being in Early Access, it feels polished to a degree that some AAA studios could learn from. I have not encountered any bugs or framedrops either. All in all, I haven't even played that much of this game, but I'm dying to play more, and I just had to write a review to express my joy for this game. Some games end up blowing you away and this is definitely one of them.[Update after the Awakening update]I'd like to update my review to say I'm actually less fond of Dreamscaper than I was initially. They added a new point/xp progression system that feels way too slow to me. You often need multiple runs to upgrade some stat to get even the smallest of bonuses, like 1% more damage. It made the game feel way more grindy to me in a way that it hasn't before. I also feel like the difficulty scaling could use some work. In the 3rd/4th map the enemies start increasing in health/damage in a way that the player can't keep up with, making the combat feel tedious after enemies turn into damage sponges and the player dying in two or three hits. It feels less like increased difficulty with new attacks or enemy types and more like number inflation, which I never am very fond of. I hope this will be looked at in future patches because I actually enjoy the game less now than when the Early Access first came out. Maybe that's just me. [Update after 1.0 release]My previous complaints were addressed, level up system was made less grindy by no longer having to invest into unlocking new options, but rather let them accumulate through total points spend. It makes a considerable difference. New maps design/levels and bosses added as well as rewarding the player for repeating bosses, rather than skipping them, and rewarding trying out new gear with the mastery system, makes the overall progression a whole lot less grindy and repetitive and a lot more enjoyable. I'm loving this game. It has the perfect balance between challenging combat, and serene and almost soothing atmosphere and music, which makes the game feel relaxing to play through. It's like soaking yourself into a warm bubble bath, the immersion and atmosphere are great. I expect to be sinking many hours into it. Wholeheartedly recommend if you are looking for a unique take on the roguelike genre. Small comment though, people keep comparing Dreamscaper to Hades, but I would say the feel and experience of the game is totally different. Dreamscaper is a surreal, almost serene and soothing experience, while Hades is super fast-paced, hectic and chaotic. I love both games, Hades being my favourite roguelike of all time, but I do not think it's fair to compare the two. Yes they both have a story- and relationship/characters- system that develops over time, as well as a stat-based progression system, but that's where the similarities end. Dreamscaper deserves it's own recognition as a unique take on the genre. Definitely among my favorite games of all time

_childDocuments_.review: DREAM. DIE. WAKE. REPEAT. That's the concept behind Dreamscaper in a nutshell. It's yet another action roguelike making its way to Steam, this time in Early Access. I've been reviewing a ton of these games, so I thought'd I give this one a look as well.So if the DREAM. DIE. WAKE. REPEAT. tagline didn't already make it obvious, this is a roguelike where the playing field is within the subconscious. It has a very clear structure. You enter a dream, explore a bunch of interconnected rooms, take down a boss, and then exit the dream back into reality before falling asleep again and repeating the cycle.The vast majority of your time will be spent in the dreaming state, where you get all the usuals found in a roguelike video game. You've got the random level layouts, the numerous different enemies with all of their unique attacks, a bunch of loot to find, and a few special rooms to add in a bit of variety. The game's got the fundamentals on lock here, the real question is how do they each feel.Well first you got the combat, which has both a bit of good and a bit of bad. It's good in that the combat has a nice sense of weight to it. Hits have proper impact and it generally flows pretty well. Then you got the responsive dodging, the block and parry mechanics, and the ability to mix up your gameplay with different melee and ranged weapons.At the same time though, the combat can also feel a bit generic. I don't want to say amateurish, but its obvious that this is not a big budget game and the combat kinda reflects that. There's not a lot of variety with the animations, the hitboxes can be a bit weird, and you pretty much deal with most enemies in the same way, regardless of the weapon you have equipped.The game also makes a few frustrating design decisions here. For example, the different shoes you can equip have different dodge lengths. The default pair has the perfect (and most realistic) roll, just slightly away from where you are standing. Then you got the special pairs that send you maybe 50% farther or so, dependent on their type. It was annoying to have to readapt my gameplay to adjust for this change, and I instead opted to stick with the default type even if I came across a special pair with better stats.The balancing is also a bit of an issue, the main problem being that most enemies simply have too much HP. It's not that they are difficult to kill, but rather that they feel like damage sponges. You're able to infinitely knockup and stun most enemies, so having to spend the time dealing 15 or so attacks to kill them does become a bit of a chore. Granted, you're able to take advantage of abilities and a ranged weapon to remedy this to an extent, but I feel like it would have been better off if each room had more enemies, but with less overall HP on each.Then you got the levels (or rooms) and how they are laid out. As for the latter, well, it's pretty much just a giant grid with rooms separated by portals, which is to be expected given the genre. The actual design of each room is where the game really shines. It's not just some flat color with random obstacles here and there, but actual locations that the protagonist has visited, or has otherwise dreamed up. This can be something like a camp site or a city street. It's really cool to see a roguelike diversify itself like this, especially when the game already looks as good as it does here.However, it doesn't come without a major downside. The levels and their design may be cool, but there is not a whole lot of them to go around. It doesn't take long before you start seeing repeats and every new run kinda loses its charm because you've already seen all of these rooms and know what to expect. This is bound to happen with any game that doesn't have randomized levels, but when I see the exact same room twice on the same floor, it kinda makes that lack of variety clear.Now onto the topic of variety, as that is something crucial to any good roguelike. As with the combat, the game does some good here, but still has some issues. For every shield upgrade that does something cool like removing your ability to block in favor of providing regenerating armor you got something a bit more boring like a sword that simply has higher dps and maybe an elemental trait to it. The elemental traits really didn't stand out to me that much and I hardly noticed the difference between them when in combat. This is something that will likely be fixed with time once the devs focus on just adding more items and abilities though.Special rooms, on the other hand, are something that the devs really need to work on. They already got a couple by way of a shop and the different puzzle rooms, but as I mentioned before, you see the same ones on practically every floor. Maybe they could add mid-bosses, challenge rooms, or some other gimicky rooms to shake things up.I haven't even touched on the social sim element to the game though. Yes, when you're not dreaming, you engage in a very light social sim of sorts. You travel to different locations, chat with strangers, and give them gifts to boost your relationship with them. This in turn unlocks a little bit of story and some upgrades that can then be taken into your next run. It's a great concept for sure, but it feels a bit shallow in its current state. It kinda reminds me of the relationship system from Danganronpa, where it's just kinda an extra thing to unlock more stuff and there's no real depth to it. It's nice to get an upgrade or two, but there really has to be something more than just "chit chat" and "give gift" to give this side of the game the weight that the devs obviously want it to have.So overall, I wouldn't say that this is a bad game, but it's also not a game I can honestly recommend, at least in its current state. There's obviously a good base here, but a lot of the core game elements just don't have the depth that they really need to warrant playing the game while its in Early Access. It might be worth a look now for diehard fans of the genre, but I would honestly recommend waiting this one out until it's at least out of Early Access. I'm interested in seeing what the game will look like at that point.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is pretty damn good. Lovely art style, nice combat mechanics. Good pacing, at least in the beginning. I think the item balance could be improved though, as some items and stats can still be the main difference between a successful run and a wipeout.The game implements a great concept of overcoming emotional trauma by fighting in your dreams. There's support characters you encounter in the overworld who are meant to help you move forward. Unfortunately, the narrative of building relationships does not really tie into the gameplay, apart from trying to upgrade a passive buff. At some point you max out your stat with each character and from there on they're basically a decoration, while you grind towards unlocking more gameplay upgrades and tackling higher difficulty dungeons.Dunegon layout is kinda similar to Binding of Isaak, but this game doesn't take full advantage of it. Some rooms have stuff you destroy with bombs. Some rooms need keys. Each level has a secret room you need a bomb to access. Other than that, there just isn't any variety. You can usually just calculate where the secret door is because it always connects to three other rooms.So, while overall the game is very enjoyable, there's still a lot of room left on the table to make the narrative more engaging. Tie the relationship progression to things that happen in the dungeon, not just guessing which gift you should give them. Add more secret rooms and minibosses. Do something to differentiate one run from another some more.

_childDocuments_.review: + Beautiful and simple aesthetics; overworld feels quaint and warm, while the dreamscape feels like a chilling, glowing...well...dream.+ Audio design is equally beautiful and really helps communicate the protagonist's story.+ The story is relatable and hits deep. It's a game about healing and self-betterment, not letting trauma and depression eat away at you, but instead reaching out for help and accepting love from those around you. This message is told through interactions with the many well-written characters that each embody certain admirable traits, as well as quite literally "fighting your demons" as you traverse Cassidy's nightmarish dreamscape.+ Lots of variation in combat through a mix of melee weapons, ranged weapons, powers, dash abilities, and shield abilities.+ Multiple customizable difficulty settings to help you find the perfect balance of fun and challenging.+ Lots of personality through the dialogue and quirky item descriptions. Also contains a handful of funny pop-culture references.+ Gives a shoutout to the game's backers whose designs made it into the game; their names are part of short descriptions when discovering certain items. It's a nice way to recognize the game's supporters and while not being obtrusive.+ Lots of nice QOL features:   * fast travel to/from already cleared rooms   * option to choose starting equipment from discovered equipment   * mini-map shows items left in the room   * defeated bosses are optional after beating them once, though with reduced rewards if skipped   * overworld shows markers for new unlocks, character interactions, and completed journal entries   * ability to toggle unlockables as spawnable or non-spawnable per run to customize the loot pool- Combat can feel a tad slow at first, but is easy to get used to. Realizing you can dodge cancel out of any animation allows for a much quicker and fluid experience.- Some dialogue with overworld characters feels a little too campy, but is mostly endearing.- Camera can make depth perception difficult in larger rooms, making it very hard to parry or dodge projectiles properly.- Can at times be hard to tell what is going on due to lots of bright particle effects and glowing backgrounds.Base game completed:  YESDLC completed:  N/ARating:  8 / 10 - Very Good

_childDocuments_.review: Soothing; that's a great word to describe this game. This one takes a very smart look at mental health challenges, trauma, fear, isolation, and a variety of other themes. It feels like everything is deeply metaphorical, and even if I can't grasp the meaning yet, there's something undeniably beautiful about the ethereal experience this game provides. Seeing comparisons to games like Hades bugs me; it's not Hades. It's not MEANT to be Hades. This is its own game, and is a rather clever take on the rogue-like genre as far as the various themes and elements involved in its design.A good way to describe the game is "slow and steady;" you're not moving at a breakneck pace like a lot of hack-and-slash rogue-likes. Combat is more tactical, where button-mashing is punished slightly with significantly lower damage than a well-timed, rhythmic hit where the optimal attack moment involves a flash of white on the character. Button-mashing is further de-emphasized by the presence of a variety of different enemies with fairly different attack patterns and rhythms of their own. While you CAN button mash to get through everything, the game most definitely rewards a tactical, slightly more deliberate playstyle. If you can master the incredibly short parry window, many aspects of combat become significantly easier. The weapons and unlockables are fantastic so far - each weapon is VERY distinct from another, from a FF7-style Buster sword, to yo-yo's, to a high-impact punching style that makes every hit feel like you have walloped the enemy with a Falcon Punch. Ranged weapons and abilities are no less serviceable to the player (my favorite is an eye beam attack that looks exactly like Cyclops' laser from X-Men). One refreshing take on the genre here is that you can start each play with a customized loadout of your favorite starting weapons and abilities, or go with random everything like normal. One of the few downsides to the game is the length of time it takes to accomplish most tasks - everything FEELS like it's just a bit too slow at times. Exploring everything on a floor may or may not yield an item you actually want or like, but permanent upgrades between rounds are so time-consuming to obtain that missing the possibility of getting an extra 25 "glass" or "inspiration" may drive you to spend the extra time searching for the "currency" you need. It's one aspect of the game mechanics that is not that fun to me, and could benefit from even slightly higher drop chances for the permanent upgrade currency. Despite this, as the theme of the game involves mental health and exploring difficulty, it's not out of place to consider that this was a deliberate choice which emphasizes the slow (and often frustrating) nature of constant self-improvement. If that is indeed the case, I can personally forgive the slowness of the game, as it truly is a fun experience all the same. I really like the developer's attention to specific details - dying in a rogue-like game is generally a punishing experience. Though this game follows that same pattern, it lessens the blow with a slightly different take on the player's "death:" you simply wake up from your dream, and proceed with a variety of healthy activities, such as meditation, daydreaming, talking with new people and connecting with friends, and developing new attitudes and experiences. What a wonderfully uplifting way of looking at life! It reminds me that I need to slow down and that its okay to take care of myself, as well. Just the simple thought of "Oh, I only woke up from the dream. I can try again!" was somehow wonderfully encouraging to me. It adds a sense of continuity to Cassidy's character that reminds me that it's okay to make mistakes, and that the end of a dream doesn't mean I failed. It just means that I learned something new. One personal gripe is that I can't personally understand why the 5th boss is portrayed with frontal nudity. There is nothing in the game before or after that fight that portrays nudity. While the argument can be made that she's not actually naked or that it's not a big deal (e.g. no nipples are visible, presence of nudity is extremely brief), it is bothersome to me to see nudity portrayed in a game about mental health and healing. It's the one thing that doesn't add up in my own book. Though I'm certain there is a metaphor there that I'm not catching, I feel like the nudity is unnecessary for the game and could be removed without impacting the core gameplay and the emotional impact of the 5th boss itself. While its slower, somber, and more deliberate pace may be a turn off to those seeking a fast hack-and-slash game, Dreamscaper is nonetheless a wonderful testament to thoughtful game design and clever incorporation of an often underutilized central theme: self-care. This unique take on the Rogue-like genre is worth noting and enjoying in between all of the hustle and bustle of daily life and the faster, flashier, yet more exhausting games of our day.

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper has an excellent, well-written story and features enjoyable characters. Battling your nightmares at night then making friends during the day (and spending meta currency to become stronger) creates a fun loop. Dreamscaper also has some QoL additions that other roguelikes would do well to copy (the ability to teleport to any previously explored room, instead of having to backtrack to heal, for instance). I really like how equipment is handled in this game. You have a melee weapon, ranged weapon, a dash, a block, and 2 special abilities. As you explore each floor you get offered lots of equipment you can swap out for what you currently have. I think the high frequency of items helps mitigate randomness (you are very unlikely to get a string of bad items). But since you can only have 1 of each kind of item, the game also prevents you from becoming overwhelming powerful, trivializing the game. I also like how items can increase in level (affecting damage) or in rarity (giving additional bonus effects). This makes choosing between items more interesting.I also think the difficulty of the game is perfect. Before you start a run, there are 4 metrics (Enemy, Damage, Size, and Boss). You can increase the difficulty of any or all of these by up 2 two (the harder you make it, the more rewards you earn), creating immense flexibility in how you want to play. I, for example, raised the Dungeon Size by 2, because I enjoyed exploring and managing resources to survive until I could find the boss. But, I was hesitant to raise the Boss difficulty because at higher levels the bosses get new attack patterns, which I thought would be too challenging for me.In summary, Dreamscaper is captivating in every way. Its story, themes, and mix between combat and conversation is unique and lovely. Its mechanics are fun and give the player plenty of interesting choices. And it iterates on some of the basic ideas of roguelikes, creating a less irritating experience. I'd recommend it to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is a thoughtful, enjoyable game, with a satisfying gameplay loop that rewards your effort with more variety of weapons, load-outs and experiences. Though the layout of each dream world will eventually become pretty predictable and familiar, being able to alter the conditions with higher difficulty levels from fairly early on helps to liven things up. The story is quiet, personal and relatable, but will inevitably be off-putting to some based on its sensibilities and some of the sentiments or morals it espouses, even in something as minor as flavor text for an equipped item. The visuals are simple and lack polish at points, especially in regards to character designs and modeling, but overall do not retract from the enjoyment of the game. Some visual design choices are fairly bizarre, such as all of the human characters (including the player) not having faces, but they also manage to create some dazzling effects for the many, many different lucid attacks, (basically your spells) such as falling meteors, pillars of flame or lightning pouring from your fingertips. The music is gorgeous and fitting for the game's melancholic atmosphere, and I'll probably be enjoying the OST for some time.  While not particularly difficult, and not necessarily having the "tightest" roguelike gameplay I've ever experienced, I consider Dreamscaper to be a fantastic and worthwhile experience for any fan of the genre and highly recommend it to anyone looking to have a slightly more laid back experience with a down-to-earth, modest story that pairs itself so well with addictive gameplay and a massive variety of powers and synergies.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: After completing this, I both was and was not surprised I had sunk 60 hours into it.Dreamscaper is a fun action rogelite telling the story of Cassidy who has moved away from her hometown and is trying to mend her life back together. There are two stages of the game. The "Waking World" where Cassidy interacts with people in her life and works on herself, and the "Sleeping World" where she fights through randomly-generated dungeons to work through her traumas and build resources for bettering herself in the waking world.Mechanically, there's a lot of diverse weapons and abilities. A ton of synergy exists, and you can complete runs in a variety of ways. It's not as balanced as some of the best in this class, but the game offers you the ability to remove some weapons and abilities from the spawn pool to offset that.However, the true standout of the game is the storytelling, the art, and emotional progression. I really enjoyed the "waking world" part of the game where I got to build on Cassidy's connections with others, and string together who she is while she works toward picking the pieces of her life back up.As I mentioned before there's a lot of fun in the sleeping world to be had once you unlock good gear and lock away stuff you don't want anymore. It can be long, runs lasting more than a couple of hours at least. The length of each run is probably the weakest part of the game. There are 6 levels of the Dreamscape. If we compare this to Hades, an average clear run is about 30 min.I appreciate that Dreamscaper is trying to tell an emotional journey, and that's one where time is part of that progress. I would have liked a slightly shorter amount of time needed for a clear run, but it doesn't detract from the game too much.Side note, the game is decently playable on the steam deck. However, if you're gunning for the harder achievements (particularly going for beating it on intensity level 6) I recommend playing on PC. There's a lot going on at higher intensities, and the text is small, so stuff can get lost. Otherwise, enjoy this game handheld.4/5, definitely recommend for the roguelite fans, and maybe for anyone looking for exactly that kind of emotional journey towards dealing with loss.

_childDocuments_.review: Changed this review to positive since devs seem attentive to improving the game, I have noted the areas I think need improving but overall it's decent for early access:Positives:- Really good soundtrack.- Cozy atmosphere and I like the diverse characters.- Only seen 2 bosses but they are good.Negatives:- Low enemy variety, stages missing bosses.- There is a break between every stage where you 'wake' to spend resource points in the real world, this feels really unnatural and disrupts the flow.- Enemies are damage sponges, especially from stage 3 onwards when there is a noticeable difficulty spike. They have no HP bars either so you're basically stunlocking them for ~30 sec and hoping they die.- Doesn't feel like there is much permanent progress, you can unlock items to the item pool, but the character upgrades aren't that powerful and you need to pick between one set of upgrades at a time (lighting damage, ranged damage etc.).- there is an animation when you cross between every room that makes me slightly motion sick.- No real video options menu to disable things like AA etc.- Combat feels kind of slow, the game feels like it should be just a little faster.

_childDocuments_.review: Poignant, exciting and endlessly replayable. This game reminds me of my therapy sessions -- it is such a safe, cozy place to process my thoughts; except, of course, my therapist does not have flashy weapons, attack companions, and bombs... that I know of. This game is truly art. Every aspect of the game was deeply explored and developed, and it just feels *good* to play. The combat is intuitive, and I love the unadulterated chaos of the ever-changing weapons and abilities. One minute I am punching baddies in the face with boxing gloves; then, I am slapping enemies around with a stick. And the movement abilities! I quite literally screamed when my character did a backflip high-kick out of nowhere. And can we talk about how beautiful it is? The colours, the environments, and the character design are gorgeous. I adore each level, from the hard winter in the beginning to the quiet nighttime in the city. This is one of the most stunning games I have ever played. This game is a journey of self-discovery, healing and acceptance. Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: My first impression of the game was not too good, I've tried it again and revised this review accordingly, be warned it may contain spoilers.There is a problem with keyboard/mouse controls. First of all, it doesn't show when there are controls that have the same keybinding and besides things like shared attack there is no need to combine keybindings, while the text ones are barely visible. For example. instead of using 'Q' and 'E' keybindings for skills by default, could use numbers 1 and 2 even if there are only two skills active (There are issues even with assigning them to numbers since it assigns to extra mouse buttons instead and even changes mid-game).So it is one thing to recommend gamepad, but it feels like you just don't care if someone doesn't like them and prefers to use mouse/keyboard or even just the keyboard when there's too much clicking involved.Another issue I had with the options was the resolution, for some reason I had some unknown custom resolution when starting the game for the first time and the cursor wasn't showing correctly while at first it didn't even let me change it, before clicking default settings.Seems like you're trying to make a game similar to Hades, but remember that in Hades the special attack is not resource dependant like the ranged weapon in Dreamscaper, while the challenge is based on chaos buffs, there is no choice like in Hades.Personally I hate the environment, with all the clutter you would think that some of it may be interactable, but it appears that there's a meaning to it only from time to time when there's some memory connected to it (instead of fishing I guess) so the destructibles which you made to stand out just make it look bizzare and lazy, while the graphics are not optimized. Even the red pit is obviously lava, though enemies don't get any damage from traps which is also stupid.Some enemies even can get off bounds and then you can't even attack them in melee (happened on last floor). Apparently not only enemies, Thundering Lounge can get you off bounds too, though you get teleported to the center of the room which can be bad if there's a trap there...I never liked mechanics such as the perfect strike which are just useless at the beginning even if later they can be very helpful with upgrades and buffs, the combat is clunky as it is with skills that you have to aim in a very limited way and traps that can hurt you even while swapping items/skills. Could introduce the perfect strike later in the game when the player is able to unlock its full potential. There's no reason to have everything at the very first run.The puzzles made me wonder if the game's major audience are small kids, like seriously, minesweeper and connecting pipes? If you wish to make it even more casual, you could add an option to mark the circles in which you think there's a bomb.On the bright side, I can say that I do like some of the items/skills which are found along the way and the variety is large, so it does add to replayability.Another good additions are the option to skip bosses and the teleport between rooms, but then again, why do I have to skip the cinematics at bosses every time? can't you add an option to toggle them on/off (for those that you've seen already), it's just a flag, not that complicated.Speaking of levels, so you have an option to save at the end of the level, but why can't you keep that save while on the floor in case that you have to leave? So people wouldn't abuse it to restart floors? It's a single player game, why do you care even if they do...The upgrade systems are nice and the stats display in inventory is informative but the tutorial is not appealing at all which is weird given the fact that you give an option to play it at any time, so I'd recommend you to add more content to it and maybe even better, add upgrades to it as you progress to act as a sandbox in which you can actually train and check various item/skill combinations. You can take it further and encourage people to use the upgraded tutorial by offering some cosmetic rewards instead of actual game progress.Otherwise you could add a compendium with all available items, skills and enemies, which would disclose the information right away or after mastering the item/skill and killing enough enemies of the specific type.The gifts which can be given to any NPC along with the extra affinity that gets obvious once you get info about their interests is good, but forcing you to watch the cinematic that way, without voice-over, is kinda boring, would rather have it saved in a journal and read it later in one go, since the stories are not really connected anyways and feel too random when the conversation comes up all of a sudden like that. Found another bug, after getting an NPC to advance another friendship level, I gave another gift by mistake and then I couldn't skip the cinematic and I couldn't do anything when it was over so I had to close the program.Another suggestion, it would be better if the challenge info would first appear at the center of the screen with a brief pause or even during the loading of the room and then move to the side afterwards. Same for things like the keepsake that destroys a random owned keepsake to give something else, cant you do a prompt for the one being destroyed? Why do I have to look through what I had in advance and then check what am I missing?Also, why is the movespeed in town so slow? Again, comparing to hades, you keep the movespeed upgrades and can even dash inside the house of hades.Oh and the secret room mechanic? The guides say that it has to be near 3 or 4 rooms but not near boss, clearly that's not the case. Though so far if there are empty rooms between 4 others, probably it will be one of them unless it's connected to a boss.So frankly, I don't see why the reviews are so high, just helping the company with the sales? Because the product just feels unfinished and I wouldn't recommend it at the current state. Even though most of the time I'm just idle in the game doing something else in real life, I'm not going to demand my money back or anything like that. Please though, stop with the discord prompt on exit, add it somewhere in the menu instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Thrill and chill can exist at the same time.Dreamscaper   you into a roguelike experience with engaging combat and upgrades all while maintaining the relaxing aesthetic of a lucid dream. _childDocuments_.review: Wow this game is cool! I heard it described as "Hades meets Life is Strange" and... um, yeah. That actually fits.The combat system is all Hades - it's an ARPG, you go into the world, fight, and die. When you die, you "wake up" (you're in a nightmare, so "death" is awakening) - and when you "wake up" you get to wander around, talk to people, buy upgrades for your next run... just like, uh, Hades. Even the fighting styles and controls are similar to Hades. The difference is in the way everything is presented. Take away the Greek Mythology, you're now a woman trying to piece together mysteries of her past and new relationships. You craft gifts for new friends to become closer to them and gain powers in the nightmare world. Very cool concept.Even with a good concept you need the art, music, and gameplay to pull it off. Gameplay is basically Hades, so that leaves us with music and art. How are they? Fantastic! The music and art styles fit the world perfectly. I've had non-gamer family members pause to comment that whatever I am playing "looks beautiful" - it's that kind of game. My *only* complaint is that it seems to crash a fair bit, and that is not an issue with my OS or computer. I'm not quite sure what causes the occasional crashes to desktop yet, but they are few and far enough in between that it doesn't put me off easily giving this game an easy recommend to friends that enjoy Hades style ARPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: I really tried to like the game since the art style is great, but after playing for 4 hours and reaching world #4 (out of 6) I have no desire to continue. The core idea and the visual presentation are good, but in terms of gameplay Dreamscaper quickly falls short.All weapons feel more or less the same, all upgrades do more or less the same (more HP, more lucidity = mana, more armor, more different rooms on the map, etc), all spells work more or less the same (aoe damage, ranged damage, short ranged dmg - we've seen this a million times in various games). So every run feels more or less the same, and the game quickly gets extremely repetitive, which is a huge NO for a roguelite.What's even worse, the deeper you travel, the more HP enemies have, but their basic variations stay the same, and also the traps and general map layouts stay the same, only the visuals change. Again, a huge NO for a roguelite. When I reach new biomes/worlds/floors, I want to see new enemies and challenges, not the same stuff, but in different color.Speaking of color, while the visuals are great, it's extremely hard to make out some items on the groud. White "sand" (currency) bubbles on white backgrounds, red HP vials on redish backgrounds, you get the idea. Even more, sometimes there's so many spell effects on screen, it's almost impossible to track your character and enemies, so you ofter take damage simply because you can't see enemy attacks and react in time.Finally, the meta progression (unlocking new weapons and upgrades) is extremely slow. Maybe due to this the game feels the same every run, but I have no desire to grind for several more hours just to potentially unlock a weapon or a spell that would play differently from what I already have.P.S. I have dozens of hours in Hades, Binding of Isaac, Returnal and some other less known roguelites. Alas, this one is nowhere near as good as the ones I just mentioned.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very good game. It has great core combat mechanics, with fast paced and fun combat, with a decent amount of enemy variety. Its art is fantastic and really nails the feeling of fighting monsters in your dream. One thing of note I think it does very well, is the progression system. In each run, you gather resources which you can spend in the real world to make yourself stronger and improve your performance. And the game has a large number of useful upgrades you can take.It does have a few problems. The story is very much of the Arty Indie Game variety, with lots of metaphors and symbolism and stuff like that. It can feel overly dramatic at times. Also, I feel like there is some balance issues with some of the weapons, gear, and powers. Some weapons have barely any range to their attacks at all and are basically pointless to use. And some of the powers aren't very good either. This is very much a fast-paced type of game, where you are constantly moving around in combat. And most of the enemies are constantly moving to. So, any power where you have to stop and aim the attacks are pretty much useless. They don't even do much damage compared to the melee weapon. Also, there is a bit of a problem with the story. See, the main idea of the story is you are metaphorically battling the main characters inner demons. There are people in the real world you can improve your relationships with to get various buffs. Similar to Persona. And as you progress with each person, you sort of go through the motions of dealing with your problems. You know, they ask you what is wrong, you respond, sometimes in a not nice or aggravated way depending on how far you have progressed. And this is fine. It's what you would expect based on the game’s premises. The problem is, that I think the game expects you to increase your relationships equally with all the people as you play the game. Because you pretty much go through the same beats in all of the relationships. Remember, the game is basically about metaphorically dealing with trauma. And you sort of see the main character dealing with this as you progress through the relationship with each person. The problem is, you progress exactly the same with each person, no matter where you are in the other relationships. So you see the main character dealing with trauma, the exact same way, with each person. It just breaks immersion a bit. And the bonuses each character gives for progressing their relationship are not at all equal. Some are great, some are crap.All in all, this is still a great game with good gameplay. I just feel it can be a bit pretentious at times. I honestly think it would have been better if it had been actual demons invading the main characters mind, and they weren’t just metaphors for dealing with trauma. English class made me hate metaphors forever. I would still recommend this game for anyone who likes a good Rouge Like.
