_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is beautiful, well-designed roguelite game that is enjoyable by one like me who generally doesn't like roguelikes and is not great at action games.  I will admit I am still working my way through the levels, but that I prefer to play it in small bursts (to avoid frustration due to my lack of skill).  But I keep coming back to it.  The music, the atmosphere, the emotional story it tells that is very human is too compelling.The various forms of meta-progression is what makes this a roguelike that works for me.  I love that there is actually a game outside of the dream world (where the main game, and all its action, takes place).  I enjoy learning about the people in the city and seeing Cassidy grow in her relationships with them.  So even as I suck at the action part (but I am improving), there is this nice break between runs that is very chill.  I also must add I appreciate that I can save between levels as I rarely have the time to try a full run.I have to say one more time how beautiful the art style is.  It is what drew me to the game in the first place and it is a significant part of why I continue to return, along with the great feeling action, and the city stories.

_childDocuments_.review: Strong Binding of Isaac vibes, but with less skill synergy and more focus on active combat.✔ a lot of active skills to choose from. Each weapon has its own combo, special and animations, making them feel distinctive✔ mechanically rich - two spells, one melee one ranged weapon, dash (many different ones to choose from), shield (with block and parry)✔ loadout - you always choose which items to start with✔ good lifepool management - should be default but a lot of roguelikes treat life as  important resource. Here it's important, but losing some of it is fine, you probably will get it back at a relatively low price❔ melee passives (those that can be called that) are very weak, while ranged are far too powerful✘ massive amount of perma progresion, that I think goes too far. _childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of Hades, Dreamscaper is the first roguelite I've played since then that really had me repeating "one more run"The art is beautiful, the music is dream-like and the UI is a delightGameplay is solid. Navigating each room is satisfying and I've enjoyed slowly picking up how different mechanics through several runs. The weapon and power variety is incredible. If you enjoyed the variety of builds in Hades, you'll feel at home here.Story so far is a very somber and slow-paced affair. Not in a bad way however. Meeting the different characters and learning about them while piecing together Cassidy's story is one of the main reasons i keep diving in for another go.My only gripes right now are minor. Combat VFX can get overwhelming to the point that its hard to see what's happening and I end up dodging to safety to reasses the situation.A few collision issues and some resource clarification issues.Overall, this has been such a steal for me. _childDocuments_.review: A lot of games these days try very hard to be Emotionally Deep, but fail to scratch the surface of the issues their metaphors are pointing at. They also tend to lack any compelling gameplay; I've lost count of how many cute-but-sad figures walk through aesthetically-pleasing-but-vaguely-gloomy landscapes as bits and pieces of their story are hinted at. Sometimes you'll get puzzles to solve, or some platforming to do, but for the most part these are just Walking Simulators where the "game" is just a medium for the creators to tell a particular story... though usually fairly vaguely, as if art is only meaningful if it's not direct.I don't mean to be derisive, all of this is fine if it floats your boat. It doesn't float mine though, especially because there are other games that go above and beyond this formula, and I think more people should know about them.One fairly famous one is Celeste, which is a really good and actually challenging platformer that has fantastic music and an emotionally meaningful story which doesn't lose any of its impact by being pretty straightforward about what it's "about."Another I've recently finished is Dreamscaper, a fairly light-weight Rogue-like that nonetheless has solid action on par with Hades, gorgeous visuals and music, and a basic but sufficient story that similarly develops between each loop.It also has a clever "self-care" vibe going through the whole thing that I found really unique. Your character has moved to a big city to get away from her grief, and as she struggles with depression and her new environment, she has a To Do list for improving her emotional and mental health, which includes things like making friends, being more physically fit, meditating more, doing creative work, etc... all of which confers in-game combat benefits. Every night you face your inner demons, and the better you do, the more Determination, Creativity, Inspiration, etc you have to work on yourself and develop your relationships the next day.It's not a complicated concept, and the execution of it is pretty straightforward (bordering on oversimplified), but it's one I haven't seen before, and it added an extra bit of emotive weight to the overarching journey. To be clear, I'm not saying the story is "deep" or complicated. Just that it's straightforward in what it's pointing at in a way I found refreshing compared to most games that try to talk about mental illness, and also feels the most like it integrates the themes and gameplay than any of them, even Celeste.I also enjoyed the flavor text for the weapons and powers, many of which are shamelessly referencing comics, shows, books, or other games that the protagonist is inspired by in her fight against the monsters in her dreams, which emphasizes the fantasy of what lucid dreaming can be like. With the right combination of pickups, you can be the Avatar, or a mutant with the power of various X-Men, or an oversized-sword-wielding fighter.Generally recommend  checking it out if you're looking for games that are "about" something without being particularly verbose, if you're looking for something to tide you over until Hades II, or both.

_childDocuments_.review: Caution: If you're struggling with mental health, know that this game contributed to my Apocalypse-class mental breakdown. So just know what you're getting into. Cool? Cool. It's mechanically complex; or perhaps complicated. Overcomplicated, if you ask me - there's an overabundance of equipment. It's nice but also... bogging things down.  Yes, although it does drag on for too long if you want to experience the story in its entirety - took me 34 hours to see the "true" ending. There also are some questionable design decisions, though in general I'd say it holds up well and does its own thing.  Yes; but the story content runs out far too quickly. So what makes it or kills it is the gameplay, in the end.That's the short version. If you'd like to know more, I'll get into the details now.Or hungry. You end up buying way more than you need, even though it seemed like a good idea at the time. This is how this game's gear system works. You have no less than 6 active gear slots (passives have no limit), and each slot has 10-20 options available. The slots are: - Melee Weapon  - Ranged Weapon - Shield - Spell 1 - Spell 2 - Shoes (aka dodge)Are you complaining that there's so much variety, you ask? No - it's nice to have so many options. But many of them are too similar to each other. Case in point: there are four short distance quick-attack weapons. Boxing Gloves, Unarmed, Biting Dagger and the Knife. From a gameplay standpoint they are almost completely identical. There are of course differences, but they don't feel too meaningful. Even bonuses and modifiers are randomly assigned - there are, however certain constants: Biting Dagger, for example, is (I think) always Poison-elemental. Ranged weapons for the most part are just "launch a projectile of varying size towards your enemy".Shields. Let's just say those feel way to similar to each other, and pretty much only differ in parry difficulty and secondary effects. Shoes - what shape does your dodge take. They affect dodge length, aftereffect, distance, all sort of stuff - it's actually a little annoying, because your muscle memory will mess with you due to sudden change in dodge distance. And then there are the spells. They actually are quite different, although there are some spell pairs which are elemental counterparts to each other. Oh, right, there's a whole element system and paying attention to it and how different elements interact is mandatory later on. That by itself adds another layer of complexity to things. And because there are just so many things, sometimes it's hard to get the build you want because of just how small the chance of getting something that works with what you have are; but it also makes it very satisfying once you do.With all that said, the gameplay is solid enough to keep on keeping on. The general structure is clearly based on Binding of Isaac - room-based map with up to four exits, bombable destructibles, walls and doorways, keys, shops, and multitude of items that modify your behaviour in some way (nowhere near as impactful as in Isaac though). The enemy variety is perhaps a little low in number, but high in quality: there are different enemy classes, which also have sub-varieties. The enemy behaviour is great; they all use their strengths tactically. F. ex. the buffer always hangs back in a corner, and when you approach to kick their ass, they'll attempt to sucker punch you and teleport away. It's great.And that's good, because to achieve the true ending, . You also need to . And sadly, the game's just not fun enough to keep at it for that long; the runs blend into one another, even with all that variety. At the time of writing, only 2.6% of players have the achievement for the true victory, and I can see why. The best approach would probably be to play this game periodically, instead of all at once. Because it is fun - it's just the drag that diminishes the experience.Since you have to play so much, minor flaws become that much more apparent. For example, there's this mechanic - "perfect attack". Instead of mashing that attack button, the game prompts you to instead tap it when the character glows for a split second mid-combo. This is great. However, for reasons I can't fathom the timing is different when you're just swinging at the air and when you're attacking something. So you can never practice it properly. And considering the fighting feels very dream-like - slow and floaty - this can cause frustration.Another thing is that whenever you reach a new level of relationship with a waking world character, the game tells you: Congrats! You unlocked Bruce's Wisdom II! Next unlock: Bruce's Wisdom III. Who thought this is a good idea? Do people not know that III is after II? If there was an explanation of what it does, it would've been helpful. But no! All you learn is that III comes after II. Oh, and the general balance is a little off. There are certain build options which are clearly superior to others, and some items I feel are almost completely useless. So the difficulty of the run will greatly depend on whether you'll find items that synergise well - far more than in other roguelikes.This game's story and general theme is finding inner peace through lucid dreaming. There's a disturbingly realistic portrayal of depression, both from the protagonist's inner perspective (dreams, state of her room) and from her friends' perspective (her treatment of others, her words and motivations, her general life situation). Each zone in the game represents a part of her life; a place and a time. The weapons and trinkets are pieces of her life. A snowman, a paper airplane, a toy car; all of them have short quips about their significance for her. And for some reason seeing life reduced down to those ever-repeating memories threw me into the deepest pit of despair I've ever been in. Is that what Nietzsche meant when he wrote about the idea of Eternal Return?For the most part, the game's storytelling is silent. Lots of story pieces are told through images; bosses representing different negative emotions and states, the dreamscapes getting warped by their emotional significance, the subtle changes in the environments. However, there are also pieces of dreams that make the protagonist reflect on that particular memory, and those are just the best. You slowly learn about her world and her life. Also, when you level up your relationship with a character, you're treated to a short-ish conversation, which grants further insight into both people's stories.So that's all good, but here's the problem: there's simply not enough of it. The world pieces run out halfway through, and there's only so much dialogue you can have with others. And it only happens when you actively progress through the story via grind. So you'll never "just stumble" upon some interesting dialogue, like you would in Hades. This undermines everything quite a bit, and makes the focus fall strictly on the gameplay. It is quite good, if stretched out. A little too grindy, a little too repetetive. The visuals and music are both fantastic; the game feels like some kind of bittersweet drama movie, and I'm saying it as a good thing here. Sadly, even those things get a little boring after a while. That's why I suggest playing it, but not all at once. Do a run or two and then shelve it, go back after a week or so. Also keep in mind what I said about that breakdown. I wouldn't wish this on my worst enemy. Hope that helps!

_childDocuments_.review: is challenging top-down action game that explores the protagonist Cassidy's present and past lives through the repetition of day and night cycles. The game entered into Early Access recently after having a  that is still available to try. The action-roguelite game is played out in the dream world. When she goes to sleep, she enters her dream dungeon every time, restarting from the beginning after a previous death, or continuing on a previous journey from before. Facing a dungeon of 6 floors, she will only tackle one floor per night, and have waking days in between. On the flip side, the waking day is limited to only between 6 and 9 PM. She has a life, moving from a small rural town to a bigger city, she has a day job and so her social life is outside of that time frame. With a strict bedtime at or before 9 PM each night, she has 3 hours at most to wander from location to location and to interact with the people in town. There are only 4 locations and 6 NPCs right now, hopefully there will be more added in the future.Why is the waking time so important for this game? Because it allow you to take some of your dream world loot and use them to craft gifts for the NPCs, who in turn give you permanent friendship progression that lead to stat modifiers or items that you can find in-game. Of course having these friendship status upgrades also allows you to learn about each individual NPC as well as the protagonist more. You do not have to craft gifts with all of your loot, as you can also choose to pick a better load-out set for the next run if you spend some of this as well. Just spending time with the NPCs will yield you friendship boosts, but giving them gifts that they love will move that bar along much faster.There's not an extensive amount of story-revealing lines, but there is enough to keep the player interested in going back to interact with the NPCs in the waking world. Though the break in the action can sometimes feel awkward, so I tend to choose to continue sleeping until the end of the run. At the end, I will do my crafting and gift-giving and try to make a few friends.I would like to see an additional option to just play a run to the end without stopping. But any time you are in the waking world, you can quit the game and it will save for you, so it's nice to be able to break up the entire dungeon into smaller chunks if you need to break for other things in your schedule. Though this also means that I typically end up with more ingredients and craft more gifts than I can travel and give out in the time available. So I am still trying to figure out how to balance between the two.In the dream world, all of the action takes place. Cassidy is exploring her childhood memories and facing her fears through brute force. You start with a loadout melee and ranged weapon, along with a shield and a special attack. You can hold up to 2 special attacks at any time during the run. You start with a dodging ability as well and can exchange for others that you come across. The melee, ranged, and dodge moves have all such different feels that you want to make sure to get used to them whenever you pick up something new. The melee and ranged weapons all have different reaches and ranges. The different dodges have different animations, durations, and also effective movement spacing, so using a room that you have already cleared to get used to them is ideal. You might want to save your ranged attacks since there's limits, but the others are unlimited. The special attacks only have cooldowns to wait through. You will be able to pick up various keepsakes that are essentially passives to make or break your run. Actually they always help. What breaks the run is typically in the later levels when the enemies are so tanky and hit so hard that they just become kind of unfair to deal with.There are six floors total and only 3 bosses, that means some floors are going to have filler enemies in place in the boss rooms. The bosses are on floors 1, 3, and 6. The game should see development toward putting new bosses into these other spaces as well. I look forward to those.Each room you enter will have its exits locked  until all of the enemies are cleared. There are special challenge rooms that if you meet the criteria given, you will also get a random drop when the enemies are cleared. The combat is also broken up by a couple of different simple puzzle rooms that also yield random drops. The puzzles are either 1. rotating pipe pieces to connect them or 2. a simple and very small  logic room.I only used a controller, it worked really well. I think I would recommend a controller for this game. The combat is fairly smooth, and the controls are very responsive. My biggest problem is parrying, I can't seem to get the timing right, but that's something for me to work on. Really nice environments in both the waking and the dream worlds. Smooth lines with 3D models in a low-poly appearance and some nice color balance work really well together. The protagonist and the NPCs have no faces, so that may take a little getting used to. But the animations used for these characters despite having no faces convey various feelings quite well. The camera angle is fixed and follows around the protagonist pretty well, In bigger rooms, this may seem a bit too zoomed out at times.Pleasant and fitting soundtrack, and the sound effects work well too. No complaints here.Current Early Access price at Launch is $19.99 base. I am 13+ hours in, and haven't even seen the final boss yet. I keep getting completely destroyed whenever I make it to the final floor just by regular enemies. The game has a good variety of weapons, passives, special attacks, shields, and dodging to make it quite interesting. What I am saying is that the content is already worth the price.-I would love to see the enemies not being so tanky later on, kind of feels unfair on the final two floors.-More environments, both worlds, and more NPCs and maybe enemy types.-Definitely needs more bosses. Fighting filler enemies in the boss rooms feel awkward.-I would like an option to toggle at the start of a run whether to run until death or to wake in between floors. I find the breaks awkward, especially if you are leveling up friendship points in between and sit through a couple of lengthier conversations. Then jumping right into a harder floor just feels wrong.-A log of the conversations recorded into the journal for the interactions with the NPCs that have already transpired, like the memories that you can find.-Various bugs. I have had the game crash on me about three times, unclear reason. I don't mind usually, but once I bought a legendary loadout item to try to conserve money for a run for that 6K achievement and it crashed. Restarting I lost my loadout and my resources, I was not a happy camper. in its attempt to mash together the action roguelite along with a story-driven set of characters that lead to in-game unlocks with actual character development in small conversation bits will create some awkward moments for sure. It's daring and overall fairly enjoyable. Some rough edges to hammer out, but I have really no major complaints for it ultimately offers great fun. Another indie gem in the making. Hopefully it will be polished to really shine.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is a highly entertaining combination of several of action roguelites, which manages to be familiar to them while definitively staying its own unique experience.Pros:- This game has a gorgeous visual aesthetic and a very moving soundtrack to back it. Ironically, though you spend most of the game in your dreams, it's the time in the Waking World where the artistic design of the game lands most strongly for me- Combat is fun and fluid, and you have a staggering number of weapons and spells to choose from. You'll never be hurting for new builds to try or options to use in combat- Borrows what works best from a number of other roguelites while keeping its own identity, making it both familiar and easy to pick up while still being fun and interesting to explore- The characters you form relationships with are quirky and interesting, but dialogue still feels pretty natural to a real conversationCons- This game could certainly stand to have some more enemy variety. What's here is great, but there comes a point when you realize that every floor deeper you go, most enemies will be the same just with one or two new/upgraded moves.- Some bosses in the mid-stretch feel a little plain/easy for the point in the run you face them at, and while you do have the option to skip any boss you've already defeated previously, it's a hard sell to do so and give up on the items and meta-progression resources you'd gain for fighting them again- A few weapons just feel totally useless given the flow of the game. Perhaps I'm using them wrong, or they work better with a build style I haven't tried, but some weapons just feel like inferior versions of others. Either too slow to be reliable or some ranged weapons are so close range for the damage they deal it seems pointless to not just use melee attacksOverall this is an easy game to recommend to any fan of the action roguelite genre. What's here is very fun and polished, I just want to see even more content and variety in future updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Cassidy lives an interesting life. By day she tries to get to know other people and socialise, and by night she fights monsters in her dreams. This concept is put together in a form of a rogue-like hack and slash game, with nightmarish dreams taking form of procedurally generated dungeons with tonnes of gear customization and loot and plenty of monsters and environmental hazards to face.This is an interesting premise. As Cassidy interacts with NPCs in the waking hours, she builds relations with them which unlocks new gear and bonuses for the dreams. At the moment there are 6 NPCs and 4 city areas. Hopefully as more are added in the future, there'll be a lot more characters to befriend and city areas to explore. The dungeons are themed and follow a certain order, but each one has a random layout in each run we do. If we lose all HP in a dungeon, Cassidy wakes up. The next time we go into the dream, we have to start over from the first dungeon again, which can feel a bit grindy and repetitive, but some will enjoy it as they get to start with new gear and abilities and have a go at the challenge again.There's lots of gear to find to customize ourselves, ranging from weapons to special abilities to armour to items with passive bonuses. This makes the fights feel quite fun and allow us to approach them in slightly different ways each time. There are also puzzles we can solve too. Though at the moment there's not much variety in puzzles and enemy types, so hopefully more will be added as the development of the game goes.I think there is potential, but it gets repetitive and grindy too early on, and the unlocks don't feel very rewarding because you don't get to use them right away. They just get thrown into the pool of items that could drop in dungeons. I think there are better rogue-likes and hack and slash games out there, but since this one is still in Early Access, it could end up becoming much better than it is now closer to the final release, and for the fans of these genres it can already provide plenty of entertainment. It's a project with a lot of passion put into it no doubt and it seems that the devs care for it to be as good as possible.For a more in-depth review and a gameplay video, check here:

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game so i could mindlessly whack stuff in a dungeon crawler and it was SO much more.It's rare every aspect of a game feel like they all work towards one cohesive feeling and theming, but everything from the music to the art style to the progression mechanics and the story really work towards their theme of a person struggling and trying to work their way out of a ♥♥♥♥ spot in lifeI've only just beat the 3rd boss, and probably on a fluke, but I can tell this game had love poured into it and i was not expecting any of this level of qualityI'll summarize the strengths and weaknesses here, but don't let any weaknesses i write deter you from getting this gameStrengths-Very coherant and cohesive EVERYTHING, from story to mechanics to music to characters. Everything adds to one strong theme and vibe-unexpected light, but good, story and characters-fairly well made and fun combat system and animations-Interesting and fun weapons, items, and abilitiesWeaknesses-It is a tad bit grindy, it hasn't bothered me much yet, but if you struggle to beat bosses too long you'll probably hit a soft progress wall-I wish i had more criticism, i normally have plenty, but this game is just unexpectedly great

_childDocuments_.review: Played the game to oblivion and I recommend it, but it has flaws. The art, writing and rogue-like gameplay are good. Balance what RNG gives you with planning to get cool builds.The length, speed and 'lock-in' on the attacks are hard to read, so don't play it as a souls-like and it will be a better experience. _childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed Dreamscaper, it's a roguelite where you try to get out of a cycle of depression. Experiencing events not by seeing them, but learning through conversations with other people as Cassidy slowly opens up to people.Combat at first feels clunky , as I progressed and unlocked way more weapons, unlocked upgrades to make perfect attacks easier to manage it felt better.The writing doesn't seem all that interesting at first, though as I learned more about Cassidy and other characters I was quite invested, and even emotional at times.Dreamscaper is a bit too grindy and takes time to to open up properly as Cassidy does.I hope you'll connect with the writing like I did.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: It's a shame I have to downvote this, because I genuinely do like the dungeons! This idea of representing one's internal struggle as a physical battle is one I've always been fascinated by, and the combat itself is tight, responsive, and provides a fast-paced intensity without becoming a sensory overload! Unfortunately, the story does very little to justify it. We are TOLD that the experiences she's having in the real world are affecting her dreams, but other than some stat boosts that you may not even notice, there's no story-relevant effect of talking to people except at the very end, which ends up feeling like there's a "goal" to building these relationships, outside of just Getting To Know Another Person. A good roguelite is a conversation between the metaprogression and the dungeon, and Dreamscaper just doesn't say much at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is poised to become the next big roguelite. It's packaged with a great emotional story, awesome gameplay, and a unique approach to meta-progression that truly enriches the overall experience. I can go on and on about the combat and how satisfying it is to smack around baddies with a pool cue, but there's one element that impressed me more than anything else: this game is flipping cozy. Cassidy's bedroom, the record store, the bar - it all feels so warm and inviting. I want to go to this city, hang out with these very peculiar people, have conversations about uncomfortable weddings, and randomly give them exercise mixtapes and hand-drawn movie posters I made in my spare time. You know, normal human being kind of stuff. I've never had a game make me long for something I've never experienced, nostalgic for places I've never been. It's crazy, and I love it. This is getting creepy, so I'll stop.TL;DR - Dreamscaper is amazing. I want everyone to play it. If you enjoyed Hades and its brand of roguelite storytelling, this one should hit many of the same notes. I wish my own dreams were this magical. Whoops. Creepy again.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: I had been eyeing this game for a while and finally picked it up on sale. The genre and art was what drew it to me initially but the gameplay keeps me coming back to keep doing runs. I find it to be more challenging than other action roguelites and the insane amount of options for all the kinds of equipment and how different they all feel is truly what's standing out for me. Meta progression is interesting too with three different currencies to trade in for various power ups/map changes as well as mastery levels for most of the equipment types. Sometimes I care about the story and sometimes I don't. I noticed something in the beginning of the game which is making some of the story predictable for me so I'm curious now to see if what I'm thinking lines up (so far it has) or there will be something unexpected. Highly recommended and great job to the devs on this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting rogue-like with a lot of heart put into it from it's developers. I watched it change from the Prologue release up to its release and so much has been added, tweaked, and adjusted, all with a listening ear from it's dev team to their community.The combat in the game calls for quick reflexes alongside quicker wits. The level designs are ethereal, fractal, and honestly perfectly suited to the idea of being lost in a dream of the main character's design. The enemies of the also world keep changing with every deeper descent to keep you on your toes, saying nothing for the bosses. The bosses feel very challenging as you progress and some that you breezed through could prove a problem later on if you decide to get into a scrape with them again for kicks, keeping you humble. With a glut of items to help pad your numbers or work new styles and attacks with, it's got plenty of content to keep you coming back for more in the dreaming world and carving your way towards the end.The waking world is where you focus your time for adjusting your stats, but it's also where you meet your over-world characters and, if it's your sort of thing, learn more about them and about Cassie's story. In my personal opinion, it's a good game with a killer soundtrack, a fantastic art direction, and a lot of open forum for playstyles of all kinds. The character writing has made me laugh out loud or cringe in dismay. All in all I think the final product from Afterburner is a fine one indeed. Definitely worth a look.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Every once in a while, I stumble upon a game that isn't very well known yet, but you can tell the developers have poured their soul into it and it's an amazing experience.Dreamscaper is one of those games.If the game developers continue to work on this game with the same love they have been working on it so far, I have no doubt it will be a huge success.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is one of the best roguelikes I've played, and I play most of them. I love how player-friendly the game is, letting you choose so much about how you head into your runs, what you can expect to encounter, and how you build out your character.Last year, Hades really blew up because it was flashy, fun, and accessible to people new to the genre. I think the same can be said for Dreamscaper, but instead of Greek mythology, it's focused on a mystery surrounding dreams and the hometown of your protagonist. Also - a TON of this game is focused on positivity and "battling your demons". If you're down in the dumps, Dreamscaper is a great way to get a mood lift.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: I had the opportunity to try the prologue, and since then I have been passionate with the story, the environment and the gameplay. This game seems to be a novel with a well written story with intertwined background and relationship growth. Will having an amazing action game, dodge, parry, melee and range attacks with a bit of salty rage/keyboard smash when the monk is healing and buffing the "minotaur". I recommend the game!
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: I couldn't get into the combat. It is very clunky with only one or two mobs on the screen at once that take too many hits while they sit there stunned. Hitting a stunned monster 10 times and waiting for it to die is not exciting for me; the gameplay feels like a long grind instead of an action-packed game. Overall the world building is great and it's a very pretty game, it just didn't catch me. I'll have to revisit it later.This is a review that took place on Early Release, so maybe there will be some changes.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is one of the most charming, relatable, beautiful, and fun games I've had the pleasure of enjoying in a long time. It's already shot to the top 5 of my favorite action roguelites. Might take the cake for being the coziest action roguelite too, which is something that I never thought I'd have to actually measure.Dead Cells was a clear inspiration when it comes to in-run progression. Items are all unique and varied and come with several modifiers depending on the rarity. The gameplay has a satisfying, crunchy feel and a very satisfying moment-to-moment loop. And to be frank, lots of the Abilities and Weapons are just damn cool to use. The Abilities/Spells have some of the best and most satisfying visuals and impacts in any game I've played for a long time.Many items, abilities, and upgrades are actually references to other games, but in each instance they're well-represented and they never beat you over the head with the novelty of "Hey look at this thing you recognize!". I happen to find myself directly in the crosshairs of the target audience in terms of writing, characterization, references, nostalgia factor, and even memes. But I have to admit it works without seeming like I'm being pandered to too heavily. Yes, there's a Buster Sword, and yes, your character holds it like Cloud, but the game never stops to draw attention to it specifically and actually using the weapon is very, very fun. I think I can live with that.In between combat sections there's a charming world-building section with realistic, varied, and (mostly) interesting characters who you gain friendship with to unlock permanent upgrades. I don't think any of them are bad, but your mileage will vary on how much you enjoy speaking to each one.A very, very pleasant surprise and hard to put down once you pick it up.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Got this game while it was in the Prologue stage, then bought it in the EA and never removed it from my PC ever since, getting back to it every now and then. A beautifully made little masterpiece that has both an enjoyable and challenging roguelite part ("dreams") and an engrossing storytelling one that progresses as Cassidy deals with her nightmares ("daytime activities"). Either is awesome in its own respects, and either complements the other in a wonderfully subtle yet very much connected way. I'm absolutely enchanted by this game.But what amazes me perhaps the most is the fact that, although it's made by a team of three people, they've really put in a lot - no, a LOT - of time, effort, and most importantly, heart and true love into this project. Regular updates, constant work on new features, listening to players' feedback and reacting to it in the most caring way I've ever seen. And as an avid follower who hasn't missed a single update yet (despite my meager 25 hours of playtime - I just come back every now and then) I can say none of those have been for the worse so far, only for the better. You guys are probably some of the best developers out there. Please keep it up, gaming community needs you.Strongly recommended for full price, you're guaranteed not to regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Oh no, another roguelike, I guess I will try it for a while and then probably quit. After a few hours I knew I was hooked. _childDocuments_.review: I picked this up in a  mystery bundle and it was GeForce Now compatible, so why the heck not? _childDocuments_.review: Quite lovely and addictive. The closest comparison I can make is the game 'Hades', although this clearly had a lower budget. I found it quite challenging, although difficulty choices are offered quite early in the game. A lot of customization of weapon and power loadouts, but just short of overwhelming. Story is drip fed and progressed between dream runs. Actions taken in the waking world help make progress in the dreaming world. The wide variety of weapons and powers encourage trying out each of them. Only wish there had been voice acting, but that desire is subjective. This is an easy one to recommend, especially if you liked 'Hades' gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the pretty good games with many bright spots to exploit. However, there are points that really make me unhappy.The difficulty is quite high, although I have played a lot of games, the difficulty level of the game will easily discourage many gamers. _childDocuments_.name: Dreamscaper

_childDocuments_.review: The game is quite fun. It looks nice, even in its minimalism. It requires thoughtful input into how you fight. There is a lot of good humor throughout. The character interactions are mostly good despite some grammatical problems.I have to say it's odd to be able to gift people objects and chit-chat with them before the "cut scene" when you're properly introduced. It also seems implicit the protagonist, Cassidy, is somehow only awake for around three hours a day, yet maintains a job despite spending those three hours having awkward social interactions. But the being awake part isn't the main draw of the game anyhow, so it's easy enough to overlook.  There are a few negatives for me.  I don't enjoy having to replay every single level after a death. I don't enjoy losing every item, and having all dreamworld progress essentially erased every time. That said, larger boss fights can be skipped instead of having to replay them, but that's the only boon you're given for completing a world. You can learn to craft items of various qualities, and set up a build before entering the dream world. In this way there is some progress that comes along with the game, but I don't enjoy having to keep setting up my build every time I go into the dreamworld. It'd be nice if the build was saved. And you lose whatever you make if you die.  Essentially, there is a lot of build maintenance required, and your resources are limited and it's off-putting to have to choose everything every time. Of course, if I was better at the game and didn't die so often, most of that wouldn't be a problem. It's a good game, and I see it improving further in its development. Even if none of my negatives end up being changed, I'd still enjoy playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Dreamscaper is a game about depression: how it affects you and affects your relationships.The protagonist, a 20-something woman named Cassidy, has moved to the big city of Redhaven from a small country town called Backhill somewhere in Canada. She's an artist by passion but has recently taken a job at some multinational corporation and is doing general office work. She's got a bedroom in an apartment and has a roommate.When she sleeps, she finds herself in a dangerous, shifting landscape made from her memories. There are six levels, inhabited by monsters and traps, and each level guarded by a boss: Fear, Isolation, Regret, Resentment, Negativity, and Loss.The main gameplay is in this dreamscape. It's an action game that needs quick reflexes and the ability to learn enemy patterns as you fight the monsters and dodge traps in each area. There is an option to turn the game difficulty down to assist with this, making the game more accessible to a wider audience. Cassidy has a melee weapon, a ranged weapon, and two magic attacks, as well as a shield and an evasion move. Some of these are pretty straightforward, and some of them are more dream-logic; Cassidy can find large swords, or fire spells, but also can find a fishing rod or attack enemies with a beard. Despite the incongruity - dream logic, if you'd like - of some of these choices, the general mood of the gameplay is serious, hectic, and overwhelming, where small mistakes can be extremely punishing.Whenever you "die" in the dream, you wake up, and then have an opportunity to move around the city and talk to up to seven other characters, Cassidy's (eventual) friends. Cassidy only has a passing familiarity with a couple of these characters to start with. By talking with them, you learn bits about them, the stories of their lives and their interests. Cassidy, in turn, slowly opens up to these friends. The stories are told as vignettes. Whenever Cassidy chats, it's clear that time has passed since the last conversation the two of them have had -- we're left to fill in the blanks as to what has lead Cassidy to this current chapter. Over the course of the game, Cassidy loses her job, has rifts with her friends and repairs them, and decides to try and follow her artistic interests and reconnect with her parents.These chapter events in the narrative are triggered each time Cassidy defeats one of the dream bosses for the first time, and unlocks the next level of the dream - and her depression.This is represented in the progression of the dreamscape. The first three levels are, in order, Backhill (Cassidy's hometown), Redhaven, and a campground that the family used to visit. As Cassidy wanders around the dream, she finds items that trigger her memories, and she narrates a bit of what she's thinking of. Memories of Backhill include places that Cassidy and Max used to play, the first time Cassidy tried ice skating, a local shopowner that makes the best ice cream, and so on. Throughout the levels, and by defeating the monsters and bosses, Cassidy also finds items she can use to improve herself, expand the dreamscape, craft items for her friends, and discover new combat and exploration items.* Inspiration: this is a currency you find to craft gifts. Each gift is preferred by at least one of your seven friends, most of them match several people. (save yourself frustration and use a guide for this -- Inspiration is in low supply, and grinding for this item in order to make story progression is one of the few places the game stumbles)* Glass: used for daydreaming, which unlocks dungeon features (challenge rooms, enchanting, better stores, better drops, etc)* Resolve: used for meditating, which gives you personal boosts (health, parry window, status effect time, initial loadout, etc)* Sparks and Ideas: you can find Ideas for new items, weapons, and attacks as rare/random drops and then use your Sparks to unlock them so that you can find them on your trips into the dreams.As you're working through your monsters, you are developing yourself and the dungeon -- gameplay gets richer as you make progress. You'll probably find a friend whose bonuses work best for you, and you'll work on that friendship, and they'll be able to support you better in turn as you head back in.The second set of levels are the same environments, but more nightmarish, and in reverse order: nightmare campground, nightmare Redheaven, and then finally ending in a nightmare Backhill.While the game never comes straight out and says it, it suggests that Cassidy has always struggled with depression. The defining event of her recent life, however, was the death of her older sister, Max. Max had been sick for some time, and her doctors had not taken it seriously. When they found out she had cancer, it was too late. Max's death affected the family terribly, and the break Cassidy had with her parents is what finally got her to move to the city and try and start over somewhere else.So there are a lot of interesting choices that help reinforce the experience of living with depression.When the game begins, Cassidy only has a few items unlocked to help her in the dreamscape. Over time, by exploring the dream, she's able to unlock more items and improve her abilities. This mirrors two fundamental aspects of depression, which are the shrunken internal world and limited ability to cope. The items she unlocks all have a connection to something of Cassidy's past -- she is remembering important things from her life. She's also able to expand the resting places in the dreamscape, and increase the chances of finding healing or other helpful items. She can develop her own health and other abilities, allowing her to survive for longer, easier, within the dream. Even as the dreamscape gets more difficult - more challenging to get to the root of her depression, this Loss - she becomes more equipped to deal with it, and her world becomes richer and more expansive in the process.The way the vignettes are structured is, in many ways, one of the primary lived experiences of depression: lost time. This is something the -player- experiences, though, not Cassidy. The player is trying to fill in the blanks and figure out how the relationship got to its current point. Sometimes the time between conversations is relatively short, especially towards the end of each narrative arc, as Cassidy repairs a break in the relationship and forges a stronger bond. Some of these breaks are from Cassidy pushing people away; a couple are due to the friends' well-intentioned but tone-deaf responses to Cassidy's pain. The vignettes deal with loss of and regaining interest in what matters to the characters, toxic positivity, being unable to accept - or even ask - for help, antidepressants (which Cassidy eventually starts, after talking about worrying how they will affect her), and loss and isolation of many types. Some of the friendships involve a lot of blunt conversations about depression. Some of the friendships, though, come at this from the side; the characters talk around things, or talk about things adjacent to the depression itself. This highlights two really important things: the need to tackle things head-on, but also the need to have places of respite where you can talk about.. something else, anything else. And it doesn't shy away from either calling out the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ behavior of Cassidy's friends, or her own ♥♥♥♥♥♥ behavior. Towards the end of each arc, Cassidy owns up to this in each case, as do her friends. It shows that breaks can be healed.I have more to say but this review hit the character limit! If you are someone who is struggling with depression (current episode or chronic), and you're okay with action games, I'd recommend giving this a try, The act of playing it is a powerful experience.

_childDocuments_.review: As of right now I would say I cannot recommend this game compared to other options.One problem the way enemies are handled it is like 1-3 sometimes it lacks any excitement of using a big skill. They still take like 7 whacks like 4 if you got a good weapon but most the time it is not like that. Spells just overpower melee so hard especially since when you are fighting enemies in higher areas they will knock a good chunk of your health bar out even with high armor. You get threw most the levels with buying a strong spell or 2 and just kiting enemies around. Melee felt so unrewarding with its damage and the risk it puts you in by being melee. Using the shield is almost a needed. So start using it unless you want to get stuck.A big glaring issue, the drops are SO rng especially the more you unlock from gifting and you dont get enough sand to buy stuff to alter your build before you are near or past halfway done before anything gets started. Not to mention you will sometimes have to drop items of your build in order to survive or deal damage.  There should be a way to fuse weapons into current ones so we can actually make builds, thats the fun of rouge games you challenge the game with different builds. You create strong or whacky builds you CANNOT do that here. What I suggest is increasing the sand count you get from enemies or just increase the amount of rooms one can explore into. Add a mini boss that is for money only. Something that can let the player use the shop to make a build. Right now its just a random roulette with no real control. And the crafting weapons, what exactly is the point of doing this? Make a Legendary Katana has 24 damage, even with the buffs it has for its rarity It gets out done by the pure damage of the weapons lying around or in the shop, on the first or 2nd level. The katana in the first level took 16 hits to kill a spear foe 16~! Do you know how boring it is to just flop the enemy in the air and just repeat hit it with the same skill.       Remedy add more damage to that crafted weapons. Or just flat out remove the system cause its useless right now.   You could also make it so any of the crafted types you make will appear more often the would help with people wanting to actually do a build.Overall the game has the foundation it is early access after all. However these are issues that in one way or another feel like they need to be addressed if you want to pull in more people. I am sure more stuff will come but the way the system just randomly drops w.e stat with no rhyme  or reason ruins a lot of the game.  I see I am in the minority here with the not recommending but for 20$ a price that can get something from a massive selection of finished games. Especially in hard times like these. I am sure if they keep at it though this game will be among those games, it just isn't right now.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't like roguelite very much and I bought this game by mistake, on a steam winter sale thinking it was a fullblown ARPG.However, i'm glad to say it was the best mistake i made, and by far.There is a lot of spells, weapons, shields, dodges and utilities. Every run is different from the other due to the huge pool of available items and the affixes system (from common to legendary) and the possibility to unloack more. The story and waking world is simple yet touching and very tastefull while the nightmare have a nice difficulty curve and fun boss fight.It's a pleasure to not mindlessy spam the dungeon crawling and get to know the NPC better, revealing parts of Cassidy personality in the process. On top of that the world is beautiful with great art direction and lovely music.Even in this stage of early access I think it was well worth the money already, and i'm impatient to see how the game will turn in the future.Good job Afterburner studio !

_childDocuments_.review: I was attracted to this game by the theme of lucid dreaming, and this theme is incorporated in an interesting and engaging way. The ability to gain buffs within the dream world by forming relationships with people in the real world is a neat way to tie the two dimensions together. I also like the puzzles and random challenges within the dream dungeons. In its current state, Dreamscaper is a bit laggy and doesn't have a lot of depth, but it does have a lot of potential.I would like to offer some suggestions to Afterburner Studios for future improvements. First, I found the controls a bit difficult to remember and use in practice; I was using keyboard controls, and I kept forgetting which key activated which ability. It would be useful to display the key next to the ability in the top left part of the GUI. Another quality of life feature could be to add a way to view the stats of your current equipment without having to find an item to swap with.I'll be following the development of this game and looking forward to the full release!

_childDocuments_.review: After following the game in Early Access for a bit now was the time to buy it. So far it gives me a lot of Hades vibes, which is a good thing! If you're into this genre of games I would definitely get this oneApart from the gameplay. The dialogues in town with the townsfolk are really intriguing and cute as well. Makes you feel good or think about moments in your own childhood which you spent with your family.

name: Kingdoms of Amalur: Re-Reckoning
detailed_description: FATE Edition The FATE Edition contains the Re-Reckoning Main-Game, the Official Soundtrack and the content Addon Fatesworn that extends the game of 5+ hours. The Official Soundtrack features 35 high quality tracks for a total of 70 minutes of music. About the Game The hit RPG returns! From the minds of the bestselling author R.A. Salvatore, Spawn creator Todd McFarlane, and Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion lead designer Ken Rolston, comes Kingdoms of Amalur: Re-Reckoning. Remastered with stunning visuals and refined gameplay Re-Reckoning delivers intense, customizable RPG combat inside a sprawling game world. Uncover the secrets of Amalur, from the vibrant city of Rathir to the vast region of Dalentarth to the grim dungeons of the Brigand Hall Caverns. Rescue a world torn apart by a vicious war and control the keys to immortality as the first warrior ever to be resurrected from the grips of death. Build the ideal character for the most intense combat, choosing from a countless combinations of skills, abilities, weapons and pieces of armor. The revolutionary Destiny system allows you to continuously evolve your character class to your style of play. Seamlessly integrate magical and melee attacks as you take on scores of enemies in grand fight sequences and finish them off with brutal Fateshift kills. Extend your experience in Amalur with all DLC from the original release, from Teeth of Naros to Legend of Dead Kel and more! Hundreds of hours of RPG play await! Travel from the vibrant city of Rathir, to the vast region of Dalentarth, and the grim dungeons of the Brigand Hall Caverns as you uncover the secrets of Amalur! Explore deep levels of lore in a universe steeped in 10,000 years of fiction created by New York Times bestselling author R.A. Salvatore. Rescue a world torn apart by a vicious war and control the keys to immortality as the first warrior ever to be resurrected from the grips of death. Explore a sprawling game world hailed as having 'more content than any single-player game deserves!' Enjoy countless side quests rich in political intrigue, romance, sinister magic, and even whimsy - all central to the primary mission. Improved graphical fidelity in Re-Reckoning.

_childDocuments_.review: Review for Amalur vets considering buying this for the very hard difficulty level like me.I'm really enjoying this so far! i bought this specially for the very hard difficulty level, having spent many many hours with the original game, and I'm loving it so far. The bear in the first area wiped 3/4 of my life off in 1 power attack, and later outside the first town I legit died to a pack of boggarts! I laughed out loud. So far the enemies seem to attack much more and faster than the original game which I think is great, and in the early game at least you need to consider each encounter even if its a few boggarts or kobolds. Initially the enemies are quite bullet spongy but I enjoy that because you find yourself doing a combo, then skill, then another combo, dodge roll etc making it much more interesting. I blew through like 8 healing potions on the first troll in the prologue, it's quite a fight! I'm really happy so far they've made it genuinely challenging with enemies taking off sizeable portions of health with their attacks and aggressiveness, now we're dark souls vets.In other words so far I'm getting exactly what I wanted gameplay-wise. Coming fresh off many hours on the original Steam Reckoning (and coming to this for the difficulty and dlcs you can no longer get + the new one), I actually really notice and appreciate the improved resolution - I can understand maybe someone coming back and not realising its sharper and being disappointed that its just a sharper and bit prettier version of what it already was, but it's all I wanted - I always thought the artwork was beautiful in the original game so happy with it as is.No bugs so far on a 1070gti (fingers crossed as I was a bit nervous seeing some of the bugs mentioned in the reviews here) but then I'm only a very short way in around Gorhart. Anything game breaking I'd update this.Worth noticing the load times are noticeably up a bit - the original I've just been playing is pretty much instant moving in and out of houses, this pauses for a few seconds. Interesting but not the worst.Hopefully the goodness continues, I'm excited as I love Kingdoms of Amalur, and removing the region level-locking and upping the difficulty is just what I'm after. Also worth noticing I bought this on sale for $40, so being in love with the original game this was more than worth the gamble.So a couple more hours in and around Dalentarth. I was going to say it's not super *hard* more of a nice medium where you have to pay attention and if you get careless you'll be battered a bit, but to be honest I've died quite a bit - sprites are currently kicking my ass and even some regular militia killed me so yea gotta say it is kind of a challenge which is great!. EDIT: Wow I just died like 6 times in a row to one group of sprites having done every quest up to this point. Admittedly I'm wearing light-ish armour as a rouge/mage but how cool is that :) Its definitely challenging, where I'm going to have to change up my approach. It ended up taking about 10 tries to beat that group. 1-2 projectiles from a sprite could kill me outright if i didn't block and their dives do a bit of damage. Wow I've never played Amalur like this - having to time roll to avoid the semi-homing projectiles, isolate enemies. This is good stuff. (Edit for that sprite fight I actually had a disease I'd forgotten about -30% dmg resistance lol..)Older thoughts are I've noticed a few more numbers in mobs, and it's fun needing to pay attention to arrows etc. as they hurt a bit. Having a good time, that gives you a bit of flavour of my experience.Very happy to say its still really difficult in Ettinmere even using blacksmithing to make some good gear for myself. I think they've nailed the difficulty level so far.

_childDocuments_.review: First couple of infos: - I didn't play the release version of 2012 - 1 end-credit playthrough, ~80% content played, reached level 38/40, ~66h - min-maxing player (level: proficient) - started on normal, last region on very hardOverall I enjoyed the game. I was surprised, when the end-credits showed that this game was originally published by EA.I don't know how much replay value this game will have. After this playthrough I feel a bit drained due to the monotone combat which is basically the only really annoying part of the game, details below.I see many comments about the "no-effort" re-release and the bugs. I have the following to say: - if you don't own the game already this is a good buy for the price - Cycle through a couple of your own save-states instead of relying on the auto-save function and you'll be fine (you should do that in every game anyway...). - nice story and underlying plots (only a couple hick-ups along the line, which are to spoilery to mention) - really nice design of the characters, enemys and the environment - while the face detail and movement are a bit 2006, the gestures and dialogue makes up for that well. - many voice actresses and actors make me feel, like I'm never talking to the same voice twice - great variety of weapon types - I really like the armor and weapons crafting/salvaging mechanic - aside from the industy-standard lockpicking mechanic (which are also nice in this game) I really enjoyed the warded chests - quests can actually be screwed up by the player! (sadly found only very few of those). Would have been exceptionally great to have many of those :) - huge variety of possible stat improvements through destinies, twists of fate, lore stones and crafting choices (sadly no proper statistic for a total overview) - walking/running/"stealthing" speed is not skill dependent and gets you around OK throughout the entire game. - the persuasion mechanic is interesting, but definitely underused. - the leveling and skill system feels a bit shallow. Max Level 40, Skill max at 10 - loot system is a bit... "unbalanced" perhaps. Sometimes the basic enemies drop set items, while bosses up to the last one don't really deliver awesome loot... - feels really weird not being able to jump ^^ - 5 tiers of items. my crafted items outperformed every last item set, begging the question why there even are sets... - melee class is as op as usual - disassembling traps yields only worthless items - nice content density in the first regions which sadly gradually declines towards the end - Couple of DLC Tasks are in the faction quest category, which annoys me - DLC Tasks provide endless high level loot. wth??? - encountered couple of bugs (thankfully few game-breaking ones like getting stuck on scenery for me) @ppl criticising the bugs: just don't rely entirely on the autosave function(it's only one slot...) and you'll be fine....... there is no software without bugs... - Combat gets really tedious after a while (I played melee class). the basic 4-slash is enough to get you through 90% of the combat. no variety required or even reducing damage output. Many skills in the tree seem to have fixed damage values which become meaningless quite quickly into the game. - not much variety on common enemies. if you have a somewhat reasonable pattern recognition and get to know enemies in the first region, you know the patterns of the stronger version of them at the end of the game - higher difficulty only increases opponents level and makes them meatier tanks. increasing the tediousness of combat - due to the previos 3 comments (and the fact that I lost dialouge audio at the end due to a bug. restarting the game didn't fix that) I basically rushed through the last region, just to get to the end of the game

_childDocuments_.review: Though my online play is about 15 minutes, I have over 250 hours into the game. I have completed all but the Travellers quests. I am level 40, (the level cap in this edition) and have seen my fair share of landscape and killed more than my fair share of fantastic beasts in Amalur.Having said that, I love this game. It is not perfect, but it is beautiful. The world is very colorful, some of the landscapes are mouth watering and make you wish rivers actually had beds of green grass, and do not erode the ground like in the real world.  The small flaws are many and varied. I have experienced a few glitches in quest logic, but it isn't super annoying. I dislike most of the weapon and armor crafting. Even as a level 10 (maxed) blacksmith, I seldom get the important base piece of a weapon or armor piece I am salvaging to remake better. You can cheat the chances a bit by saving before you salvage and if you get crap, just reload the game prior to the bungled salvage and try again. Though I have found this rarely works. Maybe it has to do with the particular Black-smithing Forge you are using. I don't know. But here is my problem - I hate the look of Prismere armor and weapons, yet that is the top tier, so far.  I play as a Warrior with a Might of 76.  I prefer the aesthetics of some of the more simplistic iron plate pieces. but they do not afford the higher base strength and protection of Prismere armor. So I salvage a low tier piece and use the best components I can to Buff it up to near Prismere level protection. Sometimes this works.The Looted and Gifted armor and weapons do have a ton of variety, but all tend to be...busy and over styled to me. But that's just my taste. Some of them have good features, but I can easily make better pieces at the forge. Not complaining - it is fairly balanced. My current fave Longsword is a salvaged and reforged Primal blade with about 200 points of damage with all of its Buff goodies.NPC interactivity is...different. I kind of wish I could hear my own character's voice...other than grunting in combat and sprinting, The NPC character voice acting is mixed. I appreciate the logic to it -the more Irish the accent, the more FAE the character. Some of the voice acting is Shakespearian - meaning very melodramatic and on the verge of being parody. In fact my ears have been trained to pick out odd audio cues as to what voice actors do -they tend to inform you subtly that they are lying, if their character is a liar. They do the same to inform you the character is truthful if the character is trustworthy.  Well, I keep hearing those "Im a traiterous bastard" cues and tend to not trust characters that end up turning out to be trust-worthy characters. I guess that's life-like though.Other characters, I know are treacherous bastards from the beginning because of the way they avoid directly addressing the truth of what they want you to do for them - or what part in the tale they intend for you to play. Of course, the treachery is reflected on them if you beat the monster, but that's the main theme of the game - defying a predestined role or destiny.And that is the biggest gripe I have about the game - the theme is...just not in my line of thinking, Not in the way it is implemented. It is an interesting and fulfilling game plot to finish, but the almost incessant emphasis on Fate by a ton of characters gets to be somewhat grating. The main quest is long, convoluted, a bit  more secretive than it really needs to be, and brings a very interesting and cool character  - Alyn Shyr (spelling?) into your life. I cannot explain why or how, but I found myself trusting her more than the most of the other Alfar in the game. And my first character was Almain, I think.  I'm playing through again as an Dokalfar just for fun - now that I know what not to do. So I played through the first time essentially as a baby since I knew nothing about the Amalur world,  except I had seen a buddy play some of it and I was enthralled by the color paplate. Caves have multiple colored light sources. The night skies are magical. It looked beautiful! I'm off my point. I think I covered it.Racism. It is a part of the Amalur world. You and others will be directly affected by this in-game. Be ready for that. You will find characters that are very complex and intelligent, and some very simplistic and stupid, some of both that harbor racist ideas, and some who generally view all people based on their actions. The spectrum of opinions expressed by characters in the game are varied and frankly realistic. But get to speak to some of them and they have reasons (some good) for hating a certain race. Sometimes it's based on shallow motivations, sometimes it's based on the loss of family member at the hands of a foreigner. You will find tension between the various races, and between the separate houses of Alfar, and towards the Fae. There is hatred of others displayed through out the world of Amalur. One thing you will notice is in many cases, the prejudice is formed due to observed bad behavior by members of the hated race. Not always. Some is based on pure elitism. Conversly most racial prejudice in the game is abated by acts of valor and good deeds, or simply being the champion you are as you fight monsters, and right wrongs. You must prove yourself a hero to everyone...much like in the old days here on Earth. All of this begs the question - and answers it - "Why do we hate others?" Because we are all different and we focus on those differences and why those differences cause suffering in others. The point of the racism in this game is reflective of racism in our own world. Hopefully it will open the eyes of players and cause them to ask questions and seek true answers. The key take away is that a person may be seen as inferior or bad due to the emotional baggage attached to their "type" or race, and they must act in a way that proves they are good, and worthy of love and respect to change that. A good lesson. Although, it seems to me, some people will never fully accept an outsider, even if they do respect them and their acts of courage.All in all, I love this game. I found many hours of enjoyable diversion in the world of Amalur. It is thought provoking, complex, challenging, sometimes annoying, and yet, for a Swords and Sorcery adventure/combat game, it is fairly relaxing to play. It isn't just practice dying. And because the world of Amalur is so densely packed with beauty, (especially the more western lands - to my eyes) the fact that you are running through it, does not take away from it at all. But then, I like a walk in the outdoors. Few places I've been compare to the magical world of Amalur, sadly. Did I mention the world of Amalur is beautiful?

_childDocuments_.review: There is really only two big problems with this game.1. For a remaster of an 8-year old game, there seems to have been very little bug fixing, with game breaking bugs being reported for many players (though as these things go, your mileage may vary)2. Things that you would normally expect from a remaster of an old game (Other than bug-fixing), ie better texture quality and quality settings and the like, have been half-arsed. The performance isn't great especially considering the specs of my machine, a Ryzen 2600x with 16GB DDR4 RAM, and a GTX 1070, which should run a game like this quite easily, consistently dropping into the 40 frames per second at 1440p with the limited settings maxed out. Because of this, right now I can not in good conscience recommend this game, however both bug-fixing and adding in more graphical settings and some decent optimisation isn't really too difficult to patch into the game later on, so it may change in the future. This should have been in the game at release (or re-release).The gameplay tweaks, though minor, are welcome but I do think that overall that the shoddy state the game was launched at easily cancels it out. If you liked the original Kingdoms of Amalur, and own it, honestly, play that. If you never played Kingdoms of Amalur before, it's a good game, trust my many hours playing it on PS3 for that (fond childhood memories right there) but maybe wait for some news on optimisation before making a purchase, and if not, well I guess get it on a good deal if you can.I want it to be clear, I love the game, and have loved it for years. The re-master just has not done it justice, and I hope it get's fixed soon, so I can change the review to reflect my opinion of the game beneath the re-master.

_childDocuments_.review: Calling this a remaster is laughable. Compared to the original, all it really offers are some quality-of-life changes and a contrast boost that gives the illusion of improved graphics, though they're hardly different from the original IGN did a graphics comparison that I'd encourage you to check out. It does include the Teeth of Naros and The Legend of Dead Kel DLCs, which are nice additions since they were unavailable on Steam when the original was still purchasable. Additionally, there's a new expansion, Fatesworn, sold separately from this "remaster." Instead of charging CDN$40 for this, it would have been more consumer-friendly to offer the quality-of-life changes and graphical enhancements as a free update, while selling the DLCs individually. Unfortunately, greed prevailed in this decision and I'm inclined to downvote it solely for this reason as this practice of minimal effort remasters is not something I support.However, despite these issues, the game itself is quite enjoyable and is by no means a bad game just as it was in 2012 & I had fun revisiting it. While it doesn't distinguish itself from other fantasy RPGs, borrowing elements from franchises like The Legend of Zelda, World of Warcraft, and God of War, it manages to create a unique world while relying heavily on familiar fantasy tropes.The gameplay is where it excels. The combat system encourages experimentation with different weapons and spell combos, reminiscent of the early God of War games but with an arcade-like feel compared to Skyrim or even Dark Souls. The crafting system, while not as deep as say World of Warcraft's, is enjoyable. Whether blacksmithing for custom gear, alchemy for potions, or sagecraft for enchantments, it all contributes to a satisfying gameplay loop. But it does feel a bit dated compared to recent games that have come out, but for the time it was passable and enjoyable.I did encounter some bugs, notably crashes when loading saves, visual glitches, and T-posing enemies. These issues were frustrating but didn't break the game entirely; thankfully, I didn't experience any save file losses, though others have reported such problems.Overall, I'd still rate it a 7/10, the same as I would have back in 2012. I recommend picking it up during a steep discount and skip the new DLC as it really is not that good much less worth the extra money.

_childDocuments_.review: *Note - I got my copy at 60% discount, and for me, that's a great value!**Also - 2 hours isn't enough time to asses whether or not "it's worth it". Try checking-out videos/streams.This game is a great alternative to scratching that Fable Itch. On that, I have to emphasize how long/extensive your quests/tasks are going to be; even the starting area has you begin a quest that takes you half-way across the map. This is one of those "collect ALL quests, and casually complete them as you go" kinda games. It can feel a bit overwhelming, and unfulfilling, if you don't use your map to fast-travel (idk if that's a new feature but it's been quite helpful). Combat feels the same as it originally did, although the dodge-roll feels less responsive, the parry feels friendlier. I haven't touched too many of the various weapons, but there are plenty to choose from, and either can be set to "Primary/Secondary" respectively, allowing for wild combinations to be experienced... save for duplicates... no Longbow/Longbow setups... Also, Magic/spells, feel quite rewarding. They take a hot-second to cast, however hit like a truck, even when resisted. You can always re-purchase ANYTHING you've sold... albeit jacked waaay-up in price... but they'll be there.Graphics are definitely cleaner... still looks like they're using older models, but the textures and lighting all seem to be sharper. There's always going to be inconsistencies, but it's a solid clean-up from an 8+ year-old game.It does feel as though experience and item capacity are a massive struggle... I don't recall ever having to deal with juggling "how much do I NEED this..." as often as I do now. I vaguely recall climbing to higher levels quite fast in the original... idk if that's part of their "difficulty adjustment".I haven't experienced any bugs/errors/glitches.... yet.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this as an excuse to toss some extra money towards THQ Nordic for the work they've put into remastering and continuing the other series that they've acquired since the THQ Nordic merger. As I already owned KoA:R I knew more or less what to expect heading into the remaster, but it seems to have failed at what they set out to do. Combat feels a little more balanced and regions no longer lock to the level you first entered them at, but that seems to be all the remaster has going for it. The big one, the graphic fidelity increase, comes at a massive performance cost. I've a 3700x, 16gb ram, and a 2070S, and cannot maintain a stable 75hz @ 1920x1080, which is unacceptable. That is to say nothing of the little bugs here and there from moves that don't deal damage properly, to texture rendering oddities that occasionally pop up (things like distorted and elongated branches, invisible rocks, ect..) as well as displaced entities (chests spawning too far left or right from their origin, and sometimes even missing the top of the chests model).All that said, I have high hopes that they will be able to patch most if not all of the problems I've encountered and those I've not. But I cannot recommend this remaster at this time.
