_childDocuments_.review: I don't know what it is about this game that I think is wonderful, but it is.  The story is really solid with nice little side quests, and some good characters here and there.  There are morals in this game, but unlike many others it isn't all black and white, nor is it all decisions that will leave you conflicted.  R.A. Salvatore created the world and is a writer for the story and you can feel his influence.  Todd MacFarlane also did art for the game, which means that it is a pretty imaginative place to be.  All these little touches add up to a fun experience that you can get lost in.  The voice acting is actually really well done, and unlike Obsidian or BioWare the chat wheel choices and character interactions aren't ambiguous or occasionally hard to understand.  There won't be a point where you will choose an interaction with an NPC and get a completely unexpected response from them.  It's an odd point to pick on, but a huge pet peeve in other RPG games for me.  You can actually act like a reasonable character in this game, and the NPCs will interact in kind.Gameplay wise this reminds me of Witcher 3 but set in a Witcher 1/2 style world.  There are skills tied to weapon types, combos, abilities tied to a 3 tree system of Might/Sorcery/Finesse.  You can mix these trees to make whatever amalgamation you desire... sort of, as long as it lines up with their Fate card system.  If you forsake matching the requirements of that system you may leave a little attack power or utility on the table.It's not open world in the vein of Skyrim or Witcher 3, but it's still a pretty "open" place to be.  You can fast travel around the map freely to key locations you've discovered.  But running around will often have you encountering side quests or items that will hint at treasures, or random caves to explore.Get the game, it's fun, it isn't the hardest game ever made, but if you are looking to RPG it up with a nice story and sub plots to explore you can't go wrong here.  This is a diamond in the rough.

_childDocuments_.review: I owned and enjoyed the original version on the 360. The world is an interesting celtic inspired fantasy setting and the game has solid systems and combat at play. I re-purchased it because I never finished it the first time and wanted to rectify that. The game is massive and very accessible. You have the ability to completely respec your character at any time, for a price, so no play style is really out of reach. This combined with a shockingly deep combat system and a very simple and flexible class and skill system leads to you very quickly finding out what works and what doesn't for you and you game experience.After that it really just boils down to whether or not you enjoy the world and the story. By far and large you won't be seeing much new here conceptually, but what the game does provide in spades is presentation. This is your typical Fantasy setting, run through a hyper saturated psychedelic filter. The environments are vibrant spectacles of color and excellent art design. The enemies all seem familiar, but they look and feel unique. There are rewards for exploration and interesting characters to meet. Dungeons are sort of bland and flat despite being visually stunning, but I think that is a byproduct of the time and technology of the day and the history of the game itself.At the end of the day this is a meaty, visually satisfying, RPG good for fans of the genre and people who are curious and want an above average, slightly complex, introduction to the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: * played on the highest difficulty setting+ freedom of class choice including mixing and cheap respecs -> combat is alright, but with the option to change your playstyle completely at any time it's actually decent (for some time)+ a lot of other comments complain about technical issues - for me the game was perfectly stable (on Manjaro using Proton)+ exploration is incentivised through e.g. lodestones, which give you experience points as well as permanent buffs after collecting a set+ a lot of characters with extra dialogue options - kinda like a light version of Morrowind dialogue system where you can ask most characters about various subjects (all voiced)+/- content quantity - best approximation of the world size are the main continents of original WoW I think - the zones are even split in similar, artificial way+/- at first it looked like it was a merge of Fable and Risen, but I quickly realized that it actually is more like single player WoW, just as people say +/- worldbuilding has some interesting ideas, but these aren't introduced in any engaging way- haven't seen much of the story, but what I saw was not interesting - single player MMO feel- restricted level design and movement - no jumping or even falling (except in very specific spots, that are even marked on minimap)- no real character stat screen (I have no clue how to check my total crit chance)- so. much. running. everywhere. And that's a problem even though you can fast travel to every location- I once encountered a boss, which simply one-shot my character with every blast. Still possible to beat it by stunlocking, but it was not fun. Cannot make a boss fight hard? -> make it deal ridiculous damage- you can go through an entire dungeon, just to realize at the end you cannot finish it because the boss at the end only spawns when you do a specific quest so have fun running back and through it again later- content quality - mostly fetch quests, but even if you avoid them it's still not good. Also the game world just feels very static and not immersive at all- quest rewards generally match neither difficulty nor the significance of the task itself- scaling monsters - they sometimes change names with maybe slight adjustments, but it feels like you fight the same monsters, but more damage-spongy versions. It feels very bad when you fight the same enemies after gaining many levels and much better equipment, you see much biggen damage numbers on hit, but it takes longer to kill the same enemy and their health bar barely even registers the damage- biggest sin of all is simply that it just gets boring after the first two/three hours and it only gets worse

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE: I'm really on the fence with this one. I'm about 85% through the game and the experience has gone from fun to terrible without changing any experience. And that's the exact problem - the game never changes. What you're doing in the tutorial dungeon will be the same thing you're doing in the end dungeon, with zero alteration aside from maybe some reskinned monsters. This is a 40-50 hour game, more with the DLC, and it only offers about 5-10 hours of original content. The first enemies you fight will be the last enemies you fight, only with more hit points. There are probably 50 or so dungeons, but only 5 different designs. Basically this game is like pancakes. You wake up, haven't eaten, and you get a plate of pancakes, they're prepared really well, and it's a great meal. That's the first 10 hours of this game.Then for lunch, it's pancakes again. Not exactly what you were hoping for but again, prepared well, they do the job. That's the next 10 hours.Dinner, pancakes. And not fresh ones, the same ones from this morning. But now it's twice as many, and you have to eat them all. That's the last half of the game. So I'm keeping this as a 'yes' because the first 10-20 hours are really, really fun. But the 2nd half of the game is all slog. You will find nothing new. Trust me, when you're playing the unlock mini-game for the 1,475th time, you'll just be pressing the 'auto-attempt' and burning through lockpicks, because money is almost irrelevant in this game, and the mini-game is way too frequent and takes way too long. "How Long to Beat" could have a separate category for "without picking locks" and the game time would be cut in half. So BUYER BEWARE, you are not getting a full game of fun, you are getting a good first half and a miserable 2nd half. So miserable, that I actually uninstalled it before even beating it. It's not worth it. It's just not worth the bland, dull, repetitive, and joyless experience. It's like the devs carefully crafted this great world, and when they were done with the first area, they were all happy and ready to move on. Then someone stuck their head in the room and said "hey, we're releasing this tomorrow, so just copy and paste what you have 5 more times to make the game 60 hours instead of 12."A clunky work of passion. Quick disclosure: I played the original on another platform, and got about 75% done. I replayed different builds, and put in over 100 hours, just never made it to the finish line. PROS: The world is well realized, almost to a fault, but not quite there, hence I have it as a PRO. Like a lot of other good fiction, you get thrown into a world with a ton of names and locations that will take a while to grasp. If you're feeling confused for your first 10 hours, don't worry, the names will start to stick. The voice acting is shockingly really well done, if at times a bit over the top. I think this may be what surprised me the most, that the voicing will REALLY hep you remember the characters. You might remember the voice more than the name. The visuals and music are both very stylized to be high fantasy. It reminds me a little of Fable, only not as sloppy. The story is adequate, nothing cringe inducing, but also not super creative. The combat is overall fun. It absolutely has flaws, but a net positive. You end up with a great set of combinations, and it can be really fun to put different things together. The open world has some holdovers from when this was going to be an MMO, and you sometimes it feels pretty empty. But the actual design itself is great for the time. CONS: Buggy, buggy, buggy. It's not so much a high frequency of bugs, but the bugs that are there can stop the game cold. And a few of them are really well known. One early quest can get locked up because the item cannot be retrieved. This is a quest that leads to joining a faction, meaning that, if you can't finish the quest, you're locked out of the faction and all its quests, of which there are a lot. The other side of combat, getting stun locked. I've heard that when you dodge roll, there are no I frames, meaning you can still get hit while dodging. Also, your combo attacks, while cool, are overanimated to the point of you leaving yourself open. Your final swing of the sword may look cool, but it certainly isn't a good way to fight. The length and emptiness of the world made it tough for me to finish. There are 5 major areas in the vanilla game, and each area has sub-areas. By the time you're about halfway through an area, you're tired of it, but still have a while to go. REMASTER PROS and CONS:Since this game is now only available as the remaster "re-reckoning", and my version was the original, I have a few things I've noticed. Not much, because not much has changed. PROS:Camera angles can be adjusted, this is probably the biggest pro because it was a real problem in the original. There are other quality of life improvement for setting the game up. Equipment seems to have been overhauled, that is, loot now seems more abundant, and more geared towards your class. No more being stealth and getting 10 hammers in a row, not yet at least. CONS:The game runs worse. It's not terrible, but you do get frame drops, and nothing in the remaster should be taxing on any system. The texture updates, while noticeable in back to back playing, aren't really noticeable in the game. Unbelievably, they did NOT fix the bugs. That's absurd. You're remastering a game and you don't address the largest game-breaking bugs? Really, THQ should've just bought the IP and re-released the original with all DLC included. No need to remaster it, just give an up to date patch that fixes the known bugs, and adds in some quality of life. VERDICT: If you own the original, I wouldn't bother with this, unless it's on a deep sale (how I got it). If you haven't played it before, and you want a decent action RPG, grab it.

_childDocuments_.review: .After 70h, playing the game in its entirety, and getting all achievements I can say my opinion about this game with no remorse. I would love to suggest this game, especially after , but the only enjoyment I actually had in the game was because , and that’s a new one for me. The FATE Edition is not a bundle and cannot be purchased after the main game. Steam will NOT detract the cost of the base game to make you pay the difference. Currently, on sale, Fatesworn alone costs almost as much as the complete package.The game started as an MMO and was converted to a single-player with some obvious remnants of it.The combat system plays with both melee and magic/abilities at the same time, and the inclusion of the Reckoning mode, which is like a rage mode from other games. The game tries to be a hack-and-slashy type of game, but even a greatsword is often not long enough making the combat frustrating. .The game has an Alchemy system, and this is the first game I played where picking up an herb is a chance of taking it instead of being guaranteed. I plucked the plant, how can I not get it it’s beyond my understanding. The Alchemy skill tree can increase the chances. Thanks…for selling me a solution to a problem you made.There is also a Gem crafting system, but I never used it as the best equipment doesn’t have Gem slots.Lastly, there is a Blacksmithing system that it’s not useful since enemies drop the loot at your level and equipment can’t be upgraded, including epic equipment.The game doesn't have a jump button but you can jump from some specific platforms that often don’t give the prompt to, and it’s a struggle to find where you can jump.In my 100% completion of the game, I did around 300 quests. For a completist, this game is a nightmare as it features uncompletable quests that are forever in your quest log. The biggest problem I have with them is that it’s mostly fetch quests going from A to B. Other than teleporting to a point of interest, you must walk to all your objectives while sprinting is barely faster than running. This makes the game a solo-walking simulator more than people ever thought of Death Stranding. Not a joke, just a fact. It gets quite lonely, especially without a soundtrack, or anything to look at. Sometimes, quests will give you a follower. They fight but I swear I never saw them deal any damage, but at least it's company. I ended up summoning a skeleton fiend to have some company while going around. The main story is nothing exciting, but it’s ok enough. You might read on websites like howlongtobeat that the main story lasts 20 hours, but truly, most will be walking in silence. There aren't many sound effects in the game, so the thing you hear the most is your footsteps. Being originally a 2012 title sometimes instead of in-game cutscenes, there are low-quality pre-rendered videos that have these beautiful background sounds, i.e. of a battle, to then cut to the in-game cutscene where it’s completely mute of ambient sounds and you only hear the characters make noises. The biggest disappointment for me though was the final boss as it was introduced so greatly, but you don’t even get to fight it. What you actually fight is some enemies until you charge the Reckoning ability and that damages the boss. Re-Reckoning presents itself as a remaster, but the real remaster work seems to be the texture upscale, which looks like it was done with Photoshop’s Preserve Details 2.0. It looks like just an upscale, and if the detail was not there to begin with, it just looks blurry. The in-game HUD has a scaling option between too big and too small while the rest doesn’t scale. I’m not a fan of the new HUD because whatever they did, now you can see color-bending in most things, especially the health bar of enemies.This new version comes with its own new and improved bugs and crashes. I had lost 9h of progress because the game would not read my profile and I saved it thanks to some tinkering that included reinstalling the game, creating new profiles, and using save managers. I suggest checking the Nexus for tools like the F2 Console as that saved me from many bugs the Remaster did not fix and from new ones that are just for the remaster, like a quest that requires 6 items for completion but the game only has 5 in it.It starts with this in-game cutscene of your character stranded on a beach, and as it stands up the devs decided to use every sound the character could make in the perfect silence of the in-game cutscene. You’ll see your character do the impossible as you moan, cough, and lament .The DLC itself is a very linear story but has a very small map that at the end of the DLC story gets re-used with side missions that make you backtrack all of it just to make the DLC last longer.There is also a new Faction where you become the Lord of a keep in the DLC, but these missions are repeatable so they never go away. You also get the chance to adopt pets like wolves, rats, bears, etc. Finally, I can stop summoning that skeleton for some livelier company. Except pets can only stay at home and give the player a permanent buff, which makes them collectibles. Being the Lord you’ll be asked to do some more fetch quests from your subjects. Last but not least, a random woman you got as part of an alliance will force you to marry her to complete the quest. Although the quest does not complete, instead, it just stays in your quest log saying “Quest completed”. The game never featured romances except for some jokes during the story, but now I can get married to a random NPC that is a woman regardless of your sex.Once in the DLC map, you can only leave by talking to the ship captain, who is a woman. I never hinted at anything, but in the dialogue where I asked her to bring me back, she hints at the fact that we had intercourse. So 10m after getting married I cheated on my wife. This DLC story is not too bad but the map is really small. In the DLC, for the first time Contract Boards refill, without notice. A quest you get from an NPC asks you to find some treasures in the DLC and bring them, except the items are .The maps are very vertical and hard to navigate, especially the sewers. You can’t climb ladders, just like in Skyrim they only teleport you to the other side, but in this DLC they decided to use them everywhere inside the map. The developers must have decided to showcase the limits of the game engine. It’s confusing for my skeletal friend too as he was always stuck at all the ladders.The DLC adds a new type of damage in this DLC: Beast damage.Good thing you read about it here cause it’ll be the only time you ever think about it.Again, in this DLC often you’ll be asked to go to the same maps for small fetch quests, which I think is just diluting more what it offers.   I started this game with the mindset of WANTING to play it, fooled by the God-of-War-y combat. Sadly, the more I went on with it the more I realized that what seemed beautiful in the demo was just smoke and mirrors. I enjoyed that in all that brain-dead fighting and walking around I could watch something, but I cannot suggest a game because it was fun to do something else in the meantime.I wanted to give it a negative review and a 6 when I was around half the main game, but the rest of it lowered it to a: .Strongly not suggested.

_childDocuments_.review: Personally, I loved the original Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning and was hyped at the idea of it being picked up and given more love. However, upon loading into this "remaster", it's pretty apparent that this was a slapdash job. Very little has been done to the game as far as "graphical updates" are concerned. True the colors are better balanced and the lighting is smoother with better contrast, but that matters very little if the game chugs like an ancient steam boat through molasses. The default settings were so poorly suited for my PC (a mid-tier gaming laptop) that the opening cutscene couldn't even play. Once in the game, everything moved in slow motion. When I went to check the graphics settings, there are all of 5 options and all but one are presented in highly technical terms that anyone who isn't really into graphics will have to google. I certainly did, and I still don't properly understand the need for a sliding bar for "anisotropy". After fiddling with it for an hour I finally found settings that let me play the game in a way that didn't hurt my eyes. From there the game is now full of new bugs - NPCs heads spin backwards like they're possessed, audio sync with NPC dialogue is way off, and to make matters worse, it seems that if you are set to borderless fullscreen there is a chance the game hard crashes when you try to quit. I'm not a tech wiz or expert, but I'm no slouch either when it comes to understanding and finding fixes to this sort of thing, but with the crash literally all I could do was reboot my computer. You shouldn't have to be incredibly in to graphics tech to play a game from 2011, no matter how much of a glow up it's gotten. I'm so disappointed because I was so hoping this would get more people into the game and it might finally get a sequel, but it's clear those hopes are dashed. If you want to play the game, go get the original - the graphics may be a bit dated, but the gameplay is just so fun and has some unique gameplay mechanics that make it a gem in the RPG world. I just wished they'd treated it that way.TLDR: Ellen is still right.

_childDocuments_.review: So far, so good, I definitely recommend it. There has been a considerable attempt at improving the textures and models. We can clearly see it while gaming. The performance dips here and there, but nothing too bad, and I still keep my frames well over the 60 mark(80 most of the time). _childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game. I have tried four times over the last ten years to get into it, and this is certainly the furthest I have gotten so far. The combat is enjoyable and the world is visually interesting. But... I'm just bored. Everything is a fetch quest. You get bogged down with repetitive side quests almost instantly. The story seems like it might become interesting at some point, but its becoming increasingly difficult to press on because I'm losing interest so quickly. I can absolutely appreciate why so many others like it as much as they do, and I imagine that had I played it to completion back when it launched I might feel differently, but it just doesn't seem to have aged very well at all. Compared to the more modern RPGs that I have played recently, such as Witcher 3 and GreedFall, I feel like Amalur lags horribly behind. I boot the game up because I'm determined to learn to love it, not because I actually want to play it, I force myself to play an hour or two, then end up shutting it off because I'd rather be doing literally anything else.

_childDocuments_.review: This is beautiful. Having played the original, I think it's important that prospective buyers of this version understand that this is a Remaster, not a Remake as there seems to be some confusion in other reviews I've read.As an owner of the original, I did get a good discount at the time of purchase on this version. If you are entirely new to the game, then the current full price tag will be worth it however if you own the console version of the original (an are not eligible for the discount), you might find full price a little steep on the PC when not on sale. This version doesn't change core mechanics, gameplay or story line. It does add some QOL and combat scaling changes. It is *just* a remaster but a stunning one at that.This game will appeal to people who enjoy the older TES games and more traditional western style single player RPGs. It has interesting skill and perk lines, fluid combat and good gear variety.  I would still like to be able to rebind the mouse buttons but that is a personal preference and does not detract from the overall experience.Personally I haven't encountered the frame rate issues some others have experienced (I'm on an AMD Ryzen 9 3900X/RTX2080 Super), however I did have the game lock up when playing in Exclusive Mode.  Fullscreen Borderless runs perfectly fine with everything set to max

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start with conclusions.Do you have the original? Get this on sale. It does look nicer, there's a few extra items(from the DLC chest and throughout the game), some extra quests, but if you already have the old version, you aren't missing $20-30 worth of content. $10-15 or lower, if you really liked it, I'd say grab it and fall in love again.Don't have the original? Why in the ♥♥♥♥ not? Get this. Right now. Stop reading and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ get this game. And don't expect to play anything else for a long time. This is easily one of the best underrated RPG's ever. Hell, one of the best, period. I'd even consider ranking it over the Elder Scrolls games, but I've settled on roughly equal ranking. I mean, technically, they aren't the same style of RPG.Ridiculous lore, huge world, tons to do(including quests that you can't get until you beat the game), factions, awesome gear, pretty great class customization, interesting gameplay features, immersive... I cannot imagine anyone who likes RPGs and/or Fantasy not loving this.Casual gamer? That's fine, easy is plenty easy.Like combat that can keep you on your feet and require you to actually be somewhat proficient? It's not Dark Souls, at all, but it there is certainly a difference between hammering through and spamming an attack and actually dodging, blocking, timing, etc.Seriously, get it any way it goes, if only to show your love for an old game brought back. Plus you do get achievements and cards off this release. If you're into that.If you want more info, I have no doubt the other reviews on this release and the original can make it clear how amazing the game is(if you ignore the ones complaining about how this doesn't change much from the original, but these are the same people that would complain about an ESIII re-release if all they did was clean up the graphics and add a couple quests and items).Dagger players, just know, the spiral attack is a bit, weird, at least it was when I first started this release. It seems fine a few levels into daggers later, but I don't know if it's a leveling thing, a bug I heard about, or what.

_childDocuments_.review: I really had my hopes up and decided to re-immerse myself into this game.The game is 1:1 what was its first release + the DLC, the textures are SLIGHTLY more HD, but in general it looks incrediblyt dated.I'm not a big fan of being scammed out of my money by having a game being advertised as "remastered with stunning graphics" and "refined gameplay" as they didn't change anything noticeable.Things that I would have expected to see improved :-Character textures (still look muddy as hell)-Improved shaders (metal looking a bit more like metal for instance, I understand it's stylized but come on)-Improve/Add new armors or weapons-Improve/expand the talent tree-Improve the environments (better environment effect, better post processing)-Improve on the 2010s Bloom onslaught.-Improve on the UI with proper scaling and better controls-Improve on gameplay (instant stagger on ANY damage is not the best definition of "fluid" combat, there is a skill that makes you immune to stagger and it's obligatory)-Improve on inventory space - THAT was a ridicolous gameplay element, a game that wants to be strong and powerful on crafting and collecting ♥♥♥♥ dooms you with a RIDICOLOUS inventory space and very little chances to increase it, it wasn't fun 10 years ago, is not fun now-you spend 90% of the time doing backtracks and walking in the same bloody areas, would have been nice to increase the amount of fast travel points or improve travel somehow (better dash perhaps)They just re-released the same exact game.Also for some reason I remembered this game to be more interesting, it turns out it's 99% fetch quests, the plot aged also quite badly as it's terribly mediocre.Shame though, I came to get an experience that was promised as overhauled and I feel ripped off with a re-release of an already mediocre game

_childDocuments_.review: I have decided to rewrite my review, this is because people cant seem to comprehend that I don't think this is game is the greatest thing ever made.To start with, in general I like this game on the surface. The combat is engaging and the "Fate Card" system is really cool.Starting with combat it definitely feels good at first, the combos are easy to perform and it doesn't take long to get into the swing of things. But my first issue with the combat is that it is sometimes forced. This was an issue for me who wanted to play a stealth character. I quickly realised how hard that was going to be when I got forced into a boss battle with not stealth approach available. Stealth in itself is fine, if a bit clunky. After my failed attempt to play an assassin I chose to path of a warrior. This was definitely more enjoyable for me, however as the game progressed I found that the combat didn't really evolve at all, leading to stale combat encounters.I really loved the "Fate" system, that being cards which you select that give you buffs towards a certain play style, I.E Mage, warrior, ranger... I especially thought the inclusion of the universalist class was super cool. However what I will again say, is that by the time I completed the game I was still two cards away from the highest level pure warrior card. Leading me to wonder what content I was missing.Levels themselves are extremely off, when I at the end of the game my best weapon was still level 13. And interestingly despite being on the hard difficulty I was still having a really easy time. This was likely due to the "Reckoning" mode. Which you can think of as your "Spartan Rage" or "Force Unleash" skill. This mode was so game breaking that the final boss became a joke because of it. All it takes is a couple "Fate" potions which instantly refill your meter.During my run I put points into persuasion which was a mistake since this skill was completely useless and served only give me more dialogue options. Alchemy on the other was an insanely busted skill which gave you infinite healing potions, and more importantly the overpowered fate potions which trivialise the game.Finally the part of this game that really let me down was the narrative. Super weak, the plot never gave me a reason to care about any of the characters apart from maybe two characters you meet right at the start and even then that may just be anchor bias.I got some smooth brain comment about how this is a hero game and that I shouldn't need a reason to want to save people because its the fantasy. To that I respond that I really felt like a hero when I betrayed my comrades in a side quest and slaughtered all of them to make a pact with a demon. Which was probably my favourite mission of the game, because it gave me a way to vent my frustrations involving the characters cardboard personalities.I'm going to finish this review with one final point, this game is supposed to me a remaster, but it looks like hot garbage for a game that came out in the last 5 years. Comparing this to the original it's clearly better, but still so far behind what we have in the modern day.Despite everything I'd still recommend this game, but they have the audacity to put a £35 price tag on this. If it was £10 or £15 sure thing, good bang for your buck. But that is so much money for this "remaster".

_childDocuments_.review: You can respec pretty much at will once you get a little bit into the game, so don't worry about screwing up your build.Blacksmithing plus sagecrafting is OP , but will put you in generic looking super-armor.The faction side quests are generally better than the other side quests.The end of tree magic spells are pretty ridiculous (meteor & tempest), especially if you have plus to elemental damage gear.Certain trainers can only train your skills at certain levels (I think you either need to have a skill of 0-3 for basic trainers, and 4-7 for advanced), and only once. If you find a trainer you can't use, keep a note of it and the next time you respec, make visiting them a priority before you redistribute your skillsThere are books that raise a skill by one. There are some classes that start with +2 in a skill. Because of this, it is possible that you can start with +2, read a book, use a basic trainer, and then not be able to use the second basic trainer (every skill gets two basic trainers and one advanced). So if you find a book that gives you +1 in the skill that you start with 2 points in, don't read it until you use both trainers.Almost all builds are viable, really. Make sure you level up the mastery skill for a weapon you have an interest in, and the corresponding ability tree for that weapon to get some powerful attacks, and then everything else is up to you. I started with a finesse-only build, for example, but then rebound my fate (or whatever the game calls it), and went with a might/finesse combo instead (bows are awesome)Good game with huge replay value!

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about Kingdoms of Amalur: Rereckoning (I have not played the Fatesworn DLC). I had played a bit of the original version of this game years ago by the seven seas and I remember liking the fusion of classic God of War style along with customizable character options.  Recently, I purchased and played the Rereckoning version and while I still enjoyed that aspect, a lot of the stuff in the game was a bit disappointing. Still, I recommend it on a discount.It has an okay story; it tries to make the choice of our fate a grand event but ends up becoming by-the- numbers “epic” story. The quests in the story only facilitates gameplay and don’t seem to have any meaningful narrative of its own. Ironically, there is too much shoving of lore in the player’s face; at times framed in a boring way. The dialogue trees with NPCs are filled with unnecessary information occasionally. Most of the voice actors feel like they are just reading lines rather than portraying characters. Although the story framing and world building is technically competent, you can describe most of the characters in the same way you'd describe a character from Skyrim: utterly dry. You won’t feel invested in the narrative experience. Even the side quests are just glorified XP farms and follow the same structure. Side quests are all the same: talk to mission giver, kill some things and/or retrieve some things, report to the mission giver. There is no memorable side quest, and the “House of Sorrows” side quest is the most painful chain of side quests I have ever played (both from story and gameplay point of view); it was only worth doing for the perk you are rewarded at the end of it which is helpful in the main campaign.There are a lot of elements that clearly mark it as a game from the late 2000’s and early 2010’s. Like being able to do every faction related activity with no real consequence,or no jumping except to traverse certain spots in the maps. Most of them are old fashioned and are products of old gaming coding practises and tech so it’s ok to accept them as things that old games tend to have, but some are mildly infuriating for gaming in the 2020’s.From the UI text to the sheen of the graphics, this game has a ‘World of Warcraft’ feel (despite being a third person game), fuelled by Western/European mythology. Classic races and monsters have different names: elves are Fae, draugurs are Faer Gorta, banshees are leanshae. Barghests, which I came across in Witcher 3, show up here too. I hope more diverse cultural tropes inspired by other parts of the globe and their respective characterizations show up in potential sequels, if there are going to be any.Character customization is limited compared to say, Skyrim. You only get a higher definition WOW style character to create and so there is not much to set, even in this remastered version. Still, I got a reasonable facsimile that I was satisfied with.The gameplay is clearly the star of the game. To enjoy the game, you should strive towards feeling like a badass who can become anything on the fly: a warrior, a rogue or a mage or any type of combination between them. You can switch weapons whenever required (depending on your inventory space) between hammers, swords, greatswords, daggers, faeblades (a pair of scythes), chakrams (discs you can hurl and get back), staffs and sceptres. Now I favoured a Kratos inspired build: a hammer-and-dagger build, quite a bit of magic to support myself, and a little bit of rogue tactics to get me out of spots. Landing hammer blows, blocking, dodging and parrying at the right time feels satisfying though. I do plan on replaying it someday as a different character to get a different experience. Combat is fast paced and leveling up doesn’t mean you are invincible; I had to struggle as I only favoured certain areas of gameplay for my Kratos inspired build. If you insist on doing everything the game has to offer, you might have an overpowered experience. The way of receiving abilities is little strange but all right: every time you level up, you receive 3 points for one set of abilities and a further three points to invest in Might, Rogue and Sorcery. It is pretty generous compared to most games, but the fast-paced nature of this game is such that it ironically doesn’t feel enough.So ultimately how does it fare as a fusion of classic God of War and Skyrim? : Worse than classic God of War and just as bad/good as Skyrim: Just as good as the PSP classic God of War games with limited combos but still satisfying hits from your player character. : Skyrim has a better tree but you get more rewarded for levelling up in KOA. I only wish they had done more with it.For all its shortcomings though, this game deserves a high-end sequel as I believe there is a lot of potential for this type of game particularly on modern systems. And the gameplay deserves a better narrative experience.TL;DR: Dated but fun game, only get it at a discount solely to enjoy this marriage of classic God of War gameplay with Skyrim gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: I just want to preface this with the following: Me not recommending the game is mostly due to the current state of the game. There are a lot of bugs and performance issues currently, so I'm placing the rest of my playtime on hold until at least some of them are addressed. Some are minor, others are obnoxious, such as saves becoming unloadable, or the constant microstuttering I began to notice about 4 hours in that was taking effect no matter what graphical settings were in use. At times I was pushing 150+ FPS, while still getting microstutters every few seconds.Once some of these issues are addressed, I'll revise my review, as I do enjoy it overall, and played the original quite a bit.: At the time of this revision, I'm about 20 or so hours into the remake. The devs have been pretty forthcoming regarding issues, and have already released a hotfix and full patch to address quite a few of them, including some fixes to issues that plagued the original. I've definitely noticed improvements in performance personally, and as such, I feel like I can now recommend it without the sour feeling in my mouth.Overall, Kingdoms of Amalur is an action-rpg that centers around your standard quest-gathering, adventuring loop. What makes it shine is simply that its actually fun to play. There are 3 major character archetypes, and you're able to mix and match between them as you see fit; One of the character customization features is known as the "Destiny" system. Based on how many points are spent in each archetype, you unlock new Destinies, giving you different passive stats, and sometimes new abilities, such as changing your dodge into a teleport for the magic related destinies. You're also allowed to respec your points spent at various locations in the game, encouraging exploration. I do at times wish that the blink dodge replacement on some of the destinies was optional, as the dodge roll IMO is simply better, but its no big deal personally.Combat is simple, with two weapon slots, and one attack button per slot. There are a few special attacks unique to each weapon type, as well as multiple skills that are unlocked in each archetype. While not anything super in-depth, its enjoyable stringing skills together and taking down enemies. It has just enough "flash" to it to remain enjoyable, but is simple enough that just about anyone can pick it up and play it. I do feel as if classes could use a few more active skills, specifically Might and Finesse builds. Mages have access to quite a few as some of their spells change completely based on if they're charged or not after some investment.Amalur is filled with lore, and many NPCs who won't shy to give you background on different subjects. Dialogue itself can be a bit on the drier side for some of the minor characters, but still typically remained interesting enough for me to want to listen to many of the topics presented during a conversation. I also appreciated that not all characters were readily willing to part with information about every topic. Quests range from the gamut of monster slaying, to finding missing persons or items. Nothing super special here, but I found when playing the remaster that I still remembered a nice chunk of the quests I ran into on my first play-through of the original, so I'd say they were enjoyable enough to be memorable in some way.One of the bigger issues is that the world itself can feel a bit empty at times. Some areas are just very large without much of interest within them outside of monsters. I personally didn't have much of an issue with it as, the combat was my biggest draw to the game.The remaster supposedly addresses some of the loot issues of the original, but, I've only got just shy of 7 hours on the remaster, so I can't say what changes truly took place.All in all, Amalur is an enjoyable game, but currently the remaster has some things to iron out before I'd suggest picking it up. If you're really itching to play it, I'd recommend picking up the original, as it still holds up quite well, just missing out on some minor tweaks and graphical updates,

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I am beyond torn to not recommend this game. Kingdoms of Amalur is theoretically a perfect game for me, yet I just couldn't keep playing it. I told myself after about 15-20 hours I would try to get through the game because I have heard so many good things from close friends and I haven't played a decent single player RPG in awhile (been stuck on multiplayer games lately), but I just can't trudge through the boredom any longer.The story and the quests you encounter can be entertaining especially if you like lore and like to read quest text. You can get invested in some of the questlines and it is satisfying to see and end to a questline that you were interested to see what the outcomes could become. Collecting Lorestones is enjoyable too because it gives you a voiceover and tells you a bit about the land or something that happened in the area.The combat was something that I was looking for too immensely. Unfortunately, I was so disappointed with how it turned out. I felt like I became too strong at a point that I just started running past enemies unless I had to kill something for a quest because I could not be bothered by spamming X and Y over and over. I played a melee build, so my combat might have been more boring than others, but it isn't enjoyable when you know exactly how a fight is going to go because you have fought the same enemies countless times before. The player can respec and change their playstyle, but I honestly feel that it would not have changed much, at least to me. Another thing to note during combat, is that the enemies can almost stun lock you into falling animations and when the character gets back up, depending on the enemies around, you can get knocked right back down. I experienced this many times with too many sprites around me or bigger enemies like Jotunn. It is not amusing get knocked over and over while you are spamming button trying to dodge or interrupt their attack. Maybe I just suck, who knows?The environments weren't anything too special. Same dungeon looks throughout the different areas. It just seemed like everything was copy pasted with maybe a couple rooms or traps added. The music was quite enjoyable, but got tiring after awhile. The sound effects of weapons and spells also got tiresome, so I ended up muting both. I did, however, leave the voice sounds on because I am very fond of different accents on characters and actually hearing that the characters are voiced over. It brought gratification hearing each character's voices, even though some were just recycled and reused.I encountered quite a lot of bugs during my playthrough, ranging from the map going completely black, to quest markers going back and forth on the map, to my character getting stuck in a random spot while I was traversing the lands, ending up in having to reload my last save. I also didn't notice a lot of graphical updates with this Re-Reckoning, so I question what this release was even supposed to be for.Overall, I would love to recommend Kingdoms of Amalur, as I am a huge RPG savant, but the boredom and the same thing over and over after about 15-20 hours literally killed the game for me. It was amazing starting off, but continuing on was brutal for my mental after trying to get through it.

The combat is smooth and similar to what could be experienced in a  game, except with a greater variety of combat options available to the player character. You can utilise traps, poisons, and spells. You can wield bows, swords, greatswords, faeblades, chakrams, staves, hammers, and sceptres. The skill, perk, and combat systems combine to provide an experience that accommodates many play styles. The settings (The Faelands, Gallows End, and Teeth of Naros) and stories are good. They won't disappoint. The main characters, factions, and their quests are adequate. The graphics of this remaster are fine. The soundtrack is epic. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: 9/10 INSTANTLY BUY ITThe best way to describe KOA is like this> Fable 1+2 and World of Warcraft had a child and it came out how you wished Fable 3 would have. (I still shudder at the thought of Fable 3, I'm not going to lie.)KOA has tons going for it:Better art style: (So much detail in structures, monsters and environments wrapped in a charming and vibrant rainbow of colors that makes you feel like you are truly in a fantasy realm. Simplified but complex at the same time, the graphics in 4k @ 60FPS with maxed settings (including settings within the Nvidia Control Panel) is still amazing on this older game. There have been several times where I had to stop and marvel at a scene, to take in it's scope and grandeur. Trust me you will not want for anything graphically. A better Story: Than Fable 1/2 and most other stories in most AAA RPG titles you have played lately. Better Crafting: OMG..way more in depth crafting, everything from the quality of metals, leathers and fabrics, to socketed Gems crafting, to breaking down weapons you find to steal their enchanted components to them combine them again to make your own Master level weapons and Armor. You can then break your own masterpieces down again and use those components again when you find better base components, better gems, and better, quality metals, ITS AN ENDLESS CYCLE OF ADDICTION HUNTING FOR BETTER EVERYTHING!! Be warned that the lust for Power in this game is real, and you can create some truly Godlike builds with the right crafting skills and components. Better Paced combat:  Plenty of time to explore, plenty of fights, plenty of boss fights, TONS of side quests, you never feel like you are rushed into completing the story, or rushed out of a side quest. Take your time, wander, stop in the middle of a quest get lost, your quest log and mini map is always there to bring you back on track after you see something shiny in the distance and lose track of the next 3 hours killing things for loot drops!!LOOT DROPS: Wow, I have never played a game where I felt I was constantly finding something better or an upgrade to what I had more than with KOA. You can find unique/set/Legendary Items everywhere. There is no specified boss that drops X sword, or monster that drops Z, shield etc. Dive in lake you might find a Set piece at the bottom. Open a chest in an Inn there might be an Epic item sitting there fresh for the taking worth thousands! There are no set rules except that you better upgrade your carrying capacity my friend, because before you know it, you are hauling back a fortune in Weapons, Armor, Components, and gems/potions. Combat: Seems simple at first then you realize you have been doing it wrong and it took you 10 levels to figure that out..Simple Complexity is the best way to describe it. Sure if you want a Fable style button mash go for it. But if you want to earn more experience and fate points, you better use all your Skills. Switch it up, shoot an Arrow into one Mob, launch a Fireball into another, and duck and dodge under a strike just in time to pull out your Shield block an attack and then Swing your Long sword, by varying up your attacks and using all your options you will get 3-4x the experience you would than by just spamming the same attack button. Honestly folks I could go on and on about this game. It is fantastic, but I will side step into a little story to end this. I have a hard copy of this game on the original Xbox 360, I own the original Steam release, and I bought this newest version as well. Whats funny is that of all the times I have tried playing this game throughout the two previous purchases, something life related got in the way and took up too much of my time and I could never get back to KOA for some reason. I started playing, would get about 20 hours in and then my attention was pulled elsewhere.. Real life you know. But this time is different.. I have 55 hours into it, and I swear I'm not even 25% complete. I am only just now level 16 today... there is a a lot more to do. I have put that 55 hours into this game in just the last 2 weeks.. So if you think about that for a moment, that's a game I really couldn't put down. Buy it and invest more than 5-7 hours and you will most likely be hooked. There are tons of Wiki Pages about the game and forums of people discussing it too. It has a large fan base. If you don't already own the original I'd say the the 39.99 Price tag is more than fair for the amount of RPG entertainment on offer here.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a lot of bad games in my time. While it's not the worst thing I've ever seen, Kingdoms of Amalur takes the cake for being the most dull and uninspired. It's bad, but not the fun kind of bad like Risen and Risen 2, both of which came out around the same time this did. Oh no, it's the other kind of bad.Let me explain where this game came from, so you can understand why it was doomed from the get-go. Kingdoms of Amalur was made by a studio called 38 Games, which was owned by Curt Schilling. If you don't know who he is, he's a washed-up former baseball player who went personally bankrupt because of this game. 38 Games was funded by the Rhode Island Economic Development Corporation, who paid Curt Schilling a crapload of money to move from Massachusetts to Rhode Island to develop this game. He in turn paid R.A. Salvatore to write this game. Salvatore is best known for a series of D&D-based "dark fantasy" novels featuring a dark elf protagonist named Drizzt who is a mary-sue at best. Seriously, his novels read like they were written by an 8 year old who got introduced to Warhammer and immediately decided it was the best thing ever. He's a laughingstock in the tabletop gaming community, apart from the kids who actually think Drizzt is a cool or well-written protagonist.Anyway, the whole idea was that Kingdoms of Amalur was going to be this predecessor to a giant MMO that 38 Studios was going to launch afterward, which I'm sure would have been amazing given how hard this game rips off World of Warcraft. Then this game bombed. Part of the reason was that there were shady backroom financial dealings going on - pretty much everyone involved with 38 Studios was sued by the State of Rhode Island, who is still paying for the mess this game created. There was even a criminal investigation at one point.So, how bad is it? Very bad. It's a direct ripoff of Fable, only without the things that made Fable a good game: you're basically Fantasy Jesus risen from the dead to murder your way through a horde of samey-looking "fey" (read: elves) who apparently are immortal. This immortality apparently extends to every other enemy in the game, since everything's a gigantic damage sponge. Just like Fable, you have three skill trees: Hitting Things With Swords, Cinematic Melee Executions, and Magic. The first one is the only viable one. Magic takes forever to recharge, has a cooldown, and in general doesn't work all that well - at least, not from what I played.Cinematic Melee Executions is another useless skill tree: it only work if the enemy can't detect you (meaning it's useless against groups) and doesn't work on bosses. Without the ability to perform a cinematic melee kill, weapons in that tree do less damage than Hitting Things With Swords and are thus useless. It's probably not a horrible idea to carry around CME-compatible weapons because they will save you a bit of time against single enemies (at least, some) but other than that they're not something you should ever bother with.Finally, you've got Hitting Things With Swords, which not only can flinch and/or stun enemies but also doesn't have any cooldowns and just kinda works. Remember kids, wizards never prosper.. unless this is 3rd Edition D&D and/or Pathfinder.What really gets me though is that everything in this game is either a ripoff or just poorly designed. The overall graphic design and art direction is heavily "inspired" by World of Warcraft. The skill trees are pretty much copy-pasted from a combination of Fable and Too Human (great choice of inspiration there, that last one) and the gear system is basically Too Human's as well: you constantly pick up new equipment and have to pause the game and go two menus deep to equip it. The equipment menu doesn't sort by effectiveness or anything so you just kind of have to tab through everything until you figure out if those boots are better than the ones you already have.There's also a durability system to ensure that you're constantly switching gear, because what game isn't improved by a durability system?Other than that though, the game feels like the developers made a checklist of everything AAA games had in 2008 (keep in mind this game came out in 2012) and decided that it was their sworn duty to check off each and every one of those boxes until they had them all checked off. Giant rats and spiders? You bet, both of them are in the first 10 minutes of the game. Wolves and bears? Check! Fetch quests? Oh, absolutely! What's a WoW clone without fetch quests? The funny part though is how it takes place in a world where all these non-human fantasy races (dwarves, gnomes, etc) exist.. but your only choices for a character are human, slightly different human, dark elf (because R.A. Salvatore) and slightly different dark elf.There's also a myriad of hilarious graphical glitches. At one point in the tutorial, my camera just kind of locked onto a random point while I was in the middle of a fight and I couldn't see what I was doing. I also had an NPC just kinda stretch his neck out like a giraffe in the middle of a cutscene. Speaking of the camera, it's another reason why magic and ranged combat doesn't work: there's no manual aiming, only a lock-on thing that only works when it chooses to.Let's be real here, this game was made because Rhode Island messed up. Thanks, Rhode Island. Hopefully they'll learn their lesson and never fund another game ever again.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played and adored the original Kingdoms of Amalur release, diving into the Re-Reckoning edition was like revisiting an old friend, albeit with a fresh coat of paint. For those unfamiliar, Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is a sprawling fantasy RPG packed with rich lore penned by bestselling author R.A. Salvatore, vibrant worlds designed by Todd McFarlane, and gameplay systems crafted by Elder Scrolls veteran Ken Rolston. Despite its star-studded creation team, the game remains a hidden gem in the RPG genre.Returning to the Faelands in the remastered Re-Reckoning edition, I was immediately struck by the graphical updates. They’re subtle but appreciated, enhancing the visual experience without altering the game's original charm. The world of Amalur is as colourful and expansive as I remember, filled with diverse landscapes and intricate designs that beckon exploration.Gameplay-wise, Re-Reckoning stays true to its roots. The combat system is where this game really shines, offering a fluid, dynamic experience that stands out from its peers. The ability to mix and match skills across different class trees—Might, Finesse, and Sorcery—allows for deeply customisable playstyles, a feature I relished both in the original game and this remaster. This level of flexibility in character development ensures that combat never feels stale, even dozens of hours in.The story and quests hold up well, brimming with intrigue and adventure. The narrative depth is commendable, featuring a rich tapestry of factions, conflicts, and characters that make the world feel alive and teeming with stories to uncover. Voice acting and dialogues maintain their quality, with the remaster enhancing some audio elements to better complement the visuals.However, it's not without its faults. The game can feel somewhat dated in its user interface and certain gameplay mechanics, a reminder of its origins in the early 2010s. Also, while the open-world is massive and filled with content, some areas and quests can feel a bit repetitive, a common issue in many RPGs of its time.Despite these minor gripes, Kingdoms of Amalur: Re-Reckoning is a testament to what makes RPGs enchanting: a compelling world to get lost in, thrilling combat, and the freedom to craft a character uniquely your own. For those who missed it the first time, and even for those who’ve already ventured through Amalur, this remaster offers a rich, engaging experience.It’s a shame that Kingdoms of Amalur doesn’t always get the recognition it deserves. As a casual gamer who has a special place in their heart for the original, I find Re-Reckoning a delightful reminder of why I fell in love with the game years ago. It manages to capture the original magic and even sprinkle a little extra on top. For anyone looking for an underrated RPG to sink dozens of hours into, look no further than Kingdoms of Amalur: Re-Reckoning.

_childDocuments_.review: Kingdoms of Amalur is a lovely little RPG but it does have a few problems. In its defence, Kingdoms of Amalur is clearly a passion project, with a great deal of effort put into it. This is an entirely new world, created with its own lore and histories, even if it does somewhat borrow from some fantasy tropes. To surmise it briefly, you are a character who was reborn after dying in a world where the only other people who can do this are the mysterious Fae, elf like creatures that revive sometime after death. However, while mostly peaceful, one large group of the Fae have gone rogue and have begun invading the peaceful Kingdoms of Amalur. It is up to you to discover the secrets of your rebirth, which have granted you the abilities to change fate (literally) and ideally, stop the bad guys.In terms of combat and character construction, the game has a lot to offer. There are three primary stats to contend with, finesse which is your standard rogue stat, might for warriors and a magic one whose name I always forget. While you can focus solely on one of these you can also quite easily mix and match. This allows you to create sub classes and gain unique bonuses, allowing you to become a hybrid ranger-mage-tank if you really wanted to! There are skills and spells to compliment your choices as well as items and different weapon types to allow for variation making combat interesting. And thanks to respecing just requiring a visit to an NPC, you can change things up when you get bored of one style. The story telling is fairly simple. The story itself is quite engaging and there are hours worth of side quests, secondary quests, little tasks and exploration to get involved in meaning you can spend hours exploring the largely entirely open world without touching the story after the intro. There are countless little quests you'll find in villages that are off the beaten track as well as dungeons you can explore and ruins to pilfer. There's also a fairly large roster of enemies, even if sometimes they are reused as mini bosses. Visually, the game is fairly pretty. Despite it apparently being a remaster it isn't that much prettier than its original release. It has a very warm, pleasant feel to it, quite like Fable in terms of its appearance. There's nothing that I have seen in game that looks ugly or poorly animated or presented, but equally there's nothing hugely impressive either. If you are like me, you'll enjoy the cozy feeling the game world has, its simple style of graphics presents a rather welcoming environment for you to explore and enjoy, you'll just never have a moment of awe with the way something looks. All in all it is a pretty good game. The only issues I had with the game is that it falls just short of being very good at everything it does. The story is good, but while it does offer you some choices, most of these are largely samey without any great difference, making it feel as if it was just a step away from being a really good story. The combat is good, but it feels sometimes like there is just a little element missing from it that I can't quite place my finger on. It looks good, but as I said above, it is just shy of being visually stunning. If you already own Kingdoms of Amalur through steam, you get a fairly reasonable 60% discount on the game. But just be aware, if you are buying it as a new game, £34.99 is quite a steep price for what is essentially just a re-release with slightly better graphics. All in all I'd say get it on sale or if you have cash to splash. As a fun little bit of information about the game, don't expect a sequel. While the game was reviewed and sold reasonably well on release, the game's budget was so high, that in order to break even, they would have needed to sell a million copies within a few weeks of launch. While the game did well, it didn't do that well and put the company out of business apparently. There's actually a really interesting youtube video about it called "Death of a game" I think.

_childDocuments_.review: I was very excited to see this re print of the original Kingdoms of Amalur, so do take my mildly biased view here into account. Initially it also came with all of the bugs and some of the stability issues of the original as well, just with some tweaks for higher end graphics cards.  Personally I hardly noticed much of a difference, but I appreciated that they did not break anything further.  Along with those minor updates Re-Reckoning has come with a series of hot fixes where the devs have been attempting to update and address some of the bugs and issues that came with the original game.  More power to them frankly, and it's nice to see them working on bug fixing.And announced with the release of Re-Reckoning was a new DLC that will at some point be added in. Release date for that not announced at the time of writing. So that will be something positive to look forward to.As to the game itself; the lore, story, and characters are still just as entertaining to me this time around as they were the first time, and I am still enjoying the different play styles that different armor and weapon sets give to you.  Not to mention the various destiny paths that choosing different skills open up.  Lots of possibilities and boosts for alternate styles of play.I have some minor gripes about not being able to tell how much of things like damage resistance or critical boosts your character has overall on the stat pages, but I am capable of doing the math and adding things together myself when I need to figure out what gear will do for me, it's just slightly time consuming.  On the whole I give this game around a 8/10 and would recommend it for anyone looking for an action oriented RPG where the primary focus is running around slaying monsters.  And I am personally looking forward to seeing what comes for this game down the road.

_childDocuments_.review: The attempt is clearly a spiritual successor to Oblivion, but you end up with something more like a worse version of Fable.The game's graphical quality, style, and gameplay all look and feel very close to Fable. Even down to how the melee combat feels strangely disconnected, the economy completely falls apart in the mid game, and the magic is too simplistic. Playing this game makes me miss Fable 1, which is a very weird feeling because Fable wasn't very good to begin with. The combat is just a game of who can stun lock who first. The focus, though, both in the game and marketing seems to be on the story. Which is very ... lackluster. It's all completely focused on fae lore and the concept of fate. And if that doesn't sound like a fun story then avoid this like the plague. Much like in Outer Worlds, the major story beats are covered very early on. Everything after that is just endless repetition of the same story beats over and over: fae stereotype, fate narrative, fae stereotype, fate narrative, over and over!The other major point you hear about this game is that it has lots of good side content. Now, there is definitely a lot of it. But it's all very boring, MMO-style, go to X and get Y quests. It's rare that I feel like a game is intentionally wasting my time, but I had that feeling here constantly. There are some interesting side quests, but they are buried under a mountain of trash with no way to distinguish them.This game is also extremely buggy. I had many quests bug and become uncompletable, or combat actions fail, or interactable objects not work, on and on. Even 3 of the major pieces of side-quest content all had major bugs that locked them completely. You can even become stuck in dunceons or terrain with literally no way out without the help of mods. While this game is trying to be like Bethesda's products they severely underestimated how much the console commands keep Bethesda's games working. There is no such option in Amalur to try and bypass their broken product.I honestly don't know who would enjoy this game. I guess if you're a really big fan of fae lore? But as an action game it is poor to play, as an RPG your narrative options are heavily restricted, as eye candy it looks mediocre, and as a quest-grinding game it's boring and buggy. You better really like fae, dude.

_childDocuments_.review: KOA:RR has been a blast to play. I enjoyed the story though it's not all that complicated.  The fighting was fun with plenty of different enemies to keep you entertained and the Boss fights usually required my full attention.  Like most RPG games, there were tons of weapons, armor and misc. items plus plenty of skills to acquire and improve.  I always wish there will be fewer inventory items to deal with when I play an  RPG game but that was not the case.  Inventory management was a major time killer.  I was a bit disappointed there were no major romance angles to pursue but there were plenty of other things to keep you busy.I could whine about the little things that could have been fixed or done better but for me, I play games to enjoy them and the game was overall interesting and entertaining enough that I played it a couple of times and had fun with it.  Occasionally a story progression seemed bugged or broken but I finally discovered most were caused by getting ahead of myself.  Once I reloaded a save and went about things in a different order, things then popped and worked as intended.  I would recommend backing up your save files.  Once in awhile when starting a session the game advised me the data was corrupt and I had to choose to let the game delete the corrupt data to proceed.  I always kept an up-to-date zipped up copy of the save folder to be safe.  I would much rather replay a couple of hours or a day than start the game over again.This is a game to have in inventory even better at a sale price, but be advised it may not seem like there were huge differences from the original version.  Bottom line for me is I've enjoyed the many hours I've played and I recommend just relaxing and letting the game come to you, don't rush it,  It's not exactly Chicken Soup for the soul but It's fun and will reward you with an enjoyable play thru if you let it.  8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: A deep and fun game, the combat feels very much like early God of War games or Dynasty Warriors where combo chaining is a big thing. Different skill trees deepen the combat styles for all the different weapons and magics.The character interactions are nuanced and various actions can have lots of wide ranging effects on the story. You could end up helping or destroying factions in the game by accident, some of them good aligned, some of them evil aligned, and some of them neutral aligned, it's all on your choices. This game actively encourages you to roam and explore off the beaten path if you want to know and experience the full story. You could main line quest it pretty easily, but that would take all the fun out of it. There are a few glitches from both the original release and new release. None of them have been game breaking in my experience. The ability to save whenever and wherever is nice. The updated graphics are ok, it mainly comes through in the lighting and color vibrancy, resolutions are really based on what your graphics card and monitor can display.All in all a solid re-release and bundling of the original DLCs. I'm looking forward to seeing what the new DLC that they have coming adds to the game. Definitely give this game a shot if you're looking for a single-player only RPG with solid storytelling, background lore and gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played much of the remaster yet, but I have about 1000-2000 hours in the original on Xbox. This is probably my favourite or second favourite game.I find the combat delightful as you can go from a sword, to daggers to magic in an instant in a really intuitive system. The destiny system allows for as many re-specs as you like, so you can really find your niche, whether that's pure magic or might/finesse/magic. I tend to play jack of all trades (the latter) so that the combat is nice and fluid. The addition of the very hard difficulty in the remaster is also really nice as for experienced players like me, hard just doesn't cut it. I wouldn't say very hard is particularly difficult for me personally, I would compare it to expert mode on Skyrim, if that helps any. The loot feels very rewarding and I like the colour system, naming system and the skills attached. I feel this game really got satisfying loot right and the balance of trash to treasure is perfect.The graphics are really pretty! I think this is one of those games where it's either your style or not. I love the bright colours and the magical feeling of the environment. Even in dull areas, though, the game manages to feel atmospheric and calming. The music fits very well with the game and I find it interesting enough, although the same combat music gets a little wearing. I don't find the apparently 'clunky and ugly' UI to be a problem, I actually really like it as it has a very Oblivion style look, which as my first RPG, is always good in my book.As for the main story, I think it's okay. I don't have any particular strong feelings about it. The faction quests such as the House of Ballads or the Travellers quests are amazing though and I really enjoy them! I would say that these and the side quests are what really shines story wise, as the side quests seem quite original, sometimes witty and just overall interesting. The DLC's are amazing too, especially Teeth of Naros. My favourite DLC's for any game I would say.Now, remaster-only stuff, there isn't much to comment on. I didn't notice any difference graphical wise, but perhaps audio-wise it sounds better and there seems to be new music and sounds which I like. I love the addition of a very hard difficulty but that wasn't particularly hard to add in I'm sure. It does feel re-balanced compared to the original game, especially in regards to loot. One thing I'm quite upset about is the fact that there's no achievement for completing the game on very hard mode, but there's one for hard mode. I can't imagine they'll make it unlock for very hard players, but if they do, I rescind my comment on that.Final thoughts. As a remaster, this doesn't currently have any content worth upgrading for. I say currently because I'm highly curious to see what they do with the new expansion in 2020. I will update my review once I play it. If you have the original game, I wouldn't recommend upgrading unless you know you'll love the Fatesworn expansion or you can get a sizeable discount. If you don't have the original game, I would recommend picking up the game off of CD keys as currently it's just £5 for the Origin platform. If you like it enough, buy the remaster.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, I've finally hit a point where I have to say: this game is RIDDLED with bugs. It's a mess. Death by a thousand papercuts.If you play this, it's going to be a mediocre not-quite-Skyrim meets not-quite-Darksiders (or similar third-person combat action game) with bugs galore and really questionable design decisions. For instance:  If you want to check your resistances, your crit chance, whatever, you have to work it all out yourself... equipment stats, ability bonuses, Destiny bonuses, Lorestone bonuses, twists of fate, all of it.Items will get stuck in inventory. Which, by the way, inventory is clunky to manage. Quests might bug and can't be finished because of nonsense reasons like "the NPC got knocked down." Even now, I'm trying to finish a side quest where I need to kill , and she just won't die. Down to one hp, won't die.I have yet to need alchemy. Sagecraft helps Blacksmithing, and Blacksmithing makes gear that puts all unique and set items to shame... not sure if that's Blacksmithing being overpowered or Unique/Set gear being woefully underpowered.Taking some weapon mastery moves can get you stuck doing an animation you don't want mid-combat. You can't really aim your bow except by its autotargeting, so no shooting over slightly raised ground, and when it auto-aims, it LOVES to target nearby crates instead of enemies. Speaking of which, maybe change your controls for switching target, or you'll have to hold X or Y AND find a way to flick the right stick.Also. google how to adjust your camera settings, because the default settings are weird and awful and have lots of drift.The issues just keep coming. I'm half-inclined to make a list, but I think I'm gonna just quit instead. Don't mind my playtime; way over half of it is me having left the game on when I was doing something else. The rest is just... boredom, mostly. As another review says, the gameplay is VERY repetitive and, especially with blacksmithed gear, you're never actually in danger. You won't get attached to characters (except maybe Alyn Shir) and almost every dungeon is just a loop.On the plus side, Dokkalfar women are hot. I know, I know, such a guy thing to say. It's true though, and I feel like I should throw the game a bone and say  nice.Edit: I forgot to say, the tradeskills are all clunky in design, and the itemization seems to be made for a looter game... with a bunch of random prefixes and suffixes... but the merchants never change their inventory.

_childDocuments_.review: Purchase this game at your own risk.Having recently become a PC gamer, from a console gamer, and reading the information out there about this game, I thought I would be safe downloading and playing it.  I had never experienced the game, so it shouldn't have mattered to me that the remaster failed to update game assets in a way that was a visual improvement over the original Reckoning.  I had never played.  So, I played.  It was fun.  Then the game-breaking bugs appeared.One entire DLC was cropped short for me when a game-breaker ended the main story of the DLC.  A magical wall that bars the players from completing the final confrontation with the DLC boss until after a wave of enemies are defeated simply didn't come down.  Left the area.  Loaded a previous save.  Returned, defeated the wave again.  Nope.  Wall still up.  Complete barrier to the remainder of the boss zone.  DLC ruined.But, it was only one of two DLC's.  I still had the other, and the main game, right.  Well, not for long.  There are hundreds of side quests in this game.  So many, in fact, that it hardly mattered if a few of them had similar quest-breaking bugs like the above.  I'd just move on.Until the main story game-breaker.  An NPC who must follow the player into a zone so she can complete a task simply failed to follow me.  I talked to her.  She said let's go.  Then stood there.  I left the area, fast traveled, came back, reentered the quest zone.  There she was.  Let's go.  Stood there.  So, I went on without her and got to the point she has to complete her task.  No way for me to do it.  She didn't come trotting up out of nowhere like I had hoped.  The quest just died with her task incomplete.  I left the zone via the rear exit you're supposed to use once the whole thing is done.  Then I entered again, but from this rear exit.  Low and behold, she was there completing her task.  I thought the main story arc would be saved!  Nope.  She completed the thing she was supposed to do after the enemy waves were defeated and stood there in that animation while the enemies spawned again.  She didn't react to them.  They didn't react to her.  I was unable to move and couldn't attack the enemies.  We all just stood there in our feckless animations as if we couldn't give the time of day to each other.  Hard to a hard shutdown of the PC.  Came all the way back into the game.  It happened again.  And, again.  Last straw.So, these crashes might not be so impossible if the game had time stamped Autosaves.  But, it doesn't.  It has one autosave slot that it overwrites.  No way to get to a previous auto save.  And it autosaves the bugs into your game history.  You can do your own saves to attempt to have a means of backing out of these bugs, but there are so many of them, you won't be able to back out of all of them.  My last straw was on the main story arc.  So my entire playthrough with that character ended.  60 hours in.  But, less than halfway through the game (since I was doing the side quests).  No path ahead.So, buy this game at your own risk.  It's fun.  Until it breaks.  And, it will break.
