_childDocuments_.review: KoA was… and still is a great open world ARPG, but this re-release is simply not good enough.- Absolutely atrocious performance, the game now runs in DX11, but the developers have completely ruined the performance from the original release, now even on powerful hardware you will see dips into the 40s. Some say it is due to the enhanced Lod which is impossible to make out, for such a small increase in visual fidelity we are hit with 3x worse performance than the original – truly embarrassing! - Numerous bugs and glitches have been introduced.- The game crashes in certain locations which it never did before, so what is the point of this "remaster"?- Minimal visual uplift with bugged anisotropic filtering and no AA option besides the horribly blurry FXAA or the performance killing (on top of the already bad performance) SSAA.The promise of new content in 2021 is not enough to excuse this remaster's many technical faults. There may have gone some quality of life improvements in the game's leveling/difficulty but at the cost of severe performance issues, numerous bugs and glitches.Only time will tell if THQ Nordic can fix this mess.As of now this is not worth the money, I feel duped for upgrading to the FATE edition as this “remaster” runs significantly worse than the original and has a plethora of new issues, not an upgrade by any stretch of the imagination.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the original, and true, on the surface, this game is identical to the original, in many ways, with only a minor graphic overhaul. But one issue that is persisant is, when they remade the game, they totally FUBAR'd the targeting system. Get ready for your attacks to pass under, around, through, and over half the hitboxes of half the enemies in the game. Get ready for sprites to be nearly impossible to hit, given their small, high hitbox. Get ready for humanoid enemies to break lockon every time they take half a step to the left, and I don't mean dodge, I mean every small movement causes your attacks to miss. Because what they seem to have done, is reduce your attack tracking to almost zero, which does not work well in a game where every attack you make is dependent upon auto-targeting, while leaving enemy tracking where it was, which is at a ridiculous level. If you play the game on normal, you might not notice. But on higher difficulties, where enemies hit like a freight train, it is frustrating. And it wasn't an issue in the original. All they had to do was overhaul the graphics, and leave the mechanics alone, but they couldn't even pull that off. This game's mechanical issues make me sure that the sequel that THQ nordic will surely make is going to be horribly flawed.

Together, you get quite the options to control the flow of a battle, options that need you to consider timing & enemy positions. _childDocuments_.review: Re-Reckoning (RR) is a remaster of the underrated 2012 RPG, , which was developed and published by different companies. I don't want to color it with fancy words so I settle for just saying this remaster is more of a compatibility upgrade for newer hardware and today's standards than a fully fleshed-out Re-work on the original game.🔸"Not the most welcoming place to wake up to, is it? Is that a pile of corpses? Fascinating..."RR follows the story of a mortal known as the "Fateless One" who having died before the game's outset, is revived in a Lazarus-like event. Now it's up to you to unweave the fate of the Amalur, slay monstrosities who terrorize the coexistence of mortals and immortals, and at the end learn the truth behind your death.For such a deep plot, the story isn't well-paced. It unfolds an inordinate number of events in one go while at other times, it sends you off on a wild-goose-chase during a story quest. That becomes less apparent in faction storylines as each offers an intriguing premise while remaining much shorter than the main story. Side quests, well, are a series of bland fetch-quests just being there to make the world feel less lifeless.🔸RR proves RPG games don't have to have subpar gameplay. I found myself utterly satisfied with how the gameplay threw every aspect of the combat and exploration at my feet from the beginning, then allowing me to elevate them to my likings. This is a breath of fresh air considering many RPG titles restrict you to a single build. Character customization, skills, and loot system are enriched with gripping elements and items.The strongest suit of RR is undoubtedly its action-heavy combat. With a plethora of sorcerous weapons at your disposal, you're free to create any hybrid style you crave. A Warhammer wielding mage in robes and slippers, or sporting a bow and arrow along with "boomerang-styled-throwing-discs" Chakrams, the possibilities are countless. The combat was once forward-looking and somehow still holds up to par with standards of the current RPG generation. The Hack 'n' Slash nature of the combat is invigorating and soon you realize dodge, parry, and a string of special moves are as important as outputting devastating damage. These abilities could be hard to master since enemies continuously throw their punches at you and their very scripted behavior proves to be unpredictable at times.Kingdoms of Amalur is a vast and magical place where each location feels distinct from one another. There are hundreds of spots that tell the secrets of Amalur in a glance. Hundreds of natives who have stories to tell and errands (you have) to run. You'll be rewarded handsomely for searching every nook and cranny, though, it's traversed all horizontally. Invisible walls over ledges and many objects deprive you of jumping around.Abilities are scattered among three dominant categories: Might, Finesse, Sorcery. While skills represent your general areas of expertise such as Blacksmithing or Alchemy, abilities are more combat-related active and passive play styles. They focus on enhancing the physical damage output, critical/elemental hit chance, and specializing the use of certain weapons. Alternatively, destiny cards unlock after investing several points in each ability tree, granting permanent buffs to your expertise as long as they're equipped.Each level XP requirement is progressively increased, except that the amount of awarded XP for killing enemies and completing quests stays the same throughout the game. But fear not, Reckoning mode is your savior. This ability is fueled by killing your foes and once it's activated, you'll be able to deliver pulverizing blows and earn a ridiculous amount of XP in each run.An example of the game's unthoughtful design is that you often find powerful gear which could be dropped by even the most insignificant enemies. Gear that you might use for the majority of the game without changing to another. Another factor playing a role in the imbalance is high-level Blacksmithing and Sagecrafting. These skills basically allow you to salvage your trash equipment and Re-forge highly potent items with the skills' benefits.🔸 had lofty ambitions and was set back by the limitations of its generation. However, the art style, vibrant colors, and gleam lightning are a treat for your eyes. You'd be traveling across enchanted forests, sandy deserts, and murky swamps that fit together naturally, and offer plenty of amazing views, if not vast ones. The only drawbacks are the low draw distance and texture pop-ins which won't be sticking out unless you want it to be.🔸This epic fantasy adventure is brought to life by the haunting music of Grant Kirkhope (who has GoldenEye 007 in his resume) and the Prague Philharmonic Orchestra. The ever-presence of ambient sounds made something unique and distinctive of traveling around the Amalur. The voice acting is a job well-done. Although, if you're hunting down the side quests, you'll be repeating to yourself: "That guy sounds a whole lot like the guy I talked to in that other town just 10 minutes ago"🔸🔸Specs: GTX1050 2GB - Athlon II X4 645 - 8GB DDR3 RAMThe game runs with all settings maxed out using about 65% of VRAM at 1050p 60hz., despite all the negative reviews, posts, and complaints regarding performance issues, I haven't had a single problem during my playtime. Given my low-end PC specs, I was able to reach 60 FPS for the majority of the game. Only small stutters occurred during heated actions, dropping down to 42-50 FPS. Also considering I've played the game on a 5400RPM HDD, loading times were still lightning fast. 10-15 seconds from the main menu to gameplay and 2-3 seconds during the game.🔸🔸RR had a chance to resurrect and did improve in many (unnoticeable) ways. It still is a worthwhile RPG that reminds you of what made the original great back in 2012. Though it no longer feels remarkable, and the more technical issues that came with this compatibility upgrade are far less excusable.

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing RPG brought back to life. Not only is it a remaster with updated visuals and lots of QoL improvements, but after all these years it is getting new content. Kingdoms of Amalur's story is crafted by prolific New York Times bestselling author R.A. Salvatore. Which just means that you know it's going to be good. Pros:- Small tweaks fixed the pacing and (lack of) difficulty curve of original- Engrossing story about defying Fate- Fantastic fast-paced combat- Tons of loot with lots of fun crafting mechanics- Massive game world teeming with quests and stories to uncover- Lots and lots of side quests makes it so you always have something to doCons:- Handful of minor bugs pop up every now and then- Lack of lock-on for combat is annoying at first- Lot and lots of side quests. The games best feature is probably one of it's worst features. There are an insane amount of side quests to the point where it can be kind of overwhelming.Over all an amazing game that any fan of the RPG genre should check out. Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning isn't the perfect game, but damn is it close.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a cash grab, plain and simple. Bugs from the original game still remain. I can't really tell the difference between the graphical upgrades and the original. The only substantial change is that you have an additional difficulty level, and a few other gameplay tweaks. That's basically it. On top of that....KoA has aged poorly. I'm sorry, but this is the truth.  The game is a composite of RPG titles of the era, mainly drawing from WoW; it comes complete with the cartoonish, over the top artwork and giant obnoxious yellow exclamation points. In many ways, you feel as if you are playing WoW for single player. This isn't a good thing. The vast majority of KoA's gameplay is you running around like a lunatic completing one inane, stupid task after another. These are classic MMORPG style quests that require you to be errand boy for the Kingdom. KoA trades quality for quantity - so many "quests" yet they amount to so little. There is little to no tension in the game as you are already Godlike when you first wake up - in fact one of the characters you meet directly says that you have Godlike powers. This doesn't bode well for RPG's where part of the enjoyment is growing in power throughout the story. There are no gameplay mechanisms to mitigate this feeling of absolute superiority. Speaking of story, KoA is paper thin. Roleplaying elements seem tacked on. Characters are shallow, the main questline is shallow and predictable. Persuasion simply amounts to a basic skill line. There are no lasting consequences to your actions. Despite these flaws, I did find some redeeming aspects of KoA. Combat is fun and feels very rewarding. The timed blocks combined with dodging and weapon combinations adds a nice level of skill to a game that feels like it was ripped straight out of an MMO (where player skill is rather limited in gameplay). I find this aspect of the game almost saves KoA, but I found myself getting very tired of the quest grind after the first zone. The game just gets so repetitive with these quests that I have no emotional investment in.

The only downside is that a lot of the story telling is pretty linear, you can't stray too far off the path as it holds your hand. Nonetheless, character customizations is yours to play with a fitting style for most people present, and every which way between. Highly recommended, even at a lofty price.

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend this game? Yep. In a heart beat. I bought this game back in 2012 but never got around to playing it. After finally beating my WoW addiction decided to get around to my single player games. This was next on my radar, but held off due to the upcoming remaster, finally go around to playing it and so far it's scratched an itch I've had since WoW's inception: a single player WoW. There's a lot to chew through, this isn't a weekend game, this isn't one you'll plow through while managing to see a good amount of the content in a 20-30 hour span. At my current rate I anticipate getting at least 80'ish hours of game play from it, maybe more depending on the side-quest burn out I may, or may not experience. I just know this, in the time I've put in, I've explored maybe 20% of the map, and in that 20% of the map I've done at least 40-45 side quests. As far as I have seen though, that's probably one third of the quests available in the areas I've explored; in other words there's A LOT to do.The graphics, while I can't say I can really compare them to the original, seem on point. A lot of people say they barely passed the muster on being considered a remake, but hell if the original looked nearly as good then they did a phenomenal job the first time around, and this is just the cherry on top.The sound is also on point, nails down that "fantasy" vibe pretty well. With my headphones on, utilizing the 7.1 component in them makes the game pretty immersive. The dialogue, to me at least, is very good. There's, what seems to be, a lot of dialogue in this game. You can tell they put a lot into the sound in this game, even if people aren't fan of the music, or sound effects, just the dialogue alone had to have taken a good amount of time to compile.Another thing is the combat.. now this is refreshing take on combat. I honestly have probably spent an hour or two just running around killing stuff just because I enjoy figuring different ways, as well as trying out different specs to find that sweet spot.  Plus a lot of the enemies have attacks that you have to keep an eye out for, making it a game where you can't just blindly slash your way to victory, some battles require a modicum of approach and strategy, Another thing I've enjoyed was being able to seamlessly change specs on the fly; granted I had the gear needed for each spec. I've found daggers to be the funnest of all the game play as it requires you to use some strategy as you're in very close proximity for roughly 90% of the fighting you're doing. Everyone else will have their preferences, they're all fun.Considering I had gotten the remake for $15, I figured what the hell give this game I bought 8 years ago a shot.. and so far I'm wondering how, and why I never got into it sooner. This version comes with all the DLC, and with a future DLC on the horizon this game, to me, is the definition of a "good deal". Like the Witcher 3, there's a lot to do and explore, and with fun combat, good lore, and  good soundtrack (to me) when I fire this game up it's easy to lose a good 5-6 hours of my day.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent remaster for a great game. The new difficulty mode was much needed (game is far too easy), small improvements to the chests in the game was great and the increased resolution/fps/shadows look pretty good. There isn't a whole lot more to the remaster compared to the original, not enough to be noticed right away at least. However the game itself is a unique WRPG with beautiful animations and art direction throughout. Story isn't groundbreaking but it has some interesting characters and writing at times. Combat is 10/10 for the time with a ton of options for play styles and builds to go for. Unique weapons (chakrams are badass) cool spells and slick combos to perform.

_childDocuments_.review: I dunno what everyone is complaining about, but this game is fun as hell. I never played it back in the day, so I'm coming into it fresh without any weird baggage I guess?Just try it for yourself though. It seems like most of the people complaining about this game don't know the difference between a remaster and a remake. If you've ever wanted to play the game Fable always wished it was, then check this game out. What a straight up just FUN video game. It's a very no bullsh*t, streamlined, fairly basic game on the surface, but has some really fun combat and systems in place that give it some surprising depth. The voice acting is entertaining and the music is great. I'm not sure what else people want from this, but I guess go play The Witcher 3? I dunno, man. But this game is just old school fun and brings me joy. It reminds me of the good feels I got when I first played Fable 1 and 2 and even reminds me of some MMOs (minus the soul-crushing grind and bland worlds). I'm looking forward to checking out the new DLC expansion for it later on! I'm not sure what happened at THQ over the past couple of years, but whoever's calling the shots there now is a genius. I'm glad to show my support to a company for bringing weird cult classics back into the spotlight with a fresh coat of paint.

_childDocuments_.review: is the best way to describe this game. It feels like the devs made this a priority.Standard fantasy RPG blended with third-person hack and slash arcade mechanics. Your skill and timing is as important as your character level, making most encounters feel fun and fresh.The best part of KOA is how it breaks the typical 'rigid' gameplay of typical fantasy RPGs. Consider it more of an action-adventure, with a (surprisingly) deep leveling system, and a vast, colourful arsenal of weapons (each with its own fighting style, skills and combos)Be it warrior, mage, rogue, or mix of all three, gameplay is always action-packed.If you do get bored of or are unhappy with your build, you can always re-spec - this will allow you to build a new class or multi-class too.Same of the above + quality of life improvements.Note: this includes all the DLC content (including the prerelease DLC) - therefore you'll start out with some overpowered equipment you might want to avoid using.The main focus of the remaster is the graphical improvements. Personally, I'm happy that the art style was not changed. KOA has the World of Warcraft style art, which to me makes a game look 'timeless' being so cartoonish, I'm a fan of that.The remaster looks great. The colourful, rich world looks brighter than ever. The supersampling option does wonders. If one can increase this to 1.5 or 2.0 - it's worthwhile.Well, as with the original release:- Music: is just 'there' and gets the job done. It's not bad, mind you, but very average. I usually mute it and put on a Spotify playlist of medieval fantasy music from someone like Adrian Von Ziegler.- Lore: while it does have a few original ideas, the lore is quite forgettable overall. This is no Dragon Age. It mostly feels like a mishmash of ideas: A little bit of Elderscrolls here, a little bit of dragon age here, then a little lord of the rings there, etc...- Loading times: I've installed this on an SSD, and load times are still too long by today's standards.- Price: For returning players - This remaster is not worth the full price. Wait for a sale or discount (as I did) For new players - Yeah, it's worth the full price IMHO. It's quite a large RPG, focused on fun and does not take itself too seriously.

_childDocuments_.review: I've put in some hours now. I think its a fun RPG. I like the visual upgrades to the game, especially the spells! Sorcery > Finesse or Might IMHO.. (only bcuz the visuals with spell casting and sorcerer weapons look so amazing) As for game mechanics, Its weird not being able to jump. No jumping and no stepping over a tree branch. You must stay on the ground and navigate around tree branches, and only jump at designated "jump" platforms.. LOL! but ok, i can live with that, just be aware of it during combat (pull mobs into open areas and avoid closed in spaces). The fighting requires some skill. its not button mash.  (Use a controller, its not QWERTY friendly, i tried, heh). Combos and new techniques introduced as you level up are fun to acquire. There are many quests! but, at least one, is buggy. Ie: Spider quest giver in spider region, which was supposed to be fixed with re-release, but is not. I have dead quest giver laying on the ground and im stuck lugging around spider guts (at least -1 inventory slot). So, Its buggy for something that is a re-do.. but i can sorta live with that.  Inventory management could be handled better but, isn't that the case with every RPG ever?  The game is entertaining with good story lines and RPG vibe. Id like to give the dead guy my spider guts tho. So, 3outta5* for dated game mechanics and at least one bugged quest  "morrowind-ish/wow-ish". Overall, if you enjoy offline, solo adventure, RPG, then i would recommend. KoA-RR is fun and worth getting while on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a difficult review for me to write, as I grew up playing this game and had a strong sense of nostalgia for it. However, as I replayed it in full recently, I saw how unremarkable this game really is. One of the things I noticed is how much this game resembles an MMORPG in everything but the multiplayer aspect, which makes sense because that's what this game was meant to be before it was reworked into a single player RPG. You have lots and lots of loot and gear sets with randomized drops, which is pretty unnecessary for this type of game. There is an excessive amount of quests, lots of them your standard fetch quests, and that also means that there is a staggering amount of voiced dialogue that you must skip at risk of losing your mind. Even the way the map is arranged and how enemies become invincible when they go outside their spawn zone points to this MMORPG past.Couple all of this MMO stuff with combat that is flashy but repetitive and simple, a lack of or very simplified (good/evil) choices you can make in the story, entire skills and game mechanics that you may never touch because they're useless and you're overpowered anyways, and lots of jank...At the end of the day, the biggest flaw of this game is a pretty simple one: it's just not fun.

Salvatore's writing is where one might expect, and the gameplay itself (I've only really gone into the spells section thus far) is fluid and there's something immensely satisfying about dropping a meteor onto the unsuspecting heads of your opponents. That said, prefer the lightning storm for mana efficiency.Game obviously has some bugs, but I've run through the main story line, most of the factions that I've found thus far AND done the DLC that I'm aware of. More than worth the buy, but I can understand why people who bought the original could be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah so full of potential, good levelling system, fun story, lots of loot, side quests that give you bonuses at the end. So why don't I finish this game? The combat. Lack of abilities? Nope, lots of those. Lack of weapons? There are chakrams in this game, so hell no. The problem being is that the combat was out of date even when this game was new! Every. single. enemy. will. STAGGER. you. From lowly boggarts to mighty Yotuns! No matter your level or epic heavy armour you will be staggard by the lightest hit. You and enemies are animation locked, so its difficult to interrupt your own attacks and movements to respond, so there is no reward for quick reflexes. Same as your enemies, once they get their attacks going, they gotta finish them. You can counter, but can ONLY counter their INITIAL attack! Not if they are already half way through the attack set. These admittedly small issues create major breaks in combat rhythm, you can't build momentum or ever really feel powerful. Its just a headache.Its all the more unfortunate as this game is very good, just let down by odd and dramatically out of date (even by its own time) combat design.

_childDocuments_.review: I think when considering this game, it's best to start with what it's not..It's not a cutting edge open world RPG with photo realistic graphics and new and innovative mechanics. It's not a AAA game from a studio with a huge budget that's trying to launch an IP that will carry the studio for decades.What it is, is an open world RPG with a stylized look that while not 'cutting edge' has a unique artistic charm that actually holds up well with age. It's a game that promotes any type of play style from the powerful melee focused warrior, to the spell slinging magic user to the swift and deadly rogue. The game features an impressive cast of voice actors and for those that like to dive into lore, you will find plenty here. The game is simply put.. fun. It's not a huge IP, it's not a huge studio, it's not a blockbuster.. it's just.. fun. If you like open world RPG's with strong lore and voice acting coupled with diverse and fun game play, this is the game.Nothing however, is perfect. The game is older and the engine is dated. You will sometimes get stutters, frame drops and pauses even on high end hardware. Not enough to deter your game play, but something you will occasionally notice. The world while vast, is in many places somewhat empty. Also, the number of quests don't keep up with your level, so if you're the type that likes to do every quest you see, you will be massively over leveled for the main story line. You will sometimes have to just decide to move on to a new area as there are so many quests that doing everything would level you way beyond the story level for that area. I personally wish the game had an option to scale quest levels to the player, I know not everyone likes that, but it would be nice as an option you could turn on or off.Overall, it's a flawed and somewhat clunky game that is just overall fun to play and can create a great sense of immersion. When on sale, it's usually very low in price and it's absolutely worth the gamble. If you're thinking you might like this game.. honestly, you probably will. The combat system alone is worth the purchase price.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok let me start by saying I never review things but I felt obligated here.I played the 1st game way back when and liked it but never finished (18 hrs total). Holy crap does that make the game 20x more enjoyable. My biggest gripe about fighting the camera is gone. I pushed that slider up and it felt so much better.  - Native 21:9 widescreen support. This is a rarity especially with older games. 1 quick setting change and I was hoping into the action. - Although its an older game the art style makes it not feel as old. Is it impressive? No, but I don't mind at all. This is coming from someone who historically does not play old games because I'm so spoiled by modern title graphics. Is this a groundbreaking remake? No, but they've added good QoL improvements. Is this game fun? Yes, very much so.Do I think it was worth the $15-20?  Yes Would I pay $40 for it? _childDocuments_.review: I hope THQ Nordic picking this up is a sign that we'll see more Amalur games in the future.It's an open-world RPG with an interesting and unique setting. While the combat isn't the most polished among action RPGs, it feels pretty satisfying and has a decent amount of variety. It's not super well balanced and you can get silly OP (especially if you use ). There's lots to do without getting buried in radiant quests (an issue I have with other open world RPGs), and while the overarching story isn't super deep, the lore of the world is pretty interesting to pick up as you play.They updated the graphics just enough to make it look really nice and fixed a lot of the jankiness. The game runs much better now--I can't test, but based on how it runs on my current PC, I suspect it actually functions on potatoes now without running in slowmo. The art/animation style, core features (skills, ability trees, etc.) have not changed, nor have the story, questlines, and voice acting.  If you like the original, this is a pretty nice update. If you have the discount for owning the original, you're basically paying for a small upgrade and any DLCs you didn't already own. Without the discount, it's only worth if you don't already own the game in some form.

_childDocuments_.review: So, Steam has asked me if I would recommend this game to anyone and I've selected No! There's a few reasons why, mainly because of all the bugs in the game. While the devs have thrown a fancy few "improvements onto the game they somehow managed to completely ignore every single bug that was in the original game AND added a whole bunch of brand new bugs into the game! There are some nice improvements over the original, but there are far too many things that aren't working quite right. Quest items that don't get removed from your inventory when you complete the quest; the game crashes somewhat randomly; you sometimes get an infinite loading screen and then there's the HUD options that they added. You get three options for the HUD: Default; Hidden and Small. The problem is that Default is just too big, it occupies a big chunk of screen space and Small is actually Tiny, it's so small that it's hard to see. Apparently they are working on adding another HUD option that will be somewhere between Default and Small in size, but no time-frame on when that might be added.Which brings me to my actual recommendation: as it stands now I would say avoid this version of the game. If you have the original Kingdoms of Amalur Reckoning then stick with that for now. If you've never played the original then buy that instead of this! Hopefully, with a few more patches they'll fix more and more bugs and make further improvements, if they do then I'll happily return and change my recommendation, but as it stands right now I simply cannot recommend this game to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: There's some hardcore crust when it comes to audio. The lightning staffs decimate your ears and the pre-rendered cutscenes blare over the in-game ones.That being said, this is probably the single best designed game I've played. I found the art direction appealing enough to ensnare me in wanderlust. I wanted to explore, to linger in areas just to admire them, yet push ever forward to see what else the world held sub rosa. The combat was always fresh. New skills opened new avenues by which to diffuse groups and their variants. Said variation of enemies in a group kept the unfortunately unvarying cast unwonted by their interactions and synergy (or lack thereof).Despite the previous complaint about the audio, the score was quite nice. It knew where it was needed, and it flourished. A nicety when repose was center and a resounding command of attention during climaxes.As far as story goes, it's a video game. I didn't expect too much, and didn't really get much in the long run.  However, the details and characters were certainly not sub par.  The lore and races weren't too terribly generic. The fae themselves waxed to be a bit more interesting. Their politics reminded me a bit of dune, most specifically during the House of Sorrows quest line, It's been a long time since I've woken up excited to turn on my computer and play a game. The last game to have pulled such a response from me was Divinity: Original Sin 2, ~4 years ago. I realize this isn't a new game, but I loved it nontheless.If you love fantasy,If you've a wanton need for adventure,If you're okay with sort of mediocre dungeon layouts,Play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game will punch you in the face with how boring it can be within the first hour or two, and it has some seriously bad sound design and map layouts (along with bugs and issues).However, if you can look past that, and the rather lackluster story, and just embrace it as a generic fantasy adventure - it will surprise you. Some of the side quests are genuinely more interesting than the main quests, and as far as general fantasy goes, this is some of the better variety out there.Give it a shot when you're not busy with other things - it's really nice.

_childDocuments_.review: While I understand many negative comments about this game (pricing and graphics come to mind); ultimately, if you like the original Kingdoms of Amalur and wanted more, this Re-Reckoning version offers the vastly superior experience and that's what really matters to me. There are three features that really standout in this Re Reckoning version: the added Very Hard mode; the new loot drop system that better suits your playstyle; and the new enemy level system that doesn't punish you for wandering into new zones early. All of these changes are great quality-of-life changes that make the gaming experience more refreshing and exciting. As a returning fan I am truly very happy to play this updated version of the game and I only hope the developers will keep improving the game from this point on.

_childDocuments_.review: Kingdom of Amalur is an open world RPG with an MMO style grind and hardcore fast respawns but without the community and friends you could have in a MMO. This game was definitely one of the most annoying games i ever played in my life. Most of the segments of the game just try to annoy the player and the list is just so long that I don't even know with which to start first.The game's start was solid and promising. The beginning is never easy in an RPG. You don’t have gear, everyone hates and the whole world is against you. Some of these will change as you progress through the game, only the hate of the developers will stay with you until the best part of the game, which is the uninstall button. But don’t get that far yet. So after you experience the world a bit you will realise enemy groups will be bigger and bigger. While dodging was funny at the beginning, where you were able to die and get some damage, it became the main part of the game. Oh well, if you could at least stop dodging… IF you do, then you can experience the best feature of the game. CHAINSTUN! Yes, you get stunned all the time, but it just never ends. The game doesn't want to kill you, it just wants you to spend as much time in combat as possible. Most of the time I wasn't even bothering to dodge anymore, I just spammed the mouse button so sometimes between the stuns and knockbacks my character finally managed to execute an attack and so slowly killing enemies was possible. All that, on hard difficulty. Unfortunately, by time and progress not only the enemy number in groups increased, but the required time to kill each of them. Why? Well, first of all enemies level up with you (up to a maximum value defined for each region, but that usually not reached when exploring that area) but gears not. Vendors selling predefined low level items. Item drops do not scale up. So enjoy the grind on lvl 50 with your lvl 16 weapons and armors :-)If there would be at least some variety among enemies, but no, that is not happening. The same few enemy types over and over again, just reskinned. Also their abilities are not changing, stun/knockback with minimal damage.The game totally lacks basic Quality of Life features. That is understandable, that your inventory is not limitless. Not sure how many items I was able to carry with me at the beginning, i think it was 40 or 50, at the end i had 150. The big problem is, that not every item counts as an item which should take a spot and the even biggest problem is, that the game is not telling you which takes a slot and which not. For example, while I had a 150 capacity at the end, just the misc category had ~350 various items in it. Some are obvious spot takes, like armors, weapons, but as you progress in the game you loot up many small things, which are hidden in misc and in other categories and taking up spots. Now imagine how annoying it is, when you have 80 backpack slots and after selling armors, weapons, useless consumables and you have only 10 open from that 80. You try to figure out what takes slots, selling stuff to get space and about 20 hours later, when you can’t finish a quest, you need to realise you sold a quest item. Luckily, it was only a side task which was picked up at the very beginning of the game and there were no achievements tied to it.The following part might be a fiction, but this is how i imagine the creation of the Fatesworn DLC:So the investors tell the developers that they want a DLC for a higher price, so they expect a good 20h+ playtime with it, but the available story allows maximum a 10-12h playtime, even with the combat, which was designed to lengthen the game. One more important thing, it should be developed in the most cost effective way. GRIND, yes that is the solution. But in which form? Then a developer, who just completed a retro game, mentioned that the DLC should be related to chaos realms and creatures and so, just like in Elder Scroll Oblivion, the player should be forced to close dozens of chaos realm portals. All of them look the same, same monsters, easy, fast, cheap method to extend playtime. 25 will be enough? Sounds good right? Hmm, wait, what if the user is forced to close rifts around each chaos portal before the player is allowed to enter the portal? Nice, a few more extra hours of gameplay! Hmm, let’s place these portals to the map of the main game, and the chaos creature will be friendly to the forces of nature (bears, wolves, regular human bandits, etc)! After all, chaos and nature love eachother so much in each fantasy! Nice, players need to fight now not just the chaos creatures, but also regular monsters from the base game, again. Few more extra hours of gameplay! Dear investors, we are done, and now you can advertise the DLC with a lot of fun playtime :-(There are still more left, but this game annoyed me so much that I want to end my suffering and just erase even the memory of it. I not saying, that it can’t be enjoyable for some, but for me it was clearly one of the most annoying game i ever played while I still forced myself to complete it, because the endless optimist inside me it kept telling: “It will be better, go on”Lore was clearly spot on, just like voice acting. So there were some good parts in the game. Too bad creativity ended up there. Yes, Fatesworn required. One playthrough is enough but there are missable achievements, which could be annoying in a 80-100h game, so save frequently. There are actually only 5 achievements, which you need to check beforehand:That's it, everything else should be unlocked during regular gameplay or could be cleared up after completing the game. 7/10 and perfection score is mostly for resisting the repetitive tasks of the game. ~80-100h

_childDocuments_.review: Man - gamers are such a snotty bunch nowadays. I don't get some of the sheer hate of a few of these negative reviews. One dude downrated it because he was too stupid to understand how to rebind his keys. It's literally in the options.With that said, I get SOME of the negative sentiment. I would say if you played the normal version this isn't QUITE worth a 40 dollar purchase. But at 15 bucks it's really a steal. Just fixing the friggin camera allowing you to zoom out to me is worth the price alone. In the original the camera was so zoomed in combat became frustrating and the fun factor was severely reduced. The map and health bars were so massive they covered 20% of your screen. Now you can reduce the size nice and small so you can see more of gameplay, which is great.As for the graphics - I get some complaining here, it's not night and day. But it definitely looks better. It has a new coat of paint is all, textures are sharper, less blurry, geometry is a bit more detailed, there's more fidelity, widescreen looks good, your character looks solid. It's tough to sorta say on video, but during your play youll notice. They definitely coulda pushed the envelope more though, I'll say that. I'm still not a fan of the cartoon WoW look, but it is what it is and is not that bad. Instead of a 2009 game it looks like a 2015 game. I mean I booted up DO:Inquisition the other day and I'd say it's honestly on par with it, maybe minus a few letter grades.Here is where this game really shines for me - the gameplay / combat. It's honestly one of the deepest combat systems in an RPG I've come across. I was really thinking on games to compare it to see if that statement held up, and lets see: Dragon Age 3 combat sucked, Tales games while fun and somewhat deep, is basically one combat over and over with a terrible dodge mechanic, Code Vein is straight trash. Putting this on Very Hard gave me serious challenge where I must time parries and dodges almost perfectly with very little room for mistakes, a few hits kill you. Combat animations are fun and flashy, with so much varying skills and weapons you can switch up your play all the time. Weapons and armor look great on your character and all have deep stats that work with your build. Some people complain about the UI and inventory management, and while it isn't the greatest, it's really not bad. It's a basically a list but you are never really OVERLOADED with loot where it gets unwieldy. It's solid.So the story, for me it wasn't earth shattering, but it's interesting. I played the game on PS3 (4hrs) and PC (10hrs old version) and I definitely read and listened to the story beats. Though Dragon Age 1 is still my favorite RPG ever. Amalur does get more interesting as time goes on, but to me it wasn't dragon age levels of intensity and edge of your seat character development. The secondary characters were passable, except the hot elf that joins you. No leliannas or Allistairs here. The world lore is deep and you can read all sorts of beats if you want, but anything that wasn't related to the story I was only passingly interested in. Admittedly I haven't beaten the game and only have 20 hours total with the story so take that what you will.Content wise, I mean you're getting between 70 to 200 hours of gameplay really. Whether it wears off at the 40 hr mark I can't say, but just what I've experienced I can see me playing a lot over time, just like I did with Tales of Berseria. Got about 60 hours over a few years lol. The two older expansion packs are included, but the new one coming in 2020 isn't in the base game.Overall - is the game worth 60 bucks? No, I don't think so. Possibly if the new expansion was included at release and really added some new elements. Is it worth 40? I'd say if I didn't play it already - possibly, I wouldn't regret my purchase and get my 40 bucks worth. Is it worth 15, yes, just for the slight graphic upgrade and camera zoom alone.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm honestly torn whether I would recommend this to other people or not. I wrote yes because I'm not saying it's a bad game but ultimately... it's bland. When I was younger, I used to play this a lot and enjoy the hell out of it because I had an old PC that couldn't run anything else properly. Since it was the only game I could play, I engrossed myself into it and to be fair, I really loved it.Now that I played many other games, I honestly think this game lacks depth. Sure, it has a lot of lore but it turned NPC's into chatterboxes without personality, whose only purpose is to throw the mountain of lore at you. However, most of this lore is not well connected to each other, and you don't get the "bigger picture" unless you interact with many, MANY npc's which can get boring very quickly.I also heavily dislike the lack of roleplaying. You want to condemn the village to death for allowing innocent Fae to be harmed? Dream on. You want to condemn Fae, or outright make the village and Fae hate each other? No way. There is only one way to play this game, and it's as a good character which makes "roleplaying" in roleplaying game pointless. However, I have enjoyed certain things in this game. For example, I made a Varani mercenary who specializes in electric magic, and then I've randomly found this Varani pendant made specially for those of Varani who use both magic and finesse. Since I picked the god Bhelen, who is the God of Death, it was quite fitting first two shrines I prayed to belonged to that god. To that end, I've realized there is a lot of "depth" you can give to your character, you can really imagine any backstory you want because a lot of the things regarding deities and history of the race you picked are left to interpretation. Whether this is a good thing or not, I'm not sure, but it can be good under certain circumstances. Also, one very good thing is side-quests. Unlike certain games where the only point of sidequests is to kill ten creatures and return for payment, developers of KoA tried their best to make every little side-quest meaningful and interesting. One final thing is the graphics. While original KoA was... okay for its time, it aged since then. KoA Re Reckoning added some graphical fidelity, yet it didn't really do much. Still, surroundings are beautiful, although nothing that wasn't already seen. To conclude my review, I would say you should give it a try, but wait for the sale to get the lower price because ultimately, game isn't worth its full price. Or even better, get a demo and see what the game is all about. Maybe it will be your cup of tea, who knows?

_childDocuments_.review: Back when I played the original Kingdoms of Amalur, I absolutely hated it. The world, despite having all these nice monster and armor designs, was a world that was boring, mundane, and uninteresting. The combat was some of the worse I played in an action RPG - one-button attacks and skills that didn't feel like they sped up the flow of the monotonous, smooth-brain combat that plagues KoA. I didn't feel like I was getting stronger as the game progress, just more durable, as I leveled the enemies still took the same amount of time to fight. The story was not at all memorable at all to me, as the main villain just doesn't leave an impression on you, and that unfortunately goes for all the other villains in this game. There was never any cool loot to find , just weapons and armor that, while I admit did look nice, were either weaker than what I already had or just barely an improvement in stats, upgrading what I had a snails pace and never finding anything truly build-defining or cool. All I could see were flaws that made KoA an immensely mid game.When I got the remastered edition of KoA in a Humble Bundle, I figured I could give it a second chance, and boy did this game not deserve it. All the gripes I previously had with the game were still true in this new edition, and nothing was improved except the graphics, and that's not even something I care about. The bugs weren't fixed from the last game, as I had to deal with a character that wouldn't revive after combat and just laid on the floor until i replayed the long, tedious quest over several times.Even if you're a die-hard fan of the original Kingdoms of Amalur with bad enough taste to have given it an 11/10, I absolutely cannot recommend getting the Re-Reckoning edition. Neither the slight improvement in graphics nor the terribly padded Fatesworn DLC justify the repurchase; stay the hell away from Kingdoms of Amalur: Re-Reckoning.

Alright, so all I am going to say about the remaster is that I am aware of all it's issues but in the end the original was still a damn good game. A game which was overshadowed by the time it was released and the company issues surrounding it. Now, let me say why I fully recommend this game and why I feel confident that THQ Nordic isn't simply being lazy. Firstly, this 'remaster' is fairly typical of THQ's tactic when they purchase a new property and release a 'remaster'. What is happening is essentially they are testing the waters to ascertain whether people are still interested in the game and if the feedback is positive enough they'll devote their resources into a proper sequel. Usually these sequels they make are pretty damn good and significant improvements over the original games. (At least in my personal opinion.) So, in summary, I recommend this game due to how good the original was and my confidence in the company to make a damn good sequel should this test go well. ^_^

_childDocuments_.review: A poor effort at bringing the game up to modern standards. Frame rate is absolutely insufferable in some areas paired with the fact that a plethora of new and old bugs are still in the game. The only positives is that Re-reckoning has convenient in-game camera settings (which had to be done using a 3rd party program in the original) and improved loot level scaling. The biggest addition in the base game is the very hard difficulty, the original game got extremely easy after you built your character up. Very hard aims to amp up the difficulty, but does so in the most mundane, lazy way possible and (in my opinion) is actually a hindrance to an otherwise enjoyable game. What changes does very hard bring, does it change the enemy ai to make them more unpredictable, or add new attacks? No one of that, all it does is multiply enemy health pools and damage, as well as increase the level cap that zones and enemies will scale to the player. Very hard ironically makes the game very hard to actually enjoy because every encounter will be stretched out, you'll end up just dodging the same attacks over and over again until you've won the fight, It plays the exact same as normal and hard does, except fights last longer. The negatives outweigh the positives, stay away from this at least until it's fixed, if it ever is.

_childDocuments_.review: This was the first game I helped Kickstart, and its been on my hard drive continually since it was originally released, I enjoy it that much. I wasn't an MMO player then, and I'm really still not a committed one, but you can see where 38 Studios (the original dev) was going with this title, and maybe that helped push me into the MMO world a little bit. TL:DR - This is a remaster of an older title which really didn't need much remastering! The original title was tremendous fun, well-written, well-designed and well-produced (which is a rarity in my experience).My first playthrough was the hardest path - a pure mage build - but I finished the game with it and had so much fun I kept coming back even though there's nothing procedural about this game (only the treasures are random). The game is very well planned-out and the progression is beautifully balanced for any class. Not to mention the writing is top-notch, although the plot is a bit thin, but the writing is definitely worth it and the voice acting is, imho, better than average for a title like this one, especially given the developer's plan to evolve this into a full-scale MMO. It would have been easy to skimp on the voice talent as so many others have done. So, recommend? Absolutely. If you're a fan of ARPGs in general, or well-designed and well-produced ones in particular, yes, pick this one up.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game just a few days ago, played it for over 30 hours, beat it, finished most of the big quest-lines with one or two remaining, and my biggest compliment I could ever give to this game is that it's just... fine. Don't get me wrong, getting me to waste that many hours in the span of just 5 days has already proven that the game has done something right to get me hooked on it, but sadly, for every right thing this game managed to do, it also did many things wrong, which led to many frustrating moments that could have been easily avoided.First, the elephant in the room: Now,:This game does not respect your time. Even though 30 hours is short for an average RPG, my adventure through the Faelands felt dreadfully long. The moment I beat the very underwhelming final boss, I even questioned myself whether or not this time was even well spent for me. Many hours were wasted traversing an empty, boring world by foot because there is no mount in this game. 90% of the quests are MMO level fetch quests that are just extremely boring and tedious. Even the main quest, DLC, and faction questline are guilty of this. Just when the quest was starting to get interesting and you were just starting to feel invested in it, the game would force you to activate like 5 stones that span across the entire continent. Backtracking, whether in the "open world" or inside a dungeon, appears a lot, which is expected from Oblivion's designer.The designers were obsessed with quantity, and it ended up sucking all the fun out of doing a quest. If the world was trimmed by half, if the number of quests was cut to just like one third, this could have been an incredible experience. One of the highest points in the game for me was when I could cut the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stuff out and just get immensely invested in a questline. And for me, that questline was Dead Kel. The main quest and some faction questlines do have many noticeable moments, but the Dead Kel quest was just super well done from the moment it started to when it ended.When I first glanced upon this game to finish the opening sequence, my first impression was that this was Fable met Elder Scrolls, two of my favorite RPGs of all time. But at the end of the day, it didn't have the interactivity and sandbox-ness nature of the world of The Elder Scrolls, nor the humor and charm of Fable. Kingdom of Amalur tried to be both and ended up with none.This has been a very critical review of this game, and for all the negative things I have said about it, I still had many memorable and fun moments that came from the game. And for that reason, my review will be recommended as long as you grab it on sale, even though I would have picked mixed if that was an option.  ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: A steady stream of updates has been happening, and while I still have some crashes, it's become less frequent and makes me confident of future stability. I'm changing to Recommended, as I said I would. The better leveling, better loot scaling, added difficulty all combine to make this a really fun open world RPG that is just absolutely MASSIVE. The story still reeeeeks of cliches left and right, but now the gameplay lives up to the potential of the fantastic combat system.Was excited immediately cause the original I felt was so close to being good. This remaster is unfortunately VERY buggy at the moment. I hope they will patch it up speedily and stop all the crashing. The difficulty has been upped and the XP has been smoothed out and the loot is better scaled. That said, it looks near identical to the original, so yes the people whining about the graphical 'update' are correct, but that's not really what I was looking for anyway. The game is no longer 'too easy' if you play on 'very hard' mode. In fact, I've dropped down to hard a couple times just to beat some of the bosses... tho granted I was underleveled. I think THQ did a good job identifying a title that could be quite good with just a little push in the right direction... and they've done that. What I can't get past is the CONSTANT crashing and bugs every few minutes. Especially in an older game where autosave is more sporadic and it's built for controller so you can't mash F5 every ten seconds... it's infuriating. Hopefully they'll smooth that out soon. When they do, I'll recommend it for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: I have plenty of hours in the original game, but haven't beaten it yet. Had laptop issues back in the day so I stopped playing. Decided to get this because of the discount from owning the original version and the hope that I would get the best Kingdom of Amalur experience. Disappointed with the final product, although still enjoying it. Biggest issues:1. File size is significantly larger than the original game. Again, considering how little has changed, this is annoying. 2. The graphics settings have very few options. This was an issue with the original game, but you would expect much more from a remaster. 3. Strange bugs and glitches which didn't seem to exist in the original game (I could be remembering wrong). I would see distant character models floating in a T-Pose until I get closer and then they fall down and their physics start working. Happens very rarely, though. Most of the bugs and glitches are just visual and aren't game-breaking, but again, you'd expect more from a remaster. 4. Barely any changes. Not much of a remaster, more like a re-release. Would have been much better if it were released as a free update for those who already own the original game like it was for Skyrim Special Edition. Skyrim Special Edition is a vastly superior "Remaster", yet it was free for those who owned the Legendary Edition on Steam. I do understand that corporate changes are behind the pricing model, but this relates to my complaints about barely having any changes. If they wanted to re-release it as their own product, much more should have been done to make it an attractive option for those who want to buy it again. Some positive things: 1. There is a new customizable camera option which I think is really helpful. Has FOV slider as well. Tweaking the camera and how it moves really improved my experience of playing the game. I remember how the camera was a bit wild and annoying at times in the original game. My preferred setting is to disable camera smoothing, follow, and enemy focus while keeping the camera height and distance reasonably high. Have much more control over the camera and positioning this way. 2. Enemy and loot scaling has been adjusted to follow character level. This was an issue in the original game where you would quickly out-level the region you're in making the enemies very weak and loot useless to you. 3. I didn't realize this at first, but the game has a new "Very Hard" difficulty setting which I found to be really enjoyable to play. It's actually challenging and requires strategy, precision and timing. The most notable difference is the increased aggression from the enemy AI. There's a smaller window for offence, you can't just mash buttons.However, this mode is not for everyone. The biggest issue is how high the enemy HP has become, making combat take longer than it needs to be and it can end up feeling very tedious at times. But for me, it's just the right amount of tedious considering how much more careful and prepared you have to be for combat. Makes things feel more tense and rewarding. I don't remember the original game being difficult, I hardly ever died even at the highest difficulty. Died a lot in this new one, which mostly felt like fair deaths because of me making bad choices in combat. Later on in the game, it becomes easy again, though, especially if you build characters that have crafting skills. Your high-leveled character can still sweep the floor with most of the enemies later on. 4. Apparently, the game has more skill slots for you to bind skills. But I immediately played with a controller so I didn't realize this.From here you can see that my complaints with the game are mostly technical stuff and the actual "remastering" of the game. However, when it comes to the game itself, it's still a very fun Action RPG game with solid combat. The build variety and flexibility adds so many different approaches to how you would play the game. The story is okay, nothing special, although the whole Fate concept is kind of cool. All in all, this is a bare bones remaster of a great game. If you loved the original game, the quality of life changes made here would really improve your enjoyment of the game. I actually believe that overall, Re-Reckoning is a better product than the original, despite its technical issues. However, if you got bored with the original game, there's nothing here to see, really. If you've never played the game before, play it, it's overall a very fun game if you completely disregard the "remaster" status. And as I stated before, the Re-Reckoning version is  slightly better than the original version.Edit: Just started playing the game again recently and the performance seems fine. One of the complaints I had early on was the performance, but it looks like it's all been sorted out. So, performance is no longer an issue. The rest of my points remain unchanged.

_childDocuments_.review: I have bought KoA:R multiple times, originally on EA: Origin and then again when it was on sale on Steam.   I was happy to see that THQ Nordic had finally done something with their purchase of the IP.   I know that there are people upset that unlike Skyrim's remaster it wasn't free to prior owners, but at 60% off for current owners (at least on Steam) it was a pretty good deal.  I went ahead and picked up the Fate Edition as I thought having the soundtrack would be nice and the future DLC (though it sounds like it will be short) will still be a nice bonus, and still it is worth the asking price for 4k and some slight bug fixes.   I would have liked to seen more Quality of Life changes but all in all the game was pretty solid when it came out and honestly I didn't think then, nor now that there really needed to be a ton of changes made to the game over all.   I think it is worth throwing some money THQ's way in hopes of seeing more future DLC or even KoA2 one day.   I think the game is still rock solid and in the 4 1/2 hours I have played the remastered version I haven't ran into any bugs or crashes.   Would I have paid $55, having already owned the original (multiple times), no but it was more than worth it for the discounted price.  Some people just want things given to them.    I agree THQ didn't do a lot for the remaster, but then again they didn't have to do anything and could have just sat on the IP and let it go to waste.  At the end of the day, no one is forcing anyone to buy the remastered version and other than 4k, some bug fixes opening up access to the future DLC and at least to me what appears to be much stabler performance on SSD and quicker load times you could still play the old copy being fully happy with your old purchase.   So for those that are on the fence read more about what it is before you let the mixed reviews turn you off.  It is worth the money if you loved the original and want to support hopefully the IP going ahead further in the future and seeing some performance and slight graphical gains.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah yes, Kingdoms of Amalur: ResellingI had such a crush on Alyn Shir when I first played this back in the day. Given the chance I would do unholy things to her… Agarth can wreck me too.Kingdoms of Amalur: Re-Reckoning is a blast from the past. It’s like World of Warcraft meets God of War. It is the Western equivalent of Dragon Quest: a colourful and nostalgic fantasy RPG from an earlier age of gaming. If any of those comparisons interest you, it is absolutely worth your time. The combat and the atmosphere... Its like straight out of a Tolkien novel. The world design is so magical and the soundtrack makes it even better. This is a good game that suffers from a lack of variety, poor side missions and repetitive bloat that makes it great to start but very tough to finish. It's not the worst thing that's happened to Rhode Island but it's probably the most 7/10 game of all time. When it came out there were much better options like Skyrim and Dragon's Dogma. It's worth playing if you like the genre but don't expect it to wow you. Felt a lot like a single player MMO in terms of quest design and environments.Despite the MMO-like gameplay, Kingdoms of Amalur wasn't planned as one. It was meant to be the single-player prequel to an MMO codenamed Project Copernicus with an epic backstory spanning millennia. It's like the most generic MMORPG possible was turned into a single-player game. It's a lot of fun, while suffering from old style game mechanics but it's part of the pleasure I suppose if you have any nostalgia for that era.Yes at first it appears like they spent more time on coming up with the new title than actually remastering the game, but they actually made a lot of changes. They're just more under the hood and quality of life changes as opposed to big overhauls. The remaster has slightly better graphics and includes all of the original DLC. The new Fatesworn DLC will only work with Re-Reckoning as well. They also changed how areas level with you to make it more dynamic or like how loot is generated and how levels of mobs in areas are calculated. They added a new difficulty, and a lot of smaller changes and details that add up to something better than the original. It's the little things that make a difference.Amalur isn't hard to get into at all. It's one of those entry-level RPGs that anyone can play. You talk to NPCs in villages and cities and accept quests from anyone with a giant gold ! over their heads. They'll send you around the current zone or a neighboring one, sometimes into linear dungeons to clear, and then you return to them for the reward on top of all the loot you picked up along the way. It's a huge world with a ton of side content and multiple factions to join alongside the main storyline.You also have complete freedom to build your character however you want. There are seven Destiny class lines to explore, each of which represents a different playstyle. I did Might/Sorcery (a battlemage tank) on my first playthrough, for example. Now I'm looking at Finesse/Sorcery (a glass cannon rogue) next.The combat is bloody hack-and-slash action in the vein of Devil May Cry, God of War, and Darksiders. There are weapons ranging from traditional swords and bows to twin scythes called faeblades and magical discs of doom called chakrams which turn you into Axel from Kingdom Hearts. There's even a Spartan Rage-style powerup called Reckoning mode that slows time and grants you extra EXP as you execute enemies in especially brutal ways. It's awesome.I played this remaster with my kids and we all loved it because it's so self-aware of its own cheesiness and has familiar themes reminiscent of swashbuckling nonsense from the last century. The hammy voice acting is also superbly hilarious given the cheesy script, it's a real hoot for sure. Definitely not flawless and definitely not for everyone. The story has neat ideas but is underwhelming, a vast majority of the quests are MMO fare, the zones can be dull to get around it, and enemies are overused. But despite all that, I still enjoyed it. Playing it is like eating plain tortilla chips. It's not a particularly life-changing experience, and I never find myself thinking "wow I really crave plain tortilla chips right now". However, sometimes I find myself with a bowl of plain tortilla chips in front of me. I eat chip after chip thinking "I should probably go grab some salsa or queso. Maybe heat up a can of refried beans or something". But I don't. Amalur is a difficult game to find time for in my backlog, but whenever I want to just chill for a few hours a bit less than sober it's a solid choice.For all its flaws, I still don't think Kingdoms of Amalur is a bad game. But I did start thinking of it as the Western equivalent of Dragon Quest. This is the opposite of Soulsborne games. In something like Amalur, you're not being challenged at all; you're there for the mindless hack-and-slash action and traditional fantasy setting. It's video game comfort food.In conclusion, Kingdoms of Amalur: Re-Reckoning is an artifact of days gone by. It can be both refreshingly simple and frustratingly outdated. But for all its flaws, this is still a really fun game. I hope the devs extend the good game concepts to a new game with similar elements in the future.Finally, remember guys. The Maid of Windemere did nothing wrong.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Update:  I still love it!  I have not had a single issue with a crash or bugging game mechanics.  I can honestly say this game runs better than it did for me originally and looks sharper and cleaner.  I am loving it and can not wait to finish the story and get the next chapter.  I keep reading all of these bad reviews due to performance and crashes and I have yet to have one and I never really had one in the original either.  Not sure what those folks are doing or trying to run, but...no issues for me thus far.If you enjoyed the original, you will love the remaster.  I owned and played the original back when the studio responsible was promising the MMO version of this world.  I loved the look and play mechanics. The graphics at the time were, to me, gorgeous and stylized.  I loved the look and wanted to see more of the world.  Unfortunately, the studio folded and had some issues with a certain state and the MMO was never realized and the single player game was forgotten about.  Until now.  Thankfully a publisher is picking it up and have the intent to add to the universe and hopefully utilize the IP for even more.  I owned the original and when Steam acquired it with some bonus materials, I bought it again.  Now, I purchased it yet again for the remaster.  The remastered graphics do not add things that were not in the original, instead what they do is sharpen and clean them up.  The colors seem to be more vibrant and the details seem to stand out more.  The main thing I noticed was the improved UI elements and how they look.  Everything just seems cleaner.  The fonts have been changed and enlarged and some of the onscreen help pop ups seem to have different wordings now.  It just comes off as cleaner looking and I did notice a difference despite what a lot of folks are saying about it.  The game also runs just fine for me.  It runs the same as the original did for.  Smooth.  I am not sure what is going on with everyone else having frame rate issues and poor performance, but I have yet to encounter such an issue...it feels the same.  On the actual game play side, the changes they have made come in the form of slower level progression and loot scaling to you as well as the enemies.  It really gives it a modern feel and I am loving the random loot drops from some of these chests early on.  Definitely nice improvement there.  All in all, it is a very well done remaster.  You can only do so much with the existing game engine, but I believe they cleaned it up and made it pop a bit more.  It looks like a modern RPG/MMO with a stylized graphic set.   If you want to continue playing in this universe in the future and possibly get more DLC for it, you are going to have to upgrade to the remastered version.  I really don't think they will update and patch the old version.  For that reason alone, pick up a copy now while they have the huge discount for previous owners.  Bottom line is this is well done, it runs well for me (and I don't have a high end PC or card right now) and it  opens up the chance to get more content or games out of this IP.  Do it!

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this "remaster" simply because I have a certain fondness for the original and getting it for 60% off felt fair enough. I find Kingdoms of Amalur hard to describe - it invokes a peculiar feeling that's difficult to put into words. It's not what I'd call visually breathtaking, but I like the aesthetic and the environments. The story reads like generic fantasy, but has some interesting concepts and you can tell that an effort was put forth to make it stand out from other games in the genre. The soundtrack was done by the legendary Grant Kirkhope and feels like a departure from much of his work, but it's very pleasant.What really makes this game stand out to me is the combat. It doesn't have the complexity of something like a Platinum game, but as RPGs go, it's far more satisfying than something like Skyrim. You have three basic classes ("Destinies" in-game) that are like roots that branch out into more complex ones. You start with the Warrior, Rogue, and Mage Destinies and you can probably guess what they do without me telling you - Warriors use big swords and hammers to slash and smash, Rogues have daggers and are better at stealth, and Mages cast spells and use elemental staves to get the job done. As you progress, you can unlock Destinies that are combinations of the aforementioned classes. Each Destiny has different skill trees and uses different combinations of weapons, so it's fun experimenting with each of them to find one that suits your playstyle. Along with combat skills, there are passive ones such as Lockpicking and Persuasion if you'd like your character to have sticky fingers or a silver tongue.From a technical perspective, the game runs fine on my ageing PC (GTX 980, i5-4670, 8GB RAM) and so far I haven't experienced any crashes or bugs, aside from some graphical ones that I believe were in the original release as well. On that note, there don't seem to have been any major graphical changes that I can notice, but I haven't played the original game in quite some time.If you're an action RPG fan, I'd say it's worth checking out. I have the most fun with this game when I've had a long day at work and just want to stop thinking and slay some monsters.Oh, and if you're like me and care about this sort of thing, they did include the armor inspired by Shepard from Mass Effect along with a ton of other weapons and armor that I believe were preorder exclusive.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game when it first came out on the xbox 360. If you asked me back then if I recommended it, I probably would have said no. There were many other Fantasy RPGs out at the time that were immensely better than this game and still are(Elder scrolls, Fable, Witcher... ETC). However, in this modern age of complex, hard to "pickup" RPGs with overbearing microtransactions, this remaster felt like a breath of fresh air for me.The game is well optimized and will run on just about anything, you pay one price and you get access to a solid 50-60 hours of decent open world RPG gameplay. About 2/3rds of the quests feel boring and uninspired, they are the basic "go here and grab/kill this thing and come back" type of gameplay. Because of this, I can see why many of the people on here are not recommending this game when there are so many better options out there. The other 1/3rd of quests are actually really well done. The faction quests connect well to the overarching story of Amalur and each have their own unique culture and storyline that feels well thought out. The different environments and enemies are varied enough to keep the interest of the player throughout the game.In terms of the combat mechanics, the game does a great job of hooking the player early on, but the limited weapon variety and low amount of spell options means you will start getting bored about halfway through the game. Luckily, the game lets you reset all your skills whenever you want for a vary low amount of gold. Meaning you can experience all the game has to offer in just one play through, although this means there is not much depth in terms of replay-ability.Overall, if you are tired of overbearing/timeconsuming modern RPGs and have already played many of the classic fantasy RPGs like Skyrim or Fable, this could be a good option if you are looking for "more of the same thing." However, if you are searching for a game with "new" mechanics that you have not experienced before with highly dynamic gameplay and deeply thought out story/quest lines, I would highly suggest you search elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've never played the original, this is absolutely worth it. If you have the original with all the DLC, there's no reason to buy this. I loved the original but never got the DLC, so I figured I'd give this a try.It's 98% the same game as Reckoning. The only noticeable change seems to be the way enemies scale to your level in a more fluid manner, which is a nice improvement but nothing revolutionary. It also feels like they tweaked the lockpicking and dispelling minigames to be slightly more forgiving, but that's a very slight change if any. That being said, there wasn't a lot that needed changing. The graphics still hold up very well, especially the character designs and visual effects. The music and voice acting are great, and the plot is fantastically detailed and well fleshed out for what ended up being a one-shot game franchise. Combat is refreshingly visceral and fluid, with attacks and combos having a very satisfying weight to them, and the three different specializations all have some fun, distinct mechanics.The one aspect that's probably aged the worst is the level design, which clearly shows the MMO aspirations of the studio - most areas are basically boxes for the player to run around in with things to click on and enemies to fight. They're pretty-looking boxes, certainly, but compared to other open world games it feels kind of flat.It's definitely disappointing they didn't do a little more with this re-release. The crafting and character advancement systems are a little obtuse and could do with a bit of balancing and streamlining. Character skills vary between potentially game-breaking (blacksmithing, sagecrafting) and virtually useless (lockpicking, stealth). All of these are fairly minor problems though, and at the end of the day it was and remains a very fun hack-and-slash RPG that will provide plenty of hours of enjoyment.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a weird one, but for all its flaws and dated aspects, it is surprisingly charming.The first thing you need to understand is that this is from the era of games when Skyrim was a big new thing. If you try to compare this to something modern like Breath of the Wild, it just won't hold up. That's the raw truth of the matter.But for the time it came from, the game has aged remarkably well- better than Skyrim has, though that's from someone who's soured on Skyrim a lot over the last almost-a-decade: You're still mostly checklist-questing, caring about objective markers you can knock off more than actually what you're supposed to be accomplishing, but the combat system is actually pretty fun, the world is, if not actively engaging, at least thought-provoking, and when they present you with an actual character who's important to the story, they tend to be reasonably charming and interesting to have around. The game has character, and the setting is interesting for how it tries to explore the idea of destiny, and how a chaotic player character can utterly shatter that.But combat is fun, the world is beautiful, thanks to some strong art direction and a willingness to just make the whole thing much larger-than-life. And, you know, because we're talking it's immediate superiorities to Skyrim, it doesn't run on spit, prayers and glitches, but actually seems to work most of the time. It does stutter occasionally and almost feels like it's about to glitch out, then corrects itself every once in a blue moon, but honestly, the game seems more stable than most of the open world RPGs of its era.The game is dated, but it holds up surprisingly well, and I'm having fun with it. More than I expected to, actually.
