_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has never put any time into the original game, despite owning it for literally years, I am astonished by the fact that I slept on this game until the re-release.The story is pretty generic in most instances, especially the core plot. It begins with the usual "You must be the legendary chosen one the world has been waiting for" trope and that is the thread that connects just about all the major sub-plots together in a fairly lackluster way. But there is a huge asterisk to this. If you're like me, most of the time spent playing will be doing as many side-quests as you can. Thankfully, it's clear that the vast majority of the side-quests were designed and written with heart and soul. Some of them are simple, and a little generic but a lot of the larger quest lines are actually really quite interesting and well-written. This has allowed me the chance to really sink into the game, and over time has made me more and more interested in the overall world building, which is incredibly robust. You can chat with almost every NPC and they have plenty to say on a bunch of topics, offering their perspective on the matter. It allows the world to feel populated by people rather than just blank NPCs and allows you to learn more about the world with everyone you speak to. Barring some small issues I have pertaining to how the camera pans in lieu of a lock-on system and when you're approaching a loading zone to a new area, the game play and combat are as smooth as butter. The combat especially has a learning curve to it which really surprised me. When I started the game I jumped right into Very Hard difficulty because I've beaten Dark Souls, and was surprised to find that the game was ruthless about kicking my teeth in. I felt like I was shedding Health Potions like a second skin, and for some time I thought that it was just the way they balance Very Hard mode. However, with more time and plenty more experience under my belt, I realize that the combat is about learning enemy patterns and attacks, and utilizing every tool you have at your disposal for both offense and defense. There are combo attacks that are difficult to simply dodge, for example, but much easier to dodge and/or parry. The combat looks clunky on paper for an RPG, but it has a sort of Devil May Cry combo system and each weapon feels completely unique, allowing for a huge variety of play styles based entirely on personal preference. Once you get the nuance of combat down, you'll feel rewarded against just about every enemy with parries, counters, and the such. An integral part of any RPG, the game can fall flat on its face if the character progression is really bad for whatever reason. It's safe to say that KoA doesn't have that problem. It uses a Classic WoW sort of talent tree system with 3 major trees to build into, Might, Finesse, and Sorcery. Might is your typical melee warrior in big armor swinging heavy weapons that do big damage. Finesse is your rogue build focused on stealth and tricks rather than brute force, and finally Sorcery is your Mage build. You get 3 talent points on each level-up and can spend them however you see fit. Just keep in mind that each tier of talents requires a certain amount of talents in that tree to unlock. So if you want to invest into all 3 trees you will end up in a "jack of all trades, master of none" sort of situation, which isn't at all a bad thing. Personally I have experimented with a hybrid Might/Sorcery build, as well as a straight Sorcery and Might build and I personally find the no-frills Might build focused on Long Sword/Great Sword to be the best for me. Magic has a tendency to feel very underwhelming and a lot of the spells feel really more focused on utility rather than raw throughput. However, using them in tandem with the Mage-style weapons feels really good and has a flow to it that makes me believe the developers really took time and care with designing how all the pieces fit together. The combat is probably the game's strongest appeal next to its world-building for any story-focused lore buffs. So I wanted to touch on this because some people may find the inventory management tedious. Each stack of items you have takes up an inventory space which can feel very restrictive. You can unlock a personal stash to store items you want to save, but that's hidden behind a wall of side-quests a few hours into the game, at least. In the meantime, every reagent you pick up and potion you brew takes up inventory space in stacks up to ten. For example, if you have one healing potion or 10 healing potions, the stack takes up 1 inventory slot. If you have 10 potions and you pick up potion 11 that creates a new stack in your inventory and now occupies 2 total inventory spaces. Each weapon and piece of armor takes up 1 inventory slot, as well as books, repair kits, and so on, so inventory management is something you'll need to be conscious of throughout the game, taking frequent trips to a merchant to empty bags, or constantly being breaking down junk, which is tedious since there is no streamlined way of doing it. The gold-making feels like most RPGs where you start out flat broke, needing to really be stingy with your gold for the first few hours, before suddenly reaching the point where you're selling so much gear you don't need and looting so much gold in the world that you couldn't spend all your money if you tried, reaching a point where gold is basically trivial and you may as well be made of gold coins. This is compounded further by the fact that the game throws so much loot at you that you'll almost never need to buy gear from merchants, and even if you see an upgrade you're considering, it's highly likely that after doing a couple of quests and exploring the world, you'll find something way better anyway. Point is, after about 10 hours you should never feel wanting for gold or gear. KoA is a ridiculously impressive title well worth the money you'll drop on it if you're a big fan of single-player RPGs with rich lore and really polished combat with virtually complete freedom in how your player develops over the course of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT 9-13-20: If I could choose a neutral rating I would. It seems they fixed none of the bugs from the original, despite being well documented for years, and they actually added some new ones. On top of that the optimization is atrocious and lags in some parts of the game especially the Teeth of Naros dlc. Will they fix these bugs? I don't know but obviously I hope they do. On the other hand we got some massive quality of life improvements over the original, the biggest one being a new very hard difficulty. They also adjusted loot and enemy scaling to make it much harder to outlevel areas, and lowered the exp you get so you don't level up too fast. Lastly we got fov and other camera options. If the new features I just listed don't interest you, then stick with the original. Otherwise buy this if you will be willing to put up with the bugs, and then buy only on sale 50% or more.EDIT: Doing some more looking, it seems the vast majority of bugs that have been around since the original release have not been fixed, such as going permanently invisible (just don't save while stealthed), and the Battle Frenzy not resetting bug, and more. There's a chance they may fix them in the future, but they were common knowledge for 8 years and THQN didn't fix them before release so it really looks like they don't care. It's still worth it I feel because it's a pretty solid game regardless.KoA is a great game and this release is worth it whether you've never played it before and thus are paying full price, or already owned the EA-published version and get this on sale. To me the new very hard difficulty alone is worth it. No longer can you mindlessly button mash the whole game on hard; now you have to actually think and dodge/parry. They've also reduced the exp you get so you aren't max level halfway through the game. Enemy and loot scaling are also calculated each time you enter an area instead of being locked forever on first visit.Pretty much all the negative reviews are by entitled, spoiled brats who are whining they aren't getting this for free. News flash: THQN made no money off the original release and need some way to make their money back. They aren't rich like Bethesda or CDPR. The other complaint is that the graphics upgrade is hardly noticeable. The game's art style still looks good today so there wasn't much work needed.My only real complaint is that they didn't update the keyboard controls. How it is now you have to use 1-0 to select a skill, then RMB to use the skill, then press another number key if you want a different skill. Why can't the pressing of the number key activate the skill? Why can't there be two keyboard buttons to use your two weapons instead of needing a specific key to swap them? Keyboard is still useable, but as it is now a controller is the best way to play.Buy this game!

Which this remaster has done. I find everyone saying it's the same game to be incredibly disingenuous and frankly an outright lie. Is it the same game visually? Pretty much! Has it been completely rebalanced? Also yes! Did they ever say they were doing more than that? NOPE! They have been very specific and upfront about what they are doing with this remaster.There is also a great jokester saying 8 years still can't rebind keys. I think he doesn't know how to use a menu you can rebind keys in the first release too.To other people saying they don't notice a difference with graphics? What are you expecting? The game has a distinct art style that is timeless there isn't much they could do without completely REBUILDING all of the models in the game. And even if they did that if they stayed faithful to the art style it wouldn't drastically change.Overall I love the story/setting/art/gameplay of this game and I hope enough people will recognize that this game is well worth the 40 dollars (or 16 if you own the original) for all the of the original content and dlc.

_childDocuments_.review: Dear THQ and all companies associated with the re-release of this game,Please take this review as a token of my deepest apologies.  I played the original Amalur, didn't like it, and wrote a thumbs-down bad review here on Steam.  In a nutshell, I complained that the lore was boring, the story didn't make sense, and the gameplay ridiculously easy.But then I picked up Re-Reckoning as part of a bundle.  I've finished the main story and all the DLCs except Fatesworn, which I admit is trying my patience a bit due to the repetitiveness of the penultimate missions.But I realize that my prior review was unfair.  This game is profoundly entertaining. I have had a fantastic time in the game world!  I've come to realize that it was me, not you.  Maybe it was bad timing, or perhaps I just wasn't emotionally ready to engage the game.  But with hindsight, I can now admit that I was wrong.I put the game in very hard mode, and the combat became challenging.  The story makes sense and is compelling with a great denouement.  I enjoyed every one of my 96 hours in the game.Sure, I can be a little critical of a few things.  I don't think I fully listened to a single line of dialog in the game.  Although, to be honest, the only games where I have listened thoroughly to dialog are the Witcher and Mass Effect series.   And some of the enemies were damage sponges (which, if I got really irritated, I solved by simply lowering the difficulty level).  And yes, the dungeons are a little repetitive, what with their combat rooms all tied together by hallways.But, what a blast I had exploring the game, upgrading my character, seeing the beautiful vistas, and slaying the bad guys.  For ARPG lovers, this is the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: So far so good. Don't listen to the others, the game runs at higher resolutions (including ultrawide, I'm running it at 3440x1440). The anti-aliasing methods suck (only FXAA is available). Do what I did and turn AA off, and use supersampling, which IS an option.The texture resolutions and lighting appear improved. The game looks pretty gorgeous for what is a dressed up 2012 remaster. Don't expect modern graphics otherwise.Framerate could be better but overall I'm not dropping below 60FPS on a 1080ti. 3440x1440 with supersampling at 1.25-1.5x resolution. Indoors I hit my refresh rate of 100 fps and outdoors it varies between 60-80 fps.The FOV slider is a god send and honestly makes the game a refreshing experience visually.I'm playing on Very Hard difficulty, the new difficulty, and with all the tweaks they've done so far it's a decent challenge.If you enjoyed the original, it's a no brainer.

_childDocuments_.review: This game deserves to be noticed and experienced! If you are a fan of huge open world RPG's with so many dungeons and things to do, discover, and fight for, then don't hesitate; this is a game for you! Originally, this game came out at a bad time (Dragon's Dogma came out at the same time and others) and went unnoticed mostly. But I played it on the PS3, and got it on the pc as well. I had lot's of fun with the different fighting styles and the huge amount of equipment to discover, not counting all the crafting you can do in this one. One problem with the original game was that you could access quite a lot of big areas at a low level and set the difficulty level for the rest of the game in them so that they quickly became to easy. In this remastered, this has been solved as the difficulty is set to your level every time you enter these regions. My monitor is able to display 4k and I do find improvement with the visual and the frame rate, making this upgrade really enjoyable. The loot also has been adapted to your level and playstyle. Considering that this remastered also contains all the  original dlcs, I find the price to be quite fair knowing how many hours I will spend on KOA-re-reckoning! Plus you have a descent story as well! Final word on this: don't miss out on this excellent CRPG!

_childDocuments_.review: It's the same game that you nostalgia so hard about, minus the enwrapping EA tendrils. Pretty much a 1:1 re-release, but for some rebalancing and camera/UI tweaks. Buy it only to reaffirm your love for an IP that was cut short before it had its full due, perhaps with an eye toward its future expansion (and maybe sequelization) by THQ. _childDocuments_.review: Yet another game that I wish steam had a "Maybe" rating for.If you haven't played the original, it had a very rocky development, and as a result the game feels unfinished at times, and definitely gets worse the more it goes on. The amount of things to do and see per zone sees drastic decreases, majorly hyped bosses end up being pretty much the same as the regular enemies you've been fighting, the story unravels itself more and more, and the game doesn't have a great sense of progression. That being said, it's easy to see why this is a cult classic, as there's a lot of potential to be seen and the core combat is quite fun - it very well could be up your ally.What makes me mark this as a No though is specific to the re-release: Although there are some great improvements over the original including ultra wide resolution support and fixes to the worst of the camera issues, as well as some improvements to textures, lighting, etc; major bugs from the original game are still here and not fixed, and what's worse, the re-release has new bugs entirely. Some are harmless like the engine not understanding how to properly render basically any fae chest or a number of interior world geometries, but often they are a real problem causing quests to completely break. There's also the fact the game runs like absolute garbage for really no reason - at times (especially in the DLC areas) I would get single digit frame rates with the camera aimed in toward a level, even with an extremely low resolution and post processing off. The game was also seriously unstable for me and would crash literally every single time I attempted to sell more than 20 items at a time. It would also randomly crash when attempting to load zones or auto-save, and at one point near the end of the game I got stuck in a loading loop were the game would finish loading and then immediately start again on the first frame of me being in a new area. As with most of this game, these problems got much worse the longer I played.If these issues are fixed, it very well could be worth your time if you like wonky niche hack'n'slash RPGs, but overall finishing this unfortunately started to feel like a chore for me near the end - exacerbated quite a bit from the technical issues.

_childDocuments_.review: Generally beautiful game, there were some utterly gut-wrenching moments (House of Sorrows??? Made me cry). Combat is extremely finicky, enemies can easily continue their ults that knock you off balance when a single hit from them interrupts your own. Ridiculous bugs breaking the gameplay (the book collection one that means if I sell them by accident I will be unable to finish this quest???). I will have to go back and undo another six hours of played time as I foolishly thought while doing the Chaos portals quest that I could complete them in one go, only to find out that it won't register more than five at a time. What an idiot I was to think that this game might be set up for such a thing...It drags in places, to be honest. There were several times when I was just rapidly skipping through parts just so I could move on. Also, let me be clear: there is no reason why you should not be able to teleport from the Dead Kel DLC worldspace to the main worldspace after the end of the questline. It's a ridiculous and tedious limitation. None of the other DLCs have this limitation. Also, the storage in your house being maximum 300 and not being able to be upgraded when there are so many uniques to collect and books in the game is bizarre.

_childDocuments_.review: Performance is a little shaky, and it doesn't seem like it ought to be for what's on screen, but the game is actually a lot of fun. I bought the original when it first came out and I never got into it because it was too easy and I felt like I was being punished for taking the time to craft powerful weapons as I tore through everything and never received a challenge which made the game a chore, but this remake added a "Very Hard" mode and it feels much more balanced. I've been having a lot of fun working my way through the game and even some of the small things that irked me like how linear it is, and that empty mmo feeling it kind of has have grown on me. There's a pretty insane amount of content, the combat is satisfying and feels fair, I'm a fan of the art style and the systems are pretty deep and offer a lot of customization and replay value. The only real knock I have is that the performance should be better as it looks basically identical to the original game but runs at less than half the framerate. Aside from that, it's a blast and definitely worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: The old style play aside (The whole almost nwn / baldurs gate style of look/play), the graphics are pretty top notch. Rich story line.Easy to use controls.Decent graphics.Mostly well done cut scenes (there are occasionally times where they glitch out camera angle wise)Decent leveling system (Though it honestly stops short at 41 leaving you less than halfway done with your characters skills and abilities, no idea why devs do this in any game. The graphics are good for the intended design and there are lots of awe inspiring areas. The npcs are fleshed out with conversations and such (at least the quest givers). Level cap for no apparent reason.I don't really get how some of the abilities work, it would most likely work well with a game pad.The third person style used is reminiscent of 90's to early 2000's games (This isn't always a bad thing)All in all I can't really find much that's wrong with this one other than some basic cosmetics. name: If Found...
detailed_description: If Found… is a game about searching for connection. On December 31st 1993 in the crumbling ruins of a mansion on Achill Island, Kasio destroys her diary. It tells the story of her return home to the West of Ireland, her conflict with her family, the friends she makes, and the challenges she goes through. Everything leads to this night when a black hole will destroy the entire world. Where did it come from? Is there any way to stop it? With brand new gameplay mechanics, beautiful hand-drawn art, and a stunning soundtrack, players will relive Kasio's experiences and see the moments both happy and painful that make up the month of December 1993. Features include: awkward crushes, the planet Jupiter, many kisses, a punk concert, confusion, happiness, a cute dog, and a break in.

_childDocuments_.review: I was never a big fan of clothes. When I went shopping, I would look with a hint of revulsion at the clothes piling up in the basket: they belonged to someone, but not to me. It should be no surprise, then, that I came to despise anything to do with fashion and expression through it. At most, I could understand wearing items indicative of your hobbies, like band merch or art from video games, but anything else was beyond me. Clothing seemed to me a deception, something you wore to conceal who you really were.  Then, something happened. After a conversation with a friend, I began questioning my own identity. In three weeks, all the characteristics that previously defined me were blurred. As my mind raced over past events, I realized that, for years, I had had a feeling of something not being quite right. I had been a walking question mark. In that moment, I understood I was not preordained to forever be the quiet person in the corner, the one whose inexpressive attire blended in with the world around them. I could see a path where there had been none. In , 23-year-old Kasio flees home. Kasio is trans and has recently been confronted by her mother, who will have none of it. “Look, you’re going to have to face the facts. Settle down with a nice woman and get your life in order,” she berates in an early scene. Taking place in 90s Ireland,  transports us to the island of Achill. Kasio’s hometown is the kind where grassy fields run rampant along the edge, the post office is the social hub, and the center of conversation is last Sunday’s mass. In this locale, there is no place for people like her. While her mother shows some degree of concern, her brother is cold as winter, and Kasio becomes a target of his derision. Kasio’s mother is not a bad person, but the death of her husband—coupled with a life spent in rural Ireland—has given her a rigid mind, a fear of concepts foreign to her own understanding. Deep down, she wishes the best for Kasio. In moments of desperation, we see her try to comfort her, but she is ultimately held back by her obstinate beliefs. Her characterization displays a rare sympathy. It would've been easy to depict every being who opposes Kasio as a monster, something less than human; to go instead for a nuanced account requires courage and maturity.Eventually, Kasio has had enough. Without packing even an extra set of clothes, she runs away at night, the nocturnal stars her only guidance in the darkness. Soon, though, she finds hope. She’s introduced to the Bandshee, a constellation of freeloaders who spend their time practicing for prospective music gigs in an abandoned, aristocratic mansion referred to as “the big house.” Kasio is first intimidated by the other’s energy and carelessness, but as she spends time with them watching TV shows, cooking, and listening to their amateurish music, she finds in them a community. Kasio’s one escape from darkness is a notebook. Here, characterizations of friends mesh with intimate moments; text and dialogue with hand-drawn minimalism, a personal panorama of all that mattered and matters. It’s also the medium you experience her story through. Equipped with an eraser, you scratch away memories painful, mundane and affectionate in cathartic motions. You erase the past. And then, when all that remains is a mountain of eraser crumbs and blank paper, something emerges. The stroke of a pencil. The creation of something new. The more upsetting the events, the faster you erase. In  most intimate moments, I savored each scene like a rare treat, the eraser a vignette swathing it in the colors of the subsequent drawing. In the painful moments, my mouse skirted across the slippery table, resulting in a cadence matching the anger and tumult felt by the characters. The eraser is more than a mechanic. It's an emotion. The strokes convey feelings—Kasio's pain, the player's pain—and then use the action of moving your mouse to  these. Gameplay empowers narrative; narrative empowers gameplay. It's a circle, a synthesis. That's why the experience is so cathartic.A game is more than gameplay. It’s the narrative, the art direction, the sound design—and it’s when these aspects are combined with the gameplay that the game is born. In this fusion, the elements possess far more power when they talk to one another, when the idea of the  is replicated in both gameplay and presentation.  You could even say the gameplay is its own narrative. A narrative that’s far more meaningful when it aligns with the narrative of cutscenes. If the gameplay revolves around shooting people and the story around the protagonist being a pacifist hero, the game loses its sense of purpose, or it is at least weaker thematically. But suppose the gameplay incentivized or required you to show mercy. Suddenly, there’s a connection. Of course,  is a visual novel, and these scenarios would not find themselves in a game like this. Still, it goes beyond the conventional mechanics and implements a way of interaction that complements the story it’s trying to tell. It chooses based on what it wants to be; not what its genre is.  While Kasio struggles to figure out her identity, a black hole closes in on Earth. In intermittent segments, you take control of Cassiopeia, an astronaut investigating this phenomenon and its potential cause. In contrast to the beige pages of Kasio’s diary, these sections are painted out with spacey purple and blue, colors that contribute to a cataclysmic aura. You can immediately draw parallels between the two stories. Kasio attempts to come out; Cassiopeia watches the space anomaly approach. Kasio finds temporary respite; Cassiopeia’s investigation moves forward. Kasio is thrown into consternation; the black hole draws closer, corrupting everything around it and threatening to swallow the planet. Not to mention that Kasio and Cassiopeia are two very similar names… Eventually, their stories cascade. And with this meeting of two worlds, we reach a climax. Up until this point, I’ve remained vague about the change I recently went through. The truth is, self-discovery can feel like the end of the world. Suddenly, there’s a discrepancy between who I am  and who I am . Yet this new person has always existed. They were the person missing in the mirror; the one masked on school photographs; the one the family did not see. Always there, hidden beneath fake flesh and a forced smile.My mind has become a clash between these two individuals. On one hand, I want to embrace my new self; on the other, I’m afraid what might happen if I do so. And this fear leads to doubt. Am I really who I think I am? Maybe I’m just making this up? If I wait a month, will these feelings disappear? Well, folks, they haven’t.  When I booted up , I’d been aware of this new person for about two months. I was at this point more confident in the direction I was heading in, but I still needed that final push, that last thing that’d tell me I was in the right. The game did that for me. It’ll be tough, but I’m starting to think I might make it. And so, I’d like to take the first step. By erasing something myself.

_childDocuments_.review: Earlier this week I did the impossible - I came out to a family member. One of my two sisters, in specific.I was nervous but relieved to know she accepted and supported me - and thought, you know, perhaps we should call and talk about some things. We had that call this Wednesday and I expressed a lot of my resentment towards my family - being stuck at home with some of my family, more specifically my , has completely wrecked my mental health. I'm still closeted from them and I live with each passing day, worried  reject me - for being non-binary, for dating a trans person, for disappointing .My sister told me that  only hears what  wants to hear, that  only thinks about what  wants to see in  kids despite often saying otherwise. From her experience,  seemed to be a very not open and is often a close-minded individual. Coming into If Found..., I had only broke down early Thursday morning as my many months of frustrations and anxieties finally given the voice it needed.If you've played the game it'd make sense if I told you that Kasio's experience with her parents in If Found... hurt reading for me - it genuinely hurt. Seeing her mom's first letter and annotating it with "She's trying. But she has all these ideas of how I should be." and "She didn't even consider she might need to apologize too." was something I sat at for a long time, probably longer than any other part of her journal that I was erasing through at a normal pace.Moments like that made me realize that this game is something I never knew I needed - a realization that hey, think about the move out you're doing in a month as rebuilding - as leaving the past behind. That there isn't anything wrong with that, and that you can really be yourself once we're out there, together. That family doesn't have to be bound by blood and it's really about the people who's there for you, even at your absolute worst. That I don't need to seek acceptance through others - but rather be more accepting of myself.There's people I can think of who need to read and see this.If Found... left me with hope - and it's leaving me with a lot to think about. Thank you so much for this game, DREAMFEEL. I wish I could articulate this game better like other people have - but it's been a lot lately and I need to rest - if you're coming across this review/text you should without a doubt play it, especially if you've felt similarly trapped like both me and Kasio did.P.S. - If you find the eraser mechanic to be a little strenuous you can increase the size of the eraser in the options!

_childDocuments_.review: Two intertwining stories. One, an epic tale of a space explorer setting out to save the universe from a black hole; the other, a young woman struggling with her identity and seeking acceptance in ‘90s Ireland.Short and linear, ‘’ is an emotional rollercoaster of a visual novel. Told through journal entries, sketches and conversations this game is stunning to look at, with vivid colours and dazzling light shows. When those were over the calm melancholic neutrals of the journal pages offered respite, room to breathe and take in the next part of the story. The soundtrack perfectly matched the highs and lows of the imagery on screen. There were times when I audibly went ‘wow’ and times where peering into the more intimate side made me want to cry.I personally found the ‘erase’ mechanic to be quite genius, it is actively having the player engage directly with the words on screen. The novelty of the gimmick does wear off towards the end but I still think it’s a nice change from the usual method of moving forward in visual novels. It goes without saying that this is an LGBTQ+ story. The subject matter is handled delicately and in such a way that the protagonist's struggles can be understood and relatable for anyone who is willing to listen. The game is not afraid to shy away from Irish slang to have the conversation feeling natural but still keeps inclusive by offering references to what they’re actually saying. I highly recommend , especially to those who enjoy exploring diversity and alternative storytelling mediums.

_childDocuments_.review: : Some scenes could be upsetting to a trans person who has experienced family members shunning their true self. A 23-year-old  trans woman struggles with her mother not knowing how to accept her true self while also feeling as though she has no where to belong, as sometimes even her peers struggle to fully understand her. As a means of escapism, she keeps a journal and writes stories about an astronaut and space explorer named Cassiopeia.     • Trans/enby representation.    • Aro/ace representation? I don’t know if the dev has clarified on this, but it’s my interpretation of the protagonist anyway.     • Creative game mechanics. The player erases entire scenes away or journal entries, then later, can write (choose where written words appear).    • Extremely stylized. It’s simple art, but the presentation and coloration of it makes it very unique.     • Lots of Irish terms and slang to learn. There’s even a glossary. There’s also an amusing achievement for playing the game in Irish.     • Speaking of languages, there are 12 languages available for the game!    • Encourages people to seek out help from those who are willing to give it.     • “Making Memories Disappear” achievement. It involves doing excessive erasing for no real reason. Definitely not a fun reason. While there is some suffering for the protagonist, she does get a happy ending.  All queers deserve happy endings.I absolutely recommend this awesome interactive story-rich game to all the queers of the world.

_childDocuments_.review: If Found… is a visual novel with a compelling hand-drawn art style and an interactive gameplay experience, as you follow Kasio’s story from Ireland in December 1993, the darkest moments of her life. The events have already taken place, and now Kasio is reflecting on her Auld Lang Syne and erasing it in order to move forward. The gameplay also reflects that, and it’s very simple: you are reading Kasio's diary about what had occurred, her family, close friends, and the emotions she had gone through during all that time; only now you have to erase it all with your mouse cursor becoming an eraser. Although it is repetitive having to delete everything from the beginning to the end, the captivating story and character development themselves are engaging enough for players to look past it. A common mistake in the media is to make a minority character and throw them into the mix for the sake of it, with no personality or interesting characteristic traits at all, a.k.a “Shoehorning’. It is the worst fate that could ever happen to any fictional character, particularly the minority ones, as it harms the viewing of, or even downright demoralizes the group of people that the character is symbolizing.Thankfully, that’s not the case in If Found…. Even though Kasio herself is an individual belonging to a small and not (yet) rightfully acknowledged portion of the population, her story is handled very carefully and naturally so that everyone - not just the people in that group - can relate to both. There’re actually just two words in two instances, in her entire diary, suggesting that Kasio is a minority character. Just by replacing those words, you will have a story about overcoming the traditional expectation of the family for their children - which is something most youngsters like Kasio have to go through during their youth.There is a saying that music touches us emotionally, where words alone can’t, and it perfectly describes how I felt while reading Kasio's diary. Every situation and portion of her story has suitable music from Ireland around the 1990s, which is a neat little detail that I would not expect. Towards the end, I couldn’t help but keep erasing faster and faster to know what would happen, as the music just sped things up, and my heartbeat went up with it too. As much as I enjoyed playing, I had to blink a lot more than usual during the story, and my eyes were actually sore in the end. There are a lot of moments with flashy and fast-flickering images, but there isn’t an epilepsy warning from the beginning or anywhere in the game. This is probably the biggest issue, as it may put off many people, so the lack of a warning is risky for both the game and the players.This is my first game where the protagonist comes from the same community as I. I tend to stay away from media works (movies, games,etc) that claim to have lead minority characters but only ruin them.That being said, I’m very pleased and happy with this title, as it not only does representation right and respectfully, but it is also a one-time experience of looking back at my past to see how far I've come and how much I've grown.Everything Kasio did and went through back in 1993 all the way over in Ireland is nearly identical to what I had been through during the beginning periods of my early adult life. There’s even an extra side story about her alternative persona that happened along with the main story as a metaphor for what’s going on, which I think is a nice touch.  It’s amazing how we're so far apart in distance and time, but still manage to sympathize with each other. The game is very short, with a two or three hours playtime in one session depending on your reading speed, and achievement afk-grinding, it’s still an experience worthy of note though. Whether you are from our community or not, this is a story about overcoming the expectations of a traditional family, becoming the person who you want to be, having the life you truly deserve, and finding connection to your loved ones by closing the generation gap. It’s something that everyone will encounter, sooner or later.If you are looking to find a good game to get to know more about minority characters, If Found… visual novel is the right one. This title is definitely worth the full price, even better if it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: If found might be one of those games you stumbled across, unsure if it might be worth your while, your cup of tea, something that fits your taste in games. While I cannot make sure that this is a game for everyone, I will emphasize that everybody should play it. The story about Kasios, a transgender woman who is struggling to fit into her old home, might be one of the most emotionally touching arcs I ever witnessed. It is without a doubt very well written, empathic and honest to an extent that really makes you sit and think about how she and her friends must have struggled. There are actually two stories intertwined: one of Kasios brief return to her home on Achill Island, Oileán Acla, and the journey of Cassiopeia, a female astronaut who tries to save earth from the inevitable destruction by a black hole. The latter is more on the philosophical side but in the end, both might lead to a conclusion that naturally falls into its place. The mechanics used to tell the story are not overly complicated but very unique. You are erasing Kasios memories, or rather her words, written in her diary. Everything she has to tell about her friends, her family, her past, present and future struggles will be lost once your eraser touches the screen. The artstyle is gorgeous and I was only taking very few screenshots because I eagerly anticipated what was behind this lovely canvas that already shone through the page. I played If found on my Steam Deck and the use of the touchpad felt like what was always meant to be combined. While your trying to fight your tears, cry and laugh with Kasios and her friends, you might also notice the amazing soundtrack from 2Mello. There is not a doubt about how wonderful the music compliments the story on screen. 1993 was the year when Ireland finally decriminalized homosexuality. Before that there were still laws from the 19th century in place. I'm a typical cis white male and I did not know about this prior to playing If found. It did however encourage me to look up the facts and open my mind even further to what it might have felt for Kasios and her friends, living in a time that started to look more brightly but was also still filled with prejudices and people who struggled to understand that their old ways of doing things harms others. I'm just putting this in here to show what a game that barely played out for 2 hours is capable of telling without forcing anything onto the player. Pick a cozy spot and shut off your phone for 2-3 hours because there is a very emotional journey ahead that deserves to be experienced with full attention for every detail. This is by no means a mere visual novel but a colorful, gentle and warm slice of life with the occasional punk-music on top.

_childDocuments_.review: If Found…is a 90-120 minute interactive graphic novel by DREAMFEEL and the publisher Annapurna, who is known for games like "What Remains of Edith Finch", "Journey", "Stray" and many others dealing with the topics Identity, queerness, coming out and the resulting conflicts with friends and family.In the story of Kasio, a transgender, we experience the last 28 days of December 1993 in Ireland as a silent partner, with the most important people in his life not even bothering to understand them. Even escaping into a new life cannot mend this hole and so Kasio's entire life literally falls apart in our fingers.The gameplay switches back and forth between diary sequences and picture dialogues, whereby it seems that the graphics consist more of unfinished and sketchy pictures, which is probably intentional and in this form really fits this novella very well. Unlike some other visual novellas, the game doesn't leave much freedom of choice and the interaction takes place here exclusively with the mouse, in which we wipe out images or parts of text with a finger swipe with an eraser. As a result, something new is revealed behind every movement and you stay more focused than if you only have to press a (mouse) button.The game shows us everyday moments of bliss but mostly moments of sorrow, as well as intimate moments that could have been avoided with a little more tolerance and compassion. So it is up to us to "wipe away" the dark heavy clouds hanging over Kasio.If Found... is a daring game with strong narrative and visuals that seems a bit strange at first, but is nevertheless easily accessible and makes it possible to understand Kasio's problems and conflicts well.However, in my opinion, the game is not aimed at the general public, but rather at people who want to deal with this type of gameplay or are interested in the topic covered. The game isn't really an active game and you can't influence the course of events, nor are there multiple endings.It happens as it happens and it can happen that one or the other time you ask yourself why? Actually everything was good!I think the length is okay, but the game doesn't offer any replay value.An important thing is to set the eraser a little larger so that you don't have to erase so much and then hurt your hand.Just don't set it too big, otherwise there is a risk of erasing things too quickly that you may not have read or seen in full. A change is possible at any time via the well-equipped menu.The existing achievements work perfectly and most of them are obtained automatically while playing. The rest are not difficult to catch up on. If you still don't know how, there is a small helpful  here and there are also trading cards.✅ strong narrative and visuals ✅ Interesting new way for a novella❌ nothing (for me)

_childDocuments_.review: This game, which could have easily been mundane or boring within the visual novel genre, uses an innovative and clever mechanism: an eraser that directly and actively engages the player in the story. In this way, I erase the old pages as if peeling away deep wounds and relieving my pain, as if forgetting past memories. My eraser removes the scars etched with anguish and the wounds marred by sorrow. And finally...고통 속에서 위안을 찾을 거야, 지우개로.

_childDocuments_.review: There were parts of "If Found..." that were resonant for me, although I am a cisgender, heterosexual male.I, too, come from a small town that is both repressing and repressed - one that urges all its inhabitants to subscribe to specific views and that compresses outsized identities into a smaller box. It is this force that Shans succumbs to, and that Kasio spends much of the story fighting against. Achill is indeed a metaphorical black hole, and one that could destroy a fragile, budding life.I also understand that strange "graduate school" space that Kasio finds herself in, where you are seen as an adult but feel anything but, while at the same time understanding that you possess an emotional intelligence greater than that of those just leaving teenagerhood.While parents can be sometimes be the source of our strongest sense of rejection, there also seems to be a part of us that never stops seeking their approval or being comforted by their embrace. Witnessing such an embrace between Kasio and her mother led me to shed the few tears that I did while playing the game.I also liked the game's central erasing mechanic. I still write almost exclusively with a mechanical pencil, and I have one of those large, pink erasers in my office. There's something very satisfying about erasing, in the creation of a new clean slate, and that feeling emerges while playing as well.However, there were certainly other parts of the game in which I found it harder to "anchor." Four individuals with uncommon sexual identities, from a culture somewhat alien to me, living together in a dilapidated mansion seemingly owned by nuns? I found it challenging to find an entry point into this world. Additionally, there were times in which Kasio (to me) expressed almost asexuality, which almost represented another barrier to empathy.I can certainly recommend the experience, despite the difficulty that I found in relating to the characters from time to time. The trans- experience is not well-represented in media, and so I think it's significant for stories like this to be told.

_childDocuments_.review: It happens quite often that someone finds themselves trapped in the wrong body and then their loved ones don't support them. If Found... is a game about going home, coming out and erasing everything. If Found... tells a story of a young woman named Kasio. She just wants to be accepted by her family as who she is. If Found... is not much of a "game," more so a journal you read through while erasing parts, so just know what to expect. Basically, your interaction would be the equivalent of turning a page in a book. This game reminded me, and I am sure many others, that no matter how hard things get, and no matter what happens, it'll all end up okay eventually. Happy Pride Month to all of those who celebrate it! 🌈💕

The voice it's written in really lends to the atmosphere.- Colm- Made me cry a little bit.CONS:- Made me cry a little bit.- Ending can come across feeling a bit abrupt- It's sometimes a little inconsistent with how much you have to erase to progress. This will give your arm a workout.- The Irish-dialectical-English explanatory notes seems to think global audiences need help to understand the concept of a hot water bottle, but not 'The Debs' (it's our Prom, there you go). Yes, this is a joke.Play it, set aside a couple hours.

_childDocuments_.review: The dislike reviews are absolutely absurd. All of them are upset with it "Not being a game" because it doesn't follow their narrow views on how to tell a story. This is one of the most beautiful games I've ever played both visually and to boot an amazing dynamic soundtrack that blends itself perfectly with the core mechanic. It's core story touches on topics of family and identity in a serious and realistic way covering topics most games are too scared to. 10/10 fantastic experience akin to "What remains of Edith Finch" in its fantastic way to tell a story.

_childDocuments_.review: This game really means something to me. And at least at the time of writing this after playing, it means a lot. I'm trans myself and god I can't think of a piece of media that's resonated so deeply, so personally, as much as If Found has. At times it hurt to read. Hurt deep. Being trans is tough. I was closed off from everyone for a long time. Living with my mom too became harder and harder as time went on. Couldn't get a job. I would have walked out too if I had literally anywhere else to go. My mom says shes accepts and supports who I am but.. I'm still called by a name I don't want. I want to believe she's trying but I truly don't know. But my takeaway isn't all doom and gloom. I feel some hope. Hope things'll get better. Hope my mom will finally get my name right. Hope for the future in general, as scary as it can be. It's okay to leave the past behind. I hope this game sticks with me for a long long time.

_childDocuments_.review: As a straight white male elder Millennial I luckily had just enough neuroplasticity in my brain left to genuinely enjoy this.The ages 16 - 25 or so are incredibly formative in which we seek to solidify our identity and share it with the world. Kasio's journey in this task is a difficult one. The game does so well not to cram  down your throat, which might feel too politicized for many (including myself), and instead takes you into her head gently, step by step. It's so subtle that I must ashamedly admit there were times where I questioned if Kasio was just an odd woman, criticized for her choice of career, dress, and personality. I wish there were more games like this; narrative adventures that bring you into the world of another person, in another land, living a different life. In experiences like these, we realize the thing we share is hardship. It may come in different forms, but they are there. Whether that experience is Kasio's, or your own. They are human experiences, and sharing them keeps the humanity within us healthy.I want to see more of these, specifically from this studio and in this style, or a similar style. A beautiful game. Please keep it up.

_childDocuments_.review: is a visual novel, though it's not a true interactive novel as you can do little to influence the way the story unfolds, except in some minor ways right at the end. It's a sensitive exploration of one person's search for identity and acceptance, and some of the challenges they face. You don't have to be LGBTQ+ to relate to many of the feelings and scenarios. The messages—if you want to see them—are worth hearing. The character building is good, and there's at least one character that you'll hate! The atmosphere is excellent, both the weather and the portrayal of life in western Ireland. The dynamic glossary is useful for understanding some of the dialect. I was disappointed with the novel's sci-fi aspect. I didn't find it convincing, and I don't think it meshed well with the rest of the story. On the other hand, some of the visual effects to illustrate it are very good. The game's main mechanic for developing and changing scenes is to use an eraser to wipe stuff off the screen. The novelty of this wears off quickly, and maybe hovers on the border of irritating some of the time. On the other hand, you can make a game of guessing how much you need to erase. And the novel itself is short—less than 4 hours—so it's not too bad, though that leads into a discussion of whether it's value for money. I recommend this game, though I feel it could have been even better. I hope  develop many more like it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you, like me, have been trying for years to scratch the itch left by exclusively reading Jacqueline Wilson books your entire childhood, stop reading my review and go play the damn game! You'll be glad you did.If Found tells a wonderful story. As someone who's Irish and who spent their childhood in a nothing-town like Achill, and experiencing the hardships that can bring, this game and its story spoke to me more than it might for you. Nonetheless, If Found's story focuses on several universal themes, such as identity, outgrowing your childhood, and the meaning of family. I loved every minute of it. The way the story is (quite literally) revealed to you keeps you invested throughout the experience, although the delay between erasing certain overlapping scenes was a tad too long, and began to disconnect me from the game at certain key moments. However, the game is still 100% worth playing despite this flaw. The art throughout the game is gorgeous, although at times it struggled to convey who was speaking in certain scenes, which made certain scenes difficult to follow. The games soundtrack was everything I could have asked for. Some tracks gave me major Christobal Tapia De Veer vibes, and they always conveyed the emotion of the scene with haunting accuracy. It's a soundtrack I will be frequently returning to.Overall, this game is an experience I wish I could have again for the first time. What time I spent playing it will not soon be forgotten, and I would hope that having read this review, you'll treat yourself to it also.

_childDocuments_.review: The first thing that hit me about this game was the visuals. But then the story came and it definitely hit me in a lot of feels, in different ways.I'll probably be processing those for a while, tbh. I really love the characters and how relatable- and in other ways, how understandable- they are, to me. As someone who is trans, this game is a rollercoaster- a good one- with things that I've experienced similarly or differently- from family, belonging (and not belonging), material insecurity, etc. The setting- 1993- or in a small Irish town- is also unique and (at least regarding the small town part) relatable.The game wears its Irish-ness on its sleeve. I find it endearing and admirable, and also an interesting look into the mundane, everyday aspects of Irish life(? I assume, anyways- and I'm not saying it as a bad thing at all but rather as a good thing/better thing). While I'm a history/anthropology/sociology/etc nerd, I'm not Irish, so I guess I'd say the look at that- and at experiences from people who were roughly my age, around the time I was born- is also nice to see.I wish more VNs were (immersive?) like this, in presentation, flow, and gameplay mechanics. I also absolutely love the story and characters, and will likely pry around the different chapters (particularly the ending) a bit to see if there's much change- it seems there is- between options. I guess all I'd say is, thanks DREAMFEEL and Annapurna for making this beautiful game.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't enjoy this game but i think you should try it. I finished the game and the comments below are only subjective.Visuals are the main focus of the game and they are really amazing. The soundtrack is great as well. But the story is sloppily put together. The writing doesn't remotely match up to artistic level of the visuals. It has somewhat good ideas here and there, but the execution is really unsatisfying. It doesn't provide any real value except being relatible. On top of that, It slaps you in the face whenever possible with the *look at me, i read science-fiction and i am quirky* narrative. Maybe the story is meant to be written this way to capture a teenager's mind, but it bothered me nevertheless.   Bigger problem for me is that the creator team didn't capure the full potential of this game. This is an interactive content but nearly always the only thing the player does is to observe. It lacks creative ways to move the story. Erasing is a fine mechanic, but pretty quickly it feels like a chore to continue to the next chapter. Maybe i have really high standarts when it comes to art, or maybe i expected more from a game with Annapurna stamp on it. Either way, i will probably return this game and buy it again on sale just to support Annapurna Interactive and the visual artists.

_childDocuments_.review: A tentative "Yes" on this one, but just barely. "If Found" could have easily been a much better experience without the weird future astronaut crossover silliness. _childDocuments_.review: I am honestly so grateful to have played this game and meet the characters, this game really sets the bar for me when it comes to LGBTQ+ representation. As a queer person myself, I was able to relate to the characters in a way that was close to my heart. This game is a visual novel and moves a little slow the first time around, but by my second playthrough I was able  to capture the full experience while having a full understanding of the mechanics at the same time. _childDocuments_.review: + This short story packs a real narrative punch.+ Cool graphics, with a deliberate scribbly style to ape the main character drawing in her journal+ Fantastic soundtrack- No way to "scroll back" if you've missed something by accident- The erasure/drawing mechanic is unique and adds flair, but sometimes it felt like I was fighting the controls or it moved on before I was finished reading. You can auto-erase by pressing F, but it's not always available.A gentle, sometimes painful story about queerness and family—both the one you're born into and the one you find for yourself. There are two dual narratives, one about Kasio, a trans girl returning home for the first time in a while uncertain of what she'll be doing next, and one about Cassiopeia, an astronaut(?) from another planet(?) trying to save the universe from a black hole(???).As you can probably tell, I didn't quite follow the second narrative line, and I'm still not totally sure how it ties in to the other one or how much of it is a metaphor, or meant to be Kasio's imagination. I didn't need to understand that part to have an amazing time with the main storyline, however.If Found remains cozy throughout, despite sometimes being heartbreakingly bittersweet. It's about surviving past when your life and relationships fall apart, finding love and community in the people around you even when you can't love yourself. The characters are lovable, the atmosphere is on point, and the only reason the story isn't the best I've read lately is because I just came from the also-excellent Citizen Sleeper. If you love narrative-driven games and don't mind having limited opportunities to make choices, nothing should stop you from picking this up immediately.

_childDocuments_.review: I was very happy with my time spent with If Found and for those looking for an interesting story and beautiful art I think you will be as well.To begin though my greatest complaint is the gameplay, and by that, I mean that the term gameplay is extremely generous. The story is unbelievably linear with the first 80-90% of the game not having choices at all and the last 10-20% providing choices, but they only adjust what you read, not any meaningful outcome. I have given lesser visual novels negative reviews for this same issue, if you are going to use a game as a medium at least give me branching choices. BUT this game has many saving graces. The first one is the erasing the image to progress the story mechanic. Maybe it is my autism, but my brain finds great pleasure in just cleaning the screen and trying to cut around things that I think look good. It is fun to me and the way it interacts with the art is phenomenal. The other saving grace is that though the part with the interactive choices has little impact I got invested enough in the story that I was interested in the way it changed the interactions in the story.Speaking of story, it is a separate yet converging story of a transgender Irish young adult trying to adapt to the hardships of family life in the 90s and a space explorer finding an anomaly. Though it sounds like an odd combination the story is phenomenal. I preferred the stuff taking place in Ireland though, it definitely was the larger of the two stories and honestly, it did not need the other in my opinion. I also appreciated that throughout the story it gave context about Irish culture and slang, though it is slightly annoying the little popups to be read so you get some of the contexts I loved learning about it all so I was unbothered by the slight loss of immersion at times. I was surprised by how well the emotions were conveyed in the story, like honestly, it was top tier. The characterization is believable, all interactions are really well done, journal entries feel as such, stakes are reasonable yet high, emotions are tense, and best of all there are no villains, just humans being humans. I am a huge fan overall of the story though I do have a complaint about the ending.  Though that complaint is notably wordy, I do actually consider it minor though it just deserves a lot of explanation.One of the largest accents to the whole story though is the game’s music. Barring the ending song I loved it all, in fact, I loved it enough to buy the soundtrack for the game once completing the game. The emotions that the music creates for the player are phenomenal. I found my emotions being guided by the music a whole lot, it was so cool. You would have a scene where the colors were light the tone of the story was relaxed and the music was calm. Then you would continue forward; the colors darken, the music intensifies and becomes slightly dissonant, and the story moves in a darker direction. Soon enough the image is dark and messy, the music brings a pit to your stomach and the scene has reached its dramatic climax. I have seen very few games utilize their art, music, and story so well; it is impressive on a level that I struggle to describe.Though the music was used well, the best part of this experience has to be the art. I have never taken so many screenshots in a game. I really enjoy simple and rough art, and this game nails it. It leaves details sparse and lines are rough to appear like a journal sketch while always providing enough to get the full feeling of the image. These feelings are also built up by color, this game's color palette is wide and vibrant and it is utilized constantly in unique and beautiful ways often as a way to build emotions. It is astounding to me how they utilized their art, all the images were colored thoughtfully to create emotions that were intended to be complemented by music. Their images are simple yet telling offering the bare minimum to create an image in many cases, yet they never have too little, and they merely assisted in the player’s imagination. They then use the erasing mechanic to create this subtractive art that often the player facilitates in its creation. All of this creates what I could easily say is one of the best (if not the best) looking games I have ever had the pleasure of playing. Lastly, I always try to hit on controls as parts of my review. They are limited, one button (f) to clear screen mouse click to clear/create selectively. It generally works well, but the eraser somewhat moves on its own and that is annoying.Overall this game has become one of my favorite experiences that I have ever encountered. I hesitate to call it a game, yes, but there is enough there for me to say that it is. Even if I couldn’t call it a game though I could call it art. Some have argued that games are not art, I offer this, what I would say is perhaps one of my favorite pieces of art ever made. This game deserves praise. I will give out steam keys, recommend it, and talk about it. At the time of writing, this is probably my favorite visual novel of all time. Buy this game even at its full price even if you do 100% of the achievements in under 4 hours like me the experience is worth it. They deserve your money I promise.

_childDocuments_.review: is a visual novel about a girl named Kasio, who has to come home to her family. The thing is that she hasn't come out to her family yet and has no clue how to do it. You, player, learn about this period of her life through her journal and erase her entries while doing it. Actually, this little detail was the one that convinced me to buy the novel. To be honest, I didn't feel like it has added anything to the experience, but the idea feels nice. The main part of the story didn't touch me at all — perhaps the reason is that I've never felt anything close to Kasio's experience. I mean, it's okay, and as far as I can see, for some people the story felt touching and relatable. If that's really true, I'm glad I've caught a glimpse of life from their point of view. But the story is very short, it doesn't really go too deep. It shows the struggle of being not accepted or understood by your family but it ends there. To be honest, I've expected something more, because there are many stories about that already. But I can't blame the game for not meeting my expectations.The really cool thing is that the story happens in Ireland in a small town and you can learn something about their culture a bit. A short phrase here, a word there. It's not much, but I loved it.All in all, I liked the game but not to the extent so that I would vote for it in "Games for Impact". Hope to see something new from this team of developers, because I'm interested in what else they have to say.

_childDocuments_.review: If Found... as a game is not that engaging. It is just holding down the mouse and moving it across the screen for a few hours, . If Found...’s B plot is also not engaging, despite the threat of the end of the universe from a black hole, there is very little to actually talk about due that story consisting mostly of two characters talking over a radio . If Found...’s main plot however, is one of the most engaging stories of loneliness and acceptance I have seen in a visual novel. All of the characters, both that are likeable and antagonistic leave a memorable impact on the player, in personality and artstyle. The creators of the game know when to have scenes carried by visuals of scenery and when to have scenes carried by the dialogue of characters. Upon looking more into the game, I found out that the main narrative is somewhat inspired by (inspired by, not based on) personal events of one of the creators, and even without knowing that, there were several strong emotional scenes that made that clear. As someone who went into the game with certain expectations, the game was able to subvert them in a very satisfying way, particularly . The only issue I have is that the ending may seem a bit abrupt . That said, if I had the ability to experience this story again for the first time, I would gladly take it.This is not a game for people who want deep mechanics, or are interested in complex science fiction. But if you want an emotional narrative about feeling alone and finding acceptance, this will not disappoint you.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me tell you about this stunning indie visual novel called If Found... It's a deeply emotional and unique experience that revolves around erasing and rebuilding. The game beautifully weaves two narrative threads together, one about a young scientist named Cassiopeia in a sci-fi fantasy, and the other about Kasio, a stargazer returning home to Achill Island.The gameplay is simple yet incredibly effective. You use an eraser as the cursor, and by erasing, you reveal the next part of the story. As you progress, the eraser shrinks, leaving marks on the page, and this becomes a metaphor for the characters' lives, where erasing is both literal and symbolic. The hand-drawn art style adds to the intimate feel of the game, making you feel like you're peeking into Kasio's personal journal.The narrative is emotionally impactful, touching on themes of family, friendship, and the struggles of coming to terms with one's identity. Kasio, a trans woman, faces the challenge of coming out to her mother, and her journey is heartwarming and relatable. If Found... doesn't shy away from real-life complexities and portrays queer stories with depth and nuance.The beauty of the erasing mechanic is that it gives you space to experience the story at your own pace. You're faced with the decision of what to erase and what to preserve, just like in life where we make choices about what to hold onto and what to let go. It's a thought-provoking experience that keeps you engaged and invested in the characters' lives.The story unfolds gracefully, and the revelation of why Kasio is erasing her past is both moving and profound. It ties into the larger mystery of Cassiopeia's journey in space, creating a powerful connection between the two threads.If Found... is not just a visual novel; it's an emotional journey of erasing and rebuilding. It reminds us that sometimes, in order to move forward, we need to let go of the past. It's a must-play for anyone looking for a poignant and thought-provoking indie game about self discovery expression and how that not impacts you but those you hold bonds with.

_childDocuments_.review: is an interactive visual novel, is a coming of age story about connection, isolation and self-discovery that centres around Kasio, a young Irish woman, destroying her diary in the remains of a crumbling old mansion. It is an emotional experience, dealing with a range of sensitive subjects; it is rife with both touching and heartbreaking moments, all delivered in an honest and relatable way.This game is a heartfelt and emotive interactive novel but its abstract double narrative is an unnecessary and unwanted distraction from an otherwise sincere and engaging story. While there is some replayability in the form of achievements and missable diary entries this is limited and as such the price tag feels a little steep for the short playtime. That being said, it is an enjoyable, thought-provoking experience with stunning visuals and some great music that I’m happy to recommend to fans of the genre.You can read my full detailed review of this game and other Dreamfeel titles at .

_childDocuments_.review: GOOD+ Great leading lady, aka Kasio.+ Heartfelt and realistic story about a transwoman.+ Creative story telling methods from click-and-drag to "erasing."+ Cursor changes as the story progresses, adding foreboding and a hint to the story length.+ Colors, shifting art style, and end music perfectly capture tidal wave of emotions Kasio endures.NOT SO GOOD- The sci-fi story, while a neat tie-in, feels out of place.- Option to erase via "F" key goes away around the end, which can leave players with a sore finger and/or wrist from nonstop click-and-drags.- Text in journal entries tend to bleed into other entries, making players read out-of-order without knowing it.- Not much player input through choices compared to most visual novels.RANDOM~ Many story segments felt like they were plucked from my own past, which made certain scenes hit harder than expected.~ God, I hated Kasio's blood relatives.~ Mainly Fergal.~ ESPECIALLY Fergal.~ It's silly, but I have a theory that the sci-fi story is actually a story from Kasio's journal.OVERALLWhether you're trans, non-binary, or cis, I recommend giving this game a shot *if* you can handle uncomfortable themes like depression and horrible blood relatives....it might also help if you do wrist exercises beforehand.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible, usually I'm not a fan of visual novels with gimmicks (for example Emily is Away's typing mechanic which I despise) but the presentation of If Found... is beautiful and enjoyable, without wasting time to progress the story, the idea of erasing ones past comes through within the game play, without being obnoxious and feel like you're wasting time, unlike many of its contemporaries.The story is enjoyable, its not something I specifically am able to relate to not being a member of the LGBT+ community or as someone who hasn't been ostracised within a community quiet like what is seen in If Found..., but it brought fourth emotions nonetheless. Finding a place and people who make you feel like you belong is hard no matter who you are, but If Found... tells its players to never give up, even in the darkest of times, and that not everything is going to make perfect sense about oneself, its okay to still explore yourself and who you are as an adult, and I think that's a beautiful message.I've already stated that I believe the visual design of If Found... is masterful, but the accompanying score fits the game perfectly and helps emphasise key emotions and climax points within the narrative.I encourage everyone to give If Found... a chance, especially so if you are someone who doesn't fit the conventional mold of whats considered 'normal' within society, as I think If Found... may speak to you in a pronounced way unlike many other stories.
