_childDocuments_.review: If Found is by far the sharpest aesthetic experience of all the 2020 games I've played. Words hardly do justice for how impressive the visuals are, especially considering how there's a lot of contrasting imagery in tone and subject, and that the game still manages to make it all cohere. The ethereal soundtrack ebbs, flows, and crashes along with those visuals to sustain soft and steady scenes and punctuate climactic narrative moments.The story is deeply personal and affecting, with an honest take on the unique joys and heartbreaks of growing up queer in a conservative family, finding your people, and all the messiness in between navigating these different relationships. It's grounded in the reality of 1993 Ireland with all the political, cultural, and economic context that comes with that setting.The use of actual Irish terms and slang make it all the more real. There's also a handy glossary for these Irish terms to ensure the player always gets what's being talked about or referenced and can pronounce certain words correctly, which I highly appreciate as a person who gets annoyed at how flippant a lot of Americans get about words that are foreign to their own vocabulary.Such specificity in the storytelling is what makes the game resonate. A good deal of artsy indie games that try to tackle serious topics fail to make much of an impression for how broad they go. If Found... doesn't fall into that trap. I could see a version of this making that same mistake since it actually has a parallel sci-fi plot of this space-traveling doctor named Cassiopeia on a quest to save the world from a black hole running alongside the straightforward biography of Kasio. I get what that part of the game is trying to do, and it mostly works to underscore the cosmologically apocalyptic feelings one might struggle with as a young person whose very identity is under siege. It's just nowhere near as compelling as the parts with Kasio reliving her memories of being with family and friends. At the very least, Cassiopeia's astronomical adventures serve up stunning starscapes.What sets it apart from other visual novels is its core mechanic of erasure. You're erasing entries in Kasio's journal, and you're also erasing very lovely paintings and sketches to make progress. There are times when you erase to recontextualize scenes, and it's these points where the game feels the most magical, so much so that I actually wish the game were more deliberate about the use of this mechanic.Most of the time you're really just doing it to push the game forward, erasing entire events in the process. I understand the intent of explorating this metaphor of erasing the past to make space for the future, and it's particularly fraught with complexity in the context of a trans lived experience. I just feel like there's a disconnect between the supposed act of erasure, which for me is to remove things from reality, as if to say those events didn't happen at all, and it's difficult to square that with what you're actually experiencing in the game where you, as Kasio, are directly confronting and living through these memories, and in doing so highlighting just how important they are in shaping Kasio into who she is now. She isn't actually discarding any of these memories in the same way you're mechanically (and physically???) removing these entries from her journal.Maybe that tension is the actual point, that it's redefining what "erasure" means, but then I go back to parts where the act of erasing is specifically done to add to and/or recontextualize scenes, revealing certain truths, while there are a lot of other parts where you're just erasing everything without bringing anything new. The metaphor just feels strained at times.It's all the more apparent when the game I can admit that this could all be just me completely missing the point, and maybe that seeing this from a cis person's perspective could also be a major factor in that misunderstanding. I'm very much open to being called out on that aspect if I'm just straight-up wrong here.That quibble I have with the mechanics not quite jiving with the themes is what's keeping me from saying If Found... is a resounding success. Everything else though, from the art to the music to the writing, is superb that the game is definitely one of my favorites of 2020 titles and one I highly recommend. Only took me 2 and a half hours to finish, which I'm sure is a plus for many of y'all!

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitely a tough one for me to review. I think the story and the intention are lovely and it's great that this platform will introduce people to the story that they might not otherwise have picked up as a graphic novel but I found the gameplay and story progression mechanism to be very frustrating. Essentially this is a visual novel that to progress you must erase the current screen. The problem is that the repetivitve back-and-forth gets really tiresome after a while. You need around 2.5 hours to get through the main story and it takes a toil on the wrists. I ended up switching mouse hands a couple of times to take a break. I think I would have preferred the option to turn this mechanic off after a little while. The other issue I had is that sometimes you don't trigger the next screen and it takes a while to find the right place to click to do so. Twice I actually had to quit and restart the game because it kept getting stuck in a specific frame (the bit where Kasio is smelling bacon in the big house). I've also now played the epilogue 3 times but it keeps getting stuck at one point. These small issues only add to my dislike of the progression mechanic. The story, as I said, is lovely and one that doesn't get much airtime outside of Ireland proper. I have some friends in the queer community that come from Ireland and I don't doubt this story for a minute. If this comes out as a graphic novel I'd recommend that instead. 5/5 stars for the story, 2 for the gameplay.EDIT: I appreciate the devs reaching out. It was a bit ♥♥♥♥♥♥ of me to not report the bug I was seeing and I'm glad they're making an auto-erase function. As such have changed my recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: I accidently stumbled upon this game. Having a fondness for games that have a strong focus on the narrative, this proved to be a golden picking. Visually at first sight it is a lot like games like Florence or When The Past Was Still Around, yet it is actually in a league of its own. One progresses the story in this visual novel by erasing the story. And the erasing happens quite literally... with an eraser. As it is a story of coming to age, the story really touches upon those emotions that go in all directions all at the same time during those formative years. The interaction design on this game is brilliant. The process of erasing the story is not just a gimmick but it is also a metaphore for... well, you will have to discover that yourself.I don't want to ruin anything of the great yet short story, but i do want to say this: i laud this game for adressing a queer topic without spelling it out as queer.  What makes it so compelling is the subtlety of the story telling, it isn't necessarily about just being a young trans woman, it is a story that speaks to anybody who went through a period of soul searching and experimented with carving out a space for their own.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 This game will comfortably fill 6-8 hours, has some replayabilty to it, and features excellent soundtracks and artistic direction which illustrate beautifully this deeply personal story. This game is more of an interactive visual novel, in which you'll progress through the story by erasing away sections of the screen to reveal what lies beneath.I thoroughly recommend If Found.... This is a lovingly detailed story of a young girl from the west of Ireland, struggling to come out to her family and to find friends who will accept her for who she is. Parallel to this story is another, in which an astronaut travels to try understand and stop a cosmic anomaly, with only a mysterious voice over her radio for company. The two stories are connected, and unite at their conclusion.The dialogue has a lovely natural flow to it which will draw you in and leave you excited for more. Many moments in this game are poignant, emotional, and powerful, which brought me to tears on several occasions, while others are heartwarming, and even downright hilarious (don't forget to click the bottom left of your screen if you can't understand the scraps of Irish language and slang peppered throughout the game, they added a lot to the character and immersion of the game for me as someone from Ireland myself).

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly can't begin to state the profound effect this game has had on me.From the very first time I told my parents that I was trans they told me that I was making life so much harder for myself.I'm narrowing my dating pool.I'm forfeiting job opportunities.What will it do to my body?What if I change my mind?What will other people think of me?It's a beautiful story. It's a deeply profound message and I think that everybody should play this game. Gay, straight, trans, cis, whatever. This game is an experience that everyone needs.

_childDocuments_.review: This was the first visual novel game I have ever played, and I wasn't expecting much. But wow, I was deeply moved by this game. The interactivity was simple yet engaging. I was immersed in the world and felt like I really knew the characters despite no voice acting and very little animation. The art style is gorgeous and I loved swiping away every frame. Many of Kasio's emotions are conveyed through the sketchbook-style art, and especially loved the erratic and chaotic sketches that appeared when her emotions grew darker. I can relate to many of Kasio's feelings in the game, which probably aided my enjoyment of it, but I think you could get a lot out of the story even if you are not trans. It's more of a story of feeling like an outcast and wanting to be accepted for who you are, and what it means to have a home. It made me cry multiple times in the 2 hrs it took to play, especially at the end. A game hasn't made me feel so much in so little time. My only negative would be that I didn't fully understand some of the ways the plot comes together at the end, but I think it is maybe just up for interpretation. Amazing game, would highly recommend, especially for anyone LGBTQ+.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who doesn't typically have the patience for visual novels I really enjoyed If Found. I absolutely love the visual style and animation, and found the erasing to be a really clever mechanic that kept me engaged throughout. The story is obviously very personal, but I was disappointed with how unemotional the storytelling was in parts, with the protagonist often recalling the events very linearly objectively with little commentary. Overall I found the story to be serviceable if somewhat uneventful, and thought the visuals did a great job of conveying a lot of emotion and personality. This seems like a great purchase for those interested in queer representation or unconventional storytelling methods, although I might consider getting it while it's on sale given it's only about two hours of gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: If Found...

_childDocuments_.review: If Found is a story of layers.  Wipe away one and dig deeper and deeper until you reach an inevitable core.  It uses it's mechanic of erasing in interesting ways that show this is not just a novel, but a simple game with story and light puzzles.  It is perfect for a quick sit down story.  The music is fitting throughout and offers a stellar ambient mood in just the right spaces, while also pulsing rock and beats in dingy dark places.  The art is fantastic.  Along with the story it truly is what drives the game.  While there is so little to do and in a way explore, what is offered is so unique, heartfelt, and pure.  It takes a lot of strength to write and produce so a personal story and the author here has done it in such a way anyone can find a connection or relatable bit.  The team behind it also seems fantastic and watching Annapurna grow into a possible solid indie game company is really fun.  Please go and support these folx.

_childDocuments_.review: If found is a story driven game where you play with a very simple mechanic: you erase memories from a journal . Story: Kasio, the main character of the story, is a human being struggling with finding her way of life. A graduated from college she came back home to her little town in west Ireland. Set in the early 90, Kasio has problem with her family and society for being part of the LGBTQ+ community, and stars drifting  away of her true idea of future.  With a variation of scenes, the game shows different situations of her life in a very stylistic way, also making feel in love with the characters. A story that can affect anyone, the struggle of life choices and feeling not part of a community is one of the fears of every living human being.Gameplay: Very simple mechanics: erase of doddle your way from page to page or visuals.Art Style: This is one of the most important parts of the game, the combination of the gameplay with the art make it feel as you are the person holding the paper. It has one of the most beautiful sequences i have seen this year in gaming. The Gig and The Opening are brilliant.Music/ SFX: It has some memorable songs but its mostly for ambient, the sound effects are a great addition to it.If found its one of those stories that is gonna stick for awhile. its gonna remind you of those early years, for myself are not long ago, where every decision takes you where are you today. A very important game for anyone struggling at the moment. If you play this game, try to share it, you never know if someone needs it.We need to never forget that everything is gonna workout at the end and this game explain "how".

_childDocuments_.review: If Found..., by developer DREAMFEEL and publisher Annapurna Interactive, is a moving coming out story about a trans-individual and connection told through an interactive novel. Throughout the story, Kasio returns to her home in Western Ireland, comes out to her parents, and faces many trials and tribulations that come with that. She is met with opposition in many parts of her journey. This game is a highly creative way of telling Kasio’s story, and it has many other valuable lessons including family not necessarily being blood, acceptance, understanding without judgement, unconditional love, and friendship.The novel begins with an astronaut falling through a black hole, trying desperately to get help as the “Big Event” approaches the horizon; the novel keeps going back to that aspect of the story every now and again, with a smaller countdown each time. The graphics in If Found... are incredible, with vibrant colors, beautiful artwork, and realistic sketches and handwriting on Kasio’s diary (which she slowly destroys through erasure). I almost didn’t want to erase some of the scenes because of how well they were drawn, but I would never have gotten to progress through the interactive novel if I had done that.As you play the game, you are given an eraser to erase from scene to scene, wiping away memories and moments that Kasio wants to forget. Along the journey, the eraser shrinks more and more until the end of the journey for Kasio accepting herself as she is, without fear of anyone else’s judgement. Once the eraser is gone, it is replaced with a pencil, rewriting Kasio’s life with new memories, and creating a clean slate and rebuilding her life, including only those that she wishes to be a part of it. Every time that Kasio got upset or experienced moments where she felt that she didn’t fit in, the music would get louder and more obnoxious as if they were crowding her head and the player was inside of her head with her.The only way to quiet the scene back down again is to erase that scene and move onto the next, either by talking to one of her friends, or by leaving her alone. The people in her life who couldn’t accept her to begin with, eventually came around and are written into her new story as well.This interactive novel is a very inspirational expression for the LGBTQ community, or anyone who is struggling with becoming their true self. Rewrite your own story how you want it to be written. Nobody should get to decide how you live your life but you, and you alone. I played through almost this entire game in one sitting; I wanted to know what would happen next along Kasio’s journey, and I was pleasantly surprised by how much real emotion went into making this, I felt like I was right there beside her the whole time. If Found... definitely deserves high praise and I’m giving it a 9 out of 10 rating.
_childDocuments_.name: If Found...

_childDocuments_.review: The basic mechanic is very simple - two animated canvases and an alpha channel, and you get to erase the alpha channel. But they really, really, work hard to make this interesting. There are lots of little changeups in the mechanics, and everything is always animated, just so much work.   At first it feels like a gimmick, but soon you're just erasing like mad and it's extremely satisfying to see what's next.Do not think too hard about the sci-fi aspect. It is very soft sci-fi like Interstellar, and if you view it as anything more than a storytelling device - like CS Lewis's Perelandra trilogy - it will make you upset.  Just enjoy the past Ireland story. You may get upset at dumb choices, but that's what being young is about.  You may also be upset about the general theme if you're a bad person.  I found it a really nice change from your normal visual novel, especially the concert scene.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't review games often but I couldn't not leave a review. This visual novel is beautiful, profound, and meaningful. I can't say much on the story without going into spoilers but it is a wonderful experience of self-discovery, development and acceptance. Bring a box of tissues as it is beautifully heartfelt. _childDocuments_.review: What a beautiful story. I could easily say too much and spoil the experience, but I won't do that. Instead I'll just say this.If you're trans, get this game and play it all the way through as soon as you can. It will make you feel all of the things.If you aren't trans but you're fascinated by people and complicated relationships and emotions, and just want to experience something profound, I think you'll really like this too.About the game itself, If Found is a visual novel with probably the coolest and most interesting visual storytelling mechanics I've ever seen. Everything about the design just works so well, from the art to the music to the way you interact with the story. If you care about visual novels, I think the way this was done is something truly special. Sit back with some tea, relax and get immersed in this one. It's an experience you'll be glad you had.

name: Hundred Days - Winemaking Simulator
detailed_description: In Hundred Days you will have complete control of a new Winery. First choose which vines to grow, learn how to grow them and when to harvest. Then following the entire winemaking process deciding on the type of wine you want to produce or the market requires. You will also have to sell the wine produced to allow your company to expand. As in reality, every choice made, from the vineyard to the sales, will be able to influence the wine produced both in quantity and quality . A quality wine will increase the reputation of your company worldwide, it may have come at a higher price and will allow you to grow better and faster. Simulative and realistic approach suitable for both beginners and more experienced players The ability to cultivate different types of vine Analyze the soil and choose the grape variety that best suits those characteristics Organize work in the vineyard such as pruning or chipping Protect your vines through specific treatments depending on the type of disease Check the state of ripeness of the grapes and decide when to harvest Follow the winemaking processes and enhance the characteristics of your wine Select the yeasts and bacteria used during fermentation Decide how and which of your wines age with aging Customize your bottles by choosing their shape, color and other aesthetic characteristics Create your sales network and adapt the characteristics of your product to the type of customer Manage marketing and social activities to increase the reputation of your company

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to review this game first as a player and second as someone with a degree in oenology and viticulture, as well as an Italian wine specialist of sorts.As a player:The game opens up in what I'm going to choose to view as paying homage to Stardew Valley, rather than blatantly ripping it off that game's narrative. Your protagonist is working a boring corporate job when you receive a letter from a mysterious winemaker nicknamed the Old Man. He is quite dead, and has left you his estate in the Langhe. You quit your boring job and go off to make wine, despite not knowing anything about wine.The game's chief resources are wine, money, and tile spaces. You have a board area that you lay tile pieces in to complete actions (some of which also cost money). When your board is full, you can't do anything else until some of your current actions are finished. Just like at a real winery, there is quite a lot to do, so the game never feels like it is on cruise control.The tutorial part of the game does a fairly inadequate job of explaining menu options, how to navigate the various parts of your winery, etc. Some tool tips on menu items would be a welcome addition to the game.It takes a fairly long time to accumulate enough resources to make any real progress in the game. You can buy upgrades to the size of the board, as well as for your winery/equipment/vines. However, many upgrades end up being themselves a drain on your resources. My first game ended after 3 hours when I tried to purchase a new vineyard so that I could plant a new variety, leaving my winery too cash strapped to bottle the next year's wine.Overall, I felt the game was enjoyable. Several hours disappeared rather quickly, though that was probably aided by my own enthusiasm for the subject matter.As an  "expert" on wine:This is by far the most realistic winery simulation game I've come across. It is very clear that the developers either know a lot about the wines of the Langhe or they had very good subject matter experts. The result is a game that has the potential to be quite educational, as well as enjoyable for people who already have strong wine knowledge.Obviously, as a video game, 100% accuracy is unattainable while still making a game that is enjoyable. But this still comes as close as you can get. I was thrilled when I saw that the game requires you to spend actions cleaning the winery equipment after it gets used, one of the less glamorous aspects of winemaking that never the less makes up the large majority of a wine maker's time in the cellar.The names of the subzones, the grape varieties that grow well in them, and the relative prestige (as reflected in the cost of purchasing a vineyard in them) are all fairly accurate. (For example, buying a parcel in Bussia costs significantly more than buying one in Principe.)I've seen a lot of other reviews talk about how rude and condescending much of the dialogue in the game is, and I will say that this too is 100% accurate. Your character is a foreigner being gifted some of the most highly prized (and expensive) vineyard land in the world. In Barolo in particular (where much of the game takes place) there is virtually nowhere left for aspiring winemakers to purchase land to develop, or for existing wineries to expand. Everyone who wants to make Barolo or wants to expands their operations literally have to wait for someone to go out of business or die. Non-Piedmontese Italians who buy wineries in the area are looked at as foreigners. Non-Italians who buy wineries there are seen something like invading aliens, a sure sign of the end times. So the fact that everyone is a giant ass to your character is really probably the most realistic thing in the game. The only way that it could be more accurate is if every elderly man or woman on the street stared daggers at you like they suspected you of killing their grand father during the war.Overall, I recommend this game very much for anyone who already has a passion for wine, or who is looking to learn more about wine in general or Italian wine specifically. It is also great for people with some product knowledge who are looking to learn a little bit more about the production side of the wine business, as it does a very good job of discussing some of the realities of that world.

_childDocuments_.review: The fact that this is a puzzle educational game and not a sim REALLY needs to be clearer. From the video and pictures, it looks like a standard farming game. _childDocuments_.review: Similar to at least one of the people who wrote a review before me, I can rate this both as a player and as somebody who owns a winery in real life and about to obtain a degree in oenology and viticulture. I cannot say that Italian wine specifically is my strong suit, but we share a lot of similar problems where I come fromAs a player:The game is enjoyable but definitely not intuitive. I did not realise you can do research until after the story was already done and finished, and I feel like that is definitely something that should be touched on in the tutorial.The board representing time is actually somewhat accurate, it's often really, really hard to manage time in an efficient manner in a business like this.As a winemaker:Seriously, a lot of time you spend in the cellar is making sure it's as immaculate as possible and thus cleaning takes up a lot of your time. I would actually say the game allows you too much in this regard as not washing your equipment for a season is a surefire way of making absolutely atrocious wine the year after. Of course, you have to balance enjoyability and accuracy, and I think this game hit the nail on the head as far as that goes.Tipicity is an attribute to your wine that the game doesn't really explore well either. Simply put, it's how well the wine you make measures up to what is expected of wine made from the grapes grown in that region, as the region influences the final product a lot more than people realise, both as far as nature and cultural practices are concerned.There is something that rubbed me the wrong way when they describe aging. I distinctly remember the game mentioning larger barrels change the aromatic profile of your wine more, which is blatantly false. Smaller barrels have a higher surface to volume ratio and thus have a higher compound exchange rate.I never really considered the characters in the game being rude to you. The one who teaches you is expecting you to abandon the winery as soon as possible and thus feels it a waste to spend the time and resources teaching you. The rest were frankly far more polite than expected, considering you're getting land they've been waiting decades to obtain. As FatherKraken mentioned, land is in low supply but very high demand in regions where the grapevine is grown and it is truly a pain to expand.Summary and final thoughts:The game truly strides the line between enjoyable and accurate as well as I could hope. I feel it confers enough knowledge to a fledgling winer that they would be able to care for a vineyard and wine cellar to a reasonable degree. Definitely a worthy game if you want to learn something about how wine is produces, less so if you're expecting an engaging story. If you have little or no interest in wine, seriously do not bother.
_childDocuments_.name: Hundred Days - Winemaking Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, a disclaimer: I am Italian, I am a wine sommelier and I have a passion for game simulations, starting from Civilization. Hundred days is a brilliant game, in my view, with room to become a better game with a few updates. The most important one (and I hope that the developers read this) is to add keyboard shortcuts because the game play implies too many mouse clicks (just that actually).The second suggestion is to provide a more developed tutorial.I am playing a game in endless mode. It is well structured, maybe a bit boring as the different phases of winemaking repat themselves, but this is what happens in real life.There is a clear logic sequence in what to do in the game: expand the board first, invest in basic winemaking techniques (malolactic fermentation and aging), go for a second vineyward to produce a white wine. Only after that start to invest in the commercial side of the business (office and wineshop).All in all, I am having fun and... congrats for the Brunate vineyard colored Chapel... it is the first time I play a game with a real place I know well!Looking forward to see the next releases and the fine tuning of the game.Thank you!Marco Baccaglio

The aesthetics are great, the gameplay is quite unique and the developers seem to have done their research. The puzzle aspect of the game is not hard but still quite fun. No bugs and the game runs great.Cons:The story is bland, consists of too much text that is not very fun too read. Every character is quite rude. _childDocuments_.review: This game could, and should, be good - there are brief moments where you see elements which work really well, but the flaws and poor decisions that brought them together make it disappointing to play.FIrst, the story mode dialogue is terrible. It's volume of text could make visual novels blush and almost all of it is just fluff - serving no benefit to learning how to play and only trying to make you feel something for your character that you haven't seen, have little interest in and becomes increasingly aggravating as you progress. For large swathes of the novel, sorry, game, you are sat watching your character get into dumb arguments with others. This looks like it's supposed to be funny - it isn't. If you've ever heard a teenager get into a vitriolic name-calling match with their middle-aged parents about gosh knows what, you know the type of exhausting petty fighting that you are in for with Story Mode.In addition, elements of the "Story" appear seemingly randomly and when they do appear, they don't actually teach key parts of the game (no indication of how to buy new equipment, or how to repair it - mandatory steps to improve your vineyard).if you choose to ignore Story Mode (or even if you try to follow the steps in Story Mode for the most part), you'll find the UI is unintuitive with key features hidden away. You are left to find the research screen and how to sell on your own, with the top-right most button barely suggesting it's function for this. When you research something, you dump so much cash into it that you commit yourself to another 10-15 minutes of mindless clicking before you can do anything else, but that doesn't even benefit you as you need to purchase it. Where do you purchase it? In your buildings of course, which at NO POINT is ever mentioned to be an interactable object.Finally, the pace of the game is incredibly slow. Not in a good "making steady progress to move to the next phase of my vineyard" kind of slow, but as in "I've made this same wine for the last 5-6 in game years and have only been able to afford one upgrade that doesn't change how I make my wine, so I might as well do the same thing again". The game can be good, but only when you have the research and tools to choose how to grow your grapes or how to ferment them. For literal hours, I've made the same 2 wines over and over with almost no change because a) the income (which you have to tediously click each individual customer to sell to) is so poor that you can't afford to buy new features or b) the features you've bought don't help with the wine you are making, so you just repeat the same steps over and over in order to buy something else and see if that feature is more funHonestly, I believe the devs can make this game good, the principle is really nice, the art style I love, but having to repeat day-after-day-after-day of "place tetris piece, click sell button 5 days, click next day button" is not a fun game. If it wants to be a management sim, it needs to let you step back, automate some steps and let you improve more at a better rate. If it wants to get into the weeds a bit more, then it needs to give a reason to slow down, dig into the story or finer details rather than just clicking next, next, next for more money

_childDocuments_.review: Time Played: 40Hrs General Thoughts: Cute art, fun but unpolished niche game if you love spreadsheets, expensive for being unfinishedPros:- Art is cute- Choices have consequences and you have to make adjustments every year - Each wine has its own personality and quirks to how to create it - I like having to make mistakes and suss out which wines have to be made which way- I like taking notes and refining my process - Chill game and late game is very relaxed- Devs are patching and incorporating suggestions- I do genuinely enjoy playing itCons:- Story mode dialogue is annoying and characters are super passive agressive for no reason- No choices to be made during the story mode (not even dialogue options)- Story is short, feels pointless, and ends abruptly - Feels kind of like an endless rush to keep my cellars stocked with wine then selling out in 1 or 2 turns- Game is still buggy with lagging issues and ghost clicks (I also got an error where I loaded the game with a bottling step on the board and then ended my turn and got a buffer overflow and ended up with a 25856 turn bottling operation)- Some of the tech trees are kind of useless, especially the marketing efforts (late game I'm selling out so fast I have no need to market)- Some choices seem to have effects but don't tell you (bottling choices apparently count towards quality?)- Some vineyards/grapes have clear planting choices but Ginestra has alkaline soil and none of the grapes like alkaline and end up with "unsuitable terroir"?- Hard to plan ahead with which grapes to plant where (what each grape likes is incredibly hard to find) - Even with custom yeast and 100% scores some of my wines don't have any flavour :'(- UI is confusing and stores information in about 40 different places making you click around endlessly during early gameSuggestions for Improvements/Balance Issues:- Wish I could rename my vineyards or that the grape varietal was the clearer item on the card (for example if i have 3 fields of chardonnay they will need to be harvested at the same time and I hate having to remember which fields they're in / check my spreadsheet)- Auto sell needs more parameters and to auto sell to restaurants/grocery stores (for example let me auto sell if the price is > x or discount is < than y)- Should have the option to "randomize" wines to some extent when starting a new endless game (like maybe Barbara will randomly be assigned an ideal sweetness between 2 and 4 so that there is still some experimenting for replayability)- wish i could customize my winery as I upgrade it - even like the colour of the roof and choosing some of the plants out front would feel like I had some impact- everything takes money and it feels in short supply early on - wish i could trade tech points for the tech and then buy the equipment because paying for it twice feels annoying - "journal" feels useless - i should be able to access all the wines i've made for each varietal through the journal and see a chart of what I did and what the score was so that I can compare what is working - Fame points feel pointless right now - I feel like they should be able to be traded in for perks or temporary boosts (or even cosmetic upgrades) - I should be able to do some light terraforming on vineyards I own (like adding more sand/clay/loam, or adjusting the PH with additives)- Malolactic and aging processes are a bit too "strong" - wish adjustments were more granular (sometimes i need to adjust the acidity by 1 but the minimum MLF with the weakest yeast is going to adjust by 2)

_childDocuments_.review: The game looks beautiful and I, as a huge fan of business simulation games, was very intrigued by managing my own vineyard, learning something about winemaking and being able to organize the logistics and production on the beautiful map.The disappointment with this game led me to return the game, which is something I have never done before.The beginning of the story is boring, not only can you not chose your character and you are being forced to play as this annoying Emma, but also are the dialogues way too long and basically made me skip them all. There was just no value in them.The biggest disappointment in this game is the overall game mechanic. You CANNOT actually BUILD your own vineyard. Every turn you get puzzle pieces (like in Tetris) in from of cards that you then can play out and place them in a square. This has nothing to do with building and managing a realistic vineyard operation. I am sure that there is a lot of value and knowledge about winemaking further down the line. But I absolutely hate the overall gameplay mechanic.If you are into strategic puzzle games, this is might be interesting. If you are looking for an actual realistic business simulator, I don't recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from someone who loves wine, is getting a degree in enology, works at a winery, and taking sommelier classes, this is a great game. There is so much to wine making that makes it an art and a science, so I really hope the developers keep updating the game, and give us more options in the wine making process. I love the little details too! 10/10 I hope they continue to amaze me with further updates.Even if you don't know anything about wine, this is such a good entry into it and, all in all, a great game.

_childDocuments_.review: Too long don't read:❌Not so intuitive UI. ❌Passive-agressive characters.❌Not the bible but a lot of text.❌Story a bit short. ✔️Beautiful graphics and music.✔️Gain knowledge, you're essentially playing winekipedia.✔️Lots of translations.✔️Huge potential.Let's start with the bad aspects, then the good ones.The interface is not so self-explanatory, you have to find your way through pretty much alone. If you are not really familiar with internet and gaming stuff the beginning is going to be a big question mark for you. So making the UI a bit more intuitive won't hurt. The story is great, the characters traits and personalities are good and well thought, but some are quite harsh and honestly I'd feel better if the characters encourage me and teach me without passive-agressive behaviour. Consequentely there's the amount of text, let me explain: I started to play this game to have a basic understanding on winemaking and didn't want to read long texts that I'd forget past two days so I wanted the learn-by-playing thing, and in this game there's plenty of learning, but also a lot of text, not the notes on the diary, those are necessary so you don't forget what are you doing, but the conversations could have significantly less text. Story is also not so long, and when you learnt everything about wine in the game it feels repetitive. Last and least, the translations (to spanish) are not complete and some are mistaken, also translating the voice texts would be awesome and more immersive to non-english speakers (still I understand this because it's just released). The aesthetics are beautiful, both the music and the visuals give you a tranquil and calm place atmosphere. You learn a lot in a fun way, even if the text is a lot, you learn and have fun with it. The research made is noticeable, it's like playing wikiwine. The game is hard, not because of the UI but you go slow till you get the hang of it. Hold my beer but I love the main character, the story is great if you can go past the harsh characthers. And about the translations, even if they are not complete, there are a lot of languages already translated and the game released just last week, that is something. The game feels repetitive at the end, but it has a lot of potential, if you buy it it will be worth the price and the time that I hope the developers need to read us and improve this beautiful game.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Really wanted to enjoy this game but unfortunately it feels like it's an excellent idea and theme but plagued by design decisions that restrict player choice & a story-line that gives you no reason to get behind the main character. The combination of a Tetris style work-order grid combined with seasonal changes and challenges to develop wines is a great idea and I suspect when all the options are open this game could really be something special. Unfortunately even having sunk a huge amount of time into this game I haven't even got close to that point. As other reviewers have said to unlock more options you need to not only pay to unlock the technology but also then pay for the development of this new item, effectively doubling (or tripling) the cost to unlock new options within the game. Thematically this makes very little sense (why did thinking I should have a shop cost me 10,000?!) but would be fine if those costs went in line with the amount of cash you were able to pull in. Even with optimised wine quality or quantity this will take you hours and hours to afford. In reality this means you'll just need to turn your brain off and click through the seasons for at least 10 hours - but you can't just idle this you need to be clicking manually to make sales every turn until you unlock and build the shop, at which point you can at least completely turn your brain off - I'm not sure how much longer it takes before the work-order and options open up enough to get interesting but it's longer than i'm willing to devote to this title. The story mode does help unlock things more quickly through some free unlocks but the character you're playing as is one of the most annoying people ever written, basically a spoiled trust fund brat who's rude to everyone and yet you're somehow expected to cheer for them. This combined with a huge amount of writing you have to click through without any game-play consequences means you have to deal with a lot of frustration either way. Despite all the above i do have some glimmer of hope that this game could still be great. If the devs considered making the technology turn dependant rather than cash dependant that may help solve the issue. Alternatively tie the unlocks to story beats and then allow us to skip the story-line. An even better option might be for all the challenges to come with all technology and land unlocked so you can immediately move to the end-game (where i suspect this game would work really well).

_childDocuments_.review: Simulation games – and especially tycoon games - usually come with one big caveat: they can’t reproduce the details or the grit of what they’re attempting to reproduce. All they can really do is give you a visual representation for the passage of time, and essentially present turns lost or points left unspent as failures in scheduling or task management. You start a cycle of larger, tentpole projects within the game, complete a series of conditions, release the finished product and then wait for the consequences. In Hundred Days, Broken Arms Games finds a new candidate for a game mechanic acting as surrogate for managerial decisions – Tetris.As strange as it might seem, you’ll chiefly spend your time in your winery arranging pieces geometrically within a limited board, effectively symbolizing your ability to multitask or delegate. Each piece represents a specific step in the winemaking process, all of them painstakingly sourced from the actual occupation and replete with triggers and conditional effects to attain, values to tweak and optimal settings to reach. In a very weird way, balancing a Nebbiolo’s sweetness and tannins is an act of precise minmaxing if you have access to the best versions of your tools, whereas your first Chardonnay’s likely to come across as drinkable no matter if you haphazardly arrange your pieces, mash the Next button and keyboard-smash your way to naming your first bottle and putting together your first official wine-tasting session. More complex operations are securely gated behind Tech tree expenditures and later purchases, which is perhaps one of the bigger problems of the title. I can understand that this represents your not only learning certain skills but also investing in their required hardware, but it makes seemingly easy unlocks deceptively expensive, which can bork your budget if you’re not careful. Similarly, visits to your actual Winery, your Tool Shed or Warehouse all come with an upfront cost that exponentially increases the more you invest in them and upgrade your resources. That makes the routine concept of peeking into side-menus for a refresher a costly operation, and you’ll very much want to keep track of what goes where and what is used for which operation. All of your hardware and tools decay over time, and the Repair card and tetrimino don’t always spawn as expected, past a certain threshold. The game seems to expect you to freely peek into your buildings to click on your rustbucket and forcefully draw the Repair card, but this involves sapping on your budget in an increasingly severe manner and skipping most of a season as your rigs get pampered. If you haven’t developed the practice of expanding your playspace whenever possible, it’ll come back to bite you in your oenological heinie.On the flipside, the game never enters Panic Mode. Urgent budgetary or temporal situations don’t result in music ramping up or the scenery changing, and your overdraft protection seems rather generous, at about three thousand Euros prior to the game declaring you bankrupt. If you keep moving and keep a steady stream of wine releases going, you’ll never bump into this lower limit. You might not release quality wines consistently and there are times where profit is obviously going to win over the artistry of it all, but it’s rather obvious that a string of cheap BYOB-worthy red ones serves to line the pocketbook and prepare your finances for that one seriously drinkable objet d’art you’d maybe like to work on. Add to this a decidedly chill soundtrack and a visual language that feels ripped from the golden years of Clipart vector art, and you’re left with a deeply relaxing and unabashedly casual experience that’s looking to make you process its offered challenge differently. Leave your twitch reflexes in your other blazer, Hundred Days wants you to stroke your chin and spend long, long minutes wondering if adding endogenic enzymes to your Barolo for the tiny down-tick in Acidity it gives you and the slightly bigger uptick in Body you’re left to manage in the last few stages of the fermentation process. You realize that wine’s like coffee, in a sense: everyone says they like a rich, dark roast, just like everyone loves to swirl a supposedly full-bodied wine they’ll only daintily sip at. Sometimes, you’re better off polishing a series of supermarket-worthy Vinho Verde bottles with fancy-pants label design, or knocking back that exact set of Cuvée F;AFKEAFDASDF 2026 you know’s going to go well with the neophyte bloggers.So crack one open – or better yet, splurge on some fancy foreign potato chips from that local Turkish supermarket you’ve never actually stopped in but always glanced at before, pair that with something slightly heady and that doesn’t let too much light through, and try this out for yourself.Oh, and don’t drink and play too much, obviously – you don’t want to look back on last evening’s worth of simulated years and see all the dumb, unfiltered crap you can entirely use as a set of valid names for a tri-annual product. Maison “Oh, sh!t, I ♥♥♥♥♥♥ it up, how do I cancel?!” 2023 apparently pairs really well with red meats and sauces.

_childDocuments_.review: Circle Peg, Meet Square Hole. The Game. Just with Pretty Farming Graphics.This is exactly the type of game that I do like, incrementals, farming, merchanting, and it looked perfect in the screenshots. But, I had no idea from those pictures that this is actually a tetris-like card game. You get to choose from 1-2 cards, and you can only ever really put 1-2 things on the board and no matter what you choose, you will be waiting. Do you remember that pre-school toy that is a wooden block bucket with a lid that has cut-outs to insert a circle, star, and square wooden pegs? That's what this mechanic is like. And it's funny because as you play through the game, the entire mechanics are like that: "PICK A OR B. BUT DEFINITELY, YOU SHOULD PICK A. NO, NO, NOT B. I MEAN, YOU CAN. BUT YOU SHOULD PICK A." It's almost as if this game was really designed for toddlers with tablets, just missing all the arrows pointing at where you should click. I bought my second field and then gave up. This game is a slog. There is no place where the game lets go of the hand-holding and lets you really play. You're tied to this system where the dialog is supposed to be the interesting thing that keeps you playing, while you skip through turn after turn with nothing to do, and the things that there are to do are only busy-work that exist in the game because it's "educational". The storyline is not enough to hold this game together.Supposedly there are more in-depth mechanics for doing the wrong thing, lol, but they are hidden behind screens that you don't use. There's never enough wine, and saving bottles feels as pointless as talking to your ex-wife about joining alcoholics anonymous, again, because you know all those bottles will be gone in, like, 3 days, tops. This game feels like a confused mess of an educational video game grant where the funders kept changing their minds about what they wanted their 4-year old to play and at the last minute decided to add more adult dialog and put new ways to fail where no one would find them. I just had such high hopes from the beautiful customization intro, from the screenshots, and then bam, paradox shift back to the bucket-and-wooden-block-game where you only get 1 or 2 wooden shapes at a time.

_childDocuments_.review: Hundred days has a strong atmosphere, interesting characters and deep mechanics. However, there is little in the game that is truly captivating. The writing feels novice, failing to convey the emotional highs and lows that the story is supposed to convey. And the plot progresses of its own accord with zero player input. What the player does control is clearly deep and well thought out, but the story ends long, long before the player has gained access to all the tools needed to create great wines. This leads to the dissonance of the story reaching its climax while the player is still muddling through the beginning of their winemaking career. It is not explained how to create the best wines, either. I know that my bricco needs more body, but I don't know how to get it. I'm sure the tools I need are buried somewhere in the technology tree, but the game has no intention of explaining exactly how to do that, and instead simply forges ahead on a pre-written story that explains only the very basics of the game's mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: A game that has lots of potential but needs a lot of work to get there. My biggest issue with this game is that I have to hunt to try and figure out anything. You wine needs more body? Okay, how do we do that? No idea after 5 several hours of playing the game. You would think it would have to do with the press but the tool tips don't tell me that it does. You want to make a great wine? Wine scores are seemingly at random and I have no idea why. I do the same steps to the same starter wine and eventually my wine went from 86% down to 60 something. I'm cleaning the machines, doing everything I can think of and nothing.Then there is the interface itself. The X button of the alert pop-ups needs a sniper's aim to hit them every time otherwise you are getting put into a menu that you don't want. Sure, you can not click them, but once again this shouldn't be that hard.Then there is the economy. Money rules, of course. To sell most of your wine at a good price you need these vendors that want specific types of wine. To make the wines they want you need money. To get money you need to sell them wine. Sure, you can trash their cards for a cost of losing levels, but after trashing the cards for 4 turns straight and still not having anyone wanting the beginning wine I have I was running out of farm levels. I've tried some of their mechanics like opening a store in my warehouse. This seemed to get me more customers, but at the cost of $500/month. This worked out to me losing money on average.I did enjoy the look of the game. The art was exactly what I would have hoped for and I think they nailed it. I named my ducks Scrooge and Quackers. All in all a frustrating experience that I'm no longer willing to put the hours into learning. I wish the developers luck.
_childDocuments_.name: Hundred Days - Winemaking Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: It really isn't all that fun, which is a shame since a vineyard simulator is something that would be interesting. The mechanics are more flashy than anything else, having to play 'cards' down on a board and figure out how to fit them in Tetris style, but there's really no substance behind them. The varietals you have access to are very limited and the actual growing and fermentation process leaves a lot to be desired.I've seen a few others criticize the story mode/tutorial, and rightfully so. If the developers wanted to do world building, then they failed at it by having every character be either dull or unnecessarily abrasive. If the developers wanted to cleverly introduce and explain mechanics, they failed as they present everything with a wall of text. I was only able to fumble through my first bottling because I knew enough of the terminology.As it stands, if you're looking for a wine making simulator on Steam, your better bet is Terroir. At least that one focuses more on the process and less on gimmicky mechanics that only detract from the overall experience.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: There has been a significant amount of post-launch support, and the developers are moving the game in a good direction. I'm happy to switch this review to positive.~~~I'm at a stage in my life where I can throw away this kind of money, but I still don't know what I was thinking. This is essentially a very polished flash game from 2007 Newgrounds. Or maybe it's a 2021 early access title on Steam, masquerading as a final product. The core gameplay loop is very interesting, and the devs have done a very good job with the audiovisuals. However, QoL is non existant, and the UI is a complete slog (in addition to ghost clicks and bugs). Most of this game is opening the workshop menu, watching the transition animation, clicking on "clean tractor", clicking it again since it didn't register the first time, exiting the menu, watching the transition animation again, dragging the "clean tractor" card onto the board. And repeating this process every single turn for cleaning your silos, cleaning your press, cleaning your bottling machine, etc. Every item in the game gets dirty after being used, so you literally have to do this every turn. Who is this game for? I guess if you are used to pre-2000 strategy games with miserable levels of micromanagement, you're interested in wine in general, and you care about the graphics/soundtrack slightly more than about gameplay - then maybe the game is for you. But the price tag is still outrageous.

_childDocuments_.review: (TLDR: Game simple, but fun. Me no like $$$ for tech. Me wish game make me wine smart)At a base level this game hits home.  It covers the basics of fermentation and wine making and the nuances that go into it's production.The mechanics are simple but still fun, albeit not specifically challenging.The tech tree is my only major qualm with game-play. Example: $20,000 spent on aging technology to then.... spend $15,000 on actually purchasing the barrel that I just  purchased the technology for.Meanwhile, I'm making $1,000/day (early game), and there are 5 days a season... I'm not reinventing the wheel here. I'm using OG wine making techniques. WTF am I doing with a tech tree that I have to PAY for. Why not simply use fame as the sole barometer for tech progression?The game had such a beautiful opportunity to educate players to the wine as well as the wine making process while still having a relatively fun game-play mechanic.Education is where the game falls flat for me.Each time I pick it up I am looking to learn how to make better wine. Not perfect wine, but better, or different. Mess with flavor and season and time of harvest. Mess with terrior to make a new strange wine variety.You can get good notes from your wine which are vaguely described, but off flavors, like "Reduction" are simply... present.No explanation of what that is, what it tastes/smells like, where it came from. The game basically says ..."sometimes your wine sucks" and moves on.Educate me. Have more about the grape varieties. Have more about the faults and notes. Explain to me what I SHOULD be tasting if I were to drink this specific style of wine. Teach me how to drink wine IRL so when I do I can be better prepared for it.You've cornered a niche market on wine making games. You spent a lot of time and effort in making it nuanced enough to have soil composition and even have a grape variety maker. I can check the grapes and see the color and powdery mildew on individual clusters.And you then tell me "Sometimes your wine has faults" with no extra information.You've got a cool game, you can make it a great one. Educate us.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd want to like this game, but I don't and I can't recommend it. On the other hand, I appreciate the fact the developers innovated and tried to invent something new. The content of the game seems to be quite solid too.There's a very annoying bug with buttons. Some buttons (especially sell buttons) usually don't work at the first few clicks. Multiple clicks are necessary. In my opinion such annoying bug is not acceptable for a release version. This just killed my patience and I gave up.Apart from this annoyance, I'd summarise my opinion saying "the game lacks of common good sense". Why my fame/reputation should depend mostly on random meaningless special requests from buyers? Why should I produce a bad quality wine in order to increase my fame/reputation (because I have to fulfil a meaningless request in order to avoid an heavy fame penalty)? Why is my technology tree blocked by fame instead of money or lab investments/infrastructure/employees? Etc...Finally, maybe I din't get things right, but playing about 5 hours I was still stuck with early stages of the game. I think the game doesn't have the complexity and deepness to justify having such a slow pace.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a neutral option. This game has many positive traits and isn't horrible by any means.There are a lot of variables that seem to be hidden or not explained concisely. I'm all for having a sense of randomness in a game, but at the same time the stakes of the game need to be balanced to make it enjoyable. I do not feel that this game is well balanced in that regard. It is a game that is slow to develop, but easy to mess up and even simple mistakes, or random variables, tend to compound. This is coupled with an autosave system that only keeps one save at a time, so unless you strategically manually save you're out of luck and you are starting from the absolute beginning. That cycle makes this game less peaceful than I would personally like. If the autosave was tweaked to have multiple slots, the experience would be better imo and you could explore the variables of the game with more safety. As it stands now, you are punished for experimenting, at least in the beginning stages of the game. There are mechanics in the game where essentially 2+2 doesn't equal 4 each time, but it's out of one's control and coupled with the slight grind of the game, it's just unpleasant at times. I have not unlocked much of the game because of this fact and it is a bit frustrating to be doing things as right as you can, get messed up by some random variable, and have to start all over again. You're simultaneously boxed in to doing the same things repeatedly, but also if you don't try new things you'll eventually spiral into losing. That's what my experience has felt like with this game. Overall the game isn't bad. It is a fairly chill experience and you can kind of veg out while playing. It would be nice though if it were a little more forgiving. I do not feel that this is a game that has the same replay value as say Stardew Valley, or other similar games, and it is more punishing for no real reason.

_childDocuments_.review: THIS IS NOT A CONVENTIONAL SIMULATION GAME. It's more of a puzzle/management game with simulation aspects. It is also very grind-y. You will repeat the same actions with slight variations based on RNG.With that being said, I like Hundred Days a lot! It's challenging enough that I don't get bored playing it, but chill enough that I can put a show on in the background and wind down. I like the aspect of world seeds for vineyards, where different sections of the vineyard will be best for growing a certain grape. I got a world seed with literally the perfect field for growing Chardonnay!I also feel like I know more about wine now than I did going in. However, I say this as someone who only knew wine was alcoholic. I knew nothing at all about it beforehand :pThe main downside of this game is that it's miscategorized. This is more of a tetris-like puzzle game that focuses on managing a vineyard. People see the word "Simulator" and go into Hundred Days with certain expectations that are not met.To sum it up: Hundred Days is overall a good game. It's just the right mix of chill and challenging, and also provides information about wine you might not know beforehand. If you don't mind the grind (or the whims of RNGsus) and want a unique experience, this is the game for you.

The game’s intricate systems and charming presentation make it a standout for fans of simulation and management genres. Perfect for those who want to dive into the art and science of winemaking from the comfort of their own home.
_childDocuments_.name: Hundred Days - Winemaking Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: As a real life enologist in the Langhe I really enjoyed this game, in few words everything is on point and quite realistic. I understand that it may lack some content about other kind of wines and some other minor things, or that the story may result a bit flat, but for someone not knowing anything about wine this is a very nice way to learn. I've read in other reviews some critics about the UI, however I think it is well done and quite intuitive after the first 10 min.Also I would like to point out the effort put in the description of all the action cards either for the vineyard management and in the winery. The wine word is so vast that it would be impossible to have everything in just one game, also this is the only game that exist of this kind, where you have to manage a wine business.The developers have done a beautiful job and i hope to see some updates in future because it has a lot of potential.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo to this game sometime during the early COVID times and fell in love. When it launched, I bought it but had to wait to play due to real life obligations. This weekend I sat down to play and found myself wondering, "What happened?"I admit I can't remember everything about the demo, but the full extent of the gameplay wasn't available then. And that was to the demo's credit. My biggest peeve with Hundred Days is the clunky attempt to gate progression through your money and fame. The ability to grow more varietals, buy a trailer, hire people, establish sales operations, etc. can be found on a "Technologies" tree which typically asks for 500, 10000, 20000, and so on for progression along each of the four separate branches of your operation. In addition to those costs you'll need to have fame (which is earned through special orders) and to upgrade your buildings. It sounds like it makes sense initially, but when your starting amount is 50,000 and you find yourself scraping together money in the first 10 years of your business growing Barbara and Chardonnay, it kills any sense of discovery.Hopefully the developers will consider an alternate format; something like action cards with unique/difficult shapes that require your vineyard to dedicate time. Thematically it makes sense- business owners need more for equipment and expansion, but it doesn't cost us 10,000 to figure out I need a trailer to sell grapes. It would take time to research the best models within our price range and purchase it. I also find it hard to believe that some operations are limited to how well known the business is. Surely a relatively unknown winemaker could source Nebbiolo grapes if they had the money or connections.Which brings me to another disappointment, the Story mode. It's probably better to think of it as the "tutorial" mode. Most of the NPC conversations serve to give you tips on winemaking or some of the game's features. The plot is suggested and then resolved quickly with no real effort on the player's part. There were a few moments where I thought that there would be features that would allow me to persuade or negotiate for marketing, storage, tools, etc., but that never came to pass.  No crisis for the player and no consequences either. The game is most enjoyable when you play on "Very Easy" mode which is with a wealth of starting cash. True to real life! Even when I nerfed my ability to earn and keep fame and increased the frequency of diseases it was preferable. The Story and Endless Mode are light on general winemaking advice, so this helps understand the mechanics better when you can play longer without going bankrupt. At this time I haven't been able to find or definitively determine if the game takes into account how long you wait to harvest, press, or crush your grapes. Does the rainy weather impact different varieties of grapes? Can winemakers attempt to amend the soil to optimize a variety's growth? Aside from the Story mode it doesn't appear there is a comprehensive explanation of how deep the winemaking can go.I did check to see if the DLC addresses these concerns, and even if it did, I think Hundred Days is difficult to recommend. The music, art design, and concept are fantastic! But I suspect a lot of gamers may find themselves discouraged by the lack of explanations and progression in gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Hundred Days - Winemaking Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: After 15 or 20 minutes in campaign mode, I've been insulted non-stop, I have no idea how the game works, I've made zero decisions, and I've clicked through hundreds of incredibly boring and pointless dialogue screens that have nothing to do with wine or advancing the game narrative. I got lost in some menus once and found my way out, but I wasn't clear why I was sent to a screen where I can't do anything. When you get a turn, you're given a single card to play, and all the cards are always playable, so there are no decisions to make. You can choose to plop it in one of several positions, but it has no bearing on the outcome. So, you play your only card, click next turn, play card, click next turn, etc. Then Anna comes and tells you about her mani/pedi, and some old guy tells you he hates you and he wishes you weren't here. Message received, I'm gone.

_childDocuments_.review: Its a great little management sim about winemaking.What stands out:+it has a nice colourful smiplistic artstyle and is obviously made with a lot of care and attention to detail.+It teaches you a lot about the process of winemaking and is very detailed and it feels sufficiently deep but not overly complex.+It has a unique system for managing your time: Tasks have certain shapes and you have to arrange them on a board of growing size to reflect what you are able to do each turn. I was skeptical at first, but after a while it really feels like a very organic way of slipping through a minigame in a very sneaky way that has actual benefits when done efficiently.+It is in a mature state of development and runs stable.Things I have to wrestle with:-QoL could be improved a lot. Why cant I see if a plot has been harvested just by looking at it? Why can't I pin special orders so I have their requirements in the main screen? Instead I have to click around into a second submenu every time I have finished a certain step in production of a batch, because i again forgot what the requirements are. Its a very constant annoyance, especially in late game. Why is there no quick way to check in the encyclopedia what Wine-Aspects I have yet to discover? Its also very tedious to do, everything is hidden in several menus, and you are constantly running around and trying to find the information you need instead of having it in a convenient place.-Story mode is more like a tutorial with a lot of text, I found that the story had only a very low influence on the actual gameplay, which is not bad per se, but I found it not that engaging.Nonetheless, I had some really fun hours with the game, I like the concept and idea a lot and the mechanics are also well done.
_childDocuments_.name: Hundred Days - Winemaking Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: This game captures perfectly the tedious juggling of competing priorities that is winemaking, along with the grind it takes to stay in the black. However, I found none of the joy in this game that I did working at real wineries for many years. I salute them for a beautiful game with a clever, well-thought-out play style, but unfortunately it just gets dull and repetitive too quickly to justify the cost. At this point I can't recommend it to people.
_childDocuments_.name: Hundred Days - Winemaking Simulator

_childDocuments_.name: Hundred Days - Winemaking Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: This isn’t a puzzle or strategy game, it’s a poorly written visual novel with barely any gameplay. The very few times you actually get to put any puzzle pieces together between the slog that are the walls of filler dialogue, it’s trivially easy. No sufficient tutorial followed by constant hand-holding and dialogue, and a puzzle that doesn’t even make your braincells wake up from REM sleep. Played this with my partner, and we could hardly keep our attention on the screen, at some point I started skimming through the pretentious dialogue in hopes of getting to do any, ANY gameplay for more than two turns. No choices, no variety, nothing interesting. I really wanted to like it, it was on my wishlist for ages. The seemingly deep menus, the lovely artstyle, the idea of working on my own wine. But even the story wasn’t immersive or remotely engaging, because instead of the game letting you just insert your own name, you’re forced into the boots of whiney and boring as oatmeal Emma. Monotone filler story, hardly any gameplay, incredibly limited gameplay if you ever get to it, menu overload for the sole purpose of making the game seem more interesting than it is.Genuinely enjoyed the very first office section more than any of the wine-related gameplay, that one was actually a sliver of fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Hundred Days - Winemaking Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- Pretty addictive gameplay loop- Just enough attention to detail so you don't feel like drowning in information- Good value for moneyThe cons for this game are a bit difficult to sum up. First for some background; I am currently doing my masters in Viticulture in South Africa which means I do have a decent knowledge of winemaking but might lack some context to the Italian winemaking scene which this game is based off of. While the game does a good job of giving surface level info of all the processes and nuances associated with winemaking, it doesn't feel detailed enough so that I would consider it an educational tool per-say. Like more detailed explanations of the grape or wine properties, reasons as to why certain soil or management decision are important. The story-mode/tutorial of the game keeps mentioning textbooks and notes the character has but I'd love to see those notes or reccomendations instead of having to figure out the ideal wine properties for myself. There are some features that I would have liked to have but might potentially break the balance of the game or interfere with the gameplay-loop.  I would have like a feature to do a proper grape analyses before harvesting to see the exact amount of sugar and acidity instead of just levels/or ratios. I would have also like double the ammount of time per season just so I don't blast through multiple vintages in say 30 minutes. Also being limited to yeasts based on research seems weird since in reality you usually just get it off of a catalogue.  But then again It seems the devs did have to strike a balance between retaining the game aspect while retaining some bit of realism.Ultimately pretty fun game ideally for people that allready know a good bit about wine-making but don't want to play a hardcore simulator

_childDocuments_.review: Ugh!  The theme and subject matter are intriguing, and there's a lot to learn about viniculture here.But the core gameplay loop is awful.   The player is asked to repeat the same minimalist Tetris puzzle, whose actions don't change, the narrow tech tree is step-locked, and so progression offers no interesting choices.  The most unforgivable sin of Hundred Days: The Grind.   Hundred Days's Grind is absolutely merciless.   You will repeat the same mindless task for hours just to unlock one new puzzle piece (say, a barrel to age wine in).   To afford the buy the puzzle piece, you will grind some more.   Then more.  And more.     You have to save up for hours to buy a Shop so you earn the mercy of clicking 10% less!   If I didn't know better, I'd say this was an exploitative F2P game; they just patched out the Energy bar and slapped a $25 premium game tag on it.The game clearly has some love behind it; the visuals are pleasant and the subject knowledge of wine is impressive: I definitely learned something.    But it just takes too damn long to do so.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT1: After 2 updates from the devs and being in the discord server, I have to say that they are incredibly responsive and are quick with important fixes to the game to make the gameplay more fluid. They acknowledge the balance issues and actively make changes to fix them, my problems below are mostly fixed or on the way of being fixed. This is great to see.Now, I do believe that it deserves full price. ORIGINAL: Played the story and continued until year 2040, story is MEH but this game isn't a story game, story is there to introduce us to the mechanics. I really like the concept and the design of this game, I think it is replayable and enjoyable to some degree. For wine + strat games lovers this game is like a delight with it's premise.You can tell that the devs put a lot of effort into the aesthetic and music as well.There are a few bugs, I noticed that the "sell" button for customers require double or triple clicking sometimes, which is normally just one. The tetris-y layout sometimes doesn't recognise the tiles when they're in the correct place, you just have to hover again to fix it though, which fixes it. BUTI have to say that this game is extremely grindy, I played it for 4 hours and I have some experience with this type of games, but it requires so much repetition to actually make some money to upgrade your stuff. I get it that in a way, that is more realistic, creating a vinery takes generations but as a game, this requires so much patience. Which I don't really have.I feel like this game could use more play testing and player feedback to increase the speed a little bit, so we don't get bored. For example, to actually place a shop to your warehouse, you have to first purchase the TECHNOLOGY then the actual shop, so it ends up double the price. When you combine this for everything, it drastically slows the game.You also can't just leave it be and wait for them to harvest, it requires you to do everything which means constant repetition for the first few hours of the game, there isn't 50 different tasks as well, it's more like, next day, put tiles on the ground, next day, repeat. Including going to the sales page to manually sell each bottle until you have I think 50k to spend, just to automate this process. Which will also increase your monthly expenses.This game becomes more of a "how can I safely grind the money to get the upgrades I want as quickly as possible", which I don't really enjoy. I ended up mostly bulk selling because it was just more convenient, especially for bigger lots. I feel like it is a case of too much realism takes the fun away a little.(right now)I am not disappointed in the fact that I did wait for this game for a year, it literally got released today so balance issues are fine, but it does need some tweaking.So I do recommend this game but on sale, I hope the game will become better and will maybe see more features in the feature and doesn't get abandoned. Because I love the concept.I'll probably spend more time on it to see HOW I can actually be quicker to get these expensive upgrades, because I did enjoy it. It just tests my patience a little.

_childDocuments_.review: As a wine enthusiast, student of Bacchus, and general private school prig, I absolutely adore this game. It's a brilliant time filler and is actually designed by genuine Oenologists. Ok so the actual storyline is a bit like a E-book, in a sense that is the actual tutorial. It talks you through the processes and what each step needs and does to the end product. After you complete the storyline (and remain solvent) the actual game begins!In it's core sense it is a management game, much like the real thing in life, granted I'm no Vintner or Vineyard expert, but I enjoy passing the time, making my own little brand, in some obscure region of Northern Italy.Also the Devs are genuinely invested in this little curio, responding extremely quickly to any question or ideas from the community to help this game grow.You look at any of the negative reviews they all possess the stale and heartless judgement of people that don't quite understand the actual community this game has fostered, and actually given a voice to.I sincerely hope with all my heart this game continues to grow, and it has my full support and endorsement.
