_childDocuments_.review: Spent 5 hours with this game last night, and overall was pretty happy with the game. I did have a few issues, which I think may have stemmed from what was ultimately a lacking tutorial.+ Informational and educational+ Very much a "one more turn" type game, where I found myself doing 100+ more turns after I was planning on going to bed+ The tech tree, expansion, etc. all make sense- Some things (like the cleaning room) don't actually seem to work? Or maybe that's only for tractors and not wine making equipment?- This game needs a lot more keyboard shortcuts. Let me get in to the menu to sell my wine more easily.- The shop only gives you the ability to sell to private customers, or nobody. Shops aren't included. It's not immediately clear how to set the selling priority ($$ vs. # of bottles, etc.)- Cleaning and repairing equipment isn't super well explained - do you NEED to clean it every time, or can you let it degrade for a while and then do it? Why does the pop up only happen some times and not others?- I feel like it's extremely difficult to get out of the 2 plot rut. It takes a really long time to unlock the ability to expand your board enough to allow for 2 simultaneous harvests, and I feel like that's going to constrain a lot of players from expanding to that 3rd farm and beyond (or maybe I'm just bad, idk).Overall, I had fun with this game last night, and I'm sure I'll be firing this up a few more times to try something new. _childDocuments_.review: So, I stream and record a lot of Rpgs and Simulation games to give opinions and to give criticism. This game is, interesting, in a good way. The good of this game outweigh the bad and what is here has a good foundation. Initially, this is a solid wine making game. The concept is simple enough, the complexity will keep you trying again and again to get it right, and it is also pretty tough. It feels simple enough, but, if you're not careful, you will bankrupt before you can even go big.The bad: The story is not very good. The characters are bland, they don't really give you ANY insight into what you're doing unless you understand a bit of viticulture yourself (luckily I do), and the ability to expand is incredibly difficult if you are not FULLY SURE of what you're doing. The mechanics surrounding special orders is not good either, as they as for wines that you really have no chance of producing and in order to clear your special orders, your reputation gets penalized for it. Now, its only a -2 when you gain a +4 or +5, but this drags the whole experience down when you see special orders for wines you either cannot make, or know that if you did, they would be near impossible to sell and would have a low rating below 40.The meh: This game is hard, which is not an issue, it is the means in which the game itself is hard. A lot of it is lack of descriptions of what the various yeast strains do, what some of the equipment and expansions to the various buildings would do for me, and the cost of expansion anywhere in the game is incredibly high, and as someone else stated, you then have to buy the item you unlocked (which is fine, you have to have a solid income to do this effectively, but it is quite difficult for a new player and the story mode doesn't really help with this concept).The good: It is a hard wine making game. The clicky complaint, to me, falls on dead ears because if you watched the promo video I mean, what did you expect. It's not a clicker game by any stretch of the imagination, but it is a tile placement game, almost as if this could be a board game. The way you make the wine is pretty accurate to real world viticulture and it is somewhat relaxing when you have an idea of what to do and where to spend your money in specific upgrades. I was able to make 100k a year in game with two plots of land growing Barbara and Chardonay. I had to uproot the starting vines and grow both plots to be dense, but it gave me more grapes then my warehouse and winery could handle, and with some more fixes and upgrades, was able to produce and sell enough to operate smoothly. From there, expanding was a little difficult, but ultimately it is going to be trial and error to see how to upgrade the facilities and how to expand safely without bankrupting your winery.This is a solid game, you just have to try and learn the mechanics of it through a little bit of trial and error. I enjoy the endless mode more than the story mode and I do recommend this if you enjoy the theme of wine making and if you like a strategy game that has complex mechanics and is unforgiving in it's own way. Perhaps a few patches and expansion of the story would correct a lot of issues that people are complaining about. Even a more expansive tutorial OR (and my opinion better) make sure every upgrade in the game has a clear definition of what it does. Does it help make your wines less sweet? Does it decrease acidity, does this age my wine more than the last upgrade, why should I buy this upgrade etc...I agree, this game is a wee bit pricey, 15 bucks is a recommended amount to spend on this for sure, but buy it outright if you really like the wine making theme for the most part.(Quantity over quality gets you a long way. Buy a field and make it DENSE with grapes, that way you can max out your warehouse and always have some kind of revenue, then expand your warehouse to meet the amount of customers you will bring in. Make sure you are ALWAYS producing this wine and you should have a steady flow of cash to buy all the upgrades that seem out of reach. It is time consuming, but it generally works.)

_childDocuments_.review: I want to love this game, and to an extent I like it, however, it is hard to say that I love it as it is. I have a few reasons why I like it, and a few reasons why I can not state that I love it. For the people that do not want to read the full thing here is my point. The game is likeable because;However, it's bad sides are;I recommend it, but it is not going to be for everyone. However, it is worth a try if you like to play management games that are more on the simple side.As to why I like it,  I want to state that the game UI is very good looking. The artstyle is very consistent, where nothing looks like "well this looks out of place.". It shows that the dev team put a lot of effort towards the game being but artistic and also having very simple UI. If you pick up this game, you wont have any issues locating the game features on the UI. A winemaking game where you are trying to achieve the best wine you can make through trial and error, as well as upgrading your vineyard. This creates an atmosphere where you could be easily spending hours on the game going "just one more batch of this Chardonnay, I'll surely get it this time.", which allows normally annoying features like trial and error, and grinding much more appealing, which is sometimes absolutely unbearable in management games. First of all I must mention, I am no wine connoseur, I like to enjoy a nice wine with friends, but when I am alone, anything goes as long as it is accompanied by nice atmosphere, so I am in no way qualified enough to say whether the game is completely true to reality or it is very simple, however, I can say that it  like it is inclusive enough that I am doing something a real winemaker would somewhat do. Makes the experience much more immersive since I can say, "Ah yes because I let my Chardonnay grapes grow until fall, they will be much less acidic and much more sweet, allowing me to accurately balance the sweetness to the acidity at the fermentation stage.", and so on, you get the idea.Now, with all good things, come the bad (and the ugly hehe). I would like to mention the things that drag this game down. It surely allows you to play the game on a very basic level. Things like how to buy a farm, how to harvest grapes and how to make a wine are explained in the tutorial. However, the game boasts some hidden mechanics, such as, like I mentioned before, harvest mechanics, in which the time at which you harvest your grapes determines their stats, wine qualities depending on the barrel and the yeast you use, and bad wine qualities, which are almost always  left unexplained. It makes you say, as a complete stranger to winemaking, "My wine just got 60/100 from tasting scores even though its stats were fairly accurate because it was uhh  What is mercaptan? How do I deal with it??" No Idea, never explained.  Throughout your game, you will have many opportunities to spend your hard-earned wine money. One place you can spend them on are your technological upgrades, however, especially the board expansions which allow you to perform more actions at once, are way tooo late game oriented. Honestly after the first few upgrades, it will be really hard for you to see value in them until you can bulk buy them. 50k on 2 squares? Even though there is literally like 1 action in the entire game which is 2 squares. You may say; "well the squares allow you to try on different orientations, increasing your effectiveness even though the size increase is not much.". Technically yes, but not really since the small tasks are already all do-able with a small board, and the big task that is harvesting, you will not get any value out of the board for them until you get the biggest board available. That is correct, until you get the biggest board available, you can NOT harvest two farms at once, and considering the fact that the time at which you harvest your grapes are very important, this is very rough. It makes it so that you practically can never high quality wines of anymore than two types of wine, even though there are like, what, 6-7 types of grapes. Since you can not make those high quality wines, they sell for less, meaning that you are much more slower at getting the board up to its maximum level, meaning that you will be stuck with one harvest at a time, with very lackluster ways of speeding it up, which practically only working for a single year of harvesting before needing repairs to work which take even more money. It is a boring and repetitive cycle that prevents the player from feeling the reward of making a good wine. Marketing upgrades are also pretty much pointless beyond the shop upgrade, as they only lead you to lose weekly income with very little gains since every action requires your precious board, which is already small enough to only allow one harvest at a time.One other way to spend money is to buy land. This is a bit weird, because obviously lands would be expensive, but some land are SOOO expensive with no apparent benefits, it seems like they are grape oriented more than cost-reward efficiency oriented. Even then, the beggining land is a sub-par area to grow your beginner grapes (barberra), you often get unfit land trait on your wines and lose quality, due to something the gmae provided you and you had no choice over. And this issue never really goes away, there are some small, very small (and very expensive) ways of improving your lands, but overall, if you have a bad land, you are pretty much stuck with it. Not much the say here, the story is very short, not very deep, full of stereotypical characters and lines, and coupled with the lackluster tutorial, it gives the player a power trip which goes away when the player starts and endless mode and loses within 10 years due to lack of knowledge in all departments. I get that the main point of the game is not the story, that is why I am not very critical of it, but honestly, I can see that you could make a much more engaging story where you first start to regionally gain fame and then move on to the global market.Overall, I like the game enough to recommend it to people into management games without the hassle of it. However, the few problems it has are glaring once you get into it.

Story mode needs some work and better writing but the gameplay itself is great and as a winemaker the thought and purpose given to the content was excellently done. They incorporated winemaking knowledge from the vineyard and cellar aspects and managed to do so while making a fun game. Had to go meet a friend yesterday and found myself clicking the next turn button telling myself just one more turn let me bottle this wine oh one more turn let me deal with this vineyard issue. Saw one complaint about how the wine scores don't make any sense and it's not clear how to adjust certain traits of wine. Honestly welcome to winemaking! After a few seasons you figure out how to make your wine perfect for each variety as you grow it, and how every step of the process affects the final product. _childDocuments_.review: Overall Rating: 4/5Gameplay: 3/5 The game is complex, as it's meant to be. It is somewhat repetitive, and is all about managing many aspects of the business. There is room to grow here (it has just been released after all) The tile action system makes sense, and sometimes has you leaving a space open to maximize your value. I can't wait to see future patches for the game, and how it grows from here. Theme: 5/5I love the vineyard background and it changing with the seasons and with what you have planted. The tone of the game is just right, with only small challenges between you and the goal of making a delicious wine. Managing a business means sometimes things have to wait, which happens often when completing certain actions. Making your own bottle and making a label is a nice touch, though they still need to add more graphics for label making. Challenge: 2/5This is not a challenging early game, there is a bit of a recipe for balancing all the things, but once you get over that small hill, it becomes easy. _childDocuments_.review: I deeply enjoy this game and its chill relaxed atmosphere and explorative, problemsolvint, managment gameplay. Highly reccomended if you enjoy taking your time and relaxing with a game. Do not expect to understand everything at once, even when you get a good grasp on the game there will be years when weather or simmilar rng issues mess up you product. One big tip, don't expand to quickly, all equipemnt is very excpensive. Unless it is really nessesary, hold off untill you really need.Some improvements i think could make the experience more enjoyable are, moving the timeline backwards. It takes years and years to build up capital to be able to expand. _childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty solid management game! It does get a fair bit into the nuance of winemaking and as I progress in the game I'm opening up a lot of new options. I've seen some reviews criticizing the writing of characters and such in story mode; for what it's worth, I think the writing is significantly above average and I've enjoyed the story mode so far.The card and grid system are neither the best nor the worst way I've seen to organize a management game like this. I'm neutral on it so far. It has a bit more character than a straightforward system of time tracking, employee payroll and available machinery, but it's less transparent. There's no real concrete reason why one step is one sort of tetronimo or another so sometimes the things you want to do don't fit together in one turn for no particular reason.The game has some rough edges and clunkiness, especially around saving, but it's more polished than I usually expect an indie game of this complexity to be at launch. I am having a good time.I have some complaints about how advanced information is communicated to the player. The basics are covered reasonably well in the story/tutorial but there is a lot more to the game than that.

name: Call of the Sea
detailed_description: Buzz About the Game It is 1934, in the far reaches of the South Pacific. Norah has crossed the ocean following the trail of her missing husband’s expedition and finds herself on a lush island paradise - a nameless, forgotten place, dotted with the remnants of a lost civilization. What strange secrets does it hold, and what might Norah unearth in her quest for the truth? Explore a stunning tropical island (meticulously modelled in Unreal Engine 4), brimming with fantastic sights, lost ruins and occult mysteries. Experience a charming character study of a woman on her quest to discover the truth of the disappearance of her husband and to find out who she really is, fully voiced by Cissy Jones (Firewatch, The Walking Dead: Season 1). Immerse yourself in a story-driven adventure full of emotion, suspense and surreal surprises. Investigate the clues left by a previous voyage, piece together what happened, and solve a variety of clever puzzles.

There is a TL;DR below for each game, but I played them back to back and you might want to review each if you are truly in a comparative strategy.TL;DR - Hobs Barrow > Call of the Sea. It all comes down to voice activity and narrative expectations. Legitimately one of the only games I have not followed through on and completed. It just felt odd, and janky. It also genuinely felt like the game developers weren't going to show me anything new throughout my playthrough. **Spoilers** -  I went ahead and read the synopsis and have personally decide that I did not miss out on much. If you played the bethesda CotC game or have read any Lovecraft story, this doesn't amount to much more than a propped-up "okay"  version of it. Frankly, it could have spent more time and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ got there sooner and I probably would have enjoyed it more. Play Hobs Barrow, Dagoth, or Bethesdas CotC before playing this game. Hobs BarrowAn expertly told occult-oriented story where the narrative beats are present and appreciated, as well as the voice acting is on-par and nails the tone of each character.The lingering, long-moments after the story are properly felt and each moment is earned with a sufficient build-up.Call of The SeaNOTE: I DID NOT FINISH THIS GAME.I wish I did, but the VA for the game was distracting and it pulled me out of the game enough that I didn't care to see how it ended.The narrative beats were interesting, the stories and puzzles intriguing, but the guiding, driving narrative was flat out bad.Comparative between both:Hobs Barrow: Arrive in a podunk town, based on the letters of some ♥♥♥♥, and find out that this town holds onto a bunch of weird superstitions surrounding this mound that you need to excavate. As the narrative progresses the VA and the cutscenes show the main character unraveling as more plot points prove to be uncanny.Call of the Sea: Story starts with a deeply personal connection being missing, with radio science for MONTHS. Main character conscripts a local charter for a boat, wild ♥♥♥♥ unravels, and the VA and cutscenes do not unnerve the character at all.STAKES - SPOILERSHobs Barrow - Throughout the game, the highest the stakes are raised is one dead person and one incapacidated person.Call of the Sea - Multiple dead people before the second and third act.Response to Stakes - SPOILERsHobs Barrow - I need to ge to the bottom of this. If not for my own will and triumphing over this superstition, but also for my father who has succumbed to this power.Call of The Sea - I have already been infected with whatever the ♥♥♥♥ inhabited here, my husband is probably dead since all I've done  is unravel uncanny deaths of his crewmates and I'm just perpetually chipper about the madness taking hold of the survivors. _childDocuments_.review: If you search for Lovecraftian games on Steam, you’ll find a ton of games on offer. But one thing that seems almost near universal is that most of these games tend to fall into the horror category in some fashion. And I don’t blame them, Lovecraft’s stories did most often deal with existential dread, so it’s hard to imagine something Lovecraftian that would deviate from that. So imagine my curiosity when I stumbled across Call of the Sea.It's obviously inspired by the stories of Lovecraft, particularly those relating to the fish-god Dagon. But unlike many of the aforementioned Lovecraftian games, Call of the Sea is not an overt horror experience. It draws more inspiration from pulpy early 20th century adventure stories. And while Lovecraft’s narratives were more about the bigger picture of humanity’s insignificance in the face of overwhelming cosmic terror, Call of the Sea is a very character focused piece.The setup is that you play as Norah Everhart. Norah suffers from an unspecified disease. And since this is a pulpy adventure tale, the obvious route to deal with it was for her husband Harry to set out into the wide-open world to find a cure. To that end he organized an expedition to a remote island near Tahiti. Now at this point, you can already guess how that went, because whenever you hear the term “expedition” in a piece of media, you know that things didn’t turn out well by the end. At some later point, Norah receives a package containing some instructions to also head to that island, which is where the actual gameplay happens.The game is mostly exploration based, meaning that you have to walk around this island a lot. Though fear not, this isn’t just another one of the plethora of walking simulators. For one, you’re given a much-needed run button, which I’m very grateful for. But more importantly, you also have to solve a bunch of puzzles to beat the game. What I like about the puzzles is that they strike a perfect balance between challenging but not impossible. Each puzzle section is completely isolated, there’s no inventory management to figure out where the few things you can pick up are required and in general, the environment along with Norah’s narration and her notes in her notebook give you enough hints to tell you what you’re supposed to do. Overall there’s a decent variety of puzzles on display, though I have to say the final stretch of the game felt a bit too repetitive by being asked to solve the same puzzle 5 times but slightly differently. And the game has a bit of a habit of sending you all over any given puzzle’s map to find clues on what to do next, which probably eats up more time than would be strictly necessary.As is typical with these pulpy adventure stories, most of the puzzles are ancient contraptions built by some kind of long-dead civilization. As such it did strain my suspension of disbelief a bit, but I guess if you want to experience this type of entertainment, it’s part of the price of admission. You just have to accept that these old mechanisms still work and that they somehow rearrange themselves after opening a path forward so the next person to come along finds it in its original state. Because I can’t imagine Harry resetting all these contraptions for Norah to find later on, they don’t serve an inherent purpose in the narrative.Said narrative is told in two parts. On the one hand it’s Norah’s internal monolog that accompanies everything you do on the island. Every object, letter or photograph you examine elicits a reaction from her. Sometimes this can be a bit overbearing, since whatever she’s saying is at times just clarifying what you’re seeing or reading yourself, so that wouldn’t have been necessary. The second half of the story is told by Harry through letters strewn about as well as the various scenes you can encounter at the campsites where you find the aforementioned letters.It's in those letters and scenes where you get to experience most of the Lovecraftian horror influence as the group of explorers start breaking down over time and losing their sanity. But Norah’s story is refreshingly different from that, in that it’s mostly about self-discovery. As you can tell, I’m trying to not get into too many details regarding the story because that would spoil it. And given that I want to recommend this game, I’m hesitant to put spoilers in here and instead urge you to go and play the game yourselves.But what I will say is that you shouldn’t expect grand cosmic horror here, like I said, it’s very much character focused. And that’s a positive standout feature of the narrative. The way the narrative gets unfolded and how the eventual conclusion unravels had me pausing for a moment at the finale when it’s time to choose an ending. What I like about the choice you get to make is that It’s not a good vs. bad ending sort of thing. Both endings make thematic sense and both endings are positive and negative in some sense. It’s not a moral choice you get to make here, it’s a human choice, in the sense that you have to decide the fate of two lovers and how they’ll spend the rest of their lives. What helps make this choice very powerful is the strong characterization of the two leads. By the way Norah talks about her unseen partner and the way Harry talks to her through his letters, you get a sense of their strong emotional bond. Harry risks his life and sanity to find a cure for his ill wife, which is a grand gesture if there was ever one, but his choice to save Norah through a far greater personal sacrifice is what really elevates the emotional tone of the game.Now while I would recommend the game based on the neat puzzles and the strong narrative alone, the beautiful aesthetics of the game are a neat bonus. Walking around the islands many gorgeous vistas is an absolute treat. And once you make your way deeper into the realm of the ancient inhabitants it takes on a fittingly ominous and dreamlike tone. But as I said, the Lovecraftian feel is only there to give you a sense of otherworldliness. And that’s what I really like about the game. It feels like over the years, Lovecraft has become such a strong influence in a lot of modern horror entertainment that people have forgotten how to do anything other than the same things Lovecraft already did with his works. Call of the Sea puts a refreshing new spin on things and manages to tell a gripping emotional story about its characters, instead of just focusing on the doom and gloom of our cosmic insignificance. It’s a compelling tale that takes just enough from the Cthulhu mythos to add some flavor without letting it overpower everything else.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the storytelling, especially the mixture of ancient murals, journal entries and protagonist's memories.It also completely subverted my expectations. Without spoiling any of the story, it's clear from the outset that there's something very old and very dangerous hidden on the tropical island you spend most of the game exploring. So naturally I expected the tone of the story to slowly descend into horror and darkness. And then it didn't. Instead it stayed stunningly beautiful and occasionally downright cozy till the very end.There are no chases, no fights, no jumpscares, just a calm stroll across a beautiful island .. and beyond.The puzzles are on the easier side, essentially exploring the area for clues and then using those clues to advance.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an absolutely beautiful entry in the Lovecraftian "horror" games. I put "horror" in quotes, because although there are elements of horror in it, it's not scary. Creepy, perhaps, as you uncover the remnants of your husband's doomed expedition and keep hoping the next grave you find won't be his. But mostly this is the story of Nora's discovery of herself, and it's beautiful. The acting is terrific, the setting is gorgeous, and the music is likewise wonderful. I played through both endings. (I highly recommend saving before going through the doors, so you can go back and try both of them.) Each is satisfying, though bittersweet. My only gripe is the puzzles. They're HARD. And even when I looked in the guide for solutions (there's a good gradual hint website), I often didn't understand how we got from point A to point B. But others might enjoy that aspect of the game more than I did. I was enthralled by the story and characters, so I still loved it.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. Well written, with great art, music, and voice. Only took a few hours to finish, and only a few more to 100%. The story flows quite neatly, with an ending that make logical sense . The narration the character makes is excellent, without being superfluous, and nearly perfectly matched what was going through my own head. Excellent system of taking notes of the puzzles in ways that act as 'hints,' but do not spoon-feed you the answers.Most of the puzzles were fairly basic, but they don't repeat unnecessarily. Most of the puzzle types are only seen onceNo real replay value, except to get 100%. Thankfully when you replay a chapter, the notes and log are filled with everything you had already gotten. It was nice to be able to focus on getting only what was missing, without having to go through the entire story.I did find a few spots where the game would freeze upon picking up a piece of paper or photograph, . Strangely, taking a screenshot usually fixed the issue.I recommend this to anyone who enjoys a good simple puzzle game with a well written story.
