_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea~~~~~~~~~~~~Call of the Sea is a unique story-driven, puzzle-adventure experience. Call of the Sea’s world revolves around Norah Everhart and her journey to uncover the truth behind her husband’s expedition to an uncharted island. As the Call of the Sea’s story progresses, Norah will discover more about herself, her incurable illness, the mysteries of the island, and her husband’s unfortunate expedition. Plot: its 1934, and Norah Everhart is on a voyage to meet her husband, Henry. Norah is very excited; it has been a while since Henry left on his expedition. Henry’s expedition was of great importance to him; Norah is unwell, and her symptoms are getting worst day by day. He is optimistic that he will find some sort of answer to cure his beloved Norah. Shortly after the captain called, “Miss Norah, we have arrived,” Norah ventures out alone to reunite with her beloved. But to her dismay, she finds an abandoned camp, with no clue about the whereabouts of Henry and/or the crew. Something has surely gone wrong, as a letter and a note from Henry indicate. Hoping that Henry and his team are all right, Norah decides to move inland. As she starts to move inland, she’s blown away by the island's beauty; she discovers local manmade structures, temples, puzzles, and complex mechanisms. As Norah progresses through the island, she discovers more and more about the mysterious island and how all this is related to her illness. She discovers a black substance, which Henry is calling black OoZe. Henry can’t really explain what this substance is.  It is surely something magical, or even evil; the doctor interacted with this black OoZe, and he soon perished, as did the others.She starts to uncover all the mysteries and the fate of the expedition.Norah finds notes, drawings, and letters by Henry and the other crew members, which lead her to the answer, puzzle by puzzle, piece by piece.Henry was right all along! He knew he would find something of great importance here, something that would surely save his beloved, even if he would need to sacrifice it all. Gameplay: The gameplay of Call of the Sea greatly compliments the amazing and creative story of the game. The gameplay is simple and effective and allows the player to take his/her time to explore the beautiful island and all its features. The basic WASD is slow and elegant, although it felt annoyingly slow sometimes when I was done exploring a particular area, or if I was revisiting it, which you have to do often in this game. The game also features a diary, which logs Norah’s adventure, her discoveries, and important details throughout the game. Norah also draws down clues as she discovers or goes through new areas, which later play an important role in solving the puzzles. Discovery and problem-solving play the most important role in this game. The game insists that the players go through every area to explore, collect clues, drawdown important details, and find notes and letters from the expedition. However, there’s really not much to explore.  The playable area seems large (it certainly gives that impression), whereas in actuality, you play through a limited area.  Finding clues and puzzle pieces is easy, which in the case of this game, is good and done very well. Voice acting and narration: Both voice-overs for Norah and Henry were very well done and gave the story a great flavor.  So did the narrations by Norah, which were consistently happening throughout the game, and at no point of my playthrough did I think that it was getting too repetitive or boring. Kudos to the actors who played these roles for doing a great job. Puzzles: Now let us get to the main course, the puzzles. Call of the Sea nailed it when it comes to puzzles, in my opinion; the game features a good balance of difficulty. Puzzles don’t have to be stupidly difficult to be enjoyable; well-balanced, well-placed and a good variety of puzzles has a far better outreach. And Call of the Sea did just that! The game features a good number and a good variety of puzzles, and each is well-designed and well-placed. Some were easy to solve yet hard to get clues from, while some were hard to solve and needed some close attention to figure out.  What they all have in common is that they are not too difficult to solve, and are very rewarding for those who like to explore the world and discover all the details, both in the open and hidden. What did make the puzzles a bit tedious or annoying is the fact that the movement speed is rather slow, and you have to explore and revisit multiple locations to gets clues or discover all the hidden details. World design: Absolutely gorgeous world design, full of different elements, colors, regions, structures, and many more. I loved it how the devs designed and divided the island into regions with minor changes at a time, rather than just throwing the player right into a unique region without any transition. The slow buildup of different elements before transitioning into a brand new area or region is much appreciated. Music and sound effects: A very well-put-together song features at the end of in this game; I absolutely love it! And it’s performed by the same actors who play Norah and Henry; they did a great job with the performance and gave the game an excellent touch. As did the sound effects and background ambient noises. Right from the get-go, I was stunned to hear how well they implemented all those sound effects and ambient noises without getting in the way of narrations. Considering all aspects of the game, Call of the Sea turned out to be a great indie title with a great touching story, voiced by a couple of talented actors, set on a beautiful island, with some great sound effects work. However, I must mention some minor issues that I faced with the performance; although the game is not that demanding, it felt quite sluggish at times, with minor lags. Positives: + Great Story+ Beautifully designed world + Brilliant narration + Good music selection + Brain-tickling puzzles + A great exploration experience + Great art style Negatives: - Sluggish performance at times with minor lags- Some clues and puzzles were not well explained - No custom settings, only graphical presetsHelp Norah Everhart in her search for the truth and for her beloved. Explore the mysterious island to uncover its secrets. 9/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very nice light lovecraftian exploration game. It strikes a weird balance, actually being lovecraftian (with many references to the mythos, but also some moments of existential dread, great atmosphere, and a fitting story), but yet including some wonder and magical moments (that's what I meant by "light lovecraftian" XD). Relatively easy puzzles, very nice easter eggs (although at least one of them would have been practically impossible to get without a walkthrough), straightforward gameplay with some amazing animations, nice ambiance and beautiful artistic scenery throughout, an interesting display of Polynesian culture, nice voice acting, soundtrack and sound design, and an entertaining, albeit cliched and predictable story. Playtime was right, and getting the achievements I missed was easy and even enjoyable once I had finished the game (you have a chapter select feature, and once you've beaten the game, you keep the logs of all the answers to the puzzles, so speedrunning a chapter to get a specific achievement is easy enough; easter eggs are pretty cool).Overall, it's definitely a well-rounded, nicely polished, sufficiently interesting and engaging, story-based, partly lovecraftian and partly wonder-filled adventure game.

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is a well-written, engaging story game brought to life by quality voice acting.  The voice actress who plays the main character really brings her to life, and she's a delightfully wry, yet emotional companion for your adventure exploring the island.  While you explore, you find abandoned campsites left behind by your missing husband, and you slowly piece together a larger story about the island and its history.  The graphics are beautiful, thought the tents do start to look overly familiar by the end, and the strangeness of the island is really well captured by the game's presentation.However, even though the game is an excellent story game, it doesn't play very well as a puzzle game.  Most of the puzzles are pretty similar, basically just roaming an area for symbols until you have the sequence to punch into the elaborate locks around the island.  Each puzzle is self-contained to one chapter and area, and serves more as an obstacle to the storytelling rather than enhancing it.  While I had several satisfying "Aha!" moments while solving some of the puzzles, most were pretty simple.  It doesn't help that the main character will jot down everything you need to solve the puzzle as you discover it, which renders paying attention to clues and figuring things out almost moot.That said, there's definitely some good kernels of puzzles in the game.  At the end, I found myself wishing I could play the game from Harry's perspective so that I could figure out the codes for myself, instead of having them all halfway solved by my husband.Spoilers aheadFor example, one puzzle in Chapter 4 deals with the diamond language of the people who live on the island.  The language, though limited, has some interesting structure to it, combining symbols to make new meanings.  But the meaning of every single symbol has already been deciphered and written down on loose pieces of paper scattered around the puzzle solving site.  This language is also only used in this chapter, as each chapter has its own symbols to decipher.I just imagine how a puzzle could have gone if one language was used throughout the game, slowly teaching the player how to read more and more complicated ideas.  For instance, if we had learned the diamond symbols for sun and water and animal in Chapter 1 instead of it being a completely different symbolic language.  Then other puzzles could build on that, increasing your vocabulary, and then the puzzle in chapter 4 could simply have Harry introduce the idea that symbols could be combined to essentially form compound words, and let you figure out how to read the murals yourself.  Or if the diamond numbering system from Chapter 3 had been introduced, instead of Harry telling you everything, as a counting game or series of math puzzles to figure out the numbers.  Or even just design, say, a base 8 number system or something and teach the player how to read it, maybe by having the numbers correspond to the number of people in a mural.  There are so many ways the puzzles could have been made more interesting, mostly just by giving the player less blatant information about how the puzzle worked.  Instead, it's one step removed from finding the necessary code on a piece of paper.  It's finding each digit of the code on it's own piece of paper.  And no need to try and correlate the information because the game will do that for you.  The puzzles aren't bad, but they are uninspired, and the player is given way too much help to figure them out.On the whole, this game is an enjoyable experience.  I really liked the character writing and lore of the world.  But it does function as a glorified walking simulator, which isn't my style.  If that is your style, absolutely check this game out.  If you buy this expecting a Myst style island puzzle adventure, maybe pass.One last gripe.  The voice acting is good, but I really hated the rest of the sound design.  There's rarely any music in the game, though what is there is also pretty.  Usually, you're just treated to the sounds of nature.  Sometimes these can be inoffensive, but other times it's just unbearable.  Do I really need the incessant river and waterfall sounds playing?  Absolutely not.  And having the thunderstorm sound loop going for all of chapter 3...I wanted the voice acting, so I kept the sound on, but I was really tempted to mute the game at multiple points just to stop the annoyance.  The sounds are mixed way too loud, and add nothing to the experience.  I'd like to continue pretending that waterfalls don't make noise, like in most video games.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Call of the Sea and am glad I played it, but I ended up liking it less after finishing it than I expected I would when I started. I would recommend it if you enjoy mystery narratives and puzzle solving gameplay (I would classify the puzzles as easy, at least compared to a typical "puzzle game"; they seem designed to keep the player engaged in the story but not stuck, and there is a built-in journal that sometimes felt overly helpful).Also, as a bit of an anti-recommendation: There is a strong literary influence that I wasn't expecting (I didn't know about it before playing); I won't spoil it here because it's fun to discover, but if you already know about it and are interested in this game solely because of said surprise influence I would warn you that although the game has lots of fun easter eggs it doesn't really feel like what you might expect tonally. As I said before it feels like a mystery where you progress by solving puzzles, and if that doesn't appeal to you then you might be disappointed if you are expecting something more similar to a certain literary influence.In very broad strokes the framing narrative is that it is the 1930s, your husband went on an expedition, and you are now following in his footsteps to try and find him. You will thus be both finding clues from his expedition but also piecing together the clues that they found in order to keep making progress. This is the kind of thing that I love and I was really excited when the game started. As I alluded to in the opening paragraph, however, I didn't quite feel like the story or puzzles lived up to the strong potential that I had sensed when I started, which is a shame. There are several puzzles, for example, that have elements of having to decipher strange languages, but then this never really happens; instead each puzzle like this is self-contained and despite the "skin" ends up being a traditional puzzle (and any actual deductions about what you find are delivered in expositional voice-overs, rather than something that the player has to figure out). In terms of narrative, as another example, there are a bunch of things (some subtle, some not) that led me to believe that a certain kind of story was being set up, but then this ended up mostly happening "off screen" and feels very distant (this is even explicitly acknowledged multiple times by the character that you play, which I thought was amusing).None of what I've complained about above means that Call of the Sea a bad game; on the contrary, I quite enjoyed my time with it. But for the first hour or so I felt like something extraordinary was being set up, and by the end it felt like a nice game but one that I will probably not think about much now that I'm done with it. If you like this kind of game I feel very comfortable recommending it. If the setting or the pretty art style appeals to you I also think it's pretty easy to recommend. If you're feeling on the fence, however, there might be other games that you would enjoy more.

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is a cozy, narrative, puzzle adventure set in 1934 Polynesia. The story is interesting and unique. The graphics and textures are beautiful. The main character narrates often, so I didn't feel a sense of loneliness while exploring a desolate, shipwrecked island. There is a lot to "collect" and achievement hunt (I 100%'ed the game in my 10 hour playtime). The puzzles are very intuitive- an added bonus is that all relative information that the MC interacts with is logged in a journal. It is entirely possible to complete this game without a guide (I used one for achievements and a couple smooth brain moments).I was relatively stress free while playing, however I was anxious in the deep water areas, so fair warning to anyone who is ocean phobic. There are only a handful of instances that had me stressed, but the awareness that nothing will harm you in the game should help (aka yes approach the spooky things).

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is a beautiful and deeply immersive adventure I highly recommend if youre a fan of shorter form puzzle games with weaving plots. Almost every aspect of this game is well executed and I genuinely found it hard to find stopping points as I was so eager for more. The voicing is amazing, the aesthetic is also really visually pleasing with lots of lore to find and a clear deep admiration for cosmic fiction writers such as Lovecraft and sci fi cult mags of the 70s and 80s, all while feeling refreshingly unique. Each piece of lore you find is accompanied with related dialogue, demonstrating a deep attention to detail. During my playtime I did experience occasional texture slows in the heavily detailed scenery, but none that impeded play or significantly took me out of the game. The puzzles are unique and fascinating, but did often rely on finding some crucial clue (usually fairly well indicated), but I did find myself having to use walkthroughs for a few of the puzzles (the organ puzzle had me spinning). Overall when I see smaller studios putting out work with level of care and attention it makes me want to support them all the more and I suggest you do too. Thanks for the ride Out of the Blue!
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Would put this more as a mixed.Basically it's far too short for the asking price but the contents isn't terrible.The puzzles aren't really that difficult and most of them are just inputting a code that they've provided for you.Story line is decent. Visuals are really good.No bugs that I found beyond some places where your view clips through a surface so you can see under the map.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: For me, this game was truly one of the best experiences I have ever had with a video game. I have tons of positive things to say about this game in particular. The story was wonderfully crafted and I loved how this game was obviously inspired by authors like H.P. Lovecraft and Jules Verne. The atmosphere to this game was very immersive with its bright and beautiful settings. I was sucked into this game and its stories with its characters the moment I started playing, and it's one experience I shall never forget. Awesome job!
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: 7.5/10The game has a great story and atmosphere. I really enjoyed the visuals, it's a very nice game to look at. The island and the underwater scenes are just dreamy. Unfortunately, I had some problems interacting with objects – sometimes you have to move back and forth until the icon appears which makes it very easy to miss objects that are interactable. And in this game, finding the right objects and interacting with them is essential. Regarding the puzzles, I found especially the second chapter a bit confusing because you discovered some puzzles before you were even able to solve them. Most of the puzzles in the game aren't solvable by "common sense", you need to find the right clues first. But the game never tells you that and even though I didn't miss the hand holding most of the time, I did get stuck at one point just because I was trying to solve the puzzles in a different order than it was intended and therefore I was missing the clues I needed. However, I think the rest of the chapters were fine and I did enjoy the second half of the game more. So overall, even with a few rather frustrating moments, it was a good experience and I can recommend this mysterious adventure game to everyone who likes story driven puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: A charmingly animated game about a quest to find your husband, though your quest is not all it seems? Cute animation, lovely voice acting and a story that really pulls you in at the end. Short, only takes about 4.5 hours to play through but still pleasant and worth the time. Fun puzzles, though a few could use a bit more exposition to get across what they'd like you to do. I enjoyed it, and found myself tearing up at the love story between our main character and her hubby, something I rarely do.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea reminds me of a mixture of The Witness, with a strong dose of the exotic and relaxing locales of the 1990's golden era of adventure titles. In an adventure title, you should feel a touch of the surreal, and Call of the Sea has this richness many adventure games lack. If you're a fan of the genre, this is an excellent title.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful game. Beautiful to look at and a great story. I took a few breaks with the game open, so my 8 hour playtime is a bit inflated. _childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful walking sim/puzzle game with an interesting story (seems like Lovecraft inspired), with stunning stylized graphics, it was a pleasant experience. Game runs very smoothly with everything at max settings on a RTX 3090 TI, at 4k. Puzzles are easy/medium, nothing you can't figure out on your own. Got it at a discount and the price I paid certainly was worth the ride. Looking forward to see more similar games from this dev. Just wished there was some happy ending, both endings are depressive, and there is really no point in having two endings.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: I had high hopes and I think it could be an incredible game. _childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: It sure is full of vibrant colours but it ain't a 9/10 stuff (oh wait..that's from Ignorant Gamers' Network, silly me). It starts off rather well but goes downhill pretty fast. It's just half-baked. Bloom, emissive maps and volumetric lights are nice but they don't make a good game. Story wise it's really lacking. You know what's up pretty much by chapter 2. As always, the devil's in the details. E.g. once Norah delves deeper into the unknown goo land she would've deffo felt whole lot better and be able to sprint faster, jump and climb since she claims to feel great. Voice acting doesn't change one bit the longer she stays on the island, if the "sickness" was truly overtaking her very being we'd hear some deranged rants or see intermittent visions without having to interact with anything. _childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very sweet and exciting game. Perfect for beginner puzzle players because the puzzles aren't too difficult, and everything gets written down automatically in a journal so you have all the information you need. A fun a story as well, with some darker themes, although it left me with a lot of questions at the end! I hope they make another one to tie some of the loose ends together.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is a great adventure game. I played it with a friend and we finished it in 7.25 hours. The puzzles were great. Some are easy, some are harder, and you need some time to think about them and solve them. The main actor and the voices of all the actors are great! All puzzle solutions were comprehensible for us.The game was exciting and the whole 7 hours we ehr had great fun playing.We also liked the story very much. And for the puzzles, it was really cool that they were perfectly integrated into the game and the game story.Congratulations to the developer and the whole team! Great game!
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: I picked this game up on a very good sale and for the value I paid (like an euro) it was worth it ! But it is honestly not worth anything near the normally listed price. I enjoyed the little puzzles and short story! _childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game, with a fun twist to the "Shadow out of Innsmouth" story. Fans of the Cthulhu Mythos will definitely enjoy the story in this game. _childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Its a good puzzler. _childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Here's the thing. For an exploratory, clue finding game, its pretty linear in terms of where to go and what to find. You're not gonna NOT be able to figure out where the main clues are, they make themselves pretty apparent from fairly far back, your cursor will change to an eyeball. The in game art was cool, reminded me of sea of thieves. The cut scenes though were really just watercolour paintings, still shots, not much to see. The puzzles weren't all the difficult, but because of the movement speed, they were annoying. Lots of ground to cover and some backtracking through the stages.The character moves horrendously slow. You can press shift to go a little faster, but why? Just make her go max speed! There's no "sneaking" or anything in this game. Just run already!Finally the story, yeah it was pretty obvious what her "illness" was less than halfway through the game. So not really a great mystery, more like a "lets see what happens when she..."Overall, Id expect an exploratory, clue finding, mystery game to have more exploration, harder to find clues, and a better mystery.  Fail on all 3.Mostly, I felt annoyed while playing.

_childDocuments_.review: is an absolutely fantastic narrative-driven puzzle game. The developers nailed the look, feel, and mystery of an old school adventure game. Supplemented by the wonderfully written and voiced main character, it is a treat to explore each chapter and uncover the various clues hidden within. As someone particularly bad at puzzles, I was pleasantly surprised that I didn't need to whip out a walkthrough often, and that each head-scratcher was challenging yet satisfying.Each clue and story beat is taken note of in Norah's journal automatically, which means that (1) it's hard to get lost or forget things and (2) that there's no need to take physical notes yourself (which I don't miss). The story is compelling, the visual design is striking and colorful, and the soundtrack pairs perfectly with the environment and themes. Norah's and Harry's stories are flawlessly intertwined, making for some truly touching moments, especially if you resonate with characters in a strong relationship.Whether you're a puzzle-lover or no, I thoroughly recommend you give this a go. Folks who enjoy similar games such as , , , and  will be right at home.

_childDocuments_.review: This was on my  radar the moment I saw the trailer; the game is breathtakingly beautiful. Each chapter is beautifully designed. Voice acting is spot-on. _childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Loyal to the Lovecraftian originals and also mind-expandingly creative, Call of the Sea is one of the best Lovecraftian game I've ever played. Tinkered with temporally accurate soundtrack and voice-acting, the game recreates the experience of watching a film classics. But Call of the Sea isn't merely a film work. What lets it transcend a common, Lovecraftian film work is its dazzling scenery and architectures. As otherworldly as they may seem, they gives a strange yet satisfying sense of harmony and beauty that pulls you in and makes you want to stay. The story was made clear enough for anyone to comprehend; it's unnecessary to educate yourself on Lovecraftian novels before playing. On top of that, the story built upon the original canons and told something of its own, something that those with some prior knowledge to this worldview (like me) can still awe at and enjoy.The difficulties of the puzzles were appropriate. I do occasionally find myself stuck on a puzzle, but it usually turns out that I just missed out some clues. The map was large and it could feel repetitive when you overlook a certain path or clue and had to run back to take it down, but other than those situations, the game usually records everything you need for you so that you won't have to go back and forth. You also won't be in the same area for a very long time, so the repetitiveness never persists for long.On the downside, the game isn't the most optimized story-driven game in the world. (Though it might be my fault for using a laptop that merely satisfies the minimum requirements.) Occasionally you may see models glitching in and out of existence, weird spots of light on not-so-reflective materials, and - if you're using a laptop as bad as mine - the fan constantly working its life out. Those, added with the fact that dialogues sometimes sound out-of-place, made the game less immersive than perfect.Even with a setup as low-end as mine though I still had a very good time taking part in the game's story, and I'm even looking forward to experiencing that again when I feel ready. I recommend this game to anyone interested in Lovecraftian literature, 20th century filmography, or just general story-driven games. Call of the Sea may be a bit different from the other ones you've played, but you will enjoy it.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know what I was expecting with this game. At first I thought things were fine. The story telling is fabulous for the most part. However, the gameplay with the walking is very slow and cumbersome. Some of the puzzles were pretty pointless and others cumbersome. I also had issue with the graphics. The game kept crashing on me. Finally, I was hoping for a happy ending here but I got no closure. It all seemed like a pointless ride. You're better off saving your money and put it towards something else.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game - beautiful sights, lovely voice acting and music, and a compelling story. I found the puzzles ranged from fun to genuinely confusing, though once you understood the trick of each one, even the tough ones were relatively easy to solve. Toward the end, I felt like the puzzles get less complicated and more tedious. _childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing. If you enjoy story-rich puzzle adventure games with a hint of mystery and suspense, this is definitely a game for you. Full of gorgeous visuals, fun and interesting puzzles, and a genuinely compelling narrative, I think Call of the Sea is worth the asking price, even despite it's overall shorter runtime.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: A visually stunning game for enjoyers of puzzle solving and Lovecraftian lore. I loved the graphics and the story and I felt accomplished when I managed to solve some puzzles even without all the clues. _childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: This is more of a visual novel with some decent puzzle elements and some very slow walking and ladder climbing.The story and art - this is where it shines. I enjoyed the voice acting and the visual style of it, especially towards the end of the game. The story had some good details, most of which are discovered by looking at every scrap of paper or mural in the game. I just enjoyed this the most and it kept me going.The puzzles - This was a mixed bag. A few of these were cool, some were Myst-like in that you say "oh, I guess these unrelated things are connected because whatever." A few just felt unfinished. Like the "puzzles" of the water jets. There also just weren't that many of them. Just enough to support the story, I guess.Walking - Walking is So. Slow. After a half hour or so I was searching for mods to just sprint faster in the game. This is especially tedious in the last half of the game where there are puzzles that require you to use objects that are spread out. Ladders were also tedious, but at least there are only a few of those.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: All in all a nice and polished game. pros:-good story, very linear, yet well told-good pacing-excellent voiceactors-smooth performance, no bugs that I saw-good graphics and soundcons:-the puzzles are pretty easy and oldschool. I like to go to escape rooms a lot, and the puzzledesign reminds me on the first ones I have been to over 10 years ago. They are not up to date, at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Exquisite game. I always get a little concerned when a game seems to feature only white characters but... From the first moment, I was enamored with Call of the Sea. It's visually stunning, like walking through a hyper-realistic, yet almost impressionistic watercolor painting. The lighting is beyond stunning. The developers ought to win some sort of award for this game. I've rarely seen lighting that is at once so real, and so ethereal at the same time. Hell, I've only seen such amazing lighting in nature maybe twice in my 40 years of living. As for the story. Just... wow. It's thoughtful, emotional; SO well written. It's beautiful. Now, I DO sort of wish there was a third ending option. A... happier... ending. None of the endings are sad exactly, just rather bittersweet. But this isn't a game made by The Mouse's studio. It has a rawness, and a realness to it that I really appreciate. The voice acting is superb. Music, also superb. Game-play, virtually flawless. I've heard some people had some glitches here and there, but my play-through was perfect. The puzzles are well thought out and meticulously designed. Once you work out what the solution to solving each puzzle is, actually solving it feels like child's play. Before the light of realization dawns though, you're liable to feel like a complete simpleton trying to piece together all the clues. I *did* have to get a little help with two of the puzzles. The one with the sea organ still has me stumped, but I'm going to play through again and see if I can figure out what I missed. The other, inside the fish statue, as soon as I realized what I'd missed, clarity came crashing in and it was super easy to figure out. I'm looking forward to my sister playing through this and getting her impressions. She's generally far better at puzzle-solving than I am, so I'm interested to see how she fairs. To sum it all up: I LOVED this game. It feels like it was crafting lovingly. With care that isn't often apparent from bigger game studios. I am very much looking forward to what this bunch of creators has in store for us next! I will definitely be buying their next game, assuming they make another one. Well, unless it's zombies. I might have to pass if it's zombies. lol Otherwise, I'm on board for whatever amazing adventure they cook up next. I can hardly wait. I truly hope Call of the Sea makes them enough that they can easily afford to start their next project soon, if they haven't already. Or, even a continuation or spin-off of this. This world is one I'd be happy to visit again and again.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea piqued my interest at first with its pretty art and interesting premise, especially since it seemed to perfectly scratch my Lovecraftian itch. I just didn’t know when I picked it up that it would so quickly become one of my favorite indie games! I simply fell in love with the game almost instantly, and let me explain why.You play as Nora Everheart who is looking for her husband after he’s gone missing on a mysterious island while searching for a cure to Nora’s strange disease. The premise itself is captivating enough, but the way the story unfolds is simply brilliant. Instead of just being told what happened, you get to piece it all together by exploring this beautiful island and checking the letters and campsites left behind by Nora’s husband and his crew. You find out what happened bit by bit while slowly getting attached to the characters and becoming immersed into the events of the story. It feels like you’re part of the journey, uncovering secrets and untangling mysteries right alongside Nora. And let me tell you, the more I found out, the more I became curious! And the way it all ties up together in the end is simply beautiful and heartbreaking that it just brought me to tears.Other than exploration, the game consists mostly of puzzle sequences which always felt fresh and unique every time. The puzzles were just the right mix of challenging and satisfying: never too obtuse or too simple. I admittedly looked up a guide a couple times during the game, but I don’t think it spoiled the fun at all. It was usually stuff I didn’t notice in the first place anyway. For the most part though, it definitely made me feel super smart when I solved the puzzles myself which was incredibly rewarding.To say that the atmosphere is one of the game’s strong suits would be an understatement. As soon as you step on the island, there’s an air of mystery and eeriness all around you. But as you explore the island, it transforms into this insanely beautiful landscape with attention to detail that just takes your breath away. The soundtrack and especially the voice acting were also wonderful and helped me become totally immersed in this world. All in all, Call of the Sea was a total gem of a game. I simply couldn't put it down once I had picked it up! Also, finishing up all the achievements was a breeze, so it's a win-win for us completionists. If you're into mystery, puzzle-solving, or just plain good storytelling, this game's a must-play. Seriously, do yourself a favor and give it a go!
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: I came to this game for this interesting visuals, but got bored with it pretty quickly. The only reason why I stuck it out to the end was because the game does start to get interesting around the 1-hour mark, which was a bit late to actually hook me in. The game's problems simply boil down to uninteresting characters and plot. Some of the puzzles require backtracking and can feel tedious, especially in the earlier parts of the game. The game also feels very slow, including your walking speed and interaction animations. Considering how my first playthrough only took about 4.5 hours, I'm convinced this was done to pad the playtime. I will say, however, that the game does get better as it goes on, both in terms of the story and puzzle design. The integration of the Lovecraft universe should be interesting to anyone who likes his work or works related to it. I'd say if this is on sale for cheap or if you're a big fan of Lovecraft, you can check this game out, but in general, I wasn't very impressed.

_childDocuments_.review: I had a good time !What drew me into this game was the fact that it looked so pretty, and this was no disappointment. Also, i like puzzle-adventure games, and i was happy to get into that once again. I have a few critics about Call of the Sea though : - . It's like following a rail. _childDocuments_.review: A little heads up: If I could rate this game neutral, I would do so. If you want to skip all the details you can scroll to the end and read about why it's only neutral. And for what kind of people I would recommend this game.First of all, I want to take a second to adress all of the "I didn't went into this game knowing it's H.P. Lovecraft inspired" reviews. In case the name of the game wasn't a big hint already, the 5th picture on the store page pretty much shows this fact as clear as it is humanly possible. Even the trailer spoils this fact. So yeah, there is that. Now let's talk about the actual game.----------------------------------------------------------The overall visuals of this game are really cool. Especially the beginning looks and feels awesome with it's lush green jungle areas. But also later parts, where the lovecraftian aspects push through more, are really nice to look at.The story itself is, should you be familiar with Lovecraft's stories, on point but very predictable. And for everyone not familiar with it, the game works perfectly well as an entry point to the whole myth. Some of the hints and easter eggs to find during your playthrough are a bit too much "on the nose" to make sure, that even the last person realizes what's really going on. Again, if you already know the stories, you sometimes might find yourself rolling your eyes because it is so obvious. This also means that there is no real ground breaking revelation at the end. Should you be looking for an all new and surprising story to experience, this game will probably disappoint you.One big issue with how the game tells it's story, is the protagonist. Everything that happens is commented by your character. Even the obvious. It also doesn't help that she writes everything down in her notebook. And I mean EVERYTHING. Doesn't matter how insignificant something is. You find yourself constantly in situations where you explore a new area, your character points something out while you also get a new notebook entry that points the exact same thing out - again. I have to admit that I stopped reading all updates in the book early into the game. It is a nice "catch-up" feature, should you not play for a week or two between sessions. But considering how short the main story turns out to be, this is probably a non-issue for most people. The whole notebook would be negligible if it wasn't for it's second use in the game. Your character also writes and draws everything down that is realted to puzzles. It would have been cool when the "story recap" part, also included the puzzle hints. This way the player would need to think about what parts are important for progression and what is not. But this is not the case. In fact, most puzzles are more or less auto-solved by this feature. All the informations needed are neatly organized next to each other. Only thing you need to do is copy the solution from your notebook. The game even let's you know when you solved a puzzle by putting a checkmark next to the book entry. Even if you decide to ignore this feature all together and make your own notes, the protagonist sometimes straight out tells you what to do.Writing a bit more about the protagonist... Her voice actor is really good and pleasant to listen to. Her character however, is hit or miss depending what you are looking for. She has this constant child-like wonder about everything. Sometimes it really feels out of place. Small spoiler. If you don't want to read this, skip the following part.----------------------------------------------------------At one point you are basically auto controlled and your character walks straight at a giant sea creature. For a moment the protagonist has some hints of panic in her voice that is completely gone a couple of seconds later when she realizes that she can breath underwater now. We went from "Oh god please no!" to "Huh... That's cool and unexpected! Let's explore a bit more!" in the span of maybe 30 seconds. The child-like character pushes through so heavily that we even have to dive directly into the dark of the deep sea and towards two glowing eyes. Without even a hint of the panic she experienced seconds before that.----------------------------------------------------------Another big problem with having only the protagonist as a character and noone else is, that she knows too much. Every time you read a note written by someone she never met, she will tell you how this character felt while writing these lines. And she is never really shaken up by any information. Like reading about the death of someone. You followed the final days of this persons life through reading their notes that are scattered everywhere. And when you finally find their grave she is like "The poor guy... Anyways! I have to find my missing husband." She doesn't really care about any of the events that happened before she arrived. And this makes it hard for me, as the player, to care for them as well.Speaking of the complete lack of other characters. The gameplay constantly comes to an hard stop because you find another 4 to 6 notes. All right next to each other that you can neatly read them in order. You will also realize, that the group of people you more or less follow, obviously never talked to each other in person. Why else would you find a note of character A asking something, and the note next to it is character B replying to the question? Considering the story setup, the devs could have used visions for example. To keep the story engaging. It's always better to show your players something, instead of just writing about it. The notes itself are really short. Most of the time just one sentence. Your characters comments to each and every note is sometimes longer than what is actually written on it.The gameplay itself is mostly fine. You can walk, walk faster and interact with things. Basic, but it get's the job done. Even tho climbing ladders is infuriating slow. And should you get stuck at certain puzzles, even tho your notebook pretty much tells you what to do, you sometimes find yourself slow walking through big areas. Not exactly the most thrilling experience.----------------------------------------------------------My opinion about this game can be considered "pure neutral". It's never really bad in the sense that I didn't want to continue. But it's also nothing to write home about. The puzzles are ok for the most part. Not too difficult because of everything I already mentioned. The story is ok and overall enjoyable for Lovecraft fans and people who just got into the myth. It's never really good, or really bad. It's just perfectly in the middle.So... Who should buy this game? Well... Everyone who wants to experience a darker story, with very few real horror elements and no jump scares. Also people who just want to dive into a nice looking virtual world for a couple of hours, without the need to use their brain too much.This game is not recommended for everyone who is looking for hard puzzles or a "never before seen" story.Expect this game to be a perfect entry point, should you not have any experience with puzzle games and/or lovecraftian stories. But please don't make the mistake to think of it like "babies first puzzle adventure" you can get for your kid to have some puzzle fun. The setting is certainly not made for kids.

_childDocuments_.review: LISTEN UP. What I am about to write is 100% true, and without exaggeration. You walk so slow in this game, that I actually watched YouTube videos on my laptop while traversing from puzzle element to puzzle element… just so I had something to do during the incredibly slow travel time. And yes, I had my finger on the run key the entire time. It didn’t matter. Still absurdly slow.There’s one puzzle in particular, where you have to press some switches in a set order. But if you mess up, the entire puzzle resets. The switches are very far from each other. I knew the solution, but I mis-clicked twice, resetting it 2 times. I got it on my 3rd try… and in that time, I got through an ENTIRE 17 MINUTE VIDEO. I spent 17 straight minutes moving from switch to switch because I mis-clicked twice.I understand it’s my fault, since I knew the answer and messed up… but imagine if I didn’t know the answer. If I was doing trial and error, or testing things out, I might’ve wasted an hour or more on in-game traversal alone.All of the positive aspects cited in other reviews are legitimate. It’s a cool story, nice graphics, voice acting, etc. But man, the slow movement really kills the fun factor. To quote AVGN: “What were they THINKING??!”

_childDocuments_.review: My gameplay of this game was undoubtedly effected by the 4 standard drinks I had before playing each session. A very short puzzle mystery in which the puzzles are deceptively simple (look complex but are in reality quite simple) and the mystery flows well with the rest of the story. Expect no thrilling surprises or unpronounced turns. The story tells itself quite well and allows itself room to develop in a open manner not locking down till the very end.  For myself the focus remained on the puzzles which if I hadn't been slightly tipsy would have been quite enjoyable. In my tipsy state I did miss or failed to connect some of the elements within certain puzzles together thus reducing my overall enjoyment. But otherwise for a mystery puzzler. Its not overly complex but complex enough to provide a challenge for a brief period. It definitely doesn't try to hide itself behind the typical mystery flaw of hiding details from the player/viewer, instead making explicit its logic and allowing the player/viewer to compare the own to the stories.

_childDocuments_.review: "Call of the Sea" is a quite remarkable title with many twists on the traditional way its genre is presented. Atleast to my knowledge when it comes to movies and videogames. To put it frank, it's beautiful, stunning and touching in every sense. One might think, a light-hearted romance story on a mysterious island seems rather dull on a first glance, but! The more you progress, the better the pieces of the story start to collect like a charming puzzle and you descent abruptly into a suspenseful narrative with wonderful visuals and a delightful presentation. The game takes some inspiration of H.P Lovecraft's novels but focuses on a more bright approach story-wise. Nonetheless, many of its genre-typical atmoshpere doesn't get lost by this! Therefore, I really enjoyed it since I love the lovecraft-universe as a whole and easily got lost in the vast narrative. Even how the "hud" is handled is perfectly splendid to immerse yourself quite literally more into the world of "Call of the Sea". Opening your journal, scribbling hints and notes here and there to occasionally look them up, again and again in order to solve riddles and problems the game throws at you is such a nice way to keep you invested in the character. Besides the well written dialogues, or should I say, the monologues for most of the time, which in my opinion is a good thing because it makes the conversations even more impactful for the relationship and plot. Lastly, even the ending feels rewarding. It's heartwarming and emotional through and through, depending on how you feel about Norah's and Harry's outcome. Although with ease a worth conclusion to its story! And it will leave goosebumps, trust me pal! So, dear old Pal! What you say? With no doubts and any regrets, I can highly recommend "Call of the Sea" to anyone who likes story driven games like "Firewatch" and "Edith Finch" and want to explore a fascinating island, full of mysterious secrets and fantastical contraptions!Now if you wouldn't mind, I might take another trip! Farewell and adieu my dear old pal of mine.Enjoy your journey!

_childDocuments_.review: For the life of me, I cannot understand how Call of the Sea is as highly reviewed as it is. This game was an utter disappointment. A beautiful shell with an empty interior, it's only real upside is the sheer graphical fidelity.Let's start with that good part, the graphics. The game is gorgeous.  I have barely any complaints on the graphical department. You have epic set-pieces, serene natural paths, and a great deal of environmental variety. Plenty of spots are perfect for just admiring, and at no point does the art style itself detract from the experience. Something I will come back to later though, is the lack of any actual character models. Nora is the only actual 3d character we ever see moving, and we only ever see her hands moving. There are 3d animated things, but actual 3d human characters just not there. The audio design is a more mixed bag than the graphics. The voice acting is just... not good. You have the only real good part of it being (big surprise) Yuri Lowenthal, with the rest of the cast being a  worse at emoting and expression. The UI sounds are also just terribly annoying, with it sounding like a drop of water falling in a pond except it's happening right in your ear over and over again. The good is the music design and Yuri Lowenthal. Music is good, and Yuri did a great job with this role.The gameplay though, is just baffling. It's a mix between a walking simulator and a puzzle game. The issue is that the puzzles are wildly inconsistent in quality, the walking is so incredibly slow, and it's never  Let's start with the walking part. You move at a snails pace, and  just makes you move at a normal video game's walk speed. You also interact with things at a slow pace, with ladders being the most egregious offender. Do you like ladders being something that you interact with? Do you like the ladders having a 3 seconds animation of you getting on  off them, and do you like moving up and down them being a slow process? Also there are puzzles past the ladders so I hope you don't mind not being able to complete a puzzle yet so you have to keep going up and down the ladder every time you think you've found the right answer. The puzzles are just bad too. As previously said, Puzzles are both never fun and are wildly inconsistent in terms of quality. The puzzles range in difficulty from "a 5 year old could solve this easily" to making literally no sense at all.  They also aren't at all interesting. I can forgive a puzzle game for having easy puzzles if the game either is incredibly unique or if it has a good story. We'll go over the story last, but this game is not incredibly unique at all. Games like Superliminal, Manifold Garden and Viewfinder are games that don't have difficult puzzles, but they make up for it in the sheer experience they offer. Evan's Remains is a good example of a game that doesn't have difficult puzzles but has a good enough story to make up for it. Call of the Sea does not impress on the puzzle front, at all.Also good to note, that if you enjoy actually  your puzzles then Call of the Sea is not for you. Nora, your player character, will literally spell out what you need to do for half the puzzles through her dialogue. For the other half she'll jot something down in a journal that is accessible almost anywhere and at anytime, and tells you exactly what you need to do.  I know for a fact that people get upset when you're struggling with a puzzle and the game decides to just spell out the solution for you because it wants you to move on, God of War got a little flack for this itself. But for some reason this game is highly reviewed even though it does that for The story isn't much better. It wants to be clever but, much like the puzzle "hints", it spells everything out the moment it becomes relevant. Nora will literally say exactly what is happening out loud for you to hear, removing any mystery from the situations and preventing you from having any "ah-ha!" moments of piecing things together. It's like she's reading you out a novel about her life, except she's all alone on an island and she keeps spoiling the story for whoever is listening. Seriously, whoever wrote Nora's dialogue, please never write dialogue again. Ever. There's also lovecraftian elements, tribal cultures and a love story but given how short the game is, none of it ever get's enough time to get interesting. It also is less than 4 hours long, for a $20 game, and you can 100% it in that time. Yikes.I do wonder how much of the budget was spent on the graphical fidelity and on getting Yuri Lowenthal on the voice cast. Did they run out of enough money to, I don't know, make interesting puzzle or hire and actual writer? Did they not have enough budget to make 3d characters? Or was all this just thrown together because of some corporate mandate? Is the impossibly slow walking there to prevent the game from being under 2 hours so you can't refund it after finishing it? I don't know.What I do know is that I did not enjoy this game and that I do not recommend it, at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: If you like visually appealing, story-driven puzzle games, this one is for you. I really enjoyed the art style and general aesthetic of the game. I found the writing and story line to be pretty decent, but the visual design and fantasy elements helped elevate it and make it more interesting for me. The pacing of the story and cut scenes felt about right; it's maybe about 6 hours of gameplay for one playthrough. (I bought it on sale, so that doesn't seem like a bad value at all to me.) The abundance of written notes and recordings all over the campsites is a bit silly if you stop to think about it, but it's easy enough to forgive as a necessary narrative mechanism. The puzzles never feel repetitive, and with the automatic journal notes as clues, they generally feel appropriately challenging. Enough to make you think about it, but not enough to keep you too long from carrying on with the story. Only one of them ended up feeling a bit tedious, mostly due to the amount of walking back and forth to complete it. Overall, the story, the style, the setting combine to make for a quality game that I enjoyed.

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the SeaI thoroughly enjoyed this game. 10/10.Call of the Sea is a beautiful walking tour/puzzle game in the vein of Fire Watch, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, The Park, and, to a lesser extent, Myst. Call of the Sea has a wonderfully affecting and personal story to tell that is fabulously paced. The 1930s aesthetic, palpable at every turn, maintains the immersion of the story giving the whole game a fabulously pulpy feel. Lovecraft’s Cthulhu mythos has a presence in this game, contributing to the foundations the game is built on, but not overshadowing it like in The Sinking City and Call of Cthulhu video games. The gameplay was fun. While your character’s speed leaves a little to be desired, she is admittedly an adventuress of the '30s, in heeled boots and a full length skirt on a wild tropical island. The puzzles grow more challenging as the game progresses without becoming obtuse or opaque. Similarly, the biomes of the island are fabulous and only add to the storytelling while keeping the feel consistent but not same-y.    All in all, this is a great game with enough detail to make it worth playing again to see all the little bits of foreshadowing that were sprinkled along the way and putting together the early puzzle pieces for a more complete story. ------Spoilers ahead!!!!!!!!------ Once I knew the twist, it threw a fascinating light on the aesthetic of the game for me. In most games set in the Cthulhu mythos, you play a protagonist traveling to an isolated, dangerous, alien, and often savage place to seek a cure for your sick loved one or yourself, only to find ancient ruins and eldritch horror. But here you play that sick loved one looking for the person that went searching for your cure. In those other storylines, the sick character is slowly changing into a monster that will inevitably be called to the sea to join others of their bloodline that have “returned home” before them. Without a cure, this person has no hope other than insanity and a slow, wasting death, or the aforementioned transformation.But here in Call of the Sea, you are that sick, slowly transforming person. After traveling across the world, you too end up at the same isolated place to find ancient ruins, but instead of a savage danger and alien horror, you find tranquility, beauty, and mystery. The only horror you find is in the evidence left by the people you are looking for, in what they did to the land and what they did to each other. This is most evident and wonderfully portrayed in the difference between the island exploration levels that are tranquil, bright, and full of life, and the civilized camp level that is dark, trash-strewn, and desolate. This level was the only part of the game in which I felt like something might truly attack me. This level was the one that was alien and dangerous. This level, full of the trappings of civilization, was the place of savage danger.I loved this: a mythos story from the perspective of someone becoming Other and finding the home of their ancestors--being called to it, and welcomed by it. I was really taken with the idea that it is beautiful and welcoming because the character belongs there, and that she sees it that way because she is wanted there. It makes me wonder--what was it like for those she searches for? She sees a tranquil beach leading to a coolly-shadowed jungle, with rays of sunlight dancing through the trees. They see a beach that is the last refuge before an ominous jungle with the ephemeral shafts of light from above providing the only safety. (Heck, their first camp on the beach is so far from the jungle that it is almost in the water.) She sees a peaceful glade by a river filled with indigenous buildings and art. They see the only safe haven in a jungle filled with the remains of a cryptically vanished people and threatening totems to the unknown.She sees the awesome ruins left by ancient people--monuments to their perseverance and craftsmanship, covered in murals, a testament to their culture. They see alien design and purpose in a place no indigenous person could have built. I found it fascinating that the environment could look so different to each group because she belonged and they didn’t. How that would affect the way they interacted with and perceived its purpose was a welcome layer to the game. It also made me think more about how other mythos stories might look from the other side.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember when Portal came out and first person adventure/puzzle games exploded and there were so many interesting takes on the subgenre. Some evolved the traditional Myst-like gameplay, some started mixing mechanics and ideas from other genres, some played with physics objects a lot… But for the past 5 or so years, I’ve been mostly ignoring these types of games. There are way too many of them and yet, vast majority of the games seems to fall into two main types: either story driven games with almost pointless adventure elements slapped on top or incredibly complicated puzzle games that make Myst look like an obvious and easy game for children.Call of the Sea got my attention because it seemed like it could be at least slightly more engaging than a typical “slapped on top” type of adventure. And for the first hour or two, that’s almost what it was. But then it turned into one of the most tedious and poorly designed first person adventure games I’ve played in a while.The game plays like one would expect from the genre – you explore locations from the first person perspective to find clues and solve puzzles to progress, while a story unfolds. In case of Call of the Sea, the story takes the Cthulhu mythos as a basis for the plot and something Jules Verne-inspired for the mood. This mix is somewhat surprising and doesn’t seem to quite work. There are countless moments that seem to aim at building tension and being scary, but they’re not. And at the same time, the game often portrays itself as something wonderous and exciting during the most dry and uneventful sections. None of this is helped by the fact that whomever wrote the script seemed to believe that main characters can’t stay silent for longer than half a minute, so our main heroine explodes into infinite trite monologues every couple of steps you take in the game.Maybe it wouldn’t be as jarring if the story itself was any good, but it’s just uninteresting, despite starting out with a promise. And the final 10 minutes of the game include a… “plot twist”? I guess? I mean, imagine if you were reading a book about a character named Harry and then the final 15 pages of the story decided to shock you, with countless explanations and flashbacks to earlier scenes, that the character name is actually Henry. Even though that changes absolutely nothing about the story or the character or anything at all. It’s baffling and feels like a result of designing an interactive ending first and then writing a story that needed to lead up to the ending but didn’t.Yet, even though it is a story driven adventure, it could still work as an adventure/puzzle title set in really pretty looking levels. But even here things start at inoffensive and end up tedious and annoying. First half of the game is full of puzzles that you solve without much thinking, while appreciating that these puzzles exist, as simple as they are. But later the game essentially switches all puzzles to horribly tedious busywork tasks, where you see the puzzle, understand the puzzle solution, but have to run around for 15 minutes and collect the puzzle pieces so you could finally move on. Then a really complex but exciting sounding puzzle, where it turns out you just need to do what the game shows you. Then you get an even bigger location where the puzzle is “press buttons”. Then poorly designed Simon Says. Then the exactly same timing puzzle repeated several times. Then another incredibly primitive puzzle, except you need to run around another large level each time you complete one section of it simply to unlock another section. All while the main character continues with her pointless introspection.While playing the first half of the game I thought that it will end up being the “eh, I guess it’s pretty and you can check it out on sale, then forget about it” type of game. But then the later half of the game happened and even though apparently it lasted for about 2 hours, to me it felt like 6 and I started hating my time with the game more and more as it went on. So, yes, it is pretty, but no, I won’t recommend playing it even if you see it on sale. There are countless far better games that have more respect for player time and either have stories that are far better written, or stories that you can safely ignore without them getting in the way.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Neat little indie-adventure. Puzzles are just right, without being too easy but also not too hard so they don't slow down the story progression. Story has clear lovecraftian inspiration but without being horror. Beautifully crafted game world. Graphics aren't always super crisp but that is not the goal of such a game. _childDocuments_.review: I am a huge fan of puzzle adventure games, particularly the Myst series, and this game definitely scratches that itch. The game does a better job of integrating the puzzles into the world than something like The Talos Principle or Faraway, so many puzzles feel like they have a connection to the story. The environments are beautiful and lushly detailed, which comes at the slight trade-off of the levels feeling a little bit on the small side.In terms of difficulty, this game is on the easier end. Any object you can interact with, or information source you can inspect or read, is clearly marked when you approach it, and the main character writes down any puzzle-relevant information in her journal. The notes left by others that she comes across are fully marked-up already - important terms are circled or underlined to make clear what the player is supposed to take away from each scrap of paper. She also talks to herself extensively, offering her own realizations that reveal the links between different information in ways that help the player along towards a puzzle solution.On the one hand, this avoids the frustration of overlooking subtle visual cues or having to parse out the important information from lengthy journals, as is sometimes the case in Myst games. On the other hand, it does feel a little like the protagonist connects most of the dots herself, leaving the player only to make a few remaining connections to complete the solution. It also affects the game length - the game is much shorter given that the protagonist essentially narrates a partial walkthrough as you play it.On the whole, this was an enjoyable game with interesting puzzles in a beautiful world. Fans of real head-scratchers might be disappointed with the modest puzzle difficulty, but on the whole I think most players will enjoy the adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: 6.2h (100% achievement, finished the game) No. Yes (22 achievements). No. follows the story of Norah Everheart, a woman that is trying to find her husband that is searching for a cure for her strange disease. You'll have to explore the beautifully-made landscapes and solve simple puzzles to get closer to the truth.- Beautiful looking landscapes and some scenes where you just need to sit and enjoy the scenery- Backtracking to gather what you miss can be easily done through chapter select- Some texts are hard to see, especially the notebook that has no option to show the text in another font- Slow walking and running speedIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650There is only one word that is fitting to describe the visuals: beautiful. I mean, I didn't even play in the highest setting - I switched to medium after I see how beautiful the game looks at the first scene and I was afraid that my laptop won't handle it for a long session. The sea looks creepy with the dim lighting, and although I had to adjust to its brighter look in the medium setting, they still look great in some scenes. I even unconsciously think that it would be great if I could experience it in VR.I couldn't help but stop and stare at how well done the scenery looks in some of the areas. The night sky is one example. The in-game sky might look brighter and has more stars in it, but as someone who like to stare at the night sky when I was little, I missed being able to see stars in the sky, and the game just brings me back to that time. There are even some areas where you can just sit and watch the beautiful-looking scenes while the game moves you to the next destination. I like how these are all designed, and if you like to take a screenshot, I believe that you'll spend your time doing that most of the time. The story blends itself between finding the main character's husband and the mystery that surrounds the area. It blends perfectly since you need to find the trails that were left by your husband, which was trying to explore the area with his team. Since you only find clues in the form of letters and images, it's easy to digest the whole thing while focusing on what matters the most: the exploration. is one of the games that didn't feel like telling much but is able to tell a lot at the same time. Part of it might be because I unconsciously process what was being spoken by the main character as I scoured the area, but finding the clues, hearing the main character's remarks, and looking at the scenery is enough to understand the worldbuilding to some extent. It feels as if you are experiencing what the main character does yourself. As I said before, the gameplay basically focuses on exploration. You need to scour the area and find some interactable objects that might hold some clues. However, although the game marks the interactable objects, it can be hard to see since the mark is just a tiny dot that will expand if you focus on it. Luckily, you can guess which are the interactable objects to some extent, making it easier to find the clues.The areas might not be vast, but I still wish for the character to have a faster walking speed. The running speed was still slow, and even if it doesn't, it can be tiring to press the sprint button every time I walk. Some areas might not be spread far from each other, although there are times when I wish that I can walk faster. I like how the game tracks clues and logs, though. The logs were written in such a way as to let you know what can't be translated by what you see through text, and the clues help to solve some of the puzzles. You just need to be more aware of your surroundings to find everything, and although some puzzles take a bit of thinking, they are pretty simple once you know what to do.I finished the game in 6.2h. There are times when I didn't know where I was supposed to go, but it was more because I missed some interactable objects on my way. Puzzles will be blocking your progress most of the time, and although I also had trouble with one, I still enjoyed how unique it was from each other. Each puzzle uses a different mechanic to solve, and since it has no instructions, you need to figure out how to solve them based on some clues that are drawn in your notes.Achievement hunters won't need to worry about completing the game. Each chapter is short and the chapter selection shows what you have missed in that chapter. If that's not enough, there are a lot of guides that you can refer to.It can be hard to read the handwriting in the journal and there is no "Read" option to show the text in a different display.As someone who hates walking simulators,  didn't bore me at all. I liked how it paced itself between exploring and puzzle solving, and exploring is still made worthwhile since you need to find clues. Moreover, the main character's remarks on the exploration always help to some extent, especially with how good the voiceover is - the voice was clear and soothing to the ear. I could recommend it to anyone who likes to enjoy the scenery in a game and doesn't mind doing some puzzles in between.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid, story-driven walking simulator with light puzzles!About 4 hours of content, so $5 an hour. The puzzles are nothing to write home about, if you're paying attention and going through all the items/notes in a scene then you should be able to breeze past most of them. But that doesn't make them unsatisfying!The scenery in this game is just downright gorgeous. There were a couple of times I stopped progressing and went back to a scene just to take it in one more time. The art team absolutely nailed it!I have a few notes of constructive criticism though:1. It may have been a bug, but about half of the scenes in the game have an almost Vaseline-like blur to them. The resolution was right, changing graphics/accessibility settings did nothing to help.2. Toggle-sprint is important for accessibility. People with disabilities like carpal tunnel can have trouble holding it down as much as one needs to in this game.3. Always on mouse acceleration/heavy smoothing is often poorly received. But for a game like this, it adds a certain cinematic charm  in my opinion and at least the timing puzzles didn't have it. A toggle would be nice.4. Story spoilers:

_childDocuments_.review: This is better as a story rich walking sim than what I want from a puzzle game, but the story as mostly told from the female protagonist is hit & miss, so I can't recommend this game even at historic low price.Here is what you need to know:+You play Norah who explores a beautiful wonderous island in search for her husband who led an expedition to find a cure for Norah's illness.-Half the time she talks it helps build the narrative and the infection fits the current tone, but other times it is brain dead observations of things you make her interact with and a vocal inflection to match.-Half the puzzles were intuitive, and the other half were obtuse in how to ultimately figure them out. _childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is a colorful Cthulhu Mythos inspired First Person Puzzle Adventure Walking Sim.That was a mouthful.For those that don't want to read: I give this Game a 6.5 out of 10. Not bad. Not groundbreaking.The Game is a highly stylized but pretty looking Game apart from some clipping issues here and there.You probably have seen this particular artstyle in Games before, but still, it was quite fitting.The Voice Acting was good (they had Yuri Lowenthal), not extraordinary, but good.You will hear the main characters voice a lot because she comments on everything and talks to you constantly but I didn't find it annoying.The Music was also pretty good, very fitting to the theme of the game.Storywise in a few words: You go on an expedition to find your missing husband who is looking for a cure for your "mysterious" illness in polynesia. The thing is, if you know your Lovecraft and Cthulhu and Dagon Stuff, the "twist" at the end is apparent right from the beginning in the prologue. But that's okay.The Game is very puzzle heavy and in my opinion some puzzles were kind of hard sometimes. And since I am pretty stupid (I mean, I went to University but still...), for some puzzles I looked up a gaming hint website or just looked up the solution outright. Still I solved a chunk myself. I know looking up solutions in a puzzle Game kind of defeats the purpose of playing that kind of Game but sometimes I just want to finish a Game quick(er)...What bugged me a little was the translation. Some words didn't fit or there were some grammar errors. And sometimes in a text heavy Game, mistakes like that - especially when there are plenty - can take me out of the immersion a bit.Also I found it kind of strange that she calls her husband her "dear old pal" and so does he with her. Overall I had kind of fun...I think!? Not really sure. I mean, the story was okay, typical lovecraftian Dagon type of story. Atmosphere was also pretty good. I dunno. I have no strong feelings in either direction.So yeah, with looking up a few things it took me 5.6 hours to complete and see both endings ().It will probably take you 1-2 hours longer without looking anything up. Also, 20 of 34 Achievements in my playthrough, I checked them afterwards and it seems even though I was kind of thorough I still missed plenty of secrets.Recommended if you want more Lovecraft, this time a little bit more lighthearted, packaged into a romance story...
