_childDocuments_.review: Less of a walking sim than a modernized version of 90's point-and-click adventure games. It is colourful, well-written, heartfelt, has solid puzzles, and is absolutely worth your time.You play as Norah, looking for her missing husband on a remote south Pacific island after receiving a letter from him. It's first-person navigation that will have you traversing the island looking for story/puzzle clues and solving said puzzles. It keeps a good pace, never having you go too far without giving you something to do. Fans of H.P. Lovecraft will be in familiar territory, despite not being a horror game. It takes place in Lovecraft's universe, and explores some themes common to his work; fans will notice lots of nods and references to his writings. However, the story is original, and no familiarity with Lovecraft's work is needed to enjoy and understand it. I've seen this game described as a "walking sim", and I don't think that quite fits. I think what separates it from that genre is:- It is primarily a puzzle game; and- Most of Norah's narrations are optional, based on objects you examine. The end result is it feels like a 2020 version of Myst, just with more dialogue outside of cutscenes and with free-form movement, though it is restrictive in where you can go. While the environments may consist of several interlocking paths, you won't be able to stray far from said paths. There are hidden objects to find and achievements to unlock, in addition to lots of discarded bits of paper or stone carvings off to the side that add to the game world. When examined, Norah will not just say "there is a stone carving here" - she will connect it to something else she has seen, or talk about how she feels about it. It all feels meaningful and relevant (aside from one or two obvious jokes), and adds an extra layer to the gameplay and to the world.Fortunately, given that the game places its emphasis on puzzles, they are challenging and satisfying. Norah keeps a notebook to record story beats and puzzle clues, which you will need to reference to solve the case at hand. Sometimes the solution is outside the box, and sometimes it's obvious - it keeps you on your toes without being too easy nor frustrating. I would say they're more complicated than a typical puzzle game, but they aren't mind-melting either. The visuals always keep things colourful and interesting, and run the gambit from serene, to ethereal, to surreal. The sound design is largely subdued as well - the game is largely quiet with ambient environmental sounds, with a few standout musical moments, sometimes used to solve puzzles. The voice acting is convincing, especially with Norah - hearing her comments and internal monologue feels natural and adds to the game world, rather than feeling like it's trying to club you over the head with narrative themes or drama.While the game runs smoothly, I did experience some technical issues, none of which were game breaking. On two occasions, the game froze while I was on a ladder; the autosave resolved that quickly. More puzzling was when an achievement triggered and the screen cut to earlier in the game for a moment (I thought it was meant to be a flashback); curious what it was, I tabbed out to see, only for the achievement not be on my list. I looked it up, only to see that it was an achievement I couldn't have triggered in that moment. Overall, I would recommend this to anyone looking for a good story and/or challenging puzzles. The beautiful location adds to both of those things. I thought this game was fantastic; considering it's the first game done by Out of the Blue, it's an excellent start, and I will be watching for their next title.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games you could end 2020 with. Call of the Sea is extremely engaging in all of its aspects. The atmosphere created by the sounds and music makes you enter this world and stay in it along the incredible adventure of Norah.The characters and the story are well developed, thanks to the different items you find all over the place that give you details of how these characters were and what happened to them. Not to mention the incredible voice acting it has.The puzzles are varied in their style: from timing to rhythm, memory, and spatial reasoning.It's a must-play for anyone that enjoys exploration, story-rich, puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: If you like beautiful puzzle games and Lovecraftian world you probably are going to like it.However the puzzles are not great designed. They mostly do not respect your time.You walk around, find clues that get automatically jotted down in the journal and then you just have to put the things inside the journal together.  This lead for me to a disconnection of the world and the puzzles - I never really had to think on my own, because I just had to gather all the stuff for the journal and then do a puzzle that had nothing to do with the world. There are many puzzles where you have to walk a few times between the same locations, while the walking is very slow.  At the same time there were some puzzles that were not completely clear because you can understand the hints in different ways. Reading the solution in a guide cleared up the confusion. Which should not be necessary imho.(Spoiler: ). For me it is not enjoyable mapping symbols to numbers 3 times in my brain - that's not an interesting puzzle to me it just takes some energy and in the end feels kind of like work.So in the end i stopped playing, although i like the topic and the atmosphere, it's just that the puzzles are very annoying to me.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game from start to finish.Immersive visuals, engaging puzzles, gripping story. That it's placed in the Mythos of H.P. Lovecraft isn't essential to its value, but the cosmic backdrop and Lovecraft easter eggs are definitely a plus.7.5 hour playthrough, and we took our time to soak it in. Worth the $20 full price, and definitely worth the $9 sale price right now during the Fall sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: (8/10)I wasn't sure what to expect with this game going in to it but I like puzzle adventures in general so I figured I'd give it a shot. It turns out its actually quite a bit more like Ethan Carter or Edith Finch than it is like a game such as The Witness.  In that vein its very story driven with the primary drive being to uncover what happened to a lost expedition to a lost pacific island.The locations are well realized and ambiance is pretty strong overall for that early 20th century adventure story vibe.  You deal with mystical things, and steampunkish technical contraptions and unravel a pretty wild story by the time things wind down.  Audio and visual fidelity is not photorealistic but its not trying to be.  Its going for a more stylized vibe and pulls it off quite well.The story comes via a combination of clues you find and narration from the main character and thankfully as in many games when the majority of the clues are hand-written, they do have a quick access to just the text to make reading easier especially on smaller screens like the Steam Deck.None of the puzzles was too challenging but they serve more as a way to thoughtfully break up the narrative elements and get you to explore a little more and that is perfectly suited to a game like this. Overall if you like narrative driven adventures and don't mind simulating maybe just a bit of walking, this is a pretty solid game for you.  If you want something a little higher octane, then look elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: See update*******************I really wanted to like this game. I love puzzles, and REALLY love Lovecraft (except for his racist parts), and I love retro/vintage stuff. I even work with old people for a living. However, this game was just painful. The puzzles were not pleasant to me. I had to look up game guides, often on 2 or more sites, just to know how to proceed. (I never got past chapter four sadly, so this review will focus on those chapters only.)To be honest, even when I did the puzzles right, there was way too much back-tracking for my liking, and random answers that just killed it. I couldn't figure out the logic behind the puzzles. Even the solutions presented on the game guides were things like "the first symbol she writes in her journal goes on the top." Well, what's the logic behind that? Ancient/alien beings somehow knew the order in which Norah would write the symbols down in her journal, and oriented the solution around that? It's frustrating AND makes no sense. To be honest, I was wiling to bite the bullet and play from the game guides because the game is really beautiful and immersive (except her footsteps, which seriously sound like a rhinoceros to me, and she walks SO SLOWLY). However, I finally got to a puzzle that defeated me. You are supposed to push certain buttons on a wheel, and there's no indication that I could see of how you are supposed to do this in the game, other than Norah repeating every time you go into the puzzle "Oh, this seems to adjust the water flow." (THANKS NORAH.) For this puzzle one of my trusty game guides (doing their best, surely) explained: "Each button can turn other buttons on and off, so you will need to play around with them until they are all lit." Well, mesdames et messieurs, after fifteen minutes of pushing random buttons willy-nilly, I just can't take any more. I am resigning in disgrace.I wanted to like this game and honestly at the very least I wanted to FINISH this game, but I can't take any more. God bless you if you figured it out or got lucky. I hope the ending was amazing. I will never see it.*****************Update: I logged back in and somehow got past the puzzle and played the rest of the game. Since I finished it, I'm changing my review from not recommended to recommended but with the caveat that I had to look up solutions to many of the puzzles, and the issues I mentioned above persisted. However, the artwork and sound is just so immersive, I have to admit I did enjoy the game for most of the time.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful graphics, immersive environment, interesting story, but so... so.... slow.... to walk around. Got fed up and used a walkthrough for the last chapter as I wanted to see how the story resolved, but with such obtuse puzzles that were either strangely straightforward and a chore to walk between buttons to push, or too weird and I needed some tips to get me through. Cissy Jones, originally from Boise, Idaho, USA, voiced Norah, the lead character, with the weirdest British/English accent I've ever heard. American media often gets somone to do 'a British Accent' that sounds cut-glass posh and like no-one who's ever set foot in the UK. As far removed from the silver-spoon set as you can get.  I've no idea what region of the UK it should be from, and took me out of the game whilst I constantly tried to work out why some parts of sentences sounded reasonably attempted and then some words were very strangely pronounced.If you have patience to wander round these lovely environments and are a lot better at grinding between buttons in walk-about puzzles than me, you'll enjoy this. _childDocuments_.review: Nice story, fairly dynamic gameplay. Overall, a very well crafted game that I think is worth a look at with gameplay videos or if you feel the need to purchase and play for yourself, by all means, I would encourage that too. _childDocuments_.review: Slow-paced and interesting storyline that keeps you engaged throughout all chapters. Riddles are generally not too hard with the occasional harder riddle sprinkled in. I liked that many parts of the game were narrated and that the game takes notes for you in the ingame log. _childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is a walking sim game with strong emphasis on puzzle solving. You play as Norah, a woman who travels to a beautiful, but mysterious Polynesian island looking for her husband and his expedition crew who disappeared under mysterious circumstances. The story is surprisingly Lovecraftian, one I did not expect when I started the game. There are references to Lovecraft stories, especially The Shadow Over Innsmouth and Dagon.The artstyle is absolutely breathtaking. It's beautiful and colorful, while also being somewhat cartoony, yet realistic. It makes the island look beautiful, both the normal, natural parts and the weird ancient architectures. In my opinion, more videogames, especially walking sims, should try to achieve this kind of look rather than the typical "next-gen realism" everyone seems to be obsessed with. And as a Lovecraftian game, kudos for not making it dreary and depressing, yet still retaining the mysterious atmosphere.Gameplay-wise, I like how this game feels so user-friendly. You can save and load everywhere, not relying on checkpoints, and there are chapter select which carries over your collectibles, in the form of journal logs and notes. If Norah takes a note of something, chances are it's a clue to a puzzle in the area. Most of the puzzles are pretty easy, but some can be confusing due to lack of clear direction of what to do, but you can always look up a walkthrough.If there's a weakness to this game, for me it's the length, and the lack of cloud saving. The game is too short, and I really wished it was longer. I'd love to see more beautiful, colorful, and mysterious vistas. Call of the Sea is an excellent walking sim, and definitely one of the best I've played, so if you like puzzles, walking sims, and/or Lovecraftian stories, you should try this beautiful game.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: First, let me say that I really enjoyed this game, This game has wonderful voice acting and stunning visuals. (Most of) the puzzles are complex enough to keep you entertained without feeling unfair, and there are plenty of hints on where to go next from where you are. There are lots of achievements, but the game is still a nice, medium length (I ended up spending about 7 hours on it). The music and environmental sounds are out of this world, and I would gladly listen to many parts of the soundtrack again.The first four and a half chapters are really good, and the story is compelling, but after those chapters, there is a steep drop off in quality. Something that really bothered me was that Norah kept ♥♥♥♥ talking Harry/her husband for trying to find a way for them to be together after . While it is true that he does some questionable things, she acts as if he is doing them in his right mind instead of becoming more and more desperate as . Meanwhile, Norah is having the time of her life, even forgetting Harry at some point after , but she outright says that she can't understand . Her attitude towards Harry persists for the rest of chapter five, and most of the last chapter, . This attitude gets tiring very fast, and I was frankly disgusted with how hypocritical she was being and her lack of any understanding or empathy that she showed for the situation (made even worse by the fact that she showed both understanding and empathy towards it in previous chapters).On top of this, my biggest complaint is chapter six in general. The majority of the time in the chapter is taken up by an extremely long, tedious puzzle that matters very little to the actual story. There are also some plot holes here, as it is implied that Norah can only complete this puzzle as  so it is unclear how Harry could have even finished it in the first place. The plot holes aren't a deal breaker for me, as I'm willing to overlook them, but the puzzle is pretty annoying. To be honest, and without spoiling too much, the plot twist is a slap in the face. At no point is it foreshadowed, and it makes the game seem much less impactful, as it means that . Both endings are bad endings. .Call of the Sea is an okay game. If its on sale, you like puzzles and a hint of mystery and don't mind a steep drop off in quality for the last 1/4 or so of the game, I would buy it. If any of those are a deal breaker for you though, I wouldn't recommend this game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a must-buy, even for the full price (though I grabbed it on sale)! The story is amazing! It all ties together, and the mysteries  are solved in the end. The voice acting is great too, professional quality, and doesn't make you cringe listening to it. And the soundtrack? Oh my god. Such a  soundtrack, I'm glad I got the deluxe edition (which includes it).This game is six chapters long, and they're all unique in their own way with their settings.If you're unsure about whether or not you want to get this, trust me, it's well worth it. I'm replaying it to get 100% completion, and am enjoying playing through it again. And if you're worried about going back to complete everything like me, don't worry as there's a chapter option you can go to at  time.In order to get full satisfaction when playing this game, it's best to go in completely blind. If you have to look up how to solve some puzzles, go ahead, I certainly had to .The only "dislike" I had (if it even counts) is it  told more backstory, but the way the storytelling is it's made to leave some questions, so I'm not really mad or anything. You just have to fill in the gaps yourself I guess.Also, this is the first time I'm writing a review on Steam, so take that as you will.

Nice music too.There are no enemies to fight in this, it is purely a Lovecraft mythos investigation game with puzzles and exploration. _childDocuments_.review: A fresh take on the Cthulhu Mythos/Cosmic-horror inspired puzzle game.  Very stylish, good pacing and real easy presentation.  Not too difficult as far as puzzle-driven adventure games go, and the chapter replay makes it easy to go back and get any missed items or story-beats.  More compelling and mysterious than scary, and short enough to play through in a few hours.  All in all, a great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: This already seemed like a game I would enjoy as it is a story-driven puzzle game, but Call of the Sea delivers beyond expectation. The puzzles are quite easy, but the amount of storytelling built around them makes up for that. The most unexpected thing about this game is that it borrows a lot from the Lovecraft mythos. There are references everywhere and there is a building eerie atmosphere as you progress through the story. This is not, however, a horror game by any means, which just makes it more interesting. Another aspect that really elevates Call of the Sea is the voice-acting. Cissy Jones does a wonderful job of making Norah a likeable character. As puzzle games go, I feel this one is a bit underrated or overlooked. Call of the Sea is definitely worth your time.

The puzzles are not difficult and the story follows the theme just fine. The only problems with the game are minor immersion breaking designs. One of the puzzles, I wondered why I need to run back and forth between two very close puzzle elements. The elements could have just been combined. Some objects have odd design, like objects that clip through one another. Things like a gap being bridged by three evenly spaced planks of wood, signs of game development rather than how the actual characters would place things. _childDocuments_.review: Gorgeous graphics and initially captivating story line don't mask the truth that it's more walking simulator than puzzle/exploration game. The second half of the game devolves into basic pattern matching and the final puzzle is easily one of the most straightforward in the entire experience. The message the game gives in it's endings is touching but is not a worthy payoff when so much of the inner details of the whole experience are left completely ignored. It would have been nice to explore Norah's lineage further through the island and mysteries it holds, but instead Call of the Sea is just a walk from one gated area to another looking for shapes or symbols to align correctly to proceed.Well made game that simply lacks the depth of others in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: is a short, cozy little puzzle walking simulator in the vein of  or the original , centering around Norah, a woman with a mysterious terminal illness, tracing the steps of her missing archaeologist husband and his trip to an uncharted island in search of a cure.  It pulls heavily from 1920s and 30s adventure serials like  and , which lends to the cozy tone, but it shouldn't surprise you or any other gamer that with a mysteriously-blighted narrator pursuing an ill-fated expedition, the game swiftly turns towards its most enduring and obvious inspirations, H.P Lovecraft's  and .Where most 'Lovecraftian' games go hard on the slavering Mythos beasties, though,  remains perpetually in this colorful, wistful space -- the game itself describes its tone as 'homesick' -- that emphasizes the fantastical elements of the unknown more than it emphasizes the horrific elements.  It eludes being a cosmic horror tale, and remains a character-driven drama throughout, told through constant narration by Norah herself in the fashion of Lovecraft's own very self-expository protagonists.Thankfully, Norah remembers that this is a puzzle game, and so she wisely shuts up and defers to the player's wisdom when confronted with the game's eight or nine elaborate, brain-tingling puzzles.  Each level fits roughly the same cadence, where Norah will walk around the level picking up clues and expositing about their narrative meaning, and then silently leave the player to assemble those clues in mechanical terms in a way that will get them around some obstacle.  When the game begins these obstacles are fairly rudimentary and intuitive, like matching symbols on a totem to corresponding symbols on a dial lock, but as the game gets more supernatural they can get very involved.  Most of my 'a-ha' moments were in these later levels, where I was frequently presented with a series of clues that didn't make sense together as a puzzle until I noticed some overlooked environment element that tied everything together into one context.It's neither the most touching story a walking simulator has ever had, nor the best puzzles, nor the most lush environments, but the game hits a solid third-base run on all three of those, which is all the more impressive since this is developer Out of the Blue Games' first time at-bat.  It's an excellent game package and well worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is an atmospheric story/puzzle game set in the 1930's with a clear Lovecraftian theme and plot. The gameplay loop consists primarily of exploring new areas for notes, objects, pictures, and other clues, and using those to discover the story and solve puzzles that block advancement. There is no real action to speak of and the spooky/creepy/uneasy level is low, but there. So how does Call of the Sea fare in what it sets out to do? It fares quite well!+Gorgeous visuals+Immersive notes, objects, environments+Solid voice acting+Puzzles that require some thinking!+Good Lovecraftian story+Somewhat sp00by-Controls could be a bit tighter-Story isn't mind-blowing-That one puzzle...-Not  sp00byCall of the Sea really nails the atmosphere and visuals. I went in thinking this was a horror-lite game but it's not at all. The game feeds you some uneasiness but it's far from truly scary. The voice actress does a great job and the supporting cast does too. The puzzles really make you think and some of them left me scratching my head for a minute until an "aha" moment. The story is a good intro into Lovecraftian tales but it's not mind-blowing or groundbreaking. Still, it's solid and I enjoyed it. My biggest complaint with the game lies with the controls. They feel a touch off. The camera is a bit sluggish. Your character moves a bit sluggish. I appreciate it's more of a cinematic game, but movement felt "over-smoothed" and not crisp. It's not a gamebreaker by any means but it is slightly annoying.Towards the end of Chapter 3, there is an infuriatingly difficult/misleading/poorly explained puzzle. Everything leading up to the puzzle is fantastic! And even the first couple attempts to solve it are great. But then, nothing seems to work. It took me 30 minutes to get nowhere. My advice is to try the puzzle a couple times and then use my hint if you're not getting anywhere. If the hint doesn't help, just lookup a guide. It's not worth the frustration. I'll leave my hint here: If you want a game focused on discovering a story and solving puzzles, you'll be happy. Don't expect to be scared, don't expect any action, and don't expect a groundbreaking story and you won't be disappointed. I enjoyed the game and will recommend it to others!

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is a beautiful game, that above all is evocative of its themes and immersive in its presentation.The story is relatively straightforward, but nontheless interesting, and sucks you in as a player in pursuit of the central mystery of the game.The beautifully crafted puzzles are the central gameplay element of the game and are very interesting to solve, even if for my taste at least a little bit to easy at times. Overall the game is also rather short and does not really provide any replay value apart from revisiting chapters to search for a few hidden items and journal entries. I finished my playthrough at 5 hours. That makes it hard to recommend in terms of value for money, when you take a look at other cheap games that can provide hundreds of hours of fun.Still Call of the Sea is a wonderful exploration of its genre, that is polished and well crafted, and is well worth it if you are a puzzle fan and want a straighforward cinematic experience that never feels boring, unfair with its puzzles or overindulges on itself with unnessecary padding.Overall a great game made by a small team of developers, whose love for the subject can be felt on every step of the way!

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is a story-driven puzzle adventure game. You play as Norah, a woman on a quest in 1934 to find her husband, who led an expedition months ago to a remote Polynesian island near Tahiti in search for a cure to your strange illness. Starting on the beach of the island, you follow the expedition's trail, uncovering clues, solving puzzles, and learning more about the island and the events that transpired during your husband's expedition.At times this game feels more like a "walking simulator" than a puzzle game, as there are only a few major puzzles per chapter, and none of them are very mind-bending. Most of the objects you end up examining only serve to fill in bits of story, so it's quite a bit like games like Gone Home or What Remains of Edith Finch in that regard. As for the puzzles, they're not terribly difficult. But they're not really tedious either. Not a lot of item collecting, fitting a gear you picked up five minutes ago into a machine to make the door open, sort of stuff. In fact, you don't have to even take notes or write down clues, as the game does it for you in Norah's journal, which certainly is helpful in streamlining things. What would streamline things even more is if they allowed you to move at a decent speed. You can make your character "run" but it's really more of a fast walk. And regular walking is a snail's pace.It took me around 8 hours to complete the game, so if you snag the game on sale you'll get your money's worth. It's an interesting enough story with decent but not fiendishly difficult puzzles that will occupy your time adequately if this is the sort of game you're into.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite usually enjoying this type of game and setting and looking forward to this a lot; I found Call of the Sea very slow and frustrating.Whilst it has a nice art style, an intriguing story and at times, an atmospheric setting a number of elements of this game started to immediately make the experience of playing it unenjoyable for me.One of the big irritations was just how bad it feels to navigate the world - despite having a decent PC there is a lot of screen tearing for no particular reason. I tried using both controller and mouse but either way everything feels very sluggish and awkward. You move around at an agonising, lumbering slow pace - there is a run button but this is the equivalent of walking in other games. There is nothing gameplay wise you haven't seen before done better - explore a small area, read audio logs, solve a few puzzles and move on. Take BioShock, remove all the gameplay, throw in some puzzles and fit the player with some extremely heavy lead shoes and you'll start to get an idea of how it feels to play this.Some of the puzzles are quite frustrating too - one of them made no sense to me even after I'd looked up the solution.I also found the main character (a posh lady from the 1930's) very uninspiring and her constant vocalisation of her inane or obvious thoughts immediately started to grate. Regularly she would be making some pointless comment on notes I'd literally just picked up before I'd even had a chance to read what she was referring to.Drawn on by the story I found myself rushing through the puzzles because I wanted to see the conclusion. As I started to expect as the end drew near - there was no big satisfying reveal and I didn't feel it was worth the effort.In summary: very overrated and mediocre. If Steam let you rate games I'd give it a 2.5 out of 5.

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is a beautiful game with an engaging story line and pretty good puzzles. I would recommend this to anyone who would likes logic puzzles and a good narrative. Took me about 5 hours to finish, and i tried to take my time with it. PuzzlesThe puzzles are completely doable and doesn't require extra paper or resources. The difficulty really just comes from needing to observe everything the game wants you to see and making sure you don't miss anything. I only looked up a couple hints just to realize there was an area/item i didn't look through and then solving the puzzle was straight forward. Most of the puzzles are logic/observation puzzles, a few timing puzzles, and there was one audio puzzle that i just looked up the answer cause the sounds were way to similar to separate from each other. Other than the audio puzzle, they definitely filled the puzzle itch of a Nancy Drew Game Fan.Story/Replay-ability Finished the game in like 3 sittings and have no desire replay it unless it was to play with a friend to show the story. The story was mysterious but gave enough answers to make you feel satisfied at the end. Also there's no jump scares in this game, so while the game may get a bit tense there isn't anything really scary. If anything I wish the story would go into more world building and more details of the back-story but I'm sure they don't over explain to keep an air of intrigue.

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is one of those games that you play in awe because the visuals and pastel colors are so beautiful that it immerses you immediately.Game's general style can be described with Firewatch, Vanishing of Ethan Carter or Annapurna-like style games. Since In The Valley of Gods got sacked by Valve/Campo Santo, Out of the Blue might as well fill that area easily with their talent because this it the closest we can get. They did a stellar job.There's a lot of walking and narrative talking but when Cissy Jones voice acting the main character, that's not a problem but instead a pleasure. You may remember her from Firewatch as Delilah. Animations, art style, music and Lovecraftian story is actually fascinating and it got pretty gloomy at the end. Puzzles weren't incredibly hard and I liked that personally since hard puzzles actually irritates the player, or me, and breaks the immersion. Game looks incredible in some areas and it's soothing to listen the rain while slowly walking, puzzle solving and let the story unfolds. Liked it very much.Harry and Norah's love coincided with Valentine's Day and left me kind of empty. The song at the end was a perfect touch.Out of the Blue did a wonderful job and I personally will follow them for their next project. Recommended.P.S.: I personally thank to developers and publisher for a wonderful regional pricing as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I love this game. I liked the puzzles and the story, albeit both being a little slow. Without spoiling, I do kind of get the sense that the developers didn't super know where they were going with this story until they got there, as it seems kind of jumbled. The beginning chapters were amazing and seemed really well thought out, but it was as though they hadn't fully thought out what direction they were going to take the story in afterwards based on how latter chapters were executed. The main character shows a great deal of empathy and adoration towards her husband in the beginning of the story, but by chapter 6 it's like that has all gone out the window. In summary, if you really like puzzle games and the story is secondary to you, this is a great fit. The story is good, but there is a decline as the story goes on that may be disappointing to some people. Me personally, I don't mind, and I still enjoyed the game overall. Definitely worth a play and I think the developers 100% have a lot of potential.

_childDocuments_.review: When played without preconceptions stemming from the overly broad and generic genre classifications,it is hard to find any fault with Call of the Sea, and as such the game is very worthy of a recommendation.But beware: most summaries and short descriptions are naught but lies. Call of the Sea is not an adventure game like Monkey Island. It is not a puzzle game like Myst. And it is no psychological horror game even tho its story has "lovecraftian" elements.In actuality, and my opinion, Call of the Sea is a sweet story about a woman with a peculiar heritage and feeble health, who embarks on a journey to find her missing husband, eventually following in his footsteps through a lush, vibrant tropical island. The game feautures a variety of puzzles, all of which can be solved without guessing. The built-in notebook automatically collects any hints found throughout the environment, eliminates external notekeeping, and presents hints in a way that makes logically deducing the solution easy without actually giving the solution away.Call of the Sea strikes a curious balance between relaxation, mystery and puzzles-olving, and provides four to eight hours of solid, low-effort entertainment. Even if you consider yourself a "true gamer", this is the ideal game to play with your mom during your holiday visit (or your non-gamer significant other).

I won't spoiler anything, but it combines a sense of wonder, mystery and cosmic horror in a beautiful way.- Sometimes I felt lost, but it actually feels like a + to me so... I don't know, it's just a great game. :)

_childDocuments_.review: I don't typically play puzzle games, but this game managed to keep me interested from start to finish. The game's Lovecraftian vibes, and engaging storyline kept me playing. The twist at the end was especially memorable, Harry is a real sweetheart.the game had really good visuals and the accompanying music, both of which played a significant role in making me want to see more. _childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is a beautiful and captivating game that takes players on an unforgettable journey to a mysterious island in the South Pacific. The game's stunning visuals and immersive storytelling make it a must-play for anyone who loves adventure and exploration.    The game begins with players taking on the role of Norah, a woman searching for her missing husband on a remote island. As players explore the island, they will uncover its secrets and learn more about the ancient civilization that once inhabited it.    One of the standout features of Call of the Sea is its gorgeous art style. The game is set in the 1930s, and the developers have done a fantastic job of capturing the feel of the era. The environments are lush and beautifully detailed, and the character designs are unique and memorable.    The game's puzzles are also well-designed and provide a nice challenge without being too difficult. They are integrated seamlessly into the story and help to advance the plot.    Overall, Call of the Sea is a truly wonderful game that offers a rich and engaging experience. It is a must-play for anyone who loves adventure games, and it is sure to leave a lasting impression on players.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a labor of love, and goes the extra mile to create character immersion and theme. The art style is vibrant and reminiscent of pulp fiction, and slowly delves into the eldritch science fiction of the Cthulhu mythos. The music is great, and the soundtrack is an excellent purchase for anyone that runs tabletop RPGs.The designers drew inspiration from The Shadow Over Innsmouth, and take it in a completely fresh direction. The protagonist, Norah, feels exactly like I am playing an Investigator out of the tabletop RPG Call of Cthulhu, solving puzzles and looking for answers to her husband's disappearance. My absolute favorite part of this game is the amazing use of suspense horror around the Deep Ones. It is present the moment you dock your motor boat on the island, and builds into a spectacular plot as the island becomes one giant "Escape Room". The game took me 9 hours to complete and unlock the achievements. That said, there is an easy 12+ hours of content here if you play any of the Cthulhu tabletop RPGs, as the designers created so much lore that one can run a prequel (of Harry's expedition team) and sequel campaigns (with the island's family tree) using this game's amazing story and characters. For anyone going this route, the art book is a must buy for use as rpg game props.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: It's "The Shape of Water," Indiana Jones, 1930s nostalgia, Pacific island adventure, and a love story, with a little bit of "Myst." If none of those options interest you then perhaps this isn't the droid you're looking for. I loved the look of the game and the sound design is fantastic. The artwork is beautiful too. I used a walkthrough for some of the puzzles simply to cut down time and to avoid repetition. I got the game on sale and it was money well spent. I clocked up 9.7 hours and enjoyed it. Your turn...
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty good.  Certainly worth the price if you like puzzle and story games.I'm not a puzzle expert and I found all the puzzles in the game complex without being frustrating.  There was only one where I got frustrated and looked up a hint for.The game has a pleasant stylised look, with good sound and voice acting that makes a great atmosphere.  The atmosphere itself is occasionally a little unsettling but is usually as pleasant as its appearance.  Which may seem an odd choice for the otherworldly elements but it works for the story and the character's situation.  It managed to get some genuine emotion from me at the climax.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: The atmosphere in the game is incredible, it's worth the price of admission as a walking simulator alone. But, it's more than just a walking simulator, it's also a story-rich puzzle adventure. There are some logic puzzles that will require a little bit of thought to figure out, and the story that you uncover along the way through voice narration, notes and photographs, as well as environmental storytelling, is captivating. Some areas are even a little bit scary or unnerving, but it's not a horror game and you're not being chased by monsters or anything like that. You can take your time, which is great considering there is so much atmosphere to soak up along the way.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: is a visually stunning and narrative-driven puzzle adventure that embarks players on a captivating journey through an enigmatic island filled with mysteries and secrets. The game's art, storytelling, and puzzle-solving elements come together harmoniously to create an engaging and immersive experience. While it has its strengths, some minor shortcomings prevent it from reaching its full potential.:Visually,  is a very pretty. The hand-painted art style and vibrant colours breathe life into the mysterious island setting. The attention to detail in the environments and character designs is commendable, creating a world that is both beautiful and haunting. The game's ability to evoke a sense of wonder and curiosity through its visuals is a definite highlight.:The game's narrative is its driving force, taking players on an emotional journey through the protagonist's search for her missing husband. The intriguing plot slowly unravels, revealing layers of mystery and suspense that keep players invested in the story's outcome. The game's voice acting also adds depth to the characters and their emotions, enhancing the overall storytelling experience.: features a variety of clever puzzles that challenge players to think outside the box. The puzzles are well-integrated into the narrative, offering a sense of satisfaction upon completion. However, some puzzles can feel overly simplistic, and a few lack the depth and complexity that puzzle enthusiasts might seek. A bit more balance in difficulty would have elevated the puzzle-solving aspect further.:While the story and puzzles are strong, the gameplay is where  falls a bit short. The movement and controls can feel clunky and imprecise at times, leading to frustrating moments during exploration and puzzle-solving. Additionally, the lack of interaction with the island's environment limits the sense of immersion, hindering players from fully experiencing the richness of the world.:The game's audio design complements the overall atmosphere, with a hauntingly beautiful soundtrack that heightens the emotional impact of the story. The ambient sounds and voice acting add to the sense of immersion, creating a well-rounded auditory experience.: offers a relatively short gameplay experience, which might disappoint players looking for a lengthier adventure. However, the quality of the storytelling and the captivating visuals make it a worthwhile journey for those seeking a memorable and emotionally engaging experience. Replay value is limited considering that the game is a linear puzzle-solving narrative experience.In conclusion,  is an enchanting and visually captivating puzzle adventure that weaves an intriguing narrative on a mysterious island. While its art, storytelling, and audio are standouts, minor gameplay and puzzle shortcomings hold it back from reaching higher heights. Overall, it provides a satisfying and memorable journey for players who appreciate immersive storytelling and atmospheric exploration.

_childDocuments_.review: This game made me physically ill navigating through the game.  I was fine on the 1st screen, but got to the island and had to stop playing and deal with the intense nausea that had built up within 10 minutes of island.  I changed the graphic setting, windowed the screen.  Navigated through the overly simple 1st couple puzzles, and got ill again.  This plays like a game from 2005 when we were still figuring out that graphics could cause nausea.the up-down, forward with side to side motion is awful.The graphics are decent, simple, and the color pallet is off too much yellows and scarlet red.  The voice actress, is a bit dull, but the idea of the game.  The plot, era, theme is very interesting.  I very much wanted to play this game, but and I'm sorry the developers didn't listen to QA when it became obvious that  it was nausea inducing.

_childDocuments_.review: In the interest of full disclosure, a friend gave me this game. The controls are a little janky, and the walking part of the walking simulator was real picky about what it would walk on sometimes. But those are tiny, tiny nitpicks in the sea of amazingness that is this game. The vibrant colors, the stellar voice acting, the worldbuilding and lore, everything was so beautifully put together. Highly recommend to anyone (especially those who like a Lovecraftian bent to their gaming experience).
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Immersive simulation and puzzles are both game genres that I enjoy. Saw Call of the Sea on someone's stream and thought this is right up my alley and I managed to grab it during good sales. However, after completing the game plus all the available achievements, while my playing experience is decent, I think the final verdict is that i probably won't be recommending it.Cons: I like the art direction and the graphics when i saw it on stream and also on video reviews. But playing it on pc with a 24", 1080p, ips monitor on Max settings, i just have this lingering feeling that the game is built for the console, couch viewing with a max resolution of 960p in mind.. FOR ME, everything just felt abit underwhelming, can be abit sharper and more detail. For the puzzles themselves, they also never quite give me a nice sense of satisfaction after solving them like many of such similar games did. They are just ok and again the same underwhelming feeling. There are only 2 possible endings and I don't quite like both of them.. lol Also there are a number of mysteries still left unexplained after the game has ended.Pros: The puzzles I imagined if it was real life can be considered to be very realistic as there was very little hand-holding in the game. The background music is good. If you enjoy steam achievements, you can "easily" complete all of them for this one~Conclusion: While i won't recommend Call of the Sea, I also didn't regret playing it. For me it was a decent, pleasant although somewhat underwhelming experience. 6.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty and relaxing. If you came for the sights, you'll be very satisfied. Climbing ladders feels the same way, even when the main character is talking about how invigorated she is!I still think it's worth playing for the beautiful setting, but just know that this game really only has one speed.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is simply put, not worth it.I experienced it as nothing more than a walking simulator - a very slow one too.The game has puzzles, yes, however they do not reward any form of intuitive thinking at all. The puzzles are almost always solved by backtracking long distances to find something to help you with the puzzle.The story is also terribly written. _childDocuments_.review: Bought this game on sale, no regrets. This was my first puzzle / adventure game, but I enjoyed it. _childDocuments_.review: Very nice puzzle game, most of the puzzles are clearly communicated with ingame hints about their rules so I only had to look up one of them to progress further.Visuals are amazing, love this style of art!Writing and self-narration is extremely on the nose and was horribly cringy in the beginning, it gets better once the exposition is mostly out of the way, but a very rough start.Voice actress is great but sounds a bit too old to my ears, extremely minor thing but combined with the self-narration I got some cognitive dissonance.Minor tip (no spoilers): You can "toggle" running by holding the sprint key/trigger, opening the main menu (release hold) and closing the menu.Just press it again to get back to normal.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: This is a VERY mid review with a LOT of complaints!So let's get the good stuff out of the way, if you like walking sims with a light puzzle element, and appreciate great atmospheric vistas, levels, and interesting stories, this is definetely something to consider playing. The genre is underrepresented and I am happy that this game was quite successfull, because despite all the critizism I will lay out shortly, this game shows the work of a dedicated indie team with a lot of potential for future titles, which is why I am overall still giving it a recommendation.That out of the way, here is what makes this game very frustrating to play:Writing: Whilst the story itself is quite interesting the execution in writing is horrible. Our main character is just a walking talking exposition dump. She has very little personality, and that is not the fault of the actress, voice acting overall is fine for a game of this size. But just reading these lines as subtitles really hurts your head. Everything is so on the nose, gets repeated hundreds of times to the player, none of the jokes work, and in some scenes our main character will just keep talking forever, like reading out the summary of the last chapter so that we still remember everything. It gets annoying VERY! FAST!I know they don't have the budget for big cutscenes but you can work around that. Show don't tell is a good rule for a reason. The game sets us on a hunt for a cure for a disease that we're never shown the consequences of! Like she's mentaly capable of solving puzzles and fit enough for this expedition but we're just supposed to believe that the spots on her arms are killing her?A personal gripe here would be the ending: Puzzles: They are mediocre at best and most of the time not very well presented to the player. Like none of these are real brain twisters, but that doesn't mean that solving them should be expected from the player. Most of the time I looked up the solution and whilest that always sounded easy on paper, I never had the means to come to that conclusion. It's just poorly communicated to the player, and in one puzzle you're taking a note of an order of buttons, and I'm expected to read that order from bottom to top... what?It's sad because the visual presentation of the puzzles always fits the level and the scenario we are currently in, but they are just so frustrating, artificially overcomplicated or just involve an unnecessary amount of backtracking. I also loved that level that followed a "power the generator puzzle" up with a "power the generator" puzzle, that made me chuckle.That combined with slow movement, overall clunky traversal some minor bugs, it just makes this game unnecessarily frustrating. Again, I still liked a lot of things that I saw, and I am looking forward to playing future titles of this developer, but only if they improve on these things, because for a price tag of 20 bucks, especially right after I finished a game that did a better job at all of the above at a 10 Dollar price tag, this is really disappointing.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Game looks alright, that's about all that's positive about it.The puzzles are kinda hit and miss (some very easy, some a bit too convoluted), but most of them the game just solves for you by writing it down in your journal anyway. Character moves painfully slow making these moments you have to backtrack to solve a puzzle 1000 times worse. But the worst part is by far the voice-acting and dialogue (or rather monologue). The main character cannot stop throwing exposition at you like a robot with some of the most annoying voice acting I have ever heard. Never have I hated a protagonist this much just because of such terrible voice acting. Funnily enough they even advertise the VA on the store page by saying she was in The Walking Dead Season 1. I checked who she voiced (turns out it was several side characters) and she was pretty much the worst VA in that game by far lol. Absolutely awful and made the constant exposition dump that much more unbearable. Like she seriously won't stop talking. Imagine being alone on a mysterious island and not shutting up for 2 seconds to stop talking about your dead mom or your missing husband or the letter you just read or the architecture or literally anything without pause. The story is nothing special (typical Lovecraftian stuff), but it would have been alright if it wasn't ruined by the most unlikeable main character I remember playing in recent times, who won't shut up ever to just let you enjoy the mysterious island you're exploring.

_childDocuments_.review: At first I thought 'This is nice; the ol' point and click adventure' and make no mistake the graphics are pretty good and the moving around is clean - but I soon got very frustrated with the amount of complex puzzles that meant a lot of repetitive assessments of e.g. huts, columns, tikis etc.  - and finally I was disappointed with the lack of any animations apart from the sea. _childDocuments_.review: One of the most beautiful games I have ever played.  I wasn't expecting much when I downloaded it and man it blew me away.  There are so many, "wow that's beautiful" moments in this game.  The pace is kind of slow, but the area around keeps you looking around in every direction.  Not to mention an absolutely beautiful soundtrack and interesting story littered with grim references to Lovecraftian lore. So, I'm giving it thumbs up, because it's an OK adventure. But, I don't recommend it if someone is looking for a scary or Lovecraftian game.

_childDocuments_.review: A charming game and clever tonal subversion of the source material / trope conventions of the genre. If you are at all familiar with the Mythos and find even a few of the secret items linked to Norah's family history you know where the story is going long before she figures it out. This didn't really detract from my enjoyment as the themes of acceptance or rejection of your fate and eternity versus entropy are well handled. The game has some stylistic similarity to Firewatch as well as sharing a voice artist along with some tangential themes. The puzzles vary in difficulty considerably which is not a problem as Norah's comprehensive notebook makes solving even the harder ones manageable. Her comprehensive notebook puts the difficulty somewhere between a walking simulator like Firewatch and a conventional puzzle adventure such as Obduction.The game is not long and can easily be completed over a weekend such I did. It feels like the right length and considering the price point is perfectly reasonable. As with a short story, more would have made it less.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very reluctant thumbs up, basically if you like hp lovecraft you should play this but if you don't you probably shouldn't. I find the puzzles to be fairly obtuse and connected in a way that makes not much sense. For instance (spoilers ahead) why does the tiki puzzle need 1 piece from each tiki in the camp? Why is there only 1 right solution to a certain star puzzle even though you can make the shape multiple ways? Why are the frequencies of those floating stones connected to the pipe organ? Why can you only hear the pipe organ play when you have the right answer (I though I still needed to find a master switch because music still plays even if the notes are wrong)? The other big issue with this game is the speed. She walks slow, she runs slow, the world is really big, and given the nature of some of the less intuitive puzzles you will be running around trying to figure out what you are even supposed to do. It takes forever. For one water level puzzle even when I found the right answer I was a bit miffed because I knew I had to go all the way to the top, then back down, then I could finish it. It was just annoying. And some puzzles are criminally easy but that speaks for itself. It's less like a puzzle game and more like a confusing mechanical obstacle course with a story I like because lovecraft. The story is ok but a bit basic. Thinking back on it, why and how did they get to another planet? Also, it's only some but not all since you have fish blood ancestry or whatever and the ship gets taken down by a giant sea monster so yeah. They make an offhand comment about the continent sinking also, but these are fish people wouldn't that be a good thing?

_childDocuments_.review: Love the 1940's-era vibe and overall aesthetic going on here but, honestly, this is a walking simulator with some puzzles thrown in. Far too much voice over exposition. Far too sluggish movement speed for such large-scale "puzzles" that require a lot of back-tracking, If the play areas were smaller I'd be more likely to troubleshoot the puzzles myself, but instead I resorted to a few YouTube walkthroughs just to bypass the monotony. The payoff at the end is decent, but doesn't quite reach the emotional highs that the game devs were clearly aiming for. Regrettably, I'd give this one a pass.

_childDocuments_.review: A good Cthulhu mythos-lite adventure. Light to medium level puzzles. Game is presently a little glitchy/wonky with the note-taking system, but good overall. Voice acting is very good but the voice direction is all over the place. For example, the main character will learn a thing at one point in the story then 10 minutes later in gameplay will say something like, "why is this happening?!" Huh? You just learned why! Other moments the main character will "figure out" a story element or acknowledge that something has happened that they have no way of knowing and it's very jarring to the immersion, which is why I play a game like this.For a game with very linear exploration and no puzzles to get lost in you would really hope for a more solid story. Still, I'd give it 7.5/10. Fun for a day but almost zero replay value.

I didn't honestly expect that. I'm also glad there was two ending choices. I would have loved to see more of that under-water city.4/5 Turtles
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't expect to be recommending this when I first started playing the game. Its prologue is clumsy, clunky, and contains some horribly inorganic exposition. The game also had this problem early on of just being... Slow and untrusting of its player; forcing you to look at the animations of machinery and the like.That all changes by the time you're investigating a jungle camp, though. After that point, the game improves dramatically. Far more exploration and opportunity for piecing together what happened in your own head. The story starts to show, rather than tell, and you quickly start to feel yourself immerse in the story.The big selling point is the atmosphere, which the game sells extremely well after it gets going. In this particular kind of story, all the bright colours and luscious greenery are a real change from the usual drab New England vibe, and it really reshapes the tone away from horror and dread into fascination.For twenty bucks, I recommend it. The first 15 minutes are a little bit of a slog, but the remaining 4.5 hours that follow are fantastic, so it's well worth your time for the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: A bit of a slow burn and the puzzles are a tad on the easy side but atmosphere and story are good enough to receive my recommendation though they're probably not for everyone. Some puzzles were a bit hard to understand (one i didn't understand even after looking at a guide) and there are some visual bugs,but I can forgive these issues since it is the first game made by this studio from what i can tell.Overall i would totally recommend this game, especially if you don't know about what happens in the ladder half of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely beautiful - it is vibrant and full of life.The story is fairly short, with 6 chapters and about 4-6 hours of game play. Whilst being short, the story is rich and narrative and does a fantastic job at painting the mysteries that you are trying to uncover.I found myself struggling to get into the game at the start, but this is honestly a characteristic of somebody like me with a short attention span. However, I was quickly captivated by the story and wanted to continue to the end to find out more about the expedition that you are tracking.Some of the puzzles are easy, and some are rather challenging. I admit, I took to google to find some hints and tips on a few of the puzzles but found good satisfaction when I was able to complete them. Whilst I am not a huge fan of puzzle games, this was thoroughly enjoyable and kept my mind stimulated and engaged.The only thing I can honestly complain about is how slow it feels to move around the environment. Whilst there is a "run" button, it does little to speed you up. I understand these kinds of games often have a slow walking pace, however it can remove some of the enjoyment out of the game when you are forced to constantly go back and forth between clues and areas at such a slow pace of movement. I will say that it was tolerable, perhaps only because of the beautiful graphics and enticing story. I certainly became attached to Norah and Harry.I would recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is a satisfying, thematic puzzle/exploration game that I can definitely recommend.Although the graphics at times feel simple, Call of the Sea conveys a sense of wonder and beauty through the visuals. They serve their purpose in supporting the story and add to the plot. A consistent visual theme is maintained which keeps the player grounded and conveys important information while helping subconsciously filter out background details. This really helps highlight the key details in puzzle and exploration sections of the game. The locales feature big setpieces to draw the player’s attention and really sell it as being larger than life. The audio is well done. The voice acting is good and the characters feel real, you can hear the emotion when the characters speak. The only complaint I have is that at times, especially near the beginning, a lot of exposition is conveyed through dialogue and it feels a tiny bit forced. The environmental audio helps keep the player in the moment and sell the setting.I can’t say much about the story or plot without spoiling it, since the entire game revolves heavily around it. It’s somewhat cliche but it’s well executed and tugs on some emotional strings. The story is compelling, interesting, and keeps the game moving forward. I enjoyed it and I think it’s got some potential as an allegory if you interpret it that way. The pacing is good and it kept me interested the whole way.Call of the Sea focuses on puzzles and exploration, which it does well. It starts fairly basic at the beginning and gets more complicated as you progress through the game. They're enjoyable and don't get so complicated that I was overwhelmed, but were pleasantly challenging. There were one or two instances where I felt slightly stuck and had to step back, recheck areas I had previously explored, or rethink a puzzle from a new angle, but for the majority of the game it flowed well and made me feel good about This game is a short one, my first playthrough took about 5 hours. The pacing felt good and it was satisfying to finish the game within a single evening. There are 34 achievements, 23 of which I was able to get on my first playthrough without hunting for them. There’s definitely room for multiple playthroughs to hunt for the rest of the achievements if that’s your vibe.Size on Disk - 11.84GB.Overall I really enjoyed Call of the Sea. It was short but sweet, it made me think but didn’t confuse me. Definitely worth the asking price ($22 CAD at time of writing).

_childDocuments_.review: I always found short, narrative-driven adventure games to be a really special niche, probably the most accessible genre if you plan on showing a non-gamer the degree of sophistication and merit  videogames can achieve, as an artistic medium.Just think about it. Portal, SOMA, Firewatch or Limbo are games that require absolute no prior experience with a controller, deliver strong storylines and end before they have a chance to overstay their welcome. Interactive novelettes, if you will, with puzzles sprinkled throughout. I’m delighted to add Call of the Sea to that list, perhaps the most lush and colorful work of art to ever be inspired by Lovecraftian literature. 	Norah Everhart never had it easy. A hereditary disease is slowly killing her, with her blotted hands, hardly a pleasant sight, forcing her to don gloves whenever she goes out in civilised society. Even that is the least of her concerns in her current predicament: freshly landed on an island where her “Dear Old Pal” Harry went missing, trying to find a cure for her illness. The expedition’s dwindling party left behind notes, clues and journal entries, and your time will be split between reconstructing the story of the missing explorers and solving Myst-type puzzles to unlock the island’s secrets.The sort of self-contained, brief but detailed experience that follows is something you’ve doubtlessly experienced before: an immersive walking simulator with a couple of eureka moments and engaging writing that is worth every penny. Like any good indie game, Call of the Sea makes the most out of minimalistic literary devices to stimulate the player’s imagination on multiple levels: Norah’s story is only the tip of the iceberg, and by the time you get to the credits you’ll have unveiled the ultimate fates of Roy, Frank, Cassandra, Teaharoa, Dr. DeWitt and Harry while understanding the origin of the island itself on tablets left behind by its original inhabitants, the Naacal. Everything ties in together, all the details matter and there’s a really good suspense curve - you only start figuring things out about halfway through the story, and the pacing of the revelations is spread out enough that you won’t need multiple playthroughs to understand everything. The mystery story aspect is interwoven with really streamlined exploration and walking sections (some of these sequences are absolutely breathtaking, their colorful underwater spectacle giving a bit of momentum to an otherwise fairly slow tempo) and the puzzles are simple, clever and varied enough to never become tedious or feel formulaic.While the space and freedom granted to you seem very limiting, exploring every nook and opening up Norah’s notebook to revisit old clues will become second nature as you have small epiphanies regarding the solution to your next big puzzle. Each of the six chapters has one big mechanic, and while some involve the sort of mechanical common sense you would apply when fixing an appliance at home, others lean on your ability to interpret abstract symbols and associate them with figures you see plastered on the walls. Considering there’s only about six big puzzles in total, it’s pretty impressive how elaborate some of them can get while maintaining a sort of simplicity and elegance you expect from well designed mind games. Furthermore, you need to interpret most of the clues yourself, as they are mostly just icons and sketches, and there’s very little actual instruction attached. In fact, one of the game’s strongest design decisions was to not provide a lot of handholding. You will always have all the tools required to understand what is required of you without it being spelled outright - make sure you explore every clue left behind and check your journal and you should never get stuck more than a few minutes on any puzzle. There is no way to die or reach an unsolvable state: you can relax, explore and take everything in at your own pace.I would recommend this game to anyone who wants to see a hopeful, lighter shade of Lovecraftian storytelling with accessible puzzles and great tempo, knowing that it’s a single-serving experience (most of the collectibles are in your way, anyway) that will end in less than four hours. That said, they will be some of the better and more memorable four hours you can choose to spend on an interactive story.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game very fundamentally misses what I feel are really important aspects of this genre. The core of this genre is usually giving players narrative intrigue that drives the clue gathering, which inform one's ability to solve puzzles, and then find more narrative leads. These then become a self-reinforcing loop of discovery. This game isn't one of those.Let's start with the storytelling. The clues dropped by the other characters are not particularly interesting, they very obviously lay out the story and then on top of that, your character monologues over each and every one. She essentially repeats what the thing just said with extra explanations that are so un-subtle it feels like the author constantly whispering in your ear.Imagine if you came across a note that said 'I'm going to have some toast', and then your character says 'Huh, he was going to have some toast, seems like he was hungry'. Imagine that, but for basically every item pickup, for hours. I felt like I was never really able to think or feel about the story on my own, I was always being told *precisely* what's going on. It was also incredibly annoying.The puzzles rarely make the world feel like a real world because they're not attached to the game world in any meaningful way. They're mostly very arbitrary and combined with the journal system, it fits you in a passive groove where you're sliding around objects until the pages are full of notes. Once the pages are full, you have all the instructions you need to 'solve' the puzzle, almost no thinking required. And then you proceed to the next area where you do the exact same thing but just a little more complicated.Together, these elements result is a game where I'm on autopilot. The game doesn't want me or need me to contemplate, examine or feel for myself about anything, it's a series of straightforward visuals, interactions and dialogue pieces that wash over me.This game is so fundamentally lacking in subtlety and cohesion that even if you wanted to say, turn off the character's dialogue (I tried because of how annoying it was), the world-building is so lacking that you can't make it through or understand certain things without her voice chaperoning you the whole time. The puzzles are so arbitrary and disconnected from the world, you *need* the journal system to be your instruction manual for opening the doors.I played through the whole thing and I felt like at no moment was my own curiosity actually rewarded. That's a really big failure for an adventure game.This game was also a fundamentally tiring and annoying experience. I really don't want to have to say that about a game, especially one that clearly looks like it's had a good amount effort put into it, but nice graphics do not make a good game and it completely misses what makes this genre compelling. I'm actually kind of shocked by how much it misses.
