Personally, I didn't have to put much thought into any of them and my 7 or so hours of play should be pretty much what to expect out of this game if you don't look at hints (and you shouldn't need any).I recommend it...the puzzles are simple and don't present anything that hasn't been seen in other puzzle games, but the game does carry itself well.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: The production value is extremely high and the story has some nice twists that keeps it fresh. The puzzles seem very cryptic at first, but with enough exploration they become approachable and do not lack internal logic. The walking parts can become tedious especially around chapter 3 where the levels get bigger, but the amazing graphics make it bearable. I recommend this game to any Myst fans and people with a soft spot for British colonialism.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Right up front, this game is slow. It's more of a walking simulator with puzzles. The puzzles themselves aren't especially difficult (with one possible exception), and you have a journal that autofills with every clue you need to solve them. But, the atmosphere is great, and it's a very pleasant 5-6 hour hike.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent, Lovecraftian take on a semi-serious medical issue that simply doesn't get the representation it deserves: pathological feminine odor. You play as Norah Everhart, a beautiful and charming victim suffering from the aforementioned condition. Your husband sails across the ocean to the other side of the planet in a desperate attempt to find a potential cure in exotic lands, and likely also to escape said odor. When communication with your husband stops, you then set out across the ocean yourself in order to find the love of your life who has been there with you through thick and thin, through fresh and not-so-fresh. You soon find, as your husband also did, that your vaj isn't the only overwhelmingly fishy thing of interest wandering the seas. And in fact, you just may find that what seemed to be nothing more than a bit of stink in your pink is actually a remnant of an ancient, extraordinary bloodline that flows through veins and out your beaver. The "Call of the Sea", indeed. 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is very much like old-school point-and-click adventure games, except from first-person perspective in full 3D world. Some might call it a walking simulator with puzzles, but it has a certain nostalgic charm to it. The art and sound design as well as voice acting is very good, and manages to get you invested in the characters and the story. I bought it from Steam Summer sale, and it was well worth the price of a movie ticket.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: It was fine. Not amazing but also not terrible. The visuals were decent, the story was ok, the puzzles were mostly ok. My complaints are that the story pacing can be quite slow. Also, some of the puzzles were tedious due to the walking speed (you walk really slowly!) to the point that I ended up using guides a little bit to finish the game because I could not be bothered waiting out the time to walk back and forth to solve puzzles (Specifically chapter 5 water level puzzle) . Without the guides I would have quit and watched it on youtube to get the story closure. So all in all, perhaps I just wasn't in the right mood or it wasn't for me. I only recommend this game if you really like slow story and slow walking sims.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just what I needed: a nice change of pace and stress relief. You follow the experience of protagonist Norah who is trying to find her missing husband and begins to see that there was more to his expedition than anticipated. The puzzles were fun, the art was beautiful, and the story was interesting. Having no background knowledge coming into this game worked well because some of the themes were pleasantly unexpected.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Puzzles fine, quite logical and straightforward for the most part, just my level of slightly tricky but nothing to get stuck by for too long, if you ever get stuck you've either overlooked something or haven't gathered the notebook clues yet (two sides of the same coin I guess).Great visuals, highly enjoy the vibrancy of the game, leaving the horror elements to the mind and the story itself. And since the story elements and acting really wasn't all that scary, it was really just a chill game, perfect for someone like me that don't like horror games anyways.Walking speed could do with some finetuning, I get that they don't want you to lose immersion by going too fast, but it's a videogame and 2-3 of the puzzles are literally just walking quite far distances back and forth to solve it, it' completely wasted downtime that adds nothing to the game.Now then, main gripe is that the voice acting and storytelling of the game is quite... bad. The emotions of the character is expressed 80% through words and words only, the actual voice acting reflects no emotions whatsover most of the time, she will remain cheery and unaffected by both the terrors of the world and the unfolding story. You know how RPGs have this absurdity where you might just have experienced a story piece where the character is torn to pieces and just lost the love of their life or whatever? Yeah and then immediately follow it up by interacting with an NPC and cracking a jolly good joke like life is just sunshines and butterflies? It's basically that, there is no consistency, there is no development in the emotional state of the character.It doesn't help that narration is easily cut off, in the speaker section of the game I had the character interrupt themselves 2 times in a row. First interruption was simply from just deciding to walk the moment I could walk after "waking up" from the cutscene, like just, playing the game. The second interruption happened just because I KEPT WALKING. They seriously need to queue their voice triggers, play out the sequence before starting anew. This also happened after having triggered a flashing cutscene with the black bowls, my characters reaction to that was abruptly cut off because of a reaction to some markings. Simply losing the story because you do not stand perfectly still and let the game just narrate like an audio book, not what I call a good design.The story itself was... whatever to me, didn't feel like it really said much of anything.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: It's alright. It's a slow walking simulator with puzzles.Graphics are nice for the most part, story is frankly forgettable, but whatever.My biggest complaint is just how slow the game is. The movement speed is slow and doesn't feel that good. There are several spots where you can get stuck, unable to walk up a tiny ledge. Mouse look is insanely smoothed out for no good reason.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: There are high-quality games out there, where both design and story and also the visual and audio aspects fit together and work like the mechanism of a swiss watch.Then there are video game studios full of good, professional and creative people.When you have both, you get a team like Out of the Blue with a game like Call of the Sea.A must have if you enjoy puzzle games and adventure stories with a Lovecraft twist in the recipe!
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the game's story, and the puzzles. The story has you following in the footsteps of your missing husband; your husband led an expedition to an uncharted island, hoping to find a cure for your mysterious affliction, and has gone missing. As you play you'll work to uncover the answer to three questions: what befell your husband's expedition, what is the cause of your illness, and what is the true nature of the island? These threads come together in a satisfying way, and I was interested in the story throughout my whole playthrough.I thought the puzzles in the game were well crafted, and varied. They're difficult enough to make you feel clever once the answer "clicks", but not so difficult that they feel obtuse. I was able to complete all puzzles without a guide, although some did take a few tries before I found the right solution -- I thought the difficulty was balanced, feeling rewarding but not frustrating. The variety of puzzles was also welcome: you'll encounter puzzles that deal with sound, the actual physical orientation of the game space, and logic puzzles.  The story and gameplay are both tied together by some fantastic art and setpieces. I loved the look of the island, and the locales you'll visit in the story are varied and stunning. The game is on the shorter side (I finished the game in just under 4.5 hours), but I don't think this is necessarily a bad thing. I had fun with the time the game took, and thought the experience was well worth the price of admission.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: A stunningly beautiful game with well-designed puzzles There's perhaps a slight overreliance on the classic adventure game trope of "Get the ancient machinery to work", but I didn't ever find myself stuck for long.Call of the Sea's plot has a lot in common with Amnesia: Rebirth, though lacks most of the horror element that defines the Amnesia series. As in Rebirth, you play a woman who is searching for her missing husband amongst supernatural goings on.I only ran across one bug, though it was an annoying one. Later in the game there are interfaces for changing water flow, but backing out of these interfaces seems to cause them to disappear, preventing progress of the game and forcing a reload. Fortunately I didn't lose any progress, but the potential is there.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: I'd only recommend this game if you enjoy spatial/mechanical puzzles, because that's the only kind you'll find here - no logical deductions, no solving of mysteries, just moving/rotating elements of the world to align with patterns and inscriptions. The landscape is very pretty and the story is genuinely intriguing, but I found most of the puzzles tedious. The constant expository comments also took me out of the experience somewhat (at one point Norah actually says 'exposition' instead of 'expedition' - Freudian slip?). The gameplay is a bit clunky (long walking distances, awkward ladder climbing, cursor blending into surroundings, lack of clarity in what you're meant to achieve). If you're super into Lovecraft and rotating objects in your mind, go for it, otherwise I'm not convinced this game's strengths are enough to compete with its weaknesses.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- GraphicsCons:- Puzzles weren't really engaging. I particularly didn't like one in chapter 4.- Story wasn't great. Narration from the protagonist was necessary for me to understand what was going on at the end - ideally it would have been obvious from the in-game events. I didn't find the plot/central mystery interesting (subjective).- Abysmally slow walking speed.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: The story was kinda . Norah was slow to control, even when sprinting. Multiple times did the game not register clues and not write them down in the journal. To fix that I had to follow online guides. Some of the puzzles didnt make much sense. Multiple times the game crashed because it got stuck on a ladder or geometry on the ground.  Multiple times I had lighting issues and I couldnt see anything I was supposed to. The game is very pretty but it certainly has issues.If I were to rate the game out of 10, it would be a 3.5 . Cool idea but very poor execution. This game would greatly benefit from better controls, better puzzles, and faster animations.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Two of my favorite games are Myst and Riven. This is the first game to really capture that sense of wonder and exploration that I loved about those two. You can see the love that went into it. The scenes were stunning and the story was touching. The puzzles were a good range of difficulty, and most made sense within the plot and environment. There was one in particular that I had to look up because the clues weren't well laid out. But the rest were fun to solve.Overall, I enjoyed thinking and discovering my way through this charming game.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: What a treasure of a game. Call of the Sea is a first person adventure game, set in the 1930s. It's beautifully vibrant, with a solid story, decent voice acting and overall a great feel and atmosphere to it. Riddles and puzzles aren't weird or, hehe, out of the blue, plus the game has sort of a hint system that I just love. Normally when playing adventure or point&click games I make notes on paper so that I don't have to keep going back and forth. Here, Nora, our heroine, does the work for us in her journal. Simply grand.Music is there, it's nice, doesn't come to the foreground too often, but is a pleasure to listen to. So is voice-acting, though 90% of it is Nora speaking.Game is absolutely beautiful, with vibrant colours and fairytale like graphics. 10/10, would set screenshots as wallpaper.The only bad thing? Game is too short, I wish we had few extra hours on the island.And, risking some SPOILERS here, I gotta say, the best part of the game for me was the fact that it's a Call of Cthulhu game for scaredycats like me. Thank you.Positives (+):+ beautiful graphics+ solid story+ decent voice acting and music+ so many pretty colours....+ good puzzles and the journal mechanic, absolutely LOVE ITNegatives (-):- kinda short- there doesn't seem to be a chance for a sequel
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: This game gave sort of mixed feelings. I totally liked the visuals, atmosphere and sound design. But the puzzle were too hard and obscure. There are puzzles which had big areas and needed constant trekking up and down. And doing those with how slow the character moves even while running and slow ladder climbing animations is the only thing I hated in the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: This game seems to have gorgeous artwork, but I had to stop playing after about ten minutes, because I got to be badly motion sick. You control the direction you look with your mouse, and rotate as you wish with it. That makes it very wobbly, and for people who get easily car sick and need Dramamine as soon as they travel, I don't recommend it. Which is a bummer. I wish I had know before buying it...
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: call of the sea is a short and sweet walking simulator with some puzzle aspects. the puzzles can be a bit tricky to figure out, but won't cause you too much trouble. the story is fantastic and worth going through, though the final act is a bit underwhelming after the strong setup.definitely check this game out if you're into the walking simulator genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not scary nor complicated in puzzles but tell a good story. I'd not say this game is classic Lovecraft style story but rather a suspense story involved elements from Lovecraft.I spent three nights slowly completed the game and discovered every corner I could go. There weren't lot of things being hidden beside the information you need for solving puzzles, however, I did enjoy how they construct the scenes and their art style.I'd say the story itself worth playing, buying it during the sale should be great for any people who like short puzzle game.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Its a puzzle walking simulator basically. The puzzles are pretty easy, the visuals are colourful and lovely, I did encounter one glitch that required a restart but was only an annoyance, but the story line is pretty weak. Subtle is not a word to describe the main character. Nothing is left ambiguous. Every little thing you see or touch she will explain in unnecessary levels of detail, leaving nothing to the imagination. Because of that, everything becomes very predictable. If you don't mind that, then theres some fun to be had solving the puzzles and just wandering around the beautiful setting.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Having solved all the puzzles and worked through the mysteries of Call of the Sea, I'm left satisfied. This fairly linear game, set vaguely in the world of HP Lovecraft's Cthulu, is beautifully made and full of reasonably challenging puzzles required to progress. Most puzzles involve translating symbols or replicating spacial patterns. I also enjoyed slowly uncovering the mystery of the protagonist's husband, left in clues scattered throughout the environment. It was a fun little experience, which took about eight hours of play to leisurely complete.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics 10/10Music 10/10Voice acting 10/10Story 8/10What a gem of a game. Fully immersive and captivating, I highly recommend.The scenery and music within the game is phenominal.You play first person, as Norah, who is searching for her husband on an island in the middle of the ocean.Traversing through lush greenery, beautiful caves and underwaterscapes, there are plenty of places to explore and find hidden notes and items to help you with your quest.With an easy to follow notebook that jots down pretty much every clue and image you come across, provides helpful and useful reference material when trying to solve the many puzzles that you encounter.I found that the story could have been elaborated a little more and felt like there was something missing, however, was still entertaining and should not put you off playing the game. With a couple of pretty well to do voice actors on the cast, I was extremely impressed with the full voiced script.  The music and ambience is wonderful and fits perfectly with each scenario. Finally, the graphics are out of this world. So realistic and pretty to look at no matter which direction you're facing. There is no expense spared. Even in the corners of the map, where no one would really look, the attention to detail in the foliage, buildings, caverns etc is phenominal.Definitely would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Some of the puzzles are a liiiiittle difficult to get into, and finding all the possible journal entries isn't a trivial task, but the game is very fun and mostly enjoyable with some very minor frustrations should you get stuck.  The music is gorgeous, and the ending is very satisfying.  Beautiful artwork, too.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: A fresh take on Lovecraft's mythos. As someone in it for the story more than the puzzles I personally enjoyed the level of difficulty they present, but someone who plays games like this for the brain challenge might find it lacking. Story and voiceacting is great though, even if the game feels a bit short.Also, wiggle that taint.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the aesthetics, both the art style and the sound design. The puzzles could be finicky and even if you had the right idea, you might not be able to complete them if you hadn't uncovered the correct story pieces beforehand.  But the puzzles were just the right amount of challenging so far as I was concerned, and the story was lovely. I would have preferred that it were longer and had gone into more about what happened to the non-human componentry of the story (trying not to spoiler), but really enjoyed it overall
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Mesmerisingly beautiful game and the artwork/style is superb.  For me at least, a perfect blend of some of my favourite games over the years which takes me back to good places - The Witness, Broken Sword and I get Black Flag vibes.  Minimal in-game interactions, however the story and journey is enough to keep you engaged throughout. Music is wonderful and the dialogue/voiceovers aren't excessively long. Excellent game and would happily replay the game again and again.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: What a fun game! Before I purchased it, based on the reviews, I assumed it would be a walking sim with simple puzzles. While part of it is that, it turned into so much more! The puzzles got more difficult and creative. The story went off the chain branching from an early 20th century mystery into a Cthulhu-themed quest! I highly recommend it for anyone who is interested in a good story and mild to moderately interested in difficult puzzles. Bonus if you are a Lovecraft fan.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Cthulhu fiction that I enjoy actually. Lovely art direction and.. basaltic technology. Was running really well, glad that it runs on Unreal.Liked the story and the protagonist. The puzzles were interesting.Would like devs to make Verne-inspired game, but I am looking forward into American Arcadia. o/
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: This was a truly visually stunning game that continuously blew me away with the sheer scope and size and beauty of it's environments.  The puzzles were a bit of a mix; some were a fun, hearty challenge, while others were somewhat illogical or just difficult and time consuming for what I assume what the sake of adding to the length of play.  My only real complaint would be that the ending(s) were so so sad that I actually cried.  Even so, I would highly recommend this game.  It is quite easy to control and play through, yet pleasantly complex in its story and worlds.  Easily 4.5/5.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable game, pretty to watch and the puzzles are fun. Rarely did I feel the need to use a guide and only got lost in one area (more so because I missed an intractable item). Did get it on sale, but still enjoyable to buy if ya want a good scenic puzzle game. Oh, and the story is pretty decent too.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game play. Sometimes the puzzles are either a bit obtuse or so obvious that it makes you think you can't possibly be doing it right. Game is visually beautiful and the endings are heartwarming but also bittersweet. The puzzles in this game did have somewhat of a Nancy Drew vibe for those looking for a game to play with a similar vibe.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: This was a really fun game. Good audio and soundtrack, and although the visuals were clipping a bit at certain areas the overall look of the game was very aesthetically pleasing. The story is intriguing, the atmosphere in this game is on point and the puzzles get trickier as the game progresses. I would recommend this game to anyone who likes story-driven puzzle games, as this is easily one of my favourites in that category.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: I love puzzle games and I got this game in a humble bundle. The trailer video enticed me into playing this game, and I am glad I did. The story was really enjoyable and I didn't know what to expect to be honest. A heads up, there is a lot of walking between finding clues for you journal notes and logs, and puzzles in each chapter. However, this wasn't a deterrent for me, I do wish you could walk a little faster, but that's just me. This game is Lovecraft inspired for sure, and my friend who was watching me play, made comments about this. It was a little suspenseful, and for some reason I kept expecting something to pop out and scare me, even though this is not a horror game lol. Overall, really enjoyable! The story drew me in, and I almost finished playing it in one sitting. However, I did end up going back at the end to get those last achievements ;) Don't forget to save! I did and it was a bit more puzzling to repeat to finish certain achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game. I didn't know PC games could be so fun and it ruined my sleep schedule. I was desperate to finish and had so much fun pushing myself to uncover each clue.  Make sure to play with a mouse and to adjust your settings first bc the experience got even better after that. I was so amazed at the detail that went into this game and how it made me feel like I was on the exotic adventure of a lifetime. I literally told my partner I was mad that I had finished it so fast and that I wished I could erase my memory and do it all over again. Now I struggle to find a game that will ever match this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: I was in the mood for this one and it didn't disappoint.The 20's/30's setting was unique for me and the voice actor did a sterling job.On one level it's a perfunctory walking sim with the requisite puzzles and exploration.  On another level it's a joy to explore this mysterious island, picking over the remnants of a failed expedition and finding your own path past it.Sure, it gets a little bizarre and a couple of the puzzles needed looking up, but the game as a whole was satisfying and the itch was scratched.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is an outlandishly pretty adventure. It captures the classic tropes of pulp adventure in exotic locales without falling into the trap of racist depictions of indigenous people so common to the genre. And it tells a pretty wild story, if a bit overnarrated.The puzzles, though, leave something to be desired. They can get pretty obtuse, and that makes a nasty combination with the large expanses the game sometimes expects you to trudge back and forth across. You'll be doing a lot of trial-and-error trying to figure out what individual puzzle elements do, and the time running between them adds up. There's also a fair amount of puzzles that challenge your spatial relationships or require setting a bunch of toggles correctly -- the kinds of things that will be easy for some and an utter roadblock for others.  At least the protagonist, Norah, is extremely thorough in taking notes and making diagrams of all the visual elements you'll need.Overall, if it's puzzle quality that draws you to point-and-click adventures, take or leave Call of the Sea. But it's a neat enough story and a screenshotter's dream with all its beautiful scenes.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished my first play through. I honestly don't know what to say. Yes it is short, but it is very much worth it in every way that you can think of it. You like puzzle games? This game has some of the best puzzles I have ever seen. You like "Walking Simulators" that focus on an interesting story? This games story is brilliantly written. You like Cthulhu / HP Lovecraft style mystery? This game is just that mixed with just the right amount of Adventure to keep you guessing at time. This is one of the most beautiful, best acted games I have ever played and my top 1 for this year all ready. I recommend it to everyone. This is a MUST-PLAY with a story that will make you feel amazing at times, but it hits very, very hard in the end if you let it get close to you.I am going to replay this and probably 100% it. It really is THAT good!Edit: I did it.... it was worth o so very much! If you play this (which you should!) do verything you can!This is a story that everyone can relate to on a personal level and the choice at the end feels like a gut punch either way. Really go job and I can't wait to see what you guys do next....Or should I say: "What was that? A vision to another world..... or a vision of the future?"
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is a mixed bag, but for me its good qualities didn't make up for its weaknesses.Pros:*   The scenery is vibrant and distinctive; a joy to look at.*   The overall arc is interesting, and if it were told well, I'd be into it.* As first-person environmental-exploration games go, this one is pretty good for blind people.Cons:*   They're crafted competently enough, and may hold a novice's attention, but veterans with games like Riven and The Witness under their belts will be snoozing.*   It can't decide how dark it wants to be (I wish it had gone darker).  The pacing is uneven, with stakes being raised erratically.  This second point may be a consequence of the first -- a result of a rushed or incomplete major edit to change the tone, perhaps?*   It's presented as your character's (Nora's) inner monologue (or else she talks to herself constantly), and Nora makes three main types of comments.  The first are comments about her husband (the search for whom is the game's driving force), giving you a sense of what their relationship is like.  These are fine.  The second are observations about the puzzle elements you find in the environment.  These (along with the in-game journal) serve as an aid (I'd say a crutch) to help you avoid missing anything important.  Telling you exactly what's significant removes part of the challenge, unfortunately.  The third category are idle remarks about the environment, of the "My, what a beautiful sunset!" variety.  The purpose of these, I can only suppose, is to let you know what you should be thinking if the environment artists have done their jobs.  The thing is, they  done their jobs.  You can see the sunset, and it  beautiful.  Hearing it said out loud destroys the immersion.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: A gorgeous to look at, gentle and gently paced puzzle game. Despite the 'otherworldly' storyline in there, this is _not_ a scary game. It's also not an action game, and all puzzles (except for 1) are without time pressure, because there is nothing lurking behind you to eat you or anything. I really enjoyed it. It took me about 9 hours to play through it entirely, and I would consider myself neither excessively fast or extremely slow. I might go back and start achievement hunting for a bit, because it's pretty enough that I wouldn't mind spending a bit more time with it :) Are there downsides? Of course. First of all, as other players mention in reviews: there is very much a reason the 'motion sickness' post is pinned in the Discussions forum here on Steam. I, too, had some serious issues with that when I started playing on standard settings. In my case, following the recommended course of action of switching off head bobbing and smooth movement in the Graphics menu really helped. After that, I had no issues with motion sickness anymore. Secondly, some of the puzzles are so straightforward, I missed the solution because I thought 'it couldn't possibly be that linear', and then I completely flubbed others because they seemed to me needlessly complicated. Though, to be fair, about halfway the game I got the hang of how the game wanted me to think, which made it easier. Thirdly, it's pretty slow sometimes, especially when you can _see_ the solution to a puzzle but you still need to run around picking up all the little elements you need.Did any of these downsides really detract from the game? Well, the motion sickness obviously, but I solved that. The 'over/underthinking the puzzles', well, that's probably a me-problem. The slow gameplay - yeah, that can be a bit of an annoyance. Then again, forewarned is forearmed, so now you know and can adjust your mindset accordingly: just take it easy and enjoy the view ;-)
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: If I had to describe this game I would call it a story/puzzle based walking simulator. As you can tell from the screenshots, the art style is great, and all the locations are beautiful, the game is a pleasure to look at. The game has puzzle elements, but don't expect a challenge where puzzles are the core of the gameplay. To me, it felt like the puzzles were there simply to enhance the exploration, as all of the puzzle solutions can be easily found by simply navigating the area. The story and characters were pretty good, enough to keep me engaged, but the story isn't one that will stick with me for long. The game is also fairly short, and can be beaten in 1 or 2 sittings. I alt-tabbed a bit during my playthrough, so it's definitely beatable in under 5 hours, even if you fully explore each area. If you're rushing, you can probably beat this in 3-4 hours. I would ultimately recommend this game if you like the art style and the screenshots make you feel like this is a world you'd like to spend a couple hours in. However, due to the length, I would feel better if I paid 10-15 dollars for this game instead of 20. 7/10 overall for me
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: PC owners beware. Like many others (see discussion thread, `Tips for playing on PC', I've had increasing problems with disappearing or non-functioning hotspots. Due to this I've abandoned the game near the end of chapter 2. Unfortunately Steam tell me I'm not eligible for a refund because I've exceed the game time limit - ironically, due to repeated failed attempts to solve puzzles that involve the said malfunctioning hotspots. Because of this I can't possibly recommend the game to PC owners (nb I have Windows 10, 64 bit). Even without this problem I found the game a little disappointing due to the fairly simple puzzles. It's great if you want lush visuals and nothing too taxing in the gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not even certain I will be able to sufficiently put into words what makes this game special. Part of me fears that my words would echo and sound empty. I will simply say that Call of the Sea has a lot that makes it an excellent game, that I am shocked more people aren't talking about the game, and that once you have played through the game, and *know* what awaits, then there is no more after the end.A magnificent art style with equally magnificent animations that bring the world to life. An excellent plot that has twists and turns (oh my god, the twists and turns!), thrills and intrigue. Superb puzzles that are hard enough to give you that oh so good dopamine drip, and yet they are designed in such a way that they respect your time and effort (save maybe one that involves timing). And the tugging of your emotions and heart strings, for not only Norah and Harry but nearly every member of Harry's expedition.I love this game so much. It can't usurp Outer Wilds for my #1 game of all time. I don't know if any game ever will. But for me personally Call of the Sea is up there alongside Chrono Trigger and a growing number of other masterclass games that hit you in the feels without restraint. Buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I am quite torn between giving the game a recommendation or not, but in the end, I do believe that its merits outweigh its flaws, albeit by a slim margin.  Not exactly a glowing recommendation, to be sure, but I hope to explain why.For most of the game, its strengths carry it forward.  First off, you'll note that the game is stunningly beautiful.  The art direction is absolutely top-notch and players will find themselves traversing beautiful and haunting vistas all across the un-named island as Norah Everhart on a quest to find her missing husband.  I once posited years ago that we are at the point where art direction is arguably more a stylistic choice these days rather than a technical one and this game definitely argues in favor of that.  The team also made sure to bring on top-notch talent like Cissy Jones and Yuri Lowenthal to breathe life into the handful of characters that make up the cast.  The result is that the game often feels like the epic it sets out to be, albeit with the help of a few invisible walls, taking you through a fascinating (YMMV) narrative that is part pulp adventure, part mystery, and a little bit of Lovecraft for good measure.It goes without saying that the game is focused on its narrative (perhaps invasively so as Norah just won't shut up) and ensuring you get through it, so its main mechanism of solving puzzles to proceed is more often logical within the narrative (e.g. stuff mostly makes sense in the game world) as opposed to completely obtuse challenges for diehard puzzlers (e.g. Myst).  The result is that the puzzles can be challenging at times, but I was able to complete the game without consulting any guides at all and I'm the first to go to one if someone wants me to solve un-fun math puzzles, so none of that crap here.  Moreover, something I enjoyed - but others may chafe at - is that Norah will document all discovered clues into her journal so you don't have to take your own notes.  As you explore locations, anything that might be useful will be collected, in detail, in her nifty book to be consulted at any time with a single button.  At times this can make solving puzzles or figuring out what to do a bit too easy as you'll never question if something is valuable or not, but for some puzzles it's a godsend, especially when you would have to backtrack great distances otherwise or meticulously draw diagrams yourself.Speaking of backtracking, one of the things that really pads out the game length is Norah's walking speed.  Narratively, there's a good reason for why she walks so slowly, but we are playing a  here and I think most players would appreciate some way of adjusting this.  This goes for  of these kinds of games, you hear me?  Let's just stop with this trash.  At no point did I ever let go of my shift key to stop the minor speed boost and I can't imagine that none of the testers didn't mention this.  I can't imagine anyone playing this ever let go of their shift key, either.  You're slow enough as it is while "sprinting", let alone turtling  normally around wide-open areas and it gets worse towards the end of the game where you spend more time traversing the environment than solving the next puzzle.  And you want me to go find secrets??  Eat balls.  YOU go find secrets.How you go about most of this game, whether you're discovering secrets or clues or puzzle mechanisms, is  by wandering around and touching hotspots like a good old-fashioned point-n-click adventure.  Anything that requires your attention will have a floaty dot that manifests when you get close enough, and morphs into the appropriate contextual action when you get even closer.  It's not difficult in any sense of the word, but because of the aforementioned pace of the character, it can be a slog if you're just looking for that last bit of information to move forward or worse yet, if you really  want to find those secrets (which are little more than out-of-the-way items like notes or pictures that you click on to pop cheevos).  Otherwise, you're solving puzzles and while they run the gamut from, "Really, that's it?  That's not even a puzzle!" to "Holy hell, what am I doing wrong?!" most of them make logical sense once you suss out what logic they're following.  At first, a lot of these are engaging and pique your interest, following the loop of wander around, get the clues, figure out how to apply the clues, profit.  Some are localized to one spot and some require the use of the entire environment.  It's great... until the latter half of the game when the puzzles mostly solve themselves or require you to simply brute force them because they're no longer following a logic and are just following some random timing stuff.  Oh, and have I mentioned that the latter half is also where you're doing a whole lot of nothing, but moving slowly forward?  Yeah, there's that, too.So it's with all this in mind that this is a cautious "recommend."  If you're in the mood for a gorgeous, combat-free puzzle game with a great narrative hook to tickle your adventure and sleuthing skills, you'll find what you're looking for mostly in the first half or two-thirds of the game.  It's great at making you feel like a puzzle master even though most of the puzzles aren't all that difficult if you give them some time, and the journey is quite good... up until it isn't.  You have to be prepared for not quite a full collapse, but more a loss of wind in the game's sails as it gets into this third act, so to speak.  It stops feeling like an exciting adventure and more like chore you push through to get to its mostly-satisfying endings (don't worry, you can save scum and see them both without spending hours retreading covered ground).  Oh let's again mention the obvious padding that is the character's walking speed... I can't complain about that enough, really.  Devs need to stop that or at least make it adjustable like aim sensitivity ought to be.  At the very least, give me an "always run" toggle!  This isn't multiplayer competition and video game narratives are never so sacred as to require wasting your time by making you move slow...  I digress.   has a lot of good going for it, so if the negatives don't seem like showstoppers for you - and for the record, they weren't for me - go on and give it a shot.  You might really enjoy yourself and get immersed in the adventure because it's about that more than it's about anything else.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best puzzle games I've ever played. The puzzles are complex enough that you do have to use your brain, but they're never so obscure that you can't trust that you'll eventually figure it out with enough trying. I also appreciate that knowing the solution to a puzzle is always enough to execute that solution- there's never a time when you could get stuck knowing the solution but being unable to, say, make a tricky jump in time. My only complaint is that the game asks a lot from your working memory. It's nice enough to provide a journal that notes all the clues you pick up as you get them, but any time the journal is open, it takes up your whole screen, so you can't quickly glance between it and what you're working on. If it was possible to slide the journal over so that one page of it took up half the screen while you could see your surroundings with the other half of the screen, that would be nice. I ended up just taking pictures of some clues with my phone.

_childDocuments_.review: In this day and age, it often takes a diamond in the rough to out-shine the production value of triple-a development titles. But Spain based developer Out of the Blue has managed to do just that.Their flagship game Call of the Sea is a beautiful example of executing a vision to near perfection, while also focusing on quality rather than quantity. Call of the Sea is a first person adventure/puzzle game where you travel to a gorgeous island off the coast of Tahiti in a bid to find your missing husband. In order to find him however you — playing as the mild mannered art professor Norah Everhart — must progress through the numerous puzzles left behind in the wake of an ancient civilization. All the while uncovering the truth of Norah’s mysterious disease that has plagued generations of her family.Firstly the plot is backed up by the game's distinct visual style.The visuals of the island you are exploring are exceedingly beautiful and well made. As well as saturated colors of the foliage and cel shaded details in the multiple murals and wall reliefs you come across are eye catching. Each water area that you traverse is packed to the brim with bright primary coloured coral and statues that evoke a sense of curiosity when you examine them. This feeling of curiosity is pervasive through the game from start to finish. Which is fitting as the visuals are a backdrop to the multiple puzzles you are presented with throughout. The puzzles are the main mechanical draw of Call of the Sea, clearly taking inspiration from fellow island based puzzle game — 1993’s Myst. On the whole they are relatively simple logic based puzzles that generally revolve around observing the virtual world around you. These puzzles were never incredibly challenging, in fact the puzzles are all rather easy — I only got hung up on one late game puzzle myself. However, these puzzles benefit from being easy, never was I increasingly frustrated to the point of wanting to put the game down. Plus the frequency of how many puzzles that I encountered gave me enough satisfaction to keep going on to the next one.Rather than a grueling mental struggle, this game was more akin to a refreshing mental workout. Puzzles often came down to a sort of meditative formula: Find visual clues in the world, read notes for contextual solutions and use logic to finish the puzzle. I often felt like I was partaking in an escape the room flash game. Additionally  just like an early 2000s flash game, Norah’s dialogue, voiced by Cissy Jones of Darksiders III fame, is to the point of hilarity all external. For example, at the very beginning of the game Norah explains ad nauseum the entire contextual basis for why the events of the game are in motion. As if she were cast in a Shakespearean play and monologuing to the crowd. Thankfully this is the only time such a monologue feels out of place and disjointed, so it is quickly forgotten. The rest of the game is beautifully narrated, with some interjections by Norah’s husband Harry played by veteran voice actor Yuri Lowenthal.The real draw of the game however is not its stunning world, or its numerous puzzles, but instead it’s story. On the surface it is a simple MacGuffin story, explore and traverse the island and its secrets, find your husband and perhaps even the cure to your illness along the way. The story is presented to you through many different documents, items, and murals. With these you are constantly making connections between locations, objects, sounds and symbols. With your trusty journal by your side that is written and illustrated by Norah, it is always interesting to read as it feels sometimes that she might have figured out some solutions before you had. But beneath the surface of the contextual clues and puzzling contraptions is a story hiding so much more. The themes of this game are steeped in a kind of Lovecraftian mysticism. Instead of invoking the endless and ceaseless horrors of H.P. Lovecraft’s work — Call of the Sea instead would rather use Lovecraft’s mythos as a lens to view ideas of personal growth, love, wonder and acceptance. The inherent unknown present in eldritch horror is related to the unknown of slowly discovering who you truly are, an experience that can be exciting and terrifying at the same time. Call of the Sea strikes this emotional balance between fear and excitement incredibly well. Often  I was so enraptured in the joy of discovery that I at times forgot about the main objective of the game itself. I always felt compelled to explore what the next area had to offer and inspect its many items along the way. It was truly a wonderful experience from beginning to end. All in all, as a flagship game goes this is a brilliant opener for Out of the Blue. Their vision was executed masterfully for a new independent studio and that truly shines through in every facet of the game. I would recommend this for anyone who is a fan of puzzles, and short story games as it is a masterful example of those genres. Do not let this diamond fall through the cracks, as it is one of the brightest that 2020 has to offer.Final Thoughts:- Beautifully crafted world to explore- Puzzles that will keep you engaged throughout- Great voice acting that never overstays its welcome- Numerous secrets and easter eggs to find- Genuinely touching story interwoven with Lovecraftian themes

_childDocuments_.review: This game does not really qualify as a "game". It is mostly a linear story, with long cuts (you basically have very limited control), lots of monologue, and many puzzles that are very easy, every detail is given you, sometimes multiple times, and one extremely hard, without any build-up or hint.Plus: beautiful render and music. Pure awesomeness.Minus: awful and limited control, you are very limited of where you can go and what you can do, too much explanation of the story (some details are repeated 3-4 times), most of the time is just navigation or listening to the monologue. About 5% is interesting. On the promo pictures and videos this game looks like open world, well, you have only limited paths, kinds of a pre-2000 solution.Extremely minus: the monologue of the lady. Completely nonsensical how she keeps repeating how she loves the guy. FFS. Also, comments that are absolutely irrelevant to the environment. And the tone as well. _childDocuments_.review: Call of The Sea is a nice, narrative rich, puzzle game, in a pleasant environment, that does not overstay it's welcome.   I found most of the puzzle to be just challenging enough, but not too hard. It's mostly walking around, collecting notes and pasting them in your journal, looking at artifacts or murals and drawing them in the journal (which works really well to keep track of puzzle elements).  Walking pace is little slow, even when "sprinting", especial in the puzzles that require some backtracking.  The "hotspots" of some of the murals and other notables can require some fiddling to find.The art style was pleasant and constant quality. Well voiced narration and immersive sound effects.  Overall well worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of games that let you explore beautiful scenery while solving light puzzles, this game will entertain you. It's a neat story told well enough, and the environments you move through are well made. You can tell the developers put some love into this, and I feel bad that while I enjoyed it, there were some weaknesses to the finished game that prevent me from giving this a carte blanche recommendation. Because while fans of the genre will enjoy it, I'm afraid others will find it a touch lackluster. The storytelling isn't quite as compelling as others. The scenery - while beautiful - not as great as other, similar games. The puzzles aren't always quite fitting -- is this a puzzle game with a strong story? Or a story game with some puzzles to solve? The game's never quite sure. And just overall, the game feels like it never quite delivers on its promise.However, all of that is quibbling detail, and it boils down to my opening remark: fans of the walking sim/exploration adventure genre will like this. Others may not. Kudos to the creators to taking us back to the 1930s for some light Lovecraftian drama. I'm sorry I didn't love your game more, I really wanted to.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Call of the Sea is one of the most beautiful games I've ever played, the puzzles are on the easier side and your character moves kind of slow, but the story is very engaging. _childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is a first-person adventure and puzzle game set during the 1930’s.After years and years of appointments and medical referrals, the doctors have all but given up on Norah’s unusual and rare condition. In pain, and suffering from horrible nightmares and visions, her husband Harry decides to embark on a quest to solve the riddle behind her affliction. The trail takes him to a remote island in the South Pacific that the locals fear and have named “The Island of Death”. When Harry goes missing without trace, Norah musters all her energy and travels to the island to investigate.  I just didn’t want to stop playing it.The atmosphere is superbly done with layers and layers of lore, intrigue and mystery added to the mix at just the right times. There is even a short, but informative, seven-part prequel story in the news section to wet your appetite and introduce you to the two main characters. Check it out before you start! I really enjoy good character development and the relationship between the two main characters is what drives the story forward. Norah and Harry are as deeply in love as the day they met, and this is portrayed wonderfully through voiced cut scenes, and letter correspondence between the two of them. The game manages to convince you that they have the perfect relationship and would do anything for each other. There are lots of different types of lore lying around to enforce this notion, from inscribed photographs showing special memories to events in their lives that we witness. I really enjoyed this part of the game as it made it feel like more than just a puzzle game loosely tied together.  where you cared about the characters and you wanted to know what happened to Harry and you wanted Norah to find him. There is plenty of exploration to do, and lots of objects to examine. Objects that can be examined will invoke either a text-based summation and/or a voiced comment from Norah. Inspecting objects will add to the lore and reveal parts about the story and island. It is all cleverly layered and keeps the intrigue high. Puzzles were imaginative but quite difficult I thought. I managed to solve them without any guides apart from two. One of these puzzles is broken and the other was slightly misleading. The puzzles were cleverly entwined around the story, which is mostly Polynesian based, and added to the immersion and feeling that the puzzle was part of finding Harry rather than a disconnected puzzle for the sake of it. Some puzzles required making notes, even though there is a diary where all important clues and puzzle notes get added. The diary can only be brought up on full screen however which means you are flicking between puzzle and diary. I would have liked the option to have the diary visible alongside the puzzle so that you refer to it and solve the puzzle simultaneously. I think most people will struggle with these puzzles. They take a bit of exploration to find the objects needed to provide the clues and when you have all the clues, it takes a fair bit of brain power to work them out. Personally, they hit just the right difficulty level with me and although I struggled, it was immensely satisfying when you reach that Eureka moment. The island setting is beautiful and voice acting is superb. Cut scenes are dramatic and have a high production feel. The whole game feels mysterious and eerie.  Characters are strong and well developed with wonderful music and sound effects accompanying it. There are six chapters and I played through the game twice to gain all the achievements. It took me around twenty hours to do so. You play as Norah Everhart, devoted wife to Harry Everhart. In search of your missing husband, you arrive on a mysterious island and must explore for clues to Harry’s whereabouts. Along the way you will find evidence of your husband’s progress in trying to find a cure for your illness, and clues to his whereabouts and what happened to his party. Norah has a journal where she notes important finds, and documents clues to puzzles which block her progress. You can refer to the diary at any time which provides invaluable help. The diary has a notes section which recaps the story and a log section which places all clues to puzzles. If an object is examinable, then an eye symbol will appear. The object can be rotated which sometimes reveals more information. Norah will comment on the object and any important information is noted. Sometimes Norah will find a letter that Harry has written for her. This produces a small cutscene detailing Harry’s efforts in finding a cure and his concerns and worries. The notebook page should be full if you are harboring all valuable evidence so if there is a gap on the page you’ll need to keep looking.  Using the evidence in your notes and logs you’ll need to solve the puzzles at hand. You do not have an inventory as such but occasionally you will pick up objects that will be automatically used on the correct puzzle. The puzzles are varied and interesting and can be quite challenging. There is a mixture of smaller and easier puzzles along with bigger ones with multiple facets. One of the first puzzles you’ll encounter is actually broken and referring to a guide proved this. If you get stuck on the lens aligner puzzle then you’ll need to look up the solution until it’s fixed. Keyboard or controller can be used. There are lots of interesting achievements to gather.The graphics were beautiful. The game felt polished and professional. I did get some screen tearing in the early chapters though but this seemed to resolve itself later. The island is well detailed and they’ve put a lot of effort into the Polynesian look and feel. Voice acting was superb and there is a wonderful orchestral tune played for dramatic effect when required. Curator Info:

_childDocuments_.review: This is a wonderful and very meaningful puzzle adventure game, where you, playing Norah, a very brave and loving lady, is happily married and in love. As you play through the game, you, as Norah, find out more and more about who she is and where she came from.The story is lovely and emotionally deep, and will leave a lasting impression.The graphics are beautiful and colorful, with deep and subtle colors and artwork. The sounds are also great, with wonderful music. I suggest you play in a darkened room to allow you to experience them in all their glory.Some have complained that the puzzles are too easy. Yes, I have played many tough puzzle games, but this game would be ruined with too difficult puzzles. This simply is not the right game for super difficult puzzles. I believe they are well thought out here, not too hard and not too easy. Also, I believe the walking speed is spot on as well.If there's any criticism I have with this game, it's too short. I love adventuring through the game and finding out more about the island and the race Norah is exploring, and I wish there was more to see. There HAS to be more about this race than what was shown, and I was really hoping to find out much more. Even if nothing more than optional levels or text to read, I just want to find out more! If the developers could even release some post release text on this, I would be ever so thankful. Yes, the game is rather short, and I believe more could have been added.Still, this is a beautiful and very meaningful adventure, which is worth exploring.NOTE: Be sure to look at every note and every mural, and walk around every area. You'll unlock all the collectibles doing so.I would love some kind of sequel that explores this race more and more

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the sea is a callback to the golden age of point-and-click adventure games with a hefty dose of puzzles and exploration thrown into the mix. The story follows Norah Everhart, a young woman struggling with an inherited terminal disease that led her loving husband Harry to go on a quest to find a cure on a forbidden tropical island where he and the entire expedition mysteriously goes missing. In the beginning of the game Norah receives a package with a few mysterious items from the lost expedition and embarks on a quest to find out what happened to her soulmate Harry. On the way we are treated to lovely environments, engaging puzzles and a genuinely heartwarming story that is narrated via the internal monologue of the main character. So the story as you might have figured out from the trailer is heavily influenced by Lovecraft yet takes it on a somewhat of a spin in the end and makes it a truly satisfying conclusion. Personally I think this might be one of the better versions of this type of story yet to come to digital media. First of all the environment and atmosphere in this game is spot on. Every chapter has its own unique look and feel to it and it brings up a wide variety of strange surroundings, weird pictograms, clever insertions of lore into the game via found logs and small cutscenes. The narration is perfect and the encountering of clues via logs and photos are fitting. The puzzles are well constructed and even though a few were a bit convoluted we finished most of the game without clues. All in all this is a wholesome story of a sick young woman looking for her lost lover in a strange land and on the way stumbles upon things that make her question her place in the world. I strongly recommend this game for the story alone yet the environments, the puzzles and the feeling of otherworldliness takes this game to a whole new level. I encountered no bugs or glitches of any kind and generally had a fantastic time with this game. 10/10, Would surely swim out to that brooding reef  again and again and again..

_childDocuments_.review: Wow!  What an absolutely gorgeous ride.  Half of it is like playing through a colourful and expensive theme park attraction, while the other half is very much not that, and I adored every minuteIt looked pretty and I was after something short and sweet. I was expecting some simplistic puzzles, a couple of basic setpieces and little else. It really looked like the sort of game where you don't even move and puzzle boxes just unfold in front of you to solve, I really wasn't expecting muchWhat I got was a solid 7 hours of being constantly awestruck. The ruins are breathtaking and complex, the water is beautiful, the colours and lighting enhance everything so strongly, the puzzles are well designed (some gentle frustration but I always got through without help) and the journal notes down everything in as much detail as you needThe story is light but heavy at the same time, I didn't think I was invested, but I was and didn't realise it.It's a good balance, it's linear with free exploration within each section, you don't move very fast and there's no jump button but there never feels like there should be a reason the game should be changed to be otherwise.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the Sea is a little different to the usual Lovecraftian works we get these days. Less of a focus on the eldritch horror and mind flaying incomprehensible creatures. As a puzzle game, Call of the Sea also stays away from fixing all your problems with a shotgun and dynamite.Instead Call of the Sea is an adventure of the unusual and alien, but also the wonder and notions of alienation or belonging. On top of this, we get to explore an island full of vibrant colour rather than a drab barnacle covered fishing district.Call of the Sea has absolutely wonderful art direction, music, and story ideas. As a game it has what it needs - the puzzles can be a little hit and miss, some have a refreshing amount of environmental integration or letting the player put two and two together, others are straight forward or just require you to pick up the final clue that puts it all together for you.Overall Call of the Sea is quite pleasant. A thoroughly refreshing and colourful adventure, though perhaps two hours or so too much walking.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty lukewarm on this game. The best part of the game is definitely the art direction and graphics. The set pieces were great for immersion with really vibrant colors. Puzzles were good. A blend of finding and entering symbols, timing puzzles, and logic puzzles. There was only a couple times I was stumped but I don't think you'd ever need to look up hints. Story is pretty decent but cliche.  Overall if you want a pretty good immersive walking simulator + good puzzles + a decent story, I'd say give it a play.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: Call of the sea is a great game. Visually stunning, I really enjoyed the vibrant colours they chose to go with instead of the dark and dreary colours most Lovecraft games end up going with. The puzzles are pretty solid, I only end up googling one of them that I was pretty stuck on for a while, and when I realised what you had to do it all became clear, just for some reason it didn't click with me from the get go. The story/atmosphere is good, keeps you involved all the way though. For Lovecraft fans this is a must for your collection, for everyone who's not into the lore should get it too as there's enough of a story with out it going to in depth of the mythos.
_childDocuments_.name: Call of the Sea

_childDocuments_.review: A weird tale of otherworldly mystery. Call of the Sea is a first-person adventure puzzle game set in the 1930s that tells the story of Norah, a woman on the trail of her missing husband's expedition. The search takes place on a strange but beautiful island in the South Pacific, filled with secrets waiting to be unearthed. It is an otherworldly tale of mystery, adventure, and self-discovery.

name: Orangeblood
detailed_description: 199X, New Koza It's the end of the 20th century, on a historic timeline different from that which we know. A manmade island off the coast of Okinawa is humming with a dirty, exotic vibe - and it's awesome! Rust and faded concrete glisten in the morning sun and the late-night neon, showing off the various faces of the island. Amazing Soundtrack Let yourself go to the subtropical sun, the sound of the waves, and the scent of dank weed, and let some real deep cuts and unknown classics of 1990s hiphop take you away. It doesn't matter whether you're chilling on a couch on a rooftop, having a drink at the bar, or capping fools in a firefight in some sketchy alleyway - these dope-ass tracks are gonna get you moving! Four 'Kawaii' Soldiers Hey you! Do you like hardcore adventures where you take on the role of an even harder-core badass tasked with beating the crap out of a bunch of demons? Well, so do I, but sometimes it's fun to try out something a little different, you know? These four cute Asian girls couldn't care less about little photo stickers... They'd rather play with some 7.62x39mm rifles and filthy, filthy cash! Simple-yet-deep Turn-based Gunfighting Use simple controls to take down evil gang members and killer robots! In New Koza, you can purchase randomly-generated and extremely powerful guns, 24/7. Load up a shotgun so powerful you'd burn yourself to toast if the gas leaked and some brand-new fireproof sneakers, find a group of psychotic yakuza thugs, and personally deliver a handwritten invitation to BEATDOWN TOWN! There's a Dog, Too! Ruff!

_childDocuments_.review: Astounding art direction with spritework that is aggressively detailed and stylish. The world is gorgeous and surprisingly engaging to explore, with lots of intractable elements. Despite getting sucked in by the stellar presentation, the gameplay chewed me up and spat me out. I've only put around 4 hours into the game, and I can still leave a review in confidence that I've experienced all that the loop has to offer. Randomly generated firearm based gameplay in a turn-based RPG is an interesting concept I'm glad the game took the effort to explore, but the balancing leaves a lot to be desired. Most of the equipment borders on uselessness which incentivizes grinding whenever you come across a roadblock in progress. The characters don't recieve new skills on level up, making battles feel astoundingly stagnant aside from when you play the Bigger Numbers game with your gear's stats. The story and dialogue mostly only shows up inbetween dungeons, and it's all pretty terrible. I'd hate to use the term "edgy" in a review I'm trying to pass off as halfway formal, but oh my God - it's a very jeuvenile attempt to capture the essence of urban crime fiction. I don't think I've ever played a game that uses the F-word more. It started off a little endearing but quickly becomes mindnumbing as you slowly realise it's trying to be "badass".Genuinely wish I could recommend this, I've been looking forward to it for months, but I'd rather just admit I'm let down and wash my hands of it. Credit where it's due, it's stunning to look at. I'll be keeping an eye on this crew's future projects.

_childDocuments_.review: Good soundtrack and pretty art, but that's it. Story fails to be funny or interesting, cringey dialogue, text off-screen, missed translations and I also noticed a few bugs. Gameplay is really unbalanced, I beat the game using the same weapons and the same tactic because I never found anything better. Main game is about 6-7 hours depending on how much grinding you do, but there is also some post-game content that I didn't get around to finishing (Would require hours of grinding).

_childDocuments_.review: Orangeblood is an incredibly pretty, turn-based RPG, in which you control a foul mouthed hotshot gangster [female] in a quest for something.  You eventually get three other party members who could be described completely in a few words each.   NPC dialogue is sometimes funny, usually irrelevant. The game was definitely able to get a laugh out of me a few times during the main story, but definitely not on any sort of consistent basisOrangeblood has plenty of it. From the great beats to it's setting of an artificial island city, there's definitely a potential for something here. The graphics are great and detailed, but most people will probably enjoy them the most if you turn off its awful filters. But that's the only thing going for orangeblood as it trips over itself completely.The loot in this game is completely random, a diabloidlands of exile, so to say. There's different categories of weapons and armor and different mods to them. Treasure the useful stuff, and throw away the bad. There's multiple shops in the game, but very rarely do they offer anything of value.  The most important modifiers tend to be skill damage.Every character has 1 (one) [ichi] {roman numeral: I} unique skills to them. Wow. There are some generic skills, 5, if i'm not mistaken. These are support skills that you can only use once every 5 turns or so. There's not a lot going on in this game.  You give a character or two defensive items and the other characters offensive items. It feels unfinished, boring. A complete chore to play. There's no challenge to the game (outside of just not dropping it for something else) outside of boss fights, since against standard mobs you can start the battle with enough SP to use your skills and kill them turn 1.The games story, and events are irrelevant, just to give you an excuse to go somewhere else.  There's about 1 recurring NPC you talk to.  Other people have mentioned the dialogue as being juvenile. They're not entirely wrong; I feel like they were going for a campy over the top gangster kind of story, but they just weren't good enough to pull that off.  Pulp fiction this is not.  The translation feels lazy at times, the text boxes overflowing on some items.  The playable area in the game is pretty small, not to mention the game just highlights treasure on your map. You can easily finish this game on a single saturday. The game and characters feel more like an art project that a game and script was hastily stapled to.  Oh, there's a post game area where the enemies are listed as level 61. I finished the game before even hitting 30 (which means no items above level 30). I wasn't about to waste time grinding levels or items to get through it.You'll have more fun watching the preview video on the store page than actually playing this kuso.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game. However, I will not do so without SOME talking points.First - The art is amazing. However, it becomes very jarring when moving around inside of zones the fog of war and tilt shift become VERY hard on the eyes.I STRONGLY suggest that anyone wanting to play the game mess with the settings at length.Make sure the bottom three settings are OFF (Tilt Shift, Chromatic Aberration, and CRT) and the color scheme is set to something easy on your eyes like Flat or Cinema. Vivid works as well but will be slightly more straining.Also, the combat focus motion is very hard to stomach so I suggest turning that off as well.The game excels in the aesthetic department but it is hard to tolerate without fine tuning.Second - The music. The audio in this game is amazing! However, some zones like the Tier 4 zone has NO audio at all. Not sure if it's a bug or glitch or what have you but it produces no sound. Also, anytime you spend a certain amount of time in a specific area the music ends. It's almost as if it isn't set to loop infinitely. Not a big problem but if you're slow and heavy on exploration you could be left in silence for a bit.Third - Combat and balance. Combat is actually my favorite part of the game. Super clean and fast paced (with focus turned off) but I will say that the game is EXTREMELY unbalanced.The game has a RANDOM LOOT system. Any time you get ANY piece of weapon or gear it will be randomized. So, the two guns you receive at the very beginning out of the crate can be a whole litany of different weapons. Now, factor this in to every enemy, boss, and crate drop for the entirety of the game and you can have some playthroughs where you are just ridiculously overpowered and some where you just have NOTHING good comparatively.I love random loot systems. It's a super fun thing. However, like Diablo and other similar systems, the game is usually balanced off of the most common drop. In this game I'd imagine that's blue/white gear. The drops, though, don't seem to be all that common. In fact, I seem to get rare and super rare (purple, gold) gear very frequently. This makes the difficulty curve near nonexistent as enemies in the game scale with you to a degree (Supervisor boss, random encounters, etc). In short, the drop rates need to be re-evaluated for better than the balance line equipment or the difficulty of combat needs to be increased.TL;DRBuy this game, especially if on sale. You will have 6-10 hours of a super fun time once you dial in the settings to make the visuals less jarring. Don't expect super difficulty as the drop system is unbalanced. Music is amazing and the dialogue is quite humorous and "punk"Not a waste of your time in any sense, I loved it, but has its own quirks that make it apparent that it's an indie/rpg maker game.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey onii-san. Right click the game in your library -> Properties -> Set launch options -> add in  "--in-process-gpu" without the "  made the steam overlay and my Xbox One controller work.Haven't gotten that far yet. Was expecting more of story focused game, but instead got more of a looter shooter inspired rpg. The guns/gear and the abilities in them seem powerful for once though. Like I found a unique shotgun that kills one enemy in one shot(at the beginning anyway), but needs to be constantly reloaded. To support that I found an another unique shotgun that stuns all enemies with a high chance. So the other gal blasts enemies while the other one keeps them stunned. I did have to switch it around little for a boss fight. Remember Machiko's passive heal.The visual style and music are easily the highlights here. The main hub is a little messy to get around at first, but it will become easier to get around soon. It would be nice if the map and/or UI elements could be hidden for screenshots. There are also some colour filters offered at the menu to change how the game looks.Haven't had any crashes so far myself which is great since the developers made the decision to not allow you to save the game freely inside dangerous zones. There are checkpoints however should you fall in battle and there are vending machines to cheaply recover your lost hp(inside dungeons too). A cheap consumable item will also quickly let you leave a danger zone, but will not let  you return to where you were.Overall it's a charming little game with a vulgar main character, but hey so is the world around her. I think the price might be a little steep for what is offered, but I found it impossible to resist girls with coloured eyelashes.Come on in.
