_childDocuments_.name: The Coma 2: Vicious Sisters

_childDocuments_.review: To start, I didn't play The Coma: Recut. You don't really need to in order to understand what is going on in this game. This game is scary and interesting with twists and turns. Eventually, the game becomes repetitive. A lot of fetch quests, trying to find notes, running back and forth in VERY large areas, and hoping you don't run into same like two creatures that are roaming around. I really loved the creatures at first because you can HEAR them moving around hunting for you. However, that quickly becomes an "Oh god, it's you again" experience and you just groan as you run away from them. After a while, you're just waiting for it to get to the ending which wasn't very satisfying and left a lot of my questions unanswered. I had fun but I didn't enjoy doing the same thing over and over again for 11 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: The Coma 2: Vicious Sisters

_childDocuments_.review: This game directly continues after the events of the first game. It is a very nice 2D atmospheric horror game. The graphics and environment are nicely rendered and are really better than the previous game. Environments are more complex and diverse. The art style is similar to the previous Coma game, but more polished. Music and sounds are good. The story and atmosphere are very good. There are more characters and there is noticeable development. Everything has moved on from the previous game for the better. The gameplay and mechanics are also good, not too hard, not too easy. Especially the last parts are really hard. If you like survival horror games and don't mind 2D. this is probably the game for you. What are you waiting for?! Grab your school bag on the run before the killer gets you!
_childDocuments_.name: The Coma 2: Vicious Sisters

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game twice - One with a general ending, the second was for the true ending. I had fun having to collect all of the notes and reading the lore. The game is challenging and unpredictable at times. But that's the whole point of the game - to keep you on your toes. I played a few side-scrolling horror/thriller games but "The Coma" series has not disappoint me yet. If you can get it on sale, the game is worth the wait. Play it in the middle of the night, the atmosphere is intense. Also, use a headphone, don't rely on your speakers; this will enhance the gaming experience. I also appreciate the port in Steam because I had bad experiences with "The Coma: Recut" in Nintendo Switch, and the port did no justice for the Switch Pro controller. The gameplay in "The Coma 2 Vicious Sisters" in Steam is great. Sound: 5/5Graphics: 4/5 (improved from "The Coma:Recut" but some spites look wonky)Controls: 5/5 (Great with gamepads/controllers)Atmosphere: 5/5 (Use a headphone and don't be stingy with the volume. Make sure you can hear incoming footsteps; this will make the gaming experience better)Lore: 4/5 (I personally think the lore so far is good, but some parts are repetitive because it caters for players who may not play "The Coma:Recut". That is fine. Yet, there are some parts of the lore that is still vague. Not sure if this is the devs' way of hinting a part 3? Either way, I enjoyed the storyline.)

_childDocuments_.review: Darn this game is good.  It does a REALLY good job at what is meant to do, scaring the living crap out of you. Highly recommend this title if you are looking for a good horror game that will have you on your tip toes.

_childDocuments_.review: The Coma 2: Vicious Sisters is a huge upgrade in comparison to the first game. I love Mina and how quick-witted she is throughout this horrific nightmare. The story is very mysterious and intriguing, but I feel the ending was a little disappointing. Overall, if you enjoy fun point & click survival horror, this is the game for you! So I wasn't invested in what was going on.I couldn't finish it, I didn't find it scary anymore, I didn't care about the main character or her plight :(

_childDocuments_.review: A decent adventure horror game. The art is nice, especially the static art, but the breathe cycles are a little rough. The gameplay is fine, with the player walking around vaguely dangerous spooky settings looking for objects. To that end, it ends up being a bit more of walking back and forth than I think it needs to be. The lack of significant danger or a time limit means that the tension is generally pretty low and the lack of meaningfully different gameplay means the game feels like it runs a bit long, even with it's rather short 5-7 hour runtime. A decent story, worth picking up on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Well this game is quite complicated ! I would say it's a survival horror with well done mechanics . The main character is an adorable girl which is constanty chased by her psycho teacher! But first you can hear high heel steps so you could hide. Sometimes the encounters are unavoidable but there is an intersting thing that if we re not on the right path possibility of encounter is very low! Also there are other types of enemies with some attacks that cause negative effects: poison or bleed! This can be prevented by using items badage or cure. There is also health bar and stamina bar. You cannot run forever! There are also QTE sequences! So the game mechanics are not that simple ! However overall this makes the game not simple " run for you life" rather stay calm re -think your actions.   10/10!
_childDocuments_.name: The Coma 2: Vicious Sisters

_childDocuments_.review: It's a cool game.☑ Buy the game on DISCOUNT unless you wanna support devs work☑ Games not bad. It's just not challenging. ☑ Story could probably have been better☑ It's pretty and the art specialists appear to really have put some work on this game☑ Do you feel like you dont want to invest too much on a game and its mechanics? Good, this game has no mechanics, consumables are ♥♥♥♥, and you can beat the game even if you play once today and then continue in 3-4 weeks.That said, and therefore recommending the game, I feel like I should make my harsh criticism mainly towards the game's bad boring mechanics:- The story could have been better. That doesn't mean its bad, it's just not super awesomely written for my taste. It's a little bit ... dull.- The art is beautiful and immersive. If someone is to congratulate in this game, it's the artists. You could have made a whole comic out of this game and it's good for them.- Game and game mechanics could feel more immersive. Why?     a) Consumables feel almost useless most of the time. I had to use alcohol to cure poison only one time in the entire game. And it still didnt feel like necessary. It was just a way to make the game less challenging.    Water bottles were used only 1-2 times to run away from an enemy. They were mostly used just because I wanted to run more as my low stamina slowed me down.    c) Dying in this game barely feels like dying. Just means you have to go through same unskippable scenes over and over again (especially last quest). Or that you have to go to the room next floor. So, using the items, feels like losing something you could have just not used anyway, as the game doesn't challenges you in using them anyways.    d) Craftable items .... I literally beat the game without no craftable items. And I had no trouble in beating the game. Just like with consumables which first give you a sense of "survival", then you just start to realize, they're not really important in beating the game. They're just .... there. Only to protect you from losing 30 seconds after you die and go back to last save.    Which I by no means mean that the game should be punishing you with saves/checkpoints that are too long in between. That would be no fun. To take a good example of challenging but fun design, just look at Dark Souls. The game is not considered hard AND fun because checkpoints are too far in between, but because it feels challenging to beat the monsters and even if you die, it will still feel challenging and fun to reach the boss again. It feels fun dying only because you have to use the same fun mechanics to get to the boss that you used to get there before, beating monsters with good fun mechanics.     In "The Coma 2" that is rather not the case. If you die, its very likely you already know how to get to the next level without dying again, it's not challenging you with fun "mini games" in the process.    e) Enemies are not challenging, nor scary after a certain point, and are repetitive. They barely appear, and when they do, finding a place to hide is really easy. Just find the first or second door, and you'll certainly find a locker or a table to hide. Now, just wait for the quick time events. Aaaaaaaaaaaaand repeat that x10-20 times till you complete the game. Yes, x10-20 times, the enemies won't really challenge you. Not that I mean, repeating this more times would make the game more fun. And I think they understood that this was the only mechanic they had for their "most scary boss" enemies and it would be really not fun for the user to repeat them even more. But that makes the "super scary enemies" ... really much less challenging, tiresome and less scary.Anyway ... that all said, game's not bad. Just not worth the full price for me and it's good I got that in Humble Bundle. The game just feels less like a game with its boring repetitive mechanics and more like a medium for the artists of this game to present their beautiful art and story.
_childDocuments_.name: The Coma 2: Vicious Sisters

_childDocuments_.review: If you like horror stories, survival games and mystery puzzles, I think you'll absolutely love this game.Continuing the story of the previous installment, The Coma 2 takes the core gameplay of its predecessor and improves it almost beyond recognition. The previous title was good, but this one is much better! Big visual and gameplay improvements, new mechanics, more diverse areas, new characters, more interesting lore and stronger narrative. All aspects of this game are not just polished, but they complement each other so well. It never felt boring, repetitive or stretched.In The Coma 2, encounters are rarer, but more dangerous than in its predecessor. QTEs, cripples and deadly grabs will keep you engaged and depending on how you prepare for some situations, you may suffer permanent injuries (reflected in your appearance as well as your HP cap - and they stack)! The pursuers will leave your area once they lose track of you, however, so you don't feel stuck in a hiding spot or constantly on the run and you can constantly progress through the game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Coma 2: Vicious Sisters

_childDocuments_.review: What at first looked like a unique game turned into easy gameplay with nice atmosphere but nothing much else. It takes around 4 hours to finish it, so you might get to the end before you start getting bored. It is positive for me, because I rarely get to play something like this, but it is not a game I would be remembering for a long time.
_childDocuments_.name: The Coma 2: Vicious Sisters

_childDocuments_.review: MAJOR UPGRADE from the first game, and even continued the story. Artwork is great, I loved that we had multiple maps this game whereas the first was just the school maps. The notes were in order this time so I was able to backtrack and look at which map I needed to go back to. It seemed at first we were really going to get to know the friend but then we just have a couple flashbacks. Then the guy that likes her who is a bully is used in the same way but we never get to know him. Overall it took me about 14 hours, and I really enjoyed it and only took breaks when I got annoyed with being killed over the killer spawning when I changed floors.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a little hesitant to purchase this because i'm not a fan of side-scrolling style but I was immediately in love with the animation that I forgot all about my judgement. The environment is rich and beautifully rendered. The sound effects are haunting and alarming. I played twice just to get the different endings and enjoyed it as much. if not more, on the 2nd go. I was able to take in more of the atmosphere and just enjoy the story. I spent most of my first play through screaming and running for my life and dying...often. I highly recommend this game for a terrifying, fun immersive experience.
_childDocuments_.name: The Coma 2: Vicious Sisters

_childDocuments_.review: Nothing short of amazing.Game is like around 10 hours or so experience so even at base price of 15 bucks it is well deserving of that amount.Good horror elements are used in the game also it has a decent story that u get invested in.Some lore is covered in journal entries while others are introduced in raw gameplay. _childDocuments_.review: A nice sequel that fixes some problems that the previous game had, like the awkward dodge and stamina management.The new portraits and art are part of its charm and the story is fairly good. Some problems would be having to go back and forth looking for where to go sometimes, also backtracking once you have items to access other areas it can be annoying since the map will draw the places where you can't go blocked by the tentacle walls but it won't show the same for the stairs, so you might end up running around looking for the not blocked stairs up or down. The lack of a difficulty setting might be a turn off for some. I hadn't played the first game for a long time and even so I managed to breeze through the game barely spending any of the money, not getting hit till a lot later just running through basically all enemies. The addition of quicktime events when you hide is nice since it's not just you hide and it's over. Since there are many lights on around it's quite pointless to take back the hold your breath to hide in plain sight mechanic so finding a place to hide is more important now. Also you can speedrun it skipping quests at the cost of losing 1 HP each time, so the game becomes harder until you have to play perfectly.Overall recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: You follow Mina Park this time around, picking up shortly after the events of the first game. A short introductory tutorial starts things off, to introduce our new protagonist and some of the basics, before dropping you right into "the coma", a dark and twisted version of our own world that you will get to know fairly well as you explore the different locations.A lot of the lore is given to you in the form of notes, spread across the locations you explore, but you can still follow the story just fine through the dialogue and comicbook-like cutscenes you encounter.With simple controls, and easy to learn gameplay. A great soundtrack to set the atmosphere together with beautifully drawn art that has lots of detail. And an interesting story and lore for those that are interested. I would absolutely recommend this game.I don't think it has much replayability value outside of getting 100% achievements. But you'll get around 5-10 hours out of one playthrough depending on your playstyle.

_childDocuments_.review: Better than CM1 in some things, worse in others. But for people who liked CM1, they should play CM2 aswell.For newcomers, it's really a matter of whether what you see in the videos interest you as the game itself is quite simple, with a relatively good story.I preferred the animation and art of the older title a little more but both are graphically nice to look at. The introduction of the quick action test(?) where you press a series of buttons that appear in the screen, while sound in concept itself - ie, succeed in an action such as holding your breath - is a bit boring in execution as it lacks in challenge.Overall, CM2 presents itself decently as a more polished version, we get more variety in terms of hiding places that provide different levels of cover, and therefore, different chances of detection but the mechanics are essencially inherited from CM1 and retained the series essence.

_childDocuments_.review: This sequel is an improvement from the first game, which I negatively reviewed two years ago..MechanicsThe same as the first game with little improvements in mechanics. Same basic concepts running and dodging. However, the additional hide in the background while holding breath has been removed for hiding spots. (thank god)The game mostly frequently utilizes quick time mini-games while doing certain actions such as hiding and crafting.Speaking of crafting:You're given the option of crafting a useful item per chapter until the last. These decide the fate of the MC throughout the story..GameplayThe same exact *unscary* enemies as the first game. With one or two insignificant traps such as falling bodies and a claw which are *EASILY* dodged. As a matter of fact, *AN EXPERIENCED GAMER CAN FINISH THIS GAME WITHOUT LOSING A SINGLE DIGIT OF HEALTH*.Every single enemy is dodgeable most of which except one won't give chase so you can leisurely stroll away from them after a quick dodge.The main enemy is a chaser type persurer, which chases you from corridor to corridor but can be escaped by doing or hiding in a locker or under a desk. *NOT SCARY OR CREEPY*.ItemsNo improvements on items in this game. They all do the same except the addition of Spectral matches, which dispel monsters allowing you to open previously locked bags. Other items are collectibles or health/stamina items.A new unique item, "Mace," bought from vending machines is a one time deterrent to the main enemy. No upgrades on inventory again in this game, leaving you with only about four slots that don't stack, so items have to be consumed or left behind..BugsDidn't find any in my 6-hour run. Unlike its predecessor.Story The story continues right after the first game and is mostly told through pages you collect throughout the different locations. I'm not a huge fan of reading walls of text on a game I don't care that much for, so I personally didn't read it, but it seems to be more crafted and less of a collection simulator as the first.This game includes achievements; unlike the first game; however, you get achievements for simple breathing. Every other second you receive an achievement, and within an hour, I kid you not, you can have at least 10.TL;DR: A flawed yet improved Achievement simulator. 6/10Buy on-sale the game is so short I wouldn't pay $15.00 for it. The game can be completed in a 3-hour speed run.
_childDocuments_.name: The Coma 2: Vicious Sisters

_childDocuments_.review: An improvement on almost every level from the first game, (first syndrome for me on the artstyle difrences between the two games though xD), theres voice acting this time!.-But yeah, if you liked the first game to any degree, this sequel will only improve on that experience massively.-Controls are super responsive, had no issues playing this with a 360 controller.-Oh yeah, the game is super worth it at full price, i couldnt wait any longer after finishing the first game, so i bought the sequel with no discount, no regrets, quality game with a solid 11 hours for a first playthrough, and thats not counting the stuff i left behind since the bonus menu isnt complete, getting the deluxe edition for future runs on this xD.-

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot possibly recommend this game enough. I haven't been so addicted to a game in a long time. I literally had to finish it in 2 days and a half, despite the fact that it took me 12 hours (go figure how much I spent per day on it).It improves on almost everything from the first game, and it is genuinely a really fun experience to go through. Consequently, it is one of the indie survival horror games that comes closest to absolute perfection. The gameplay is extremely addictive, as there are countless secrets and hidden pathways that you can always discover, locations to explore, and mysteries to solve. The writing is absolutely stellar, and I have rarely (or perhaps never) seen a game that fuses typically-anime (I'm aware that this is more akin to manhwa, but "anime" might sound more familiar) fantasy and superhero motifs with tales of trauma, abuse, friendship, and survival in such a convincing and moving manner.Therefore, if you are into survival horror or simply into anime/manga/manhwa (and don't mention a creepy and gory story), you MUST try this out. You won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't normally enjoy these type of 2D visual novel games, but something about the art initially attracted me and I thought I would give it a try.  9 hours later after beating it I can say that I really enjoyed it.  The puzzles can be a bit frustrating, requiring you to revisit areas you already explored, but that's probably because most games nowadays hold your hand and show you a blip on a map and you just follow along mindlessly.  I thought the story was good and despite a few frustrating moments of having to backtrack several times to figure out what I missed, all while having to constantly dodge the same enemies over and over again, I would recommend it to anyone.If you are interested in playing the first game (The Coma:  Recut), I would say you can skip it. _childDocuments_.review: The total playtime should roughly be around 4 to 6 hours on your first time depending on how fast or slow you take things. Along side these that I mentioned, there's also interesting story and little side stuff to do.I do in fact have some small complaints, like the new "visibility," mechanic that really doesn't go deep into itself (it introduces itself by saying something like "if you have your lighter on you'll be visible from a further distance," sorta thing, really wish they also could've done more with this and added a stealth mechanic so you wouldn't have to always go into a different room to completely avoid her) sometimes, maybe a bug or glitch, Dark Song will appear right next to you when you enter/exit a room, I sorta wish that the ominous footsteps came with some laugh or giggle to creepify Dark Song even more, the amount of stamina this high school girl has is sorta concerning, When you go UP, or DOWN you don't hear Ms Songs footsteps anymore, but she's still walking by.10/10, must experience. _childDocuments_.review: Coma 2 is a total improvement of the previous game, and one of the best games developed by a Korean studio. Coma 2 shares similarities with Clock Tower saga, using a 2D aesthetic to create a relentless hide and seek against an immortal stalker. The graphic is really gorgeous, between a manga and a cartoon, well cared in every detail, from the characters to the complex background. The level of detail and polish is incredible, also focusing on rewarding the player. For example, several achievements after being unlocked will reveal a gorgeous concept art or an artwork.This time, the game is not only set in a dark version of a school, but will bring the player roaming around the shadow version of hospitals and markets. The gameplay is based on the exploration of the settings, collecting items and notes to advance in the story and to meet new characters. Secondary quests are also available, helping to break the linearity of the plot.In this case, the main stalker is the dark version of a teacher, hunting her students with a knife, helped by another more brutal and deranged version of herself. A stamina bar helps to outrun the devilish teacher, but also other strategies are possible. The main character can hide in bathrooms or closets, but only by completing a quick time event, the player will stay hidden without making any noise. There are several traps and minor monsters along the way, which will generally cause negative effects. Different attacks can bring to status alterations, such as poison or bleeding, creating an additional level of threat. Avoiding spoilers, there are also specific events that could lead to the permanent loss of a chunk of the health bar.Managing the limited inventory is also a crucial task, which will add even more survival vibes to the core gameplay. Is it better to bring items to cure health or stamina? Also, the many negative effects could strike at any distraction, driving the player into a desperate search for a remedy forgotten somewhere in the level.Being developed by a Korean team, Coma 2 also offers an interesting view of modern Korea. Schools and student life is well portrayed, with many details revealed by posters and notes. But the interesting lore expands toward more traditional locations, such as a food market, enriched in detail and places. The shadow world is also a place of forbidden traditions and dark arts, with strong connections with more ancient and mystical times, also reflected in the outfit of some of the characters. Glyphs and ritual items are scattered around, in a silent and mad world where not even the corpses are ordinary. Folkloric characters will also make their appearance, such as the Dokkaebi, a sort of mischievous Korean goblin.The Coma 2 is how every sequel should be, and one of the best horror experiences for fans of the first Clock Tower, from the art-style to the gameplay.More info on horror games based on Asian folklore in my article:

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic and phenomenal! Incredibly better than the first game! The Coma 2: Vicious Sisters story wise is alot more compelling and interesting, when the first game came out i was like, alright, its a bit cliche. A Kid trapped in school, yada yada But this game takes it up a notch! I'm very impressed with how the story came to be. How we were able to go beyond just the school and visit other areas of the city. This game has alot of qtes and stealth gameplay, which alot of people didn't like. But I actually liked doing the qtes, im most likely one of those rare people who liked it. Also the Ai, has improved. Ms.Song's AI wasn't incredibly annoying as the previous game from my experience. My most favorite part of this game was definitely going through Mina's friendship with Da-Hyun and finding out her backstory. Though i wonder how Mina will make it up to Da-Hyun and actually be with her, through thick and thin. In the beginning i didn't particularly like Mina because of her indecisiveness to Myung-Gil's love and Da-Hyun is right, and i agree with her. I don't like girls who don't know what they want and they're not straight. But it's really good, Mina goes through a ton of character development in this game.Which made me like her alot Also reminds me, even the side characters backstories are explained through all of the notes! They're fully fleshed out and i'm impressed on how much the devs put so much effort to solve the questions i had, and they made sense! Cons/Disappointments/Nitpicks: There weren't alot of things i disliked about this game surprisingly Though I disliked the True ending, it was very understandable for Youngho. Because of it, I think Youngho would most likely end up being together with Yaesol. I didn't care much about her honestly. _childDocuments_.review: Oh boy, I don't even know how to start this "review".Well, I'll start from a general impression! I have enjoyed this more than a first game.What have I liked: (comparing it to the first game)1) 2 endings instead of 4 from the first Coma, so you can unlock all achievements in 2 runs.2) Instead of just one school we have different locations so you don't get too bored with the level design.3) More usable inventory items and even a crafting system (though quest related)!4) More characters to interact with!5) The story goes smoother and the lore is explored better.6) customization for the main character (though via DLC)!7) I liked the story more than in the first game.8) The graphics are "indie" of course but they are still MUCH better and atmospheric than in the 1st Coma.9) The game is neither shorter nor longer compared to the first one.10) Achievements are here!What I didn't like:Not much really. I just wish that closed doors would get marked on the map. Also I want to be able to re-read the unlocked notes from the main menu.Verdict:Let's put it this way. If you have liked Silent Hill Shattered Memories then you would probably like this one. The gameplay is kinda similar, you don't fight, just explore and run\hide. The story isn't "gory", it's not a visceral horror (which I personally think is good!), the game's spirit is more light hearted. And if you have liked the first Coma then you will like this one too. _childDocuments_.review:
Mina Park, a student of Sehwa High, awakens at night in her school. It isn't long before she realizes that something is amiss. The once-familiar school where she spends her evenings studying looks twisted by something dark and sinister. She finds herself pursued by someone or something that looks eerily like her teacher. To survive, Mina must venture beyond the boundaries of her school and into the surrounding district. There, she will encounter strange creatures, mysterious strangers, and uneasy allies.

The Coma 2: Vicious Sisters is an atmospheric, story-driven game. Immerse yourself in the warped Sehwa district as you encounter an engaging cast of characters, solve puzzles, discover revealing clues, and fight for survival against a relentless psycho.

Heroines, forced to confront their worst fears, rarely emerge unscathed. Over the course of the story, Mina will encounter dangerous scenarios from which she could sustain permanent damage. Craft items to anticipate future dangers to avoid injury.

Dark Song is now more fearsome and powerful than ever before. Falling into her grasp could spell instant death. Running and wielding your flashlight makes you an easy target. You must precariously balance the urgency of exploration with your absolute need to survive!

_childDocuments_.review: This game looks and plays like a pirate skinned Slay the Spire, and well, that is pretty accurate and not a bad thing either. It does mold and craft its own unique image in both the style and gameplay. Some of the game design choices would actually make me think it is more of an Anti-Slay-the-Spire at times as it makes deliberate design decisions to stray from the path of its inspiration.While you can craft some pretty OP builds still, it can be a lot harder to achieve some of the broken builds of stacking poison to 999 or such - largely because the status system in this pirate game is quite different. Only one status is allowed to be active at a time. So if your enemy is poisoned, they can wipe their poison stacks clean by buffing their self with an attack increase. Because buffs can erase debuffs and vice versa. However, this goes for the player too. There is even a boss battle that will absolutely wipe the floor with you if you don't have some kind of way to buff yourself. He will keep raising your injury (this game's version of poison) stacks on you and they will just get higher and higher unless you wipe it with a buff. Not much different than how Slay the Spire bosses can hard counter some of your decks. But at the same time it is just different and feels unique. I wasn't so sure about the status system at first but it grown on me quite a bit. Which I think brings me to the next major difference.In Pirates Outlaws, you cannot skip a reward, without some workarounds. In Slay the Spire, a lean deck full of good cards usually works best and you will want to skip cards that do not add anything to your deck. The same kind of deck building philosophy still applies to Pirates Outlaws but with the added challenge of there not being a skip button to just skip card rewards. It is really frustrating at times when you don't like any of the card options. But there are some workarounds. You can spend some of the game currency to reroll the rewards. Also the rewards will include both relics and cards so preferable to just pick a relic when you don't want a card. Unwanted relics are still useful as you can actually skip those when full - or if you have a free slot can just sell it later. Recommend to reroll only once or so and not go too crazy as it gets expensive, Selling a relic will cover the cost of those rerolls generally making it worth it in the end. But even when you are forced to take a card due to bad rolls there are still some ways to keep your deck lean. There are cards that remove themselves when played - like exhaust. Those generally aren't too impactful to take since the second time through your deck will be faster with them out of play. Then there are consumable cards - they do not just exhaust from the battle, but will be gone from your deck completely until you find another one. Such consumable cards are great picks when you are happy with your cards already since you can just play them then never see again. In some cases, it may be a great strategy to keep them and use duplicating cards to copy them and spam their effects over and over. A great way to have healing sustain with a healing consumable for example.But sometimes even all that fails and it can get frustrating to take cards you really don't want. But I actually kind of like the challenge of having to be forced to pick rewards. It's a bit less stressful to me than picking whether or not to skip cards. Plus, there are way more options to remove cards in Pirates Outlaws than in Slay the Spire. It stays at a cost of 50 gold per visit to a tavern - and you can remove multiple times at one tavern trip although in that case it will increase in price per extra remove. Now -- what really surprised me is I think I may actually like this game more than Slay the Spire. It is just so full of content and reasons to replay. Maybe I am weird, but I never really liked climbing the ascensions in Slay the Spire all that much for its replayability.  What Pirates Outlaws does differently is instead have multiple "spires" to play through and 14 characters to choose from. There are six "spires" and they are basically each new themed lands with whole different sets of enemies. Each land consists of 3 stages with 3 possible bosses at the end of each stage so 9 bosses per land where you will see 3 of them each run. That's a lot of unique enemies to learn and fight against with new cards and relics per land as well; many of them specialized to deal with new enemy types such as the undead or beasts. (I have only played through the last few lands once or twice so far - so not sure if they continue the pattern of 3 bosses, but there's at least 2 variants per stage). The lands are kind of an ascension in a way in that the first land is categorized as "Normal" the next 2 as "Advanced" and the last 3 as "hard" and I would agree with those ratings based on the challenges they present. And if you still haven't had your fill, there is a sort of 7th land called the "Arena" which is really a different sort of gameplay option. There is no choosing your path through a map. Instead its a 100 battle gauntlet with options to claim rewards or spend gold to upgrade/heal after each battle etc. Every 10th stage is a boss unique to the arena and are some of the most difficult challenges I've encountered - especially floor 50 and beyond. I still have not yet reached the end.And if you still haven't had your fill, there is also a quest system where you can go to specified nodes on a map to fight unique battles or events. These quests have various rewards. Some unlock cards, some skins for your characters, and at least one quest actually unlocks a character. The hero quests are definitely worth doing for the skins and unique relics/cards that unlock for the characters, generally a sort of "ultimate" card/relic for the character.Now -- back to when I first started this game. I found myself continuously playing first to unlock and try out each character. Each run took about an hour or so since I tend to stop and think a lot. A run can probably be optimized to be closer to half an hour.  Perhaps after ever two runs or so I would unlock a new character to try out! Some of the first few characters don't feel entirely too different with some shared starting deck cards, but they really do play quite differently. The initial character Gunner is a good introduction to the game and its ammo system in place of energy. Basically, melee cards do not cost ammo and can be played freely. They generally only target the closest enemy though as a drawback. Ranged cards require ammo which can be reloaded through ammo cards. There is no passive energy reload like in Slay the Spire unless its a hero's ability or card effect (Gunner for example will always reload 1 ammo end of turn). The next character, Sword Master is where the game really starts to get fun I think since she is the opposite and prefers melee rather than ranged. Her ammo is usually best spent buffing herself and then use cards to reposition enemies and melee them to death. Her only drawback is she cannot gain block/armor. Her damage mitigation instead comes in the form of her buff (dodge) and some abilities to lifesteal on attack. She is pretty fun and will probably be a lot of people's first victory since she seems much easier to play than Gunner.I will mention each of the other characters and  my other thoughts in comments since my review got too long.I do think the game is worth a purchase at its current price, and especially on sale. If you want a cheaper alternative, then I would recommend the mobile version but the definitive Steam version is probably more my cup of tea. Or mug of rum rather, pirates and all.I also just absolutely love pirates so maybe I am biased.TLDR: Pirates cool, game good, play curse captain and laugh at enemies giving you curses and making you stronger.

_childDocuments_.review: Pirates Outlaws is a roguelite deckbuilder where the player is the captain of a pirate ship in search of fame and fortune, and must fight against Human pirates, skeletons, ghosts and monsters. The game mechanics will be very familiar to anyone who played other games in the genre such as Slay The Spire or Neoverse, although of course Pirates Outlaws has its own unique twists.Combat is turn based, with the player’s actions being represented by the cards drawn into their hand, and you’ll see what action each enemy intends to take on their turn. Melee attacks can only target the enemy closest to the player (unless the card says it damages all enemies) but are usually free to play. Ranged attacks can target any enemy but they cost ammo to play. Other cards can give the player armour (which can be carried forward to the next turn), restore health, apply status effects to the player or enemies, change the position of an enemy, or have other special effects.Unlike other games in the genre, in Pirates Outlaws most characters don’t automatically gain ammo at the start of a turn, they need to play specific cards that have a reload effect, which makes ammo management crucial. I’ve had turns where I couldn’t play any cards at all.You can only have one status effect at a time, which means when the enemy applies a negative status to you such as bleed or weak, you can replace it with a positive status like dodge, and likewise you can use a negative status to remove an enemy’s positive status. If the same status is applied multiple times it will stack, making the effect last for several turns.There are 14 playable characters who have unique abilities and playing styles. For example the Swordmaster can’t gain armour but has more ways to regain health by leeching back from damage done to enemies, while the Bear Tamer fights alongside a big brown bear who can attack enemies or give armour to their master, and the bear’s abilities become more powerful the longer a fight goes on. New characters are unlocked by earning reputation points from each playthrough.The main game mode follows a familiar three act structure. The player spends action points to sail between islands, with each island being either a battle, random event, tavern or market, and each act ends with a boss fight. Occasionally you’ll find a maelstrom which will instantly transport you to another part of the map. You can heal, restore action points, and remove cards at the tavern, while the market lets you buy or upgrade cards, and buy or sell relics. Relics provide powerful passive bonuses, and being able to sell relics that don’t fit your character build, or that only have a one time use, and put the money towards something else is a nice option that other games don’t allow.There are 6 maps unlocked through reputation points, which increase in difficulty and feature different enemies and bosses. The layout of each map is randomised during each run. A single complete run takes around 40 minutes, but there are many hours of replayability from trying to win with every character. There’s also an arena mode where every stage is a fight, judging by the achievements there are at least 100 stages, and every 10th is a boss.The only thing I don’t like about Pirates Outlaws is that the game is not good at giving useful information to the player. For example, many bosses have a special ability – one is immune to damage until you kill their minions (and they can infinitely summon more minions), one increases their damage every time you hit them, one inflicts a stackable bleed status effect every time you hit them – but you’re not given this information. Its like if you had to fight Slay the Spire’s Time Eater without knowing that every 12th card will end your turn and increase his strength. So the first time I encounter a new boss I feel like I’m pretty much guaranteed to die just because it takes a few turns to figure out what they’re doing, and in future encounters you have to work from memory (and you’ll have to remember the abilities of 9 bosses x 6 maps = 54 different bosses).Another example of where this lack of information is a problem is when you’re offered a card/relic that puts another card in your hand. Other games in the genre would allow you to hover the mouse pointer over the item and find out what that other card does, but not in Pirates Outlaws. It tells you the name of the card, but nothing else. So again, the first time you take that item you’ve no idea whether its actually worth it, and every time afterwards you have to remember what it does (or maybe find a website to look it up).Maybe this is part of the challenge that the developers want their game to have, but personally I don’t like having this information hidden from me.Despite that minor complaint, Pirates Outlaws is a good game that I’ve mostly enjoyed playing so far, the variety of playing styles offered by the different characters has kept the game interesting, and its worth picking up if you’re a fan of roguelite deckbuilders.

Large variety of enemies.Many different bosses. (at least nine per map)Large card selection, some adventure specific, so there are lots of new combos to discover.They have added new game types, basically arena with drafting.Every month or so they add something new.Cons:Not very much information on what some abilities and enemy intentions are. _childDocuments_.review: I liked this game at first until I noticed all the heroes draw from the same huge pool of cards. This does not only mean there's not a lot of variety between heroes, it also means the luck of the draw is that much more important. The more cards you unlock in the game the less chances there are of finding cards that have synergy with each other. In other words in contrast to other roguelikes this game because harder and harder the more you play. Not because the enemies require more strategy to beat but because the odds of getting good cards and items get worse and worse. And you can't skip rewards. You can however change the rewards by paying 25 coins, but then you're 25 coins poorer and you still need the luck of drawing good rewards. I'm sure someone smarter than me can probably find a way to gain the advantage in this game but it's not accessible to say the least.

_childDocuments_.review: is a roguelike deckbuilding card game that is in Early Access. It's a decent game and fairly well-designed, though the asking price for the current Early Access build is a bit high, given how many other deckbuilding card games are out there.The game has an in-game tutorial and is very easy to learn.The game starts off on a map that you can choose different paths to different islands. Every path will lead to an end boss, and in similar such games, you can expect each island to help or hinder your progress. On some islands, you will encounter battles, on others, some random events, taverns, or markets.There is a limit to how much you can travel though, so you will have to consider this a limited resource as well. You will find relics or new cards along your way, or you can remove cards, etc.The battles are done with cards. You have basically 3 action points available at the start of your fight for attacking or defending. These action points are labeled as "Ammo" and if you use them, you will have to "Reload." Some cards allow for reloading, while each turn, you will reload automatically one of these "Ammo" rounds. Cards that you play will rely on "Ammo" and you have to use your limited resources. Some cards do not cost anything, so you can play even when you have zero rounds left. There are 3 chapters and each has a few stages, along with 40 in-game achievements. However, there are no Steam achievements as of this time. It would be nice to add those as well.The game in its current state already contains so many things to unlock, such as new chapters, new skins, new cards, new heroes, more storage, as well as an arena mode. Some you will need Repute which you will earn by playing the game, while others you will unlock when you reach specific goals.Everything looks bright and clear. The artwork is in the style of paper cut outs. I really like the general appearance of the game.The music is befitting of the theme, and the sound effects are fine. But after a while, you might find the continually repetitive theme a bit too much.The game can be fully played with a mouse.Here's where the game feels like it's over-reaching a bit. I do think that the base price is a bit high. Base price of €16.79 EU/$19.99 US while the game is in Early Access means that the current build should have more content, gameplay, and polish than a lot of similar deck-building roguelikes/lites just based on the price. I do think this game is fun, but it's not offering so much as that. And the planned price will be higher after release.With the right price tag (€9.99 in my opionion) it would probably sell more copies and get some more positive feedback. Instead, it's a price tag along with the Early Access tag that tends to drive a lot of potential players away. is a fun deckbuilding roguelike with fun gameplay. But there are too many other similar card games released on Steam with better pricing that are also solid games. If the price were better, I would have given it a full out recommendation, because it is very good. Though as the way things are with the pricing in Early Access, I would say that waiting for a sale is probably a better option for most people.There are in-game achievements, but no Steam achievemeents yet, that will hopefully get added.Overall a really good game and can be good in short bursts or it can draw you in for lengthy sittings.

_childDocuments_.review: This game came out on mobile a while back, and I've loved the mobile version.  I've unlocked mostly everything in the mobile version, along with all but 2 achievements, and really don't get tired of it.  It ties in the randomness factor of a dice-rolling game into something with strategy and pattern recognition when playing with the AI.  Recognizing moments when not attacking is the best option, and when not defending is the best call makes each playthrough of the game slightly unique from the last time.  The different characters to choose from have different pros and cons to them, with some having a higher curve than others.  It's what I would consider to be a well-rounded game, and one that I've assisted with finding and reporting bugs on.The Development group seems quite responsive to bugs and feedback from players, and I would recommend it to people that are looking for a game that you can putter away at, put away, and pick up again later right from where you left off.  Experiences can range from 20 minutes for a map to 60-120 minutes for the arena mode.  The drive to unlock more cards and then play again with anticipation of using the newly unlocked cards gives some enthusiasm to play it repeatedly.  And even after unlocking all the cards and relics, trying to get just the right combo of cards to try something crazy out is a fun time.I would recommend this game to anyone with a Desktop or mobile platform to play it on.  You will have frustrating moments that will make you rage quit the game for a bit, but you will likely come back to it, eager to try something new.  The game isn't perfect, but that doesn't mean it's not approaching perfection.7 stacks of injury out of 7 for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I love card games as I played MTG for a big amount of time and have a bit less than 150 hours in Slay the Spire. This game attracted me first by the pirate theme and made a huge change from StS. Is it better now? I won't say it is better because it is different. I believe I still prefer StS (in my opinion it is the master of it's own genre), But Pirates Outlaws does everything great as well.First of all let's make a list of the major differences the game has versus StS:- Energy to travel : when you travel on the map between stages and levels your ship has a limited amount of energy that allows you or not to travel from a point to another. This leads you to try and predict which path you want to go and put a little bit of difficulty when you need to face various problems and change the route you chose.- Reload system : in StS every character starts with 3 energy and restores on the start of each turn. Here in PO, you have a limited amount of bullets and you need to use the bullet card to reload when you use too much ranged attacks. Pistols blasts and some other ranged attacks costs bullets to play, where melee attacks costs nothing. This can lead to create different types of decks when you play along those two mechanics.- Armor stays between turns : the title says it all. In StS, if you gain armor but take less damage or nothing at all, the exceeding armor will disappear at the beggining of your next turn. Here, in PO, you sustain the exceeding amount or protection between turns. This allows you to prevent dying like a noob if you think about it some turns in advance (and as a huge noob myself, it is very helpful).- Mini-bosses : as I traveled alongs maps, I noticed there was no mini-bosses or elites, as StS would have call them. This is the main difference that makes gaining relics a bit harder in PO. Where in StS you need to defeat elites to get relics or buy them at the shop, in PO it seems like you can only buy them or find them while looting enemies. Which is not bad, but makes the relics a bit more rare.- Importance of the money : the money you gain from combat is hella important. Everything is done with money. Of course, you can loot cards and relics for free after a combat, but when you need to rest or to upgrade cards, it is mostly done with money. There are events that allows you to chose between both of these options for free, but in my experience they have been a bit more rare. You also can buy cards and relics, which, again, makes the money very important.- Re-rolling loot : an awesome mechanic that dosen't exist in StS as far as I know is when you win a battle, you get to choose one card/relic among 3 that are presented to you. But, if you are unsatisfied with the choices you have, you can reroll the loot and get now propositions. Although you can only reroll by paying money which makes my last point even more important.- Skipping loot : in StS, when you get to loot enemies, you can skip the loot that dosen't fit your deck. Here, I did not see any options to do so and this pushes you to reroll and lose money everytime the loot dosen't fit your deck. That makes the game a bit more RNG based and could, with a lot of badluck, ruin a run. HOWEVER, someone who knows how to makes changes to their decks to adapt to their loot will have no problem moving forward. For me, it is a negative point, but definetly not a dealbreaker.There are probably a lot more differences between the two games, but I might just not think of them for now. I want to mention that as I write this review, I have only played 1.5 hours and did not progress too far in the game. This is more of a "surface" review. Anyway I managed to die in the tutorial so this is written from a noob perspective.Moving forward, now, let's talk about the pros and cons :Pros :- Great soundtrack- Simple but nice and classy graphics- Innovative mechanics that makes the game very different of others- Large amount of characters and playstyles, plus every character has a large amount of skins you can unlock while playing- Runs *very well* on my potato pcCons :- Maps are kind of short and you don't run out of energy too often, making the mechanic sometimes useless- In the short experience I have, I feel like enemies are repetitive, but I could be wrong- Relics in general are a bit too hard to get for the bonus they give you- Not being able to skip loot when I don't want to reroll is a bit weird to meIf I had to point out what could be improved (these are not cons for me, more like flaws that may be easy to fix) :- According to the first boss Red Beard, I feel like it lacks of mechanics and feels like a normal enemy. The combat is still challenging as he deals a lot of damage and has a big life bar, but still feel like a random enemy.- Making relics more efficient and various ways to get them without paying- Making a little bit more enemies which would help the encounter be various (and give special mechanics/abilities that makes every enemies different from one another)- PLS ALLOW ME TO SKIP REWARDS T^T (and everything else in the cons list I've made up there)Conclusion :A very fun game that costs a reasonnable amount of money (I paid it 11$ at 50% promotion). It brings a couple of new mechanics and the variety of character you can play makes runs differrent from each other. Love the ambiance, music and graphics are very well done.The game feels like it's creators put love and work in it. I definetly would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: At first I really liked this game. It had an interesting art style. There appeared to be a lot of meta progression. The combat, while very similar to Slay the Spire, had some interesting differences related to enemy positioning.However, 20 hours in, I am starting to really not like this game. So far, every unlockable character is a joke and basically unplayable. There is WAY too much reliance on chance, to the point where your runs are essentially just flipping a coin over and over. Bosses (and enemies as well) tend to scale preposterously, though there seems to be no cards that scale for you. Some other things: - the ammo as energy system is cool, but ill conceived when you take into account that your deck continues to grow (you can't skip rewards), but you only have your starting ammo. (I've yet to see a way to get draft more ammo cards...maybe unlocked after 100 hours? lol) When your blocks takes up ammo too, it's just a matter of time until you hit a bad turn and die.- the money and AP system add no enjoyment to the game. Your boat sails around until you run out of AP, then it will sink. You can get more at Harbors, but you can only refill to 100% and it's always 100 gold. Imagine going to a gas station and it always cost a flat amount to refill. Well, you can wait to the last minute to get max value and run out of gas. Or go early and lose value. Yes, there is strategy there, but it doesn't feel good. Especially since that money your wasting is money that you NEED for upgrades, healing and card removal. Managing money is thus impossible, and  you can't even see how much AP the total path is. You're always poor and it always feels bad.-Just too much RNG. You can grind through the progression and presumably unlock more powerful stuff, but it's all just total luck whether you win a run or not, and it's not enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyable card game, it's not frustratingly difficult like most others in the genre. I was very pleasantly surprised and enjoyed it alot for the first few hours. However, there are some rather silly design decisions that sour the experience.You can only have one buff/debuff at a time. That means that if you buff your character with Dodge, the first enemy can still hit you with a debuff that overwrites your Dodge, and that leaves the 2nd and 3rd enemy free to mollywhop you.I'm also having a hard time understanding the choice to make Dodge and Blind only 50%. Play as the Sword Master where dodging is your main defense, the fact that it only works half the time if you're lucky, makes for a rather aggravating experience. I'd rather strategize my way to winning, rather than praying RNG doesn't kick me in the nuts.Edit: Gave the game another try, and actually had quite a bit of fun - was considering changing my review despite the crap that is the Buff/Debuff mechanic...Untill I came upon the Sentinel boss-fight. What's the point of something that can only be won by building your deck a very specific way, and on top of that, only with certain champions.

_childDocuments_.review: I've got almost 200 hours into this game on my phone and this is a pretty good port. There are differences between the two games (most notably pay-to-unlock is available in the mobile version and not here), but the gameplay is the same. The challenge of starting over appeals to me as well -- the cards are a bit different than on the phone, though, so there's a very minor adjustment for those players who come over from the mobile version. Also, in-game card upgrades are more expensive on the PC in "coins" than they are in the mobile version.Gameplay is smooth, very quick and, as many have mentioned, it's a lot like STS. Some of the complaints I've seen about the game in terms of managing deck size are a little spurious -- the clever player can manage desk size through selection of one-off or cards removed after a single use. You need to think ahead.In all, though, a very satisfying purchase and as much fun as the mobile. Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: My first impressions of this game were that it was too simple. There's no saving cards in your hand for the next turn, there's only one buff/debuff allowed at a time. I actually refunded it the first time, but then decided to give it another try because I did really like the art style and the pirate setting. My first impressions were very wrong. This game is complex, and you have to actively work at managing all resources (including your buffs/debuff and any "curse" cards), particularly for certain heroes you may play as. There is a fair RNG element to the game in which loot you get and which bosses you encounter, but I find that it gives it a challenge, and the game gives you ways to prune decks or items as you progress. I like the Slay the Spire format, and I love the pirate theme. Worth the money!PS, excellent on steam deck!

_childDocuments_.review: Let's be honest, most of you are here because you love Slay The Spire and you are looking for another game that can scratch that itch. WELL LOOK NO FURTHER. TL;DR... this game is AWESOME and it is well worth the money. If you want details, keep reading.This game takes the STS formula and multiplies it by 10. Now, a lot of games claim to do that but they get so lost in their own mechanics it just feels like a different game. Which is fine. This game however is the exact STS formula but improved in every way. Because you are already familiar with STS, you will feel right at home diving into this game. I'm going to do a quick pros/cons, please be aware these are direct comparison to STS.Pros -- 1) Where STS gives you 4 unique characters, this game gives you 16 if I counted correctly. Yes, each with their own decks and dynamics, just like STS. So a LOT more character variation which adds tons of strategic options.2) Characters also have different skins you can unlock, giving a light bit of customization to the experience.3) Card affects are explained just like in STS. Just hover over the card, it tells you what the card does, and includes descriptions of any special modifiers or effects. In some other STS inspired games, the card UI is so terrible it takes away from the enjoyment. Not in this game. You won't get confused in the mechanics. 4) In STS you have a 3 tier ladder with unique bosses at the end. Same here. The difference with this game is, it has multiple worlds. Each with unique enemies and dynamics. And each world has multiple difficulty levels. So the gameplay is expanded greatly in this game. I am 40 hours in as of this writing and I have unlocked maybe 20% of what I can and haven't even played every world yet. 5) FREAKING PIRATES YO! YARRRRRRRR!!!!Cons -- 1) STS has better graphics. Hopefully there will be updates to this game to improve on that in the future. This game is really more about your strategy playing, which is excellent and super fun. But if you are expecting eye candy as far as battle animations, you will be disappointed. I understand with the vast array of characters, worlds, and enemies this game offers, that may have had to take a back seat in development. But it is worth mentioning, and improving on this would elevate this game to one of the best in the genre. 2) The main hud can be a little confusing going in. Fear not, this is a minor annoyance, and after playing for awhile you will get used to it and things will make more sense. But I feel like the hud design could use some minor improvements. Which if the devs read this, I would be happy to elaborate on. All of that out of the way, I freaking LOVE this game. It's addicting, there is a ton to unlock and explore, and it is very very fun. Great job to the devs and I hope this game will do well enough for you that you can continue making great games, because gameplay wise this is one of the best in this genre I have encountered. In many ways, superior to STS, and deserves to be in the conversation when ANYBODY discusses these types of games.  Thanks for reading gamers, cheers.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty alright, even if somewhat on the repetetive side. Doesn't break any new ground, as it doesn't have any new exciting mechanics to speak of other than the management of a single non-replenishing resource used for a lot of cards, but I'd say it more than makes up for that with the boatloads of content. _childDocuments_.review: This game is addicting! I have trouble playing games because I'm picky, this game has 10/10 art direction and the gameplay is fun as well. Usually the artsier the game the worse the gameplay but this game manages to do well with both. The rougelike-ness of the game keeps every session fresh and I'm having such a great time with it. There's also a lot of content which is nice as well and the pirate theme is pretty dope as well.EDIT: So I've played now for about 12 hours and I keep dying on the first mission. I thought that my progress would be rewarded but this game can be very unfair and it's really stingy about giving you any sort of rewards for anything. Even after a while I noticed that I wasn't able to build a deck with the cards I was unlocking. Even some of the bigger prizes that come from just playing the game for a while were too bad to justify the hours of playtime. For example I played for 10 hours dying on the first baord trying to get to the 3rd area and I finally earned enough points from losing to get a ship upgrade. This upgrade that I worked for 10 hours; apparently all it does is give me a 20% chance of spending less money on something that's usually not even an issue... Like the game is really stingy and I want to play more but it's really frustrating to play for 12 hours and not get any better. Especially I'm making HUGE plays and trying really hard when I play only to die from unavoidable things. It just doesn't feel like this game rewards the time you put into it so why should I bother playing? It feels like the game does as little as possible to improve your starting cards or situation no matter how much work you put in, and the game is really really hard. It shouldn't be this hard to beat one quest.RE-EDIT: So I'm still playing the game and I've kind of just become okay with losing. I've won a few times now with Gunner. As it turns out the game gets easier for Gunner as you unlock more cards. I also found a couple helpful tips online. All in all this is a great game and I'm still playing it for as long as I feel it will be fun. The losses sting less when you care about improving your overall skill. Winning feels amazing and well earned. I do wish there were more upgrades to unlock with higher repute because currently it does feel like you will just lose a lot more than you'll win. But then again I'm still playing and there's tons to learn still. I've put almost 24 hours into this game in the last few days and it's been an extremely rewarding game to play.

_childDocuments_.review: 4.3/5 good neo-roguelike card with decent vector graphics and some interesting mechanics. Needs a 'restart battle' button like Across the Obelisk -- too many fights are lost due to uneven random card draws, especially at harder levels.Other flaws include it being too expensive to remove cards and related inability to skip card pickups.  Th game plays hints including keeping deck tight, which is not really an option.  Also the monsters and bosses should have more visual/textual hints to remind one of their special abilities. Designers want it to be obscure, but it's too obscure. Fights can be  restarted with new random seed by quitting mid fight, but it's annoying. Absolutely necessary for enjoying the late game: even the best deck with top artifacts and perfect play , one can lose badly to weak monsters -- Tedious and frustrating.But, overall, good game.

_childDocuments_.review: Wish there was a 'meh' option.It's Slay the Spire, except everything has been adjusted to disadvantage the player. You MUST pick up a card after every fight, you occasionally have to give up gold or encounters to patch up your ship, all cards from all builds are in one excessively gigantic pool, you're limited in how many relics you can carry, you have a hand size of five and cannot increase it, and your energy does not regenerate by itself. _childDocuments_.review: + Well executed and original art direction+ Many characters and builds+ Nice for chilling- Ridiculous grinding (to unlock characters, regions, etc)- Repetitive gameplay, most enemies don't require specific strategies (only boss and few normal monsters tbh)- Poor gameplay, low amount of tactic required beyond the deckbuilding partShallow waters.... shallow gameplay. The deckbuilding mechanics are the only important part of the game, rest relying on luck and spamming your cards. There are few options in fights as a lot of cards demand amunitions, but these choices become very easy and obvious as time pass. Most enemies feel the same because of a lack of impactful mechanics, at the exception of most bosses and few enemies. One advantage of this is that I could chill while playing, and that's it.There is no story, but a meta progression that is quite boring : you just play the game, and every run give you x coins (depending on win/lose), it automaticaly unlock something. Wow, incredible.Talking about coins, the game is a f***** grind machine. I have played 15h and yet not unlocked everything, not to mention quests that are equally grindy (do this thing on this region that you have already played 100 times :).I really enjoy the minimalistic graphisms overall. All cards look good, so do characters, enemies and battlegrounds. The UI does its job well.The soundtrack is somewhat good, but way too short in content in regards to the amount of grinding hours required to finish the game, and the sound design is really cheap for the most part. Most sounds don't feel any close to realistic, and fail to grasp the fantasy of a pirate world.I was really enjoying the game as a chilling method after work, but I got bored at some point. The game pretends to have a lot of content, but this is not the case actually, most of it being blocked by "grinding barriers" anyway. I do not recommand this lazy game that took Slay The Spire and mixed it with addiction//grind methods.Personnal note : 4/10

_childDocuments_.review: Pirates Outlaws:~~~~~~~~~~~~~Ahoy, me hearties! Arrgh … Arrgh! Are you ready to take to the sea, sailors? Arrgh…. But it won’t be easy sailing, let me tell you! There is plenty of gold for the taking, as well as dangerous islands to pass through, and terrifying enemies to defeat.  Locate the largest island, find a way to navigate there and beat the hell out of the big boss. . .  Arrgh! What!? You already beat one! And you think sunbaking on the beach looking like a lobster is a good idea? Get to your ship and ravage all the islands in Pirates Outlaws!   Pirates Outlaws is a turn-based / casual roguelike card game developed by Fabled Game and published by BlueStacks on the 28 August 2019 on the Steam platform. The game is also available on mobile devices on Google Play and the Apple App Store. However, my review is based solely through the Steam version gameplay.As you launch the game, you’ll be prompted by a minimal tutorial and then will arrive on the main menu page. On this screen, you’ll be presented with a few options. First, you can choose which hero you’d like to play. They are nine in total, but at the start of the game, you’ll only be able to select one until you reach a certain number of reputes to unlock the other characters. Each of these characters will have a specific ability (some have a few), health points, ammo (which are yellow spheres, usually three but some have two), and a number of coins they will start the game with. They will also have an exclusive pre-set deck of cards (10) each. There are skins to unlock too, but you must beat the game on each of the game modes to unlock them.The game modes are the Arena and Navigate. Only the navigate will be available on your first go. There are three maps available for selection, but only one will be accessible at the start. And yes, you need to have a specific number of reputes to unlock the other two. The gameplay is fun and addictive. In this mode, you’ll have two screens; one will be the map (with islands, rocks, markets and taverns) and the other one is the cards turn-based combat. On the Island map, you’ll have to move your ship either right or left towards the next island, rocks or shipwreck until you reach the top island to face the big boss. Each time you move your ship, it will cost you several moving points; you can track your remaining points below the boat wheel on the bottom left of your screen. If you run out of movement points, your next move will have a 25% chance of your ship sinking, and this will double each turn. So, death will arrive in the next three moves unless you manage to visit a tavern. There, you’ll be able to purchase movement points, health, sell relics or remove one or more unwanted cards from your deck. When you reach a market, you’ll be able to upgrade cards, and/or purchase cards or relics if you have enough coins. If you decide to move toward rocks and shipwrecks it will trigger an event. Most of the events end up with great goodies, but others can cost you many health points, and you might even receive a curse to top it off! The combat screen is straightforward. Under your character there will be either two or three yellow spheres (depending on the character you selected at the start of the game). That represents your ammo. At the bottom of the screen you’ll have 5 cards which will be randomised at the start of each turn. Some of the cards will have a yellow sphere with a number in it on the top left, which will indicate how much ammo you need in order to use these cards. Cards that don’t have a yellow sphere are basically free to use. At the end of each battle you’ll be rewarded with coins and presented with three cards, from which you must select one. You may have a relic card within the mix, too, and it could be a good one! As you battle your way to the big island, your deck of cards will grow, causing the game to become harder and harder to play along the way.    The Arena mode is a dual-mode type of gameplay where you will face between one, two or three enemies per round, and the main goal is to win 30 rounds in a row. However, this mode will be locked until you reach a certain number of reputes.  Charming and polished graphics and the game is fun and addictive. What I like is that each run is randomised in terms of what relics and new cards you collect during that gameplay. It’s even better when you start unlocking new characters. In terms of settings you can select up to 2560 X 1440 in resolution, and the game has been translated into nine languages: German, French, Russian, Spanish, Chinese, Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Korean and of course English. In terms of controls, you can play this game entirely with a mouse. A robust Early Access.Positives:~~~~~~~+	Colourful and polished graphics+	Easy to play and very addictive+	Two modes of play+	Nine different characters+	300 cards and 100 relicsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	No achievements-	No trading cards as yetAn excellent, addictive turn-based / casual roguelike card game! Ahoy, me hearties, it’s time for you to experience Pirates Outlaws!7/10 Key provided by developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: Most reviews cite Slay the Spire, of which this is a poor copy that seems worse at both more and less. Pirates Outlaws is heavily rogue-LITE, in that there is A LOT to grind and unlock. The "real game" is mostly hidden past a timewall, one hopefully long enough to get you out of Steam refund's policy. As opposed to the mobile version that asks you to pay to skip the grind, the Steam version just charges up front ... and then leaves in the grind. Maybe it's even grindier on mobile.The mechanics have less synergy than competitors like Slay the Spire, in part by dumping all the cards into one pool rather than per-character, in part with its mechanic of allowing just 1 buff or debuff on a character. This is a potentially interesting mechanic that effectively requires players to carry buffs and debuffs but not rely on them. A classic poison or bleed deck will not work when blinding the enemy instantly cures its poison, as does getting drunk, as does the enemy buffing itself.The mechanics that are not obvious are not really documented. Keywords show their definitions, but cards do not show what cards they create. Bosses get around the one buff issue by having undocumented buffs that you can work out through trial and error, like damage immunity or a thorns aura. There ARE visual indicators, but those are the visuals of the characters themselves, not anything like an icon. The icons themselves are going for language independence, which is convenient for selling a game in multiple countries but problematic when the icons are not always present or useful indicators.Early on, there do not seem to be enough customization options, as opposed to grinding runs to unlock the options that make the game interesting and/or balanced. All I see at this point is a long horizon of potential grinds, and there are better games to grind. I have requested a refund rather than go further and hope it gets better.

_childDocuments_.review: I have this on mobile and have played it for years. While I've gotten a lot of enjoyment and hours out of the mobile version (which is $0.99 I believe but has MANY available in-app purchases that would add up to about $15-20ish if you bought them all), I agree with other reviewers who complain about the balance of the game and the shared card pool between all heroes. I recently picked this back up on mobile after returning the Steam version and am working on completing quests and unlocking things, and it just gets harder as you unlock more cards to find the ones you want for any particular build. I tried doing a drunk build on Explorer like five or six times last night and couldn't make it happen because the cards and relics never lined up. Heroes having their own card pools (with some shared cards between heroes) would make this a 1000x better. The game is HARD, which is ok but a lot of the hardness comes from reliance on luck rather than strategy. I was stoked to have this on PC because I'm tired of playing games on my phone but I found the controls with the controller quite wonky. The keyboard/mouse controls are probably fine but with my setup I am pretty much controller only nowadays.If you find it on sale for like half off, I'd say it's worth giving a shot. But the $20 is a lot considering it's mostly taking into account optional in-app purchases to get to that price and the issues with balance and the controller.

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely fun deck building rouge-like. Wonderful swashbuckling atmosphere and art. Unlocking characters and cards, and then building powerful card synergies are all very addictive. Definitely worth getting on sale. Alternatively, but the game for a few bucks on a mobile app-store. (Almost all content is available to unlock for free on mobile, but the progression is slower. And imo, is more rewarding this way)For those complaining about not being able to skip reward cards that are given, there are workarounds. (But honestly, this is a Rouge-like game. Each play through is different and forces you to adopt new strategies and card synergies. If you aren't prepared to improvise then I suggest you reevaluate if this genre is for you. )Firstly, The RNG card reward-er is not as random as you might think. It often offers you cards with themes you have already built on (like "shield," "reload," "multi-hit," or "injury") so pick your first couple cards wisely. They will likely affect your "random" options down the road. You can also spend 25 to re-roll rewards or spend 50 to remove cards at taverns. Try picking relics (to sell later), consumable (single-use) cards, or a "self-removing" (once-per-battle) card for temporary or minimal effects on deck composition. Keeping "self-removing" cards in your deck makes you more likely to receive them in the future as well.If you are a beginner, don't worry. It gets easier as you unlock more powerful cards and relics with more play-throughs.

Altered from the StS mechanic of having bad starting cards and limited card removal, thus encouraging an ever growing deck to bring up the average value of cards, instead the meta becomes ALWAYS to choose relics whenever possible from these rewards unless a card HAPPENS to fit into the strategy you are trying to play into.
