_childDocuments_.review: When I first started this game, I was confused that there are no difficulty sliders or ascension mechanics like in other roguelike deckbuilders.I soon discovered that the reason for this is that the difficulty of each run is utterly random, and even the best card picking ability will only marginally affect your chance of survival.I should preface that I have played and thoroughly enjoyed StS and several other deckbuilding roguelikes, against which this one simply does not stack up.The two biggest offenders:1) All characters share the same card pool, and that card pool is . There are more than ten characters, and except for the first two, I have not seen a single card that supports the character's gimmick. For example, one character has the gimmick that she has an animal companion that can be ordered to do certain actions. Turns out, apart from her starting deck, there are ZERO cards in the game (at least in the first 41 hours of continually unlocking stuff) that reference the animal companion at all. Basically, if you want to use the companion, you have to stick with the starting deck throughout the entire game.This problem applies to all the characters except the first two, whose gimmicks are compatible with basically any playstyle (and consequently make for 1000% easier runs than the other characters).2) The game wants to be an exploration game. Granted, there are TONS of unlocks and quests and whatnot, which is fun. But the devs also extend the exploration aspect to the player, to a point that is decidedly not fun anymore. Most mechanics are not explained, and a majority of buffs and debuffs are invisible. Did that boss use his  buff two times or three? Better make sure you counted, 'cause the game sure won't tell you! This elite just used a buff. What does the buff do, you ask? ♥♥♥♥ if I know! You can have this relic, but it will give you the curse . What does  do? Why don't you take the relic and find out, hahaha!Sure, this is cute and fun the first few times it happens, but after the hundredth run or so that ends because you picked a card where the game  and it turns out that card somehow kills you? It starts being tedious. (For example, the aforementioned curse makes it such that you .)All in all, I concur with other reviews here: the game is kind of fun for the first few hours while you are playing the two tutorial characters and exploring new things with a sense of wonder. After about 20 hours it turns into a pure RNG-fest where the game essentially does stuff to you and you watch while the devs every once in a while point at a piece of storytelling and go 'hey, look at this stuff! Isn't it neat? Wouldn't you say my collection's complete?'. No, that's Arielle. But you get my point.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay I played for about 8 hours today I have played slay the spire for about a couple hundred hours and can say that this is a similar game. The graphics are kind of meh compared to the ones on slay the spire there are not really any animations in STS but the colors pop and draw your attention. This game does look good in its own way and is still very enjoyable to look at but can use some more work in that area for sure. The cards are all pretty simple you can build some nice decks and do a couple different strategies like STS without as much difficulty or confusion. Now where this game does excel and beat STS is its characters there are so many more out already than STS and they all have their own unique synergies with the cards as well as their own playstyle. The game also introduces a reward system for playing giving you things like more health and relic space ECT. I do not like the part that restricts how many relics you can have that kind of ruins the experience for me I like to make GOD like runs with tons of relics but its still do-able. I would give this game a 6 out of ten as it stands right now it is in early access so hopefully the developers will fix and update some of the issues. The game overall though has a lot of promise. I would say it is worth the 15 I got it for not sure if 20 would be worth it but if you like rouge lite games give this a shot 100%.

_childDocuments_.review: While it looks very cool, has nice music and runs very smoothly, this is a copy of Slay the spire. And it would be a decent one, even better perhaps. But imagine playing chess without knowing the rules. Yes, it's fun, it's exciting, it's action all the time. Until you lose. Now, I don't mind losing like a normal person. But what makes this game awful is you don't know WHY you lost. Because rules aren't explained. Opponents aren't explained. Abilities are barely explained. Mobs are there just to frustrate you: try this, oh no, that did nothing, try that, oh my, fail again, well now you're dead. Try to solve this mystery and get back to us. No. I won't. This is the worst format of gaming. Just die several thousand of times and you report back. Oh, you're losing HP and you don't know why? Tough! Suck less! If you don't mind spending weeks on forums, wikia, or such, sure, this could be a good game. Without it? No. Look at the global achievements. You will get those achieved by more than 50% players in 10 hours. Because no one will play this after that. If you like frustration and have several hundred hours to spend, this is the game for you, I hope you enjoy it, I didn't! Have a nice day!

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another game that is similar to 'Slay the Spire'. However, card effects are rather uninspired and there are few synergies. Since only a single (de)buff can ever be active on yourself or a particular enemy, exciting combos are almost impossible. As a result, luck of the draw is a significant factor leading to a rather frustrating experience.Also, in the beginning only a single character is playable. _childDocuments_.review: Just play Slay The Spire.  That game did things correctly.  This one tried a different approach and it didn't work.So, after a (LONG) while of hating this game, I gave it another shot.  It's better but still no where near fair or balanced.  The problem is that I like the concept but I hate the execution.  It falls just short of being "good" IMO.Another thing: there is no true "random."  Everything is heavily weighted and different characters have different weights on cards and artifacts so the most useful ones almost never show up.  Ammo cards are too often hoarded by the game and given at the least opportune times (often all at once).  If the enemy has very little health left, the game will draw out the fight one more round by holding back your attack cards.  If you're about to take mortal damage, the game will hold back your armor cards...etc.  Also, "dodge" (50% chance to avoid damage) procs about 15-25% of the time for the player but 75-90% of the time for a Boss and if your health is low, you can all but forget about it working where as a Boss will be near impossible to hit.  Boss with 15 hit points left dodged 7 attacks in a row.  Yeah, sure, game, what ever you say.  I'd call it bad luck on my part but it's to the point where it's predictable. You also can not get your character's cards as combat rewards.  Every character's rewards are from the same pool.  It gets very generic.  There's also almost no way to get copies of your starting cards (the only unique cards each character gets) unless you use a "copy card" option in the game (does not show up often).  Which means that the Fortuneteller's unique cards (the ones she is based around) are always buried in a deck of generic bloat.  There's no reason to have a character with a unique deck if you've got 10 unique cards and 59 generic ones.  It's bad design.Also, avoid the mobile version.  It's a paid app with Free To Play mechanics and "gotcha" moments (times when the game just gives you the finger and you loose) out the wazoo.  Paid app with the best cards/features locked behind a pay wall is a scumbag thing to do.

_childDocuments_.review: This game saved my life.I am 37.My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old.When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide.After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ing minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay.After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as.Today, I am close friend with my kids mother. We don't fight, or argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents, and friends.I now have 3 kids. My third child is, wait for it, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my own separation, and we just stumbled in to each others life unexpectedly. We have been in a relationship for a year now, and are very happy together.Moral of the story, you never know what life holds in store for you, and if I would have given up when all the odds were stacked against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. _childDocuments_.review: My 4-minute review video can be seen here: Pirates Outlaws is a fast paced deckbuilding roguelike which lets you control unique characters accompanied by extremly diverse cards, in a simplisticly stylized world with various different maps and enemies to face. The first impression of the games simplicity can be deceiving since the combat speed and the strategic weight each of the limited hand cards has combines perfectly in one of the three modes and results in a rather addictive gameplay loop. In the first mode we start every run with one of 16 drastically different heroes and work our way through more islands than the One Piece manga, facing numerous enemies, encountering various events, shops and taverns on our way to the final endboss of three levels. Reaching each island chips away from our ships endurance in form of action points, this resource has to be taken into account when planning out a route since a lacking management skill can result in a quick ending. Finishing a run unlocks further cards and rewards us with repute which works together with milestones we can reach. These milestones unlock further characters we can play as well as new maps, enemies and bosses to face. Taking on these enemies is done in a turn and card based as well as a heavily hand and bullet limited combat system. Each hero has melee, range and skill cards working together in sinergy and need to be cleverly used, which at first seems dawnting but due to the mentioned limit of hand cards strategies and sinergies are being formed naturally. This results in a satisfying learning curve and sees us quickly ramping up the repute we need for more heroes. Having a large roster of creatively designed heroes to choose from offers enourmous amounts of replayability. Two perfect examples could be the alchemist who can combine cards temporarily creating completely new ways to fight, while the carpenter stacks up a damaging buff which renders him useless the next turn when reaching a certain number. Each hero requires us to experiment with its skillset to work around their strengths and weaknesses. This results in hours of fun since any felt monotony can be brilliantly avoided by just picking another hero. Apart from the various cards we obtain with every battle, we can further equip our hero with relicts which can fundamentally change our playstyle. With a particular set of skills (TAKEN) I mean relicts we can equip we further enhance our progress during a run by enhancing our cards or remove unwanted ones. The games combat system changes up the usual style by two small differences with the armor being carried over to every round and only one buff being applicable. This allows us to strategically manipulate our own buffs and debuffs as well as the enemies. We have a huge bleeding debuff, no worries, a quick sip of rum and we are drunk instead, which as we all know is a form of alternative medicine.Reaching a high repute score sees us unlock two more modes with the arena and the tavern brawl. The former puts us against a constant stream of battles while after every finished fight we get a number of choices to enhance our character and deck for the upcoming battles. These fights number up to 100 while every 10th battle puts a boss in our way.The Tavern Brawl is slightly different with only three battles to fight, while our heroes deck is filled with cards from themed packages accompanied by a relic. The first two battles have one further rule namely that we are facing five waves of enemies in one go, while the last encounter puts us in front of the tavern keeper, a challenging boss with three stances and an alcohol problem.These three game modes would suffice to provide a great amount of replayability but the game has one more addition with quests and bounties. These give us further goals we need to reach during a run in one of the maps of the main mode, while the rewards mostly are beautiful new skins for our heroes. Those skins are not limited to our heroes but can give our ship some style.This choice of three different modes, a roster of 16 unique heroes, 700 diverse cards and over 60 bosses lets Pirates Outlaws stretch out the term of replayability. With a simplistic yet charming artstyle and shanty esque music the game delivers a relaxing ambient. The sound design however fell flat for me regarding the constant sound every single card and action made, culminating to a barrage of sounds. Luckily we can turn off those soundeffects giving us the chance to brilliantly immerse ourselves into the pirate theme.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a Rogue-lite card battler similar to Slay the Spire. At first glance, I thought the game was decent, but not great. There's a wide variety of captains you can choose, and they all have completely different strengths and weaknesses. There's a fair amount of relics and a boatload of card options. There's a number of levels, and each one has a unique biome, and unique enemies and bosses. It wasn't until I got into the quests that I really started enjoying myself. They forced me to try out the different captains instead of just the ones I was immediately interested in playing. Some of them grew on me. Others I just learned to despise. The game does variety really well. There's a ton of different playstyles and builds that will work. But since there's so much content, sometimes getting what you need to be successful is difficult, so you'll fail simply due to RNG. My #1 gripe with this game is just what makes some of the combats difficult: They like to add negative cards to your deck, or give you effects that restrict your plays. I really don't like it when strategy games restrict your agency. Why would I want to go through all the effort of making a great deck only to have it massacred via unstoppable card mechanics? It's also why I very much disliked the curse captain. Going whole rounds without making a card play seems like the antithesis of strategy. TLDR: I got 100 hours in the game. Well worth the $20 I paid for it.  I loved the art style.  I enjoyed the quests, and I loved how many captains there were to play. All in all, a pretty good game. No where near the level of STS, but still pretty good. Who knows, in the future I might go back to it.

_childDocuments_.review: Pirates Outlaws is a very fun and addicting deck building roguelike that plays very differently from other deck building roguelikes such as Slay the Spire.Why on Steam: Correct me if I'm wrong but this game is actually a Steam port of a free-to-play google play game that's 99 cents. You might be thinking "Why should I buy this on Steam then?" The answer, no mobile monetization bs to shift through. The Steam version let's you unlock everything instead of buying loads of dlc. If anything you unlock things too fast in the Steam version but that might just be me.Other reasons, steam sales exist so you could consider this a $10 or even $6 game on the right day and it has workshop support. It's origin as a mobile game works in it's favor because it's super quick and responsive to play.The Gameplay: You choose a character, choose a map, then travel up a very Slave-the-Spire map system. Though you do have to make sure your ship has enough AP to make the journey. Where the game differs is in deck building and combat. Each character has their own starting deck but share the same pool of card options after the battle. Additionally, you have a limited number of relics (items with passive effects) and have to choose a reward at the end of each combat. The lack of an option to skip rewards changing decision making drastically. You might want to avoid combat just so you don't hoard too many cards, perhaps pick a useless relic as an option to either be discard or sold later (btw you can sell relics). It gives money more value by letting you refresh rewards so you aren't forced to pick a terrible option for your build.The Combat: Combat has some weird quirks to it. First your mana in other cards games is now your ammo which doesn't refill to full at the start of each turn and instead only fills back up with certain ammo cards and relics. You have to be very strategic with when you spend your ammo, but on the bright side there are plenty of melee cards that cost nothing to play though most of them only target the first enemy. Status effects are also very weird. The player and enemies can only have one effect at a time and that effect can either be positive or negative. So you can cleanse a negative status effect by giving yourself a positive one or vice verse. There is only one con and it's that the mechanics for certain enemies and bosses are hidden, forcing the player to trial and error until they figure it out (which can be really annoying for final bosses of an area).The Unlockables and Modes: There are a lot of things to unlock in the game. There are plenty of characters each with their own unique passives and starting cards that causes them to play different despite sharing the same pools of cards. There are a variety of maps to explore (7 to be exact) and each character has a skin for beating all of them (except the doctor). All the skins look great because this art style is very appealing. There are quests that give you a bit more direction, some give you the currency to unlock things, some are character specific quests that will unlock a new card or item exclusive to that character, or a quest to unlock the 7th Sea. There's an arena mode that I haven't quite reached the end of and a Tavern brawl which I'm not sure what it is, I'll get back to you on that.The Characters: I'll make this brief but I absolutely love the characters in this game. The starting one, The Gunner, serves as a nice little introduction to the game and pairs really well with ranged cards. The Bear taming gives you a sixth card that uses the bear to attack/defend. Use the bear enough times and that card becomes a free action. Even the ones that haven't gotten around to playing look really interesting.In conclusion: This game is a must for any fan of deck building roguelikes and is looking for a new spin on the formula.

_childDocuments_.review: I like the variety in the playable characters. There are lots of different ways to build a successful deck. One thing I wish was better is the information provided to the player. The game does an okay job of this, but there are other games out there that do a MUCH better job of informing the player about what something means. For example lets say that "Card A" has the following text: "Create 'Card B' and then an enemy gains injury 1." The game will not tell you what 'Card B' does, but it will explain what injury 1 means. It is up to the player to use "Card A" to learn what 'Card B' does and then remember what 'Card B' does from then on. This only bothers me a little, but I recognize that it is annoying and that it may be a bigger deal to other players. Despite this shortcoming, I do really enjoy playing this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard to review this and ignore "Slay the Spire", as the two games are very close to each other. Surprisingly, I would give "Pirates Outlaws" the upper hand, though.Pros:+ nice graphics, good theme+ several "campaigns", heroes, quests, item and card unlocks+ all unlocks happen gradually, at a reasonable pace (grinding is definitely here, but it's not exaggerated)+ high level of replayability+ receives updates and some additional contentCons:- weird use of English (I'm not a native speaker either, but some of the text seems strange to me)- not all features are available from the beginning, some grinding is necessary- quests are definitely nice, but I think that the implementation can still be optimized a bit- devs need to expand on the hero descriptions and explain their PROs and CONs in much more detailOverall I would give it a strong 8.5/10 - very well worth the asking price on a Steam sale.

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay...On the plus side it has plenty of content, unfortunately it feels really grindy to unlock said content. There are a lot of characters and maps but all the battles feel the same and don't feel especially 'fun'.Certain bosses will wipe you unless you have a specific deck to counter them which means you'll feel either cheated or railroaded depending on your choices leading up to the battle.Limited relic slots plus an ever bloating deck is theoretically interesting but in reality it just means you don't get to play interesting combinations.Ammo system is cool but the ever bloated deck feels like it limits the use of 'ranged' cards.Tool-tips are hit+miss (mostly miss) you can't see what a card does in the shop. For example: so with the 'hook' artifact you know it spawns a hook card but not what the hook card does....until you buy that relic and find out. Also bosses have special abilities which is cool but not knowing what they are until you've worked it out...then you have to remember when you restart the journey and fight it again.Over all it's a bit of a kitchen sink of ideas, if you like card battle games like this then give it a try (on sale).

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty lightweight StS clone with a pirate theme to it. It's an interesting take on it since your mana is ammo, and melee attacks don't consume ammo. If you're into Slay the Spire or similar games, then this is probably right up your alley. I'm pretty sure it's a mobile game ported to PC, but I haven't had any bugs or issues with it. They also removed MTX from it and made everything progression based instead, so that's very good.There's a lot of characters in the game, but I haven't really played with much else other than the Swordsman, as you can essentially ignore Ammo on her (?) and just spam away with melee cards and infinite lifesteal. I do think the ammo-based cards need more power to them, as you need to play cards to recharge ammo (doesn't reset every turn). Basically if you end up with a bunch of ammo-spenders and no ammo-recharge you're screwed. As such, imo the balance is lacking and could use a rework or significant buff to ranged/ammo-based attacks to make up for their inconsistency.Overall though, not a bad card-based rogue"lite".

_childDocuments_.review: Love this game. This is a very casual card battler that does not require you to build a overly-prepared deck from the beginning. It feels a lot like Dicey Dungeons due to the fact that you can build your deck and learn along the way. I'm very mediocre at card battlers, so this one took me 12 hours to beat a full play through. I thought it was well worth the time.Also, pirate themed games rule.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game with a highly interactive gameplay. I'm not joking when I say that I genuinely enjoyed this game and spent a lot of time in it. Well, at least much more than what I originally expected. The amount of things that you can explore is incredible. Since the game is kind of raw, it is lacking in certain aspects like sound design or a lack of unique animations. I would love if it would go in the Darkest Dungeon direction here and did splash art for each move. That would be sick and would make the feel of the game 100 times better. But if you played some of those deck-builder rogue-likes like Slay the Spire and you liked them, I highly recommend you try this one out too. It has so much spirit and uniqueness in it. Maybe it's my childhood me speaking, the one who loves the pirate theme and the simplistic design and picture, but it's still worth checking out. 9/10 do recommend. :)

_childDocuments_.review: A simplified Slay the Spire with a pirate theme.Differences worth mentioning:It takes longer to unlock cards and other characters.You don't lose block/shield at the end of each turn.Less deck-archetypes to build (However I'm still early on in my playthroughs)More characters to unlock but they aren't as vastly different as they are in StSOverall, still an enjoyable game and worth picking up.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a blast. This is such a great game. Unique look, unique mechanics, a lot of cards and items to unlock, several game modes and quests, more than one map! This is great.While using familiar mechanics, there are a lot of unique twists like: ammo doesn't recharge unless you play ammo cards, you are forced to take a card after each battle and you can draft items instead but you have limited inventory, status effects replace each other so buffs and debuffs are a huge resource to handle. _childDocuments_.review: Really enjoying this game a lot. At first it can be a bit hard to get into but as you unlock more cards and have better and better games it gets addictive. A couple days ago I beat the first island for the first time using the Curse Captain and unlocked three achievements at one time, which really pulled me into the game a lot more. _childDocuments_.review: If you're a slay the spire (StS) addict like I was, this game's a pretty good next-in-line. While it might not revolutionize the genre, what it does do is bring fantastic character design to a tried-and-true game formula. Once you're far enough along in the game to make both character and card choices from what you've painstakingly unlocked via grinding, it's strong competition with StS. Some of the mechanics are a bit frustrating (status effects override each other, making some deck builds quickly obsolete or frustrating to play.) But the balancing of mana and positioning of enemies is a neat level of complexity to the StS formula. I recommend the game for genre die-hards!

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoying this so much that I thought I'd leave a rare review, Finally a worthy successor to Slay the Spire! Tons of unlockable content, a bunch of player classes that play significantly different from each other, lots of relics and secrets to discover....this game is the complete package! I can't stop playing the damn thing. I finally beat the first world and punched the air in triumph, the last battle was just fantastic: and I have two more final bosses to discover! And that's just the first world! The best value for content I've gotten for a game in ages, totally worth full price. Thank you, game devs for seeing the Slay the Spire formula not as a trend to cash in on but a framework for serious, polished game design.
_childDocuments_.name: Pirates Outlaws

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game, for $20 it is an absolute steal in terms of value, and with even more content coming down the pipeline, it truly is hard for me to believe that this game is in early access. This is an easy must-own for anyone who enjoyed Slay the Spire, I had it recommended to me, purchased it on a whim, and I've not regretted it for even a moment. However I do think that this game does have a few issues that require some attention: First of all, the fact that you can't double click on a part of the map to travel there instantly is pretty annoying but a simple fix. Next is the fact that all of the keywords are separated by their own "Glossary" tab, as opposed to tooltips that tell you what each keyword means, this is especially annoying for the Carpenter, whose keywords aren't even in the Glossary tab(please fix that). Additionally, I wish there was more conveyance on enemies and what they do, bosses especially, for example Red Bear(one of the earliest bosses) when he's in his second phase, his damage increases each time you hit him, but you won't know that until you actually commit to attacking him, which can lead to some cheap deaths, because it denies information to the player if they don't know/remember it going into the fight. Even regular enemies, I didn't know which attack will be raw damage and which one will debuff me and damage me until I noticed the difference myself, this is what might be the aspect of the game the is in greatest need of fixing. Finally, my personal biggest issue, the characters, or at least how they're handled, I don't know if it's just because I'm not deep enough into the game yet, but from what I've been seeing so far it does not look like this issue clears itself later in the game. That issue being the card pool, now there are alot of cool cards and cooler characters with alot of variety for builds and strategies, which is good, however, what I don't like is the distinct lack of character-specific cards. The only character specific cards in the game are in each characters starting decks, which is fine for the simpler characters(Gunner/Swordmaster) but for characters like the Vigilante and the Carpenter(him especially) I would love to see separate progression tied to each character(much like how there is card unlock progression tied to each stage), that unlocks cards unique to that character that can be found in later runs, because even though each caracters unique abilities do help to set them apart from the rest, I think a few more character specific cards would do wonders for the game and its variety(it might also give the Carpenter more ways to get rid of his fervor without overloading).

name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth
detailed_description: Story Three heroic explorers wander the post-apocalyptic desert on a mission to save their village from despair. They soon find a dark, twisted tower that has risen from the depths of the planet and seemingly holds the key to their survival. In order to ensure their victory, one of them has made a secret pact with the Titan of Death, Epimetheus, allowing them to reincarnate until they have accomplished their mission. But what fate lies in store for the heroes and their village? Death is Only the Beginning Astalon: Tears Of The Earth is an action-platformer set in a dying world where life is cruel, but death can be a stepping stone to victory! Use the unique skills and weapons of Arias the fighter, Kyuli the rogue, and Algus the wizard, to surmount the mysterious tower and find the answers to their survival. Slay terrible monsters, discover powerful artifacts, and solve fiendish puzzles, reaching new heights in the tower with the aid of a Titan. Follow a story about friendship and sacrifice, building up the courage to take down giants to protect the weak and powerless. Strengthen your party and change their fate by embracing death. Discover the countless secrets of the Tower of Serpents! Features Relive the glory days of 8-bit action-adventure through beautifully detailed, authentic pixel art set in a dark, fantastic world! Astalon features the progressive exploration of an interconnected world with the swiftness and quick rhythm of a room-by-room action platformer. Original character design by Ryusuke Mita, creator of world-famous manga Dragon Half! Play at your own pace -- explore thoroughly and build your characters strengths, or use risky methods to slice your way up the tower furiously! Switch between your heroes and utilize the unique abilities of a warrior, archer and wizard to progress through the game. Battle against a large assortment of different enemies, giant monsters, and epic bosses! Choose the right hero to find the weaknesses of the creatures that stand in your way! Upgrade your characters’ abilities and change the course of destiny by making deals with Epimetheus -- the Titan of Death. Collect a variety of incredible artifacts such as the “Sword of Mirrors” that will bestow your characters with new abilities and open new possibilities. Use campfires to save your progress, change characters, and discover details about the heroes’ pasts. Hundreds of rooms to discover -- hours of challenging exploration with a plethora of unlockables and secrets to reward the most inquisitive players! Experience an exciting soundtrack of chiptune music composed by Matt Kap, spanning over 30 pieces of music!

_childDocuments_.review: This is great game and I really enjoyed playing it, yet it has couple of flaws that can cause some misunderstanding with the players. I've read some of the reviews, and, well, some folks didn't like it due to various reasons. The main problem in my opinion - is that people expect it to be a "modern era" metroidvania, which this game is not, yet, I'll get there. Buckle up.Let's talk why is it great first:- it has a big varied map which is actually fun to explore, because there are literally dozens and dozens of secrets.- it has cool unlock/progression systems where you can level up your characters and/or party by purchasing stuff from a store, bestiary with a ~90 entries (where each entry has to be killed certain amount of times to complete), etc.- it has a varied set of abilities that will allow you reach locked out spots (duh, like any metroidvania would) plus a set of combat abilities that enhance each of your character combat style- it's a really chill game, that doesn't demand you to grind your skill/resources/time to be good at it (yet there are portions of the game where you would actually need to Git Gud, yet those are optional)- juggling multiple characters a time - is a nice idea and it works really well in terms of exploring the world/combat variety.Then what is wrong with the game, you ask?Well, let's say I would advertise it slightly different to avoid confusion. People got used to so-called "modern" metroidvanias, they are used to have save spots replenish life, better flow in backtracking and so on and so forth.Yet this is a homage to the older ones - from graphics to some gameplay elements. Yes at times it's really unfair, and I must agree - the public would much prefer some better and more merciful solutions when it comes to navigating around game map (teleporting and stuff), better healing system, ability to leave pins on map, etc. But this is what it is:  newmade oldschool attempt with modern elements. (Sounds confusing so far, right?)- the amount of healing is limited per random heals at bonfires (that are limited and come up only when you achieve plot points), some minor healing by breaking candle pots (limited, regenerates if bought at store), random drop from mobs (if ability bought from store, small chance). <- this makes the game harder and longer than it should, but that's the way it is.  - navigation on world map can be a pain. There's a limited set of elevators (teleporters) on a huge map, meaning if you want to get to that room and check out if there's something left - welcome to helluva running through 20+ rooms.  Could be better, you could get an item that allows you to teleport between save spots in last quarter of the game for easy backtracking and less frustration, yet this is what it is. - I saw people complaining that backtracking is hard because when you bump into a character specific block - you have to run all way back, to a savespot, where you can switch the active character and run back yet again to unlock the thing. Well, this is not really true, because one of the first items you unlock is a thing that allows you to switch chars on the flight. Honestly speaking - most of the frustration causes will have an item that serves exactly to ease that frustration (healing item, can't reach there, char switching, etc)  Except teleporting around - that's a pain. Yes. - Oh, and one more. Each time you die - you respawn at the same room at the very beginning of the game, not at your last visited save spot. And that actually (frustrating again, yes, I know) makes sense if you follow the story, as the characters are... NO SPOILERS! :)Overall: a great game that took me 16.0 hours to 100% the main story. Full of secrets, fun to explore, great value of upgrading/unlock systems, good controls and pretty nice pixel art. Definitely recommend to genre fans, yet be sure to read the Cons section above, as the game might tick off all the boxes you expect it to have. If not - it's a great game that you will definitely enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: There are truly few things as gratifying as a well put-together metroidvania. The persistent popularity of the ancient Metroids and Castlevanias from which this awkward moniker was taken should be testament to that, but so many recent indie attempts have been just as captivating, if not moreso. Astalon definitely deserves a place among these modern adventures, with its gorgeous, detailed pixel art and creative upgrades. It’s got plenty of interesting design decisions that set it apart from others of its ilk, too, though not all of them may have been the best ideas. Still, there’s so much good about Astalon that I couldn’t help but dip into its bonus modes, even after taking the time to 100% the main game, and that’s something I don’t normally do.Astalon Episode II (it’s doing a Star Wars thing, you didn’t miss anything) chronicles the adventures of Algus the mage, Kyuli the archer, and Arias the knight. In their post-apocalyptic world, the ancient ruins of those that came before are re-emerging, and a nearby tower has poisoned the water of our plucky party’s village. Together, these would-be heroes climb the tower to uncover the secrets of this blight. Inside they’ll find all manner of grim creatures serving the gorgons, great stone beasts sealed within. They’ll need a host of powers to overcome the challenges before them, and not all of these powers will come from mortal sources.One immediate draw of this game is the many unique hooks it has for its story and structure. I had to mention the gorgons because they’re a new and creative adversarial force for a game like this, rather than vampires or demons or evil AIs. The continue and upgrade systems are also tied into a neat story element that gets introduced almost immediately; your buddy Algus has a deal with Epimetheus, the Titan of Death, who refuses to let the party die until the bargain is complete. He’ll even grant you new powers in exchange for the souls you hoover up while exploring the tower, what a guy! But really, it’s these elements along with the exciting discoveries you make as you ascend that helps Astalon stand out from other metroidvanias.If you’ve played more than a few metroidvanias, I’m sure you’ve had that moment where you got a new power and it changed your very perception of the game world. Games like Hollow Knight and Axiom Verge do this, and I was pleased to see Astalon do it several times to great effect. There’s one particular power I got that I was not expecting at all, and it felt like it opened up the game in so many ways. It also helps that there are a vast array of secrets to find as you ascend the tower, none of them particularly torturous to find but some of them impressively expansive. This is a game that’s a pleasure to explore, especially if you’re keeping up with your character upgrades to ensure you can dispatch enemies quickly and efficiently. The combat in Astalon is thankfully quite good, and offers you several approaches to battle that are sure to include something that you’ll find fun.I will say there are parts of this game that don’t quite live up to the others, and the big one for me is the map. Metroidvanias live and die on their map designs, because if you hate trying to get around the world, you’re going to run out of steam real fast. Astalon doesn’t have a bad map, and like I said, some of the secrets are really quite interesting to uncover. However, this is one of those games where the map might show three exits out of a room, but only two of those are connected. The tower is intensely maze-like, and several sections of it don’t connect like you’d expect they would. If you’ve ever played the middle child of Castlevania on the Gameboy Advance, Harmony of Dissonance, Astalon has a lot in common with the twisting castle there.It’s also worth mentioning that the health system is a bit unusual, and while I won’t spoil it, I will say that it can be hard to recover from heavy losses. Coupled with the proliferation of traps like spikes in this game, I can see health being a frustration for some, though ultimately it never was for me. I was having too much fun teasing out the tower’s secrets for any of these complaints to really bother me, and I think that’ll be the case for most people who give Astalon a chance. It took me about a dozen hours to 100% complete a normal playthrough, and that opened up a whole host of bonus modes, included a New Game + that actually mixes up the map a little. With solid gameplay, unique hooks, and a gorgeous presentation, I can definitely recommend Astalon to anyone needing a new cursed tower to explore.Did you enjoy this review? I certainly hope so, and I certainly hope you'll check out more of them at  or on my !

_childDocuments_.review: Having heard a lot of praise for this one, I began this game with fairly high expectations. While I *did* enjoy my time with this game (and it is insanely impressive for such a small team), it didn't quite live up to the hype. I'll explain some reasons why I enjoyed it, and some things that I think could be improved.First, let's talk about some good things:- I think one of the areas where this game excels the most is level design. The puzzles are fun, there are tons of shortcuts, and the fast travel points are fairly well distributed. Each area has its own unique atmosphere, complete with gorgeous artwork and a banging soundtrack. Honestly, I fail to understand how so many MVs consistently have excellent soundtracks, and Astalon certainly keeps this bar set high.- Astalon features tons of hidden areas and pathways. I would frequently uncover a hidden pathway that looped back on some earlier part of the level I'd already been to—if I had just known it was there to begin with then I could've taken it right from the start! I think this sort of level design is great, as it adds a real sense of connectedness to the map. There were also a few areas with their own really cool gimmicks, e.g., the bubbles in The Serpent Path, and the Darkness area.- Enemy design is fairly diverse; I enjoyed fighting most things in this world. I also didn't mind the way the character upgrade system was designed.- Some of the abilities you unlock are quite creative IMO, and they work well with the party member system by making each character useful in certain scenarios. - Things seemed fairly expensive at the beginning (as well as at the end), but currency scaled up well throughout my journey...although, I believe it was absolutely necessary for me to always buy that upgrade upon death that results in 10% more orb drops. I had that stacked up to 20 or so by the end game, and every time I'd die I'd have a few thousand orbs.Now, let's talk about things that could be improved (or that I just *wish* were done differently):- First, starting at the beginning of the tower every time I died got really old really quickly, even after unlocking some fast travel stations. The reason why is that even after unlocking shortcuts, I'd sometimes still have to traverse 10+ rooms to get back to where I was when I died; that is not challenging in any way, it's just tedious. I would have had a much better time if there was a way to respawn at the last campfire you saved at...e.g., maybe that could've been an ability unlocked mid-game, or maybe you could have paid Epimetheus some orbs to place you there. I think the fast travel stations were placed well from an exploration point of view, but not from the point of view of "every time you die, you'll have to effectively restart from one of these"- Next, while the party member mechanic was cool, I had a few issues with it. (1) I didn't feel like I got to know any of the characters AT ALL, except maybe for Algus. So by the end of the story, if I'm supposed to feel something for any of them, that was completely lost on me. (2) I felt that this game encouraged a play style where you "main" Algus, and only play as other characters situationally (when you need their unique abilities). While this is not terrible, it became a bit annoying as the party grew because rotating between members became cumbersome. Also, Algus becomes way too OP way too quickly IMO, and the balance is trivialized in the player's favor as early as 30% into the game. I only struggled with the first 2 bosses, everything after that was a cakewalk. I don't think games have to be hard, but at the same time, it was exceedingly clear to me that Algus was far more powerful than any of the other party members and that most bosses + mobs were not balanced around him. I think nerfing Algus by like 4x, and making the campfires checkpoints would've been a great way to balance the game better. This would force you to engage in enemies and bosses in a more thoughtful manner, but would've mitigated the punishment by allowing you to die more often without feeling like you were losing too much progress.- The next point I mention touches on two things at the same time: campfires and ability upgrades. Basically, I noticed that once I got the bell, the campfires became almost entirely useless. However, it also occurred to me that a player who *didn't* find the bell early enough would end up having a pretty frustrating time trying to get through the rest of the game, before realizing they were missing a key item somewhere (but where?). This concern actually came to fruition for me much earlier on in the game, during my first 2 or so hours. I had found one blue key in the starting area, and used it to unlock a random blue door (couldn't tell you which). On my way to fight the first boss, I passed an elevator and was so excited...but, of course I couldn't actually use it. I thought that was bizzare. Promptly fought the boss and died. Tried the boss again with a different character, same outcome. About 4 or 5 tries later (and after realizing Algus was my best bet), I beat the boss...but that process was thoroughly annoying because I had to run through the entire level every time I died. I later found more blue keys and eventually found my way to the door that gives you the elevator ability, but I couldn't help but feel it was overly punishing to not give you the ability to use an elevator as soon as you found it. It makes it way too easy to "screw up" the first area (the part that has to be good to keep most players hooked!) by making the trek back to the boss super annoying. Another example that affected by playthrough was the ghost-killing ability. I think the puzzle for unlocking this is fairly well explained at the beginning of the game (when you first discover the puzzle), but as I went exploring I completely forgot about it. Then there came a time (towards probably 75% of my way though the game) where there were certain enemies I had to kill, but I was so used to not killing them that I thought they were just part of the environment. I was so stumped and I had to look up a guide for the area, which led to me realizing I had completely forgotten about that puzzle from the start of the game. All in all, my point here is that some *crucial ability upgrades* are likely too well hidden for the game's own good.- I also found it unfortunate that I could not place custom markers on the map. There were too many times where I kept going back to a few rooms that had items in them, only to realize I didn't have the correct ability upgrade yet (but I wasn't able to keep track effectively of *which* ability upgrade I needed). A system like this could've also helped me keep better track of "quests"/puzzles like that one I just mentioned about unlocking the ghost-killing ability. If I had been able to place a marker on my map in the central room for that puzzle, I wouldn't have forgotten about it so easily.- Finally: the morningstar is unlocked wayyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy too late. I can't emphasize that enough!!!!! So much backtracking upon death would have been mitigated if we had it by mid-game. Better yet, why even bother having so many of those breakable blocks in front of key pathways? It was just plain frustrating to hit so many dead ends until I was like 90% of the way done the game and finally got that ability.All in all, Astalon was a really cool experience that brought a lot to the table, but was a bit rough around the edges. Despite some questionable design decisions, I think these devs have what it takes to be among the best in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Astalon is a totally recommended, awesome 8-bit-inspired Metroidvania, but it has some issues you need to be aware of. You can work around most of them if you understand from the beginning how the game works, which I didn’t lol. Don’t let the bad reviews keep you from enjoying the game. I’ll mention the problem and give you a solution/workaround for it. When you die, you get sent all the way to the very beginning of the game. Any progress you make is “saved”, but you have to work your way back to where you died. Campfires (save points) are mostly for decoration. You get to switch characters at them, and that’s about it. Now here’s the solution. Every area has one or two elevators (for fast travel). They are usually located just before the area boss and either next to or very near a save point. Once you activate them, you can quickly access most areas of the game. However, if you die before reaching the elevator, you’ll still have to do some backtracking. There are also two warp portals within some areas. You can use them to quickly move from one to the other within the one area you’re in.  You start the game with your full HP level and need to hope it’s enough to get to the end of the area/save point. There are scattered candles around all areas, but they barely refill anything and they’re gone once you break them. Solution: every time you die, you get access to the “shop” and can buy upgrades and assorted items. Make sure you buy Candle Light. It restores all candles throughout the game. You will never be able to fully restore your HP because there aren’t enough of them, but at least you get some relief. The surprises may add to your gameplay, but I hate it. Just google it so you know what you’re buying. Every room is exactly one square, so you get to see everything going on as soon as you enter it. For the map, that means the rooms are all bunched up like a hotel and it’s very difficult to tell them apart. There are hardly any empty spaces between anything, which makes it pretty difficult to place a mental mark on specific rooms you need to go back to later. Mitigation steps: You can (and definitely should) buy items that add information to your map, but it’s still not ideal. This is just me, but I had to do a ridiculous amount of backtracking searching for keys because there are some doors that don’t need to be opened. I accidentally touched one of said doors and lost the last key I had. Then, after fighting and barely surviving my way through a tough area, I got to the room just before the save point/elevator and was greeted with a door for which I had no key. I was ready to ditch the game for good since I was over 20 hours into it and most of it was backtracking. “Solution”: I got myself a guide map listing all items and went searching for keys. Maybe you’re a better player than I am (very likely) and will find items on your own, so this might not even be a problem. There are more keys than doors, so you’ll never be permanently stuck. Because I’m not super good at catching hints and finding all items, I had to do a lot of backtracking, and that made the game pretty difficult for me. The dungeons themselves get tough at times, but never NES-era difficult. Because of all the backtracking, I got frustrated and in a hurry to get back to where I last died, so I made lots of mistakes. Solution: get a guide or become a better player lol. If you can find all the items you need, the game is not difficult. The bosses are mostly easy, especially if your characters are fully upgraded. I beat several of them on the first try without full HP. The game looks beautiful overall, but I felt that most of the dungeons were the same thing with a different color palette. That’s not to say they’re bad. Everything looks great, but nothing looks remarkable. Another unfortunate thing is that some helpful items are found way too late in the game. There’s an item in the last area that would’ve helped me tremendously throughout the entire game, and I was able to get it literally 5 minutes before fighting the last boss. You can get it earlier, but way past being useful.Now that you’re aware of some of the issues you’ll find, you can go in with open eyes. If you can deal with them, you’ll have a blast playing Astalon.The story isn’t super captivating or deep, but the cutscenes just before and after the last boss were particularly impressive and beautiful. I got 100% (map and items) and will definitely play it again in the future. Again, if you can get past the disclaimers, you’ll love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I found this to be a mostly grating and annoying experience. I was charmed at the outest by the visuals and I liked the introduction of skill progression. That said, my issues with the game crept in early. Much of my backtracking was a result of the game's respawn and health replenishing mechanics. You respawn at the starting room of the entire game AND enemies barely drop any health pickups after paying for it in the store. I did make it to the final boss, but by that point just wanted to roll credits. Youtube shows me that the final boss has like 4 life bars, yeah, no thanks. _childDocuments_.review: I feel like this will be a nice little hidden gem that nobody really ends up playing which is a shame. It's a great metroidvania with a retro aesthetic. You'll often find yourself revisiting areas to find new items or characters. You start off with 3 but can get up to 5 and they all have their own strengths and weaknesses that you will have to switch between to solve rooms. The exploration is a lot of fun. The game is a bit difficult at first and can be a bit tedious early because dying sends you back to the beginning but you'll unlock fast travel points as you progress. Every time you die, you'll be able to purchase upgrades at a shop to make yourself stronger and get through tough sections you may keep dying at.The game is a decent length for a metroidvania. It'll probably take you about 15-20 hours to 100% it and there are unlockable game modes for some added replayability if that interests you. Overall, it's a really neat retro game that definitely deserves a playthrough if you're into retro games.

_childDocuments_.review: I first played Astalon during the February Steam Game Festival and was impressed with the retro art style and the different playable characters. Now that I’ve had time to play the full release, I can safely say the game is up there with Cyber Shadow for my ‘Best 8-Bit Game of the Year’. The developers of the game have nailed the look and feel of the NES era perfectly, from the selectable CRT scanlines, to the chiptune soundtrack.  There are three things that I feel really make this game stand out from the crowd: 1: The Plot. Plots for platformers are usually either non-existent, or a convoluted mess. However, Astalon’s plot engaged me from the off. In a post-apocalyptic world, a demon has poisoned the water supply and the three companions must ascend the twisted tower of serpents to save their homeland. Unbeknownst to the others, Algus has made a Faustian bargain with the Titan of Death, Epimetheus, allowing them all to reincarnate every time they die. This secret pact raises the stakes somewhat and adds a tension to the plot. To save everyone else, there must be sacrifice.  After each death, characters can be upgraded, and new items bought, making you stronger next time. I found this mechanic similar to many roguelites with permanent upgrade features, and like those games, death is more of a learning curve than a hinderance.   2: The Three Playable Characters: Algus, Arias and Kyuli. Algus is a wizard with a wand that fires projectiles to defeat enemies and activate stone statues. Arias is a swordsman, perfect for close combat, plus his sword can cut down overgrown vines blocking the path. Kyuli is an archer. She has a long-ranged attack and can jump off walls, allowing her to reach places the other two can’t. You can switch characters at campfires (which double as save points) scattered throughout the map. Unfortunately, characters can’t be switched on the fly, which often means backtracking to control the character you need to get past a certain point.  3: The Level Design. Astalon is a puzzle platformer that has metroidvania elements. The game features a meticulously crafted vertical map, which reveals itself the more you play. With action taking place in a mysterious tower, you start at the bottom and work your way up. Rather than most metroidvanias where you explore in all directions, without any real clue of where the end point will be, I found the vertical tower structure quite original, as you know to work your way upwards.   Shortcuts can be unlocked, so returning to previous areas never feels onerous.  With invisible walls, hidden notes and cryptic clues, there are plenty of secrets to discover, some of which reminded me of games like La Mulana.  Astalon is a sizeable game, chock full of interesting areas, creative puzzles and inventive boss fights. It’s a wonderful modern retro platformer that channels the original NES Metroid, Castlevania 3, and even Team Cherry’s ‘Hollow Knight’. It steals things from many of the classics, but manages to mix everything together to feel unique as a whole.  Astalon was my Indie Game of the Week for May 31 - Jun 6:

_childDocuments_.review: All the colors of the Necco Wafer rainbow await thee in this:  a massive, multi-character metroidvania greased for arcade speed, in which treasures gleam in every corner, and any of the chibi champions in your one-at-a-time rotation is sufficiently interesting to star in his or her own game.  You'll be Algus, a mage with short-range projectile power and a dirty secret; Arias, a swordsman who plies his blade with the flickering rapidity of a meth-possessed prison shanker; and Kyuli, the Red Riding Boobs of the bunch, whose arrows streak on a flat trajectory all the way across the screen, but take some time twixt nockings.  There are others, too, but you'll have to uncover these adventurers over the course of your tower climb.The map is sprawling, almost certainly one of the biggest, varied enough to keep the plate of novelty spinning, and fairly logical too (insofar as the contents of a poison-dispensing monster tower in a video game can be deemed such).  Intriguingly, the effect of size is magnified by the dearth of healing items and lack of save zone fast-travel -- though there do exist an elevator of deliciously forboding make, and six demon skull teleportation portals to shrink the distance -- with every death taking you back to the tower entrance.  Since the devs made the deliberate choice  to punish players with permadeath or an experience point tax, they had to encourage careful play in some fashion -- and this works about better than anything for a game of 's type.  You'll be forced to learn the layout.  You won't slip into sloppiness.  You'll actually feel threatened . . . with the superficial ebb of progress, but it threatens all the same!  The lower-level monsters you'll thrash on the way back to your former places of rest will give you a periodic reminder of just how much you've grown.The "bad" (for the sake of Devil's Advocacy) is represented by a handful of grammatical glitches in the presentation of the perfectly serviceable fairy tale story, and in one, count 'em,  graphical glitch that flashes on Bram's sprite when he melees immediately after lobbing an ax.  And that's it.  Not too shabby, eh?Soulful and without pretension,  is one of the recent best in the metroidvania genre.  This is somebody's baby, somebody's carefully cut gem -- and you see that in the , not just the intent.(After you beat the main game, you can play through as the Black Knight or a flying gargoyle, either of whose beefed up powers allow you to get to the top of the tower in a fraction of the time your original team could.  Pretty fun!  Also, there's the ubiquitous New Game+ for completionists, with remixed item locations -- but after three climbings, I'd already had plenty of Serpent Tower.)

_childDocuments_.review: I've been following the development progress of this game since it's first announcement, and I'm really impressed at how it turned out! There were of course various tiny bits that I could nitpick about, but in summary I loved 98% percent of the whole game. Even if I felt disappointed at certain things, it always found ways how to compensate those shortcomings with an amazing art direction, the whole strange universe concept and with it's silly-cute horror charm.-----------------The Positives:-----------------There is something warmly special about generic fantasy settings done right, don't get it wrong, Astalon is not lacking in terms of creativity in any way, but the premise is so simple and catchy, the way it presents you the main aim of the game is enough to feel interested and it does a great job at getting your attention. It's like you feel a naive kid again, no philosophical/existential deep ass plot, just go on a noble adventure and have fun. I mean.. A mysterious massive tower full of dangers and secrets to solve and overcome? Sign me in. I've seen numerous times the concept of exploring ''evil towers'' in JRPG games more than multiple times before, in such titles as ''Ys Origins, Pandora's Tower'' or in the anime called ''The Tower of Druaga'', makes me think that it should be it's own genre already, and Astalon is an amazing addition to the list!So you have an initial standard trio group which consists of a fighter, magician, archer and later on you get some extra weirdos jumping in, but their addition felt a bit irrelevant. Because the chemistry at the beginning is beyond good! I loved the way each character has been balanced well enough for different play-styles, let's say the most primitive example would be that the archer has the farthest reach, but her attacks are also the slowest, while the knight has barely any reach, he is the fastest at dealing damage. The difference is how you want to proceed and what type of tactic suits you best. It might sound obviously banal, but I really liked how they all have their own personalities and image that is being portrayed through blue/yellow/red colour palettes, as I mentioned before the simplicity in it's design and vision is where this game shines. Heck, it even has a huge variation of tiny chibi characters showing up in the corner of the loading screen. Makes you feel that Astalon feels comfortable enough in it's own style to experiment and find subtle ways to squeeze bits of story there and there.This brings me to the topic that I'm mostly excited to talk about is the main villainous creatures called ''Gorgons''. At the very beginning I didn't really paid much attention to the setting that I'm in, and it does a fantastic job at giving you almost zero clues who the heck the villain is, or what exactly is going on or what I'm going against. But I've never seen such an amazing and refreshing interpretation of various creatures from Greek mythology before.. Gorgons in Astalon are some sort of nasty demigods or entities.. Their designs are twisted/illogical.. Deceiving? One thing they all have in common is that they share cold-like, lifeless elements, while hiding their true monstrous form.. Their role felt like solely parasitic, menacing and repulsive.My favourite part of the environmental design, regarding Gorgons was definitely all the visual art, through architecture, murals, decorations. While you explore and ascend the tower bit by bit, you will come across lots of innovative depictions of the owners of that place. Sometimes it even sets the tone of a gruesome dark fantasy. I guess no way child-eating abominations would want to see themselves in a brighter tone. And it really did a brilliant job to keep me interested to see what else is there to see. If anyone who played Elder Scrolls before and was hooked into discovering everything that there is regarding the lost ''Dwemer'' race, will definitely get an idea. Such subtle details made me question if I should start treating this game more seriously.. and not just for the gameplay value but it made me fall in love with the world that I'm in. Gorgons are such awesome ''baddies'' that I would want to see more crazy stuff in the sequel!Music is straight A+ in Astalon, it's catchy, melodramatic, heroic with bits of melancholy popping up when you least expect it, sometimes you even want to perfectly kill enemies in time while matching to the rhythm, squeeze those hits in a sync with the beats. I always felt empowered and determined to keep on going while jamming to those sick chiptunes. -----------------The Negatives:-----------------Apart from tiny scattered visual bugs and occasional glitches, I wished the main three characters received more interaction between each other, comfy chit-chats by the campfire were sweet but I wished they expanded more on such moments. Also the glass candle-heal thingies were really weird, I ended up in different situations, where I could not progress because there were simply no ways to restore HP, so I would rather just die and start again with full HP.  Because what's the point, to make a long journey somewhere where you know you gonna get KO'd in one hit and just waste time. Those roguelike elements felt a bit unnecessary, I would say it was more tedious than challenging. But nevertheless I admire the intention to experiment and expand the genre. My biggest disappointment lies within extra game modes and especially in ''Boss Rush'' mode, which is beyond absurd.. You get instantly all 5 characters, 2 of them which serve barely any good purpose, because in the main game, their skills were primary related to solving puzzles instead of combat. And I doubt anyone would want to use them against bosses, so they just occupy space and it delays the process to quickly switch between characters, because of that you feel more encouraged to stick to just one, instead of having fun to mess around while trying to squeeze more use of their various abilities.And here is another problem, once you clear a boss, you may choose 1 out of 3 random items while preparing for the next encounter, and those items are complete joke, why they decided to throw useless garbage into the mix is beyond me, but imagine you desperately need an upgrade to have a chance at the upcoming boss and you get an artefact which in the main game is used to destroy blocks, or to make a block to access higher places.. how in the hell are you gonna use that against boss? It's a joke, so you better arm yourself with lots of patience and wish that luck is on your side. Because of devs illogical decisions, you may end up fighting three bosses in a row with total junk, which you can't use, and just die in vain at the 4th one, because you simply don't have anything to fight with. Even though I already got all the achievements I really hope that they will fix this somehow or avoid practising such poor ideas. Challenges are amazing when they require skills, not luck..-----------------The Verdict:-----------------Strong 9/10 from me. It's far from perfect, in the same way it's far from horrible, but the potential is huge and since both the sequel and prequel were announced I hope this will turn into a series! ^^

_childDocuments_.review: Astalon is an excellent game that could've been even better with some small tweaks.Visuals, music, controls and the general flow of gameplay are completely on point.  Level design is very good and full of a bunch of micro shortcuts, honestly feels very La-Mulanish-ish in that manner.  Unfortunately, that's where the the game's biggest problem comes into play.  When you die, you respawn at the beginning of the tower, and yes, while there are elevators to different levels and and the aforementioned micro shortcuts, it just doesn't work well in the game's overall level design.  The elevators are often too spread out for a game that features the amount of intended backtracking Astalon has.  The game is also hurt by a weird by-product of the respawing at the beginning of the tower by the player realizing it is often more beneficial to just intentionally die at times, especially when backtracking, in order to spawn near the opening elevator rather than maneuver through a dozen or more rooms just to get to an elevator.  The strange thing is the game has save points that would easily serve as check points but doesn't employ them as such.  In the end, respawing at the beginning of the tower either feels like a vestigial aspect of the game's design that should have been removed or something added late in the process.  It just doesn't work in a satisfying manner.A 100% playthrough of the game will probably take around a dozen hours or so and there's a bunch of extra content.  There are two modes where you play as a generic monster and villain through the same map, but they're only okay and are kind of frustrating, as they feature some health regen annoyances, in particular the monster.  Both modes are much shorter than the main game since there's no real reason to explore the map since both characters start fully kitted out.  You basically main-line the game.NG+ is actually quite fun.  You keep your store-bought upgrades but the map features a large number of tweaks and remixed item locations.  I really enjoyed it and did not expect to play through it at first but next thing I know,  I finished it 100% in around half the time it took me to play through new game.Some other niggling annoyances in the game include the forced switching of characters at campfires.  This is one of those things like respawing at the beginning of the tower that don't really work but the devs eventually realize this and around 1/3 of the way through the game, you get an item that lets you switch on the fly.  Another issue some have, but I didn't mind, is this does not feature traditional healing mechanics found in most games.  For the most part, you can't heal, but enemies at least seem balanced around this (they aren't very difficult).  Areas are a war of attrition and you aren't supposed to just face tank enemies and spikes like some other games.I spent a lot of time on complaints in this long-ass review, but that's only because I think Astalon is soooo close to being absolutely excellent.  It really nails some ambiguous sense of just feeling how a video game should be to me.  Definitely interested in whatever comes next for the devs.P.S. TO THE PUBLISHERS, the art book for the game is not listed on the store page dlc for whatever reason.  If you want people to buy it, you probably should rectify that.

_childDocuments_.review: The backtracking, character switching, and health mechanics are insane. You cannot fast travel between save points, and you go back to the literal beginning of the dungeon every time you die. Health replenishment is nearly non-existent. Worse, each of the three characters is needed to clear different obstacles in the world, and you can only change characters at save points (and no, they don't have different health bars either). You constantly go through a cycle of reaching a new room, discovering you need a different character, and then trying not to die while you go back to a save point and then back again to clear the obstacle. I really want to like this game, but it is incredibly frustrating to play. What were they thinking?! Apparently there is an item that lets you change characters whenever, but it's a long way into the game...provided you can stand it long enough to acquire the item.

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend Astalon, but with some caveats. The game starts out pretty fun, and the central two gimmicks (getting resurrected when you die, and swapping party members) are interesting, particularly the party members. I'd say this fun lasts most of the way to the first boss. The boss is pretty tough, so you may well find yourself dying repeatedly, and the runback gets tedious, although nowhere near as tedious as runbacks will get later.The first boss, though, is the beginning of the frustration period of this game, which lasts until you get a very key upgrade partway through the area after the second boss. This period is where the character swapping mechanic starts to lose its shine, as you make your way through paths, only to find you need a different character, have to backtrack to a camp, and swap. Over and over again. Combine this with the runbacks after death, which always takes you back to the beginning of the tower, and you get a period of a couple of hours where the game honestly kind of sucks to play.However, once you get the key upgrade I mentioned, things improve considerably, and the game gets more fun with pretty much every upgrade from there. Later areas feel more generous with shortcuts you can unlock to make the runbacks quicker. You'll get more orbs from later enemies, meaning more upgrades for your characters and less dying. Once I bought some of the key general upgrades, I dumped the majority of my orbs into making Algus a powerhouse, as he has some upgrades (both found and purchased) that make his DPS ridiculous, and his range, although not as long as Kyuli's, is still a huge asset.I will admit, the frustrating portion I mentioned nearly got me to quit the game. I was probably another half an hour of annoyance away from dropping the game entirely. I'm glad I didn't, though, as the mid and late game are really quite good. I didn't quite have it in me to 100% the game, ended with 96% map completion and 90% item completion, but I did get all the major upgrades, and had a good time doing it. If you are able to get past the hour or two of jank early on, you'll find an experience well worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Astalon: Tears of the Earth - A Triumphant Climb (with a Few Stumbles)Just conquered the twisted tower of Astalon: Tears of the Earth, and let me tell you, it was an adventure! It's a challenging Metroidvania with a dark atmosphere and a cool way to explore. Here's the lowdown on my journey:Teamwork Makes the Dream Work:•	Three Buddies, One Goal: Astalon lets you control a trio of heroes: Arias the fighter, Kyuli the archer, and Algus the mage. Each has special skills you gotta use smarts to get through the tower. Switching between them to overcome obstacles keeps things fresh and exciting.•	Secrets Around Every Corner: The world of Astalon is dark and mysterious, filled with hidden passages and treasures to uncover. Exploring feels super rewarding - you might find powerful upgrades or lore bits that explain this messed-up world.•	Prepare for a Challenge!: This ain't no walk in the park. Astalon throws tough enemies and mind-bending puzzles your way. Combat requires quick reflexes and using your characters' abilities strategically. Be ready to learn from your mistakes and come back stronger!A Few Minor Bumps on the Road:•	Retracing Your Steps: Sometimes the level design can feel a bit repetitive. You might have to backtrack a bunch to use a specific character's ability to move forward. This can slow things down a bit.•	Inventory Tetris: Managing your inventory with limited space can be a bit of a headache. You'll be constantly swapping items in and out, which can disrupt the flow of combat.•	Story Buried in the Shadows: There is a story, but it's more like whispers in the dark. You gotta piece it together from the environment and item descriptions. If you crave a super clear narrative, you might be left wanting more.The Final Verdict:Astalon: Tears of the Earth is a challenging but rewarding Metroidvania for players who enjoy a good test of their skills. The unique three-character system and the dark, atmospheric world are its highlights. While some backtracking and inventory juggling can be annoying, and the story takes a backseat, the sense of accomplishment from conquering the final boss with your heroic trio is awesome!If you're looking for a tough Metroidvania with a unique twist and a dark atmosphere, then Astalon is definitely worth checking out. Just be prepared for a challenge and a few bumps along the way. But hey, that sweet victory at the end will be all the sweeter!So, how'd your adventure in Astalon go? Did you master the teamwork and conquer the darkness, or did the backtracking and inventory stuff slow you down? Let me know what you think!
