_childDocuments_.review: This game is 99% tedious backtracking and "where the ♥♥♥♥ do i go?"I say this as a HUGE fan of metroidvanias (i've played every metroid game multiple times, Hollow Knight, most castlevanias, etc.)The lack of some very basic QoL considerations saps all the fun from the game.Update: Developer left a comment on this review asking for more detail on my QoL complaints.- The map is frustrating to navigate with, because although each room exit is marked on the map, whether you can traverse between any two exits is not. I frequently found myself stuck 10 rooms deep in what looked like a path to my destination, but was actually a dead end.- I found the world layout necessitated a TON of backtracking. I have 7 hours in this game by the time I threw in the towel and most of it was backtracking. In most metroidvanias, you can more or less complete an area and get a significant upgrade or item the first time you visit it, i didn't find that to be the case in Astalon. Even with the dead maiden's ring, the thing that marks items on the map, and the thing that marks locked doors, i STILL found it frustrating.- The above complaints are made ten time more obnoxious due to the scarcity of health and healing, the fact that you always respawn at the first screen of the game, and that you can only fast travel to vanishingly few waypoints, and only from those specific waypoints. I get that this game is aiming for a retro feel, and the punishing nature of exploration plays into that, but i think it's at odds with its own design. Either reduce the punishment for dying by spawning you at the last used campfire, or reduce grinding required just to backtrack through the map.Yes, damage and defense upgrades exist, but these are very expensive, far too expensive to make traversal less annoying.- I really hated having to run back to a campfire to change characters, but the timing of when you get the bell that eliminates this as an issue was pretty much spot on in my opinion.Suggestions:- On death, spawn at the last used campfire. If you want to keep the punishing deaths, use a Continue system with like 3 campfire respawns before you're booted back to the entrance of the tower. This alone would go a VERY long way to reducing the tedium and frustration. I get that there's a lore reason for spawning at the entrance, but come on.- An option to allow fast travel from any campfire to any other campfire would mitigate 90% of my complaints.- I don't think there's a clean way to make the map easier to parse and clear up the "Where the ♥♥♥♥ do i go?" issue, at least not without a ton of work, but reducing the cost of dying by either/both of the above changes would go a long way to reducing the frustration of not knowing where the ♥♥♥♥ do go. It would be a lot less frustrating to explore and engage with the very interesting world layout if the punishment for doing so wasn't literally being kicked back to the first room of the game.The actual gameplay, art, story, and music are all fantastic. The game itself is fantastic.The problem is i never got to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ play it because i was always wandering through the same 20 rooms i had already been in 500 times trying to figure out where i needed to go to progress the story.I dropped this game after 7 hours and picked up UNSIGHTED instead.UNSIGHTED is a metroidvania that is infamous for its awful and obtuse map navigation. It's still a billion times less frustrating than Astalon because it has decent fast travel and respawn mechanics. UNSIGHTED is probably even worse than Astalon in terms of "Where do i go?" issues, and it has a time limit as well. And it has Souls-Like corpse runs.And yet, just being able to get back to near where you died without much fuss more than compensates for all of it.I am begging you to make death and navigation less obnoxious because i really do want to finish Astalon, and I want to flip this review to a thumbs up. Everything else about this game is amazing, but the few flaws it does have are so egregious that it ruins the entire experience.

_childDocuments_.review: What a rad little game. Picked this up in the AGDQ Humble Bundle in 2023 and was very pleasantly surprised at how much it marries the old and the new. It's got all this Metroidvania + Lost Vikings + Roguelite DNA in it. The overall narrative framework was really interesting as the mage/warlock's pact with a creepy god provides narrative rationale to respawning while also mechanically giving the opportunity to purchase Roguelite upgrades for your next travel up the tower. There was also so much tasty pixel art where even if the characters are channeling Megaman, the backgrounds can occasionally have these really complex Metroid looking creepfests in them. The bosses were generally well-designed even if my eventual commitment to upgrading Algus, the mage, seemed to allow for some real brute forcing.My few quibbles would be that I wish there were more upgrades to the map as it got a bit hard to parse later on, so at a certain point I just pushed to the ending instead of doing cleanup. Also, the music can definitely get a little repetitive as it seems each entire zone has just one song.

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely go for a 100% achievements completion for games, but I did for Astalon!An axcellent metroidvania with retro style pixel art (with big selection of filters if you desire to use them) and music.The core gameplay is simple - you have a jump button, an attack button and a special ability button. However, the depth of platforming and exploring the levels comes from switching between multiple characters.There are slight roguelite elements, in a sense that when you die you get a chance to spend accumulated currency on permanent and temporary upgrades. In theory the game can be completed without dying once, and subsequently with no upgrades, if you're a god gamer.Dying sends you back to the beginning of the game. However, as you play, you'll unlock shortcuts, fast travel points, and more traversal options for your characters, making backtracking easy and fun. There are lots of secrets to find as well as 3 additional game modes after you beat the game.Astalon is definitely worth its price! It's a blast of a game!

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Castlevania, you’ll really like this game because it’s basically just Castlevania. Responsive controls, interesting level design and a good combat system with the three characters all being surprisingly equal in strength, either attacking crazy fast, attacking quite fast at a decent range, or attacking slowly with an infinite range.The main gimmick of the game is that you can only reliably heal through dying, as the other healing method-- breaking candles-- only heals you for 5 health and has to be bought from the death shop to respawn. The death shop is the secondary gimmick, you buy upgrades there ranging from minor perks to stat increases and new abilities when, obviously, you die. This naturally leads to retreading rooms that you've already been through, but the level design is excellent and you're constantly rewarded with shortcuts for progressing far enough, and the enemy design is such that they telegraph their attacks so you can dodge so you can progress quite reliably as long as you play well. Furthermore, the levels are absolutely sprawling and reward exploration with death shop currency and rarely new items/upgrades, so you're strongly encouraged to not just blindly press forwards down the same path you've just been down.The one issue I have after playing a good 25% through (just beat the second boss) is that the keyboard controls are bricked. Space is ALWAYS bound to pause, even if you bind it to something else like jump, and for some reason you can’t bind shift to anything at all. XMousebutton Controller was a lifesaver, can’t recommend it enough. Apparently today they've fixed this though, so yay, no complaints then.

_childDocuments_.review: I beat the game (it's pretty easy, just way too tedious); I even unlocked the additional characters after I beat the boss (which only took me two attempts with zero grinding), and I think it was massively overhyped by the metroidvania community. The game overall is okay (I guess); it has some cool platforming and exploration, but the developers made some pretty terrible mistakes/questionable decisions. In my opinion, these decisions were so detrimental to the game that I'm simply not going to recommend it because of how annoying it was to play. 1. For the majority of the game, you can only apply upgrades when you die (this is not a roguelike/lite, so why would you this?) *2. When you die, you start at the beginning of the dungeon instead of the save points (like every other metroidvania since SOTN), so the save points are virtually meaningless. *3. For how few fast travel points there are, there is way too much unnecessary backtracking.4. The bosses look cool, but they are way too easy. Arguably the easiest part of the game. To sum up, there are much better metroidvanias available on Steam that are more worth your time and money. I've played and reviewed a ton of them. These include but are not limited to: Blasphemous, Grime, Tou Hou Luna Nights, Bloodstained: ROTN, Record of Lodoss War-Deedlit in Wonder Labyrinth, Midnight Castle Succubus DX, Infernax, FlipWitch, The Messenger, Islets, and many many more.

_childDocuments_.review: Everything you want out of a Metroidvania.Fantastic art and music, with a huge and interesting map to explore. I'd say that compared to other games in the genre, Astalon's focus lies primarily in exploration, navigation and platforming. Especially at the start, when you are trying to find your way and get your footing, the game's map can feel labyrinthine - in a good way. You'll discover that one central element of making progress comes from discovering and unlocking shortcuts - plainly visible and hidden ones alike. Whenever you die, you are set back to the very entrance of the Tower of Serpents, so these shortcuts can be huge time-savers in regaining your progress.Some might find that approach frustrating, but I appreciated the way it essentially asked you to master an area before you could easily bypass it. It feels like the game rewards your knowledge about it, rather than encouraging a grind of upgrading your characters' stats. Speaking of characters, the fact you can control multiple ones probably is one of the game's most unique aspects. While there are plenty of situations that call for the use of specific characters' abilities, it overall feels like you're able to pick a favorite and stick to that one.  This is especially true at the start of the game, where you cannot change characters except at save spots and it feels more like you're sending specific characters on solitary excursions. It's an interesting mechanic, and I appreciated the way it unfolded over the course of the game, though it came with a few minor downsides.One - it could be a bit annoying having to cycle through the characters (once you unlocked an ability to swap them on the fly) to quickly get to the one you wanted.Two - at least for the character I favored, Kyuli, it felt like it made a lot of the boss fights somewhat underwhelming. Her bow and arrow attack has the ability to shoot from far across a room, which lets you keep a safe distance easily. On one hand, I appreciate that this was an option (and I guess if I wanted a bigger challenge, I could have used a different character), but on the other, the boss fights did suffer from it. My strategy throughout all of them felt like it never needed to adapt much, which is a shame. Especially the final boss fight felt anticlimactic (in challenge, certainly not in presentation - all the visuals for each fight were brilliant!). It's likely that this was due to me having explored all of the map and purchased plenty of upgrades beforehand. Though it's certainly not something I am going to hold against Astalon - as it's an issue that a lot of games in the genre have.Again, I consider these minor downsides, and I really enjoyed my time with Astalon overall. But I wanted to point them out so that if you favor combat and challenging boss encounters in a Metroidvania, I would recommend adjusting your expectations of the game around that. Its challenges were much more akin to a marathon - getting to a boss fight unscathed (obstructed by platforming and lower level enemies; assisted by unlocked shortcuts) often felt like the much bigger challenge than the fight itself. That said, once you finish the game, you unlock some additional modes that feature new characters. I did not finish these, only briefly tried to see what the new characters feel like. It's entirely possible that a bigger challenge can be present here, if that's what you're looking for. There also is a New Game+ mode that shuffles the map around, which certainly feels more involved and interesting than a lot of other New Game+ modes that simply let you carry over abilities from your first game. Overall, I would say Astalon is of a medium difficulty. Especially when I started out, the game reminded me a lot of La-Mulana (in particular how secrets were hinted at in the environment, and how you could discover shortcuts). The key difference is that it's A LOT more approachable and easy - in particular regarding puzzles (Astalon is very light on them). So if you've bounced off of La-Mulana due to its difficulty or obscure nature, but enjoyed the overall vibe, I would heartily recommend Astalon.And to every other Metroidvania fan - you will not go wrong with this game either. It's definitely one of the best around. Its length (around 20 hours for me to 100% it) hits that perfect sweet-spot. The art is fantastic, with countless unique sprites that give the entire game a truly handmade feel. There's more of a story present than in a lot of other genre contenders, and its presented well. The music is banging, and the gameplay feels incredibly satisfying - again, especially if you favor exploration and are okay with less challenging boss fights.

_childDocuments_.review: Astalon is outstanding.  10/10.  I got Astalon in a Humble Bundle.  I hadn't heard of it before, and went in with no expectations.  It just looked like a nice NES-style platformer.   What I didn't expect was a top-class Metroidvania with excellent dungeon design.  Areas aren't too long, and puzzles aren't too cryptic.  There are a few mild difficulty spikes here and there, but death isn't ever an issue, as it brings you to a screen where you cash in the orbs you've collected to upgrade your characters.  There are very few negatives:-While the game runs at a locked 60fps, it stutters and doesn't feel as responsive as it should.  There is a mod to unlock the framerate, which works very well, but also makes some objects and enemies run at breakneck speeds.  There's a spider enemy late into the game that flies at you at mach speeds, so that's probably really not funny at all if you're arachnophobic.  -Some unlockable abilities aren't even explained until after you buy them.  Why?That's it, really.  The game is spectacular.  I can't wait to see the next thing from Labs Works.

_childDocuments_.review: I Played Astalon for a couple hours, made it through a few areas, and let me tell you, it was not a couple hours of joy. It was two hours of abject frustration. Movement is stiff and clunky and imprecise. All three characters feel awful to use. The game has me running through the same sections over and over again, with a lackluster map (you need to use leveling currency to give the map even the slightest hint of value), constant and aggressive gating, not behind interesting gameplay items, but just locked behind at least five different colors of keys. Map design consists of "climb tower A for a button to open a door in tower B. Go through door in tower B to open a further door in Tower A. Go back through A and flip another door in tower B. Now you can proceed through Tower B." Enemy placements are frustrating and obnoxious, and "surprise!" spikes pop up under you with intentional cadence. You effectively can't heal, but dying holds no penalty, and getting around is so tortuous that often the best way to get from point B to point C is to intentionally kill yourself and respawn from point A. Even if you're on the right path, if you're near a (rare) elevator you should kill yourself anyway just for a free heal. It's a classic anti-pattern.Then there are the little things, like how when you kill a nearby enemy it sends the coins out flying in all directions, purposefully over your head, so every enemy killed means backtracking and playing some 52 pickup (don't even get me started on the treasure chests. Never has uncovering a room of treasure chests elicited such dread). Items are not described, some even after you buy them, you'll spend 200 gold on something and it gives you an icon at the top of the screen like it's activated, but you've got no idea what it does. Switches will be flipped with no indication of their doors, and doors will be found with no indication of their switches. Upgrade prices increase between purchases at seemingly random and chaotic intervals. The game will frequently trap you into near certain death. Often, you'll run halfway down a level, only to see a blue door that can only be unlocked by the melee schmuck so you'll have to run all the way back to the campfire, switch to the blue guy,and run all the way back again (killing the same enemies for a 3rd time now) just to unlock the door. Oh, and long and unskippable cutscenes, some of them playing again at the start of each boss. The characters are strangely balanced. The character with the only long range attack is also the one that does the most damage per shot and has the only mobility skill available. Why ever use anyone but her? Your other options are an old guy that has no mobility skill, deals less damage, and has a medium range attack (but he attacks slightly faster), and a melee guy with a pathetically short range attack that you'll avoid for everything except opening blue doors.The art hits that feel of "maybe they went back in time a little TOO much", and lacks the finesse of the game's obvious inspiration, Shovel Knight. I found the music anywhere between non-offensive and mute-levels of bad, but even the non-offensive stuff starts to trigger PTSD when you find yourself running again through the same hallway and hearing the same tune again for the 50th time.I appreciate the effort that was made here, but I found the game comes up short in nearly every category. 5/10

_childDocuments_.review: I didn’t have Astalon on the radar until some people on the Metroidvania Review Discord were starting to talk about it so I checked it out and fell instantly in love. It’s by Matt Kap (who previously did Castle in Darkness, a masocore metroidvania-ish platformer) and some others he teamed up with. Visually the game is a love letter to NES games although while it looks like a NES game it has a modern heart beating inside it.Usually, I’m not too fond of games where you have to switch characters to progress, I prefer the whole unlock-ability gameplay loop to do that. Astalon has that as well but added character switching that you can do early on in the game at campfires, which you find generously strewn throughout the tower you explore. Later on, you will find an item/ability to switch on the spot but honestly, it never bothered me to go back to a campfire to switch as the game is so well designed that it usually has a campfire nearby if you need one. You can also unlock 2 more characters later on with their own abilities.Some people have used the roguelike moniker when talking about the game which initially confused me as there’s nothing roguelike about it. What it does have is a system similar to Rogue Legacy where dying allows you to spent your well-earned money on upgrades so that upon respawning you’re stronger than before. This is in theory a great system and worked really well in Rogue Legacy as its random castle generation could lead to some really tricky situations but here it somewhat trivializes difficulty. Halfway into the game (or even earlier) the bosses will become complete pushovers utterly getting annihilated by you. While not a K.O. criterium for a metroidvania, the Igavania games are notorious for how easy it is to cheese difficulty, it does lessen somewhat the enthusiasm for boss fights.But the game scores in the category most important for any metroidvania, and it scores big time there. The dungeon design is incredibly dense with numerous secrets to discover around almost every corner, fake walls, hidden abilities, various keys, invisible treasure chests, and so on. It’s often worth killing all monsters in each room just to see if it opens a gateway or discloses something else. You have various shortcuts, a normal elevator that you unlock with reaching its specific gate screen, you have two-way portals connecting various parts of the tower, and a teleport system working similarly in closely connected rooms. And depending on which abilities you have unlocked (or characters with abilities) you can cross barriers or scale heights to take entirely different paths through the tower.By the end of the game, it’s not so much about beating it which by that point will be so easy as not to be really all that interesting. No the real challenge lies in getting to each room, to open all doors and get to any unexplored corners of the map. And there’s quite a bit to explore with countless different sections each with its own theme and its own enemies. Like in Hollow Knight and many other games you can fill out a bestiary by killing a certain number of every enemy type but then you’ll discover that certain enemies can only be killed by a specific character and his specific skill. At that point, I found I had completely overlooked a secret from the beginning that allows you to slay ghosts. Though there’s one enemy that can only be killed by the special ability of one character and it’s not the ghost banning spell nor the block throwing stuff.Astalon also has a story that’s quite solid though it’s not exactly the driving force here. Almost more amusing are the character interactions you get at key scenes and on campfires when you’re allowed to rest (which happens rarely and mostly to advance the plot a bit). Once you’ve beaten the main game and maxed out every character and filled out the bestiary, you still have stuff to do. You can unlock three modes, a boss rush mode and two extra modes where you play through the entire game either with the Black Knight or a random gargoyle, both of whom handle quite differently than any other character.The Black Knight has a massive jump and can only replenish health when he stands still in areas with blood on the floor. While this approach is slightly more challenging than the main game as death means death here, it’s really the Gargoyle playthrough that takes the cake. While he can fly endlessly (though it feels more like flappy bird than a majestic flight) the only way to replenish health is by getting random food item drops from enemies and these don’t happen too often. Both the Gargoyle mode (which looks a lot like playing as Firebrand from Gargoyle’s Quest) and the Black Knight mode allow you to go for a bit more difficult experience which is really nice. A lot of games do this, many of the Igavania do, but there are few games where I’m actually motivated enough to actually dive right back into the game. But Astalon has just such a well-designed level architecture that it’s fun to play through all over again.For a game, I didn’t know anything about beforehand Astalon pretty much managed to become my metroidvania of the year and probably is in my top 20 list of all-time great metroidvania. Truly great experience, it’s the one metroidvania to check out this year.

_childDocuments_.review: Astalon: Tears of Earth is a very good Metroidvania, that takes a lot of inspiration from the game Trine.  As with Trine, you switch between 3 different characters to solve puzzles.  It also incorporates elements of RPG's, Roguelites, and Soul'slikes.  It really is a great game... after you get past the opening section. The first few hours of this game are a brutally punishing slog where you have to play threw the same sections over and over again.  You have little health, poor movement, no evasion, and no defensive abilities.  Plus all three characters move ever so slightly differently, so if you get used to the timing and jumps with one character, the others play just different enough that your going to miss jumps and fall into attacks.  You are always taking all but unavoidable damage.  You die FREQUENTLY and every time you die you respawn all the way back at the start of the game Rogelike style, only to have to retrace your steps and take the same unavoidable damage every loop.  If you are lucky you get a few rooms farther, and maybe get an upgrade or enough in game currency to buy a few skill points.  Honestly after 30 or 40 minuets I was frustrated and gave up for my first 5 total hours I played this game.  I would love to see the devs adjust the opening difficulty possibly giving the defensive knight character a few more hard counters or evasion for the rogue when the game starts. After that I got to the mid game (i.e. enough upgrades to survive) I really started to enjoy my time with Astalon.  When you are not repeating the same sections ad nauseam, exploration is amazingly rewarding. The art is spot on for a NES inspired game, and the graphic filter options are the best I've ever seen.  Normally I'm a crisp chunky pixel guy and never uses filters, but Astalon have several that I fully endorse.  Sound design is again very solid.Overall I recommend Astalon: Tears of the Earth as the mid and end game are fantastic.  You just have to be ready to slog threw the miserable first few hours to get there.  If this is a compromise that you are willing to deal with, you will enjoy the game.  If you do not have the testicular fortitude to beat your head against a wall for half a day... there are other far more approachable Metroidvanias out there for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This is pretty good, as an NES-era inspired metroidvania. sufficent content, decent graphics within the style and all that.The game's biggest problem, however, is not being bad, but the fact that the genre is filled of better games.  It's as if the game design decisions were NES-era, as opposed to modernized, and it shows:- The bosses are often far less challenging than navigating the maze- The idea of very minimal healing, leading to restarts, doesn't lead to better decisions, or roguelike tension.- You get to heal at campfires... sometimes? This makes no sense. This is also the main way to move the story forward, but it also wastes heals.- The developers can make good scene pixel art... but mostly skip doing anything special in said mid dungeon story beats?- Character utility is very unevenAll fixable things with time, but it seems like a game that was marked as finished with a whole lot of polish left to do. It's still perfectly functional, and would have sold great if it wasn't in a genre full of games with four times the polish and production values.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: What is Astalon: Tears of the Earth?Released on June 3rd, 2021 (on PC, Switch, PS4, and XB1), this retro-styled metroidvania follows a classical aesthetic while having a more modern methodology. Leading to an overall fun experience. This might be one of the few games where I honestly pick up the OST. The music is really good!Created by Labworks. This is a stellar entry by a largely unknown studio. I'm interested in knowing more about this world and I hope Labworks get the support they need to continue doing that. It's very clear they know what they're doing and how to create a modern feeling game with a retro look. The game follows a simple cycle. Explore the Tower, kill enemies, gather orbs, collect items, perish: upgrade your heroes and repeat. There's not much to it, but what is there is polished to a fine sheen. The game feels great to play and is responsive. I think the only thing people might have an issue with it, is that when you jump: you are committed to the direction you are looking when you jump. It's a classic product of it's era, but I can imagine that might be the only thing that might irk some people. You'll get used to that quirk eventually. Other than that, the game also does not tell you what upgrades do. Which is another product of the era and the design philosophy behind this era of gaming. So I can find some people might not like that. This is not a rogue-like. The Tower is clearly and carefully designed. There isn't much in terms of replayability, outside of some bonus modes. However, that shouldn't dissuade you from picking it up. For it's 20 dollar price tag, I got nearly 22 hours out of it, with a keen desire to play more. This game is not terribly challenging, but it is not a complete pushover either, at least initially. While it is retro-styled, it is not as punishing as games from that era. This is a game where it can be beaten eventually. The slope in terms of difficulty is pretty steady with no real sudden spikes in terms of challenge. By the time I got to areas that were challenging, I largely felt prepared for what I had to go through. Even making it through one of the hardest areas in one shot!All in all, it's a good little gem and I hope it gets the opportunity to shine. Give this one a go!
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Great metroidvania overall, and runs great on Steam Deck.The art style is consistently great throughout, the cutscenes are fantastic, the music is enjoyable.The game has an OKAY flow throughout. The games main gimmick is dying and going back to the start, but you get stronger each time. You also unlock various ways to navigate the castle throughout, like portals (tied to one another) and the elevator that essentially teleports you to the start and end of each floor. Healing is a scarcity throughout, so you are expected to die.This generally works great...but earlier on this may frustrate you. Each character feels very different, and allows you to access different things. To swap characters, you need to trek to a campfire.  This works fine for the MOST part.   You unlock a way to swap at will later in the game (about halfway) that makes everything a lot smoother.My biggest gripe, and a small spoiler:I do want to put a small note that it's very flashy, even with the accessibility option to make it flash less. My girlfriend has epilepsy and she was wanting to watch me play, but that was not an option. Some enemies flash a TON when you kill them. Besides that, the game kept me compelled and took me over 15 hours to 100%. It's a solid game!

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid Retroidvania game. It's basically Trine if it came out in 1991, and was made as a collab between Capcom and Konami with a dollop of Souls and Roguelite trends from the future and a smorgasboard of other 80's and 90's game references including Ys III and Milon's Secret Castle. The main gimmick is that this game has a Souls/Rogue respawn system where health pickups are extremely limited and you can only upgrade your character on death and start over from the start, while also have multiple characters to switch between as you assault an evil tower. Some particulars:> The game feels particularly big because the character sprite to screen size ratio is on Mega Man levels, and the map is composed of a LOT of screens, so it really *feels* like a huge game, although if you play it for a bit it's much more manageable than it at first seems. > The death system will force a lot of back-tracking early on when you're especially weak, which could be a bit frustrating over the course of a game. > There are more map zones than bosses, by a fair amount, which feels a bit odd and really there just aren't enough bosses generally. The ones they have are good, so it's a shame there aren't more.> The difficulty is basically entirely player driven, which could be a good or bad thing depending on your tendencies. You start extremely weak but can make this game extremely easy through upgrades. If you want a more directed difficulty curve and can fall in to a tendency to overlevel or grind you'll probably find the game too easy too quickly. > The upgrade shop doesn't give you enough information on what the items you're buying actually do, which is an opaqueness that doesn't add to the game because there aren't actually any penalties to buying anything, and you're either going to look up what an item does or you're going to learn what it does on purchase, so it's just obfuscation for obfuscation's sake. Definitely a recommend if you like Metroidvanias and/or Retro styled indie games. This one seems particularly suited for the 30-something crowd that grew up in the NES era as there are a surprising amount of references and nods to games from that era that I don't think zoomers would ever actually get simply due to their obscurity.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: What a weirdly paced emotional rollercoaster of a game that was. Astalon starts off pretty strong. The striking NES-coded visuals with their matte color-palette of beautiful orange and blue tones, the boppin’ chip tune music and vintage yet charming story presentation hyped me up pretty instantly. Within the first couple of minutes of gameplay, the game lays down the basic formula for the entire playtime. That formula is a creative mix of traditional metroidvania, puzzle elements and rogue-lite progression. As a player, you can switch between 3+ characters all with different abilities, slightly different move set and attack modes; it’s the old and well-established divide into warrior, archer and sorcerer that you can choose from. You progress through a dark tower, motivated by a simple plot of saving your home village from the evil  who have poisoned the waters and overrun the lands with tyranny and terror. It’s a neat setup that is anything but original but was enough for me to spark my curiosity. The first hours that followed irritated the hell out of me. I love the search-action genre and I count games like Symphony of the Night (SOTN) among my absolute favorites. I do prefer the more modern takes on the genre with game elements introduced by Super Metroid and SOTN. However, I do not discriminate against more traditional  that usually present themselves as more linear but also unforgiving or outright brutal. I expected Astalon to be a modern search-action game with all the “progress” made in the last decades, offering quality-of-life features like save-points, level-ups, teleporters and an open level structure. I thought that the 8-bit look of the game was purely an aesthetic choice that wouldn’t extend to game mechanics. The thing is, all of these features I just mentioned  in the game but somehow, Astalon still feels super archaic in its design at times. Most of my frustration with this game comes down to the lack of features the map provided, at least initially. This is one of the most rudimentary maps I’ve ever seen in a search-action game. Save-points are marked, as are teleporters and elevators. The rest is for you to figure out and – most importantly – memorize. You do unlock more features for the map as the game progresses, like items and key locations, but even then, the map remains rather basic. There is one little nitpick that I need to point out because it bothers me so much. As is usual in this genre, there are secret passageways between rooms, like hidden openings in a wall. Once you find one, the map . Naturally, when you check the map later you see a solid separation between rooms where there is actually a secret path you already unlocked, not a fan of this. In general, the game just expects you to keep a lot of information in mind or to take notes on your own for later reference. As you keep playing, there will be a plethora of small and not-so-small secrets in pretty much every room you’ll have to keep track of. So many times would I re-enter a room looking for an item that was supposedly hidden there only to find out that I couldn’t access it at the time. The game doesn’t allow you to put your own markers on the map which would have been greatly appreciated. The backtracking in general is a real pain in the butt, especially at the beginning. Within the first 4 to 5 hours of playtime, I felt like I made little to no progress. This game has rogue-lite elements and is designed around you dying a lot and starting again from the very beginning. It is rather forgiving as you basically keep all the progress made. The map-sections you visited remain uncovered, you keep all the items and even the crystals that function as currency to obtain upgrades for your characters. Still, in the early hours, I died really easily from environmental traps or the occasional over-the-top room filled with way too many enemies. So, I ran through the same set of rooms over and over and over again feeling like losing my mind. Elevators and teleporters are sparse and even in the later stages of the game, it usually takes a while to get where you want. I nearly dropped the game here as it felt more like a chore than a pleasure. But something kept me coming back. For when you  make progress in Astalon, it feels significant, it feels rewarding. I got a rush of adrenalin whenever I found a shortcut or an elevator. My mind was racing with all the new ways to interact with the world upon unlocking a special ability that enabled me to access new areas. It’s that old-school design philosophy of restricting the player so much that every little success feels like a huge milestone. You may hate that or you may love it but I definitely get the appeal. Bosses are a mixed bag. The first major boss kicked my butt so hard, I thought I’d never defeat that guy. Going back to previous areas and leveling up my characters helped a lot though and I finally got the better of him. Every other boss that followed was a walk in the park. I would go so far as to say that bosses get successively  as you play which is not what I expected. I pretty much spammed the final boss to death without any kind of strategy or tactical maneuver in a few seconds. The pacing is just weird like that. You spend the first 5 hours barely making any progress and hitting a rock wall with the first boss only to blast through the second half of the game like bulldozer and getting super overpowered; it’s one of the weirdest difficulty curves in the genre.There is a lot to love about Astalon. On an audiovisual level, the game is pure bliss. The little animations are really cute, the campfire chats between the characters are super charming and once the game clicks, you don’t want to put it down until you’ve seen it through to the end. But there is just as much irritating stuff and weird game design decisions to be found here. The map is just a pain to deal with, backtracking is way too emphasized in the first half of the game, bosses are rather simplistic, the story doesn’t do anything special and the game throws unlockable characters at you at a time when you’re almost done with the game which is like… why? I would still absolutely recommend getting this if you’re at all interested in the genre and are fine with some esoteric game design choices. It surely isn’t for everyone but believe me, if you give this game a proper chance and don’t drop it within the first couple of hours (and I don’t condemn you if you do), you will find a lovely little gem of an indie title underneath the rubble.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game as part of the AGDQ 2024 Humble Bundle. I'm not well-versed in the design of (or especially good at) Metroidvanias, but I nevertheless enjoyed Astalon -- I played it to completion! -- and thought I'd write a review in recommendation of it. I'd be hesitant to recommend it at full price, mostly because I am a cheapskate, but if you can find it as part of a bundle, it's worth picking it up.+ The character designs are appealing, and both the PC and monster sprites all have good animations.+ The post-apocalyptic setting is fascinating, and I wanted to learn more about .+  is a stroke of genius. Not only is his design impressive, but his role in the world's lore also becomes an interesting mechanic, since . So many times when playing a game, I might be tempted to ask myself, "In the context of the world they live in, how did these characters become so powerful?" Not here. He's a perfect example of how to properly merge form and function in game design.+ As expected for a quality Metroidvania, there are lots of neat little secrets to discover, many of which reveal story or add variety to gameplay.+ Good music.+ Fighting, as it should, feels really good, especially when you've collected all the bells and whistles for the playable characters.• Movement feels okay for the most part. I used a controller to play and occasionally struggled with getting my character to face the right direction when attacking. Some characters are more maneuverable than others, but they're also less overall powerful, unfortunately.• Although you're given a wide range of characters, you will likely find yourself sticking with one or two of them, switching to the others only when you need their special abilities. It's a shame that they're not all equally viable in combat.- The game could have used an editor. Some of the dialogue contains misspelled words or incorrect grammar. It's distracting -- but not to the point of being a deal-breaker.- Some of the campfire scenes were out of order for me. (For example, in my playthrough, .)- When making use of the campfire to rest, I saw the same dialogue repeated over and over again. That felt like a missed opportunity, especially given that none of the scenes includes .- The boss rush mode is particularly difficult and annoying because many of the items you're offered aren't helpful in the slightest, and the fights take forever -- especially the animations after a boss is defeated.- The number one complaint others seem to have about the game is that it requires a lot of backtracking -- more than usual for other Metroidvanias -- and I would agree with that. It's easy to feel lost, since having an unexplored part of the map does not necessarily mean that you'll be able to progress in that direction.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the great art direction, atmosphere, and level design, this game is held back by "tunnel vision" in game design around the game's gimmick.In this game, when you die, you are sent in some demonic realm which serves the purpose of the game's shop, and after your shopping spree is over, you come back to life. In theory a very good concept, but the execution is awful and ruins the entire experience. The game's progression revolves so much around "farming, dying, buying upgrades" loop, only made extra tedious due to absurd game design decisions such as being unable to restore health in any way other than dying and respawning, shop upgrades not telling you what they do until you buy them, and you always respawning at the beginning of the dungeon no matter what.In practice, this quickly makes you hate the good level design because you will end up doing the same rooms dozens of times due to forced backtracking, campfires are seemingly useless as you cannot use them to heal on demand, and even if you use them as save points, they don't work as respawn points. Every single chip damage from enemies is devastating, as you will not be able to be full health where you last died, often resulting in your completing about two extra rooms, and taking a death again, repeating the rooms you just did again. In the 90 minutes I spent playing this game, I probably spent 20 minutes exploring new rooms, and 70 minutes redoing rooms I've already completed.The last straw for me was when I blind purchased an "upgrade" in the shop with my hard earned and scarce money, only to find out I just increased the enemy's damage output. Yeah I'm out.This game features so many questionable game design decisions which I feel could have been fixed if they didn't host the beta test campaign I was a part of just a mere week before launch. I cannot recommend this game in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: I was enjoying this at first, but there are just too many things that keep me from recommending it. Unexplained mechanics, powerups that are both expensive but lack any kind of description as to what they do, way too much dialog, and the most annoying thing- constant backtracking to get to the campfires. What finally made me quit was when I got to the first boss- it was immediately clear that I had no chance whatsoever of defeating it (my attacks did almost no damage). Faced with the prospect of dying a lot, and backtracking a lot, all to level up my attacks to where they might actually do something sounded like the opposite of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: An impressive Metroidvania, with lovely pixel art and quite unique game mechanics.The difficulty is not too high, but offers enough challenges to keep you on your toes, and even though you will die frequently, it is never a punishment, because you don't lose any progress. You constantly purchase various buffs and new talents, so if you lack skill as a player, you can make it up by grinding a bit and buying upgrades.The game has lots of secrets and collectible items, genuinely making every new find impactful.I strongly recommend it, for this price it's a steal.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun, average-length metroidvania with some DNA from La Mulana and Lost Vikings. Doesn't hold your hand, but reveals itself as you progress, with a good distribution of special items and new abilities throughout the adventure. The secrets and riddles for solving puzzles can be fairly devious but not frustratingly so, if you find something you can't figure out, just keep exploring and something will click.In addition to the main game there are unlockables: NG+ mode with a remixed map, Boss Rush, and two other campaigns with different characters/abillities. It's quite good overall.I did encounter one bugged puzzle late in the game but simply reloading the save fixed it, was the only time I got really "stuck".Some characteristics of the game become a little imbalanced towards the end. The power creep is very gradual, as most obtained ability items have very subtle or specific effects, in particular the coveted traversal abilities which actually grant you access to later-game areas all take some doing to acquire, this is done well and gives you occasion to familiarize yourself with the complications of the map. The early game is fairly difficult, with an interesting mechanic on managing health which is hard to recover, and also once you find the option to sacrifice some of health in exchange for more xp from enemies. However, late in the game if you bother to max your stats (why wouldn't you), even the bosses become kinda trivial especially if using the right character. But NG+ does significantly increase the difficulty, mainly in terms of damage received, but also with new enemies, traps and routes to explore, you acquire the ability items in a different order -- I appreciate when games do this.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: it is with some hesitation I recommend Astalon: Tears of the Earth.I enjoy some of its main features:But I didn't enjoy everything.Common first complaint from me on recent indies -- the Title doesn't really fit. This game is about a dungeon filled with giant evil statues you have to kill. Tears of the Earth are never relevant except for lore you can ignore, and doesn't really have to do with the main problem in the game. Maybe the title is an homage to Japanese fantasy games or something. But I know this is a minor nitpick. The result of the negatives I listed is that just getting around the big Metroidvania map is a chore, and the game makes you do it a lot. There is some of this that's expected in a Metroidvania game like this -- the whole map is kinda supposed to be a big maze; it's supposed to feel mazey. But when you die in this game, you go back to the start, and can only rely on sparse fast-travel points to get quickly back to where you were. You'll come back with upgrades, so it'll be easier, but you're still retreading the exact same paths. And it's almost impossible to restore health for most of the game, so you'll die frequently just by tallying up inconsequential platforming mistakes (or occasionally getting hit by things during the screen transitions that you couldn't possibly predict).There are a lot of quality-of-life upgrades to earn in-game, but you won't get them until you've grinded a lot or getting really far into the game. They really should've front-loaded the QOL upgrades -- I like them being upgrades, and I like earning them. But I didn't need to play for 10 hours before I could appreciate them.The map indicators, as I said, aren't good enough to tell you what path you'll need to take. So unless you memorize the layout of every grid you've been in, you'll run back into some dead-ends you've run into before, making re-traversal even more tedious. The paths visible from the map leading one sector to another can be outright misleading.The later, harder areas of the game seem to deliberately have less fast-travel access, and getting to them is harder and more time consuming. So you end up re-treading the exact same floorplans a lot.Ultimately I feel like I understand what they were going for. It's similar to the roguelite formula, and Metroidvanias often require a lot of retraversal for secret hunting / unlocking new areas anyway. Seems like a perfect match, right?But Roguelites have procedurally generated levels for a reason - so that when you retread the same path, you're not bored to tears. Astalon doesn't do that. And I think they knew, wisely, that having too many fast-travel points would trivialize the death penalty -- but the re-traversal just usually isn't fun. So they're left holding the bag. They added more, and more tedious, retraversal to an already retraversal-heavy genre, and it's not an improvement in that respect.All that whining aside, a big part of me is happy that they did something a bit new with the death mechanics to make death more consequential. Maybe with a bit less of a punishing map maze, I would've appreciated it more. They're taking risks, and so ultimately I'll leave a positive review, since I'd rather indies take some risks than not. Hoping they're taking notes and learning some lessons along the way.If you can get over the grind of just getting through the map, there's a lot of fun ideas in this game, and I don't regret my time with it. I could've just done with about 3 hours less running into the same dead-ends.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of people are comparing this (accurately) to Legacy of the Wizard on NES. If you like that game and 'metroidvanias' in general, this is a no-brainer to pick up.It has the classic feel of Metroid and Super Metroid, where you find puzzles and pathways that you can't access just yet, but there's no indication that you'll get the equipment or power-up to ever access it. Move on, you'll find the power-up. Or you'll backtrack later and realize you just didn't clear the room, or you had to approach from a different direction. The exploration is phenomenal is what I'm saying.It uses the Legacy of the Wizard gameplay loop of using different characters with different abilities that have strengths and weaknesses against different enemies and abilities you'll need to swap out to traverse certain areas of the map or address certain puzzles. It also starts you at the beginning if you die. A lot of people are complaining about this, and I disagree with them wholeheartedly. For one thing, instead of picking a character and sticking with that character until death or return to homebase to swap, you can swap at 'camp' locations all over the place and eventually whenever you want (you get this ability rather early on...well before halfway through). And there's a fast travel point...RIGHT AT THE BEGINNING OF THE MAP. I swear, the people saying they are fans of metroidvanias that complain about the lack of fast travel points and needing to backtrack the map...have never played a metroidvania. This game's map is not huge. Hollow Knight asks more backtracking from the player than this game does, and every enemy defeated provides resources you need so without a little backtracking you'd be seriously underpowered for different areas. These complaints are baffling.Pick this bad boy up, don't listen to the naysayers whining about fast travel.

_childDocuments_.review: Check out my full gameplay review video for Astalon: Tears of the Earth. I go into great depth about the Story, Graphics, Audio, Gameplay, and other noteworthy things I feel needs to be mentioned:  So Astalon: Tears of the Earth is an action platformer with rpg elements that plays like a metroidvania. The game starts with our three main protagonists entering a tower in hopes of ridding their village with the evil poison spewing out of the building.There’s Algus, the mage who kicked off this whole adventure by making a pact with a demon for great power, the Knight Arias who is brave and wants to live up to his family’s legacy, and Kyuli, a ranger type class who is along for the ride in order to help her village from further corruption.The game starts you off with a quick introduction then throws you right into the action. Right off the bat you can start exploring the tower. Just like most metroidvanias you start off pretty weak but after finding new items, equipment, and skills you’re able to survive easier and explore more of the blocked off passages.Each of the characters have their own strengths and weaknesses. You can play as only one of them at a time, but you can switch out who you control at bonfires, which also doubles as a save spot.To give you an example for each characters uses, the knight has more defense, boasts a fast melee attack and can reflect projectiles, the mage has mid range ranged attack that they can pass through blocks and activate switches, and the ranger has a screen wide range attack but it is slower, she can also bounce off walls to reach higher places.These characters can also be upgraded in various ways. As you defeat enemies and complete challenges you’ll obtain currency used to upgrade their skills and stats permanently. Some of these changes are universal for all characters while some are class specific and compliment their playstyles.You can increase attack, defense, health, invincibility frames, collect radius, improve map features, and way more. You unlock many skills to buy throughout the game and there’s even permanent stat increases and skills to find in the tower itself. The big feature this game has that makes it stand out among other Metroidvanias of this style is how the death mechanic is used here. Every single time you die you end up at the skill shop to spend your currency. Buy what you want or maybe save up.After that you are brought back to the beginning of the tower at the very first room. As you get further and further along the map you’ll start to unlock more shortcuts, secrets, and teleports. Astalon: Tears of the Earth is a very well made action rpg metroidvania. The constant character progression is addicting and frequently rewarding. The exploration aspect is fun with puzzles to solve and figuring out which character is best in which situation.The graphics and animations are very nice to look at. The music is amazing with a chiptune feeling but also harboring an overall sense of epicness. The story, while not at all impeding your gameplay, is there and is pretty unique and will want you to keep playing in order to find out how the characters react to the situations.The only thing I personally had an issue with is the controls. I played an earlier version of the game so I’m not sure if it will be a problem in the release but my character would sometimes glitch out and walk on their own after inputting a direction.They would continue to slide even after jumping unless I wiggled the stick around a bit. I’m not sure if it’s my controller or maybe the game is sensitive to sticks but it was better playing with the D-pad. I have no opinion on keyboard and mouse though.The controls, though the combat is fun, the movement doesn’t feel as tight as you would expect it to be. It’s not as stiff as let’s say Castlevania 1 or anything, nor is it as well implemented as a Mega Man X game. It feels floaty and just a bit off. It could just be me though.Overall, Astalon: Tears of the Earth is well worth the money and I easily recommend this game. I love metroidvanias and this one has all the right mechanics that will keep you addicted to not only see how powerful these characters get, but exploring the tower is satisfying, the death mechanic is challenging but rewarding, and the main driving story plot is competent. Definitely check this game out.Disclaimer: I received this game for free. I was not paid to promote or write a review. All thoughts are solely my own. Thanks!

_childDocuments_.review: Its a damn shame that this game isn't being talked about more.  This is a top-tier metroidvania.  If you enjoy SOTN, Metroid, Hollow Knight, etc you wont be disappointed.  It has beautiful NES-style graphics, a sprawling map, awesome music, great characters, interesting boss designs, and secrets upon secrets.The story has you following 3 adventurers who are trying to figure out who poisoned their village water supply.  You can swap between the 3 characters to navigate different obstacles in the tower.  As you'd expect you unlock new abilities as you progress that allow you to reach previously inaccessible areas.The only minor gripes I have about this were a few graphical/hit detection bugs.  None of these were game breaking.  The other thing is it starts off a bit slow.  Traversing the tower can be a bit of a slog at the beginning.  Once you start gaining new abilities it really picks up though.This game combines old and new with great results.  If you're a fan of exploratory 2-D action games dont sleep on this one!

_childDocuments_.review: Well, hot dog!      This game is everything I love about old games from bygones past but with no limitations on graphics or system memory so you don't get flickering and tons of slowdown like you might remember back in the day.    It's a Metroidvania/RPG hybrid, where death is only the beginning. That's right, you actually die in order to level up in this game! For those that are worried, this IS NOT a rogue-lite or rogue-like, so you don't have to worry at all about losing your items or the rooms suddenly changing around when you die.      As for the story and characters, it has a very serious and dark tone reminiscent of old school RPGs of the 8-bit and 16-bit eras, with a post-apocalyptic world where high fantasy magic rules. There is some dry and dark humor to be had in the way the characters interact with each other. Something worth noting is that, depending on what character you're using, when you inspect various objects in the tower or face a boss, they all have unique dialog!     Finally, the graphics and art style of this game are phenomenal. Rysuke Mita, the mangaka who did "Dragon Half" back in the late 80s, did the character designs for this game and they are full of charm and personality. The characters move about as little chibi 8-bit characters but with fluid animations.      One thing I love about modern hardware with the retro aesthetic is that the concept of lovely pixel art can be more fully realized by game designers and graphic artists and it certainly shows in . There are flowing tattered curtains, dripping water (and other substances), detailed stone work as you climb/descend to the different areas of the dark tower and it simply oozes atmosphere. There is a juxtaposition between your cute 8-bit characters and the grim environment full of corpses, blood-soaked traps, and grotesque statues of monsters. The enemies are very interesting because some of them might be familiar RPG/D&D, but there are other designs that defy description, in the best way possible.     I can't recommend this game enough, and I bought it twice so that I can play it on multiple systems as I like. Will keep an eye out for future releases from this dev for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: A really great "metroidvania", one of the most enjoyable i ever played.Very charming 8-bit style with good tunes and great gameplay. A bit on the tough side but the challenge is what makes the game fun to play. The controls are very responsive and the gameplay with the multiple characters gets a bit more depth that what it looks on the surface. The map (one of the most important thing in the genre) is great to explore, full of secrets and challenges. The game also has loads of content if you go for full completion (besides the main game that is about 15h long), and it doesnt really get boring.Absolutely recommend it for the fans of this genre and style.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the perfect example of a dev who grew up playing retro games and Metroidvanias and knows exactly what they want. If you've played games back to the NES days, I'd say this is a combination of Faxanadu and Legacy of the Wizard (with a lot of modern improvements).I will say before my actual review that I helped play-test the game for the publisher, so there's that. But I honestly believe that this game is amazing and is deserving of high praise, and sincerely hope that LABS Works puts out a sequel.Pros:+ You can switch characters frequently, and each character has their own set of unique abilities suited to different combat situations and puzzles.+ The game map is MASSIVE and there are TONS of secrets to be found.+ Control feels smooth and very responsive.+ The graphics look amazing. Player characters were designed by Ryusuke Mita, creator of the manga Dragon Half.+ The music is fantastic, and you'll never get tired of listening to the soundtrack.+ Upgrade system allows for customization of your favorite characters.+ Plenty of unlockables including staples like a Bestiary and Music Player.+ Very fair and well set up difficulty curve.+ Multiple endings.+ Several new game modes to unlock.+ The color palette is like Shovel Knight. Very close to the original specs for NES games, but they add a few colors here or there that wouldn't have been possible back in the day.Cons:- The current build still has a few bugs in it. Characters will get stuck walking on flat platforms. There are a few places where you can softlock using Kyuli's wall jump ability.- The story is interesting, but it feels somewhat lacking. Bad thing is happening, heroes must go stop it. There is a unique twist, but that goes into spoiler territory so I won't say it here.If you're a fan of retro games? Go buy this. If you're a fan of Metroidvanias? Go buy this. If you like fun games with tons of content for $20? Go buy this. Seriously, what are you waiting for?!
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: A very retro metroidvania that is heavily inspired by the castlevania series on the NES. While it has quite a few  QOL improvements over games made in the 80s it doesn't have enough and this can only be recommended specifically to those who have a tolerance, or even a desire, for retro-style meroidvania gameplay. The world itself is truly excellently designed with secrets within secrets within secrets but because of the lack of the aforementioned QOL improvements you're probably going to need a map from the internet at some point. The ability to add marks on the map would have prevented the need to use a map from the internet but it is what it is. Japanese developers have been slow to learn from the innovations of western developers in recent years.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so frustrating. It has so many good parts, but so many flaws that are just bewildering.The good...- It has a really big map, with tons and tons of secrets and optional areas, even recruitable characters- The controls are great- The visuals are just fantastic. It's fairly true to the NES, but also has some downright haunting imagery.- Music is pretty good too- Combat is usually pretty fun and exciting- Lots of stuff to collect- A few interesting cutscenes, though not a particularly deep storyThe BAD- Ohhhhh boy, the healing. Well, I should say, lack of any healing whatsoever. There are only three ways to heal in this game.1) Candles, one time use (unless you PAY to refill them!), heals only 5 HP2) Green orbs, extremely rare drop even with the upgrades, and heals ONLY ONE HIT POINT3) Regeneration item... THAT WAS IN THE VERY LAST ROOM I EXPLORED, AT THE END OF THE GAMEThat's it. You end up just having to make it to the lifts, and then die so you can start off at full health. Oh, and when you die, you always go back to the first room of the game. Lovely.- Many of the "power-ups" seem like things that should have obviously been a regular part of the game. One of the power ups is just descriptions of items. Why would you ever make that something you need to upgrade? What? In addition, there is no description for them, so you have no idea what they do until after you buy them, and sometimes I still couldn't figure it out.- In platforming, crumbling blocks do not respawn on their own. This forces you to leave the room, and then come back in, respawning every enemy.- In a similar vein, some platforming sections involve you making jumps that bring you to the next screen up, and then falling back down, which respawns all the enemiesIt's a shame that this game is held back by the bad. It's so frustrating, because it can be so fun, but its obvious, bewildering flaws randomly take you totally out of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Super Metroid is my favorite game of all time, and I love Metroidvanias.Astalon: Tears of the Earth is an 8-bit (by design) metroidvania which sort of weaves in RPG elements with a roguelite mask over them. You can only heal by candles for the large majority of the game, and so dying brings you to the game's shop, where you spend your currency earned by killing baddies on upgrades and new abilities/buffs to make your next playthrough easier. This is cool because you know that you can upgrade every time you die, and it also takes the pressure away from dying, because dying is generally a good thing (like most Roguelites), you can progress by dying. The game spawns you at the entrance to the tower each time, but the next room over is an elevator (lift) that will take you to the start or end of each area, so that you're usually not too far from where you died.Gameplay: 9/10The game rewards you for dying instead of punishing you which is super cool. You would really have to grind hard to upgrade everything all the way, so instead it's got more RPG overtones, where you can choose to level up everyone fairly equally (what I did) or save up to make one character super buff (what I did at the end with Arias). One thing this game does very well is that it has a LOT of powerups scattered throughout the world. At no point in the entire game are you thinking "OK I'm fully upgraded now there's nothing new to get besides health upgrades this is boring." Up until the very end of the game you are still getting new abilities or passive powerups. This keeps the game fresh for me.There's mostly great level design throughout. There are some cheap enemies and hazards in some room transitions but that's arguable, and even then with no fear of death it's not a very big deal.I would say the bosses are much too eary. I died on 2 bosses in the game and 1 miniboss. Usually it was due to low health. The first boss I died twice on. Most bosses I killed on first try. This could have been me being Mr. Exploration and getting tons of powerups, but I never felt like I needed to go grind monsters or collect orbs to get some buffs to have an edge on a boss. Once you learned boss patterns they generally had a good warning of attacks, and weren't too difficult to dodge.Music: 10/10Excellent, catchy tunes throughout. You can tell the game creators have made 8bit music before, or had heavy influences from 8bit era of gaming. The sound effects, music, everything is A+Graphics: 10/10Really excellent models, animations, sprites, level design. Some level design seemed redundant, like the bricks in the outer rooms of the tower being identical from area to area, with a mere palette change. That's totally something you would see in a NES game, but I would expect this game to have more original tiles since it doesn't have the size limitations of a NES game.Story: 9/10The story is pretty cliche. It's serviceable, and it has some original elements strewn about the cliche'd ones. It's not a story I would tell my grandkids about, but it gets the job done. We don't really play Metroidvanias for story do we?Overall: 9/10Great game. If you like Metroidvanias and aren't bothered by it being 8bit, this is one you definitely won't regret playing. I beat this in like 2 weeks, so you can tell from 29 hours (with not a lot of idle time) that I played it very heavily while I was.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great, quite high difficulty metroidvania. I find it high difficulty not in the combat or bosses, but working my way through the map. I think in 7 hours I've seen less than 50% of the map.I've seen plenty of people commenting "LOOKS LIKE THE DEVS FORGOT TO SAY THIS IS A ROGUE-LITE!"This game is not a rogue-lite in any conceivable way. Nothing about the game is random. Yeah, you upgrade when you die. So what? If you die in dark souls then use your soul items to level up does that make it a rogue-lite? No, it doesn't. You don't even have to die to upgrade. It ain't a rogue-lite. That being said, you will die. Quite a lot.The only negative I have about this game is that item descriptions are extremely lacking or even completely absent, even after buying the item description upgrade. People have said that they blindly bought an upgrade which made the game harder. While technically true I mean... the upgrade makes enemies do 10% more damage and you get 10% more currency. Pretty minor difficulty ramp up considering almost every enemy I've seen, including bosses, do less than 10 damage. I'm taking 4.4 damage instead of 4? And it goes away when you die? Damn dude... brutal... (But yes you *should* fully be aware of this before you buy the upgrade, but the lack of descriptions makes it tough)
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a very good game, nice visual style, dope music, fun exploration, solid controls, etc..Not without its flaws, notably most of the upgrades are very vague about what they do and how they work.Honestly one of the things that made me uncomfortable about this was its core mechanic of death not being final; I'm hard wired to feel that dying is failure, so I want to grind healing instead of respawning with full health. It's a weird position the game puts you in.One thing in particular I have to praise about it, your wizard character Algus feels like a legendary figure; in most games magic feels mundane, in this it feels SPECIAL, like Gandalf type of special.

_childDocuments_.review: This runs perfectly on the Steam Deck. I’m changing my review as I powered through the first boss and then it turned into one of my favorite games I’ve ever played.The art style, music, enemy designs, and level designs are fantastic. If you manage to push on past the first boss it gets much easier as you level your character up. Running through the dungeon is very annoying at times, especially when you have to throw yourself against the same place over and over. The campfires truly don’t make sense to me as they’re basically a point at which you can save, not at which you’ll ever respawn. They aren’t not checkpoints. _childDocuments_.review: Great game with some minor faults. It's more puzzley than other metroidvanias, which was a plus for me, although I would have liked some puzzles to be a bit more obtuse. There's a puzzle with teleports that makes no sense in terms of pathing, as solving the riddle will basically get you to a place you've already visited. On the other hand, that says a lot about how open the map is.Also, the characters aren't too balanced; one of them is certainly much better than the others due to sheer damage and range (Castlevania Man) while another is only used for three or four puzzles in the game, as his kit is not really that good for the level design (Zeek).The bosses are somewhat easy, the first few are probably the hardest since you get to them with very few resources, but once you can reflect projectiles most of them become probably way too easy.The map layout is very nice, with memorable rooms, but the minimap is a bit iffy, as sometimes the rooms contain two comlpetely separated paths that you cannot see when the map only shows exit points.Still, it's a very fun game. Exploring the tower is very rewarding, it makes you feel like you have a big brain when you find some hidden path or some spot that spawns orbs. In a way, it does the reverse of what many soulsvanias do nowadays, where most of the difficulty comes from the bosses while the path to them is somewhat bland. In Astalon, the journey is the fun part.Easily the most fun I've had with a game in 2021 so far. Very recommended if you like the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: There is no such thing as a game that caters to every type of gamer. Some of us love RPGs but hate Racing games. Others may love Sports but hate Horror titles. This is a truth that's starting to make more and more sense to me as I get older. Me? I love Metroidvanias. I love having a huge map filled with secrets to discover and new abilities to acquire which leads you to even more goodies. However, while I wanted to give this one a chance, after spending what time I have with it I'm afraid I can only recommend this one if you're willing to endure ALOT of hardship for very little reward. In other words, if you want a game that's mostly just challenge and not much else, this is for you.Now, I do not mind a challenge in my games. I mean, I love the Dark Souls games and I love Doom Eternal, and those are some really hard titles. However, this game? It pushes the difficulty to such an extent that I legit just ended up being bored out of my mind by the end and just not caring all that much. Dying...carries some pretty heavy penalties in this game, and yes, I know death is a key part in what little story this game has but that doesn't make it any less frustrating. You die, you get a chance to spend your currency on improvements and upgrades in the hopes your next run will go a little easier. However, you're also sent all the way back to the starting room of the game, meaning you could lose a considerable amount of progress. Also, said upgrades can get VERY expensive, meaning you may need multiple runs by the end just to acquire one or two upgrades, and as of writing this, I only now found out the best way to farm currency so...yeah.Sure, you can unlock teleporters and elevator stations to help cut down on the amount of backtracking and getting to places but I found that only goes so far. Plus, even after I acquired almost all the gear and most of the upgrades in this game, I didn't really feel all that stronger than I did at the start. Not helped by how my greatest enemy ended up being those blasted spikes. Seriously, not only do they take a big chunk of your health, but you get all of ONE SECOND to jump off before they spring back up. Like, wow, that is incredibly strict in my book. To the point it feels needlessly cruel. Also, I just learned getting the best ending requires you to get a 100 percent completion, so...yeah. Considering how much of a boring slog I found this game to be, I'm not sure I'll be going through the effort. HOWEVER, this is all just MY opinion. You may play this and it'll be one of the best games you ever played. Remember, all of us have our own tastes, and what one person enjoys doesn't always mean someone else, and there is nothing wrong with that.  Be open to trying something new, and if you don't end up liking it? Well, at least you're now a little wiser thanks to the attempt.

_childDocuments_.review: Kind-of a good game, but it fools you as to what it really is. The general look and feel of this game is superb, but the things that bother me REALLY bother me.The only thing the 3-character system does is make you backtrack more, and it adds nothing but more frustration to the game. It would also be nice to start where you saved last instead of all the way back at the beginning. The prices for upgrades could be lowered a good 10% at least to make the game less of a grind as well. The worst part about this game is the constant backtracking- every room is a puzzle. Some people may not like that aspect, or think this is more of a casual game until they find out what it really is. Me personally- I would have preferred a more casual game without 90% of the puzzles.This game could have been a gem, but the backtracking and puzzles make it only about a 7 out of 10. This is not a casual game that you can play whenever you want with some free time here and there- this is a 'memorize every room and play the whole game in one sitting' kind of game.I had to change my review to negative for the following reasons: there is nothing but 2 options for rating, this game has too high of a rating in my opinion, and I can't find the energy to play this game again considering that I forgot what I'm supposed to be doing and it's been many months since I played it (I gave up).
