_childDocuments_.review: I just finished this with 98% map completion. I'm loving this boom in metroidvanias over the last few years and I've played all the ones that have good review scores. This is one of the best. The world is huge and filled with secrets. Many of the items you find add meaningful changes to gameplay. The different characters have great variety. The art looks great and has a really creepy feel at times. Quality chiptune music that doesn't get old. Worth every penny at full price!
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't beaten the game yet, but... holy smoke do I love this game. I do love me a good metroidvania,  and this game scratches that itch. The Good: The music is great, the gameplay itself, is fun, and it is pretty tough overall. We are not talking La Mulana hard, but still tough. The RPG aspects are almost roguelike and the story is pretty great. The cons: the ONLY issue I had... is the lack of HP regen early on. Later in the game its not as bad with death orbs, but its very minimal. That is me trying hard to find any cons with it though.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: A sometimes tough but rewarding Metroidvania. The game excels in it's level design, which it stands a head above its contemporaries. The spritework is gorgeous, the truckload of CRT emulated modes with appeal to the NES purists, and the soundtrack is a treat for the ears.  Well worth the asking price.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Astalon is a roguelite game with a fun and simple graphical style.  Some of the tunes are quite earworms and reminded me of Megaman 3 a couple times.  The overall dungeon feel evoked a lot of memories of Faxandu: an old NES game.  I can't articulate why it does.  Overall, I enjoyed the feel and the flow of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: What a great surprise: Addictive metroidvania with a roguelite twist in that dying gives you the opportunity to upgrade your characters - there's three of them with distinctive skills and you can switch between them fairly freely. The production values are top-notch (esp. if you like high-res NES graphics), and the game has been receiving frequent polish updates since launch. If you like exploration-heavy platformers, this is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an wonderful homage to msx style games like la mulana one. Overall, its a brutal game that blends metroidvania exploration, light puzzle solving, precise platforming , and a roguelike progression system.The game is massive and it took me almost 16+ hours to find everything. Oddly enough there is one criticism I have for the game. Some of the later bosses are a little too easy. I hope the developers make another game and they crank up the difficulty to absurd levels.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: A metroidvania that is overflowing with secrets, items, Easter eggs, bosses and probably the best damn soundtrack you will ever hear! I had some reservations about the game the first hour or so in but anything that seems like a problem becomes fixed as you upgrade. Incredibly satisfying exploration and tight controls make the game a joy to play. You can tell an immense amount of detail and thought went into the map layout and it is difficult to full 100 percent ( i only made it to 97% ). My only issue was there were times in the game where it made more sense to die and restart than to back track. However, backtracking usually feels fine because of how dynamic the upgrade system is. you can level your characters and buy plenty of upgrades and the upgrades actually make you feel more powerful and they are very rewarding! If you are fan of old school games like Zelda II Links adventure, NES Castlevanias or Megaman this game will make you feel right at home. The team did an amazing job with this one and Ill say it again the music is just *chefs kiss!
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Simple mechanics put to the test by brutal difficulty that's reminiscent of the old days. This difficulty is somewhat lessened by the fact that every time your party dies, you're taken to a shop of sorts to upgrade your characters to improve them in battle and exploration.Although some characters feel more useful than others do, you cannot say that a character is completely useless (by virtue of the game's design and in terms of each character's skill set). It will take some getting used to, swapping between this cast of characters that share a health pool and constantly dying in an unforgiving environment that requires full awareness of each character's skill set, but the exploration it offers because of this system is a tad too addicting--a credit to its design.There are a few bugs -- namely, how characters sometimes need to jump off ladders before they count as off the ladder, and a few bugs that prevent character switching. The checkpoints few and far between also hurt when backtracking to areas (and you WILL be backtracking), but overall, this game is great. Definitely worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Game is great, very reminiscent of many great classic games like megaman, shovel knight, super metroid etc. The gameplay is fun, the platforming is crisp and the game has a really good difficulty curve; It felt challenging, but always fair and it never got too difficult. The map is huge with plenty of secrets and places to explore. it's a proper metroidvania map too, too many metroidvanias i've played use small cordoned off sections of the map laid out in a grid and don't feature the sort of interconnectedness and intracacy that makes exploring those maps fun. Highly recommend if you're at all interested in the metroidvania genre because this game has some real legs.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty delightful little metroidvania experience. Cute NES-style graphics and music, with pretty tight controls and interesting variety of mechanics and items. Even the story is pretty interesting, not that it's the important part about an action adventure! The difficulty level isn't too punishing, and since you do get a chance to get stronger when you die, you can substitute persistence for luck and skill (which is a godsend for someone like me who appreciates a casual adventure).The biggest downside is that there's a lot of backtracking -- if you die, it's back to the very first room. Without spoiling too much there're many ways to expedite returning to where you were, but even with that you're gonna be going over certain areas over and over, and that makes the gameplay feel a bit on the grindy side at times. I don't mind too much personally, but something to consider.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: While probably better described as a Rogue-like-Metroidvania, it has a good story and makes you think through the puzzles/requirements at least at first. There are some minor bugs, but nothing gamebreaking. Figuring out the strengths of each character is a must, as they will all be required to complete the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: A decent old school Metroidvania that ultimately I got near to completing, but didn't really feel all that compelled to. You reach the "final boss", long before the map is anywhere close to 100%, and I can't for the life of me figure out why you would want to rush off and do so. There's not really incentive, and that's a pretty big flaw in a metroidvania. The map is also really annoying to follow, with a poor legend and failure to mark hidden pathways into other rooms once you have found them. Also, some warp areas don't even show up on there at all, which is just awful.Asides from that, the gimmick of having to switch players to better traverse the game is pretty neat. I don't think it was fully utilized - especially when the game suddenly decides you need to have the power to switch at will, essentially making the thought process of going through long stretches with one character rather redundant. The game would have been better off with much more lenient warp spots, and keeping the character switching limited to camps.If you're looking for a recommendation, I'd say it's worth playing, but there have been better options this year. Notably, Ender Lillies
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: - Great Metroidvania that's packed with content. - Difficulty ebbs and flows but leans toward challenging through-out most of the play-through. - Plenty of secrets to find, most of which can be seen with a perceptive eye or keen intuition. - Each character has strengths and weaknesses, each bringing something different to the party. - The map is sprawling and has many nooks and crannies to explore. - The story is minimal, but what's there I found interesting enough to seek out. - Additional game-modes after first completion.It took me roughly 11 hours to beat my first 100% file completion, and that was after a preliminary 6 hours on a previous file. Great game, and I can't recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT*******  Still a thumbs down game and now about 8 hours in and 7 of it is spent back tracking to get the right character and trying to remember how and where to go to use that characters skill to progress a further 1% only to die and have to backtrack from the start all over again.   Really the multi character and death backtracking ruin a somewhat fun game.  It's a chore and work to continue backtacking so much without QOL improvements on how the game is traversed is the biggest reason why it gets a thumbs down.  The second reason is the spike traps and drip drops and enemy missle are inconsisent and i feel like they track where your going and not where you are.  If you scroll a screen the platforms for jumping are gone or a spike trap will kill you and its time to start walking from the begining again. I just really wish i could get my money back this feels like work and isn't fun after a few minutes/hours just a big dissapointment and let down.There is a lot to like here but overall the pain in the butt of restarting in the very beginning and having to do SO MUCH BACKTRACKING if you aren't using the right character or died you spend the first couple hours just walking to the first gorgon boss to die and repeat.  The spike traps are timed weird, same with the projectiles on the enemies.  Sometimes it feels timed correctly, other times the timing feels purposely off to kill you.  I love metroid/castlevania style games but Astalon is more of a chore than a fun game.  Just really poor controls and grinding gameplay with so much back tracking its not fun at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Out of all the side-scrollers that I had played throughout my entire life, this is by far one of the best. Controls are simple, story is easy to understand and engaging, and the variety of powers/abilities are also simple in those regards as well. I love the variety of levels presented, and the BGM for each one definitely brings it all to life. The only dislike that I have is that I feel like the two characters that you get in the game later on, should have been power-ups :/They add almost nothing to the story - save for having their own background story to briefly tell and that's it. Now, they are fun to use but it can be a hassle to keep switching between them either at the bonfires or when you obtain a certain item to switch on the fly.Overall... 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: I was waitig for this game. In general I liked the game and it's plot. Nice work. But it lacks some style.At the current state it reminds more of a big maze with swarming minor monters and hidden passes where you die more likely from searchig for an entrance to another level than in a boss fight. Currently savepoints are not working, so that can be frustrating.Liked the legend of Gorgons, but they are weak now, their power and cruelty are not implemented in full constent. Not all them have two forms (stone and demonic), no dengerous abilities. Locations also has no unfluence on their appearance or abbilities. Almost no evidences of their hunger, only few corpses somewhere in the deadends. The first cutscene with the dark knight is rather a silly joke, because in real he is weaker than any mini-boss in the game. There are also a lot of rooms with inactive stone heads and statues of monsters which could be major obstackles or puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. It hits all the right notes. Crystalis, Maze of Galious, Dark Souls, Metroid, Castlevania, and a few others. But it's executed very well, the gameplay is crisp, the powerups are meaningful without being overkill, and the difficulty isn't so punishing that you get mad at the game. It's just fun all the way through. Soundtrack and art are great. It's even got a Willow reference.Skip the super arrange soundtrack though, the instrumentation on that is Not Good.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Astalon is one of the better Metroidvanias I've played recently. The story is intriguing and the world is captivating. There are some cool puzzles and exploration is rewarded with upgrades and a handful of secrets. I enjoyed the challenging platforming, evolving combat, and mysteries. There is a central mechanic where you can level up and buy upgrades upon death, but the game is not a Rougelike/Rougelite (so don't worry if that isn't your thing). The game has secret characters and multiple endings. My only criticism is that sometimes you complete business in one section of the castle and would like to warp somewhere else right away to find a missed item, but the only not-slow way to do that is to kill yourself. So instead of reversing through the maze in the direction of a warp point--which will take at least a couple of minutes--you start looking for a way to die, which (depending on your stats) also takes more time than you would like.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Individual rooms are generally pretty fun, but the overall design of the castle leads to constant backtracking and aimless wandering to find newly-reachable areas and items every time a new ability is unlocked. (There is an item that helps mitigate the backtracking to some extent, but it takes much too long to get that item and it only partially solves the problem.) Upgrading heroes is also way too grindy and slows game progression significantly.The game's almost good and I really want to like it, but in the end most of the time with the game just feels like padding, retracing steps through the same rooms over and over again. It ends up feeling like a roguelite except without any of the map randomness that keeps those games feeling fresh. Here you're just dying repeatedly, leveling up a bit each time, but then replaying the exact same map with the exact same enemies. It's fun for a bit but gets tedious and annoying pretty quickly.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: The game forces you to backtrack through the entire dungeon every time you die. Save points only serve to save and quit. I feel like I don't have to write anything else. This alone is such an incredibly stupid, poor design decision that it alone trumped all the things that are really good about this game, because no one in their right mind would waste a player's time like that.Just don't even bother with this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: I've tried to push myself a little here because it seems like it's a relatively decent game. But I don't really understand where the praise is coming from. It definitely doesn't stand up against other metroidvania games that people keep referring to.There's 2 big issues, stemming from how you get your upgrades. The first is that you gather currency by killing enemies, forcing a grind. If you like grind, this may not be an issue. You don't necessarily have to keep going in and out of one room over and over and over. But there are items like HP+1 Attack+1 Attack Speed+1 with 20 odd ranks to get yourself to a maximum, with an increasing cost. None of these items tell you what they do, you'll need to look up a guide - I don't know why, there's no fun in guessing how to spend your hard earned money - and you can only upgrade when you die. You can buy an item that lets you buy at certain points in the game while you're alive, but this doesn't make a whole lot of sense either, because you'll have less money to spend by the time you get there.The second problem is the metroidvania-esque upgrades you find lying around. Most of them aren't at all satisfying. I have about 10 upgrades which I think is about a quarter of these types of upgrades in the game, and about 3 or 4 of them are just effectively keys to progress. Doorway-openers. One is a music test. That's not rewarding. A couple of interesting-looking items are used only by the melee character which seems to me to be the weakest of the three, so those are items I almost never use.Another problem is that you can't really heal. There are fairly-rare candlesticks where, when broken, heal you for a few points, but then you have to pay 50 coins per candlestick you've broken to restore them. In other words, if you want to heal, it costs you your progression. And hopefully you won't need to heal before you're able to repay that debt, otherwise you're trapped in healing limbo. Killing enemies doesn't heal you. Camping/switching characters doesn't heal you. Dying heals you, but you're meant to avoid dying, sort of.I like the pixel art style, but don't like the music.I'm photosensitive and there's a disclaimer about flashing lighting at the beginning of the game, but all of the flashing is unnecessary. There's an accessibility option to change this between "Moderate" and "Full", but even on Moderate, the main menu has a hard flash and certain portals in game flash fast nonstop until you leave the screen, and I have to assume there's more like this. This is particularly odd because of how avoidable these situations are. There's an option there for it and they only go half way? It doesn't contribute to the atmosphere of the game to keep in this kind of flashing, photosensitive or not.Look, it's fun enough if you've got nothing better to play, but if you're after a new metroidvania, I just can't rate this one higher than average on the list, even given its positive aspects, especially not at full price, but probably not even at half price.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: It's ok. Although there are a lot of very rough design decisions. It begins with the save system. You have to manually save at checkpoints, not that uncommon, but if you die you start at the start of the game. So no matter where you died you have to walk all the way back. It has a lot of short cuts so it wont take too long but still. You can't use the save system to exploit the game (by buying something for instance to see what it does and then reload) because the game autosaves after death. That means the only time the game doesn't auto save is when you are in a hurry and want to close the game without having to backtrack to a save point. What's the point here? Why not autosave on exit? Then there are your 3 heroes: Red Archer, Orange Mage and Megaman. You can only swap them at save points which gets very tedious very quickly. I run down a hallway as the archer (because the archer is the strongest character) only to see a thing that needs to be unlocked by the mage. So I run back to get the mage instead, open the thing, go into the next room and see a wall that needs to be destroyed by megaman. So I run back and get megaman and go back. That's the game. I don't know if they ever going to justify not being able to switch characters on the fly, by having certain areas you can only traverse as one of them for instance, but if not then the should have changed that. Especially since HP is shared between all characters so you can't even switch to restore health. Later on you can switch at will but before those are tedious ten hours. The store doesn't tell you what each item does. It really hurts when you spend 666 orbs on a "gift" if all it does is give you the ability to buy upgrades without having to die first... when dying and respawning is easier than having to walk to one of the rare shop locations. And some buffs only last until you die, not that the game bothers to tell you about that before hand. There even is a "knowledge" item that gives you better item descriptions (they still don't tell you what they do but in more words this time). In general the game is very VERY grindy. You have to embrace the walking in and out of room farming.But the exploration and progression through the map is very fun and there are many unexpected gameplay changes and upgrades.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: 1/10You can be a fantastic metroidvania with excellent graphics, animations, sounds, and music. You can have an interesting map that invites exploration, a story that leaves you with some questions, and excellent controls.But all of that is for naught if you abandon your game while it contains the absolute worst game mode of any game I’ve ever played. The Boss Rush here is a travesty. It destroys any good will you might have with the game. It is slapped on, yet required, and throws all of the good dev practices seen thus far out of the window. It’s incredibly slow. Runs can take 30m or longer. You have to sit through incredibly long intro, outro, and phase change animations, EVERY TIME. You have to wait while the dead boss spits out money at you, very slowly, EVERY TIME. You get three random items after each boss, except some don’t even have a use in this mode, while others are so important you may as well forfeit if you don’t get them. In short, it’s the cheesiest, most frustrating, most poorly thought out game mode I’ve ever played. I’ll probably get this “somehow”, but it has destroyed any good memories I have of this game.Also, the game has a habit of crashing right on initial game load on the Steam Deck. It has had this problem for three years now. Good luck to any potential Steam Deck users.I won’t buy any more games from Dangen after seeing the state this game was left in when it was abandoned.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This is a well-crafted metroidvania, with an interesting twist on death and upgrade mechanics.Like any good metroidvania, the emphasis is on exploration and unlocking various movement abilities that help you reach further parts of the castle.The twist comes from the way leveling up and death are treated in this game.  There's very few effective ways to heal yourself while playing.  Occasionally you'll get to rest at save-points after major events or find orbs that restore a few hit-points, but for the most part any damage you take is permanent.  Once you die, you're taken to a shop where you can spend resources to purchase various upgrades for your characters.  These range from simple stat upgrades, to meta enhancements like marking locked doors on the map.Dying also throws you back to the beginning of the level.  Thankfully you unlock shortcuts, portals and elevators that will help you quickly get back to where you were before.  I've seen some complaints about this system in other reviews, but it never took longer than a few minutes to get right back to where I was.  The character switching mechanic is fun with each character excelling at certain roles.  All in all, this game gave me the same feeling some of the best metroidvanias do.  It keeps you going, wanting to see what's on the next screen, and leaves you feeling slightly sad when it's over.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: I'm giving this a no not because it seems really bad, but - man, I've played a lot of metroidvanias and other ones look better, play better, have better soundtracks, this one really is at the bottom of the list just about. Bad things I would say are the controls, the graphics, the fact that save points don't do anything and you have to backtrack a bunch when you die, the story seems lame. I only played it for like 45 minutes but was done at the end of the 45 minutes. Three games with a similar sort of vibe and gameplay that I enjoyed more are Castle in the Darkness, Aggelos, and Odallus the Dark Call. I'd play those three before you play this.All that said if you're a metroidvania addict you could do worse. It's just not good compared to others I've played and I won't be picking it up again.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of good encased in a lot of bad.This game had (and still has possibly) a lot of potential, but overall I feel like it fails to execute what it wants to do.  It tires to be a platformer, but the controls are not responsive enough. It tries to be a metroidvania/dark souls combo, but overall it just feels lacking.  I tried to enjoy this game, and I put a lot of time into it to like it, but in the end I found it more tedious and aggravating instead of fun.Spoilers:The black knight mode is what finally made this a 'no' for me.  It gives you the option after (very painfully) getting 100% on the first game to play as the villain.  However, there is only 'one' way to heal yourself in this mode, and that way is extremely few and far between. Plus, when you die, you die for good and have to continue from last save (unlike the original where you keep everything you got and whatnot).
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: When you die in this game, you do not return to the most recent save point -- you go back to the beginning of the game.Backtracking is usually something I enjoy in Metroidvanias, but not when you have to do it for every single death.  That's just adding needless tedium to the game.Also, upgrades are expensive and have vague descriptions (or none), so it's difficult to decide what to purchase with your limited currency.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: The gam could have been much better, but it is a no from me.Pros;+playing with 3 different characters is boring at first, but after you get the "Switch whenever you want" item, it is better.+Exploring can be rewarding.Cons:- Roguelite system is bad because it requires an enormous amount of grinding. Also, due to this system, there is a terrible design choice to start from the beginning, instead of the last save spot.- I said above, but I will say it again. Skills are too expensive. Attack-defense skills are separate for each character and I think this is ridiculous.- You start at the beginning every time you die. And fast travel points are too scarce for this system.- For a game without a way to heal yourself (apart from very rare monster drops of 1 hp), there are a ridiculous amount of traps like spikes. And these melt down your HP very fast if you are a little careless.-Oh yes, you cannot heal yourself in the game. Only after boss fights, you get to heal yourself one time, about %50 of your HP- Backtracking is bad because there are a lot of rooms where you need to cross a terrible amount of spikes just to find out that you cannot go there from your location. And since you cannot mark that room, you go there again and again during gameplay, just to find out that you still cannot cross the room.NO.

_childDocuments_.review: It was a decently pleasant metroid.If the developers made a few changes this game would have went from mildly good to excellent. The four biggest of which are:1. Nerf spike damage, increase monster damage (Later in the game i simply ignored mobs and was basically playing a platforming game with orb collecting).2. Add a few extra elevator checkpoints (I found myself repeating the same rooms a little too many times trying to remember where to go and as a result ended up overfarming before most of the bosses).3. Prevent the player's characters from being overpowered when facing bosses (Implement some sort of softblock on how many times the player can level up his character before facing x boss).The first 2 bosses were kinda lame and not fun to fight against while the other ones seemed to be well designed but died within 10 seconds to my overfarmed characters.4. Having the good ending be unlocked by finding certain items/doing specific things in game not 100% discovery of the map which includes secret rooms (I only made it up to 96%). _childDocuments_.review: One of if not the best looking 8-bit games I've ever played. But wow does it lack some things other modern search-action games have (metriodvania games). Before the negatives, which are easier for me to talk in length about, I really do love the room/ map design in Astalon ep2. Great enemies, challenging platforming, wonderful art, and even the occasional puzzle, or joke/ oddity. However, when zooming out there are some big problems I started to notice, especially as the game dragged on at the end.1) My biggest gripe is with the bosses, or more so the leveling system that lets you out-scale the bosses later in the game. This makes the earlier bosses the hardest, and the later ones a joke. 2) My second biggest problem with Astalon ep2 was the lack of meaningful fast travel options around the quite large map. This was also more of a problem in the later half of the game when it just seemed better to die and go back to the starting room sometimes. The  was the type of item I wanted more of, maybe something like a  would have fixed this for me.2.5) Oh, also, please mark important rooms that I have already discovered. Such as the 3) This one hurts personally, and maybe should be higher up? But wow does this game need more music. The good tracks that Astalon ep2 does offer get so so repetitive, and as a whole the game sadly doesn’t even come close to the deep OSTs that many other games in the same genre/ art style offer.All in all I liked this game, and do recommend it, but honestly not just to anyone. _childDocuments_.review: A fun game, controls well, and the level design is mostly spot on.But two complaints;First one is the two unlockable characters. _childDocuments_.review: Astalon's level and enemy design are pretty competently made. It doesn't try to aggressively push what it does have, though, so Astalon ends up being defined by what it DOESN'T have: reasonable numbers of fast travel nodes, healing, and mobility upgrades. This is a game that doesn't respect your timing and expects you to put up with its failed three-character gimmick that's so dire (forcing you to backtrack to campfires to swap characters normally) that it just gives up entirely and gives you an item to cheat the gimmick completely. The wizard is the only character worth upgrading and using, with the other two having crippling drawbacks that make trying to use them a mistake.If you're a fan of the genre you might get something out of it. Do not touch this game if you aren't - this is not a good foray into the Metroidvania genre and you should be playing something cool like Axiom Verge or Hollow Knight instead.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game but it got frustrating after a while. Traversal abilities are too slow to come by and just not fun to use at all. Fast travel points are sparse. Puzzles can be obtuse. Combat is limited. The worst aspect is the map design. Parts of the map are too sectioned off and you're forced to take detours and backtrack too much. And the mini map is lousy. For example, it may show that you can go up 3 rooms straight but actually one of the rooms gets permanently walled off in the middle and you have to actually walk through 6 rooms instead. When combined with lackluster traversal abilities, the game just became really tedious in the long run.Compared to Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night, Ori 1 & 2, and Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown, this game is just... meh and overrated.

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome metroidvania with a massive tower to explore. Lots of powerups to both find and purchase and new baddies/bosses keep coming to keep things fresh. _childDocuments_.review: The art grabbed me with its charm and readability. It's animated beautifully, and the game recommends a soft anti-aliasing to give a lovely, fuzzy pixelated look. The artist gets it. I love the art  — it deserves a better game to go with it.My hour with the game saw me standing on one side of a screen and slowly shooting enemies. Or taking damage because the enemies' movement patterns feel jerky. Or hitting spikes because falling follows a strange arc. Or accidentally double-clicking in menus or cutscenes because button registry seems to be hyper-sensitive. Or dying and trekking back to where I had just been from the start. Death has some of the most draconian penalties I've ever experienced. It asks you to replay parts I would just as soon not see again. Yes, the game unlocks shortcuts and has a form of progression that lets you skip certain sections after you've made enough progress, but, man, it is just a drag to navigate those rooms.For comparison's sake to illustrate why I think Astalon just doesn't work, I also died a lot in Infernax or Faxanadu, but getting back to where I died each time was satisfying. It was challenging, and I had to memorize patterns and navigate the world carefully. Progress felt meaningful, a la that Dark Souls kind of meaning (or like learning to play the piano and mastering one section of a song until it all comes together). Astalon was hard, yes, but in a way that seemed like that's all there was to it. I felt no joy in progressing because I didn't feel any better at the game, and I didn't feel like the game wanted me to engage with it. It didn't have interesting patterns to memorize and it allowed me to choose the uninteresting way of progressing. Again, I sat on the edge of the screen slowly shooting at enemies or got swatted by enemies with strange jerky motions that were at odds with the soft, sensitive movements of the characters. Rather than deeply and patiently testing and polishing the game with love until it shined, the game wanted me to like it simply because it was a shallow reflection of better games that I already like.Unfortunately, I can't recommend Astalon despite its promising appearance. I think that it's the sort of game that works better on paper than in practice. The developers didn't seem to want to kill their darlings. It's a game that needed more cooking; more time with each room with someone asking, how do we make the experience of playing this game as magical as it has the potential to be? How do we pare things down to make each system meaningful and not there just because they are cool in the abstract? How do we get the player to deeply engage with the game and play authentically? How do we make something that is our own and not a hollow facsimile?
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really enjoyed Astalon: Tears of the Earth. It does so many things amazingly well. In short, the game is a Metroidvania where 3 adventures head inside a tower in search of who poisoned the water and you progressively unlock more abilities and areas where to progress to.The presentation and story are done so well and they draw you in. The game leans heavily in amazing gothic aesthetics and it's the consistency of how good the areas look that turns the tower into a character of its own. It makes your imagination run wild which for me at least partly feeds into the story of the game as well. There is a nice and consistent thematic throughline in the design even when you are unlocking areas that look very distinct on their own. The story and cutscenes are smartly done; there is not much of it and it acts a bare minimum to push you through to the end but what they have is focused on the characters. There's no long clumsily written exposition but instead, it tries to hit a few emotional beats with absolutely minimal writing. Which I think is smart here because it's allowing things to play more in your mind and does not take you out of the experience.The exploration and upgrades are also very well done. New abilities open up new areas and allow you to backtrack to old areas to discover previously inaccessible places and treasures but I noticed multiple places where an upgrade would have made advancing easy but it was possible to progress even without an optional upgrade. It would just require more skill and you to be more observant. There are areas which you can miss altogether and it strikes a good balance of giving you freedom in which order to complete areas, how to do it and with what ability sets while at the same time pushing you towards the end if you are not interested in exploring. The game design here is really good.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: When it comes to itching my 8-bit nostalgia, Astalon: Tears of the Earth couldn't have done it any better. The world created here is a blast and proves yet again that this era of gaming is alive and stronger than ever!

_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty game ultimately hampered by awful design choices. I like it, and I hate it.The good:* The sprite work is gorgeous and the music is spot on. The game FEELS like you're playing it on an NES.* The map design is great. Each area feels different, navigation weaves you through different screens multiple times. Exploring new areas feels fun.* The combat is generally engaging. Most of the time when you die it's your fault, though I've had a few cheap deaths due to falling onto spikes from an adjacent screen or being transitioned facefirst into an unwinnable encounter.The questionable:* No real way to restore health in the middle of a run. Enemies don't drop health, and the limited fixed health pickups cost money you won't have.The bad:* The fast travel in this game is AWFUL. For a game supposedly oriented toward making mistakes and dying, the game punishes you horribly for it. Each time you die you restart at the very beginning of the game, which means you'll spend the majority of your time just tracing your steps to get back to the exploring fun part. You have to _unlock_ fast travel to use it, and unless you're playing with a guide there's a good chance you'll miss it altogether. (It's behind a locked door you probably won't have a key for.)* A lot of necessary upgrades are generally hidden or require hidden keys. The fast travel unlock is a major one, but the upgrades to increase the number of orbs you pick up are also necessary and are in hidden side rooms-- you have to do something not obvious to actually get them.* The shop system only being accessible upon death makes sense, but I can't tell what anything does until after I buy it. Why?* The "save point" system. There are campfires spread through the game but they don't restore your health and you don't restart from them when you die. So the only point to having them is to force you to backtrack if you need to stop playing. Why would you design a game like this?Ten hours in, not yet finished, and after multiple frustrating deaths trying to reach another fast travel point in Ruined Ash I'm putting this one down. It's pretty, it's just not fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Astalon is one of the best Metroidvania titles to come out in a long time. You can tell how much love the devs put into this 8-bit world at every corner. Each character and their abilities are critical to progressing through the tower, and you will find so many secrets just by exploring and you never get lost or frustrated with countless ways to approach each new run. With hours of replayability, characters and items to discover, stat progression, and a ton of other unlockables, Astalon sets a new standard for retro indies and for the price is a steal.

_childDocuments_.review: Astalon Tears of The Earth is a game developed by LABS Works and published by DANGEN Entertainment. It is a punishing 2D Platformer Metroidvania, where your mistakes will send you right back to the entrance of your castle, your only hope of returning in any sort of appropriate time, being the games Dark Souls-esque shortcuts.For people who enjoy series like the aforementioned Dark Souls, which derives most of its difficulty from contrivances, such as janky parkour mechanics, undue punishment, poor hitboxes and laborious runbacks and backtracking through all of said jank, this game will probably scratch just the right itch.The game markets itself as a Metroidvania, with NES-stylings, which is quaint enough on its own, and there is nothing wrong with it on the surface. Unfortunately, the developers of games such as Astalon, too often forget why we moved away from this era of gaming mechanically speaking: We've come a long way in terms of game design. And while many indie games use nostalgia only to their visual and auditive advantage, using said elements for evoking a certain feel, style and, on a meta level, time in the history of gaming, others, such as Astalong, decide to forget all game design lessons learned throughout the last decades too.Nostalgia is a fickle thing, and a nostalgic product lives or dies based on the premise of "does it make you feel like you're playing one of those old games?" or "does it make your remember why those games are old and archaic?" When a game, such as Shovel Knight, brings in certain stylings, and matches them with an appropriate level of identity, quality of life and intelligence, the end product is greater than a mere replica of a faded, bygone era. Astalon innovates in no way shape or form, its controls are sloppy at best, its backtracking is purely tedious, its health drops are non-existent, most upgrades have no description to them, until you purchase them, meaning you can either spend your hard-earned money on important things, or on things that are less than useful to you, only a small icon and vaguely poetic name to accompany you during your purchasing decision. I seemingly have just unlocked the ability for enemies to drop health orbs, so maybe it can eek out a few more hours from me."Where do you purchase these meta-progression upgrades?" You might be asking. After dying, of course. You do not get to spend your money or see the games' uneventful shop until you die. Don't worry, it will happen a lot, because everything does a lot of damage and healing is sparse to the point where it might as well have been removed from the game entirely (at least so far during my play). After purchasing your upgrades, you get revived by some ancient god... at the very entrance to "generic castle nr. 22356", the game's very signature location (mind the sarcasm). Thankfully, you unlock Dark Souls style shortcuts to your destinations, but they don't help make up for the tedium of first unlocking them, and you still have to actually run to or through the shortcut/elevator/warp to access them.You have three characters, two-ranged characters, and one with a pitiably short sword, whom you will only use if the game really makes you. How will it make you? By placing various obstacles down, which can only be bypassed with a specific character. Sounds neat, right? Pretty classic game mechanic, featured in many different games before this one. Well, what ends up souring the whole thing, is that Astalon: Tears of The Earth has the brilliant idea, that no game I've ever played with this mechanic has had, of allowing you to switch characters only at campsites (the game's save point system), adding not only an unnecessary layer of extra tedium to the already exhausting proceedings, but also making you question why the ancient god constantly bringing you back to life, wouldn't just revive you at the campsites? Adding to my gripes with the combat, many enemies exhibit weird, downright spasmodic movements. The first boss (the only one I have thought as of the time of this review) was barebones, basic, and had only one, annoying attack, which made up his entire difficulty. Though I must admit his design was neat and a few of his animations were great, as well.Dialogue in this game can be easily accidentally skipped, by simply pressing inputs to have it progress, as you would in any other game, cause the dialogue boxes are stupefyingly sensitive to any controller input, prompting me to skip most of the rest of it, due to already lacking content, and from what I was allowed to read, the characters have no personality and the story has a vain attempt at intrigue inside of an otherwise milquetoast, par-for-the-course narrative.Some additional remarks: The game is also apparently a Metroidvania, but has lacked any progression upgrades so far, apart from its cryptic, boring death shop. Also, if I didn't make this clear enough, the game nails its aesthetic (to say at least one positive things).Astalon: Tears of The Earth is certainly a game I will continue playing, until I fully run out of steam, in order to see if it gets any better. I recommend it only as a passing curiosity, to indie game enthusiasts such as myself and people who have run out of each and ever good Metroidvania to play otherwise. : Though my words have been harsh, I hold nothing but respect and admiration for the developers and independent artists like them, throughout the entirety of the industry.

People say this about any game with rpg mechanics, but refuse to either A) play better or B) use the games systems and mechanics properly. I never once felt that grinding was the only answer. Definitely in the upper echelon of modern retro games and a labor of love.

_childDocuments_.review: Astalon is wonderfully made 8bit/16bit looking game, that exceeds many games of those past eras with its sagacious puzzles and sprawling maps that makes it interesting to traverse and discover.  It is built upon a uniquely, forgiving level up system that encourages you, at times, to die, which allows you to spend your xp points with the god of the underworld, and the only punishment is you are returned to the entrance of the map.  There are Gorgon bosses you need to defeat at important crossroads of the map, and you earn helpful power-ups as you destroy them and reach new areas of the map.    You will find engrossing art in the background, and some obscure areas that you may not know what you are to do.  The game is well made, but you can easily get lost trying to find your way back to an area, or to find paths to new areas.  For retro comparison, I would compare the game play and map idea of Astalon to like Castlevania Symphony of the Night, or to one of my favorite NES games Legacy of the Wizard with its secret, sprawling passages, and using multiple characters abilities to open new areas of the map.  Astalon is not a side scroller, but is made of single screens each with its own gauntlet to pass into the adjoining screens, which makes a well connected game world.   Astalon has enjoyable game play, and artistic flavor that beautifully blends into a unique game.ControlsYou have a team of 3 unique characters that each have specialized skills that allow them to traverse the underground world.One can jump higher and shot an arrow across the screen, one can break barriers with his sword, one can shot projectiles through walls. Most of the controls are tight, and responsive, with a wall jump that works way better than most games, and you do not hit your head easily on ceilings as abruptly as some games.  The only control downside is you cannot quickly turn while attacking, but most of the controls are fluid.   It took a bit to get the controller PS3 style to work, but it worked when I went to the controller options to "Enable Steam Input Translation".Atmosphere praiseThe art for many rooms in this game are impressively detailed. There are a motley assortment of gothic statues with their mouths clenched or agape, and they add a sinister feeling to the back ground.  The music is well done with repetative, driving, 8-bit rhythms, and yet the songs change at different areas of the maze to keep a good variety. There is one beautiful song in the falling cave section that stands out as uniquely expressive.DifficultyThe game is not very hard as you will be able to beat the bosses on a few tries, and you do NOT need to be amazingly tight with the controls to handle the platforming and attacking.  A lot of enemies can be killed by using the specialized attack of each character and some enemies you can just pummel before they kill you.  The bigger challenge of the game was getting lost on the map and trying to remember how to reach a room, or where to access a new area.  There is replay value with "NewGame+" that retains your earned levels but you need to rediscover all items.  "Boss Rush" mode is exceedingly difficult since you lose all your levels and your Hit Points reset to 30, and suddenly the controls feel non-agile and sluggish in comparison to the how error free you need to play. I only beat the 1st boss rush, and stopped because it is super difficult.  For the regular game, I enjoyed the game's difficulty, since the power-ups make you feel dynamic and powerful without having to be perfect.Map ChallengeAs the game map expands, it can get a little frustrating to feverishly return to dead end areas only to realize you still cannot get through. Each room has branching passages that connect to adjacent rooms, so you will need to have a great memory or make your own map notes.  A few of the areas place an obstacle that matches each character, so that you need to bring each character one at a time to try to open an area.  Astalon can be completed with some variation in the order of items, or by not getting certain items at all. I completed the game, without knowing how to remove the Yellow block barriers.  The flexibility allows freedom, but I would prefer that the game make sure that you need most items so that you do not skip too many areas without the player realizing it.OverallAstalon is a stellar game in many ways, with its well designed maze, solid controls, and character switching system.  The moderate challenge makes it fun to traverse the screens, and to beat the Bosses, even if you need to retrace the areas a few times to find where to go.  The game limits the punishment for dying, by allowing the player to level up and get stronger, so that your team can competently defeat all enemies.  I am reaching for what could be improved, but maybe the game would feel tighter if all the items were required to be found so that you do not miss areas of the game, and feel like the complete world puzzle fits together. I would welcome other adventures like this one since it did most everything with high end artistic quality and enjoyable game play.

_childDocuments_.review: A very charming 8bit metroidvania. _childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent old school metroidvania with a great 8-bit anime aesthetic and solid chip tune soundtrack.It has the standard 3 pillars for the genre: exploration, combat and platforming, but the latter two are on the easier/average difficulty side of things. There are only 6 or so total bosses in the entire game, so if fighting tough-as-nails bosses is what attracts you to these titles this one will disappoint in that regard. Exploration and level design are where the game really shines. There are tons of secrets and shortcuts to find. Your health pool is limited and thee are very few ways to regain health as you explore so attrition eventually will see you dead. This makes the shortcuts particular rewarding because when you die you're returned to the entrance of the tower (although you always keep any items or shortcuts you've found.) These shortcuts make getting back into the action pretty quick, so death is not terribly punishing. The story line was serviceable. More of an effort was made here than in other metroidvania titles, but it's still pretty basic. There are a couple features that set the game apart from a standard metroidvania. Killing enemies gives you a currency that you can spend upon death on permanent meta-upgrades (similar to a roguelite). Rather than play as a single protagonist, you're given a team of 3 heroes, each with their own attack and traversal ability. Many of the puzzles require you to switch between the heroes to figure out a way to proceed through the tower obstacles. It took me about 20 hours to 100% the main game and there are 3 additional unlockable modes, including boss rush, once you beat the game. I didn't delve into the additional modes at all so this review is aimed at the core game. It's a good value for the money, especially if you get it on sale, but it is worth the full asking price.Astalon is very reminiscent of older NES titles and does hit the nostalgia button pretty hard, but it brings enough quality of life features to the table that it feels modern in all the right ways. If you like exploring large maps, solving puzzles and finding secrets with a bit of platforming and combat sprinkled in to liven things up I can wholeheartedly recommend the game!

_childDocuments_.review: Charming game with simple but tight controls, easy to learn, yet difficult enough to keep you on your toes. This game doesn't hold your hand, as some rooms requires a thorough investigation in order to locate key items. This may be a detriment to some, but I personally didn't mind it once I understand the layout, and had enabled higher levels for the elevator to use as short cuts. This game is a dime piece that had me hooked from beginning to end, and was an absolute masterclass in level design.

_childDocuments_.review: Astalon is a hybrid roguelite/metroidvania, and it does a really good job of balancing the two genres. It has a huge interconnected map that will surprise you with its secrets even if you've played a lot of MVs before. Upgrades can only be purchased when you die, and you restart at the beginning of the map every death. And you'll die a lot, because the game is quite difficult. The world does have persistent features that make it less tedious than most roguelites - bosses and minibosses stay dead and switches stay pressed even between runs. It does get significantly easier over the course of the game because a lot of the upgrades are OP, and you can get pretty absurd amounts of money later on. The only real bad design ideas I've found so far are that the  is hidden out of the way (and it's a huge pain getting around without it), and upgrades have zero description of what they do. I just used a guide for that. Otherwise it's a great game and well worth full price - I got 100% map and items at around 17 hours playtime.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all: DO PAY ATTENTION TO THE FLASHING LIGHTS WARNING. THIS GAME IS NO JOKE ABUSING THE ♥♥♥♥ OUT OF THAT EFFECT, AND IT IS HEADACHE INDUCING EVEN IF YOU DON'T HAVE PHOTOSENSITIVITY.With that said, I did enjoy the game, but felt somewhat unpolished.The game has a nice concept going on for it, heavily encouraging you getting killed if not extremely sure of what you're doing, which is purposefully made to have the player engage with the game's main mechanic: upgrades upon death. Exploration is good, as the fact that it is mostly just a tower with different colors is countered by some really good art design for the backgrounds, and the enemy variety I feel is fair enough for the game's overal lenght. You even have some anti-frustration measures in the ability to purchase the map layout after having exploded a sufficient amount of the world, so you don't feel the need to just go into a wiki for that. That said, some of the physics at place during exploration are straight up broken: the "grab" mechanic is of particular note, as it is glitchy as all heck, but there's also things like the minibosses not recovering health when abandoning the fight, or how some of the scene transitions when jumping with Kyuli have obstacles in the between or that need to be dodged right before, causing the screen to go back and forth like 3 times.The controls are kinda weird, and one of my main frustrations. They are responsive in regard of the character movement on itself, but characters lock themselves in direction they're facing when attacking, which is a double edged sword, as it makes it easy to spam attack and dodge big stationary targets, but frustrating to change direction to attack multiple targets or smaller ones that you had to dodge. Kyuli is particularly bad in this regard because she has a weird setting in which she keeps direction on ground but switches in the air, which can take you out of the loop. But why would you even use Kyuli in a situation in which you're close to the target instead of abusing her long range to kill the Black Knight and it's braindead AI, you might ask? Simple, because your party rotation (which is tied to an item in order to artificially increase the lenght of the first half of the tower) only goes one way, so it is quite possible that in trying to switch a character in a hurry to get a vertical source of damage or quick swap to Arias for projectile reflection, you might not land in what you want and have to deal with whatever you had at that precise moment.Bosses are rather simple, with the second Gorgon being a problem and the Black Knight battle being poorly thought out. The upgrades, though, can make all battles much simpler, and letting Algus get a pet effectively transforms him into a monster capable of decimating everyone by abusing the direction lock stated above.All in all, it is a fine game, heavily carried by it's art style, but nothing spectacular on its mechanics (and some of them need some more love to work right). Also, I forgot to mention, the game is yet another victim of the "Indie devs think they need to add a sequel hook on everything" syndrome that ravages the industry. Not exactly sure why they even did that, when the story of the game barely matters other than it's simple premise. There are some attempts at world building, but they contribute nothing to the overal narrative, and some are ambiguous for no good reason.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm still not finished with the game, but here's my impressions so far.When the game hits its flow, it's incredibly fun. I usually prefer softer, calmer games, but I got this on a whim and I love the flow state of the movement. I just recently figured out how to do some pretty wild tricks with the warrior character's dash.I will say there are some things that brought down the quality of the game. The first boss is unreasonably difficult compared to what you might expect (and indeed, compared to the second boss), and for a Metroidvania, there's an awful lot of backtracking. Not because of the usual "use the abilities you got in old areas to unlock new stuff", but because of "I died and now I need to spend 5 minutes finding where I was again". Being able to warp to campsites, or at least set a campsite as your checkpoint instead of always going back to the dungeon entrance would have alleviated these issues.I also think being able to swap between party members should have been a feature from the start. As is, there's a lot of pains in the early game as you realize you need to trek all the way back to the campsite to swap to overcome an obstacle. It didn't feel like a challenge, it felt like padding, forcing me to redo the same areas over and over again. Again, being able to warp to a previously visited campsite would have resolved a lot of these issues, as well as some adjustments to level design to make each run through an area with a different character feel different.I streamed it with a friend through Discord and he immediately picked up a copy himself and put 18 hours into it, so he's ahead of me at this point. One thing we agree on is that the warrior character feels painfully weak early on until he gets the extra range from the sword upgrade and the dash. Letting him start with the dash rather than just the ability to cut through the weird blue vines would give him a more interesting quality when dealing with the terrain (as a counterpart to the archer's wall jump and mage's ability to hit through walls) while also giving you a reason to use melee when two very competently-executed ranged characters are playable.Those I think are the big issues, but other nitpicks aside, this is a great game. The music is a bop, I love the retro art style (and the ability to adjust the settings to mimic old monitors!), and when the game hits its moments, you feel so good about what you overcame. My friends cheered with me when I finally overcame the first boss. Loved the game. 7/10, would love to see updates.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes this is a fantastic game that you should play if you have the patience and this game could've been one of my absolute favourites, but there are a few baffling design choices that make this game considerably less fun to play than it could've been. First off, just to get this off my chest, there are some "puzzles" that don't need to be in the game, like paths you can open by hitting a bunch of easily reached switches. The real problem is that much of my game time, maybe 1/3, is just me trying to find my way back to where I died so I can keep doing what I was doing before I died. There is no fast travel except for about 5 or so elevators you can open as you ascend very big floors, health is extremely hard to come by, and characters all share a pool of very important health. Worst of all, when you die, you need to run back to the elevator from the start and get back to the floor you were on. I know there is supposedly a "canon" explanation why you don't respawn at a campfire, but that could be written however they want, so it's not an excuse.Probably what really drives the last nail in for this game because of the above issues is that there are hundreds of rooms and the map does nothing to remind you how each room is laid out, only whether it opens up to other rooms. So you may spend ages moving from room to room, trying not to get hit because you know it'll mean starting from the entrance of the last elevator you found (and failing because stuff can be hard to dodge), only to find you actually used the dead-end path and you have to go several screens back and around. The Messenger also struggled with the map problem and we just need to let devs know that making your map hard to use is not making your beautiful old-school game any better.The same question of "why?" keeps popping up when I'm playing. Why make it hard for me to know what a room will look like and how I should navigate the map? Why kill the fun and not let me respawn at the latest campfire? Why can't I teleport to other campfires I've unlocked? Why not let me heal more than a single chunk of damage at a time with a torch (which you pay to restock)? What's the point of making it hard for me to heal and then have me run the entire gauntlet again? It doesn't add anything to the experience but exhaustion.

_childDocuments_.review: Thumbs up. Had I known that Astalon is related to Castle In The Darkness, I'd have bought and played this sooner. What I particularly enjoyed:- Basic mechanics and controls are just as fun, as tight and as precise as in CITD.- The initial setting throws likeable, goofy friends into a dark and dramatic adventure.- The RPG elements are fun, exploring is worthwhile.- Rooms are unique enough to recall them whenever you come by.- Given the limitations of the 8-bit style, graphics are rather nice and have a good choice of colours.- The soundtrack isn't as great as the CITD one, but still good.- Occasionally, Astalon made me think that the devs can't be serious --- just for the game to hand me a solution shortly thereafter ().Aspects I didn't like:- The second half of the story is botched and tame. There is no drama, no conflict, no climax. I also noticed a few dialogue bugs --- some campfire chats were out of order () and the  dialogues played repeatedly.- Level design is flawed. There is no hint on the next goal and some power-ups are at unpredictable locations, so progression appears directionless and random. Conversely, some off-beat areas serve near to no purpose ().- I got past half the puzzles by accident (without knowing there was a puzzle) and the other half I figured out by brute force. It doesn't have to be La Mulana, but puzzles should be more challenging.- Difficulty is balanced for sloppy completion. If you explore exhaustively --- a premise for any Metroidvania --- the game gets progressively easier towards the end. I killed the final boss in seconds, which just felt unrewarding.- Apart from ability gates, there hardly is any reason to switch characters.- The unlockable characters feel like an afterthought. They don't integrate into cutscenes and dialogues, their skills are mostly useless and skipping through the extended party roster is tedious.- As in CITD, the deadzones for analog sticks are too small, so you'll inadvertently climb ladders as you walk past.- As in CITD, fast-forwarding dialogues is broken --- if you hold the button to fast-show text, you'll regularly skip the entire line. I don't know what exactly is amiss, it just feels different to usual conventions.Minor nitpicks:- What, in good graces, is up with the plethora of cyclops minibosses everywhere? They even get their own music cues, but are really easy to kill. If this is some sort of joke, I don't get it.- The Gorgon Tower is more of a tall castle. For a tower, the map is too wide and too holey and the connectivity is too horizontal. It doesn't help that the elevator rooms aren't aligned atop each other.- The optional game modes are a novelty, and a broken one at that (e.g. they have bugs where you get stuck to walls or in pits you can't jump out of). I'd have ignored them, but they must be completed for the final ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, very nice progression, loads of shortcuts and secrets to find, solid soundtrack and charming characters.However, I do think the ability to swap characters on the fly should be more obvious and given sooner, or perhaps even available right from the start. It's not fun when you see something you need a specific character for and have to walk back to get them, or when the game starts assuming you have that item and you think you're making progress only to run dead stop into another hurdle that requires a different character. Also, the ability to destroy tan blocks should be available off the beaten path during the midgame, and not hidden in an optional late game area. The ability to create shortcuts and uncover secrets throughout the tower is really hampered when those shortcuts are no longer useful and you have to backtrack a ton to find the secrets. Perhaps they should've also given the ability to destroy tan blocks and pick up blocks to the main cast, as swapping between them all for one rare use case, and another rarer still, gets cumbersome. All said, I did still enjoy my time with Astalon. Its strengths outweigh those two weaknesses.

The music is fine but it gets repetitive pretty quickly due lack of variety and track duration.My main issue with it is that you spend a large amount of time backtracking and redoing areas over and over again due to the respawn mechanic and not having enough fast travel points. Being able to quick travel to save points as well would've made traversing the map significantly more enjoyable in my opinion.Arias as a playable character is pretty much pointless except for a few instances. He has barely enough to do in the game except for  The balancing is also way off, Arias is overall the worst character playable character in the game up until you  You basically use Algus and Kyuli 90% of the time due to their improved movement and attack range.Another big issue is that switching between characters become quite tedious, this is fixed around 3/4 into the game, but at that point you'll likely have There's also some weird jump in the story (it could be a bug), but at some point in the game all the other characters Just be aware that if you're not a fan of grinding then you might not enjoy this game. _childDocuments_.review: A retro metroidvania with modern feelingAstalon is a fairly inexpensive game that is well worth the cost.  If you like retro styled games, you'll like this.  If you like Metroidvanias, you'll like this.  If you like games with lots of exploration and secrets, you'll like this.Really, there are only two draw backs to this game: 1. it can be extremely tedious at times due to how the game works.  Every time you die, you get sent back to the start of the dungeon.  Luckily, you unlock abilities that make exploring and moving easier, and every shortcut you unlock stays unlocked.  In addition, you unlock an elevator that has multiple stops along the map.  While this is all true, it can still really drag out the play time with you re-doing the same things over and over again.2. The game asks a lot of you and your time to see all the story has to offer, but the story isn't quite good enough to warrant it.  It's not a bad story, but to get the True ending, you need to 100% complete the map and items.  Once you complete the game, it asks you to complete it twice more under special circumstances to reveal a sequel teaser.  These modes weren't nearly as interesting as the main game but take a good chunk of time to complete.  So, between the main games tedium and the separate playthroughs it asks you to complete, I'd recommend checking out the teaser on youtube.All in all, this is an amazing game, but if the one thing you don't like about metroidvanias is the backtracking and "padding" this is one of the worst offenders I've played through.  If this doesn't bother you, this is well worth your time

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game, and I think there are enough reviews on here already to tell you why that is. However, I have a few quite annoying nits to pick that I would like to  caution people against and haven't seen mentioned elsewhere:1. As you can read in about every other review, when you die, you go back to the beginning of the tower. Now that in itself doesn't bother me. Yes, the backtrack can be quite lengthy at times, and yes, there are more than a few rooms that look completely connected on the map with no indication that only one other exit is connected to the one you are trying to use, which makes it a bit annoying. But this aspect works well with the general scarcity of healing in creating a pretty tense atmosphere especially in the later areas, when you're getting low on health and hoping for the next lift, gate or shortcut unlock at every screen transition. So that part is fine and even desirable.But all of the backtracking is ruined by the fact that all rooms with retractable spikes start out with the spikes hidden, only for them to pop up after a second. If you have ever played games with screen transitions, you are accustomed to using these to scan the room in advance so you can plan your movement. This is especially important in this game, where you just want to rush past the rooms that you have already traversed 500 times in order to pick it up from where you died last time. There are many rooms like that, so that it is impossible to memorize all the sucker punch rooms. So you will just run into spikes (which, by the way, seem to scale their damage with your total health pool so that touching them will never become just a minor nuisance) over and over again.What can you do against this? Wait for a second at every room entrance to make sure this doesn't happen. There is no challenge in it, no skill involved, it just slows down the very frequent backtracking and makes it way more annoying than it should be. And it could all be easily avoided by just showing the easily dodgeable spikes already during the screen transition. The way it stands, it is an annoying and disrespectful gotcha that adds nothing but frustration to an otherwise excellent game. Shame.2. The characters are not balanced well. For most of the game, Algus is just the best choice for nearly every fight, which will cause you to spend most of your upgrade points on his stats, which will make him even more superior to the others. You will want to put something aside to spend on Arias' defense, though, since he is the one character with a dash and will be your go-to backtracking aid, so he'll need to be able to withstand touching the occasional hidden d*ck spike without losing half your Health every time.All the other characters pretty much only exist for those moments when their movement or pathmaking abilities are required to proceed, or the rare occasion when a specific character's attack pattern can cheaply hit dangerous enemies from a safe position without retaliation. Very late in the game, when/if you max out all the characters, that becomes less of an issue for normal progress since all characters will end up doing good dps eventually. But you will still want to use Algus exclusively for the boss fights because of his superior combined attack range and speed, unless you want to challenge yourself.But it's just a pity that there is one clearly optimal upgrade strategy for 90% of the game. This is a wasted opportunity for adding replayability through different equally viable upgrade paths. Although you will most likely end up wasting most of your orbs on useless bonus abilities anyway that do not indicate at all what they are going to do until you buy them, and sometimes not even then. Bloodlust, anyone?3. The difficulty curve is weird. The beginning is properly linear, but then it gets quite hard mid-game all of a sudden, only to become rather easy again after you get a few key abilities. Very late, the game just trivializes itself by . I was looking forward to a challenging final boss, but in the end you can just Algus deathspam it to pieces like all the other ones while just tanking all its damage. Again, wasted potential.Apart from these few points of criticism, though, the game is fantastic, and if you think you can bear those, you should definitely get it, anyway. I did, and I am not disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This is just about my favorite labyrinth action game at this point. Three playable characters right from the start, every room is dense with combat or platforming or has an item you'll definitely need, secret rooms everywhere and entire areas kept secret, secret characters, movement and combat are brisk, it's amazing.I know the idea of starting over from the tower's beginning sounds terrible, but you'll get an elevator key in the game's first area that lets you travel throughout the tower as you find rooms with elevators. I would say the longest it took me to get back to where I was before I died was three or four minutes tops. There's also plenty of contraptions you can activate to open up shortcuts so you're not retreading through the same rooms and getting chewed up by enemies, too. And there's also void chasms, yet another way to travel between two distinct points. Also, there is a certain feature that multiplies the number of orbs you earn from enemies, so look carefully around the tower because there's three of them, and they stack. So with all three of these found and destroyed, an enemy that drops 100 orbs would then drop 800. And you're going to need a  of orbs if you plan out maxing out everyone's strength defense, and your total HP. Check for walls you can pass through, there's a ton of them.The only real criticism I have of this game is that you don't always know who to have as your character before you go exploring in the first three areas, leading to some backtracking as you find a bonfire to swap out characters. After the second major boss there's an item you can get that lets you swap between characters anywhere and anytime you want, but it just seems strange to me to make that an item and not something you do from the start. I don't recall any rooms early on that using multiple characters would have allowed the player to access any overpowered items. It wouldn't have made the game any easier if you could have rotated through your characters from the start, why do it?Other than that, everything else about the game is rock-solid. The developers are currently a sequel to their first game, Castle in the Darkness, and I'm curious as to how much they'll take what they learned from making this one.
