These include combat and traversal abilities, and many of the upgrades found apply to only one of the characters.-You can't easily regain HP. If you break an HP-restoring candle, it doesn't respawn on its own.-If you die, you go back to the beginning! No, don't worry. It's the first room of the game, but you don't lose any progress on things you've collected or ways you've altered the world. If this game is to be compared to Souls in some way, this is it: Progress is obtaining things and opening paths.-See, one of the party has secretly made a Faustian bargain with the Death Titan, selling his soul in exchange for his party being revived as many times as needed to finish their quest. Said Titan also runs a shop. He'll sell you upgrades post-mortem, although he won't tell you much about what some of them do.So all in all it's a bit of typical Metroidvania, a bit of La-Mulana Lite, but all really good and fun. Two complaints I have are that the Rogue is needed all the time compared to other characters, due to jumping and ranged combat abilities, and I had to resort to a guide at one point when I found almost everything  the last traversal upgrade, opener of shortcuts in every third room, and the key needed to access the area leading to it. The key was in a hidden room, which is not great when you've been scouring the entire game world for it and finding nothing but stat upgrades.Anyway, great game. Play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Astalon is one of the best metroidvanias released this year. The culmination of a deceptively big map, choke full of secrets, head bopping soundtrack and classic but effective gameplay makes it a great pick for any metroidvania fans. If you're looking for that type of exploration you loved from Hollow Knight, you'll get that here. Everywhere you go you'll find secret rooms, paths, upgrades and more, it was honestly such a joy to just go around with no hand-holding and get lost in the worldIt's just a big shame the game has a few glaring issues that prevents it from ascending to the pantheon of the elite.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most enjoyable games I've played in a long time! It's captures the exploration and progression of a Metroidvania, with a few Roguelite progression elements thrown in. The sense of exploration and progression is exceptional. Starting back at the beginning with each death makes every run feel tense, but the shortcuts and ability upgrades make even a failed run feel meaningful and worthwhile.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: 1. Good pixel art, but I must admit the portraits look odd2. Great synth music. They clearly put their soul into this.3. It doesn't replenish your health at save points, which is unusual for a metroidvania game.4. Keys are perishable. You will always find enough to beat the game, but sometimes you're taking a short cut and making a smart decision, other times you've made a bad decision and you're just wasting keys for absolutely no reason.5. Overall this is still a good metroidvania game. Though there are better ones out there.(and worse ones)
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: A fun metroidvania with old-school style graphics and chiptunes, Astalon is a great play for anyone looking for that retro NES feel, but with modern game balance, style and achievements.  A tale of 3 friends who enter into a monster-filled tower to save their village, Astalon: Tears of the Earth features an initial three playable characters, all with different abilities which you'll need to navigate and explore the tower.  Two additional characters will be unlocked through the main quest, along with various bonus modes and optional areas.  Astalon features plenty of exploration and secrets, and is a fine time for gamers like me, who thrive on such things.  The bosses are all fairly easy for those experienced in the 2D platformer genre, and won't be much of a challenge compared to the likes of Cuphead or Environmental Station Alpha.  Most of the game's challenge comes from getting around the dungeon, replete with traps and monsters.  I would recommend this game to any fans of the genre and style.  8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: I'm about 5 hours in, the map say's its 20% completed, and so far I'm really enjoying it! It's much denser than I expected, which is always a pleasant surprise. The map design is peak metroidvania, with many shortcuts and secrets. I've only fought two bosses so far, and I guess my only criticism is that they were a little boring. Hearty recommendation from me! (PS I found this game by randomly trying the demo on the Switch, seeing it was on sale on steam and immediately buying it here. Demos are awesome!)
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: One of the better metroidvanias I've played in recent memory. Astalon nails the NES-era aesthetic and gameplay, while maintaining enough modern conveniences to largely avoid the frustration that true old school games came with. The map is fun to explore, though the backtracking is a bit much at times. The difficulty is highest at the beginning and sharply drops off later if you've been exploring and upgrading consistently. Still, I had fun the whole through and felt the game was the right length. Highly recommended for fans of the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: It's not awful, but it's more like a 7/10 than the 9.5 reviews would indicate.The game clearly had potential, parts of it are really good, but as a whole it doesn't hold up. It's got very obvious bugs, the basic gameplay mechanics and map design are flawed, and it mostly just borrows from other games but fails to use what it borrows properly. It's probably worth picking up if you love the genre and are dying for more content, but there are many other games I'd recommend over this with worse scores and often cheaper pricetags.Bugs include but are not limited to: Very frequent total silence when music should be playing, clipping into walls, visual glitches, approximately 1/4th of the entire story clearly being played out of order, spoiling itself, and assorted minor bugs related to combat. The music and plot ones are by far the worst.The art is nice in some places, with lots of unique stuff in the background. Unfortunately, the enemy variety is quite poor, with most enemies being palette swapped and reused dozens of times throughout the game. The little animated cutscenes are nice.The map layout is mediocre. It's got some genuine branching paths and entirely optional areas, which is rare to see and improves the game a lot. Unfortunately, that aspect doesn't show up until fairly late in the game, just a few hours before you can win. And believe me, I was looking for alternate paths very hard. The map also has significant problems with connectivity, which leads into...Gameplay is, honestly, kinda bad. To start off with, the way dying, respawning, and travelling work together means that more often than not, it'll be literally 5-10 times faster to find the nearest spikes and stand in them until you die rather than actually find your way to the nearest travel point. Until about halfway through the game, you can expect to backtrack through the same room up to EIGHT times in a row as a result of needing to switch characters at a campsite to handle 3 different puzzles, in a specific order, in a nearby room. Even later in the game it just feels clunky and annoying stopping and switching between characters to get around basic obstacles you've dealt with dozens of times before, when part of the joy of this genre is the feeling of freedom unlocking new powers gives you, trivializing old obstacles. The game falls into the trap of making many of it's items have no real gameplay effect besides functioning as a fancy key. Some of the upgrades really do change the gameplay, but others do things like solve a single puzzle in the entire tower. Getting items like that feels very bad. Many of the upgrades are slight improvements to the map, which is honestly pretty hard to read and sometimes inaccurate.The music, when it's there, is kinda meh. I've got hundreds of tracks from games in my collection, including chiptunes from old games. This isn't close to making the cut.The combat doesn't feel good. After the first few hours it gets very repetitive, as nothing new really unlocks to change things. There's no charged attacks or dash slashing or anything of that sort. You just mash your attack button while standing in the spot the enemy can't hit you. Which is easy to find because the enemies are very simple, most just pacing back and forth or not even moving at all. They don't jump or block hits or have multiple attacks. There's a handful of bosses in the game, but aside from the last couple, they're pretty dull affairs as well. The final boss was great though, better than all the rest combined honestly.Honestly, it feels like a 10-15$ game, and not a great one at that. If it had been getting reviews around the 85% positive mark, I probably wouldn't have bothered writing this at all, but I felt kind of duped after seeing reviews on the cusp over overwhelmingly positive and people claiming it's the best game ever. It's got more flaws too, but I feel like I've gotten the point across. Pick it up if you can't find anything else similar that you're curious about. I liked it enough to finish the game, but really wish I'd spent the time and money trying out something else in the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: For a retro throwback, this has a surprisingly smooth difficulty curve. No ice or minecarts here! I also like that each character has certain fights where they're the best choice, but there aren't many fights where one character is the ONLY choice. (A couple of the minibosses do need the swordsman, though.)
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly excellent Metroidvania that also adds some novel mechanics to the genre, like switchable characters at bonfires, each with unique abilities or roguelite-like upgrades system that is available after death. But first of all, Astalon shines with its excellent map, filled with puzzles, secrets, and interesting shortcuts to unlock. The shortcuts are essential for progression since teleport points are sparse in this game, and dying always returns you to the very first room of the game, which also adds a little thrill to the exploration. On top of that, the game has great retro art direction, atmosphere and a simple but nice story.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This is an awesome game in the spirit of old 8-bit classics from the 80's. It feels like a mash-up of a bunch of different games including: Metroid, Castlevania, Megaman, Super Metroid, Legacy of the Wizard, Ys, and Actraiser. The soundtrack is similarly styled (for that era) and is both enjoyable and fitting for the genre.Long story short, if you have an appreciation for the 8-bit/16-bit classics I mentioned earlier, I think you will find this title very much to your liking.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: I've enjoyed a lot of platformers over the years and this is a very solid entry. Another poster mentioned that this has some of the Metroidvania elements of games since the 1980s but with more modern mechanics and quality of life improvements - agree. I do not look at this as a roguelite. I enjoyed going back to find all the secrets in the game, and found that this is a game that you could 100% in a reasonable time. Easier than games like hollow knight, and closer to Ori in terms of difficulty. You can really tweak your characters out if you want to invest the time, and roll over things by the end of the game. Only negative was the portraits for the rogue character - at least give her alternate portrait some more clothes! I don't post reviews often, but found this game really enjoyable - give it a go! I look forward to the next entry by Labs.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This is a positive review with quite a few annoyances.First of all, play the game, it's definitely a great deal. It's an interesting take on Metroidvania, forcing rogue-lite elements to it. You will die many times, and each time you get stronger. The art is great, the music is nice, there are lots of interesting enemies and platforming, though in the end it gets a bit repetitive.That said, there are a lot of issues with the game as well.- You will need to backtrack. A lot.- Why are so many important items and content hidden in secret rooms? That makes no sense. Secret rooms are for optional upgrade, but here you cannot enjoy the full game unless you check every single nook and cranny (or look up the amazing 100% map).- I got locked out of fully completing the game because I did things in the wrong order and was missing a certain key.... Maybe I missed something, but that's exactly the issue, the map is massive and if you miss a secret room your completely screwed. - To unlock some important things you NEED to pay attention and hunt down the smallest details - There are still bugs, mostly minor with moving platforms, but I wasted 20 minutes walking around because some necessary platforming bubbles didn't spawn in a room the first time...- The upgrades are so slow, and some of them don't make any sense. Also there's no reason to hide the description of what you are buying in the store before buying it...- This game really needs a better fast travel system. As it stands it doesn't respect your time and at some point I just quit.Again, even with all of that, it is still a good game. I definitely don't think it's a game of the year contender though.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This should be in any metroidvania fans' top 10 list for sure. Controls are tight, gameplay is solid. No idea about the music as I don't listen to it. The story is pretty standard, but it gets the job done. Plus, there are 2 special modes to play through the tower again in different ways! In the main mode, every time you die, you're able to use the orbs you've collected from defeating monsters to upgrade your stats and unlock new combat abilities, in addition to the standard movement type abilities you'll acquire from exploring the tower. This definitely helps in case you ever feel like you're stuck. Just grind for a while and you can improve your stats or get another helpful bonus.  Only thing I would've added would be an item to teleport from anywhere to an elevator to avoid some backtracking, but if you don't like backtracking, why are you in the metroidvania tag?
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: As something of a veteran of Metroidvania games I cannot recommend this game enough, I had an absolute blast playing this game and exploring the map. It was pretty difficult at first but learning the ins and outs of a game like this is extremely satisfying especially when it's well done. Great soundtrack, interesting story, and the controls felt exactly like what I'd want from a game.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really, really good. I'm not a fan of the 8-bit pixel thing in general, so I was hesitant to get this one despite the rave reviews, but eventually I got bored and said 'why not' and I'm really glad I did.I got all the way to the point of no return in front of the last boss and realized I only had like 50% of the map discovered, so then I started exploring more seriously and realized there was a LOT more game here than I thought. There are a few nitpicks I have, like the fact that the map won't show you special rooms you need to come back to later, but overall this is a strong recommend. The story is decent. The character dialog is written pretty well, at least. There are some things going on in the premise that feel a bit 'extra', like the fact that it's a post-apocalyptic wasteland outside of the magic tower you spend the whole game inside, but it's fine. The music is never intrusive but never really outstanding. The game plays really well, never quite feeling like you need twitch reflexes but just hard enough that you have to make an effort to get through. Lots of hidden stuff everywhere, including some big surprises because I never read any spoilers and didn't realize you could unlock... two... things.Overall, the game shows an above-average level of love and care, coupled with some very sensible design choices and careful, deliberate gameplay. If you like metroidvanias, IMO this is a must buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great retro metroidvania.  It will likely take you 9 or 10 hours for your first playthrough, with another handful of hours to 100% the first game mode.  There is some replay value, though, because new game modes are unlocked after that.  While this may not crack the top five in my list of favorite metroidvanias, i think it's likely in my top ten.  It has been a while since i've played a game that i really didn't want to put down.There are a few small annoyances with this game, some of which actually get remedied as you continue to play.  Initially, you begin your adventure with three characters, each with different abilities that are required to move through the world.  However, you can only swap in certain spots, and this means a sigh, an eye roll, and some back tracking when you realize you need to switch to someone else.  While this is mildly irritating, this is one of those annoyances that disappears a bit later in the game.Another annoyance is just the world design as a whole.  The map can be misleading.  If you're trying to navigate from one room to another across the map, you might initially see what appears to be a convenient path to get there.  The map shows where rooms connect, but what it doesn't show is that you may actually have to detour five rooms away and come back via a different route in order to actually access one of the exits to a room.  In other words, some exits shown on the map will only actually be accessible if you enter the room via a particular direction.  This isn't necessarily a bad thing - it certainly makes exploration more of an intricate process - but even late in the game you will find yourself groaning as you realize "you can't get there from here".Other than those small complaints, the game is really fun.  The art is neat, the enemies varied and interesting, the map is huge, and it's all littered with secrets to find.  This absolutely deserves more attention than it has gotten.  Give it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible map design. I think a lot of people misconstrue the difference between level design and map/world design. The interconnected world in this game is top class. There's a ton of secrets, shortcuts, and interesting things to discover. It is very cleverly designed. On the other hand, the level design - the actual content of the rooms - is just okay. The rooms don't get overly creative. A ton of enemies that borders on enemy spam, with some serviceable but not noteworthy combat. This game is all about exploration. There is cool stuff to find in here. Upgrades start a little boring but quickly become really interesting. A really enjoyable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite games this year, and one of the best metroidvanias I've played.The exploration in this game is superb. The way the areas connect to each other, it all fits together so well. And you are constantly rewarded for poking your nose in every nook and cranny, powerups, keys, and new weapons and abilities are hidden everywhere. I love the way every square on the map is a new room, and each room is it's own self contained challenge with platforming, combat, or a mix.You control three characters who each have their own unique abilities for moving through the tower, and you can switch out who you're controlling at campfires. There is also an exp system, and the way that is implemented is very unique. Death sets you back in that you must work your way back to where you died, but you keep all items you found and can now spend your souls(experience points) for character upgrades!While plenty of progression is gated by abilities discovered, most is gated by keys. Blue keys for optional stuff, white keys for major progression, and red keys for some of the biggest secrets. This might sound not very interesting, but early on you will be having to make choices as to which door to open, and this is always exciting as you never know what to expect. There are plenty of keys hidden about too, so don't worry too much about missing out.Enemy encounters aren't too difficult, most are obstacles instead of difficult fights. The bosses, on the other hand, are all a wonderful spectacle, and imaginative in design. Especially the Gorgons themselves, I loved seeing their giant stone heads appear every time. Expect plenty of minibosses as well, they are scattered all throughout the tower.Unless you want to make a beeline for the end, expect to backtrack plenty. But that's what this game does so well, encapsulates that feeling of "Aha!" as you realize you can know reach something, or solve a platforming obstacle you remember from before. You will even learn how to spot the hidden doors in each area, for there are many!The music is top notch, I regularly have different tracks stuck in my head on repeat. There's mysterious and moody pieces that really immerse you in the atmosphere, and faster tracks to get your blood pumping as you move through a new section of the tower.And I'd be remiss if I didn't mention the graphics. I absolutely adore the look of this game. I am constantly impressed with how much detail they crammed in using this 8-bit style. Crumbling demonic statues and monstrous faces adorn the stones of the tower, and provide so much atmosphere. In other places dozens of spinning gears in the background power god knows what, while literal veins grow up through floors like the tower is a living creature. And you never forget you're climbing a tower! Some of the rooms off to the side let you climb out into the night sky, seeing the horizon below and the wind rushing past.I won't talk too much about the story, for there isn't too much, but what is there is pretty compelling, I enjoyed the fireside chats the characters have every so often, their personalities really shine in these.If you have any interest in metroidvanias, do not miss this game. If you like classicvania, but are maybe iffy on the newer ones, you should STILL give this game a shot. If you like platforming, exploraiton, or moody gothic pixel art, try this game! I won't say it's perfect, I wish the campfires were a bit more useful, and some of the upgrades could've really used better descriptions(thankfully there is a very detailed guide to these here on Steam), but it's one of the best of these types of games I've come across. It feels very unique despite it's obvious influences. I've truly enjoyed all of my time with it and really hope to see a sequel. I desperately need another gorgon slaying adventure.This game is definitely going on my curator page.

_childDocuments_.review: Astalon is an exceptionally fun metroidvania. My favorite thing is probably how snackable it is. You're constantly discovering new pathways, getting a new upgrade or finding new items. So each time you start it back up, you're bound to make some kind of progress. The death mechanic adds an interesting extra wrinkle because it gets you think about optimal routes and things to check out on your way back to where you died. Even though you're sent back to the beginning of the castle upon death, the game doesn't devolve into excessive backtracking due to a multitude of shortcuts that let you skip over large areas of the map. So, at best, it challenges you to think about how to efficiently navigate its world; at worst, you're just a few moments away from getting back to where you were. Conveniently, each boss encounter  has a way to quickly return to it. So, it's not Dark Souls or Hollow Knight levels of boss runs, and it's not a rogue-like either where you're reset back to square one.As you defeat enemies, you gain a currency that's used for acquiring various unlocks that'll ease your quest and let you upgrade the characters' stats. Even if you don't spend them all, they carry over when you respawn. It mostly feels like a way to let you make some micro progress each run, so even when you messed up you get to go back in a little bit more powerful. I expected this aspect of it to be a greater point of friction, but it really wasn't -- more comfy than it is punishing.Astalon's platforming and combat are just right in terms of challenge, I feel. Overall, it's a relatively easygoing experience as long as you stay on your toes and pay attention to traps and enemy attack patterns. At a more basic level, the play simply feels really good in your hands. Animations are mostly quick and cancellable, and your characters are very maneuverable. So even though it has that retro look and you'd expect a more rigid-playing game like classic Castlevania, it actually is very responsive The world is quite large but not overwhelmingly so. Aside from being filled with lots of neat little trinkets and upgrades to find, the process of navigating its maze-like levels and figuring out each room's little combat or platforming challenges is very satisfying. Astalon gets fundamentals like this really well. It feels like the designers spent a lot of time looking at other highlights in platforming and search-action games, and then put a great deal of thought and work into fine-tuning the framework that the rest of the game's built around.So yeah, a fun game top to bottom that's well worth the time and money. Don't let this one pass you by.

_childDocuments_.review: two words: amazing game. that's it, review done! go buy it. ok, here's a bit more: fun platforming with tight, responsive controls, huge map, secrets to reveal, upgrades to buy, several endings, four game modes, great visuals and music - it's all there. the game is polished, exploration is rewarding, and while the story might be simple, it's nicely presented with few little surprises here and there. all in all astalon has a lot to offer and is definitely worth its (very reasonable) price.  game loop is simple: kill enemies and collect orbs, die, buy upgrades, start again to progress further. every elevator you find is very welcomed milestone which allows you to skip areas, so you really don't have to make it from the bottom of the tower to its very top in one go. sure, it may not be for everyone, but thanks to this approach the game doesn't have to make assumptions about your skills. if you struggle, make sure to destroy as much stuff and enemies as you can and level up your characters. if you feel like your life is too easy, keep buying death wish upgrades only (or unlock and play other game modes, they are more challenging). it's up to you. i love that characters actually grow as you play. you start with a pack of slow weaklings and end up with murderous warriors breezing through the rooms and killing with ease almost everything in sight. it's glorious. and a lot of fun. i hope this is just a start and there will be more astalon games in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy metroidvanias or retro games, pick up Astalon. If you enjoy both, pick it up right now.Click on my video to see gameplay and watch my first impressions as they happened. Astalon puts you into the boots of Arias, Kyuli, and Algus, three heroes bent on saving their village from the poisoned river. The twist? Algus has made a deal with the devil-god-titan Epimetheus, raising your heroes from the dead each time they perish. Astalon is built around this mechanic, placing save points and elevators few and far between, enemies everywhere, and spike traps commonly. A shared health pool makes things all the trickier. Critics will point to this as Astalon's flaw. But if you can get past it--or if you enjoy the challenge of retro style games--then there's much to love here.Each time you meet Epimetheus, you can spend souls (experience points) on upgrades of your choice. Many items have no described effect, so there's a bit of trial and error (or walkthrough-checking) involved. In my opinion, it adds to the retro charm. Astalon's map is also surprisingly open. After the first couple of bosses, most of the castle tower is open to you. And that's another point in Astalon's favor: while most of the game's inspiration is drawn from Castlevania, its map focuses more on the verticality more commonly felt in Metroid. On the downside, each screen is an individual room: there are no long hallways or tall climbs here. Yet at the same time each room feels memorable. Astalon doesn't fall into the copy and paste trap of the titles that inspire it.Combat is satisfying, starting you with three distinct characters that you can switch between at save points and later on the fly after discovering a certain upgrade. There's quite a bit to discover in Astalon's map, in fact, and anyone hoping to 100% on their own should take notes. Hints, false walls, items that can't yet be obtained, and more can be discovered and forgotten by the time it comes to reach them.It's no secret that metroidvanias are my favorite games, and Astalon scratches that retro metroidvania itch so well, bridging the gap between retro difficulty and modern conveniences as unlockables. It's a great treat and a game I highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is almost a perfect Metroidvania. Good music, fun boss fights, amazing exploration and the map is large and doesn't waste much space. That being said, the difficulty presented by the game's gimmick, no healing and dying takes you back to start, is tedious and frustrating. Save points have let you save and swap characters, but not heal or set a spawn point, feel mostly useless, especially as you progress. I think they could have had a better system.The game alleviates this by letting you unlock shortcuts as you go, and having a shop when you die so that you can improve your characters. It works, altho retracing your steps only to get back to where you were at half life due to the environmental hazards or random chip damage from enemies is tedious and frustrating. The game also ramps up the difficulty after the 2nd boss, and man, that was a pain.Then there's the stuff the game does right. Exploration, unlocking new features that let you explore farther, cool enemies and abilities, the way that each character plays a little differently, it really opens up and gets super fun as you go along. I kind of wish some of the powerups and abilities had come much sooner, or had been in from the start. Towards the end of my time playing, I really felt like it the vision the devs had for how to play the game really came together nicely, and if the entire game could have been that way, I think this game would easily be an instant classic.Overall, I'd give it a 8/10. I got my money's worth, and you probably will too. Trudging through the early parts sucks, but it does come together really nicely.

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely pleasant surprise. I loved this game. A great action-platformer combining elements of Metroidvania with some roguelite elements - namely somewhat frequent deaths and upgrade mechanics. The tower you're exploring here however has a fixed and well crafted layout, and your party of characters each have set unique capabilities that grow as you progress.The art is a little inconsistent in spots but for the most part I thought it looked great and fit really well with the overall vibe of the game. Some of the boss characters and background details in particular really stood out. The game for some reason defaults to an unbearable super blurry anti-aliased mode, but you can easily swap it out for a more reasonable option.Great soundtrack as well that hits on a lot of Mega Man, Metroid, and Castlevania notes.

_childDocuments_.review: The two big things I didn't like is you can't change characters on the fly for the first half of the game, which really adds to the backtracking and these games are already backtracking heavy.  And that some rooms it feels like you have no choice but to take a hit to get through it, there's this one area in particular that during my backtracking in Ruins of Ash (you will probably die a lot here, there is a long stretch without an elevator) I was always getting hit by a demon's fireball no matter what I did.  But I'm sure someone will come along to do a no-hit run and prove me wrong.  Not as hard as Castle in the Darkness, spikes don't kill you in one hit (they do a decent amount of damage though) and the platforming isn't hard.You're still going to die frequently, but again some of those will feel like the game making you take hits sometime, those adding up on really good runs (where you dodge most attacks) and that getting you killed.  But you're always opening shortcuts each attempt (at least I was always making *some* progress), and this makes it easier to get back to where you left off.  There's also an upgrade you can buy that gives you more HP when you break an orb that's placed in the room you last died in, so that gives you a boost.  Right now the game doesn't have descriptions on items until you buy them, but there's a community guide for that now... I also had a bug three or four times where I would land on a moving platform, go invisible, then fall through the moving platform, usually into an enemy or pit of spikes, giving me some damage.  Frustrating but didn't happen often enough to make me want to stop playing, and most of the platforming in this game is pretty easy.  I also had another bug where I couldn't change characters with the bell or at the camp - this was before I got Zeek - but a game reboot fixed it and it never happened again.The soundtrack is pretty good, and it's worth checking out the Super Arrange version.  Threads of Fate is my favorite track.Tips for new players:  Get Orb Seeker right away, and pick a character you will play the most to focus on for upgrades.  My favorite was the wizard.

_childDocuments_.review: An enjoyable Metroidvania that feels like a fun mix of Legacy of the Wizard and La Mulana, though it's a lot more direct than La Mulana.You take control of three characters and switch between them at bonfires to tackle different challenges and solve puzzles. Each one has strengths and weaknesses that you'll need to utilize to get by. Even at the end of the game, it never gets old, and you'll find yourself switching often to make the most out of each character's unique skillset.The death system is an inverse of Dark Souls. When you die, the game gets easier by letting you purchase upgrades and come back stronger. Eventually, if you die and grind enough, you can become an absolute powerhouse. This allows Git Gud players to flex by never dying and never getting upgrades, if you feel like doing something so tedious. Or, you can get a solid 15 hours of fun out of dying and making attempts at difficult sections until you're strong enough or skilled enough to get through.I will say that as of this writing, the game is extremely buggy. A few skills simply won't work unless you save and quit the game. Things you purchase may vanish until you reload the game. Occasionally you'll turn invisible and blink through the floor. Hopefully these issues will be resolved in the future.The main negative is the checkpoint system. You start at the beginning of the tower every time you die. The tower stays in the same state, so anything you've opened stays open. Save points are for quitting mid-session. Being unable to set a new respawn is a huge downer, even with the fast travel points. They're often at the beginning and end of zones, though sometimes there's just a single one in the middle, so trying to get around means a lot of backtracking. This can be a bonus at times, as you'll come across places to use your newer abilities and open up more of the game.There's also several extra play modes (which are only for the Git Gud crowd) to unlock. If you're a casual player, you'll find them unbelievably frustrating, especially if you relied on upgrades to 100% the main game like I did.With some quality of life improvements, Astalon could be amazing. As-is, it's a great, clever Metroidvania that die hard fans of the genre should definitely check out.
_childDocuments_.name: Astalon: Tears of the Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Finished the game after 18 or so hours with 100% map completion, items & upgrades.VISUALSThere’s been a lot of games, over the past few years, that have tried to replicate the artistic style of the 8 bit and 16 bit console era. Astalon goes for the former, even providing several different filters and aspect ratios to complement its 8 bit art style. The developers have nailed the look but that’s only half of it.There’s a huge difference between devs using pixel art as a crutch for lack of artistic expertise, and talented artists working within the confines of that era’s aesthetic. In Astalon’s case it is most definitely the latter, the pixel art here is great with character designs by noted mangaka Ryūsuke Mita. Animation is smooth and the environmental art really gives the tower a sense of place.STORYThe narrative here is quite interesting, especially in how it plays into the gameplay loop (more on that later). In short, the story revolves around 3 adventures, Algus, Kyuli and Arias who must work together to infiltrate the Gorgon tower and stop the source of the poison that is infecting the people of their village.The leader of the party, Algus, has made a pact with a Titan/God of Death. The pact allows him and his friends to be revived upon death, until they complete their mission, although Algus is the only one aware of this. That’s the initial setup. The story gets more interesting as you get further into the game and is sometimes revealed in surprising ways.GAMEPLAY/MECHANICSAstalon is a Metroidvania with a twist; instead of just one character, you play as three. Each character has their own set of skills (I’ll avoid mentioning upgrades for spoilers sake); Arias is the Swordsman who can slash through certain blocked doors and has a fast attack speed. Kyuli is a Rogue, she has a bow and arrows, so she’s good for range but slower to attack and timing is more important. She also starts with a wall jump ability making her the most mobile of the 3 and likely to be the character you will spend most time as during general exploration. Finally, you have Argus the Mage. He starts with a projectile spell that can go through walls and activate certain switches. In order to progress you’ll need to use all three characters. This isn’t Lost Viking's though; you can only control one character at a time and swapping is only possible at campfires initially.These campfires don’t behave in the way you might expect (i.e. the Dark Souls bonfire way). You can save your game at them and, occasionally, eat a meal to recover some health while getting some exposition from the characters. Health recovery can’t be triggered anytime though but it seems to be possible after big events like bosses. Mostly you will only use bonfires for saving and swapping characters. This brings me onto how death and character progression works…Astalon has an interesting way of handling death. As with many action RPGs these days, you collect currency (souls) when killing enemies. When you die in Astalon, you do not lose your currency. Instead, Argus is transported to the Titan of Death with whom he has made his pact. Here you can spend currency on various permanent upgrades to make your journey easier. These range from stat boosts to special abilities among other things. This is where I have my first gripe with Astalon; while some of the upgrades are self-explanatory, some have names that offer little insight into what they do. Only when you buy them are you informed of their use. I am sure this is intentional, the game likes a bit of mystery, but not every “upgrade” is necessarily desirable and a bad pick could lead to frustration. Upgrades can get expensive too, so if you intend to try and brute force your way through the game you can expect a fair bit of grinding. I’ve been able to get through with minimal grind so far.Anyway, once you select your upgrades it’s back to the start of the tower; don’t expect to be respawning at that last campfire though! At first this seems like bad design but no, this isn’t a roguelike, all your progress within the tower, including shortcuts/items is saved. Early on it can feel like you are running the same areas repeatedly if you’re dying a lot. Then you find your first big shortcut and realise that saving time is a matter of making careful progress through each section. The more you explore, the more ways of zipping about the tower you’ll find. Level design is excellent in Astalon and extremely well crafted; it’s full of secrets and clever shortcuts. Seasoned Metroidvania fans will lap it up, but I can imagine some people will dislike the way Astalon handles death, especially not being able to heal easily during a run or not being able to warp between campfires. It really forces you to find, and make good use of, shortcuts and play a bit more carefully.So, the gameplay is great but a couple of design aspects still jumped out at me. Firstly, in the very first section of the game there are water droplets coming from the ceiling, the game shows you that these are harmless when stepped under. However later in the game there are droplets, that to all intents and purposes look identical, that will damage you. It’s a nit-pick but irritating if you die to one!The second is the map which is always a tricky aspect to get right in a Metroidvania. Right now I think Astalon's could use a bit of work. Eg. If a room has two locked door colours, show both on the map. If the player visits a room with a POI , show it on the map (some POIs never appear). The aim is to reduce aimless wandering without killing the sense of exploration. Marking things the player has already seen is simply removing manual work they could do themselves on paper.AUDIOAstalon’s music is enjoyably reminiscent of the 8 bit era with some very nice chip-tune work, and the sound effects are just fine too.DEMOGRAPHIC10 and up I would say. Some elements could be disturbing for very young children.SPECIFICATIONSI’m playing on a relatively high-end rig but you should be able to play this on your average tater. File size clocks in at just under 0.5GB on the disk.DIFFICULTYThe game is somewhere between medium to hard challenge wise. I haven’t found anything rage inducingly difficult so far and the curve is just about right if you do some light grinding for skills and upgrades. Just don’t be turned off in the early areas before your first big shortcut.BUGSGameplay wise I only encountered 1 definite bug and 1 potential bug:The first one I have seen reported in other reviews. It was very rare for me but now and again my character would just keep walking despite letting go of the movement controls. This happened when using analogue sticks or D-pad.The other thing, I’m not sure if it’s intentional but if so, it makes no sense. MILD SPOILERS: There’s an upgrade you can buy that will show the location of God of Death statues for Argus to speak to him even without dying. However, once you find the God of Death statue, the location is removed from the map making it nigh on useless.GRINDAs mentioned, some mild grind might be required for most players to even the odds. Brute force grinding is discouraged by gradually inflating upgrade prices Vs time taken to grind them out.DURATIONTook me around 18 hours to finish my first run with 100% map completion and all items and upgrades. Two extra modes were unlocked and I've just started to play those. There's a ton to get through.PRICEFor any serious Metroidvania fan this is a no brainer at full price, you will definitely get your moneys worth here, and fans of platformers n general should give it some serious consideration.OVERALLLABS Works have crafted an amazing game here that’s well worth your time and may even make you forget about Silksong for a while! (the highest praise!)Final Score: 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: I got this key from the devs to make content about and just opened my stream to test it out, zero expectations. The game is absolutely amazing. Beautiful and detalied pixel art graphics. Perfect gameplay dynamics with a cool character swap system but not like Bloodstained where you swap wherever you want. You have to find your friends on the mpa to switch between characters. Music is cool. Could be perfect though, but it's just good. Also I don't really enjoy the save system. You save your progress but not your location (like a Castlevania por isntance) but as far as I'm concerned, this is the only down side so far... Great game. Buy.

_childDocuments_.review:
Uphold your pact with the Titan of Death, Epimetheus! Fight, climb and solve your way through a twisted tower as three unique adventurers, on a mission to save their village from impending doom!

Three heroic explorers wander the post-apocalyptic desert on a mission to save their village from despair. They soon find a dark, twisted tower that has risen from the depths of the planet and seemingly holds the key to their survival. In order to ensure their victory, one of them has made a secret pact with the Titan of Death, Epimetheus, allowing them to reincarnate until they have accomplished their mission. But what fate lies in store for the heroes and their village?

Astalon: Tears Of The Earth is an action-platformer set in a dying world where life is cruel, but death can be a stepping stone to victory! Use the unique skills and weapons of Arias the fighter, Kyuli the rogue, and Algus the wizard, to surmount the mysterious tower and find the answers to their survival. Slay terrible monsters, discover powerful artifacts, and solve fiendish puzzles, reaching new heights in the tower with the aid of a Titan. Follow a story about friendship and sacrifice, building up the courage to take down giants to protect the weak and powerless. Strengthen your party and change their fate by embracing death. Discover the countless secrets of the Tower of Serpents!

name: Eternal Threads
detailed_description: Warning This game contains flashing lights and images from the very beginning which may not be suitable for those suffering from photosensitive epilepsy and other similar conditions. Player discretion is advised. About the Game Eternal Threads is a single-player, first-person story-driven puzzle game of time manipulation, choice and consequence. As an operative tasked with fixing corruption in the timestream, you have been sent to the North of England in May 2015, where six people died in a house fire. Prohibited from simply stopping the fire, you must instead manipulate the choices made by the housemates in the week leading up to it so that they all survive the event. From the outset, you have free and complete reign to explore the seven day timeline before the fire. You can watch and alter the significant events from the entire week as many times as you like and in whatever order you wish. Some decisions will have only minor effects on the timeline, moving objects around the house or revealing deeper stories and secrets. Major changes however, rewrite the timeline by changing existing events, adding new events and even replacing other events entirely. You must traverse up and down this timeline, changing decisions at different moments throughout the week so that their effects interact and combine together to save all six housemates. However, it is not just the housemates who have choices. Each of them can be saved from the fire in multiple ways, with each outcome having a profound effect on their lives in the future. Will you just search for the quickest and easiest solution, or can you find the best possible outcome for everyone? Ultimately, everything is about choices and consequences. Features Choose how you want to follow the game’s story The complete narrative follows the six main characters through multiple decisions across multiple timelines and you can experience these in any way you choose. You can concentrate on just one particular character’s storyline at a time, following their choices across the timelines and then go back to the start and follow another character. You can approach the story like a forensic detective, observe the final outcomes of the story and then work backwards along the timeline – essentially observing the effects and then determining their cause. Or you can just watch things in chronological order, experiencing the timeline unfold as you observe and change the decisions that the characters face as the week progresses. Watch and change things as many times as you like Can’t remember exactly what happened in an event? Changed a decision and you’re not sure you like the consequences? That’s fine. Just pop back along the timeline and watch and change whatever you like, whenever you like, as many times as you like. Change the past to affect the future Setting up temporary base in the house mere hours after the fire, provides a unique perspective on events. As you look back through the timeline, past events play out in front of you in ghostly form, with the smoke and fire damaged house a constant reminder of what is to come. In addition, as you manipulate the past, the environment can be reset around you to match the changes taking place. Some new objects will appear, others will move around the house and the contents of rooms can change substantially as you change the past.

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid game! Highly recommended if you enjoy games featuring time travel or choices impacting the direction of the story. It's nothing terribly ground-breaking but it's a solid, well-written piece of media that I enjoyed. I would say however it's probably not worth 30 dollars, I'd suggest 20 or 15, so wait for it to go on sale.I do have a few complaints, it doesn't use the 'items getting moved or generated as a result of your interference' gimmick to its fullest, there's maybe 4 or 5 puzzles tops that go beyond a scene that just shows you a hidden area you couldn't touch until you saw it in a cutscene. But what few there were I really enjoyed. Beyond that, the character models could have been better. The environment, by contrast, is very well detailed and if you pay attention minute things shift around depending on how you've changed the timeline such as a window being broken and a hammer being brought up to repair it without the story ever drawing attention to such little details, it helps make the world feel alive and like your choices are really changing things. The character models could have maybe used some love in this regard showing bruises or marks from previous days.This is not an objective point but I also enjoyed the main character, he (or she) is a silent protagonist but they've got a fair amount of personality with how they title each of the cutscenes sometimes even joking around with a life or death scene for the victims but what must be fairly mundane for a time traveling fixer. It got a fair amount of giggles out of me how they acted.And...that's kinda it. I'm really hoping to see something else from this developer! The game has a good template that can be dropped onto other stories and circumstances to great success I feel. I'm hoping the next one is a setting that's a little bit more important/life or death with regards to the stakes! I'd be a fun escalation from this one!
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: 11.1h (100% achievement, finished the game) No. Yes (7 achievements). No. is an adventure game with a time travel element where you have to make decisions for the 6 characters living in the same building. You need to watch how the story unfolds and influence their decisions over 8 days.- Multiple endings based on your decision- Easy to change your decisions without having to watch the cutscene again- Events are segmented based on timeframe to make it easier to remember- You need to walk around the house to watch the cutscene- It can be hard to deduce how to unlock an event- It's hard to figure out the correlation between the perfect and normal ending for each characterIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650The first thing that comes to mind regarding the visuals is that the house is spooky. You are exploring an abandoned house when a storm is going out outside, meaning that you have to hear thunder while exploring a dark place. It gives a spooky atmosphere that horror games usually have, especially with the echo and occasional sound like thunder and water dripping in the bathroom. I was almost surprised when I heard the latter one.I like the design choice that the developer makes with the characters. It shows all characters in hologram-like visuals to indicate that they were events from the past. The decision to make the room darker to brighten up the holograms is also done perfectly to make you immersed in it.To be honest, I didn't find the correlation between the premise and what you are doing. The game starts by giving an introduction about how you have to go to the past and save the world, but it doesn't seem to match what you are supposed to do. The ending might give some sort of room for a sequel, but even that hardly connects with the story of the 6 characters.Well, if you can ignore the premise, the story is nice. It gets boring at first, especially since there are a lot of introductions and you have to remember a bunch of characters at once. Moreover, the game starts a bit slow with the story, showing a lot of unnecessary events about the daily life of the 6 characters. That being said, it was designed nicely over the course of 8 days. Conflicts and traumas will come up one after another, sometimes with or without your interference, and things will change based on your decision. Sadly, you don't watch the ending of the characters - you only read a summary of it.In , you are given a timeline interface where you can watch an event that unfolds in it. However, you must go to the area where the event happened to watch it. This can be tedious if you have to go to different areas all the time, especially when you are just starting and don't know where most areas are.Some timeline events will give you choices that you can change which will cause a butterfly effect on future events. However, you "forced" a character to make a choice with a machine, which doesn't explain how that can change a person's decision. That being said, the game will give an indicator of which events it can change, although you can't do it the other way around. It was disappointing since I needed to figure out how to unlock the rest of the events by guessing and making random choices.It can be confusing to figure out which decisions you make. There are just a lot of choices that can change a character's life and death. Since you will be changing these a lot to figure out the optimal ending, it can be hard to keep track of the ones that you want. I don't even understand how you can get a perfect ending for a character since I felt like I didn't change anything from what I previously did.I like how easy it is to make a choice. As a game that is focused on different choices, you don't have to watch the cutscenes from the beginning to do it; you can just change it in your timeline. Moreover, the events are cut nicely to make you remember which is which without having to replay it. Heck, there is even a summary told both in text and voice if you are that lazy to replay the scene.I finished the game with the perfect ending in 11.1h. The game has no replayability value; I feel that your end goal is always to get a perfect ending for all of the characters. There is no difference in the ending except for the character's fate at the end of the story, though. Trying to watch all events blind might give you trouble, especially since some events' unlock requirements can be vague, and changing decisions blindly to find choices that might trigger it can also cause headaches.Also, if you are a scaredy-cat like me, you might feel a bit scared when you are exploring the house, but there isn't any jumpscare in the main game at all. The only jumpscare it got lies in one hard-to-find easter egg that you can find post-game.The game doesn't start well with me. I don't like slow-paced stories, and the game's pacing is exactly that. It picks up a bit later on, although it wasn't anything extreme. The story feels like something that can happen in our daily lives, with traumas and issues, and how you can try to get through it. It wasn't that bad as long as you forget about all of the premise that doesn't make sense. I suggest buying it at a sale if you like games where your choices matter. It was done perfectly without making all future choices look odd.
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: The Invisible Hours. Tacoma. Her Story. The Return of The Obra Dinn. Gone Home. If you've played and enjoyed any of those games, then you're going to love Eternal Threads! Piecing together the story of what happened the week before a house caught on fire, and the interwoven lives of these 6 people, is quite interesting. And how one decision can change the course of further events.I only wish that it was a bit easier to keep track of which choices lead to which outcomes, since I'm trying to see all events, but still want to save everyone. I highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: ⚠⚠ This Game Has An Unskippable "Photosensitivity Warning" That Will Waste Approx. [8] Seconds Of Your Time Each Game LaunchI bought Eternal Threads without really knowing what kind of game it was.  It's risky to not watch any trailers, view any gameplay footage or read any reviews, but sometimes I like going into a game that's obviously not formulaic for a given genre and figuring it out for myself.I found out that Eternal Threads is a very specific kind of game.  It's totally focused on its narrative, so much so that I hesitate to even place it in the Adventure game genre and it definitely isn't a puzzle game.The point of the game is to view the story, not to interact with game mechanics or explore environments.  The game is about these six characters from the past, not your player character.  The entire game takes place in a house with around 20 rooms/areas.  This game has the structure of a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure® book.  The only game mechanics are choosing historic scenes to view with a hologram projector and some of the scenes let you choose between two outcomes.  This is the so-called "time manipulation."It didn't really feel like I was manipulating time in Eternal Threads, because almost all of the effects were abstract.  They applied to the holographic scenes I was viewing and to the user interface for the timeline.  It's not like most time travel stories where character actually goes back and directly interacts with the world of the past.  The player in Eternal Threads is alone in an abandoned house.  There were precious few instances when decisions I made about the timeline actually affected the "real world" in any way.  Again, I think "choose-your-own-adventure" is a better way to describe the interactivity in Eternal Threads than "time manipulation."  I was always a spectator, separated from any actual events.I think the basic systems of Eternal Threads could have had supported robust puzzle gameplay, but it doesn't have any.  It really is like watching a TV show or a very long movie.  The story and characters of the people that lived in this house is the main (and only) attraction.I could write a detailed essay on what I thought about the story & characters of Eternal Threads.  But we all know that would be a wasted effort, so even though I took notes on these topics, I'll avoid doing that.  General characterizations will rule this day!Despite the apparent sci-fi stylings of this game's initial presentation (the title screen, while very cool, is misleading about the nature of the game), it's like the Assassin's Creed games where there's a layer of "real world" on top of the historic events that are the main setting of the game.  In Eternal Threads, 98% of the game is following the activities of housemates in the UK who are thoroughly contemporary and completely ordinary.These characters are a collection of the varieties of young degenerates produced by modern society.  I didn't like or respect a single one of them, but they were all very well acted and successfully carried the game for me.  The characters were motion captured and interacted with the environment in a very nice way.  Unfortunately, the developers didn't do any performance capture for faces, so characters always have flat expressions and usually no mouth movements.  That's alright, I started played video games in the mid-1990s and I still can use my imagination to fill in the blanks.As for the story.... it's amazing that the developers were brazen enough to add the "sci-fi layer" on top of their story about the totally mundane lives of young adults living in the United Kingdom.  It's kind of misleading to entice people with the thought of a fantastical futuristic game about time manipulation, when what the game is really about is a group of unremarkable people whose problems largely boil down to needing to see some kind of "professional."Bringing back the "choose-your-own-adventure" comparison, those books may not have as much detail or as many individual choices as Eternal Threads, but they tend to have branches that go in significantly different directions.  Eternal Thread's choices stick closely to a central progression of events.  By the end of the timeline, it all collapses down into whether or not characters survive the housefire.This is the way the player interacts with the past events that he otherwise can only watch.  "Potential Corruption Points" appear in certain scenes that have two choices which affect the availability of scenes down the timeline.  The whole timeline is available from the start, but there's no reason to view to story out of order, especially since events will be locked until corruption points are changed, or particular scenes are viewed that will allow entry into new rooms in the "real world."There are over 150 scenes and obviously that is way too many to keep in my head at once.  Thankfully there's a feature called "Event Lock" that assists by showing scenes that influence, or are influenced by, the selected scene.  Usually, it was very helpful but there were times it didn't work properly.  I struggled to find how to enable a scene called "Handsfree Packing" because none of the scenes suggested by event lock could activate it.  I had to go outside of the event lock, and back several days, to find the relevant decision point: I wish there was a rhyme or reason to the corruption point decisions, but not really.  It causes things to play out in different ways that usually can't be anticipated by knowledge of the past, of the future, of character personalities, or anything else.  In Eternal Threads, you've just got to watch every scene and try every possibility.  This is why I reject characterizing Eternal Threads as a proper puzzle game.I saved all six characters, not by reasoning or applying earned knowledge, but by watching this TV show/movie from start to finish and observing what sequence caused characters to survive.  Aiming for particular outcomes was a process of trial-and-error.  For the final goal of saving characters from the housefire, it mostly comes down to .  There's a bonus objective to resolve each character's personal struggles.  I figured out how to do this for a few characters, but solving the rest would have been trial and error.  I had an idea of what their big struggles were, but not how to manipulate the specific events necessary to resolve them.  I spent a while trying to make that happen, but decided it was too tedious and just completed the game with only 2 or 3 optimal outcomes.  I assume there's a different ending, so I might go back (with the solution!) and check it out.Like I said a thousand words ago in this review (as usual, I didn't mean for it to be this long!), this is a specific kind of game.  It has elements of all the things the developers added as tags, such as "puzzle," "investigation," "thriller," "choices matter," and "mystery," but the only tags that describe the game in a comprehensive way are "Narrative," "Story Rich," "Choose Your Own Adventure" and basic technical stuff like "First Person" and "Drama."  I never felt "Emotional" but I imagine some people might if they're able to connect with these characters more than I did.And I really did have a bunch of notes about specific characters and story developments.  Even without using any of them, this review is still long as hell.  I'll stop it now.  Bye.

_childDocuments_.review: It is very much like a good choose your own adventure book that you read through once and then back track to get a good ending. The story is very touching and you really feel for the characters and want to help them get the best outcome. I could not put it down and played it all in one sitting. About 9 hours to beat it, or 12 to get the perfect ending. I really enjoyed the style of gameplay and want more! I hope there is some DLC or a sequel in the works!

_childDocuments_.review: First off, this is a proper game. Usually games which focus on unique mechanics fall short of fleshing out the actual game and can feel like a demo, this is not the case with Eternal Threads, this is a complete story with many place to go in the future.I suggest playing the game like this; find a decision thread (could be someone keeping a secret) and just go off on a tangent of the timeline how that secret is kept or revealed all the way to the conclusion. I destroyed a long term relationship in 5 seconds flat and it was much more fun than going through the timeline in order.Your choices genuinely affecting the entire course of the characters (not just the ending!) without punishing you for choosing a certain path. You can zip along the timeline to the point you feel things for a certain character started to go wrong and try again.The objective of the game is to find a combination of solutions that save everyone. At first I thought the "right" choices were obvious as with many decision tree games, play lawful good is encouraged however very cleverly you need to investigate all the potential outcomes to have access to certain branches that hold the ultimate solutions.I have achieved the optimal ending but I don't think that affect the replay-ability because in a few months starting from scratch there is no way I get there again with no retries and that is a good thing.Once I had uncovered the timeline from start to finish my understanding of the timeline's causality was 1/10, then I saved 1 person and another and another but I just sacrificed 2 people back to square 1; slowly slowly I understood more and more and as frustrating as it was this only proved the decision tree actually affects the gameplay.There are very satisfying Eureka! moments in the late game when you graduate from trying to brute force a single character's salvation to thinking how each character's feelings are connected to each other.I wish they increased the scariness / thriller factor somehow, more of the pit in your stomach feeling you have at the start and end of the game. The ending has so many implications, very excited to see what is next for Eternal Threads.
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: Very happy with this one. Mechanically somewhat reminiscent of Obra Dinn in that you progressively unlock and witness little character vignettes, gradually piecing together the story. Many positives:* Above all, an understandable chain of events that you influence in a logical, reasonable way. You can't always fully appreciate the changes your choices make but you can usually make a pretty good guess and rarely find yourself 'flipping switches' without some kind of plan or idea.* Especially enjoyed the initial experience of gradually unpicking the original timeline, which can be approached in several different ways (for example, strictly chronologically, or by following a single character through their individual story, or even working your way backwards from the fire).* Professional, convincing voice acting across the board.* Realistic character behavior and motivation.* Good attention to detail, for example, stored messages on cell phones that shift around based on your decisions.* A smattering of eerie events in the 'present' that create an uncertain atmosphere and keep you on your toes.* Overall a satisfying and well-written story, although perhaps it stumbles a bit with the cliff-hanger final ending.Easy recommendation to anyone who likes mysteries to unravel, exploration, or a good story with light but meaningful game elements.
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: This review is spoiler free.I'm a big fan of detective games - Obra Dinn, Painscreek Killings, Paradise Killer - and found Eternal Threads a good entry of the genre. It isn't too hard to complete but takes time and patience if you want the best outcome. There are no real puzzles to solve and you act more on how much information you uncover than anything else.Some of the criticisms levelled at the game I'm quite surprised at. Some people found the voice acting wooden or weird but as a Northerner who has lived my years in shared accommodations, the variety of regional accents was very accurate, as was the painfully polite small talk and awkward jokes. We're just...like that unfortunately! I also was really impressed with the vocal performance particularly of Neil; specifically when he trashes his room and when he's calling for his sister near the end.For the 'bad bits': this game is a lot of standing around and listening to people talk without doing much about it for ages. I don't mind this at all, but I can see how some players would hate the inaction and information overload. If you're one of these people then Eternal Threads may not be for you.There is also a jump scare if you go for the photograph Easter Egg - while its telegraphed a little it did really get me, and I really could have done without it in the game. However, it is hard and specific to find so you can avoid it comfortably.I was very intrigued by the overarching world building, and will be checking in the future for more titles from this developer. I hope this review was helpful!
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: I tried, couldn't get into it. Should have probably played the abridged version. The idea of going back in time to prevent death while changing the future as little as possible is intriguing, but a game revolving around a single mission where you're hanging around for several days in the life of six randos and getting way too involved in their mundane lives, I lost interest. Make the setting more interesting and the characters more intriguing and I'd be down for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: So, where to start? I love this game, oh man, I do, but and it's a big one, I will not recommend this. At least not now, and for one specific reason, the save system. I don't understand this nowadays, don't devs know how to program a save system anymore? Do I have to see the same thing over and over and over and over again because for the life of me, the game only saves when it wants?? I work quite long hours and many times I'm not allowed to see throughout a full sequence until the devs decide I can save the game. So, this way, I've played the initial 15 minutes about 4 times now. 4 times. And no skipping as well. No, you have to watch the all bloody thing, because hey, s...w the player if he has to go somewhere in a rush. And no cloud save either, if I want to play between the Deck and PC. So, until the save system is tweaked, avoid it, or, if, unlike me, you have plenty of time, I totally advise it. It's a gorgeous game, that maybe one day, I'll be able to see past the first 15 minutes.
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: I gave this game a really good chance, as I wanted to love it, but as it is I can't recommend it.There's not enough meaningful choice or investigation involved. For example, you have to figure out how to unlock a bunch of doors. I thought okay, let's look at events right before the door gets used, or try to be clever following people around, etc. But actually the location of at least two of those doors is revealed through mostly random events that I don't think could logically be tied to the doors. It makes me feel that what I really have to do is just watch alllllll the events (there are maaaanyyyy events) and flip them around until everyone lands in the right place. Which brings me to...The controls are somewhat tedious and make the game seem longer than it is. There's no way to skip through dialogue on first encountering a scene, and you have to move around through the house to watch events where they occurred. But because of the lack of real choice, this mostly means: select an event, move around to the location, watch the event, repeat.The portion of the story I've seen so far isn't super compelling. The writers clearly made an effort to have very different and engaging characters, and their personalities definitely come through. However, what's happening with them isn't super interesting, and saving them involves such small changes that it doesn't feel like a huge accomplishment.On the plus side, the writing and the voice acting are both really good. If you are in the mood for a somewhat relaxed slow paced game, this could be just the ticket. As for me, after a good 10 hours I'm bored and don't care anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: VERY underrated tbh. I'm not finished yet but I'm very close to the end and this game has moved me in many ways.The attention to detail is amazing, the flowchart system works super well, the writing is perfect and so is the acting, this game deals with a lot of very deep issues, trauma, abuse, lost of loved ones, relationship issues, societal issues etc. in very realistic ways, everything is so well written, I've been immersed in the plot so much, especially because of the several timelines mechanic, it keeps you hooked up fr. If you like games like Life is Strange and Zero Escape you'll love this, I never thought I'd say this but I think I found a game that handles the flowchart/different timelines mechanic better than Zero Escape, and that's the best compliment I could give any game.This game deserves wayyy more recognition, there's so much content and it works so well, the story is very complex but also easy to follow, the flowchart system is so well put together you'll never get lost tbh, this could've ended up being a total disaster very easily, but the devs did everything right, can't wait to see more from them.In short: 10/10 best thing I've played in a long while.

_childDocuments_.review: As an operative tasked with fixing corruption in the timestream, you have been sent to the North of England in May 2015, where six people died in a house fire. Prohibited from simply stopping the fire, you must instead manipulate the choices made by the housemates in the week leading up to it so that they all survive the event.You must traverse up and down this timeline, changing decisions at different moments throughout the week so that their effects interact and combine together to save all six housemates.However, it is not just the housemates who have choices. Each of them can be saved from the fire in multiple ways, with each outcome having a profound effect on their lives in the future. Will you just search for the quickest and easiest solution, or can you find the best possible outcome for everyone?Setting up temporary base in the house mere hours after the fire, provides a unique perspective on events. As you look back through the timeline, past events play out in front of you in ghostly form, with the smoke and fire damaged house a constant reminder of what is to come. In addition, as you manipulate the past, the environment can be reset around you to match the changes taking place. Some new objects will appear, others will move around the house and the contents of rooms can change substantially as you change the past.Eternal Threads comes together as a solid, engaging narrative that keeps things simple, with a cleverly implemented time manipulation mechanic that easily allows you to jump back and forth through every possible outcome- Excellent Storytelling- Enjoyable voice acting- Clever use of the time manipulation concept- Atmosphere keeps you on the edge- Puzzles outside of the time map could have been more elaborateDISASTER | BAD | MEDIOCRE | OKAY | GOOD | GREAT |  | MASTERPIECE

_childDocuments_.review: 5.5 hours. 6/10. Alright. Wholesome. Good. Walking simulator trying to connect timelines. Sound of rain mostly. None.ᶠʳᵒᵐ ᵐʸ ᶠᶦʳˢᵗ ᵖˡᵃʸᵗʰʳᵒᵘᵍʰIt's a walking simulator in which you walk around with your hi-tech gear that can show you short glimpses of past events so that you can reconstruct the timeline of the house (in reality the "reconstruction" is choosing 1 of 2 choices for each compatible scene). The story revolves around 6 characters each with their life problems, the decisions of which you affect, and in the end their fate is based on these choices. If you want to achieve the perfect (it's called 'optimal') outcome for the characters you'll have to resolve their issues in addition to saving their lives, again by changing choices. If you're not walking to your destination (one of three floors), then you're either watching a scene or spending time in the timeline menu. For the most part I found the experience relatively enjoyable, and the story was wholesome at the end with Ben being the best guy ever.It's not a masterpiece and it's not on the same level as "Return of the Obra Dinn", but it can be considered of the same category. One optimal outcome here didn't make sense to me and by pursuing it the process became more trial and error rather than logical conclusion.
