_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a neutral option but since there isn't I will lean towards the Not Recommended option.Eternal Threads starts out well. I generally love games like this where you need to watch the events unfold in order to piece together what happened and why. Especially welcome is the ability to change the outcome.However the underlying story and the ending lets this game down. I especially loathe cliffhangers in any media unless a sequel is guaranteed. In this case the meta story was established at the start of the game but fails to wrap anything up and instead introduces more questions than answers. There is no guarantee of a sequel and I feel like these kinds of stories should be wrapped up inside the game and sequels should just naturally flow on from the original game to extend the story further.I was also a little disappointed with how the final conclusion is portrayed. I feel like some sort of flash-forward mechanic could have been used to show us the fate of the characters rather than relying on us to just read what happens in their character profiles. After investing almost 10 hours of gameplay into watching these characters and trying to get their best outcomes, I'm left feeling a bit deflated and dissatisfied. The concept is great but the execution just falls flat. I'd recommend waiting for a sale if you're still curious or just watch a playthrough on youtube instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Eternal Threads attempts to blend gaming and interactive storytelling, but unfortunately falls short of its ambitious goal. From the outset, it's clear that this experience is more akin to an interactive TV show than a compelling game. The premise holds promise: guiding the fate of a house's former inhabitants and, in a bizarrely stretched sense, the fate of the world itself.However, the execution leaves much to be desired. Much of your time is spent scrolling through a timeline, selecting from a series of banal encounters. Regrettably, the majority of these interactions lack any meaningful impact, rendering them more like poorly acted scenes from a low-quality soap opera. Occasionally, a nugget of potential interactivity emerges – a key, a hidden object – briefly teasing at a deeper level of engagement that the game consistently fails to deliver. It's a missed opportunity that's hard to ignore, and it's disappointing that the developer didn't capitalize on these moments to create a more captivating experience.After a grueling two-hour investment, I found myself on the verge of abandoning ship. The hope that the experience might improve was the only factor that kept me going. To give credit where it's due, it did... but only marginally.   Pushing on for another two hours was a daunting task, and noticing that I was only about 40% of the way through the timeline, I had to uninstall it.  I have other games to play, other books to read, other films to watch... and for a 'game' so focused on manipulating time, Eternal Threads just felt like a complete waste of mine.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for June 2023, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before July 4th, 2023, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A game where choices matter.Eternal Threads is a strange game where players time-travel back to a night when six people died in a fire.  The goal is simple, save everyone, and the only way to do this is to view events and sometimes make choices.  Those choices will change which events happen, and potentially the fates of characters.  While this is a straight story-based game, you’ll be able to explore the house as you learn more about each of the characters.At the same time, the game feels like it wants to be a horror game, except it’s not.  Like not even trying to be, it just has this feeling of horror for some reason.    The acting in the game works, but it feels a touch cheap and could have been better, the same is true for some of the animations, and a few times the naming of the scenes feels callous.Pick this up if you like story games, especially that voyeuristic style that Her Story and Immortality has, or games like Gone Home and What Remains of Edith Finch.  It doesn’t reach those same levels, but it still is an interesting experience, and I hope this team will be able to produce a second game in the genre because this is pretty unique, and with a larger budget, this would stand out as something very unique.If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel: After having played almost all the game, I can confirm my review, it's a solid game, and an interesting story with a few flaws.  Still I have enjoyed my time.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey kids, if you ever become a time traveler and need to save someone from a house fire, remember you can always get them drunk and make them cheat on their failing marriage. That saves a bunch of people real fast.Jokes aside, I really loved the fact that the choices made across the board change how the story plays out in a realistic way. The story is also quite realistic, the characters feel genuine, and the two-story home in England with gallons of rain to match was quite nice too. I was really invested in saving all six characters throughout the story and it never became boring.Now for the bad stuff: The controls are a bit janky, I got stuck in an animation a few times, the time control menu is obviously made for console and unwieldy for PC, especially where you need to pick a different event at the same timezone (psst, you need to click the event with your mouse the arrow keys don't work) The price tag is also hefty. And the game ends in an irritating cliffhanger, although that's a nitpick.Anyway, great game, worth buying but I would buy it at a discount because I'm poor.

_childDocuments_.review: It was a beautiful ride playing this game. The gimmick of the game is a very interesting one, there's many events in a 7-day timeline outta which you as a time-traveller can access, view and change any event outcome as you please. It's a gorgeous way to show the butterfly effect, but it also isn't something crazy like spit out a chewing gum and 2 days later the president dies.  The writing was pretty strong in how these events are linked, how the changes you make affect the characters and how the changed characters interact with new events. However, the writing fell short of praise in the conclusion of the game. Without revealing any direct spoilers, However, I would not recommend the game for someone on a budget, since there isn't much replayability once you 100% the game (in about 10-15 hours) so the playtime-to-bucks ratio is pretty low. However, if you've got the money to spend, definitely go for it!

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game for Pay or Play 2nd Cycle of 2024 and it was picked for me by La Volpe.As an operative tasked with fixing corruption in the timeline, you have been sent to the North of England in May 2015, where six people died in a house fire. Prohibited from simply stopping the fire, you must instead manipulate the choices made by the housemates in the week leading up to it so that they all survive the event.Eternal Threads is a single-player, first-person story-driven puzzle game of time manipulation, choice and consequence. You watch through scenarios to unravel the personal stories of the six people you are tasked to save, while changing their choices along the way to make sure they survive the night of the fire. You can also work through their personal issues while you are at it, which leads to a "perfect ending".It's definitely an awesome storytelling game that is well written and it combines the ordinary together with the futuristic mundane. It was really hard to just stop playing and I felt like I could have played it from start to finish in one setting if I had the time. The stories of the different characters were very good and really had me hooked. The burned down house was at times creepy and gave a little bit of suspense to the whole game while playing.The game wasnt too difficult to 100% and I really had a blast while playing it. It's definitely a good game to play if you enjoy choices, time manipulation and a good, well written story. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: This game has an intriguing premise - You alter past events and see the consequences of those changes on the timeline and in the present day in an effort to save the future from a temporal apocalypse.Where it falls down is the execution.  The past events you're manipulating are a single week in the domestic life of an English shared home apartment.  Sure by the butterfly effect, this might somehow save the future, but it's not immediately clear how.  Worse, since none of the subject matter is particularly gripping, the game has to live or die on the strength of its performances and they are... generously... fine.  Mechanically, the game loop is that you select an event you want to see, then run around a tiny apartment until you find the scene and watch it.  Sometimes you make a choice between two outcomes, which affects what events you can select going forward.  Barring some light "hidden" object searching, there's very little reason we wouldn't have just selected the events to watch and cut out the middle man.Long story short, there's a seed of a good game here, but it's buried deep under some truly baffling design choices.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like butterfly-effect-type games, this is worth your money. If you like what-went-wrong-here mysteries, this is worth your money.I suspect some people may not want to pay this much before they know if the writing is any good, so let me put those fears aside: nobody is an idiot; nobody makes decisions based on crazy moon logic; changing the outcomes of certain scenes affects other scenes in  ways. This is a well-written story.I will avoid spoilers, but here's an example: there is a hidden room in the house, and you will form a theory about what's in that room long before you can investigate it for yourself. The game trusts you to come up with that theory; it does not try to double-bluff you. When my theory was confirmed, it made me feel like a good investigator, and it make me appreciate this game for presenting a  puzzle and allowing me to trust my intuitions.First and foremost, this game reminds me of : watch “recordings” of scenes overlaid on your environment, learn things from them, use that knowledge to progress. Unlike , there's only one small setting; but, also unlike , you actually have the ability to change the past, thus addressing the most common complaint about the “walking simulator” genre of game.I like that there's not a single perfect version of the timeline; some various combinations of decisions will produce the same outcome. I like that you have to pursue some outcomes that  sub-optimal before you see how they might be for the best. I like that you have to temporarily pursue some outcomes that  sub-optimal in order to gain access to certain places.Most of all, though, I appreciate the timeline view. It makes it possible to think (e.g.) “hmm, I haven't seen Possibility 192 yet; how do I get that to happen?” — and then be able to find out, because the timeline view tells you which previous events it relies on  telling you which choices you need to make for those events. That feels like just the right amount of assistance. Any less help and I wouldn't have bothered to go for the “viewed every scene” achievement; any more help and I would've felt robbed of the satisfaction of figuring it out on my own.Like another reviewer said, I was intrigued with the change-the-past-to-change-your-current-environment mechanic, and wish there had been a bit more of that. But that's only a minor gripe for me.I am thrilled at how the “investigation” genre is finding an identity. For me it's about understanding all the elements of a story over time, pieced together puzzle-style, and without much effort to explain away the gameplay concessions needed to make that possible.  is nominally a science-fiction game, but only because it needs to envision a world where you can change the past and observe the outcomes.  is a game about finding out what went wrong on a boat, and the supernatural element exists just so the player understands how it's possible for a person's dying moments to be captured. The premise is just a bit of hand-waving that needs to be accepted by the player before they can disappear into the fun part: piecing together how something happened.Like , I think there's eventual replay value here, but I'd have to wait at least a year so that I can forget enough of the plot for it to pose a challenge again. I'd love to use these same mechanics to play different stories, though I know that involves new voice actors and new motion capture.

_childDocuments_.review: Think of Eternal Threads as 3D visual novel – with superb voice acting, by the way, and some elements from “walking simulators” - where you follow the lives of 6 housemates in the week leading up to their untimely demise, no thanks to several potential corrupted points in the timeline. Naturally, you'll be able to alter these moments in the timeline by choosing one out of two available decisions, some of which may seemingly look innocent enough, but may have serious ramifications later down the road. If you like the idea of that, then you might want to at least give Eternal Threads a try. Personally, I've only managed to save the lives of 2 out of the 6 housemates - the easiest 2 IMHO - but I'll definitely stick with it until I get all 6 :)Editing my review to point out that yes, the game does have a slow start where you get to know the characters, but the party was pretty eventful and that was on Day 3! By my count, I've managed to get to Day 4 within the first 2 hours by following the entire timeline from start to finish, and not narrowing it down to individual characters.

_childDocuments_.review: The time-travelling 'set right what went wrong' adventure is one of my favourite types of game, and 'Eternal Threads' is a great new entry in the genre. You play an anonymous time-traveller from a grim dystopian future, brought about by too much meddling with the timeline. Your task is to travel back to a single household where six people 'wrongly' perished in a fire in 2015, and - by altering their decisions over the course of a single week - save all of them from their grisly fate.What makes 'Eternal Threads' interesting and unique is that you can view the entire timeline right from the start of the game. If you prefer you can jump right to the end to view the characters' deaths, and work backwards to find the first decision that changes their fate. Alternatively you can watch all events from the beginning in strict chronological order, or choose a particular decision tree and follow it through to its conclusion. However, certain events are dependent on previous decisions or objects you'll find while exploring the house, so you can't just choose the 'best' path right from the start.Gameplay is pretty intuitive, and the timeline helps you keep track of how different decisions and events are linked together. The 'correct' decisions are usually fairly obvious, and different decision chains will often lead to the same ultimate outcome. I'd have liked to see a little more complexity here, e.g. having to make sub-optimal choices early on to gain information that will help you later - perhaps something to consider for a sequel.I should also stress that a huge part of the game consists of watching scenes play out with very little input. With almost 200 events on the main timeline (plus multiple endings), if you're keen to view every scene in order to find the best outcome for each character, you'll easily get your money's worth here. If you're only interested in skipping through the story to reach the ending as quickly as possible, you may well be disappointed. Personally I was hooked from the start; I found the characters likeable and sympathetic (if occasionally a little clichéd) and couldn't wait to uncover everything about their histories, desires and secrets.My biggest complaint is with the ending - while the main characters' fates are resolved, the game ends on a massive cliffhanger regarding the 'framing story' of the time travellers. Sequel hooks are one thing, but with a new IP from a relatively unknown developer, there's no guarantee of when - or even if - we'll ever actually see a second game. I hope 'Eternal Threads' does sell well enough to fund a sequel, as it's a great concept that definitely deserves to be re-visited.

_childDocuments_.review: I had a great time with Eternal Threads. It's an solid storytelling game with convincing voice acting most of the time - which is good, since you cannot speed up line delivery - and a theme that serves the gameplay very well and vice versa. I have seen some comments to the effect that the characters' storylines are mundane and not that deep, but they're not the one with the stakes the game is supposed to be about - that's you, the silent protagonist, and your quest to find the right combination of decisions to get the best outcome for the characters is a lot of fun.Yes, this is all about the events that occur, and so you will do a lot of listening - a slowed down version of the reading a visual novel would give you. Honestly, though, I found I enjoyed a game that forced me to take it at its pace, rather than rushing through to complete it as quickly as I could. (Tacoma is a great comparison to this in many ways.)My one issue is that the patterns are fairly easy to figure out. The challenge level does not come from beating the game - that's pretty easy, all in. There is a bigger challenge in beating the game with the best ending for each character, especially since an obvious best decision for one character might actually preclude another character from having their best ending.The biggest challenge is in finding all the letters and listening to the voicemails - a couple of the letters and most of the voicemails require fairly specific events to have happened. In several cases, they also can't have been overwritten by subsequent events also. This leads to much more of a puzzle, but one that has no real clues to it. You don't know who is going to leave each character a voicemail or why, and so I gave up with the collecting puzzles and used a guide to find them. Note: You actively have to hit the "read" button to read the letters - you can't just pick them up. I found all but two without help, but would not have received the achievement as I did not clock that. It makes these two achievements a little irritating, and was the one tiresome part of the game for me.This is not for everyone. If you don't like significant character-building, especially given the fact that the stakes - at least until the fire comes into play - are not life or death, but more true-to-life issues like happiness or divorce, then you won't enjoy this. Even the tragic ends some characters can meet months after the events of the game are relegated to a text box you might not even read until towards the end of the game. HOWEVER, if you want a game that will engage you with its characters no matter their personal stakes, and challenge you to save them all from their impending deaths, then you'll have a good time with this one, and I recommend it highly as a fun experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: I have two issues with this game: one is core mechanic and another just the way it's made. 1) I had to watch hours of in-game events, before I could start making any serious changes. Talk about sluggish start. 2) The game is dark. It doesn't have to be, there is no reason for that, but it's the way it is. There are hundreds of significant and minor conversations. Making decisions (or changing them later) will re-write parts of the timeline, where the new scenario either improves (you save people) or worsen (poor bastards die).The problem here - I don't care about these neighbours. It's an absolutely plain gathering. A girl hides her pregnancy and her boyfriend cannot decide about career opportunity.A lad jumps between drinking and playing games, occasionally bursting into anger, while his sister struggles with marriage. Another guy's unable to ditch crazy girlfriend and the 6th person has childhood trauma. I appreciate the complexity of these six people communication and consequences, but their personalities and story just below casual.
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game expecting a compelling mystery-based time-travel narrative, but that's not really what this game is. It's more like a short series of a TV drama / soap meets a choose-your-own-adventure book, draped in a supernatural horror atmosphere for some reason. (I clarify what I mean by this below).I actually quite liked the writing, the characters and the voice-acting, and it's not a BAD game, but I can't recommend this game because:1. It's actually pretty tedious watching similar scenes over and over, hoping that one of them will reveal a new choice to branch the narrative further. The game does incorporate some ways to 'skip' scenes, but sometimes even 'new' scenes will repeat dialogue from old scenes (because the new and old scenes are in different branches of the timeline).2. The supernatural horror atmosphere makes the game unnecessarily tense, and I didn't realise it would be like this before I bought it. There's no clear reason for this atmosphere, except that it was originally intended to have horror-like elements that were cut.If I were to give advice to my past self before I played the game, I'd tell myself to try the abridged version first, and not to bother trying to find and watch every single scene.To clarify regarding horror elements: Nothing in the game is actual horror outside of a jump-scare in an easter egg that you have to really go out of your way to find (you have to finish the game, then find multiple secret objects in the house - check the guides for more info). The "TV drama" stories your character watches aren't horror stories either. However, your character spends the whole time wandering a darkened house, you mostly see by torchlight, there's a storm the whole time, suspenseful music, and there are some minor scares, like a picture falling off the wall or a dog barking loudly on the other side of a fence. When your character sets up a scene from the "TV drama" to watch, the characters are projected like ghosts, which by itself can be startling.Regarding mystery and time-travel and genre elements: - It's not a mystery - or at least, the mysteries aren't compelling - because you can immediately jump to the end scenes of the 'tv drama' and find out how everyone died. - It's barely time-travel or sci-fi, because those elements are just used as a wrapper to explain why and how your character can summon scenes from the narrative in any order you wish. - It has some very light puzzle elements, in the sense that you have to figure out the right combination of narrative choices that lead to your desired conclusion - like a choose-your-own-adventure book.
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: This must be the dumbest, braindeadest take on time travel I've ever come across. The original premise sounds interesting enough - time travel exists and that existence itself fwcked up the timeline. So you're sent from an unspecified future to something like 2016 to right a small wrong: six people died in a house fire that shouldn't have, so you need to save them. You can't prevent the whole fire, because reasons. Cool, I've read Eternity's End, let's do this!Except... no. You appear in the house in question AFTER the fire. The house hasn't burned to the ground and most people were killed by smoke, so fair enough. You can run around the house and you have a "timeline" view showing "events" from a week before the fire to the night of. You pick an event, find its trigger point in the house, then use your thingamajig to view the even. By which I mean a holograph of the characters standing around and talking. Pick next event, repeat. Took me three hours of gameplay just to go through all available events. The last ones follow each character individually and shows you how they died.Some are not available, because a few rooms are locked and you can't reach the trigger until you find the key  or code. And some event are only potential and become available when you change the timeline. Which is really the whole point of the game. If you thought you'd go deeper into the past to, say, hide someone's car keys, so they're l;ate for work, you will be very very disappointed, like I was. No, you are still viewing the talks from AFTER the fire, but some events have a possible branch. You can somehow reach into the past and screw with a character's free will and change what they said. Like "is there something in the mail for me?" YES/NO. Or "Do I drunk text my crazy ex?" YES/NO. Which will, of course, change the timeline, open new events and close some of the current ones. You win if you can save all six people.But the stupidity doesn't end there, the whole thing sucks. Minor spoilers ahead, if you're still interested.There is one couple sleeping in the same bed and he takes some sleeping pills just before the fire. She desperately tries to wake him and/or drag him away, but she can't and suffocates. Which is about the only thing that makes sense. Others are sleeping in their rooms, alone, and just suffocates. Nobody except this lady wake up from the smoke and those last events show them coughing in their sleep until they stop. Now I've changed some events and caused the couple to have a huge fight, with the guy sleeping downstairs in the living room (sans pills). So now he survives, yay! But she's alone upstairs and doesn't do the whole rescue thing, she should be fine, as well, right? Wrong. She dies. And even the devs know this is a pile of oxen feces, because in this new timeline, she doesn't get a death scene. She just dies without an explanation.I don't think I will have the stomach to continue this stupidity. No, do not recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has an interesting concept- time travel, this house of people all died horribly, alter details to fix it.  Unfortunately, it's let down by its scale.  It ropes you in and hooks you with a Flashpoint Paradox-style "This timeline is not well, we made a time jump and all these other unrelated things changed, we need to fix it!"  It was a little tropey, but it had me invested and ready to save humanity.  Then I spent the next six hours watching a C-tier British soap opera.  Like Gone Home, it hints at some supernatural elements to keep you invested, and like Gone Home this turned out to be a red herring and not relevant to the plot whatsoever.The game does get points for not pulling the usual choices-matter card "Woah-hoa, you thought picking the right thing to do would be the right thing to do, but it actually ruined everything!"  Unfortunately, it loses those points when just generally picking the "don't be an emotionally-unavailable jerk" options were nearly always the right ones.  I went sequentially through the events picking the options to just generally be nice to people, and saved everyone with 3/6 of the perfect endings before I'd even finished with all the events.  There weren't any difficult decisions; it was always "should I be honest, or be awkward and quiet?" or "should I be a ♥♥♥♥ or not be a ♥♥♥♥?"The timeline is also bogged down with events that even the timeline screen acknowledges have no impact on anything else.  It felt like just an obligation to have something in a slot.  Sometimes this was to give the characters some room to shine, and properly get us invested.  Most times it was absolutely irrelevant; like an entire event dedicated to one of the housemates having lost the remote and being ultimately unable to find it.If I'd been invested, I might have been willing to pore back through the timeline to figure out what precise choices would leave everyone with a happily-ever-after, but I just did not care about these people.  It's nice that they lived, but I'm not crossing the street for them, let alone the timestream.I like investigation games, and I have no problems with games that expect you to get emotionally invested, but after blowing its load in an opening text crawl, this game just did not keep me interested; in the end, I finished it mostly out of a sense of obligation.  Your six hours are likely better spent elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: What is this? Essentially it's "Everyone is gone to the rapture" story rich walking simulator meets "Detroit : becoming human" high amount of branching. Interestingly enough, it plays out in reverse. When in other games you're asked to make decisions (House of Ashes, etc) then discover the outcome, here, you discover the outcome, then get a chance at trying out all the branches until everything "clicks". It's quite clever and well executed upon. It's in fact .This will be controversial to players, but the fact that a massive 30% managed to finish the game AND complete all storyline to perfection shows that if you have OCD, this is the title for you :) Because experimenting is encouraged, you'll find yourself trying out pretty much all potential combinations. It ends up being quite addictive to 'unlock' all the possible storylines. One downside of this is that as per usual in this type of game, these changes often end up being one character interupting the action of another - the "choice" is changing the character that caused the interruption, without any apparent consequences. There are some good surprises throughout the game that I won't spoil and if you like "meta" jokes or easter eggs, you'll enjoy the half dozen spread within the game. One major concern for me is that towards the end, I wasn't trying to save anyone (the goal of the game) - but instead trying to watch every possible cutscene. While tempting, (there's an achievement for it) , I had to force myself to first finish the game, and THEN and only then rewind to get all the outcomes. Some of them can be quite obscure, very obscure in fact, at first glance. This clashes with the seemingly straightforward appraoch you might think is applicable to game. Note that an ingame-help is available if you press esc while in pause mode, and you should 100% use that feature if you want to see the game to the end while getting a 'perfect' score.On an RTX2080 coupled with an i9900, the game runs in 32:9 (5kx1440p) on ultra with SMAA enabled at 55fps average. There's no ray tracing, so no DLSS, and there's not much options to customize. Bottom line, either you have a rig that can play it, or you'll have to downgrade the quality drastically. Personally I was happy with the outcome based on my specs, which are 2 generations behind now. The graphics are solid without being sumptous. We know since "oberver: system redux" that walking simulator can have better gfx than AAA entries. This one however, doesn't qualify. Think functional. So is the UI and the menus, although the 32:9 support is very welcome to manage the gigantic timeline the game is based around.The game presents no bug or glitch, is well voice acted, graphics are decent, the soundstage is good to great, especially on 7.2, but even stereo still had me jumping out of my seat on several occasions. This is a walking simulator with some detective angle (think the Paincreek killings)The story is decent and I'm about 1/3 through because I want to collect everything. I'm rather sure this can be speedrun in about 4h. But you'd be missing out. There's also a "simple mode" for those that don't want the headaches associated with a gigantic set of storyline branching.A solid entry in the genre even though it's not phenomenal like other titles, but one that's guaranteed to be very divisive due to it eventually turning into 'trial and error' process than the outcome of a deductive conclusion.As for myself, I was able to save all 6 members, get 2 perfect endings, and will use youtube to watch the altenatives. To try all the other alternatives is just too repetitive when i could be playing something else, and with 13+h on the clock, i had my money's worth.Thumb up, but try the demo first.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was positively lovely and I'd be darned if i saw it get slept on.Pros:- Fully realised characters with human reactions.- Choices Matter can make small and large differences but ALSO are easy to change back- Multiple endings for saving everyone vs giving everyone their best possible livesCons:- Could benifit with a fast forward mode for scenes incase you have to re-watch something/2nd playthroughs- Finding keys by changing choices can be a little tidious- Some of the different paths feel a little to similar.I absolutely loved this game and was so happy I gave it a shot. _childDocuments_.review: it huts me to low score indie games but...1. shallow storylines: shallow scenes, dialogues that are pure filler, no underlying mistery or sideline story besides "save everyone" which is pretty simple in terms of story telling. no clues or hidden objects to find when you what the scenes, nothing to pay attention to. if the game had richer , deeper story and less scenes it would be good2. the timeline layering: you dont have one action affecting other action and then span two timelines and so let's say create exponential timelines. that would be insane for many choices grouped together but not for 1, 2 or even 3! here the game only goes with one choice and builds on it. nothing more. no timeline layering complexity3. the timeline navigation: i think the dev wanted to keep it simple or want to make you see similar event unfolding according to your choices but they are just all mixed up in one single linear display. not even the option to unfold the different timelines you already discovered. i think this is a must in terms of user experiencei guess some people enjoy the game, it has positives reviews but i cannot lie according to my own opinion, the game is nor bad nor good. mediocre, quite mediocre. im just gonna play it because im bored, but im sure at this point im not gonna find any twist or anything to change my opinion, though if i found something worthy my review may changeagain i dont like bad scoring indie games, but man, this is so shallow, a wasted opportunity

_childDocuments_.review: ETERNAL THREADS is a tough recommendation, because while I enjoyed the conceit of time traveling to an English house in 2015 to save the lives of six ordinary housemates by making tiny changes to their timeline, the whole thing comes off... a little boring? There are almost 200 timeline events to view and about a fifth of those are manipulable, which cause events down the timeline to change due to the ripple effect of choice and consequence. That is entirely too many, especially given most of the events are just fluff.Now, to be fair: you need fluff to see what the everyday lives of the housemates are like so we can connect with them on an emotional level (and I did!); but to also be fair: some of these events are really boring and either needed to be edited down or just removed completely. I really do not need to see another event where a character walks into a scene, meets another character, they say "hi what you up to" and then go about their business - you can just show what they're up to if they're in the house, otherwise I just don't really care.There *is* a stripped down version of the game which reduces the number of events to two-thirds of that 200 (almost as if they realised how boring and superfluous a lot of it is!), but it also locks you out of the supposed best ending of the game. Which is a bit crap, honestly. That said the best ending involves you  Now that I've told you what it is, maybe you could... not bother? It really isn't worth it.I mean. I say all that, but I also unlocked all the acheivos for ETERNAL THREADS so who's the real foolish one here, ey? TWAS ME WHO TWAS THE FOOL

_childDocuments_.review: Title is a bit hyperbolic but I couldn't resist the pun. :PBasically what you do in this game is watch hours of cutscenes of ordinary people with ordinary problems. The time travel metaplot is present but out of focus most of the time, and it doesn't feel meaningful when your "gameplay" consists of guessing how to thread the needle so that all the people survive, and maybe work through their issues if you feel like it. Ultimately it's not even that hard. Most of the time, characters are set to Decision track "A" by default, and you just need to switch them over to "B". Encourage healthy behaviors and stronger bonds between characters, and things will mostly work out. When that doesn't work, swap decisions around until you see new events appear on the timeline. Sometimes a character needs to make a mistake or two to realize they need change, but I did not find the process to be too complicated. Besides that, there are no real puzzles, not much gameplay to speak of. It feels tedious when most of what you do is walk from room to room, push a button, wait and see if there's a decision to make, say A or B, and then repeat the process. It's like a visual novel, except your progrss is locked to the voice actors' line delivery instead of your reading speed.  I took to standing up from my computer and wandering off to do chores while everyone was talking, which shows my level of engagement. I advise buying on sale or not at all. Unless you really, really loved "Gone Home", or felt like "Tacoma" would have been more fun if there were no puzzles in it, in which case you'll be just fine.

_childDocuments_.review: In my first steps into the game I thought it was another horror adventure with a sci-fi feel. Since the tale takes place inside a building vacated due to an enigmatic arson, they only leave vestiges of rooms sunk in darkness where its lodgers once lived. But I realize that its story goes further: it offers an acceptable narrative where the drama of the characters expressed in their daily lives is emphasized as its plot thread for the game. Although this theme may be repetitive, what differs is in the way of telling or developing its story.Before entering the game menu, it informs a story of some experiments that were accomplish with time. Which some unidentified group resorted to time travel to surgically repair certain changes in events. The history was contaminated with chrono radiation. They also noticed that particular less important events trigger extremely important events, highlighting the butterfly effect. So the mission consists —embodied in agent 43— of fluctuating such events in order to rescue the dead lodgers in the building, whose demises were «untimely». To do this we interact with the characters for almost a week.As I indicated above, something clichéd can be told well. Generally we’re used to living great stories with large-scale events. The narrative formulation of this game involves of inverting and reversing from an important event to a simple or «insignificant» one. I ensue a story of everyday along with their decisions. This is what the game is about: how can I give a different decision to each character to realize a good consequence as part of completing the mission. Well, their ending or mission is that everyone lives and, at the same time, they succeed to overcome their personal dilemmas.The entire adventure develops with a common story. The way the characters are presented is through holograms as equivalent to ghosts. They relate us their actions as their own life or related to someone else. However, such characters are in motion despite being spectres sheltered as echoes in such events. The script is well performed, each of them has their own behaviour and I enjoyed their diversity of tones of the voices. It has its touch of humour and melodrama. They provide an impact of shock when comprehending their personal stories through home problems.The structure of the plot plays an important role. The game takes place in a single place: the building. It’s gloomy, atmospheric (the basic resources of the Unity graphics engine); with artless details which is lit by little drones. Time: almost a week. What changes is the story. To appreciate this, just look at the chronological map. The main plot is a straight line of cause and effect. But inside it there’re nodes that enclose events. Some of them reveal what’s happening at that moment. While others may have a chance to change it and, later, it’ll affect the action of one person or with another. Since I constantly have to select, each incident is represented with a geometric figure and some title —many of them have curious names. One alternative may be more substantial than another.Depending on decisions, the effect will change. Even a feature is, depending on the modifications, some things change places or disappear (such as opening doors or discovery documents that weren't there before). Although many times it’s barely perceptible. On the other hand, we can go from one event to another in partial freedom, moving along the timeline. Although it’s prudent to follow the narrator's advice, as he offers a basic tutorial. We can move from event to event with strides, but if we don’t have order we can get confused and end up tangled without knowing its story. Because the purpose is to untangle it in sequence to make good decisions that lead to a judicious outcome for all the characters. There’s already an ending, but we can give it a different one.Part of the gameplay is realized in the chronological map where they display possible actions as well as their changes. This way we can navigate to move an action that is detrimental or favourable to everyone together according to their connection between persons. Hence the game's title, threads. We must pull those strings in the conjecture of eternity. It’s more contemplation and movement of the map than interaction with the characters, since sometimes a secondary event allows us to see a consequence of a previous decision and so on. Such an action can be done on the map without repeating the scene dramatized by the characters.On the other hand, the interaction with them will be through a device. I choose the happening, it will indicate me the location within some room. It shows me the action of the subjects. I'm in the swing of space-time. As I said, they reveal themselves as ghosts, they’re reverberations of the possible past. They no longer interact with objects, except by telling us something. From the same tool, it’ll expose a possible alternative if the node has it. Without that apparatus we’d only be walking through an almost meaningless building. Although I found it a little annoying that it said my position data all the time, but I guess it's part of the narrative in some way.The gameplay scheme is simple, but it’s entertaining to draw the threads to find out when the characters are alive or still dead. The game has the potential to develop an even profounder story. Or, to perform a second part or a new story, since it has the necessary elements to be able to offer something different and captivating through an originality approached from another angle about time travel. It lacks a soundtrack (except it appears in the start menu) as well as a suitable development of the introduction and conclusion, since it seems like a sandwich. The game is quite short. But if you like stories —like I did— this could be a good option. One small thing can change a decisive moment, like the flutter of a butterfly's wings can create a hurricane. The plot is already there, you can see each event that makes it up and, in the end, make the decisions to give a happy ending to everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming off of the success of non-linear puzzle/detective games like Return of the Obra Dinn and Outer WIlds, developer Cosmonaut tries their hand at a modern-day web of deductions with their game Eternal Threads. Set inside a British house shared by six people, you are a time traveler named Forty-Three tasked with saving these six from a house fire that will take all of their lives. To do this, you must manipulate a variety of major and minor choices in their lives over the previous week, creating subtle rifts in spacetime and influencing them all to save themselves by the time the fire arrives. It's an excellent premise that is immediately interesting and slightly unnerving. The entire 8 hours spent in Eternal Threads keeps you in its contained domestic setting, slowly unlocking doors and secrets as you learn more about the house and the people inside of it. Right at the top of the game, you are given a device that can visit many events that lead to the current timeline, which you can tackle in any order. I chose to see events mostly in chronological order, but there's nothing stopping you from jumping ahead to see the fates of the residents change based on your actions. Once you choose an event you want to watch, you must find its location in the house and then watch the scene play out. In some events, there is a binary decision which can alter the timeline, like choosing to drink or not, telling someone a secret, or choosing how to spend a morning. One of the most fascinating elements of the game is trying to deduce how certain choices will lead to a better or worse outcome and how far do the choices allow for new opportunities. Besides the choices, there isn't much interaction with the characters or the world. Your character is viewing everything through holograms, so you aren't directly influencing the characters, just the choices they make. Ostensibly, the game is just watching over a hundred scenes and picking which decisions carry you forward. This lack of tactile interaction would be fine if not for Eternal Thread's awful UI. The menu you use to select events is laid out so you can easily see the events on the timeline in order, with potential events found on alternate paths blocked out. You can easily change decisions without having to re-view the scene, but there is no menu or tracker of what decisions you've made, so skimming through the massive timeline is cumbersome. It's all too easy to forget which decisions you've left active also, especially if you return to the game for another session. Thankfully, the writing overall is pretty good with some standout moments between characters. Vocal performances are hit and miss, but generally the scenes aren't boring if there are multiple people in them. All of this concludes in an ending that is wildly unsatisfactory, even when achieving the best possible outcome. The game has some truly incredible revelations hanging on its outer edges, but never tries to find a payoff or a valid reason for it all to be there, and instead opts for a cliffhanger that feels out of place and unearned for the stakes previously presented. I was really enjoying the last few hours of Eternal Threads and the actual path to the end completely deflated all desire to 100% complete every scene and collectible. I wish I had more positives to give this game, For 7 of the 8 hours played, I was having a fantastic time, but unfortunately, this genre rides upon how it puts the pieces together, but currently those pieces are from two completely different jigsaw puzzles. I cannot fully recommend Eternal Threads, but lightly suggest trying it out if you like general drama or if you don't mind following through to the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: Cool concept but ultimately boring and messy. Eternal Threads is about saving 6 people from a house fire by watching the last week of their lives and changing some of their decisions in scenes that feature 1-6 characters. My approach was to start from the beginning and view every scene in chronological order. Some scenes were locked out due to the current timeline choices, so I went back to change decisions, rather than keep going. But doing it this way meant the story was a jumbled mess after a few hours. I no longer could remember what decisions had taken place and no longer cared. Although since some decisions are only minor, scenes were 90% the same anyway, so I'm rewatching things multiple times and getting more and more bored. Progressing this way also meant I stumbled into ways to save characters. Also I fixed all their personal issues by accident too. Sounds like my fault, right? Let me be clear, I’m still glad I did it this way because many saving/fixing decisions felt arbitrary; a character will live or die depending on whether you let them drink at a party several nights before the actual fire that kills them. So doing it the other way would mean I’d end up going back and randomly picking options and then I’d have the problem of forgetting where in the story everything takes place.What else is there to say? The game is 90% watching cutscenes, many of which seem overly protracted and a waste of the player’s time. Often I found myself just leaving my PC to do other things while these scenes played because they are similar or overly long. The device you use to watch scenes also has to type out the scene name before you can pick another scene, so there’s another 5 seconds of your life wasted (over 190+ scenes). I ended up using this dead time to return to the middle of the house so it would potentially reduce walking time to the next random scene location. There are notes to read, and a few hidden/locked areas. One of the early secrets turns out to be surprisingly boring when I was hoping for much more. The dialogue isn’t even bad just not usually exciting. Ian is the standout best character who has a few good lines but isn't part of the six main cast members. But it really needed a huge compression to the tune of 50% off. If you do play it, I would recommend the abridged option since normal felt far too long, even though it only took me 6 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: I've always been a sucker for visual novels and story telling games with branching time lines, so for me Eternal Threads scratches that itch. The story is decent, the characters are well told, and I ended up more then a few times becoming rather invested in certain story lines to the point that I'd end up skipping entire events just to see what happens next. The atmosphere too was rather enjoyable. A few times I expected this to turn out to be a secret horror game in disguise, and even the small details like the movement of items when someone is or isn't dead is nice. I'd recommend it, but with some caveats.The game left me itching for more. The whole time travel altering the past thing is very minimal. Its strange that so many options really just have no affect to the story, and aside from the major major story parts even the options that do effect the story don't really effect the story. No matter how you end up getting to the end, most of the time the ending will be the same. You HAVE to save them all, and some may or may not have perfect endings but all of that is hidden away in their bio, something I didn't even realize until I had reached the ending with each of them optimal. The atmosphere is great but so little is done with it. After I found the special item in the safe, I half expected to start seeing people staring at me from outside the windows, stuff left on the walls, markings that said someone was there with me but it (kinda) never came. I went down to the basement to fix a light and... nothing. It was just me fixing a light. It feels like they had planned on having something else but scrapped it mid-way, leaving only traces, and the constant back and forth back and forth as you go up and down buggy stairs or rush into a room only to have to go back to the room you were just in became tedious, leading me to only really stick it out because I was invested in the characters by then. The ending was by far the worst part about the game. If the game had left it off at all of them getting out and being treated, then maybe it wouldn't have been so bad but instead I was left with a sequel bait for some future game or product that may never come, and a feeling that I missed something major that just doesn't exist. Despite all that I would recommend it. If you can ignore the ending, if you can ignore the tedious running around, if you can ignore the wasted potential, its a fun story. If you do end up making a sequel to this game, I hope you expand on the idea of branching time lines. I hope you have drastically different endings based on what you do. Hell, I hope you lean into that horror atmosphere more. I just really really hope you don't leave us guessing at the end of it.

_childDocuments_.review: This was an enjoyable game.  I was able to learn as I went along and it was a smooth ride.  Usually I'm not a fan of rewind time games but the way it was laid out made it easy to understand the mechanics and play along.Basically you have a group of flatmates living their lives and your goal is to have them survive the final event by manipulating their everyday choices to their best advantage.I especially liked that their stories were not over dramatic but gossipy enough to keep me interested.  A few good hidden secrets were especially fun to uncover and one timeline in particular took me a fair bit of puzzling before i was able to suss it out.Voice acting is wonderful and the visuals, though a little dark, in no way impede your exploration.  You have subtitles and all notes can be written out for you to read, so a very user friendly game.All in all something to add to your wishlist.
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: If you like narrative games, where most of the gameplay is piecing the story together, you should not miss this one.  I like a quality story, but being a game, I love it even more when a story is told in an innovative way.  This game provides both.Also, in most narrative games it is relatively straightforward to find one ending, but punishingly difficult and tedious to find the best ending.  Here, I managed to do both with some effort, without it ever becoming dull and repetitive.  It is in part because of the very intuitive user interface.Most reviewers complain about the ending.  While I see their point, and it does indeed open up the possibility of some kind of continuation (please do it!), I definitely did not feel cheated by it.  I feel that the things I was most interested in got resolved.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to say, this was a fantastic experience from start to finish. The actual puzzle solving is daunting as all heck when you are first thrust into things. I'm not sure if it was the atmosphere, the web of wants and needs that everyone in the house was woven together with, or just the act of finding out and developing care for these people with their lives in your hand- it was a blast. I can't wait to see what else these developers bring to the table next. ;)
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: I was really torn between giving a thumbs up or down for Eternal Threads but I think in the end, there aren't many that I would recommend this game to for a few reasons. The core story about saving 6 people from a house fire by manipulating smaller events is great and well thought through. All of the characters were compelling in their own ways and it was fun watching them interact. The time manipulation element has the same issue that most of these kinds of games have where jumping back and forth can feel tedious although I will say that this game avoids the butterfly effect issues that most games suffer from where your choices feel like they make arbitrary and random changes later on. Honestly, I give the devs props for this.Ultimately though, each of the characters really just have one actual problem that needs solving to get their optimal ending and they each feel a bit two-dimensional by the end because of that. While it's fun to discover these traits early on, by the halfway point, it starts to be less and less interesting. Some of the characters also take significantly more work to "fix" than the others. Neil and Linda take a bit of work but Ben and Jenny, I just solved by accident. I would have liked it if there were a few more plot points to discover and the characters had a bit more going on. Plus, if some of the puzzles were a bit harder to piece together, that would be nice. I started off taking notes, thinking that would help, but everything was pretty surface level so that never really came into play, personally. Taking off the training wheels that was Control just telling you how to solve puzzles would be nice.I still would recommend this game to fans of the genre though if it weren't for the framing story. Don't get me wrong, there is a lot of series potential here and maybe years from now, this won't be as much of an issue. For now though, there's a ton of worldbuilding and setup that doesn't really go anywhere. I'll be vague here to avoid spoilers but be warned that there may be some minor spoilers in the next couple of sentences but just jump to the next paragraph if you want to avoid even that. With all of the dialogue that occurs between Control and the main character, the various events that occur throughout your time in the house like the light going out and a picture falling, the mystery about the former tenant and the occupants of the hidden safe, and the strong implication that one of the characters sees visions of the future and alternate timelines, the ending is frustratingly vague and never ties any of this together. Maybe some future entry in the series will explain it but until then, we're just left with no answers at all. For a plot thread that gets so much screen time and even has an achievement titled "Final Revelation", it's frustrating that it doesn't actually reveal anything and just adds additional questions that may or may not ever be answered.If you are a huge fan of games like Steins Gate, 999, Forgotten City, Outer Wilds, Gone Home or anything like that, Eternal Threads is a fun way to spend ~10 hours. It also has a ton of potential going forward and I hope to see more later on. For now though, for the price and the issues, I'd have a hard time recommending it to anyone but the most diehard of genre enthusiasts begging for something new.
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun little game, not too long. I should point out that it isn't so much a "game", as it is an interactive movie. Think like Black Mirror's Bandersnatch. The cool hook of this game is that you get to view the story completely nonlinearly, and changes that you make can drastically change events that take place later. This game could definitely be a first entry into a series, although some improvements could be made. Primarily, I wish there was a bit more puzzling and discovery to be had. The 4 locked rooms were given pretty obvious answers of how to get in once you play the correct scene or scenes, made extra simplified by the narrator basically spelling out the solution to you afterwards. I also wish there was a bit more branching stories towards the end, as it felt like there was only like 3 possible outcomes per character (although I do enjoy how they interacted and changed other outcomes). The story was pretty nice, interesting enough to be engaging with some mystery throughout. Overall for a little indie game I think it is worth your time and investment

_childDocuments_.review: Recommending this game came down to a coin flip, or would have, and that is what lead me to NOT recommend this game. A good game would not need a coin flip, it would speak for itself.The choose your own adventure nature and style of the game has been done before. The timeline was useful, to a point and eventually it becomes the primary way you are looking at the game as you go to pick up your final cheives. The game falls badly at its own promise about the events, however. The text and synopsis of the game leads you to believe that the branching narrative matters. What I can tell you after 11 hours of watching the same scenes with minutely subtle differences over and over is that they really don't. No matter your choices, the only person's fate truly decided anywhere other than the last minute is the bird.  No characters can die early and thereby remove themselves from interaction later on. The game alludes to multiple interesting endings as well, but really it boils down to lots of watching people die almost peacefully in their sleep because they were too drunk to wake up during a fire.The man characters (Control, 43) talk about wielding a scalpel in fixing things. I guess. What it boils down to is you watch a LOT of the same thing, not even from different people's perspectives, but with minutely different changes in dialogue. Some so subtly different you feel, "Well, why bother?" and some scenes had no reason at all to be in the game except as a scene to pick up and watch. Twice we see different characters in the bathroom having little pep-talks in the mirror. Multiple times we focus on a single character doing nothing of any import what so ever. The scenes play with all the sincerity of a high school student changing spacing on the paragraphs to make the page length requirements of a paper. And on sincerity: every single actor in this game reads the lines well enough, but the models used for the characters smack of early 2000's movement and expression. Everyone is staring off into the thousand yard mark with blank expressions in eyes, faces, etc. Mouths clearly do not line up with scripts, heads and arms move as though there is a single bone/joint in them and track poorly.  The bad models suck the very life and soul out of the performance, and lets face it, there isn't a ton of action on screen already. We are supposed to give a fart about these people, to want to right all the issues and fix their broken stupid lives (if you want the good ending!) and they can't seem to give a wet fart about their own issues. I'm entirely willing to forgive scene elements not lining up with the action. THAT at least makes sense because 43 is viewing the burned out home after and the device is laying over a hologram. Unfortunately, the hologram aspect only really serves to further the uncanny gulf between the viewer and the game. The full start to finish is not that long, but digging though the permutations for the last few cheives is like nails on a chalkboard. You find yourself really wishing for a fast forward or skip to see the scenes without having to watch them to clear them all, and in a game that really wants you to pay attention, read between the lines(?) and see the whole picture.All in all, the ending is painfully anticlimactic and the sting for the perfect ending is predictable and sets up for a follow-on that looks to be as unoriginal as the story delivery vehicle.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game.  The concept is really good, and I love story and dialogue based games. I will say, however, to its credit, it is a beautiful game with great animations.

_childDocuments_.review: An EXTREMELY pleasant surprise and a game I really wasn't expecting too much out of but manages to wring every penny out of its probably meagre budget and elevates itself significantly from its very limited setting to make for something memorable and interesting.The game isn't that much of a looker and you're confined to a single house for its entirety but it manages to make every part of the house fairly interesting with a bunch of notes and actual environmental storytelling. There's also ways the gameplay itself shapes the house that I'll get into later. The voice acting leaves a fair bit to be desired sometimes but is mostly serviceable. This isn't a theatre play or some grand tale. It's just a bunch of people living in a house for which the voice acting is adequate. There's not much music to speak of and the game is mostly quiet but the ambient sound design works wonders in keeping you fairly tense.On the gameplay side of things, you're working in first person and working your way through snippets of the events that transpired in the one house before something pivotal happens. You're required to investigate a timeline and see the sequence of events that led to what happened and also explore what happens when you force changes in some of the decisions. The game is pretty much strictly this so if you've played something like Tacoma then this would be right at home. I found a good deal of polish in how you navigate through the timeline, especially the cool way in which it shows you all the events that are changed by the decision you just made which was a massive help. This even changes the placement and presence of items in the house, for example, you could have posters up on the wall in the present depending on if you asked the landlord to clear the stuff from the old tenant away which is neat-o. There are a fair few issues here though, especially the lack of a conversation log, requiring you to continually walk up and down the house, no playback options for the events and some minor lack of polish with triggering them. I found it quite annoying how much walking I'd had to do and wish there was an easier way to get around the house and view the events.The story itself is not a particularly complicated one. It's mostly the lives of a few distressed folk who're trying to get by and you sort of have a hand in how they're going to react to the situations they end up in within the house to try and make their "ending" better. Most of the conversations flow naturally and feel like people talking rather than any stage direction though the voice acting does let it down in spots. It's a simple story told in a complex way but the delivery makes it much more engaging to discover all of it. It's also just fun to watch the characters sometimes since most of them are very likeable and have a fair few things going on.I didn't expect to like this one as much as I did, especially when the initial hour is a bit of a slog and the timeline looked extremely daunting. But the game lets you in slowly and I found myself entertained all the rest of the way. If you're a fan of games like What Remains of Edith Finch and Tacoma, this is a solid recommend from me.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have light induced seizures avoid this game. Or Eternal Threads is a Unity based time travel puzzle game. You must change the course of events to change the outcome.Early time travel experiments caused a massive release of chronal radiation into the time stream altering history. Your job is to travel back in time and repair the damage by making small changes in an effort to have those changes effect larger changes in the timeline.Like many games this game has light induced seizures warning. Unlike most games, this will hit you fast and hard in the beginning of the game with frequent events with strobing lights.You go back in time to a boarding house where six people died in a fire. Your task is to change minor events that occurred over the previous week so that the six people survive. Optimally you also resolve their personal issues.You start in the future and are transported back to the past. You set up tripods around the house to increase the images of the past. After the tripods are set up you can experience different events on the timeline. Certain events have two options for what can happen. Your job is to select the correct option in order to cause the events to change enough that all six people survive. You will see a status change when your change causes someone to survive the fire.The images you see are "ghost" images, so change you make to the environment do not affect the scenes you witness. However, the same is not true the other way around. Some things require specific scenes in order to access them. While I agree with this for some items, like the combination to a lock. It makes no sense for finding keys to things. I shouldn't have to see the scene showing me where the key is hidden in order for me to find the key.In order to view the scenes you have to be in the room where the scene occurred. While this makes sense, it does frequently require you to move across the entire house to move from scene to scene. There is no way to sort the scenes by where they happen. You can isolate the scenes that a specific person or group of people are in.In additional to the scenes that can change the story there are also "filler" scenes that will fill you in on the character's backstories. This will allow you to unlock things like the combination to the lock. There are also various documents and phones laying around to allow you to piece together the full story.I did have an issue where I could save all of the people, but was unable (even using multiple walkthrough) to get Neil's story resolved. The item that seems not to register is that he admits having an issue as the resolution for him specifically says that he doesn't admit, even though that conversation is set to him admitting he has a problem. Despite that issue I enjoyed playing through to find, and adjust the story for all of the characters.A good mystery game, where you have to figure out what aspects of the story to change in order to get the desired outcome.Intel i7-8086K Coffee Lake 6-Core 4.00GHz CPUCrucial Ballistix Sport AT 2666 MHz DDR4 RAM (16GB x 2)ASUS GeForce RTX 2080 Overclocked 8G GDDR6Or

_childDocuments_.review: Very unique take on interactive story telling. Being able to move back and forth and effect the story while moving FORWARD, is really nice. Typical pathway games are nice, path A vs path B, but there needs to be more than that to be a perfect blend of movie experience and game experience. I think this is a fine example of better balance. The main story is fine, realistic story. The atmosphere and the detail really hold everything together. But, the "world story" is the real interest. With the intro, ending and details throughout the game, I want to know about the dystopian future that this takes place. I hope there will be more of this series, it is on the right path.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game more in theory than in practice.Despite the sci-fi framing device the game is really more about watching characters in their day to day lives influencing their decisions to come to the best conclusion.The big issue I have with this title is that for a game that starts with someone stating something as grandiose as "we broke the world", the actual story you're going to be dealing with, is pretty mundane. Yes, any real person dealing with these issues would find them difficult, no doubt. But saving a marriage, dealing with childhood trauma - that's pretty low stakes when you consider the main conceit of the game is that the player is involved in fixing a world-ending crisis. This would be easier to ignore if the drama you are supposed to be invested in was written better. What we get here is soap opera level and mostly doesn't ring true to life. Characters just seem to be waiting for this one week to resolve their issues / help others resove their issues. And while it's nice to help the characters find their happy ending, the actually interesting questions go unanswered. Finally, the game mechanic ends up being a bit unwieldy at the end. I really wanted to see all the events, but simply didn't have enough information (or the patience) to find the right combination of decisions.I played the demo first and was lured in by the promise of some darker mysteries ... but those just never surfaced. I still recommend this game, because I'd rather see a hundred games like this - made by developers trying to do something different and not quite getting there instead of a hundred uninspired games by developers trying to play it safe.
_childDocuments_.name: Eternal Threads

_childDocuments_.review: You will be playing as a temporal agent, giving a unique perspective to this interactive drama. The voice acting, music, and graphics, were all quite pleasing. I found myself caring for each character more than I expected to based on the trailer. I would have liked more room to physically explore, or multiple settings, however for the limited setting, it was executed very well. Would recommend to anyone with a curious bone in their body, who enjoys decision-based games, and would love to see what else these devs get up to.

_childDocuments_.review: The game was ok.  It took awhile to finish playing it because when you toggle certain timelines off and back on it would change the status of other events later in the timeline.  This didn't happen for most of the timeline events but it happened for a few of them so even though I perfected Linda's timeline first before I perfected anyone elses, I couldn't remember exactly which timeline options I had chosen to get back to it since a later events reset from just toggling events to try to find other characters timelines and so her timeline was also the last one that I perfected.This isn't any kind of revolutionary game or profound story, but if you like playing things like jigsaw puzzles and hidden object games and you also like visual novels then there's some entertainment for at least several hours here.  The voice acting and the sound quality seemed pretty good and that's important for a visual novel.I achieved 100% completion with only having to look up the location of two of the letters I couldn't find from a guide, so it seemed pretty reasonable as far as how difficult it is to locate the hidden stuff in the game.I got this as part of the Humble Choice bundle so ultimately it cost me only a few dollars and that seemed fine for the amount of entertainment I got out of it.  I give it my thumbs up if you can get it for perhaps $5 or less.

_childDocuments_.review: You don't get a huge introduction but you don't need one. The game begins in such a way that you can figure things out without hand-holding, but you still have your 'instructor' in your ear making commentary at very specific moments.You are the protagonist, known as #43. When they view a scene/choice, they type in a title for those scene/choices and some of those titles are funny.I liked all of the characters, in the end. Initially I was more interested in getting the right outcomes but then I became invested and interested in the characters and their lives. I managed to unlock all their secrets and all the doors without too much trouble, but Neil is a hard one to save. I admit I cheated a little bit with him... and discovered (as I cheated with the walkthrough) that at one point I'd come very very close to perfection.I do like the way the choices connect with one another, and after unlocking them, that you can press a button and see where and how they connect. This must've been a devastatingly confusing game to tie together, but it has been done extraordinarily well.The voices, music, setting, storyline are all amazing and help you become immersed. The story can have a satisfying ending with room for sequels (other events to fix, plus there's something else that happens that implies more can come)I hope that there is an Eternal Threads 2.

_childDocuments_.review: The narrative style of Eternal Threads won't be to everyone's taste - this is more akin to a visual novel than a game, despite some puzzle-solving elements.Eternal Threads pulled me in, with a low-key story (belied by the time travel concept and opening voiceover), about the relationships between characters and their own personal problems. Though these were small in scale, I did end up interested to see how the story played out, and I'm upset to have reached the end.It was also nice to have decidedly British characters in a game for a change. In a way, it was like watching a drama on television, and I appreciated that.I'd say Eternal Threads is worth the play, and at its non-discounted price point. It brings an interesting story and an innovative concept, and manages to pull it off without either being overly complex, meaningless or overly ambitious.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally, a "Choices Matter" "Multiple Endings" "Story Rich" game where all three of those are actually accurate!Eternal Threads isn't a showstopper visually, but what it lacks in that department it makes up for with a puzzle that had me scratching at my brain for a good while. Considering how some actions butterfly out to affect others is really fun, and I ended up making 9 separate steam notes just to track my thoughts and what was going on. Twists and turns and unexpected events abound! Characters are believable and feel grounded in reality, especially when they all make terrible decisions in their default timeline. My girlfriend was laughing to herself about my walking around exclaiming "Well if she tells him about the baby then, they don't have sex and he dies!" Great game, working on that 100%.
